notes: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, and prune annually to an open center for good air movement. Achilles is a mildew-resistant red gooseberry developed at England's East Malling Research Station, valued for pairing heavy, reliable cropping with much better resistance to American gooseberry mildew than older varieties like Leveller. The medium-large, smooth berries ripen to a deep pinkish-red with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor good for both fresh eating and cooking. Its upright, moderately vigorous bush is easier to manage and pick than sprawling heirloom types, making it a practical choice for smaller home orchards.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; agarita is a classic native Texas evergreen shrub with small, three-lobed, holly-like leaves (each with sharp spines) arranged in a distinctive trifoliate pattern — it looks like a small holly with fierce spines and makes an impenetrable wildlife barrier hedge. In spring it produces clusters of small, intensely fragrant yellow flowers, followed by brilliant red tart berries in late spring that are relished by birds and made by Texas foragers into highly prized jelly. The flavor is tart-sweet, similar to a currant. The berries ripen and fall quickly — traditionally harvested by spreading a tarp under the shrub and shaking the branches. Deer browse it rarely due to the spines. A tough, beautiful, and ecologically valuable native for difficult dry spots in zone 6–9.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to maintain productive fruiting wood. Alachua is a University of Florida-released black muscadine bred and selected specifically for the low-chill, high-heat, high-humidity conditions of Florida and the Deep South, where it produces large, high-quality fruit reliably even in areas too warm for many Georgia- and Carolina-bred muscadine cultivars. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, bearing medium-to-large black fruit with good sweetness and flavor well suited to both fresh eating and processing. Its Florida-focused breeding makes it a particularly strong choice for muscadine growers in the warmest parts of the Gulf South, zone 7–10.

common_name: Alachua Southern Highbush Blueberry (Florida-Bred Low-Chill Blueberry)
notes: Amend the planting bed to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines before setting out dormant bushes in winter, and mulch well to conserve moisture around the shallow root zone. Alachua is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for the state's mild winters, producing medium to large, firm, flavorful berries on a vigorous bush that ripens over a solid midseason window. Its very low chilling requirement makes it a dependable choice even after an unusually warm winter along the Gulf Coast, where higher-chill varieties can bloom poorly or fail to set fruit. Plant with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination and yield, fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain strong production.

Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Alapaha is an early-ripening rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Georgia and named for the Alapaha River region of south Georgia, bred to combine early harvest timing with better-than-average tolerance of Septoria and other leaf-spot diseases common in humid Gulf South summers. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and firm with good flavor for an early variety. Fruit set improves noticeably with a second rabbiteye cultivar planted nearby, since Alapaha is only partially self-fruitful. The upright, vigorous bush needs little training beyond removing old unproductive canes each winter. Mulch generously with pine bark or pine straw and avoid overhead irrigation late in the day to further reduce leaf-spot pressure in humid climates.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun; Alapaha is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for exceptional berry quality — the fruit is large, light blue, and has a dessert quality with a sweet-tart balance and crisp texture that earned it high consumer preference ratings in taste trials. Released in 2001, Alapaha is among the newer rabbiteye cultivars with improved fruit quality over the older varieties developed in the mid-20th century. It ripens early in the rabbiteye season (late May to mid-June in zone 8–9), overlapping with Premier and producing well with 300–400 chilling hours. The moderately vigorous, upright-to-spreading shrubs are productive and show reasonable resistance to late-season water stress.

Alpine currant is an extremely tough, compact, mound-forming shrub long used for shade hedging in cold climates where few other woody plants tolerate dense shade and dry soil so well. Plant in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil; it is not particular about soil pH or fertility and shrugs off urban pollution and road salt. Inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in spring, and female plants (this species is dioecious, so both sexes are needed for fruit) set small, glossy red currants in midsummer that are edible but tart and bland, used mainly by birds or for jelly rather than fresh eating. Prune after flowering to maintain a formal hedge shape, since it tolerates shearing extremely well and rarely needs spraying for pests.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; American barberry is a thorny, deciduous Appalachian native shrub with small, spine-tipped leaves, drooping clusters of small yellow flowers in late spring, and bright red, elongated berries that ripen in fall and persist into winter, providing food for birds when little else is available. It is a genuinely native, non-invasive alternative for gardeners who want the ornamental berry and thorny-hedge qualities of barberry without planting the widely naturalized and ecologically disruptive Japanese barberry. Because Berberis species can serve as an alternate host for wheat stem rust, avoid planting it in large numbers near commercial grain fields, a precaution that led to historic eradication programs targeting common barberry in agricultural regions. Otherwise easy to grow and largely trouble-free, it works well as an informal barrier hedge, wildlife planting, or specimen in a naturalistic border.

Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun, planting two different cultivars for cross-pollination; American elderberry is a fast-growing native shrub of floodplains and woodland edges that produces large, flat-topped clusters of tiny, white, fragrant flowers in early summer followed by hanging clusters of small, dark-purple to black berries in late summer that are among the most nutritious and medicinally valued native fruits in North America — the basis of elderberry syrup, wine, pies, jams, and traditional immune-support preparations. Never eat raw elderberries in quantity (mildly toxic); cooking destroys the problematic compounds. The flowers are also edible and delicious battered and fried or infused into cordials. Excellent wildlife plant, supporting over 50 bird species. Named varieties 'Bob Gordon', 'Adams', and 'Nova' have larger berries and heavier yields.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun — American gooseberry is the native gooseberry of the northeastern US and Canada, one of the most productive edible native shrubs for cool-climate food gardens. The tart-sweet berries (ripening from green to reddish-purple in midsummer) are excellent for pies, jams, preserves, and fresh eating when fully ripe. The shrub tolerates partial shade better than most fruiting shrubs and produces reliably in conditions too shaded for currants and jostaberries. The stems bear short, sharp spines at the nodes; wear gloves when harvesting. American gooseberry is more resistant to powdery mildew than European gooseberry (R. uva-crispa), making it easier to grow in humid climates. Best in zones 3–7; does not perform well in hot, humid summers of zone 8 and south. Check state regulations on Ribes planting before ordering.

American highbush cranberry is a native Viburnum — not a true cranberry — bearing clusters of bright red, tart berries in fall that persist on the shrub into winter, providing critical food for wildlife during cold months. The berries have a distinct musky aroma when raw that largely disappears with cooking; they are high in pectin and excellent for jellies, sauces, and syrups as a cranberry substitute. Do not confuse with the European cranberrybush (V. opulus), which produces lower-quality, more bitter fruit. Prune out the oldest canes at the base every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and an open, multi-stemmed form.

Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, planting at least two shrubs to ensure cross-pollination; American highbush cranberry is not a true cranberry but a native viburnum that produces bright red, translucent, cranberry-sized berries in clusters from fall through winter that birds love and that can be made into preserves, sauces, and jellies with a flavor resembling true cranberries. The lacy white flower clusters in late spring are attractive, and the three-lobed leaves turn brilliant red-purple in fall. Plants are also important wildlife habitat shrubs for nesting birds. The native var. americanum is preferred over the European V. opulus (which escaped and has naturalized invasively in some areas).

Set out rooted suckers or container plants in spring on poor, sandy, or saline ground where its vigorous, nitrogen-fixing roots and suckering habit can be left to spread without crowding cultivated beds. This silvery-leaved North American native tolerates conditions few other fruiting shrubs can, needing no supplemental fertility once established. Small, fragrant yellow flowers in early summer give way to silvery, mealy berries that ripen in fall and are used for jam, drying, and winter forage for birds. Unlike the related autumn olive and Russian olive, American silverberry is a true native across most of its range and behaves far less aggressively, making it a sound choice for windbreaks, erosion control, and reclamation plantings.

'Anne' produces exceptionally large, pale-yellow fall-bearing berries with a sweet, apricot-like flavor. Grow in rich, moisture-retentive soil and support the tall canes with a two-wire trellis to keep fruit off the ground. As a primocane variety it can be mown down each winter for a single autumn crop, simplifying pruning. The soft golden fruit does not ship well, making it an ideal home-garden and fresh-eating selection.

'Arapaho' is an early-ripening erect thornless blackberry with medium-large berries containing small, unobtrusive seeds. Its self-supporting canes need minimal trellising, making it well suited to compact plantings and home gardens. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and provide even moisture during the fruiting period for best size and flavor. Remove floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to five or six vigorous shoots per plant.

Actinidia kolomikta is the hardiest kiwi species, tolerating temperatures to -40°F in zone 3, and is grown for its small (1 in), sweet, smooth-skinned fruits that ripen in late summer. The vine is ornamentally striking due to pink-and-white variegated foliage on male plants. It is dioecious and requires both male and female plants — one male per 4–6 females. Cats are intensely attracted to the plants and will damage young vines, so protect new plantings with wire cages. Prune each dormant season to maintain a framework of lateral arms on a sturdy arbor or fence.

Aronia is exceptionally hardy and tolerates wet, poorly drained soils, making it suitable for rain gardens. It is self-fruitful and rarely needs a pollinator, though yields improve with a second plant nearby. Prune by removing the oldest, thickest canes at the base every 3–4 years to encourage vigorous new growth and better light penetration. Harvest clusters in late summer when berries are very dark purple-black; the astringent flavor mellows after a light frost or processing.

common_name: Aurora Blueberry (Very Late Season Northern Highbush Blueberry, Season-Extender Blueberry)
notes: Plant in very acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil; maintain pH 4.5–5.2 with acid fertilizer; mulch with pine bark; Aurora ripens very late (late August through September) producing large, firm, light blue berries with outstanding flavor — considered by MSU researchers to have among the best flavor of any northern highbush variety; plant early-season varieties (Duke, Bluecrop) alongside for cross-pollination and a full-season harvest. Aurora blueberry is a Michigan State University-released variety (2003) that has become highly regarded among serious home blueberry growers and specialty producers for its combination of very late ripening season and exceptional berry quality. The variety was specifically developed as part of MSU's late-season breeding program aimed at extending the Michigan commercial blueberry season into September, reducing market glut during the peak July–August production and commanding higher prices for September-ripening fruit. Aurora ripens the latest of any major highbush blueberry variety — typically 4–6 weeks after early-season varieties like Duke and 2–3 weeks after Jersey (itself a late variety), making September fresh blueberries possible in zones 4–6 where frost would otherwise end the season. The berries are large to very large, firm (excellent handling and shelf life for a highbush variety), and have a notably good flavor — sweet, aromatic, and complex — that is consistently rated among the best of all highbush varieties in blind flavor tastings. The very firm texture also makes Aurora berries excellent for fresh eating (they snap satisfyingly rather than bursting), baking, and freezing. An excellent choice for home orchardists wanting to extend fresh blueberry season as late as possible into autumn.

common_name: Aurora Honeyberry (Late-Season University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
notes: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Aurora is self-infertile. Aurora was released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the leading haskap breeding program in North America, and is valued for its large, elongated berries with a sweet, well-balanced flavor closer to blueberry than the tart, sometimes bitter flavor of earlier haskap introductions. It blooms and ripens later than earlier-generation cultivars like 'Borealis', which helps the flowers dodge late spring frosts, and the fruit holds on the bush longer without dropping, extending the harvest window. Like other haskaps, Aurora is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F and flowers that survive down to about -8F, but it is poorly suited to hot, humid climates and performs best in short-season, cold-winter regions. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes.

Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Austin is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the University of Georgia breeding program, selected as an early-to-midseason ripening variety that fills the harvest window alongside Climax, extending the picking season before the midseason varieties come on. Berries are medium-large, light blue, and firm with good flavor, borne on vigorous, upright, productive bushes that establish quickly. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Austin is not self-fruitful and should be planted with at least one other compatible variety within about 50 feet for cross-pollination and full crops. Remove flower buds the first year or two after planting to direct the plant's energy into root and cane development rather than fruit; full production typically begins by year four. Mulch generously with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity, and irrigate consistently during fruit swell, since rabbiteye blueberries have shallow, fibrous roots that dry out quickly in Gulf Coast heat.

Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist. Austin is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry that ripens just after Climax in the early part of the season, producing medium-to-large, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It extends the early harvest window when planted alongside Climax and Premier, and its dependable, heavy cropping habit combined with good disease tolerance has made it a standard early-season choice for Gulf South home orchards and u-pick plantings. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Autumn Magic Aronia (Compact Ornamental Black Chokeberry)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Magic is a compact black chokeberry cultivar selected primarily for landscape use, staying notably smaller and more rounded than seed-grown Aronia melanocarpa while still producing a good crop of glossy black, antioxidant-rich berries. The shrub is a genuine multi-season landscape plant: clusters of white flowers in spring, clean dark green summer foliage, and some of the most vivid red-purple fall color of any Aronia selection, making it a strong choice for a foundation planting or mixed border that also happens to produce useful fruit. Berries are highly astringent eaten raw and are best processed into juice, syrup, or dried additions to baked goods and trail mixes. The self-fertile, adaptable shrub tolerates wet or dry soils and both full sun and considerable shade, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems to stay dense and well-shaped.

Autumn olive is a nitrogen-fixing Asian shrub with extremely high yields of small red-speckled berries that are rich in lycopene and have a sweet-tart flavor; it is among the most productive fruiting shrubs per acre in temperate climates. However, it is considered an invasive species across much of the eastern U.S. and is prohibited or discouraged in many states — verify legal status in your jurisdiction before planting. Named fruit-producing selections such as 'Garnet' or 'Red Wing' are more compact and productive than seedlings. Harvest by hand-stripping clusters in fall when berries are fully red; fruit quality improves after light frost.

common_name: Avonblue Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early Florida-Bred Blueberry)
notes: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in winter into acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) heavily amended with pine bark or peat moss, and mulch to keep the shallow root zone cool and evenly moist. Avonblue is one of the older University of Florida southern highbush releases and remains valued for its dependable early ripening, largely self-fruitful flowers, and tolerance of Florida's sandy, warm-winter growing conditions. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and mildly tart, produced on a moderately compact, rounded bush well suited to smaller home garden plantings. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water deeply during dry spells, and prune out old unproductive wood each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.

Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive conditions rabbiteye blueberries need. Baldwin is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for ripening quite late in the season, extending the blueberry harvest well past earlier cultivars, with small to medium, firm, dark blue berries that hold their shape and flavor well, making them useful for fresh eating, freezing, and machine harvest alike. The plant is vigorous, productive, and well adapted to the acidic, sandy soils typical of the Gulf South, requiring a second compatible rabbiteye variety nearby for good cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with vigorous new fruiting wood.

Beach plum is a native Atlantic coastal shrub that thrives in sandy, salt-spray-exposed sites where few other fruits survive, making it invaluable for coastal and xeric gardens. The small (0.5–1 in), round fruits range from red to purple to blue at maturity in late summer and are traditionally used for preserves and jams on Cape Cod and Long Island. Plant at least two named cultivars such as 'Autumn' and 'Premier' for adequate cross-pollination, as seedlings are variable and often infertile. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape; heavy pruning reduces fruiting the following year.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; bear huckleberry is a deciduous native shrub of the high-elevation Appalachian forests from North Carolina to Tennessee, naturally growing in the understory beneath oaks, hemlocks, and rhododendrons. The shiny black berries ripen in late summer and are eaten by bears (which explains the common name), black bears being primary dispersers in its mountain habitat. The berries are edible by humans as well — sweet and flavorful, similar to blueberries but with a distinctive tang. Like all huckleberries, the plant is challenging to cultivate outside its specific acidic, woodland conditions; it does not tolerate alkaline soil, dry soil, or full sun. Excellent for native woodland gardens in the southern mountains.

Plant in acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, in full sun with a compatible early-season pollinator nearby. Beckyblue is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry bred specifically for the low winter chill of the Deep South and Florida, ripening among the earliest of the rabbiteye cultivars and giving Gulf Coast growers a jump on the blueberry season. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and pleasantly mild-flavored, borne on a vigorous, spreading bush. Because it flowers early, plant it in a site with reasonable air drainage to reduce frost risk to the blooms in years with a late cold snap. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, mulch well to conserve moisture, and prune out old wood each winter to sustain strong early yields.

Grow in full sun on well-drained, acidic soil and mulch with pine bark or sawdust to hold moisture around the shallow, fibrous root system. Berkeley is an older, widely planted mid-season highbush cultivar valued for large, firm, pale sky-blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and good resistance to cracking. Its spreading, vigorous bushes are heavy and reliable producers over a long lifespan, and the plant also offers attractive orange-red fall foliage. Because it dislikes waterlogged soil, raised beds or amended rows are worthwhile on heavier ground.

Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Berry Blue is not reliably self-fertile. This is one of the earlier commercially available honeyberry cultivars in North America, forming a compact, tidy bush well suited to small gardens and mixed borders, with round-to-oval berries that ripen a bit later than the earliest University of Saskatchewan releases, helping spread out the harvest window when several cultivars are planted together. Flavor is tart with a mild blueberry-like undertone, better suited to jam, syrup, and baking than to fresh eating for most palates, though fully ripe fruit sweetens considerably. Berry Blue is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating winters well below -30F, but struggles in hot, humid summer climates and is a poor match for zone 8-10 gardens. As with other haskaps, avoid heavy pruning in the first several years and then renew the oldest wood periodically to keep the bush productive.

common_name: Big Lifeberry Goji (Large-Fruited Compact Patio Goji)
notes: Plant in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0 in full sun; goji tolerates poor, alkaline soils where other fruiting shrubs struggle. Big Lifeberry is a modern breeding-program goji selection producing notably larger berries than seed-grown goji, on a more compact, better-branched plant that fruits at a younger age and fits large containers as well as garden beds. Its bushier, less sprawling habit than wild-type goji makes it easier to manage without the loose, arching growth typical of the species. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals; harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers rather than pulling on the fruit directly, since the sap can stain.

Bilberry is a low-growing European relative of blueberry that differs in producing berries singly rather than in clusters; the deep purple-red flesh (unlike blueberry's white flesh) stains heavily and has an intense, slightly tart flavor. It demands strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) with high organic matter and cool, moist conditions, making it challenging to grow in most American gardens but worth attempting in zones 3–7 under high shade or at elevation. Minimal pruning is needed; shear plants lightly every 3–4 years to rejuvenate. Harvest in mid- to late summer when berries are fully dark blue-black and tender.

Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Biloxi is a very low-chill-hour southern highbush blueberry developed by USDA and Mississippi State University, requiring only 150–200 chill hours — among the lowest chilling requirements of any productive blueberry and making it suitable for the warmest areas of zone 9 and parts of zone 10. The medium-sized, light blue, firm berries ripen in April–May in zone 9 — among the earliest-ripening blueberries of the season — with a mild, sweet, and slightly tart flavor. The early ripening window allows Biloxi to produce before summer heat stresses the plant and before peak blueberry pressure from insects and birds. The vigorous, upright plant habit is well-adapted to Gulf Coast conditions. Biloxi was tested and released as a variety specifically suited to the Gulf South and Florida, giving it a track record of success in the climate conditions that characterize zone 9a and 9b.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Black Beauty is a University of Arkansas release bred specifically for fresh-market eating, producing very large, glossy black berries with a tender skin and mild, sweet flavor that is less musky than many older muscadine varieties. It is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though nearby vines improve fruit set. Vigor is strong and disease resistance is good across the humid Gulf South. Because berries ripen unevenly over several weeks rather than all at once, plan on repeated picking passes through the harvest season for the best quality fruit.

common_name: Black Butte Blackberry (Oregon State Extra-Large-Fruited Bramble)
notes: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a trellis, pruning out fruited floricanes each year after harvest to keep new primocanes productive. Black Butte was released by the Oregon State University blackberry breeding program in the 1980s and is best known among Pacific Northwest growers for producing exceptionally large fruit, with individual berries often noticeably bigger than those of Marionberry or most other trailing types. The berries ripen early in the trailing-blackberry season, are glossy black with good flavor, and their large size makes hand-picking notably faster than with smaller-fruited varieties. Because the canes are thorny and quite vigorous, Black Butte requires the same sturdy trellising and winter pruning used for other trailing blackberries grown in maritime climates.

Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in virtually any soil — moist or dry, acidic or neutral, clay or sand — in partial shade to full sun; black chokeberry is one of the most adaptable native shrubs in North America, thriving under conditions that defeat most other fruiting shrubs. Aronia melanocarpa produces stunning clusters of small white flowers with prominent pink anthers in May, glossy, dark-green summer foliage, and massive clusters of small, dark-purple to near-black berries in August and September that persist into winter; the berries are extremely high in anthocyanins and antioxidants — among the highest recorded for any fruit — with an astringent, tart flavor excellent for juices, syrups, and wine. Fall foliage is a brilliant scarlet-red. The plant is essentially bulletproof once established, tolerating wet soils, clay, drought, and partial shade; it spreads by root suckers into dense thickets over time.

Black currants fruit most heavily on one-year-old wood, so annual renewal pruning is critical: remove one-third of the oldest canes each late winter to stimulate vigorous new shoots. The berries have a strong, tannic flavor prized for jams and juices; harvest when the entire strig has turned glossy black. Choose blister-rust-resistant cultivars such as 'Consort' or 'Titania' where regulations permit. Verify local restrictions before planting.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; prune hard in late winter to maintain shape and vigor. Sambucus nigra (black elderberry or European elder) is the classic European elder — a fast-growing, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub or small tree long cultivated for its remarkable botanical generosity: in late spring it produces large, flat-topped, highly fragrant clusters (corymbs) of tiny, cream-white flowers with a distinctive musky-lychee-pear elderflower fragrance; by late summer these transform into heavy, drooping clusters of small (1/4-inch), jet-black, glistening berries. Both flowers and berries are culinary staples in English and Scandinavian cooking: elderflower cordial (steeped flowers, sugar, lemon, citric acid) is one of England's most beloved summer drinks; elderflower 'champagne' (a lightly fermented drink) and elderflower fritters are summer traditions. The berries are made into elderberry syrup (rich in anthocyanins and vitamin C, widely sold as an immune-support supplement), elderberry wine, elderberry jam, and in Scandinavian juices (hyldebær saft). CAUTION: Raw flowers and berries contain mild cyanogenic glycosides — cook berries before eating in quantity; flower clusters are generally safe raw in cordials and wine but not in large raw amounts. The cultivar 'Sambuco' and 'Haschberg' are selected for large berry yields; 'Black Beauty' and 'Black Lace' are ornamental dark-leaved forms.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; black highbush blueberry is native to wet coastal-plain woodlands and pocosins and tolerates wetter soil than most cultivated blueberries. Vaccinium fuscatum is a tall, southeastern coastal-plain native blueberry with small, urn-shaped white to pink flowers in spring followed by sweet, dark purple-black berries in summer that are edible and attractive to wildlife, growing naturally in the moist, acidic soils of pocosins, bay forests, and wet flatwoods from the Carolinas to the Gulf Coast. Its tolerance for consistently damp soil and light shade makes it a good choice for a rain garden, pond margin, or the moist, partly shaded portion of a mixed berry planting where standard rabbiteye or southern highbush blueberries would struggle. It benefits from a second blueberry species or cultivar nearby for improved pollination and fruit set, following the same acidic-soil culture as other Vaccinium.

Black huckleberry (Gaylussacia baccata) is a native eastern North American shrub distinct from Vaccinium huckleberries, bearing shiny blue-black berries in summer that differ from blueberries in having 10 large, hard seeds rather than many tiny seeds. Plants form slow-spreading colonies via rhizomes in dry, acidic soils (pH 4.0–5.0) and are extremely fire-adapted and long-lived. The berries have a rich, complex flavor prized for pies and preserves — often considered superior to blueberries by foragers. Difficult to cultivate commercially; best suited to naturalistic plantings in appropriate native habitat.

common_name: Black Satin Blackberry (Classic Thornless Semi-Erect Blackberry)
notes: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the sprawling semi-erect canes onto a sturdy two-wire trellis. One of the earliest widely available thornless blackberry cultivars, introduced in the 1970s, Black Satin remains valued for its reliable, heavy production of large, glossy, firm black fruit with good flavor, ripening over a fairly long midsummer season. The semi-erect canes need more support and tying than fully upright modern cultivars, but the plant is vigorous, dependable, and tolerant of a range of soil conditions. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting productive and make room for new fruiting canes.

Plant bare-root or container canes in early spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; blackcap fruits on second-year canes, so tip-prune first-year primocanes in summer to encourage branching and next year's crop. Rubus leucodermis is a western North American native bramble with arching, prickly canes coated in a whitish, waxy bloom, producing small white flowers in spring followed by dark purple-black, dome-shaped berries in early to midsummer that are tart, seedy, and excellent for jam, syrup, and baking. It tolerates lighter, drier soils and more shade than most cultivated raspberries, and its thicket-forming habit makes it useful for naturalized plantings, wildlife hedgerows, and erosion control on slopes as well as a home fruit patch. Remove spent floricanes after fruiting each year to keep the planting productive and manage its spreading habit.

common_name: Blue Belle Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
notes: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Belle is self-infertile. Blue Belle was one of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Bird, and Blue Moon) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that brought large-fruited modern haskaps into wide North American cultivation. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening two to three weeks ahead of standard blueberries in most climates. Like other haskaps, Blue Belle is exceptionally cold-hardy, surviving winter temperatures to -40F with flowers tolerating brief dips to about -8F, but it is not well suited to hot, humid summers and performs best in cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit forms on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing branches for the first three to four years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the shrub productive.

Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Blue Chip is a low-chill-hour dwarf southern highbush blueberry selected for compact growth habit — typically reaching only 3–4 feet tall and wide, making it the most container-appropriate blueberry variety and an excellent choice for small gardens, patios, and raised beds where standard blueberries are too large. The moderate-sized, sweet, firm berries ripen in May–June in zone 9 with good flavor and production relative to the small plant size. Blue Chip's dwarf habit is not a compromise in productivity — the plant concentrates its energy into fruit production rather than excessive vegetative growth, and a mature container-grown Blue Chip in a large pot can produce 2–4 pounds of fruit annually. The ornamental value is also high: the spring white flower clusters, glossy summer foliage, and brilliant orange-to-red fall color make Blue Chip a true four-season specimen for containers and small gardens.

Plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; blue elderberry is the western counterpart to eastern black elderberry, native from British Columbia to New Mexico, producing large flat-topped clusters (corymbs) of tiny white flowers followed by abundant powder-blue to nearly black fruits with a distinctive waxy blue bloom. The berries are somewhat sweeter and milder than eastern elderberry and were a major food plant for over 50 indigenous nations of the Pacific Coast and interior West — eaten fresh (ripe only), dried, made into jam, syrup, wine, and elderflower cordial. Like eastern elderberry, unripe or raw berries can cause nausea; cook before eating in quantity. An exceptional wildlife plant and one of the most productive native fruiting shrubs.

Plant in any moist to well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — blue elderberry is the western North American native elderberry, native from British Columbia to Baja California and east to the Rocky Mountains, producing large, flat-topped clusters of dark blue to blue-black berries with a distinctive waxy, blue-gray bloom (giving both plant and fruit their names). The berries are slightly sweeter than American elderberry (S. canadensis) and are used the same way — in jellies, juices, wines, elderflower cordial, and traditional medicine. Blue elderberry is significantly more drought-tolerant than American elderberry, adapts to alkaline soils, and grows in the dry, sunny conditions of western landscapes where the eastern species struggles. It is an important food and medicine plant in the traditions of dozens of western Native American nations. Plant where spreading by suckers is acceptable.

common_name: Blue Lake Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Purple Dooryard Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing good airflow through the canopy. Blue Lake is a purple Florida bunch grape carrying strong resistance to Pierce's disease, one of a small group of University of Florida-recommended cultivars able to shrug off the bacterial infection that limits most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South. Unlike several of its Florida-bred counterparts, it typically grows well on its own roots and does not need grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in alkaline soils, simplifying establishment for home growers. Its purple berries are used both for fresh dooryard eating and for juice and jelly making, ripening in midsummer shortly after the earlier 'Stover' cultivar. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and maintain a preventive fungicide program to control the fungal fruit rots that are the main remaining disease threat in Florida's hot, humid summers.

common_name: Blue Moon Honeyberry (Original University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
notes: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Blue Moon is self-infertile. Blue Moon was part of the founding quartet of haskap cultivars (alongside Berry Blue, Blue Belle, and Blue Bird) released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, the introductions that established large-fruited modern haskaps in North American gardens and orchards. Berries are elongated, dusky blue, and sweet-tart with a flavor often described as a cross between blueberry and raspberry, ripening well ahead of standard blueberries and giving cold-climate gardeners one of the first fresh berry harvests of the season. Like other haskaps, Blue Moon is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures to -40F with flowers surviving brief dips to about -8F, but it performs poorly in hot, humid summers and is best suited to cooler, shorter-season climates. Fruit is borne on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning in the first three to four years to removing dead or crossing branches, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes.

growth_habit: Eastern Australian ornamental fringed-flower berry tree
notes: Plant Elaeocarpus reticulatus in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment and in dry periods; mulch to maintain soil moisture and acidity; grows well in coastal gardens with some protection from strong wind. Blueberry Ash is one of the most ornamentally multi-season of all Australian native trees — providing year-round interest through its attractive, elliptical, fine-toothed leaves; the exquisite spring flowers (white or blush-pink, tiny fringed bells hanging in clusters, earning the nickname 'Fairy Petticoats'); and the persistent, brilliant cobalt-blue to blue-violet, blueberry-sized drupes that can be present on the tree year-round and are avidly consumed by parrots, doves, and other birds. The blue fruits are technically edible for humans but very astringent and are not eaten except in famine conditions; birds have no such reservation. Elaeocarpus reticulatus is a small to medium rainforest tree (20–40 feet in the wild) that adapts well to cultivation in garden situations, particularly in the humid, subtropical Gulf Coast climate. It makes an outstanding specimen, street tree, or privacy screen for zone 9–11 gardens; the year-round blue berries make it perhaps the most effective bird-attracting tree available for subtropical plantings.

Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; bog bilberry absolutely requires constantly moist to wet, strongly acidic, poorly drained peaty or boggy soil and will not succeed in drier, neutral conditions. Vaccinium uliginosum is a circumboreal subarctic and subalpine species found in bogs, tundra, and moist mountain heaths across North America, Europe, and Asia — the hardiest of all Vaccinium, surviving temperatures to -60°F; it produces small, round, blue-black berries with a sweet, mild flavor and exceptionally high antioxidant content (higher than commercial blueberries). The berries are an important subsistence food for northern indigenous peoples and are used in jams, pies, and fresh eating. Best suited to cold, wet, acidic sites in zones 1–6 where it is invaluable for bog gardens and moist native plantings.

Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil, incorporating pine bark fines to boost organic matter and moisture retention. Released by the University of Florida in 1985, Bonita is one of the earliest-ripening rabbiteye cultivars available, typically flowering and fruiting several weeks ahead of midseason types like Tifblue. It requires a compatible rabbiteye pollinator such as Climax or Beckyblue blooming at the same time to set a good crop, and while modern mid- and late-season rabbiteyes have generally surpassed it in overall yield, Bonita remains a useful choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible rabbiteye harvest. The vigorous, spreading bush performs well across the humid Gulf South once established in properly acidified soil.

Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Boreal Beauty needs cross-pollination from another haskap cultivar to crop well. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program as part of its 'Boreal' series, Boreal Beauty ripens later than the earliest haskap introductions and produces firm, elongated, deep-blue berries bred to hold well on the bush without dropping, making it well suited to mechanical or delayed hand harvest. Like other haskaps, it is exceptionally cold-hardy and thrives in short, cool-summer growing seasons, but it is not well adapted to hot, humid climates. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then shift to renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep the bush productive.

Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, as Boreal Blizzard will not set a meaningful crop without a compatible pollinizer nearby. Part of the University of Saskatchewan's 'Boreal' haskap series, Boreal Blizzard produces a heavy crop of good-flavored blue berries and blooms at a time that makes it an effective pollen source for several other Saskatchewan-bred cultivars, so it is commonly planted in pairs specifically to boost yields in a mixed haskap planting. The upright, vigorous shrub is extremely cold-hardy, tolerating deep winter cold typical of the Canadian prairies, but struggles in hot, humid summer regions. Limit pruning to removing dead or crossing wood while the bush is young, then begin renewal pruning of older canes once the planting is established.

common_name: Borealis Honeyberry (Large-Fruited University of Saskatchewan Haskap)
notes: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, since Borealis is self-infertile and needs cross-pollination to set fruit. Released by the University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program, Borealis produces some of the largest berries of any haskap cultivar, with a sweet-tart flavor often compared to a cross between blueberry and raspberry, and ripens in late spring, about two to three weeks before strawberries in most climates, making it one of the earliest fresh fruits of the season. Flowers open very early and tolerate temperatures down to about -8F, but a hard late freeze can still reduce fruit set, so plant in a site that avoids obvious frost pockets. Like other haskaps, Borealis is bred for cold-winter regions and struggles with root and crown health in hot, humid summers, so it is a poor fit for the Gulf Coast and performs best in short-season northern gardens. Minimal pruning is needed for the first four to five years beyond removing dead wood; thereafter remove one or two of the oldest, thickest canes annually to keep the shrub renewing itself.

Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; boulder raspberry is one of the most beautiful ornamental native shrubs of the Rocky Mountain foothills — an entirely thornless, arching shrub with attractive, deeply lobed, maplelike leaves and stunning large (up to 2.5 inch), pure white, rose-like flowers in late spring. The species name 'deliciosus' was reportedly given because the flowers are so delightful, though the fruit (small, dry, sparse drupelets) is technically edible but far from impressive compared to other raspberries. The magnificent white flowers in May and June make boulder raspberry outstanding as a flowering ornamental in dry, rocky garden situations in zones 4–8. Completely thornless — unlike virtually all other Rubus — making it safe for high-traffic areas of the garden. The state flower of Colorado (not officially, but very emblematic of the Front Range foothills). Drought tolerant once established, appropriate for xeriscape plantings in the Rocky Mountain West.

common_name: Box Huckleberry (Long-Lived Evergreen Creeping Shade Shrub)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, and mulch with pine needles or leaf litter to maintain acidity and moisture. Box Huckleberry is a rare, low, evergreen, boxwood-like shrub native to scattered sites in the eastern United States, forming slow-spreading clonal colonies that are among the longest-lived plant clones known, with some wild colonies estimated at over a thousand years old. Small, glossy, leathery evergreen leaves cover the low, dense mat of stems, and it bears small pink, bell-shaped spring flowers followed by sparse but edible, sweet, dark blue berries in summer, similar in flavor to other huckleberries though the plant fruits lightly in cultivation. Because it tolerates deep shade and stays low and evergreen year-round, it makes a distinctive, slow-growing woodland groundcover for shaded native gardens where few other fruiting shrubs will grow; give it consistent moisture and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizome mat once established.

Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant a second, genetically distinct viburnum nudum nearby to ensure heavy fruit set, since this species needs a compatible cross-pollinator. Brandywine is a Southeastern native shrub selected for its extraordinary berry display: clusters of pink berries that ripen through shades of rose and blue to a deep, glossy blue-black, often showing several colors on the same cluster at once, held above glossy, dark-green, disease-resistant foliage that turns burgundy-red in fall. It tolerates consistently wet soil better than most flowering shrubs, making it a strong choice for rain gardens, pond edges, and low, poorly drained spots where many shrubs struggle. The berries are an excellent food source for songbirds, who typically strip them soon after they ripen.

Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil in full sun; Brazos is a thorned, semi-erect blackberry developed by Texas A&M University and released in 1959 — for many decades it was the dominant commercial blackberry variety in Texas and the Gulf Coast South. Though newer thornless varieties have largely replaced it commercially, Brazos remains prized by home gardeners and farmers' market growers for its exceptional heat adaptation, flavor, and productivity on the alkaline soils that characterize much of central and south Texas. Berries are large, elongated, and very flavorful, ripening from late April through June in zone 9 — among the earliest major varieties. Unlike the University of Arkansas thornless releases (Natchez, Ouachita), Brazos tolerates alkaline soil pH (7.0–7.5) and calcareous caliche significantly better, making it the variety of choice for gardens on tight, rocky Hill Country soils or coastal prairie clay. Canes require trellising due to vigorous, semi-trailing growth. Wear heavy gloves when pruning. Remove fruited canes after harvest and select 4–5 of the strongest new canes per plant.

Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark; Brightwell is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1983 that became the dominant commercial rabbiteye variety in the southeastern US for its outstanding combination of yield, adaptability, and suitability for mechanical harvesting on u-pick and commercial farms. Mid-season ripening (late June to July in zone 8–9) follows the early-ripening Climax and Premier, extending the harvest window. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, firm, with a dry scar and mild, sweet flavor that improves with heat — they tend to sweeten noticeably as they ripen fully over 2–3 weeks, making daily picking rewarding. The upright, vigorous plants are productive and show good disease tolerance under Gulf Coast conditions. As with all rabbiteye blueberries, plant at least two compatible varieties for cross-pollination. Mulch deeply with pine bark or wood chips; never use fresh hardwood mulch as it raises pH.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Brightwell is the most widely planted rabbiteye blueberry variety in the southeastern United States, valued for its consistent mid-season production, outstanding flavor, and broad adaptability across zone 6–9. The medium to large, light blue berries ripen in June–July in most Gulf Coast plantings and hold well on the bush, extending the harvest window over 4–6 weeks. Brightwell's moderate chilling requirement (350–400 hours below 45°F) suits it perfectly to zone 8–9 conditions where high-chill northern varieties fail. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain consistent moisture through summer, and fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) at bloom and again after harvest. Avoid lime applications, which raise soil pH above the acceptable range.

Plant dormant or container bushes in winter in raised, sulfur-acidified beds where native soil is not already acidic, and keep a permanent layer of pine bark mulch over the root zone. Britewell is a University of Georgia rabbiteye selection valued by growers for consistently heavy, reliable cropping of firm, medium-blue berries with good flavor on a moderately vigorous, upright-spreading bush, ripening in the mid-season window alongside cultivars like Tifblue. Plant with a second mid-season rabbiteye for cross-pollination and fuller berry set, and feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest. Renewal-prune the oldest wood out each winter to keep young, productive canes coming and sustain the heavy yields the variety is known for.

Silver buffaloberry is an extremely cold-hardy nitrogen-fixing shrub native to the Great Plains, valued for its bright red, tart berries that have historically been used by Indigenous peoples of North America for pemmican and sauces. It is dioecious and wind-pollinated, requiring male and female plants; purchase sexed plants, as seedlings cannot be sexed until flowering at 3–5 years. The thorny, silver-leaved plants thrive in alkaline, dry, or infertile soils where other fruits fail. Harvest by spreading a tarp and gently shaking or beating branches after a light frost, which softens the bitterness; berries are very tart raw but excellent cooked.

Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun; Caddo is a more recent University of Arkansas thornless blackberry release, bred for a compact, upright plant habit that is noticeably shorter and tidier than older erect thornless cultivars, making it well suited to smaller home gardens and even large containers. It ripens early in the season, ahead of many other thornless varieties, with large, firm, glossy black, well-flavored berries. The compact habit reduces the need for trellising and makes hand harvest easier. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest few per plant to maintain good air circulation and fruit size.

common_name: Camellia Southern Highbush Blueberry (Mild-Flavored Productive Blueberry)
notes: Amend planting beds to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines before setting out dormant bushes in winter, and keep roots consistently moist with a thick mulch layer since southern highbush blueberries have shallow, fibrous root systems. Camellia is a University of Florida release known for very high, consistent yields of medium to large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, low-acid flavor that many home growers find especially easy-eating fresh off the bush. The upright, vigorous plant tends to hold its crop well without excessive splitting in Gulf Coast humidity. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to renew fruiting wood, and fertilize lightly with an acid-forming blueberry fertilizer split between early spring and shortly after harvest.

Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Cape Fear is a southern highbush blueberry released by North Carolina State University and selected for an early ripening window combined with a comparatively low chill requirement, which lets it set a full crop even after mild Gulf South winters that shortchange higher-chill northern highbush types. Fruit is medium-large, light blue, and firm with good classic highbush flavor. Cape Fear is only partially self-fruitful, so plant a second southern highbush or rabbiteye cultivar nearby to improve fruit set and berry size. Because southern highbush types have shallower, less drought-tolerant roots than rabbiteye, keep a thick layer of pine bark or pine straw mulch over the root zone and irrigate through dry spells, especially in the first two years after planting.

'Captivator' is a nearly thornless American-type gooseberry producing sweet, teardrop-shaped reddish-purple berries that are pleasant for fresh eating. Its low thorn count and good mildew resistance make it one of the most user-friendly varieties for home gardeners. Grow in full sun to light shade in cool, moist, well-drained soil with a thick organic mulch. Prune lightly in winter to remove old and crowded wood, keeping the bush open and productive.

Plant dormant, thorny bushes in fertile, well-drained soil in a spot with cool root conditions, mulching to conserve moisture and prune to an open framework to make harvest through the spines easier. Careless is a traditional English culinary gooseberry long grown for its heavy, reliable crops of large, pale green, thin-skinned berries that are quite tart when picked early for cooking but sweeten as they ripen toward translucent pale yellow-green, making it equally suited to pies, fools, and preserves or later fresh eating. The vigorous, somewhat spreading bush is one of the most widely planted gooseberry cultivars in British gardens and allotments. Prune in the dormant season to an open, airy shape to improve light penetration and reduce mildew pressure on the ripening fruit.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Carlos is a bronze-skinned muscadine developed by North Carolina State University and released in 1970, and remains one of the two or three most widely planted muscadines in the southeastern US because of its exceptional adaptability, consistent yields, and suitability for both fresh-eating and bronze muscadine wine production. The medium-sized, bronze-gold berries ripen uniformly in mid-season and have a mild, sweet musky flavor that is less pronounced than Scuppernong — making Carlos wines and juice more accessible to people new to muscadine flavors. Self-fertile, so it produces well as a single plant, though yields improve with a black muscadine variety nearby. Carlos is resistant to Pierce's disease, downy mildew, and other diseases that devastate European wine grapes in the humid South — no spray program is needed in most home garden settings. Prune in late winter, leaving only short spurs on permanent cordons. Harvest when berries slip from the cluster at a gentle tug.

'Caroline' is a vigorous fall-bearing red raspberry prized for large, intensely flavored fruit with high antioxidant content. Plant in full sun in fertile, slightly acidic soil and irrigate consistently during fruit development. Prune as a primocane type by cutting canes to the ground in late winter for one large fall harvest. Its heat tolerance makes it a strong choice for warmer parts of its range, though it benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.

Amend soil to a strongly acidic pH 4.5–5.0 with peat moss or sulfur before planting; Centurion is a USDA-ARS-released rabbiteye blueberry prized as one of the latest-ripening varieties available, extending the harvest well past Tifblue into late July and into August in zone 8–9 and stretching the fresh-picking season for home growers and u-pick operations alike. It is also among the more cold-hardy rabbiteye selections, tolerating winter temperatures further north than many older varieties. Berries are small to medium, dark blue, firm, and flavorful, holding well on the bush without softening even in late-season heat. Plant with an early- or midseason variety such as Climax or Brightwell for cross-pollination, since rabbiteye blueberries including Centurion set little fruit without a compatible partner nearby. Established Centurion bushes are vigorous and heavy-bearing; renew a portion of the oldest canes each winter by cutting them to the ground to keep the bush productive and to encourage fresh, high-yielding new wood.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun; Centurion is a late-season rabbiteye blueberry that ripens in July in zone 8–9, extending the pick-your-own season after mid-season varieties like Brightwell have finished. The large, firm, dark blue berries have excellent flavor and shipping quality, and the upright, vigorous shrubs can reach 8–10 feet at maturity. Centurion requires approximately 400–500 chilling hours, making it suitable for zone 7–8b but less reliable in the mildest parts of zone 9a where chilling accumulation can be inconsistent. Plant as part of a multi-variety planting to achieve full-season harvest from late May through mid-July. The firm, large berries are particularly well-suited to fresh markets and U-pick operations where shelf life matters.

common_name: Champanel Grape (Extremely Vigorous Pierce's Disease-Resistant Grape)
notes: Plant in average to poorly drained soil in full sun on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis able to support very vigorous growth. Bred by Texas grape pioneer T. V. Munson in the late 1800s from a cross of the wild Vitis champinii with an American labrusca-type grape, Champanel is renowned for tolerating conditions that kill most grape vines outright, including heavy soil, occasional flooding, and Pierce's disease, a bacterial illness common in the humid South. The large, dark purple-black berries are tart and seedy, better suited to juice and jelly than fresh eating, but the vine's toughness makes it a dependable arbor and shade grape where other varieties fail. Prune to a permanent framework each winter to manage its rampant growth.

Site bushes in full sun on acidic soil amended with peat or pine bark and mulch heavily to keep shallow roots cool and moist. Chandler is famous for producing some of the largest berries of any highbush blueberry, often nickel- to quarter-sized, with a mild, sweet flavor and a very long harvest window since ripe fruit holds well on the bush. Its extended ripening period spreads picking over several weeks rather than concentrating it into a short flush. Vigorous, upright canes benefit from a second pollinator variety nearby to improve fruit set and size.

Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5); Cherokee is one of the earliest University of Arkansas thornless blackberry releases, introduced in the early 1970s and long a standard against which newer thornless varieties are measured. Canes are erect and self-supporting, requiring only light trellising, and produce medium-to-large, firm, well-flavored black berries in a concentrated early-to-mid season harvest. Because it is an older release, Cherokee is generally less productive and somewhat more disease-prone than modern Arkansas thornless cultivars like Natchez or Ouachita, but its cold hardiness and long track record still make it a dependable choice. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 per plant to keep the planting productive.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the vigorous semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Chester is one of the most widely planted thornless blackberry cultivars in North America, valued for a rare combination of good cold hardiness, strong resistance to cane blight and other diseases, and reliable production of large, firm, mild-flavored fruit that ripens later in summer than most cultivars, extending the blackberry harvest season. Its tolerance of colder winters than many thornless blackberries has made it a standard choice well beyond the Gulf South, though it performs well there too given adequate summer water. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for the next season's fruiting canes.

Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun and trellis the vigorous, thorny canes for support and easier harvest. Chickasaw is an older University of Arkansas blackberry release valued for its very large fruit size and vigorous, productive canes, ripening in the early-to-mid part of the season. Unlike the newer thornless Arkansas releases, Chickasaw retains thorns, so plant it where hand-picking around thorny canes is acceptable in exchange for its exceptionally large, firm, flavorful berries. Prune out fruited floricanes immediately after harvest and thin new primocanes to the strongest 4-6 canes per plant to sustain vigor and berry size in subsequent years.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chilean guava is a compact, evergreen shrub with small, dark-green, aromatic leaves that produces masses of tiny, deep-pink to red berries with an intensely sweet, aromatic flavor reminiscent of strawberries and vanilla — reportedly Queen Victoria's favorite jam fruit. The plant makes an excellent evergreen hedge or foundation shrub in mild climates and tolerates light frost to about 12–15°F once established. Harvest berries in fall when they are fully ripe and very dark pink-red. Excellent for jams, jellies, and fresh eating. The closely related Ugni candollei (Chilean strawberry guava) is very similar with slightly different flavors.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade — Chinese wolfberry is similar to goji berry (L. barbarum) but more cold-hardy and shade-tolerant, producing red-orange elongated berries with the same sweet-astringent, tart-sweet flavor. In traditional Chinese medicine, the leaves (often cooked as a vegetable), young shoots, and berries are all used. The dried berries (gou qi zi) are a fundamental ingredient in Chinese tonic soups and herbal preparations, used for eye health and as a general tonic for centuries. Fresh berries are also edible and pleasant. The arching, thornless-to-spiny stems produce attractive light purple flowers in summer before the berries. Remarkably adaptable to difficult soils including alkaline, clay, and dry soils, and more shade-tolerant than most full-sun fruiting shrubs. Note that it spreads by roots and seeds; manage accordingly.

Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, acidic soil; Choctaw is an erect, thorny blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in 1980, one of the earliest-ripening blackberry varieties available and long valued in the mid-South and Gulf Coast for extending the harvest season ahead of later thornless varieties. The medium-sized berries are glossy black, firm, and exceptionally sweet with small seeds and outstanding flavor, considered by many Southern growers among the best-tasting of the University of Arkansas blackberry releases even decades after its introduction. The erect canes are self-supporting and highly productive, though the thorns require more careful handling at harvest and pruning than newer thornless varieties. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; tip primocanes at about 36 inches in summer to encourage the lateral branches that carry the following year's crop. An excellent early-season partner for later-ripening varieties like Ouachita or Natchez to extend the blackberry harvest across the whole season. Zone 6–9.

Amend soil with peat moss, pine bark, or sulfur to achieve pH 4.5–5.5 before planting; rabbiteye blueberries like Climax will not thrive in neutral or alkaline soils. Climax is a rabbiteye blueberry (Vaccinium ashei) released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1974 and remains one of the most widely grown rabbiteye varieties in the Deep South because of its early season (it ripens in late May to early June in zone 8–9, the earliest of the major rabbiteye varieties), consistent productivity, and excellent fruit quality. Berries are medium-sized, light blue with a mild, sweet flavor and small dry scar. Plant in groups of 2–3 varieties for cross-pollination (rabbiteye blueberries are not self-fruitful). Remove flowers the first 2 years to direct energy into root establishment; full crops develop by year 3–4. Mulch 4–6 inches deep with pine bark or wood chips to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Climax is notably upright in growth habit and tolerates the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast well.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Climax is one of the original rabbiteye blueberry cultivars released by the USDA and University of Georgia, selected for very early ripening — typically the first rabbiteye to color in a planting, beginning to ripen in late May in zone 8–9. The medium-sized, firm, light blue berries have good flavor but a somewhat thicker skin than later-season varieties; this firmness improves shipping quality. Climax's moderate chilling requirement (350–400 hours below 45°F) ensures reliable bloom in zone 8–9 without risk of late-season freeze damage. The upright, vigorous shrubs are productive and long-lived. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain acid fertilization with ammonium sulfate, and keep soil consistently moist through the production season.

Clove currant (Ribes odoratum, syn. R. aureum) is a tough, drought-tolerant native prairie shrub with intensely clove-spice-scented yellow spring flowers and glossy black berries in mid-summer. It tolerates alkaline, clay, or droughty soils far better than European currants, making it the best Ribes choice for the Great Plains and intermountain West. The berries range from mild to somewhat astringent depending on selection; look for named fruit-producing cultivars such as 'Crandall'. Prune by removing the oldest canes at the base every few years; the plant suckers moderately and can form a thicket if not managed. Verify state restrictions before planting.

Plant rooted tip cuttings in moist, well-drained sandy loam in full sun to light shade; southern dewberry is a low, trailing Gulf Coast and Southeastern native bramble that hugs the ground rather than growing upright, with slender, prickly canes that root wherever the tips touch soil. It is among the earliest brambles to flower, opening white blooms as early as late winter in the Deep South, followed by glossy black, sweet-tart drupes ready to pick weeks ahead of upright blackberries. Because canes trail and root freely, give it room to spread or confine it with a mowed border, and expect it to naturalize readily in sunny, sandy fields, roadsides, and open pine woods edges. After fruiting, cut back spent floricanes to tidy the patch and encourage vigorous new primocane growth for next year's crop.

common_name: Columbus Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Large-Fruited Southern Blueberry)
notes: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Columbus is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry that ripens late in the Southern blueberry season, extending fresh harvest well past most mid-season cultivars while still producing large, flavorful fruit on vigorous, productive bushes. Pairing Columbus with earlier-ripening cultivars like Austin, Alapaha, or Premier gives a Southern blueberry planting a long, staggered harvest from late spring through midsummer. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Columbus requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean, alkaline to slightly acidic soil in full sun; common barberry is drought-tolerant and adaptable to poor soils but is an alternate host for wheat stem rust (Puccinia graminis) and is prohibited in many wheat-growing states — confirm legality before planting. Berberis vulgaris is a thorny, deciduous European shrub producing clusters of small, oval, bright-red berries (barberries) in fall with an intensely tart, citrusy, slightly astringent flavor rich in vitamin C; they are used in Persian cooking (zereshk polo — barberry rice pilaf) where they are a quintessential flavoring, and for making barberry jam, juice, wine, and candy throughout Europe and western Asia. The bright-yellow wood and bark contain berberine, a traditional medicinal compound. The berries are also an important food source for birds in winter.

Plant rooted cuttings in fall in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; manzanita absolutely requires excellent drainage and summer drought — it will not survive in humid climates or wet soils and is best suited to Mediterranean-climate gardens in California and similar dry-summer climates. Arctostaphylos manzanita is a large, beautiful, evergreen California native shrub or small tree with signature smooth, mahogany-red bark that peels to reveal bright, polished inner bark; it produces masses of urn-shaped, pink-white flowers beloved by hummingbirds and native bees in late winter through early spring, followed by small (1/3 inch), round, apple-like fruits (manzanita means "little apple" in Spanish) that ripen red to dark burgundy in summer. The edible fruits are tart and mealy, used by California Native Americans for making a refreshing cider-like beverage by soaking in water, and for making pinole (ground dried fruit). The exfoliating bark is one of the most beautiful features of any native western shrub.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, and avoid the hottest afternoon sun, which can scorch the glossy, holly-like leaflets. Compactum is a dwarf selection of the Pacific Northwest native Oregon grape, staying under 3 feet tall and wide — roughly half the size of the species — while still producing the same fragrant, bright yellow spring flower clusters followed by dusty-blue, edible (if tart) berries beloved by songbirds, and the same spiny, holly-like evergreen foliage that turns purple-bronze in winter cold. Its smaller stature suits it to foundation plantings and shaded borders where full-size Oregon grape would eventually crowd the space. Prune only lightly, if at all, since its naturally compact habit needs little maintenance to stay tidy.

Grow this cold-hardy American grape on a two- or four-arm kniffin trellis, pruning heavily each winter to keep fruiting wood renewed and clusters well spaced. It produces the same deep blue-black, musky-sweet slip-skin berries prized in classic Concord grape juice and jelly, but without the seeds that fill traditional Concord fruit, making it far more pleasant for fresh eating. The vines share Concord's toughness and reliable heavy cropping in short-season northern climates, though clusters are typically a bit smaller and looser than the seeded parent. It is self-fruitful and widely adapted to home gardens outside hot, humid grape-growing regions.

common_name: Conquistador Grape (Disease-Resistant Black Juice and Jelly Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Developed from breeding lines descended from T. V. Munson's disease-resistant Texas grape stock, Conquistador produces vigorous vines with strong tolerance to Pierce's disease and other conditions that limit grape growing in hot, humid regions. The medium-sized black berries are tart and well suited to juice, jelly, and homemade wine rather than fresh eating out of hand. Because vines are vigorous and productive, prune firmly each winter to a permanent set of cordons and thin fruit clusters if growth becomes crowded, which improves air circulation and reduces fruit rot in humid weather.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cowart is an early-ripening black muscadine developed by the Georgia Experiment Station (now UGA) and released in 1974. It is widely valued as a dual-purpose black muscadine: the large, jet-black berries (larger than Noble) are excellent for fresh eating with a rich, sweet, full-flavored muscadine taste, and also produce outstanding dark wine, juice, and jam. As one of the earliest-ripening black muscadines, Cowart extends the beginning of the black muscadine season and is frequently paired with Noble and other later-ripening varieties to spread harvest over a longer window. The thick skin makes berries more durable and longer-lasting after harvest than most muscadines. Cowart is self-fertile and requires no pollinizer, though yields increase with nearby compatible varieties. Disease resistance is excellent across the humid Gulf South. Harvest in late August when berries are fully black and slip freely from the stem with gentle pressure.

Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun, spacing plants to knit together into a solid groundcover; established plantings tolerate light foot traffic and need only occasional shearing to keep them tidy. Creeping Raspberry is a low, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen trailing bramble native to Taiwan, grown chiefly as an ornamental groundcover for its glossy, crinkled, bronze-tinged leaves, small white flowers, and small orange-red, raspberry-like fruits produced in late summer that are edible, if mild and seedy, and readily eaten by birds. Its dense, mounding, self-rooting habit makes it useful for covering slopes, edging shaded beds, or spilling over walls in areas too shady for turfgrass, and unlike upright brambles it stays low and thornless-feeling underfoot. Cut back hard in late winter every few years to renew growth and prevent the center of the planting from thinning out.

Train young vines onto a permanent support system and prune annually in dormancy, since fruit forms on the current season's growth from one-year-old canes. Crimson Seedless bears elongated, crisp, pink-to-red berries with a mild, sweet flavor on large, well-filled clusters that ripen late in the season. It is a late-season companion to earlier seedless grapes, extending the fresh-eating harvest into fall, and tends to color best where nights cool down as the fruit matures. Like most vinifera grapes it prefers a long, warm growing season and struggles in areas with high humidity and fungal disease pressure.

Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting; Croatan is a historic North Carolina State University highbush blueberry release from the 1950s, bred specifically to bring highbush fruit quality to areas with milder winters than the traditional northern highbush belt, and it remains one of the lower-chill highbush options that can crop reasonably well in zone 8-9. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, firm, and sweet with the classic highbush flavor that many gardeners prefer over rabbiteye. Croatan is partially self-fruitful but produces heavier, larger-berried crops with a second southern highbush or rabbiteye cultivar blooming nearby. The compact, rounded bush needs consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil to perform well in Gulf South clay, so raised beds or heavily amended planting holes give the best results.
