Prune out the oldest wood each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.

Plant in acidic, moist, sandy or organic soil in partial to full shade; Dangleberry tolerates and indeed thrives under open pine forest canopies where acid soil and dappled light create its native habitat. Gaylussacia frondosa is a native deciduous shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, found in longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods, and sandy pine-oak barrens from Maine to the Gulf Coast — a classic component of the native understory throughout zone 7–9. The small blue-black berries, ripe July–August, are sweet, distinctly resinous in flavor, and historically among the most prized wild fruits gathered by indigenous peoples and early settlers throughout the Southeast — often preferred over blueberries for their more complex flavor when made into jams, pies, and preserves. Dangleberry is closely related to the Black Huckleberry (G. baccata) but tends to be taller, more open in habit, and more shade-tolerant. The plant spreads by underground stolons to form loose colonies that provide excellent wildlife habitat — birds, black bears, and small mammals rely heavily on huckleberry fruits. In zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes with acidic, sandy soil, it is an outstanding native understory berry for shaded woodland gardens where blueberries struggle in too much shade.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Darlene is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) bronze muscadine released by the University of Georgia for home garden and commercial production, valued for combining good fresh-eating fruit quality with the self-fertility that allows a single vine to produce a full crop. The medium to large, bronze-gold fruits have a sweet, mild, pleasant muscadine flavor with less of the strong musky note that some consumers find overpowering in older varieties. The tender skin and mild, sweet flavor make Darlene one of the more approachable fresh-eating muscadines for people new to the variety. The self-fertile habit is particularly valuable for home gardeners who have space for only one vine; unlike female-flowered varieties that require a separate pollinator, Darlene sets fruit reliably on its own. In zone 9 the vigorous vine grows readily in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and produces consistently.

Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and train the vigorous, self-supporting canes onto a wire trellis to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. Darrow was developed by USDA breeders and released in the late 1950s, named in honor of the noted small-fruit breeder George M. Darrow, and it was bred specifically for cold hardiness beyond what most erect blackberries of the era could tolerate. The berries are large, firm, glossy black, and tart-sweet, produced in heavy clusters over a mid-to-late season harvest window that extends the bramble season after earlier varieties finish. Its thorny, upright canes and strong winter hardiness have kept it in cultivation as a dependable choice for northern growers who need a blackberry that survives cold winters without cane dieback.

common_name: Darrow Blueberry (Evergreen Blueberry, Native Florida Blueberry)
notes: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich, sandy to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun; amend with peat moss or pine bark to increase acidity; mulch heavily with pine straw. Vaccinium darrowii (Darrow blueberry or evergreen blueberry) is a native Florida and southeast Georgia blueberry species — one of several native blueberries of the southeastern coastal plain — producing small, 1/4-inch, intensely flavored, blue-black berries in April–May with an extraordinarily rich, sweet-tart blueberry flavor that many consider superior to commercial cultivars. The small, semi-evergreen to evergreen, blue-green leaves are among the smallest of any blueberry species; the white, urn-shaped flowers in February–March are especially important for native bee pollinators emerging early. This species is a parent of several southern highbush blueberry cultivars (including 'Sharpblue,' 'Gulf Coast,' and 'O'Neal') bred for low-chill southern climates. Darrow blueberry is extremely low-maintenance in native soils — requiring no supplemental irrigation once established and producing reliably in the conditions of the coastal plain with minimal care. It is rarely available commercially but is outstanding as a native wildlife plant — birds and small mammals consume the berries eagerly.

common_name: Daytona Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Pink Dooryard Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy. Daytona was released in the early 1980s from the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program and is grown chiefly as a home dooryard grape, valued for its pink-blushed fruit and for standing up to Pierce's disease and downy mildew far better than European wine grapes in Florida's hot, humid climate. It does remain somewhat susceptible to anthracnose, ripe rot, black rot, and powdery mildew, so an ongoing fungicide program through the growing season is worthwhile even on a resistant cultivar like this one. Fruit is best suited to fresh eating off the vine rather than commercial wine or juice production. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and reduce disease pressure in humid weather.

Deerberry is a native eastern North American Vaccinium species bearing clusters of small, blue-green to purple berries that ripen in midsummer with a flavor ranging from tart to mildly sweet depending on provenance and growing conditions. Unlike most blueberries, the flowers have exserted stamens (protruding well beyond the petals), giving them a distinctive open, star-shaped appearance that attracts native bees. The plant is very drought-tolerant once established and naturalizes well in dry, acidic woodland margins. Berries are edible fresh or cooked but have variable palatability; select superior-tasting wild ecotypes or named cultivars when available.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Delight is a long-established North Carolina State University bronze muscadine cultivar known for consistent production of medium-sized, sweet, thin-skinned bronze berries with good flavor for fresh eating, well ahead of the peak-season bronze varieties like Fry. Vines are vigorous and reliably productive, and the early-to-mid-season ripening window makes Delight useful for extending the start of the bronze muscadine harvest when paired with later cultivars. It is self-fertile and needs no separate pollinizer, though yield improves with additional muscadine varieties nearby. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that limit bunch grape production in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input once established. Harvest as berries color fully and detach easily from the stem; train vines to a sturdy two-wire trellis and prune annually in winter to keep fruiting wood renewed.

Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur well before planting; Delite is a USDA-ARS rabbiteye blueberry released from the small fruit research station at Poplarville, Mississippi, and prized among Gulf South gardeners for having the sweetest, lowest-acid flavor of the classic mid-century rabbiteye releases. Berries are medium-sized, dull blue, and ripen over a fairly long mid-to-late season window, making Delite a good choice for spreading out the fresh-eating harvest rather than a single heavy flush. Plants are vigorous and productive but need a compatible rabbiteye pollinator within about 50 feet, since Delite sets poorly on its own. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system from Gulf Coast summer heat, and avoid phosphorus-heavy fertilizers that blueberries tolerate poorly.

common_name: Delite Rabbiteye Blueberry (Extra-Sweet Midseason Southern Blueberry)
notes: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter into acidic, well-drained soil worked with pine bark or peat, and mulch well since rabbiteye blueberries root shallowly. Delite is an older University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for producing some of the sweetest fruit of any rabbiteye cultivar, with medium to large, light blue berries that ripen midseason. Like other rabbiteyes it needs cross-pollination from a second rabbiteye variety blooming at the same time to set a full crop, and its moderate chill requirement fits well within the zone 7-9 range common along the northern Gulf Coast. The upright, moderately vigorous bushes are long-lived and low-maintenance once established in properly acidified soil.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Dixie is a large, dark-skinned muscadine released by the University of Georgia, producing very large, round, dark purple to black berries with a sweet, rich flavor and thin, relatively tender skin that makes fresh eating more comfortable than older tough-skinned muscadine varieties. As a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) cultivar, Dixie sets heavy crops reliably without a pollinator vine — a significant practical advantage for home gardeners. The late-season ripening (September–October in zone 9) extends the fresh muscadine harvest into fall when most other fresh fruit has finished. The vigorous vines are productive once established and show good resistance to the common muscadine diseases including black rot and angular leaf spot that can be problems in the humid Gulf South. Dixie pairs well with Triumph (bronze) for a complementary planting that provides both dark and bronze-skinned muscadines from the same trellis system.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Doreen is a bronze muscadine released by Mississippi State University in 1979 and named for a long-serving clerical employee at the university's experiment station. It is the most widely used late-season bronze muscadine, valued by commercial growers and home winemakers for extending the harvest season past Carlos and Scuppernong into late September and October. Yields are among the highest of any self-fertile bronze variety, making Doreen important for commercial production where volume matters. Berries are medium-sized, bronze-tan at maturity with a pleasant, mild muscadine flavor and good sugar content that makes excellent late-season wine. The plants are very vigorous and productive with strong disease resistance. Doreen is often planted in combination with Carlos to extend the bronze muscadine season from mid-August through October and to provide a range of flavors for blending. Prune heavily each winter; leave only short spurs on permanent cordon arms.

common_name: Dorman Red Raspberry (Heat-Tolerant Deep South Trailing Raspberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun and trellis the long, trailing canes on a two-wire support, since this variety sprawls rather than growing upright. Selected in the Deep South specifically to withstand summer heat that kills most raspberry cultivars outright, Dorman Red is one of the few raspberries that reliably fruits in zone 8-9 gardens where standard northern types decline within a year or two. It produces a single crop in late spring on second-year canes, with medium-sized, tart-sweet red berries that are excellent for preserves as well as fresh eating. Prune out spent floricanes immediately after harvest to make room for the current season's new growth, and keep roots mulched to buffer summer soil heat.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Downing is a nineteenth-century American gooseberry, a Houghton seedling introduced in the 1850s and still one of the most widely planted heirloom gooseberries because of its reliable production, vigorous growth, and good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many European gooseberry cultivars. Berries are medium-sized, pale green, and tart, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, picked slightly underripe for cooking or left to fully ripen for a milder, sweeter fresh-eating berry. The self-fertile bush needs no separate pollinator and bears reliably from a young age. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the thorny bush productive and open enough for easy harvest, and site with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides.

common_name: Doyle's Thornless Blackberry (Vigorous Trailing Thornless Bramble)
notes: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the long, trailing, thornless canes onto a sturdy multi-wire trellis, since this cultivar's vigor can overwhelm a light support structure within a couple of seasons. Doyle's Thornless was developed and patented by an amateur grower in Illinois and marketed directly to home gardeners rather than released through a university breeding program, and it became known for extremely heavy per-plant yields once established, with growers regularly reporting a single mature plant can produce many gallons of fruit. The berries are medium-to-large, sweet-tart, and hold their shape well for fresh eating, freezing, or preserving, ripening over an extended midseason window. It is self-fertile, though many growers plant more than one to maximize the already generous yields typical of the variety.

Plant in dry to well-drained, acidic, sandy or rocky soil in partial shade or dappled woodland light; dryland blueberry is a compact native Vaccinium of eastern US woodlands and acidic ridge tops that earns its common name from its exceptional tolerance of dry, lean, acidic conditions — it is among the most drought-tolerant blueberries in cultivation. The white to pink bell-shaped flowers in spring are followed by small, intensely sweet blue-black berries in midsummer that are prized for fresh eating and bird fodder. Excellent fall color in shades of orange, red, and burgundy. Unlike highbush cultivars, no irrigation or supplemental fertilizer is needed once established in appropriate soil. Plant several individuals for cross-pollination and heavier berry crops. An underused native for dry, shaded slopes and woodland gardens.

'Duke' is a highly reliable early-season northern highbush blueberry with firm, mild-flavored berries that ripen over a concentrated window. It blooms late but ripens early, helping it dodge spring frosts while still producing an early harvest. Plant in full sun in acidic soil with a pH of 4.5 to 5.5, amending heavily with peat moss and mulching with pine bark. Provide consistent moisture, avoid lime, and prune out weak twiggy growth each late winter to maintain vigor.

Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf huckleberry is a low-growing, colony-forming native shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain longleaf pine ecosystem, spreading by rhizomes across the forest floor of dry, sandy pine flatwoods and scrub habitats. The small, black to deep blue-black berries are edible and flavorful — similar in taste to other huckleberries but produced on a very low-growing plant. The sticky, gland-dotted leaves are a distinctive feature. In the garden, it makes an excellent low, spreading ground cover for dry, sandy, sunny, acidic sites in zone 9a where few plants thrive. It is fire-adapted and rebounds strongly after prescribed burns in its natural habitat. An underused native ground cover for longleaf pine ecosystem restoration and dry, acidic, native plant gardens.

common_name: Ebony King Dewberry (Heirloom Self-Fruitful Southern Dewberry)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a low wire trellis to keep fruit clean and easy to pick. Ebony King is an early twentieth-century Southern dewberry selection once popular from Texas through the Gulf South for its dependable, self-fruitful cropping and glossy black, firm, sweet-tart berries that ripen ahead of blackberry season. It largely fell out of commercial favor as upright, easier-to-manage blackberry cultivars became available, but it remains a hardy, low-input option for gardeners wanting the distinctive early-season flavor of a true dewberry. Cut fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes onto the trellis for the following year's crop.

Elderberries are fast-growing shrubs that fruit on current-season wood arising from two-year-old stems; cut one-third of the oldest canes to the ground each late winter to keep the planting vigorous. Plant two or more cultivars for cross-pollination — solo plantings produce far fewer berries. Harvest entire umbels (flat-topped clusters) in late summer when at least 95% of berries in a cluster are dark purple-black. Raw berries and green plant parts contain cyanogenic glycosides; always cook berries before eating.

Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and cut new canes back after their first season to encourage strong lateral branching for the following year's crop. Eldorado was discovered as a chance seedling in Ohio in the early twentieth century and went on to become one of the most widely planted home-garden blackberries in the eastern and midwestern United States for much of the century, valued above all for its reliable cold hardiness and productivity without needing a second variety for pollination. The berries are medium-sized, glossy black, sweet, and nearly seedless-tasting compared to many older thorny types, ripening over a fairly long midseason picking window. Eldorado's erect, self-supporting thorny canes tolerate harsh winters better than many later thornless introductions, which is why it persisted in northern gardens long after flashier commercial varieties came and went.

Elliott's Blueberry is one of the most valuable native blueberries for the warm, humid southeastern coastal plain, native to the moist to dry, acidic, sandy soils of pocosins, pine flatwoods, bay swamp edges, and woodland margins from North Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, where it grows in association with other ericaceous plants on acidic, well-drained soils. A vigorous, upright to arching shrub that can reach 8–12 feet in favorable conditions, it produces an abundance of small, sweet, dark blue berries in spring (April–May, depending on location) that ripen earlier than most highbush blueberries and are highly palatable to wildlife and humans alike. One of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the native blueberries, it is an excellent choice for the Gulf Coast region where northern highbush varieties struggle; it requires consistently acidic, well-drained soil and benefits from cross-pollination with other Vaccinium species. Plant multiple shrubs for cross-pollination and heavier fruiting; mulch with pine bark or pine needles to maintain soil acidity.

Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in spring in any well-drained, alkaline to acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; European hackberry is remarkably adaptable to poor, dry, rocky soils, alkaline conditions, and urban pollution. Celtis australis is a long-lived (500+ year), medium to large tree of the Mediterranean basin and southern Europe, producing small (1/3 inch), round fruits that turn from yellow to orange to dark-purple-black when fully ripe in autumn, with a sweet, date-like flavor and a single large seed; the fruits were widely eaten by Mediterranean peoples since antiquity (the "lotus" fruit referenced by Homer that caused forgetfulness, though the identity of Homer's lotus is debated). The tree's beautiful, long-petioled, rough-textured leaves, tolerance of drought and heat, and picturesque form make it an excellent ornamental in zones 7–11; it is one of the best shade trees for very hot, dry, alkaline landscapes.

Plant in well-drained, acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; European mountain ash is a graceful ornamental tree with pinnate, ash-like leaves that delivers three seasons of interest — clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring, abundant bright orange-red berry clusters from late summer through winter, and orange-red fall foliage. The profuse berries are eaten by waxwings, robins, thrushes, and other songbirds so eagerly that trees can be stripped within days of peak ripeness. The berries are edible to humans but contain parasorbic acid when raw (causing nausea) and must be cooked or frozen to destroy this compound; cooked berries make excellent jelly with a tart, cranberry-like flavor. Prefers cool, moist climates and does not perform well south of zone 6.

This everbearing mulberry yields sweet, plump berries over a long season on a compact, shrubby tree that is easy to manage. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates a range of conditions and is quite drought resistant once established. Prune in winter to keep it at a pickable height and to open the canopy. The fruit ripens over many weeks, so harvest regularly and expect birds to compete for the crop. Note that ripe berries stain, so site it away from patios and walkways.

common_name: Evergreen Blueberry (Darrow's Blueberry, Lowbush Evergreen Blueberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy or amended soil in full sun to partial shade; in hot zone 9 climates, afternoon shade improves fruit quality. Vaccinium darrowii (Darrow's Blueberry or Evergreen Blueberry) is a native, low-growing blueberry species from the coastal plain flatwoods and sandhills of the Southeast, ranging from South Carolina through Florida to Louisiana. It is unique among native blueberries for being semi-evergreen to fully evergreen — retaining most of its small, bluish-gray leaves through mild winters — and for requiring very few chill hours (100–200 hours below 45°F), making it one of the most reliable blueberries for warm zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where the commonly-planted Rabbiteye types (Vaccinium ashei) may not receive enough cold in mild years. Vaccinium darrowii is also an important breeding parent used by blueberry breeders at the University of Florida and USDA to develop the Southern Highbush blueberry series — its drought tolerance, evergreen foliage, and minimal chill requirement were bred into commercial cultivars. The wild species produces small but sweet, intensely flavored berries that are beloved by wildlife. It tolerates the high heat, humidity, and wet-dry cycles of Gulf Coast flatwoods better than most northern blueberry species.

Evergreen huckleberry is a slow-growing Pacific Coast native prized both as an ornamental evergreen shrub and as a source of small, sweet-tart black berries that ripen from October through January — one of the few edible fruits to ripen in the Pacific Northwest winter. Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5 with pine bark or sawdust mulch. The plant is extremely slow to establish from container stock and may take 5–7 years for significant fruit production. Florists prize the glossy foliage as a cut green; pruning for floral use also serves to shape the shrub.

Plant in well-drained, rocky or gravelly, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen sumac is one of the finest drought-tolerant evergreen shrubs for dry Southwest and Texas Hill Country landscapes, holding its glossy, leathery dark-green leaves through winter and providing year-round structure. Small creamy-white flowers bloom in late summer and attract bees and other pollinators, followed by dense clusters of deep-red, slightly sticky fruits that are documented as a food source for over 100 bird species including mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and Montezuma quail. It thrives on neglect once established and is an excellent choice for wildlife gardens, slopes, or as a large screening hedge. Avoid overwatering and heavy soils, which are the primary causes of decline.

Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur several months before planting; Excel is an early-season rabbiteye blueberry from the University of Georgia breeding program, selected to open the harvest window ahead of standard mid-season varieties while still carrying good rabbiteye vigor and heat tolerance. Berries are medium to large, light blue, and firm, with a mild sweet-tart flavor typical of early rabbiteyes. Excel's relatively low chill requirement makes it reliable in zone 8-9 Gulf South winters that sometimes shortchange higher-chill northern varieties. It is not self-fruitful, so interplant with Climax or another early-blooming rabbiteye within about 50 feet for good fruit set and larger berries. Mulch with pine bark to keep roots cool and moist, and skip lime and phosphorus fertilizers, which blueberries handle poorly.

'Fall Gold' is an extra-hardy everbearing yellow raspberry that produces very sweet amber berries on both first- and second-year canes. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil amended with organic matter and keep evenly moist. It bears a summer crop on overwintered canes and a fall crop on new primocanes; leave floricanes standing for two harvests or mow for one large fall picking. Suckers freely, so contain the planting with regular removal of wandering shoots.

Plant in well-drained, lean, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established, requiring no irrigation in the Southeast. Vaccinium arboreum (farkleberry or sparkleberry) is the largest native Vaccinium in the southeastern United States — a multi-stemmed, deciduous to semi-evergreen large shrub or small tree reaching 6–15 feet with smooth, reddish-brown exfoliating bark that is ornamentally attractive year-round. It is native to the dry, acidic soils of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, piedmont, and lower Appalachians, tolerating drought, sandy soils, and poor fertility far better than cultivated highbush blueberries. The small (1/4 inch), dark blue-black berries are technically edible, but are mealy, seedy, and quite astringent when eaten fresh — quite different from cultivated blueberries. They are far better suited to drying (they were used extensively by southeastern Native Americans as a dried fruit), cooking into jams and pies, or fermenting. Birds and wildlife consume the abundant fruit crops enthusiastically. As a garden plant, farkleberry is an underused native with beautiful four-season interest: white urn-shaped flowers in spring, glossy foliage in summer, brilliant red-orange fall color, and attractive bark in winter.

common_name: Farthing Southern Highbush Blueberry (High-Yield Midseason Blueberry)
notes: Plant container-grown or dormant bare-root bushes in winter into raised, sulfur-amended beds if native soil is not already strongly acidic, and mulch with pine bark to conserve moisture through summer heat. Farthing is a University of Florida southern highbush release valued by Gulf Coast growers for its exceptionally heavy, reliable yields of medium-large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, well-balanced flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It ripens over a fairly long midseason window, which spreads out the harvest and makes it a strong choice for home orchards wanting an extended picking period. Feed lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and after harvest, and renewal-prune out the oldest wood each winter to sustain the heavy fruit set.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, providing good air circulation to reduce fungal disease pressure. Favorite is a seedling selection of Black Spanish (Lenoir), one of the historic Gulf Coast grape varieties long grown for its exceptional tolerance to Pierce's disease, a bacterial infection spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European wine grapes within a few years in the warm, humid South. It produces blue-black, juicy berries used for both fresh eating and home winemaking, ripening reliably where Vitis vinifera varieties fail. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and airflow through the canopy.

Schisandra chinensis is a vigorous deciduous twining vine native to northeastern China and Russia, bearing pendant clusters of small, brilliant red berries in late summer whose juice is famously described as simultaneously sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent — hence the common name wu wei zi ('five flavor fruit'). The plant is predominantly dioecious, so plant at least one male and one female vine for fruit production, though some cultivars bear perfect flowers. Train on a trellis, pergola, or fence with afternoon shade; the vine prefers cool, moist, slightly acidic woodland conditions. Prune to control size after fruiting; berries are used medicinally and in herbal preparations worldwide.

Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Flordablue is a very low-chill-hour southern highbush blueberry developed by the University of Florida, requiring only 150–200 chill hours — one of the standard blueberry varieties for zone 9 and zone 10 gardens where inadequate winter chilling prevents northern varieties from producing. The medium-sized, firm, dark blue berries ripen in March–May in zone 9, among the very earliest blueberries of the season. Flordablue produces reliably in the mild winters of north-central and north Florida and the Gulf Coast, where more northerly varieties like Bluecrop or Blueray would fail to receive adequate winter chill. The flavor is mild, sweet, and pleasant — not as intensely flavorful as northern highbush varieties grown in their optimal cool climates, but very acceptable for fresh eating and processing. As a University of Florida release, it has an extensive track record of performance in Gulf Coast conditions.

Florida Serviceberry is a native shrub of moist to wet, sandy coastal plain habitats from Virginia south to Florida, producing clusters of small white flowers in late winter to early spring — among the first native flowers to open each year — that provide a critical early nectar and pollen source for emerging native bees and butterflies at a time when little else is blooming. The sweet, dark blue-purple berries that follow in late spring and early summer have a mild flavor reminiscent of blueberries and are avidly consumed by mockingbirds, catbirds, Baltimore orioles, cedar waxwings, and over 40 other bird species during the critical spring migration feeding period. The smaller, more compact stature compared to the familiar Downy Serviceberry makes Florida Serviceberry well suited to smaller gardens and naturalized plantings in the coastal plain Southeast. Plant in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Florida Serviceberry tolerates the wet, sandy, coastal plain soils that can challenge other native fruit shrubs.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun alongside a self-fertile pollinizer variety; Fry is a bronze muscadine developed by the Georgia Experiment Station and released in 1972, consistently regarded as the best fresh-eating muscadine available — the benchmark for table-quality muscadine grapes. The berries are extraordinarily large (up to 1.5 inches in diameter, one of the largest of any muscadine), bronze-gold at maturity with a beautiful appearance, excellent mild-sweet flavor, and thinner skin than most muscadines, making fresh eating more pleasant. Fry's principal limitation is its lack of self-fertility: it will produce essentially no fruit without a compatible self-fertile pollinizer planted within range. This has made it less popular commercially where single-variety plantings are common, but in home gardens where a pollinator is easily added, Fry is unmatched for fresh table quality. The vines are vigorous, productive once pollinated, and disease-resistant. Harvest when berries are fully bronze-gold and yield to gentle pressure.

Fuzzy kiwi (the standard grocery-store kiwifruit) requires a long, warm growing season and is best suited to zones 7–9 with at least 200 frost-free days. Like hardy kiwi, it is dioecious and requires male and female plants — one male pollinates up to 8 females. Train vines on a T-bar or pergola trellis and prune hard each dormant season to manage the vigorous growth. Harvest in late fall before hard frost when the seeds have turned black and the flesh is tender; fruit ripens off the vine.

Goji berries are highly adaptable, tolerating poor, alkaline soils where other fruits fail, but perform best in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0. The arching, slightly thorny canes can be left as a shrub or trained to a central leader with a stake. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals. Harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers — ripe fruits are bright red-orange, soft, and drop easily (avoid touching them, as the sap stains).

common_name: Golden Shadows Pagoda Dogwood (Variegated Rainbow Pagoda Dogwood)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Shadows is a variegated sport of native pagoda dogwood selected for leaves edged in bright golden-yellow around a green center, a combination that brightens through the season and glows in the dappled light of a woodland-edge planting. It retains the species' distinctive tiered, horizontal branching habit — the source of its 'pagoda' name — along with small, flat-topped clusters of white spring flowers and blue-black summer berries relished by songbirds, but it stays noticeably smaller and shrubbier than the green species, usually 8-12 feet tall. Like the species it is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker, so avoid trunk injuries, provide good air circulation, and keep it out of hot, reflected-sun locations where the variegated leaf margins scorch.

Gooseberries tolerate partial shade better than most fruits and prefer cool, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0–6.5. Prune to an open-vase structure each late winter, removing canes older than 3 years and any crossing branches to reduce disease pressure. Pick berries early for cooking (when green and firm) or allow them to ripen to red, yellow, or white for fresh eating. Note: check local regulations, as Ribes species are restricted in some U.S. states due to white pine blister rust.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; provide consistent moisture during fruit development. Ribes hirtellum (hawthorn gooseberry or Appalachian gooseberry) is a native North American gooseberry species found naturally in cool, moist woodlands, bog margins, and rocky slopes from Labrador to Missouri — the most widespread of the native American gooseberries and a parent of many modern gooseberry cultivars. The shrubs are compact and moderately thorny, producing clusters of small, 1/2-inch, green to red-purple, translucent fruits in June–July with the characteristic sweet-tart gooseberry flavor excellent for preserves, pies, fools, wines, and chutneys. Unlike European gooseberry cultivars (Ribes uva-crispa), which often struggle with mildew in humid eastern North American summers, R. hirtellum and its native cultivar hybrids have better disease resistance in humid climates. An important distinction: Ribes species (gooseberries and currants) can serve as alternate hosts for white pine blister rust; planting within 1,000 feet of white pine stands is regulated or prohibited in some states — check local regulations. In zone 9, gooseberry requires deep mulching and consistent moisture and is marginal at the southern edge of its range; best in cooler climates.

Plant in very well-drained, sandy, infertile, acidic soil in full sun — gopher apple is native to the xeric scrub and dry pinelands of the southeastern coastal plain and is exceptionally drought-tolerant, thriving on soils too poor and dry for most plants. The small, low-growing shrub produces white apple-like edible fruits about 1 inch long that are sweet and mild when fully ripe, eaten by gopher tortoises (for which the plant is named), bears, deer, and other wildlife. A critically important food source for gopher tortoises in Florida. Spreads slowly via an extensive root system; once established, this tough native is essentially maintenance-free. Excellent for butterfly gardens and native scrub restorations in the deep South.

Goumi is a nitrogen-fixing shrub from East Asia that produces abundant small, cherry-red, speckled fruits with a sweet-tart flavor reminiscent of cherry. It is remarkably drought-tolerant once established and fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, making it a valued plant in permaculture systems. Prune lightly after fruiting to shape the plant and encourage denser branching; heavy pruning stimulates excessive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit. Harvest when berries are fully red and slightly soft — ripe fruits have little to no astringency and taste excellent fresh or dried.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; extremely adaptable — drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and fixes nitrogen. Elaeagnus multiflora (goumi berry or natsugumi) is a deciduous shrub from China and Japan producing one of the earliest ripening berry crops in the edible landscape — the elongated, cherry-red, silver-speckled fruits ripen in late May to June (in zone 6–7), several weeks before blueberries or raspberries, filling a gap in the fresh fruit calendar. The fruits are tart-sweet, somewhat astringent when slightly underripe, with a pleasant fresh berry flavor when fully red; they are rich in lycopene (higher concentration than tomatoes), vitamins A, C, and E, and flavonoids. Unlike its aggressive invasive relative autumn olive (E. umbellata), goumi is not considered invasive in most regions — it produces less seed, spreads less aggressively, and is widely grown in permaculture and food forest systems. The roots fix atmospheric nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis, making goumi a valuable soil-building companion plant in the food forest understory layer. The attractive silvery-green foliage and small, fragrant, creamy-yellow flowers in spring are also ornamentally pleasing.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Granny Val is a Mississippi State University muscadine release bred for exceptionally large, glossy black berries with a good balance of sweetness and the classic musky muscadine flavor, ranking among the largest-fruited black muscadine cultivars available for home gardens. The large berry size makes it a favorite for fresh eating and an eye-catching addition to a mixed muscadine planting, and vines are vigorous and reliably productive once established on a sturdy trellis. Granny Val is self-fertile and does not need a separate pollinizer, though nearby compatible varieties tend to improve overall yield. As with other muscadines, it shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases and Pierce's disease that make bunch grapes difficult to grow in the humid Gulf South, needing minimal spray input. Harvest as berries turn fully black and detach easily from the stem, and prune annually each winter to renew fruiting wood and keep the vigorous vine in bounds.

Plant in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade, providing a sturdy trellis, fence, or shrub for support; Grape Honeysuckle is a non-invasive native alternative to the notorious Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) that offers nearly all the same wildlife value — tubular yellow flowers for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees in June–July, followed by clusters of red berries consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and other songbirds in fall — without any of the aggressive, smothering growth habit that makes Japanese honeysuckle a serious ecological threat. One of its most distinctive features is its perfoliate leaves, where paired leaves fuse at the base so the stem appears to pass directly through a single disk-shaped leaf, giving the foliage a sculptural, unusual appearance. It is substantially more cold-hardy than most ornamental honeysuckle vines, thriving in zones 3–8, and is well-suited to the upper Midwest and Great Plains where few ornamental vines are fully reliable. Established vines are drought-tolerant once rooted.

Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in moist to wet, acidic soil along streambanks, pond edges, or other consistently moist sites in full to partial sun; gray alder establishes vigorously in wet conditions and should be sited where roots will have reliable access to subsurface moisture or periodic flooding. Alnus incana is a fast-growing native tree of northern North America, prized for its ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with Frankia bacteria and to stabilize eroding streambanks with its dense, fibrous root system; male catkins emerge in early spring before the leaves, providing an important pollen source for early-flying native bees. The persistent small woody cones that remain through winter supply seeds to goldfinches, siskins, and redpolls, and the bark and foliage support a rich diversity of Lepidoptera larvae including many specialist moth species of northern forests.

Prepare acidic soil to pH 4.5–5.0 before planting; Gulf Coast is a Southern highbush blueberry developed jointly by the USDA and the University of Florida and released in 1987, specifically bred for the lower-chill coastal regions of the Gulf South including Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and the Florida panhandle. It requires 200–300 chill hours and produces reliable crops where northern highbush varieties fail to fruit. Berries are medium-large, blue, firm, with a dry scar and good sweet flavor that develops best with warm, sunny ripening conditions. The plant has a naturally spreading habit and is fairly tolerant of the heavy clay soils found in coastal areas if drainage is adequate — raised beds work excellently. Gulf Coast is also noted for tolerance of the wet winters common on the Gulf Coast, as long as roots are not waterlogged for extended periods. An excellent variety to pair with Climax rabbiteye blueberry to extend season: Gulf Coast ripens 2–3 weeks before Climax begins.

common_name: Gulfcoast Southern Highbush Blueberry (Original Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)
notes: Plant in raised beds or native soil amended to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines, setting out dormant bushes in winter and mulching well to protect the shallow root system from summer heat. Gulfcoast was among the first University of Florida southern highbush releases bred specifically for the state's mild winters, and it remains a reliable, vigorous producer of medium, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on an upright, spreading bush. Its very low chilling requirement makes it dependable even after unusually warm winters along the Gulf Coast, where many northern blueberry varieties fail to set fruit. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water during dry spells to support fruit sizing, and prune out old wood each winter to keep the planting productive.

Half-high blueberries are crosses between highbush and lowbush species, combining the large-berry quality of highbush with the extreme cold hardiness of lowbush — cultivars such as 'Northblue', 'Northcountry', and 'Polaris' survive to -35°F when snow-covered. Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.0 and mulch heavily with pine bark or sawdust. Cross-pollination between two compatible cultivars improves berry size and total yield. Pruning is minimal for the first five years; thereafter remove the thickest, oldest canes each late winter to encourage fresh productive wood.

Hardy kiwi vines are dioecious — plant one male vine for every 6–8 female vines or choose a self-fertile cultivar such as 'Issai'. The vines can take 4–7 years to bear fruit but become very productive once established, requiring a pergola or heavy-gauge trellis rated to hold at least 200 lbs. Prune to a permanent framework of main arms and renewal spurs each late winter, cutting lateral shoots back to 2–4 buds. Harvest when smooth, grape-sized fruits yield slightly to pressure and taste sweet.

Plant Haskap in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; always plant two or more compatible cultivars for cross-pollination; water regularly during establishment and fruit development; berries ripen 2–3 weeks before strawberries and should be harvested promptly. Lonicera caerulea var. edulis and its cultivated selections (Honeyberry or Haskap) represent one of the hardiest edible shrubs in cultivation — tolerating temperatures to -40°F or below in adapted varieties, and withstanding late spring frosts during bloom thanks to early-season cold-hardiness of the flowers. Two compatible cultivars are essential for reliable fruiting, as the species is largely self-incompatible; many named Canadian and Japanese breeding program selections are available for pairing. The elongated, dark blue-black berries are nutritionally similar to blueberries but with a distinctly more complex flavor — sweet-tart with blueberry, raspberry, and elderberry undertones and a pleasant tartness. The shrubs are extremely long-lived (50+ years), begin bearing in year 2–3 after planting, and require minimal pruning beyond removing deadwood. Excellent for northern gardens where blueberries struggle, and the extremely early ripening season makes them valuable for extending the fresh-fruit season.

Hayward is the classic commercial fuzzy kiwifruit cultivar behind nearly every kiwi sold in grocery stores, prized for its large size, bright green flesh, and well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. Like all fuzzy kiwi it needs a long, warm growing season and is best suited to zones 7–9 with at least 200 frost-free days; it is dioecious, so a compatible male vine (roughly one male for every 6–8 female vines) must be planted nearby for pollination, since Hayward itself is a female-fruiting cultivar. Train vines on a sturdy T-bar or pergola trellis and prune hard each winter to control the vigorous growth and keep fruiting wood renewed. Harvest in late fall before hard frost once the seeds have turned black, and finish ripening the firm fruit indoors at room temperature.

Plant in consistently wet, moist-to-saturated soil along stream edges, pond margins, or low wet areas in full sun to partial shade; hazel alder is a multi-stemmed native shrub or small tree that thrives where few plants can, colonizing eroded stream banks and stabilizing them with a dense fibrous root system. Like other alders it hosts nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria in root nodules, enriching surrounding soil and supporting the broader riparian plant community. Reddish-purple male catkins emerge as early as February before any leaves appear, providing critical early-season pollen for queen bumblebees and other overwintered insects. The persistent woody seed cones persist through winter and are eaten by redpolls, goldfinches, and other seed-eating birds.

Plant rooted cuttings in spring into moist, organically rich soil at the base of a large, sturdy support structure, watering thoroughly and mulching to retain moisture through the first growing season while the root system establishes. Heartleaf peppervine is a vigorous deciduous vine native to floodplain forests and bottomland thickets of the southeastern US, recognized by its broad, bold, heart-shaped leaves and the showy clusters of small berries that ripen from green through turquoise to blue-black in fall, providing an important food source for mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and other songbirds. This large-scale native vine is well suited to covering fences, large arbors, and the trunks of substantial trees in moist, lowland sites where vigorous growth is desired and space is not limiting. Once established on fertile, consistently moist soil, it requires no supplemental care and will cover its support structure rapidly; direct new growth as needed to keep the vine on its intended structure.

common_name: Herbemont Grape (Historic 1800s South Carolina Wine Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Herbemont is a historic wine grape dating to the early 1800s in South Carolina, one of the older American hybrid grapes still valued today for its strong tolerance of Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection that has limited European wine grape production across the humid South for two centuries. It produces small, dark, sweet-tart berries used historically and still today for wine, offering a taste of the region's viticultural history along with genuine disease resilience that many modern hybrids still aim to match. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and airflow.

Plant 'Heritage' canes in well-drained loam enriched with compost, spacing them 2-3 feet apart in rows. This reliable everbearing (primocane) variety fruits on first-year canes in late summer and again the following early summer. For a single heavy fall crop, mow all canes to the ground each late winter. Provide a trellis or T-post support and keep beds mulched to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil and provide a pollinator vine; Higgins is a Georgia Experiment Station-released muscadine variety renowned for producing fruits of extraordinary size — large white (bronze-skinned) muscadines reaching 1.5–2 inches in diameter, among the very largest in the muscadine world. The large, pale bronze-gold fruits have a sweet, rich, floral muscadine flavor and a tender skin that makes fresh eating considerably more pleasant than older tough-skinned varieties. Higgins is primarily a fresh-eating variety; the impressive fruit size creates visual impact at farmers' markets and U-pick operations. As a female-flowered (pistillate) variety, Higgins requires a perfect-flowered pollinator nearby — without cross-pollination the vine sets little or no fruit. Plant alongside Ison, Triumph, or another self-fertile muscadine for reliable production. In zone 9 the long, warm summer provides ideal conditions for the large fruits to develop to their full potential size.

Blueberries require acidic soil with a pH of 4.5–5.5; amend with elemental sulfur and use acidic mulch such as pine bark or wood chips 3–4 in deep. Plant at least two cultivars for cross-pollination and better fruit set. Prune out old canes older than 6 years at the base each late winter to stimulate productive new wood. Harvest when berries turn deep blue and detach with minimal resistance, typically 7–10 days after color change.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool; mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune to an open framework each winter to ease harvest among the thorny stems. Hinnomaki Red is a Finnish-bred gooseberry cultivar prized for combining reliable productivity, good mildew resistance, and outstanding fruit quality — the medium-sized berries ripen from green to a deep red-burgundy with a rich, sweet-tart flavor considered among the best of any gooseberry for fresh eating out of hand, as well as excellent for pies, jams, and fools. The compact, upright bush is more manageable and less sprawling than many older gooseberry varieties, and its Nordic breeding gives it strong cold hardiness alongside dependable disease resistance in cool, humid summer climates. Best suited to northern gardens with cool summers; in hot, humid zones the plant struggles with heat stress and powdery mildew regardless of afternoon shade. Zone 3–7.

'Hinnonmaki Red' is a hardy Finnish gooseberry with dark-red, aromatic berries that are tart when green for cooking and sweet when fully ripe for dessert. It shows good mildew resistance and thrives in cool, moist conditions. Grow in full sun to partial shade in rich, well-drained soil and mulch to keep the roots cool. Prune to an open-centered bush in winter, removing crossing and low branches, and wear gloves when harvesting the thorny stems.

Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool and pruning to an open vase shape each winter for easier harvest among the thorns. Hinnonmaki Yellow is the golden-fruited counterpart to the widely grown Hinnonmaki Red, bred in Finland from the same mildew-tolerant lineage and sharing its compact, upright, spiny habit. The translucent amber berries ripen a little later than the red form and carry a milder, honeyed sweetness many gardeners prefer straight off the bush, while both hold up well cooked into pies and preserves. Best suited to cool-summer climates, since heat and humidity bring on powdery mildew and fruit stress.

Plant in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; hoary blueberry is a native Appalachian species of high-elevation heath and forest understory communities, distinguished by its distinctly hairy (hoary) twigs and leaf undersides — the fine hairs give new growth and undersides a grayish, woolly appearance. The plant is closely related to rabbiteye blueberry but adapted to cooler, higher-elevation sites. The blue-black berries are edible and well-flavored. In the garden, it performs well in moist, acidic shade conditions that suit other ericaceous plants like rhododendron and mountain laurel. An excellent native for the acid woodland garden in zones 5–8.

Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade, allowing generous spacing for the broad, arching form; hobblebush requires cool summer temperatures and consistent moisture, and is best suited to northern gardens or high-elevation sites where summer heat is moderate. Viburnum lantanoides produces large, heart-shaped leaves on low-arching branches that root where they contact the ground — the source of the name 'hobblebush,' as the rooted stems can trip unwary woodland walkers — and bears flat-topped clusters of showy white flowers in April and May followed by berries that ripen from red to black and attract thrushes, cedar waxwings, and other wildlife. Fall foliage color is among the most dramatic of any native shrub, turning rich crimson to claret-red in September, making hobblebush a multi-season standout for shaded northern woodland gardens.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and include at least one Honey Bee or comparable pollinizer whenever planting fruiting haskap cultivars, since nearly all commercial haskaps are self-infertile. Honey Bee is a University of Saskatchewan haskap cultivar bred primarily as a universal pollinizer rather than for its own fruit production, chosen for heavy, well-timed flowering that overlaps with most other haskap cultivars' bloom windows. Its berries are edible and pleasantly flavored but smaller and less abundant than dedicated fruiting cultivars like Borealis or Aurora, so it is typically planted as roughly one bush in five or six. The bush is extremely cold-hardy and easy to grow, tolerating the same conditions preferred by other haskaps.

Plant two or more different cultivars for cross-pollination in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–7.0) in full sun; honeyberry is an edible-fruited honeysuckle native to boreal regions of Russia, Japan, and Canada that produces sweet-tart blue berries resembling elongated blueberries in late spring — the first fresh fruit of the season in cold climates. Plants tolerate temperatures to -40°F and the flowers survive spring frosts to -8°F. Fruit is borne on second-year wood, so avoid heavy pruning in the first three years. Cultivars 'Tundra', 'Indigo Gem', and 'Borealis' are among the most productive for North American gardens.

Honeyberries are among the earliest fruits to ripen — often 2–3 weeks before strawberries — and flowers can survive temperatures as low as -4°F, making them ideal for short-season climates. Two compatible cultivars from the same breeding group must be planted for cross-pollination. Minimal pruning is needed for the first 5 years; thereafter, remove a few of the oldest, thickest canes annually to renew. Harvest when berries are entirely blue-purple inside (cut one open to check), as color alone can be misleading.

common_name: Hull Thornless Blackberry (USDA Semi-Erect Thornless Bramble)
notes: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and tie the semi-erect, arching canes to a two-wire trellis to keep fruit clusters accessible and off the ground. Hull Thornless was developed by USDA-ARS breeders at Beltsville, Maryland and released in the early 1980s as part of a program aimed at combining the thornless trait with better cold tolerance and fruit quality than earlier thornless releases. The berries are medium-to-large, glossy black, and notably sweeter than many of its thornless predecessors, ripening over a fairly long midseason window with good yields once the semi-erect canes are established. Because it tolerates cooler winters better than many thornless trailing types, Hull Thornless became a popular home-garden choice for growers who wanted thornless canes without moving to a warmer climate zone.

common_name: Illini Hardy Blackberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Erect Blackberry)
notes: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5). Illini Hardy is an erect, thorny blackberry developed at the University of Illinois specifically for reliable cane survival in cold northern winters where most blackberry varieties suffer significant winterkill, tolerating temperatures well below zero without winter cane protection. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening mid-to-late season with good yields once established. Because the canes are self-supporting and very cold-tolerant, Illini Hardy is a dependable choice for northern growers who want blackberries without the trellising and winter mulching that tender varieties require. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 6-8 per plant to keep the planting productive and manageable.

Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis or fence for climbing; Incense is a USDA hybrid passionflower combining native maypop (Passiflora incarnata) with the more tender South American Passiflora cincinnata, bred to combine maypop's reliable cold-hardiness with larger, showier, more intensely fragrant deep-purple flowers than the straight native species. Like maypop, the vine dies back to the ground in winter through much of its hardiness range and resprouts vigorously from the roots in late spring — do not disturb or remove the crown before new growth appears, as it can be slow to emerge. Flowers are followed by egg-sized, aromatic fruit with sweet-tart pulp similar to tropical passionfruit, though fruit set is often lighter than the straight maypop species; plant more than one vine to improve cross-pollination and fruiting. Incense is also an important larval host plant for Gulf fritillary and variegated fritillary butterflies, adding pollinator-garden value beyond its fruit and ornamental flowers.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Indian plum is a Pacific Northwest native deciduous shrub prized for being one of the earliest-blooming woody plants — small clusters of fragrant white flowers appear in February or March before leaves emerge, often while snow is still on the ground, providing an invaluable nectar source for early bees and hummingbirds. Small oval drupes (like tiny olives) ripen to blue-black with a single large stone; the flavor is astringent and bitter raw but palatable to birds and was eaten sparingly by many Native peoples. An excellent choice for wildlife habitat gardens, riparian buffers, and native plant landscapes in the Pacific Northwest and northern California.

Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Indigo Gem sets almost no fruit alone. Bred at the University of Saskatchewan from Russian breeding stock, Indigo Gem is one of the earliest widely planted North American haskap cultivars, valued for its productive, compact bush and elongated, deep-blue berries with a tart, slightly grape-like flavor closer to the wild species than the sweeter modern releases. It is among the earliest fruits to ripen each year, often ahead of strawberries, which makes it a useful season-opener but also puts its early flowers at some frost risk in variable spring weather. Like all haskaps, it is extremely cold-hardy but performs poorly in hot, humid summers, so it is best suited to northern gardens and short-season climates rather than the Gulf South. Fruit forms on second-year and older wood, so limit pruning in the first few years to dead or crossing branches before starting renewal pruning of older canes.

Plant in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and interplant with a different, overlapping-bloom cultivar such as Indigo Gem or Aurora for reliable pollination and fruit set, since this cultivar is self-infertile. Indigo Treat is a midseason haskap from the University of Saskatchewan breeding program, selected for a sweeter, less tart flavor than earlier releases like Indigo Gem, with large, elongated, deep-blue berries. The upright, extremely cold-hardy bush breaks dormancy early, so late spring frosts during bloom are the main risk to cropping rather than winter cold itself. Expect fruit to ripen a week or two after the earliest haskap cultivars.

Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and provide consistent moisture during fruit development for the best size and flavor. Indigo Yum is one of the later-flowering cultivars in the University of Saskatchewan's Indigo series of haskaps, bred for a milder, sweeter flavor than earlier Indigo-series releases. Because its bloom period does not fully overlap with the earliest Indigo cultivars, it should be paired with a similarly timed pollinizer, such as Aurora or Borealis, to ensure adequate cross-pollination and fruit set. The compact, productive bush produces large, oblong blue berries with thin, tender skin well suited to fresh eating, jams, and baking.

'Invicta' is a heavy-cropping green culinary gooseberry with outstanding resistance to American gooseberry mildew. The vigorous, spreading, and notably spiny bush yields large pale-green berries excellent for pies, jams, and preserves. Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil and space generously for airflow. Prune to an open goblet each winter to ease harvest among the sharp thorns and shorten leading shoots to encourage fruiting spurs.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ison is one of the most widely planted muscadine varieties in the Southeast, selected by Ison's Nursery in Georgia for its combination of very large, sweet, black-bronze-skinned fruits and self-fertility — the perfect-flowered habit means a single Ison vine sets full crops without requiring a separate pollinator vine. The large, round to slightly oval fruits ripen to deep bronze-black with a rich, sweet, complex muscadine flavor and relatively low tannin compared to older varieties. Ison is used for fresh eating, juice, wine, and muscadine jelly, where the large fruit size and good juice content are advantageous. The vine is vigorous and productive once established, with crops of 30–60 pounds per mature vine in good growing conditions. Unlike some muscadine varieties that have a thick, tough skin, Ison's skin is more tender and the slip-skin characteristic less pronounced, making fresh eating more pleasant.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis, and plant a self-fertile muscadine variety nearby for pollination, since James produces only female flowers. James is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still widely grown, a historic bronze cultivar prized for very large, sweet berries with the classic musky muscadine flavor, harvested for generations across the Deep South for fresh eating, jelly, and wine. Its long track record in Southern gardens speaks to its reliability and adaptability across a range of soils and conditions. Like other muscadines it resists Pierce's disease and the major fungal diseases of the humid South without a spray program. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster.

common_name: Jersey Blueberry (Classic Northern Highbush Blueberry, New Jersey Standard Blueberry)
notes: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat moss or pine bark; maintain soil pH at 4.5–5.2 for healthy growth and production; mulch heavily with pine bark or acid wood chips; fertilize with ammonium sulfate in early spring; Jersey ripens in August (late season) producing large, firm, light blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and excellent storage quality. Jersey blueberry is one of the oldest and most historically important highbush blueberry varieties in American commercial and home garden production — developed by Frederick Coville at the USDA Beltsville Agricultural Research Center in 1928 from deliberate crosses with wild Vaccinium corymbosum selections from the Atlantic coastal plain. Jersey was one of the first named highbush blueberry varieties released and became the cornerstone of the New Jersey commercial blueberry industry (the first commercial blueberry industry in the United States), for which it was specifically developed. For several decades, Jersey was essentially THE commercial highbush blueberry of the American East Coast, dominating production in New Jersey, Michigan, and the other blueberry-producing states before the development of newer varieties with earlier ripening or larger fruit. Despite its age (nearly 100 years of commercial production), Jersey remains popular for several reasons: its late-season ripening (August) extends the fresh blueberry window after most other varieties have finished, its very large, firm, light blue berries store and ship exceptionally well (better than softer-berried varieties), and its mild, sweet flavor is reliable and consistent. Jersey is considered somewhat milder in flavor than Bluecrop or Elliott but produces reliably in a wide range of conditions.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and mulch to keep roots cool, since this hybrid inherits its cool-climate preference from both currant and gooseberry parents. Jostaberry is a thornless hybrid bred in Germany from a cross of blackcurrant and gooseberry, combining the vigor and disease resistance of both parents into a productive, easy-care shrub that bears large, smooth, dark purple-black berries with a flavor described as a cross between the two — richer and less tart than gooseberry, milder and less musky than blackcurrant. The thornless canes make picking far easier than with true gooseberries, and the shrub is notably resistant to the powdery mildew and rust diseases that trouble many currants and gooseberries. It performs best in regions with cold winters and mild summers, generally struggling with the heat, humidity, and mild winters of the Deep South, so it suits cooler parts of the transition zone and the upper South far better than true Gulf Coast gardens. Prune out the oldest third of canes each winter to encourage strong new fruiting wood.

Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; Kiowa is a thorned, erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 1996 as part of the same breeding program that produced Natchez and Ouachita. It is distinguished principally by its extraordinary berry size — among the largest of any blackberry variety, often exceeding 10–14 grams per fruit — and its exceptionally long harvest season that can extend 6–8 weeks through June and July in zone 8–9. Flavor is sweet and complex. The upright, thorned canes are self-supporting and vigorous, producing heavily. Kiowa shows good adaptability to the South and mid-South, performing well in humid, hot climates where some varieties decline. The principal trade-off is the thorns — unavoidable when harvesting and pruning — but many growers consider this worthwhile for the combination of size, yield, and long season. Prune fruited floricanes to ground level after the last berries are harvested; tip primocanes at 36–42 inches in summer to promote lateral branching.

Kiwiberry is a compact-fruited selection of hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) grown specifically for smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruits that are eaten whole without peeling — they have the same flavor as standard kiwifruit but ripen 3–4 weeks earlier. Self-fertile cultivars such as 'Issai' and 'Ken's Red' allow single-plant production, but yields are higher when a male pollenizer is present. The extremely vigorous vines require a heavy-gauge trellis or pergola capable of bearing hundreds of pounds of vine and fruit; prune hard each dormant season to renewal spurs. Harvest when fruits yield to gentle pressure and taste sweet with no starchiness.

growth_habit: East Asian compact edible mulberry shrub-tree
notes: Plant Morus australis in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment, then reduce as the plant is drought-tolerant once established; prune in winter to shape and control size; harvest berries as they ripen and turn deep purple-black, as they stain readily. Korean Mulberry is the smallest-growing of the commonly cultivated mulberry species — typically maturing as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 5–15 feet tall — making it better suited to smaller gardens than the more vigorous White Mulberry (Morus alba) or American Red Mulberry (Morus rubra). The abundant small to medium berries are very sweet and richly flavored, ripening over several weeks in early to midsummer; birds are strongly attracted to fruiting trees so netting may be needed for a full harvest. In East Asian traditional medicine systems, the berries (sang shen), leaves (sang ye), bark (sang bai pi), and twigs (sang zhi) are all used in herbal preparations for treating conditions ranging from hypertension and diabetes to tinnitus and gray hair. The leaves are used for silkworm (Bombyx mori) cultivation like other mulberry species. Compact enough for container growing in large pots; prune annually to maintain size and maximize fruiting wood.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Krewer is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for its notably late ripening window, extending the fresh Southern blueberry harvest into midsummer after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, a valuable trait for home gardeners and market growers wanting to spread out the harvest season. The vigorous, productive bushes bear medium to large berries with good flavor and firmness. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Krewer requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other, choosing early- and mid-season partners to spread bloom timing and further extend the overall harvest. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Lake Emerald Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Florida Wine Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing extra space between vines since Lake Emerald is a vigorous grower recommended for wider row spacing than most other Florida bunch grapes. Developed by the University of Florida's bunch grape breeding program at Leesburg, it is prized for strong resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by leafhoppers that has historically limited grape growing across the humid Gulf South, and it does not require grafting onto a resistant rootstock except in soils with a naturally high pH. It produces light green, juicy berries used mainly for wine and juice or jelly rather than fresh eating, ripening in midsummer just after the purple 'Blue Lake' cultivar. As with other Florida bunch grapes, a preventive fungicide spray program through the growing season is important to control the fungal fruit rots that thrive in hot, humid weather, and vines should be pruned hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons.

common_name: Lane Muscadine Grape (Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Lane is a modern University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its very large, glossy black berries with a thinner, more tender skin than many older black muscadines, along with sweet, richly flavored flesh well suited to fresh eating. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, ripening in the mid-to-late season, and its improved skin quality and berry size have made it a popular choice for both home gardens and u-pick plantings across the Gulf South. Keep vines well watered during fruit development for the best berry size, and thin overcrowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid weather.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Late Fry is a University of Arkansas release bred as a black-fruited counterpart to the popular bronze variety Fry, producing very large, glossy black berries with the same thin skin and high sugar content that made Fry a favorite for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and ripens late in the season, filling out the tail end of the muscadine harvest after earlier black varieties are finished. Vigor and disease resistance are good across the humid Gulf South. Because it is one of the last muscadines to ripen, protect ripening clusters from birds and other wildlife, which concentrate on the few varieties still fruiting late in the season.

common_name: Leatherleaf Mahonia (Chinese Mahonia, Leatherleaf Oregon Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf mahonia is a bold architectural evergreen shrub with some of the most striking foliage in the shade garden — stiff, upright canes bearing enormous compound leaves (18–24 inches) of dark, holly-like leaflets with viciously spiny edges that create a dramatic tropical effect in the deepest shade. Fragrant yellow flowers appear in winter in drooping grape-like clusters, followed by powdery blue-purple berries in spring that are edible (tart, used for jelly and wine). It is one of the few large shrubs that truly thrives in deep, dry shade — an outstanding barrier plant and shade specimen. NOTE: Mahonia bealei is listed as invasive in several southeastern states including Texas and Georgia — check local invasive species lists before planting; the native alternative Mahonia trifoliolata (agarita) is an excellent substitute in Texas.

Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch well to maintain the moist, acidic soil conditions blueberries require. Legacy is a USDA release bred from a cross between northern highbush and southern highbush parentage, giving it unusually broad climate adaptability — it performs well from the upper South through much of the Gulf region, bridging the gap between cultivars suited only to cold winters and those needing very low chill. The semi-evergreen bush produces heavy crops of firm, sweet, richly flavored medium-sized berries over a fairly long mid-to-late season, and its vigorous, upright growth habit makes it easy to manage and harvest. Its adaptability and reliable production have made it one of the more versatile blueberry cultivars for gardeners uncertain whether a northern or southern highbush type suits their exact climate. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself with productive new wood.

common_name: Lemony Lace Elderberry (Golden Cutleaf Ornamental Elderberry)
notes: Lemony Lace is a compact, rounded ornamental elderberry selected for finely dissected, lacy, bright chartreuse-gold foliage held on contrasting near-black stems, a dramatic color and texture combination for a mixed border or foundation planting. Flat clusters of pinkish-white flowers appear in late spring, followed by small red berries that, like other red elderberries, are mildly toxic raw and should be cooked before any culinary use, or simply left for birds. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than wild red elderberry, needs only light shaping after bloom, and performs best where summers are not extremely hot and humid, since foliage color and vigor decline in the most intense Deep South heat.

Plant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into fertile, well-manured soil, since Leveller needs steady moisture to size its fruit. This Victorian-era English dessert gooseberry, first raised in the 1850s, is still grown for its very large, pale yellow-green, thin-skinned berries with an exceptionally rich, sweet flavor once fully ripe. It is a vigorous, somewhat spreading bush that is more prone to American gooseberry mildew than modern disease-resistant releases, so good airflow matters in humid climates. Best reserved for dedicated fruit growers in cool-summer regions willing to manage its mildew susceptibility for the sake of exceptional flavor.

Plant in well-drained, loamy to rocky soil in part shade to full sun along a trellis, fence, or forest edge; Limber Honeysuckle is a native twining vine found across northern and central North America from Quebec to British Columbia and south into the Ozarks and Appalachians, scrambling up shrubs and small trees along forest margins where it is an important nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds during their spring and early-summer residency. The flowers range from orange-yellow to red and appear in May–June in clustered whorls at the stem tips, followed by translucent red to orange berries in late summer that are eaten by thrushes, vireos, and other woodland songbirds. Like Lonicera prolifera, it has perfoliate leaves near the stem tips where the uppermost pair of leaves fuse into a disk, though in this species the leaves beneath the flower clusters are typically distinctly bluish-green. It is non-invasive and well-behaved in the garden, rarely exceeding 15 feet, making it one of the best native vine choices for small to medium trellises in northern gardens.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; locustberry is frost-tender and native to the pine rockland and coastal habitats of extreme South Florida and the Keys.
