Small, glossy, leathery leaves and delicate clusters of small flowers that open pink and fade to yellow give this native shrub extended seasonal interest, followed by small red berries that ripen to nearly black and are eaten by birds, while the foliage serves as a larval host plant for several native butterfly species. Highly tolerant of poor, rocky limestone soil, salt exposure, and drought once established, it is a valuable, low-maintenance shrub for a South Florida native landscape, coastal planting, or pollinator garden, requiring essentially no irrigation or fertilizer beyond its first year. Prune lightly to shape if a more formal habit is wanted, though it naturally maintains an attractive, open form without regular pruning.

Lowbush blueberries require strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) and spread by underground rhizomes to form colonies. Manage in a two-year cycle: mow or burn half the planting to the ground each year so alternating sections produce a full crop annually. Harvest in midsummer when berries are deep blue-purple and sweet. Drought-tolerant once established, but irrigation during fruit fill improves berry size.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy loam and train the sprawling, thorny canes onto a low trellis or wire to keep the large fruit off the ground. Lucretia is one of the oldest named dewberry cultivars still grown in the South, prized in Texas and the Gulf region in the early twentieth century for producing unusually large, glossy, sweet-tart fruit far earlier in the season than blackberries. Because dewberries flower and ripen so early, protect blossoms from late cold snaps and expect a short, intense harvest window rather than the extended cropping of modern blackberry cultivars. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to keep the sprawling planting from becoming an unmanageable thicket.

Plant in full sun in any well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Magnolia is a USDA-developed self-fertile bronze muscadine grape, bearing medium to large bronze-to-copper-colored fruits with a mild, sweet flavor and thin, tender skin — one of the more elegant-tasting muscadine varieties for fresh eating, without the strongly musky, foxy character of older selections. The perfect-flowered Magnolia vine can pollinate female-only varieties like Carlos and Fry planted nearby, making it doubly useful as a multi-variety vineyard anchor. Fruits ripen in late August to September in most zone 8–9 plantings, later than some early-season varieties. The vines are vigorous and productive, typically yielding 15–20 pounds per vine at maturity. Train on a 4-wire trellis system, prune back to 2–3 buds per spur in late winter, and fertilize lightly in early spring.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; maqui berry is a Chilean native shrub prized for its small, intensely purple-black berries with the highest reported anthocyanin content of any known berry — significantly higher than acai, blueberries, or pomegranates, giving it extraordinary antioxidant properties. The berries have a pleasant sweet-tart flavor with herbal overtones; they are eaten fresh, made into juice, jams, and wine, and used extensively in Mapuche traditional medicine. It grows naturally in the coastal and Andean ranges of Chile and Argentina, tolerating mild frost, and adapts to a Mediterranean climate with dry summers. An emerging superfood crop with increasing commercial cultivation in Chile.

Marge is a prolific European elderberry prized for heavy yields of dark berries used in syrups, jams, and wine. Plant in full sun in moist, fertile soil and keep it well watered, as elderberries are shallow-rooted and thirsty. Fruit set improves dramatically with a second, different elderberry variety planted nearby for cross-pollination. Prune out the oldest canes each late winter to keep the plant vigorous and productive. Always cook the berries before eating, since raw fruit and other plant parts can cause stomach upset.

common_name: Mars Seedless Grape (Cold-Hardy Disease-Resistant Blue Table Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Bred at the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in the 1970s, Mars combines good disease resistance with genuinely seedless, blue-black berries and a sweet, fruity, slip-skin flavor reminiscent of Concord but milder. Its compact vine habit and strong resistance to common grape diseases make it far easier to grow without a heavy spray program than European wine grapes, especially in humid climates. Prune hard each winter to a few renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation.

This slender, nearly thornless bramble stays compact and shrubby rather than sprawling, and it holds its foliage through mild winters where hardy, making it useful as a shade-tolerant edge planting under fruit trees or along a woodland path. It flowers and fruits nearly continuously in warm climates, producing small, soft, sweet-tart red raspberries that are eaten fresh, though they are more delicate and less productive per cane than temperate raspberries. Give it half-day shade and evenly moist soil, and thin out older canes each year to keep new fruiting wood coming. It offers gardeners in humid subtropical and tropical shade gardens a genuine raspberry-family fruit where classic raspberries fail from heat stress.

Maypop (Passiflora incarnata) is a North American native passionflower that is cold-hardy to zone 6, distinguishing it clearly from the tropical Passiflora edulis (passionfruit). The ornamental lavender flowers are stunning and the egg-sized yellow-green fruits have sweet, aromatic pulp similar to tropical passionfruit. Plants die back to the roots in zone 6–7 winters and re-sprout vigorously in late spring — do not remove the crown before new growth appears. Plant cross-pollinators nearby (more than one plant) for reliable fruit set. Harvest when fruits turn yellowish-green and fall or detach easily.

common_name: Meadowlark Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry)
notes: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in winter into acidic, well-drained soil enriched with pine bark fines, and mulch to protect the shallow root system. Meadowlark is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for only about 200 chill hours, so it reliably leafs, blooms, and ripens even after unusually mild Gulf Coast winters that leave higher-chill cultivars sparse. It is one of the earliest-ripening blueberries available, often ready well ahead of standard rabbiteye types, though it benefits from a second early low-chill cultivar nearby for best pollination. Prune out old canes each winter and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring to keep plants vigorous.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moderately moist soil; Mexican elderberry is more drought-tolerant than eastern common elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) once established and adapts well to the neutral to alkaline soils of the Southwest, California foothills, and the intermountain West. Sambucus mexicana (syn. Sambucus nigra subsp. cerulea) is the native elderberry of California, the Southwest, and the Pacific Northwest mountains, forming a large, fast-growing, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with massive, flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) of creamy-white blossoms in late spring that are irresistible to native bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. The flowers are followed by heavy drooping clusters of small, powdery-blue to blue-black berries in late summer — excellent for elderberry syrup, jelly, wine, and traditional medicine. CAUTION: cook berries before eating; raw berries, bark, and leaves contain cyanogenic glycosides. An outstanding wildlife plant — the berries are consumed by dozens of bird species including waxwings, robins, and thrushes.

common_name: MidSouth Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Mississippi Bunch Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the moderately vigorous canopy. MidSouth was released by Mississippi State University in 1981, tracing back to USDA breeding work begun in the late 1930s at the Meridian, Mississippi field station, and it remains valued today for its exceptional tolerance of Pierce's disease across Mississippi, Louisiana, and neighboring Gulf South states. Its self-fertile vines produce clusters of dark blue-purple berries covered in a heavy waxy bloom that ripen in late July to mid-August in the southern part of its range, with a rich, sweet-tart flavor carrying a hint of raspberry; the seeded, slip-skin berries are best suited to jelly and juice rather than fresh table use. The vine is more susceptible to fungal disease and root-knot nematodes than to Pierce's disease itself, so a regular fungicide program and nematode-aware site selection help keep plantings productive. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons to keep cluster and berry size from declining.

Plant rooted cuttings or nursery liners in spring in sandy, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving light afternoon shade where summers run hot. This low, spreading Australian bush-food shrub produces small white flowers followed by white, red-freckled berries with a spicy, blueberry-like flavor over a long summer-to-fall season, forming a durable, drought-tolerant edible groundcover once its roots are established. It has almost no frost tolerance, so treat it as a container plant that can be moved under cover anywhere winter lows dip much below freezing. A light shearing after each fruiting flush keeps the mat dense and encourages the next round of flowers.

A sprawling, semi-woody vine-shrub of Florida and Gulf Coast maritime hammocks, milkberry produces small fragrant white tubular flowers followed by glossy white berries that persist through much of the year and are relished by birds. It scrambles over neighboring shrubs or can be kept as a loose mounding groundcover shrub with occasional pruning. Grow in partial shade to filtered sun in humus-rich, well-drained soil typical of coastal hammock understories, and provide some wind protection when young since it is not a true front-dune plant. Its salt and drought tolerance once established make it useful as a naturalizing understory shrub in restored maritime forest plantings.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in part shade; water with rainwater or filtered water — chlorinated tap water and alkaline water damage the plant. Synsepalum dulcificum (miracle berry or miracle fruit) is a West African evergreen shrub that produces the most remarkable edible berry in the botanical world: small (1-inch), red, olive-shaped berries containing a glycoprotein called miraculin, which temporarily binds to sour taste receptors on the tongue and causes sour, acidic foods to taste intensely sweet for 30–60 minutes after eating a single berry. The berries themselves have virtually no sugar content and a bland flavor — the effect is entirely on taste perception, not on the food itself. After eating a miracle berry, lemons taste like lemon candy, vinegar tastes sweet, sour cream becomes sweet cream, and Tabasco sauce tastes like hot doughnut glaze. Miracle berry parties (where participants eat the berry and sample unusual flavor combinations) have become a culinary novelty. The plant is native to West African rain forest understory and requires the same acidic, humus-rich, moist, part-shade conditions as blueberries — it is extremely pH-sensitive and will decline rapidly in alkaline soil or water. In zone 10–12, it can be grown outdoors; in zone 8–9, best in a pot brought indoors in winter.

common_name: Miss Blanc Grape (Mississippi-Bred White Wine Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Miss Blanc was released by Mississippi State University in 1982, bred by USDA researcher N.H. Loomis specifically for Pierce's disease tolerance, and produces white grapes well suited to wine and juice production across the Gulf South where the disease limits most traditional wine grape choices. Its interspecific hybrid parentage gives it the disease resistance needed to thrive in the region's warm, humid growing conditions without the heavy spray program European wine grapes require. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve fruit quality and reduce fungal disease risk.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Missouri gooseberry is a thorny, arching Midwestern and Great Plains native shrub found wild along woodland edges, fencerows, and thickets, tolerating more shade than most fruiting berries while still producing a reliable crop. Small, greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers in early spring give way to smooth, purple-black berries by early summer that are tart-sweet and excellent fresh once fully ripe, or cooked into pies, jams, and preserves while still slightly underripe and firmer. It is notably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than European gooseberry cultivars, and its wide native range makes it naturally adapted to variable continental climates from hot summers to severe winters. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to renew vigor, and watch for the sharp spines at each leaf node when harvesting or pruning.

common_name: Montgomery Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Mid-Season Southern Blueberry)
notes: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Montgomery is a vigorous rabbiteye blueberry cultivar developed for Southern growing conditions, producing a reliable mid-season crop of medium to large, firm berries with good flavor. The bushes are notably vigorous and productive, establishing quickly and bearing well once mature, making Montgomery a dependable choice for filling out a mid-season harvest window alongside earlier and later rabbiteye selections. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, it requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

Mountain huckleberry naturally colonizes the filtered light beneath conifer forests in the Pacific Northwest and Rockies, so give it acidic soil, steady moisture, and the dappled shade of nearby trees rather than open, exposed sun. Established plants spread slowly by underground rhizomes and reward patience with intensely flavored, dark purple berries in late summer that are considered by many foragers to be the finest of all the huckleberries for pies, jam, and eating fresh. It is notoriously slow to establish from nursery stock, so plant it where it can be left undisturbed for years. This is a true forest-floor crop, offering a genuinely shade-adapted alternative to sun-loving blueberries.

Propagate from hardwood cuttings taken in late winter and root in a well-drained propagation mix under plastic film, or take semi-softwood cuttings in early summer; plant rooted cuttings out in spring after the last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Multicaulis mulberry is a vigorous, large-leaved variety of white mulberry selected in China for its enormous leaves — up to 12 inches long — that historically supported the silk industry; in the food garden it channels that same vigor into abundant, sweet white to pale-pink berries that ripen weeks ahead of most mulberries. The tree tolerates a wide range of soils including clay, heat, and urban conditions, and once established is drought-resilient while performing best with consistent moisture during fruiting. Harvest berries over several weeks as they ripen unevenly, spreading a sheet beneath the canopy and shaking branches gently to collect ripe fruit.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly, coastal-type soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established; avoid clay or poorly drained soils. Kunzea pomifera (muntries, emu apple, or native cranberry) is a prostrate, ground-hugging Australian native shrub from the coastal heathlands, mallee scrub, and sand dunes of South Australia and western Victoria — one of the most remarkable and underappreciated Australian native food plants. The plant spreads slowly as a low (6–18 inch), dense, aromatic groundcover with tiny, dark-green leaves and small white bottlebrush-like flowers, eventually producing clusters of small (1/4–1/2 inch), round berries that ripen from green to red-purple in late summer. The berries have a unique, complex, sweet-spicy flavor combining apple, cinnamon, and a subtle eucalyptus note — quite unlike any other berry. Nutritionally, muntries are exceptional: ORAC (antioxidant) values four times higher than blueberries by weight, with high vitamin C, flavonoids, and polyphenols. Aboriginal Australians historically ate muntries extensively as a major food source across the southern Australian coast. In the modern Australian native food industry, muntries are used in jams, sauces, ice creams, and gourmet berry products, and are increasingly available from specialty nurseries. As a garden plant, muntries serves as an excellent low-maintenance native groundcover that also produces an edible crop.

Muscadine grapes are native to the southeastern U.S. and far more heat- and disease-resistant than European or labrusca types. Train to a single trunk with two permanent lateral cordons on a high-wire trellis at 5–6 ft; spur-prune cordons each dormant season to 2–3 bud spurs spaced 4–6 in apart. Many cultivars are not self-fertile, so check pollination requirements before purchasing. Harvest by shaking or hand-picking individual berries when they reach full color and slip easily from the skin.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Mysore raspberry is the premier fruiting bramble for subtropical gardens — the only raspberry-type fruit that thrives and produces abundantly in zone 9–10 conditions where standard raspberries fail from summer heat and disease. Native to the hills of South Asia, it produces arching, thorny canes 5–8 feet tall with attractive silver-backed leaves and large clusters of small, dark-red to black berries with an intense raspberry flavor from October through April. Unlike temperate raspberries, it fruits on second-year canes (floricanes) but in a warm-climate evergreen pattern. Cut canes to the ground after fruiting; the plant regrows vigorously. It can be invasive outside cultivation where conditions suit it — avoid planting near natural areas.

Nanking cherry is one of the hardiest fruiting shrubs available, reliably surviving temperatures below -40°F and tolerating poor, dry, or alkaline soils. The abundant small red cherries ripen in early summer and have a sweet, slightly tart flavor excellent for jams, juices, and fresh eating. Two or more plants are needed for cross-pollination; plants flower very early in spring and may need frost protection of blossoms in zones 3–4 during cold snaps. Prune after harvest to remove dead wood and open the canopy; the shrub is generally very healthy with minimal pest and disease problems.

Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; nannyberry is one of the most shade-tolerant native viburnums and grows naturally as a large shrub or small tree at the edges of moist woodlands and thickets. Viburnum lentago is a large native viburnum of the northeastern and central United States, producing shiny, deeply veined, finely toothed leaves and flat-topped clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring that are outstanding for native bees; the abundant, blue-black, berry-like drupes in fall and winter provide critical food for migrating and overwintering songbirds — particularly cedar waxwings, robins, and thrushes — and are also edible for humans, with a sweet, date-raisin flavor when fully ripe. The fall foliage turns rich wine-red to purplish-red; the plant often sends up suckers and gradually forms a thicket.

Root hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; natal plum is a South African native shrub with glossy, dark-green, oval leaves armed with forked spines, fragrant white flowers like large jasmine blooms, and cranberry-sized red to deep-crimson fruits that are among the finest edible berries available in zone 9–11 landscapes. The fruit has a rich, sweet, somewhat cranberry-like flavor and is excellent for jams, jellies, juices, and fresh eating. Plants bloom and fruit nearly year-round in frost-free climates. Salt-tolerant, drought-resistant, and excellent as a security hedge or coastal planting. Note: only the ripe red fruits are edible — all other plant parts including unripe fruits are toxic.

Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5); Natchez is a semi-erect, thornless blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2007, widely considered one of the finest named varieties for the Gulf Coast and mid-South. It is the earliest-ripening major thornless variety, typically producing its first berries in late May to early June in zones 8–9 — a full 2–3 weeks before Ouachita and other Arkansas releases. Berries are very large (9–12 grams), elongated, jet-black, sweet, and aromatic with excellent fresh-eating quality. Yields are high, and the self-supporting semi-erect canes need only minimal trellising. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select 4–6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for next year's crop. Natchez is susceptible to double-blossom rosette disease in areas with high disease pressure; avoid overhead irrigation. In zone 9a, provide afternoon shade or plant on a north-facing slope to reduce heat stress during fruiting.

'Navaho' is an erect, thornless blackberry that produces firm, very sweet berries with excellent shelf life on self-supporting canes. Because it grows upright it needs little or no trellising, though a single wire helps in windy sites. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep suckers thinned to maintain a manageable hedgerow. Prune out fruited floricanes each fall and tip new primocanes to encourage branching.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood on a two-wire trellis or arbor. Nesbitt is a University of Georgia-released muscadine selected for its combination of very large, deep purple-black fruit, vigorous productive vines, and reliable self-fertility, making it a popular home-garden choice that needs no separate pollinator vine. The fruit has a thin, tender skin for a muscadine, sweet juicy flesh, and good flavor for fresh eating, with fruit size among the largest of the widely grown self-fertile varieties. The vigorous vine bears heavily once established and holds its crop well, tolerating the humid, disease-prone conditions of Gulf South summers better than bunch grapes. A dependable, high-yielding choice for a home muscadine arbor in zone 7–9.

The nessberry is an old dewberry-raspberry cross developed for the hot South, producing dark, wine-red berries with a sprightly flavor. Its trailing canes benefit from a low trellis and adapt well to heat and heavier soils where standard raspberries struggle. Plant in full sun in well-drained ground and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Remove spent floricanes after the summer crop and train fresh primocanes for the following season.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Noble is a black-skinned muscadine released by North Carolina State University in 1971 and named for James Noble, an early muscadine researcher. It is the standard against which black muscadine wine varieties are measured: the deep purple-black berries are extraordinarily high in anthocyanins, resveratrol, and other polyphenols that give muscadine wine and juice its distinctive deep color and purported health benefits. Flavor is rich, musky, and complex — more intensely flavored than bronze varieties — producing deep-colored wine, juice, and jelly with earthy, berry notes. Fresh-eating quality is good but not as mild as bronze types; the thick skin and seeds are more pronounced. Noble is self-fertile and produces consistently high yields even as a single vine. Its exceptional disease resistance and adaptability make it one of the best black muscadines for the humid Gulf South. Harvest when berries are fully black and yield easily to gentle pressure.

common_name: Northblue Blueberry (Half-High Cold-Hardy Highbush Blueberry, Northern Half-High)
notes: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.2) with excellent drainage; mulch with pine bark 3–4 inches deep to protect roots and maintain moisture; fertilize with acidifying fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) in spring; Northblue ripens mid-season (July in Minnesota and Wisconsin) producing large, dark blue berries with excellent highbush flavor — larger and better-flavored than lowbush but hardier than standard highbush. Northblue blueberry is one of the University of Minnesota-developed half-high blueberry varieties that transformed blueberry growing in zones 3–5 of the upper Midwest, making reliable blueberry production possible in climates where standard highbush varieties (which are typically hardy only to about -20°F with snow cover) suffered severe dieback or winter-killed entirely. The half-high blueberries were developed by crossing standard highbush Vaccinium corymbosum (for berry size and quality) with the ultra-cold-hardy native lowbush blueberry Vaccinium angustifolium (for hardiness) — and Northblue represents one of the earliest and most successful results of this breeding work. Northblue plants grow 2–3 feet tall — intermediate between lowbush (6–18 inches) and highbush (4–6 feet) — and produce large, dark blue berries with a distinctly better flavor and larger size than wild lowbush berries, closer to highbush quality. The combination of cold-hardiness to -35°F (with some snow cover and mulching), compact size, and genuinely good fruit quality (not just acceptable — actually good by highbush standards) makes Northblue one of the most important blueberry varieties for cold-climate gardeners. Cross-pollination with another half-high variety (Northcountry, Northsky, Polaris) is required for best fruit set.

common_name: Northcountry Blueberry (Half-High Minnesota Cold-Hardy Blueberry, Twin Cities Blueberry)
notes: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.2); mulch heavily; fertilize lightly with ammonium sulfate; Northcountry ripens slightly earlier than Northblue (late June to early July in Minnesota), making it valuable for extending the blueberry season from the beginning; berries are medium-sized, sky-blue, with a mild but pleasant flavor and good sweetness; the plants have attractive red-orange fall color. Northcountry blueberry is a companion half-high variety to Northblue from the same University of Minnesota breeding program, released together as a pair that complements Northblue's mid-season ripening with an earlier season (typically ripening 1–2 weeks before Northblue). The pairing of Northcountry (early) with Northblue (mid) or Northsky (late) is the standard recommendation from University of Minnesota Extension for home blueberry plantings in zones 3–5, providing a 3–4 week fresh blueberry season from one combined planting. The cross-pollination between these varieties also improves fruit set on both plants. Northcountry plants grow slightly more compact than Northblue (typically 24–36 inches rather than 36–48 inches), with a dense, mounded habit that makes them particularly attractive as landscape shrubs in addition to their edible fruit value. The berries are medium-sized (slightly smaller than Northblue), sky-blue in color, with a good sweet-mild flavor and good shelf life for a half-high variety. The extreme cold-hardiness — tested to -30°F with snow cover — and early ripening season make Northcountry one of the most important blueberry varieties for northern Minnesota, North Dakota, and other severe cold-climate gardening situations.

Sow seeds in fall after rubbing away the waxy seed coating, or provide a 60–90 day cold stratification period before spring sowing; northern bayberry grows naturally in coastal dunes, sandy thickets, and open woods from Newfoundland to North Carolina and thrives in lean, acidic, sandy or loamy soils with excellent drainage. This nitrogen-fixing native is highly tolerant of salt spray, wind, and drought, making it an exceptional choice for coastal landscapes and difficult sites where more refined shrubs fail. The aromatic, blue-gray waxy berries cluster tightly along the branches and persist into winter, historically rendered for bayberry candles; in the garden they provide excellent winter interest and food for birds such as yellow-rumped warblers. Northern bayberry spreads slowly by root suckers to form naturalistic colonies and requires both male and female plants for berry production.

common_name: Norton Grape (Cynthiana, Flagship Ozark Native American Red Wine Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the vigorous canopy. Norton, also sold under the name Cynthiana, is a pure native American grape (Vitis aestivalis) with exceptional resistance to Pierce's disease, black rot, and other diseases that limit many other wine grapes across the humid South and lower Midwest, and it served historically as the flagship red wine grape of the Ozark and Missouri wine industry before Prohibition. It produces small, dark, high-acid berries that make deeply colored, full-bodied red wine, though the fruit is generally considered too tart and seedy for fresh eating. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, since Norton is a vigorous grower that needs regular canopy management to keep fruit quality high.

Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist through the long southern summer. Ochlockonee is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry named for the Ochlockonee River in the Florida Panhandle, valued for ripening late in the season, after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, which lets home growers stretch fresh blueberry harvest into July. The vigorous, upright bush produces firm, medium-to-large, good-flavored berries in heavy clusters, and its low chill requirement makes it well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and remove old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous fruiting wood.

Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full to partial sun; odorless bayberry is a coastal plain specialist that naturally inhabits wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bay swamps and performs best in consistently moist to seasonally wet conditions. Myrica heterophylla is a semi-evergreen to evergreen native bayberry of the southeastern coastal plain, closely related to wax myrtle but lacking the characteristic aromatic fragrance; it produces similar small waxy berries that attract overwintering songbirds and provides dense cover in wet to moist habitats where few other shrubs thrive. This species is an excellent choice for rain gardens, wet swales, and pond margins in the Southeast, where its compact form and wildlife value make it a workhorse of native planting designs.

Grow this low, wiry-branched shrub in gritty, well-drained, acidic soil that mimics its native volcanic cinder habitat, and avoid rich garden soil or heavy watering that can encourage rot. Ohelo produces small, tart-sweet, cranberry-like berries in shades of red, yellow, or orange, borne alongside dainty urn-shaped pink or yellow flowers typical of the blueberry family. Native to high-elevation Hawaiian volcanic slopes, it tolerates poor, rocky ground and strong sun but is sensitive to wet, poorly drained conditions and to frost. The tangy fruit is traditionally used fresh or cooked into jams and sauces.

The olallieberry is a trailing blackberry hybrid (a cross involving loganberry and youngberry parentage) popular along the California coast for its rich, sweet-tart flavor. Its long, sprawling canes must be trained onto a trellis and are best separated by fruiting year for easier pruning. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with regular irrigation through the dry season. Prune out fruited canes after the early-summer harvest and tie in the new canes for next year.

common_name: Onslow Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Productive Southern Blueberry)
notes: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Onslow is a rabbiteye blueberry cultivar released for the Southeast, valued for exceptional plant vigor and consistently heavy production of medium to large, good-flavored berries. Its strong growth makes it well suited to establishing a productive planting relatively quickly, and it performs reliably across the range of soil conditions typical of Southern blueberry patches, provided the acidic, well-drained requirements common to all rabbiteye types are met. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Onslow requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Optimus Blueberry (Machine-Harvest Early-Season Southern Highbush Blueberry)
notes: Plant dormant bushes in winter in well-drained, acidic soil amended with pine bark, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Optimus is a University of Florida southern highbush release bred for a very low chilling requirement of roughly 150 to 200 hours, an early bloom period, and good natural leafing, all of which suit the mild, unpredictable winters of the Gulf Coast. The firm, round, medium-sized berries were selected with machine harvesting in mind, and the vigorous, disease-tolerant bushes have shown good field resistance to stem blight and Phytophthora root rot. Home growers get the benefit of a reliable, early-season crop on a tough plant that shrugs off the humid Southern growing season.

Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Oregon Champion is a nineteenth-century American heirloom gooseberry long favored in the Pacific Northwest for combining decent mildew tolerance with the classic tartness of European-type gooseberries. The medium-sized, pale yellow-green berries have a smooth, faintly fuzzy skin and hold their tang well, making them as useful for pies and preserves as for fresh eating once fully ripe. The vigorous, spiny bush handles the region's cool, damp summers better than many English exhibition varieties.

Oregon grape is a native Pacific Northwest evergreen shrub with holly-like spiny leaves that produces clusters of tart, powder-blue berries in midsummer — one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant edible-fruiting shrubs available. The berries are too tart to eat fresh in quantity but are excellent for jellies, syrups, and wine when sweetened; they are high in berberine, a compound with traditional medicinal use. Plant in groups of three or more for best cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune by removing the oldest, leggiest canes at the base every few years to encourage compact, multi-stemmed growth.

Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; oriental photinia is adaptable to a range of soil types and is notably more disease-resistant than the commonly planted red-tipped photinia. Photinia villosa is a deciduous shrub or small tree from East Asia offering outstanding multi-season interest: flat clusters of small white flowers appear in spring, followed by persistent bright red berries that last well into winter, and the foliage turns a brilliant red-orange in autumn that rivals the best fall color of any shrub in the temperate garden. Birds, particularly thrushes and waxwings, relish the persistent berries through late winter, making this an excellent choice for a wildlife-supporting mixed shrub border.

common_name: Orlando Seedless Grape (First Pierce's Disease-Resistant Seedless Bunch Grape)
notes: Plant grafted vines in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, since Orlando Seedless requires grafting onto 'Tampa' or 'Dog Ridge' rootstock for satisfactory growth and yield rather than growing on its own roots. Bred from interspecific crosses at the University of Florida's Agricultural Research Center in Leesburg, it was the first bunch grape to pair genuine seedlessness with resistance to Pierce's disease, the leafhopper-spread bacterial infection that devastated Florida's historic bunch grape industry. Its white, seedless fruit has good eating quality and fresh-market appeal, though the variety is notably more susceptible to anthracnose than other Florida-bred cultivars and can suffer berry shattering as clusters mature, so a consistent fungicide spray program from bud break onward is important. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to reduce disease pressure and improve berry size.

common_name: Osceola Blueberry (Southern Highbush Large-Berry Low-Chill Blueberry)
notes: Plant in highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil; acidify if necessary with sulfur or peat moss. Mulch with pine bark or pine straw. Osceola is a southern highbush blueberry developed in Florida through the University of Florida breeding program — a hybrid of northern highbush (Vaccinium corymbosum) and the native southern rabbit-eye relative (Vaccinium darrowi) that produces a plant adapted to the warm, humid conditions and low chilling hours of the Gulf South. The challenge of growing blueberries in the Deep South is chilling requirement: most northern highbush varieties need 800–1,200 hours below 45°F per winter to break dormancy and fruit properly, a requirement never met in zone 8–10 winters where chilling hours typically run 150–400. Osceola and other southern highbush varieties were specifically bred for low chilling requirements (150–200 hours), allowing reliable fruiting in zone 8–10 where northern varieties fail. Osceola produces large, firm, high-quality berries with excellent flavor — among the largest of the southern highbush varieties — ripening mid-season (May–June in zone 9). It is one of the most widely planted commercial and home garden blueberries in Florida and along the Gulf Coast.

Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained acidic soil; Ouachita is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2003 — one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in the mid-South and Gulf Coast because of its outstanding combination of productivity, fruit quality, and disease resistance. Berries are medium-large (7–9 grams), glossy black, firm, and mildly sweet with a pleasant balanced flavor and small seeds. Yields are among the highest of any named blackberry variety, and the plants show good resistance to orange rust and anthracnose — a meaningful advantage in the humid South. Canes are self-supporting but benefit from a simple T-trellis for row plantings. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; thin primocanes to 4–6 per plant and tip at 36 inches in late summer to encourage lateral branching that will carry next year's fruit. Ouachita's mid-season ripening (about 2 weeks after Natchez) makes it an excellent partner variety for an extended harvest window.

Native across the cool coniferous forests of Alaska, the Pacific Northwest, and northern Japan, this blueberry relative is remarkably tolerant of dense shade and thrives in the same acidic, mossy understory conditions that defeat most fruiting shrubs. Its pale pink spring flowers give way to soft blue berries by midsummer, among the earliest wild blueberries to ripen, with a mild sweet flavor traditionally gathered fresh or dried by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific coast and interior. Keep the soil consistently moist and acidic and avoid any lime or wood ash near the roots. For a genuinely shade-loving berry crop under established evergreens, this species outperforms almost any cultivated blueberry.

Plant in full sun in strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to protect the shallow root system. Ozarkblue was developed by the University of Arkansas and stands out among northern highbush blueberries for its unusual heat tolerance and adaptability to warmer regions that would stress most other northern highbush cultivars, while still delivering the large size, firm texture, and excellent, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor the group is known for. It ripens late in the blueberry season, extending the harvest window when planted alongside earlier-ripening cultivars. Cross-pollination with a second highbush cultivar improves fruit set and size. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water deeply during dry spells, and prune out old canes each winter to keep the bush productive.

Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda dogwood is shade-tolerant and adaptable but is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker disease — provide good air circulation and avoid injuring the bark. Cornus alternifolia is the only native eastern dogwood with alternate (rather than opposite) leaves, and it produces one of the most distinctive and elegant branching patterns of any native tree — distinctly horizontal, tiered layers of branches that create a pagoda-like architectural silhouette outstanding in winter; its small, fragrant, flat-topped white flower clusters are followed by showy blue-black berries on red pedicels that are consumed by dozens of migrating bird species. Four-season interest: layered winter form, white spring flowers, summer fruit, and red-purple fall foliage.

Passionfruit is a vigorous, tendril-climbing vine requiring a sturdy wire trellis or fence. Train the main stem vertically and allow lateral shoots to drape horizontally from the top — these laterals bear the flowers and fruit. Prune heavily after fruiting to rejuvenate the vine and maintain productive growth. Harvest when the fruit skin begins to wrinkle and the fruit falls or detaches easily; purple cultivars are generally more cold-tolerant than yellow types.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and give the vine generous trellis space; Paulk is a self-fertile muscadine released by the University of Georgia breeding program and has quickly become popular for producing some of the largest berries of any muscadine cultivar, with glossy black-purple skin and a sweet, mild flavor good for fresh eating. Vines are notably vigorous and heavy-bearing, often needing more aggressive winter pruning than older varieties to keep the canopy in bounds and light penetrating to the fruiting spurs. Train young vines to a single trunk and permanent cordon along a wire, then prune all lateral growth back to short spurs each winter, since fruit forms on new shoots from that spur wood. Harvest from late summer into early fall as berries turn fully black and detach freely from the stem; because Paulk berries are large and thin-skinned relative to older varieties, pick promptly at ripeness to avoid splitting after rain.

Amend soil to pH 4.5-5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Pearl River is a rabbiteye blueberry released by the LSU AgCenter specifically for Gulf South dooryard and commercial plantings, selected for consistent production under Louisiana's mild winters and low-to-moderate chill hours. The medium-sized, light blue berries ripen mid-season and have a firm texture and mild, sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating and freezing. Plants are vigorous and moderately disease-tolerant, though they benefit from mulching with pine bark or pine straw to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. Not self-fruitful, so plant with at least one other rabbiteye cultivar within 50 feet for reliable cross-pollination and full-sized fruit. Prune out the oldest, least productive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.

common_name: Phoenix Tears Goji Berry (Compact High-Yield Goji Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained loam with a pH of 6.5–8.0 in full sun; goji tolerates poor, alkaline soils where other fruiting shrubs struggle. Phoenix Tears is a named goji cultivar selected for heavy, reliable fruit production and elongated, bright red-orange berries with the tart-sweet flavor typical of the species, on arching, slightly thorny canes that can be left as a loose shrub or trained to a central leader with staking. Prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting laterals for the following season. Harvest ripe berries by gently rolling the stem between your fingers rather than pulling directly on the fruit, since the sap can stain skin and clothing.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. Pineapple is a self-fertile bronze muscadine grown by home gardeners and small vineyards for its distinctive flavor — a mild, sweet, tropical pineapple note layered over the classic musky muscadine taste, unusual enough among muscadine varieties to have earned the fruit its name. Being self-fertile, one vine sets a full crop without a second pollinator variety planted nearby, making it an easy choice for a single-vine home planting. As with other muscadines, it resists Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make European wine grapes difficult to grow in the humid South, so no regular spray program is needed. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest berries as they ripen and slip easily from the cluster.

Pink currants are naturally occurring or selected mutations of red currant (Ribes rubrum) producing pale rose-pink to blush-colored berries that are milder and sweeter than the typical red forms — popular cultivars include 'Pink Champagne' and 'Gloire de Sablons'. Culture is identical to red currant: plant in cool, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0–6.5 and prune each late winter to retain 8–12 mixed-age canes, removing any older than 5 years. The translucent pink strigs are ornamentally striking and ripen slightly earlier than most red currants. Check state Ribes restrictions before ordering.

'Pink Lemonade' is an ornamental rabbiteye-type hybrid bearing translucent pink berries with a mild, sweet flavor that deepen in color as they ripen. It offers attractive white-pink spring blooms and fiery fall foliage in addition to novelty fruit. Grow in full sun in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) kept evenly moist with a pine-bark or pine-needle mulch. Yields improve with a second blueberry variety nearby for cross-pollination; prune lightly after the third year to renew fruiting wood.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in hot climates. Pixwell was bred specifically to make gooseberry picking less painful, holding its pale green, ripening-to-pink berries on longer stems that dangle clear of the thorny branches, unlike older cultivars whose fruit clusters tightly among the spines. The berries have the classic tart gooseberry flavor, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, and the plant is vigorous, cold-hardy, and self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive, and site with some afternoon shade in warmer climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the upright canes onto a simple two-wire trellis for support. Released by the University of Arkansas breeding program, Ponca is one of the newer thornless erect blackberry cultivars, notable for exceptionally high sugar content and small seed size that give it outstanding fresh-eating flavor compared to older, tarter cultivars. The compact, upright canes need less trellising than sprawling semi-erect types, and the plant produces a concentrated harvest over a relatively short picking window in early summer. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to make room for the canes that will fruit the following season.

Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch and reduce mildew pressure). Poorman is a long-cultivated American gooseberry hybrid, valued for combining good disease resistance with berries that are sweeter and milder than many European gooseberry cultivars, making them pleasant for fresh eating as well as pies, jams, and preserves. The medium-sized fruit ripens from green to a rosy red-pink blush, and the bush, while still thorny like most gooseberries, is comparatively less vicious to harvest from than many older European types. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on both old and new wood; prune out the oldest canes each winter and thin crowded growth to improve air circulation, since gooseberries are prone to powdery mildew in humid, poorly ventilated plantings. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; possumhaw holly is a multi-season native shrub that blooms with small white flowers in spring attractive to native bees, then develops abundant bright-orange to red berries that ripen in fall and persist through winter to provide critical food for cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other frugivorous birds. A male pollinator must be planted nearby for fruiting; nurseries often sell named female selections (Warren's Red, Council Fire) paired with a male. Tolerates the periodic flooding and clay soils common to Gulf Coast lowland sites. Exceptional as a wildlife garden shrub, in rain gardens, and along creek margins.

common_name: Powder Blue Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Heavy-Bearing Gulf South Blueberry)
notes: Plant in acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil at the same depth as the nursery container; mulch 4–6 inches deep with pine bark or pine straw to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Do not fertilize with standard garden fertilizers — use acid-specific fertilizers (ammonium sulfate or azalea/camellia formulas). Powder Blue is a rabbiteye blueberry (Vaccinium virgatum, formerly classified as V. ashei) released in 1978 by North Carolina State University — one of the most widely planted and highest-yielding rabbiteye varieties across the Southeast. Rabbiteye blueberries are the blueberry species native to the Gulf South — the wild Vaccinium virgatum grows naturally throughout the coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana — and they are dramatically better adapted to the heat, humidity, and acidic sandy soils of the Gulf South than the northern highbush blueberries that dominate the commercial blueberry market. Powder Blue produces very large berries for a rabbiteye — medium-firm, light blue (giving the variety its name), with a mild, sweet flavor. The late-season ripening (July in zone 8–9) means Powder Blue fills the end of the Gulf South blueberry season after earlier-ripening varieties have peaked, extending the household fresh blueberry window into midsummer. Established rabbiteye plantings (plants reach bearing age in 3–5 years and can remain productive for 30–50 years) are highly cost-effective long-term investments for Gulf South home fruit gardens.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Powderblue is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry valued for its vigorous, upright, disease-resistant growth habit and dependable, heavy production of firm, small-to-medium, powder-blue berries with excellent shelf life and a mild, sweet flavor well suited to both fresh eating and freezing. It ripens mid-to-late season, several weeks after Climax and Premier, helping extend the rabbiteye harvest window into July in most Gulf Coast plantings. The upright, vigorous canes tend to sucker less than some rabbiteye varieties, keeping the planting tidier, and the bush shows good tolerance of the humid, disease-prone conditions typical of southeastern summers. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain consistent moisture through fruit development, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer at bloom and again after harvest. Zone 6–9.

Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.0) amended with pine bark, peat, or sulfur; Premier is an early-to-mid-season rabbiteye blueberry released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1978, valued particularly for its very large berry size — among the largest of the rabbiteye types — and excellent fresh-eating flavor. Berries are light blue, mild, sweet, and ripen from late May through June in zone 8–9. The spreading, vigorous plant is one of the more open-canopied rabbiteye varieties, giving better air circulation that reduces disease problems. Premier is a perennial favorite for u-pick operations and home gardens in the Gulf Coast South because the large berries are showy and harvest quickly. Fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or cottonseed meal) in early spring and again in late spring; avoid high-nitrogen applications after July. Prune to remove crossing branches and old unproductive wood after the third year of growth.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark in full sun; Premier is the standard early-season rabbiteye blueberry for zone 7–9, producing large, light blue, mildly flavored berries beginning in late May in most Gulf Coast plantings — up to 3 weeks before mid-season varieties. The upright, vigorous shrubs can reach 8–10 feet with age and are among the most productive of the early-season rabbiteyes. The berries have a larger size than most other early varieties but a thinner skin than mid-season types; harvest promptly after coloring to prevent skin softening. Premier has a chilling requirement of approximately 350 hours, making it reliable in zone 8–9 without the risk of premature bloom during January warm spells. Cross-pollinates well with Brightwell, Climax, Centurion, and Tifblue.

Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Prima Donna is a southern highbush blueberry selected by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery for its combination of high fruit quality and strong plant vigor in warm-climate conditions. The medium-large berries are firm, flavorful, and sweet with a pleasant balance of sugar and acid that makes them superior for fresh eating. Prima Donna's primary advantage is a high-quality, consistent fruit that stores and ships better than softer varieties — the firm texture retains quality for 2–3 weeks under refrigeration, significantly longer than some other southern varieties. In zone 9 home gardens this means less pressure to consume the harvest immediately after picking. Prima Donna is popular in commercial pick-your-own operations in the Southeast precisely because the firm berries withstand handling by customers without bruising. The plant habit is vigorous and upright, producing good yields without excessive vegetative growth.

'Prime-Ark Freedom' is the first thornless primocane-fruiting blackberry, capable of bearing very large berries on first-year canes. It offers an early summer crop on floricanes and a late-summer-to-fall crop on new primocanes. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, and support the canes on a trellis in windy locations. In hot climates the fall crop yields the sweetest fruit when temperatures moderate; soft-tip the primocanes to boost lateral fruiting.

Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Prime-Ark Horizon is the newest primocane-fruiting blackberry from the University of Arkansas breeding program, meaning that unlike traditional blackberries it fruits on the current season's new canes in addition to the usual second-year floricanes, extending the harvest window into fall. It produces larger fruit with a good sugar-to-acid balance and was bred to push the primocane fruiting season later than the earlier Prime-Ark releases. Because it retains thorns, unlike Prime-Ark Freedom and Prime-Ark Traveler, handle canes with care and consider glove use during pruning and harvest. To get both a summer floricane crop and a fall primocane crop, leave some canes unpruned; for a fall-only crop, mow all canes to the ground in late winter.

common_name: Prime-Ark Traveler Blackberry (Thornless Machine-Harvestable Primocane Blackberry)
notes: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and provide a sturdy trellis, since this vigorous primocane-fruiting cultivar produces fruit on first-year canes in addition to the traditional second-year floricane crop. Bred by the University of Arkansas specifically for firmness that withstands mechanical harvesting and shipping, Prime-Ark Traveler also performs well as a home-garden thornless blackberry, producing a first crop on primocanes in late summer and fall in addition to the normal early-summer floricane harvest. Because it fruits on both first- and second-year wood, pruning decisions affect which crop you prioritize: cutting all canes to the ground in winter sacrifices the floricane crop but still allows a fall primocane harvest, while leaving some canes standing provides both crops.

Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Ranger is a mid-20th-century erect, thorny blackberry from the early era of USDA bramble breeding, valued today mostly for its toughness, cold hardiness, and productivity under low-input conditions rather than for the largest berries. Fruit is medium-sized, firm, and tart-sweet, well suited to jam, jelly, and cobbler more than fresh eating. The upright canes are self-supporting in home gardens, though a simple wire trellis keeps rows tidier and eases picking. Prune out spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest and thin new primocanes to 4-6 per plant, tipping them at about 36 inches in late summer to encourage the lateral branches that carry next year's crop. Its old-fashioned toughness and reliable cropping make Ranger a good pick for a low-maintenance hedgerow planting rather than a showcase bed.

Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Rebel is a southern highbush blueberry developed by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery, released specifically for its combination of very large fruit size and excellent flavor — the berries are among the largest available in southern highbush blueberries, and their rich, sweet-tart, complex flavor rivals northern highbush varieties that are not adapted to zone 9 conditions. The vigorous, productive plant produces heavy crops of these exceptional large-caliber berries with a firm texture that holds up well in packing, shipping, and storage. Rebel's fruit quality has made it popular among commercial pick-your-own operations in the Southeast where premium large berries command top prices. In zone 9 home gardens it provides exceptional fresh eating quality — the large berries are satisfying to pick and eat fresh from the bush. Cross-pollinate with Flordablue, Biloxi, or Windsor for maximum crop set.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; red barberry is a dense, spiny-leaved evergreen shrub of the desert Southwest, its holly-like, blue-gray foliage giving way in spring to small, fragrant, bright yellow flower clusters that draw bees. Clusters of tart, juicy red berries follow in summer, edible fresh in small quantities and traditionally used to make jelly, syrup, and a tart, refreshing beverage similar to that made from the related algerita (Berberis trifoliolata). The dense, thorny branching makes it a useful barrier or wildlife hedge planting, offering cover and food for birds while deterring foot traffic. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant once established and requires minimal care beyond occasional shaping, needing supplemental water only during the driest extended stretches.

Red chokeberry (Aronia arbutifolia) is a taller, more upright native shrub than its black-fruited relative, bearing bright red berries that ripen in fall and persist well into winter, providing exceptional wildlife food and four-season ornamental interest. The berries are intensely astringent fresh but soften after frost and are suitable for jellies, juices, and wines with added sweetener. The cultivar 'Brilliantissima' is widely grown for its especially vibrant fall foliage and heavy fruit set. Prune oldest canes to the ground every 3–4 years to control suckering and maintain vigor.

Red currants fruit heavily on spurs of wood two years old and older; prune each late winter to keep 8–12 canes of mixed ages and remove any cane older than 5 years. They tolerate more shade than most fruits and appreciate afternoon shelter in hot climates. Harvest entire strigs (clusters) when berries are uniformly bright red and slightly translucent. Check state restrictions on Ribes planting before ordering.

Red Elderberry is a fast-growing native shrub of cool, moist forests, rocky slopes, talus, and ravines across the northern United States and Canada, valued for its dramatic pyramid-shaped white flower clusters in spring and vivid red berry clusters in early summer that ripen weeks before American Elderberry. The berries are relished by over 50 species of birds including thrushes, waxwings, grouse, and tanagers, making Red Elderberry among the most important native berry shrubs for wildlife in northern gardens. Unlike the closely related American Elderberry, Red Elderberry berries are mildly toxic when eaten raw due to cyanogenic glycosides and should be cooked before any culinary use; fully cooked berries have been used for jams, wines, and syrups in both traditional and modern kitchens. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Elderberry is more shade-tolerant than American Elderberry and thrives at cool woodland edges and in dappled understory light.

Red huckleberry is a Pacific Northwest native that naturally colonizes rotting conifer stumps and logs, requiring extremely acidic conditions (pH 4.0–5.0) and excellent drainage with abundant organic matter. The bright scarlet berries ripen in summer and are tart — excellent for jams, syrups, and pies — and are an important wildlife food for birds and bears. Established plants spread slowly by rhizomes and require minimal pruning; remove only dead or crossing branches in late winter. Difficult to transplant as a wild specimen; use nursery-grown container stock for best results.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the red mulberry is the only mulberry native to eastern North America and produces berries superior in flavor and nutrition to the introduced white mulberry — richer, more complex, and deeply red to black when fully ripe. It is an ecologically critical plant, providing fruit for hundreds of wildlife species at a critical early-summer period. The berries are edible fresh or made into pies, jams, wine, and dried fruit; harvest is best done by spreading a tarp and shaking the branches, as berries stain everything they touch. Red mulberry is distinguished from white mulberry by its leaves, which are rough on the upper surface (smooth in white mulberry). It unfortunately hybridizes readily with the invasive white mulberry where the two grow together, threatening the genetic integrity of pure wild populations; purchasing certified native red mulberry trees from reputable nurseries is important.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Regale is a University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its large, glossy black berries with a thinner skin and juicier, sweeter flesh than many older black muscadine cultivars, making it well suited to fresh eating as well as juice and wine production. Vines are vigorous and productive, ripening a heavy mid-season crop that holds up well on the vine without excessive splitting in wet weather, a common problem with thinner-skinned muscadines. Regale is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, though as with other muscadines, planting several varieties together tends to boost overall yield. It shows good disease resistance typical of muscadine grapes in humid Gulf South conditions, requiring far less fungicide input than bunch grapes. Harvest as berries turn fully black and detach easily from the stem with gentle pressure; expect the vine to reach full production three to four years after planting on a sturdy two-wire trellis.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Developed by the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program, Rosborough was selected specifically for reliable performance in the hot, humid conditions of Texas and the Gulf South, producing good yields of medium-to-large, flavorful berries in early-to-mid summer. It has thorns, unlike many newer cultivars, but its regional heat tolerance and disease resistance have made it a long-standing favorite among Gulf Coast growers who prioritize proven regional performance over the novelty of thornlessness. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting vigorous and productive.

'Royalty' is a hybrid of red and black raspberry yielding large, richly flavored purple berries excellent for jam and baking. The tall, sturdy canes do not sucker as aggressively as red types and are best tip-pruned in summer to encourage lateral branching. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and remove old floricanes after fruiting. Plant at least 300 feet from wild or black raspberries to reduce viral disease pressure.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. RubyCrisp is a modern University of Georgia muscadine bred to address the main complaint fresh-market shoppers have about muscadines — thick, tough skin — with noticeably firmer flesh and thinner, more tender skin that make the deep red-to-black berries far more pleasant to eat out of hand, closer to the experience of a bunch grape while keeping the intense, musky-sweet muscadine flavor. Like other muscadines it is naturally resistant to Pierce's disease, downy mildew, and the fungal diseases that plague European wine grapes in the humid South, so home gardeners can grow it without a spray program. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety nearby if RubyCrisp is female-flowered, or check with the nursery on flower type at purchase, since muscadine cultivars vary between self-fertile and female-only. Prune hard in late winter, leaving short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as individual berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; running serviceberry is the low-growing, colony-forming native serviceberry of the northeastern US and Appalachians, spreading by stolons to form attractive low thickets 1–3 feet tall on rocky slopes, woodland edges, and open forests. Like all serviceberries, it produces masses of white flowers in early spring that are an important nectar and pollen source for early-emerging native bees, followed by sweet, blueberry-like June berries in early summer that are excellent fresh, dried, or cooked into pies and preserves. The low, suckering habit makes it more useful as a shade-tolerant groundcover or erosion control plant than as a specimen shrub. It colors brilliantly orange-red in fall. An ideal native edible shrub for shaded slopes, woodland edges, and low-maintenance natural landscapes in the Northeast and Appalachians.

Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established; the plant fixes nitrogen through Frankia bacterial symbiosis. Shepherdia canadensis (russet buffaloberry or soopalallie) is a deciduous native shrub of Canada, Alaska, and the northern United States — one of the most cold-hardy native fruiting shrubs on the continent, thriving in zone 2–6 conditions where few fruiting plants survive. The plant produces small (1/4-inch), translucent, red-orange to yellow, elliptic berries in summer that are bitter and astringent when eaten raw due to saponin content, but become edible after frost or cooking. The most famous traditional use is as 'sxusem' or 'soopalallie' (in Chinook jargon) — the indigenous peoples of British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest whipped the raw berries with water to produce a frothy, bright-red, bitter-sweet foam similar to meringue, traditionally sweetened with berries or honey and eaten as 'Indian ice cream.' The high saponin content is what enables the foam to form — the same compounds that make dish soap foam. The berries are also used for jelly, syrup, and beverages. Shephaerdia canadensis is a dioecious nitrogen-fixer (requires separate male and female plants, and fixes nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis), making it valuable in cold-climate food forest systems as a soil-building shrub with an edible berry crop.

Sow seeds in fall directly in the garden or cold-stratify for 60–90 days before planting in spring; plant in dry, rocky, or sandy soil with excellent drainage in full sun, as russet buffaloberry naturally colonizes forest edges, rocky slopes, and open woodlands from Alaska to the northeastern United States. This dioecious nitrogen-fixer requires both male and female plants to produce its small, tart red berries, which ripen in midsummer. The berries were a prized food source for many indigenous peoples and can be whipped with a small amount of water and a touch of sweetener into a stable foam traditionally called 'sxusem' or Indian ice cream. Established plants are extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once rooted, making russet buffaloberry an excellent low-maintenance native for challenging northern and high-altitude sites.

Salal is an evergreen native shrub of the Pacific Northwest coast, found beneath conifers from central California to Alaska, where it forms dense thickets on acidic, well-drained forest soils. The dark blue-purple berries are similar in size to a blueberry but have mealy, mildly sweet flesh and were an important food source for coastal Indigenous peoples, eaten fresh or dried into cakes. Salal is propagated by division or from container-grown nursery stock; seed germination is slow and unreliable. The glossy foliage is commercially valuable in the floral trade, and home growers can cut leathery stems for arrangements without harming the plant.

Sand cherry is a small, sprawling native North American shrub bearing small dark purple to black cherries in midsummer with a flavor ranging from pleasantly tart to bitter depending on provenance and ripeness stage. The fruits are consumed fresh, dried, or processed into pemmican and preserves and were an important food source for Plains Indigenous peoples. The plant is extraordinarily cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, spreading by root suckers to form low thickets excellent for erosion control. Harvest when berries are fully dark and soft; cross-pollination between multiple plants improves fruit set significantly.

Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full shade to partial sun; dwarf smilax is a coastal plain specialist adapted to the dry, shady conditions beneath longleaf pine and live oak canopies where few other evergreen groundcovers thrive. Smilax pumila is a low, trailing, spiny evergreen vine native to the pinelands and oak hammocks of the southeastern coastal plain, producing attractive glossy foliage that remains green through winter and showy clusters of bright red berries in late winter and early spring when wildlife food is scarce — making it exceptionally valuable for birds and small mammals during the hungry gap. Use it as a weed-suppressing groundcover under open-canopied native trees, where it will spread gradually into dense mats that require virtually no maintenance once established.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and train onto a single-wire or double-curtain trellis; Scarlett is a self-fertile muscadine released by the University of Georgia breeding program, selected for its reddish-bronze skin color, above-average berry size, and reliable self-pollination, making it a good choice for a home planting with limited space for a separate pollinizer vine. The flavor is sweet with the classic musky muscadine character, and the vine is vigorous and productive once established, typically bearing its first meaningful crop in year three. Prune hard every winter back to spurs on the permanent cordon, since muscadines fruit on new growth from the current season's canes. Harvest berries individually as they ripen and detach easily from the stem, over a multi-week window in late summer, and provide consistent moisture during fruit swell to reduce splitting after heavy rain.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; elderberries tolerate wet sites better than most fruiting shrubs and are well suited to low or seasonally damp spots in the garden. Scotia is a Nova Scotia-origin American elderberry selection valued for its very early ripening and large, showy fruit clusters of small, dark purple-black berries, borne on a vigorous, suckering shrub. Berries must be cooked before eating, as raw elderberries and other plant parts contain compounds that can cause stomach upset; ripe, cooked fruit is traditionally made into syrup, jelly, wine, and pie, and the broad, flat flower clusters can also be used fresh or dried for elderflower cordial and fritters. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to renew the shrub, since elderberries fruit best on relatively young wood, and cut the whole planting back hard every few years to keep it a manageable size.

Sea buckthorn is a thorny, nitrogen-fixing shrub that thrives in poor, dry, sandy soils where most fruits struggle. It is dioecious and requires male plants for pollination — one male per 5–7 females; sex is not identifiable until first flowering, so purchase sexed plants. The tiny berries are borne directly on the branches in dense clusters and are difficult to harvest without damaging the plant; a common approach is to cut fruiting branches in fall and strip berries indoors or by freezing and shaking. The tart, orange berries are extremely high in vitamin C.

common_name: September Sun Arctic Beauty Kiwi (Variegated Fruiting Kolomikta Kiwi)
notes: Plant a rooted cutting of September Sun in spring against a sturdy trellis or fence in humus-rich, well-drained soil, and pair it with a male Actinidia kolomikta vine nearby since this cultivar is a fruiting female that needs a pollinator to set fruit. Give it a site with dappled or filtered light rather than harsh all-day sun, which keeps the foliage's dramatic pink-and-white variegation from scorching while the vine still ripens its small, smooth-skinned, sweet kiwiberries in late summer. The grape-sized fruit tastes like a sweeter, thinner-skinned version of grocery-store kiwifruit and can be eaten skin-and-all straight off the vine. Because it thrives with part-shade protection and doubles as an ornamental accent, September Sun suits a partly shaded arbor or fence where both fruit and foliage color are wanted.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–7.0) in full to partial sun; serviceberry tolerates wet sites and woodland edges better than most fruiting shrubs. No cross-pollinator is required, though planting two or more selections increases yield. Fruits ripen in late spring to early June, turning from red to deep purple-blue when fully sweet — birds will compete for them, so netting is advisable. Prune crossing or crowded stems in late winter to maintain an open, multi-stemmed form and remove root suckers to control spread.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; shadblow tolerates wet, poorly drained sites better than most Amelanchier species — excellent for rain gardens, streambanks, and moist woodland edges. Amelanchier canadensis (shadblow serviceberry or downy serviceberry) is one of the most widespread native Amelanchier species of the eastern United States, growing naturally in bogs, streambanks, wet woods, and swampy thickets from Maine to Georgia and inland to the Great Lakes. The plant flowers in earliest spring — often the first woody plant to bloom, sometimes even before forsythia — with spectacular clusters of pure white, 5-petaled flowers on bare branches that open as the leaves begin to emerge. The flowers are followed in June by small (1/3-inch), round, purple-black to dark blue-purple berries with a mild, sweet, almond-apple flavor distinctly different from blueberries — produced abundantly enough that a mature shrub can yield several quarts of fruit. The berries are excellent fresh, in pies, jams, pancake syrup, and anywhere blueberries are used. The name 'shadblow' (also written shad-bush or shad-blow) derives from the colonial observation that the tree bloomed when alewife and shad fish began running up rivers from the sea — a reliable calendar indicator for early spring fishing. Notable for better tolerance of wet soils than smooth serviceberry (A. laevis).

Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.5) amended with peat or composted pine bark; Sharpblue is a Southern highbush blueberry developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program and released in 1976 as one of the first cultivars specifically bred for extremely low-chill environments — it requires only 150–200 chill hours and thrives in zone 9–10 where rabbiteye varieties often fail to fruit consistently.
