This makes it particularly valuable for gardeners in coastal zone 9b, south Florida, and similar climates where winter chill accumulation is marginal. Berries are medium-sized, dark blue, very flavorful and aromatic — quality rivals highbush varieties grown in cooler climates. The plant is slightly tender and may be damaged by hard freezes below 15°F, though it recovers quickly. It is nearly evergreen in frost-free areas and can produce two crops per year in very warm locations. An excellent container blueberry for patios in the deep South.

Shiny Blueberry is the low-growing native blueberry of the Florida peninsula and southeastern coastal plain, native to the dry, sandy, fire-maintained flatwoods, scrub, and longleaf pine savannas from South Carolina to Florida and west to Mississippi, forming dense, rhizome-spreading colonies under open, sunny conditions. The small, glossy, dark green leaves are evergreen in zones 8–9, giving the plant its common name, and the small, sweet, dark blue berries ripen in spring — earlier than most other blueberries — providing fruit for birds and gardeners alike. Unlike the taller highbush blueberries, Shiny Blueberry is a groundcover-scale plant that works well as an edible lawn substitute in acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; it requires the same highly acidic soil conditions as all blueberries and benefits from cross-pollination with additional plants for heavy fruiting. Excellent for edible native landscape designs in the lower South.

Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; silky dogwood grows naturally in streamside thickets, wet meadows, and pond margins and is one of the best native shrubs for stabilizing stream banks and rain gardens. Cornus amomum is a loosely branched, multi-stemmed native shrub with soft, somewhat silky-haired leaves, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in June that are outstanding for native bees and small butterflies, and blue-black berry-like drupes in fall that are among the most heavily consumed native fruits by migrating songbirds — particularly wood thrushes, robins, and waxwings; the red-purple winter stems provide dormant season interest. Plant in groupings for best berry production and wildlife impact.

Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; silver buffaloberry is a spiny, thicket-forming native shrub of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain West with distinctive silvery-gray foliage and clusters of brilliant orange-red to red berries that ripen in summer and fall. The plant is dioecious — male and female flowers appear on separate plants — so both sexes must be planted for fruit production. Berries are tart but edible, historically used by Plains nations to make pemmican and sauce for buffalo meat (hence the name). Plants fix nitrogen through root nodules, tolerate extreme cold, drought, alkaline soils, and salt — among the most rugged food-producing shrubs for difficult Great Plains conditions. Excellent wildlife hedge.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), lean soil in partial shade to full sun; small black blueberry is a dwarf, spreading native vaccinium of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine flatwoods, closely associated with longleaf pine habitat. The small, very dark blue-black berries ripen in early summer and, while tiny, are intensely flavored and sweet — eaten fresh or used in preserves and baked goods in the traditional Southern way. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form low colonies and provides important food for dozens of bird species. In the native range, it grows in the precise habitat type (sandy, dry, very acidic) that is among the most threatened ecosystems in North America. An excellent species for naturalized longleaf pine ecosystem restoration in the Gulf Coastal Plain.

Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; viburnum nudum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites and thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, and low areas where standing water occasionally occurs. Viburnum nudum produces one of the most spectacular fall berry displays of any native shrub: the abundant berry clusters transition through pink, rose, blue, and finally blue-black as individual berries ripen at different times in September and October, creating a multi-colored cluster that is breathtaking and irresistible to migrating songbirds; the berries are consumed within days of full ripeness by cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and dozens of other species. The glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen foliage turns rich burgundy-red in fall; white, fragrant flower clusters in May attract native bees.

Southern highbush blueberries are interspecific hybrids bred for low chill-hour requirements (150–500 hours below 45°F), making them the only highbush-type blueberry suitable for Gulf Coast, Florida, and mild-winter California climates. Maintain soil pH at 4.5–5.5 with pine bark mulch and acidifying fertilizers; do not use lime. Plant two or more cultivars for cross-pollination and improved fruit size. Prune lightly for the first three years, then begin removing the oldest, least productive canes each late winter to stimulate vigorous new wood.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy arbor or pergola, where the vine doubles as an ornamental landscape feature. Southern Home is a distinctive interspecific hybrid between muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) and traditional bunch grape (Vitis vinifera), bred at the University of Georgia specifically for its uniquely ornamental, deeply lobed, almost oak-leaf-shaped foliage that sets it visually apart from the simple rounded leaves of standard muscadine varieties, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for a decorative fruiting arbor. The self-fertile vine produces medium-sized, black, muscadine-flavored fruit in loose bunches more reminiscent of a traditional grape cluster than the typical loose, few-berried muscadine set, and it carries good resistance to Pierce's disease inherited from its muscadine parentage — a critical advantage over standard bunch grapes in the humid Gulf South and Southeast, where Pierce's disease kills most vinifera and many hybrid grapes outright. An excellent choice for gardeners who want both fruit and ornamental landscape value from the same vine, zone 6–9.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Southland is a University of Georgia release valued for its large, dark reddish-black berries with a thin skin and sweet, rich muscadine flavor good for fresh eating as well as juice and wine. It is self-fertile, vigorous, and consistently productive, with solid disease resistance across the humid Gulf South. Mid-season ripening makes Southland a dependable companion to earlier black varieties like Cowart and later ones like Ison, spreading harvest over a longer window. Prune annually in late winter while dormant to renewal spurs to keep the vine productive and manageable on the trellis.

Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest parts of zone 9, and mulch well to keep roots cool. Southland is one of the few red raspberry cultivars bred specifically for adaptation to mild southern winters, with a low chilling-hour requirement that lets it flower and fruit where standard northern raspberries decline within a season or two from insufficient winter chill. It produces a light-to-moderate crop of medium-sized, sweet-tart red berries in late spring, with some plants also producing a smaller fall crop on primocanes. Yields are modest compared with northern raspberry cultivars grown in their ideal climate, but Southland remains one of the more dependable options for gardeners in zone 8-9 who want to try growing red raspberries. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to maintain airflow and reduce disease in humid conditions.

common_name: Springhigh Southern Highbush Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Blueberry)
notes: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun, and pair with another early-blooming southern highbush variety for best pollination and fruit set. Developed by the University of Florida's blueberry breeding program, Springhigh was selected for an unusually low chilling requirement that lets it flower and fruit reliably in the mild winters of the Deep South, where many northern blueberry types fail to break dormancy evenly. It ripens very early in the season, often the first blueberry to color up in the garden, giving growers a jump on the market and on fresh eating alike. Keep soil consistently moist during bloom and fruit development, since southern highbush types have shallow root systems that dry out quickly in sandy Gulf Coast soils.

Plant in partial shade in consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Squashberry is native to the understory of boreal and subarctic forests and performs best where it receives filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade. Maintain even soil moisture, especially during summer, by applying a generous layer of organic mulch around the root zone. Clusters of translucent orange-red berries ripen in late summer and were historically harvested by indigenous peoples of the north for fresh eating, jam, and pemmican. Propagate by softwood cuttings taken in early summer, treated with rooting hormone and kept in a humid environment; division of established clumps in early spring is also effective.

common_name: Star Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early-Ripening Low-Chill Blueberry)
notes: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and provide consistent moisture through spring fruit development for the best berry size. Star is a University of Florida southern highbush release valued for its very early ripening, often among the first blueberries ready to harvest in Gulf South gardens, bearing firm, flavorful, medium to large berries on a vigorous, productive bush. Its low chill requirement and early season make it a good choice for extending the front end of the blueberry harvest, particularly useful when paired with a mid- or late-season rabbiteye or southern highbush cultivar to spread the crop over a longer window. Plant with a second compatible southern highbush variety for the best fruit set, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush productive.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) in full sun on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis. Sterling is a self-fertile bronze muscadine released jointly by North Carolina State University and USDA-ARS, bred with juice production as the primary goal — the berries are consistent, productive, and well suited to pressing, though they are equally good eaten fresh. Being self-fertile, a single vine sets a full crop without a second pollinator variety nearby, simplifying the planting for a home gardener who only has room for one plant. Like other muscadines it shrugs off Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make European grapes difficult in the humid South, needing no regular spray program. Prune hard in late winter to short spurs on permanent cordons, and harvest as berries ripen and slip easily from the cluster; a light dropcloth under the vine makes fallen ripe fruit easy to gather during peak harvest.

common_name: Stover Grape (Early Self-Fertile University of Florida Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing plenty of airflow through the canopy. Stover was released by the University of Florida in 1968 and remains a standard early-ripening bunch grape for the Deep South, producing self-fertile crops of white-to-green, tart-to-sweet fruit good for table use, juice, and wine, ripening well ahead of many other bunch grape cultivars. Its early season lets growers harvest before the peak of summer disease and pest pressure builds. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and reduce fungal disease risk in humid weather.

Plant in moist to wet, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Celtis laevigata is an exceptionally adaptable native tree tolerating periodic flooding, clay soils, silt, calcareous substrates, and seasonal drought once established — one of the few large trees naturally adapted to Gulf Coast bottomland conditions. Celtis laevigata (Sugarberry or Southern Hackberry) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous native tree of the southeastern United States, ranging from the coastal plain of Virginia and Maryland south through Florida and west to Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas — a dominant tree of river bottomlands, floodplains, moist woodland slopes, and disturbed sites across the South. The common name 'Sugarberry' references the small, round, thin-skinned, reddish-orange to dark-purple to black fruits (technically drupes) that ripen in late summer and fall — sweet, date-raisin-like in flavor, tiny but edible and historically eaten by indigenous peoples across its range. The wildlife value is extraordinary: the berries are consumed by at least 25–30 bird species including mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, wood thrushes, bluebirds, and yellow-rumped warblers, and by raccoons, opossums, foxes, and white-tailed deer. As a native habitat tree, Sugarberry also supports the larvae of several butterfly species including the Hackberry Emperor (Asterocampa celtis) and Tawny Emperor (A. clyton), whose caterpillars feed exclusively on Celtis foliage. An outstanding choice for native wildlife plantings, riparian buffers, and restoration plantings in the Southeast.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune to a well-spaced fruiting framework each winter. Sugargate is a University of Georgia-released black muscadine grown almost entirely for exceptional fresh-eating quality — its large, tender-skinned fruit carries the highest sugar content and richest, sweetest flavor of any widely planted muscadine cultivar, making it a favorite among home growers and muscadine enthusiasts who prioritize taste over yield. The vine is somewhat less vigorous and productive than heavier-bearing varieties like Nesbitt or Supreme, so it is often planted as a specialty dessert selection alongside a more prolific cultivar rather than as the sole vine in a planting. Give it full sun, good drainage, and attentive care to get the best from its outstanding flavor, zone 7–9.

Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Summit is a southern highbush blueberry released by the University of Georgia for its outstanding combination of large, flavorful berries and good disease resistance to the humid-summer conditions of the Southeast. The large, firm, dark blue berries have excellent flavor — sweet and complex with good sugar-to-acid balance — and a dry scar that reduces the tendency to leak after picking, improving storage quality. Summit is specifically bred for disease resistance to mummy berry (Monilinia vaccinia-corymbosi) and to stem blight, which are the primary fungal diseases limiting blueberry production in the humid Gulf South. This disease package makes Summit particularly valuable in zone 9 conditions where wet summers favor fungal diseases. The mid-season ripening (late May–June) slots Summit between the earliest varieties and the latest-season types, contributing to an extended home harvest season when planted with Biloxi, Flordablue, and Windsor.

'Sunshine Blue' is a compact, semi-dwarf southern highbush blueberry that is self-fertile and needs only about 150 chill hours, making it ideal for warm regions and pots. It tolerates a slightly higher soil pH than most blueberries but still performs best in acidic, well-drained media. Grow in full sun, water consistently, and feed with an acid-formulated fertilizer during the growing season. Its tidy habit and showy pink-to-white flowers make it a productive ornamental for patios and small gardens.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with a perfect-flowered pollinator vine; Supreme is a USDA-released dark (black-skinned) muscadine producing the largest black-skinned fruits of any commercially available muscadine variety — round to slightly oval berries reaching 1.5–2 inches in diameter with deep blue-black to jet-black skin and rich, deeply flavored, sweet-tart purple flesh. The combination of very large fruit size, deep color, and late ripening (September–October in zone 9) makes Supreme particularly valuable for extending the fresh muscadine season after most other varieties have finished. The deep color indicates high anthocyanin content and the associated antioxidant capacity that has made muscadine grapes a focus of nutritional research. Supreme is primarily a fresh-eating variety; the very large individual berry size and attractive appearance make it outstanding for fresh market and U-pick use. As a pistillate variety, it requires a self-fertile pollinator nearby for any fruit production.

common_name: Suwannee Grape (Early Disease-Tolerant University of Florida Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy to help manage humidity-driven fungal disease. Suwannee was released by the University of Florida in 1983 as a companion to Stover, matching its early ripening while offering comparable resistance to Pierce's disease, anthracnose, and powdery mildew, making it a dependable bunch grape option for the Deep South where European wine grapes typically fail. Fruit is used for fresh eating, juice, and home winemaking. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and reduce disease pressure in humid weather.

Plant in strongly acidic, well-drained soil generously amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Suziblue is a University of Georgia-bred southern highbush blueberry selected for a relatively low chilling requirement suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South, ripening its crop of large, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor early in the blueberry season, ahead of many other southern highbush varieties. Like all blueberries it needs consistently acidic soil and will struggle or fail in neutral to alkaline ground; test soil pH before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed. Plant it with a second, compatible southern highbush cultivar nearby to improve pollination, berry size, and total yield, since cross-pollination generally outperforms a single variety planted alone. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, and water regularly during dry spells and through fruit development.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp fly honeysuckle is a native shrub honeysuckle of northern boggy habitats — a deciduous shrub with paired, yellowish-white flowers in late spring and attractive paired red berries in summer. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle vine (Lonicera japonica), this is a well-behaved native shrub that does not spread aggressively. The berries, while not favored as human food, are consumed by numerous bird species in summer and early fall. The shrub provides nesting structure for a variety of native birds in boggy habitats. An excellent native choice for consistently moist to wet, acidic, partially shaded sites in the cold-hardy northern zones 2–6.

common_name: Sweet Jenny Muscadine Grape (Very Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Sweet Jenny is a University of Georgia muscadine release notable for producing some of the largest fruit of any black muscadine cultivar, with sweet, mild-flavored flesh and a skin tender enough for easy fresh eating rather than just juice or wine. The self-fertile vine is vigorous, productive, and ripens over an extended mid-to-late season window, making it a favorite for home gardeners who want big, showy fruit without needing a second pollinator vine. Water consistently during fruit sizing for the largest berries, and thin crowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid Gulf South conditions.

common_name: Sweetcrisp Southern Highbush Blueberry (Crisp-Textured Low-Chill Blueberry)
notes: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.5 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch heavily with pine bark to maintain the moist, acidic conditions southern highbush blueberries require. Sweetcrisp is a University of Florida southern highbush release notable for its unusually firm, crisp berry texture — distinct from the softer bite of most blueberries — paired with high sugar content and good flavor, along with very low chill requirements that make it one of the most reliable blueberry choices for the Deep South and coastal Gulf region. The compact, productive bush ripens over a fairly long mid-season window, and its firm texture holds up especially well for fresh eating and short-term storage. Plant with a second southern highbush cultivar for best cross-pollination and yield, and prune out old, unproductive wood each winter to keep the bush vigorous.

common_name: Sweetie Pie Blackberry (Rosette Disease-Resistant Thornless Trailing Type)
notes: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, providing a trellis for the trailing canes to climb; Sweetie Pie is a thornless trailing blackberry developed at the USDA-ARS Southern Horticultural Laboratory in Poplarville, Mississippi, bred specifically for resistance to rosette disease (double blossom), a fungal disease that deforms flowers and ruins fruit set and is one of the most serious blackberry problems across the hot, humid South. It produces sweet, well-flavored berries on canes that need training to a trellis since the trailing habit does not stand upright on its own. Because rosette disease spreads through infected plant tissue and is difficult to control with fungicides alone once established, Sweetie Pie's genetic resistance is a real practical advantage for Gulf South growers who have struggled with the disease in other varieties. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and train new primocanes onto the trellis for next year's crop.

Table grapes require a robust trellis capable of supporting 15–30 lbs of fruit per vine; the two-wire Kniffin system or a pergola are common choices. Train a permanent trunk and 2–4 fruiting arms during the first 3 years; thereafter, annual dormant pruning should remove 90% of the previous year's growth, leaving spurs or canes with 2–4 buds each. Thin clusters after fruit set to improve berry size and airflow. Harvest when berries reach full color, the tendrils nearest the cluster have dried, and sugar is confirmed by taste.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Tara is a University of Georgia-released bronze muscadine grown for its consistently high fruit quality — large, uniform, golden-bronze berries with sweet, richly flavored flesh and a relatively tender skin — combined with a self-fertile, productive vine that bears reliably without a separate pollinator variety. It ripens earlier in the season than many bronze muscadines, extending the harvest window when planted alongside later-ripening varieties, and the fruit holds well on the vine without excessive cracking or splitting in humid weather. Widely recommended for both fresh eating and home winemaking, Tara is a strong choice for a Gulf South home muscadine planting, zone 7–9.

Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or elemental sulfur before planting, and mulch well to retain the consistent soil moisture rabbiteye blueberries need for good fruit size. Tara is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release prized for its early ripening and consistently light, sky-blue berries with excellent flavor and a small, dry picking scar that resists splitting and leaking, an important trait for fresh-market and pick-your-own plantings. The bush is vigorous, productive, and well adapted to the sandy, acidic soils of the Gulf South, extending the early end of the rabbiteye blueberry season when planted alongside later-ripening cultivars. Plant with a second compatible rabbiteye variety for good cross-pollination, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush productive.

common_name: Texas Elderberry (Mexican Elder, Blue Elderberry, Tapiro)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil; Texas Elderberry adapts to a wide range of soil types from sandy loam to limestone caliche, and is more drought-tolerant than the Eastern Common Elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) once established. Sambucus mexicana (also listed as S. nigra subsp. canadensis var. mexicana and S. caerulea in western references) is the native elderberry of Texas, the Desert Southwest, Mexico, and Central America, ranging from the western Edwards Plateau of Texas through the Rio Grande Valley. It overlaps geographically with S. canadensis to the east but is adapted to the more alkaline, hotter, drier conditions of central and south Texas and the Mexican highlands. The plant produces large, flat-topped clusters of small, creamy-white flowers (excellent nectar source for native bees and butterflies) followed by clusters of small, blue-black to dark purple berries similar to common elderberry. The berries ripen in late summer–fall and are used to make elderberry wine, juice, jelly, and the traditional folk medicine elderberry syrup for immune support. CAUTION: Raw berries, bark, leaves, and roots contain cyanogenic glycosides — cook berries thoroughly before consumption; do not eat raw.

Set vines against a sturdy trellis or arbor in deep, well-drained soil, spacing plants widely to allow for vigorous cane growth, and prune hard each dormant season to renew fruiting wood. This old California cultivar, also known as Sultanina, produces small, oval, amber-green berries in loose to medium clusters with no seeds and thin, sweet skin. It is the classic grape dried into raisins and is equally popular fresh, but it needs a long, hot growing season to ripen and size up well. Vines are vigorous and productive but more cold-tender than American-type grapes, so winter protection is worthwhile at the cooler edge of its range.

Prime-Ark Freedom is a thornless, primocane-fruiting blackberry that bears large, sweet berries on first-year canes, giving a summer crop that can extend into fall. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and provide a trellis or support for the vigorous canes. Because it fruits on new wood, you can mow floricanes to the ground in late winter for a single heavy late-season crop, or leave them for two harvests. Keep soil evenly moist during fruit development and mulch to suppress weeds. Feed in early spring with a balanced fertilizer.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Thunderbird is a more compact, heavier-fruiting selection of evergreen huckleberry bred for improved garden and orchard performance. Small, glossy, dark evergreen leaves emerge bronze-red on new growth, covering a naturally more compact, dense shrub than the wild species, which produces small, sweet-tart, dark purple berries in late summer and fall prized for pies, jams, and fresh eating, historically an important traditional food for Pacific Coast Indigenous peoples. Native to coastal forests from British Columbia to California, it thrives in the dappled shade and acidic, humus-rich soil of a woodland understory, and its glossy evergreen foliage is also cut and sold commercially in the florist trade. Mulch with pine needles or acidic compost to maintain soil pH, water regularly during establishment and fruit development, and expect the heaviest fruit set with a bit of morning sun.

Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Tifblue is a rabbiteye blueberry developed by the Georgia Experiment Station (Tifton, Georgia) and released in 1955, becoming the most widely planted rabbiteye blueberry variety in the world for most of the 20th century. Though newer varieties (Climax, Premier, Brightwell) have larger or earlier-ripening fruit, Tifblue maintains a loyal following as the definitive late-season rabbiteye: its berries ripen in late July through August in zone 8–9, extending the blueberry season 4–6 weeks past early varieties. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, mildly sweet, with a firm texture that makes them excellent for shipping, freezing, and baking where texture is important. Tifblue is also one of the most important pollinators for other rabbiteye varieties, its abundant, late-season pollen highly compatible with Fry and other non-self-fertile varieties. Plants are vigorous, productive, and cold-hardy for a rabbiteye (surviving 10–15°F without significant damage in established plants). As a historical benchmark variety and reliable late-season producer, Tifblue remains valuable in zone 7–9 blueberry plantings.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark in full sun; Tifblue was the rabbiteye blueberry standard for decades — a large, vigorous, upright shrub with good berries and excellent adaptability. Released by the USDA-ARS Tifton, Georgia station, it produces medium to large, light blue, firm, mild-flavored berries in late June to July, extending the harvest season after early and mid-season varieties have finished. The berries have excellent shelf life due to their firm texture. However, Tifblue's higher chilling requirement (500–600 hours) makes it a less reliable choice in the warmer parts of zone 8–9 where chilling hours may not accumulate sufficiently in mild winters. Best suited to zone 6–8 where more consistent chilling ensures reliable bloom and full fruit set.

Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Titan is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry celebrated for producing exceptionally large berries, among the biggest of any rabbiteye cultivar available, with good firmness and a pleasant, mild sweet-tart flavor that makes for an impressive fresh-eating harvest. The vigorous, upright bushes are productive and ripen mid-to-late in the rabbiteye season, extending the harvest window when paired with earlier cultivars like Alapaha or Premier. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Titan requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Top Hat Blueberry (Dwarf Container Blueberry, Patio Blueberry)
notes: Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.5) or containers filled with peat-based mix; fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or azalea fertilizer) in early spring; Top Hat requires two plants for best pollination and fruit set; berries ripen mid-season (July in zones 5–6) — medium-sized, sweet, and flavorful; does not need pruning for first 4–5 years. Top Hat is the most widely grown dwarf container blueberry and the standard recommendation from extension services for gardeners wanting to grow blueberries in containers, small raised beds, or on patios where the 4–6 foot size of standard highbush varieties is impractical. The variety is a University of Michigan-developed dwarf highbush × lowbush half-high cross that was specifically selected for its unusually compact habit — plants grow only 18–24 inches tall and wide, far smaller than either highbush (4–6 feet) or lowbush (6–12 inches, spreads widely). This intermediate compact size makes Top Hat ideal for large container culture in a way that no other named blueberry variety achieves: large enough to be productive, small enough to manage easily in a 15–20 gallon container, and cold-hardy enough to survive winters outdoors in zones 4–7 on a patio or protected corner. The berries are medium-sized, deep blue, and well-flavored for a half-high type — sweeter and more aromatic than wild lowbush berries and with good quality comparable to standard highbush varieties. The plants are also attractive ornamentally: brilliant red fall foliage makes Top Hat an attractive container plant throughout the growing season. One of the most important blueberry introductions specifically designed for urban and suburban small-space gardening.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in extremely well-drained, lean soil — avoid summer irrigation once established; Toyon (California Holly, Christmas Berry) is a large, handsome, evergreen shrub native to California chaparral and oak woodland, producing spectacular clusters of brilliant red to orange-red berries in November–January — the traditional holiday decoration plant of coastal California and the plant thought to have inspired the name 'Hollywood.' The berries have a slightly bitter, astringent flavor when raw but become edible and pleasant when fully ripe and soft after frost or light cooking; indigenous Californians ate them roasted, fermented into cider, or dried. The white flower clusters in summer attract bees, and the winter berries support mockingbirds, waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds through the season when few other fruiting plants are active. Toyon is one of the most ornamentally rewarding California natives for gardens in the dry western zones and Mediterranean climates; its tolerance of the Gulf Coast requires excellent drainage and restrained irrigation.

'Triple Crown' is a thornless semi-erect blackberry famed for high yields of large, sweet, glossy-black fruit in mid to late summer. Train the vigorous canes onto a sturdy T-trellis and tip the primocanes at about four feet to promote fruiting laterals. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with consistent summer moisture during ripening. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for next year's fruiting wood.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Triumph is a bronze-skinned (white) muscadine grape selected by the University of Georgia for large, sweet, bronze-gold fruits with an exceptionally sweet flavor and low acidity — one of the sweetest muscadine varieties available and a benchmark for fresh-eating quality among bronze muscadines. The large, round fruits (1–1.25 inches) ripen to a deep bronze-gold color and have a thin, tender skin with less of the tough slip-skin character that makes some muscadine varieties less appealing for fresh eating. The sweet, mild, slightly floral flavor with classic muscadine aromatic notes makes Triumph outstanding for fresh eating, and the golden color produces beautiful pale-gold juice and jelly. Triumph is a self-fertile (perfect-flowered) variety that sets crops reliably without a pollinator. In zone 9 the vine is vigorous and productive; provide generous spacing (20+ feet) for the mature vine's spread.

Plant two or more compatible cultivars in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for cross-pollination, since Tundra will not set a worthwhile crop alone. Released by the University of Saskatchewan breeding program as a mid-to-late-season pollinizer partner for Borealis, Tundra bears firm, mild-flavored, elongated blue berries that hold their shape well and are less prone to splitting after rain than some earlier cultivars, making them good for both fresh eating and processing. The upright, vigorous bush is easy to hand-harvest and tends to crop reliably once established. Tundra is extremely cold-hardy, surviving winter lows well below -40F, but like all haskaps it performs poorly in hot, humid summer regions and is not recommended for the Gulf South. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood for the first several years, then begin renewal pruning of the oldest canes to keep production high.

Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Tupy is a vigorous, thorny, erect blackberry developed by the Brazilian agricultural research agency EMBRAPA from Arkansas breeding lines, and it has become one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in warm-climate regions of Latin America because of its exceptional heat tolerance and productivity under conditions too warm for many U.S.-bred varieties. Berries are large, glossy black, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening early in the season with a long harvest window and heavy yields. Because canes are thorny, plan for careful pruning and picking; remove fruited floricanes after harvest and tie in 4-6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for the following year. Tupy tolerates the intense heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast better than many thornless northern-bred varieties, making it a strong choice for zone 9-10 growers.

Plant in strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0), well-drained and sandy or peaty, in full sun to light shade; velvetleaf blueberry is a low, colony-forming native shrub of the boreal forest and northern Great Lakes and New England barrens, distinguished from the closely related lowbush blueberry by the fine, dense, velvety hairs covering its young twigs and the undersides of its light blue-green leaves — a texture you can feel by running a leaf between your fingers. It spreads by shallow rhizomes into loose colonies and, like other lowbush blueberries, is fire-adapted, resprouting vigorously from its roots after burning or hard mowing; commercial growers of Maine's wild blueberry barrens manage mixed stands of this species and Vaccinium angustifolium on a two-year burn-and-harvest cycle for the same reason. The small, powder-blue, sweet berries ripen in mid- to late summer and are borne most heavily on wood that grew the previous year, so avoid heavy pruning right before a harvest season. Foliage turns brilliant scarlet-red in fall. Plant at least two genetically distinct plants for reliable cross-pollination and best fruit set. This is strictly a cold-climate plant, thriving where winters are long and cold; it struggles and rarely fruits well south of its native range.

common_name: Venus Grape (Seedless Blue University of Arkansas Table Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, with good airflow through the canopy to help manage humidity-related fungal disease. Venus was bred by the University of Arkansas grape breeding program and produces genuinely seedless, blue-black berries with a slip-skin texture and sweet, richly fruity flavor reminiscent of Concord grapes, on a vine with good resistance to the common grape diseases that plague less resilient cultivars in humid climates. Its early to midseason ripening and reliable disease tolerance have made it a popular home-garden choice for gardeners wanting a seedless table grape without a heavy spray program. Prune hard each winter to renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation.

Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Vernon is a mid-season rabbiteye blueberry bred for the Gulf South, producing an upright, vigorous, productive bush with firm, well-flavored, medium-to-large berries that hold well on the bush without excessive splitting in humid weather. It fills the harvest gap between early cultivars like Climax and later ones like Tifblue or Ochlockonee, giving home orchards a steadier, more extended supply of fresh fruit. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid high-nitrogen feeding late in the season, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production.

Plant container stock in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wax myrtle is highly adaptable and tolerates poor, sandy, wet, or salty soils and thrives in coastal and inland settings alike. Myrica cerifera is a fast-growing, aromatic, nitrogen-fixing native evergreen shrub or small tree of the Southeast, valued for its densely branched form that provides excellent year-round cover, nesting habitat, and foraging sites for wildlife; the distinctive blue-gray, waxy-coated berries produced in dense clusters along the stems attract over 40 bird species including yellow-rumped warblers, tree swallows, and bluebirds. Plant in groupings to form evergreen screens or wildlife hedgerows, and allow the plant to grow to its natural multi-stemmed form for maximum habitat value.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Welder is a heritage Texas muscadine selection, originally found growing wild along the Texas Gulf Coast, long valued by home growers for its vigorous, reliably productive vines and dark bronze-to-purple berries with the strong, musky-sweet, classic muscadine flavor favored for fresh eating, jelly, and homemade wine. Its Gulf Coast origins give it excellent heat and humidity tolerance, and it has a long track record of thriving with minimal care in Texas and Louisiana home gardens where more refined modern cultivars can sometimes struggle. Welder is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinizer, though yields benefit from having other muscadine vines nearby. Like other muscadines, it shows strong natural resistance to Pierce's disease and the fungal pressures that make bunch grapes difficult in the humid South. Harvest as berries darken fully and detach easily from the stem with gentle pressure, and train the vigorous vine to a sturdy two-wire trellis with annual winter pruning.

common_name: Wentworth American Highbush Cranberry (Early-Ripening Fruit Selection)
notes: Set out a bare-root or container-grown Wentworth shrub in early spring into moist, well-drained soil, choosing a site with a half-day of shade if the location has hot afternoon sun, since this selection tolerates woodland-edge conditions better than many fruiting shrubs. Wentworth was selected for producing earlier-ripening, larger, better-flavored clusters of tart red berries than typical seedling highbush cranberries, though a second unrelated seedling nearby improves pollination and fruit set. The berries soften and mellow after a frost and cook down into a bright, tart preserve or sauce reminiscent of true cranberry, a useful substitute in regions where cranberry bogs are not practical. Its tolerance of part shade and reliable fruit set make Wentworth a good choice for a hedgerow or forest-garden edge planting where full sun is not available all day.

Plant dormant bushes in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, in full sun or light shade, and prune to an open vase shape each winter to ease harvesting among the thorny stems. A very old English cultivar dating to the mid-1800s, Whinham's Industry remains popular for its notable tolerance of poor, heavy, or shaded conditions where many other gooseberries struggle, along with strong resistance to American gooseberry mildew. Its medium-to-large, hairy-skinned berries ripen from green to a deep dusky red with a rich, sweet-tart flavor good for both dessert use and cooking. The vigorous, spreading habit and dependable heavy cropping have kept it a garden favorite for over a century.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, average to poor soil; Grewia bicolor is highly drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry and semi-arid conditions — once established it requires little or no supplemental water in warm arid and semi-arid climates. Grewia bicolor (White Cross Berry or Crossberry) is a thorny, much-branched shrub or small tree native to the dry, open savannas, bushveld, and semi-arid woodland of sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal east through Ethiopia and south through East Africa to South Africa and Mozambique — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important shrubs of African savanna ecosystems. The distinctive bicolor leaves — deep green and glossy above, densely silver-white hairy and felted beneath — give the plant a shimmering two-tone appearance in the breeze. Small, 5-petaled, yellow or cream star-shaped flowers are borne prolifically from the leaf axils in summer, followed by round to oblong, 2–4-lobed berries — ripening from green through reddish-orange to dark brown or black — that are sweet-mucilaginous, edible raw or dried, and important bush food across the plant's range. The berries are browsed by elephants, giraffes, and many antelope species, and are eaten by indigenous peoples dried as a sweetener or fermented into beer. The roots and bark carry extensive traditional medicinal uses across sub-Saharan Africa for fevers, diarrhea, and sexually transmitted infections. An excellent drought-tolerant, wildlife-attracting shrub for hot, dry, sunny gardens in zone 8–11.

White currant is a yellow-fruited mutation of red currant sharing identical cultivation requirements: it fruits most heavily on spurs of two-year-old and older wood. The translucent, ivory-white berries are sweeter and milder than red currants and are prized for elegant fresh-eating and jellies. Prune each late winter to maintain 8–12 canes of mixed ages, removing canes older than 5 years. Harvest entire strigs when berries have turned fully translucent white-golden and taste sweet; check local Ribes restrictions before purchasing.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to average soil; Celtis africana is drought tolerant once established, growing well in a wide range of soils including clay, rocky, and alkaline soils typical of the South African highveld and bushveld — water regularly only in the first year of establishment. Celtis africana (White Stinkwood, Witstinkhout) is a large, graceful, fast-growing deciduous to semi-evergreen tree native to the forests, river margins, and bush-margins of South Africa (particularly the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, and Mpumalanga) and extending north through East Africa. The English common name 'stinkwood' refers to the smell of freshly cut wood — the dried wood does not smell strongly and is actually a fine-grained, attractive timber used for furniture and flooring in South Africa (though far less valuable than the true 'Black Stinkwood,' Ocotea bullata). Celtis africana is one of South Africa's most popular garden shade trees: fast-growing, with an elegant, slightly weeping branch structure, fine-textured, lime-green foliage that provides deep shade, and outstanding wildlife value — the small, round, yellow-orange to red-black fruits are eagerly eaten by many fruit-eating birds including barbets, mousebirds, bulbuls, and starlings. The tree supports many butterfly species and is larval host plant for the Charaxes butterfly group.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil — willow-leaved sea buckthorn tolerates poor, gravelly, or stony ground and is highly drought-tolerant once established, making it a superb windbreak tree for cold, exposed sites. Cold-stratify seeds for 30–60 days before sowing in early spring, or sow fresh seed in fall for natural stratification. Because the species is dioecious, include at least one male tree for every five to six female trees to ensure reliable pollination and fruit set; the dense orange berry clusters ripen in late summer to autumn and are extraordinarily rich in vitamin C, carotenoids, and omega-7 fatty acids. Larger and more tree-like than common sea buckthorn (H. rhamnoides), it can reach 30 feet, providing significant shade and windbreak value while producing a heavy fruit crop.

Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Windsor is a southern highbush blueberry requiring 500–600 chill hours — more than the ultra-low-chill varieties like Flordablue and Biloxi, but still significantly less than northern varieties that require 800–1,200 hours. This intermediate chill requirement makes Windsor suitable for zone 9a where winters typically provide 500–700 chill hours but unsuitable for the warmer zone 9b areas. The advantage of Windsor's higher chill requirement is higher fruit quality — the berries are larger, firmer, darker, and more flavorful than very-low-chill varieties, with the rich, complex blueberry flavor that intensifies with more winter dormancy. Windsor was developed to provide the best possible fruit quality while still meeting the reduced chill requirements of the upper Gulf Coast. The midseason ripening (May–June in zone 9) follows the earliest varieties and provides an extended blueberry harvest season when planted alongside Biloxi or Flordablue.

Wine grapes thrive in lean, well-drained soils with a pH of 5.5–6.5 and perform best on slopes with excellent air circulation to reduce disease pressure. Establish a vertical shoot positioning (VSP) trellis with catch wires at 4 and 5 ft above the cordon wire. Rigorous dormant pruning — leaving only 30–60 buds per vine depending on vigor — is essential for fruit quality. Harvest timing is cultivar- and use-specific; measure Brix (sugar) with a refractometer and monitor seed color and berry flavor.

common_name: Winterthur Viburnum (Compact Possumhaw with Multi-Season Berry Color)
notes: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites, including rain gardens and pond margins. Winterthur is a compact selection of native possumhaw viburnum producing showy clusters of berries that pass through a striking sequence of pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen in late summer and fall, often displaying several colors on the same cluster at once, in addition to attractive burgundy-red fall foliage. Its smaller stature compared to the species fits typical residential borders better, and planting a second unrelated clone nearby improves the reliability and abundance of berry set.

common_name: Womack Blackberry (Texas A&M Heat-Tolerant Thorny Blackberry)
notes: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Womack is an erect, thorny blackberry released from the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program and bred specifically to withstand the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Texas and the western Gulf South. It produces medium to large, firm, sweet-tart berries with good flavor and holds up well to summer heat that causes softer varieties to decline in quality. As an older Texas A&M release, it is a dependable, disease-tolerant option where more modern thornless varieties struggle with heat stress. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select vigorous new primocanes to tie in for next year's crop; wear heavy gloves when working the thorny canes.

common_name: Woodard Rabbiteye Blueberry (Classic Large-Berried Southern Blueberry)
notes: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. One of the older, longer-established rabbiteye blueberry cultivars, Woodard is valued for its unusually large, soft-textured, mild-flavored berries that ripen in early-to-mid season, a bit ahead of many later rabbiteye types. The bushes are moderately vigorous and productive, though the soft fruit texture makes it better suited to fresh home use and processing than commercial shipping. Keep soil consistently moist through bloom and fruit development, and mulch well to conserve moisture and maintain the acidic soil conditions blueberries require.

The worcesterberry is a North American species of gooseberry (Ribes divaricatum) sometimes grown as a productive alternative to European gooseberries because it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and American gooseberry mildew. The small, dark purple-black berries resemble currants more than typical gooseberries and ripen in midsummer with a tart, rich flavor excellent for jams and pies. Prune to an open-vase structure each late winter, keeping 8–10 canes of mixed ages. Verify state restrictions on Ribes planting before ordering, as some states still restrict the genus.

common_name: A Shropshire Lad Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1996 and named for the A. E. Housman poetry collection, A Shropshire Lad carries large, softly cupped, warm peachy-pink blooms with a light, fruity fragrance, on long, arching canes that can reach 8-10 feet or more when trained as a climber, or be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. Its vigor and long, flexible canes make it a favorite for growing over an arch or pergola, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Abraham Darby Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, compost-enriched soil and feed regularly through the growing season to support this heavy-blooming rose's vigorous repeat flowering. Bred by David Austin and named for the ironworks pioneer, Abraham Darby was introduced in 1985 and bears very large, deeply cupped blooms that open in warm blends of apricot, peach, and pink with a rich, fruity fragrance often compared to ripe peaches. Its vigorous, somewhat arching growth habit and strong disease resistance in humid conditions make it a dependable performer across the Gulf South, where it is frequently grown as a large shrub in a mixed border or trained up a pillar or low wall for extra height. Deadhead spent blooms through the season and prune hard in late winter to keep the shrub shapely and productive.

scientific_name: Ulmus davidiana var. japonica × Ulmus wilsoniana 'Morton'
common_name: Accolade Elm (Vigorous Disease-Resistant Hybrid Shade Tree)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where the tree quickly develops a dense, vase-to-rounded canopy of glossy, dark green foliage. Accolade is a hybrid of two Asian elm species introduced by the Morton Arboretum, prized for combining rapid growth, strong urban tolerance, and outstanding resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle, two of the biggest threats to elms in cultivation. Unlike American elm selections it does not aim to replicate the classic broad vase silhouette exactly, instead forming a somewhat more upright, uniform shade tree well suited to streets, parking areas, and residential landscapes where a fast-growing, trouble-free canopy tree is wanted. It tolerates heat, drought once established, and a range of soil types, and needs only routine formative pruning in its early years to develop strong branch structure.

common_name: Ace of Hearts Redbud (Compact Round-Leaf Dwarf Redbud)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where its small mature size and dense canopy can be appreciated up close. Ace of Hearts is a dwarf, compact selection of eastern redbud, reaching roughly half the size of the species, with small, glossy, heart-shaped leaves packed tightly along the branches and a rounded, tidy habit that needs little pruning to stay in bounds. Like other redbuds it flowers on bare wood in early spring with a dense flush of small rosy-pink pea-like blooms before the leaves emerge, followed by clean, deep-green summer foliage that holds its glossy texture better in heat than the species form. Its small stature makes it well suited to foundation plantings, patios, and smaller residential landscapes where a full-sized redbud would quickly outgrow the space.

common_name: Acoma Crape Myrtle (Weeping White Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Acoma is a distinctive weeping, semi-dwarf National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle with pure white flower clusters produced from summer into fall on gracefully arching branches, a growth habit unusual among crape myrtles that gives it strong specimen and accent value. Like its sibling cultivars it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and develops attractive mottled, exfoliating bark with maturity. Its spreading, weeping form makes it well suited as a small specimen tree, container planting, or bank cover where the arching branches can be shown off. Remove root suckers and prune only lightly to shape rather than heavily topping the plant.

common_name: Admiral Semmes Azalea (Golden-Orange Southern Heritage Native Azalea)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. Admiral Semmes is a long-cultivated Southern heritage selection of native azalea grown for its fragrant, golden-orange flowers that open in a heavy spring flush on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed shrub well adapted to Deep South heat and humidity. As with other native deciduous azaleas, its strong fragrance and heat tolerance have kept it in cultivation among Southern native-plant collectors even as flashier Asian evergreen azalea hybrids have dominated the broader nursery trade. Site it at a woodland edge or beneath high pine or hardwood canopy, and keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.

common_name: Adolphe Audusson Camellia (Deep Red Camellia japonica)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Adolphe Audusson is a classic, vigorous Camellia japonica cultivar valued for one of the deepest, richest red flower colors available in japonica camellias — a vivid blood-red to deep crimson-red in large, semi-double flowers with a prominent central cluster of golden-yellow stamens that creates a striking color contrast. The bold, saturated red flower color and large flower size make it one of the most eye-catching camellia selections for winter color in the shaded garden. Introduced in France in 1877 and still widely grown, Adolphe Audusson is a vigorous grower that develops into a large shrub or small tree in zone 9 conditions, with upright growth to 7–14 feet and dense, dark-green, glossy evergreen foliage. It blooms in mid-season (December through February in zone 9), with peak bloom typically in January. The bold red flower color provides exceptional cut-flower value — the flowers last well in arrangements. 'Adolphe Audusson Variegated' is a sport with red flowers marked with white streaks and spots; 'Adolphe Audusson Special' has darker red, more formal double flowers. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil; apply sulfur-based acidifying fertilizer if soil pH drifts above 6.5.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil of average fertility in full sun to partial shade, watering regularly the first year and then only occasionally once roots are established, since this East African conifer handles heat and drought far better than most needled evergreens. Fine, narrow, willowy leaves give the tree a soft, weeping texture unlike the stiff scale foliage of junipers and cypresses commonly used for the same purposes, and it responds well to shearing, which makes it a popular clipped hedge, screen, or espalier as well as an unclipped specimen tree in mild climates. It is widely planted as a street and parking-lot tree in California and the Southwest for its tolerance of reflected heat, compacted soil, and irregular irrigation, but is damaged by hard freezes and is only reliable outdoors in nearly frost-free zones.

Plant in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 10–12; African mahogany is a West African timber and shade tree in the Meliaceae family (same family as American mahogany), widely planted in tropical and subtropical regions for shade and timber. The pinnate compound leaves create a dense canopy that provides excellent shade. The reddish-brown wood is harder than West Indian mahogany but less prized in fine furniture; it is extensively used in flooring, general construction, and plywood production in Africa. In south Florida, African mahogany is widely planted as a fast-growing street and shade tree, developing a large, spreading crown that provides dense summer shade. More salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant than American mahogany and faster-growing, making it practical for large-scale urban tree planting in zone 10 coastal Florida.

common_name: African Milk Tree (Cathedral Cactus, Friendship Cactus)
notes: Grow in bright light with some direct sun, in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only after the soil has dried out. African milk tree is a fast-growing, cactus-like succulent shrub from Central Africa with tall, upright, triangular, ridged stems edged in small paired thorns and tiny leaves along the ridges; the widely sold 'Rubra' form has deep burgundy-red coloring that intensifies in strong light. Stems branch readily from the base and from pruning cuts, quickly producing a dense, candelabra-like clump that can eventually reach several feet tall indoors. Handle only with gloves and eye protection, since like other Euphorbias it exudes a milky latex sap when cut that is a potent skin and eye irritant and toxic if ingested; keep well away from children and pets. Repot every couple of years into fresh, fast-draining mix and prune to control height, using the resulting cuttings to propagate new plants after a callusing period.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil; Pterocarpus erinaceus is a drought-adapted savanna tree that requires excellent drainage and tolerates seasonal dry periods — avoid waterlogged sites and heavy clay soils. Pterocarpus erinaceus (African Rosewood, Vène, or Kosso) is a large, deciduous legume tree native to the open savanna, guinea woodland, and dry forest zones of West Africa from Senegal east through the Sudan-Sahel zone to Ethiopia, a member of the Fabaceae family and one of the continent's most economically significant and critically over-exploited timber trees. The heartwood is dense, durable, deep reddish-brown to rose-red with interlocked grain — superficially resembling Asian rosewoods (Dalbergia spp.) — and has been the subject of massive illegal logging and export particularly to China and East Asia in the 21st century for furniture manufacture, resulting in international CITES trade regulation. Before logging, trees produce spectacular, dense, terminal clusters of deep-yellow pea-family flowers in the dry season on leafless branches. The tree is a critical component of the West African parkland agroforestry system where it is retained in farmers' fields for shade, nitrogen fixation, fodder, and traditional medicine (the red-staining bark gum is used medicinally across West Africa). A valuable shade and nitrogen-fixing tree for tropical agroforestry systems where large specimens can be grown sustainably.

common_name: African Trumpet Tree (Magnificent Fernandoa, Yellow African Trumpet)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — African Trumpet Tree is drought-tolerant once established and grows vigorously in the well-drained, sandy soils of tropical coastal landscapes. Fernandoa magnifica is a medium-sized, semi-deciduous flowering tree from eastern tropical Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zimbabwe) in the Bignoniaceae family, belonging to the same remarkable family that gave horticulture Jacaranda, Tabebuia, Catalpa, and Bignonia. The tree produces large, pinnately compound leaves and bears its flowers in massive, terminal, many-flowered panicles at the tips of the branches: each individual flower is a large (2–3 inch), funnel to broadly trumpet-shaped bloom in vivid yellow-orange to orange, with five spreading, frilled petal lobes and a slightly darker orange interior. When a Fernandoa magnifica flowers — typically in spring, often producing the display on leafless or partially leafless branches — the sheer density and size of the flower clusters is extraordinary, covering the branch tips in orange-yellow bloom. The species is a significant ornamental tree in tropical East African gardens and in tropical botanical collections worldwide, considered one of the finest flowering trees of the African continent in terms of bloom impact. Underused in zone 10-11 US tropical landscapes compared to its merit.

Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; African tulip tree (fountain tree, fireball) is a large, fast-growing West African tropical tree of the bignonia family (Bignoniaceae) that produces one of the most spectacular and instantly recognizable flower displays of any tropical tree — large, upright, cup-shaped, terminal clusters of 10–20 large, flared, bright scarlet-orange to crimson flowers with yellow-edged petals are produced at the branch tips year-round in zone 10–12 tropical climates, creating a constant flaming-red display from a distance. The flower buds hold water — a trait used by children in the native range who squeeze the buds to squirt water — and are visited by sunbirds and bats as pollinators. The tree grows rapidly to 40–50 feet with a dense, spreading canopy, making it an effective but large shade tree. It has become invasive in Hawaii, Pacific island nations, and parts of tropical Florida, where it spreads aggressively by wind-borne seeds into disturbed forest areas — check local regulations before planting.

common_name: Aimee Gardenia (Very Large Flower Exhibition Gardenia from Louisiana)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Aimee (also known as 'Aimee Yoshiba') is a Louisiana-associated gardenia cultivar producing some of the largest flowers of any commonly grown Gardenia jasminoides — individual blooms reaching 4–5 inches across with many rows of creamy white, wavy, overlapping petals that create a full, formal double flower of extraordinary refinement. The flowers open creamy white and age to a warm ivory-yellow, with the same intense, classic gardenia fragrance that has made gardenias the most beloved fragrant landscape shrub in the American South. 'Aimee' grows as a vigorous, upright-spreading shrub to 5–7 feet in typical Gulf South gardens, larger and more open in habit than compact cultivars like 'Radicans' or 'Chuck Hayes'. The spring bloom (April–June) is the primary season, often with sporadic rebloom in fall if conditions are favorable. As with all Gardenia jasminoides, 'Aimee' requires strongly acidic soil for healthy growth — iron chlorosis (yellowing leaves with green veins) is the primary symptom of insufficient acidity, corrected with sulfur soil acidification and acid-forming fertilizers. The large flower size and outstanding fragrance make 'Aimee' the preferred gardenia for cut flower use, where a single bloom can fragrance a room for several days.

Alabama azalea is a rare native deciduous azalea endemic to the limestone cedar glades and sandy, acidic woodlands of central Alabama and adjacent states — one of the most sweetly fragrant of all native azaleas, its white to creamy-white flowers with yellow-orange blotches emit a delicate, spicy-sweet fragrance reminiscent of lemony honey that fills the woodland in spring. It blooms in April after the piedmont azalea but before leaves emerge, producing large, showy clusters of flowers at a time when the garden's background is still relatively bare. Alabama azalea is adapted to the warm, humid climate of the upper Gulf Coastal Plain, tolerating zone 9 summers better than most native azaleas of eastern North America — an important advantage for Gulf Coast native gardens where heat and humidity defeat many Rhododendron species. In acidic woodland gardens and under tall pines, plant in combination with native groundcovers like Carex, Pachysandra procumbens, and native ferns for an authentic Alabama woodland garden.

Alabama Snow-Wreath is one of the rarest native shrubs in North America, a monotypic genus (the only species in its genus) restricted in the wild to a handful of limestone bluffs and rocky river slopes in northwestern Alabama and a very few widely scattered natural populations in other southeastern states. In April and May it produces a cloud of unusual, feathery, white, petal-less flowers — the 'petals' are entirely absent, and the display comes entirely from numerous long white stamens — giving the shrub an airy, ethereal appearance reminiscent of its common name. An adaptable plant in cultivation that grows well in partial shade in a wide range of soils from dry and rocky to moderately moist, Alabama Snow-Wreath is easy to propagate from cuttings and is increasingly available from specialty native plant nurseries. Never collect from wild populations — purchase only from nurseries that propagate their own plants from cultivated stock.

Plant along a fence, arbor, or trellis in full sun to light shade in ordinary garden soil, giving the vigorous vine plenty of vertical room to climb by tendril. This pure-white-flowered selection of the native maypop produces the same intricate, fringed blossoms as the wild form but without the usual purple banding, and still serves as the essential host plant for gulf fritillary and zebra longwing caterpillars. Bees and other pollinators visit the large flowers freely, and edible yellow-green fruit follows in late summer. Once established it spreads by root suckers and tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought better than almost any other flowering vine on the Gulf Coast.

common_name: Alba Plena Camellia (White Formal Double Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Alba Plena is one of the oldest and most historically significant Camellia japonica cultivars in cultivation — an early-season white camellia with perfectly formed, large, formal double flowers in pure white with tightly spiraled, overlapping petals arranged in a geometrically precise rosette pattern of extraordinary elegance. The pure white flowers are exceptional for formal garden compositions, white-themed borders, and cut-flower use — few winter-blooming plants can rival the pristine beauty of fully open Alba Plena flowers. In zone 9, it blooms from November through January, making it one of the earliest reliable winter blooms in the Southern garden. The vigorous, upright growth to 5–12 feet produces dense, glossy dark-green foliage that provides excellent year-round screening and foundation value. Alba Plena was introduced to Western cultivation from China in 1792 and has been grown in Southern American gardens since the early nineteenth century — one of the most historically long-cultivated garden plants in the South. Early bloom season means open flowers may occasionally be damaged by hard frosts in zone 9 winters; siting under the canopy of overhead trees provides some protection. Maintain acidic soil pH with periodic applications of acidic fertilizer and deep organic mulch.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Alba is the classic white-flowered form of eastern redbud, a naturally occurring color break from the typical rosy-pink to lavender bloom of the wild species, covering bare branches in clean white pea-family flowers in early spring before the heart-shaped green leaves emerge. It provides a softer, more understated spring display than pink or magenta redbud cultivars and pairs especially well with purple-leafed selections like Forest Pansy planted nearby for contrast. Growth habit, size, and cultural needs match the straight species — a small, adaptable native tree well suited to the dappled light of a woodland edge or understory planting, tolerating partial shade better than many flowering trees, though bloom is most abundant with several hours of direct sun. As with all redbuds, plant in well-drained soil, since the roots are prone to rot in heavy, wet sites, and avoid disturbing the root system once established, since redbud transplants best when young and container-grown.

Plant in partial shade in reliably moist to boggy soil, mimicking its natural habitat along streambanks and in swampy woods. Dig a hole at least twice the width of the root ball and amend heavy clay with organic matter to improve moisture retention. Water deeply and consistently through the first two growing seasons to establish a strong root system. Berries attract birds in fall; plant at least one male and one female for fruit set.

Plant on a dry, rocky, well-drained slope or bank in full sun; alderleaf mountain mahogany is a tough, long-lived Rocky Mountain and Intermountain West foothill shrub with small, wedge-shaped, deeply veined leaves resembling alder foliage, evergreen to semi-evergreen depending on winter severity. Small, inconspicuous flowers in spring give way to the plant's real ornamental feature: clusters of feathery, silvery, corkscrew-tailed seed plumes that catch afternoon light through summer and fall, giving the whole shrub a soft, smoky appearance from a distance. Extremely drought and cold tolerant once its deep root system is established, it is browsed by deer and elk in the wild and provides valuable winter forage and cover for wildlife. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood, and the shrub is essentially maintenance-free in the lean, rocky soils it prefers.

common_name: Alexandrina Magnolia (Classic Large Pink-Purple Saucer Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Alexandrina is one of the oldest and most widely planted saucer magnolia cultivars, producing large, goblet-shaped flowers in rich rose-purple on the outside and creamy white within, opening on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. Its early bloom timing gives an unmistakable, showy spring display but also leaves the flowers vulnerable to browning from a late hard freeze, a common risk for early-flowering saucer magnolias, so siting away from low frost pockets helps. The tree grows into a broad, multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub with minimal pruning needs beyond removing dead or crossing wood, and established trees are otherwise low-maintenance and long-lived landscape specimens.

common_name: Algerian Ivy (Canary Island Ivy, Canariensis Ivy)
notes: Plant cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Algerian ivy is the superior ivy for Gulf Coast zone 7–10 gardens — larger-leaved, more heat tolerant, and more drought tolerant than English ivy, making it better suited to the summer conditions of the Gulf South. The leaves are 3–8 inches across, rich glossy green (sometimes with a reddish tint in winter), and distinctly larger than the familiar English ivy. The variegated form 'Gloire de Marengo' has silvery gray-green leaves with creamy white margins and is one of the most beautiful of all shade vines. Like English ivy it can climb by aerial roots and spreads vigorously as a groundcover, but has a less aggressive spreading habit than English ivy and is less likely to invade natural areas. Still, plant with care and keep away from forest edges.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alice oakleaf hydrangea is an outstanding cultivar selected and named for Alice Recknagel Ireys, a distinguished American landscape architect, by Michael Dirr at the University of Georgia — the plant's finest characteristics reflecting the horticultural standards of its namesake. Alice produces exceptionally large, upright panicle flower clusters — sometimes reaching 14 inches long — that are among the biggest of any oakleaf hydrangea cultivar, creating a spectacular mid-May to June display in zone 9 gardens. The individual flowers open pure white and age gradually to a beautiful soft rose-pink, creating clusters that simultaneously show white and pink tones. The foliage is large, bold, and deeply lobed with the characteristic oak-leaf silhouette, turning rich burgundy-red in autumn in zone 9. Alice grows vigorously to 6–10 feet tall and equally wide, making it an outstanding large-scale specimen, naturalizing under trees, or massing for a bold woodland effect. The peeling cinnamon-brown bark is ornamental in winter. Alice received the Award of Garden Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society, confirming its outstanding ornamental performance.

common_name: Alice du Pont Mandevilla (Classic Vigorous Pink Mandevilla)
notes: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a trellis, arbor, or other support able to accommodate a vigorous twining vine. Alice du Pont is a long-established classic mandevilla cultivar, valued for producing large, glossy, deep green leaves and abundant clear pink, trumpet-shaped flowers continuously from late spring through fall, with a naturally vigorous, fast-climbing habit compared to some of the more compact modern mandevilla series. It thrives in the heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer, needing only regular water and monthly fertilizing during active growth. In zone 9a it typically dies back after a hard freeze but often regrows from the roots in a mild winter; in colder zones it is best grown as a container plant brought indoors or treated as an annual.

common_name: All Summer Beauty Hydrangea (Reliable Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun and drying wind. All Summer Beauty is an older bigleaf hydrangea cultivar valued for setting flower buds reliably on new wood, so it continues to bloom through summer even in years when a late freeze damages old stems and buds, a problem that leaves many other mopheads bloomless for a season. Its large, rounded mophead flower clusters shift from blue to pink depending on soil pH, blue in acidic soil and pink in more alkaline soil, and can be nudged toward blue with aluminum sulfate or toward pink with garden lime. Water deeply during dry spells, since bigleaf hydrangea wilts readily in heat, and prune only lightly right after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

common_name: Allee Lacebark Elm (Texas A&M Drought-Tolerant Shade Tree)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Allee is a lacebark elm cultivar selected and introduced by Texas A&M University for its uniform, vase-shaped growth habit, resembling the classic silhouette of American elm without the vulnerability to Dutch elm disease that devastated that species.
