Its most striking feature is the beautifully mottled, exfoliating bark in patches of gray, green, orange, and brown that develops as the tree matures, giving significant year-round ornamental interest even in winter. It is highly tolerant of heat, drought, and the alkaline, compacted soils common in urban and suburban Southern landscapes, requiring only routine structural pruning while young to establish strong branch angles for a long-lived, storm-resistant shade tree.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil sited with some relief from the hottest afternoon sun, which helps the variegated foliage hold its pattern instead of scorching at the leaf margins. Alley Cat is a variegated redbud selection bearing heart-shaped leaves heavily splashed and streaked in cream and white over green, giving the canopy a bright, almost frosted look through the growing season, and it produces the species' typical rosy-pink, pea-like flowers on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows as a smaller, slower tree than the straight species, staying more compact and tidy, which suits it well to a specimen spot in a shaded courtyard or woodland-edge planting where the bright foliage can be appreciated up close. Plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites, and prune only to remove dead, crossing, or reverted all-green branches, since variegated shoots can occasionally revert and should be cut out to keep the tree true to type.

Plant this cold-hardy species with its roots cool and shaded, ideally at the base of a low fence, wall, or open shrub for the wiry stems to scramble through. It is among the earliest clematis to bloom, opening nodding, lantern-shaped blue-purple to pink flowers on bare stems before most other vines have leafed out, followed by fluffy seed heads. Since it flowers on the previous year's growth, prune only lightly right after flowering to remove dead wood, never cutting it back hard. Its small scale and dainty flowers suit rock gardens, low trellises, or mixed borders where a larger clematis would be too much.

Always Summer is a reblooming gardenia bred to flower repeatedly from late spring well into fall rather than concentrating bloom into one or two flushes, giving a much longer season of the classic waxy white, intensely fragrant flowers than older gardenia cultivars provide. It holds a compact, rounded, well-branched habit with glossy dark-green foliage and, like other modern reblooming gardenias, benefits from regular feeding with an acid-forming fertilizer through the growing season to fuel the repeated flower flushes. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, strongly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and watch for the yellowing (chlorotic) foliage that signals insufficiently acidic soil, correcting with sulfur or an acidifying fertilizer as needed.

common_name: Amber Jubilee Ninebark (Multicolor Orange-Gold-Red Foliage Ninebark)
notes: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; ninebark is an exceptionally tough native shrub tolerating clay, poor soil, and drought once established. Amber Jubilee stands apart from the many purple- and burgundy-leaved ninebark cultivars by cycling through a distinct multicolor foliage display: new growth emerges bright orange-gold, matures through yellow-green, and finishes deep burgundy-red by fall, often showing several of these colors on the same plant at once. Its vigorous, upright habit and season-long shifting color make it a strong focal point in a mixed shrub border. Exfoliating bark on older stems adds winter texture; prune out the oldest stems at the base every 2–3 years to keep growth vigorous and colorful.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; American basswood is one of the most important honey trees in North America — when the intensely fragrant cream-yellow flowers open in June and July, beekeepers consider it the single most important nectar flow of the year, producing linden honey renowned for its delicate, flowery flavor. The fragrance of a flowering basswood in a neighborhood can be detected at a distance of several blocks. The large, heart-shaped leaves, distinctive bract-winged fruiting clusters, and tall, straight trunk make it a notable landscape specimen. Young leaves are edible in spring salads; the inner bark (bast) is one of the best natural fibers for cordage in North America and was extensively used by Native Americans. Tolerates partial shade well, making it suitable for understory planting in very large gardens.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil; American beautyberry tolerates a wide range of soil types and performs well in woodland edges, shade gardens, and naturalistic borders. Callicarpa americana is a deciduous native shrub of the southeastern United States and one of the most visually arresting plants in the native landscape — in late summer and fall it is covered in tight, globe-shaped clusters of vivid magenta to violet-purple berries arranged in rings directly along the arching stems, creating a spectacle unlike any other shrub. The berries persist well after leaf drop and provide outstanding late-season food for mockingbirds, robins, catbirds, and other wildlife. Prune hard in late winter (to within 6–12 inches of the ground) to encourage vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production, as berries form on new wood; without pruning the shrub can become leggy over time.

Plant in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; American bittersweet is a native deciduous twining vine prized for its spectacular fall and winter fruit display — clusters of small, round capsules that split open in autumn to reveal brilliant orange-red arils (fleshy seed coverings), creating a vivid orange-and-red effect that persists on the vine through winter and is widely used in dried arrangements and holiday decoration. The small, greenish-yellow flowers in early summer are inconspicuous but attract small native bees. The fruit is a critical winter food source for many songbirds including bluebirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and mockingbirds, which eat the arils while dispersing the seeds. American bittersweet is increasingly rare in wild populations because Oriental bittersweet (C. orbiculatus), an invasive Asian relative, has displaced it across much of the East — purchase only from reputable native plant nurseries and verify the species. Female plants require a nearby male for fruit set. An outstanding native vine for trellises, fences, and naturalistic settings where its wildlife value can be fully expressed.

American Bladdernut is a large, multi-stemmed native shrub, native to moist, rich deciduous forest understories, streambanks, and floodplain edges throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to Kansas, forming thickets in the shade of oaks, maples, and ashes where few other ornamental shrubs survive. In April and May it produces drooping clusters of small, white, bell-shaped flowers attractive to native bees; these are followed in summer by the plant's most distinctive feature — inflated, papery, three-chambered seed pods resembling small green Chinese lanterns that persist into fall and rattle audibly in the breeze, turning tan and remaining decorative into winter. The opposite, trifoliate leaves resemble those of box elder and turn yellow in fall. An underutilized native shrub for difficult shaded, moist sites — excellent for naturalizing under large trees where maintaining lawn is impossible.

American Elm was for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries the most important street and shade tree in eastern North America, the classic 'cathedral' tree whose interlocking vase-shaped canopies arched over village streets from New England to the Great Plains in an iconic display of American civic beauty — until Dutch Elm Disease (Ophiostoma ulmi), introduced from Europe in the 1930s, devastated the species throughout most of its natural range and removed it from the American streetscape within a few decades. Today, disease-resistant cultivars ('Valley Forge', 'Princeton', 'New Harmony') have restored American Elm to viability in the landscape and are the preferred planting choice for new trees; these cultivars maintain the original graceful, vase-shaped habit that made the species so beloved, with resistance to DED ranging from moderate to strong. American Elm is adaptable to a wide range of soils from wet bottomlands to dry uplands and tolerates urban conditions, road salt, compaction, and air pollution better than most native trees. Plant disease-resistant cultivars in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil; provide adequate space for the wide-spreading mature canopy.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; American holly is the native evergreen tree holly of the eastern US, producing the classic red-berried, spiny-leaved holly that symbolizes the Christmas season. It grows naturally from Massachusetts to Florida and west to Texas, often in moist, slightly shaded woodland conditions along the coastal plain and Piedmont. The red berries (persistent through winter on female trees when a male pollinizer is present) are consumed by dozens of bird species, providing critical winter food for robins, cedar waxwings, and mockingbirds. It tolerates partial shade and performs remarkably well in zone 8–9 heat, making it one of the best native evergreen screening or specimen trees for the Gulf Coast garden. Hundreds of named cultivars exist — look for 'Fosteri' (compact), 'Savannah' (heavy fruiting, zone 7–9), and 'East Palatka' (Gulf Coast adapted).

American hop hornbeam is a small to medium understory tree of exceptional adaptability, tolerating everything from deep dry shade under mature oaks to moist bottomland edges — one of the finest native trees for difficult shaded sites where larger trees struggle. Its common name refers to the distinctive hop-like fruiting clusters that hang from branches in summer and fall, providing important food for ruffed grouse, wild turkey, northern bobwhite, and numerous songbirds and small mammals. The wood is extraordinarily hard and dense — historically used for tool handles and fence posts and known as 'ironwood' — and the pale, finely ridged gray bark provides year-round ornamental interest. Grow as a specimen or in groupings beneath taller oaks, hickories, and maples to create a multi-layered native woodland garden; it thrives with minimal care once established and is largely pest and disease free.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; American hornbeam (also called musclewood or blue beech) is one of the finest small native understory trees, growing naturally in the deep shade of bottomland forests and stream banks across eastern North America. The distinctive smooth, gray, sinewy bark with ridge-like muscle-like sinews makes it an outstanding specimen year-round. Delicate hop-like seed clusters in fall provide food for many finch and songbird species. Outstanding golden-orange to orange-red fall color. It grows slowly — 10–12 inches per year — but is very long lived. One of the few small trees genuinely suited to planting in deep shade under large oaks or maples. Excellent for naturalistic woodland gardens and native plant landscapes.

Sow seeds in moist, fertile, well-drained to average soil in full sun to part shade; American pokeweed is a large, dramatic native perennial of eastern North America with striking ornamental qualities — brilliant magenta-pink hollow stems, large tropical-looking leaves, long white flower racemes, and most notably the clusters of deep purple-black, shiny berries in late summer and fall that are among the most important food sources for migrating thrushes, mockingbirds, woodpeckers, and other fall-migrating birds that disperse the seeds widely. Despite being a generous wildlife resource, the entire plant — especially the roots, berries, and seeds — is dangerously toxic to humans and livestock, containing phytolaccatoxin and phytolaccigenin that cause severe gastrointestinal symptoms. The magenta pigment in the berries (pokeweed ink) was historically used to write documents, including some drafts of the US Declaration of Independence. The young spring shoots (poke sallet) have been boiled and eaten in Appalachian tradition after multiple changes of water to reduce toxins, but this practice is risky and not recommended. Best established in naturalized areas.

Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; American smoke tree is the native North American species of smoke tree — rarer, larger, and considered by many horticulturists to be superior to the European smoke tree (Cotinus coggygria) for fall color. The large, oval, blue-green leaves turn extraordinary shades of orange, scarlet, and burgundy in autumn, rivaling the best maples for fall color brilliance. Named 'chittamwood' in the Ozarks, where it grows on rocky, limestone outcrops and cedar glades. The smoke-like display in summer (from the fluffy, hair-like styles remaining after flowering) is less showy than the European species but still attractive. Extremely drought-tolerant on dry, rocky, alkaline soils. Much less commonly grown than European smoke tree, despite its superior fall color — an underused native ornamental tree that deserves wider planting in appropriate dry, rocky, well-drained garden settings across the eastern US.

Plant in partial shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil; American snowbell is a refined and underappreciated native shrub of eastern North America, bearing in May and June an elegant display of nodding, white, reflexed-petaled flowers with conspicuous bright-yellow stamens — the blossoms hang in short racemes beneath the arching stems, reminiscent of a smaller, shrubby version of the ornamental Japanese snowbell (Styrax japonicus) but entirely native and better adapted to wet sites. Styrax americanus is a multi-stemmed, loosely branched shrub native to moist, low-lying woodland margins, floodplain forests, and streambanks from Virginia to Florida and west to Missouri, making it an ideal choice for rain gardens, bioswales, and the moist edges of naturalistic woodland gardens where many other shrubs fail. The clean, elliptic leaves emerge fresh green in spring and offer a pleasant backdrop to the delicate flowers; fall color is a quiet soft yellow. A superb native alternative to non-native snowbell species for gardeners seeking an authentically regional plant with quiet seasonal beauty, exceptional ecological value for native bees, and reliable performance in wet or seasonally flooded sites.

American Sycamore is one of the largest deciduous trees in North America — with trunk diameters commonly reaching 6–8 feet and old specimens exceeding 10 feet in diameter — native to the moist, rich alluvial soils of river bottoms, floodplains, and stream terraces throughout eastern North America from Maine to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas, where its massive, gleaming white upper trunk (revealed as the outer gray-brown bark sheds in large patches) makes it visible from great distances and impossible to mistake for any other native tree. The distinctive mottled, ivory-white, cream, and gray trunk bark is among the most ornamental features of any North American tree, and the large, maple-like leaves create deep, cooling shade in summer; the spherical, golf-ball-sized seed heads hang through winter and are consumed by a variety of birds including American goldfinches. Wood ducks, chimney swifts, and other cavity-nesting species prize the large hollow cavities that develop in old sycamores. Plant in deep, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil near water features, streams, or in large park settings; it is not appropriate for typical residential lots given its ultimately massive size.

Direct sow scarified seed in fall into well-drained to moderately moist soil in a sunny to partially shaded meadow or woodland edge; nick or lightly sand the seed coat before sowing to improve germination, and inoculate seed with an appropriate rhizobium inoculant to activate nitrogen fixation from the first season. Vicia americana is a perennial scrambling vine native to meadows, prairies, roadsides, and open woodlands across most of North America, producing clusters of 4–9 purple-blue pea-like flowers from April through July that attract native bees and bumblebees while fixing atmospheric nitrogen into the soil through root nodules. It is an important larval host for the Gray Hairstreak butterfly and several other Lepidoptera, and its lightweight tendrils allow it to weave through grasses and low shrubs without smothering neighbors, making it an excellent addition to naturalistic meadow plantings.

Plant container-grown named cultivars near a very strong trellis, pergola, or fence in full sun to partial shade; unlike the invasive Asian wisterias (W. sinensis, W. floribunda), native American wisteria is well-behaved, will not escape into natural areas, and responds to pruning. The fragrant lilac-purple flower clusters appear in late spring, with good repeat bloom through summer on named cultivars. Prune twice yearly — once after the main spring bloom and again in late winter — to maintain size and encourage blooming spurs. American wisteria is naturally found in moist lowlands and swamps and tolerates wetter conditions than Asian species; do not confuse with the highly invasive Japanese and Chinese wisterias.

American Yellowwood is a superb native shade tree, native to rich, well-drained limestone bluffs, rocky slopes, and bottomland forest edges in the mid-South from North Carolina and Kentucky south to Alabama and west to Oklahoma, producing in May and June the most spectacular flowering display of any native shade tree — long, pendulous clusters of fragrant, white, pea-like flowers resembling wisteria that drape the wide-spreading canopy in a breathtaking display. The smooth, light gray bark resembles beech bark and is ornamental year-round; the bright green, pinnately compound leaves turn yellow in fall; and the wood at the heartwood core is bright yellow — hence the common name. Yellowwood blooms on alternate years or following stress, but the wait is always worth it. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; it adapts to a wide range of conditions once established and is a long-lived, virtually pest-free tree.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support structure; Amethyst Falls is the most popular and most widely planted cultivar of Wisteria frutescens — the American native wisteria — offering all the beauty of classic wisteria with critically better behavior in the garden. Asian wisterias (W. sinensis and W. floribunda) are considered invasive in many Eastern and Gulf South states and can escape cultivation into natural areas; American wisteria (W. frutescens) is a well-behaved native that produces similar, lightly fragrant, lavender-to-violet flower racemes without the invasive spreading of its Asian cousins. Amethyst Falls was selected for early bloom age (typically flowering in its second or third year, compared to 5–10 years for species wisteria), repeat blooming through summer after the main spring flush, and shorter flower racemes (4–6 inches) that are proportionally appropriate for smaller garden structures. The flowers are fragrant but less intensely so than Asian wisterias. In zone 9, Amethyst Falls blooms reliably from April through June with lighter repeat bloom flushes through summer. The vigorous twining habit quickly covers an arbor, pergola, or fence and the compound, dark-green deciduous foliage provides summer shade after bloom. Prune after bloom to control size; established plants tolerate hard pruning.

common_name: Amethyst Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dark Purple-Red Reblooming Oakleaf)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun. Amethyst is an oakleaf hydrangea selected for flower panicles that mature to a deep, saturated purple-red unusually dark for the species, extending the multi-season color display well beyond the typical white-to-pink progression of most oakleaf cultivars. The bold, deeply lobed foliage turns rich burgundy and orange in fall, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark adds winter interest once leaves drop. Prune, if needed, right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year set on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid cutting back in fall, winter, or spring, which removes next year's bloom.

Plant in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Amur maackia is a genuinely underappreciated small to medium deciduous tree from the forests of northeastern China and Manchuria, valued primarily for blooming in July and August when almost no other trees are flowering — producing upright, dense racemes of small, white pea flowers with a delicate blue cast that are mildly fragrant and attractive to bees and other pollinators. The tree is a legume and fixes atmospheric nitrogen, gradually improving soil fertility. The foliage emerges in spring with a distinctive silvery-blue sheen as leaves unfurl (a reliable spring identification feature) and matures to dark glossy green through summer. The copper-brown, peeling bark on older specimens is ornamental year-round. Highly adaptable to urban conditions, clay soils, drought, and air pollution, and one of the hardiest flowering trees available (to zone 3). Closely related to Cladrastis (yellowwood) and with a similar leguminous form. An excellent, pest-resistant, four-season small street or garden tree that remains widely unknown outside specialist circles.

Plant in well-drained, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; Anacacho orchid tree is a rare Texas native of rocky limestone canyon walls in the Anacacho Mountains of Kinney County, Texas — one of the most beautiful small native shrubs or small trees of the southwestern US. The flower display in spring is extraordinary for such a xeric plant — profuse, pure white, five-petaled, orchid-like flowers (the characteristic two-lobed leaf shape of all Bauhinia gives the entire genus the appearance of orchid plants) cover the shrub from tip to base. Unlike the tropical orchid trees widely planted in south Florida (B. purpurea, B. variegata), this species is hardy to about 15°F and adapted to dry, rocky, calcareous soils — making it far more practical for the Hill Country and Edwards Plateau. The characteristic bilobed leaf (like two fused circles) is distinctive and attractive. A rare and outstanding native ornamental.

Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to partial shade on a large, sturdy support; Anemone clematis is one of the most vigorous of all clematis species, capable of quickly covering an arbor, pergola, or fence with a dense curtain of growth and, in mid to late spring, an overwhelming flush of four-petaled, anemone-like flowers in white or soft pink, often fragrant, produced in such profusion that the entire vine can appear smothered in bloom for several weeks. It flowers on the previous year's growth, so it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned, if needed, immediately after flowering rather than in late winter — pruning in winter removes the wood that would have flowered that spring. Because of its size and vigor, give it ample space and a support strong enough to bear its eventual weight; it is not well suited to small trellises or delicate structures. Once established it is a tough, long-lived, relatively low-maintenance vine, though it prefers cooler summers and can struggle with the most intense Gulf Coast heat and humidity.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; angel's trumpet is among the most spectacular flowering plants in temperate-tropical horticulture, producing enormous (10–20 inch) pendulous trumpet-shaped flowers in white, yellow, peach, pink, or salmon that hang gracefully downward and fill the air with an intoxicating fragrance, particularly in the evening and night. With adequate water and nutrition, a well-established plant can produce 50–100 blooms simultaneously at peak season. Brugmansia is distinguished from Datura by its pendulous (not erect) flowers and woody, tree-like habit. All parts of the plant are extremely toxic — containing tropane alkaloids including scopolamine, atropine, and hyoscyamine — and should never be grown where children or pets may contact or ingest any part. In zone 8 it may die back in hard winters but regrows from established roots; in zone 9–11 it is evergreen and can be trained as a small tree. Propagate from 12-inch hardwood cuttings placed directly in moist soil.

common_name: Angel's Trumpet (White Angel's Trumpet, Moonflower Tree, Toé)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Angel's Trumpet grows most vigorously and flowers most heavily in full sun with adequate moisture and fertilization, but appreciates afternoon shade in zone 9 to prevent wilting of the large leaves during peak summer heat. Brugmansia suaveolens is a large, fast-growing soft-stemmed shrub or small tree from the Atlantic rainforest of Brazil in the Solanaceae family, extinct in the wild but widely cultivated throughout the tropical and subtropical world. The plant produces some of the largest and most dramatically beautiful flowers in the plant kingdom: enormous pendulous trumpets 12–18 inches long hanging downward in a cascade of pristine white (in the species) or in various shades of pink, yellow, orange, and peach in cultivars. The flowers are intensely and penetratingly fragrant, especially at dusk and through the night — a sweet, heavy, tropical perfume that carries for remarkable distances on still evenings. In zone 9, a well-established Angel's Trumpet in full bloom may carry dozens to over a hundred simultaneous flowers — a spectacular display. The plant was a sacred ceremonial and medicinal plant to indigenous peoples throughout South and Central America. EXTREME CAUTION: All parts of all Brugmansia species — flowers, leaves, seeds, roots, sap — contain potent tropane alkaloids (hyoscine, hyoscyamine, atropine) causing severe anticholinergic toxicity in humans and animals; fatalities have been recorded.

Sow seeds 1 inch deep in spring at the base of a fence, trellis, or woody shrub in partial shade with moist, humus-rich soil, providing a support structure immediately so the twining stems can climb as they emerge. Anglepod milkvine is a native perennial of southeastern US woodlands, thicket edges, and streamside clearings, producing star-shaped, greenish-white flowers in the milkweed family that are followed by distinctively angled, warty seed pods splitting to release silky-plumed seeds in late summer. As a member of the milkweed family, it serves as a larval host plant for monarch butterflies and queen butterflies alongside true milkweeds, making it a valuable addition to wildlife gardens in shaded or woodland-edge sites where common milkweed does not thrive. The vine dies back to a perennial rootstock each winter and re-emerges reliably in spring; avoid disturbing the root zone once plants are established.

Plant in well-drained, lean, even sandy soil in full sun in frost-free or warm winter climates; anil indigo is a tropical American shrub historically cultivated as one of the primary sources of natural indigo dye — the leaves are harvested and fermented in water to extract the blue pigment indigotin, which was the world's most important natural blue dye before synthetic indigo was developed in the 1880s. It naturalized throughout the warm coastal Southeast after Spanish and French colonial plantations, and still grows spontaneously in disturbed areas of Florida and the Gulf Coast. In zone 9, it often behaves as a self-seeding annual or short-lived perennial; in zone 10 and warmer it is a true woody perennial. The small pink-lavender flowers in drooping racemes bloom repeatedly. Yields the same dye compound as the Asian species I. tinctoria.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ann magnolia blooms later than star magnolia, helping its flowers dodge late spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering magnolias. One of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later, frost-dodging bloom, it produces rich reddish-purple, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact, shrubby, multi-stemmed plant well suited to smaller gardens where full-sized magnolia trees would be too large. Its later flowering window, roughly two to four weeks after star magnolia, gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts, which often blacken and ruin the flowers of earlier-blooming cultivars. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally, since magnolias generally need little pruning beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Annabelle is the most famous and most widely planted smooth hydrangea cultivar — a native American species selected for its exceptionally large, pure-white, snowball-like flower heads that can reach 12 inches or more in diameter and weigh enough to bend the stems dramatically in rain. Annabelle was selected from a specimen found growing wild near Anna, Illinois, and has been in continuous cultivation since the 1960s. The extraordinarily large, spherical flower heads in brilliant white are one of the great spectacles of the summer garden in shade — there is almost nothing else that produces flower heads of this size in partial to full shade. Annabelle blooms on new wood, meaning it can be cut back hard each spring (to 12 inches) and will still flower the same season — unlike old-wood bloomers that lose flowers if cut incorrectly. This makes it nearly foolproof: any pruning approach that removes old stems in late winter produces abundant bloom. In zone 9, Annabelle blooms from May through July and handles summer heat in partial shade better than Hydrangea macrophylla. The flowers dry beautifully on the plant, transitioning from fresh white to paper-white to soft tan as they age through summer into fall. Divide or transplant in fall after dormancy.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Anthony Waterer is the classic carmine-rose Japanese spiraea cultivar — one of the oldest and most widely grown selections of Spiraea japonica, introduced before 1884 and still among the most popular compact summer-blooming shrubs in American horticulture. The flat-topped, 3–4 inch flower clusters are a rich carmine-rose to deep rose-pink color from June through August (in zone 7–8), with peak bloom lasting 4–6 weeks followed by scattered repeat bloom if sheared lightly after the first flush. As with all Japanese spiraea cultivars, Anthony Waterer blooms on new wood — shear the entire plant hard to 6–8 inches in late winter or very early spring to stimulate vigorous new growth and produce the densest possible flower coverage. An established plant that is not sheared becomes leggy and produces fewer flowers; annual hard pruning is the most important maintenance practice for this species. Anthony Waterer grows to 3–4 feet tall and wide with a neat, rounded, mounding form that requires virtually no pruning to maintain shape beyond the annual renewal shearing. The new growth often emerges with distinctive cream and pink variegation, maturing to green. The plant is exceptionally adaptable — tolerating clay soil, heat, drought, and urban conditions throughout zone 9.

Plant in sharply drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Apache plume is a semi-evergreen Southwestern native shrub with small, deeply lobed leaves and a long, nearly continuous bloom of single, white, rose-like flowers from spring through fall. Each flower is followed by a distinctive cluster of pinkish, feathery, plumed seed tails that persist alongside the next flush of blooms, giving the shrub a two-toned, constantly changing appearance of white flowers and dusty-pink plumes at the same time. It is exceptionally drought, heat, and cold tolerant once established, thriving in the same lean, fast-draining, low-fertility soils that support native sagebrush and juniper communities. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain an open, airy form, and avoid rich soil or frequent irrigation, which produces lanky, less floriferous growth.

common_name: Aphrodite Rose of Sharon (Deep Pink Red-Eyed Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Aphrodite bears large, single, deep rose-pink flowers with a prominent dark red eye at the center, a bold, saturated color combination that reads clearly from a distance, blooming heavily from midsummer into fall. It is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection, setting little seed compared to old-fashioned rose of sharon and avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with seed-grown plants, while remaining a tough, heat- and humidity-tolerant shrub. It requires little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and encourage the current season's flowering wood.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Appalachian Red is a North Carolina State University introduction selected for exceptionally vivid, deep magenta-red flowers that bloom on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, standing out sharply from the softer pink-lavender tones of the wild species and from the more common purple-leafed and pink-flowered cultivars already popular in the nursery trade. Green, heart-shaped summer foliage and a classic small-tree vase shape follow the spring flower display, with attractive yellow fall color. Like other redbuds it is a valuable, adaptable native flowering tree for the understory or edge of a woodland garden, tolerating a good range of soil types as long as drainage is adequate, since redbud roots are susceptible to rot in wet, poorly drained sites. It performs well as a specimen tree, in a mixed native shrub-and-tree border, or naturalized at a woodland edge where its striking bloom color provides one of the most vivid early-spring accents in a partly shaded Southern garden.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Appalachian Spring is the most significant disease-resistant flowering dogwood cultivar ever introduced — selected from wild dogwood populations in the Appalachian Mountains specifically for its outstanding resistance to dogwood anthracnose (Discula destructiva), the fungal disease that since the 1970s has killed millions of wild dogwood trees across the eastern United States and continues to devastate unresistant trees in humid forest conditions. Dogwood anthracnose causes branch dieback, water-soaked lesions, and can kill an entire tree within 2–3 years of infection — it is the primary reason dogwood populations have declined so dramatically in eastern American forests. Appalachian Spring was selected by the US National Arboretum through a program specifically aimed at finding anthracnose-resistant genotypes among surviving wild populations where the disease had been established for decades. The flower display is classic white Cornus florida — large, four-bracted, pure white flowers in March through April — combined with the full suite of ornamental qualities: excellent fall red color, attractive horizontal branching, and fall red berries for wildlife. In zone 9, Appalachian Spring performs similarly to other Cornus florida cultivars but offers insurance against the anthracnose that has become more of a concern in humid Gulf South conditions.

common_name: April Dawn Camellia (Cold-Hardy Variegated Ackerman Hybrid Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in partial shade, and mulch well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Bred by Dr. William Ackerman at the U.S. National Arboretum as part of his cold-hardy camellia breeding program crossing Camellia japonica with the hardier C. oleifera, April Dawn produces large, formal double blooms of white heavily streaked and marbled with pink, opening in late winter to early spring on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its late bloom timing and improved cold hardiness compared to standard japonica camellias make it more reliable in the northern Gulf South and in years with a late hard freeze, since fewer flower buds are lost to cold damage. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape, and avoid heavy pruning in fall, which removes the developing flower buds.

common_name: April Snow Camellia (Cold-Hardy White Ackerman Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and mulch well to protect shallow roots. April Snow is one of the cold-hardy camellia introductions from Dr. William Ackerman's breeding program at the U.S. National Arboretum, developed to extend reliable camellia flowering into colder parts of the Southeast and mid-Atlantic than standard Camellia japonica cultivars can tolerate. It produces medium, formal double white flowers in early spring on a dense, rounded evergreen shrub, with glossy dark green foliage that provides structure and screening year-round even when not in bloom. Feed lightly with an acid-forming azalea-camellia fertilizer after flowering and again in early summer, and avoid heavy pruning except to shape, since camellias set next year's flower buds on the current season's growth. In Gulf Coast gardens, afternoon shade helps protect the flowers and foliage from scorch during hot spells.

Root cuttings in moist sand/perlite mix in summer heat or plant container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Arabian jasmine is the national flower of the Philippines and the primary source of the jasmine scent used in perfumes and jasmine tea — the double-flowered form 'Grand Duke of Tuscany' is especially fragrant, with blooms that intensify their perfume at night. Plants bloom intermittently throughout the warm season and can be trained as vines on a trellis or grown as shrubs. Fertilize monthly during active growth with a balanced fertilizer. In zone 9 grow against a warm south-facing wall and protect from hard freezes; in zone 8 and colder grow in containers. Harvest flowers in the morning for the strongest fragrance.

Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer and root them in a well-draining mix before transplanting to a permanent site in spring. This fast-growing coastal shrub thrives in sandy, poor soils and tolerates salt spray, making it ideal for seaside gardens in warm zones. The aromatic gray-green trifoliate leaves and purple flower spikes appear through summer and have long been used in Asian herbal traditions for their fragrant essential oils. In borderline zones 8-9, plant against a south-facing wall and mulch the base heavily to protect the crown through cold snaps.

common_name: Arapaho Crape Myrtle (True Red Upright Crape Myrtle with Dark Fall Foliage)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Arapaho is a later U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series release bred to improve on earlier red-flowered crape myrtles, combining true, vivid red summer flowers with strong resistance to powdery mildew and dark maroon-red fall foliage color that extends the tree's seasonal interest well past bloom time. The tall, upright habit suits it to specimen or street tree use in larger Gulf South landscapes. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Archduke Charles Rose (Color-Changing Antique China Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced around 1837, Archduke Charles is a classic China rose whose fully double blooms open pale pink at the petal edges with deep rose-red centers, then darken dramatically toward crimson-purple as they age in warm weather, so a single well-established bush can show several bloom colors simultaneously. Like other China roses it flowers almost without pause from spring through the first hard frost and carries strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, thriving in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South with minimal spray input. The rounded, bushy shrub works well massed, in mixed borders, or as an informal low hedge. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or weak wood; hard pruning is unnecessary and reduces flowering, since China roses bloom continuously on both old and new growth.

Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cold, sunny site, replicating the circumpolar arctic tundra of Alaska, Arctic Canada, and Greenland where it forms dense evergreen hummocks. Its stems are clothed in tightly overlapping, four-ranked scale leaves that give the shoots a distinctive square cross-section, and nodding white bell flowers open on slender red stalks in summer. Extremely cold-hardy but slow-growing and intolerant of heat, it belongs strictly in far-northern or high-elevation native and rock gardens with cool summers and a reliable winter snow cover.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Argentine trumpet vine (lavender trumpet vine) is a South American evergreen or semi-evergreen vine of the bignonia family that produces clusters of large, flared, trumpet-shaped, soft-lavender to pale-lilac and white flowers with violet-purple striping and veining on the throat in spring (April–May) and intermittently through the year, creating a refined and graceful floral display above its dense, glossy, dark-green, tendril-climbing foliage. The soft, delicate lavender-lilac color and the large, attractive, trumpet flower form give it a more elegant and less brash appearance than orange or red trumpet vines. It is notably more shade-tolerant than most Bignoniaceae vines and can bloom acceptably in partial-shade positions — a valuable attribute for the shadier garden where most large flowering vines fail. Hardy to approximately 20°F in zone 8, it is one of the more cold-tolerant of the tropical trumpet vine family. Excellent trained on arbors, fences, and large trellises in zone 8–11. May be invasive in some warm, moist climates — monitor for naturalization near natural areas.

common_name: Argentine Trumpet Vine (Garrocha Tecoma, Red Esperanza)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Tecoma garrocha grows most vigorously in full sun and will produce fewer flowers and become leggy in shade. Tecoma garrocha is a large, fast-growing, semi-deciduous shrub or small tree native to Argentina and Bolivia in the Bignoniaceae family, closely related to the commonly grown Yellow Bells (T. stans) but with distinctly orange-red to coral-red tubular flowers rather than yellow — a color difference with significant ornamental consequence. The plant produces compound leaves of several lance-shaped leaflets and bears its trumpet-shaped flowers in terminal clusters throughout the warm months from spring through fall, with a particularly prolific bloom in summer and early fall. The long, tubular, orange-red flowers are extraordinary hummingbird attractants — the nectar-rich, hummingbird-adapted flower form and vivid color ensures a continuous parade of hummingbirds in zone 9 gardens where this shrub is planted. Unlike many tropical-looking flowering shrubs, Tecoma garrocha is genuinely cold-hardy — cold-hardy to zone 7-8, surviving temperatures to 20°F — one of the most cold-hardy of the Tecoma species. This cold tolerance combined with its spectacular hummingbird value and long bloom season makes T. garrocha one of the most underused and undervalued ornamental shrubs for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast landscapes.

Plant in spring along desert washes, canyon bottoms, or irrigated landscape zones that mimic its native riparian habitat in southern Arizona and New Mexico canyons. Deeply cut, palmate leaves and smooth white upper bark give it striking form against arid backdrops, while its multi-trunked, twisting habit develops character with age. This sycamore provides critical shade and nesting habitat for desert wildlife along streamcourses and tolerates the region's intense summer heat as long as its roots have access to subsurface moisture. Water deeply and infrequently during establishment to encourage the deep rooting this species depends on in the wild.

Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, dry, sandy, acidic, infertile soil in full sun; Arkansas oak is a relatively uncommon, small-statured oak of the red oak group naturally restricted to dry, sandy, acidic soils in the Gulf Coastal Plain and lower Mississippi River valley, primarily in Arkansas, Louisiana, and Texas. The leaves are variable in shape, sometimes entire, sometimes shallowly lobed, with a distinctive blue-green upper surface from which the common name 'bluejack' derives. A small tree, rarely exceeding 25 feet, it grows naturally in sandy pinelands and upland scrub alongside longleaf pine. The small acorns are eaten by deer and turkeys. An uncommon and undervalued native tree for dry, sandy, acidic sites in the Gulf South where its modest size and adaptability to infertile conditions make it appropriate for naturalistic woodland gardens and pine savanna restoration.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence able to support a large, vigorous evergreen vine. Native to China, Armand clematis is unusual among clematis for its leathery, glossy, evergreen leaves that provide year-round structure, and for its very early spring bloom of small, intensely fragrant white star-shaped flowers produced in such abundance that a mature vine can perfume an entire section of garden. It grows quickly and can become large and somewhat unruly if not given enough room or occasional pruning right after its spring bloom to keep it in bounds, since it flowers on the prior year's growth and heavy pruning at the wrong time removes the coming season's flowers. It is a good choice for screening a fence or arbor with year-round foliage in the milder parts of its range.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; Armenian tea olive is a large, handsome evergreen shrub from the Caucasus and northeastern Turkey with exceptionally large, glossy, lance-shaped leaves that give it a bolder, more tropical texture than most other osmanthus species. In spring it produces clusters of small white flowers with an intensely sweet fragrance that carries far on the breeze, followed by dark blue-black, olive-like fruits. Compared to the popular Osmanthus fragrans (sweet olive), it is considerably more cold-hardy and generally less invasive in North American landscapes. It makes an outstanding large screening hedge or specimen shrub in zones 6–9, and the bold foliage provides strong year-round structure in mixed borders.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Arnold Promise' blooms in late winter while dormant, so plant it where its bare, flower-studded branches can be seen from the house on gray winter days. Hamamelis x intermedia 'Arnold Promise' is one of the most celebrated winter-blooming shrubs, a cross between Chinese and Japanese witch hazel selected at the Arnold Arboretum for its abundant clusters of spidery, ribbon-petaled, bright yellow flowers that open in late winter, often while snow is still on the ground, followed by good yellow-orange fall foliage color. It is among the latest-blooming and most floriferous witch hazel cultivars, providing months of anticipation-breaking color in a shaded winter border when almost nothing else is in flower. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, and give it consistently moist, well-drained soil, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogging.

Direct-sow into warm soil after all frost danger has passed; this diamond-leaved, small-flowered subshrub of the mallow family grows fast in full sun and tolerates poor, dry soils, self-sowing readily once established in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens. It behaves as a woody-based perennial in zones 9-11 and dies back to the root in colder winters within its hardiness range. Its main draw for pollinator gardeners is as a larval host for both the Common Checkered-Skipper and the Tropical Checkered-Skipper, which are otherwise hard to attract without a mallow-family host present.

Plant in moist, well-drained to average soil in part shade to full sun; arrowwood viburnum is one of the most adaptable and wildlife-valuable native shrubs of eastern North America, producing flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring that attract butterflies and native bees in abundance, followed by clusters of metallic blue-black berries in late summer that are among the most preferred fruits of over 35 species of birds including bluebirds, robins, catbirds, cedar waxwings, and wood thrushes. The glossy, coarsely-toothed leaves turn orange-red to purple in fall, making it a multi-season performer. It was named 'arrowwood' because Native Americans used the straight, stiff young stems for arrow shafts. The multi-stem rounded habit is excellent for hedges, shrub borders, and naturalistic plantings. Extremely cold-hardy and adaptable to clay soils.

Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in rocky, alkaline, well-drained limestone soil in full sun; Ashe juniper is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established and needs no irrigation beyond its first year or two. Dense, scale-like, dark green foliage covers a shrubby to small tree form native to the limestone hills of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau, where it is often called 'mountain cedar' and forms extensive brakes on rocky slopes too thin-soiled for most other trees. Its winter pollen, released in massive quantities from December through February, is the primary cause of the region's notorious 'cedar fever' allergy season, a significant consideration before planting near a home; mature female trees produce small, blue, berry-like cones that are valuable winter food for cedar waxwings and other birds. Established stands provide critical nesting habitat for the endangered golden-cheeked warbler, which nests almost exclusively in old-growth Ashe juniper bark strips, making mature stands ecologically valuable despite the tree's reputation as a rangeland weed when it encroaches on grazing land.

Ashe Magnolia is one of the rarest magnolias in North America, a critically imperiled native shrub or small tree endemic to the steep, moist, shaded ravines and bluffs of the Florida Panhandle in a handful of counties in far northwest Florida and adjacent Alabama, where fewer than 20 wild populations survive. Despite its rarity in the wild, Ashe Magnolia is relatively easy to grow in cultivation and is widely offered by specialty native plant nurseries; it is often treated as a dwarf or subspecies of the closely related Bigleaf Magnolia (Magnolia macrophylla) but is considered a distinct species by most authorities. The enormous, white, bowl-shaped flowers (12–14 inches across) with purple-spotted centers appear in April and May and are among the most spectacular of any magnolia — attracting native bees and beetles as pollinators. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and protect from drying winds that damage the enormous leaves; it is significantly smaller and faster-blooming than M. macrophylla, making it more suitable for the typical home garden.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; ashy hydrangea is closely related to smooth hydrangea and shares its tolerance for shade and adaptable garden soil. Hydrangea cinerea is a southeastern native shrub closely related to and sometimes treated as a variety of smooth hydrangea, distinguished by the fine, ashy-gray down covering the undersides of its leaves, with flattened clusters of small white fertile flowers ringed by a few showier sterile florets in early summer. Its shade tolerance and adaptability to typical garden soil make it a reliable native alternative to Hydrangea arborescens cultivars for a woodland border or native shrub planting, blooming reliably on new wood even after a hard late-winter pruning. Cut stems back by a third to a half in late winter to encourage strong new growth and the best flowering the following summer.

Plant in any well-drained soil in full shade to full sun; asiatic jasmine is the premier shade-tolerant groundcover for zone 7–11 landscapes — a dense, weed-suppressing mat of small, oval, glossy, dark-green leaves on wiry twining stems that fills in rapidly and maintains its deep color year-round. Unlike its fragrant relative confederate jasmine (T. jasminoides), asiatic jasmine rarely flowers in the landscape and is grown purely for its exceptional foliage ground cover performance. It is the go-to solution for the problem spots in Southern landscapes: dry shade under large oaks and magnolias, slopes that are difficult to mow, areas around tree roots where nothing else grows. Once established, it requires almost no maintenance — shear or mow to 3–4 inches in early spring every few years to remove the older, woody stems and stimulate fresh, dense regrowth. Remarkably drought tolerant, heat tolerant, and deer resistant. Variegated forms ('Ogon Nishiki') have yellow-green leaves that brighten shaded areas.

Plant divisions in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade; asparagus fern (plumosa fern, lace fern) is a South African climbing plant grown for its extraordinarily delicate, feathery, bright-green foliage — the flattened, horizontal branchlets bearing tiny, needle-like cladodes create a texture so fine and airy that it appears almost like mist, making it incomparably useful as a filler and softening element in cut flower arrangements and mixed container plantings. The plant climbs by small, hook-like thorns and in tropical gardens can ascend to 10–15 feet, creating a soft curtain of misty foliage over trellises and fences. In cooler climates it functions as a houseplant or annual container filler. Small white flowers followed by dark berries appear on mature plants. It differs from the more robust A. aethiopicus (emerald fern / Sprengeri fern) in producing a finer, more delicate, horizontal branch structure. A staple of the cut flower industry worldwide for its use as foliage filler in arrangements. Note: berries are mildly toxic.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Athens' is a yellow-flowered sport of native sweetshrub discovered in Georgia and is grown and cared for exactly like the wine-red species. Calycanthus floridus 'Athens' is a distinctive color break for the native sweetshrub, producing the same fruity, strawberry-banana-scented flowers as the typical maroon-red species but in a clear chartreuse-yellow, blooming over an extended period in late spring into early summer. Its unusual flower color and strong, sweet fragrance make it a good specimen for a shaded border or foundation planting near a patio or window where the scent can be enjoyed, and it shares the species' excellent shade tolerance and adaptability to a range of soils. Prune lightly after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on old wood and hard pruning will sacrifice the following year's flowers.

Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Atlantic pigeonwings is a native twining vine of open woodlands, sandy roadsides, and pine flatwoods across the Southeast, closely related to the tropical culinary butterfly pea (C. ternatea) but hardier and better adapted to North American conditions. The large, powder-blue to lavender-blue pea flowers are inverted on the plant — the keel points upward rather than downward as in most legumes — with a distinctive white and yellow central mark. The tubular flowers are an important nectar source for bumblebees and sphinx moths that are physically capable of reaching the nectar. At woodland edges and in partial shade gardens, it provides a delicate, trailing structure on fences and shrubs throughout summer. Dies back to persistent roots in winter and re-emerges reliably in spring in zones 7–10. An outstanding native vining legume for the dry, sandy soils typical of the Gulf Coastal Plain.

common_name: Aucuba (Japanese Aucuba, Spotted Laurel, Gold Dust Plant)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; aucuba is an outstanding broad-leaved evergreen shrub for zone 7–9 shade, producing large, leathery, glossy leaves in solid dark green or in the popular spotted 'Variegata' form with irregular yellow speckles that light up deep shade like scattered gold dust. The spotted forms are called 'gold dust plant' and are among the most striking variegated foliage plants for shade. Female plants bear large, glossy red berries in fall and winter that persist attractively; a single male plant is required for fruit production. Aucuba tolerates dense, dry shade under trees better than virtually any other broad-leaved evergreen shrub, surviving in conditions that defeat hostas, ferns, and most other shade plants. It is the ultimate plant for the dry, root-filled shade under large oaks and pines in the Gulf South.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade. August Beauty is one of the most widely planted gardenia cultivars in the Gulf South, prized for large, fully double, intensely fragrant white flowers produced over an extended season from late spring well into early fall rather than a single short spring flush. The dense, rounded, glossy-leaved shrub makes a good foundation or specimen planting near a porch, window, or path where its fragrance can be appreciated up close. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves if the soil is not sufficiently acidic, so acidifying fertilizer and consistent moisture are key to keeping it healthy and free-flowering.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aurea is tolerant of a wide range of soils and light levels once established. Unlike the many red-and-burgundy-toned nandina cultivars grown for winter foliage color, Aurea keeps its lance-shaped leaflets a soft yellow-green year-round, with creamy-white summer flower clusters followed by unusual pale yellow berries instead of the typical bright red, giving it a distinctly different look for gardeners wanting variety among their heavenly bamboo plantings. Its upright, cane-like growth habit is identical to other nandina cultivars, spreading slowly by underground rhizomes to form a loose colony over time. Prune by removing the oldest canes at ground level each year to keep the planting full from top to bottom rather than shearing, which leaves bare lower stems.

Plant container stock in spring once temperatures are reliably warm in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Australian tree fern is frost-tender and needs protection or container culture with winter shelter outside zones 9b and warmer. Cyathea cooperi is a fast-growing, dramatic tree fern from Australia with a slender, fibrous trunk topped by a crown of large, lacy, arching fronds up to 10 feet long, creating an instant tropical, prehistoric look in a shaded courtyard or lush understory planting. It is one of the fastest-growing tree ferns in cultivation, adding a foot or more of trunk height annually under good conditions, but its speed comes with a need for consistent moisture and high humidity, since the trunk itself absorbs water. In marginal zones, wrap the fibrous trunk with burlap or frost cloth ahead of hard freezes, or grow it in a large container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

common_name: Australian Wax Plant (Common Wax Flower, Hoya australis)
notes: Grow in bright indirect light to partial shade — Hoya australis blooms most freely in bright indirect to gentle morning sun and will produce few flowers in shade, but performs well as a trailing houseplant even in moderate light. Hoya australis is a vigorous, twining, semi-succulent epiphytic vine native to eastern Australia (Queensland and New South Wales), one of the few Hoyas from the Australian continent rather than Southeast Asia, and one of the most cold-tolerant commonly grown Hoya species. The plant produces long, trailing stems of paired, broadly oval to slightly rounded, fleshy, glossy, dark-green leaves that are thicker and more succulent than most commonly grown Hoyas. In summer (its natural Southern Hemisphere flowering season, now extended to warm months in cultivation), Hoya australis produces large, globe-shaped umbels of 20–40 individual star-shaped flowers — pure white with a faint pink-red corona — with an intensely sweet, musky, almost spicy fragrance that is among the most powerful of any Hoya species. The combination of vigorous growth, good cold tolerance (relative to other Hoyas), reliable blooming, and powerful fragrance makes Hoya australis one of the most recommended starter Hoyas and a valuable addition to zone 9 shaded container and patio displays. Non-toxic to pets.

common_name: Autograph Tree (Pitch Apple, Balsam Apple, Florida Clusia)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in sandy, rocky, or average well-drained soil; Autograph Tree is exceptionally drought- and salt-tolerant once established, making it one of the premier coastal shrubs for zone 10–11 Gulf Coast and South Florida landscapes. Clusia rosea is a tropical tree from the Caribbean and tropical Americas that has become one of the most widely planted landscape shrubs in South Florida, the Keys, and coastal South Texas for its bold, glossy, ovate, extremely thick, leathery dark-green leaves and tolerance of the most challenging coastal growing conditions. The leaves' remarkable rigidity — they feel like synthetic material — allows text or drawings scratched with a nail or key to remain permanently etched as the leaf expands and matures, making it a natural curiosity and the source of the common name 'Autograph Tree.' In late summer, the plant produces attractive cup-shaped white to rose-pink flowers followed by fleshy green fruits that split open to reveal red seeds — both attractive to birds. Clusia rosea develops aerial roots that eventually reach the ground, giving mature specimens a striking strangler-fig appearance. The milky white latex sap was historically used as a boat caulk ('pitch') by Caribbean peoples — hence the name 'Pitch Apple.' A large, fast-growing hedge or specimen plant for zone 10–11.

common_name: Autumn Blaze Maple (Fast-Growing Hybrid Freeman Maple)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Autumn Blaze is a hybrid cross between silver maple and red maple, bred to combine the rapid growth rate of silver maple with the sturdier branch structure and reliable orange-red fall color of red maple, avoiding the weak, storm-prone wood that has made straight silver maple less popular as a landscape tree. It grows into a dense, oval-to-rounded shade tree relatively quickly compared to most large shade trees, making it a popular choice where gardeners want a mature-looking canopy sooner rather than later. It is adaptable to a range of soils and tolerates urban conditions reasonably well, though like its silver maple parent it can have somewhat brittle wood in ice or heavy wind, and should be kept away from underground utilities and pavement given its vigorous surface roots.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; autumn cherry is a Japanese species celebrated as the parent of the cultivar 'Autumnalis', which holds the exceptional distinction of producing semi-double, pale pink flowers twice — in October-November when temperatures drop in fall, and again in early spring. In mild winters, the fall flowering can continue sporadically through winter into spring, providing flowers for weeks or months. The weeping forms (var. pendula) create graceful, cascading silhouettes, and 'Autumnalis Rosea' has deeper pink, semi-double flowers. More cold-hardy than many ornamental cherries and longer-lived than double-flowering varieties. A cherished ornamental for fall-winter garden interest, providing color at a time when almost no other flowering trees are in bloom. Less vigorous than Yoshino cherry but more refined.

common_name: Autumn Embers Encore Azalea (Deep Red Reblooming Compact Azalea)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with protection from harsh afternoon sun in the hottest part of zone 9. Autumn Embers is a compact-growing selection within the Encore reblooming azalea series, producing deep, rich red double flowers in the main spring flush and then again through summer and fall, giving significantly more color over the season than traditional once-blooming azaleas of similar size. Its smaller mature size compared to many Encore cultivars fits foundation plantings and smaller borders where a full-sized azalea would outgrow the space. Water deeply during dry spells, especially before the later bloom flushes, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom to avoid removing the buds destined for later color.

common_name: Autumn Gold Ginkgo (Seedless Male Ginkgo with Golden Fall Color)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, and water regularly through the first two to three seasons to help the young tree establish, since mature ginkgo are exceptionally tough and drought-, pollution-, and pest-tolerant once rooted in. Autumn Gold is a grafted, male-only selection of ginkgo prized for its symmetrical, broadly pyramidal form and its dependable, uniform display of clear golden-yellow fan-shaped leaves each fall, often dropping in a dramatic, near-simultaneous leaf fall over a day or two once peak color is reached. Because it is propagated from a male tree, Autumn Gold never produces the notoriously foul-smelling, messy fruit that female ginkgo trees bear, making it a far better choice than a seed-grown tree of unknown sex for street tree plantings, lawns, or anywhere fallen fruit would be a nuisance. Ginkgo is one of the most resilient shade trees available, tolerating urban pollution, compacted soil, heat, and periods of drought with ease, and it is essentially free of serious insect and disease problems. Little pruning is needed beyond removing any dead or crossing branches while the tree is young.

common_name: Avondale Chinese Redbud (Intense Rose-Purple Compact Redbud)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the multi-stemmed shrub room to develop its dense, rounded form. Avondale is a New Zealand selection of Chinese redbud prized for producing the most intensely colored bloom of any redbud in general cultivation, with deep rose-purple to magenta pea flowers packed so densely along every branch, twig, and even the older trunk wood that the bare stems all but disappear under the spring flower display. Its naturally compact, shrubby habit stays smaller and tidier than the species, and its greater shade tolerance compared with Eastern redbud makes it a strong choice for a woodland-edge planting, foundation bed, or small-garden specimen where its eye-level bloom show can be appreciated up close. Large, glossy heart-shaped leaves follow the flowers and turn clear yellow in fall; prune only to remove dead or crossing wood right after bloom.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Awabuki is the most attractive and most dramatic viburnum for Gulf Coast zone 8–10 landscapes — a vigorous, large-growing evergreen shrub or small tree producing enormous, glossy, dark-green leaves with an extraordinary mirror-like surface sheen that catches and reflects light unlike any other commonly grown landscape shrub. The leaves (4–8 inches long) have such a pronounced, lacquered surface gloss that the plant appears polished — the deep, wet-looking gloss is so intense it almost looks artificial. This exceptional foliage texture makes Awabuki a striking specimen plant and creates a more architectural, tropical effect than standard sweet viburnum. White, fragrant flower clusters (panicles) appear in spring, followed by small red berries that age to black and attract birds. The fast, vigorous growth makes Awabuki excellent for rapid screening and privacy hedges — it can grow 3–4 feet per year in zone 9 with adequate water and fertilizer. Awabuki is more cold-sensitive than standard sweet viburnum (V. odoratissimum) and can suffer significant damage in zone 8 during severe winters; zone 9 coastal gardens are ideal. Prune after spring bloom to control size — Awabuki tolerates heavy pruning and can be maintained as a formal hedge.

common_name: Baby Gem Boxwood (Compact Slow-Growing Dwarf Boxwood)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun with afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9. Baby Gem is a compact, naturally slow-growing boxwood selected to hold a small, dense, rounded shape with minimal pruning, making it an efficient choice for low edging, knot gardens, and small formal accents where a full-sized boxwood cultivar would quickly outgrow the space and require constant shearing. Its fine-textured, glossy, light-to-medium green foliage stays dense from the ground up, and the plant's naturally compact habit reduces the maintenance burden common to boxwood hedging. It tolerates Gulf South heat and humidity reasonably well with afternoon shade and sharp drainage, since boxwood roots are highly susceptible to root rot in wet soil. Watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest, treating with a systemic insecticide if infestation becomes heavy. Light shearing once or twice a season, if any, is usually sufficient to maintain its naturally tidy form.

common_name: Bahama Senna (Chapman's Senna, Mexican Senna, Coastal Senna)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy, rocky, or alkaline soil — Bahama Senna is exceptionally drought and salt-tolerant once established and thrives in the challenging coastal and limestone rock conditions of South Florida where many other ornamental shrubs struggle. Senna mexicana is a compact, evergreen to semi-evergreen shrubby Senna native to the Caribbean (Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola) and southern Florida (Chapman's Senna / var. chapmanii, endemic to Miami-Dade County and the Keys) in the Fabaceae family. The plant produces pinnately compound leaves of 4–6 pairs of oval, gray-green leaflets and produces clusters of bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers at the branch tips through the warm months and intermittently year-round in zone 10-12. The flowers are followed by flattened, dark-brown seed pods. Bahama Senna is one of the most important butterfly host plants available for zone 9b-12 gardens: Senna species are the exclusive larval host plants for two of the most abundant and beautiful Florida butterflies — the large, brilliant yellow Cloudless Sulphur (Phoebis sennae) and the Sleepy Orange (Eurema nicippe) — both of which lay their eggs exclusively on Senna foliage and whose caterpillars feed on the leaves. A landscape with established Senna mexicana will be host to these butterflies throughout the warm months. An outstanding, low-maintenance native flowering shrub for coastal zone 9b-12 gardens. Non-toxic.

Bahama Wild Coffee is a compact native evergreen shrub, native to the coastal hammocks and tropical hardwood forests of south Florida, the Keys, the Bahamas, and the Caribbean, where it grows as a common understory shrub beneath larger canopy trees in partial to full shade. Similar to Wild Coffee (Psychotria nervosa) but with smaller, shinier, privet-like leaves (hence the species epithet ligustrifolia, meaning privet-leaved), it produces small white flowers year-round that attract native bees and butterflies, followed by clusters of red berries that turn black and are avidly consumed by migratory warblers, thrushes, and robins in fall and winter. An outstanding native shade shrub for zone 9b–11 landscapes where its shade tolerance, modest size, year-round bloom, and exceptional wildlife value make it a versatile foundation plant, hedge component, or understory specimen. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; established plants tolerate brief drought but prefer consistent moisture.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Baja fairy duster is a desert shrub native to the Baja California peninsula and Sonoran Desert that produces clouds of brilliant, brushy, red powder-puff flowers consisting almost entirely of long, bright-red stamens with no conspicuous petals — a classic desert flower form that has evolved specifically for hummingbird pollination. It blooms heavily in spring and fall with sporadic flowers between, providing critical nectar for migrating and resident hummingbirds during the desert seasons when few other plants are in bloom. The fine, bipinnate, semi-evergreen foliage has a soft, feathery texture. More cold-sensitive than the pink fairy duster (Calliandra eriophylla, which is already well-known in Arizona desert gardens), it is best suited to the warmer deserts and coastal warm-winter climates of zones 9b–11. Outstanding combined with desert willow (Chilopsis linearis), autumn sage (Salvia greggii), and other hummingbird-attracting desert plants.

growth_habit: Gulf Coast native deciduous conifer swamp tree
notes: Plant Taxodium distichum in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil — it tolerates standing water, drought once established, alkaline soils, and urban conditions, making it one of the most adaptable large trees in its range; young trees benefit from regular watering for the first 1–2 years, after which they become remarkably tough and self-sufficient. Bald Cypress is among the most iconic trees of the American South — the defining image of Gulf Coast bayous, cypress swamps, and river floodplains — yet it is equally at home in ordinary garden soil and among the most pest- and disease-resistant of all large deciduous trees. Growing 50–70 feet tall with a buttressed base, strongly vertical form, and spectacular fine-textured, feathery foliage, it provides outstanding summer shade and brilliant fall color (unusual for a tree this adapted to tropical Gulf Coast conditions). The famous 'knees' — woody projections from roots that emerge above the waterline — appear primarily in flooded conditions and are thought to provide oxygen to waterlogged roots. Ancient specimens exceed 600 years old; the Montezuma Cypress (Taxodium mucronatum) of Mexico is related and evergreen. Bald Cypress is an ideal large specimen tree for rain gardens, pond edges, low-lying areas, and urban street plantings where other trees fail.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; baldhip rose is one of the few native roses that thrives in woodland shade rather than full sun. Small, delicate, single pink flowers open in late spring on slender, sparsely thorned canes with fine, fern-like compound leaves, followed by small orange-red rose hips that characteristically drop their sepals early, leaving a smooth, 'bald' hip that gives the species its common name. Native to coniferous forest understories along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to California, it is unusual among wild roses for genuinely thriving in shade, making it a valuable native shrub for a woodland garden where sun-loving roses would fail to flower. It needs little care beyond occasional thinning of old canes and provides good wildlife cover and berries for birds through fall and winter.

Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun along water features, floodplains, and wet areas; balsam poplar is the most widespread tree of the boreal forest, forming groves along rivers and lake shores from Alaska to Newfoundland. Its common name 'balm of Gilead' reflects the intensely sweet, balsamic fragrance of the opening buds in spring — one of the most distinctive and beloved spring fragrances of the northern forest. The sticky, resinous buds have been used in traditional medicine as a cough remedy and wound herb, and the bud resin has been used by bees (as propolis) and by indigenous peoples as a wound plaster. A very fast-growing, large tree requiring moist to wet soil and ample space. The female trees produce cottony seed fluff that can be messy; male cuttings are often preferred for planting.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; banana shrub (formerly Michelia figo, now reclassified as Magnolia figo) is a Chinese evergreen magnolia relative that has been a classic southern garden shrub for over a century — prized not for showy flowers but for the intensely, exotically sweet, banana-custard-like fragrance of its small, creamy-yellow, purple-edged, tulip-shaped flowers that are produced in abundance from spring through fall amid the dense, glossy, dark-green, leathery leaves. The flowers are small but individually so powerfully fragrant — a single established shrub can perfume an entire garden — that they are worth seeking out close up, where the heavy, tropical sweetness creates an extraordinary sensory experience disproportionate to the flower's size. Banana shrub grows as a dense, compact, slow-growing, rounded evergreen shrub with a formal, refined habit and requires minimal care. It tolerates partial shade well and is one of the most versatile and dependable fragrant shrubs for zone 7–11, performing reliably for decades with little attention. 'Port Wine' (deep-burgundy purple flowers with stronger fragrance) is an outstanding cultivar.
