Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; banana shrub is a classic evergreen shrub of the South, related to magnolias and producing small, creamy-yellow flowers edged in maroon-purple that emit an intense fragrance reminiscent of ripe bananas — particularly potent in warm, humid air. The fragrance carries considerable distance and can be detected from many feet away when the plant is in full bloom in spring and early summer. The evergreen foliage is attractive year-round. This plant has been grown in Southern gardens for well over a century and is among the most beloved fragrant shrubs for the warm-climate garden. In zone 9a it is a reliable, low-maintenance garden anchor that thrives with minimal care once established. A few individual flowers in a small vase can fill a room with fragrance.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; banjine (or rice flower) is a neat, compact, mounding Australian shrub from the coastal heathlands of southwestern Western Australia — producing in spring dense, rounded terminal clusters of many small, tubular, four-petaled flowers in a rich, warm, rosy-pink to deep pink, each small flower head about an inch across and the clusters collectively covering the plant in an abundant pink display. The common name 'rice flower' comes from the appearance of the dense, rounded, tightly packed flower clusters resembling a cluster of tiny rice grains dipped in pink. The compact, neat, naturally mounding growth habit and glossy, small, dark-green leaves provide attractive structure year-round, and the plant maintains a tidy, ornamental character without significant pruning. It is in the Thymelaeaceae family (the same family as daphne), and like daphne, it has a reputation for sensitivity to site conditions — it resents transplanting, requires excellent drainage, and is unforgiving of waterlogged conditions. In the right position in zones 9–11 Mediterranean-climate or warm coastal gardens, however, it is a rewarding, long-lived, compact ornamental shrub.

common_name: Barbara Karst Bougainvillea (Classic Magenta-Red Everblooming Tropical Vine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Barbara Karst is one of the most popular and widely planted bougainvillea cultivars for Gulf South gardens — a vigorous, large-scale vine producing brilliant magenta-red to cerise-red bracts (the showy colored structures surrounding the inconspicuous true flowers) through most of the year in frost-free conditions. In zone 9, Barbara Karst blooms most heavily in spring and fall when temperatures moderate; in winter (November–February) the vine may defoliate partially during cold spells and bloom is reduced. The brilliant magenta-red bract color is one of the most vivid in the warm-climate garden palette and creates an unmistakable tropical visual impact when the vine is in full bloom. Bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight stress — dry-down periods between waterings, lean soil without excessive nitrogen, and root constriction (slightly root-bound in containers) all promote flower production over vegetative growth. This counterintuitive cultural requirement (bloom more when stressed) is the most important management principle for bougainvillea. The thorny stems require careful placement away from pedestrian areas. In zone 9, Barbara Karst may be killed to the ground by severe freezes but returns from the roots; cover with frost cloth during freezes below 28°F. Outstanding trained on walls, fences, and pergolas where the massive bloom display can be appreciated.

common_name: Baronne Prevost Rose (Extremely Hardy Antique Hybrid Perpetual)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Baronne Prevost, introduced in 1842, is one of the earliest Hybrid Perpetual roses and remains prized for its extreme hardiness and large, deep rose-pink, flat, quartered blooms densely packed with petals in the old-fashioned style, carrying a strong classic rose fragrance. Its wide climate tolerance, from cold northern winters to hot Southern summers, has kept it a mainstay of heirloom rose collections for over 180 years. It blooms in a strong spring flush with some repeat through summer and fall, and benefits from richer soil and more regular feeding than tougher China or Tea roses. Prune moderately in late winter to shape and remove old wood, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage additional flowering.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Bauer's grevillea is a compact, spreading, relatively low-growing Australian grevillea — native to the rocky, somewhat shaded forest margins and valley floor habitats of New South Wales — that stands apart from many grevillea species in its greater shade tolerance, making it one of the few Proteaceae useful for planting in the dappled shade or semi-shade of woodland margins and north-facing hillsides. The flowers are in the typical grevillea 'toothbrush' or clustered style — dense clusters of small, curved, tubular red to pink-red flowers with projecting, hooked styles that create the characteristic grevillea flower cluster — produced in greatest abundance in spring but appearing sporadically through the year in favorable mild-winter climates. The foliage is small, dark green, and finely textured, creating a compact, spreading, mat-like mound that works well as a low-maintenance groundcover shrub in the right conditions. Like all Proteaceae, it requires lean soil and absolutely no phosphorus fertilizer. Named for Franz Bauer, the celebrated Austrian botanical artist at Kew whose extraordinary illustrations documented the new Australian flora in the early 19th century.

Plant in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun along the immediate coastline; bay cedar is a dense, rounded, salt-tolerant strand shrub with soft, narrow, yellow-green leaves clustered toward branch tips and small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers produced nearly continuously in warm weather. It forms a natural windbreak hedge along tropical and subtropical shorelines, tolerating direct salt spray, poor sandy soil, and drought that would quickly kill most ornamental shrubs, and it requires essentially no irrigation once established. Small, dry, corky fruit follow the flowers and float on ocean currents to colonize new shoreline, the same strategy used by many other strand-zone pioneer species. Because it is strictly frost-tender, grow it only in true frost-free coastal gardens or as a large container specimen brought under cover elsewhere; light trimming after major growth flushes keeps the naturally rounded form dense.

Plant in loose, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun on dunes or other sandy coastal ground; beach croton is a rounded, silvery-gray, aromatic native shrub covered in fine star-shaped scales that reflect intense sun and salt spray, distinct from the colorful tropical houseplant croton (Codiaeum) sold under the same common name. Small, inconspicuous cream-colored flowers appear nearly year-round in mild climates, and the plant serves as a critical host for several coastal butterfly species while its extensive root system helps trap wind-blown sand and build and stabilize foredunes. It is exceptionally salt and drought tolerant and needs no supplemental irrigation once established in appropriate sandy, well-drained soil, making it valuable for beachfront restoration and low-maintenance coastal landscaping. Avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, or regular watering, all of which shorten its life in this sand-adapted pioneer species.

Establish rooted cuttings or small nursery transplants in spring into loose, infertile, well-drained sand, since this wiry, gray-green, heather-like shrublet is adapted to the driest, most exposed dune and sandplain sites around the Great Lakes and Atlantic coast. Its tiny bright-yellow flowers open only in full sun for a few hours at a time in late spring but are visited by small native bees and flies, and its dense mat of scale-like foliage provides cover for ground-nesting insects and helps anchor loose sand against wind erosion. It requires excellent drainage and low fertility to thrive and quickly rots in heavy, moisture-retentive soils. An excellent, tough groundcover choice for a sandy, sun-baked native dune or gravel garden.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, coastal soil in full sun; beach hibiscus is a pantropical coastal shrub or small tree growing naturally at the landward edge of mangroves, sandy beaches, and coastal margins throughout the tropics. The large, round, heart-shaped leaves with their silvery, velvety undersides are distinctive and attractive, and the flowers are a rich yellow with a dark maroon center that changes to pink-red as the flowers age — the color change occurring within hours on the same flower. The wood is very buoyant and was traditionally used throughout the Pacific for outrigger canoe construction. Extremely salt-spray tolerant and useful for coastal hedging and screening. In zone 9, may be killed back by hard freezes but regrows from the base if roots are protected. The fibrous bark has traditional uses in making rope and cordage.

common_name: Beach Morning Glory (Railroad Vine, Bay Hops)
notes: Sow scarified seeds in sandy, infertile coastal soil in full sun; beach morning glory (railroad vine) is one of the most important native plants of tropical and subtropical beaches and coastal dunes worldwide — a prostrate, creeping vine that can spread 60 feet or more along the sand from a single plant, rooting as it goes, stabilizing shifting dunes against erosion with a mat of large, distinctive bilobed hoofprint-shaped leaves. The large, rose-purple morning glory flowers are produced throughout the growing season and are a beautiful ornamental bonus. Each stem can extend 100 feet, rooting at nodes wherever moisture is available. It is resistant to salt spray, storm surge flooding, and hurricane-force winds in ways that few other plants can match. An outstanding native for coastal restoration, living stabilization of beach dunes, and coastal ornamental planting. It is not invasive in its native coastal range.

Plant in loose, sandy, salt-influenced soil in full sun on the foredune or upper beach; native beach naupaka is a low, rounded, salt- and wind-tolerant shrub with thick, glossy, fleshy leaves clustered at branch tips and small, white, fan-shaped flowers that appear split in half, giving rise to the naupaka legend told throughout the Pacific and Caribbean. White, spongy, buoyant fruit follow the flowers and are dispersed by ocean currents, part of the plant's natural strategy for colonizing new shorelines. This native Atlantic and Caribbean species is an important dune stabilizer and is increasingly planted specifically to displace the ecologically invasive Pacific naupaka (Scaevola taccada), so confirm the scientific name at purchase before planting. It tolerates salt spray, sandy soil, and drought once established but is frost-tender and limited to essentially frost-free coastal sites.

common_name: Beach Naupaka (Sea Lettuce Tree, Scaevola, Beach Fan Flower)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any sandy or well-drained soil — Beach Naupaka is one of the most salt-tolerant and wind-tolerant coastal shrubs available, performing on the front line of beach dunes and oceanfront plantings where few plants survive. Scaevola taccada is a large, spreading, salt-tolerant shrub native to tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean coastlines, found naturally on sandy beaches, dunes, and coastal margins from Hawaii to Australia, through Southeast Asia, and naturalized on Gulf Coast and Florida beaches. The distinctive white to pale lavender, fan-shaped flowers — each one appearing as if cut exactly in half, with all five petals gathered on one side (a characteristic of the Goodeniaceae family that ensures specific pollinator access) — are borne prolifically throughout the warm season. The thick, fleshy, succulent-textured, bright green leaves and extremely deep root system allow the plant to thrive with saltwater spray, drought, compacted sand, and periodic flooding. Beach Naupaka spreads by underground runners to form dense, stabilizing colonies that protect coastal dunes from erosion. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, it makes an outstanding low-maintenance native or naturalized coastal shrub for beach properties, waterfront landscapes, and salt-exposed sites where conventional ornamentals fail.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; beaked yucca is widely considered the most ornamental of the tree yuccas — a slow-growing, single-stemmed Texas native from the Trans-Pecos that develops over many years into a remarkable blue-leaved specimen with a trunk to 10 feet or more, crowned by a perfect, symmetrical pom-pom of hundreds of narrow, powder-blue, rigid leaves that radiate in all directions. The color is among the most intensely glaucous blue-gray of any yucca, creating an outstanding specimen plant with a bold, sculptural presence. In late spring, a tall flower spike emerges from the center bearing a large, dense panicle of white, bell-shaped flowers that are attractive to yucca moths and other pollinators. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert limestone mountains of west Texas and northern Mexico, it is cold-hardy to zone 5 where drainage is excellent. Outstanding as a container specimen, landscape specimen, and architectural focal point — slow-growing and long-lived.

Bear Oak is a low, colony-forming native scrub oak of the acid pine barrens, serpentine outcrops, dry sandy ridges, and coastal heathlands of the northeastern United States, where it is a dominant species of the globally rare pitch pine-scrub oak barrens community from Massachusetts south to North Carolina. The small, irregularly multi-lobed leaves have a distinctive whitish, velvety underside; the abundant small acorns are a critical food source for black bears (the origin of the common name), ruffed grouse, white-tailed deer, and numerous songbirds in the barrens communities where Bear Oak's dense, fire-adapted thickets provide both food and cover. Highly fire-adapted, Bear Oak resprouts vigorously from deep rhizomes after the frequent, low-intensity fires that historically maintained pitch pine barrens and oak-scrub habitats, making it nearly impossible to eliminate once established in appropriate conditions. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Bear Oak requires the same fire-maintained, nutrient-poor conditions as its native barrens habitat.

Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; beauty bush is a Chinese monotypic deciduous shrub — the single species in its genus, and one of the last of the great early 20th-century introductions from E.H. Wilson's plant hunting expeditions in western China — that produces a brief but spectacular flowering display in late May to June when the entire large, arching, vase-shaped shrub becomes enveloped from base to tip in masses of small, pale-pink to rose-pink, yellow-throated, tubular flowers in dense clusters, creating a cloud-like, pale-pink effect that gives the plant its perfectly apt common name. After the flowers fall, the bristly, pink seed heads are themselves attractive for weeks. The shrub has a graceful, arching, fountain-like form with peeling, tan-brown bark that provides winter interest. It tolerates a wide range of soils including alkaline and dry conditions. After the spring flowering peak it is relatively plain but does not detract from the garden. 'Pink Cloud' is an improved selection with denser, deeper-pink flower clusters.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, siting them along a pond edge, wet ditch, or bog garden bed where the roots stay damp. This slender native shrub takes its name from its narrow, whorled leaves that resemble bedstraw (Galium), and it produces cheerful bright yellow, five-petaled flowers with showy stamens through the summer months. It grows naturally in wet pine savannas, pond-cypress depressions, and roadside ditches from the Gulf Coast into the Southeast, tolerating both standing water and periodic dry spells once its roots are established. Its fine texture and steady summer bloom make it a useful, low-maintenance shrub for softening the edges of a rain garden or wetland planting while feeding native bees.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; bee bee tree (Korean evodia) is arguably the most valuable pollinator tree for temperate gardens, producing massive, flat-topped panicles of small white flowers in July and August — a critical period when almost no other trees are blooming — that attract extraordinary concentrations of bumblebees, honeybees, native solitary bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects. A single mature specimen in full bloom is a memorable spectacle of insect activity. Native to China and Korea, it grows as a medium-sized tree 20–30 feet tall with large, pinnate, aromatic leaves that have an interesting citrus-like scent when crushed. In fall, the clusters of small, red to black seed capsules are ornamental and attract birds. The tree was formerly known as Evodia daniellii (or Euodia daniellii) and still appears under the old name in many references. Fast-growing, adaptable to a range of soils, and largely pest- and disease-free in North America where no major insects have adapted to feed on it.

common_name: Belinda's Dream Rose (Texas Earth-Kind Landscape Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Belinda's Dream needs little more than an occasional deep watering once established. Bred in Texas and one of the first roses awarded Earth-Kind status by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, a designation reserved for roses proven to thrive in Southern heat and humidity with minimal fertilizer, spraying, or supplemental water, Belinda's Dream produces large, fully double, clear pink, classically shaped blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance in continuous flushes from spring through frost. Its excellent resistance to black spot and powdery mildew makes it dependable in the humid Gulf South where many hybrid tea roses struggle without a regular spray program, and the vigorous, upright shrub works equally well as a specimen, a hedge, or a source of cut flowers. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new growth and the best bloom production.

common_name: Belle Etoile Mock Orange (Purple-Blotched Fragrant Mock Orange)
notes: Belle Etoile is a French-bred mock orange prized for single, pure-white, four-petaled flowers each marked at the center with a distinctive maroon-purple blotch, a striking contrast on a plant otherwise similar to standard mock orange. The flowers open in a heavy late-spring flush and carry an intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance that can perfume an entire garden corner, borne on a medium-sized, rounded, arching shrub. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune immediately after flowering to shape, since Belle Etoile blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's fragrant display.

common_name: Belle Story Rose (Soft Pink Fragrant English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and feed and water consistently through the growing season to sustain repeat flushes of bloom. Belle Story is a David Austin English shrub rose bearing large, cupped, semi-double flowers in soft blush pink surrounding a boss of prominent golden stamens, giving each bloom an open, almost peony-like or wild-rose look, backed by a strong, sweet myrrh-and-honey fragrance typical of many English roses. Its bushy, well-branched growth habit and repeat-flowering nature from late spring through fall make it a versatile choice for a mixed border or dedicated rose bed, combining the romantic form and scent of old garden roses with the modern trait of reblooming rather than flowering just once. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to encourage the next flush, and watch for blackspot in humid Gulf South summers, providing good air circulation and a preventive fungicide program if the disease has been a problem in the garden.

common_name: Bengal Clock Vine (Sky Vine, Blue Trumpet Vine)
notes: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a very large, sturdy support structure; the Bengal clock vine (sky vine) is one of the most spectacular flowering vines available for warm climates, producing pendant clusters of enormous (3–4 inch), lavender-blue to pale blue funnel-shaped flowers with white throats continuously from spring through frost in zone 9–11. The huge, heart-shaped leaves and rampant growth create a dense, cooling shade canopy over pergolas and arbors very quickly. It is an outstanding choice for covering large unsightly structures rapidly. However, this vine is INVASIVE in Florida, Hawaii, and similar warm climates — plant only where you can control its spread and never near waterways or natural vegetation. In zone 9a it often dies back to established roots in hard winters and recovers rapidly; in true zone 10+ it is a permanent, massive vine.

common_name: Benjamin Britten Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001 and named for the English composer, Benjamin Britten bears vivid orange-red to crimson, cupped rosette blooms with a strong, fruity fragrance carrying notes of blackcurrant, on a compact, bushy, disease-resistant shrub. Its vivid, saturated warm color reads strongly even at a distance in the border, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading, holding clean foliage well through humid summers.

common_name: Berenice Boddy Camellia (Cold-Hardy Light Pink Camellia japonica)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Berenice Boddy is a long-cultivated Camellia japonica heirloom valued for its soft, light pink, semi-double flowers with a subtly deeper pink center, produced over a long midseason bloom window, and for a cold hardiness that has kept it in wide circulation across Southern gardens for decades even where harsher winters limit some other camellia cultivars. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub provides dense year-round structure and glossy dark green foliage in addition to its winter and early spring flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and avoid heavy pruning except to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Berry Dazzle Crapemyrtle (Dwarf Mildew-Resistant Fuchsia-Pink Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Berry Dazzle is a genuine dwarf crapemyrtle, staying about 4 feet tall and wide, bred with resistance to powdery mildew so its foliage stays clean through the humidity of a Gulf South summer while producing a heavy show of fuchsia-pink blooms. Its compact size makes it well suited to small foundation plantings, mixed borders, or large containers where a tree-form crapemyrtle would be far too large. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through summer and fall. Because of its naturally compact habit, Berry Dazzle needs little pruning beyond removing dead or damaged wood in late winter.

common_name: Betty Corning Clematis (Fragrant Pale Lavender Bell Clematis)
notes: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Betty Corning, discovered as a chance seedling in a New York garden in the 1930s, bears delicate, nodding, bell-shaped flowers in soft pale lavender with gently recurved petal tips and a light, sweet fragrance, blooming over an unusually long season from early summer well into fall. Its refined, understated flowers and fragrance set it apart from the bolder, flatter blooms of large-flowered hybrid clematis, and because it flowers on new growth it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing bloom, a more forgiving pruning regime than many older clematis cultivars require.

common_name: Betty Magnolia (Little Girl Series Late-Blooming Reddish-Purple Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Betty is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, producing large, fragrant, deep reddish-purple, multi-petaled, tulip-shaped flowers with a paler interior on a compact, multi-stemmed tree small enough for a modest-sized yard. Like its sibling Jane, its key advantage is later bloom timing than star and saucer magnolias, helping the flowers dodge the late spring freezes that often damage earlier-blooming magnolias, and it sometimes produces a light rebloom later in the season as well. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture and avoid heavy pruning, since magnolias generally need little routine shaping beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Betty Sheffield Camellia (Iconic White Picotee-Edged Camellia japonica)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Betty Sheffield is one of the most celebrated Camellia japonica cultivars in Southern gardening, producing huge, formal to semi-double blooms in white edged and streaked with red or pink in an ever-varying, unpredictable picotee pattern that has made it a favorite exhibition flower for generations. The large, upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in mid to late winter and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its dramatic flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; big-leaf mahogany is the commercial mahogany of global trade — the source of almost all mahogany lumber in furniture, cabinets, boats, and fine woodwork worldwide. Native to tropical forests of Central and South America from Mexico to Brazil, it produces spectacular large, compound leaves up to 12 inches long that unfurl pink-bronze before maturing to glossy dark green. The enormous seed pods hang from the canopy and split to release winged seeds. The species is now protected under CITES Appendix II due to severe overharvesting, with few large trees remaining in accessible forests. In zone 10 Florida, it grows as a large ornamental shade tree, widely planted in Miami-Dade parks and neighborhoods. Planting contributes to conservation of this critically important and over-exploited tropical timber species.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in morning sun with afternoon shade; bigleaf hydrangeas are the classic summer-blooming shrubs with large mophead or lacecap flower clusters in blue, pink, or white. Flower color depends on soil pH — blue in acidic soil (pH below 5.5) and pink in alkaline soil (pH above 6.5); to maintain blue, add aluminum sulfate and maintain pH below 6.0. In the South (zones 8–9) afternoon shade is essential to prevent wilting and maintain flower quality. Old-wood bloomers (most classic varieties) should be pruned only immediately after flowering — never in fall, as this removes next year's buds. Reblooming types such as 'Endless Summer' bloom on both old and new wood, making them more reliable after hard winters.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil sheltered from strong winds in partial shade; bigleaf magnolia holds the distinction of producing the largest simple leaves of any native tree in North America — up to 32 inches long and 12 inches wide — and the combination of these extraordinary leaves with the enormous, intensely fragrant white flowers (up to 16 inches across) makes this one of the most spectacular ornamental trees in the world. The cream-white flowers in late spring to early summer have a distinctive sweet fragrance detectable from considerable distance. It grows naturally as a rare understory tree in moist, protected ravines and hollows of the South Appalachians and Gulf States. Site it in a protected, partly shaded location away from wind — the huge leaves shred easily in exposed sites. The rose-pink fruiting cones in fall are ornamental and provide food for birds.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; bigleaf maple is the dominant large deciduous tree of moist Pacific Northwest forests, producing the largest leaves of any North American maple — up to 12 inches wide with 5 deep lobes. The massive leaves produce an extraordinary large-textured canopy unlike any other temperate tree. In Pacific Northwest old-growth forests, bigleaf maple trunks and limbs are often draped in thick carpets of mosses, ferns, and licorice fern, creating some of the most magical, fairy-tale forest scenes in North America. Long, pendulous clusters of small, fragrant yellow-green flowers attract early-season pollinators. The paired samaras are large, forming a unique, U-shaped pair. Fall color is golden-yellow to bright orange. The sap can be processed into maple syrup, though production is lower than sugar maple.

Bigleaf Snowbell is a beautiful native understory shrub or small tree, native to the moist, rich deciduous forests of the southeastern United States from Virginia and Tennessee south to Florida and west to Louisiana, where it grows as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 6–12 feet tall in the shade of larger hardwoods and pines along stream terraces and ravine slopes. In May and June it produces cascading racemes of fragrant, pure white, bell-shaped flowers with conspicuous yellow stamens that cover the branches in a spectacular display and attract native bees; the flowers are best appreciated from below, where the full pendant clusters are visible against the dark canopy. The large, soft-textured leaves (up to 5 inches long) give the plant its common name and create an attractive bold texture in the shade garden. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and protect from drought; it is more adaptable to heat and humidity than Japanese snowbell (Styrax japonicus) and is a superior choice for southeastern gardens.

Plant root suckers or cuttings in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bigtooth aspen is distinguished from quaking aspen by its larger, more coarsely toothed leaves with larger, irregular, rounded teeth (reflecting the name 'grandidentata' — large-toothed). More common on sandy, dry soils and mixed hardwood-aspen forests of the Northeast and Great Lakes region. Like quaking aspen, it spreads clonally by root suckers to form groves, and the flat petioles cause the leaves to tremble in the breeze. The bark is greenish-white to cream-colored, somewhat less white than quaking aspen. Fall color is a warm golden-yellow. The bigtooth aspen grove supports important habitat structure — the trees are fast-growing pioneer species that provide early succession habitat for nesting birds and beaver activity. Excellent for naturalistic, large-scale native woodland restoration in appropriate cool climates.

common_name: Bill MacKenzie Clematis (Golden Bell Tangutica Clematis)
notes: Give this vigorous clematis a large support to scramble over and keep its roots cool with mulch or low companion plants while the top growth reaches into full sun. Nodding, bell-shaped, bright yellow flowers with thick waxy petals appear from midsummer well into fall, followed by fluffy silvery seed heads that extend garden interest into winter. Because it flowers on new wood, cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter to keep it dense and floriferous rather than bare-legged. It is one of the toughest and most vigorous of the small-flowered clematis, tolerant of poor soil once established.

common_name: Biloxi Crape Myrtle (Light Pink Vigorous Gulf Coast Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Biloxi is a vigorous, medium-to-large National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle named for the Mississippi Gulf Coast city, producing clear light pink flower clusters over a long summer bloom season on a fast-growing, upright tree. It shows strong resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem for older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars in the humid Gulf South, and develops attractively mottled, exfoliating cinnamon-and-gray bark as it matures. Fall foliage takes on orange to red tones before dropping. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune selectively to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the tree, which spoils its natural vase-shaped form.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; birchleaf spirea is a tough, adaptable native tolerant of a range of soil conditions. Rounded, toothed leaves resembling those of a birch tree cover a low, mounding native shrub topped with flat clusters of small white flowers in late spring and early summer, followed by reliable orange-red fall foliage color, native to open woods and rocky slopes across northern and western North America. Its compact, tidy, mounding habit and tolerance of a range of soils and light conditions make it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a native shrub border, foundation planting, or mass planting where a smaller-scale flowering shrub is wanted. Prune lightly after flowering to shape if needed, and expect minimal pest or disease problems from this tough, adaptable native species.

growth_habit: Pacific island sticky-seeded shade coastal tree
notes: Plant Pisonia umbellifera in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; young trees prefer some protection from the hottest afternoon sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; the sticky fruits should be considered when siting — place away from areas frequented by small birds and do not plant near bird feeders. Bird Catcher Tree is one of the more ecologically unusual trees of Pacific island forests — its narrow, club-shaped fruits are covered in an extremely sticky, clear resin that adheres to anything that brushes against it, and small birds investigating the fruit clusters can become fatally entangled. This macabre adaptation has made it a subject of scientific and popular fascination: in some Pacific island seabird colonies (particularly on Heron Island, Australia), large numbers of migratory petrels and shearwaters are trapped each breeding season. Despite its sinister seed-dispersal strategy, the Bird Catcher Tree is a handsome ornamental with very large, glossy, paddle-shaped leaves creating a bold tropical texture in the shade garden; it performs well as a specimen or screen in zone 10–12. The variegated form ('Variegata') with green and cream-white blotched leaves is particularly attractive and widely grown as an ornamental across tropical and subtropical regions.

Plant in consistently wet, poorly drained sites such as swamp edges, floodplains, or low spots where few other shade trees tolerate standing water for extended periods. Compound leaves with 7-11 leaflets turn a soft yellow in fall, and the tree's flexible wood was historically prized by indigenous basket weavers for splint material. Black ash is highly susceptible to emerald ash borer, so it is now best planted only in restoration or wetland mitigation contexts with active pest monitoring. Choose a site with year-round soil moisture, since this species does not tolerate drought.

common_name: Black Beauty Elderberry (Dark Purple-Leaved Pink-Flowered Elderberry)
notes: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade helpful in preserving foliage color in hot climates. Black Beauty produces broad, dramatic, deep purple-black leaves on a large, vigorous shrub, providing strong foliage contrast in a mixed border throughout the growing season, along with fragrant, lemon-scented pink flower clusters in early summer that mature into small dark berries. Like other ornamental elderberries it is grown primarily for its foliage impact, though the berries can be cooked into syrups and preserves; raw berries and other plant parts are mildly toxic and should not be eaten uncooked. Prune in late winter to control its substantial size and maintain good structure.

Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, well-drained riparian soil in full sun along streams and rivers; black cottonwood is the largest native hardwood of western North America, reaching 100+ feet in the riparian forests of the Pacific Coast and Cascades. The deeply furrowed, dark gray bark gives the tree its common name. The buds are large and resinous with a balsamic fragrance similar to balsam poplar. Black cottonwood riparian forests are among the most productive wildlife habitats in the western US — supporting bald eagle nesting, great blue heron colonies, beaver activity, and a rich understory of native shrubs and wildflowers. The brilliant golden-yellow fall color marks every river valley from the Cascades to the Rocky Mountains with spectacular seasonal color visible for miles. The first tree species to have its complete genome sequenced (2006), serving as the model organism for forest tree genomics.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; black dalea is a limestone-adapted Texas shrub that thrives on neglect and rots in rich, moist, or heavily irrigated soil. Fine, wiry, blue-green foliage clothes a low, rounded, woody-based shrub that bursts into bloom in fall with masses of small, rich reddish-purple to violet flowers with contrasting yellow anthers, providing an important late-season nectar source for bees just as many other xeriscape plants are finishing. Native to limestone hills and caliche flats across central and west Texas into Mexico, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established and requires no supplemental irrigation, fertilizer, or pruning beyond an occasional light shaping. Its fine texture and fall color make it a valuable structural component of a Texas-style xeriscape or native pollinator planting.

common_name: Black Diamond Crape Myrtle (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Reblooming Series)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Black Diamond is a series of crape myrtles bred for foliage that emerges near-black and holds its deep purple-maroon color through summer heat rather than fading to green, a trait that sets it apart from the many crape myrtle series bred primarily for flower color or mildew resistance. Individual selections within the series bloom in shades from pure white through pink, red, and purple, and the dark foliage makes even pale flower colors read as especially vivid by contrast. Like other modern interspecific crape myrtles (Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei), Black Diamond selections generally show good resistance to powdery mildew, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where older all-indica cultivars mildew heavily. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed, and the naturally attractive, often multi-trunked form with exfoliating bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Avoid the practice of severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, siting them where their dense form can be appreciated up close along a path or foundation bed. 'Black Dragon' is a slow-growing, densely branched dwarf selection of Japanese cedar with tightly packed, curled, near-black-green foliage that holds its color through winter without the bronzing common in larger cultivars. Its compact, irregularly conical to globose habit fits rock gardens, mixed conifer collections, and small-space foundation plantings where a full-sized Japanese cedar would quickly overwhelm the space.

common_name: Black Gold Philodendron (Melanochrysum, Dark Gold Velvet Philodendron)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Black Gold Philodendron needs consistent bright indirect light to produce its best, most dramatic foliage, but cannot tolerate direct sun which scorches the delicate velvet leaf surface. Philodendron melanochrysum is a climbing philodendron from the humid tropical forests of Colombia in the family Araceae, prized internationally as one of the finest velvet-leaved collector aroids. The leaves are large (reaching 24 inches or more on climbing specimens), elongated heart-shaped with a long, tapering tip, and velvety dark — a color so deep and saturated that it has been described as 'black-green' or 'midnight green' with a subtle sheen of bronze or gold visible in raking light, the quality that inspired the species name 'melanochrysum' (Greek: 'black gold'). The midrib and primary veins are precisely delineated in pale cream to yellowish-white, creating a striking contrast against the dark velvety surface. New leaves emerge in shades of bright copper-orange before slowly darkening to the mature near-black green. Philodendron melanochrysum has become one of the most desirable collector aroids of the current era, valued for both its exceptional leaf beauty and the dramatic transformation in leaf size as the plant matures on a climbing support. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade — black gum consistently ranks among the top native trees for fall foliage color: its leaves turn brilliant shades of scarlet, orange, purple, and wine-red as early as late August in the South, among the first of all trees to change, providing exceptionally early and long-lasting fall color in the landscape. The tree is pyramidal when young and becomes more irregular and picturesque with age; horizontal branching and somewhat layered architecture make it attractive year-round. Small, dark blue to black berries in clusters ripen in September–October and are consumed by over 30 species of songbirds and mammals. Black gum is one of the most important wildlife trees in the eastern US due to its early-ripening, high-fat fruits. Adaptable to a wide range of moisture conditions from dry upland slopes to wet bottomlands — an outstanding landscape tree for native plantings.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — black haw is a native multi-stem large shrub or small tree of open woodlands, roadsides, and fence rows throughout the eastern US, valued for four seasons of ornament: flat-topped clusters of white flowers in April, lush summer foliage, brilliant scarlet to burgundy fall color, and clusters of ripening fruit that progress from green to pink to blue-black as fall advances. The dark blue-black berries are edible and have a sweet, raisin-like flavor when fully ripe, used traditionally to make preserves, wine, and fruit leather; they are also heavily consumed by migrating birds in fall. Black haw is one of the most drought-tolerant and shade-tolerant native viburnums — it thrives where other viburnums struggle — and brings exceptional wildlife value to naturalistic plantings and food forest understories.

common_name: Black Knight Butterfly Bush (Dark Purple Buddleja)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Black Knight is the most popular dark-purple butterfly bush — a vigorous Buddleja davidii cultivar producing long (12–18 inch), conical, densely packed flower spikes in a rich, deep violet-purple to nearly black-purple color that is the darkest flower color readily available in any buddleja cultivar. The intense color contrasts dramatically with the silver-gray to gray-green lance-shaped foliage and creates an outstanding late-summer focal point. Like all butterfly bushes, Black Knight is extraordinarily attractive to butterflies, particularly swallowtails, monarchs, fritillaries, and skippers — which visit in such numbers during bloom that a well-established Black Knight shrub becomes a butterfly feeding station rivaling any other garden plant. Bloom runs from July through September (and often through October in zone 9) with regular deadheading. In zone 9, butterfly bush is a woody perennial that dies back significantly in winter and regrows vigorously from the woody base in spring. Cut back hard in February — to 12 inches from the ground — to stimulate vigorous new growth and maximum flower production. Note: Buddleja davidii is listed as invasive or potentially invasive in the Pacific Northwest and some mid-Atlantic regions; in the Gulf South it self-seeds less aggressively, but deadheading before seed set is still best practice. Sterile varieties (Buddleja 'Blue Chip,' 'Miss Ruby') are available for regions where invasive concerns apply.

common_name: Black Lace Camellia (Dark Red Anemone-Form Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Black Lace is among the darkest-flowered camellia cultivars grown, its formal anemone-form blooms opening a deep, near-black red with a center boss of small petaloids in the same dark tone, giving each flower an unusually rich, velvety intensity compared to the brighter reds typical of most camellia cultivars. It blooms in mid to late winter on a slow-growing, dense, upright shrub with glossy dark-green foliage typical of Camellia japonica. Its dramatic dark color reads best against a light background — a pale wall, light mulch, or evergreen groundcover — where the depth of the flower color is not lost in shade. Prune, if needed, immediately after bloom in late winter or early spring, before next year's buds set.

common_name: Black Lace Elderberry (Finely Cut Purple-Black Ornamental Elderberry)
notes: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade helping preserve the deepest foliage color in hot climates. Black Lace is a striking ornamental elderberry cultivar with finely dissected, almost lacy, deep purple-black foliage resembling a Japanese maple more than a typical shrub, topped in early summer by flat clusters of soft pink flowers that mature into small dark berries. It is grown primarily as a dramatic foliage accent for a mixed border rather than for fruit production, though the berries can be used for elderberry syrup and preserves after cooking, since raw elderberries and all other plant parts are mildly toxic. Prune in late winter to control size and maintain a strong branch framework, since it can grow quite large if left unchecked.

Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun; black locust is a large, fast-growing native tree of the central Appalachians that has spread across North America and much of the world, valued and controversial in equal measure. In late May to June, mature trees produce spectacular, pendulous clusters of fragrant white pea flowers — some of the most intensely honey-scented flowers of any tree — that are the primary source of the prized 'acacia honey' of Europe (where black locust is widely grown as a honey crop). In the United States, it yields exceptional amounts of nectar for beekeepers. The flowers are edible, with a sweet, floral flavor, and are traditionally dipped in batter and fried as fritters in Appalachian and Eastern European cuisines. Black locust fixes atmospheric nitrogen and rapidly improves poor soil — a valuable quality for reclamation and agroforestry. The wood is extremely rot-resistant and harder than white oak, used for fence posts, outdoor furniture, and boat-building. CAUTION: the tree spreads aggressively by root suckers and seed and is invasive in many states and countries — manage carefully. Seeds, bark, and inner wood are toxic to horses, cattle, and humans if ingested.

Black Mangrove is the most cold-tolerant and widespread of the three mangrove species native to Florida and the Gulf Coast, colonizing the mid- to upper intertidal zone above the Red Mangrove and tolerating periodic freezes that kill its more frost-sensitive relatives — a cold-hardiness that has allowed it to expand dramatically northward along Texas and Florida coasts as winters have warmed. The shallow, horizontally spreading root system produces thousands of pencil-shaped pneumatophores (air-breathing roots) that project vertically from the mud in dramatic, spiked mats, aerating the root system in oxygen-depleted estuarine sediments. Black Mangrove leaves excrete salt through special glands on their undersides, enabling survival in highly saline tidal mudflats; the flowers are an important nectar source for bees and produce the prized black mangrove honey marketed along the Gulf Coast. Plant in estuarine, tidal, or high-marsh substrate in full sun in Zones 9–11; Black Mangrove is protected in Florida and most coastal states and should only be established from nursery stock within its natural range.

Closely related to sugar maple but more tolerant of floodplain soils and drought, this tree should be planted from container stock in fall into loamy, well-drained ground. Its distinctive drooping, three-lobed leaves with fuzzy undersides and thick, fissured bark distinguish it from sugar maple, and it produces similarly vivid gold-to-orange fall foliage. It works well as a durable street or park shade tree in the upper Midwest and can also be tapped for syrup like its close relative. Once established it needs little supplemental care beyond occasional deep watering during extended dry spells.

Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; black oak is a major forest tree of the eastern United States, growing on dry to mesic upland sites from Maine to Texas and one of the primary components of the oak-hickory forest type. The leaves are large, deeply lobed, and glossy dark green, turning russet-red to orange-brown in fall. Like all oaks in the red oak group, the acorns require two years to mature and are an important high-fat food source for white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, blue jays, and many woodpeckers. The inner bark contains a yellow dye called quercitron that was historically used in textile dyeing and tanning. Black oak supports over 500 species of caterpillars and other insects in the eastern US, making it one of the most ecologically important trees for supporting bird populations. A long-lived, majestic shade tree for large properties.

common_name: Black Pearl Redbud (Near-Black Glossy Foliage Redbud)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Black Pearl is a hybrid redbud bred for the darkest foliage color available in the genus, with new leaves emerging nearly black-purple and holding that deep, glossy color with far less summer fading than older purple-leaf cultivars like Forest Pansy, which typically wash out to greenish-purple by midsummer. The glossy leaf surface, inherited in part from Texas redbud parentage, also reflects heat more effectively and resists leaf scorch better than standard purple-leaf redbuds in hot, humid Gulf South summers. Rosy-pink, pea-like flowers cover the bare branches in early spring before the dramatic dark foliage emerges, and the tree grows into a well-proportioned small shade tree with the redbud's typical graceful, spreading form. Provide afternoon shade in the hottest climates for the best color retention, and plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet sites. Prune only to remove dead, damaged, or crossing branches in late winter.

Plant in moist to moderately wet, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; black tupelo (also called blackgum or sourgum) is widely regarded as one of the finest native trees for fall color in the eastern United States, turning brilliant scarlet — sometimes the first tree in the landscape to color in early autumn — weeks before most other species. It is remarkably adaptable, growing naturally in both swampy bottomlands and dry upland ridges, and tolerates periodic flooding as well as moderate drought once established. The small blue-black fruits ripening in September are among the most intensely sought wildlife foods of the season, consumed by at least 36 bird species including wood thrushes, robins, cedar waxwings, and wood ducks. Plant while young as the deep taproot makes transplanting difficult once trees exceed 3 inches in trunk diameter.

Black Willow is the largest native willow in North America and the most important native tree for the immediate stabilization of eroding streambanks, native to the moist to wet, sandy and gravelly alluvial soils of rivers, streams, and floodplains throughout eastern North America from New Brunswick to Florida and west to Montana and New Mexico. Its aggressive, fast-establishing root system grips unstable bank soil within weeks of planting, and hardwood cuttings root readily when simply pushed into moist streambank soil in early spring — making it the fastest and cheapest native solution for stream restoration and bank protection. The pendulous, narrow, lance-shaped leaves create a graceful, weeping appearance over water; catkins appear in early spring, providing one of the season's earliest pollen sources for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Black Willow is short-lived (40–60 years) and prone to branch breakage in ice and wind storms, but its rapid establishment and wildlife value (woodpecker habitat, caterpillar host plant) make it an invaluable native pioneer for wet, disturbed sites where quick establishment is the priority.

common_name: Black-Eyed Susan Vine (Thunbergia Annual Tropical Climbing Vine)
notes: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost at 65–70°F; transplant to a trellis or support after last frost. Black-Eyed Susan Vine (not related to the native perennial Rudbeckia) is a fast-growing African tropical vine with a twining habit that quickly covers a small trellis, fence section, or mailbox post with dense foliage and continuous bloom. The distinctive 1–1.5 inch flowers have five flattened petals in a circular arrangement around a dark purple-black or white center tube — the dark center among the orange or yellow petals creating the characteristic 'black-eyed' appearance that gives the vine its common name. Colors range across orange, yellow, white, and salmon, with the classic orange-with-black-center the most recognizable form. Black-Eyed Susan Vine is particularly valuable in the Gulf South for its heat and humidity tolerance — it blooms continuously through hot summers when many other annual vines fade or slow down. The vine is well-scaled for residential use: reaching 5–8 feet rather than the 20–30 feet of aggressive vines like trumpet creeper, making it appropriate for small gardens, fences, and containers with a tomato cage for support.

common_name: Blackie Sweet Potato Vine (Deep Purple-Black Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine)
notes: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Blackie Sweet Potato Vine is a cultivar of ornamental sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) selected for its deep purple-black to near-black leaf color — the most dramatic dark foliage of any commonly grown ornamental annual, producing a cascade of deeply lobed, star-shaped leaves in a color so dark it reads as nearly black in high contrast compositions with chartreuse or white companions. The purple-black color is produced by extremely high anthocyanin concentrations in the leaf tissue — the same pigment chemistry that makes purple basil, dark caladiums, and black elephant ear dark, but at an intensity that produces the closest approach to true black available in an annual foliage plant. 'Blackie' is one of the most vigorous ornamental sweet potato vines, spreading 4–8 feet during the Gulf South growing season to create a dense, ground-covering mat of dark foliage. The vine is one of the most effective design tools for creating contrast in mixed container plantings and annual border compositions: the deep purple-black creates dramatic negative space against which brighter flowers and lighter foliage appear to glow. In zone 9, Blackie grows as a warm-season annual, though the storage tubers sometimes survive mild winters in protected positions. Outstanding paired with 'Margarita' (chartreuse sweet potato vine), 'Diamond Frost' euphorbia, or bright orange and yellow tropical flowers.

Blackjack oak is the signature tree of dry, sandy, impoverished 'blackjack' soils across the southeastern United States — its distinctive club-shaped, three-lobed leaves with a broad, rounded top and narrow base are immediately recognizable, and the tree is virtually impossible to establish in rich or moist soils, thriving only in the driest, poorest, most acidic conditions that prevent most trees from growing. Often found alongside post oak in the 'Cross Timbers' forest of Oklahoma and Texas, blackjack oak commonly forms dense, almost impenetrable thickets on sandy, infertile ridges that are habitat for some of the most specialized dry-land wildlife communities in the South. Despite its demanding site requirements, blackjack oak is a highly valuable wildlife tree: its small acorns are consumed by wild turkey, whitetail deer, and at least 30 species of birds, and the crooked, gnarled dead snags are prime nesting habitat for cavity-nesting birds. In landscapes with genuinely poor, dry, acidic, sandy soils, it is one of the most reliable native trees for creating a self-sustaining, wildlife-rich oak woodland.

Set out container-grown plants in fall into lean, sandy or gravelly, sharply drained soil in full sun, ideally against a dry wash or rocky slope similar to its native Mojave and Sonoran Desert habitat. Bladder sage produces small tubular violet-and-white flowers favored by hummingbirds and native bees, followed by its namesake inflated, papery seed capsules that persist and rattle through summer, adding ornamental interest after bloom. It is a wiry, intricately branched shrub that is nearly leafless in dry periods, an adaptation that makes it extremely drought tolerant once established. Avoid summer irrigation and heavy soils, which quickly cause root rot in this true desert specialist.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; bleeding heart vine is one of the most exquisitely beautiful flowering vines available for shaded tropical and subtropical gardens, producing pendant clusters of flowers that are truly bicolored — the white, inflated, papery calyx (the balloon-like outer part) encloses a brilliant red corolla with protruding red stamens, creating a striking red-and-white contrast that gives the plant its common name. After the red corollas drop, the white calyces persist for weeks and gradually turn pinkish-purple, extending the display. This semi-twining vine blooms most heavily in spring and again in fall and prefers the bright, filtered shade of a pergola or porch where the flowers can be enjoyed up close. In zone 9a it needs winter protection or overwintering indoors; it thrives outdoors year-round only in frost-free areas. Keep it slightly root-bound in containers for best bloom.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blood of China is an old, historic camellia cultivar valued for its dependable, vivid red winter bloom. One of the oldest camellia cultivars still commonly grown, dating to the early nineteenth century, it produces semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a vivid, saturated blood-red that opens over a long bloom season from fall through winter on a vigorous, upright shrub with glossy, deep green foliage. Its long history in Southern gardens and reliable, generous flowering have kept it in cultivation for two centuries, and it remains a benchmark red camellia against which newer introductions are still compared by collectors. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid overhead watering which can spot the flowers, and prune lightly after flowering finishes to shape if needed.

common_name: Bloodgood Japanese Maple (Red Upright Japanese Maple)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade; Bloodgood is the single most widely planted and most reliable upright red-leafed Japanese maple cultivar in American horticulture — selected for excellent dark reddish-purple leaf retention through summer (resisting the tendency of many red-leaf maples to fade to greenish-bronze in summer heat), attractive upright-spreading form reaching 12–18 feet, and reliable deep scarlet-red fall color. The five-lobed, deeply cut leaves emerge rich reddish-purple in spring and hold good color through the growing season with adequate moisture and afternoon shade. Bloodgood's vertical-upright branching pattern creates an elegant, architecturally refined form that provides seasonal interest year-round — spring leaf emergence, summer purple foliage, scarlet fall color, and attractive branching structure in winter. In zone 9, Bloodgood requires careful siting with afternoon shade, moist but well-drained soil, and protection from hot dry winds to prevent summer leaf scorch. It performs reliably as a landscape tree in zone 9 with correct placement — east-facing exposures or locations under tall trees providing dappled afternoon shade are ideal. Consistent moisture during summer heat stress periods is the key to success in zone 9. The reddish-purple bark on young stems adds winter interest.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, though this series tolerates considerably more direct sun than older azalea types once established. Bloom-A-Thon is a breeding series developed as an alternative to the Encore line, valued for a more continuous rebloom pattern through the growing season rather than distinct spring, summer, and fall flushes, along with a naturally more compact, mounded habit that needs little pruning to stay tidy. Cultivars are available across a range of flower colors including hot pink, lavender, red, and white, all sharing strong heat tolerance and repeat flowering suited to long Gulf South growing seasons. Water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to shape the plant without removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Bloom-A-Thon Hot Pink Azalea (Reblooming Compact Vivid Pink Azalea)
notes: Bloom-A-Thon Hot Pink carries vivid, saturated hot-pink flowers on a compact, naturally mounded shrub, part of a breeding series developed as an alternative to the Encore line with a more continuously repeating bloom pattern through the growing season rather than distinct spring, summer, and fall flushes. Its tidy habit needs little pruning to stay in shape, and like other Bloom-A-Thon selections it tolerates considerably more direct sun than older azalea types once established, extending its usefulness beyond the deep shade typically required for reliable azalea bloom. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to avoid removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Bloom-A-Thon Lavender Azalea (Reblooming Compact Lavender-Purple Azalea)
notes: Bloom-A-Thon Lavender carries soft lavender-purple flowers on a compact, naturally mounded shrub, offering a cooler-toned option within the Bloom-A-Thon series that pairs easily with pinks, blues, and white companion plantings. Like its siblings in the line it reblooms nearly continuously through the growing season rather than flowering only in short flushes, and its tidy habit needs little pruning to hold shape. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to avoid removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Bloom-A-Thon White Azalea (Reblooming Compact White Azalea)
notes: Bloom-A-Thon White carries clean, pure white flowers on a compact, naturally mounded shrub, providing a versatile neutral that brightens a shaded bed and pairs with virtually any other color in a mixed planting. It shares the series' hallmark near-continuous rebloom through the growing season rather than a few short flushes, and its tidy habit needs little pruning to hold shape. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, water deeply during dry spells to support the extended bloom cycle, and prune lightly right after the heaviest spring flush to avoid removing developing buds for later color.

Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; BloomStruck tolerates more direct sun than most bigleaf hydrangeas, though afternoon shade is still beneficial in the hottest Gulf South summers. Part of the Endless Summer series, BloomStruck was bred for improved heat tolerance, sturdier dark red-purple stems, and better resistance to powdery mildew than older reblooming hydrangea cultivars, along with vivid rose-pink to purple mophead flowers that shift with soil pH. It flowers on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year, so a late spring frost that damages old buds does not prevent a strong summer and fall rebloom. Flower color ranges from blue-purple in acidic soil to rose-pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

common_name: Bloomerang Lilac (Reblooming Dwarf Lilac with Spring and Summer Flushes)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and deadhead spent spring flower clusters promptly to redirect energy into the intermittent summer rebloom this series was bred to produce. Bloomerang, developed by Proven Winners, was among the first lilacs marketed specifically for reblooming, opening a full flush of fragrant purple-lavender flowers in spring like a standard lilac and then continuing to produce scattered new blooms on current-season wood through summer and into fall. Its compact, rounded habit fits smaller gardens and foundation plantings better than large old-fashioned lilac shrubs, and it shares the family's need for a real winter chill and good air circulation to perform and stay free of powdery mildew. Light monthly feeding and consistent moisture through summer support the extended rebloom cycle better than the sparser feeding a once-blooming lilac needs.

Set out young trees in fall on dry limestone slopes or upland alkaline soils, where its distinctive four-angled, winged young twigs and thick corky bark set it apart from other native ashes. This species shows somewhat greater tolerance to emerald ash borer than other North American ashes, making it a more resilient choice for restoration and specimen plantings where ash trees are otherwise declining. Its dense, rounded canopy provides good shade for dry, calcareous sites that few large shade trees can handle. Historically its inner bark sap was boiled down to produce a blue dye, giving the species its common name.

common_name: Blue Butterfly Bush (Sky Flower Clerodendrum, Uganda Clerodendrum)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Blue Butterfly Bush adapts to most soils and responds well to regular fertilization and moderate watering during active growth periods. Clerodendrum ugandense (now sometimes reclassified as Rotheca myricoides) is a large shrub from the highlands of East Africa — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania — producing one of the most charming and distinctive small flowers in the tropical plant world. Each individual flower consists of four pale blue petals spreading like wings and a single deep violet-blue lower petal curving downward, creating the unmistakable silhouette of a small blue butterfly perched on the stem. The flowers are borne in loose, airy panicles at the branch tips throughout the warm season in zone 9, with the most spectacular flushes in spring and fall. The overall effect of a plant in full bloom — dozens of tiny sky-blue butterflies hovering in clusters at every stem tip — is extraordinary and unlike any other flowering shrub available in zone 9. Blue Butterfly Bush is a fast grower that responds well to hard pruning, which stimulates vigorous new growth and repeat blooming cycles. Excellent as a container specimen on a sunny to partly-shaded patio.

common_name: Blue Cascade Distylium (Spreading Groundcover Evergreen Shrub)
notes: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, spacing plants to allow the low, wide-spreading branches to knit together into a dense evergreen groundcover over a couple of seasons. Blue Cascade is a low, mounding, ground-hugging distylium selection with fine-textured, blue-green foliage that cascades over walls, banks, and slopes, sharing the parent species' resistance to leaf spot, scale, and deer browsing along with tolerance for both wet and dry, sunny and shaded sites. Its width-over-height habit makes it a durable substitute for juniper or low spreading yew in Gulf South landscapes, where those traditional groundcover shrubs often struggle with heat, humidity, and root rot. Requires little to no pruning beyond removing an occasional wayward branch to keep the mounded outline tidy.

'Blue Chiffon' Rose of Sharon is a deciduous flowering shrub with large, double, lacy blue flowers borne from summer through fall. Plant in spring in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil, giving it room to reach its mature size. Water regularly the first year to establish, after which it becomes fairly low-maintenance and tolerant of heat. Prune in late winter or early spring to shape the shrub and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. The long bloom season and hardiness make it a reliable summer backbone for borders and hedges.

common_name: Blue Chip Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile Compact Buddleja)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth. Blue Chip was one of the first true dwarf butterfly bush cultivars introduced, staying under 3 feet tall and wide — a fraction of the size of older Buddleja davidii selections — while still producing lavender-blue flower spikes continuously from summer through frost. Its compact, mounding, sterile habit fits containers, small borders, and mass plantings where full-size butterfly bush would need constant hard pruning to control, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds heavily despite its small stature. It tolerates heat and drought well once established, needing little care beyond the annual cutback.

Plant cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; blue dawn flower (blue morning glory) is one of the most spectacularly beautiful ornamental vines for warm climates — producing abundant 3–4 inch diameter, vivid violet-blue to deep blue-purple morning glory flowers (changing color slightly through the day from bright blue in morning to blue-purple by afternoon) from spring through fall on a vigorous, twining vine that can grow 10–15 feet or more in a season. Unlike many morning glories, this is a perennial vine (in zones 9–11) that builds a woody base and becomes more vigorous each year. Spreads by self-seeding abundantly and can be invasive in warm coastal and subtropical climates — listed as invasive in Hawaii and Florida. A magnificent flowering vine for trellises, fences, and arbors in zones 8–11 where its aggressive nature can be managed. The vivid blue is particularly rare and striking among flowering vines. Hummingbirds visit the flowers.

common_name: Blue Diddley Chaste Tree (Compact Lavender-Blue Dwarf Vitex)
notes: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Diddley is a compact chaste tree selection, staying 3-6 feet tall, considerably smaller than the classic 10-20 foot vitex species, making it easier to fit into a residential foundation planting or mixed border. It produces the same fragrant, gray-green foliage and lavender-blue flower spikes as larger vitex selections, blooming from summer into fall and tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil well once established. Its smaller stature means it needs less aggressive pruning than full-sized vitex; simply cut back lightly in late winter to encourage fresh growth and maintain a tidy shape.

common_name: Blue Maid Holly (Compact Female Meserve Hybrid Blue Holly)
notes: Blue Maid carries the blue-green, glossy, spiny foliage typical of the Meserve hybrid hollies on a somewhat more compact plant than Blue Princess, with a dense, well-branched habit suited to a smaller hedge or foundation planting. Once pollinated by a compatible male such as Blue Prince blooming nearby, it produces a heavy crop of bright red berries that persist through winter and provide food for birds. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter before new spring growth begins, since Meserve hollies generally hold their form well with minimal shaping.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; blue mist shrub is a compact, late-summer flowering shrub that fills a critical role in the garden: just as most spring and summer shrubs have finished blooming, caryopteris erupts in August through October in dense clusters of small, intense china-blue to violet flowers covering the tops of the aromatic gray-green stems. The blue color is unusually saturated and clean, closer to true blue than almost any other hardy shrub. Bumblebees, honeybees, and other pollinators mob the flowers throughout the extended bloom period. The plant has a pleasant minty-sage fragrance when the foliage is brushed. It thrives in hot, dry, full-sun conditions with excellent drainage and poor soil — conditions that kill many other shrubs. 'Dark Knight' and 'Longwood Blue' are outstanding cultivars with deep blue-violet flowers. Caryopteris is outstanding combined with ornamental grasses and late perennials like sedums and asters.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support structure; Blue Moon is the most outstanding American wisteria cultivar available — a selection of Wisteria macrostachya (Kentucky wisteria, native to the central United States) that combines the non-invasive native wisteria's better behavior with several remarkable additional qualities: exceptional cold hardiness (to -40°F, reliably hardy to zone 3 — far hardier than any Asian wisteria), spectacular long racemes (8–12 inches) of silvery-blue-lavender fragrant flowers, and most remarkably, repeat blooming — producing a main spring flower flush in May followed by two or more additional bloom flushes in summer, a quality almost completely absent in single-blooming wisteria. The ability to bloom multiple times per season gives Blue Moon a greatly extended flowering season (May through August) compared to the single brief bloom of Asian wisteria. Like all W. macrostachya selections, Blue Moon is well-behaved — it does not spread invasively into natural areas as Asian wisterias do. In zone 9, it blooms most reliably with adequate chill hours (zone 9a); the floral display is exceptional in zones 3–8. Established vines bloom at a younger age than Asian wisteria and require less time to become established performers.

common_name: Blue Muffin Viburnum (Compact Native Arrowwood with Heavy Blue Berries)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally with a different arrowwood viburnum clone nearby to improve cross-pollination and berry set. Blue Muffin is a compact selection of native arrowwood viburnum bred specifically for heavy, reliable production of vivid, deep blue berries in fall, a standout food source for birds and a striking ornamental display against the shrub's red-purple fall foliage. Its smaller mature size compared to the wild species fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and hedgerows where a full-sized arrowwood would need more room. It is highly adaptable to a range of soil conditions from dry to moist and needs only occasional structural pruning to maintain shape.

Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, dry, rocky to clay, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; blue oak is named for the distinctive bluish or glaucous hue of its deeply lobed, somewhat wavy leaves, which is an adaptation to intense summer sun and drought. It is the dominant oak of the California foothills, forming extensive blue oak woodlands on dry, rocky slopes at 200–3500 feet elevation throughout the Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills. The tree is semi-deciduous — losing leaves early in summer drought and regaining them with fall rains in addition to the standard spring flush. The relatively sweet acorns were a food staple for numerous California indigenous cultures. Extraordinarily drought and heat tolerant — the blue oak's ability to survive summers with essentially no water after establishment is exceptional among deciduous trees. A landmark species for ecological restoration of California foothill habitats.

Plant scarified seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; blue palo verde is the state tree of Arizona and the signature large tree of the Sonoran Desert — a spectacularly beautiful, low-branched, naturally multi-stemmed small tree whose entire trunk, branches, and even branchlets are photosynthetically active and bright blue-green ('palo verde' = green stick in Spanish). The trunk synthesizes chlorophyll, allowing the tree to photosynthesize even when it drops its tiny leaves during drought. In spring, the tree produces a breathtaking, completely enveloping display of brilliant yellow flowers that cover every branch tip, creating one of the most spectacular natural flowering events in North American desert landscapes.
