The edible seeds (large, protein-rich) were a staple food for the Tohono O'odham and other desert peoples. Extremely drought tolerant and fast-growing for the desert. The flat seed pods are also edible when young and green. An essential native for Sonoran Desert gardens, xeriscape, and low-water landscape plantings in zones 8–11.

common_name: Blue Plumbago (Sky Blue Everblooming Gulf South Shrub for Sunny Borders and Hedges)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Plumbago is one of the most valued and widely planted flowering shrubs for Gulf South landscapes — an evergreen to semi-evergreen South African native that produces clusters of small, five-petaled, sky blue to pale periwinkle-blue flowers nearly continuously from spring through frost in zone 9, creating one of the most sustained flowering displays of any commonly grown landscape shrub. The sky blue flower color is genuinely unusual in the warm-season landscape palette and is particularly valuable as a cooling contrast to the warm orange, yellow, and red tropicals that dominate Gulf South summer gardens. The slightly sticky calyx is a minor nuisance (small pets and children can find seeds sticking to fur or clothing) but not a significant garden problem. Plumbago is fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, salt-spray tolerant for coastal plantings, and adapts to a wide range of soil types including the poor sandy soils common along the Gulf Coast. In zone 9, the tops are often damaged or killed by hard freezes but plants return quickly from the roots in spring, producing new growth and beginning bloom by late spring. The fast regrowth after frost damage makes Plumbago one of the most resilient landscape shrubs for zone 8b–9 gardens. Cassius blue butterflies use Plumbago as their primary larval host plant — an important ecological function that makes Plumbago doubly valuable in Gulf South butterfly gardens.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Prince is a male pollinator cultivar and produces no berries itself but is needed nearby for female Blue Girl or Blue Princess holly to fruit. Small, spiny, glossy, blue-green leaves cover a dense, compact, exceptionally cold-hardy holly bred by crossing English and evergreen Japanese holly species, holding its rich blue-green color and dense form through harsh winters that damage many other broadleaf evergreen hollies. As the male counterpart in the popular Blue-series holly pairing, it produces no berries of its own but is essential for pollinating nearby female Blue Princess or Blue Girl hollies, which cannot set their showy red berries without a male plant within pollination range. Plant one male for every three to five female Blue-series hollies, shear lightly to maintain shape if a formal hedge is wanted, and provide the same acidic, well-drained soil other hollies prefer.

common_name: Blue Princess Holly (Meserve Hybrid Blue Holly)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant a compatible male pollinator such as 'Blue Prince' within about 30–40 feet, since this female cultivar needs cross-pollination to produce its signature berries. Blue Princess is one of the most widely planted Meserve hybrid hollies, its glossy, spiny, blue-green leaves and heavy crop of bright red winter berries combining the cold-hardiness of Ilex rugosa with the refined, lustrous foliage of English holly, making it more reliably cold-tolerant than English holly alone. Its dense, pyramidal, evergreen form works well as a specimen, foundation planting, or informal hedge, with the winter berry display providing strong seasonal interest and food for birds. Prune, if needed, in late winter before new spring growth begins.

common_name: Blue Puffball Chaste Tree (True Dwarf Leaf Spot-Resistant Vitex)
notes: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Puffball is a genuine dwarf chaste tree, staying about 3 feet tall and 4 feet wide, a fraction of the size of the straight species, and bred with resistance to leaf spot that keeps its fragrant, gray-green foliage looking clean through a humid Gulf South summer. It produces the same lavender-blue flower spikes as full-sized vitex selections on a compact, rounded form suited to small beds, foundation plantings, or large containers. It blooms on new growth through summer into fall and tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil well once established. Cutting back lightly in late winter encourages fresh growth and continued heavy flowering.

common_name: Blue Sage (Eranthemum, Directweed, Blue Sage Shrub)
notes: Plant in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; Eranthemum pulchellum is one of the few shrubs that produces its best blooms in shade and actually prefers protection from direct afternoon sun in zone 9. Eranthemum pulchellum (Blue Sage or Directweed) is a small tropical shrub from India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia in the Acanthaceae family, notable for producing its vibrant, true-blue flowers during the cool season — December through March in zone 9 — at a time when blue-flowered plants are exceptionally rare. The individual flowers are small (1/2 inch) but borne in numerous terminal spike clusters that cover the plant in a haze of brilliant sky-blue to deep blue color, providing exceptional winter interest in the Gulf South garden. The deep green, quilted foliage is attractive year-round and the plant tolerates the dry shade under oak trees that defeats most other flowering ornamentals. Eranthemum performs remarkably well as a container specimen on shaded patios and porches, bringing winter blue-flower color to spaces that otherwise have no flowering plants. In zone 9a it may freeze to the ground in hard winters but typically resprouts. Prune hard in early spring after the main bloom flush to encourage bushy new growth.

common_name: Blue Satin Rose of Sharon (Azurri Blue Satin, Large Blue-Purple Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Blue Satin bears some of the largest flowers of any rose of sharon cultivar, single blooms up to 5 inches across in a rich blue-purple with a small red eye at the center, opening from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, well-branched shrub. Its bold flower size and saturated color make it a strong summer focal point in a mixed border or informal hedge, and like other modern rose of sharon selections it sets relatively little seed compared to old-fashioned, seed-grown althea. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, needing little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens against a strong pergola, fence, or arbor in full sun; blue sky vine is one of the most spectacular flowering vines for Gulf Coast landscapes, producing pendant clusters of enormous sky-blue trumpet flowers 3 inches across from summer through fall on vigorous vines that can grow 20–30 feet in a single season. The large, heart-shaped leaves and cascading flower clusters create an exotic tropical effect. In zone 9 plants die back after frost but regrow from the roots in spring; in zone 10–11 they are evergreen and bloom nearly year-round. Plants can become invasive in tropical areas; monitor spread. The species is sterile and does not set seed, so spreading occurs only by root suckering and vegetative growth.

common_name: Blue Star Juniper (Dwarf Silvery-Blue Mounding Juniper)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Star will not tolerate soggy or heavy clay soil and needs sharp drainage to avoid root and crown rot. This dwarf, mounding juniper produces dense, star-shaped sprays of intensely silvery-blue, prickly foliage on a slow-growing, irregular mound that stays small for many years, making it a mainstay of rock gardens, foundation plantings, and mixed conifer borders where a low, textural, blue-toned accent is wanted. Its fine, dense form needs little to no pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward branch, and it is extremely low-maintenance and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor, rocky soil that would stress most other shrubs. Deer generally avoid it, and it holds its blue color year-round in mild climates.

The Blueberry Pie butterfly bush produces dense clusters of deep blue-violet, sweetly fragrant blooms that draw butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds all summer. This vigorous flowering shrub is easy to grow and provides months of pollinator activity in the sunny border. Plant a potted shrub in full sun with well-drained soil and water moderately until established. Deadhead spent flower spikes to prolong bloom and prune hard in early spring to keep the plant compact and full of new flowering wood.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bluebird mountain hydrangea is more cold-hardy and reliably reblooms after a hard pruning better than many bigleaf hydrangeas. Delicate, lacecap flower heads ring a center of small, fertile blue (or pink in alkaline soil) flowers with a fringe of larger, showier sterile florets, a more refined, airy bloom than the tight mophead clusters of standard bigleaf hydrangea, on a compact, well-branched shrub with narrower, more textured leaves. As a mountain hydrangea it tolerates more cold and sun than typical bigleaf hydrangeas and blooms on both old and some new wood, making it more forgiving of pruning mistakes and late spring frosts that can eliminate the year's flowers on old-wood-only cultivars. Amend soil pH to control flower color — more acidic soil produces blue tones, more alkaline soil produces pink — and mulch well to keep roots cool and moist through summer.

common_name: Bluebird Rose of Sharon (Clear Blue-Violet Red-Eyed Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bluebird is a widely grown, older rose of sharon selection carrying clear blue-violet, single flowers with a small red eye at the center, considered one of the truest blue tones available among rose of sharon cultivars, blooming heavily from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. It is tough and easy to grow in average garden soil, tolerating heat and humidity well, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and water only to establish, since summer irrigation on settled soil is the leading cause of root rot and premature death in this famously drought-adapted shrub. Blueblossom ceanothus is one of the showiest California native shrubs, producing a spectacular late-winter to spring display of dense, powder-blue to deep cobalt flower clusters that smother the glossy, dark evergreen foliage and draw enormous numbers of native bees. It grows quickly, often 2 to 3 feet a year while young, reaching large shrub or small multi-trunked tree size along the coast, and works well as an informal hedge, slope stabilizer, or specimen where its rapid early growth and long-term drought tolerance can be put to use. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since old wood does not resprout reliably, and avoid heavy pruning into bare wood.

Bluejack Oak is a distinctive native tree of sandhills, xeric upland forest, and fire-maintained scrub across the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Texas, immediately recognizable among oaks by its blue-gray, paddle-shaped leaves with pale, hairy undersides that give the small tree a frosted, silvery appearance unlike any other eastern oak. Adapted to the driest, most nutrient-poor sandy soils of the coastal plain, Bluejack Oak is extremely drought-tolerant and fire-resilient, regenerating rapidly from its extensive root system after low-intensity fires that historically maintained the sandhills where it is one of the dominant trees. The small acorns ripen in fall and are a critical food source for white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, small mammals, and Florida Scrub-Jays in dry upland communities where larger mast-producing oaks may be absent. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun — Bluejack Oak will not tolerate clay, excess moisture, or shade.

Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; bluff oak is a medium to large white-oak group oak of the lower Piedmont and Gulf Coastal Plain, naturally growing on rocky bluffs, dry slopes, and upland sites from North Carolina to Georgia and Alabama. The leaves are variable but typically club-shaped with rounded lobes, resembling a smaller or more graceful white oak leaf. Like all white-oak group oaks, the sweet acorns ripen in a single season and are immediately germinated by squirrels and blue jays. The tree provides important acorn mast for wildlife and supports the full suite of moth and butterfly caterpillars that depend on native oaks. Relatively uncommon in cultivation and underused compared to its relatives, bluff oak is a dependable, drought-tolerant native for dry, upland settings in the Gulf South.

common_name: Blush Noisette Rose (The Founding Noisette Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Blush Noisette is historically significant as the original rose of the Noisette class, raised from seed in Charleston, South Carolina around 1811-1817 by rice planter John Champneys and further developed by nurseryman Philippe Noisette, making it one of the very few major rose classes bred in North America. It produces large clusters of small, soft pink, sweetly fragrant blooms in nearly continuous flushes through the growing season, on a vigorous, arching shrub that can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a modest climber. Noisette roses remain some of the best-adapted roses for the heat and humidity of the Deep South, and Blush Noisette needs little more than a sunny site and occasional shaping to perform for decades.

common_name: Blush Pink Nandina (Soft Pink New-Growth Compact Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Blush Pink is a dwarf, mounding nandina selected for new foliage that emerges soft candy-pink before maturing to green, giving a softer, pastel-toned flush of color than the red new growth typical of most dwarf nandina cultivars. Its compact, dense habit fits foundation plantings and mixed containers, and the plant is sterile, producing no berries and avoiding the self-seeding that has made standard nandina an invasive problem in parts of the Southeast. Little pruning beyond removing occasional damaged canes is needed to keep its naturally tidy shape.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bobo is the most compact of the widely available panicle hydrangea cultivars — a dwarf selection staying just 2.5–3 feet tall and wide while producing flower panicles nearly as large as those of full-size cultivars like Limelight. This unusually large flower-to-plant-size ratio gives Bobo a heavily blooming, almost top-heavy appearance at peak bloom that creates a dramatic visual impact from a very compact plant. The large, cone-shaped flower panicles open pure white in mid-summer and transition through blush-pink to dusty rose as fall approaches — a 3–4 month evolving color display. Bobo's compact, mounding habit and relatively sturdy stems that hold the large flower heads erect without flopping make it one of the most practically useful panicle hydrangea introductions for residential landscape use. Like all Hydrangea paniculata cultivars, Bobo blooms on new wood and is pruned hard in late winter (to 12 inches or shorter) to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum flower production. This new-wood blooming habit means the timing of pruning is not critical — unlike the French hydrangeas that must be pruned at precisely the right time or lose the season's bloom. In zone 9, afternoon shade helps maintain flower color and extend the display season through the intense summer heat.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Bodinier's beautyberry is the Chinese species most widely considered superior to the American beautyberry (Callicarpa americana) for ornamental use, producing extraordinarily vivid, metallic violet-purple berries in very large, densely packed clusters along the arching branches in October–November — the intensity of the color approaches an almost unreal, electric quality that is one of the most striking autumn fruit displays in temperate horticulture. The clusters are larger, more densely packed, and the berry color more metallic and saturated than the American native. The cultivar 'Profusion' is the most widely planted and has become a standard of the British and American garden for its exceptional berry production. Unlike the American species, Bodinier's beautyberry is hardy to zone 5 without dieback. The pink to lilac summer flowers are small and inconspicuous. After frost removes the leaves, the vivid purple berry clusters on the bare, arching branches are an extraordinary sight that persists into winter and is eaten by birds.

Set transplants in well-drained soil amended with compost, spacing them 4 to 6 feet apart to allow the arching branches to develop freely. Water regularly through the first growing season to establish deep roots, then reduce irrigation as the shrub becomes more drought tolerant. Cut stems back by about one-third in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and the most prolific berry production the following autumn. The metallic violet-purple berry clusters persist on bare stems well into winter and are a standout in the landscape.

Plant in acidic, consistently wet, peaty soil in partial shade; bog laurel is a low, wiry, evergreen shrub of northern peat bogs, with narrow leaves that are dark green above and whitish underneath, and in late spring produces clusters of small, saucer-shaped, rose-pink flowers held above the foliage on the current season's new growth. Growing naturally in permanently saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic bogs alongside sphagnum moss, it is a plant for a true bog garden or an engineered rain garden basin kept consistently wet and acidic, not an ordinary moist border — normal garden soil and drying out are both fatal to it over time. Like its relative mountain laurel, all parts of the plant contain grayanotoxins and are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from grazing animals and out of reach of children and pets. Where conditions genuinely suit it, bog laurel needs essentially no maintenance once established.

Bog Rosemary is a native circumpolar evergreen shrub of the coldest, wettest, most acidic sphagnum bogs and arctic tundra of the Northern Hemisphere, prized among bog garden enthusiasts for its attractive, narrow, blue-green, rosemary-like evergreen leaves with rolled margins and beautiful clusters of small, pink, globe-shaped flowers in spring. Like other members of the blueberry family adapted to the specialized bog environment, Bog Rosemary requires extreme growing conditions — permanently saturated, strongly acidic (pH 3.5–5.0), nutrient-poor peat — and is entirely unsuitable for conventional garden soil or climates south of Zone 6. All parts of the plant contain grayanotoxins and are toxic to livestock; the specific epithet polifolia ('gray-leaved') refers to the glaucous appearance of the foliage. Plant rooted cuttings in permanently wet sphagnum peat in full sun; Bog Rosemary is an outstanding native specimen for cold-climate bog gardens, peat gardens, and tundra-habitat restorations where its specialized conditions can be maintained.

Plant container-grown transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bolivian fuchsia is frost-tender and grown as a container specimen brought indoors for winter outside zones 9b-11. This large, vigorous, shrubby fuchsia from the Andean cloud forests of Bolivia and Argentina produces long, drooping clusters of slender, tubular, deep red flowers in nearly continuous bloom through the warm season, drawing hummingbirds in large numbers to even a single well-grown plant. Its bold size and shrubby, almost tree-like habit set it apart from the more compact hybrid fuchsias typically grown in hanging baskets, making it a striking specimen for a large container or the back of a shaded border in mild climates. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain its heavy, continuous bloom.

Bonica was the first shrub rose to win the All-America Rose Selections award and remains a benchmark for easy-care landscape roses. It bears clusters of soft pink, lightly fragrant double blooms almost continuously from late spring to frost, followed by ornamental orange hips if deadheading is skipped late in the season. Give it full sun and average garden soil; established plants need only light pruning in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood. Its disease resistance and dense, rounded habit make it a reliable choice for hedges, borders, or mass plantings.

common_name: Boscobel Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Set plants in full sun with at least six hours of direct light and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply and regularly during the establishment year. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season for continued bloom. Boscobel is one of David Austin's more disease-resistant English rose introductions, bred to hold clean, healthy foliage with minimal spraying even through humid summers, an advantage for Gulf Coast gardens where black spot pressure is heavy. Its rosette-shaped, salmon-pink to peachy-apricot double flowers with a light myrrh fragrance are held upright on strong, slightly arching stems, giving the shrub a neat, well-mannered look in the border rather than the floppy habit of some older English roses. It repeats reliably through the growing season with regular deadheading and moderate feeding.

Plant in almost any soil in full sun to full shade; Boston ivy is the quintessential self-clinging wall vine of ivy-covered colleges and historic buildings, native to China and Japan and widely planted worldwide for its ability to cover brick, stone, and concrete walls with a seamless carpet of foliage. The simple, three-lobed leaves (variable in shape) are overlapping and smooth-textured throughout summer, then transform in autumn to some of the most spectacular fall colors of any vine — brilliant crimson, scarlet, and burgundy, rivaling the finest maples in intensity. Unlike English ivy, Boston ivy is deciduous — letting winter light through the wall and providing summer cooling by shading the masonry while becoming bare in winter. It climbs by tiny, disc-tipped adhesive tendrils that grip masonry firmly without growing into mortar. The small blue-black berries in fall are an important food source for birds. Unlike its cousin Virginia creeper (P. quinquefolia), Boston ivy's three-lobed leaves have a slightly smoother texture and the vine tends to stay flatter against a wall.

Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in deep to part shade; bottlebrush buckeye is one of the most dramatic large shade shrubs in American horticulture, producing spectacular 8–12 inch cylindrical flower spikes (panicles) of densely packed white flowers with long, prominent, reddish-pink stamens in midsummer — hence 'bottlebrush' — at precisely the time when most shade shrubs have finished blooming, filling a critical gap in the summer woodland garden. The bold, tropical-looking, palmately compound leaves (5–7 leaflets each to 8 inches long) create dense shade and turn clear yellow in fall. Native to the understory of moist forests in Alabama and Georgia, it is one of the rare large shrubs that performs as well or better in dense shade as in sun. Spreads by suckers to form broad, dramatic colonies. Hummingbirds and large bumblebees are the primary pollinators. All parts are mildly toxic if ingested.

Plant in very well-drained soil in full sun; bougainvillea is the quintessential tropical vine of warm-climate gardens, producing massive displays of brilliantly colored papery bracts (the true flowers are small and white at the bract center) in shades of magenta, red, orange, pink, white, and bicolor from spring through fall — especially spectacular in late winter and spring in zone 9. The plant is a vigorous, thorny scrambler that must be trained on a strong trellis, arbor, or fence; it is not self-clinging and must be tied. Light stress (slight drought, slightly root-bound) dramatically increases bloom production. In zone 9, it may suffer frost damage in cold winters but typically regrows from the base; in zone 10–11 it blooms nearly year-round. Prune after each major bloom cycle to encourage re-blooming. Extremely heat, drought, and salt tolerant once established — one of the most spectacular flowering vines available for Gulf Coast landscapes.

common_name: Bougainvillea Spectabilis (Great Bougainvillea, Paper Flower, Bugambilia)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Bougainvillea blooms most prolifically in full sun with moderate stress — overwatering and over-fertilizing produce excessive vegetative growth at the expense of flowering. Bougainvillea spectabilis is a massive, vigorous, thorny, woody climbing vine native to eastern and central Brazil, widely regarded as one of the most spectacular flowering plants in the subtropical and tropical world. Like all Bougainvillea, the apparent flowers are actually highly colored papery bracts (modified leaves) — magenta, purple, crimson, orange, pink, white, yellow, or bicolor depending on cultivar — surrounding the tiny, inconspicuous true flowers within. The bracts persist on the vine for months and are produced so profusely that a specimen in full bloom is literally buried under color. B. spectabilis is one of the two primary species (along with B. glabra) from which nearly all cultivated Bougainvillea hybrids have been developed; it is distinguished by its larger, pubescent (hairy-textured) bracts and more vigorous growth than B. glabra. The iconic vine of Mediterranean and tropical architecture — covering walls, pergolas, gateways, and entire buildings in swaths of brilliant color — Bougainvillea is the definitive plant of zone 9b-11 Gulf Coast, South Texas, California, and Florida landscapes. Sharp, stout thorns require care when pruning.

common_name: Bower Vine (Bower of Beauty, Pink Bower Vine, Jasmine Pandorea)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Bower Vine blooms most prolifically in full sun but performs well in partial shade and actually benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Pandorea jasminoides is a vigorous, twining, evergreen vine native to eastern Australia (Queensland and New South Wales) in the Bignoniaceae family, one of the finest Australian native vines for subtropical and warm-temperate gardens worldwide. The plant produces attractive, pinnately-compound leaves with 5–9 leaflets that create a fine-textured, airy, dark-green canopy on whatever structure the vine covers. In spring and intermittently through the warm months, the vine produces clusters of funnel-shaped to trumpet-shaped flowers in shades of white to soft pink, typically with a distinct deep rose-pink to rose-red interior throat — the clean, elegant color combination has made Bower Vine one of the most popular ornamental vines for zone 9-11 gardens, walls, and arbors. The flowers are lightly fragrant in warm conditions. Multiple cultivars are available: 'Rosea' (deeper pink), 'Lady Di' (pure white with no pink throat), and 'Rosea Superba' (larger, deeper flowers). Bower Vine is relatively free of pest and disease problems in zone 9 conditions, making it one of the most reliable and beautiful low-maintenance ornamental vines for Gulf Coast gardens.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — Bowman's root is a graceful, airy native perennial of eastern woodland understories, producing a cloud of delicate five-petaled white to pale pink flowers on reddish-tinged branching stems in late spring to early summer — one of the most elegant of all native shade-garden plants. The leaves are trifoliate (three leaflets), giving it the specific epithet, and color attractively to orange-red in fall. It grows naturally in moist, rich, rocky woodland slopes and ravine banks from Ontario south to Georgia. Unlike most shade perennials it has a somewhat shrubby, upright structure rather than a mounding habit, adding height and structure to the shaded border. Bowman's root serves as a host plant for several native moth species and provides nectar for hummingbirds. Once established it is long-lived and low-maintenance. An outstanding native for the woodland garden in zones 4–9.

Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; box honeysuckle is a Chinese evergreen shrub grown as a boxwood alternative for formal hedging in shade and difficult conditions where true boxwood (Buxus) struggles — its small, paired, glossy, oval leaves and dense, twiggy growth habit create the same refined, fine-textured, formal effect that makes boxwood so desirable, but it tolerates more shade, heat, drought, and alkaline soil than boxwood. Small, creamy-white, fragrant flowers appear in spring, followed by small, translucent, purple-red berries. It clips beautifully into formal geometric shapes and responds vigorously to shearing. 'Elegant' and 'Maigrün' (Golden-tipped new growth) are improved selections. An underused, extremely tough alternative to the blight-susceptible boxwoods increasingly being replaced across North American gardens.

Boxelder is a native maple unlike any other — with pinnately compound leaves (3–7 leaflets) that bear no resemblance to the classic maple leaf — native throughout almost the entirety of North America east of the Rockies and naturalized well beyond, growing in river floodplains, bottomlands, stream corridors, and disturbed urban habitats with the same casual colonizing energy as cottonwood. Often dismissed as a weed tree in horticultural circles, Boxelder provides important ecological services that more ornamental trees cannot match: it is the only host plant for the Boxelder bug (Boisea trivittata), a harmless true bug that is a significant food source for many native birds; female trees produce abundant samaras (paired winged seeds) that are an important winter food for evening grosbeaks, finches, and other seed-eating birds; and the fast-growing tree provides rapid canopy cover for riparian restoration. Tolerant of flooding, drought, poor soils, and urban pollution, Boxelder is effectively impossible to kill once established and self-seeds prolifically — use it intentionally in naturalistic, riparian, or wildlife plantings where its resilience is an asset.

common_name: Bracken's Brown Beauty Magnolia (Cold-Hardy Southern Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Bracken's Brown Beauty is one of the most exceptional named Southern magnolia cultivars for cold-climate performance — consistently hardy in zone 5 with reliable protection and zone 6 without protection, significantly colder than most Southern magnolia cultivars. It was selected by Ray Bracken of Bracken's Greenhouses in Easley, South Carolina, from seedlings grown at the Secrest Arboretum in Wooster, Ohio — selected specifically for cold hardiness in a climate where Southern magnolias are not traditionally grown. Despite its northern origin, it performs beautifully in zone 9 and throughout the Southeast. The leaves are particularly distinctive: smaller and more densely arranged than many cultivars, with an exceptionally rich, dark cinnamon-brown to rusty-red woolly undersurface (indumentum) that is thicker and more prominent than most selections, creating year-round visual interest as the wind moves the leaves to reveal the contrasting undersides. The medium-sized flowers (5–7 inches) are intensely fragrant and produced prolifically from May through September in zone 9. Bracken's Brown Beauty grows to full tree size (20–30+ feet) and is appropriate for medium-to-large landscape plantings.

Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; bracted hydrangea blooms later than most hydrangea species, from late summer into fall, avoiding damage from late spring frosts that can nip earlier bloomers. Hydrangea involucrata is a Japanese species notable for its unusual flower buds, which are wrapped in showy, papery bracts that peel back as the lacecap-form flower clusters of pale blue-lavender to pink open in late summer, later than nearly any other hydrangea. Its late bloom time and distinctive bud structure make it a valuable addition for extending hydrangea interest into fall in a shaded border, and it stays relatively compact compared with many other hydrangea species. Give it rich, evenly moist soil similar to bigleaf hydrangea, and protect from harsh winter cold at the northern edge of its hardiness range.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with support to climb; bracted passionflower is a smaller-flowered Texas and northeastern Mexico native passionvine, distinguished from the showier maypop by its more finely three-lobed leaves and modest, pale greenish-white to cream flowers backed by a distinctive ring of leafy bracts. Like other native passionflowers, it is an essential larval host plant for gulf fritillary and other passionflower-dependent butterflies, and the vine is often grown specifically for that wildlife value rather than for its comparatively small, less palatable fruit. It spreads by root suckers to form a thicket over time, which is useful for naturalizing a butterfly garden corner but should be watched in smaller, mixed borders. Where winters bring hard freezes, expect the top growth to die back, with new shoots emerging from the roots once the soil warms in spring.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bracted viburnum is a rare native selected for good garden performance and drought tolerance once established. Flat clusters of small white flowers open in mid-spring on a dense, upright shrub with dark green, toothed leaves, followed by blue-black fruit that provides food for birds into fall, a garden performance similar to more commonly grown viburnums but from an uncommon Georgia native species discovered along the Savannah River in the twentieth century. Its combination of good drought tolerance, dense habit, and reliable spring bloom and fall fruit makes it a worthwhile, less common alternative to more commonly planted viburnum species for a native shrub border or wildlife garden. Water during establishment, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and prune lightly after flowering if shaping is needed.

Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial to full shade; Brazilian plume flower is a South American native soft-wooded shrub that delivers one of the most spectacular flower displays possible in a shaded landscape — dense, upright, plume-like clusters of tubular rose-pink to deep magenta flowers from late summer through frost, and again in spring. The large, oval, dark-green leaves are handsome throughout the year. Hummingbirds visit the flowers repeatedly. Requires consistent moisture and resents drought; water deeply during hot, dry spells. Cut back by one-half to two-thirds in early spring to promote vigorous, floriferous new growth. In zone 9 it may be killed to the ground by hard frost but re-sprouts from the base; mulch heavily in winter.

Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Brazilian red cloak is a bold, fast-growing tropical shrub grown for its striking upright flower spikes, in which large, deep red-maroon bracts overlap like shingles and part to reveal pure white, tubular flowers, creating a strong color contrast that blooms heavily from late summer into winter in frost-free climates. Large, glossy, dark green leaves give the shrub a lush, substantial presence even between flowering flushes, quickly filling out a tropical border or privacy planting where winters stay mild. It grows rapidly and can become leggy without regular pinching or a hard pruning in early spring, which encourages the dense, well-branched form that shows off the flower spikes best. Where frost is a risk, grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter, or mulch heavily and expect it to die back and resprout from the roots after a light freeze.

Plant Duranta stenostachya in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; prune after flowering to maintain compact shape; more cold-hardy than Duranta erecta, tolerating light frost to about 28°F. CAUTION: the berries are toxic to humans and pets. Brazilian Skyflower is a close relative of the widely grown Pigeon Berry (Duranta erecta) but with a distinctly different character: where D. erecta is a large, sprawling, vigorous shrub or small tree reaching 15 feet, D. stenostachya stays compact and rounded at 3–6 feet, making it much more manageable in typical garden situations. The flower spikes are narrower and more erect than D. erecta's cascading clusters, giving a slightly different visual effect; the violet-blue to lavender flower color is similar. Originally from the cerrado and forest-savanna transitions of interior Brazil, it is adapted to the seasonal drought and lean soils of tropical savannas — making it more drought-tolerant than D. erecta once established. The compact form makes it an excellent choice for informal hedges, mixed shrub borders, and foundation plantings in zone 9–11 gardens. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the flowers just as reliably as they visit D. erecta. The yellow-orange berry clusters are ornamental through winter and much appreciated by mockingbirds and thrushes — but should not be eaten by people or pets.

Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Brazilian tree fern develops a short, scaly trunk over time and produces striking architectural fronds up to 3 feet long with a distinctive ladder-like arrangement of leaflets. New croziers and expanding fronds emerge in vivid copper to red tones before maturing to dark, glossy green. The contrast between the dark mature fronds and the red new growth is especially dramatic in spring. It thrives in sheltered, humid, shaded positions in zones 8b-11, excellent at the base of a building wall or among large tropical perennials in a sheltered courtyard garden.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Brazilian yellow sage (yellow jacobinia, golden justicia, golden plume) is a Central American tropical shrub of the family Acanthaceae that produces dense, upright, cone-shaped spikes of bright-yellow, tubular, two-lipped flowers in the fall and winter months — at a time when yellow-flowering shade plants are exceptionally rare. The golden-yellow flower spikes, clustered densely at the tips of the arching stems, provide a vivid autumn-to-winter color display in the warm-climate garden that is nearly unmatched among partial-shade flowering shrubs. The large, soft, oval, velvety-hairy leaves are attractive and provide bold foliage texture in the shade garden. Like other shade-tolerant members of the Acanthaceae, it performs remarkably well in the dappled light of open tree canopies — one of few large-growing shade-tolerant shrubs that produce ornamental spikes of flowers rather than solitary tubular flowers. In zone 9 it freezes to the ground but regrows vigorously in spring. Cut back after flowering to encourage compact regrowth.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; breath of heaven is a South African Cape fynbos shrub prized for two complementary qualities: the fine, soft, needle-like, heather-like aromatic foliage that releases a sweet citrus-like scent when brushed or touched — earning the common name 'breath of heaven' — and the winter to early spring flowering, when the entire shrub becomes covered in hundreds of tiny, five-petaled, pink to white-pink flowers so numerous and so densely covering the fine, feathery foliage that the plant appears dusted with confetti, giving the alternative common name 'confetti bush'. The flower display in late winter and early spring, when the fine-textured shrub is smothered in small, clear-pink flowers against the bright-green, aromatic, needle-like foliage, is one of the most cheerful winter garden displays available in zone 9 landscapes. The aromatic foliage is attractive year-round and the light, fine texture provides a delicate contrast to bolder neighboring plants. It demands excellent drainage — the primary requirement for success — and lean soils. A valued landscape shrub in California and in Gulf Coast Mediterranean-style gardens.

Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Plumeria pudica, commonly sold as Bridal Bouquet, is a distinctive species with elongated, glossy, dark green, fiddle- or spoon-shaped leaves entirely different from the broad, oval leaves of standard Plumeria rubra hybrids, giving it a unique tropical texture even when not in bloom. Unlike most plumeria, it is evergreen and nearly ever-blooming in frost-free conditions, producing clusters of pure white flowers with a soft yellow throat and a mild, pleasant fragrance almost continuously rather than in a single seasonal flush. It also branches and fills out more readily than many plumeria, forming a fuller, bushier plant at a younger age. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors before temperatures drop into the 40s, since it tolerates cold poorly even compared to other plumeria, and reduce water in winter if kept in a cooler spot. Outdoors in frost-free zones it makes an excellent low-maintenance flowering hedge or specimen.

common_name: Bridal Wreath Spiraea (Plena Old Fashioned Bridal Wreath)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Spiraea prunifolia, the Bridal Wreath Spiraea, is one of the oldest ornamental shrubs in continuous cultivation in American gardens — grown since the early nineteenth century for its exceptional late winter to early spring flower display of small, perfectly double, white, button-like flowers arranged in dense rows along each long, slender, arching branch before any foliage appears. The distinctive flower arrangement on the bare stems is unlike any other spiraea: dozens of small, round, double flowers line up in rows along the branch length from base to tip, covering the entire structure with a lacy white effect. The fully double, non-fading white flowers persist longer than single-flowered types. Unlike the more common Vanhoutte spiraea (S. × vanhouttei), Spiraea prunifolia has glossy, deep-green, relatively small leaves that turn attractive orange-red to burgundy in fall — providing outstanding fall color that S. × vanhouttei lacks. Spiraea prunifolia grows somewhat more upright than Vanhoutte (5–7 feet tall, wider than tall) with a graceful arching form. In zone 9, it blooms in late February through March — one of the earliest spring-blooming shrubs in the landscape. Like Vanhoutte, it must be pruned only immediately after flowering; pruning in fall or winter removes the old-wood flower buds essential for the spring display.

common_name: Brilliant Red Tropical Hibiscus (Classic Large Single Red Hibiscus rosa-sinensis)
notes: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Brilliant is one of the classic large-single tropical hibiscus cultivars — a time-tested variety producing very large (5–6 inch), brilliant solid-red, single flowers with the typical flared, five-petaled hibiscus form and prominent staminal column. The pure, intense red of 'Brilliant' — without the pink undertones of some red hibiscus or the orange overtones of others — is the quintessential tropical hibiscus red that defines the color archetype. Individual flowers last one day but are produced in continuous succession throughout the warm season on well-fertilized, adequately watered plants — a mature hibiscus in peak condition can produce 20–40 open flowers daily. Hibiscus rosa-sinensis is the national flower of Malaysia and a widely revered cultural symbol across Southeast Asia and the Pacific — Brilliant's classic single-red form is the type most closely associated with this symbolic status. In zone 9, Brilliant grows as a large perennial shrub in protected locations but may be severely damaged or killed by hard freezes — container-grown specimens provide the flexibility to overwinter indoors during cold spells. The continuous bloom, vivid color, and hummingbird attraction make Brilliant one of the most effective tropical accent plants for Gulf South summer container displays and protected courtyard gardens.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; brittlebush is a rounded, silvery-leaved desert shrub whose felted, gray-white foliage reflects intense sun and reduces water loss, and it is one of the most visually dominant plants of the Sonoran Desert, covering hillsides in a haze of bright yellow, daisy-like flowers on tall, leafless stalks each spring. The dried, resinous stems were historically burned as incense by Spanish missions and Native peoples, giving the plant one of its alternate common names, incienso. Fast-growing and short-lived compared to many desert shrubs, it typically declines after five to ten years but self-sows readily in disturbed, sunny, well-drained soil to replace itself. Prune out dead or woody stems in fall to encourage fresh growth, and avoid rich soil or regular irrigation, both of which shorten its already modest lifespan.

Plant in average, well-drained soil, tolerant of dry, poor, or root-filled ground, in partial to full shade; broad-leaved butcher's broom is an unusual evergreen shade shrub whose apparent 'leaves' are actually flattened, leaf-like stems called cladodes, broader and softer than those of the common spiny butcher's broom (Ruscus aculeatus), and — unlike that spiny relative — pleasant and safe to handle. Tiny greenish flowers appear directly on the surface of the cladodes in late winter, and on female plants pollinated by a nearby male, these are followed by bright red berries that persist attractively through much of the year. It tolerates deep, dry shade under mature trees better than almost any broadleaf shrub, spreading slowly by rhizomes into a low, dense, glossy-textured colony that needs essentially no maintenance once established. A useful, unusual evergreen for the most difficult dry shade in a woodland or shade garden, valued by flower arrangers for its long-lasting cut foliage.

Sow fresh seed in fall as soon as it is collected, as broad-leaved linden requires a sequential warm then cold stratification period to break its compound dormancy; germination is slow and may extend into the second spring, so mark the planting site carefully and keep it weed-free. Plant in deep, fertile, moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, where the tree will develop a stately, broadly domed crown reaching 60 feet or more at maturity. In early summer the tree produces hanging clusters of fragrant creamy-yellow flowers along winged bracts that attract bees in enormous numbers — broad-leaved linden is considered one of the most important bee-forage trees in European temperate forestry and produces a prized light honey. Harvest flower clusters when fully open but before they begin to brown and dry them quickly in a warm, airy space; the dried flowers (tilleul) brew into a delicate, mildly sedative herbal tea with a long tradition in French and central European folk medicine.

Set this narrow, columnar juniper in full sun and well-drained soil; it tolerates poor, dry, and rocky ground once established. Space plants at least 5 feet apart when used as a screen so the slender pyramidal form fills in without crowding. Water regularly the first year to establish deep roots, then reduce watering as it becomes quite drought-tolerant. Its dense evergreen foliage holds green year-round, making it a reliable windbreak or accent needing almost no pruning.

Plant rooted cuttings in spring into lean, acidic, excessively well-drained sandy soil in full sun, reproducing the coastal heathlands and pine barrens from Newfoundland to New Jersey where this rare, fire-adapted shrub grows alongside bearberry and lowbush blueberry. Its needle-like evergreen foliage and inconspicuous, wind-pollinated flowers in earliest spring give it a heath-like texture that fills a distinct niche in a dry, sandy native planting. Because natural populations are globally rare and disturbance-dependent, use only nursery-propagated plants and avoid rich or moisture-retentive soils that this dune and barrens specialist will not tolerate.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to part shade; brown boronia is legendary among Australian garden enthusiasts for producing one of the most intensely beautiful, complex, and powerful floral fragrances of any plant in the world — a rich, warm, spicy-floral scent with fruity undertones that has been compared to a combination of roses, sweet peas, and anise, extraordinarily powerful from a single small shrub and impossible to ignore in the garden. The fragrance of Boronia megastigma is considered by perfumers and garden writers to be among the finest natural plant scents, and commercial extraction of boronia fragrance compounds has been used in perfumery for over a century. The flowers themselves are small, pendant, four-petaled, in a distinctive two-tone coloring: dark, brownish-red to mahogany on the outside (giving the common name 'brown boronia') with bright yellow-green on the inside, hanging in clusters from the fine, dark-green, needle-leaved branches in spring. The visual effect is quiet and understated — but the fragrance transforms every garden space within range. Notoriously demanding in cultivation outside its native coastal peat heaths of Western Australia, but the reward of its fragrance for those who succeed is without peer.

Buckley's oak (also called Texas red oak) is a native tree of the limestone hills and rocky canyons of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Cross Timbers region — the most important red-oak-type tree for autumn color in central Texas. In October and November, its deeply lobed leaves turn brilliant shades of orange-red, red, and scarlet — spectacular fall color unusual for the semi-arid Texas Hill Country where most oaks turn only dull brown or rust. Because it grows naturally on the shallow, rocky limestone soils and caliche of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau, it is better adapted to alkaline soils than most other red oaks in its group; it is one of the few native oaks that will tolerate the alkaline, calcium-rich soils common across central Texas that cause iron chlorosis in acid-adapted species. The medium-sized acorns are consumed by white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and scrub-jays, and the tree provides important larval host resources for hundreds of native Lepidoptera. Excellent choice for limestone-soil native landscapes in central Texas and the Oklahoma Cross Timbers.

Buckwheat tree is an evergreen native shrub or small tree of the Gulf Coastal Plain, forming dense thickets in bogs, bay swamps, and along black-water stream margins from South Carolina to eastern Texas — a dominant species in some Gulf Coast wetland plant communities known as 'titi bays.' In early spring, dense racemes of fragrant white to pinkish flowers smother the branches before the leaves fully emerge, providing critical early-season nectar for native bees, including honeybees, which produce a distinctively flavored 'titi honey' prized by beekeepers. The distinctive buckwheat-shaped winged fruits ripen in summer and persist into fall, giving the tree its common name. Grow at the margins of rain gardens, constructed wetlands, or low-lying acidic areas where the soil stays moist to wet — it forms a naturalistic thicket that provides excellent wildlife cover and spring pollinator support.

Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in naturalized settings along stream margins, pond edges, and moist woodland borders; buckwheat vine is a native vine of the southeastern US in the knotweed (Polygonaceae) family, producing distinctive, unusual fruit structures — each seed is enclosed in a winged, membranous structure resembling a miniature winged seed that aids wind dispersal, giving the plant an unusual ornamental quality in fruit. The white to cream flower clusters in summer attract bees and butterflies. In moist, shaded bottomland settings it can twine vigorously through shrubs and small trees, providing textural interest at the forest margin. An unusual and underappreciated native vine for naturalistic, moist woodland garden designs in zone 9a.

common_name: Buff Beauty Rose (Apricot-Buff Hybrid Musk Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 4-6 feet apart to allow for its broad, spreading habit. Bred by Ann Bentall and introduced in England in 1939, Buff Beauty is a hybrid musk rose bearing large clusters of warm apricot-buff, fully double blooms with a strong, sweet musk fragrance, aging to a soft cream as they open. As a hybrid musk, it is more shade-tolerant than most roses, flowering respectably with as little as four to five hours of direct sun, which makes it useful in gardens where a fully open, all-day-sun spot isn't available. The lax, arching canes can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber against a wall or fence, and the plant blooms in flushes from late spring through fall with good resistance to blackspot. Prune back by about a third in late winter if grown as a shrub, or simply thin out old wood if trained as a climber, since Buff Beauty flowers on both old and new growth.

Bur oak is the most majestic and long-lived of all North American oaks — individual trees commonly live 400–600 years and may exceed 1,000 years on favorable sites, developing massive, deeply furrowed, corky trunks and broad, spreading crowns of great character and presence. The acorns are the largest produced by any North American oak, each nearly half-enclosed in a distinctive fringed, mossy cup that gives the species its alternate name 'mossycup oak' — these large, low-tannin acorns were the most important food item for many plains tribes, who harvested and processed them into flour. Bur oak's extraordinary drought resistance — the result of a massive taproot that may penetrate 14 feet in the first year — made it the tree that historically crossed the prairie/forest boundary into the Great Plains, creating the legendary prairie grove ecosystems that supported bison herds. Like all oaks, it supports hundreds of native Lepidoptera species as host plants and its acorn crops feed deer, turkeys, bears, woodpeckers, and dozens of other wildlife species. A tree to plant for future generations.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Burford holly is one of the most commonly planted landscape hollies in the South — a large, dense, rounded to broadly mounding shrub reaching 8–15 feet tall with exceptionally glossy, dark-green foliage and notably reduced spines compared to the species (most leaves have only a single terminal spine rather than the species' four-five-spined leaves). This reduced spininess makes Burford far easier to work around than typical Chinese hollies. The outstanding feature that separates Burford from all other landscape hollies is its self-fruitfulness: female plants set abundant, large, bright-red berries every year without any male pollinizer plant nearby — a critical advantage in residential settings where only one plant will be grown. The red berries ripen in fall and typically persist through winter. Burford is adaptable to a wide range of soils and extremely heat-tolerant, performing reliably in Gulf Coast zone 9 without the summer stress that affects some hollies. A dwarf form ('Dwarf Burford Holly', Ilex cornuta 'Burfordii Nana') reaches 3–4 feet and is suitable for foundation plantings and low hedges. Prune in late winter or spring after berries have served their wildlife purpose.

Plant in acidic, well-drained soil with a pH between 5.0 and 6.5, incorporating sulfur or acidifying fertilizer if your native soil is alkaline. Burgundy loropetalum establishes readily in Gulf Coast landscapes and rewards minimal pruning with its best natural form—avoid heavy shearing, which reduces flowering and distorts the graceful branching habit. Magenta-pink fringe flowers appear most heavily in late winter and spring, but sporadic bloom continues throughout the warm months. Mulch the root zone to conserve moisture and maintain the soil acidity this plant prefers.

Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun to partial shade; burning bush is one of the most widely planted ornamental shrubs in North America — famous for its extraordinary, blazing, neon-scarlet to crimson fall color, one of the most brilliant autumn displays of any deciduous shrub. The distinctive corky, wing-like ridges on the stems ('winged' euonymus) are immediately distinctive and attractive year-round. Extremely adaptable — tolerating a wide range of soils, light conditions, and drought. However, burning bush has escaped cultivation and naturalized in forests throughout the eastern and midwestern US, where it displaces native understory vegetation. Listed as invasive in Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and other states — banned from sale in some states. Native plant alternatives with comparable fall color include: native highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) and black gum (Nyssa sylvatica). If planting, choose a dwarf, compact cultivar ('Compactus') away from natural areas and remove the small orange-red berries before birds can disperse the seeds.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun along the coast or partial shade in hotter inland gardens, watering occasionally through the first two summers to establish a deep root system; bush anemone is a naturally rare California endemic, restricted in the wild to a handful of Sierra Nevada foothill canyons, yet it performs reliably in cultivation across a wide range of climates. Glossy, leathery, dark evergreen leaves set off large, fragrant, pure white, anemone-like flowers with prominent golden stamens in late spring to early summer, creating a striking display against the deep green foliage. Once established it tolerates considerable summer drought, though it looks and blooms best with an occasional deep soak during the driest months rather than complete neglect. Prune lightly after flowering to shape and remove any winter-damaged wood, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

Bush honeysuckle (Diervilla) is an easy-to-grow native flowering shrub of eastern North American rocky woods and dry slopes, producing small but cheerful, tubular yellow flowers in summer that turn orange-red as they age, providing an attractive bicolored display on the same plant; the compact habit and beautiful foliage that turns brilliant orange-red in fall add to its landscape value through three seasons. Despite sharing the 'honeysuckle' common name with the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), Diervilla is a completely different and well-behaved native genus that poses no invasive risk and is in fact declining in parts of its range due to habitat loss. It spreads slowly by underground stolons to form colonies — useful for erosion control on shaded, dry slopes where few other shrubs perform reliably — and tolerates dry shade better than almost any other flowering native shrub, including spots under shallow-rooted maples and in the dry, poor shade near building foundations. Hummingbirds and native bumblebees visit the flowers, and the autumn foliage provides late-season color in woodland garden situations.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bush poppy is a California chaparral native that produces a uniquely beautiful combination — narrow, gray-green, willow-like, glaucous leaves on an arching shrub and, from spring through summer, large (2–3 inch), bright golden-yellow, four-petaled poppy flowers that open to a pure, clear, unornamented yellow of exceptional purity against the glaucous foliage. The simple, clean flower form — each petal a perfect, softly-textured quarter-circle of yellow — combined with the silver-blue foliage creates an effect of cool, refined beauty appropriate to the dry, sunny California garden. It is native to chaparral slopes throughout the California coast ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, growing on dry, rocky, lean soils in full sun and requiring no summer irrigation once established. Seed germination in the wild is triggered by the heat and chemicals of chaparral fires. In the garden, fire-adapted plants like this one can be started from cuttings or from smoke-treated seed. Outstanding for drought-tolerant California native plantings where it provides yellow flowers and silvery foliage contrast.

This slow-growing spruce features weeping, lace-like branches clothed in soft blue-green needles for an elegant textured specimen. Plant in full sun and cool, moist, well-drained soil; it appreciates protection from harsh, drying winds. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially while young, as Engelmann spruce dislikes prolonged drought. Little pruning is needed beyond removing damaged branches, letting the graceful cascading habit develop naturally.

Plant divisions or container specimens in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial to full shade; butcher's broom is a Mediterranean native evergreen subshrub that fills a nearly unique niche — it thrives in the deep, dry shade under mature evergreens and dense broadleaf trees where almost no other ornamental plant survives, producing stiff, spine-tipped, dark-green cladodes (flattened stem segments that function as leaves) with tiny greenish-white flowers in midwinter followed by ornamental bright-red berries (on female plants only, requiring a male in proximity) that persist through winter. The plant is extremely drought-tolerant and salt-resistant once established. The stiff, prickly branches were historically used to sweep butcher's blocks. An invaluable plant for the most challenging dry-shade conditions in zone 7–9 gardens.

Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Buttercup Bush is drought-tolerant once established and thrives on neglect in sandy or rocky soils where other shrubs struggle. The cheerful golden-yellow flowers bloom for an extended season from summer into fall, providing reliable late-season forage for native bees and other pollinators. In zone 8, hard freezes will kill the top growth to the ground, but the plant reliably resprouts from its root system in spring. Cut frosted stems back to the crown in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and a tidy shrub form.

common_name: Buttercup Tree (Poro Poro, Rose Silk Cotton)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; the tree naturally defoliates in a dry season to bloom. Cochlospermum vitifolium (buttercup tree or poro poro) is a Mexican and Central American tropical deciduous tree that creates one of the most dramatic dry-season flowering displays in the tropical world. The tree is deciduous in response to drought or cooler temperatures: as it drops its large, deeply-lobed, vine-like leaves (the species name 'vitifolium' means 'grape-leaved,' referring to the leaf shape), the bare branches produce large (3–4 inch across), brilliant golden-yellow flowers with five silky, crinkled petals and prominent yellow stamens — like enormous buttercups or golden poppies — covering the entire leafless tree in a blaze of yellow. The effect is similar to a yellow Tabebuia or yellow jacaranda — a complete crown of golden flowers on bare branches — spectacularly showy. The tree is fast-growing, drought-tolerant, and appropriate for tropical dry landscapes; it can actually flower more prolifically with a dry season. Fluffy, cotton-like seed fibers in the large seed capsules provide the name 'silk cotton.' Bark fibers have traditional uses in rope and textile making in Mexico. An exceptional and underused ornamental for zone 10–12 tropical gardens.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade with shelter from late-season frosts; buttercup winter hazel is the smallest and most refined of the Corylopsis species, producing delicate, drooping racemes of pale yellow, primrose-scented flowers in late winter or very early spring — among the earliest ornamental shrubs to bloom, often appearing in late February or March alongside snowdrops and before forsythia. The small flowers are each shaped like a tiny cowslip, nodding in clusters on bare winter stems. The heart-shaped, finely toothed leaves emerge bronze-green after flowering and mature to fresh green with fine veining. More compact than other winter hazels, it is well suited to smaller gardens and shaded woodland edges where its subtle, early charm can be appreciated up close. Site in a sheltered spot to protect blooms from late freezes.

Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Butterfly Japanese maple needs protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, which scorch its variegated leaves. Small, delicate, blue-green leaves are irregularly margined in creamy white, often blushed pink on new growth, giving the airy, upright canopy a light, fluttering appearance that inspired the cultivar's name, on a naturally narrow, columnar form well suited to a smaller garden or container where wider-spreading maples would be too large. Its fine-textured, variegated foliage provides season-long interest, turning soft yellow-pink in fall, and its upright habit makes it a good vertical accent for a shaded border or Japanese-style garden without the footprint of broader cultivars. Site out of hot afternoon sun and strong wind, which quickly scorch the delicate variegated leaf margins, and water during dry spells, especially for the first few years after planting.

Nick the hard seed coat, soak seeds overnight, then start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in well-drained potting mix at 70–80°F; transplant after last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in zone 9–11. Butterfly senna produces masses of bright golden-yellow flowers from fall through early winter on arching branches with compound, ferny foliage — one of the showiest fall-blooming shrubs for Gulf Coast and South Florida landscapes. It is a critical host plant for cloudless sulphur butterfly larvae, and the adult butterflies nectar heavily on the bright flowers. Growth is fast and may require pruning to maintain shape; cut back hard in early spring before new growth begins to keep the plant compact. The related Senna alata (candlestick plant) blooms in candle-like spikes and is equally effective in zone 9–11.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; buttonbush is an essential native shrub for wet, seasonally flooded, or permanently moist sites — pond margins, rain gardens, wet swales, and creek banks where it thrives in conditions that eliminate every other large shrub. The spherical, white, pincushion-like flower heads appear in midsummer and are one of the finest native pollinator plants available, attracting an extraordinary diversity of native bees, bumblebees, skippers, and swallowtail butterflies that few other native plants can match. The round, persistent seed heads provide winter food for waterfowl and songbirds. An outstanding choice for rain garden perimeters, bioswales, and naturalized wet areas in zone 5–10 landscapes.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest climates. Buttons is a compact, low-growing gardenia cultivar that produces an abundance of small, single, star-shaped white flowers rather than the large double blooms of classic gardenia varieties, and while individual flowers are smaller, plants bloom so heavily that the effect is a dense, sweetly fragrant flush of white against small, glossy dark-green leaves. Its dwarf, dense habit makes it well suited to low borders, container growing, and small-space gardens where standard gardenias would need frequent pruning to control size. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer during the growing season, keep soil consistently moist but well-drained, and watch for the whitefly and scale issues common to gardenias in humid climates.

Buttonwood is a native coastal tree or large shrub of the upper tidal fringe and coastal upland that transitions from saltwater to terrestrial habitats, growing at the landward edge of mangrove forests along both coasts of Florida, the Florida Keys, and throughout the Caribbean. Though often grouped with mangroves in coastal conservation contexts, Buttonwood is not a true mangrove but a member of the Combretaceae family that grows in the mangrove associates zone and shares the extreme salt tolerance that characterizes its habitat. The small, button-like seed heads that give it its common name are distinctive; the dense, slow-growing wood is exceptionally hard and was historically used for fuel, charcoal production, and as a building material. Highly salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and wind-resistant once established, Buttonwood is an excellent native landscaping choice for coastal South Florida homeowners seeking an attractive, low-maintenance native tree or large hedge plant for Zone 9b–11.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun to partial shade; Caddo maple is a naturally heat-tolerant and drought-adapted selection of sugar maple (Acer saccharum) collected from the Caddo-Kiowa country of the Wichita Mountains in southwestern Oklahoma — the southern edge of the species' native range. Plants grown from seed collected at this southerly provenance are significantly better adapted to the summer heat and periodic drought of the southern plains and lower Midwest than sugar maples sourced from Pennsylvania or Vermont nurseries. The fall color is the brilliant red, orange, and yellow typical of sugar maple. Used in street tree trials in Kansas and Oklahoma where its heat tolerance has proven superior to northern-sourced maples. The best available choice when a true sugar maple is desired for gardens in zones 6–8 in the transition-zone South.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart for a dense flowering hedge or mass planting. Caldwell Pink is a 'found rose' — a once-common variety that fell out of the nursery trade but survived for decades at an old homesite before being rediscovered, propagated, and named by Texas rose rustlers for the town of Caldwell, Texas, where it was found. It produces a profusion of small, fully double, medium-pink pompon blooms in dense clusters nearly continuously from spring through fall, on a compact, well-branched polyantha shrub. It is extremely disease-resistant and largely free of the blackspot and mildew problems that plague many modern roses in humid climates, needing no spraying and very little care beyond an annual light shaping. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and heat, making Caldwell Pink one of the most reliable low-maintenance flowering shrubs for Gulf Coast gardens.

Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; California black oak is the largest and most widely distributed of the California red-group oaks, growing from the Oregon border to Baja California in the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges at mid-elevations. The deeply lobed, bristle-tipped leaves (characteristic of the red oak group) are large and bold — up to 8 inches long — turning brilliant gold, orange, and russet in fall for some of the finest fall color of any California native. The large, nutritious acorns were a dietary staple of numerous Sierran indigenous cultures including the Miwok and Paiute, providing a high-calorie starch food after leaching of bitter tannins. California black oak is an important food source for Steller's jays, band-tailed pigeons, acorn woodpeckers, mule deer, and black bears in mountain habitats. A magnificent landscape tree for large-scale California and Pacific Northwest plantings.

Plant in lean, sharply drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; California buckwheat is a foundational chaparral and coastal sage scrub shrub prized above nearly any other plant for the sheer volume and diversity of native bees, wasps, and butterflies its flowers support. Narrow, gray-green, needle-like leaves cluster along woody stems below rounded umbels of tiny white to pink flowers that bloom from late spring through fall and dry to attractive rust-brown seed heads that persist through winter and add off-season texture. It thrives on neglect once established, needing no summer irrigation and often declining if watered on the same schedule as lawns or border perennials nearby. Leave the dried flower heads standing through winter for seed-eating birds and structural interest, then lightly shape in late winter before spring growth resumes.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this adaptable shrub tolerates clay, sand, and loam equally well once established. Water regularly for the first two summers to help roots reach deep moisture, then taper to infrequent irrigation or rely on winter rainfall alone. The berries ripen from green through red to near-black, providing a long season of color and food for birds. Lightly tip-prune after fruiting to maintain a tidy shape if desired, or allow to grow into a large screening shrub.

common_name: California Gold Bougainvillea (Golden-Orange Vigorous Tropical Vine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun on a strong, permanent trellis, arbor, or wall, since mature vines become heavy and woody over time. California Gold produces masses of vivid golden-orange papery bracts, the true flowers being the small white blooms tucked inside, covering the vigorous, thorny vine through the warm season, especially heavily when the plant is kept on the dry, slightly stressed side, since bougainvillea blooms more prolifically with somewhat restricted water and root space than when pampered. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and is one of the more cold-hardy bougainvillea colors for the warmer parts of zone 9, though hard freezes will still cause dieback that regrows from the roots in spring.

Set out a container-grown, cutting-propagated plant in fall so it can root in before the rainy season, giving it a trellis, fence, or shrub to twine up and part shade in hot inland gardens (it tolerates more sun near the coast). Growth follows the old nursery adage of "sleeps, creeps, then leaps" — expect a slow first year or two before the vine takes off, and it drops its heart-shaped leaves and goes dormant in summer heat. This species is the essential, near-exclusive larval host of the Pipevine Swallowtail throughout coastal and interior California, and conservation groups actively promote planting it to rebuild local populations.

Plant in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; California privet is one of the most widely planted formal hedge shrubs in North American landscape history, valued for extremely fast, dense growth, glossy semi-evergreen foliage, and outstanding tolerance of hard, frequent shearing into tight formal hedges, screens, and topiary shapes. Small white flower clusters appear in early summer with a strong fragrance some find pleasant and others find heavy, followed by small blue-black berries that birds spread widely — this vigorous self-seeding has made California privet a documented invasive species in wooded and disturbed areas across much of the eastern and midwestern United States, where it forms dense thickets that crowd out native understory plants. Where hedging is still desired, shear regularly before flowering to reduce berry production and self-seeding, or consider a non-invasive alternative such as Podocarpus, Distylium, or Ternstroemia for new plantings near natural areas. Established hedges tolerate poor soil, pollution, salt spray, and neglect better than almost any other hedging shrub.

Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial shade; California spicebush is the western native counterpart of the eastern Carolina allspice (Calycanthus floridus) — a large, suckering deciduous shrub from the stream banks and moist canyon slopes of California's Coast Range and Sierra Nevada foothills. The unusual, dark burgundy-red to brownish-red flowers are unlike those of most ornamental shrubs — large, with many strap-shaped petals in overlapping whorls like a water lily, with a distinctively spicy-fruity fragrance. All parts of the plant have a spicy, slightly vinegar-like fragrance when crushed or cut — the bark was used by Indigenous peoples as a spice and medicine. The large, dark green, sandpaper-textured leaves (rough on the upper surface) are attractive through the growing season. A natural companion to other California riparian and canyon shrubs in mixed planting. More heat-tolerant than the eastern sweetshrub, adapting to hot, dry-summer California coastal and inland valley gardens with summer irrigation.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil with consistent moisture; California spicebush is native to riparian corridors, streambanks, and canyon bottoms in California and performs best where roots can access consistent moisture — it is more drought-sensitive than its eastern relative Calycanthus floridus and should not be allowed to dry out completely during summer.
