Calycanthus occidentalis produces large, uniquely structured flowers from late spring through summer — burgundy-red to maroon, multi-petaled blooms with a warm, spicy-sweet fragrance resembling red wine and cloves, making it a standout sensory plant in woodland gardens and shaded borders. The bold, rough-textured, aromatic leaves turn yellow in fall. An excellent large-scale native shrub for shaded rain gardens, streamside plantings, and California native gardens in zones 6–9; pairs beautifully with native ferns, Ribes species, and Cercis occidentalis.

Transplant container-grown trees in spring near stream banks, drainage swales, or large open lawns where this California and Southwest native's thirsty, wide-spreading roots have room to run. Its mottled, exfoliating white-and-tan bark and massive, often multi-trunked, gnarled form make it a dramatic focal point in western landscapes and riparian restoration projects. Large maple-like leaves provide heavy dappled shade in summer, and the tree tolerates seasonal flooding as well as the region's dry summers once its roots reach groundwater. Provide supplemental irrigation for the first several years until the tree is deep-rooted and self-sufficient.

Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 4 weeks before) in well-drained, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; canary creeper prefers cooler conditions than garden nasturtium (T. majus) and blooms most freely in partial shade and cool summers. Tropaeolum peregrinum is a vigorous annual climbing vine from the Andean cloud forests of Peru with deeply five-lobed, gray-green leaves and profuse, small (3/4 inch), bright-golden-yellow flowers with two large, fringed upper petals that create an extraordinary resemblance to small yellow canaries or birds-in-flight, giving the plant its charming common name. It is an outstanding annual climber for a partially shaded trellis, fence, or pergola and is useful where full-sun annuals fail; it provides nectar for hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees. Less commonly grown than garden nasturtium but more refined and tolerant of shade and cooler conditions.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Canary Island dragon tree is extremely drought-tolerant once established and tolerates brief light frost but is best suited to zones 9-11 outdoors. Thick, stout, gray trunks branch dichotomously (splitting into two at each growth point) into a distinctive umbrella-shaped crown of stiff, sword-like, blue-green leaves, an ancient, sculptural silhouette that can take a century or more to reach the tree's full mature form. Native to the Canary Islands and named for the dark red resin, called dragon's blood, that oozes from any wound in the bark or trunk, it is exceptionally long-lived, slow-growing, and drought-tolerant once established, making it a striking, low-water architectural specimen for a xeriscape or Mediterranean-style landscape. Water only occasionally once established, avoid overwatering which is the most common cause of failure, and grow young plants in a large container to move under cover during any hard freeze.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade; Canary Island foxglove is a tender, shrubby relative of the true foxgloves (Digitalis), native to the laurel cloud forests and scrublands of Tenerife and Gran Canaria in the Canary Islands. Unlike the familiar biennial foxglove, it is an evergreen shrub 3–6 feet tall producing firm, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves and tall upright spikes of densely packed, tubular flowers in a distinctive shade of warm orange-yellow to tawny-amber — one of the few foxglove-family plants producing orange flowers. The flower color is unique among foxglove relatives and is particularly striking in the warm half-tones of the late afternoon light. The flowers are visited by sunbirds in their native habitat and are attractive to hummingbirds in cultivation. Related to Digitalis but classified in the separate genus Isoplexis. A collector's plant of considerable distinction, excellent in mild coastal gardens in zones 9–11 as a specimen in dappled shade.

common_name: Candlestick Senna (Empress Candle, Ringworm Bush, Seven Golden Candlesticks)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Candlestick Senna grows rapidly — a spring-planted seedling often reaches 6–8 feet and begins blooming by August–September in zone 9. Senna alata (Candlestick Senna or Empress Candle) is a stunning tropical shrub or sub-shrub native to tropical America and now naturalized throughout the world's tropics, producing one of the most dramatic flower displays in the subtropical garden: erect, rigid, conical flower spikes 12–18 inches long closely packed with bright golden-yellow individual flowers that open progressively from the base upward — the unopened buds at the tip are enclosed in overlapping orange-brown bracts that suggest golden candle flames, inspiring the common name. Multiple spikes arise simultaneously from each stem tip in August–November in zone 9, creating an extraordinary golden spectacle when the plant is in full bloom. The large, pinnately compound leaves are architectural and attractive even out of bloom. Senna alata is also famous for its potent antifungal properties — leaf extracts have been shown effective against Microsporum canis, Trichophyton species, and other dermatophytes responsible for ringworm and tinea infections, hence the folk medicine name 'Ringworm Bush.' An outstanding butterfly plant as well — Orange-barred Sulfur and Cloudless Sulphur butterflies use it as a larval host plant throughout the Gulf Coast.

common_name: Canyon Creek Abelia (Copper New-Growth Arching Abelia)
notes: Canyon Creek is an abelia selection prized for foliage that emerges a rich copper-orange in spring, matures to yellow-green with darker green centers through summer, and warms again to bronze-copper tones in cool fall weather, giving three-season color on the same graceful, arching, cascading branch structure typical of larger abelia cultivars. Small, fragrant, white, tubular flowers appear in loose clusters from late spring through frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds, and the plant's spreading habit makes it a good choice for a mixed border or slope where its weeping branch tips can drape naturally. Like other abelias it tolerates clay soil, heat, humidity, and drought once established, needing only an occasional thinning of old wood after the main spring flush to keep it looking fresh.

Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, calcareous or sandstone soil in partial shade in the canyon microclimate; canyon maple is the native maple of the Rocky Mountain and Great Basin canyons and the Edwards Plateau of Texas, producing spectacular fall color — brilliant orange, red, and scarlet tones — in otherwise largely dry, autumn-green landscapes. It is the maple that colors the walls of Lost Maples State Natural Area in the Texas Hill Country each October in brilliant red and orange, one of the most spectacular fall color displays in Texas. The tree grows naturally in sheltered canyon walls and north-facing slopes where moisture and shade moderate summer heat, and it is adapted to calcareous, rocky soils unlike the acidic-soil preferences of eastern maples. The small stature (10–30 feet) and excellent fall color make it the ideal native shade tree for small alkaline gardens in central Texas.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; canyon sage is a compact, shrubby perennial salvia from rocky canyon habitats of the Chihuahuan Desert in west Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, producing a long succession of vivid violet-blue flowers throughout the warm season. It forms a dense, dome-shaped subshrub of small, aromatic, gray-green leaves with persistent woody lower stems and soft herbaceous upper growth. The flowers are intensely blue-violet — among the most saturated blues in any salvia — and are produced in whorled spikes throughout spring, summer, and fall with particular abundance after rains. It is a hummingbird magnet throughout its bloom season. Canyon sage combines extreme drought tolerance with outstanding ornamental quality and a refined, compact habit that fits into almost any garden setting. In humid Gulf Coast climates, excellent drainage in lean soil is critical to long-term success; it performs excellently in raised beds, rock gardens, and containers.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; cape honeysuckle is a South African evergreen scrambling shrub-vine that is one of the most reliable and versatile hummingbird plants for Gulf Coast and southwestern zone 9–11 gardens, producing clusters of long, tubular, brilliant scarlet-orange to orange-red, honeysuckle-like flowers in flushes from fall through spring — at the opposite end of the warm season from most summer-blooming hummingbird plants — when migrating and wintering hummingbirds most need reliable nectar sources. It grows as a large, lax, sprawling shrub or a climbing vine if given support, and can be trained against walls, over fences, or left to sprawl as a groundcover on banks. Tolerates partial shade (blooming acceptably in open tree canopy), drought, heat, poor soil, and alkaline conditions once established. In zone 9 it may freeze back in hard winters but recovers quickly from established roots. 'Aurea' (clear-yellow flowers, more refined in habit) is an attractive alternative to the standard orange form. Excellent as a slope cover, espaliered vine, and sprawling hedge.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cape plumbago is one of the most beloved and widely used flowering shrubs of Gulf Coast landscapes, producing continuous clusters of sky-blue to powder-blue flowers from spring through the first frost — a color rarely achieved by other summer-blooming shrubs in the heat. The arching, semi-scandent stems naturally mound and sprawl, making it ideal for slopes, large containers, espalier on fences, or informal hedges. It is remarkably drought tolerant once established and thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 9. A white cultivar ('Alba') is also widely available. Prune back by one-third in early spring to encourage fresh, dense regrowth and a compact habit; in zone 9 it remains evergreen year-round. An outstanding long-season butterfly and bee plant, particularly attractive to swallowtail butterflies.

common_name: Carajuru (Chica Vine, Blood Vine, Bejuco de Indio)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Carajuru blooms most prolifically in full sun and produces attractive foliage display in partial shade. Fridericia chica (formerly Arrabidaea chica, Bignonia chica) is a vigorous, woody, tendril-climbing vine native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and tropical South America (Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela) in the Bignoniaceae family — one of the most historically significant ornamental plants of the tropical Americas for a quality beyond its ornamental flower display: its leaves yield 'carajuru' or 'chica,' a brilliant red-orange to brick-red natural dye that has been used by indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin for body decoration, face painting, textile dyeing, and ceremonial preparation for thousands of years, and that remains in use today. The vine produces clusters of attractive, rosy-pink to magenta-pink, 1.5-inch, tubular trumpet flowers with five spreading petal lobes, produced through the warm months and attracting hummingbirds. The compound leaves (2 leaflets + tendril) contain the carotenoid pigment bixin and related compounds responsible for the red dye — the same class of compound that gives annatto its orange color. Beyond its ethnobotanical significance, F. chica is a fast-growing, flowering tropical vine with genuine ornamental value in zone 10-12 warm garden conditions.

common_name: Cardinal Creeper (Red Morning Glory, Hybrid Cypress Vine)
notes: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms; nick or soak seeds 24 hours before planting; the vine grows quickly to 6–15 feet with minimal care. Ipomoea x multifida (cardinal creeper or cardinal vine) is a naturally occurring hybrid between cypress vine (I. quamoclit) and red morning glory (I. coccinea) — combining the most appealing ornamental features of both parents. From cypress vine, it inherits the deeply pinnately cut, feathery, bright-green foliage that creates an extraordinarily delicate, lacy texture. From red morning glory, it inherits slightly larger, more robust flowers (3/4–1 inch across) of the same intense cardinal-red as its parents. The result is a vigorous, fast-growing, annual ornamental vine that covers trellises, fences, and arbors with a curtain of delicate, feathery foliage and an abundance of small, brilliant-red, star-shaped tubular flowers from summer through fall. The flowers are irresistible to hummingbirds, which visit constantly throughout the day. The vine self-sows readily in warm climates and can be treated as a perennial in zone 9–10. A classic hummingbird garden plant that requires almost no care once established on a trellis.

Plant Odontonema tubaeforme in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment and through summer; cut back hard in late winter (before new growth emerges) to encourage compact, bushy growth and prevent woodiness; propagate easily from stem cuttings. Cardinal's Guard is one of the most valuable shade-garden flowering shrubs for the Gulf Coast — its spectacular scarlet-red flower spikes in fall and winter create color in shaded spots at a season when most other plants have stopped blooming, and the flowers are an important fuel stop for hummingbirds during fall migration. The plant performs remarkably well in the partial shade of large trees, where most other fall-blooming shrubs fail to flower well; in deep shade, it will grow vegetatively but reduces flowering. In zone 9, it dies back to the ground after hard frost and re-emerges from the roots in spring, re-establishing quickly to bloom again by October–November. In zone 10–12, it grows as a substantial, multi-stemmed shrub year-round. The tall, elegant flower spikes with their waxy, bright-red individual flowers are also excellent cut flowers. An indispensable plant for Gulf Coast butterfly and hummingbird gardens.

common_name: Carefree Beauty Rose (Cold-Hardy Own-Root Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Bred by Dr. Griffith Buck at Iowa State University and introduced in 1977, Carefree Beauty is one of the best-known results of his decades-long program to develop tough, own-root roses that survive harsh Midwestern winters without protection and resist disease without spraying — goals that happen to also produce excellent performance in the hot, humid Gulf South. It bears large, semi-double, clear pink blooms with a light fragrance in generous flushes from late spring through fall, followed by an abundant crop of showy orange-red hips that provide fall and winter interest and feed birds. The vigorous, upright shrub shows strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew and needs minimal care once established. Prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, and leave some hips on the plant through fall for ornamental and wildlife value.

Root stem cuttings (caution — wear gloves, latex is a skin and eye irritant) or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; Caribbean copper plant is a tropical American shrub or small tree grown entirely for its spectacular, deep-mahogany to wine-red, rounded foliage — the constantly produced, oval, alternate leaves emerge in brilliant coppery-red and mature to deep burgundy-maroon, maintaining their rich coloring throughout the season. In the tropical garden it provides a bold, jewel-toned color anchor that contrasts dramatically with lime-green foliage (aralia, euphorbia tirucalli 'Sticks on Fire'), silver-gray plants, and orange-flowered tropical perennials. It is fast-growing to 10–15 feet in tropical climates, functioning as a screening shrub or specimen small tree; in cooler zones 9 gardens it may be damaged by hard frost but resprouts from the roots. Insignificant yellowish flowers. All parts contain toxic, milky latex — handle with gloves and avoid eye contact. Excellent as a bold color contrast in mixed tropical borders.

Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; caricature plant is a tropical shrub from New Guinea and the Pacific Islands that is grown entirely for its extraordinary variegated foliage — large, shiny, oval leaves boldly streaked, blotched, and suffused with yellow, cream, rose-pink, or purple-red markings on a dark-green background, with the irregular patterning suggesting (to imaginative observers) the exaggerated features of cartoon faces or caricatures, giving the plant its common name. The color intensity and pattern of the leaf markings vary with the amount of light — plants in brighter partial shade develop the most vivid contrasts, while plants in deeper shade become more uniformly green. Small, tubular, purplish-red flowers appear occasionally on mature plants in tropical conditions but are secondary to the foliage display. Widely grown as a houseplant and greenhouse specimen in cool climates; in zone 10–12 it functions as a year-round outdoor foliage shrub of considerable ornamental impact.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Carissa is a compact, slow-growing Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta) cultivar with a distinctive characteristic that sets it apart from all other Chinese holly cultivars: its leaves have only a single terminal spine rather than the multiple sharp spines of standard Chinese holly. This makes Carissa the most maintenance-friendly and user-safe holly cultivar for residential settings — plants around walkways, children's play areas, and high-traffic zones where the multiple sharp spines of Rotunda, Burford, and other Chinese holly types would create hazards. The deep, lustrous, dark-green foliage is more elongated and less glossy than some Chinese holly types but still attractive and evergreen year-round. Carissa is a female clone and requires a nearby male Chinese holly for berry production — when pollinated, it produces attractive red berries. The compact, naturally mounded habit (3–4 feet) requires minimal pruning to maintain in typical landscape situations. Extremely tough — tolerating clay soil, drought once established, heat, and partial shade without significant performance loss. Essentially pest-free, deer-resistant, and pollution-tolerant, making it practical for urban and suburban foundation plantings.

Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina allspice blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates significant shade and is one of the few large flowering shrubs that performs well in light to moderate shade. Calycanthus floridus is a deciduous native shrub of the southeastern United States with a rounded, spreading habit and remarkable, deeply fragrant, strap-petaled flowers with brick-red to burgundy petals that resemble no other flower in the garden; blooming from late spring through summer, the flowers have a complex, spicy-sweet scent compared variously to strawberries, banana, and pineapple, and the aromatic quality extends to the crushed leaves and bark. The plant suckers gently from the base over time and can be used as an informal hedge, woodland shrub border specimen, or under-planted beneath large trees; it is completely carefree once established in zones 4–9.

Plant young container-grown trees in fall in wet to seasonally flooded, poorly drained soil in full sun to partial shade, since Carolina ash naturally roots in cypress-tupelo swamps, sloughs, and pond margins where standing water lingers for much of the year. It stays small compared to other native ashes, usually developing a multi-trunked, shrubby to small-tree form with glossy compound leaves, and its inflated, corky-winged seed pods float on floodwater to disperse, giving the tree its 'pop ash' nickname. Inconspicuous spring flowers provide early nectar for native bees before the leaves fully emerge, and the seeds are eaten by waterfowl and other wetland wildlife. It is a dependable small shade tree for the wettest corners of a Gulf Coast landscape, including pond edges, rain garden basins, and low spots that hold water after heavy rain.

Plant in well-drained to moist, acidic, sandy or poor soil in full sun; Carolina bayberry is a southeastern native shrub closely related to but distinct from the wax myrtle (Morella cerifera) — it is more compact and cold-hardy, with narrower leaves and slightly smaller, waxy gray berries on the female plants. Like all bayberries, only female plants produce berries, and one male is needed per 4–6 females for berry set. The fragrant, waxy berries were historically used to make bayberry candles, soap, and as a flavoring. The aromatic foliage is evergreen to semi-evergreen, releasing a pleasant spicy-resinous scent when crushed. Excellent for dry, infertile, sandy, acidic sites, roadsides, and coastal landscapes in zones 5–9 where it fixes nitrogen through root associations and requires virtually no care once established.

common_name: Carolina Buckthorn (Native Understory Tree with Red-to-Black Fruit)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it as an understory or woodland-edge tree where it naturally occurs. Carolina Buckthorn is a native small tree or large shrub found across the southeastern and south-central United States, valued for its clusters of small berries that ripen through a striking progression of colors from red to dark purple-black over summer, providing an extended food source for birds and other wildlife as different berries in the same cluster ripen at different rates. Its glossy, deep green foliage and neat, rounded form make it a good choice for naturalized plantings, woodland gardens, and wildlife landscaping, and unlike the invasive European buckthorns it is a well-behaved native that does not spread aggressively. It tolerates a range of soil types and light conditions once established and needs little maintenance beyond occasional shaping if a more tree-like form is wanted.

Carolina Cherry Laurel is an evergreen native tree or large shrub of the coastal plain and piedmont from North Carolina to central Florida and west to Texas, where it grows at forest edges, in disturbed sites, and along stream banks in full sun to partial shade. The glossy, lance-shaped evergreen leaves, fragrant white flower clusters in early spring, and dense branching habit make it one of the most popular native plants for hedges, privacy screens, and naturalized windbreaks in the Southeast, especially in Zones 8–10 where it grows vigorously year-round. Clusters of glossy black drupes ripen in fall and winter and are eagerly consumed by mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, robins, and other fruit-eating birds, though all parts of the plant contain hydrogen cyanide compounds and must never be eaten by humans or livestock. Plant in well-drained, loamy to sandy-loam soil in full sun for best flowering and fruiting; established plants tolerate extended drought, moderate clay, and salt spray in coastal settings.

Carolina Holly is a native deciduous holly of the coastal plain and lower piedmont from the Carolinas south to Florida and west to Texas, growing as a large shrub or small tree at forest edges, hammock borders, and along stream banks in partial shade to full sun. The small but vivid red to orange-red berries, held in clusters along the bare winter branches after leaf drop, are an important food source for robins, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, hermit thrushes, and other fruit-eating birds during fall migration and winter. Like all native hollies, Carolina Holly is dioecious — both male and female plants are required within pollinator range for berry production — and its modest size compared to American Holly makes it suitable for smaller gardens where the larger species may overwhelm the space. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants tolerate moderate drought and require little maintenance.

This evergreen vine covers fences, trellises, and arbors with fragrant, bright yellow trumpet blooms in late winter to early spring. Plant in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil and provide sturdy support for the twining stems. Water regularly while establishing, then it tolerates moderate drought once mature. Note that all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so site it away from areas frequented by pets and children; prune lightly after flowering to control size.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens on a trellis, fence, arbor, or mailbox post in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Carolina jessamine is an evergreen, twining native vine that produces a spectacular display of bright, golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped, sweetly fragrant flowers in late winter to early spring — often the first vine to bloom, sometimes as early as January in zone 9. The glossy, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves are handsome year-round. The vine grows vigorously to 10–20 feet and can be allowed to cascade down banks, scramble through shrubs, or climb structures. All parts of the plant are highly toxic — do not confuse with true jasmines and never allow children to put flowers in their mouths. Valuable early-spring nectar source for native bees and hummingbirds returning from winter.

Plant in well-drained, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Carolina laurelcherry is fast-growing and can be pruned as a formal hedge or allowed to grow as a multi-stemmed small tree. Prunus caroliniana (Carolina laurelcherry or cherry laurel) is one of the most useful and fastest-growing native evergreen plants for Gulf Coast privacy screens, hedges, and windbreaks — a glossy-leaved, fast-growing shrub or small tree native to the coastal plain from North Carolina through Florida and Texas, producing small clusters of fragrant white flowers in spring followed by small, black, cherry-like fruits (the 'mockingbird berry' that Northern Mockingbirds consume voraciously). The dense, lustrous, dark-green, lanceolate leaves give it a formal, refined appearance well-suited to clipped hedges and screens; it grows 2–3 feet per year when young and can form a dense privacy screen within 3–4 years. CAUTION: The leaves, seeds, and stems contain amygdalin (prussic acid precursor) and are toxic if ingested in quantity — the mature black fruits are consumed safely by birds but should not be ingested by people. Carolina laurelcherry also volunteers prolifically from bird-dispersed seeds in the Gulf South; it can become weedy in natural areas near plantings.

common_name: Carolina Midnight Loropetalum (Near-Black Purple Fringe Flower)
notes: Carolina Midnight is a vigorous, large-growing loropetalum selected for exceptionally dark, near-black purple foliage that holds its intensity through the growing season better than many purple-leaf loropetalum cultivars, which tend to fade toward green in summer heat. Frilly, spidery, deep magenta-pink flowers stand out sharply against the near-black leaves in a heavy spring flush, with lighter rebloom into fall. Its large mature size makes it best suited to a screen, background planting, or small tree form rather than a tight foundation bed; like other loropetalum it tolerates heat, humidity, and normal garden soil well as long as drainage is adequate, and should be pruned, if needed, right after the spring bloom to avoid cutting off the next flush of flower buds.

Plant in average to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade at a woodland edge or naturalistic fence where slender twining stems can climb through shrubs or simple supports. Carolina Milkvine is a softly hairy, heart-leaved native perennial in the milkweed family (Apocynaceae), producing small, star-shaped, dull brownish-purple flowers in summer that are followed by spindle-shaped seed pods splitting open to release seeds with silky white plumes. Like other milkweeds it exudes latex sap when cut and supports generalist milkweed bugs and potentially monarch butterflies as a larval host plant. It is an underused native vine well suited to naturalistic woodland garden settings where it weaves through existing shrubs without smothering them.

Carolina rhododendron is one of the most compact and garden-worthy of all native North American rhododendrons — a small-leaved, dense, evergreen shrub from the high-elevation heath balds and rocky slopes of the southern Appalachians that produces masses of rose-pink to white flower clusters in April and May that can cover the entire plant in bloom. It is notably more heat-tolerant, drought-adaptable, and pest-resistant than the large-leaved rhododendrons (R. maximum and R. catawbiense) and adapts to typical garden conditions more readily; its compact size (2–6 feet) makes it appropriate for small-space native gardens and foundation plantings where large rhododendrons would overwhelm the space. The tiny, dark-spotted dots (puncta) on the leaf undersides give it the alternate name 'punctatum' and help identify it in the field; the small, leathery evergreen leaves roll upward in cold temperatures as a water-conservation mechanism, creating a distinctive winter appearance. One of the best native rhododendrons for shaded rockeries, acidic slopes, and native woodland gardens in the mid-Atlantic and upper South.

Carolina Rose is a slender, drought-tolerant native of dry open woods, meadows, and roadsides throughout eastern North America, thriving in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soils where more vigorous shrubs struggle. Plant rooted cuttings or suckers in spring into a sunny, open site, spacing plants 3 to 5 feet apart to allow air circulation and natural colony spread. In June, the arching stems bear fragrant, single, pale to deep pink flowers about 1.5 to 2 inches across, followed by small, persistent red rose hips that feed mockingbirds, thrushes, and waxwings well into winter. No spraying or heavy pruning is needed; simply remove dead wood in late winter and allow the plant to spread slowly by suckers into an informal, wildlife-friendly thicket.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly to moderately acidic soil in partial to dappled shade; Carolina silverbell performs best in the cool, moist conditions of forest understory and does not tolerate drought or heavy clay well. Halesia carolina (syn. H. tetraptera) is a beautiful native small tree of the southern Appalachians producing cascading clusters of pure-white, bell-shaped, 4-petaled flowers covering the bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, creating a breathtaking floral display; the flowers are followed by ornamental, 4-winged, tan seed pods that persist through fall. One of the most spectacular spring-flowering native trees of the Southeast, excellent as a specimen or in mass plantings along woodland paths; the flowers are particularly lovely when viewed from below against a blue sky. Outstanding companion for dogwood, redbud, and rhododendron.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade under the canopy of taller trees; Carolina Silverbell is at its absolute best as a woodland understory tree receiving dappled light rather than direct afternoon sun. Halesia tetraptera (also listed as H. carolina) is a native deciduous tree of the Southern Appalachians and Piedmont, with populations extending to the Gulf Coastal Plain of Louisiana and Mississippi, where it grows in moist ravines, bottomland hardwood forests, and shaded creek banks. In April–May (earlier in zone 9), the branches are literally covered with pendant clusters of pure white, four-petaled bell-shaped flowers just before the leaves emerge — the display earned it the common name 'Snowdrop Tree,' as the dangling white bells cascade along every branch with the appearance of snowflakes frozen in time. The flowers are followed by winged, four-ridged fruits (the source of the species name 'tetraptera,' meaning four-winged) that persist into winter and are eaten by wood ducks, wild turkeys, and songbirds. The tree grows relatively quickly for an understory species — 12–15 feet in 10 years in good conditions — with a naturally attractive multi-stem or single-trunk form, attractive exfoliating bark on mature specimens, and clear yellow fall color. In zone 9 Gulf Coast woodland gardens, Carolina Silverbell provides spring floral interest under large live oaks where most ornamentals fail.

common_name: Carter's Sunburst Camellia (Striped Pale-Pink Exhibition-Form Japonica Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; Carter's Sunburst is one of the most immediately recognizable Camellia japonica cultivars — producing large, semi-double to peony-form flowers in pale pink to soft blush with overlaid deep pink stripes, streaks, and blotches distributed across the petals in patterns that are never exactly the same flower-to-flower. The striped and spotted flower coloring is distinctive enough that Carter's Sunburst is among the most frequently identified camellias by home gardeners and garden visitors — the unpredictable pink-on-pale-pink pattern creates visual complexity that solid-color camellias cannot match. The flowers are large (typically 4–5 inches across), combining good exhibition size with the informal charm of variegated coloring. Carter's Sunburst is a mid-season bloomer (typically February–March in zone 9), flowering after the earliest camellias and before the latest, filling a useful mid-winter bloom window. The plant grows as a medium-to-large, dense, upright evergreen shrub with the characteristically glossy, dark-green camellia foliage that provides attractive year-round structure. In zone 9, Carter's Sunburst is a reliable perennial landscape shrub requiring primarily acidic soil, consistent moisture, and protection from afternoon sun that can bleach the pale-pink flower color. An outstanding specimen plant near garden entrances where the distinctive striped flowers can be seen closely.

Plant rooted cuttings or nursery-grown container stock in fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil along a streambank, seep, or shaded slope, mimicking the subalpine forest openings and avalanche chutes of the Cascades and northern Rockies where it grows wild. Unlike most rhododendrons, its cream-white flowers open along the stem below the newest leaves rather than in a terminal truss, giving it a distinctive, informal look in a woodland or native shrub border. It struggles in hot, humid summers and is best reserved for cool-climate gardens with reliable moisture and good air movement.

Plant container-grown stock in spring into consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a cool, partly sunny site, recreating the snowmelt-fed subalpine meadows of the Cascade and Olympic Mountains where it forms low, spreading mats. Bell-shaped pink flowers appear in early summer followed by sweet, powder-blue berries considered among the best-flavored of the wild huckleberries and are eagerly sought by birds, bears, and foragers alike. It resents summer drought and heat, so it performs best in cool-climate gardens or high-elevation native plantings with reliable soil moisture.

Plant in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Cascade Oregon grape is more drought and shade tolerant than the better-known tall Oregon grape (M. aquifolium) and is superior for naturalizing as a ground cover in dry, shaded forest settings under conifers or other dense trees. Mahonia nervosa is a low-growing western native evergreen shrub 12–24 inches tall with long, pinnate, holly-like leaves with many narrow leaflets, clusters of yellow flowers in early spring before many other shade shrubs bloom, and blue-black berries that are loved by birds and used to make preserves and a tart beverage in the Pacific Northwest. The evergreen foliage turns wine-red to bronze in winter, providing year-round interest. An excellent, underused evergreen ground cover for the Pacific Northwest and adaptable dry-shade situations in western gardens; deer resistant.

Divide root masses or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; cat's claw vine (cat's claw creeper, yellow trumpet vine) is a Mexican and Caribbean deciduous to semi-evergreen vine of the bignonia family (Bignoniaceae) that clings to walls, trees, fences, and masonry with remarkable tenacity through specialized, three-pronged, claw-like tendrils at the leaf tips — the claws can grip and penetrate the most vertical, smooth surfaces and provide virtually no-effort climbing capability. In spring, before or as the new leaves emerge, the vine produces a profusion of large, bright-yellow, funnel-shaped, trumpet flowers in spectacular abundance covering the entire plant. The vine is extraordinarily tough, drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and adaptable, and recovers quickly from hard freezes that kill it back to the large, persistent underground root system. It is, however, aggressively invasive in many warm-climate regions, spreading by seeds and underground tubers into natural areas and difficult to eradicate once established. An impactful, low-care vine for contained, fence-line, and masonry situations in zone 8–11 where its invasive spread can be managed.

common_name: Catawba Crape Myrtle (Deep Purple Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Catawba is a National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle producing one of the deepest, richest purple flower colors available in crape myrtles — a vivid, true violet-purple that holds color through the heat of the Gulf South summer without fading to pink or lavender. Purple is among the rarest and most sought-after crape myrtle flower colors — most purple-claiming cultivars prove to be lavender, mauve, or reddish-purple — but Catawba's color is among the most reliably true purple in cultivation. The flowers are produced in large, compact clusters from June through September in zone 9, covering a medium-sized multi-trunked tree to 10–15 feet with vivid purple bloom. Fall foliage transitions to attractive orange-red. The exfoliating bark develops an attractive mottled pattern of gray and tan with age. Like other National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, Catawba shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Its medium size makes it appropriate for the majority of residential landscapes where the large tree-form Natchez and Muskogee would eventually overwhelm the space. Catawba is an excellent choice for the gardener who wants a distinctive crape myrtle that stands apart from the dominant pink and red cultivars. Never top or severely prune — proper pruning removes only dead and crossing branches.

Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun for wildlife habitat restoration; catbrier is a common native greenbrier of dry woodlands and woodland edges throughout eastern North America, distinguished from other Smilax by the glaucous (blue-white) coloring on the underside of the leaves. Like all greenbriers, it is an armed, scrambling vine with stout, curved thorns and tendrils, climbing through shrubs and into tree canopy. The blue-black berries that persist through winter are critically important food for numerous thrushes, mockingbirds, and other fruit-eating birds. Dense catbrier thickets provide nesting cover for ground-nesting birds including bobwhite quail and wild turkey. The young shoots in spring are edible, resembling asparagus in flavor, and have been used as a spring vegetable by indigenous peoples and early settlers. The starchy underground tubers can be processed into a flour-like starch. Primarily a wildlife planting rather than a garden ornamental.

Catclaw acacia — nicknamed 'wait-a-minute bush' because its small, curved, cat-claw-like thorns snag clothing and skin, halting passage — is a native shrub to medium tree of dry washes, rocky slopes, and desert grasslands from south Texas to California and south into Mexico. Despite its formidable armament, catclaw acacia is one of the most important native bee plants in the Chihuahuan Desert and south Texas, producing abundant cream-colored, cylindrical flower spikes in spring that support hundreds of native bee species and are the source of a prized honey; it is considered the single most important native honey plant in the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts by commercial beekeepers. The long, flat seed pods ripen in summer and fall and are consumed by deer, javelinas, and large-seeded birds; the dense, thorny structure of established shrubs creates impenetrable wildlife brush habitat essential for quail, roadrunners, and nesting songbirds throughout south Texas. Best suited to xeric native plantings, dry washes, and wildlife habitat gardens where its thorny nature is an asset rather than a liability.

Cedar Elm is the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant of the native elms, native to the river bottoms, limestone floodplains, and upland limestone woods of Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Louisiana, where it frequently grows adjacent to cedar (Juniperus species) — hence its common name. Its most distinctive habit is bloom timing: unlike all other North American elms that bloom in late winter before leaf-out, Cedar Elm blooms in late summer and fall (August–October), producing tiny, inconspicuous flowers followed by small, papery, winged seeds; this unusual timing means it can be confused with a disease-stricken elm (sparse fall foliage is normal, not worrying). A tough, adaptable native shade tree that tolerates the alkaline limestone soils, compaction, and summer heat of Texas landscapes with exceptional resilience, Cedar Elm is one of the most widely recommended native shade trees for central and south Texas gardens. Grow in full sun in any well-drained to moist soil; it adapts readily to both alkaline limestone and acidic sandy soils.

Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Celadine is a plumeria cultivar bearing soft, creamy yellow flowers brightening toward a deeper yellow throat and edged in white, a gentle color combination carrying the strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance the genus is famous for. It is a reliable, free-flowering cultivar favored by plumeria collectors for its consistent bloom production through the warm season. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to prevent stem rot. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes. Excellent drainage is essential year-round.

Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline soil; cenizo is the iconic native shrub of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau and one of the most drought tolerant and xeric shrubs in the South — its silver, feltlike leaves reflect heat and reduce water loss, allowing it to thrive in the hottest, driest conditions where other shrubs fail. The lavender-purple tubular flowers burst open in response to humidity — most dramatically in the 24–48 hours before a summer rain — giving it the folk name 'barometer bush.' Bloom cycles repeat with each moisture event from summer through fall, covering the entire silver shrub in purple. Cultivars include 'Green Cloud' (dark green leaves, rich purple flowers), 'White Cloud' (white flowers), and 'Compact' (dense, 3–4-foot habit). Never overwater or fertilize — excess moisture is the primary killer. Outstanding for xeric, native, and wildlife gardens in zones 8–11.

common_name: Center Glow Ninebark (Glowing Bicolor Foliage Ninebark)
notes: Center Glow is a large, vigorous ninebark selected for unusual bicolor foliage: new leaves emerge with wine-purple margins surrounding a glowing chartreuse-to-orange center, an effect most pronounced on fresh spring and summer growth before the whole leaf gradually deepens toward purple with age, giving the shrub a constantly shifting, luminous look through the season. Clusters of small white-to-pink flowers in late spring draw pollinators, followed by reddish seed capsules and, once leaves drop, attractive exfoliating bark for winter interest. Like other ninebarks it is exceptionally tolerant of clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems at the base to stay full and vigorous.

common_name: Center Stage Red Crapemyrtle (Black-Foliage Cerise-Red Compact Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Center Stage Red bears near-black foliage that provides dramatic, season-long contrast to its clusters of vivid cerise-red flowers, standing out from the many crapemyrtle series bred primarily for flower color alone. Bred for good disease resistance, it holds its foliage well through a humid Gulf South summer, and its compact 10-12 foot mature size fits more readily into a residential landscape than older, larger crapemyrtle varieties. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood, preserving the plant's natural vase-shaped form.

common_name: Center of Attention Distylium (Upright Burgundy New-Growth Evergreen Shrub)
notes: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow the upright, vase-shaped form to develop into a screen or informal hedge without crowding. Center of Attention is a First Editions distylium selection with a notably taller, more upright habit than typical mounding distylium cultivars, producing burgundy-red new growth that matures to glossy dark green, along with small maroon flowers along the stems in late winter. Like other distylium, it shares the species' rare tolerance for both full sun and full shade, wet or dry soils, and strong resistance to the pests and diseases that trouble many broadleaf evergreens in humid Gulf South summers, along with being seldom browsed by deer. Its taller, narrower form makes it particularly useful as a living privacy screen or vertical accent where a low, spreading distylium would be the wrong shape, and it needs only occasional shaping to maintain its natural upright form.

Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ceylon leadwort is a sprawling, semi-scandent subshrub found through the tropics and subtropics of Asia and Africa that bears loose spikes of small white flowers with a slender green calyx, blooming most heavily where it gets some relief from the hottest afternoon sun. It spreads slowly by root suckers to form an informal, arching mound and works well tucked under high tree canopy or along a shaded fence line where fewer flowering shrubs perform. It is drought tolerant once established and needs little care beyond an annual cutback in late winter to control size and encourage fresh flowering growth; wear gloves when handling cut stems, since the sap can irritate sensitive skin.

common_name: Chalice Vine (Cup of Gold, Hawaiian Wedding Flower)
notes: Plant in fertile, rich, well-drained soil in full sun; chalice vine is one of the most spectacular large-flowering plants in the world, producing enormous chalice-shaped flowers 8–10 inches across in golden yellow with purple veins and a powerful, tropical, coconut-like fragrance, strongest at night. The massive, woody vines with large, glossy evergreen leaves can eventually cover a large wall, pergola, or building. It is one of the showiest of all tropical vines for zone 10–11 landscapes and a traditional feature of California and Florida coastal gardens. Established plants are surprisingly drought tolerant. Bloom is typically heaviest in late winter through spring and again in fall. Caution: all parts of this plant, including the nectar, are highly toxic — the active alkaloids can cause severe poisoning. Do not plant where children, pets, or livestock can access the plant.

Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; chalk maple is a small-to-medium native understory maple of the Southeast Appalachians and Piedmont, closely related to sugar maple but significantly more heat-and-drought-tolerant and better suited to the zone 7–9 garden than its more famous relative. The common name comes from the distinctive light-colored, chalky-white to pale gray bark. The 3–5 lobed leaves turn magnificent shades of yellow, orange, and scarlet in fall — one of the best native maples for fall color in the South. It grows naturally as an understory tree on rocky slopes and bluffs with well-drained, calcareous soils. An outstanding and underused native small tree for shaded gardens in the Southeast where sugar maple and Japanese maple both struggle with the heat and humidity.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; champaca is a large tropical tree from the eastern Himalayas and Southeast Asia that produces some of the most intensely fragrant flowers in the botanical world — the golden-orange, magnolia-like blooms have a complex, fruity-floral-spicy scent used in 'Joy' by Jean Patou (once called the world's most expensive perfume) and numerous other fine fragrances. The flowers are sacred in Hindu and Buddhist traditions and used extensively as temple offerings across South and Southeast Asia. In India, garlands of champaca flowers are worn in the hair. The essential oil, extracted by enfleurage or solvent extraction, is extraordinarily expensive. In the home garden in zone 9, grow as a large container specimen moved indoors in winter, where even a few flowers will perfume an entire room.

common_name: Champaka (Joy Perfume Tree, Yellow Champak, Magnolia champaca)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — Champaka grows most vigorously in full sun but benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Magnolia champaca (formerly Michelia champaca) is a large, fast-growing evergreen tree from the Himalayan foothills of India and Southeast Asia in the Magnoliaceae family, cultivated throughout the tropical world for one of the most celebrated flower fragrances in perfumery. The small (2–3 inch), creamy-white to golden-yellow flowers are produced in extraordinary abundance from spring through fall on established trees — typically dozens to hundreds of flowers open simultaneously — and release a fragrance variously described as combining orange blossom, ylang ylang, jasmine, and spice in a complex, penetrating, euphoric composition. Jean Patou's 'Joy' perfume (once the world's most expensive perfume per ounce) was built substantially around champaka absolute. In South and Southeast Asia, the flowers are woven into garlands for religious offerings in Hindu and Buddhist temples and worn as hair adornments at weddings and festivals. The flowers are among the most revered in Asian botanical culture. In zone 9-10 Gulf Coast landscapes, Champaka is a fast-growing ornamental tree that blooms for months and fills garden spaces with its remarkable fragrance.

common_name: Champneys' Pink Cluster Rose (Original Noisette Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a fence, arbor, or trellis, allowing 4-6 feet for its spreading, semi-climbing habit. Bred around 1811 by rice planter John Champneys of Charleston, South Carolina, by crossing the musk rose with an early China rose, Champneys' Pink Cluster became the founding parent of the Noisette class — the only major class of roses developed in North America — after cuttings were shared with a Charleston nurseryman named Philippe Noisette, who sent seedlings on to his brother in Paris. It bears large, loose clusters of small, semi-double, soft pink, fragrant blooms in repeated flushes from spring through fall on long, lax canes best trained on a support. As an early hybrid between a China rose and a musk rose, it carries strong heat tolerance and repeat bloom, traits that were unusual in roses available in Europe at the time and that make it well suited to the modern Gulf South garden. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to shape and remove spent wood, training new canes onto the support as they grow.

common_name: Chandleri Elegans Camellia (Antique Anemone-Form Pink Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Chandleri Elegans, introduced in England around 1831, is one of the oldest camellia cultivars still widely grown, prized for large, anemone-form flowers with a ring of broad, rose-pink outer petals surrounding a dense central cluster of smaller, irregular petaloids, a distinctive form quite different from the neat, layered rows of formal-double camellias. Occasional flowers show attractive white mottling or streaking. Its long cultivation history and reliable performance have kept it a fixture in historic and heritage camellia gardens across the South for nearly two centuries. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it flowers in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

common_name: Chapel Hill Gold Lantana (Cold-Hardy Sterile Gold Lantana)
notes: Plant nursery starts after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Chapel Hill Gold is a landscape lantana bred at North Carolina State University for two traits at once — root hardiness well into zone 7b, letting it return reliably as a herbaceous perennial in much colder winters than most lantana can survive, and functional sterility, meaning it produces few to no viable seeds and so does not spread into surrounding natural areas the way common seed-producing lantana cultivars can. It covers itself from late spring through frost in rounded clusters of clear golden-yellow flowers that are a magnet for butterflies and other pollinators. Once established it is highly drought tolerant and needs little supplemental water. In zone 9, expect the top growth to die back to the ground after a hard freeze; cut the dead stems back close to the ground in late winter and new growth will resprout from the crown in spring. Avoid overwatering and rich soil, both of which encourage leggy growth at the expense of flowering.

Plant container shrubs in spring in moist but well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; Chapman's rhododendron is a rare Florida Panhandle endemic best purchased only as nursery-propagated stock from growers who cultivate it responsibly, never wild-collected. Rhododendron chapmanii is a federally listed endangered evergreen shrub found only in a handful of sandhill and scrub sites in the Florida Panhandle and southwest Georgia, with small, leathery leaves and clusters of rose-pink, funnel-shaped flowers in early to mid-spring. Unlike most rhododendrons, it is naturally adapted to sharply drained, sandy soil and considerable sun exposure, making it more drought-tolerant than typical evergreen rhododendrons and a good candidate for a well-drained Gulf Coast native garden. Growing this rare species in cultivation from nursery-propagated stock helps support conservation of the species by reducing pressure on its few remaining wild populations, so buy only from reputable native-plant nurseries with documented cultivated origin.

Chardonnay Pearls is a slender deutzia selected for bright chartreuse-gold foliage that lights up a shaded border through the growing season, topped in mid-to-late spring by small, pearl-like white flower buds that open into star-shaped white blooms, giving the shrub a two-tone gold-and-white display. Its low, mounded, well-behaved habit fits foundation plantings and mixed borders where a compact flowering shrub with season-long foliage color is wanted, unlike plain-green deutzia cultivars that offer interest only during the spring bloom window. It tolerates partial shade better than many golden-leaved shrubs while still coloring and flowering well, and needs only light pruning right after bloom to keep a tidy, rounded shape.

common_name: Charles Darwin Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001, Charles Darwin bears very large, deeply cupped blooms in a distinctive mustard-bronze to old-gold color that deepens as the flower ages, with a strong tea fragrance, on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its unusual bronze-gold tones set it apart from the more common clear yellows and pinks in the English rose palette, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; chaste tree is a fast-growing, multi-stemmed deciduous large shrub or small tree with deeply fragrant, spicy gray-green palmately compound leaves — a strong, pleasant sage-and-lavender scent — and tall, upright spikes of lavender-blue flowers from summer through fall that make it one of the most valuable summer-blooming ornamentals for hot, dry climates. It blooms profusely on new growth; cutting back hard in late winter to 12–18 inches above ground produces vigorous new shoots and the best flower display. The dried fruits were historically used as a spice and medicinal herb (the name 'chaste tree' refers to its historical use to reduce libido). 'Shoal Creek' (large, deep blue spikes) and 'Abbeville Blue' are outstanding selections.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; chenille plant is one of the most unusually beautiful tropical flowering plants, producing long, pendulous, fuzzy catkin-like flower spikes in brilliant crimson-red that dangle like fluffy chenille tassels 12–18 inches long — an unmistakable and astonishing floral display unlike anything else in the garden. The flowers are produced nearly year-round in frost-free zones. It thrives in the warm, humid conditions of zone 10–12 and is used as a summer annual or large container plant in cooler zones; in zone 9 it may be grown as a seasonal annual or overwintered in a greenhouse. Bright filtered light or morning sun produces the most flowers while preventing leaf scorch in the afternoon heat. Regular watering and monthly fertilization during the growing season keeps the plant vigorous and blooming well. Propagate from 6-inch stem cuttings in late spring.

common_name: Cherokee Brave Dogwood (Deep Red Flowering Dogwood)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cherokee Brave is the finest red-flowering dogwood cultivar — a selection with deep rosy-red to crimson-red bracts that are noticeably darker and more intensely colored than older red dogwood cultivars like 'Cherokee Chief.' The deep, saturated crimson-red bracts create one of the most spectacular spring flowering displays available for the partial-shade Southeast garden in March through April. Like the native species, Cherokee Brave is an understory tree — it evolved growing beneath the canopy of larger hardwoods in the forest edge, making it one of the finest specimens for sites that receive morning sun and afternoon shade. This understory adaptation is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the intense afternoon sun and summer heat stress full-sun dogwoods. The spring floral display is followed by attractive horizontal branching with dark-green summer foliage and excellent red fall color. Glossy red berries in fall provide bird food. In zone 9, dogwoods perform best in the northern portions and in protected, afternoon-shaded positions — mulch heavily around the root zone to maintain cool, moist soil. The striking contrast between the dark red bracts and white-centered bracts creates a bicolor effect that distinguishes Cherokee Brave from solid-red cultivars.

Cherokee Brave opens deep pink spring blooms with reddish new foliage, followed by red fall color and berries that attract birds. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, siting it in part shade or where it gets afternoon protection in hot regions. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, as dogwoods are shallow-rooted and dislike drought. This selection shows improved resistance to powdery mildew; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

Cherokee Chief bears rich rosy-red bracts in spring on graceful horizontal branches, with glossy foliage that turns red in autumn. Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and give it part shade or afternoon protection where summers are hot. Maintain even soil moisture with mulch, since the shallow roots suffer in dry conditions. Prune sparingly right after bloom to shape the canopy and remove any damaged wood.

common_name: Cherokee Crape Myrtle (Red-Flowered Dwarf-to-Medium Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); Cherokee is a bright red-flowering crape myrtle from the U.S. National Arboretum's early tribe-named breeding series, producing dense clusters of vivid red crepe-textured flowers through the heat of summer on a dwarf-to-medium multi-stemmed shrub. Being a straight Lagerstroemia indica selection rather than one of the later indica x fauriei hybrids, it carries more susceptibility to powdery mildew than mildew-resistant selections like Natchez or Tuscarora, so give it full sun and good air circulation to minimize disease pressure. Its more compact size compared to the largest crape myrtle cultivars makes it a fit for smaller landscapes or foundation plantings where a full-size tree form would be too large. As with all crape myrtles, never top or hard-prune the main framework — a practice sometimes called 'crepe murder' — since it ruins the natural vase-shaped form permanently; instead prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or crowded twiggy growth.

Cherokee Princess is prized for its heavy set of large, pure-white spring bracts and a well-branched, rounded form. Plant in moist, acidic, organically rich soil in part shade, protecting it from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind. Mulch to keep the shallow root system cool and consistently moist. Enjoy red fall foliage and berries that feed birds; prune only lightly after flowering to maintain the tidy structure.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Cherokee rose is a large, vigorous climbing rose native to China that naturalized across the Deep South and is now Georgia's state flower. The single, 3–4 inch white flowers with prominent golden stamens are produced in extraordinary abundance in March–April, covering the long canes with a spectacular display that has made this rose a Southern garden tradition for over two centuries. The hips that follow are large, pear-shaped, red, and persist through winter — they are extremely high in vitamin C and were historically made into rosehip syrup and tea. The evergreen to semi-evergreen foliage is attractive year-round and the thorny canes form impenetrable barriers that deter deer and intruders. Requires almost no care once established; thrives on neglect.

Plant in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial to full shade; cherry laurel is a vigorous, broad-spreading, broadleaf evergreen shrub native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia, grown for its large, glossy, deep-green leaves and upright spikes of small, fragrant white flowers in mid-spring, followed by cherry-like fruits that ripen from red to glossy black. Few other evergreen shrubs of comparable size tolerate the deep, dry shade cast by mature trees as well as cherry laurel does, which has made it a staple hedge, screening, and foundation plant throughout the maritime Pacific Northwest and the British Isles for generations. Compact cultivars such as 'Otto Luyken' and 'Zabeliana' stay low and spreading for foundation use, while 'Schipkaensis' (Schip laurel) is notably more cold hardy for zone 6 gardens. Because it self-seeds readily in the deep shade it favors, cherry laurel has naturalized aggressively in woodlands in parts of the Pacific Northwest and the United Kingdom, so spent flower spikes should be sheared off before fruit ripens in gardens near wild or natural areas, and all plant parts other than the ripe fruit pulp should be kept away from children and grazing animals.

This bigleaf hydrangea produces color-shifting blooms that mature to rich cherry-red tones from spring into fall on a compact, rounded shrub. Plant in part shade with morning sun and afternoon protection in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil. Water deeply and regularly, especially in heat, and mulch to conserve moisture. It blooms on both old and new wood, so prune only to remove dead stems in early spring for the most reliable flowering.

common_name: Cherrybark Oak (Swamp Red Oak, Elliott's Oak)
notes: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic bottomland or bluff soil in full sun; cherrybark oak is generally regarded as one of the finest and most beautiful of all North American oaks — a majestic timber tree reaching 80–120 feet with a straight, clear trunk and distinctive shaggy, plated bark reminiscent of black cherry (hence the name). The deeply lobed, very large leaves have outstanding scarlet to orange-red fall color. The abundant small acorns are a critical food source for deer, turkeys, wood ducks, and squirrels. Unlike many red-group oaks, cherrybark oak is intolerant of flooding and requires the rich, well-drained ridges and terraces of bottomland hardwood forests — the 'cherrybark ridges' of bottomland forest. It is the fastest-growing of the large southern oaks (4–5 feet per year when young) and develops into an impressively large, long-lived specimen tree.

Plant young trees in fall on well-drained, rocky or sandy slopes where this ridge-loving oak naturally thrives, since it tolerates drought and poor soil far better than bottomland oaks. Its thick, deeply furrowed bark and coarse, chestnut-like leaves give strong winter and textural interest in naturalized or restoration plantings. Because it resists rot and drought stress once established, it is an excellent long-lived specimen for dry hillsides, ridgetops, and low-maintenance shade areas. Acorns are relatively large, low in tannin, and readily eaten by wildlife.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; chestnut rose is unusually disease-resistant and tolerates heat and humidity well compared to many old garden rose species. Fine, ferny, glossy foliage and attractive, peeling, cinnamon-colored bark give this Chinese species rose year-round ornamental appeal beyond its clear pink, single to semi-double summer flowers, which are followed by distinctive, spiny, chestnut-bur-like orange-red hips that give the species both its common name and a striking, unusual fall and winter feature unlike the smooth hips of most roses. Notably resistant to black spot and other common rose diseases that plague many garden roses in humid climates, it is an easy, low-spray option for a Gulf South or humid-climate garden where disease pressure on roses is often severe. The edible, vitamin-C-rich hips are also used in some regions for jams, jellies, and traditional preparations. Prune minimally, mainly to remove old or damaged canes, since it flowers on both old and new wood.

common_name: Cheyenne Crape Myrtle (Semi-Dwarf True Red Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cheyenne is valued among National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles for its true, vivid red flower color, a shade less common among crape myrtle cultivars than the many available pinks, lavenders, and whites. The compact, semi-dwarf size fits foundation plantings and smaller landscapes better than the large tree-form crape myrtles, and it shows good resistance to powdery mildew typical of the National Arboretum breeding program. Fall foliage takes on attractive orange-red tones. Remove root suckers and prune lightly to remove dead or crossing branches rather than heavily topping the plant.

Chihuahuan Globe Mallow is a compact, velvety-soft native mallow shrub of the Chihuahuan Desert and adjacent Texas Hill Country, its stems and leaves coated in dense, silky white hairs that give the plant a striking silver-gray appearance year-round. From summer through fall it produces cheerful, bright yellow, five-petaled mallow flowers about 1-1.5 inches across, the golden blooms providing a vivid contrast against the silver foliage. Plant in very dry, poor, calcareous or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; wet or clay-heavy soils quickly lead to root rot, so excellent drainage is non-negotiable. Once established it requires minimal supplemental irrigation and is an outstanding choice for Texas xeriscape designs, Chihuahuan Desert gardens, and other arid Southwest landscapes.

Plant in spring or early fall in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Leucophyllum species suffer in waterlogged or heavily amended acidic soils and must have excellent drainage to thrive. Chihuahuan sage (L. laevigatum) is the most compact and finely textured of the native Texas sage species, with smooth, small, grey-green leaves and a naturally mounded, nearly spherical habit that makes it one of the most refined-looking drought-tolerant shrubs for formal and informal use in hot, dry landscapes; like all Leucophyllum, it responds to humidity and soil moisture by bursting into bloom with masses of small, lavender to purple tubular flowers — a phenomenon known as 'barometer bush' behavior because blooming is triggered by summer monsoon rains. Essentially maintenance-free once established and highly tolerant of alkaline caliche soils.

Start seeds indoors early and train on a trellis in full sun; Chilean glory flower is a vigorous tendril-climbing vine from Chile and Peru producing masses of small (1 inch), tubular flowers in brilliant orange-red to scarlet (with yellow and orange-yellow forms also available) in long racemes from summer through the first hard frost — an extended, prolific bloom display on a fast-growing vine that reaches 8–15 feet. The small, bright flowers resemble a more refined version of Eccremocarpus, with the tubular shape irresistible to hummingbirds during migration. It climbs using leaf tendrils over trellises, fences, shrubs, and netting with remarkable speed. In zones 8–10 the roots may survive winter to resprout; in colder climates treat as an annual started from seed each spring. A good combination vine with purple-flowered plants such as Cobaea scandens or morning glory, where the orange-red flowers create striking complementary color.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Chilean jasmine is the most cold-hardy and most fragrant of the mandevilla vines — significantly more cold-tolerant than the showy tropical Mandevilla sanderi hybrids commonly sold in summer, surviving reliably to zone 7b and making it a viable perennial vine for gardens far colder than those where tropical mandevillas must be overwintered indoors. The flowers are produced in summer in loose clusters of 3–5, each flower a large (2–3 inch), pure-white, funnel-shaped, five-petaled blossom with a slightly twisted, windmill-like arrangement of the petals and a powerfully sweet, intense fragrance that is often compared to jasmine but with a richer, more complex depth than most jasmines — one of the most fragrant summer-climbing vines available for temperate gardens. It twines vigorously and can reach 15–20 feet on a sturdy support over several seasons. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it performs as an outstanding, reliable perennial climber with an extended summer bloom season. The white flowers and sweet fragrance make it ideal for placement near porches, pergolas, and garden seating areas.

All parts other than the flowers should be treated as inedible, since this is a relative of the potato — grow it strictly as an ornamental screen. Plant this fast-growing, semi-woody scrambler against a sturdy wall, fence, or pergola in spring, tying in new growth as it develops since it climbs by leaning rather than by tendrils or twining. Large, fragrant clusters of blue-purple, star-shaped flowers with bright yellow centers open from summer into autumn and continue even in a partly shaded position, though bloom is somewhat fuller with a few hours of direct sun. Cut back hard in early spring where winters are borderline, since it often regrows vigorously from the base after cold damage.

common_name: China Boy Holly (Compact Male Meserve Hybrid Holly)
notes: China Boy is the male counterpart bred alongside China Girl in the Meserve holly line, sharing the same compact, dense, glossy dark-green, spiny foliage but producing no berries of its own, since only female holly plants fruit. Its main garden role is as a reliable pollinator planted within about 30-40 feet of China Girl or other compatible female Meserve hollies to ensure a heavy berry set on the female plants, though it is also a handsome, fully ornamental evergreen shrub in its own right for a hedge or foundation planting. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter before new growth begins.

Plant container-grown trees in spring, spacing them well back from structures in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water regularly through the first two seasons while roots establish. China fir forms a broad pyramidal tree with stiff, glossy, dark green needles borne in dense whorled tiers, and old bark exfoliates in long reddish-brown strips that add winter interest. Unlike many needled conifers it resprouts vigorously from cut stumps and tolerates the humid summers of the southeastern United States, where it is grown as a large screening or specimen tree rather than the timber crop it forms across much of China. Lower branches often decline with age and can be limbed up to reveal the trunk on mature specimens.

common_name: China Girl Holly (Compact Female Meserve Hybrid Holly)
notes: China Girl is a compact, self-branching Meserve hybrid holly with glossy, spiny, dark green leaves and, once pollinated, a reliably heavy crop of bright red winter berries, making it a popular and dependable evergreen shrub for foundation plantings, hedges, and mixed borders. It is more heat-tolerant than some other blue holly selections, an advantage in warmer regions where straight Meserve hollies can struggle, but as a female cultivar it needs a male pollinator such as China Boy blooming nearby to fruit well. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter before new growth begins.

Plant in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun, with awareness of invasive potential; chinaberry is an Asian deciduous tree widely naturalized across the US Gulf South, Caribbean, and tropics worldwide. The fragrant, lilac-purple flower clusters in spring are highly ornamental and have given the tree the names 'Persian lilac' and 'pride of India.' The clusters of small, yellow berries that persist through winter are striking ornamentally but are toxic to humans, dogs, and livestock (though consumed by birds, which distribute the seeds widely). The tree is drought and heat tolerant, fast-growing, and adaptable to almost any well-drained soil — characteristics that, combined with prolific bird-dispersed seeding, make it invasive in many parts of the South. Used in agroforestry in tropical countries for natural insecticide compounds (azadirachtin relatives from the same Meliaceae family as neem). Caution: do not plant near natural areas.

common_name: Chinaberry Tree (Bead Tree, Pride of India)
notes: Plant in any well-drained, moist to dry soil in full sun; chinaberry grows in almost any condition and requires minimal care — it is extremely fast-growing. CAUTION: Invasive in the southeastern United States — verify local regulations before planting. Melia azedarach (chinaberry or bead tree) is an Asian tree that has naturalized across the entire Gulf Coastal Plain and has been a fixture of southern rural landscapes for generations, valued for its extraordinary fast growth (5–10 feet per year), deep, cooling shade, and clusters of fragrant, lilac-purple flowers in April–May that make it one of the most ornamentally beautiful trees in bloom despite its weedy reputation. The clusters of small, round, yellow-white berries persist into winter and are eagerly consumed by American Robins and other fruit-eating birds, which has facilitated its spread. CAUTION: The berries are toxic to humans (causing gastrointestinal distress) and especially to pigs; all parts of the plant contain triterpenoids and limonoids. Chinaberry is listed as invasive in Florida, Georgia, and much of the Gulf South. Historically important as a fast-growing 'pioneer tree' for farmstead windbreaks and shade, and the hard berries have been used for rosary beads and crafts (giving it the 'bead tree' name).

common_name: Chindo Viburnum (Award-Winning Large Evergreen Screening Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Chindo is a selected, more cold-hardy form of sweet viburnum that earned a Gold Medal Award from the Georgia Botanical Garden for its outstanding performance as a large, fast-growing evergreen screen. It has bold, glossy, deep green leaves considerably larger than most viburnums, white spring flower clusters, and showy red fruit that matures to black, all on a dense shrub that quickly reaches privacy-hedge size or can be limbed up into a small multi-trunked tree. It tolerates heat and humidity very well, making it a Gulf South landscape staple for fast screening, and needs only occasional shaping to control size in a smaller garden.
