common_name: Chinese Chaste Tree (Monk's Pepper, Negundo Chastetree, Five-Leaf Chaste Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; Chinese Chaste Tree is drought-tolerant once established and adapts broadly to soil types including clay and alkaline calcareous soils prevalent across the Gulf South. Vitex negundo is a large aromatic shrub or small tree from tropical and subtropical Asia (India, China, Southeast Asia) that is one of the most widely-used medicinal plants in Asian botanical medicine traditions — the berries (used as a spice in China), leaves, and roots are employed for numerous traditional remedies and the berries are considered a substitute for black pepper (hence 'Monk's Pepper'). In zone 9 Gulf Coast and Southern gardens, it is grown primarily as an ornamental for its fragrant, silver-gray, divided foliage and long summer flower spikes of small, lavender-blue, tubular flowers that attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators in profusion from June through September. The pleasantly aromatic, camphor-like foliage repels some insect pests. Chinese Chaste Tree is closely related to the common American Chaste Tree (V. agnus-castus) but produces more narrowly divided leaves (often 5–7 leaflets rather than 5), adapts better to Southeast Asian humid conditions, and is reportedly somewhat more drought-tolerant. Hard pruning to 12 inches each February keeps the plant vigorous and maximizes flower production.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese climbing hydrangea is closely related to Japanese climbing hydrangea (Schizophragma hydrangeoides) but considered by many to be the more ornamentally impressive species, producing even larger, more spectacular flowerheads with broad, pure white sterile bracts that completely surround the central fertile flowers. The individual lacecap-like flower clusters can exceed 12 inches across. It clings to trees, walls, and trellises using aerial rootlets — no support structures needed. Like its relatives, it is slow to establish but becomes a spectacular, long-lived climber that requires no pruning to maintain. An outstanding shade vine for large masonry walls, mature trees, and shaded pergolas in zones 5–9.

Plant acorns in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Chinese cork oak is the Asian counterpart of the European cork oak (Quercus suber) — and in many ways a superior ornamental and more cold-hardy version of its famous cousin. Native across a huge range in Japan, Korea, and China, it develops a similarly distinctive thick, deeply furrowed, corky bark, but is deciduous (the European cork oak is evergreen) and considerably hardier to cold, surviving to zone 5 compared to zone 7-8 for cork oak. The chesnut-like toothed leaves are attractive and larger than the European cork oak's leaves. The acorns are covered almost entirely by the shaggy, bristly, elongated acorn cup scales — one of the most distinctive acorn features of any oak. An excellent ornamental for large gardens in zones 5–9 where the dramatic corky bark texture and bold silhouette are desired. More versatile climatically than cork oak but rarely grown in North America.

Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese evergreen oak is a handsome, moderate-sized evergreen oak native to China, Japan, and Korea, producing long, narrow, slightly wavy-margined, glossy dark green evergreen leaves with distinctive reddish-bronze new growth — creating a refined, almost tropical appearance more reminiscent of a Southern Magnolia relative than a typical oak. One of the most ornamental and well-behaved evergreen oaks for humid subtropical gardens in zones 7–9, more tolerant of the heat and humidity of the Southeast than many evergreen oaks from the Mediterranean. The slender leaves and upright, oval crown make it suitable for smaller garden spaces where live oak would be too massive. Produces small, elongated acorns. Increasingly available at specialty nurseries and becoming recognized as an excellent evergreen street and garden tree for the Southeast.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; loropetalum is one of the most popular landscape shrubs for the Gulf Coast and Southeast, prized for its burgundy to purple-bronze foliage that holds color year-round and its showy fringe-like flowers in spring and sporadically through the year. The purple-leaved forms ('Plum Delight', 'Burgundy', 'Purple Diamond') are especially striking contrasted against green neighbors. It tolerates summer heat and humidity better than most ornamental shrubs. Prune immediately after the main spring flowering to shape; do not shear into tight balls — this destroys the natural graceful arching habit and removes flowering wood. Apply a slow-release, acid-forming fertilizer in early spring.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese fringetree rivals the native white fringetree in spectacular spring flower display, producing dense, drooping clusters of slender, white, four-petaled flowers that cover the entire tree in a frothy, fragrant cloud of white in May and June, giving the tree the appearance of being draped in snow. The flowers are both fragrant and profuse enough to be visible from a great distance. Male trees tend to produce heavier floral displays than females; female trees produce attractive clusters of dark blue-black berries beloved by birds in late summer and fall. Compared to the native Chionanthus virginicus, the Chinese species blooms slightly later, is notably more heat-tolerant and adaptable in zone 8–9, and has a tidier rounded habit. The large, glossy, leathery leaves are attractive all summer and the gray, furrowed bark is interesting in winter.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chinese hat plant is a Himalayan shrub grown for its uniquely structured flowers — each blossom has an expanded, saucer-shaped orange-red calyx (the 'hat') surrounding a smaller tubular corolla, giving each flower the appearance of a Chinese mandarin's hat. The flowers appear in arching terminal clusters from fall through spring in frost-free climates when hummingbirds and sunbirds seek them out. The plant is drought-tolerant and blooms most prolifically during cooler, drier periods. Prune hard after bloom to rejuvenate and shape. In zone 9 protect from frost or grow in large containers.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — Chinese hibiscus is the quintessential tropical flowering shrub, producing the largest and most spectacular flowers of any landscape shrub: blooms 4–8 inches or more across in virtually every color of the rainbow — red, pink, orange, yellow, white, lavender, and complex multi-toned combinations — blooming from spring through frost in zone 9 and nearly year-round in zone 10–12. Flowers last only a single day but the plant produces so many buds that the display is constant. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom; apply slow-release fertilizer every 4–6 weeks during the growing season. In zone 9, mulch heavily in fall and expect some stem dieback in hard winters, but established plants resprout reliably from the base. Essential for the tropical-theme summer garden in any zone as a magnificent container plant moved outdoors in summer.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese holly is the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant of all the landscape hollies — an essential, tough, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub for Gulf Coast and southeastern landscapes that tolerates summer heat, poor soil, clay, drought, and partial shade far better than English holly (I. aquifolium). The leaves are rectangular with four characteristic spiny corners, giving them a distinctive, blocky appearance different from other hollies. Most cultivars set heavy crops of large, brilliant red berries without a pollinator tree. 'Burfordii' (single terminal spine, heavy berries, classic selection), 'Needlepoint' (narrow, single-spined leaf, columnar form), 'Dazzler' (heavy berry producer), and 'Rotunda' (compact, dwarf, no berries) are widely grown selections. Remarkably tough and long-lived once established in the landscape.

Soak seeds in hot water and allow them to cool overnight before sowing directly into prepared ground in spring after frost danger has passed. Plant seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained soil and keep evenly moist until germination occurs. Transplant seedlings to their permanent location while still small, as the taproot establishes quickly and resents disturbance. Allow generous spacing to accommodate the wide canopy this tree develops at maturity.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese ixora is an East Asian evergreen shrub of the coffee family (Rubiaceae) closely related to the common tropical ixora (I. coccinea) but producing its characteristic, dense, rounded, terminal clusters of small, tubular flowers in a soft-pink to rose-pink or white color rather than the vivid red-orange of the common species. The flowers are produced continuously from spring through fall, with some intermittent bloom at other seasons in frost-free climates, creating a long-season display of soft-pink color that is more easily incorporated into refined garden color schemes than the intense red-orange of common ixora. Chinese ixora is notably more shade-tolerant than its common relative, blooming acceptably in partial shade conditions — making it one of the few continuously-blooming flowering shrubs useful in shaded positions in zone 9–12. Like all ixoras, it requires strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) for best performance; alkaline soil causes interveinal chlorosis. It is more cold-hardy than I. coccinea, surviving temperatures to approximately 28°F in zone 9.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese lantern abutilon grows into a tall, upright, somewhat leggy shrub with maple-like leaves and pendant, bell-shaped flowers in orange with distinctive dark red veining, the coloring that earned it the nickname candy corn plant among collectors. It blooms over a long season, often nearly year-round in essentially frost-free gardens, and is a reliable, easy-care source of hummingbird nectar with minimal pest or disease trouble. Pinch young plants regularly to encourage branching, since unpinched stems tend to grow tall and sparse rather than full and floriferous. Where winters bring hard freezes, expect significant dieback, with recovery from the roots likely if mulched; alternatively, grow it in a large container that can be moved to a sheltered spot for winter protection.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath high, open tree canopy; Chinese leatherleaf mahonia is a tall, architectural evergreen shrub with long, upright canes topped by whorls of narrow, spiny-toothed, leathery leaflets, giving it a bold, almost tropical silhouette unlike the lower, mounding mahonias more commonly grown. In late fall into early winter it produces dramatic upright racemes of bright yellow, faintly fragrant flowers held above the foliage like candelabra, opening earlier than most other mahonias and providing valuable nectar for pollinators and hummingbirds during the coldest, leanest part of the year; blue-black, grape-like berries follow and are relished by birds. Its strongly vertical, sculptural habit makes it a striking accent for the back of a shaded border or a shady courtyard corner rather than a foundation planting. It is the parent, along with M. japonica, of the popular hybrid Mahonia x media selections such as 'Charity' and 'Winter Sun'. Prune out the oldest canes at ground level after flowering if the clump becomes leggy, to encourage fresh basal growth.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Chinese mahonia is a more refined, less aggressive alternative to Oregon grape (M. aquifolium) for warm-climate shade gardens, producing an upright, narrow form with elegant pinnate leaves bearing multiple narrow, deeply toothed, dark-green, glossy leaflets and dense clusters of fragrant yellow flowers in fall followed by small, blueberry-like, powdery-blue fruits. It is specifically more shade-tolerant and heat-tolerant than the popular Oregon grape. The evergreen foliage provides year-round structure in the darkest parts of the shade garden. Valuable for winter interest with both flowers and persistent fruits. Excellent in formal shaded landscapes and Japanese-inspired gardens.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Chinese parasol tree (fenghuang tree or phoenix tree in Chinese, critical in Chinese mythology as the only tree on which the mythical fenghuang/phoenix would perch) is a fast-growing deciduous tree from China and Japan with extraordinary ornamental character — the smooth, bright gray-green bark is distinctive and attractive year-round, the enormous 3–5 lobed, maple-like leaves (up to 12 inches wide) create a bold, tropical appearance, and the unusual fruits (split open as boatlike follicles with edible seeds attached to the margins) are unlike any other temperate tree fruit. The seeds have a mild flavor and are eaten roasted in China. Widely planted across the southeastern US and has naturalized in many areas. The botanical family Malvaceae places it with hibiscus, cotton, and cacao. Beautiful spring flower spikes of greenish-yellow flowers. The pale gray bark is particularly attractive in winter, glowing almost white against a dark background. A dramatic, fast-growing ornamental but aggressive self-sower.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun with good air circulation; Chinese photinia is the large-growing photinia species that serves as the parent of the more commonly planted Fraser photinia (Photinia × fraseri) — a robust, large evergreen shrub or small tree growing 10–25 feet tall with broad, leathery, serrated, glossy dark-green leaves and dramatic new-growth red coloration when young foliage first emerges in spring. The new growth displays the vivid red coloration characteristic of all photinias — a flush of bright red new leaves that contrasts dramatically with the existing dark-green foliage in spring and provides several weeks of striking seasonal color. Chinese photinia is more cold-hardy than Fraser photinia and grows substantially larger, functioning as a true screening tree or large specimen shrub rather than just a foundation shrub. It is notably more resistant to Entomosporium leaf spot disease (the fungal disease that disfigures many Fraser photinias) than its hybrid offspring. White flower clusters in spring are followed by red berries that attract birds. The tall, screening habit makes Chinese photinia valuable for privacy screens and large property divisions — it can reach tree proportions over decades. Provide excellent drainage and good air circulation to minimize leaf spot.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese pistache is widely regarded as the single best fall-color deciduous shade tree for the Gulf South — one of the very few trees that reliably produces brilliant orange, scarlet, and red fall color in zone 9, where autumn temperatures are too mild for most fall-color trees to perform. While maples, oaks, and sweetgums produce muted or inconsistent fall color in zone 9, Chinese pistache reliably transitions to vivid orange-red in late October through November even with the mild, late arrival of cool nights in the Gulf Coast region. The tree grows 30–40 feet tall with a broad, rounded canopy that provides excellent shade, and it is well-suited to the challenging conditions common in Gulf Coast urban landscapes — clay soils, alkaline soil pH, extended summer drought, reflected heat from pavement, and periodic wet periods all fail to deter established Chinese pistache. Female trees produce ornamental clusters of small red berries that transition to blue-purple in winter and are attractive to birds. Trees are dioecious (separate male and female trees); most nursery trees are grafted males selected for form, or named females. Exceptionally low-maintenance once established — no serious pest or disease problems affect Chinese pistache in the Gulf South.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor, alkaline-tolerant soil; Pistacia chinensis is drought tolerant once established and adaptable to clay, calcareous, and compacted soils — an ideal street and parking-lot tree for hot, dry southern climates where few trees provide reliable autumn color. Pistacia chinensis (Chinese Pistachio) is a large, handsome, deciduous tree native to the mountains and valleys of central and western China (Sichuan, Hubei, Shaanxi), a member of the same genus as the edible pistachio nut (P. vera) and closely related to the mastic tree (P. lentiscus). Its primary ornamental value is its outstanding, consistent, brilliant autumn foliage — turning vivid combinations of red, orange, scarlet, and yellow that rival New England maples in color intensity, but dependably in climates from zone 6 through zone 9 including the Deep South, Gulf Coast, and Texas where true maples produce disappointing autumn color. The tree is extremely tough and adaptable: drought tolerant once established, alkaline soil-tolerant, heat-resistant, relatively pest- and disease-free, and tolerant of urban pollution and compacted soils. Small, blue-black drupes on female trees (pistachio-like but not edible commercially) are attractive to songbirds. Chinese Pistachio has become one of the recommended utility and street trees for Texas, Oklahoma, and the Gulf States precisely because of its reliable autumn color and toughness under extreme summer heat and drought.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese plumbago is a shrubby, deciduous perennial from western China producing clusters of brilliant, clear-blue, five-petaled flowers from midsummer through fall — one of the best sources of true blue color in the late-season garden. The vivid cerulean-blue flowers are distinguished from hardy plumbago (C. plumbaginoides) by the upright shrubby form and slightly larger flowers. In autumn, the dark green foliage turns brilliant burgundy-red simultaneously with the last flush of flowers, creating an exceptional combination of blue flowers and red foliage. Hardy to zone 6, it dies back to the ground in cold winters and re-sprouts from the roots. In zone 9, it may remain evergreen in mild winters. Combines beautifully with ornamental grasses and late-season yellow wildflowers in fall gardens.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Chinese redbud is a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree from central China that produces an extraordinary spring flowering display on bare branches in early spring — densely packed, vibrant rosy-purple pea flowers covering every branch, twig, and even directly on older wood (cauliflory) before a single leaf emerges. The intensity of the floral display is arguably greater than Eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis) because the flowers are deeper in color (deeper rose to violet-magenta) and the shrubby habit places them at eye level where the bloom can be most appreciated. The cultivar 'Avondale' (from New Zealand) is considered among the finest woody ornamentals in cultivation, with unusually intense, deep rose-purple flowers. Chinese redbud is more shade-tolerant and more compact than Eastern redbud, making it more manageable in smaller gardens and better suited to underplanting in partial shade. The heart-shaped leaves are large and glossy, turning yellow in fall. Long-lived, disease-resistant, and exceptionally showy in spring.

Chinese snowball viburnum produces some of the largest flower clusters of any hardy landscape shrub, with sterile snowball-shaped heads 6 to 8 inches across opening lime-green in mid-spring before maturing to pure white. Because the flowers are sterile, the plant sets no fruit, trading wildlife berries for weeks of striking bloom display. It grows into a large, rounded, semi-evergreen shrub in the Gulf South (fully deciduous in colder zones) and works best as a specimen or large screening plant where its considerable mature size is an asset rather than a problem. Give it room, water it well while establishing, and resist heavy pruning except right after flowering.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Chinese stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance. Smooth, flaking, multicolored bark in patches of gray, tan, and cinnamon provides outstanding winter interest, complemented by white, camellia-like summer flowers with prominent yellow-orange stamens and rich orange-red fall foliage color, giving this small ornamental tree four full seasons of garden interest. Related to camellias and prized among collectors for its combination of showy summer flowers, exfoliating bark, and vivid fall color on a manageable small-tree scale, it makes an outstanding specimen for a shaded woodland garden or Asian-style planting. Provide consistent moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, mulch well to keep roots cool, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established, since stewartias transplant and establish slowly.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some shelter from strong wind and the hottest afternoon sun; Chinese sweetshrub is a striking relative of the familiar American Carolina allspice, bearing much larger flowers — broad, white-to-blush, waterlily-like blooms with a yellow-streaked interior — in late spring, a dramatic step up in size and showiness from the smaller maroon flowers of the American species, though with only a light fragrance rather than the American plant's strong spicy scent. Glossy, deep-green, oval leaves turn a clear yellow in fall. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than American Carolina allspice and appreciates a sheltered woodland-edge position rather than full, exposed sun. A choice, uncommon specimen shrub for a partly shaded border, valued more for the size and elegance of its individual flowers than for fragrance. Prune only lightly after flowering to shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial shade; Chinese sweetspire is the Asian counterpart of Virginia sweetspire (Itea virginica) — a graceful, slightly larger evergreen shrub from the forests and stream banks of central and southern China, with similar (but somewhat larger and more leathery) glossy green leaves and long, fragrant, white flower spikes in summer. More heat- and drought-tolerant than Virginia sweetspire, and evergreen in zone 7–10 rather than deciduous. The long (4–6 inch), slender, fragrant white flower spikes are produced in summer and have a pleasant, sweet scent. Fall color in mild climates is less spectacular than Virginia sweetspire (which turns brilliant red), remaining more greenish-yellow in warmer zones. A refined, shade-tolerant evergreen shrub for the mild, humid Gulf Coast and similar climates where an elegant partial-shade shrub with fragrant summer flowers is desired. Less commonly grown than Virginia sweetspire but valuable for its additional heat-tolerance and evergreen quality in the South.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese sycopsis is an uncommon and underused member of the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) from central China, providing year-round ornamental interest through its dense, holly-like evergreen foliage of dark, glossy, spiny-margined leaves. The late-winter flowers — small, yellowish, without petals — are unspectacular individually but appear in late January or February before most woody plants show any sign of life, providing early-season pollen for queen bumblebees. The compact, dense growth habit makes it an excellent formal evergreen screening shrub or hedging plant. More shade-tolerant than most Hamamelidaceae relatives and particularly well adapted to the woodland garden in zones 7–9. Rarely available in US nurseries but worth seeking from specialist growers for a distinctive, refined addition to the winter garden.

common_name: Chinese Trumpet Vine (Chinese Trumpet Creeper, Grandiflora Trumpet Vine)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Chinese Trumpet Vine blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates and even benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat, extending the blooming season. Campsis grandiflora is a vigorous, deciduous, woody climbing vine native to China and Japan in the Bignoniaceae family, closely related to the American Trumpet Vine (Campsis radicans) but producing flowers roughly twice the size — 3–4 inches across rather than the 2-inch flowers of its American relative. The large, trumpet-shaped flowers are borne in terminal clusters of 6–12, in vivid shades of orange-red with a salmon-orange interior tube — somewhat less intensely red than C. radicans and more orange-apricot in tone. The flowers bloom from mid-summer through fall in successive flushes and are extraordinary hummingbird attractants. Unlike C. radicans, which clings to surfaces via aerial holdfast roots, C. grandiflora generally lacks strong self-clinging ability and requires tying to support structures — a quality that makes it more controllable in small garden spaces. The intergeneric hybrid Campsis × tagliabuana 'Madame Galen' (C. radicans × C. grandiflora) combines the best features of both parents and is one of the most widely planted trumpet vines in US gardens. Zone 7–9 hardiness makes C. grandiflora a better Gulf Coast choice than the more cold-hardy but aggressively spreading C. radicans.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy or sandy loam soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese tulip poplar is the Asian counterpart of the American tulip poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera) — the only two species in the genus, separated by millions of miles of ocean yet producing very similar leaves and flowers. The leaves are distinctively more deeply notched (2 lobes per side rather than 1 in North American tulip poplar) and slightly smaller, giving a more intricate, finely cut appearance. The flowers are smaller and greener than the North American species' bold orange-and-yellow flowers, but share the same tulip-like form. Chinese tulip poplar grows more slowly and at a smaller ultimate size than American tulip poplar, making it more appropriate for gardens of moderate size. More tolerant of heat and humidity than North American tulip poplar in zones 7–9. Of great botanical interest as a 'living fossil' — a relict of the ancient flora of the Northern Hemisphere from the Cretaceous period, now restricted to two isolated populations on opposite sides of the Pacific Ocean.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Chinese Virginia creeper is a shade-adapted relative of the American Virginia creeper (P. quinquefolia), notable for its strikingly beautiful foliage — the dark green leaves are marked with silver-white veining along the main veins, creating a distinctive, elegant variegated effect. The velvety texture of the leaves enhances this decorative quality. In shade, the silver veining is most pronounced; in full sun, the plant is less attractive and the variegation less distinct. The vine clings to walls, fences, and tree trunks using adhesive tendrils. In fall, the leaves turn rich red-orange even in shade — unusual for a variegated plant. An outstanding shade vine for covering north-facing masonry walls where few other vines perform well.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Chinese winter hazel is a large, multi-stemmed shrub native to mountain forests of central China, producing long, pendulous racemes of soft yellow flowers with a light, sweet fragrance in late winter or very early spring before the leaves emerge. Each drooping chain of 15–20 small flowers resembles a string of yellow bells, and a well-established shrub in full bloom creates a spectacular curtain of pale gold in the February garden. The large, boldly veined, heart-shaped leaves that follow are attractive through summer, turning yellow in fall. One of the more cold-tolerant Corylopsis species, surviving reliably to zone 6 and worth trying in sheltered zone 5 microclimates. The variety var. calvescens 'Spring Purple' has purple-flushed new growth; 'Wisley Red' has red-tinged new leaves and calyces.

Plant grafted plants in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun with very strong permanent support; Chinese wisteria is one of the most spectacular flowering vines in temperate gardening — in full bloom in April and May the plant is covered with cascading, pendulous clusters (racemes) of fragrant, violet-purple flowers up to 12 inches long that open all at once in a breathtaking floral display. The fragrance is sweet and pervasive. However, Chinese wisteria is classified as an invasive exotic pest plant throughout the southeastern United States, where it has escaped cultivation to smother trees and native forest understory in a manner similar to kudzu. It twines clockwise (Japanese wisteria, W. floribunda, twines counterclockwise). The vines become massive with age — potentially requiring structural reinforcement of pergolas and arbors. For gardeners seeking wisteria bloom without ecological risk, the native American wisterias (Wisteria frutescens, W. macrostachya) offer similar floral display with smaller racemes and WITHOUT the invasive risk. Confirm wisteria regulations in your state before planting Chinese or Japanese wisteria.

Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese witch hazel dislikes wet, waterlogged soil or heavy clay — ensure adequate drainage; it is the most cold-hardy of the Chinese witch hazels and reliable in zones 5–8. Hamamelis mollis is the best of the Chinese witch hazels and one of the finest winter-blooming shrubs for temperate gardens; it produces exceptionally large, softly golden-yellow, strap-petaled flowers with an extraordinarily rich, spicy-sweet fragrance — one of the finest natural perfumes of any flowering plant — on bare stems in January and February when the garden is otherwise dormant. The large, soft, round leaves turn butter-yellow to orange-yellow in fall before dropping; and the plant has a distinctive, broadly spreading, vase-shaped form. The cultivar 'Pallida' (pale sulfur-yellow) and 'Goldcrest' (deep golden yellow with red centers) are among the finest selections.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chinese witchhazel is one of the most fragrant of the witchhazels, producing its spidery yellow to orange flowers in the dead of winter (January through February) with an intensely sweet, warm, spicy scent that carries remarkable distances on cold air. The flowers are frost-resistant and remain attractive even after mild snow and ice events. Chinese witchhazel (H. mollis) is a primary parent of the popular Hamamelis x intermedia hybrids that dominate nursery trade — including 'Arnold Promise' (yellow), 'Jelena' (orange), and 'Diane' (coppery-red). The large, rounded leaves turn a clear golden-yellow in fall. Slow to establish but very long-lived and low-maintenance once settled.

common_name: Choctaw Crape Myrtle (Large-Flowered Bright Pink Indian-Series Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, allowing ample room for this tall, tree-form cultivar to reach its mature size. Choctaw is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, prized for its clear bright pink flowers borne in exceptionally large clusters, among the largest of any crape myrtle cultivar, on a tall tree reaching up to 30 feet with age. It ranks among the most mildew-resistant cultivars in the Indian series, an important trait in the humid Gulf South, and develops attractive exfoliating bark for winter interest. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

Christmas senna is a semi-evergreen, fast-growing tropical shrub from the Caribbean and Central America that earns its common name by producing showy clusters of bright canary-yellow flowers from October through December and into winter — blooming abundantly when most other landscape plants have shut down for the season. It is one of the most important larval host plants for cloudless sulphur butterflies and orange-barred sulphur butterflies, with adults laying eggs on the foliage throughout the warm months and caterpillars consuming the leaves until the plant is bare, then quickly regrowing — a cycle that makes Christmas senna an outstanding butterfly garden plant. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, it grows rapidly to form a large, billowing shrub that can be cut back hard in late winter to maintain a manageable size and stimulate vigorous new growth; it tolerates poor, sandy soils and drought once established, making it low-maintenance in suitable climates. Note: it can naturalize and spread by seed in zone 9b–11 — monitor and remove seedlings in ecologically sensitive areas.

common_name: Chuck Hayes Gardenia (Cold-Hardy Reblooming Double-White Gardenia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade; Chuck Hayes is a standout gardenia cultivar selected for two key improvements over standard Gardenia jasminoides: superior cold-hardiness (zone 7 reliable, versus zone 8 for most gardenias) and a rebloom tendency that produces flowers in both spring and fall rather than the single spring-only bloom flush of the species. Named for the North Carolina gardener who selected and propagated it, Chuck Hayes represents a significant horticultural improvement that extends gardenia culture northward and provides a longer bloom season throughout the Southeast. The flowers are classic double-white gardenia — the iconic, deeply fragrant, creamy white multi-petaled blooms that represent the pinnacle of floral fragrance in the American garden — produced in April–June and again in September–October in favorable conditions. The compact, rounded habit (3–5 feet) is more manageable than standard gardenia, fitting typical residential border spacing without crowding. The cold-hardiness improvement makes Chuck Hayes the preferred choice for zone 7b-8a gardeners who have lost standard gardenias in severe winters, and provides additional security for zone 9 gardeners in the rare extreme cold events that affect the Gulf South. Gardenias require consistent moisture and strongly acidic soil — iron chlorosis from insufficiently acidic soil is the most common cultural problem.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; chuparosa is a sprawling, nearly leafless desert shrub of the American Southwest with slender gray-green stems that carry out most of the plant's photosynthesis, an adaptation to extreme drought and heat in its native washes and rocky desert flats. Tubular, bright red-orange flowers, rich in nectar, are produced heavily in late winter and spring and again after summer rains, and are one of the most reliable early-season hummingbird nectar sources in the low desert, giving the plant its Spanish common name meaning 'hummingbird sipper.' It tolerates reflected heat, poor rocky soil, and long dry spells that would kill most other flowering shrubs, needing supplemental water only to establish and during the driest extended stretches. Prune out dead or frost-damaged wood in spring, since plants may drop leaves or die back partially in a hard freeze but generally resprout well from older wood.

common_name: Cinnamon Girl Distylium (Bronze New-Growth Evergreen Shade Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to full shade — distylium is one of the most adaptable evergreen shrubs available, thriving in nearly any light level and tolerating both drought and occasional wet soil once established. Cinnamon Girl produces new growth flushed a warm coppery bronze-red before maturing to lustrous dark green, giving season-long color contrast on a dense, mounding, wider-than-tall shrub that functions as a low-maintenance, deer-resistant alternative to boxwood or Indian hawthorn. Small, inconspicuous red flowers appear in late winter but are not the plant's main ornamental feature. It requires little pruning to hold its naturally tidy, rounded form, and tolerates heat, humidity, and both sun and shade with equal ease, making it a versatile foundation or mass-planting shrub across a wide range of garden conditions.

Plant this compact shrub rose in spring in a sunny, well-drained bed, spacing plants for good airflow. Cinnamon Hearts forms tidy mounds topped with clusters of fragrant cherry-red blooms from spring into fall. Water deeply and regularly during the first season to establish roots, then keep soil evenly moist. Prune lightly in late winter and remove spent blooms to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Cinnamon-Scented Hoya (Lacunosa Hoya, Porcelain Flower, Trough Wax Plant)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Hoya lacunosa blooms most freely in bright indirect light and will produce few flowers in dim conditions, but it is one of the more adaptable Hoyas and can tolerate lower light without the decline that affects less robust species. Hoya lacunosa is a compact, trailing to twining epiphytic vine from South and Southeast Asia (India, Malaysia, Thailand, Java, Borneo, Sumatra) in the family Apocynaceae, producing smaller leaves than most Hoyas — elliptical, dark-green, waxy, with a distinctive pitted or trough-marked surface texture (the specific epithet 'lacunosa' means 'marked with pits or troughs'). The primary ornamental appeal is the flowers: small, waxy, white to cream, star-shaped flowers with a yellow or pale center, arranged in tight, globe-shaped umbels of 15–30 individual florets, produced at the tips of the characteristic persistent flower stalks (peduncles). The flowers produce an intense, sweet, spicy fragrance often described as pure cinnamon or warm vanilla-cinnamon — far more pronounced than the subtle fragrance of most other commonly grown Hoyas. The fragrance is most intense in the evening and on warm days, filling a room with a pleasant bakery-like scent whenever a cluster is in bloom. Hoya lacunosa is considered one of the easiest and most rewarding Hoyas for beginners, blooming freely with minimal care. Non-toxic to pets.

Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Cityline is a series of compact bigleaf hydrangeas, named for individual cities, bred for a dense, rounded, well-proportioned habit that stays under 3 feet and holds its large mophead blooms upright on strong stems rather than flopping under the flower weight, a common problem with older, taller hydrangea cultivars. Its compact size makes it especially well suited to foundation plantings, small gardens, and large containers where a full-sized hydrangea would be too large. Individual cultivars within the series bloom in shades from blue and purple to pink and red depending on soil pH, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, adjustable with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune lightly if needed, since bloom occurs primarily on old wood formed the previous season and heavy pruning removes next year's flower buds.

common_name: Claire Austin Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing support if training the vigorous canes upright as a short climber. Introduced by David Austin in 2007 and named for his daughter-in-law, Claire Austin carries large, cupped, pale creamy-white to soft lemon blooms that fade toward pure white as they open, with a strong myrrh fragrance that intensifies on warm days. Its vigorous, somewhat lax growth habit allows it to be trained against a fence or pillar for extra height, or kept as a large freestanding shrub with regular pruning, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; clammy locust is the ornamentally superior native locust of the southern Appalachians, producing large, elegant clusters of rose-pink (not white like black locust) flowers that are among the most beautiful of any native North American tree in spring. The species name 'viscosa' and common name 'clammy locust' refer to the distinctive sticky, clammy glands on the leaf stalks, branchlets, and seed pods that make the plant sticky to the touch. More compact than black locust and less aggressive in spreading — a significant advantage in the garden. Nitrogen-fixing, drought-tolerant once established, and tolerant of lean, poor soils where other trees struggle. The pink flowers make it a far better ornamental specimen than black locust for garden use. Spreads by root suckers like other locusts but less aggressively. An underused native ornamental small tree.

common_name: Clara Indian Hawthorn (Compact White-Flowered Indian Hawthorn)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates partial shade with somewhat reduced flowering. Clara is a compact Indian hawthorn selection valued for its clean white flower clusters in spring, a crisper look than the pink tones of most other cultivars, held against the same leathery, dark green, disease-resistant foliage typical of the species. Its naturally tidy, rounded size fits foundation plantings and low borders without the size Majestic Beauty or other larger selections eventually reach. Like other Indian hawthorns it is outstanding for coastal Gulf gardens, tolerating salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil, and needs only a light shaping prune right after spring bloom.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Cleopatra is a vigorous, upright Camellia sasanqua cultivar producing single to semi-double, rose-pink to deep-pink flowers with prominent golden-yellow stamens from October through December in zone 9. The medium-pink flower color is clear and saturated — a classic, feminine camellia pink that combines well with white-flowering companions, silver-foliage plants, and the dark evergreen foliage of camellias and hollies in the fall garden. Cleopatra is one of the more sun-tolerant sasanqua camellias, performing well in 4–6 hours of direct sun that would stress most japonica camellias, and it is more vigorous and faster-growing than many sasanqua selections. The upright, dense, somewhat narrow-columnar habit (6–12 feet tall, somewhat narrower than its height) makes it useful for screening and hedge applications where height is needed in a limited horizontal space. As with all sasanqua camellias, the fall flowers are mildly fragrant — pleasant but not overwhelming. Cleopatra was one of the foundational sasanqua cultivars widely planted across the Gulf South in the mid-twentieth century and remains a reliable, proven performer for zone 9 camellia gardens. Fertilize with azalea-camellia acidic fertilizer in spring and early fall.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Cleveland sage is a California native aromatic shrub with one of the strongest and most complex sage fragrances in the genus — deeply resinous, herbaceous, and intensely medicinal. The gray-green, deeply textured leaves are used as a culinary sage substitute (particularly appropriate with poultry and game) and were traditionally used by Kumeyaay and other indigenous peoples for ceremonial smudging. It blooms profusely in spring with whorls of lavender-blue flowers on tall spikes that are outstanding for hummingbirds and native bees. In summer-dry Mediterranean climates and warm dry gardens, it is one of the best ornamental shrubs available — extremely drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and low-maintenance once established.

Plant in moist, slightly to moderately acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — cleyera is one of the most refined and underused evergreen shrubs for southern shade gardens, producing elegant, glossy, dark green leaves with reddish new growth on a naturally pyramidal to oval form. The small, creamy-white, fragrant flowers in spring are followed by dark red to black berries that attract birds; the plant is sacred in Shinto tradition in Japan, where it is planted at shrines. Cleyera is an outstanding foundation plant, informal hedge, or large specimen for the shaded, acidic, humus-rich conditions under tall pines and oaks throughout zone 7–9. It grows more slowly than many companion plants (camellias, gardenias) but eventually becomes a large, refined, long-lived shrub requiring almost no maintenance beyond an occasional light shaping. Excellent companion plant for camellias and azaleas in woodland garden compositions.

Plant container stock in fall into rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, matching the limestone canyons and rocky slopes of the Southwest and southern Rockies where cliff fendlerbush grows wild. In late spring it produces an abundant flush of four-petaled, white to pale-pink, sweetly fragrant flowers resembling mock orange blossoms, drawing native bees, hawk moths, and hummingbirds to an otherwise sparse rocky landscape. It is highly drought- and cold-tolerant once established and needs no supplemental irrigation, making it well suited to xeriscape and native rock-garden plantings. Deer tend to browse it lightly, and its dense, twiggy branching provides good cover for small birds.

Plant Bomarea multiflora tubers in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; provide support for the twining stems to climb; keep consistently moist through the growing season; in zone 8–9, mulch heavily in winter to protect the tubers from frost. Climbing Alstroemeria is a genus of tuberous, climbing vines closely related to the familiar Alstroemeria (Peruvian Lily) of florists, but with a distinctly different growth habit — the stems twine and scramble through surrounding vegetation to heights of 3–6 feet, decorated with alternate, bright-green, resupinate (twisted) leaves. The large flower clusters at the stem tips bear 10–30 individual pendant, tubular flowers in brilliant orange to deep red-orange (B. multiflora is one of the most vivid-colored species) with a contrasting yellow interior and brown-purple speckling. The genus Bomarea comprises some 120 species throughout the Andes and tropical Americas — an undeservedly neglected group that most temperate gardeners have never encountered despite the extraordinary floral display. Native to the cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador at elevations of 6,000–10,000 feet, B. multiflora prefers cool to mild temperatures — making it better suited to the mild climates of the Pacific Coast and zone 8–9 Southeast than strictly tropical conditions. Hummingbirds are the primary pollinators in its native range.

Climbing aster is the only vining aster native to North America, an extraordinary scrambling perennial from the Gulf Coastal Plain and Florida that clambers 6–15 feet through shrubs and fences to display enormous masses of small, lavender-to-pink flowers with yellow centers in late fall, often blooming well into December in zone 8 and 9 gardens. Because it flowers so late in the season — October through December in the Deep South — climbing aster serves as a critical last nectar source for late-migrating monarchs and queens, sulphur butterflies, and overwintering native bees that remain active through early winter in the Gulf Coast region. Plant it where it can scramble through a wax myrtle, yaupon holly, or native shrub border; its somewhat weedy scrambling stems are hidden by surrounding plants while the spectacular late-autumn bloom is the garden's last big show before frost. Cut back hard in late winter to control spread and encourage vigorous new stems for next season's bloom.

Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade at the base of a trellis, fence, or scrambling support; climbing bleeding heart is a unique native biennial vine of moist, rocky, shaded slopes and forest margins in the Appalachians and northeastern North America. The lacy, glaucous blue-green foliage is extremely finely divided and feathery, resembling the leaves of bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos/Dicentra) or corydalis, and the plant climbs by means of clinging petioles to reach 6–10 feet. The small, nodding, tubular flowers — white to pale pink — are produced in summer of the second year in clusters from the leaf axils, resembling tiny bleeding hearts. Self-sows freely in appropriate conditions to form a naturalized colony. An unusual and beautiful native vine for shaded woodland trellises and shrub edges, little known in cultivation.

Climbing dogbane is a rare native alternative to the widely planted Confederate jasmine (Trachelospermum jasminoides), naturally found in the moist bottomland forests, swamp margins, and stream banks of the Gulf Coast from Virginia to Texas — it is the only species in its genus native to North America. Unlike its Asian relative, climbing dogbane adapts to shaded conditions under bottomland oaks and cypress, making it one of the few woody ornamental vines that will thrive in genuine shade; it produces clusters of small, fragrant, yellowish-white five-petaled flowers in early summer that are visited by native bees and butterflies. The milky latex sap makes it unpalatable to deer, and the plant is host to several specialist milkweed butterflies and moths in the family Apocynaceae. While less commonly available commercially than Confederate jasmine, climbing dogbane is worth seeking out from native plant nurseries for shaded trellises, arbors, and woodland garden structures where a fragrant, native evergreen vine is needed.

Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; climbing fetterbush is an unusual native Gulf South evergreen shrub with small, glossy, dark-green leaves and clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers similar to its relative Pieris japonica, but famous for a remarkable habit in the wild — in its native cypress and blackgum swamps, it grows as a true climber, sending stems up underneath the loose, fibrous bark of the host tree, invisible except where leafy branchlets emerge through cracks in the bark many feet up the trunk. In ordinary garden cultivation without a suitable host tree, it instead grows as a low, sprawling, spreading shrub, still worthwhile for its evergreen foliage and flowers in a wet, shaded native plant garden. It needs the same reliably moist, acidic soil as its swampy origin and struggles if allowed to dry out. A conversation-piece native shrub for a bog garden or swamp-margin planting within its narrow Gulf South range.

Plant Mutisia clematis in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide shrubs, netting, or a trellis for the modified leaf tendrils to grip; keep evenly moist in the growing season; protect from hard frost below 25°F; propagate from stem cuttings in late spring. Climbing Gazania (Mutisia) is one of the most remarkable genera in the Asteraceae (daisy) family — unlike virtually all other members of the daisy family which are herbaceous or non-climbing, Mutisia species are climbing, tendril-bearing, woody-stemmed scandent shrubs that scramble through Andean cloud forest and shrub margins by means of modified leaf extensions acting as tendrils. The large, solitary daisy-like flowers — brilliant orange-red in M. clematis with a golden-yellow center disc — are produced repeatedly at the stem tips and are genuinely spectacular on close inspection, resembling a large, elegant gerbera daisy held by a climbing vine. The approximately 60 Mutisia species are distributed along the length of the Andes from Venezuela to Patagonia; most are challenging to cultivate but M. clematis is considered one of the more tractable in mild climates. A genuinely unusual and conversation-worthy plant for mild, coastal garden climates in zone 8–10 where cool temperatures, consistent moisture, and good drainage can be provided.

Start seeds early indoors and train on a trellis or other support in full sun to part shade; climbing gloxinia is a Mexican native vine producing large (2–3 inch), softly tubular, trumpet-shaped flowers in clear, warm rose-pink to soft magenta — a flower form and color closely resembling gloxinia (Sinningia), hence the common name, on a freely climbing vine 6–10 feet long. The hairy, somewhat gloxinia-like leaves contribute to the resemblance. The flowers are abundant from summer through fall and the whole plant has a pleasant, cottage-garden quality — softly colored, generous with bloom, and adaptable to growing up fences, trellises, tripods, and into shrubs. Previously classified as Asarina erubescens, it belongs to the snapdragon family and shares some visual qualities with that family. 'Magic Dragon' is a widely available seed strain in the nursery trade. An excellent companion to softer-colored annual and tender perennial vines on a mixed-planting trellis or fence.

Climbing hemp weed is a vigorous native twining vine of the aster family (Asteraceae), native to wetland margins, pond edges, freshwater tidal marshes, and moist thickets across the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern United States — despite being little-known in cultivation, it is one of the highest-value native vines for late-season pollinators. Dense clusters of small, fluffy white to pinkish flowers cover the vine from late summer through fall and are magnets for migrating monarchs and a remarkable diversity of native specialist bees; it is among the most important native late-season nectar sources in Gulf Coast wetland habitats. The vine climbs and twines quickly in warm seasons, making it useful for rapidly covering trellises, fences, and chain-link at the edges of rain gardens, constructed wetlands, and moist riparian restoration plantings. In zone 9 and south it remains semi-evergreen; in zone 8 it freezes to the ground but returns vigorously from the roots each spring.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to part shade; climbing hydrangea is among the most valuable vines for shaded positions — one of the few vigorous, ornamental climbers that succeeds and blooms in substantial shade. It clings to walls, tree trunks, and structures by tiny adhesive aerial rootlets without damaging sound mortar and masonry. In June and July, established plants produce large, flat-topped flower heads (lace-caps) up to 10 inches across — creamy white with ornamental sterile flowers surrounding a center of tiny, fertile flowers — in breathtaking abundance that is one of the showiest June spectacles possible on a shaded wall. The bark on mature stems exfoliates in thin, cinnamon-red sheets, creating beautiful winter interest. The broadly oval, glossy leaves turn bright yellow in fall. Native to Japan and Korea, it is slow to begin growing after planting (famously described as 'the first year it sleeps, the second year it creeps, the third year it leaps') but is exceptionally long-lived and essentially maintenance-free once established on a suitable structure.

This vigorous woody vine climbs walls and trees by aerial rootlets, covering surfaces with heart-shaped leaves and fragrant, lacy white blooms in late spring. Plant in part shade to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; it also tolerates morning sun with steady moisture. Be patient, as it is slow to establish but grows rapidly once settled, eventually reaching great heights. Provide strong support and prune after flowering only to control size.

Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in part to full shade; climbing hydrangea vine is a native eastern North American alternative to the Asian climbing hydrangea (H. anomala subsp. petiolaris), found naturally in moist forests and swamp edges from Virginia to Florida and Louisiana. It climbs trees, walls, and structures by clinging aerial rootlets, and in late spring produces clusters of small, sweet-fragrant, white flowers without the large sterile bracts of the Asian species — more modest but very sweetly scented and genuinely attractive to pollinators. The leaves are glossy, dark-green, and semi-evergreen to evergreen in zones 7–9, making it useful for year-round coverage of shaded surfaces. It tolerates deeper shade than most vines and is one of the few self-clinging climbers native to the southeastern US. Outstanding for climbing shaded tree trunks, stone walls, and other structures in moist, shaded southern gardens where Asian vines perform poorly. Supports the ecology of the forest system it comes from — its berries are eaten by several bird species.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun along a fence, trellis, or through a sturdy shrub; Climbing Milkweed (also called Honeyvine) is a vigorous twining native perennial in the milkweed subfamily, producing smooth, heart-shaped leaves and dense clusters of small, sweetly honey-fragrant white flowers from July through September that are outstanding nectar sources for monarch butterflies and many native bees. It is native to moist, open, disturbed ground, fencerows, and thicket edges throughout the eastern and central US, and produces classic milkweed seed pods that split to release plume-tailed seeds. Climbing Milkweed can spread aggressively from both seed and rhizomes in favorable conditions and is best suited to naturalistic or wildlife garden settings where its habit of covering fences and scrambling through shrubs is welcome rather than a problem.

Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 60–70°F; transplant after last frost into partial shade to sun in moist, well-drained soil; climbing snapdragon (Asarina procumbens) is a charming, soft-hairy, trailing vine-like plant native to rocky cliff faces and limestone walls in northeastern Spain, producing snapdragon-like pale yellow flowers with cream-yellow throats throughout the summer. The self-clinging petioles allow it to scramble over rough surfaces and through other plants; it is especially beautiful draping over stone walls, tucked into rock garden crevices, or spilling from containers and hanging baskets. In zone 7–10 it is perennial and can be propagated from cuttings; in colder zones grow as an annual. Distinguished from the related climbing snapdragons (Lophospermum) by its pale yellow flowers rather than pink or red.

Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; this slow-establishing evergreen vine rewards patience with years of low-maintenance coverage once mature. Glossy, leathery, evergreen leaves cling self-sufficiently to a wall, tree trunk, or fence by aerial roots much like climbing hydrangea, producing frothy, creamy-white clusters of small flowers in late summer when few other climbing shrubs are blooming. Native to forests of China, it is slower to establish than more vigorous climbing vines, often taking several years before it begins climbing in earnest, but once established requires little maintenance and holds its evergreen foliage through mild winters better than deciduous climbing hydrangea relatives. Provide consistent moisture during establishment, be patient during the slow early years of growth, and site on a shaded wall or trunk where its self-clinging roots can attach.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; provide a strong trellis or allow to scramble through a supporting tree. Artabotrys hexapetalus (climbing ylang ylang or manorangini) is a tropical Indian and Southeast Asian climbing shrub in the custard apple family (Annonaceae) that climbs by means of distinctive hooked, curved peduncles (flower stalks) that become woody and hook-like as the flower develops — anchoring the plant to supporting branches without true tendrils or twining. The plant produces small, pale yellow-green to yellow flowers in clusters, with six tepals (three outer, three inner) — the flowers have an extraordinarily powerful, sweet, heady fragrance almost identical to true ylang ylang (Cananga odorata) — intensely sweet, floral, slightly fruity — and are among the most powerfully fragrant flowers in the tropical garden. The scent intensifies dramatically at night, making this plant outstanding for outdoor seating areas in the tropics. In South India, the flowers are used in temple garlands, hair decorations, and in traditional perfume making — the essential oil extracted from the flowers is used in Ayurvedic preparations and in the perfume industry as a low-cost ylang ylang substitute. A remarkable and underused tropical fragrance plant for zone 10–12.

Take semi-hardwood cuttings 4-6 inches long in late spring or summer, remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and insert into a warm, humid propagation environment with bottom heat near 80°F. Once well rooted, harden off and transplant to a permanent location with robust support, as the vine climbs by means of strong hooked stems that anchor to host structures. Water consistently during establishment, then reduce frequency once the plant is settled; mature plants tolerate brief dry spells but flower most profusely with regular irrigation and monthly balanced fertilization from spring through fall. Prune lightly after each flush of bloom to encourage branching and additional flowering, and position near seating areas or windows to take full advantage of the powerful ylang-ylang fragrance that intensifies in the evening.

common_name: Cloud 9 Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming Compact White Flowering Dogwood)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, siting it in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Cloud 9 is a compact, exceptionally heavy-flowering flowering dogwood selection, producing such a dense covering of large, pure white bracts each spring that the tree can appear almost solid white, an especially prolific bloom that has made it one of the most popular white dogwood cultivars in nursery production. Its smaller, more compact mature size than the species also suits it to smaller residential landscapes. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, since dogwoods are shallow-rooted and stressed by drought; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering, and watch for powdery mildew and dogwood borer in humid climates.

common_name: Cloud Nine Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming White Flowering Dogwood)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cloud Nine is one of the most widely admired white flowering dogwood cultivars — selected for its unusually profuse bloom (the bracts cover the tree so densely at peak bloom that the branches are nearly invisible), its somewhat horizontally spreading branch structure that creates a wider than tall profile, and its ability to bloom as a young tree in its first or second year rather than requiring 5–7 years before flowering as is common with seedling-grown trees. The large, overlapping, pure-white bracts (each slightly overlapping the adjacent bract, creating a solid canopy of white) cover the entire tree at peak bloom in March through April in zone 9 — the flowering display has been described as looking like the tree is covered in white clouds, giving the cultivar its name. The wider-than-tall spreading form gives Cloud Nine a distinctive silhouette even when not in flower — an elegant horizontal branching pattern that is attractive year-round. Excellent red to maroon fall foliage color and red berries for wildlife follow the spring bloom. In zone 9, plant in morning sun and afternoon shade on the north or east side of structures to minimize summer heat stress on this understory native.

Coast azalea is a compact, stoloniferous native azalea of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain's sandy pine barrens and oak scrublands — producing one of the most intensely fragrant flowers of any native azalea, with white to pale pink blooms that emit a strong, sweet vanilla-clove fragrance in April and May before the leaves fully expand. Unlike most native azaleas that form upright, single-stemmed shrubs, coast azalea spreads slowly by underground stolons (horizontal stems) to form broad, low colonies — a growth habit that makes it one of the finest native azaleas for use as a naturalized groundcover or mass planting under open pinelands and dry oak canopy. Its compact, low stature (rarely over 4 feet) and tolerance of dry, sandy, nutrient-poor acidic soils make it more versatile in the landscape than taller species; it is also more heat-tolerant than northern azaleas and performs reliably in the upper Gulf Coastal Plain. Several hybrid azaleas have been developed from this species for their fragrance and compact habit.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic soil in full sun; coast banksia is one of the most adaptable and cold-hardy Australian banksias, a coastal tree of eastern Australia growing 10–30 feet with distinctive pale-green leaves that are dark green above and silvery-white below — creating a two-toned effect as leaves move in the wind. The characteristic cylindrical banksia flower spikes (4–6 inches long) are produced primarily in autumn and winter in soft, pale-yellow, and are among the richest natural nectar sources of any flowering tree — overwhelming in the volume and concentration of the nectar they produce. This makes them critical wildlife habitat for honeyeaters, lorikeets, bats, and a vast array of insects including native bees. The hardened, woody seed cones that follow the flowers can persist on the branch for years before opening to release seeds in response to fire (a key ecological adaptation). One of the most cold-tolerant banksias and the best starting species for gardens in zones 8b–11 seeking Australian native character.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Erythrina caffra is drought tolerant once established — water deeply and infrequently during summer in Mediterranean and subtropical climates and rely on winter rainfall in coastal California conditions; avoid heavy clay with poor drainage. Erythrina caffra (Coast Coral Tree or South African Coral Tree) is a large, semi-deciduous tree native to the coastal forests and river margins of Eastern South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape) that has become one of the defining ornamental trees of the Southern California street landscape, the official city tree of Los Angeles. Trees lose most of their leaves in late winter and simultaneously burst into spectacular bloom — the dense, columnar racemes of bright coral-red to orange pea-family flowers covering the bare, spiny branches from January through March create an unforgettable winter floral display unmatched by almost any other tree in temperate gardens. The flowers are rich in nectar and attract hummingbirds, lorikeets, and sunbirds across its global planted range. Erythrina caffra is more cold-hardy than the related E. variegata — tolerating brief periods near 25°F when established in well-drained soil — which has made it the standard large coral tree for zone 8b–9 California and Southeastern gardens. A nitrogen-fixer that enriches surrounding soil; useful for large spaces, street medians, and parks.

Coastal Doghobble is a graceful, arching, broadleaf evergreen native shrub, native to moist, acidic, shaded streambanks, ravine slopes, and moist, sandy forest understories of the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi, where its arching stems weave through the understory to form dense, impenetrable thickets — hence the 'doghobble' name, as hunting dogs became entangled in the arching stems. In April and May it produces racemes of small, white, urn-shaped flowers along the undersides of the arching branches, followed by attractive dark green, leathery, lance-shaped leaves that turn burgundy-red to bronze in winter, providing excellent cold-season color in the shade garden. One of the most shade-tolerant native broadleaf evergreen shrubs available, Coastal Doghobble thrives under dense tree canopy where azaleas and camellias struggle; provide consistently moist, acidic soil and avoid alkaline conditions or prolonged drought.

Plant in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; inkberry is a versatile native evergreen holly of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain with glossy dark green leaves and small black berries that provide essential winter food for over 35 bird species including bluebirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and hermit thrushes. Unlike many hollies, inkberry tolerates wet, seasonally flooded sites and even some saltwater intrusion, making it ideal for rain gardens, bioswales, and poorly drained sites where most shrubs fail. Numerous compact cultivars have been developed for landscape use, including 'Compacta' (3–4 ft), 'Shamrock' (3–4 ft, very cold hardy), and 'Nigra' (4–6 ft with good fruiting). Both male and female plants are needed for berry production; one male ('Nordic' or 'Strongbox') pollinates several females.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coastal jugflower is grown almost exclusively for its foliage — one of the finest-textured, most silvery-soft, most ethereally beautiful of all Australian native shrub foliages. The leaves are divided into multiple, extremely fine, thread-like silver-gray segments covered in silky, lustrous, silver hairs that catch light from every angle and create an overall impression of a plant made from fine, soft, silver-gray floss — a shimmering, luminous, soft-silver cloud of extraordinary fine texture. Each leaf has multiple, feathery, thread-like lobes covered in the lustrous, silky hairs of the species name 'sericeus'. The whole shrub creates a medium-to-large mound of incomparably fine, silver-gray, soft-textured foliage that provides year-round textural and color contrast with nearby bold-leaved or dark-leaved plants. In spring it produces small, tubular, red flowers in the leaf axils — pleasant but not the primary ornamental point. Native to the coastal sand dunes and heathlands of southwestern Western Australia where its silver, reflective foliage may reduce water loss and reflect intense sunlight. Outstanding as a silver foliage specimen or contrast plant in zone 9 Mediterranean-climate gardens requiring excellent drainage and lean soil.

common_name: Coastal Plain St. John's-Wort (Atlantic St. John's-Wort)
notes: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the seasonally flooded pine flatwoods and pond margins where it grows wild. This small, upright, semi-evergreen shrub has fine, needle-like leaves and produces a summer-long succession of bright yellow flowers with a prominent tuft of stamens at each branch tip, attracting native bees and other small pollinators. It tolerates standing water for extended periods yet also handles the seasonal dry-down typical of Gulf Coast wet pinelands, making it a resilient choice for the fluctuating water levels of a rain garden or pond-edge planting. Use it as a filler shrub among taller wetland trees or massed along a ditch or bioswale where few other woody plants can establish.

Coastal Plain Staggerbush is a native evergreen shrub endemic to the dry, sandy, fire-maintained scrub and flatwood habitats of the Florida peninsula, where its dense, leathery-leaved growth and small white to pink urn-shaped flowers in spring make it a characteristic component of the open, sunny, infertile sand communities dominated by oaks and palmettos. Adapted to the same xeric conditions as Florida Rosemary, Scrub Hickory, and other Florida scrub specialists, Coastal Plain Staggerbush requires excellent drainage and periodic low-intensity fire to maintain the open, competitive-free conditions it requires. Like other Lyonia species, the foliage contains grayanotoxins and is toxic to livestock if consumed. Plant in dry, strongly acidic, sandy, well-drained, infertile soil in full sun — Coastal Plain Staggerbush thrives in the nutrient-poor, fire-managed conditions of its native habitat and requires no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established.

Coastal Plain Willow is the most abundant native willow of the coastal plain wetlands, stream banks, tidal margins, and disturbed wet soils from Virginia south through Florida and west to Texas and the Caribbean, forming dense multi-stemmed thickets that provide critical cover and nesting habitat for waterfowl, shorebirds, and muskrats. Like all willows, it produces copious pollen and nectar in early spring that are among the first resources available to emerging queen bumblebees, native sweat bees, and early butterflies; the foliage hosts the caterpillars of Viceroy, Mourning Cloak, and numerous native moths. Propagate easily from hardwood cuttings taken in late winter before bud break, inserting 8–12 inch stems into moist, wet soil in full sun; rooting is rapid, establishment reliable, and fallen branches that contact moist soil root naturally. Coastal Plain Willow spreads aggressively by root suckers in wet areas and is best used in large, naturalized riparian settings where its vigorous growth habit is an asset.

common_name: Cockspur Coral Tree (Ceibo, Cry Baby Tree, Fireman's Cap)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Cockspur Coral Tree is quite drought-tolerant once established and tolerates a wide range of soils including sand and alkaline conditions. Erythrina crista-galli (Cockspur Coral Tree or Ceibo) is the national tree and national flower of both Argentina and Uruguay — its spectacular, intense red flowers are also depicted in the coat of arms of Argentina. The flowers are large (2–2.5 inches), waxy, brilliant red, and clustered into drooping racemes at the branch tips in spring and summer; the characteristic 'crista-galli' (rooster's crest) refers to the hooded shape of the large standard petal. In warm climates the tree blooms March–June and again in fall, attracting hummingbirds, orioles, and numerous other nectar-feeding birds. In zone 9, the plant dies back to the root system after hard frost each winter and regrows to 5–8 feet by the following summer, blooming on new wood — acting effectively as a large, spectacular die-back perennial. In zone 10-11 it grows into a 30-foot tree with massive flowering displays. The thorny branches and trunks are a defensive characteristic; all parts of the plant are toxic if consumed. 'Compacta' is a dwarf cultivar reaching 6–8 feet suitable for smaller gardens.

Cockspur hawthorn is a native small tree or large shrub of the eastern United States named for its long, curved thorns (3–4 inches) that resemble a rooster's spur and made it one of the most effective barrier hedges historically used to create impenetrable property boundaries before barbed wire. Its extremely wide, horizontal branching creates a distinctive, picturesque silhouette that provides year-round interest: white flower clusters in May, glossy red fruits persisting through winter, and spectacular scarlet-to-orange fall foliage color. As a wildlife tree, it is exceptional: the long-persistent red fruits are consumed by cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, robins, and bluebirds through winter when other food is scarce; the dense, thorny structure provides the safest possible nesting habitat for catbirds, thrashers, and wood thrushes. A thornless cultivar ('Inermis') is available for locations where the formidable thorns would be a hazard, providing all the wildlife and ornamental benefits of the species without the thorns.

common_name: Coco Magnolia / Dwarf White Jade Orchid
notes: Take semi-hardwood cuttings in late spring or early summer, wound the base lightly, apply rooting hormone, and root under intermittent mist or inside a humidity tent at 75-80°F with bright indirect light. Transplant rooted cuttings into organically enriched, well-drained soil and avoid heavy clay or sites prone to waterlogging, as Magnolia coco is sensitive to root rot. Unlike most magnolias that bloom in a single dramatic flush, this compact species produces its nodding, creamy-white, intensely sweet-scented flowers from spring through fall, making it especially rewarding near a patio, entryway, or courtyard window. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and midsummer, and deadhead spent flowers to keep the plant tidy and encourage the next wave of bloom.

This iconic conifer forms a stately pyramid of silvery-blue needles, serving as a striking specimen or windbreak. Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained soil and give it space, as mature trees grow large. Water regularly while young to establish deep roots, then it tolerates cold and moderate drought well. Avoid crowding to reduce needle-cast and canker problems, and prune only to remove dead or damaged branches.

common_name: Comanche Crape Myrtle (Coral-Pink Mildew-Resistant Indian-Series Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Comanche is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, an interspecific hybrid of Lagerstroemia indica and Lagerstroemia fauriei released in 1978 for improved powdery mildew resistance over older all-indica cultivars, bearing large clusters of coral-pink flowers through summer on a medium-to-large tree.
