Like other Indian-series crape myrtles it develops attractive exfoliating bark and good fall foliage color, adding multi-season interest beyond the summer bloom. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Common Boxwood (American Boxwood, Large-Growing Species Boxwood)
notes: Plant in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest parts of zone 8–9; common boxwood is the classic large-growing species behind centuries of formal garden hedging, topiary, and knot gardens, producing dense, small, glossy evergreen leaves on a shrub that, left unclipped, eventually reaches 15–20 feet — considerably larger and faster-growing than the compact 'Suffruticosa' edging boxwood more often used for miniature parterres. Regular shearing two to three times during the growing season maintains a tight, formal hedge or topiary shape; boxwood tolerates hard pruning well and can be shaped into nearly any form. Good air circulation is essential to reduce boxwood blight and leaf spot diseases, both increasingly serious problems in humid climates — avoid overhead watering and dense, unpruned growth that traps moisture. Provide consistent moisture, especially the first two years, and mulch to keep roots cool, since boxwood roots are shallow and sensitive to both drought and waterlogging.

Plant in moist to wet, or even periodically flooded soil in full sun to partial shade; buttonbush is a native shrub of swamps, pond margins, and floodplains throughout eastern North America, producing creamy white spherical flower heads resembling pincushions in July and August that are among the most intensively visited flowers by butterflies, native bees, and hummingbirds. The round seed heads provide food for waterfowl and songbirds through winter. It is one of the premier plants for rain gardens, bioswales, and pond edges where periodic flooding occurs. Prune in late winter to shape and stimulate new flowering wood; it can be cut back hard if it becomes too large.

Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; common correa is the most widespread Australian Correa species — occurring naturally across the entire southeastern corner of Australia from Queensland to South Australia, in habitats from coastal cliffs and heathlands to mountain forests — and producing in winter and early spring the pendant, tubular, fuchsia-like flowers that give all the correas their common name 'native fuchsia'. The flower form is characteristically correa: a pendant, narrow, tubular or slightly flared tube with four petals that reflex (turn back) at the tip, the whole flower dangling downward from the stem like a small, pendant, delicate bell. The flower color in the wild type is typically red to green-and-red bicolor — a vivid red tube with reflexing green petal tips — but the species is exceptionally variable, with white, pink, salmon, and pure green forms occurring naturally and several selected cultivars now in the trade. The winter bloom timing provides nectar for winter-active honeyeating birds; in cultivation it serves hummingbirds. More shade-tolerant than most Australian natives, growing well in the dappled shade of light-canopy trees. One of the most adaptable and garden-worthy of all correas.

Plant in moist, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil with afternoon shade in zones 8–10 to prevent leaf scorch; gardenia is prized for its intensely fragrant, waxy white flowers that bloom in late spring to midsummer and makes one of the most effective landscape shrubs in the Deep South when sited correctly. Maintain consistent soil moisture but never allow roots to sit in standing water — drought stress triggers bud drop. Fertilize monthly from spring through summer with an acid-type fertilizer; yellowing leaves between the veins (interveinal chlorosis) signal iron or manganese deficiency and respond to applications of chelated iron. Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in late summer for propagation.

Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any reasonably fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to full shade; common greenbrier climbs by tendrils and should be given a sturdy support or allowed to clamber through shrubs in naturalized garden areas, as the stout, prickly stems are difficult to remove once established. Smilax rotundifolia is a native vine of eastern North American forests, woodland edges, and disturbed areas; it produces stout, green, thorny stems that climb vigorously by paired tendrils, bearing glossy, round to heart-shaped, evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves, small, greenish, insignificant flowers in spring, and clusters of blue-black berries in fall that are important wildlife food for many species of birds and mammals. The young shoot tips, new leaves, and rhizome tips are edible and have been used as food by Native Americans; the berries are edible but insipid. Best used in naturalized, wildlife-friendly gardens where its aggressive colonizing habit is an asset rather than a problem.

Plant on a trellis, fence, arbor, or other sturdy support in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; common jasmine, also called poet's jasmine, is the classic hardy climbing jasmine species long grown for its intensely sweet-scented white, star-shaped flowers, produced in flushes from late spring through summer above delicate, deep-green pinnate foliage. It is the species most associated with the essential oil used in perfumery and is more cold-tolerant than the tropical jasmines popular in warm climates, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once established, though it dies back in a hard freeze and resprouts from the base. The twining stems climb readily onto any support and can also be trained as a loose, informal groundcover or espalier if left untrellised. Prune immediately after the main spring-summer flush to shape the vine and control size, since it blooms on the current season's new growth. Consistent moisture and a sunny to lightly shaded spot with good air circulation encourage the heaviest, most fragrant bloom.

Site in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, and prune spent flower clusters immediately after bloom since next year's buds set almost right away. The intensely fragrant purple, lavender, pink, or white florets are a classic foraged edible flower, stripped from the woody stem and used fresh in salads and desserts or infused into sugar, syrup, jelly, and shortbread; only the petals are eaten, as the green calyx is bitter. Established plants are long-lived and drought-tolerant once rooted, and old, overgrown shrubs respond well to renewal pruning by removing a third of the oldest canes each year.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; common net bush is a large Australian shrub of the southwest with a distinctly unusual flower arrangement — unlike the symmetrical bottlebrush spikes of Callistemon, in which flowers radiate from all sides of a terminal spike, Calothamnus (and its flowers are embedded along the woody, older stems and oriented predominantly to one side of the stem — the 'one-sided bottlebrush' habit that makes the genus immediately distinguishable. The crimson flower bundles appear in spring along the older, needle-leaved, dark-green stems at intervals, the scarlet to crimson stamen bundles projecting to one side of the stem in a bold, contrasting display of rich crimson on dark, needle-like foliage. The effect is unusual and distinctly architectural — red flower bundles appearing at intervals along the dark, spiky-leaved, one-sided bottlebrush stems — and quite different from the familiar symmetrical bottlebrush form. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established, enduring the hot, dry, lean conditions of southwestern Australian coastal scrub without supplemental irrigation in Mediterranean-climate zones. A distinctive choice for water-wise zone 9 gardens seeking Australian flora with unusual flower arrangement.

common_name: Common Privet (European Privet, Classic Deciduous Hedge Shrub)
notes: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; common privet is the traditional European hedging shrub behind centuries of formal garden and farmstead hedgerows, valued for tolerating hard, frequent shearing, poor and alkaline soils, and urban pollution better than most flowering shrubs, growing dense and twiggy with small, dark-green, semi-deciduous leaves that persist late into fall. Clusters of small, strongly scented white flowers appear in early summer, followed by small black berries that are mildly toxic if eaten and are spread widely by birds — this readiness to self-seed has made common privet a documented invasive species escaping into woodlands and fencerows across parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States, where it crowds out native shrub-layer plants. Shear two to three times during the growing season to maintain a tight, formal hedge, and consider deadheading or shearing before flowering to reduce berry production and self-seeding where invasive spread near natural areas is a concern.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, phosphorus-poor, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; common sunshine conebush is the most adaptable and widely grown Leucadendron species, a South African fynbos shrub producing lance-shaped leaves that flush brilliant yellow-green to gold in winter and spring — the yellow color intensifying with cooler temperatures and brightening the garden in the season when color is most needed. Male and female plants are distinct (dioecious); female plants produce small, scaled cones surrounded by the colorful bracts; male plants produce more colorful upright flower heads. Many named hybrids including 'Safari Sunset' (dark red), 'Wilson's Wonder,' and 'Cloudbank Ginny' are popular in the cut foliage trade. Like all protea family plants (Proteaceae), leucadendrons require excellent drainage, lean soil with very low phosphorus, and minimal irrigation once established. Outstanding in California Mediterranean climates and dry subtropical gardens; a major component of the international cut-foliage industry.

Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; common witch hazel is highly shade-tolerant and grows naturally as an understory tree in mature eastern deciduous forests. Hamamelis virginiana is the source of the distilled witch hazel extract used in skincare, first-aid, and medicinal products worldwide, and has extraordinary ornamental value as a native shrub/small tree that blooms with wavy, spider-like, bright-yellow fragrant flowers directly on bare branches from October through December — the latest-blooming native woody plant in eastern North America. It also provides outstanding fall foliage color in shades of yellow to orange-red, is a critical late-season nectar source for witch hazel bees (Andrena astragali) and other fall-active insects, and the ballistic seed capsules that eject seeds up to 30 feet give rise to its folk name. Extremely adaptable, cold-hardy, and long-lived.

common_name: Common Yellow Plumeria (Traditional Hawaiian Yellow Frangipani)
notes: Grow in full sun in fast-draining soil or a large container, since waterlogged roots are the main cause of failure; along the Gulf Coast this cultivar is best grown in a pot that can be moved to a garage or greenhouse for winter dormancy. Common Yellow produces intensely fragrant white flowers with golden-yellow centers from late spring through fall and is among the most widely propagated and lei-grade plumerias in Hawaii and the tropics. Withhold water almost entirely once the plant drops its leaves and goes dormant in winter storage, and resume watering only after new growth appears in spring.

A French introduction from the early twentieth century, this reliable clematis produces abundant mauve-pink flowers with a subtle darker central bar and golden stamens over a long summer bloom period. It belongs to pruning group three, so cut stems back hard to a healthy bud pair near the base in late winter to keep the vigorous vine tidy and encourage maximum flowering. It tolerates a range of soils better than many large-flowered hybrids as long as drainage is adequate, and it is often recommended as an easy, forgiving choice for beginners. Pair it with a host shrub or sturdy trellis, since its long stems can reach considerable height in a single season.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; confederate jasmine (not a true jasmine but a related genus) is one of the most beloved and widely planted fragrant vines in Gulf Coast landscapes, producing masses of small, pinwheel-shaped, pure-white flowers with an intoxicating, sweet-spicy fragrance that perfumes an entire garden in spring bloom. Glossy, dark-green, evergreen leaves on twining stems provide year-round foliage interest. It is remarkably adaptable — trained on trellises and arbors as a vertical element, allowed to sprawl as a groundcover, used as a sprawling shrub, or pruned as a low hedge. In zone 8–11 it is fully evergreen and essentially indestructible once established, tolerating heat, drought, poor soil, and salt spray. Prune back after flowering to keep it tidy and encourage dense regrowth. One of the most reliable and rewarding plants in the Gulf Coast garden.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; confederate rose is one of the most spectacular autumn-blooming flowering shrubs of the American South, producing enormous (4–6 inch), double, peony-like flowers that open white in the morning and gradually deepen through pink to rose and finally deep red by evening — the color change of a single flower over one day is one of the most remarkable visual effects in horticulture. Single-flowered forms also exist. Blooming from late summer through frost, confederate rose provides critical fall color just when other shrubs are fading. The plant grows very large — a true shrub-tree — and propagates effortlessly from cuttings, which root in a cup of water on the windowsill. It was passed from garden to garden across the antebellum South this way for generations. Prune to 2–3 feet in late winter; the plant regrows vigorously each season and blooms on new wood.

Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Confetti is a compact variegated abelia selected for small, glossy green leaves edged in creamy white through the growing season, with the margins flushing rosy-pink in cool fall and winter weather for striking three-season color even without flowers. It still produces the small, fragrant, pale pink to white tubular blooms typical of abelia from summer into fall, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds, but its main appeal is the compact, dense, mounding habit and reliable foliage color. Like other abelias it tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and a range of soils once established, needing only a light shaping after the main bloom flush and removal of any winter-damaged stems in late winter.

common_name: Constance Spry Rose (First David Austin English Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the long canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1961, Constance Spry was the first rose in what became the English Rose line, bearing huge, cupped, clear pink peony-like blooms carrying a rich, unusual myrrh fragrance that David Austin had not previously found in a modern rose. Unlike most later English roses it blooms only once, in a spectacular, heavy flush in late spring, on a large, vigorous, thorny shrub or short climber, so it is best sited where its single dramatic display and handsome foliage justify the space; some gardeners underplant it with later-blooming perennials to extend seasonal interest.

common_name: Conversation Piece Azalea (Multi-Color Reblooming Robin Hill Azalea)
notes: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Conversation Piece, the first-ever Louisiana Super Plants selection, is a Robin Hill series azalea known for a genuinely unusual trait — individual flowers on the same plant, and even within the same cluster, open in a range of colors and patterns, from soft pink to near-white to boldly splashed and variegated blooms, so no two flushes ever look quite the same and the shrub is a real conversation starter in bloom. It flowers in spring and often produces a second, lighter flush in fall, extending the display beyond the single spring bloom typical of most azaleas. Like other azaleas it needs consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil and benefits from a partly shaded site protected from hot afternoon sun. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom if shaping is needed, since next year's flower buds set on the current season's growth.

Plant in deep, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade, choosing a permanent location since beech roots are shallow and easily damaged by digging or soil compaction nearby. Copper Beech is a classic purple-leaved selection of European beech, prized for foliage that emerges deep purple-bronze in spring and generally holds a rich copper-purple color through summer before turning bronze-gold in fall, providing dramatic color contrast as a specimen or shade tree. It grows into a large, dense, majestic tree with smooth gray bark that stays attractive through winter, and its lower branches sweep gracefully toward the ground if left unpruned, though it can also be limbed up for a more traditional shade-tree form. It is a slow to moderate grower that rewards patience with great longevity, but it needs a real winter chill and struggles with the heat and humidity of the Deep South, performing best in cooler temperate climates well outside zone 9.

common_name: Copper Canyon Daisy (Mountain Marigold, Lemmon's Marigold)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; copper canyon daisy is one of the finest large perennial flowering shrubs for zone 8–11 gardens — a sprawling, aromatic shrub covered in masses of small, bright golden-yellow daisy flowers in fall and winter (and sometimes spring) when very little else is blooming. The deeply divided, fernlike leaves are pungently aromatic (a strong citrus-mint-marigold scent that is powerfully deer repellent) and retain an attractive gray-green color through much of the year. It is outstanding for fall color, butterfly attraction, and combining with blue salvias or purple ageratum for a stunning gold-and-purple fall combination. Prune back by one-third after each bloom flush to keep the plant compact; an unpruned shrub can spread to 6 feet or more. In zone 8, top growth may be killed by hard freezes but roots resprout reliably.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; copperleaf holds its most vivid foliage colors in full sun — in shade the color becomes less intense. Acalypha wilkesiana (copperleaf or Jacob's coat) is a tropical Pacific Island shrub grown worldwide as a tropical foliage plant for its spectacularly colorful, large (3–5 inch), copper-red, bronze, maroon, red-orange, yellow, or multicolor variegated leaves in an enormous range of named cultivars — each leaf is often a mosaic of two or three colors in irregular patterns or in distinct margins. The effect in mass plantings is bold and tropical, creating intense color impact that few other foliage plants can match in summer heat. Common cultivar groups include 'Mosaica' (rich coppery-red), 'Marginata' (green leaves with copper-red margins), 'Musaica' (orange to bronze), and 'Tricolor' (red, pink, and green). In zones 9–12, copperleaf grows as a perennial shrub; in colder zones, root cuttings in fall and overwinter indoors. It thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity and is essentially pest-free in those conditions, making it one of the best choices for low-maintenance tropical-themed summer color.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it as a low-maintenance evergreen hedge, foundation shrub, or mass planting where deer pressure is a concern, since distylium is rarely browsed. Coppertone is a First Editions selection of distylium prized for its striking bronze-copper new growth in spring, which matures to glossy dark green, giving the shrub a two-toned seasonal display on a mounding, medium-sized evergreen frame, with small maroon-red flowers appearing inconspicuously along the stems in late winter. It shares the exceptional adaptability of the species — thriving in full sun or full shade, wet or dry soil, and resisting the leaf spot and scale problems that trouble many broadleaf evergreens in humid Gulf South summers. Requires only occasional shaping, as its naturally dense, mounded form rarely needs hard pruning.

Prized for its glowing coral-red winter bark, this Japanese maple also offers soft green spring foliage that shifts to golden-yellow in fall. Plant in part shade with rich, moist, well-drained soil, protecting it from drying wind and intense afternoon sun that can scorch leaves. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist. Prune minimally in late winter to reveal the colorful stems and maintain the graceful branching form.

Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; coral bean is one of the most striking native shrubs of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, producing brilliant scarlet tubular flowers in long spikes in spring before the leaves emerge — they are among the most important hummingbird nectar plants in the Southeast. In fall the pods split open to reveal vivid coral-red seeds that are highly ornamental but extremely toxic if swallowed. The stems bear recurved spines that deter browsing; the plant dies to the ground in hard freezes in zone 7–8 but regrows rapidly from an established root crown. It tolerates partial shade, sandy soil, drought, and salt spray — making it an outstanding native plant for difficult spots in Gulf Coast gardens. The red seeds were traditionally used as ornamentation and have important Native American cultural uses.

common_name: Coral Bells Azalea (Classic Coral-Pink Masses-of-Bloom Kurume Azalea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Coral Bells is a classic Kurume azalea cultivar — one of the Japanese Kurume (city of origin, Kurume, Japan) hybrids that are among the most widely planted azaleas in the American South, characterized by small, glossy leaves, compact mounding habit, and spring flowering so profuse that the foliage can be completely obscured by flowers. The spring bloom display of 'Coral Bells' — masses of small, hose-in-hose (double) to single, coral-pink to warm rose-pink flowers covering the entire plant simultaneously — is one of the quintessential signs of Gulf South spring alongside dogwood and wisteria. The hose-in-hose flower form (one flower nestled inside another, giving the appearance of a double flower with extra petals) is characteristic of many Kurume cultivars and adds ornamental complexity to each individual flower. In zone 9, Kurume azaleas perform as reliable evergreen foundation and landscape shrubs that require only occasional pruning after bloom to maintain their compact, mounded habit. The small, glossy, dark-green leaves provide attractive year-round structure. Strongly acidic, humus-rich soil and consistent moisture are the most critical requirements — chlorosis from insufficient acidity is the most common cultural problem, corrected by soil acidification with sulfur and acid-forming fertilizers.

common_name: Coral Berry Ardisia (Christmas Berry, Hen's Eyes, Marlberry)
notes: Plant in partial to deep shade in any well-drained soil — Coral Berry Ardisia is one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant small shrubs available, performing in conditions of deep dry shade under large oaks that defeat nearly all other ornamentals. Ardisia crenata (also listed as A. crispa) is a small, upright evergreen shrub from India, Southeast Asia, and Japan in the Primulaceae family that produces one of the most striking winter ornamental displays in zone 9 gardens: during November–February, pendulous clusters of bright coral-red to vivid scarlet round berries the size of small pearls hang in dramatic arching sprays below the dark, glossy, wavy-edged, evergreen leaves. The berries persist on the plant for months, and fully loaded plants in December–January are extraordinarily ornamental. The plant blooms in summer with small, inconspicuous white to pinkish flowers that are followed by the developing berries. White-berried ('Alba') and pink-berried forms are available. CAUTION: Classified as invasive in Florida, Texas, Louisiana, Georgia, and other Gulf and Southeast states — birds devour the berries and disperse seeds freely into natural areas where the plant displaces native understory species. Remove berries before they fall if planting in areas with access to natural lands.

Carolina Snailseed is a twining woody vine native to woodland edges, thickets, and fencerows across the southeastern United States. It produces small, heart-shaped to kidney-shaped leaves and inconspicuous greenish flowers on female plants in summer, followed by dense clusters of brilliant red berries in fall that persist into winter and provide important food for mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and hermit thrushes. Grow in average to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; it tolerates a range of soil conditions once established. Note that the berries, while highly attractive to wildlife, are toxic to humans — plant where children will not have unsupervised access to the fruit.

Plant rooted cuttings or small container plants in spring once the soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; coral creeper spreads by rooting stems as it grows, forming a low, dense mat useful as a border edging or filler beneath larger shrubs and trees. Salmon-pink to coral-red tubular flowers appear in flushes almost year-round in frost-free climates, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds, and the semi-glossy foliage stays attractive in light shade where many flowering groundcovers thin out. It is easy to propagate and quick to fill in a bed, but is strictly tropical and tender, dying back or dying out in any real frost.

Set plants in full sun with good drainage, watering deeply during establishment and only occasionally afterward thanks to the shrub's compact, drought-tolerant root system. A light shearing in late winter keeps the low mound shape neat and stimulates fresh bloom cycles. Semi-double coral-orange flowers with hints of yellow at the base cover the small, dense mounds of foliage from late spring through frost, a hallmark of the Drift series bred for continuous bloom and reduced disease susceptibility compared to older groundcover roses. It works well cascading over walls or spilling from raised beds and containers.

Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle this native species is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. The long, tubular scarlet-to-coral flowers bloom heavily in spring and continue sporadically through fall, providing the long-tube nectar that ruby-throated hummingbirds require. Prune in late winter or just after the main spring flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood. In the deep South it is semi-evergreen and may retain foliage through mild winters; in colder zones it loses leaves but regrows vigorously from the base in spring.

growth_habit: landscape shrub rose, Knock Out series
notes: Set plants in full sun with well-drained, fertile soil, watering consistently the first year to establish a deep root system. An occasional light pruning in late winter maintains a compact, well-branched shape and promotes vigorous new flowering wood. Single, coral-orange blooms with a lighter reverse open in flushes from late spring through fall on this compact member of the Knock Out series, bred for strong disease resistance and minimal care. The warm coral tone stands out among the more common red and pink Knock Out selections, and plants rebloom reliably without deadheading.

common_name: Coral Plant (Coral Physic Nut, Multifid Jatropha, Physic Nut)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Coral Plant is drought-tolerant and thrives in the poor, well-drained soils of zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes, tolerating the summer heat and periodic drought that challenges many tropical ornamentals. Jatropha multifida is a large, architectural shrub or small tree from tropical America (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean) grown throughout the subtropical world for its striking combination of deeply lobed, palm-like leaves and vivid coral-red to scarlet flowers. The foliage is dramatically ornamental: large (up to 15 inches across), deeply cut into 7–11 finger-like lobes reminiscent of a Cannabis or Ricinus leaf, on long, flexible petioles that give the plant a bold, tropical sculptural quality. The flowers are borne in flat-topped clusters of tiny, brilliant coral-red, star-shaped blooms that appear prolifically at the branch tips throughout the warm season, attracting butterflies and occasionally hummingbirds. The interesting three-lobed fruit capsules that follow contain large seeds that, while potentially useful as a biofuel crop in some tropical production systems, are highly toxic and should not be consumed. In zone 9, Coral Plant is a fast-growing tropical accent that provides months of flowering interest and bold architectural foliage through the summer and fall.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; coral plant is drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms more heavily under mild drought stress. Russelia equisetiformis (coral plant or firecracker fern) is a Mexican native producing a dense, weeping, fountain-like mound of slender, rush-like, bright-green to gray-green photosynthetic stems (reduced leaves — hence the species name 'equisetiformis,' meaning 'horsetail-like') hung with hundreds of slender, 1-inch, bright-red tubular flowers from spring through frost. The effect is of an almost waterfall-like cascade of green stems and red flowers — one of the most graceful and romantic ornamental shrubs for tropical and subtropical gardens. Ruby-throated hummingbirds and butterflies visit the tubular flowers extensively. Coral plant is exceptionally heat, drought, and salt-tolerant once established, performing well in coastal gardens, under dry overhangs, and in containers on sunny patios. In zone 9, it dies back in hard freezes but resprouts reliably from roots; in zone 10–12, it is an evergreen perennial. It roots quickly from stem cuttings and can be propagated freely for mass plantings.

Plant tubers in well-drained soil in full sun on a fence, trellis, or arbor; coral vine is one of the most beloved and reliable vining plants of the Gulf South — a fast-growing, drought-tolerant vine from Mexico that covers itself in sprays of small heart-shaped pink to magenta flowers in summer through frost, creating a solid curtain of pink that is irresistible to bees, particularly bumble bees and honeybees. The vine climbs by tendrils and can reach 20–30 feet when established. In zone 7–9 the tops die back in hard frost but established tuberous roots resprout vigorously each spring, often growing 10–15 feet in a single season. The flowers and tubers are edible (tubers roasted like sweet potatoes in Mexico). A white-flowered form ('Album') is less vigorous but charming. A fixture in traditional Gulf South gardens for generations.

Divide suckers or plant container specimens in well-drained to dry, average to poor soil in partial to full shade; coralberry (Indian currant, buckbrush) is one of the most valuable and underused native shrubs for the most difficult landscape challenge: dry, deep shade under dense tree canopy where most plants refuse to grow. Coralberry not only survives in these conditions but thrives, spreading steadily by suckers to form colonies of arching, wiry stems bearing small, oval, bluish-green leaves and dense clusters of small, coral-pink to rosy-red berries that persist through winter — important food for bobwhite, pheasant, grouse, cedar waxwings, and other wildlife. Unlike most native shrubs, it tolerates alkaline soil, clay, and root competition from established trees. Its stoloniferous spreading habit makes it excellent for erosion control on shaded slopes and embankments. The cultivar 'Foliis Variegatis' has yellow-variegated leaves that are effective in lightening dark shade. Often overlooked by gardeners in favor of showier shrubs, it is irreplaceable for solving the deep-dry-shade problem.

Plant in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; cork-stemmed passionflower is a compact, small-flowered passionflower with distinctively corky, ridged stems that distinguish it from other species. The tiny greenish-white to cream flowers are inconspicuous but produce small, dark purple to black berries that are important food for white-eyed vireos, gray catbirds, and other frugivorous birds. Most significantly, it is an essential larval host plant for multiple Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and Julia heliconian butterfly species — its small, tri-lobed leaves are consumed voraciously by caterpillars. In zone 9a, it is a reliable perennial vine that provides critical butterfly habitat with almost no maintenance.

Corkwood is one of the rarest and most botanically unusual native shrubs in North America — a monotypic genus (Leitneriaceae family) with no close relatives among living plants, native to the tidal swamps, brackish marshes, and wet bottomlands of scattered, disjunct localities in Georgia, Florida, Texas, Arkansas, and Missouri, where it forms thickets in periodically flooded, organic soils. Its most remarkable characteristic is its wood, which is lighter than cork — making it the least dense wood of any known North American woody plant — and the plant occupies a phylogenetically isolated position in the evolutionary tree of flowering plants. Catkin-like male and female flowers appear on separate plants in spring before the leaves emerge. Despite its rarity, Corkwood is adaptable to a range of wet to moist soil conditions in partial shade to full sun and is occasionally available from specialty native plant nurseries; plant male and female specimens together for seed production. Listed as threatened in several states and on NatureServe's watch list.

Sow fresh seed at a depth of 0.5 inch in moist, well-drained potting mix and maintain temperatures above 72°F to achieve germination within 2-4 weeks; allow seedlings to reach 6-8 inches before transplanting to a permanent understory or semi-shaded garden position. Corky bark polyalthia establishes most successfully in organically enriched, consistently moist soil with good drainage, and benefits from a layer of organic mulch to retain moisture and suppress weeds during the first growing season. Once established, this unusual custard-apple family shrub requires minimal maintenance; its small cream to yellow-green flowers attract pollinators and are followed by small black fruits that draw birds, adding wildlife interest to tropical garden compositions. The deeply furrowed, corky gray-brown bark develops distinctive textural character with age, making it a conversation piece as a specimen shrub or informal screen in zone 10-11 tropical and subtropical gardens.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Covey, marketed as Lavender Twist, is a distinctive weeping redbud cultivar with strongly cascading, contorted branches that arch and twist downward to create a dense, umbrella-like curtain of growth, completely unlike the upright vase shape of standard redbuds. In early spring, before the heart-shaped leaves emerge, the weeping branches are covered top to bottom in the same rosy-lavender pea-family flowers typical of redbud, creating a striking waterfall effect. Because it is usually grafted onto an upright standard trunk, young trees need a stake to help the leader gain height before the weeping side branches are allowed to cascade freely; without staking, the tree can sprawl low to the ground. It stays considerably smaller and more compact than a standard redbud, making it an excellent specimen for a small garden, courtyard, or as a dramatic focal point near a patio. Like other redbuds, it tolerates partial shade well and needs well-drained soil, since the roots are prone to rot in poorly drained sites.

Plant container-grown coyote brush in fall into well-drained soil in full sun; it is one of the most adaptable evergreen shrubs of the California coast and coastal ranges, tolerating fog, wind, salt spray, clay, and extended drought once established. Plants are dioecious, and though wind-pollinated, the male and female flowers that appear in late fall are an outsized late-season nectar and pollen source for migrating butterflies, native bees, and beneficial insects at a time when little else is blooming. Low, spreading cultivars are widely used as erosion-control groundcovers on slopes, while the upright species form makes an excellent informal hedge or wildlife screen. It requires essentially no irrigation once established and tolerates hard pruning to control size.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, thin, rocky or sandy, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; crabwood is a native evergreen tree of south Florida tropical hardwood hammocks, typically growing as an understory to mid-canopy species in the diverse, dense hammock forest. The small, dark green, elliptical leaves are glossy and leathery, and the plant produces dense, attractive foliage year-round. The catkin-like flower spikes are inconspicuous. Small, black fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons, the indicator bird of the south Florida hammock ecosystem. The wood is dense and hard, used historically for tool handles and small crafts. Crabwood is an important structural species of the Miami-Dade hammock ecosystem — a habitat that has been reduced by over 90% from original extent. Suitable for naturalistic south Florida landscaping under and around larger hammock trees.

Plant in wet to moist soil in full sun near water features, ponds, streams, or drainage swales; crack willow gets its name from the brittleness of its branches, which snap off at the joints in storms — a trait that is actually part of its natural dispersal strategy, as fallen branches root wherever they land in moist soil. A native of Europe and western Asia now widely naturalized in North America, it grows extremely fast (5–8 ft per year when young) and provides rapid screening and streambank stabilization. The lance-shaped, glossy green leaves appear very early in spring and provide important early-season forage for willow aphids and the beneficial insects that prey on them. Keep well away from septic systems and water pipes, as the roots are highly invasive toward water sources.

common_name: Cramoisi Supérieur Rose (Crimson Antique China Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1832, Cramoisi Supérieur ('superior crimson') bears cupped, fully double, rich crimson-red blooms with a light fragrance, borne in small clusters against dark green, glossy foliage typical of the China rose class. It blooms in nearly continuous flushes from spring through the first hard frost and shares the exceptional heat, humidity, and disease tolerance for which China roses are prized in the Gulf South, needing little to no spraying to stay healthy through the growing season. A climbing sport of the variety is also grown, but the shrub form remains the most widely planted, working well in borders, mass plantings, and as a low, informal hedge. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; heavy pruning is unnecessary since flowering continues on both old and new growth.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; crape jasmine (pinwheel flower, East Indian rosebay, Adam's apple) is a widely grown South and Southeast Asian tropical shrub that produces pure-white, waxy, pinwheel-shaped flowers with five overlapping, twisted petals throughout the warm season, releasing an intensely sweet, jasmine-like fragrance especially in the evening — making it one of the most fragrant flowering shrubs available for the Gulf Coast and tropical garden. The glossy, deep-green, oblong leaves and neat, dense, rounded growth habit make it attractive even out of flower as a foliage shrub. The double-flowered form, 'Flore Pleno', with ruffled, rose-like double flowers, is the most widely sold cultivar and is particularly ornamental. The plant exudes a milky sap when cut (it is in the Apocynaceae family, related to oleander and plumeria) and all parts are mildly toxic. It is sensitive to frost and is killed back by temperatures much below 32°F, but recovers from the root in zone 9 if given winter protection. Used extensively as a specimen, informal hedge, and container plant throughout tropical and subtropical regions.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; crape myrtle is arguably the most important ornamental tree of the Gulf Coast, the mid-South, and California, producing dramatic clusters (panicles) of crepe-textured flowers in white, pink, red, lavender, or purple from July through September — among the longest bloom periods of any flowering tree — on plants that range from 3-foot dwarf shrubs to 30-foot trees depending on selection. The modern hybrid varieties (L. indica x L. fauriei) also offer spectacular exfoliating bark in cinnamon, gray, and russet that is ornamental year-round, plus brilliant orange-red fall color. These hybrids are also substantially more mildew-resistant than pure L. indica. Sizes range from true dwarf cultivars ('Petite Embers,' 'Tonto') to large trees ('Natchez,' 'Muskogee'). All are extremely heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and long-lived in zones 7–9. Spring pruning should be limited to removing dead wood and crossing branches — severe topping destroys the natural form permanently.

Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or plant container specimens against masonry, stucco, or wood surfaces in partial to full shade; creeping fig is a vigorous East Asian climbing fig that attaches to vertical surfaces by tiny adhesive rootlets, blanketing walls and fences in a dense, neat carpet of small, heart-shaped, dark-green, juvenile leaves — one of the few true shade vines that thrives in deep shade and provides the distinctive ivy-covered wall effect so prized in formal garden design. Juvenile foliage is small and refined; if the vine is not trimmed, the older climbing stems eventually produce larger, leathery, elliptic adult leaves and even figs, but most gardeners trim annually to maintain the juvenile foliage texture. Excellent for covering bare masonry walls, garden structures, and shaded embankments in Gulf Coast landscapes. Can become very large and difficult to remove once established — roots deeply into masonry. Tolerates brief cold snaps to 15–20°F.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, gravelly soil in full sun; creosote bush is the dominant, defining shrub of the Mojave, Sonoran, and Chihuahuan Deserts, with small, resinous, dark green leaflets that release the sharp, distinctive scent of rain on the desert (petrichor) when wetted, the source of the plant's common name. Small yellow flowers appear after rain in spring, followed by small, round, fuzzy white seed capsules, and the plant can flower opportunistically after any significant rainfall throughout the warm season. It is exceptionally slow-growing but extraordinarily long-lived and drought tolerant, surviving on minimal rainfall by way of an extensive, far-reaching root system that also chemically suppresses competing plants nearby. Give it plenty of room and avoid any supplemental irrigation once established, since regular watering shortens its life and encourages the same root rot that kills most other true desert natives when overwatered.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; the crimson bottlebrush is one of the most versatile and widely planted Australian natives in Gulf Coast and California gardens, producing spectacular cylindrical flower spikes 4–6 inches long with hundreds of bright crimson stamens that give the flower its distinctive bottlebrush shape. The nectar-rich flowers attract hummingbirds and butterflies and appear primarily in spring and often reflower in fall. Unlike Callistemon viminalis (weeping bottlebrush), C. citrinus grows as a dense, upright to spreading shrub rather than a pendulous tree. It tolerates poor soils, salt spray, drought, and occasional standing water — making it one of the most adaptable ornamental shrubs for challenging coastal and urban conditions. Excellent as a screen, foundation plant, or specimen.

common_name: Crimson Fire Loropetalum (Deep Red Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Crimson Fire is a compact, mounding loropetalum introduced by Monrovia Nursery that combines some of the most intense foliage color in the genus — deep crimson-red to dark burgundy-red new growth that matures to a rich dark purple-red — with a manageable size of 2.5–4 feet tall and wide that fits foundation plantings and shrub borders without requiring constant shearing to control size. The deep pink to magenta fringe flowers appear in spring and intermittently through summer and fall, standing out vibrantly against the dark foliage. Crimson Fire holds its foliage color better through summer heat than some loropetalum selections, maintaining richer red-purple tones rather than fading to green-bronze. The compact size and naturally dense, mounding habit reduce the maintenance requirements that make larger loropetalums problematic in typical home foundation plantings. Loropetalums are some of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant ornamental shrubs for zone 9 and are largely free of serious pest and disease problems in the Gulf South. Provide good drainage — waterlogged soils cause rapid root rot. No pruning is required but plants respond well to light shaping immediately after the main spring bloom.

common_name: Crimson Pygmy Barberry (Dwarf Mounding Deep Red-Foliage Barberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, where the deep burgundy-red foliage color develops most intensely; shaded plants tend to green out and lose color saturation. Crimson Pygmy is one of the longest-established and most widely planted dwarf barberry cultivars, forming a tight, low, rounded mound of small reddish-purple leaves that holds its color from spring through fall, with small yellow spring flowers and red fall berries adding secondary interest. Its dense, thorny, compact habit makes it useful as a low hedge, foundation accent, or color contrast in mixed borders without the size of full-scale barberry cultivars. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant, low-maintenance, and rarely need pruning beyond an occasional shaping cut, but gardeners should confirm local invasive-species regulations before planting, since Japanese barberry naturalizes readily and displaces native understory plants in much of the eastern and midwestern US.

common_name: Crimson Queen Japanese Maple (Red Weeping Japanese Maple)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade; Crimson Queen is the most popular and widely planted laceleaf (dissectum) weeping Japanese maple with red foliage — a mounding, cascading, mushroom-shaped small tree reaching 6–10 feet tall with an even wider spread, producing deeply dissected, lace-like, rich crimson-red to burgundy-red leaves that maintain better summer color than most dissectum Japanese maples. The extremely finely cut, feathery foliage drapes from gracefully weeping branches in a soft, cascading curtain of crimson-red — one of the most visually dramatic and elegant small trees available for woodland garden or specimen use. The weeping, mounding habit creates a naturally sculptural form without pruning, and mature specimens become increasingly dramatic focal points over decades. In fall, the foliage transitions to bright scarlet. In zone 9, Crimson Queen requires careful siting to succeed — morning sun and afternoon shade in a location with moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil are the minimum requirements. Plant near water features, in east-facing beds, or under the high canopy of larger trees. Provide consistent moisture during summer. In the right location, Crimson Queen is reliably successful in zone 9 and is widely grown in Houston, New Orleans, and coastal Mississippi.

Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; crimson-spot rock rose is the largest-flowered of the Mediterranean cistus shrubs — producing blooms 3–4 inches across in pure white, each petal bearing a prominent crimson-maroon basal blotch that creates a ring of five vivid spots within the white flower, giving each bloom the quality of a hand-painted botanical illustration. The flowers last only one day each (the petals falling by late afternoon), but are produced in such lavish succession from May through July that the plant appears constantly in flower for weeks. The sticky, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves produce labdanum resin with a distinctive, warm, ambery-woody fragrance that has been harvested for use in perfumery since ancient times — the gum being collected by raking the hillside goats' beards after they browse among the plants. Outstanding as a drought-tolerant flowering shrub for lean, rocky, or sandy soils in hot, dry gardens in zones 8b–10.

common_name: Crocus Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2000, Crocus Rose bears soft apricot-yellow buds that open into rounded, rosette-shaped flowers fading gracefully to a warm buff-cream, carrying a light, sweet tea fragrance on a compact, bushy, disease-resistant shrub. Its manageable size and reliably healthy foliage make it well suited to a smaller border or foundation planting, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Plant in spring in moist, well-drained soil against a sturdy trellis, fence, or tree trunk in partial to full sun; cross vine attaches by tendril-tipped branching structures that grip masonry, wood, and chain link effectively without damaging most structures. This southeastern native semi-evergreen vine produces spectacular clusters of 2-inch, trumpet-shaped flowers in reddish-orange with yellow throats that attract hummingbirds in profusion during its main spring bloom, with scattered rebloom through summer and fall; the glossy, compound leaves remain attractive year-round in zones 7–9 and turn burgundy-red in winter. Cross vine tolerates partial shade remarkably well and is an excellent choice for growing up the trunk of a large tree or covering a shaded fence where other flowering vines would fail. Prune lightly after spring bloom to maintain size and shape.

Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring or fall against a sturdy trellis, arbor, fence, or mature tree in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; crossvine is a vigorous native evergreen vine of the Southeast that produces masses of large, trumpet-shaped, orange-red to yellow flowers in mid-spring that are a critical early hummingbird nectar source just as ruby-throated hummingbirds return to the Southeast from their Caribbean winter. The bicolor flowers (orange-red outside, yellow inside in the species; brick-red in the cultivar 'Tangerine Beauty') cover the mature vine in late April to May in a stunning display. It climbs by adhesive tendrils to 30–50 feet and is semi-evergreen in zone 6–7, fully evergreen in zone 8–9. Once established it is drought-tolerant and self-supporting on any surface it can grip.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to part sun; protect from direct afternoon sun in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, but too little light causes diminished color intensity. Codiaeum variegatum (croton or garden croton) is one of the most spectacularly colored tropical foliage plants in cultivation — a Malaysian native producing thick, leathery leaves in an astonishing variety of shapes (lobed, ribbon-like, twisted, spiral, oak-leaf, or fiddle-shaped depending on variety) in colors ranging from bright yellow and orange to red, maroon, bronze, and multicolor combinations of all these, often changing color dramatically as leaves mature. No two leaves on an established plant may be the same color. Over 100 named cultivars exist including 'Mammy' (twisted red, orange, and yellow leaves), 'Petra' (classic red and yellow lobed leaves), and 'Gold Dust' (green leaves spotted yellow). In South Florida and zone 10+, croton grows as a perennial landscape shrub 3–8 feet tall; in zones 8–9, it is used as a summer patio plant and overwintered indoors. Croton sap is a skin irritant — use gloves when pruning. The sap and seeds are toxic if ingested.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; crown flower is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives on neglect; CAUTION: All parts except outer petals are toxic — wear gloves when handling. Calotropis gigantea (crown flower, giant milkweed, or mudar) is a large tropical shrub to small tree native to South Asia and Southeast Asia — one of the most important ornamental, cultural, and medicinal plants across the tropics. The plant produces large, thick, ovate, silver-blue-green leaves coated with a waxy, white powder, and spectacular clusters of waxy, star-shaped flowers with a distinctive crown-shaped secondary corona — each individual flower resembling a tiny crown, in white or lavender-purple. In Hawaii, crown flower (particularly the white form) has been the classic choice for making long, fragrant leis for over a century; Queen Lili'uokalani was famous for wearing long white crown flower leis and the plant is deeply associated with Hawaiian royalty. In Hindu tradition across South Asia, the flowers are sacred offerings to Lord Shiva and are used extensively in religious ceremonies and temple garlands. The milky white sap (latex) is toxic and irritating; the bark fiber has traditional uses in rope-making. A magnificent, bold-textured, drought-tolerant ornamental for zone 9–12 that combines ornamental beauty with deep cultural significance.

common_name: Crown of Thorns (Christ Plant, Christ Thorn, Euphorbia milii)
notes: Grow in full sun in very well-drained, gritty or sandy soil or potting mix; Crown of Thorns is extremely drought-tolerant and will rot quickly in wet, heavy soils or from overwatering. Euphorbia milii is a semi-succulent shrub native to Madagascar, heavily armed with long, sharp spines on the zigzagging, grayish stems — a characteristic thought to have inspired its Biblical associations with the Crown of Thorns worn by Jesus at the Crucifixion. Despite its formidable armament, Crown of Thorns is one of the most popular and widely cultivated succulent ornamentals in the world, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions where it is grown as an outdoor hedge, container specimen, and cut flower plant. The true flowers are tiny and inconspicuous, but they are surrounded by brilliantly colored, petal-like bracts in vivid scarlet, pink, orange, yellow, salmon, cream, or bicolor combinations — and the plant blooms nearly continuously in warm climates, making it one of the longest-blooming ornamentals available. Modern Thai hybrids (often marketed as 'Giant Euphorbia') produce much larger, showier bracts than the original species and are available in an extraordinary range of colors. CAUTION: The milky white latex sap is highly irritating to skin and eyes and toxic if ingested by humans or pets.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — cucumber magnolia is the largest and most cold-hardy native magnolia of eastern North America and the only magnolia native to the Great Lakes region and far north, surviving to zone 3. The greenish-yellow flowers (2–4 inches) in spring are not the showiest, but the distinctive cucumber-shaped bright red-pink fruiting cones in summer that split to reveal brilliant orange-red seeds are highly ornamental. The tree develops an impressive pyramidal to broadly rounded form 50–80 feet tall — one of the largest deciduous trees in the native flora. Crucially, it is a parent in the development of numerous hybrid 'yellow magnolias' such as 'Elizabeth' (with Magnolia denudata), which have transformed the magnolia world. The tree produces a yellow pigment in the wood historically used by Native Americans. An excellent choice for large-scale landscape planting and ecological restoration in zone 3–8.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Cumberland azalea blooms later than most native deciduous azaleas, after the leaves have fully expanded, giving a different seasonal effect than earlier-blooming relatives. Rhododendron cumberlandense is an Appalachian native deciduous azalea producing vivid orange-red to deep red, funnel-shaped, mildly fragrant flowers in early to midsummer, well after the spring flush of most other native azaleas has finished, extending the native azalea bloom season into summer. Its late timing and fiery flower color make it a valuable addition to a native shrub border or open woodland garden planned for a long succession of bloom, and it tolerates the acidic, well-drained mountain soils typical of its native range. Give it consistently moist but well-drained, acidic soil and dappled shade, avoiding both deep shade, which reduces flowering, and hot, dry, exposed sites.

Start seeds on their edges in moist compost and transplant to a strong trellis or arbor after last frost; cup and saucer vine is a fast-growing Mexican native that can cover 15–20 feet of trellis in a single season, producing an abundance of large, bell-shaped flowers with a prominent ribbed green 'saucer' calyx that makes each flower look like a flower-in-a-cup. The flowers open green-white, then rapidly age to deep purple, so the plant carries both colors simultaneously in an interesting contrast. They are intensely fragrant, with a sweet musky scent. Tendrils at the leaf tips cling to virtually anything with great strength. In zones 9–11 it grows as a perennial woody vine and becomes even more vigorous in its second year.

common_name: Cup of Gold Vine (Golden Chalice Vine, Hawaiin Lily)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide extremely strong support — this vine becomes enormously heavy; CAUTION: All parts are toxic. Solandra maxima (cup of gold vine or golden chalice vine) is a rampant, large-leafed tropical climbing shrub from Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean — a member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) and one of the most impressively large-flowered ornamental vines available for zone 9–12 gardens. The flowers are exceptional: enormous (6–9 inches across), goblet or chalice-shaped, with five creamy-yellow to golden petals fused into a spectacular cup form, each petal marked with a deep-purple to chocolate-brown stripe running from the center to the tip — an elegant and unusual color combination. The flowers have a powerful, sweet, vanilla-coconut fragrance that perfumes the garden, especially in the evenings. The main bloom period is late winter through spring, when the heavy vine covers itself in the golden chalices. The thick, glossy, leathery leaves are bold and attractive when not in flower. Solandra requires an extremely strong support structure (heavy wooden pergola or steel framework) as established plants can reach 40+ feet and become enormously heavy and woody. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are poisonous; the plants produce tropane alkaloids similar to Datura and Brugmansia.

common_name: Cupani Sweet Pea (Original Fragrant Heirloom Sweet Pea)
notes: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Cupani is the historic parent of all modern sweet pea cultivars, first sent from Sicily to England in the early 1700s by the monk Franciscus Cupani, and it remains treasured today for having by far the strongest, sweetest fragrance of any sweet pea, since much of that intense scent was gradually bred out of later, larger-flowered modern cultivars in favor of bigger blooms. The relatively small, bicolor maroon-and-violet flowers are less showy than modern hybrids but reward growers with an exceptional perfume, especially valuable for cutting and bringing indoors. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before the heat of summer ends the season.

Plant container stock in fall or early spring into rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil on exposed, sunny sites, since curl-leaf mountain mahogany is a slow-growing, long-lived evergreen native to dry foothills and mountain slopes throughout the Intermountain West. Its inconspicuous spring flowers are wind-pollinated, but the shrub's dense evergreen cover and abundant, twisted-plumed seed heads make it critical winter browse and cover for mule deer, bighorn sheep, and small birds. It is remarkably drought- and cold-hardy once established, tolerating shallow, rocky soils where little else will grow, and needs essentially no irrigation after the first two seasons. Growth is slow, so choose the planting site carefully, as this long-lived shrub can persist for centuries.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket, or mount on a slab, in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Curtis's hoya is a small, slow-growing miniature best suited to a small pot, terrarium, or mounted display. Tiny, thick, silver-speckled, heart-shaped leaves lie closely along thin, wiry, creeping stems that root as they spread, forming a dense, low mat or a delicate curtain when allowed to trail from a small hanging pot. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it is among the smallest and slowest-growing hoya species commonly cultivated, making it well suited to windowsill, terrarium, or miniature garden displays where larger hoyas would be out of scale. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright filtered light for the best leaf speckling, and avoid overpotting this slow-growing miniature in too large a container.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; cutleaf stephanandra is a graceful, arching Japanese shrub in the rose family producing elegantly divided, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves with a refined, lacy texture that gives it its common name. In spring it produces clusters of small, white star-shaped flowers along the arching branches, attractive but secondary to the exceptional foliage. In autumn the leaves turn orange, red, and purple before dropping. The compact cultivar 'Crispa' is particularly valuable as a groundcover — growing only 18 inches tall while spreading 3–4 feet wide, with crimped, finely cut leaves that form a thick, weed-suppressing mat in shade. Branches that touch the ground root themselves (layering), helping the plant colonize large areas under trees where grass and other groundcovers fail. Among the finest shade-tolerant ornamental shrubs for the difficult zone between trees and planting beds, providing excellent weed suppression and year-round ground cover.

Nick or soak seeds overnight in warm water before direct sowing after last frost in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; cypress vine self-seeds prolifically in warm climates and can become invasive — deadhead if naturalization is not desired. Ipomoea quamoclit is a delicate, fast-growing annual vine from tropical America with extraordinarily fine, feathery, deeply pinnate leaves resembling cypress foliage and a long succession of small (1-inch), brilliant scarlet, star-shaped flowers with a white eye from summer through frost that are irresistible to ruby-throated hummingbirds. In zone 9–10 it self-seeds vigorously and can naturalize along fences and into disturbed areas; it has been listed as invasive in some southeastern states, so monitor seedling spread and remove volunteers if they escape the garden area. An outstanding container or trellis plant for attracting hummingbirds.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; D.D. Blanchard is one of the most magnificent Southern magnolia cultivars — distinguished by exceptionally dark, glossy, almost black-green upper leaf surfaces with a rich, coppery-orange to russet-brown underside that is among the most vivid and attractive of any Southern magnolia selection. The underside color is a significant ornamental feature: when a breeze stirs the branches, the leaves momentarily reveal their orange-bronze undersides, creating a shimmering two-tone effect that no other tree quite replicates. D.D. Blanchard is a large tree with a naturally pyramidal form, growing 30–50 feet tall with a 20–30 foot spread — a specimen tree with an imposing, stately presence appropriate for large residential landscapes and commercial settings. The giant, creamy-white, intensely fragrant flowers (8–12 inches across) bloom from May through July in zone 9, with intermittent bloom through summer. Like all Southern magnolia cultivars, D.D. Blanchard produces large, cone-like fruits with brilliant red seeds that are consumed by birds and wildlife. An outstanding selection for the Gulf South where the tree is most at home — performing magnificently in zone 8–10 heat and humidity.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun — dahoon holly is one of the most beautiful and ecologically important native trees of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, growing naturally in the understory of bottomland swamps, cypress heads, wet pine flatwoods, and stream banks from Virginia to Texas. Female plants (a male nearby is needed for pollination) produce abundant clusters of small, brilliant red to orange-red berries that persist from fall through winter, providing critical food for robins, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and dozens of other fruit-eating birds during winter when food is scarce. The narrow, elliptic, dark evergreen leaves are attractive year-round. It tolerates flooding and wet soils better than almost any other tree in cultivation and is outstanding for rain gardens, wet low spots, pond margins, and other challenging wet sites in zone 7–11. An excellent winter-interest tree for the shaded, wet areas of Gulf Coast landscapes.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Daikagura is a centuries-old Japanese camellia cultivar prized for exceptionally large, formal peony-form flowers, densely packed with irregularly waved and twisted petals boldly streaked and mottled in rose-red over a white background, a strikingly variegated pattern unique to each bloom. The dramatic size and coloring make individual flowers a focal point in the winter garden, and the plant's dense, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage provides year-round structure. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it blooms in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9, when little else is in flower. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, which scorches the glossy leaves, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, deep soil in full sun; daimyo oak (emperor oak) is the boldest-textured oak in the world, producing enormous, deeply lobed, paddle-shaped leaves that can reach 18 inches long and 10 inches wide — the largest leaves of any temperate-zone oak, creating a strikingly coarse, tropical-looking canopy texture completely unlike the small-leaved English oak. Native to mountain forests of China, Korea, and Japan, it is a relatively small to medium oak suitable for residential gardens where its dramatic foliage creates a bold statement. The leaves turn bronze to red-brown in fall and often persist on the tree into early winter before dropping (marcescent). Relatively slow-growing compared to other oaks. The species is the host plant for the silkworm Antheraea yamamai (the Japanese oak silkworm) which produces golden 'tussah' silk. An outstanding specimen tree for gardens where dramatic large-leaved texture is desired.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Dakota prairie rose is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant, well adapted to harsh northern plains conditions. Fragrant, single pink flowers cover this low, suckering native shrub in early summer, followed by bright red hips that persist through winter as valuable food for birds and wildlife on the harsh, wind-swept northern Great Plains where it grows natively. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, it spreads slowly by root suckers into loose colonies that help stabilize prairie soil, making it a valuable, low-maintenance native shrub for a prairie restoration or naturalistic planting in cold, dry climates where more tender roses would not survive winter. It needs no fertilizer, spraying, or winter protection, dying back partially in severe cold and resprouting reliably each spring.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; among the most heat- and drought-tolerant native shrublets available, thriving in conditions that kill most perennials outright, but requires perfect drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained gardens. Chrysactinia mexicana (damianita) is a small, rounded, woody-based evergreen shrublet native to the limestone hills and rocky slopes of the Trans-Pecos, west Texas, and northern Mexico, with fine, needle-like, resinous, aromatic foliage that releases a pungent, camphor-like scent when brushed or crushed. From spring through fall, and especially heavily after rain, the plant is smothered in small, bright golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers that draw bees and butterflies and make a vivid mounded splash of color against its dark, textured foliage. Its extreme drought and heat tolerance make it a staple of xeriscape and rock garden design across the drier parts of Texas and the Southwest, and it also tolerates the humidity of the Gulf South reasonably well provided the drainage is sharp. An excellent low-water accent plant for a sunny rock garden or gravel bed, zone 7–10.

common_name: Darcey Bussell Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2006 and named for the celebrated British ballerina, Darcey Bussell produces deep crimson-red, fully double rosette flowers with a fruity, slightly musky fragrance on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub noticeably smaller and tidier than many older English rose cultivars. Its manageable size and rich, saturated color make it a strong choice for a smaller border or mixed planting where a full-size climbing English rose would be out of scale, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, though established plants tolerate deeper shade under high tree canopy. David viburnum is a low, mounded evergreen shrub from western China valued for its leathery, deeply three-veined, glossy dark green leaves that hold their color through winter, forming a dense architectural groundcover unlike most deciduous viburnums grown for flowers or fall color. Flattened heads of small white flowers appear in late spring, and where a male plant grows nearby, female shrubs set clusters of long-lasting, metallic turquoise-blue berries that are one of the more unusual fruit colors in the shade garden. Its tidy, spreading habit suits it to massing along a shaded foundation, edging a woodland path, or filling a bed beneath taller understory trees.

Dawn redwood is a fast-growing deciduous conifer often called a living fossil, prized for feathery fern-like foliage that turns coppery orange before dropping in fall. Give it full sun and consistently moist, well-drained soil; it tolerates wet sites and even seasonal flooding better than most conifers. Choose a location with abundant vertical and horizontal space, as mature trees reach 70 to 100 feet with a broad conical form. Water deeply during establishment and through dry spells for the first few seasons. It needs no pruning to develop its naturally elegant shape.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, in a sheltered spot away from harsh winter wind that can brown open flowers. 'Dawn' is an upright, multi-stemmed hybrid selected at Bodnant Garden in Wales, prized for clusters of small, tubular, rose-pink buds that open to pale pink and release a strong, sweet fragrance intermittently from late fall through late winter, often on bare wood well before other shrubs stir. The dull, coarsely toothed leaves emerge bronze-tinted in spring and take on modest red tones in fall, but the plant's main season of interest is the depth of winter, when little else in the shaded border is in bloom. Renewal-prune older stems back to the base every few years after flowering to keep the shrub from becoming leggy at its base.

Plant transplants after last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; day jessamine self-sows readily in warm climates and its white berries are toxic if ingested, so site away from grazing animals and small children. Clusters of small, tubular, greenish-white flowers open by day, unlike the related night-blooming jessamine, releasing a mild, sweet fragrance through the daylight hours before giving way to small white berries that persist into fall and winter. Native to the Caribbean and long naturalized across the Gulf South, it grows quickly into a loose, twiggy shrub tolerant of a range of soils and light conditions, but its toxic berries have caused documented livestock poisoning in Florida cattle, so it is not recommended near pastures. Prune to control size and self-sowing, and remove volunteer seedlings promptly in naturalistic areas to prevent it from spreading beyond the intended planting.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Daybreak's Flame loropetalum holds its intense burgundy foliage color best in full sun. Deep, rich burgundy-purple foliage provides season-long color contrast in a shrub border, punctuated by a heavy flush of vivid magenta-pink, fringed, spidery flowers in spring with lighter repeat bloom through the growing season, a bold, reliable color combination that has made loropetalum a mainstay of Southern landscaping. Its vigorous, adaptable growth and strong dark foliage color make it a versatile choice for a hedge, foundation planting, or specimen shrub, tolerating heat, humidity, and a range of soil conditions across the Gulf South and greater Southeast. Prune after the main spring flush to shape, and provide full sun for the darkest, most saturated foliage color, since shade causes the leaves to green up and lose intensity.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Debutante is one of the most beloved and widely grown Camellia japonica cultivars — a long-cultivated Southern garden classic producing early to mid-season (December through February in zone 9) flowers in a gorgeous soft light-pink peony form with rows of neatly layered petals that create a formal, rose-like, fully double flower of exceptional elegance. The soft light-pink color — a warm blush to light rose — makes Debutante one of the most feminine and refined camellias for traditional Southern landscape and cut-flower use. The upright, vigorous growth to 6–12 feet tall with dense, glossy dark-green evergreen foliage makes it an outstanding foundation shrub and informal hedge plant for shaded or partially shaded locations. Debutante is known for reliable, abundant bloom production even in zone 9's mild winters — bloom quality does not depend on cold temperatures to trigger flower set. In zone 9, Debutante typically begins blooming in late November and continues through February, often with peak bloom in January. Plant in partial shade — morning sun is acceptable but afternoon shade is essential in zone 9 to prevent sun scorch of the glossy leaves. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil conditions camellias require.

common_name: Dee Runk Boxwood (Narrow Upright Columnar Boxwood)
notes: Dee Runk is a narrow, upright boxwood cultivar valued for holding a clean columnar to slightly conical shape with less regular shearing than most boxwood needs to stay vertical, making it a practical choice for a formal hedge, allee, or paired accent planting where a consistent narrow profile is wanted over many years. Its dense, deep green, fine-textured foliage gives year-round structure, and its somewhat broader base than the very narrowest columnar cultivars gives it a bit more visual heft as a specimen. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush keeps the form crisp if a more formal look is wanted.

Nick or hot-water-soak the hard-coated seed before sowing to mimic the fire scarification this chaparral pioneer needs in the wild, and plant in fall so seedlings establish with winter rain. It grows quickly into an airy, broom-like subshrub on lean, disturbed, or sandy soils and fixes nitrogen, which makes it a favorite for post-fire restoration and slope stabilization in California gardens.
