Few plants support as many small butterfly caterpillars at once: it is a documented larval host for the Acmon Blue, Bramble Hairstreak, Silvery Blue, and Funereal Duskywing.

common_name: Delta Jazz Crapemyrtle (Dark Burgundy Foliage Hot-Pink Bloomer)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Delta Jazz stands out among crapemyrtles for its dark burgundy, distinctively cupped foliage that holds its rich color through summer heat, providing dramatic contrast against clusters of hot-pink blooms from summer into fall. It is heat-tolerant and generally resists deer browsing better than many other landscape shrubs, making it a durable choice for a Gulf South foundation planting or mixed border. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season. Prune lightly in late winter to remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches rather than heavily topping the plant, which sacrifices its natural form and delays bloom.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; dense St. John's wort is a native shrubby Hypericum of moist streambanks, pond margins, and wet woodland edges across the eastern United States. It produces abundant clusters of small, bright yellow flowers in summer that attract specialized pollen-collecting bees. Unlike the herbaceous St. John's worts used medicinally, this is a woody, multi-stemmed shrub that can reach 6 feet, providing structure in the wet garden. The tiny, linear leaves are produced in dense, crowded clusters along the stems — giving the species its name. It tolerates seasonal flooding and grows naturally in the same wet habitats as cardinal flower, swamp milkweed, and ironweed. An excellent shrub for rain gardens, bioswales, and wet meadow edges where it provides summer blooms and serves as a nectar source for native bees.

common_name: Desdemona Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2015, Desdemona produces ruffled, blush-white buds that open to nearly pure white, cupped rosette flowers with a strong myrrh fragrance carrying hints of almond, held on a compact, well-branched, disease-resistant shrub. Its pale coloring and refined flower form make it a versatile pairing with almost any companion color, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Plant rooted cuttings of a male, non-seeding cultivar such as 'Centennial' in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; desert broom is a broom-like, nearly leafless southwestern native shrub of green, rush-like stems that photosynthesize year-round, giving it an evergreen effect in the low desert. Male plants produce inconspicuous cream flowers in fall that feed late-season pollinators, while unselected female plants can seed aggressively and are best avoided in cultivated landscapes. It tolerates extreme heat, poor caliche or disturbed soil, and long dry spells with no supplemental water once roots are established, making it a workhorse screening or bank-stabilization shrub in Arizona and West Texas xeriscapes.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; desert honeysuckle (hummingbird bush) is a native Southwestern shrub with an extraordinarily long season of tubular, orange-red flowers that are among the most powerfully attractive hummingbird plants in the xeric and arid Southwest. Blooming from summer through fall with each successive flowering flush triggered by summer monsoon rains, the plant produces dense masses of 1.5-inch, orange-red tubular flowers that provide rich nectar for migrating and resident hummingbirds. It is extremely drought tolerant and actually declines in fertility and blooming if given rich soil or excess water — thriving in the hard, dry, alkaline conditions of the Southwest and Edwards Plateau. Cut back hard each late winter before new growth begins. The species A. wrightii (flame anisacanthus, Wright's desert honeysuckle) has similar requirements and is equally outstanding as a hummingbird plant; both are outstanding native choices for xeric wildflower and butterfly gardens.

Plant in a sunny, open location with fast-draining soil; this desert-adapted shrub excels in rocky, alkaline, or caliche-laden ground where many plants fail. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in midsummer, or cold-stratify seed for 30 to 60 days before sowing in spring. Water to establish during the first growing season, then transition to deep, infrequent irrigation or rely entirely on natural rainfall. Dense branching provides cover and nesting habitat, and the dark blue-black fruits ripen in summer, attracting a wide range of bird species.

common_name: Desert Sage (Mojave Sage, Gray Ball Sage)
notes: Plant in spring in extremely well-drained, dry, alkaline to neutral, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; desert sage is intolerant of heavy clay or summer moisture and is best treated as a xeriscape plant that thrives on neglect in dry, arid conditions. Salvia dorrii (desert sage) is a beautiful, fragrant native sage of the Great Basin, Mojave Desert, and interior mountain ranges of the American West, forming compact, rounded shrubs 18–36 inches tall with densely silver-woolly, aromatic foliage and brilliant purple-violet flowers in spring and early summer that are among the most intensely colored of any western native shrub; the strong, camphor-sage fragrance of the foliage is cleansing and memorable, particularly after rain. Extremely cold-hardy for a desert plant (surviving zone 4 conditions) and exceptionally drought-tolerant once established — it evolved in habitats with 6–12 inches of annual rainfall and grows best in similar lean, dry conditions. An outstanding plant for western xeriscape gardens, rock gardens, and dry borders.

common_name: Desert Willow (Flor de Mimbre, Willowleaf Catalpa)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; desert willow is one of the most beautiful flowering native trees of the Southwest and South Texas, producing masses of showy, orchid-like flowers in pink, lavender, rose, white, or bicolor from late spring through fall in multiple flushes — a spectacular hummingbird and butterfly plant. Despite its name it is not a willow at all but rather a member of the Bignonia family, closely related to catalpa. The long, willow-like leaves emerge late in spring and drop early in fall. It is remarkably drought tolerant once established, thriving on natural rainfall alone in zone 7–11. The decorative seed pods hang on through winter. Many named cultivars are available with different flower colors and forms; 'Dark Storm,' 'Bubba,' and 'Art's Seedless' are popular selections for southern gardens.

Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; devil's walking stick is one of the most architecturally dramatic native plants in eastern North America — a large, coarse shrub or small tree with massive bipinnate-to-tripinnate compound leaves (sometimes 3–4 feet long) arranged in a palm-like whorl at the top of unbranched, viciously prickle-armed stems. The effect in the landscape is aggressively tropical and primitive — unlike anything else in the native plant palette. In late summer, enormous flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers (12–18 inches across) provide a spectacular nectar feast for dozens of native bee and butterfly species. The dark purple berries in fall are consumed by more than 100 bird species during fall migration. It suckers to form dense colonies in moist woodland edges — give it space or contain it.

common_name: Diabolo Ninebark (Classic Dark Purple-Black Foliage Ninebark)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Diabolo was the original widely popularized dark-leaved ninebark cultivar, producing deep purple-black, maple-like leaves on a large, vigorous, arching shrub, topped in late spring with clusters of small white-to-pink flowers that draw pollinators, followed by reddish seed capsules and attractive exfoliating bark that provides winter interest. Full sun brings out the darkest foliage color, while shadier sites shift the leaves toward a more muted green-purple. It tolerates a very wide range of soil conditions and needs only occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems at the base each year to keep the shrub full and vigorous.

common_name: Diamond Spire Gardenia (Narrow Columnar Fragrant Gardenia)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest Gulf Coast gardens. Diamond Spire is a narrow, upright gardenia selection bred to give the intensely fragrant, double white summer flowers of a classic gardenia in a tight, columnar footprint suited to narrow side yards, foundation plantings, and vertical accents where a standard wide-spreading gardenia wouldn't fit. Glossy dark evergreen foliage clothes the upright stems from top to bottom, and the strongly perfumed blooms open over the summer, filling the surrounding air with the classic gardenia scent. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in spring and again in early summer, keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and watch for whitefly and sooty mold, common gardenia pests in humid climates. Prune only lightly right after flowering to maintain the narrow form.

common_name: Diana Rose of Sharon (Sterile White Althea)
notes: Diana was introduced by the US National Arboretum as part of a breeding program aimed at improving on old-fashioned rose of sharon, and it remains one of the best white-flowered selections available. Its large, pure white, 4 to 5 inch flowers stay open later into the evening and remain open longer during the day than most rose of sharon cultivars, and as a sterile triploid it sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older althea. Bloom runs from midsummer into fall on new wood, giving a long season of clean white color when many other shrubs have finished flowering; site it as a summer anchor in a mixed border or informal hedge.

common_name: Diane Witch Hazel (Red-Flowered Winter Witch Hazel)
notes: Diane is the most widely grown red-flowered witch hazel, producing clusters of narrow, spidery, ribbon-petaled flowers in a deep coppery red that opens in late winter while the shrub is still bare, one of the earliest and most distinctive flower displays of the gardening year. Its fall foliage color, orange to red-purple, is also considered among the best of the intermedia witch hazels, giving Diane strong two-season interest beyond the winter bloom. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogged soil.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; dipladenia (mandevilla, rocktrumpet) is a Brazilian tropical twining vine widely sold throughout the garden industry as a patio and container flowering plant for its large, trumpet-shaped, glossy-petaled flowers in vivid shades of red, deep-pink, rose-pink, and white, produced continuously throughout the warm season on new growth. It is one of the most extensively-sold container flowering vines in the American nursery trade, marketed under the names dipladenia (for the more compact, less-twining forms) and mandevilla (for the larger, more vigorous climbing forms). The glossy, deep-green, oval leaves and shining, varnished-looking flower petals give the plant a distinctive, tropical-polished appearance. As an outdoor perennial in zone 10–12 it grows vigorously on trellises and arbors; in cooler climates it is used as a summer annual or overwintered as a container plant indoors. The compact cultivars (sold as 'Dipladenia') are bushy and non-vining; the larger forms (sold as 'Mandevilla') climb to 10 feet or more. The plant exudes milky sap; wash hands after pruning.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil in part shade; disanthus is a monotypic genus in the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) — a single species from mountain forests of Japan and central China that is grown primarily as one of the elite autumn-coloring shrubs. The broadly rounded, heart-shaped leaves closely resemble those of Cercis (redbud) in shape, turning in autumn to some of the most spectacular colors achievable in a garden shrub: brilliant combinations of crimson, orange, purple, and claret, often with all colors simultaneously visible on a single leaf. In October, tiny, deep wine-purple flowers appear directly on the bare and falling-leaf branches — so small and dark that they are easily missed but distinctive and curious up close, with reflexed petals in pairs. A slow-growing, understated but ultimately magnificent shrub for the woodland garden with moist, acidic conditions, outstanding autumn color, and a refined year-round form. Often cited by plantsmen as one of the most desirable garden shrubs, despite remaining little-known outside specialist collections.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Distylium racemosum is a Japanese evergreen shrub in the witch hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) that is gaining significant recognition as one of the most adaptable and low-maintenance broadleaved evergreens for zone 7–10 landscapes. It produces glossy, leathery, dark-green leaves on spreading, arching branches and bears unusual, petal-less winter flowers with prominent red stamens that emerge in February–March in zone 9, providing early-season color before most shrubs bloom. The strongly adaptable nature of distylium is its defining quality — it thrives in full sun to dense shade, in dry or moist soils, in clay or sandy soils, and in both acid and moderately alkaline pH ranges. This adaptability makes it invaluable for difficult landscape situations where few plants perform reliably. Named compact cultivars have made distylium increasingly available in the trade: 'Cinnamon Girl' (4–5 feet, copper-bronze new growth), 'Vintage Jade' (4 feet, spreading), and 'Coppertone' (2.5–3 feet, compact) are among the most widely sold selections. Distylium is completely free of serious pest and disease problems in zone 9, requires no deadheading or shaping, and is highly deer-resistant — a compelling combination for the low-maintenance Gulf South garden.

Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Distylium is a genus of evergreen shrubs and trees in the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) from China and Japan, emerging as one of the most important new landscape shrubs for the mid-South and Southeast. The species D. myricoides produces small, glossy, dark green leaves with a neat, compact, spreading habit and unusual winter-to-early-spring flowers — red stamens without petals that create a purplish-red haze across the plant in late winter. Exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established and resistant to deer browsing. Widely used in current Southeast US landscaping as a low-maintenance foundation plant; cultivars including 'Vintage Jade', 'Linebacker', and the Coppertone series are widely available. Thrives in part shade and full sun with minimal care. Disease and pest resistant.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in deep to part shade; mulch with pine bark or pine needles to maintain soil acidity. Leucothoe fontanesiana (dog hobble or drooping leucothoe) is an elegant native Appalachian understory shrub growing along shaded stream banks and moist forest floors from Virginia south to Georgia and Tennessee. The plant produces long (3–5 foot), gracefully arching stems clothed in glossy, lance-shaped, evergreen leaves — in summer a rich, dark green, transforming to dramatic shades of burgundy, bronze, and red-purple in winter (especially in cultivars like 'Rainbow' and 'Girard's Rainbow'). In late spring, drooping clusters of urn-shaped, white flowers (resembling lily-of-the-valley flowers) line the undersides of the arching branches — fragrant and attractive. Dog hobble earns its common name from the impenetrable tangles it forms along mountain creek banks, through which hunting dogs cannot easily pass. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form colonies. As a shade garden plant, Leucothoe fontanesiana provides outstanding year-round interest: spring flowers, summer foliage, and winter color in sites too acidic and shady for most other shrubs. The cultivar 'Scarletta' has especially vivid scarlet winter color.

Plant in a sunny, open location with well-drained soil; Dog Rose tolerates poor, rocky, and chalky conditions and does not require amendment or fertilization. Take hardwood cuttings in late autumn or early winter, root them in sandy compost, and overwinter in a cold frame before transplanting the following spring. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and requires little supplemental watering. Prune out oldest canes after flowering to maintain an open framework and encourage vigorous new growth bearing the following season's blooms and hips.

common_name: Donation Camellia (Classic Pink Williamsii Hybrid Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer. Donation is a Camellia x williamsii hybrid, a cross between C. japonica and the more cold- and sun-tolerant C. saluenensis, and it combines the best traits of both parents: a vigorous, upright, densely branched habit smothered in late winter to early spring with large, semi-double, clear orchid-pink flowers. It is widely regarded as one of the finest garden camellias ever raised, prized not only for its heavy, reliable bloom but also for cleanly dropping its faded flowers on its own, sparing gardeners the tedious deadheading that camellias with browning, persistent blooms require. It tolerates more sun and cooler conditions than many Camellia japonica cultivars, though afternoon shade still helps prevent leaf scorch in hot Gulf South summers, and it needs little pruning beyond light shaping right after bloom.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; double flowering plum is a Chinese shrub producing double-flowered, rosy-pink blooms so profusely that stems are completely hidden under flowers in very early spring. The popular cultivar 'Multiplex' has fully double, deep rose-pink flowers with a ruffled, peony-like form. This is one of the most spectacularly spring-flowering woody plants for cold climates — reliably cold-hardy to zone 3 with outstanding early season color. Often confused with double flowering almond (Prunus glandulosa) in the garden trade; both are excellent ornamental spring shrubs. The flowers appear before leaves, making the bare-stem flower display especially dramatic. Prune hard immediately after bloom to maintain compact shape and maximize next year's flowering. Short-lived (10–20 years) but easy to propagate from cuttings.

Plant this double-flowered althea in full sun with well-drained soil, spacing shrubs 5-8 feet apart to allow their broad upright habit room to mature. It blooms late summer into fall on the current season's growth, so prune in late winter or early spring to shape and encourage flowering wood. Water regularly the first two seasons until the roots establish, after which it tolerates heat and short dry spells. The full, layered pink blooms are sterile, so this cultivar reseeds far less than single-flowered forms.

common_name: Double Play Gold Spirea (Reblooming Gold-Foliage Compact Spirea)
notes: Double Play Gold is a compact, part of Proven Winners' reblooming Double Play spirea series, valued for bright gold foliage that emerges with orange-red tints in spring and holds its color through summer, topped by rounded clusters of pink flowers. Unlike older spirea cultivars that bloom in one spring flush, Double Play selections rebloom through summer, especially if the spent flower clusters are sheared off after the first round fades, giving a longer season of both foliage and flower interest from a low, tidy mound. It is extremely tough and low-maintenance, tolerating drought, heat, and poor soil once established, and a single light shearing after the first bloom flush is usually all the pruning it needs.

common_name: Double Play Spirea (Reblooming Compact Spirea Series)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear off the first round of spent flowers to prompt a stronger summer rebloom. The Double Play series was bred by Proven Winners for extended flowering, combining colorful spring foliage — emerging in shades of orange, red, or burgundy depending on the specific selection — with an initial flush of pink to rose-red flowers in late spring and repeat bloom through summer into fall. Its compact, dense habit and long season of both foliage and flower interest make it a strong low-maintenance choice for foundation plantings and mixed borders. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor soil and urban heat with minimal care.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; doublefile viburnum is one of the most architecturally striking flowering shrubs in cultivation — its strongly horizontal, tiered branch structure creates a layered, pagoda-like silhouette that is ornamental year-round even without flowers. In spring, rows of flat-topped lacecap flower clusters are borne in pairs ('doublefile') along the horizontal branches, covering the entire upper surface of each tier in white blossoms — a spectacular display. Red berries follow in summer, turning black and persisting into winter; they are attractive to birds, which rapidly consume them. In fall the leaves often turn wine-red to purplish-red. Popular cultivars include 'Shasta' (large, flat flower clusters and low, wide habit), 'Mariesii' (the most widely grown, strongly horizontal), and 'Summer Snowflake' (an extended blooming selection). Performs best in zone 5–7; in zone 8 it tolerates summer heat with afternoon shade and consistent moisture but may be short-lived.

Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring or fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, allowing generous room to grow since this is one of the largest conifers in North America. Douglas fir carries soft, flat, blue-green to dark green needles and distinctive pendulous cones with three-pointed bracts that protrude past each scale, a reliable identification feature unique among conifers. It is among the most important timber trees on the continent and is also the most widely grown Christmas tree species in cooler climates, valued in the landscape for dense pyramidal form and a strong central leader. Performance declines sharply outside cool, humid, well-drained mountain and coastal climates, so it is a poor choice for the hot, humid Southeast or dry, alkaline plains soils.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy soil in partial shade; dove tree is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world, with a legendary history in Western botany — first seen by European plant hunters in Chinese mountain forests and described as a tree covered with fluttering white handkerchiefs or white doves perching in the branches. The 'flowers' (actually a tiny, inconspicuous cluster of flowers) are almost invisible — what creates the stunning display is a pair of very large, unequal, pure white bracts (modified leaves) flanking each flower cluster, ranging from 3 to 7 inches long. When in full bloom in mid-spring, a mature tree covered in hundreds of hanging white bract pairs in a light breeze creates an unforgettable, magical spectacle. The tree requires patience — it typically does not flower until 10+ years from seed. A legendary collector's tree planted in large gardens and arboreta worldwide for this once-yearly flower event. The fruit is a large, olive-like, edible (barely) nutlet. The legendary China plant collector E.H. Wilson nearly died collecting seeds in 1900.

Plant in a well-draining location with partial shade to full shade; this viburnum thrives in dry, rocky soils and actually struggles in rich, moist conditions. Dig a hole twice as wide as the root ball and backfill with unamended native soil. Water consistently for the first season to establish roots, then reduce irrigation — established plants are notably drought-tolerant. Flat-topped white flower clusters appear in late spring, followed by dark blue-black berries that persist into winter for birds.

Sow in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; downy indigo bush is a low, semi-woody Southeastern native legume of dry sandhills, scrub, and open pine woods, related to the taller false indigo bush but distinguished by its shorter, more subshrub-like stature and the soft, downy hairs covering its compound gray-green leaves. In summer it produces upright spikes of small, deep purple-blue flowers with prominent orange anthers, similar in form to leadplant, that attract native bumblebees and other pollinators. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it thrives in poor, sandy, infertile soil where many other flowering shrubs struggle, and it is well adapted to fire-maintained pine ecosystems, resprouting readily from the root crown after burning or hard pruning. It is drought-tolerant once established and requires very little supplemental water or fertility, making it a low-maintenance choice for a sunny, sandy native planting or a naturalized dry meadow in the Gulf South and greater Southeast.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — downy jasmine is an Indian native jasmine widely grown along the Gulf Coast for its masses of small, starry, pure white flowers with a light, sweet fragrance produced from fall through spring during the cooler months. The soft, downy-hairy leaves and stems give it an appealing, fine-textured, gray-green appearance when out of bloom. It is a sprawling, loose shrub that can be used as a large-scale groundcover, a slope stabilizer, or a mounding informal hedge; with light pruning after bloom it stays tidy and compact. Unlike many jasmines, it tolerates partial shade and performs excellently along the shaded sides of buildings and fences. In zone 9 the foliage may drop or be damaged in hard freezes but the plant resprouts quickly from roots; in zone 10–11 it is fully evergreen. Extremely drought tolerant once established, requiring virtually no supplemental irrigation in adapted soils.

Direct sow in sandy or gravelly, low-fertility soil in full to partial sun after last frost; this twining native legume vine thrives in the poor, dry, sandy soils of the southeastern coastal plain where most garden plants fail, and fixes its own nitrogen through root nodule bacteria. Slender twining stems produce small pink-purple pea flowers from midsummer through early fall that are visited by native bees, and the vine is a documented larval host plant for gray hairstreak and other butterfly species, making it valuable in wildlife and pollinator gardens. It is a true perennial in zones 7-10, dying back to the roots after frost and re-emerging reliably from the root crown in spring. Avoid amending soil with compost or fertilizer as rich soils reduce flowering and encourage excessive foliage at the expense of blooms and seed production.

Dr. Ruppel is a vigorous large-flowered clematis with pink, star-shaped blooms accented by a bold magenta bar down each petal. Give it a sunny position for the vines but keep the roots cool and shaded with mulch or low companion plantings. Provide a trellis, arbor, or fence for the climbing stems to grip, and tie in new growth as needed. This variety blooms on both old and new wood, so prune only lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead stems. Water regularly and feed in spring for the best flower show.

common_name: Dr. Tinsley Camellia (Blush Pink Semi-Double Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Dr. Tinsley is a long-cultivated camellia prized for its soft, blush-pink, semi-double to peony-form flowers that shade from deeper pink at the petal base to nearly white at the edges, giving each bloom a gentle, watercolor-like gradation of color. It flowers over a long early-to-midseason window on a vigorous, upright, free-flowering shrub, and its dependable, prolific bloom has kept it a favorite among camellia collectors and Southern gardeners for generations. Its soft coloring makes it a versatile companion to more strongly colored camellia cultivars in a mixed planting. Prune immediately after bloom in late winter or early spring, before next year's flower buds set.

common_name: Dragon Lady Holly (Narrow Pyramidal Hybrid Holly)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Dragon Lady is a narrow, densely pyramidal hybrid holly with glossy, deep green, spiny-margined foliage and, when pollinated, a heavy crop of bright red berries that persist through winter and provide food for songbirds. Its tight, upright, formal shape needs little pruning to maintain, making it a popular choice for narrow screens, foundation accents, and formal entryway plantings where a broader holly would not fit. Give it consistent moisture while establishing, and plant a compatible male holly cultivar nearby to ensure the female flowers set fruit, since Dragon Lady itself produces only female flowers.

common_name: Dragon Tail Plant (Centipede Tongavine, Cebu Blue Pothos, Tibatib)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Dragon Tail Plant adapts to lower light in its juvenile form but requires adequate light and a vertical climbing support to progress to its spectacular adult leaf form. Epipremnum pinnatum is a large, climbing aroid vine native to Southeast Asia, the Pacific Islands, and northern Australia, distributed across an enormous range from India to Polynesia in the Araceae family. The plant exhibits one of the most dramatic cases of leaf dimorphism in common cultivation: in the juvenile trailing or hanging form, it produces narrow, elongated, slightly iridescent, silvery-blue-green leaves 4–8 inches long with no lobing — the form sold commercially as 'Cebu Blue Pothos' (though not a true Pothos). When the same plant begins climbing a rough surface and receives adequate light, it transitions progressively to the adult form: leaves become dramatically larger (up to 24–36 inches), dark green, and deeply pinnately lobed along the midrib in a pattern resembling a dragon's tail or centipede — giving rise to the common name 'Dragon Tail Plant.' The adult leaves develop fenestrations along the midrib similar to but distinct from Monstera. The transformation from slender blue juvenile to enormous pinnate adult is dramatic and rewarding for collectors who provide climbing support. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

common_name: Dragon Tail Rhaphidophora (Creeping Philodendron, Monster Dragon Tail)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Rhaphidophora decursiva transitions from attractive juvenile form to spectacular adult form most quickly in bright indirect light with a climbing support, remaining in the juvenile stage indefinitely if conditions prevent climbing. Rhaphidophora decursiva is a vigorous climbing aroid from South and Southeast Asia (India, Sri Lanka, southern China, and across to the Philippines and Indonesia) in the family Araceae — not a Philodendron or Monstera despite being commonly mislabeled as both in commercial plant sales. The juvenile form produces simple, elliptical, glossy, dark-green leaves that are attractive but unremarkable. As the plant matures and climbs upward, the leaves transform progressively and dramatically: they enlarge significantly and develop deep pinnate lobing — the leaf divides into a row of distinct, finger-like segments radiating from the central midrib — eventually producing 24-inch leaves deeply cut almost to the midrib in a pattern resembling an enormous feather or a prehistoric wing, from which the common name 'Dragon Tail' derives. This adult form is often confused with Epipremnum pinnatum in its adult form (also called 'Dragon Tail') and with large pinnate Monstera species — all three can produce superficially similar adult leaves. Rhaphidophora decursiva is a fast grower that rewards patience with an extraordinary final form. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

common_name: Drake Chinese Elm (Semi-Evergreen Gulf South Shade Tree)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Drake is a graceful, fast-growing selection of Chinese elm valued for its attractive mottled, exfoliating bark, fine-textured foliage, and semi-evergreen habit that holds leaves later into fall and winter than most deciduous shade trees across much of the Gulf South. Unlike American elm, it shows strong resistance to Dutch elm disease and also tolerates heat, drought, and compacted urban soils well, making it a popular street and shade tree throughout Texas and the Deep South. Its arching, weeping branch habit gives mature specimens an elegant silhouette, and it needs only routine structural pruning when young to develop strong branch angles for long-term storm resistance.

Dream Weaver is a sasanqua camellia bearing abundant double blooms of deep pink to lavender edged in white, flowering from fall into winter. Plant it in partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, and mulch to keep roots cool. Protect from harsh afternoon sun and drying winds, especially in warmer zones. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape the evergreen form. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer in spring for lush foliage and reliable bloom.

Plant in consistently moist, deeply acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; drooping leucothoe is a graceful native evergreen shrub of mountain stream banks and ravines in the Southern Appalachians, with long arching stems clothed in lustrous lance-shaped leaves that turn bronzy-burgundy-purple in winter — one of the finest winter foliage colors in the shade garden. Tiny white bell-shaped flowers in May are fragrant and nectar-rich for early bees. The plant spreads by stolons to form a layered, naturalistic colony that suppresses weeds effectively. The cultivar 'Rainbow' has cream-pink-green variegated foliage; 'Girard's Rainbow' and 'Zeblid' (Scarletta) are also widely available. All parts are toxic. Excellent massed under rhododendrons, azaleas, or as an understory layer beneath oaks.

Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle, this native selection is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. Dropmore Scarlet is a hybrid honeysuckle noted for its exceptionally long bloom season, producing clusters of long, tubular, bright scarlet-red flowers continuously from late spring through frost rather than the more sporadic rebloom typical of straight coral honeysuckle, making it one of the most reliable season-long hummingbird plants available. Prune in late winter or right after a bloom flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood. It is semi-evergreen in mild climates, holding foliage through many winters in the Gulf South.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Drummond red maple is the variety of red maple (Acer rubrum) native to wet bottomlands, swamp forests, and pond edges of the Gulf Coastal Plain and lower Mississippi River valley. It differs from the typical red maple in larger leaves with more prominent, whitish-tomentose (densely hairy) undersides and in greater adaptation to the hot, humid, wet conditions of the Gulf South. The brilliant red fall color persists even in zone 9, providing some of the best native fall color available in the Gulf South where fall color from other trees is limited. Early red flowers in late winter announce the approach of spring. Unlike typical red maple, Drummond red maple tolerates the periodic flooding and summer heat of Gulf South bottomlands reliably. An outstanding native shade tree for wet, moist, or low-lying areas in zones 6–9.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along pond edges, wet roadside ditches, and seasonally flooded areas; drumstick sesbania is a native Gulf Coast fast-growing shrubby annual to short-lived perennial — one of the most vigorous nitrogen-fixing native legumes of the wetland margins and wet roadsides of the Gulf South. The bright yellow flowers in summer are highly attractive to native bees, especially large bees and carpenter bees. The long, distinctive seed pods rattle when shaken — a characteristic of the genus that gives one of its common names. A native plant valued for quick erosion control and soil improvement on wet, disturbed sites. Note: seeds and foliage are toxic to livestock; do not plant in pasture settings. Native to the Gulf Coastal Plain from Florida to Texas.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1869, Ducher is a compact China rose bearing clusters of fragrant, fully double, creamy-white blooms tinged with pale pink at the center, set against small, dark, glossy foliage. It is considered one of the most cold-hardy roses in the China class, extending its usefulness slightly beyond the warmest zones where most Chinas thrive, while still carrying their signature nonstop bloom cycle and strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew in humid climates. The compact, rounded shrub suits borders, low hedges, and container culture. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood; deadhead spent blooms to encourage the next flush, though the plant reblooms readily even without deadheading.

common_name: Duchess of Albany Clematis (Pink Tulip Texas Clematis)
notes: Grow this heritage cultivar of the Texas native clematis on a narrow support such as an obelisk or wire trellis, keeping its roots cool and shaded beneath low plantings. From midsummer into fall it produces slender, tulip-shaped, deep pink flowers with a candy-striped reverse that nod outward from the wiry stems rather than facing up, a distinctive habit inherited from its Texas parent species. Because it blooms on new growth, cut the vine back hard to a foot or so above the ground each late winter to renew vigor. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many large-flowered clematis, making it a good choice for warmer gardens.

Dating to 1876, this antique clematis produces fully double, pure white rosette-shaped flowers with a light green tint that carry a fresh, sweet fragrance rare among large-flowered clematis. It flowers earliest in the season on old wood, so prune lightly right after the first flush to shape the vine and encourage a smaller repeat bloom on new growth later in summer. Give it fertile, well-drained soil and a sturdy support such as a trellis or pergola post. Because its doubled flowers can be sparse in cooler climates, siting it in a warm, sheltered spot improves flower quality.

common_name: Duchesse de Brabant Rose (Cupped Antique Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1857, Duchesse de Brabant bears silky, cupped, shell-pink blooms with a light, fruity tea fragrance, held on a bushy, rounded shrub with soft blue-green foliage. President Theodore Roosevelt reportedly wore its blooms as a boutonniere, and the rose has remained a favorite of Southern gardens ever since for its dependable, near-continuous bloom and excellent tolerance of heat and humidity. It shows good resistance to blackspot compared with modern hybrid teas and asks for little beyond routine watering once established. The nodding, cupped flower form and soft coloring make it a favorite for cutting and for cottage-style borders. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; avoid hard pruning, which delays and reduces bloom.

Dura Heat is a river birch selection with creamy exfoliating bark and strong tolerance of summer heat and humidity. Plant it in full sun to part shade in moist, slightly acidic soil; it thrives in wet spots where other trees struggle. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells to prevent leaf drop. Its resistance to bronze birch borer makes it a durable landscape and shade tree. Prune only in summer or fall, since birches bleed heavily if cut in late winter or early spring.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil; Dura-Heat is a heat-tolerant selection of native river birch (Betula nigra) selected at the University of Alabama for superior performance in the hot, humid summers of zone 7–9. The exfoliating, creamy-to-salmon bark that peels in papery sheets is the tree's primary ornamental feature, providing year-round interest — the effect is most dramatic on multi-trunk specimens. Unlike most birches, which require cool summers, Dura-Heat thrives in zone 9's climate and tolerates temporary flooding, making it valuable along streams, ponds, and in rain gardens. Fall color is a modest yellow. The tree is relatively fast-growing (2–3 feet per year when young) and provides dappled shade suitable for understory plantings.

common_name: Dusky Coral Pea (Running Postman Coral Pea)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; dusky coral pea is a robust, vigorous, trailing or twining Australian native legume from the coastal scrub and dry forests of eastern Australia — producing in spring a succession of the distinctive Kennedia flower form: a typical sweet-pea-family flower with a broad, curved, deep dusky-red to dark coral-red to brick-red standard petal and smaller, darker, often almost blood-red wing and keel petals, the whole flower a rich, warm, dusky-red combination. The flowers are borne in clusters of 2–4 in the leaf axils, scattered throughout the vine over the spring bloom period. The plant itself is vigorous and fast-growing — potentially reaching considerable size as a vine or sprawling, mounding groundcover — with large, trifoliate, deep-green, somewhat coarse-textured leaves. Excellent for covering difficult, dry, sunny, rocky banks and slopes where its drought tolerance, fast growth, and nitrogen-fixing root nodules make it both ornamental and functionally valuable. The trailing stems root where they contact soil, spreading into an increasingly dense groundcover. An excellent, low-maintenance, soil-stabilizing ornamental for zone 9 coastal and inland slopes.

Dwarf Alberta spruce is a slow-growing conifer forming a naturally dense, cone-shaped pyramid of soft green needles, ideal for small gardens and containers. Plant it in full sun and well-drained soil, avoiding hot, reflective spots that can scorch the fine foliage. Provide good air circulation to reduce spider mite pressure, and rinse the foliage periodically in dry weather. Water consistently, as its shallow roots dry out quickly in pots. It rarely needs pruning thanks to its tidy, formal habit.

Plant young transplants in spring into acidic, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full to partial sun, matching the boreal barrens, subalpine meadows, and lakeshores across its wide transcontinental range from Alaska to New England. This low, tufted shrub bears small white-to-pink flowers in late spring followed by sweet, dark blue berries relished by grouse, songbirds, and small mammals. Its compact, mat-forming habit makes it a good choice for a sunny native rock garden or as a groundcover at the front of an acidic border.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Dwarf Burford Holly is a compact sport of Burford holly (Ilex cornuta 'Burfordii') that inherits most of the parent's excellent landscape traits — self-fertile heavy red berry production, single-spine leaves, glossy dark-green foliage, and outstanding deer resistance — in a much more restrained package reaching only 3–5 feet tall and wide, compared to the large-shrub to small-tree dimensions of standard Burford holly. The compact size makes Dwarf Burford exceptionally versatile for foundation plantings, low hedges, mass planting as ground cover, and container culture in situations where the full-size Burford would quickly become oversized and require heavy pruning. Like all Chinese hollies, Dwarf Burford produces the characteristic single prominent terminal spine rather than the ring of spines of American holly, making it somewhat less hazardous to plant near walkways and play areas. The heavy red berry crop matures in October–November and persists through winter, providing striking red accent color against the dark-green foliage. Extremely tough and adaptable — tolerates clay, alkaline soil, drought, and heat once established. One of the best small evergreen shrubs for the Gulf Coast region.

Dwarf Chinkapin Oak is a colony-forming native shrub oak of dry, rocky, sandy, or calcareous upland soils across the eastern United States from New England to Texas, spreading by underground rhizomes to form dense thickets in acid barrens, shale outcrops, dry prairies, and other open, infertile habitats. Though modest in stature at 3–8 feet, it produces large, sweet, low-tannin acorns with coarsely toothed chestnut-like leaves, and the acorns were historically harvested and eaten raw — without the leaching required for most other acorns — by Native Americans across its range; they remain among the best-tasting acorns of any North American oak. Spreading steadily by rhizomes to form wildlife thickets, Dwarf Chinkapin Oak provides year-round habitat value: dense nesting cover, summer leaf-litter decomposition, and a reliable annual fall acorn crop for turkeys, deer, squirrels, and many bird species. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in dry, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; no supplemental irrigation needed once established in xeric conditions.

common_name: Dwarf Creeping Gardenia (Miniature Gardenia, Radicans Gardenia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Radicans is a low-growing, spreading dwarf form of the common gardenia that stays 12–18 inches tall while spreading 3–4 feet wide, creating a compact, flowing ground cover or low shrub form with all the fragrance and ornamental qualities of its larger relatives in a much more manageable size. The small, double, white flowers (about 1 inch across) are produced abundantly in late spring and summer and carry the same intensely sweet, classic gardenia fragrance as the standard-size plants, making this one of the most fragrant plants available for a low-growing ground cover position. The glossy, dark-green, narrow foliage is evergreen in zone 9 and attractive year-round. Radicans is effective as a ground cover under trees with partial shade, along shaded walkway edges, cascading over retaining walls, and in containers where its low, spreading habit can be displayed. It requires the same acidic, humus-rich, moist soil that all gardenias prefer and is sensitive to soil pH above 6.5 — yellowing foliage (chlorosis) in zone 9 is often a sign of pH too high or iron deficiency in alkaline soils. Excellent for zone 9 where the mild winters allow it to thrive and bloom reliably year after year.

common_name: Dwarf Firebush (Compact Native Hummingbird Shrub for Gulf South Gardens)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Dwarf Firebush ('Compacta') is a compact cultivar of the native Hamelia patens (firebush), a Florida and Gulf Coast native shrub that is one of the most outstanding hummingbird and butterfly plants for subtropical gardens — producing dense clusters of tubular, orange-red to coral-red flowers continuously from late spring through fall on a more compact, manageable 3–4 foot plant compared to the 6–10 foot of the full-sized species. The combination of orange-red tubular flowers (ideal for hummingbirds), black-purple berries (eaten by songbirds), reddish new growth, and reliable heat/drought performance makes Dwarf Firebush one of the finest all-around wildlife shrubs for zone 9 landscapes. Ruby-throated hummingbirds visit constantly during migration (March–May and July–October) and resident Gulf South hummingbirds use it throughout the warm season. Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and numerous other butterfly species nectar on the flowers regularly. In zone 9, Dwarf Firebush may be killed to the ground by hard freezes but returns vigorously from the roots in spring — treat as a perennial subshrub and cut back to 6 inches in late February to promote fresh growth. In protected locations and zone 9b, the plant may remain evergreen through mild winters. The compact habit makes it proportionate for residential gardens where the full species would be too large.

Dwarf Fothergilla is one of the finest native shrubs for four-season interest in the southeastern garden, native to wet pine savannas, pocosins, and moist, acidic coastal plain habitats from North Carolina to Alabama, producing fragrant, white, bottlebrush-like flower spikes of pure white stamens in March and April before the leaves emerge — among the most beautiful of all native spring-blooming shrubs. The broadly ovate, blue-green summer leaves are attractive in their own right; they turn to exceptional shades of crimson, orange, and yellow in fall, often with all three colors on a single leaf. Easy to grow in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, Dwarf Fothergilla is compact enough for small gardens and is valuable as a foundation planting, border accent, or naturalized understory shrub. Provide acidic, consistently moist soil and avoid alkaline conditions, which cause chlorosis.

Dwarf hackberry is a small native tree of rocky limestone glades, cedar barrens, dry cliffs, and open woodland edges across the eastern and central United States — the most compact and stress-tolerant of the native hackberries, growing slowly into a rounded shrub or small tree on exposed, droughty sites where little else establishes. Like larger hackberries, it is one of the most important wildlife trees for native butterflies: the larvae of hackberry emperor, tawny emperor, and American snout butterflies feed exclusively on hackberry foliage, making all Celtis species invaluable host plants for these specialist butterflies. Its small, orange-to-dark-purple berries ripen in fall and are consumed by at least 48 species of birds — it is one of the top bird-attracting fruiting native trees for fall migrants. Its tolerance of rocky, alkaline, shallow limestone soils and exposed cliff-face conditions makes it ideal for dry stone walls, rocky native plantings, and limestone-soil landscapes where conventional trees fail to thrive.

Dwarf Hinoki cypress is a slow-growing evergreen with rich green, fan-shaped sprays of foliage that form a graceful, sculptural pyramid. Plant it in full sun to light shade in moist but well-drained soil, avoiding soggy sites that cause root rot. It appreciates shelter from harsh drying winter winds, which can brown the foliage. Water regularly during establishment and in droughts, then it becomes fairly self-sufficient. Little pruning is needed, and its naturally elegant layered form makes it a favorite for rock gardens and containers.

Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to part shade; dwarf honey bush is the compact species of the South African Melianthus genus — producing the same striking blue-gray, serrated, pinnate foliage as its larger relative M. major but in a more restrained size (2–5 feet) suitable for mixed borders and smaller gardens. The foliage has the distinctive, sharply toothed, almost claw-like leaflet margins of the genus and the same beautiful glaucous blue-gray color that reads as near-exotic in the garden. Dark maroon to brick-red tubular flowers appear on upright spikes in late winter and spring, producing copious nectar that earned the genus its common name — in South Africa, the flowers drip with honey-like nectar attractive to sunbirds and hummingbirds. The bruised foliage has an unpleasant odor (described variously as peanut butter or something less pleasant), so site away from paths or wear gloves when handling. Cuts back to the ground in cold winters in zones 8–9 and resprouts reliably.

Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; dwarf live oak is a running, rhizomatous scrub oak of the longleaf pine flatwoods and coastal scrub habitats of the southeastern Coastal Plain. Unlike typical upright oaks, this species stays very low (usually under 3 feet) and spreads by underground rhizomes to form dense, thicket-like colonies — a fire-adapted growth form that allows it to re-sprout vigorously after ground fires in its native longleaf pine savanna habitat. The small, evergreen leaves are typical of live oaks. The acorns provide food for bobwhite quail, wild turkey, deer, and numerous other wildlife. An outstanding native for stabilizing dry, sandy soils and creating dense, low wildlife cover in the longleaf pine ecosystem. Its low habit makes it useful as a large-scale native ground cover in dry, sandy, sunny sites.

Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; dwarf umbrella tree is a compact, versatile tropical shrub from Taiwan that produces the same distinctive, deeply divided, umbrella-shaped, palmate leaf compound structure as its larger relative Schefflera actinophylla but remains a more manageable size for garden and indoor use — each leaf consists of 7–9 glossy, oval leaflets radiating from a central point like the spokes of an umbrella, creating a bold, tropical texture on densely branched shrubs. In zones 10–12 it grows as a substantial landscape shrub or small tree; elsewhere it is among the most widely grown tropical houseplants, adapting to a broad range of indoor light conditions while remaining significantly more compact and manageable than the large umbrella tree. It can be pruned aggressively to maintain shape and size, trained as a braided trunk or multi-stem specimen, or allowed to grow freely. 'Trinette' (yellow-variegated), 'Gold Capella' (golden-green), and 'Janine' (cream-variegated) are popular cultivars. Toxic if ingested.

common_name: Dwarf Wax Myrtle (Compact Native Evergreen Shrub for Gulf Coast Landscapes)
notes: Plant in any well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Dwarf Wax Myrtle ('Pumila') is a compact cultivar of the native southern wax myrtle (Morella cerifera) that offers the same extraordinary adaptability and wildlife value of the species in a smaller, more landscape-manageable scale of 3–6 feet — suitable for foundation plantings, hedges, and mixed shrub borders where the full-sized species reaching 10–15 feet would be out of scale. The aromatic, small, narrow, gray-green evergreen foliage has a pleasantly spicy, bay-like scent when crushed and provides fine-textured, dense screening year-round. Female plants (this species has separate male and female individuals) produce the characteristic small, waxy, gray-blue berries in clusters along the stems — these berries are consumed by over 40 species of birds including yellow-rumped warblers, tree swallows, bluebirds, and Carolina wrens that depend heavily on the high-fat berries during winter migration and cold weather. The deep-rooted, nitrogen-fixing root system improves lean soils over time. The standard species (full-sized wax myrtle) is one of the most important multi-habitat native shrubs of the Gulf South; 'Pumila' provides the same ecological value in residential-scale plantings. Tolerates salt spray, poor drainage, drought, and coastal conditions that challenge most ornamental shrubs.

common_name: Dwarf Wax Myrtle (Dwarf Southern Wax Myrtle, Compact Wax Myrtle)
notes: Plant in any well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf wax myrtle is a compact native shrub closely related to southern wax myrtle (Morella cerifera) but naturally staying much smaller — 2–4 feet tall and wide — without requiring the heavy shearing that makes the larger species high-maintenance. The aromatic, semi-evergreen to evergreen, dark-green, spatula-shaped leaves have the same pleasant, bay-like fragrance when crushed as its larger relative. Small clusters of waxy, steel-blue berries form on female plants in fall and winter, providing essential high-fat food for dozens of native bird species — a cornerstone plant for wildlife habitat. Dwarf wax myrtle is extraordinarily adaptable: it tolerates salt spray, poor sandy soil, clay, periodic flooding, and significant drought once established, making it one of the most valuable natives for difficult Gulf Coast sites. Excellent as a naturalized hedge, mass planting, or foundation shrub where its compact size fits without constant pruning.

Scarify and stratify seed before spring sowing, or set out nursery plugs into dry, well-drained prairie soil where this diminutive shrub forms a tidy, low mound rather than the taller thickets of its relatives. Short spikes of fragrant purple flowers with prominent orange anthers appear in late spring and are worked heavily by bumblebees, leafcutter bees, and other native pollinators drawn to the sweet scent. It is especially well suited to short-grass and mixed-grass prairie restorations of the Dakotas, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, where its compact size keeps it from overwhelming smaller neighboring wildflowers. Established plants are extremely drought tolerant thanks to a deep taproot and rarely need irrigation once past their first season.

common_name: Dwarf Yaupon Holly (Schilling's Dwarf Yaupon, Nana Yaupon)
notes: Plant in any well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; dwarf yaupon holly is a compact, mounding cultivar of the native yaupon holly that stays 2–3 feet tall and 3–5 feet wide without requiring the constant shearing that maintains the rounded shape of unselected yaupon. The 'Nana' and 'Schillings' cultivars are the most widely grown dwarf forms, producing the characteristic small, slightly toothed, dark-green leaves of the species in a naturally dense, low, spreading mound that functions beautifully as a foundation plant, hedge, or mass planting. Being male cultivars, these dwarf selections do not produce berries — for berry production, plant named female selections like 'Hoskins Shadow' or unselected yaupon alongside. Dwarf yaupon is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, enduring the Gulf Coast's extreme summer conditions without supplemental irrigation in established plantings. The deer resistance and extreme adaptability make it one of the most reliable low-maintenance native shrubs for zone 7–10.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Dynamite is among the finest red-flowered crape myrtle cultivars and one of the most popular landscape crape myrtles in the Gulf South — producing vivid, true cherry-red to scarlet flower clusters from June through September on a medium-large tree reaching 15–20 feet. True red is one of the most difficult colors to achieve reliably in crape myrtles — many claimed reds prove to be pink, magenta, or dark rose under Gulf Coast summer conditions — but Dynamite holds consistently true cherry-red color throughout the bloom season without fading. It was introduced by Dr. Carl Whitcomb and is marketed with the name 'Dynamite' reflecting the explosive intensity of its flower color. The multi-trunked form develops attractive exfoliating bark with age. Dynamite is somewhat more compact than the National Arboretum large-tree series and reaches 15–20 feet — large enough to function as a specimen shade tree but manageable in typical residential landscapes with some annual guidance pruning to remove crossing branches and maintain open, arching structure. Never top or 'crepe murder' — proper pruning removes only small, dead, and crossing branches, preserving the natural vase-shaped form.

common_name: Eagleston Holly (Southern Hybrid Evergreen Tree Holly)
notes: Plant in well-drained, acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing plenty of room for its eventual size as a large tree. Eagleston is a hybrid tree holly (Ilex x attenuata), a cross between American holly (I. opaca) and Dahoon holly (I. cassine), selected for fast growth, a strong single-trunk pyramidal form, and heavy annual crops of bright red berries that persist through winter and feed songbirds. It has been a favorite specimen and street tree across the Deep South for decades, valued for reaching an attractive mature tree form faster than American holly while retaining good foliage density and cold hardiness. The glossy, lightly spined, dark green evergreen leaves provide year-round structure and screening, and the tree tolerates the heat, humidity, and clay soils typical of Gulf South landscapes once established. Like most hollies it is dioecious, so a male holly planted nearby improves berry set, though Eagleston often fruits reasonably well from pollen carried from other hollies in the neighborhood. Prune, if needed, in late winter to maintain a single leader and remove any competing double trunks while the tree is young.

common_name: Early Amethyst Beautyberry (Compact Early-Fruiting Purple Beautyberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Early Amethyst is a compact selection of Asian beautyberry prized for producing an especially heavy, early display of small, intensely violet-purple berries clustered tightly along graceful, arching branches in fall, after inconspicuous pink summer flowers. Its smaller mature size compared to native American beautyberry makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller gardens, though the vivid fall berry display is just as striking. It flowers and fruits on new wood, so a hard pruning in late winter to a foot or two from the ground each year encourages the most vigorous new growth and heaviest berry set the following fall.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; early stachyurus sets its dangling flower chains in fall and displays them through winter before opening, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds. Stachyurus praecox is a graceful Japanese shrub with arching, reddish-brown branches that hang with drooping chains of small, pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers in late winter to early spring, opening from buds that form the previous fall and remain an ornamental feature through the cold months. Its arching form and cascading winter flower chains make it a distinctive specimen for a shaded border, adding a different texture and bloom form than the more upright witch hazel or paperbush that flower at the same season. It appreciates the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil favored by camellia and rhododendron, and benefits from a sheltered site out of harsh winter wind.

Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; East Palatka holly is a naturally occurring hybrid of Dahoon holly (Ilex cassine) and American holly (Ilex opaca) selected from natural hybrid populations near Palatka, Florida, and has been widely used in southeastern landscape plantings for decades. Like Savannah holly, East Palatka is a large, fast-growing, upright-pyramidal evergreen tree, but it is distinguished by a somewhat more open branching habit and leaves with typically only a single apical spine at the tip rather than the multiple spines of standard American holly, making it less prickly and easier to handle. The single-spined leaves and the plant's natural origin deep in the Gulf Coastal Plain make it exceptionally well-adapted to zone 9 heat and humidity. Female plants loaded with small red berries in fall and winter are spectacular wildlife plants, attracting migrating and wintering songbirds. East Palatka is particularly well-suited to Florida, coastal Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana conditions where the high humidity and heat stress some landscape hollies. Requires a male pollinizer for heavy fruit production. Widely available in Gulf Coast nurseries and highly recommended by the University of Florida IFAS Extension for sustainable Gulf Coast landscapes.

Eastern Cottonwood is the fastest-growing native tree in North America, capable of adding 6–8 feet of height per year in moist, fertile, alluvial soils — a growth rate no other native tree approaches — and is native to the river bars, floodplains, and moist bottomlands of virtually every drainage system in eastern and central North America from Quebec to Florida and west to the Rockies. The triangular (deltoid) leaves tremble and shimmer in the slightest breeze due to their flattened petioles, creating a distinctive rustling sound audible at considerable distances; in late spring, female trees produce enormous quantities of cottony-tufted seeds that fill the air like midsummer snow, settling on every surface and creating what many observers find an enchanting spectacle and others find a nuisance. An important pioneer tree for streambank stabilization and riparian restoration, Eastern Cottonwood provides critical early-successional habitat for many birds and insects. Plant male cultivars to avoid seed dispersal; provide full sun and deep, moist soil near water features or for rapid windbreak and privacy screening.

Plant in almost any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; eastern groundsel tree is a large, fast-growing, fall-blooming native shrub of coastal and inland wetland edges from Massachusetts to Texas, valued primarily for its extraordinary fall display when female plants produce dense, silky-white seed heads (pappi) in such abundance that the plant appears to be covered in brilliant white cotton or snow. Male plants produce the inconspicuous but nectar-rich cream-white flowers in September and October that attract monarch butterflies, native bees, and insects before seed set. It is among the most salt-tolerant and flood-tolerant native shrubs of the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts — growing in coastal marshes, salt spray environments, and periodically inundated soils where few ornamentals survive. Equally valuable inland as a fast-growing screen or wildlife shelter shrub. The brilliant white fall seed heads of female plants are stunning in the autumn landscape. A critical ecological shrub for the coastal plain.

Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; eastern ninebark is a native shrub of eastern North America prized for two distinct ornamental features — exfoliating bark that peels and shreds in layers on mature stems (creating year-round textural interest in winter, when the orange-brown inner and grayish outer bark peel apart in curling strips, hence 'ninebark') and, in late spring, dense clusters of small, creamy-white to pale-pink flowers attractive to many native pollinators. The dark-purple to burgundy foliage cultivars such as 'Diabolo' (very deep purple-black leaves) and 'Summer Wine' (somewhat more compact, wine-red foliage) have become mainstays of the mixed shrub border, providing a bold, dark, non-green foliage contrast through the entire growing season. 'Coppertina' has coppery-orange new growth fading to burgundy. The compact cultivar 'Little Devil' stays 3–4 feet. Native across a huge range from Ontario to Georgia in river banks, woodland edges, and bluffs, it is exceptionally tolerant of difficult sites including clay, flooding, and urban conditions.

Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Eastern redbud is one of North America's most beloved native understory trees, erupting each spring in clouds of vivid magenta-pink flowers that cover the bare branches for two weeks before the heart-shaped leaves emerge — one of the most spectacular floral displays of any temperate tree. The flat, pea-like flowers are edible and can be added to salads, pickled in vinegar, or used as a colorful garnish. After flowering, the attractive rounded to heart-shaped leaves provide clean summer shade, turning golden-yellow in fall. The species is native from New Jersey to Nebraska and south to northern Florida, making it well-adapted to the Gulf Coast from zone 7 through 9 with afternoon shade; 'Oklahoma' and 'Texas White' are compact heat-tolerant cultivars excellent for the South. The weeping form 'Traveller' and the dark-foliaged 'Forest Pansy' are outstanding landscape selections.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; eastern wahoo is a native alternative to the invasive Asian burning bush (Euonymus alatus) and performs the same landscape function — stunning fall color — while supporting native wildlife instead of escaping into woodlands. In fall, the foliage turns brilliant scarlet-red while the seed pods split open to reveal dangling bright coral-pink and orange arillate seeds that attract migratory birds including thrushes, bluebirds, and waxwings. The purple-tinged flowers in late spring are modest but charming. The plant tolerates deep shade and is one of few shrubs that thrives under the dense canopy of mature oaks and maples. All parts are toxic to humans and livestock. This is the true 'burning bush' of the native landscape.

Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ebbinge's Silverberry is a vigorous, large-growing evergreen hybrid elaeagnus — a cross between Elaeagnus macrophylla and E. pungens — producing large, broadly oval, silvery-green to silver-backed leaves on arching, fast-growing stems that create a substantial evergreen screen or windbreak in one to two growing seasons. The large, silvery-underside leaves give the shrub a distinctive, gleaming silver-gray appearance in breezes when the undersides catch the light. In fall, small, creamy-white, intensely sweet-fragrant flowers are produced — remarkably fragrant for small, inconspicuous flowers — followed by small, orange-red berries in spring that are edible (sweet-tart when ripe) and attractive to birds. Like its parent E. pungens, Ebbinge's Elaeagnus is one of the most remarkably tough and adaptable landscape shrubs available: tolerating drought, salt spray, wind, poor soils, alkaline conditions, and coastal exposures that defeat most evergreen shrubs. It grows by nitrogen fixation through root nodules, enriching the surrounding soil. The fast, dense growth and salt tolerance make it outstanding for coastal windbreaks and screening. 'Gilt Edge' and 'Limelight' are named cultivars with bold golden-yellow leaf variegation.

common_name: Edith Bogue Magnolia (Cold-Hardy Upright Southern Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Edith Bogue is the most cold-hardy Southern magnolia cultivar available for routine landscape use — surviving temperatures as low as -10°F and reliably winter-hardy in zone 5 where no other Southern magnolia cultivar can be grown. The cultivar originated from a tree planted by Edith Bogue in Montclair, New Jersey, that survived severe winters that killed all other Southern magnolia selections in the area. This exceptional cold hardiness expands the range of the magnificent Southern magnolia northward into climate zones previously inaccessible to the species. Beyond cold hardiness, Edith Bogue has a distinctly narrower, more columnar to pyramidal habit than most Southern magnolia cultivars — a significant advantage in residential landscapes where the typical broad, spreading form of standard Southern magnolias would require too much space. The upright form makes Edith Bogue appropriate for tighter spaces along buildings, driveways, and in urban settings. The glossy, dark-green leaves with a lighter underside and the classic creamy-white, deeply fragrant flowers (8–12 inches across) are characteristic of the species. In zone 9, it performs superbly — the superior cold hardiness is not needed in the Gulf South, but the narrow habit is a consistent advantage.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Edward Goucher Abelia is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full to partial sun; Edward Goucher is a hybrid abelia cross between Abelia x grandiflora and Abelia schumannii, producing a medium-sized (4–5 foot), gracefully arching shrub with distinctly more colorful flowers than standard white-flowered abelia — the small, tubular flowers are lavender-pink to lilac-pink, creating a softer, more distinctly colored floral display that continues from late spring through frost. The semi-evergreen to nearly evergreen foliage has a refined, fine texture, and the new growth emerges with a bronze-red tint that transitions to dark green — adding foliage color interest beyond the continuous flower display. Abelia in general is one of the most butterfly-attractive landscape shrubs available in zone 9, and Edward Goucher's colored flowers enhance this quality — the lavender-pink flowers are particularly attractive to swallowtails, skippers, and sulphurs throughout the long bloom season. The combination of zone 9 adaptability, long bloom season, drought tolerance once established, and the graceful natural habit has made Edward Goucher one of the most classic and enduringly popular landscape shrubs for Gulf South gardens since its introduction.

common_name: Eleanor Taber Indian Hawthorn (Deep Pink-Flowered Indian Hawthorn)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates partial shade with somewhat reduced flowering. Eleanor Taber is a long-popular Indian hawthorn selection prized for its especially deep, rich rose-pink flower clusters in spring, a stronger color than the softer pinks and whites typical of the species, set against the same leathery, dark green, disease-resistant foliage. Like other Indian hawthorn selections it is outstanding for coastal Gulf landscapes, tolerating salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil with ease, and needs only a light shaping prune right after spring bloom to keep its naturally tidy, rounded form. Good air circulation helps reduce Entomosporium leaf spot, the main disease concern for Indian hawthorn in humid climates.

common_name: Eleanor Tabor Indian Hawthorn (Deep Pink Compact Indian Hawthorn)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Eleanor Tabor bears an unusually heavy flush of deep pink flowers each spring, richer in color than many Indian hawthorn cultivars, on a dense, rounded shrub with glossy, leathery, disease-resistant evergreen foliage followed by small blue-black berries that draw birds. Its bold spring color and dependable form make it a strong choice for foundation plantings, low hedges, and coastal landscape beds. Like other Indian hawthorn cultivars, it tolerates salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils well; provide good air circulation between plants to help minimize leaf spot disease in humid climates.

common_name: Elegans Camellia (Chandleri Elegans, Pink Anemone-Form Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Elegans is one of the oldest and most historically celebrated Camellia japonica cultivars in American horticulture — introduced by English nurseryman Alfred Chandler in 1831 and still one of the finest camellias for landscape and specimen use nearly two centuries later. The large, anemone-form flowers display a distinctive structure with five large, broad outer guard petals in deep rose-pink to shell-pink surrounding a central boss of densely packed, smaller, petaloid stamens (petaloids) in the same pink color — creating a unique, shaggy, high-centered flower form quite different from the flat formal doubles or simple singles of other camellias. The large flowers — up to 4 inches across — are exceptionally showy and produced in mid-season (December through March in zone 9). The shrub develops a characteristically spreading, somewhat horizontal habit that is distinctive from the more upright growth of most japonica camellias, eventually reaching 5–10 feet tall and 6–10 feet wide. 'Elegans Champagne' is a sport with white petals and yellow petaloids; 'Elegans Supreme' has ruffled pink petals. Provide morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9, consistent moisture, and acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil.

Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun to light shade; Portulacaria afra (Elephant Bush, Dwarf Jade, or Spekboom in Afrikaans) is a South African succulent shrub and small tree that is both one of the most ecologically important plants on earth and one of the most practical ornamental succulents for warm, dry landscapes. In its native South Africa's Eastern Cape, spekboom forms vast thicket ecosystems and is one of the most efficient carbon-sequestering plants known — Kruger National Park estimates that spekboom thicket sequesters 4–10 times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforest. As a garden plant, Elephant Bush is valued for its ease of care, attractive small rounded succulent leaves (resembling jade plant Crassula ovata but faster-growing and more heat-tolerant), and its edible, pleasantly sour leaves used in South African salads and stews. The shrubs grow rapidly in warm conditions (up to 3 feet per year in zones 10–12), are extraordinarily drought-tolerant once established, and root easily from stem cuttings. The leaves are eaten by elephants (hence 'Elephant Bush'), baboons, and other wildlife in the wild. Excellent as a low-water landscape shrub, large container specimen, or informal hedge in zone 9b–12; root cuttings easily to propagate. The similar-looking variegated form (leaves edged in cream) is widely grown as a decorative specimen.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; elephant ear begonia (Begonia scharffii, syn.
