B. haageana) is one of the largest and most architecturally impressive of the shrub begonias — it grows with a stout, upright, branching, cane-like habit reaching 3–5 feet, with enormous, asymmetric, heart-shaped leaves that can reach 12 inches or more in length, rich olive-green on the upper surface and vivid deep-red on the undersides, with both surfaces covered with soft, silvery-white hairs that give the foliage a luminous, textured quality in low light. Large, pendant clusters of white to pale-pink flowers with prominent yellow stamens are produced at branch tips throughout the warm season. The hairy, large-leaved, red-backed foliage and the bold shrubby habit combine to make it a commanding specimen in shaded gardens, large containers, and conservatories. It tolerates lower humidity better than most shade-growing tropical plants and is one of the easier large begonias to grow as an overwintering indoor houseplant in cool climates. An outstanding architectural shade specimen for zone 10–12 outdoor gardens.

Scarify seeds with sandpaper and soak overnight before sowing; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun; provide frost protection when young. Enterolobium cyclocarpum (Guanacaste or elephant ear tree) is one of the most massive and magnificent tropical shade trees of Central America — the national tree of Costa Rica — growing to an enormous size with a broadly spreading crown reaching 80–100 feet in diameter that provides extraordinary shade. The common name 'elephant ear tree' comes from the distinctive, flat, dark-brown, ear-shaped seed pods 2–4 inches across that resemble a stylized elephant ear. The tree produces fluffy, white, powder-puff flowers followed by distinctive coiled pods containing 6–15 seeds surrounded by edible, sweet, pulpy flesh used in traditional beverages in Costa Rica. The seeds are high in protein and have been used as animal feed. The wood is valuable for furniture and construction throughout Central America. In zone 10–12 gardens with no frost risk, the tree is a spectacular choice for large-scale tropical landscaping where its enormous size can be accommodated; it grows fast (to 15–20 feet in 3–4 years) and eventually dominates the landscape.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Elizabeth magnolia was the first yellow-flowered magnolia hybrid widely introduced to the nursery trade. Bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and released in the 1970s, this landmark hybrid was the first widely available magnolia with soft, primrose-yellow flowers, a color previously unseen in cultivated magnolias, opening on bare branches in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge, with a light, sweet lemon fragrance. Its introduction opened the door to the many yellow-flowered magnolia hybrids bred since, and it remains a garden favorite for its unusual color, upright pyramidal form, and good resistance to the late-frost damage that plagues some earlier-blooming white magnolias. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally, removing only damaged or crossing branches as needed.

Emerald Green arborvitae is a narrow, upright evergreen with dense sprays of bright green foliage, widely planted in rows for privacy screens and hedges. Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants roughly 2 to 4 feet apart for a solid living wall. Water regularly during the first two seasons to establish deep roots and prevent winter browning. It holds its color and slender form well without shearing, though it can be trimmed lightly. Protect young plants from heavy snow load and browsing deer.

common_name: Emerald Snow Loropetalum (Cold-Hardy White-Flowered Green Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Emerald Snow is a white-flowered Loropetalum chinense selection that departs from the more familiar burgundy-leaved, pink-flowered loropetalum cultivars, instead pairing clean green evergreen foliage with abundant, fringe-petaled white flowers in spring and scattered rebloom later in the season. Bred for improved winter hardiness relative to older white-flowered selections, it holds up well through colder snaps common in the northern Gulf South while retaining the vigorous, adaptable growth habit typical of the species. Its all-green foliage makes it a versatile companion for gardens that already feature plenty of burgundy loropetalum, offering contrast and a softer, more traditional look for a hedge, foundation planting, or mixed border. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom to shape, since later pruning removes developing flower buds.

common_name: Emily Brontë Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2018 and named for the author of Wuthering Heights, Emily Brontë bears warm pink, rosette-shaped flowers with a fresh tea fragrance, on a healthy, well-branched, medium-sized shrub bred for improved disease resistance over older English rose cultivars. It flowers in generous flushes from late spring through frost, and its manageable size and clean foliage make it a reliable choice for a mixed border where a compact, classic-form English rose is wanted.

common_name: Emily Bruner Holly (Large Red-Berried Hybrid Holly)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Emily Bruner is one of the finest large-statured evergreen holly trees for the Gulf South — a hybrid between Ilex latifolia (lusterleaf holly) and Ilex aquifolium (English holly) that combines the large, deep-green, dramatically lustrous leaves of the former with the heavy red berry production and classic holly appearance of the latter. The large, glossy, finely spined leaves (3–4 inches long) create an exceptionally handsome texture — more coarse and more dramatic than American holly (Ilex opaca) and much bolder and glossier than Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta). The tree grows into a broad, pyramidal to oval form reaching 10–25 feet tall with heavy, persistent red berry clusters that develop after cross-pollination from a male plant (James Swan is the recommended male pollinator for Emily Bruner). The massive red berry clusters that develop in October through December are among the most spectacular berry displays of any landscape holly — birds consume the berries through winter. Emily Bruner is excellent as a specimen tree, screening plant, or large accent in mixed shrub borders. The outstanding year-round appearance and heavy berry production make it one of the finest alternatives to American holly for large-scale landscape use in zone 9.

common_name: Emperor I Japanese Maple (Late-Leafing Frost-Resistant Red Maple)
notes: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Emperor I holds deep reddish-purple foliage color through the growing season better than many older red Japanese maple cultivars, and its notably late spring leaf-out — about two weeks behind most red-leaf cultivars — protects the new growth from the late frosts that can damage earlier-leafing maples. Its upright, well-branched form makes it a strong choice for a small specimen tree in a partly shaded border or as an accent near a patio, and its heat tolerance has made it a popular choice for warmer zones where some red Japanese maples scorch. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, protecting plants from harsh afternoon sun in the hottest part of zone 9 summers. The Encore breeding series, developed in Louisiana beginning in the 1990s, was a breakthrough because it combined the classic look of Southern azaleas with genuine repeat blooming, flowering not just in the traditional spring flush but again in summer and often into fall, greatly extending the color season of a plant long associated with a single brief burst of spring bloom. Dozens of named Encore cultivars are now available across a wide range of flower colors and mature sizes, all sharing the reblooming trait and reasonably good heat tolerance for the Gulf South. Water deeply during dry spells, especially heading into the summer and fall bloom flushes, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom to shape without removing the buds that will produce later color.

Endless Summer is a reblooming bigleaf hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, producing large mophead blooms from spring through fall. Plant it in morning sun with afternoon shade in rich, consistently moist soil, and mulch to keep roots cool. Flower color shifts with soil chemistry: acidic soil yields blue blooms while alkaline soil produces pink, so amend accordingly. Because it blooms on new growth too, light pruning is forgiving, though it rebounds best with minimal cutting. Keep it well watered, as wilting in heat is common.

common_name: Enduring Summer Crapemyrtle (True Dwarf Reblooming Disease-Resistant Series)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Enduring Summer is a true dwarf crapemyrtle series that stays a compact 4-5 feet tall, far smaller than the tree-form crapemyrtles that dominate most Gulf South landscapes, making it a good fit for small beds, foundation plantings, or large containers. It is bred with resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew and reblooms steadily through summer, especially if spent flower clusters are removed. Like other modern crapemyrtle introductions, it should be pruned lightly to remove only dead or crossing wood rather than subjected to the severe topping sometimes called 'crape murder,' which sacrifices natural form and delays bloom.

Plant container-grown vines in spring in average soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; this selection has smaller, finer leaves than typical Virginia creeper and clings tightly to masonry and wood. A finer-textured, smaller-leaved selection of the native Virginia creeper, it clings tightly to brick, stone, and wood surfaces with adhesive tendril discs, covering walls and structures densely with palmate, five-lobed leaves that turn a brilliant scarlet-red in fall, one of the showiest native fall foliage displays of any vine. Extremely tough and adaptable, tolerating poor soil, drought, shade, and urban pollution, it provides valuable dark blue berries for birds in fall and is a larval host plant for several native moth species. Prune as needed to keep growth away from windows, gutters, and shingles, since the adhesive tendrils can damage some building surfaces and are difficult to remove once attached.

common_name: English Edging Boxwood (True Dwarf Boxwood, Dwarf English Boxwood)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade with some direct sun; Suffruticosa is the true dwarf English boxwood — the cultivar used for centuries in European formal knot gardens and low hedges, producing extremely dense, slow-growing, fine-textured, bright-green foliage mounds that clip beautifully into precise geometric forms. The very slow growth (6–9 inches per decade) and naturally tidy, globe-shaped habit make Suffruticosa the traditional edging boxwood for formal herb gardens, parterre gardens, and low border edging — a role it has filled in European gardens since at least the seventeenth century. The sweet, resinous fragrance of the foliage is the quintessential boxwood scent, associated with formal gardens throughout the Western garden tradition. However, Suffruticosa is highly susceptible to boxwood blight, the devastating fungal disease (Calonectria pseudonaviculata) that has been spreading across the Eastern United States since 2011 and can kill entire boxwood plantings within a season. For new plantings in areas where boxwood blight is present, disease-resistant Korean boxwood cultivars (Winter Gem, Green Velvet, Green Mountain) are strongly recommended over English boxwood. Where boxwood blight is not a current concern, Suffruticosa remains an outstanding traditional garden plant requiring precise siting in well-drained, aerated soil with good air circulation.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to filtered sun; English holly is the classic broadleaf evergreen of Christmas wreaths and greenery, native to western and southern Europe, bearing stiff, glossy, spine-edged dark green leaves and, on pollinated female plants, abundant bright red berries that persist through winter and feed thrushes, waxwings, and other birds when little else is available. It is dioecious, so a male cultivar such as 'Blue Prince' or 'J.C. van Tol' (a self-fertile selection) must be planted within pollinator range of a female such as 'Blue Princess' or 'Argentea Marginata' for reliable fruit set. As a large, pyramidal shrub or small tree it makes an outstanding dense screen, windbreak, or specimen for shaded woodland-edge gardens, and it withstands shearing well if a more formal hedge is wanted. In the Pacific Northwest, English holly has escaped cultivation and is classified as an invasive species in forest understories, so gardeners in that region should choose non-invasive native or sterile cultivars instead, or deadhead berries before birds can disperse the seed.

Plant cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; English ivy is the classic, most widely used shade groundcover in temperate gardens — the glossy, lobed, evergreen leaves in many different sizes and variegations (solid green, silver-variegated, gold-variegated, small-leaved, large-leaved) create a dense, weed-suppressing carpet under trees. It climbs structures by aerial rootlets and has been used for centuries to cover buildings, walls, and slopes. However, English ivy is invasive in many parts of the United States east of the Rockies, smothering native understory plants and climbing trees — where naturalized, it can eventually kill large trees by girdling. Plant only in maintained, contained situations and remove regularly from any areas where it might spread to natural woodland. In zone 9a summer heat and humidity can reduce vigor; the heat-tolerant 'Needlepoint' and small-leaved varieties perform better in the Gulf South.

Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep fertile to average loamy soil in full sun; English oak is the archetypal oak of European culture — the 'royal oak,' the great forest tree of England, the sacred tree of the Celts — producing the classic, deeply lobed oak leaf and small, elongated acorns held on distinctive long stalks (peduncles, giving the alternate common name 'pedunculate oak'). English oak has been planted throughout North America in parks, estates, and arboreta for centuries, developing into magnificent specimens in suitable climates. It is more tolerant of clay soils and seasonal wetness than most American oaks. The acorns are consumed by squirrels, jays, deer, and other wildlife. Many cultivated varieties exist, including the fastigiate (columnar) 'Fastigiata' or 'Skyrocket' forms widely used in street tree plantings. A very long-lived tree — English oaks commonly reach 500–800 years of age, and individual trees are counted among the oldest living things in Europe.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; English Roseum is a tough, adaptable, cold-hardy rhododendron widely used in commercial and municipal landscaping. Full, rounded trusses of clear pink flowers open in late spring above large, glossy, dark evergreen leaves on a dense, vigorous, well-branched shrub valued for its exceptional toughness and adaptability across a wide range of climates and soil conditions. One of the most commonly planted landscape rhododendrons in North America due to its reliability, heat and cold tolerance, and resistance to common rhododendron problems, it is a dependable choice for foundation plantings, mass plantings, and shaded borders where a fussier hybrid might struggle. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

Plant with the roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs a trellis, arbor, or fence in full sun, watering regularly during dry spells to keep flowering strong. This long-blooming, vigorous cultivar produces large, glowing magenta-red flowers with contrasting golden anthers from midsummer through early fall, one of the most reliable and free-flowering of the older large-flowered hybrids. Because it blooms on both old and new wood, it only needs light shaping in late winter rather than a hard cutback, so leave the framework mostly intact when pruning. Its strong constitution and heat tolerance make it a dependable choice for covering fences and arbors quickly.

Plant in well-drained soil next to a fence, arbor, or pergola so the twining stems have something sturdy to climb, and water regularly the first season while roots establish. Clusters of tubular, richly fragrant cream to pale yellow flowers open in late spring and early summer, gradually deepening to orange as they age, and are followed by small red berries that draw songbirds. It is a vigorous, semi-evergreen to deciduous climber that tolerates heat, dry spells, and poor soil once established, making it useful for covering a large structure quickly. Prune after flowering to keep it in bounds, since it can grow rampantly in favorable conditions.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; European hophornbeam is a refined, small-to-medium deciduous tree of dry, rocky, calcareous mountain forests from southern Europe through Turkey and the Caucasus — closely related to the American hophornbeam (Ostrya virginiana) but slightly smaller and more drought-adapted. The distinctive fruiting clusters of papery, bladder-like inflated husks enclosing each nutlet hang in loose, pendulous clusters resembling hops (Humulus lupulus) — one of the most distinctive and ornamental fruiting features of any deciduous tree. The finely toothed, birch-like leaves turn gold in autumn. The wood is exceptionally hard and dense. More drought-tolerant than most other deciduous trees, making it an excellent choice for dry, alkaline, rocky garden soils in full sun or light shade. The hop-like fruiting clusters are attractive from summer through winter. An underused but beautiful ornamental tree for dry, chalky, or limestone-based soils where larger trees struggle.

Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, fertile to average, loamy or clay loam soil in full sun to partial shade; European hornbeam is one of the most important and widely planted trees in the European formal garden tradition — valued both as a large specimen tree and as one of the premier hedging and pleaching trees, because its dense, twiggy branching retains dead tan leaves through the winter (marcescence) just like beech, creating a solid, opaque winter hedge. The wood is extraordinarily hard and tough — 'hornbeam' literally means 'hard tree' — historically used for making cogwheels, tool handles, and cutting boards. The oval leaves turn gold in autumn. The fruiting catkins with their distinctive three-lobed involucres (leafy bracts around each nut) are attractive. Exceptionally pollution-tolerant and adaptable to urban conditions. The cultivar 'Fastigiata' (columnar hornbeam) is one of the premier street trees in European cities. An excellent hedge, screen, and formal pleached allee tree for gardens with the space for its imposing mature size.

Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to lean, rocky, loamy, or sandy soil in full sun; European smoke tree is one of the most widely grown and loved ornamental shrubs in temperate gardens — famous for the extraordinary summer display of its tiny flowers, which are followed by large, loose panicles of fine, hair-like, pinkish-purple styles (the fuzzy threads remaining after the petals fall), creating the effect of a misty 'smoke cloud' surrounding the entire shrub in summer. The purple-leaved cultivars ('Royal Purple', 'Grace', 'Velvet Cloak') are among the most popular shrubs in the garden center trade — the deep wine-purple foliage contrasting with the ethereal pink-purple smoke creates a striking effect through the entire growing season. Fall color in the purple forms is spectacular: scarlet to orange-crimson. Native to southern Europe and central Asia. Extremely adaptable — tolerating dry, lean, rocky, alkaline soils where other flowering shrubs struggle. The purple-leaved forms are ubiquitous in modern garden design for their dramatic foliage season-long effect.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; European snowball bush is an old-fashioned, sterile-flowered cultivar that produces no fruit. This long-cultivated heirloom shrub bears large, perfectly round clusters of pure white flowers in late spring, opening lime-green and aging to snowy white, giving the shrub the appearance of being covered in dozens of large snowballs at peak bloom, a classic pass-along plant of old Southern and Midwestern gardens for generations. Because every flower in the cluster is sterile (unlike the fertile lacecap flowers of the wild species), it produces no berries, trading wildlife food value for a much showier, fuller flower display. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's flowers; watch for aphids, which favor the tender new growth of this species.

Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; European turkey oak is a fast-growing, large deciduous oak native to southern Europe and western Asia, named for its abundance in Turkey (not the bird). It produces deeply and variably lobed, bristle-tipped leaves with variable shape, and its most distinctive feature is the acorn cup covered in long, outward-curling, mossy-looking scales — creating some of the most ornamental acorn cups in the genus. The acorns require two full growing seasons to mature, a characteristic of the red oak group. A tough, adaptable tree for poor, dry soils where English oak would fail, commonly used in Europe for woodland planting on difficult sandy or chalk soils. The fall color is variable — yellows and bronzes. Note that in the southeastern US the name 'turkey oak' refers to the native Quercus laevis, an entirely different species.

Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil, spacing plants 24–36 inches apart, and shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep the rounded mound tidy and dense. Native to South Africa, euryops daisy is a fine-textured, silvery-gray-leaved shrub that produces bright golden-yellow, 2-inch daisy flowers almost continuously in mild climates, with the heaviest flush in fall through spring and lighter bloom through summer heat. It is highly drought- and salt-tolerant once established, making it a mainstay of Gulf Coast and coastal landscaping, and is largely untroubled by pests or disease as long as drainage is sharp — soggy soil is its main weakness. Hardy as a perennial shrub only in zones 9–11; further north it is grown as a container plant brought indoors before frost or replaced annually as a warm-season bedding plant.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained, limestone-based or average soil in full sun to partial shade; Eve's necklace tolerates both dry limestone soils and the partial shade of a woodland edge. This small, graceful understory tree native to limestone woodlands and stream edges across Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana produces drooping clusters of fragrant, pale pink to rose flowers in mid-spring, followed by distinctive black seed pods constricted between the seeds like a string of beads, giving the tree its common name. Compound, locust-like foliage casts light, dappled shade, and the tree's small mature size makes it a good choice for planting under power lines or in a smaller landscape where a full-sized shade tree would be too large. It is drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established, needing only occasional shaping in its early years to develop a strong branch structure.

Ever After Ruby is a reblooming azalea that produces vivid ruby-red flowers in spring and again from summer into fall. Plant it in dappled or partial shade in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch to protect the shallow roots. Keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since azaleas resent both drought and soggy feet. Shear lightly right after the spring flush to encourage a fuller shape and stronger repeat bloom. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer in spring.

common_name: Ever Red Loropetalum (Dwarf Mounding Red-Leaf Fringe Flower)
notes: Ever Red is a dwarf, densely mounding loropetalum selection that holds a compact size well below the larger, more vigorous fringe flower cultivars, making it a practical choice for small foundation beds where standard loropetalum quickly becomes too large. Its small leaves emerge burgundy-red and hold that deep color better through summer heat than many red-leaf loropetalum selections, set off by frilly, spidery magenta-pink flowers concentrated in spring with lighter scattered rebloom later in the season. Like other loropetalum it is easygoing in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and full sun to partial shade, needing only an occasional light shaping right after the main spring bloom to stay tidy.

Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; evergreen climbing hydrangea is less cold-hardy than the deciduous climbing hydrangea and benefits from a sheltered site. Glossy, leathery, evergreen leaves cover a self-clinging vine that attaches to walls, trellises, and tree trunks by aerial roots much like its more familiar deciduous relative, producing flat, lacecap clusters of small fertile flowers surrounded by larger, showy white sterile florets in summer. Native to cloud forests of Mexico and Central America, it holds its foliage year-round in mild climates, providing continuous coverage on a north-facing wall or shaded fence unlike the winter-bare deciduous climbing hydrangea. Provide a sturdy support for the self-clinging stems, keep soil consistently moist, and mulch well to protect roots in the colder parts of its hardiness range.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; evergreen mock orange is less cold-hardy than northern mock orange species and best suited to zones 7-9. Fragrant, creamy white, single flowers open along arching, semi-scrambling branches in late spring, carrying the classic sweet orange-blossom scent typical of the genus, on a Mexican native species that holds its glossy foliage semi-evergreen through mild winters in warmer zones where deciduous mock orange relatives lose their leaves. Its sprawling, somewhat vine-like habit makes it useful for training against a wall or trellis as much as a freestanding shrub, and its milder climate tolerance broadens the range of conditions where fragrant mock orange bloom can be enjoyed. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, and provide some winter protection at the colder edge of its hardiness range.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen wisteria is a Chinese legume vine in the same family as wisteria, producing dark, wine-purple to reddish-purple flower clusters from midsummer through fall — a very different bloom time from the spring-flowering true wisterias. The pinnate leaves are glossy and retain their attractive appearance year-round in mild climates. Compared to the aggressive true wisterias, Millettia reticulata is more restrained and less invasive, making it somewhat more manageable in the garden. The deep purple to burgundy flower clusters have a spicy, grapelike fragrance. An excellent vine for providing summer-through-fall fragrant flowering interest on arbors and pergolas in zone 9a gardens, where it is reliably perennial.

common_name: Fairy Blush Camellia (Small-Flowered Pale Pink Compact Camellia)
notes: Fairy Blush produces an abundance of small, single, pale pink flowers with a delicate blush deepening toward the petal edges, held above fine-textured, small, glossy evergreen leaves quite different from the larger, coarser foliage of many camellia cultivars. Its dainty flower form and dense, twiggy growth make it useful as a low informal hedge or mass planting where the sheer quantity of small blooms creates a soft haze of color through the bloom season. Like other camellias it needs consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and a layer of mulch to protect its shallow roots; prune, if needed, only lightly right after flowering to avoid removing next season's buds.

Sow scarified seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to rocky, poor soil in full sun; fairy duster is a low-growing native Sonoran and Chihuahuan Desert shrub in the pea family (Fabaceae) — one of the most charming and ecologically valuable small flowering shrubs of the desert Southwest — producing masses of powder-puff-like flower heads composed entirely of long, filamentous, pink-white to deep-pink stamens that give the plant its evocative common name. The silky, feathery flower clusters appear in late winter through spring, just as desert wildflowers peak, and provide an exceptionally early nectar source for emerging queen hummingbirds, sphinx moths, and native bees. The delicate, twice-pinnate, tiny-leafleted, gray-green foliage is drought-deciduous (dropped in extreme drought) and creates a fine, airy texture. Fairy duster grows naturally on dry, rocky, desert foothill slopes and bajadas and demands perfectly drained, lean, rocky soil — it fails in amended or moist garden soil. Its cold-hardiness to approximately 10°F makes it the most cold-adapted of the calliandras, suitable through zone 7. An excellent xeriscape shrub for dry Southwest gardens.

common_name: Falling Waters Bald Cypress (Weeping-Form Bald Cypress)
notes: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and stake or train the leader when young if a taller cascading form is wanted, since the weeping branches otherwise spread along the ground. Falling Waters is a striking weeping cultivar of the native bald cypress, its soft, ferny, blue-green deciduous foliage draping in cascading curtains from the branches rather than the upright, pyramidal form typical of the species, turning warm rust-orange in fall before dropping. It thrives in the same wide range of conditions as the wild species, from swampy, seasonally flooded ground to ordinary well-drained garden soil, making it a distinctive specimen tree for a pond edge, rain garden, or prominent lawn feature. Once established it needs little routine care beyond occasional watering during extended drought and removal of any reverted upright growth to preserve the weeping habit.

Plant in any moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; false indigo is a large, airy native shrub with pinnately compound leaves and 3–6 inch spikes of unusual dark purple-violet flowers with bright orange anthers in early summer — a striking color combination. It blooms at a time when few other shrubs are flowering, providing important early nectar for native bees and the southern dogface butterfly, whose caterpillars feed exclusively on the plant. It is one of the most adaptable native shrubs for wet, poorly drained soils, riverbanks, and flood-prone areas, tolerating temporary inundation and spreading to stabilize streambanks. After the flowers, clusters of resin-dotted seed pods remain through winter. Prune back by one-third after flowering to maintain a compact form. Despite its common name it has no connection to true indigo (Indigofera).

Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade along streambanks, pond margins, and low-lying areas subject to periodic flooding; false indigo bush is a fast-growing, wide-ranging native shrub found from Ontario to Florida and west to the Great Plains, producing striking 3–6 inch racemes of deep purple flowers with bright orange anthers that create a vivid two-tone contrast in late spring — one of the most visually dramatic native shrubs in flower. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it actively improves soil fertility and is an excellent anchor species for riparian restoration and streambank erosion control projects. The fine-textured, pinnately compound foliage remains attractive through the season, and the plant tolerates brief inundation that would kill most shrubs. Bees — especially bumble bees and native leafcutter bees — heavily visit the flowers. In rich, moist conditions it can sucker to form large colonies, which is desirable for mass plantings and erosion control; remove suckers to keep it shrub-sized in garden settings.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; false sarsaparilla is one of the most widely grown and adaptable Australian native ornamentals outside its homeland — a vigorous twining vine or sprawling groundcover shrub that produces in late winter and early spring a spectacular, prolific display of small but densely clustered, typical sweet pea-family flowers in vivid, rich, deep purple-violet with a distinctive small, contrasting, white-and-yellow mark at the center of each standard petal. The flowers are borne in long, pendant or arching racemes of 20–40 individual blossoms, and a plant in full late-winter bloom — covered in masses of deep-purple flower racemes against the dark, leathery, lance-shaped evergreen leaves — is a very striking sight in the winter-spring garden. The bloom period (late winter to early spring) provides vivid purple color at a time when the garden most needs it, and the flowers are attractive to honeyeating birds and bees. The form 'Happy Wanderer' is among the most commonly available and most vigorous cultivars. Tolerates considerable neglect once established, making it an ideal low-maintenance vine for fences, banks, and ground-covering in zones 8–11.

common_name: Falstaff Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1999 and named for the Shakespearean character, Falstaff carries deep velvety crimson-purple blooms that darken further as they age, one of the darkest flower colors among English roses, with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous, arching shrub. Its dramatic, saturated color makes a bold accent in a mixed border, especially paired with lighter pastel companions, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Fantasy Crape Myrtle (Tall White-Flowered Fauriei Selection with Cinnamon Bark)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, siting this large, tree-form selection where it has ample room to grow into a substantial shade tree. Fantasy is a selection of Lagerstroemia fauriei, the Japanese species behind the mildew resistance and exfoliating bark of the modern Indian-series hybrids, grown less for its relatively modest white flower clusters than for its own outstanding qualities: smooth, richly colored cinnamon bark that peels in large sheets, and a fast-growing habit that can reach 30 to 40 feet, among the tallest of any crape myrtle. It is essentially free of powdery mildew, a trait inherited from its Lagerstroemia fauriei parentage. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural form; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter as the tree matures into a fine specimen or shade tree.

Fastigiata is a long-established, classic narrow upright boxwood cultivar, its name referring to the fastigiate, columnar branching habit that has made it a staple of formal European-style garden design for generations, typically used in matched pairs or rows to frame an entry, path, or formal parterre. Its dense, deep green, small-leaved foliage gives the same year-round structure as other boxwood cultivars while holding a taller, narrower profile than rounded forms. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush maintains a crisp, formal outline.

common_name: Father Hugo Rose (Golden Rose of China)
growth_habit: species shrub rose, early spring bloomer
notes: Plant in full sun with good air circulation and well-drained soil, watering deeply while roots establish and then relying mostly on natural rainfall. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's growth. This is one of the earliest roses to flower each year, covering its arching, fern-like foliage with pale yellow single blooms in mid-spring before most other roses have even leafed out. Small dark hips follow in fall, and the fine-textured foliage gives the shrub an airy, graceful habit distinct from typical garden roses.

Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind. This unusual bigeneric cross between Fatsia japonica and English ivy was first raised in France in 1912 and combines the bold, glossy, lobed foliage of Fatsia with a looser, semi-climbing habit inherited from its ivy parent. Left unstaked it sprawls and roots where it touches soil, making a good shade groundcover or informal hedge, or it can be tied to a support for a more upright accent. It tolerates deep shade better than most broadleaf evergreens, is easy from cuttings, and needs only an occasional light pruning to control its size.

common_name: Fatsia (Japanese Fatsia, Japanese Aralia, Glossy-Leaf Paper Plant)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fatsia is one of the most dramatic and tropical-looking shade shrubs for zone 7–11 gardens, producing enormous, glossy, deeply lobed leaves 12–18 inches across on bold, multi-stemmed plants that create an instant tropical feel in the darkest garden corners. The leaves hold their rich, dark green color year-round and are remarkably resistant to wind damage. Clusters of small white ball-shaped flowers appear in fall, followed by black berries. It is one of the most shade-tolerant large shrubs available and thrives under the dense canopy of live oaks and other large trees where most plants fail. The variegated form ('Variegata') has attractive white-edged leaves. Equally at home as an outdoor landscape shrub in zone 7–11 and as a bold container plant for covered patios and atriums.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; Faxon yucca is a large, dramatic, tree-forming yucca of the Chihuahuan Desert and Trans-Pecos region, with stiff, dagger-like blue-green leaves crowded at the tips of one or more thick, woody trunks that develop slowly over decades of growth. A massive, densely packed flower spike of creamy white, waxy bell-shaped blooms rises several feet above the foliage in spring, one of the showiest floral displays of any cold-hardy desert plant. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant once established and tolerates winter cold well beyond what its desert origin suggests, needing only sharp drainage and full sun to thrive for many decades as a slow-growing architectural specimen. Give it plenty of room from walkways, since the rigid, spine-tipped leaves can cause painful puncture injuries on contact.

Plant in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial shade and leave it undisturbed once sited, since daphnes resent root disturbance; February daphne is a small deciduous shrub cherished for its very early, intensely fragrant, rosy-purple to pink flowers that wreathe the bare stems in late winter, often opening while snow is still on the ground and well before almost anything else in the garden. Flowers give way to bright red berries in summer, and the plant is compact and upright, fitting neatly into a shaded shrub border or entry planting where the winter fragrance can be enjoyed at close range. It performs best in cooler summer climates with a real winter chill and can be short-lived or stressed in prolonged summer heat and humidity. Every part of the plant, especially the berries and sap, is toxic if ingested and the sap can irritate skin, so site it away from children and pets who might be tempted by the colorful fruit, and wear gloves when pruning. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and avoid disturbing the root zone once planted.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; fern-leaf philodendron climbs readily and develops its most deeply divided leaves when given vertical support. Mature leaves are cut into numerous narrow, finger-like segments radiating from a central point, giving the plant a delicate, feathery, fern-like texture that sets it dramatically apart from the broad, solid leaves typical of most philodendrons, with new leaves unfurling a coppery bronze before deepening to green. Native to Brazilian rainforests, it climbs steadily up a moss pole or trellis, and taller, more mature plants produce progressively larger and more finely divided leaves than young specimens. Keep humidity high, provide bright indirect light, and allow the potting mix to dry slightly between waterings to prevent root rot.

Set out container-grown fernbush in fall or early spring into lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun, where it establishes as a tough, aromatic shrub with finely dissected, fern-like foliage native to the dry mountains and mesas of the Great Basin and interior West. Plants produce airy spires of small white, rose-like flowers from midsummer into fall, well after most Great Basin shrubs have finished blooming, making it a valuable late-season nectar source for native bees and butterflies at elevation. Fernbush is exceptionally cold- and drought-tolerant, thriving in the same lean soils as sagebrush and pinyon-juniper, and needs no supplemental water once rooted in. Light shaping after bloom keeps the naturally rounded form tidy.

Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Fernleaf Full Moon maple prefers cooler, more sheltered conditions than sun-tolerant Japanese maple cultivars. Deeply and finely dissected leaves, cut almost to the leaf base into slender, fern-like lobes, give this full moon maple relative a distinctly soft, feathery texture unlike the more classic star-shaped leaf of Japanese maple, turning an extraordinary blend of orange, red, and burgundy in fall that is often considered among the best of any maple's autumn display. Native to Japanese mountain forests, it is more cold-hardy but less heat-tolerant than many Japanese maple cultivars, performing best in cooler climates with protection from strong afternoon sun and wind. Provide consistent moisture and dappled shade, avoid hot, dry, or windy sites that stress the delicate foliage, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.

Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fetterbush is a native evergreen shrub of pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bog margins across the coastal South, producing glossy, leathery, sharply ribbed leaves (the midrib runs parallel to the leaf margin — a key identification feature) and small pink to white urn-shaped flowers in early spring that are critically important for native mining bees and early bumblebee queens. The plant naturally grows in waterlogged, very acidic soil and is adapted to conditions that are difficult for most other plants. An outstanding native plant for bog gardens, wet acid borders, and naturally moist sandy soils in the Southeast. All parts are toxic to livestock and humans if ingested.

Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; fever tree is one of the rarest and most unusual native shrubs of the southeastern coastal plain, found naturally only in a narrow band of swampy pocosins and wet pine savannas in coastal Georgia and the Carolinas. In the coffee family (Rubiaceae), it is related to gardenias and quinine trees — and indeed the bark was historically used as a quinine substitute to treat malaria (hence 'fever tree'). In early summer, the plant produces clusters of small, tubular, rose-to-magenta flowers, each surrounded by spectacular, greatly enlarged, rose-pink to rosy-red sepals (calyx lobes) that resemble large pink bracts or petals and create a showy, ornamental display far larger than the flowers themselves — similar in strategy to dogwood bracts. The large, tropical-looking leaves give the shrub a bold texture unusual among native plants. A conservation-significant plant that also makes an outstanding specimen for moist shaded gardens in zones 7–9, appreciating conditions similar to native azaleas.

Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10–12; fiddle-leaf fig has become one of the most widely grown and immediately recognizable indoor trees of the early 21st century, prized for its enormous, deeply wavy-edged, violin-shaped leaves (12–18 inches long) in rich, dark, glossy green that create an unmistakably tropical and architecturally dramatic statement in interior spaces. Native to the lowland tropical rainforests of West Africa, it grows as a large tree to 50 feet in its native habitat. As a houseplant it requires bright, indirect light (a few feet from a south or west window), consistent watering (allowing the top 2 inches to dry between waterings), and avoidance of both overwatering (the primary cause of root rot and leaf drop) and cold drafts. It dislikes being moved and may drop leaves in response to environmental changes. In zones 10–12 it can be grown outdoors as a specimen tree in partial shade. Cleaning the large leaves with a damp cloth maintains their glossy appearance and maximizes light absorption.

common_name: Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron (Horsehead Philodendron, Panda Plant, Panduraeforme)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron produces its most dramatic and largest leaves with consistent bright indirect light and a climbing support, but adapts to lower light conditions without serious decline. Philodendron bipennifolium (formerly classified as P. panduraeforme, a name still commonly used in horticultural trade) is a climbing philodendron native to Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru in the family Araceae. The common names 'Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron' and 'Horsehead Philodendron' both refer to the distinctive shape of the adult leaves — a broad, slightly elongated outline with two distinctive basal lobes and a characteristic narrowing in the middle that creates a violin or fiddle silhouette, or, from another angle, a horse's head profile. The leaves are glossy, bright to dark-green, leathery, and held on long petioles that give the plant an open, airy structure. In the juvenile form, the leaves are much smaller and simpler; the characteristic fiddle shape develops progressively as the plant matures. As a rapidly growing, adaptable climbing philodendron with an unusual and attractive leaf form, P. bipennifolium has long been popular in cultivation and has been used in breeding the modern 'Philodendron Florida' hybrid series. All parts contain calcium oxalate and are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Fiddleleaf Morning Glory (White Beach Morning Glory)
notes: Direct sow scarified seed or root stem cuttings after the last frost in loose, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, watering only to establish since the vine is adapted to droughty dune sand. Fiddleleaf morning glory sends out long, prostrate, fleshy stems lined with distinctive lobed, fiddle-shaped leaves and opens white, funnel-shaped flowers with a soft yellow throat through the warm months. It is a close coastal relative of the pink-flowered railroad vine, and its network of trailing stems and deep roots make it an effective, low-growing sand stabilizer for beachfront and other extremely sandy, salt-exposed Gulf Coast sites. Because it spreads by rooting at the nodes, it also works well cascading over a hot, dry retaining wall or bank where little else will grow.

common_name: Fine Wine Weigela (Compact Dark-Purple-Foliage Weigela with Rose-Pink Flowers)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and prune lightly right after the main spring flush to shape the compact mound without removing next year's buds. Fine Wine is a dwarf sport of the popular dark-leaved Wine and Roses weigela, bred smaller still for tight spaces, foundation plantings, and mixed containers, with narrow, deep burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season and clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds. Its compact, mounded habit needs little pruning to stay tidy, and the dark foliage provides season-long color contrast in a border even between bloom flushes. Established plants are drought-tolerant and largely trouble-free, needing only an occasional renewal cut to the oldest wood to keep growth vigorous.

Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Fire Light was bred specifically to solve the floppy-stem problem common in many panicle hydrangea cultivars, holding its large, dense, white flower clusters proudly upright even as they age and turn deep red-pink in late summer and fall. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood, so a hard renewal pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the season's flowers. It tolerates more sun and less consistent moisture than mophead hydrangeas once established, and the sturdy stems make it a good choice for a mixed border where less rigid hydrangea cultivars tend to sprawl after rain.

common_name: Fire Light Tidbit Hydrangea (Miniature Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Fire Light Tidbit is a true miniature panicle hydrangea, staying under 2-3 feet tall while still producing the same sturdy-stemmed, upright white flower panicles that age to deep pink-red typical of the larger Fire Light selections. Its diminutive size makes it one of the few panicle hydrangeas practical for a large container, small foundation bed, or the front edge of a border, without sacrificing the reliable, strong-stemmed flower display the series is known for. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter, since it blooms on new wood and tolerates a hard cutback without losing the coming season's flowers.

common_name: Firebush (Scarlet Bush, Hummingbird Bush, Mexican Firebush)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil of any quality — firebush thrives in poor, sandy, low-fertility conditions and performs well without supplemental fertilization once established. Firebush (Hamelia patens) is one of the highest-value native flowering shrubs for wildlife-friendly Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes — a Florida native and tropical American species that produces tubular, bright orange-to-red flowers in dense, clustered cymes from early summer continuously through the first frost, creating one of the longest-lasting flowering displays of any shrub in the region. The relentless summer bloom makes firebush a magnet for hummingbirds, butterflies (especially Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and swallowtails), and native bees throughout the growing season; the small, dark purple-black berries that follow the flowers are eaten by mockingbirds, cardinals, and other berry-eating birds, making firebush valuable at multiple levels of the food web. Unlike many nectar plants, firebush blooms heavily in partial shade as well as full sun, making it one of the few flowering shrubs that reliably attracts hummingbirds in partially shaded sites. The foliage is medium green to bronze-tinged (more colorful cultivars like 'Compacta' exist) with a whorled leaf arrangement that gives the plant a distinctive tropical texture. Firebush is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, grows rapidly in poor soils, and requires essentially no care beyond occasional pruning to shape — an ideal low-maintenance native for zone 9 wildlife gardens.

Plant rooted cuttings or small container vines in spring after frost danger has passed, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun with a trellis, obelisk, or fence to twine on. Firecracker vine is named for its small, tubular, two-toned red-and-yellow flowers that resemble tiny lit firecrackers and appear in a near-continuous flush from spring through fall. It is a modestly sized, well-mannered twining vine rather than a rampant grower, making it a good choice for containers, hanging baskets, or a small trellis on a porch or patio in warm climates. Where winters bring hard frost it is usually grown as a container plant brought indoors, or replanted annually.

Firefly is a compact bush honeysuckle prized for its glowing amber-to-gold foliage and small yellow flowers borne over a long season. Adaptable and tough, it grows in full sun to part shade and tolerates poor, dry, or rocky soils once established. Its dense habit and spreading roots make it useful for erosion control on slopes and banks. Prune in late winter or early spring to renew and control size, since it blooms on new wood. The nectar-rich flowers attract bees and other pollinators.

common_name: Fireglow Japanese Maple (Translucent Red Upright Maple)
notes: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Fireglow is a compact, upright, non-dissected Japanese maple cultivar prized for foliage that glows a translucent red-orange when backlit by low morning or evening sun, a quality that gives the cultivar its name, deepening to a rich maroon-red in shadier light through summer before a bright red fall display. Its smaller, more rounded five-lobed leaves and tidy, upright habit make it a good choice where a smaller-scale specimen tree is needed near a patio, entry, or Japanese-style garden. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Firepower Nandina (Compact Brilliant-Red Winter-Color Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Firepower is a compact, mounded dwarf nandina selection producing some of the most vivid fall and winter foliage color available in any compact evergreen shrub — the fine-textured, compound foliage transitions from lime-green in summer through orange to brilliant scarlet-red in fall and winter, with the most intense red occurring during and after the coldest periods. The bright red winter color of 'Firepower' is significantly more intense than the reddish tones of most other nandina cultivars, making it particularly outstanding in winter landscapes when few other evergreen shrubs provide warm color. In Gulf South winters (mild in zone 9), the red coloration is variable — coldest winters produce the best red; mild winters produce more orange and red-orange. The compact, naturally rounded habit (2–3 feet) requires minimal pruning and maintains its shape without shearing, making Firepower one of the most truly low-maintenance landscape shrubs for Gulf South foundation plantings, parking lot islands, and mass plantings. The fine bamboo-textured foliage creates an appealing contrast with bold-leaved plants. 'Firepower' does not produce berries (it is functionally sterile), eliminating the concern about nandina berry toxicity to birds that has arisen in some regions.

common_name: Firestick Plant (Pencil Cactus, Milk Bush, Naked Lady)
notes: Plant in full sun in any very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Firestick Plant is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives with minimal water in hot, sunny conditions — overwatering or poor drainage causes rapid decline and root rot. Euphorbia tirucalli is a large, succulent shrub or small tree native to tropical East Africa (Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania) and widely distributed throughout the tropics as a traditional living fence plant, medicinal species, and petroleum-substitute biofuel candidate. The plant consists almost entirely of dense, tangled masses of smooth, pencil-thick, green cylindrical stems with virtually no leaves — the stems perform photosynthesis directly. The 'Sticks on Fire' cultivar (the 'Firestick' form) produces young stem tips in vivid orange, yellow, and red — most intensely colored in full sun and cool weather — creating the appearance of a bush on fire. The effect in winter months when the color intensifies is extraordinary. CRITICAL WARNING: The abundant milky white latex sap that immediately flows from any cut or broken stem is a potent toxin and irritant — it can cause severe skin blistering, is extremely dangerous if it contacts the eyes (potentially causing permanent damage or blindness), and is toxic if ingested. Handle with heavy protective equipment only.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade; firethorn is an evergreen thorny shrub that earns its place in the landscape through a spectacular fall and winter display of clustered, brilliant orange, red, or yellow berries that cover the shrub in such abundance they literally hide the foliage — providing one of the most eye-catching ornamental fruit displays available in temperate gardens. White flower clusters in spring attract bees. Excellent as an espalier against a wall or fence, as a barrier hedge (the thorns are fierce), or as a freestanding specimen. Cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds flock to the berries. 'Mohave' (orange-red, disease-resistant), 'Lalandei' (orange, vigorous), and 'Teton' (yellow-orange, upright) are widely grown. Berries are mildly toxic to humans; do not eat.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Fireworks Clerodendrum is a vigorous grower that can reach 6–15 feet quickly in zone 9-11, making it best suited for large spaces or where a bold statement is desired. Clerodendrum quadriloculare is a large tropical shrub or small tree native to the Philippines, Sulawesi, and New Guinea, widely grown in tropical and subtropical landscapes for its spectacular winter-to-spring floral display: large, domed to rounded panicles up to 12 inches across of individual tubular flowers, each with a long pink-to-deep-rose tube opening into 5 white to pale pink star-shaped petal lobes that spread flat — the overall effect of hundreds of these flowers clustered together in a dome against the dark foliage is precisely that of an exploding fireworks burst, earning the common name. The large leaves have a distinctive two-toned appearance — dark, glossy bronze-green above and deep burgundy-purple below — making the foliage ornamental even when the plant is not in bloom. Blooming primarily December–March in zone 9, the plant provides floral color at a time when relatively few tropical shrubs are in bloom. The suckering habit can be used to create a large informal screen or hedge; remove excess suckers to maintain a single-stemmed specimen form.

growth_habit: Pacific Island coastal ornamental poisonous tree
notes: Plant Barringtonia asiatica in moist, well-drained, sandy coastal soil in full sun; highly tolerant of salt spray and sandy soils; water regularly during establishment; the flowers open at night and fall by morning — best appreciated in the evening. CAUTION: all parts contain toxic saponins and other compounds; seeds and bark were used traditionally across the Pacific to stun fish in tidal pools for harvesting — do not consume. Fish Poison Tree is one of the most architecturally striking coastal trees of the Indo-Pacific — the large (4–6 inch), pompon-like flowers with their dramatic pink-tipped white stamen bundles open at dusk and are gone by morning, attracting nocturnal bats, moths, and hawk moths as pollinators. The fruits are equally distinctive: large (golf ball to baseball sized), square-ridged, four-winged, corky structures that float in seawater and are ocean-dispersed throughout the Indo-Pacific — one of the most remarkable examples of ocean-dispersal in flowering plants. Throughout Oceania, the toxic seed extracts were used for fishing: pounded seeds thrown into tidal pools or reef systems stunned or killed fish within minutes, allowing easy collection. The bark and leaves also have documented traditional medicinal uses across the Pacific Islands for skin conditions and headaches. A magnificent ornamental for sheltered coastal sites in zone 10–12 with evening-opening flowers that create a magical night-garden effect.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil of average to rich fertility in part shade to full sun; five-leaf akebia is an elegant, twining Asian vine producing delicate, compound leaves with five rounded blue-green leaflets that persist through winter in mild climates, plus unusual, intensely vanilla-chocolate-scented maroon-purple and pale-pink flowers in early spring — the female flowers are larger and darker purple, the male flowers smaller and rose-pink, and both appear together on the same plant before the leaves fully emerge. Two different plants must be present for the interesting, sausage-shaped, gray-purple fruits to develop — edible but bland, with a mild, slightly sweet flesh. The vine is vigorous and tolerates shade better than most flowering vines. In mild climates, akebia can spread aggressively through bird-dispersed seeds and should be monitored; select sterile cultivars or remove fruits if invasiveness is a concern in your region.

Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; flame acanthus (hummingbird bush) earns its name with brilliant orange-red tubular flowers that literally glow like flames and attract hummingbirds from the moment the plants begin blooming in late spring through fall. It is a tough, deciduous or semi-evergreen native shrub of the Texas brush country that thrives in rocky alkaline soil, extreme heat, and drought conditions that would wilt most plants. The orange-scarlet flowers are produced in profusion from spring through frost, providing hummingbirds with a nearly continuous nectar source. It is deer resistant and rabbit resistant. The plant dies to the ground in hard freezes in zone 7–8 but resprouts vigorously from established root systems. An essential and easy plant for the wildlife-friendly Gulf Coast garden.

Plant in moist, deeply acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade from taller deciduous trees; flame azalea is the most spectacular of the native deciduous azaleas, producing brilliant orange, red, and yellow flowers (often in multiple hues on the same plant) in late spring that blaze against the emerging green foliage at the peak of the Appalachian wildflower season. The flower display can range from pale yellow to deep orange-red depending on the individual plant's genetics — purchase in bloom to get the color you want. Plant with the crown above soil level and mulch lightly with pine bark or oak leaves to maintain acidity. Prune only lightly after bloom to shape.

Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; the rhizomes prefer cool soil — keep them shaded even when the top growth reaches into the sun; in hot summers the plant may go dormant. Tropaeolum speciosum is the spectacular perennial climbing nasturtium from the cool, moist forests of Chile, producing long, twining stems with small, deeply lobed, bright-green leaves and a seemingly endless succession of vivid scarlet-red, spurred nasturtium flowers followed by striking, blue-black berries surrounded by bright red sepals from summer through early fall. It is famously beautiful scrambling through dark evergreen shrubs like yew or rhododendron in cool, moist British gardens, but is challenging in hot climates — it requires cool soil, consistent moisture, and partial shade and goes dormant in heat. A collector's plant for the cool, moist garden.

Flame Thrower is a redbud selection celebrated for multicolored foliage that emerges burgundy and matures through orange and yellow to green, plus rosy-red spring flowers on bare branches. Plant it in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil, giving the best color in a spot with some sun. Water regularly during the first couple of seasons to establish its roots. Prune lightly after flowering only to shape or remove dead wood. The early blooms are a valuable nectar source for pollinators.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; flame vine (golden shower vine, orange trumpet vine) is a South American evergreen tropical vine of the bignonia family that creates one of the most spectacular mass-flowering displays of any vine in the tropical and subtropical garden — in winter and early spring (December–March in the Gulf South), the entire vine, which can cover a fence, wall, or support structure for 30 feet or more, becomes completely blanketed from end to end with thousands of long, tubular, brilliantly vivid orange-red to flame-orange flowers arranged in dense, rounded clusters, transforming the entire structure into a cascade of blazing orange that is visible from great distances. The winter flowering season is particularly valuable in zone 9–12 winter gardens when few other vines or shrubs produce color. It is a vigorous grower that requires strong support and substantial space. In zone 9 it may be killed back by hard freezes but typically resprouts vigorously from established roots. Excellent on large arbors, fences, trellises, and covering walls where its spectacular winter display can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Flame Vine (Mexican Flame Vine, Orange Glow Vine)
notes: Root cuttings in moist potting mix and plant after last frost in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; provide a strong fence, arbor, or trellis to support the fast-growing vines, which can reach 10–20 feet; flame vine produces an almost continuous cascade of small, brilliant orange, daisy-like flowers with yellow centers that make it one of the most visually stunning vines for frost-free gardens and one of the top nectar sources for butterflies and hummingbirds in the Gulf South. In frost-free zones it blooms year-round; in zone 9 it blooms spring through fall and may freeze back in cold winters. Nearly maintenance-free once established, tolerating heat, coastal conditions, and drought once rooted. Excellent for screening fences, covering arbors, and cascading over walls.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; provide trellis or arbor support. Clerodendrum splendens (flaming glorybower) is a spectacular West African tropical vine producing dense, terminal clusters of brilliant scarlet-red, tubular flowers with prominent protruding stamens in large, rounded cymes that blaze against the dark, glossy, heart-shaped leaves — one of the most intensely colored flowering tropical vines available. Unlike the better-known bleeding heart vine (C. thomsoniae, with red and white flowers), C. splendens produces entirely scarlet flowers in even larger clusters and is a more vigorous climber. It blooms primarily in winter and spring in zone 10–12 — a welcome season when few tropical vines flower. The plant is an outstanding container plant and can be grown on a warm patio or sunroom in zone 9, brought outdoors in summer and protected in winter. Hummingbirds and butterflies are strongly attracted to the scarlet flower clusters. The vine roots easily from stem cuttings in warm, moist conditions.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, dry soil in full sun with NO summer irrigation once established; flannel bush is one of California's most spectacular native shrubs, covering itself in large (1.5–2.5 inch), saucer-shaped, intensely golden-yellow flowers from April through June — on a mature specimen the display of hundreds of golden flowers against the dark, lobed, flannel-textured, gray-green leaves is one of the showiest spectacles in the native California garden. The flowers technically lack petals; the bright-yellow 'petals' are enlarged, petal-like sepals. Named for the distinctive, flannel-soft texture of the leaves and stems, which are densely covered with stellate hairs. The plant strongly prefers lean, well-drained, dry soils and dry summers — conditions that suit California native planting schemes and water-wise gardens, but make it difficult in climates with summer rainfall. The hybrid 'Ken Taylor' (F. californicum x F. mexicanum) is the most commonly cultivated, offering extra-large flowers over an extended season. CAUTION: the fine hairs are a serious skin and eye irritant — wear gloves and eye protection when pruning.

Sow scarified or soaked seed 1 inch deep in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis, fence, or shrub margin for the tendrils to grip; flat pea is a tough European perennial vine that climbs to 4–6 feet by summer and produces clusters of small pink and magenta-crimson flowers with distinctive winged stems from which the common name derives. Unlike the annual sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus), it has no fragrance, but is far more persistent — once established it returns reliably each spring and spreads gradually by seed. It is drought-tolerant and will grow in poor, thin soils where little else climbs, making it valuable on dry banks, hedgerow margins, and informal screens. Cut stems back to the ground in late fall to remove old growth and prevent untidy sprawl.

Plant near a very sturdy fence, masonry wall, pergola, or large tree in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil. Flava is a yellow-flowered selection of the native trumpet vine, replacing the species' typical orange-red trumpet flowers with clear, bright golden-yellow blooms from June through September, while retaining the same vigorous, aerial-root climbing habit and importance as hummingbird forage. Like the straight species, it is extremely vigorous, spreading by root suckers and capable of quickly covering — or overwhelming — a support structure, so it needs a genuinely sturdy structure and regular control of suckers around the base. The sap can cause skin irritation in some people; wear gloves when pruning or handling the vine.

common_name: Flirt Nandina (Dwarf Compact Red-Tipped Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 18–24 inches apart for a low mass planting or border edge. Flirt is a dwarf, mounding nandina bred to stay compact without the tall, leggy cane growth of larger nandina cultivars, producing new foliage that emerges bright red and matures to green through summer before returning to deep red-burgundy in fall and winter cold. Its small size and dense, tidy habit fit foundation plantings, mixed containers, and border edges where full-size nandina would need constant cutting back, and it is sterile, producing no berries and therefore no risk of the self-seeding that has made standard nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast. Little pruning is needed beyond removing occasional damaged stems.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Florida anise is a southeastern native evergreen shrub that is one of the very best shade-tolerant shrubs for Gulf Coast and Southeast landscapes, producing handsome, lance-shaped, glossy dark-green leaves that release a strong anise-star fragrance when bruised or crushed. Unusual dark maroon-red, multi-petaled starfish-like flowers appear in spring and sporadically through the year. All parts of the plant are poisonous and should not be confused with the edible Asian star anise (Illicium verum). Provides excellent year-round screening in shaded areas and is notably deer-resistant due to its aromatic foliage. Tolerates wet soils seasonally.

common_name: Florida Anise Shrub (Spicy-Scented Native Shade Shrub with Dark Red Spring Flowers)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial to deep shade; Florida Anise Shrub (Illicium floridanum) is a native Gulf South evergreen shrub of extraordinary shade tolerance and distinctive character — tolerating deep shade under magnolias and live oaks while producing one of the most unusual spring flower displays of any native shrub: dark red, multi-petaled, starry flowers with narrow, strap-shaped petals arranged in a loose, spidery pattern, appearing in April–May with a pleasant but faint sweet-spicy fragrance. The large, glossy, dark-green leaves are the plant's dominant feature through most of the year — broader and more tropical-looking than most native shrubs — and when crushed or bruised they release a strong, pleasant anise-spice fragrance from volatile oils, giving the plant its common name. The fragrance is from anethole compounds similar to those in culinary anise, but Florida anise shrub is toxic and must never be confused with star anise or used in food preparation. Florida Anise Shrub grows naturally in moist, shaded ravines and creek banks in the Florida panhandle and along the Gulf Coastal plain from Florida to Louisiana — it is the quintessential native Gulf South shade shrub, evolved under the same dense-canopy conditions that dominate Gulf South residential landscapes. The fast growth rate allows it to reach privacy-screen heights quickly, and the dense, branching evergreen habit creates an impenetrable visual screen. An outstanding native hedge shrub for shaded property edges. All parts are toxic if ingested.

Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Florida anise is one of the finest native evergreen shrubs for deep shade in the Gulf South and grows naturally along shaded stream banks in Florida and adjacent states. Illicium floridanum is a large, evergreen native shrub or small tree with glossy, dark-green, elliptic leaves 3–6 inches long that are remarkably aromatic when bruised, smelling strongly of anise or licorice; in mid- to late spring it produces unusual, star-shaped, maroon-red to burgundy flowers with numerous strap-like petals that are fascinating if not conventionally beautiful, and the flowers are followed by star-shaped seed capsules similar to (but not the same as) culinary star anise. It forms a naturally dense, multi-stemmed shrub that is excellent for hedges, screens, and foundation plantings in shaded sites in zones 7–10; all parts of the plant are toxic.

Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Florida azalea is one of the earliest and most fragrant of the native deciduous azaleas, producing clusters of brilliant golden-yellow to orange-yellow tubular flowers with exserted stamens in early spring before or with the emerging leaves. The fragrance is intensely sweet and carries far in the still spring air. It is native to the wooded ravines and stream banks of the Florida Panhandle, south Georgia, and Alabama and is one of the best native azaleas for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens, tolerating the heat and humidity better than northern species. Plant as a foundation shrub, in a native garden, or massed along a woodland edge. Prune only immediately after bloom if needed; never shear. The color is exceptionally vivid when purchased in bloom.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Florida Beauty philodendron holds its cream-and-green variegation best with consistent bright indirect light. Deeply lobed, uniquely shaped leaves are heavily splashed and speckled in cream, yellow, and pale green over a darker green base, no two leaves patterned quite alike, on a climbing hybrid vine believed to descend from Philodendron pedatum crossed with a variegated relative. Its unusual, deeply cut leaf shape combined with bold, splashy variegation makes it a sought-after specimen for collectors, and it climbs readily up a moss pole to produce larger, more dramatically lobed and patterned leaves as it matures. Prune out any leaves that revert to solid green to keep the plant's energy focused on variegated growth, and rotate the pot for even light exposure.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, moderately fertile soil in partial to full shade; Florida boxwood is a native evergreen shrub of the tropical hardwood hammock understory in south Florida and the Keys, bearing small, shiny, leathery leaves that superficially resemble true boxwood (Buxus), hence the common name. Though unrelated to northern boxwood, it serves a similar function as a shade-tolerant, small-leaved, evergreen understory shrub that can be sheared into hedges and formal shapes. Small orange-red to red fruits provide food for tropical birds. One of the few native south Florida shrubs genuinely adapted to deep shade within the hammock canopy, making it valuable for shaded landscape settings in zone 10. An important but little-known native for ecologically appropriate south Florida landscaping.

Set out container-grown plants in spring with roots shaded by mulch or low neighboring plants while the twining petioles climb a trellis or shrub toward filtered light. Creamy white to pale green flowers with a striking dark maroon-purple stamen cluster appear on the previous year's wood in late spring and summer, so prune only lightly and just after flowering to avoid cutting off next year's display. It is a more compact, semi-woody grower than many large-flowered hybrids, making it well suited to a shaded container or small trellis near a patio. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, especially through its first growing season.
