Florida Clover Ash — also called West Indian Clover Ash — is a native member of the Melastomataceae (melastome) family, found in the United States only in the pine rocklands and tropical hardwood hammocks of Miami-Dade County, Florida, where it is listed as critically imperiled. The lance-shaped, three-veined leaves are glossy and attractive; clusters of small white to pale pink flowers appear in spring and summer and are followed by dark purple-black berries eaten by birds including the White-crowned Pigeon. An ornamental and ecologically significant native shrub of the highly threatened South Florida pine rockland community — one of the most endangered ecosystems in the United States — Florida Clover Ash deserves wider cultivation in Zone 10–11 South Florida native plant gardens. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are drought-tolerant in the rocky, thin soils of its native pine rockland habitat.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection; mulch well to keep roots cool and never let the root zone dry out completely in the first two seasons. Rhododendron austrinum is a deciduous native azalea of the Gulf Coastal Plain — from the Florida panhandle and south Georgia west into Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana — prized as one of the most fragrant of all native azaleas. In early to mid-spring, before or as the leaves emerge, the shrub is smothered in large trusses of intensely honeysuckle-scented flowers ranging from clear yellow through orange to deep gold-orange, drawing in early spring pollinators including native bees and swallowtail butterflies. It naturally colonizes the dappled shade of bluffs, ravines, and stream banks under a high pine and hardwood canopy. Excellent as a specimen or in a woodland-edge shrub border in the Gulf South, where it is far better adapted to summer heat and humidity than most Asian azalea hybrids. Zone 7–9.

Florida leucothoe is an upright, arching, semi-evergreen to evergreen native shrub that thrives beneath pines and oaks in moist, acidic, sandy or loamy soils — one of the Southeast's most graceful shade-garden shrubs, seldom seen in commerce despite its outstanding ornamental qualities. In spring, fragrant clusters of small white, urn-shaped flowers hang along the arching branches, feeding native bees; glossy, poplar-shaped leaves persist through winter in the Deep South. Plants form loose colonies via underground runners, providing excellent erosion control on shaded slopes and stream banks in the Gulf Coastal Plain from South Carolina to Florida and Mississippi. Grow in consistently moist soil away from drought and reflected heat; pair with native azaleas, swamp roses, and Syngonium for a woodland understory that supports diverse wildlife.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic to moderately acidic, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Florida leucothoe thrives in moist, shaded woodland gardens alongside ferns, azaleas, and hostas. Agarista populifolia (Florida leucothoe or tall leucothoe) is a large, arching, semi-evergreen to evergreen native shrub forming an elegant fountain of gracefully nodding branches clothed in lustrous, dark-green, alternate, lance-shaped to ovate leaves; small, white, urn-shaped, sweetly fragrant flowers are produced in pendulous clusters in April–May, covering the branches in a frothy, white-flowered curtain. The overall effect is remarkably elegant for a native shrub, combining refined foliage, fragrant flowers, and an architectural arching form that makes it one of the finest native screening and understory shrubs for the Deep South. Florida leucothoe is found wild in moist woodland ravines and bottomlands from South Carolina to northern Florida and is especially well-adapted to warm, humid, acidic-soil gardens in zones 7–9. Though often confused with the common drooping leucothoe (Leucothoe fontanesiana), Florida leucothoe is substantially larger, more heat-tolerant, and better adapted to zone 8–9 gardens.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade — Florida maple is the southern adaptation of the sugar maple group, a medium-sized native tree of limestone bluffs, rich upland woods, and creek bottoms throughout the Southeast, providing outstanding fall color (orange, scarlet, and gold) in zone 7–9 where the northern sugar maple fails in summer heat. The distinctive 3-lobed leaves are smaller than those of northern sugar maple; trees are compact, multi-season ornamental trees with smooth gray bark, golden spring flower clusters, and the classic maple winged seeds (samaras) in spring. Florida maple tolerates the heat and soil alkalinity of zone 8–9 gardens significantly better than northern sugar maple cultivars and is the appropriate choice for fall color, shade, and wildlife value in Gulf Coast landscapes. Trees yield a small quantity of sap that can be made into a light maple syrup in the brief late-winter cold spells of zone 7–8.

Florida Privet is a tough, adaptable native shrub, native to coastal hammocks, scrub, and beach margins of south Florida, the Keys, and the Caribbean, where it grows in thin, well-drained, sandy or rocky soils under the influence of salt spray and periodic drought. Related to the ornamental privets used in hedges but native to the Southeast, it produces tiny yellow-green flowers in very early spring (sometimes as early as January) that are among the first nectar sources of the year for native bees, followed by small, dark blue to black oval berries that are important food for migrants and resident birds. An excellent native hedge, screen, or windbreak plant for coastal zones 9–11 where it tolerates salt, alkaline soil, drought, and occasional flooding; male and female plants are needed for berry production, so plant a group for wildlife benefit. Prune as needed for shaping — it is fast-growing and responds well to trimming.

Florida Rosemary is one of the most ecologically fascinating native shrubs in North America — a dominant species of the imperiled Florida scrub habitat, native to the ancient, white sand ridges of the Florida peninsula where it creates one of the strangest visual phenomena in American botany: "Florida rosemary rings," circular patches of bare white sand 3–20 feet in diameter surrounding each plant, kept barren by allelopathic chemicals (terpenes and phenolics) that the plant releases through its roots to prevent competing plants from establishing. Not a true rosemary (Rosmarinus), it bears superficial resemblance to the culinary herb with its needle-like, aromatic, evergreen leaves densely arranged on erect stems, but is a monotypic genus in the heath family (Ericaceae). Small red-orange flowers in fall are followed by tiny berries consumed by Florida scrub-jays, gopher tortoises, and other scrub species. Grow in the driest, most infertile, most acidic sand you can provide in full sun; it is intolerant of irrigation, rich soil, shade, or the weed-suppressive conditions that most ornamental plants require.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Florida Sunshine is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated selection of the Florida native anise shrub, grown almost entirely for its brilliant chartreuse-to-gold evergreen foliage, which glows in a shaded bed year-round and intensifies to a deeper yellow with cooler fall and winter temperatures — an unusually reliable, low-maintenance way to add sustained bright color to deep shade where flowering plants often struggle. Crushed leaves release the same anise-like fragrance as the straight species. Its narrow, upright growth habit makes it useful as a bright vertical accent or informal screen in a shaded border, contrasting well against dark-green companions like azaleas, camellias, or hollies. It tolerates a range of shade levels and adapts to both moist and average garden soil once established, needing little more than routine watering during dry spells and an occasional light shaping if a more formal look is wanted.

growth_habit: groundcover shrub rose, Flower Carpet series
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply through the first growing season to encourage roots to spread beneath the wide, low canopy. Once established, the vigorous, disease-resistant foliage needs little care beyond an annual cutback in late winter to renew growth. Small, bright pink semi-double flowers smother the spreading mounds almost continuously from late spring to frost, a signature trait of the original Flower Carpet introduction that popularized low-maintenance groundcover roses. Its dense habit suppresses weeds and works well on slopes, in mass plantings, or cascading over retaining walls.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; flowering almond is a Chinese shrub long cultivated in Asian gardens, producing small, double-flowered blooms so densely that stems are buried in flowers from tip to base in early spring. The double pink cultivar 'Sinensis' and double white 'Alba Plena' are the most widely grown forms. Unlike most Prunus shrubs, flowering almond has little wildlife value (the double flowers limit pollinator access and fruit rarely sets) but provides exceptional ornamental impact in the spring garden. After flowering, the plant is an unremarkable medium deciduous shrub, so site it where it can be seen from a window during its brief but spectacular early spring bloom and is less conspicuous the rest of the year. Prune hard immediately after bloom to maintain a compact, floriferous shape.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to dappled shade — flowering dogwood is one of the most beloved native understory trees of the eastern US, producing its iconic four-bract 'flowers' (actually modified leaves surrounding tiny true flowers) in brilliant white or pink in early spring before the leaves emerge, covering the tiered, horizontal branches in a sheet of bloom visible through the forest from a distance. The leaves are followed by clusters of brilliant red berries in fall that feed migrating birds, and the foliage itself turns brilliant scarlet and purple in autumn. In the South, flowering dogwood is more susceptible to dogwood anthracnose fungal disease in hot, wet, poorly-aired conditions than in the North; plant in well-drained soil with good air circulation and avoid wetting foliage to reduce disease pressure. Zone 9 specimens benefit from afternoon shade and consistent moisture during summer heat.

Direct-sow scarified seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; flowery senna (Argentine senna) is a fast-growing South American shrub that provides one of the most spectacular late-summer and fall flower displays available in the Gulf Coast garden — smothered from late August through November in clusters of brilliant, clear-yellow, five-petaled flowers that glow with exceptional intensity as other summer plants fatigue. It is critically important as the larval host plant for the Cloudless Sulphur butterfly (Phoebis sennae) and the Sleepy Orange butterfly (Abaeis nicippe) — expect to find caterpillars feeding on the foliage throughout summer, which is a sign of success rather than a problem. The plant is fast-growing, drought-tolerant, and thrives in poor, dry soil — conditions that suit it for problem, hot, dry corners of the garden. In zone 8 it dies to the ground in winter but rebounds from the root to 6–8 feet by midsummer. Excellent screening plant for late-season butterfly gardens.

Plant scarified seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun; foothill palo verde (yellow palo verde) is the smaller, stouter, more spiny, and more drought-resistant companion of blue palo verde in the Sonoran Desert — where both species often grow together on rocky desert slopes, bajadas, and wash margins. Distinguished from blue palo verde by its shorter stature, more yellow-green (rather than blue-green) trunk and branches, more prominent spines, and pale yellow flowers (slightly paler than blue palo verde's bright yellow). Like blue palo verde, the green trunk is photosynthetically active, allowing drought survival after leaf drop. Slower growing than blue palo verde and eventually smaller, making it appropriate for smaller garden spaces. The seeds are also edible. Produces the iconic Sonoran Desert 'nurse plant' relationship with saguaro cactus — more saguaro seedlings establish and survive under the nurse canopy of palo verde and other desert shrubs than in open desert. An essential Sonoran Desert native for xeriscape plantings in zone 8–11.

common_name: Forest Bell Bush (River Bells, Broad Mackaya)
notes: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Forest Bell Bush is one of the finest shade-tolerant flowering shrubs for zone 9 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes, providing beautiful lavender blooms in the cool season when most shade plants are not flowering. Mackaya bella is a glossy-leaved evergreen shrub native to the subtropical coastal forest and riverine bush of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, growing naturally in the shade of forest margins and along shaded stream banks — conditions that translate perfectly to zone 9 shaded garden beds. The attractive, large, dark-green, glossy leaves have attractive wavy margins and create an excellent textural backdrop year-round. In winter to spring, the plant produces delicate, tubular, 5-lobed flowers 2 inches long in pale lavender with darker veining — a distinctive, elegant color combination that is very different from the saturated purples of most tropical flowering shrubs. The flowers are produced in loose, airy terminal spikes over a period of 6–10 weeks. Forest Bell Bush is a monotypic genus (only one species in the genus Mackaya) in the Acanthaceae family, closely related to the Justicia and Eranthemum plants well-suited to Gulf Coast shade gardens.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Forest Pansy is the most widely grown and recognized purple-leafed redbud cultivar — selected for its spectacular, rich purple to wine-red heart-shaped leaves that emerge in spring immediately after the rosy-pink flower display and persist with deep purple coloration through summer, transitioning to orange-red in fall. The stunning spring sequence begins with the bare branches covered in rosy-pink flowers in February–March in zone 9 (before the leaves emerge), followed immediately by the emergence of the deep wine-red heart-shaped leaves — a foliage display that maintains dramatic interest throughout the growing season. The purple leaf color is most intense in spring and early summer, gradually fading to greenish-purple through the hottest summer months, then reviving to orange-red in fall. Forest Pansy grows as a small multi-trunked or single-stemmed tree to 15–25 feet tall and wide, with an elegant horizontal branching pattern. It is more shade-tolerant than many ornamental trees, performing well with 4–6 hours of sun in the understory of larger trees, though leaf color is most vibrant in full sun. In zone 9, afternoon shade helps prevent summer leaf scorch. Plant in well-drained soil — redbud roots are highly susceptible to root rot in poorly drained, wet sites.

Plant in partial shade — filtered light under tall pines or high-branched deciduous trees is ideal; avoid deep shade or full afternoon sun — in well-drained, very acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Formosa is one of the defining large Southern Indica azalea cultivars, producing massive specimens with very large (3–4 inch), vivid reddish-purple to magenta-purple, single flowers in an overwhelming spring bloom display that, when a mature Formosa azalea is in full flower, can completely cover the shrub in a solid mass of vivid purple bloom — one of the most dramatic flowering displays available from any single shrub species in the Gulf South landscape. Southern Indica azaleas (Rhododendron indicum cultivars) are among the most important and historically significant landscape shrubs of the American South — thriving in the partial shade, acidic, well-drained conditions under the longleaf pine and mixed hardwood forests that characterize the Gulf Coast region, and producing their spring bloom display in February–April when the landscape is transitioning from winter to spring. The combination of dense evergreen foliage year-round, the spectacular spring bloom, and exceptional longevity (Formosa azaleas over 50–75 years old are common in old Gulf South gardens) makes this cultivar one of the most enduring and valuable ornamental shrubs for zone 7–10 partial shade gardens.

Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; forsythia is the most widely planted early-spring flowering shrub in the temperate world — a hybrid of two Asian species producing cascading arches of branches covered, before any leaves appear, with bright, clear-yellow flowers in late February through April, depending on location. The intensity of color — pure, saturated spring-yellow on bare branches against the still-dormant landscape — makes it one of the most visually arresting events of the early garden year. After the flowers fade, the arching branches clothe themselves in dark-green foliage that provides a pleasant, medium-textured hedge or background through summer. It is among the most cold-hardy, drought-tolerant, and adaptable flowering shrubs available — growing in clay, sand, poor soil, and partial shade without complaint. The cultivar 'Lynwood Gold' (also sold as 'Lynwood Variety') is the most widely planted, with an upright habit and consistently large, fully open flowers. 'Meadowlark' is exceptionally cold-hardy to zone 4. Pruning should be done only immediately after flowering.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Fortune's osmanthus is a hybrid evergreen shrub combining the most desirable traits of its two parents — the extraordinary apricot-peach fragrance of the tea olive (O. fragrans) with the improved cold hardiness and dense, attractive, spiny-leaved foliage of the holly osmanthus (O. heterophyllus). The tiny, cream-white flowers in fall produce the same intensely sweet, far-carrying fragrance as tea olive, perfuming the garden from a considerable distance. This hybrid is cold-hardy to about 0°F (USDA zone 7) compared to tea olive's zone 8 hardiness, making it the better choice for the colder end of the zone 7–9 range. An excellent, deer-resistant, relatively low-maintenance evergreen shrub for the partial-shade garden in zones 7–9.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Foster holly is a hybrid of American holly (Ilex opaca) and Dahoon holly (Ilex cassine) selected from a population in Birmingham, Alabama, by E.E. Foster in 1954. It is one of the most widely planted landscape hollies in the South and is distinguished by a distinctly narrower, more columnar habit than most other hollies — making it ideal for tight spaces, narrow screens, and situations where a tall, slim evergreen accent is needed. The small, somewhat spiny, dark-green leaves and dense, narrow growth create a refined, formal appearance. Female plants (the widely sold 'Foster No. 2') produce abundant small red berries that ripen in fall and persist through winter, attracting birds. The narrow habit and attractive berries make Foster holly an outstanding street tree, screening plant between properties, and formal landscape accent. Male plants ('Foster No. 1') must be planted nearby for reliable berry production. Foster holly is notably adaptable to the Gulf Coastal Plain's humid, hot summers and performs well in zone 9 where it is widely used in formal residential and commercial landscapes.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; fountain butterfly bush blooms on old wood in late spring, unlike the more common Buddleja davidii, so prune immediately after flowering rather than in late winter. Long, slender, weeping branches are lined with clusters of small, fragrant, lilac-purple flowers in late spring, forming a graceful, fountain-like silhouette quite different from the more upright, spiky growth of the familiar summer-blooming Buddleja davidii, and drawing butterflies in similarly large numbers. Its early bloom time and weeping habit make it a distinctive alternative to the more commonly planted summer butterfly bush, providing a different silhouette and bloom season in a mixed shrub border. Prune immediately after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood unlike davidii-type butterfly bush, and avoid the harder late-winter pruning appropriate for davidii types, which would remove this species' flower buds.

common_name: Four Seasons Gardenia (Reblooming Double White Gardenia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade. Four Seasons lives up to its name among gardenia cultivars by reblooming intermittently through summer and into fall after its main spring flush, extending the fragrant, double white flowers well beyond the shorter bloom window of many older gardenia cultivars. The dense, glossy-leaved shrub makes a good foundation or specimen planting near a porch, window, or path where its strong fragrance can be enjoyed up close through multiple seasons. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves in insufficiently acidic soil, so feed with acid-forming fertilizer and keep moisture consistent to support the extended bloom cycle.

Plant in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; fourwing saltbush is one of the most ecologically important and widely distributed native shrubs of the arid and semi-arid West and Southwest, occurring naturally from Oregon to Texas and from the Plains to the Pacific Coast in desert shrubland, grasslands, and disturbed alkaline soils. The distinctive four-winged seed capsules that cover female shrubs in fall are immediately recognizable and are an important food source for pronghorn antelope, mule deer, and many birds. The gray-green, slightly mealy foliage is moderately salt-tolerant, making it valuable in alkaline soils and roadsides with ice melt. Native American tribes used the seeds as a grain and the leaves as a salt substitute. The plant is one of the primary components of native range reclamation seedings in the West and an outstanding drought-adapted landscape shrub for dry, alkaline, or sandy conditions.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant abelia blooms earlier and more briefly than glossy abelia but compensates with a much stronger, sweeter fragrance carried well beyond the shrub itself. Abelia mosanensis is a deciduous Korean species grown chiefly for its intensely fragrant, pink-budded, white to pale pink tubular flowers borne in dense clusters in late spring, filling the garden with a sweet scent often compared to lilac or daphne, followed by attractive burgundy-red fall foliage color. Unlike the more commonly planted evergreen glossy abelia (Abelia x grandiflora), this species drops its leaves in winter and blooms in one strong spring flush rather than repeating through summer, making it a specialty fragrance shrub rather than a long-season landscape workhorse. Site it near a patio, walkway, or window where its brief but powerful spring fragrance can be fully appreciated, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant olive (sweet olive, tea olive) is one of the most beloved fragrant shrubs of the Gulf South — a classic fixture in old Southern gardens, cherished for its tiny, creamy white flowers that perfume the air with an intense, sweet apricot-like fragrance that can carry 100 yards on a still autumn morning. The plant blooms repeatedly from fall through spring in zone 8–9, often triggered by cool snaps, and the fragrance is one of the most powerful and instantly recognizable in the Southern garden tradition. The large, dense, glossy evergreen shrub makes an outstanding screen, hedge, or specimen. It grows slowly but lives for decades and eventually becomes a small tree. The variety O. fragrans f. aurantiacus has orange flowers; 'Fudingzhu' is a particularly free-flowering white selection.

common_name: Fragrant Pink Camellia (Pioneer Sweet-Scented Small-Flower Hybrid Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; Fragrant Pink is a hybrid Camellia bred to introduce the sweet floral fragrance of Camellia lutchuensis into cultivars with the refined flower form of Camellia japonica — a cross that transformed the possibilities of camellia breeding by combining beauty and scent that had previously been impossible in a single plant. The flowers of Fragrant Pink are small to medium-sized, peony-form to double, in clear soft rose-pink — the individual flower size is smaller than most japonica cultivars, a characteristic inherited from the C. lutchuensis parent, but the sweet, true floral fragrance detectable from several feet away compensates fully for the smaller bloom size. The scent is genuine and pleasant — not a faint hint but a real, detectable, jasmine-like sweetness that makes this camellia suitable for planting near outdoor living areas. Fragrant Pink typically blooms in late winter (January–March in zone 9), filling the period when the garden has few fragrant flowering plants. The plant grows as a compact to medium evergreen shrub — somewhat smaller than most C. japonica cultivars — with a densely branched, naturally rounded habit. In zone 9, it is a reliable landscape perennial performing best with morning sun and afternoon shade. The fragrant flower characteristic and compact habit make Fragrant Pink an ideal camellia for planting near patios, garden seats, and paths where the sweet winter fragrance enhances the garden experience.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant snowbell is an underused Japanese deciduous tree distinguished from the common Japanese snowbell (S. japonicus) by its much larger, broadly rounded leaves that can be 8 inches across — giving the tree a bold, almost tropical appearance in summer. In late spring, the long, pendant racemes of white, bell-shaped flowers hang beneath the large leaves in an unusually graceful display with a soft vanilla-like fragrance that is notably stronger than S. japonicus. The combination of bold leaves and hanging flower clusters is architecturally distinctive. The tree tolerates partial shade better than most flowering trees and is excellent as an understory specimen beneath taller oaks and beeches. Yellow fall color.

Plant in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant sumac is one of the most versatile, adaptable, and underused native shrubs in North America — tolerating dry shade, rocky slopes, alkaline soil, and drought conditions that defeat most plants. The crushed leaves have a distinctly pleasant lemon-citrus fragrance. Small yellow flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge provide important early nectar for native bees emerging from overwintering. The fuzzy red fruit clusters feed dozens of bird species through fall and winter. The three-parted leaves turn brilliant orange-red and burgundy in fall — among the best native plants for fall color — and the low, spreading form makes it excellent for groundcover use on slopes. The cultivar 'Gro-Low' is a compact, 2-foot-tall groundcover form widely used in landscape planting.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, and water regularly through the first year to establish a deep root system before easing into its drought-tolerant mature habit. Fragrant Sweet Box is a rounded evergreen shrub with glossy, leathery, willow-like leaves and inconspicuous but powerfully fragrant white flowers produced along the stems in late winter, filling the shade garden with a sweet, honeyed scent when little else is in bloom, followed by showy red berries that ripen to black. Denser and more heat-tolerant than the more commonly planted Himalayan sweet box, it holds up well through hot, humid Gulf Coast summers and is an excellent evergreen backbone for a shaded foundation planting, woodland border, or beneath high tree canopy where deer pressure is a concern, since deer generally avoid it. Prune lightly after flowering only to shape, as it blooms on old wood.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fragrant viburnum blooms on bare branches in late winter, so protect from hard freezes during the flowering window in colder zones. Clusters of small, tubular, pale pink flowers open on bare branches in late winter to very early spring, well ahead of most other flowering shrubs, releasing an intense, sweet, clove-like fragrance that carries a surprising distance on a still winter day. Native to northern China, it is one of the earliest viburnums to bloom each year, providing welcome color and fragrance during the last weeks of winter dormancy, though an unusually hard late freeze can damage open flowers in colder parts of its range. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and site where its winter fragrance can be enjoyed near a door or path.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; fragrant winterhazel blooms before its leaves emerge in early spring, so site it where the drooping, fragrant flower chains can be seen against a dark evergreen backdrop. Corylopsis glabrescens is a large, rounded Japanese shrub producing drooping chains of small, soft yellow, sweetly fragrant, bell-shaped flowers in early spring before the rounded, blue-green leaves unfurl, followed by attractive yellow fall color. It is among the most cold-hardy and heat-tolerant of the winterhazels, making it a dependable large specimen or informal hedge for a shaded border where its fragrant early bloom announces the start of spring. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil favored by azalea and rhododendron, and prune only right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; allow soil to dry between waterings. Plumeria rubra (frangipani) is one of the most beloved and iconic tropical flowering trees in the world — a deciduous Central American tree or large shrub producing clusters of breathtakingly beautiful, intensely fragrant, 5-petaled flowers in an enormous range of colors (red, pink, orange, yellow, white, salmon, and multicolor) from late spring through fall on bare or nearly bare branches, with the flowers most concentrated when the plant is otherwise leafless. The legendary fragrance of frangipani — sweet, heady, exotic — has made it the quintessential tropical flower scent; the white-and-yellow P. obtusa and related species are used for Hawaiian leis, Buddhist temple offerings, and perfume across Southeast Asia. In zone 9, plumeria grows as a large shrub (6–10 feet) and goes fully dormant and leafless in winter — it should not be watered when leafless to avoid root rot. Rooted cuttings are the fastest way to bloom. Plumeria is surprisingly drought-tolerant and requires perfect drainage to avoid stem rot.

Plant in moist, acid, humus-rich, perfectly drained soil in part shade to full sun; Franklinia alatamaha is the most famous extinct-in-the-wild tree in North America — last seen growing wild along the Altamaha River in Georgia by John Bartram in 1803 and never found wild again, every Franklinia tree alive today descends from seeds or cuttings taken by Bartram before the species vanished from nature. The tree itself is extraordinary: large (3–4 inch) camellia-like white flowers with brilliant golden stamens bloom from August through October at the same time as the leaves turn flaming orange-red, producing a spectacular late-season display unlike any other temperate tree. The flowers are fragrant. It is a rare opportunity to grow a tree that would be extinct today without human cultivation — both a horticultural treasure and a living piece of botanical history.

Fraser Magnolia is a deciduous native magnolia of the southern Appalachians, native to the rich, moist cove forests and ravine slopes from Virginia and West Virginia south to Georgia and Alabama, immediately recognizable by its enormous leaves (up to 18 inches long) with distinctive ear-like lobes (auricles) at the base — the largest leaves of any magnolia native to the southern mountains. In May and June it produces large, cup-shaped, creamy-white, fragrant flowers 8–10 inches across that emit a sweet, lemony fragrance, followed in fall by striking pink to red cone-like fruit clusters that split to reveal bright red seeds, providing ornamental interest from spring through fall. Fraser Magnolia is a shade-tolerant understory tree that grows naturally in the deepest, richest, most sheltered cove forest conditions alongside cucumber magnolia, yellow buckeye, and basswood, and it translates beautifully to shaded woodland gardens in zones 5–8. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protecting from prevailing wind to prevent the large leaves from tearing.

Plant hardwood cuttings in spring in moist to wet, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along stream banks, river edges, and areas with high water tables; Fremont cottonwood is the dominant riparian tree of the American Southwest, forming gallery forests along desert rivers from California to New Mexico. The massive, fast-growing trees reach 40–80 feet, with deeply furrowed, gray-brown bark and large, triangular, bright green leaves that flutter constantly in desert breezes. In the arid Southwest, riparian cottonwood forests are oases of biodiversity — the trees support more bird species than any other habitat type in the desert, providing nesting sites for endangered southwestern willow flycatchers, yellow-billed cuckoos, and numerous neotropical migrants. The fall foliage is brilliant gold, providing the most spectacular fall color in the otherwise largely evergreen Sonoran and Mojave Desert landscapes. Named for explorer John C. Frémont who documented it in western expeditions.

Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil similar to what camellias prefer, keeping the pH between 5.0 and 6.5 and the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged. The large, white, camellia-like flowers with showy yellow stamens open from autumn through winter, providing color when little else is blooming in the garden. Protect young plants from hard freezes with frost cloth, as established specimens tolerate brief dips to the upper teens but young transplants are more vulnerable. Minimal pruning is needed; remove only crossing or damaged branches in late spring after the main flush of bloom.

Frill Ride is a bigleaf hydrangea bearing bold mophead blooms with distinctive frilled petal edges in shades that shift with soil pH. Plant it in morning sun and afternoon shade in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool. Acidic soil pushes blooms toward blue while alkaline soil yields pink, so amend to steer the color you want. Prune just after flowering, since it blooms mainly on old wood. Water generously in heat to prevent the large leaves and flowers from wilting.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Fringed Twining Milkweed is a drought-adapted native perennial milkweed vine of desert shrubland, washes, and roadsides from California to Texas in the southwestern US. It produces long, narrow to linear leaves and clusters of small, pale to rose-pink, star-shaped flowers with a distinctive fringed corona that bloom across a long summer season. Like true milkweeds it produces latex sap and classic spindle-shaped seed pods with plume-tailed, wind-dispersed seeds. It is a particularly important late-season milkweed resource for monarch butterflies on their fall migration routes through the Southwest, and should be kept dry and given excellent drainage to perform well — it declines quickly in heavy or poorly drained soils.

Frost Proof is a cold-tolerant gardenia bearing intensely fragrant white flowers against glossy evergreen leaves, and it withstands cooler temperatures better than typical gardenias. Plant it in morning sun with afternoon shade in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Keep watering consistent, as fluctuating moisture causes bud drop. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer during the growing season and prune lightly after the main bloom. Protect from harsh winter wind at the colder edge of its range.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun. As its name suggests, Frostproof was selected specifically for improved cold hardiness compared to standard Gardenia jasminoides, tolerating colder winters with less dieback than most cultivars while still producing the classic, intensely fragrant, creamy white double flowers gardenias are grown for. Its compact, naturally dense habit also makes it a good choice for foundation plantings and smaller borders where a full-sized gardenia would grow too large. Consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential, since gardenias quickly develop yellow, chlorotic foliage in alkaline or poorly drained conditions.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; fuchsia begonia is a Venezuelan shrubby begonia uniquely suited to milder and drier conditions than most tropical begonias — it produces a graceful, freely branching, shrubby habit reaching 2–4 feet with small, oval, glossy, bright-green, slightly toothed leaves and an abundance of pendant, fuchsia-like, coral-red to bright-pink flower clusters hanging on long, slender pedicels throughout the warm season and nearly year-round in frost-free climates. The delicate, drooping flower clusters have a jewel-like quality that closely resembles fuchsia flowers in their pendant form and rich coloring — hence the common name — but this plant is better adapted to warmth and partial shade than true fuchsias. It is the most drought-tolerant of the commonly grown shrub begonias, making it better suited to indoor conditions and gardens with inconsistent irrigation. An outstanding specimen in hanging baskets, tall containers, and sheltered outdoor shade gardens in zone 10–12.

Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; fuchsia-flowering gooseberry is a California native coastal shrub producing one of the most spectacular winter-flowering displays of any western native plant — long, pendant, brilliant-red flowers (dangling on slender stalks in clusters of 1–4) from January through March that are, in form and color, almost identical to a fuchsia flower: deeply red, tubular, with projecting red stamens that extend beyond the tube. These winter-blooming flowers appear on nearly leafless or semi-leafless stems and are an overwhelmingly important resource for Anna's and Allen's hummingbirds during the period when almost no other nectar sources are available. The plant goes fully dormant in summer — browning its leaves and appearing dead, which is entirely normal. The thorny stems create an excellent barrier planting and wildlife shelter. A startlingly beautiful winter-blooming native shrub for California and Pacific Coast gardens in zones 8b–10.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun. Fudingzhu is a Chinese tea olive selection bred for exceptionally heavy, repeat bloom — flowering several times a year rather than the one or two main flushes typical of standard tea olive — filling the garden with the intensely sweet, apricot-like fragrance for which the species is prized over a much longer season. Its more compact growth rate compared to seed-grown tea olive makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller gardens where the species' eventual large size would be unwelcome. Plant it near a patio, walkway, or window where the fragrance can be enjoyed on its frequent bloom cycles; little pruning is needed beyond light shaping after flowering.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fuji cherry is a Japanese alpine species from the slopes of Mount Fuji, characteristically small and shrubby compared to the large ornamental cherries, bearing small, finely cut, incised-margined leaves (incisa = cut) and a profusion of tiny white to pale pink flowers from February to March — among the earliest cherries to bloom. The small stature makes it appropriate for small garden spaces and courtyard gardens where full-sized cherries would be overwhelming. Good fall color in shades of orange and red provides a second season of interest. Important parent in breeding compact ornamental cherry cultivars, including the popular columnar 'Amanogawa' cherry. The widely planted Okame cherry (Prunus x incam 'Okame') is a cross between P. incisa and P. campanulata (Taiwan cherry).

Grow in bright light with a few hours of direct sun daily, in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil kept evenly moist but never waterlogged. Fukien tea is a small-leaved, rough-textured evergreen shrub from Southeast Asia that is one of the most popular subjects for indoor bonsai worldwide, prized for tiny, glossy, dark green leaves, naturally gnarled and easily shaped woody stems, and a long season of small white star-shaped flowers followed by tiny red berries that can appear almost year-round in good light. It is notoriously fussy about consistency: sudden changes in light, temperature, humidity, or watering routine often trigger leaf drop, so once a good spot near a bright window is found, avoid moving the plant and keep humidity elevated with regular misting or a pebble tray. Prune and wire young growth to develop bonsai form while the plant is actively growing in spring and summer, and repot every one to two years into fresh, fast-draining mix as roots fill the container.

Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and avoid overwatering, since this Texas native subshrub is highly susceptible to root rot in soggy or heavy clay conditions. Furman's Red is a superior autumn sage selection valued for its true, deep scarlet-red flowers and its exceptional cold hardiness, which allows it to survive winters in colder parts of its range that would set back other Salvia greggii cultivars. It blooms in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost, drawing hummingbirds throughout the growing season, and its compact, well-branched habit needs only an occasional hard cutback in late winter to stay dense and floriferous. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on lean soil and minimal supplemental water, making it a low-maintenance choice for xeriscape and pollinator gardens across the Gulf South.

Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; fuzzy deutzia is a Chinese and Japanese deciduous shrub that creates a spectacular late-spring and early-summer flowering display — the upright to arching branches become completely covered from tip to base with dense, upright panicles of white or pink-tinged, five-petaled flowers in late May to June, creating one of the fullest and most exuberant white-flowered shrub displays of the season. The name 'scabra' (rough) refers to the distinctive, rough, scurfy, sandpaper-textured surface of the ovate leaves, which distinguish it from the smooth-leaved species. 'Plena' with double, rose-flushed flowers, 'Pride of Rochester' with large, semi-double, white flowers with pink reverses, and 'Nikko' (dwarf, ground-cover habit) are the most widely planted cultivars. Tolerates partial shade acceptably. After a few years, the arching stems develop attractive, warm-brown, exfoliating bark that provides additional winter interest. An easy, trouble-free, and long-lived deciduous shrub that has been reliably ornamental in temperate gardens for well over a century.

common_name: Galaxy Magnolia (Deep Pink Late-Blooming Hybrid Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Galaxy is a USDA National Arboretum hybrid magnolia introduction — a cross between Magnolia liliiflora 'Nigra' (the dark-purple Japanese magnolia) and Magnolia sprengeri 'Diva' (the vivid pink Chinese magnolia) that combines the intense dark-pink to reddish-purple color and late bloom timing of the former with the large flower size and vigorous tree habit of the latter. The large, upright, tulip-shaped flowers (6–8 inches across when fully open) are deep rose-pink to reddish-pink on the exterior and lighter pink on the interior, produced in exceptional profusion on an upright, oval-to-pyramidal tree reaching 20–30 feet at maturity. The bloom timing — 2–3 weeks later than saucer magnolia (Magnolia × soulangeana) — is Galaxy's most practically important quality: in zone 6–7, late frosts frequently damage the flowers of earlier-blooming saucer magnolias; Galaxy's delayed bloom schedule moves past the most dangerous late-frost window. The upright habit and considerable height distinguish Galaxy from low-branching, spreading saucer magnolias — Galaxy has a more tree-like form appropriate for use as a street tree or in more formal landscape settings. In zone 9, Galaxy blooms in February–March with no frost risk, producing an exceptional flower display in warm winter conditions.

Set out young trees in fall on dry, rocky mountain slopes and mesas across the Intermountain West, where this drought-tolerant oak often forms dense colonial thickets from root sprouts. Its lobed, deciduous leaves turn russet-orange in fall, and its abundant acorns are an important food source for deer, black bear, and wild turkey. Gambel oak works well as a low-water specimen or naturalized thicket planting in xeriscape and wildfire-resilient landscaping in its native high-desert range. Once established it requires minimal irrigation and tolerates poor, rocky soils that few other oaks can handle.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; pinch to encourage bushiness and more prolific flowering. Strobilanthes isophyllus (Ganges primrose or India snapweed) is a shrubby, semi-sprawling tropical perennial from India and Southeast Asia in the acanthus family (Acanthaceae), producing a nearly continuous display of pale lavender-blue to soft violet, snapdragon-like (tubular, two-lipped) flowers from spring through fall in warm climates. The plant is grown primarily for its prolific flowering rather than its foliage — the leaves are glossy, lance-shaped, and dark green, attractive but not as dramatic as those of the related Persian Shield (S. dyerianus). Strobilanthes isophyllus tolerates a range of light conditions from bright indirect to quite deep shade, where it continues to flower more readily than many shade plants. In zone 9–12, it grows as a perennial; in colder climates, it makes an excellent container plant that can be overwintered indoors. The similar 'Gossip Girl' and 'Kimberley Blue' cultivars are sometimes attributed to this species or close relatives. A useful and underused shade-flowering perennial for warm, humid climates where few ornamentals bloom reliably in full shade.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade — the most vibrant leaf coloration develops in brighter light; deep shade produces greener, less intensely colored foliage. Garden croton is one of the most spectacularly colorful foliage plants in tropical horticulture, with leathery leaves that combine vivid red, orange, yellow, green, and purple in patterns ranging from fine-speckled splashes to broad blotches, depending on the hundreds of named cultivars available. Hundreds of leaf shapes exist: broad and lobed, narrow and twisted, curled, or oak-leaf shaped. It thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast and Florida in full outdoor culture in zone 9–12. Mite infestations are the most common pest problem, particularly in dry conditions — maintain adequate soil moisture and mist foliage during droughts. Crotons drop leaves readily when moved, so establish carefully. An outstanding specimen and landscape plant for bold tropical color.

Plant in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade, ideally on a slope or raised bed where water never stands around the roots; rose daphne is a low, mat-forming, evergreen shrub that in late spring smothers itself in small, intensely fragrant, rosy-pink flower clusters — one of the most powerfully scented small shrubs grown, easily perfuming an entire rock garden or path. It is a classic choice for alpine and rock gardens, where its trailing habit can drape attractively over stones. Good drainage is the single non-negotiable requirement for success; more rose daphnes are lost to wet, heavy soil than to cold, pests, or neglect. Like other daphnes, it resents being moved once established, so plant it in its permanent spot and avoid disturbing the root zone afterward. Mulch lightly with gravel rather than organic mulch to keep the crown dry.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with sturdy support for the vigorous vines; garlic vine (Mansoa alliacea) is a striking tropical vine from the Amazon basin producing clusters of lavender-purple to purple-pink, trumpet-shaped bignonia-family flowers in successive waves through the warm season, most heavily in fall and spring. Its common name comes from the pronounced garlic odor of the crushed leaves, stems, and flowers — a distinctive fragrance that has led to its use in traditional medicine in South America. The three-part leaves and decorative clusters of flowers make it an attractive flowering vine for tropical and subtropical screens and arbors; the vines climb vigorously and can cover a large fence or pergola quickly. It flowers most prolifically in full sun but tolerates partial shade and performs well in the humid heat of Gulf Coast zone 9–10 gardens. The unusual garlic fragrance is surprising and memorable in the garden.

common_name: Gatsby Gal Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact White-to-Pink Blooming Selection)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gatsby Gal produces large, elongated flower panicles that open white in early summer and take on a soft pink blush as they age, on a more compact plant than the straight oakleaf hydrangea species, making it easier to fit into a foundation planting or shade border. Like all oakleaf hydrangeas, it is a Southeastern US native fully adapted to the heat, humidity, and clay soils of the Gulf South, developing excellent burgundy-red fall foliage and attractive peeling bark for winter interest. Requires little pruning; remove only dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth by late summer.

common_name: Gatsby Moon Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large Double-Flowered Oakleaf Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving this full-sized cultivar plenty of room to reach its mature spread. Gatsby Moon is part of the Gatsby series of oakleaf hydrangeas bred for exceptionally large, densely double, pure white flower panicles that age to a soft pink, giving an especially showy, full-looking bloom compared with the single-flowered species. The bold, deeply lobed foliage turns outstanding shades of burgundy, orange, and purple in fall, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid pruning in fall, winter, or spring, which removes the coming year's blooms.

common_name: Gatsby Pink Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large White-to-Deep-Pink Color-Shift Selection)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gatsby Pink produces large, showy flower panicles that open pure white in early summer and gradually deepen to a rich, saturated pink as they age through the season, giving an extended, ever-changing floral display. Its full-sized habit fits well in a woodland border or mass planting where its bold texture and multi-season interest can be appreciated. Like other oakleaf hydrangeas, it develops burgundy-red fall foliage and attractive cinnamon, peeling bark for winter interest, and is fully adapted to the heat, humidity, and clay soils of the Gulf South. Requires little pruning; remove only dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth.

Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun, ideally with some shelter from hard freezes; Geiger tree is native to beach dunes and coastal hammocks of South Florida and the Caribbean and is exceptionally salt- and wind-tolerant, making it a signature small tree of Florida Keys and coastal landscaping. Clusters of crepe-textured, brilliant orange-red flowers appear nearly year-round in frost-free areas, followed by white, pear-shaped fruit that birds relish, while the large, rough, sandpapery leaves give the plant a distinctive tropical texture. It can be maintained as a large multi-trunked flowering shrub with occasional pruning or allowed to grow into a small canopy tree. Protect young plants from temperatures below the high 20s F, since it is one of the more cold-tender salt-tolerant natives available.

common_name: Gem Box Boxwood (Naturally Rounded No-Shear Dwarf Boxwood)
notes: Gem Box is a naturally compact, mounding boxwood hybrid bred to hold a tidy, rounded form on its own, essentially eliminating the frequent shearing that traditional boxwood hedging requires while still giving the same fine-textured, dense, dark-green formal look. It tolerates heat, cold, and a wide pH range better than many older boxwood cultivars and shows improved resistance to boxwood blight in independent trials, a significant advantage given how damaging that disease has become in Southern landscapes. Give it moist, well-drained soil and afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, watch for boxwood leafminer (the primary Southern boxwood pest), and expect to do little more than an occasional light touch-up shearing to keep its naturally neat habit looking crisp.

common_name: Georgetown Tea Rose (Found Texas Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Georgetown Tea is a Texas 'found rose' rescued by rose rustlers from an old homestead near Georgetown, Texas, and — like most tea roses that have survived generations of Southern neglect — it is exceptionally heat-tolerant and disease-resistant. It produces large, fragrant, loosely double blooms in soft pink to apricot tones that open from long, elegant buds, flowering nearly continuously from spring through fall in a warm climate. Grown own-root, it regrows true to type from the base after cold damage or hard pruning, and it needs little more than full sun, decent drainage, and an occasional light shaping to perform reliably for decades, much as it has at the old homesite where it was found.

common_name: Georgia Charm Indian Hawthorn (Compact Rose-Pink Indian Hawthorn)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Georgia Charm produces rose-pink flower clusters in spring above compact, dense, glossy evergreen foliage, followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds, on a tidy, rounded shrub sized for smaller foundation plantings and low hedges. Like other Indian hawthorn cultivars, it tolerates salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils well, making it a dependable choice for coastal Gulf Coast landscapes. Good air circulation between plants helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions; established plants need little care beyond occasional shaping.

Georgia Holly is a rare and regionally endemic native deciduous holly of the upper coastal plain and piedmont, found in a narrow range across Georgia, Alabama, and adjacent states, where it grows as a spreading shrub in the understory of moist, well-drained, sandy-loam upland forest. Distinctive among native hollies for its unusually long flower and fruit pedicels — the scientific epithet longipes means 'long-footed' — the bright red berries appear to float in space on their elongated stalks, making them more visible and accessible to birds than the closely bunched berries of many other holly species. A candidate for greater cultivation in the native plant garden, Georgia Holly is a multi-season ornamental shrub with small white spring flowers, deep green summer foliage, vivid fall berries, and clean branch structure in winter. Plant rooted cuttings in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; as with all native hollies, both male and female plants must be present for berry production.

Plant fresh acorns in fall in very well-drained, acidic, rocky, thin soil in full sun; Georgia oak is a rare, small-statured oak endemic to granitic flatrock outcrops and thin, rocky soils of the southern Appalachians and Georgia-Carolina Piedmont — one of the more restricted native oaks in the eastern United States, found primarily on Stone Mountain in Georgia, Hicks Knob in Georgia, and a few scattered Piedmont locations. It is a small tree or large shrub reaching 25–30 feet, with small, deeply lobed leaves that are smaller than most red oaks, turning a reliable, rich red-orange in fall. The compact size and superb fall color make it an outstanding specimen tree for rock gardens, rocky slopes, and smaller properties in zones 6–9 where space constraints prohibit larger oaks. A significant conservation plant with a very limited natural range.

Georgia Plume is one of the rarest and most endangered native shrubs in the United States, a monotypic genus (the only species in its family in North America) endemic to the Sandhills and longleaf pine region of Georgia, where fewer than 50 wild populations survive in dry, sandy, acidic longleaf pine savannas and turkey oak ridges. In July it produces spectacular terminal plumes of small white, four-petaled flowers in drooping clusters 6–12 inches long — an arresting display on a plant that looks unlike anything else in the native flora. The species rarely sets viable seed in the wild (likely due to the collapse of its pollinator community), and natural populations reproduce almost entirely by root sprouting; specialty native plant nurseries propagate it by root cuttings. Grow in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in partial to full sun — it is intolerant of heavy, wet, or alkaline soils. Supporting cultivation of Georgia Plume in private gardens is an important conservation act.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; germander sage is a small evergreen to semi-evergreen subshrub from the dry mountains of Mexico producing small, rounded, silver-gray to blue-gray leaves on compact, arching stems and brilliant electric-blue flowers from spring through fall — the striking cerulean-blue color of the flowers is more vivid and saturated than almost any other hardy sage. Native to rocky, limestone soils of the Sierra Madre and Chihuahuan Desert foothills at 4,000–8,000 feet elevation, it is adapted to the alkaline, well-drained soils common in Texas, New Mexico, and the Gulf Coast region. It is one of the best low-water-use ornamental plants for Texas gardens: compact, deer-resistant, drought-tolerant, and in near-continuous bloom. Excellent in rock gardens, xeriscapes, and as a low edging plant.

Set plants where they receive at least six hours of direct sun and good air circulation to limit blackspot, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. This David Austin English rose produces large, intensely fragrant, old-fashioned rosette blooms in deep pink over repeated flushes from late spring through fall. Prune hard in late winter to encourage strong new flowering canes, and feed monthly through the growing season for the best repeat bloom. It can be grown as a bushy shrub or trained as a short climber against a wall or fence.

common_name: Giant Carrion Flower (Zulu Giant, Starfish Flower)
notes: Plant in gritty, very well-drained soil in bright light with light afternoon shade in the hottest climates; this South African succulent forms a low, spreading mat of soft, four-angled, toothed, cactus-like stems that root easily wherever they touch the ground. In late summer it produces some of the largest flowers of any succulent grown in gardens, up to 10-14 inches across, star-shaped, and covered in fine wrinkled maroon-and-cream banding that mimics rotting flesh both in appearance and in scent, a strategy that lures flies as pollinators rather than bees. It is more cold-sensitive than most desert succulents and needs winter protection or container culture outside of zone 9-11, and unlike true cacti it appreciates slightly more regular moisture during active summer growth followed by a dry winter rest. Its sprawling habit makes it a striking, talking-point groundcover for raised beds, rock gardens, and container plantings in warm-climate xeriscapes.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, average to fertile soil in partial shade; giant dogwood is an East Asian deciduous tree considered by many plantspeople to be the finest and most architecturally distinguished large dogwood species — it develops a uniquely spectacular, perfectly horizontal, tiered, layered branching structure in which each layer of branches extends in a flat, table-like plane from the central trunk, creating a dramatically architectural silhouette reminiscent of a cedar of Lebanon in miniature, but made entirely of horizontal, flat-planed foliage tiers. In early summer, the upper surfaces of all the horizontal branches become covered with flat, corymb-like clusters of small, creamy-white flowers (without the large bracts of C. kousa or C. florida). The oval, alternate leaves turn deep-red to burgundy in autumn, and small, round, blue-black fruits provide food for birds. The legendary cultivar 'Variegata' (Wedding Cake Tree), with leaves broadly and irregularly margined in cream-white on the horizontally tiered branches, is one of the most spectacular variegated trees in cultivation and is widely regarded as a masterpiece of the ornamental tree world.

common_name: Giant Pelican Flower (Brazilian Dutchman's Pipe, Calico Flower)
notes: Plant in rich, well-drained soil next to a strong trellis or arbor, watering deeply and regularly through the growing season since this vine is a heavy feeder that grows fast in warmth and humidity. It produces enormous, mottled maroon-and-cream pouch-shaped flowers with a long tail-like tip that give off a faint carrion scent to lure pollinating flies, blooming heavily from summer into fall. Where winters are too cold to leave it outdoors it can be grown in a large container and overwintered in a bright, frost-free space, and it also serves as a larval host plant for pipevine swallowtail butterflies. Prune in late winter to control size and encourage fresh flowering growth.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun, mulching well to keep roots cool. One of the most celebrated Exbury hybrid deciduous azaleas, Gibraltar bears large, ruffled, brilliant orange flowers with a bold yellow-orange flare and a light fragrance, opening in vivid trusses that cover the shrub in mid to late spring and rank among the most eye-catching colors in the deciduous azalea group. Fall color adds a second season of interest, with the foliage turning shades of orange, red, and purple before dropping. Site it where the intense flower color has room to make a statement — as a woodland-edge specimen or backdrop to a shade border — and keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial sun; Girald's pearl bush is a large, arching Chinese ornamental shrub native to Shaanxi province that puts on one of the most spectacular spring flower displays of any cold-hardy deciduous shrub, smothering its long arching branches with racemes of pure white, 5-petaled flowers in mid-spring just as the leaves are emerging. The flower buds are distinctly round and pearl-like before opening — the origin of the common name. It is slightly larger and somewhat hardier than the related Exochorda racemosa and can ultimately reach 12–15 feet, so allow ample space in the landscape. Prune selectively for shape only immediately after bloom, as flower buds are set on the previous season's wood; deadwood can be removed at any time.

common_name: Globosa Nana Japanese Cedar (Dwarf Globe Sugi)
notes: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their naturally rounded outline to develop without crowding. 'Globosa Nana' is one of the oldest and most popular dwarf Japanese cedar selections, forming a dense, symmetrical mound of soft, blue-green, slightly twisted needles that take on a plum-bronze cast in cold weather before greening up again in spring. Its predictable globe shape and slow growth make it a dependable anchor plant in mixed conifer gardens, foundation plantings, and Asian-style landscapes where a formal, low-maintenance mass is wanted without shearing.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; glossy abelia is a semi-evergreen hybrid shrub that ranks among the most reliably long-blooming ornamentals for the Southeast and Gulf South, producing masses of small, funnel-shaped, white to blush-pink, pleasantly fragrant flowers continuously from late spring through hard frost — a bloom period of 5–6 months that few shrubs match. The small, glossy, bronze-tinged leaves are attractive year-round in mild climates. Hummingbirds and butterflies visit the flowers consistently. It is highly adaptable to soil conditions, tolerating heat, humidity, and urban pollution. Prune selectively in late winter to remove oldest canes and encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth. 'Kaleidoscope' (variegated yellow and green) and 'Confetti' (variegated pink-white) are popular selections.

common_name: Glossy Privet (Tree Privet, Evergreen Privet Tree)
notes: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; glossy privet is a large, fast-growing evergreen shrub or small tree with big, glossy, dark-green leaves and showy panicles of small white flowers in late spring, historically planted as a substantial screening hedge, street tree, or specimen for its handsome, dense evergreen canopy. Left unpruned it grows quickly into a 20–30 foot tree; sheared regularly it can be maintained as a tall, dense hedge or screen. The abundant, heavily fragrant flowers give way to prolific clusters of small blue-black berries that birds spread widely, and glossy privet has become a serious, well-documented invasive species across the Gulf South and much of the southeastern United States, forming dense stands in bottomland forests and disturbed woodland edges that displace native trees and shrubs. Because of this, it is best avoided in new plantings near natural areas — where a large-growing broadleaf evergreen screen is wanted, non-invasive alternatives like Podocarpus macrophyllus, Ilex, or Ternstroemia gymnanthera are strongly preferable.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath established trees or against a shaded wall; glossy sarcandra is an evergreen East Asian understory shrub grown for its glossy, deep-green, sharply toothed foliage and, most of all, for the clusters of small, bright orange-red berries that ripen in late fall and persist through winter, giving deep shade a spot of color when little else is blooming there. The tiny greenish flowers themselves are inconspicuous. Long used in traditional East Asian herbal medicine and prized in Japanese and Chinese flower arranging (ikebana) for its cut branches of glossy leaves and berries, it is grown ornamentally in the West mainly as an unusual, refined evergreen for the woodland shade garden. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native forest floor conditions; protect from hard freezes in the colder end of its hardiness range.

common_name: Glowing Embers Hydrangea (Deep Pink-to-Purple German Mophead Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun. Glowing Embers is a German-bred bigleaf hydrangea, roughly a half-century old, still regarded as one of the finest mopheads for deep, saturated flower color, ranging from rich pink in more alkaline soil to deep purple-red in strongly acidic soil, a shift managed with soil amendments if a specific shade is wanted. The large, rounded flower heads are held on a sturdy, well-branched, moderately compact shrub. Water deeply during dry spells to prevent wilting, and prune only lightly right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year form on the current season's growth by late summer.

common_name: Gold Cone Juniper (Narrow Columnar Golden-Foliage Juniper)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, since this narrow columnar juniper is intolerant of wet feet and develops its brightest gold color and tightest form with maximum light. Gold Cone is a sport of common juniper selected for a strongly upright, slender columnar habit and soft golden-yellow new growth that mellows to yellow-green with age, making it a popular vertical accent for narrow beds, foundation corners, and formal plantings where space is tight. It needs essentially no pruning to hold its naturally tidy spire shape and tolerates drought, wind, and poor soil once established, though it performs best in climates with a real winter chill and can struggle with humid, mild-winter heat. Avoid overhead watering and crowding, which encourage the fungal blights that trouble junipers in humid regions.

Plant in deep shade to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Gold Dust Aucuba is one of the most shade-tolerant large shrubs available, thriving in conditions where direct sunlight never reaches and where most ornamental shrubs slowly decline; Gold Dust is the classic variegated cultivar of Japanese Aucuba (Aucuba japonica), producing large, glossy, dark green leaves heavily speckled and splashed with bright gold and yellow markings — a bold, striking foliage pattern that provides strong ornamental interest in the deep shade conditions where the plant grows best. The gold-speckled leaves literally brighten dark shade garden areas, reflecting and amplifying available light in a way that creates a visual sense of brightness even under dense tree canopy. The combination of large, lustrous, gold-variegated foliage with the tolerance to thrive in genuinely deep shade — not just the 'partial shade' that many 'shade plants' actually require — makes Gold Dust Aucuba one of the most useful and irreplaceable shrubs for the specific problem of planting in dense shade under established trees, along north-facing walls, or in any situation where direct sunlight is effectively absent. Pollinated female plants produce clusters of bright red to scarlet berries that develop in fall and persist through winter, adding seasonal fruit color to the year-round foliage interest.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Gold Mound Duranta is a compact, golden-foliaged cultivar of the tropical Duranta that produces stunning chartreuse-to-golden-yellow leaves throughout the growing season, in dramatic contrast to the deep green foliage of surrounding plants. Unlike the standard blue-flowered Duranta erecta, Gold Mound rarely flowers or fruits, redirecting its energy into the vivid foliage display that makes it a premier landscape accent in zone 9–11. The compact, mounding habit (2–4 feet tall and wide) makes it far more manageable than the standard species, which can reach 15–20 feet without regular pruning. Gold Mound performs exceptionally well as a low border plant, foundation shrub, or container specimen in the Gulf Coast, where it provides year-round color in the landscape. The bright gold leaves intensify through summer heat, and the plant withstands the full force of Gulf Coast summers without wilting or losing color.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after flowering to keep the mounded habit tidy and encourage fresh golden new growth. Gold Mound forms a low, dense, rounded mound of bright yellow-gold foliage that holds its color through the growing season better than many gold-leaved spirea cultivars, accented by flat clusters of small pink flowers in early summer. Its compact, tidy habit and reliable color make it a popular choice for low borders, foundation edges, and mass plantings needing consistent, low-maintenance color. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, it tolerates poor soil and urban heat with minimal care.

Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Gold Star croton needs strong light to hold its bright yellow leaf speckling. Narrow, elongated, glossy green leaves are heavily speckled with bright golden-yellow spots that can nearly cover the leaf surface in strong light, one of the most vividly gold-toned of the many croton leaf-color selections and a striking accent among the deeper reds and oranges of other croton cultivars. Like other crotons it colors most intensely with abundant direct or bright indirect light, fading to duller green in low light, and it holds its foliage year-round in frost-free gardens or as a long-lived container and houseplant elsewhere. Water when the top inch of soil dries, protect from any frost, and wipe dust from the glossy leaves periodically to keep them looking their best.

common_name: Gold Star Esperanza (Cold-Hardy Compact Yellow Bells)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil after the danger of frost has passed. Gold Star is a selection of esperanza (yellow bells) chosen for a more cold-hardy root system and a more compact, better-branched habit than the standard species, which lets gardeners in zone 7b and 8a grow it as a reliable perennial that dies back to the ground and resprouts each spring, rather than needing to treat it as a tender annual or overwinter it indoors. It produces the same masses of bright golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped, hummingbird-attracting flowers from early summer through the first hard frost, but on a shrub that typically stays a more manageable 4-6 feet rather than the 8-12 feet the straight species can reach in zone 9-11. In milder zones it remains semi-evergreen; where winters kill the top growth, cut the dead stems back to the ground in late winter and the plant resprouts vigorously and blooms the same season. Prune to shape in early spring to encourage the most compact, floriferous growth.

common_name: Gold Thread Cypress (Threadleaf Golden False Cypress)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, keeping soil evenly moist, especially while young, since this species is less drought-tolerant than junipers or pines. Gold Thread Cypress forms a loose, mounded to broadly pyramidal shrub of cascading, thread-like, bright golden-yellow foliage that provides strong, season-long color contrast against green-leaved shrubs and dark conifers, with the color often deepening to a coppery gold in winter cold. Its fine, weeping texture and bold color make it an effective specimen or focal point in a mixed shrub border or foundation planting. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or damaged branches; avoid shearing, which disrupts the natural cascading form.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; the gold tree (golden trumpet tree) produces one of the most spectacular flowering displays of any tree in the world — for 1–2 weeks in late winter or early spring, the entire tree is covered in blazing, golden-yellow trumpet flowers before a single leaf has emerged, creating a vision of solid gold visible from hundreds of feet away. The display lasts only 1–2 weeks and is immediately followed by the production of deeply cut, palmate compound leaves. The species is the national tree of Brazil and widely planted as a street and specimen tree throughout the tropics. Drought-tolerant once established, growing naturally in deciduous tropical dry forest. In south Florida (zone 10), it produces its spectacular bloom in February-March — one of the great floral spectacles of the Miami-Fort Lauderdale area.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden angel's trumpet is an Andean species producing enormous, pendant, trumpet-shaped flowers up to 12 inches long in soft golden-yellow, often with a rich, sweet, tropical fragrance strongest in the evening. A single well-grown plant can carry dozens of pendant blooms simultaneously, creating a spectacular tropical accent. Like all Brugmansia, all plant parts are dangerously toxic — containing tropane alkaloids (scopolamine, atropine) that cause hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, and potentially fatal poisoning. Never use any plant part medicinally without expert guidance. In zone 9, grow as a container plant moved indoors in winter or in a frost-protected location. Fertilize heavily with a balanced fertilizer every 2 weeks during the growing season to achieve maximum bloom production. The large, pendant flowers are adapted for pollination by large hawk moths.

common_name: Golden Angel's Trumpet (Large Pendulous Yellow-Trumpet Brugmansia Shrub)
