notes: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Queen is a yellow-flowered Brugmansia (angel's trumpet) producing the spectacular large-scale tropical display characteristic of the genus — very large (10–14 inch), pendulous, trumpet-shaped flowers in warm golden-yellow hanging in clusters from the branch tips, releasing an extraordinary heavy fragrance particularly intense in the evening hours. The golden-yellow flower color of 'Golden Queen' is distinctly different from the white, peach, pink, and apricot tones of other angel's trumpet varieties — a warm, pure yellow that creates a dramatic tropical focal point in partial shade. In zone 9, Brugmansia grows as a large tropical shrub or small tree reaching 6–12 feet, blooming most heavily in spring and fall as temperatures moderate from summer extremes. The plant requires generous water and fertility to produce its finest flower display — large containers require daily watering in summer. All parts of Brugmansia are toxic if ingested and should be handled with caution; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. In zone 9b and 10, Golden Queen grows as a perennial. In zone 9a, frost may kill the top growth but the plant often returns from the roots with mulch protection; container-grown specimens can be moved indoors before frost. The spectacular flowers and fragrance make angel's trumpets one of the most dramatic ornamentals for Gulf South tropical garden designs.

Plant container-grown stock in fall or early spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; this Trans-Pecos native thrives in exactly the hot, dry, alkaline conditions that defeat most flowering trees. Fragrant, powder-puff, golden-yellow flower balls cover the fine, mimosa-like bipinnate foliage in flushes from spring through fall, especially after summer rain, drawing bees and butterflies, and the plant is unarmed (thornless), unlike mesquite or acacia. It is usually grown as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small specimen tree and is extremely drought tolerant once established, needing supplemental water only the first year or two. Hard freezes can kill it to the ground, but it reliably resprouts from the root in spring.

common_name: Golden Celebration Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1992, Golden Celebration is one of the most celebrated of all English roses, bearing very large, deeply cupped, rich golden-yellow blooms with a strong, warm fragrance often compared to sauternes wine and tea, on a vigorous, arching shrub with glossy, disease-resistant foliage. Its combination of flower size, color saturation, and fragrance made it an instant classic, and it repeat-blooms generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading, tolerating heat better than many older yellow rose cultivars.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden chain tree is one of the most spectacular of all spring-flowering trees, producing long, pendant racemes of brilliant, clear-yellow pea flowers up to 24 inches in length in May and June — so dense and vividly colored that the entire tree appears to drip with cascades of golden chains, from which the common name derives. The famous Laburnum Walk at Bodnant Garden in Wales — a 180-foot tunnel of intertwined laburnums, trained overhead to create a tunnel of golden chains — demonstrates the full theatrical potential of this tree. In smaller gardens, a single mature specimen in full bloom against a dark background or blue sky is extraordinary. Native to central Europe and tolerant of shallow, chalky soils and part shade. The hybrid 'Vossii' is the most commonly planted, with the longest flower chains. EXTREME CAUTION: all parts of the plant, especially the seed pods and seeds, contain cytisine (a toxic alkaloid similar to nicotine) and are highly poisonous — the plant should never be planted where children play.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; golden dewdrop is a vigorous tropical shrub that provides two seasons of ornamental interest — lavender to purple tubular flowers from spring through fall, followed by clusters of small golden-yellow berries that drape like strings of dewdrops and persist on the plant for months, creating the common name. The berries are the primary food source for many songbirds, particularly mockingbirds and robins. Be aware that the berries and leaves are toxic to humans, dogs, and cats. The popular weeping cultivar 'Geisha Girl' has larger, richer purple flowers; 'Gold Mound' is a compact, dwarf golden-foliage form. Prune severely in late winter to maintain a compact, manageable shape — unpruned plants can reach tree size. Outstanding as a large informal screen, espalier, or specimen shrub for zone 8–11 gardens where its rapid growth and dual seasonal interest make it highly effective.

Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Golden Full Moon maple scorches in hot afternoon sun and needs protection from strong wind. Rounded, star-shaped leaves emerge a luminous chartreuse-gold in spring and hold their bright golden color through summer better than most yellow-leaved trees, glowing especially vividly in the dappled light of a shaded garden, before turning shades of orange and red in fall for a second seasonal color display. Slow-growing and long-lived, it develops a graceful, mounded, layered branching structure over the years that makes it a prized specimen tree for a shaded Japanese-style garden or woodland border, where its bright foliage color provides strong contrast against darker-leaved companions. Provide dappled shade and shelter from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, both of which scorch the delicate gold leaves, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer.

common_name: Golden Mop Cypress (Threadleaf Mounding Gold Falsecypress)
notes: Golden Mop is a dwarf, mounding false cypress selected for stringy, thread-like sprays of bright golden-yellow foliage that spill over themselves in an informal, tousled mound, distinct from the finer, more upright Gold Thread Cypress. It stays low and rounded for many years, needs essentially no pruning, and provides year-round texture and color contrast against darker evergreens or as a rock garden and foundation accent. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest gold color, though a little afternoon shade helps in the hottest climates; established plants are low-maintenance but resent soggy, poorly drained soil, which promotes root rot.

Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; golden rain tree is very adaptable to poor, dry, alkaline, and clay soils once established and requires minimal irrigation or fertilization. Koelreuteria paniculata is a Chinese ornamental tree 25–40 feet tall that fills a unique niche by blooming in midsummer (July–August) with spectacular 12–15 inch upright panicles of small, bright golden-yellow flowers followed by ornamental papery seed pods (lanterns) that are green, then pink-salmon, then tan, remaining decorative into winter; it is among the most summer-drought-tolerant and adaptable ornamental trees for zones 5–9. The compound leaves turn yellow in fall and the form is broadly rounded with age; plant with adequate space as the canopy spreads widely. Self-seeds freely in some regions — collect seed pods before they shatter to prevent volunteers.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; golden shower tree is one of the most spectacular of all tropical flowering trees — the national tree of Thailand — producing cascading chains of brilliant golden-yellow flowers 12–18 inches long that completely cover the tree before the new leaves emerge in spring, creating a breathtaking golden cascade. It grows fast (3–5 feet per year) in frost-free conditions, reaching 25–40 feet, and tolerates drought, alkaline soil, and seaside conditions once established. The flowers are edible in some cultures (flower buds in curries). In zone 9a it may die back in severe freezes but typically regrows from established root systems; site in a protected location sheltered from north winds. A magnificent specimen or street tree for zone 9–11 Gulf Coast landscapes.

common_name: Golden Spirit Smokebush (Bright Chartreuse-Gold Smoke Tree)
notes: Golden Spirit is a smokebush selected for bright chartreuse-gold foliage that holds its color through the growing season before turning orange-red in fall, a striking contrast to the dark purple leaves of cultivars like Royal Purple and useful for lighting up a border planted with darker-foliaged companions. Airy, smoke-like plumes of tiny pinkish flowers appear in summer, giving the plant its common name, though the golden foliage itself is the main ornamental draw. Like other smokebush selections it is highly drought-tolerant once established and prefers lean, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter for a more compact, densely leaved shrub, which sacrifices that year's smoky flower plumes in exchange for larger, bolder foliage.

common_name: Golden St. John's Wort (Shrubby St. John's Wort)
notes: Golden St. John's wort is a native deciduous shrub of dry, rocky hillsides and cedar glades in the southeastern United States, producing profuse, large, golden-yellow flowers with prominent, brush-like clusters of yellow stamens for several weeks in summer — among the most floriferous and ornamentally attractive of all native shrubs for dry, rocky, or difficult soil situations. Unlike the weedy, herbaceous common St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), this species is a well-behaved woody shrub that stays in bounds without invasive spreading, making it an excellent low-maintenance landscape plant for dry sunny borders, rock gardens, and native shrub masses. The blue-green foliage and exfoliating gray bark are attractive through the growing season, and the persistent, reddish seed capsules provide winter interest; it is deer resistant and tolerates drought, heat, and poor soil with minimal care. An Award of Garden Merit recipient from the Royal Horticultural Society, it is popular in European gardens and deserves much wider use in American native plant landscapes as an alternative to non-native ornamental shrubs.

Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; golden trumpet tree (formerly Tabebuia chrysotricha, now Handroanthus chrysotrichus) is one of the most spectacular flowering trees of the Brazilian cerrado and is widely planted throughout tropical and subtropical landscapes for its extraordinary spring flower display — the entire tree becomes covered in large, vivid, deep-golden-yellow to butter-yellow, funnel-shaped, trumpet-form flowers while the branches are leafless or just beginning to leaf out, creating a breathtaking all-yellow display against the blue sky. The flowering season typically lasts only 2–3 weeks but is of extraordinary intensity. The national tree of Brazil is a related species (Handroanthus serratifolius, Tabebuia serratifolia — the Yellow Ipê), and the genus includes pink, purple, magenta, and lavender flowering species as well. Hardy to approximately 28°F in zone 9 with established trees often recovering from frost damage. Excellent as a street tree and garden specimen in zone 9–12. Also known as the golde Ipê.

Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, very well-drained soil; golden trumpet vine is one of the showiest tropical flowering plants available for Gulf Coast gardens, producing an almost continuous display of large (3–4 inch), brilliant canary-yellow trumpet-shaped flowers from spring through fall on glossy, leathery-leaved vining or shrubby stems. It can be trained as a vine on trellises and fences or pruned as a rounded shrub in formal plantings. The shrubby cultivar 'Cherries Jubilee' has deep rose-purple flowers; 'Hendersonii' bears larger golden flowers. Regular fertilization during the growing season is essential for continuous bloom. All parts of the plant are toxic — wear gloves when handling the milky sap and keep away from children and pets. In zone 9, protect from hard freezes; plants may suffer foliar damage but typically recover from established roots once warm weather returns.

common_name: Goldfish Plant (Flying Goldfish Plant, Columnea gloriosa)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Goldfish Plant flowers most prolifically with good indirect light (bright north or east window or 3–5 feet from a south window) and will produce few flowers in dim conditions. Columnea gloriosa is a trailing, epiphytic vine from Costa Rica and Panama in the Gesneriaceae family, named for its flowers: vivid orange-red, hooded, tubular blooms 2–3 inches long with a small yellow patch in the mouth that, when seen dangling from the trailing stems, precisely resemble a leaping orange goldfish — one of the most charming visual metaphors in the houseplant world. The flowers emerge from small, fleshy, hairy, brown-purple calyx tubes along the trailing stems and at the stem tips, appearing most abundantly after a brief cool, dry rest period in fall. The stems are clothed in pairs of small, thick, fleshy, dark-green, hairy leaves. In excellent conditions with good light and appropriate care, a well-established Goldfish Plant in a large hanging basket produces dozens to hundreds of the characteristic orange flowers simultaneously in winter-spring — an extraordinary display of color at a time of year when few houseplants are blooming. Widely hybridized; many modern hybrids are sold simply as 'Columnea hybrid' with flowers in red, yellow, or bicolor combinations.

Train on a trellis, arbor, or fence in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Goldflame honeysuckle is a hybrid ornamental vine producing exceptionally showy flowers from late spring through summer — the tubular flowers are an intense coral-red to orange-red on the outside with a creamy-yellow interior, presenting a striking bicolor combination as the buds open and the flowers age. The fragrance is moderate to strong, sweet and honeysuckle-like. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica), Goldflame is a controlled, twining vine that blooms repeatedly through the season and attracts hummingbirds and butterflies throughout its long bloom period. The foliage is glaucous blue-green, semi-evergreen in mild climates, and attractive in its own right. Particularly valuable for hummingbird gardens as it provides a succession of nectar-rich flowers through most of the warm season. Well-behaved and garden-appropriate for zones 4–9, it thrives even in heat if given consistent moisture and partial shade protection in the afternoon in the hottest climates.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Goldflame is the premier tricolor Japanese spiraea cultivar — producing a remarkable three-season foliage color progression that provides more sustained ornamental interest than almost any other compact shrub. The new spring growth emerges in a vivid bronze-orange to copper-red color that is one of the most striking spring colors available on any deciduous shrub; through summer the foliage matures to yellow-gold; in late summer and fall the leaves develop orange and red fall tones. The transition from bronze-orange spring → yellow-gold summer → orange-red fall provides effectively continuous color change interest from April through frost. In early summer, small rosy-pink flower clusters add additional color above the evolving foliage. Goldflame's compact size (2–3 feet, slightly wider) makes it proportionate for typical residential borders and it has become one of the most widely planted compact deciduous shrubs in American landscaping. Like other Japanese spiraea cultivars, it is extremely adaptable and tough — tolerating clay, urban conditions, drought, and the heat of zone 9 with minimal care. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush in early summer to stimulate vigorous new growth with fresh bronze-orange coloration.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to refresh foliage color and encourage a tidy shape. Goldflame is one of the older and most widely planted foliage spirea cultivars, its new growth emerging a vivid coppery orange-red before maturing to bright gold through summer and finishing with orange-red fall tones, all set off by small clusters of pink flowers in early summer. Its compact size and long season of foliage color make it a workhorse for mixed borders and mass plantings where a low-maintenance shrub with more than a few weeks of interest is wanted. Extremely tough and adaptable, tolerating drought, poor soil, and urban conditions with minimal care once established.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; goldfussia is a Thai and Myanmar native shrub that is prized in zone 8–11 gardens for two qualities rare in shade-tolerant woody plants: dramatically iridescent dark-green foliage with a blue-purple metallic sheen in certain light conditions, and a profuse display of soft, powder-blue to violet-blue tubular flowers in autumn and winter — when most garden shrubs have ceased flowering. The combination of semi-glossy, iridescent leaves and late-season blue flowers makes goldfussia an exceptionally valuable plant for providing fall and winter interest in the shaded border. The plant grows as a rounded, mounding shrub with soft, slightly hairy leaves and is somewhat frost-sensitive, typically dying back to the roots in zone 8 winters before resprouting vigorously from the base in spring. In zones 9–11 it grows as a semi-evergreen to evergreen perennial shrub. Excellent combined with autumn-blooming companions in the partially shaded border.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Goshiki (Japanese for 'five colors') is a slow-growing, spiny-leaved evergreen shrub whose new growth emerges in a mottled blend of pink, cream, and bronze over dark green, settling into a creamy-mottled variegated pattern as the leaves mature — a striking, ever-changing foliage display that provides year-round color in a shaded border without relying on flowers. Its dense, holly-like, prickly foliage also gives it useful deer resistance and makes an attractive, low-maintenance foundation or accent shrub for shaded entries and woodland-edge plantings. Little pruning is needed given its slow growth rate; shape lightly if needed after the inconspicuous fall flowers finish.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun to bright part shade; the swollen base is the ornamental feature — keep soil dry in winter to prevent rot; CAUTION: All parts are toxic. Jatropha podagrica (gout plant, Buddha belly plant, or tartogo) is a distinctive, slow-growing tropical ornamental shrub native to Central America — a member of the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae) and the Jatropha genus, widely known for its unusual and sculptural physical form. The most dramatic feature of the plant is its pachycaul (thickened-trunk) base: a grotesquely swollen, knobby, gnarled, bottle-shaped or bumpy stem base that looks like a massively enlarged, deformed joint — exactly resembling gout-afflicted knuckles (hence 'gout plant') or the pot-bellied figure of a Buddha (hence 'Buddha belly'). This caudex-like swollen base serves as a water reservoir, making the plant drought-tolerant. Above this remarkable structure, the plant produces large (8–12 inch across), deeply palmately lobed, bright-green leaves with a tropical appearance, and small clusters of vivid coral-red to vermillion-orange flowers on erect peduncles that attract hummingbirds and butterflies. Gout plant is a beloved collector's plant and pot plant in tropical horticulture for its unusual form, easy culture (very low water needs), and colorful flowers. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic, similar to other Jatropha species.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Governor Mouton is a classic, long-cultivated Camellia japonica with distinctive semi-double to peony-form flowers showing a highly variable, bicolor pattern — the base petal color is deep rose-red to carmine-red with irregular splashes, streaks, and flecks of white that create an unpredictable, painterly, somewhat informal flower. No two flowers are exactly alike, which gives Governor Mouton a loose, old-fashioned charm quite different from the geometric precision of formal double camellias like Alba Plena or Pink Perfection. This variability is part of its appeal: the informality suits cottage garden and naturalistic landscape styles. The cultivar is named for Alexandre Mouton, an early Louisiana governor, reflecting its long association with the Gulf South camellia tradition. The upright to spreading shrub reaches 6–12 feet tall and produces dense, dark-green, glossy evergreen foliage. Governor Mouton blooms in early to mid-season (November through February in zone 9), one of the earlier and more reliable bloomers in the japonica camellia lineup. It shows good vigor and adaptability to Gulf Coast conditions. Apply acidic camellia-azalea fertilizer in spring and early fall; maintain 3–4 inches of pine bark mulch at all times to protect the shallow root system.

common_name: Grace Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001, Grace bears warm apricot, deeply cupped rosette blooms with a light tea fragrance, on a vigorous, well-branched shrub whose slightly nodding flower habit distinguishes it from more upright-facing English rose cultivars. Its warm, glowing apricot tone pairs well with both cool blues and other warm-toned companions in a mixed border, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Graham Blandy Boxwood (Extremely Narrow Columnar Boxwood)
notes: Graham Blandy is one of the narrowest columnar boxwood cultivars available, growing tall and slender in a tight, almost exclamation-point form that fits spaces too narrow for other upright boxwood selections, such as flanking a narrow gate or walkway. Its fine, deep green foliage provides the same year-round formal structure as other boxwood but in a distinctly vertical, space-saving silhouette that needs little pruning to maintain. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; because its narrow form relies on strong vertical growth, avoid heavy shearing that would disrupt its naturally columnar habit.

common_name: Graham Thomas Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood; where grown as a climber, tie the long canes horizontally along a fence or trellis to maximize side-shoot flowering. Bred by David Austin and introduced in 1983, Graham Thomas was named for the renowned English rosarian and combines the rich, deep golden-yellow, cupped-to-rosette blooms and strong tea fragrance of an old garden rose with the vigor and repeat-flowering habit of a modern shrub rose. It quickly became one of the best-selling English roses ever introduced and remains a benchmark yellow rose for its combination of color saturation, fragrance, and reliable rebloom from late spring through frost. It shows good disease resistance in humid climates when given full sun and adequate air movement.

Plant transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Fully double, camellia-like white flowers open in clusters from summer through fall, releasing the classic, powerfully sweet Arabian jasmine fragrance used to scent jasmine tea, with far more petals per flower than the simpler single or semi-double forms of the species, making this one of the most ornamentally prized jasmine cultivars for fragrance gardens. Its warmth-loving nature makes it a superb container plant that can be moved to a sheltered spot or brought indoors for winter outside the warmest zones, continuing to bloom under bright indoor light with adequate humidity. Water regularly, feed during the growing season to sustain the heavy, fragrant bloom, and prune after flowering to shape and encourage bushier growth.

common_name: Grand Slam Camellia (Bright Red Peony-Form Camellia japonica)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Grand Slam is a widely grown Camellia japonica cultivar bearing large, bright, true red flowers in a loose semi-double to peony form packed with ruffled petals, one of the most vivid reds available among camellia cultivars and a longtime award winner on the camellia show circuit. The vigorous, upright evergreen shrub blooms in mid-season and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its striking winter flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Grandma's Yellow Rose (Texas Superstar Found Heirloom Yellow Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Grandma's Yellow is a Texas Superstar-designated rose identified and propagated by Texas horticulturists as a tough, disease-resistant 'found' rose — a survivor discovered thriving in an old home landscape long after the original planting was forgotten, a hallmark of genuinely tough antique and found roses well adapted to Southern conditions. It produces deep golden-yellow, repeat-blooming flowers on a vigorous, disease-resistant shrub that needs far less spray intervention than most modern hybrid tea roses to stay healthy through a humid Gulf South growing season. Like other Texas Superstar-designated found roses, it rewards low-input, minimal-spray care once established — light pruning in late winter and routine watering during dry spells are usually all it needs to perform reliably for years.

Provide a sturdy support structure such as a trellis, fence, or pergola, and plant in well-drained, dry to average soil in partial shade — this native midwestern vine prefers its roots cool and shaded while its stems climb toward sunlight. Unlike invasive non-native honeysuckles, Grape Honeysuckle is well-behaved and will not spread aggressively or self-seed excessively. Water regularly for the first growing season to establish, then scale back irrigation; established vines are drought-tolerant and thrive with little intervention. The distinctive perfoliate leaves and tubular yellow to orange flowers are magnets for ruby-throated hummingbirds and native bees from late spring through midsummer.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; grape ivy is a Venezuelan tropical evergreen vine of the grape family (Vitaceae) that has been among the most widely grown and reliable shade-tolerant tropical foliage vines for over a century — it climbs by tendrils to form dense, leafy masses of three-parted (trifoliate), broadly rhombic (diamond-shaped, hence rhombifolia), glossy, dark-green leaves with prominent, rusty-brown, finely hairy undersides that give the plant an attractive textured quality when the foliage is disturbed. The lustrous, dark-green foliage, reliable shade tolerance, and easy cultivation make it an enduringly popular choice for covering shaded walls, trellises, and structures in tropical and subtropical gardens, and as a trailing vine in large containers and hanging baskets indoors or in sheltered outdoor positions. 'Ellen Danica' (oak-leaf grape ivy) has more deeply lobed, oak-leaf-like leaflets and is slightly more cold-sensitive. Outdoors in zone 10–12 it can reach 15 feet or more on suitable supports in shade conditions where most other vines would fail to thrive.

Plant in well-drained, average, fertile soil in full sun; grape-leaf flowering maple is a fast, large-growing Chilean shrub with soft, gray-green, grape-like leaves and an abundant spring display of large, saucer-shaped, mallow-like flowers in shades of lavender, blue-violet, or white, among the showiest blooms of any commonly grown abutilon. It grows quickly, often reaching full size within just a few years, making it useful for a fast privacy screen or a dramatic single-season specimen in mild-winter gardens. It performs best in climates with moderate summer humidity similar to its native Chilean range and can suffer more from prolonged intense heat and humidity than some of the more tropical abutilon species, so afternoon shade is worthwhile in the hottest, most humid parts of its zone range. Prune after flowering to control size and shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and protect the root zone with mulch through winter at the cooler edge of its hardiness.

Set out young trees in spring on sandy, acidic, or poor soils where this tough pioneer species readily colonizes abandoned fields and roadsides. Its slender, chalky-white trunks with black triangular patches beneath each branch and its fine-textured, fluttering foliage give it strong ornamental value in multi-stem clumps. Gray birch tolerates poor drainage and infertile ground better than paper birch but is shorter-lived, typically thriving for only 30-50 years, making it best suited to naturalized or reclamation plantings rather than a long-term specimen. It requires little supplemental water once established, unlike its moisture-loving birch relatives.

Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to moderate shade; gray dogwood is one of the most wildlife-friendly native shrubs in the eastern US, producing clusters of white berries on distinctive red pedicels in late summer that attract catbirds, robins, thrushes, and over 90 other bird species. The shrub tolerates dry soil, compacted clay, and partial shade better than most native dogwoods. It spreads by root suckers to form dense thickets valuable for erosion control and wildlife corridors; remove suckers in spring if a more contained form is desired. Small white flower clusters in early summer are visited by numerous native bees and short-tongued pollinators.

Plant in any well-drained to moderately moist soil in full shade to partial sun; greater periwinkle is a vigorous, trailing, evergreen groundcover with larger, glossier, darker green leaves than the more refined Vinca minor — it covers ground more aggressively and thrives in the heat and humidity of zones 7–11 where V. minor can struggle. Sky-blue, star-shaped, 1.5-inch flowers appear from early spring through summer. Particularly valuable in the hot Southeast and Gulf Coast where its heat tolerance far exceeds V. minor. The variegated form ('Variegata', with leaves edged in creamy white or yellow) provides striking year-round foliage interest in shaded spots. Be aware that V. major can be invasive in riparian zones and warm-climate areas where it spreads into native plant communities — do not plant near natural areas or waterways in warm climates. Excellent for covering slopes, under trees, and in difficult shaded areas in contained residential landscapes.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, deep, well-drained to seasonally wet soil; Green Ash is one of the most adaptable native trees in eastern North America and tolerates periodic flooding, clay soils, and urban conditions better than most hardwoods. It is the fastest-growing native ash species and provides dense shade and important wildlife value — the winged seeds are consumed by many bird species including finches and grosbeaks. All plantings of this species should be made with full awareness of the emerald ash borer threat: consult your local extension service for current biocontrol and treatment options and consider whether site conditions justify planting. Established trees need little care beyond occasional formative pruning of crossing branches in late winter; avoid wounding the bark unnecessarily, as entry points can invite opportunistic pests.

common_name: Green Cloud Texas Sage (Dark Green Cenizo with Magenta Flowers)
notes: Plant in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Green Cloud is a named cultivar of Leucophyllum frutescens (Texas sage, cenizo, Texas ranger) — distinguished by its dark-green foliage rather than the typical silver-gray woolly leaves of the standard species. This green-leaved form creates a different visual effect: while the silver-gray species has a dusty, high-desert texture, Green Cloud has a more lush, conventional-looking green shrub appearance that may integrate more easily into traditional landscape palettes. In both forms, the flowers are identical: vivid, deep magenta-purple, bell-shaped blossoms that emerge in spectacular flushes after rain events (or periods of high humidity) from late spring through fall — a flowering behavior so reliably triggered by moisture that Leucophyllum is sometimes called the barometer bush for its ability to 'predict rain' by blooming just before or after rainfall. The stunning magenta flower display against the dark-green foliage of Green Cloud creates an outstanding ornamental effect. Leucophyllum is one of the most drought-adapted large shrubs for the Southwest and Gulf Coast — native to the Chihuahuan Desert and extremely tolerant of heat, reflected heat, alkaline soil, and periods of drought. In zone 9, it is reliably evergreen and long-lived without supplemental irrigation once established.

common_name: Green Giant Arborvitae (Fast-Growing Evergreen Privacy Screen)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing trees to allow the dense, pyramidal form to grow together into a solid screen while leaving room for good air circulation. Green Giant is a vigorous hybrid arborvitae, a cross between Western redcedar and Japanese arborvitae, developed for exceptionally fast growth and reliable performance as a large-scale evergreen screen, reaching mature heights of 40–60 feet with a dense, uniform, deep green pyramidal habit that requires little to no shearing to maintain its shape. Unlike Leyland cypress, which has become increasingly prone to canker and root disease problems in the humid Gulf South, Green Giant shows notably better disease resistance and has become the preferred fast-growing screening tree for many Southern landscapes. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, and deer browsing is generally minimal compared to other arborvitae. Water deeply and regularly for the first two years to establish a strong root system.

common_name: Green Mountain Boxwood (Upright Cone-Shaped Hybrid Boxwood)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9. Green Mountain is a hybrid boxwood bred for a naturally upright, broadly conical form that holds its shape with minimal pruning, making it a popular choice for formal accents, low pyramidal specimens, or a more structured look in a mixed border without the labor of constant shearing required by rounder cultivars. Like other hybrid boxwoods combining English and Korean parentage, it shows better resistance to boxwood blight than pure English boxwood (Buxus sempervirens) and better summer heat tolerance than English boxwood alone, while retaining rich, deep green, small-leaved foliage year-round. It tolerates the heat and humidity of the Gulf South reasonably well when given afternoon shade and excellent drainage, since boxwood roots are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet, poorly drained soil. Watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary pest in Southern gardens, which causes blistered, discolored leaves; treat with a systemic insecticide if infestation is heavy. Light shearing or hand-pruning in late winter or after the spring flush maintains a crisp, formal outline if desired.

common_name: Green Rose (Viridiflora, Novelty Antique China Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Green Rose, also sold as Viridiflora, is one of the odder curiosities in the rose world: a China rose sport whose flowers never develop true petals, instead producing dense clusters of jagged, sepal-like bracts that open bright green and age to a rusty maroon-bronze, giving the plant an unusual, almost floral-arrangement look rather than typical rose color. It has no traditional fragrance but is a favorite of flower arrangers for its novelty and long vase life. Like other China roses it blooms nearly continuously from spring through frost and shares their outstanding tolerance for heat, humidity, and blackspot, needing little spraying or care in the Gulf South. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and expect curious questions from visitors who assume the buds simply haven't opened yet.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Spire euonymus grows in a naturally upright, columnar form requiring minimal shearing to maintain a narrow hedge or screen. Small, glossy, dark green, evergreen leaves cover a naturally narrow, upright, columnar shrub that provides quick vertical screening or a tidy formal hedge without the wide footprint of rounder evergreen shrubs, tolerating regular shearing and heat well. Fast-growing and adaptable to a range of soils, it is commonly used for narrow foundation plantings, privacy screens along property lines, or formal accents flanking an entrance where a slim, columnar evergreen form is wanted. Shear lightly through the growing season to maintain a tight form, and watch for euonymus scale, a common pest that can build up on stressed or crowded plants.

common_name: Green Tower Boxwood (Narrow Columnar Formal Accent Boxwood)
notes: Green Tower is a narrow, strongly columnar boxwood selected to grow tall and slender rather than wide, holding a tight, formal vertical shape with only light shearing rather than the heavy pruning needed to force a rounder boxwood into a similar form. Its fine-textured, deep green foliage provides year-round structure for flanking an entry, punctuating a formal border, or standing as a pair of vertical accents where a wide shrub would crowd the space. Give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest; occasional light shearing in late winter or after the spring flush keeps its narrow profile crisp.

common_name: Green Velvet Boxwood (Cold-Hardy Rounded Hybrid Boxwood)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade with some afternoon shade in the hottest part of zone 9. Bred in Canada as a cross between English and Korean boxwood, Green Velvet combines the fine, dense texture prized in English boxwood with much better cold hardiness and improved resistance to winter bronzing, holding a rich, consistent dark green color through the year better than many older cultivars. Its naturally tidy, rounded habit needs only light shearing to maintain a formal shape, making it a popular low-hedge and edging plant. Like other boxwoods it requires sharp drainage to avoid root rot and benefits from monitoring for boxwood leafminer, the main pest of concern in Southern gardens.

Plant rooted cuttings in sharply drained, rocky or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun, spacing wide since a single plant spreads into a dense mat 5 to 8 feet across within a couple of seasons. Small, silvery-gray, pinnately compound leaves cover trailing, woody stems that root as they spread, and clusters of small purple, pea-like flowers appear in spring, drawing bees and providing light seasonal color over the silver foliage. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it needs no supplemental irrigation in the low desert and is commonly used as a large-scale erosion-control groundcover on slopes, banks, and parking lot islands throughout its native Chihuahuan Desert range. Prune back hard every few years to rejuvenate woody, overgrown mats and keep the silvery foliage dense and fresh.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; Grevillea robusta (silky oak) is the most cold-hardy and widely grown grevillea, a fast-growing Australian native that can reach 20–40 feet in frost-free climates and produces spectacular orange-yellow spider-like flowers in spring that are intensely attractive to hummingbirds, honeyeaters, and native bees. Smaller shrubby grevillea species (G. thelemanniana, G. lanigera, G. rosmarinifolia) are excellent for xeriscaping in zones 8–11 and produce red, pink, or orange flowers over much of the year. All grevilleas require excellent drainage and minimal fertilization, as phosphorus-sensitive root systems are easily damaged by standard garden fertilizers. Once established, they are extremely drought-tolerant.

Grey Owl is a wide-spreading, arching juniper selected for silvery gray-green foliage, taking on soft purplish-bronze tones in winter cold, on a low, informal, fountain-shaped mound that works well cascading over a wall or covering a slope. It is derived from eastern red cedar and shares that species' remarkable adaptability, tolerating heat, drought, poor soil, salt spray, and the humidity of the Gulf South better than many other juniper cultivars bred from less heat-tolerant species. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; established plants need little care beyond occasional shaping to control the spreading habit, and good air circulation helps avoid the fungal blights that can affect junipers in humid climates.

common_name: Gro-Low Fragrant Sumac (Dwarf Spreading Groundcover Sumac)
notes: Gro-Low is a low, wide-spreading selection of native fragrant sumac grown as a tough, drought-tolerant groundcover for slopes, parking lot islands, and other difficult dry sites where turf struggles. Its glossy, three-lobed leaflets resemble poison ivy in outline but are harmless and release a spicy, citrus-like fragrance when crushed; small yellow flower clusters in early spring are followed by fuzzy red berries and then a reliable orange-to-burgundy fall color display. Once established it needs no supplemental irrigation, spreads steadily by rooting where branches touch soil to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat, and requires only an occasional hard pruning in late winter to keep it within bounds.

Plant small container starts in spring into acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil under light conifer shade, matching the high-elevation forest understory of the Rockies and Cascades where this wiry, broom-like shrub carpets the ground. Its tiny leaves and green, angled twigs give it a fine, airy texture quite different from other huckleberries, and its small pink urn flowers give way to tart red berries that are a critical late-summer food source for grouse and black bears. It spreads slowly by rhizome into low colonies and is best used as a textural groundcover in a cool woodland or native rock garden rather than for significant fruit production.

common_name: Gruss an Aachen Rose (Antique Peachy-Pink Floribunda)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in Germany in 1909, Gruss an Aachen ('greetings from Aachen') is historically significant as one of the roses credited with founding the floribunda class, produced by crossing a hybrid tea with a polyantha to combine large, full-form blooms with the polyantha's compact habit and cluster-flowering vigor. Its large, fully double, old-fashioned-shaped blooms open warm peachy-pink and fade to soft cream, with a moderate, pleasant fragrance, on a low, bushy, well-branched shrub that blooms in generous, repeated flushes from spring through fall. It shows good resistance to blackspot for an early-20th-century rose and needs little care beyond routine watering and an annual light shaping. The compact size makes it well suited to borders, low hedges, and containers. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and maintain a tidy shape.

Guajillo is a large native shrub or small tree of south and central Texas brush country, producing very fragrant, fluffy white-cream flower heads in late winter and early spring when few other plants are in bloom — its abundant, sweetly scented blossoms make guajillo the most important honey plant in south Texas, where beekeepers prize 'guajillo honey' as a premium single-varietal product with a distinctive, mild floral character. The plant is unarmed (thornless), making it more landscape-friendly than many other native acacias; its feathery, twice-pinnate leaves cast dappled shade and give the plant a graceful, airy appearance throughout the growing season. Dense thickets of guajillo provide critical thermal cover and escape cover for white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and quail in south Texas brush country, and the plant is commonly used in habitat restoration on the Edwards Plateau and south Texas plains. It is highly drought tolerant once established and thrives in the caliche and limestone soils that typify the Texas Hill Country and Winter Garden regions.

common_name: Guest of Honor Camellia (Large Salmon-Pink Semi-Double Exhibition Japonica)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; Guest of Honor is a well-established Camellia japonica cultivar producing large, semi-double flowers in warm salmon-pink — a color between clear pink and peach-salmon that is warmer and more orange-tinted than standard camellias, providing a distinctive color option in the predominantly pink-red-white camellia palette. The large, semi-double flowers (typically 4–5 inches) show a loose arrangement of wide, slightly wavy outer petals surrounding a center of mixed stamens and petaloids in the classic semi-double camellia form — less formal than fully double varieties but with more visual complexity than single-flowered types. The salmon-pink color stands out clearly against the characteristic glossy, deep-green evergreen foliage of camellia and is sufficiently distinctive that Guest of Honor is consistently recognized in the landscape. Guest of Honor grows as a medium-to-large, upright, densely branched evergreen shrub with vigorous growth in appropriate conditions. In Gulf South zone 9, it is one of the most reliable long-lived landscape camellias — a plant that improves with age and can become a large, impressive landscape feature over decades of growth. Strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) and consistent moisture are the primary cultural requirements. The unusual salmon-pink color makes Guest of Honor an outstanding specimen where more typical pink or red camellias would seem repetitive.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; Guianese colicwood tolerates a range of soil moisture from dry to seasonally wet. Small, leathery, dark green leaves densely clothe an upright, multi-trunked native shrub or small tree, with inconspicuous flowers followed by small, dark purple-black berries that provide reliable food for native birds through much of the year. Native to hammocks, pinelands, and wetland edges across Florida and the Caribbean basin, it is an adaptable, low-maintenance understory shrub tolerant of both dry and periodically moist soils, useful for a hedge, screen, or wildlife habitat planting in a native landscape. It handles both sun and considerable shade well, and needs only routine watering during establishment before becoming largely self-sufficient.

common_name: Gulf Stream Nandina (Gulf Stream Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Gulf Stream is an outstanding mid-sized compact nandina cultivar that fills the gap between the very dwarf Firepower and the full-size species — reaching a tidy 30–42 inches with a dense, rounded, upright-mounding habit and exceptional seasonal foliage interest. The distinctive characteristic of Gulf Stream is its brilliant blue-green summer foliage — more intensely blue-colored than most nandinas — followed by outstanding orange to red to burgundy winter coloring. It is a semi-sterile selection that produces few berries, reducing the invasive spread concerns associated with the species. Gulf Stream was selected by the late nurseryman John Hampton Brinkley of Lewisville, North Carolina, and has been widely promoted by the National Arboretum as an outstanding landscape selection. The medium size, dense habit, and excellent foliage color make Gulf Stream appropriate for foundation plantings, mixed shrub borders, and mass plantings where neither the very dwarf Firepower nor the large standard species is appropriate. Like all nandinas, it is adaptable to a wide range of soils and light conditions, extremely drought-tolerant once established, and resistant to deer browsing.

Plant this shrub rose in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart for their rounded habit. Gumball Goody blooms from spring to fall in a candy mix of light pink, deep pink, and yellow on a compact, tidy plant well suited to borders and containers. Water deeply and regularly during establishment and the growing season, keeping foliage dry to limit disease. Prune in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and deadhead to encourage repeat flushes.

Plant hardwood cuttings or container trees in well-drained, rocky, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; gumbo limbo is nicknamed the 'tourist tree' because its distinctive reddish, peeling bark resembles a sunburned tourist. The shiny, exfoliating, copper-red outer bark peels off in thin sheets to reveal smooth new bark beneath — one of the most ornamentally interesting barks of any South Florida native. The tree is remarkably tough: hurricane-resistant due to flexible limbs, very tolerant of salt spray and coastal conditions, and one of the few South Florida hammock trees that can be grown from large cuttings — even cut limbs several inches in diameter, stuck in moist soil, will root readily. The red, fleshy fruits are eaten by numerous subtropical birds. A cornerstone of South Florida coastal hammock forest and an outstanding landscape tree for zone 10 coastal settings.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Gumpo is a classic dwarf Satsuki azalea from Japan, valued for its unusually low, spreading, groundcover-like habit and large flowers relative to its small size, blooming several weeks later in late spring than most other azaleas and extending the azalea season into early summer. Named forms are available in white, pink, and variegated pink-and-white flower colors, all sharing the same compact, mounding growth well suited to low borders, rock gardens, and container culture. Water deeply during dry spells and protect from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the foliage; prune lightly right after flowering to shape without removing next year's buds.

Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full shade in naturalistic woodland or wetland settings; hairy spicebush is a rare and threatened native shrub of the Carolinas coastal plain, naturally restricted to wet, shaded pocosins and bay swamps where it grows beneath pond pines and Atlantic white cedars. Like common spicebush (L. benzoin), the leaves, bark, and twigs are aromatic when crushed with a spicy, benzoin-like fragrance. The small yellow flowers appear on bare stems in very early spring, providing pollen for early-emerging native bees. A host plant for spicebush swallowtail butterfly (Papilio troilus) caterpillars, which use both Lindera species. More restricted to wet, acidic, shaded conditions than common spicebush and more appropriate for pocosin and bay swamp restoration. A rare plant with significant conservation value.

Plant in dry, lean, sandy, strongly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; hairy wicky is a diminutive evergreen shrub of the longleaf pine ecosystem of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, growing in the driest, most nutrient-poor, acidic white sands of pine scrub, sandhills, and dry pine flatwoods. Its characteristic small, hairy, needle-like leaves and low, spreading habit distinguish it from the large, showy mountain laurel (K. latifolia) of Appalachian forests. Despite its small stature, the flowers are disproportionately showy for the plant's size — the same distinctive cupped, saucer-like Kalmia blooms in bright pink with ten anthers tucked in pockets around the rim — produced in summer when few other shrubs bloom. An outstanding native for low-maintenance landscaping in dry, acidic sandy soils in zone 7–9 where mountain laurel would fail in summer heat.

Plant in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; halberd-leaved rose mallow is native to wet areas and thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, bioswales, and consistently moist borders. Hibiscus laevis is a native eastern US perennial hibiscus of floodplains, streambanks, and wet meadows, distinguished from the similar H. moscheutos by its distinctively halberd-shaped (like the medieval weapon — three-lobed with two lateral points) leaves and smooth stems (laevis = smooth); it produces large, showy, 5–6 inch pale pink flowers with deep red centers from midsummer through early fall, similar in scale and beauty to other native rose mallows. The plant dies to the ground in winter but re-emerges reliably from a woody crown in spring; it is particularly valuable as a native pollinator plant for large bees and hummingbirds in wet areas. Less commonly grown than H. moscheutos but equally beautiful and better suited to shaded, wet settings.

common_name: Halley's Comet Florida Anise (Large-Flowered Red Anise Shrub)
notes: Halley's Comet is a selection of native Florida anise chosen for producing a much heavier crop of flowers than typical seedling plants, with numerous, larger, deep maroon-red, multi-petaled starfish-shaped blooms that open along the branches in spring. Like the species it forms a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub with anise-scented foliage when bruised, thrives in the deep, acidic shade under pines and hardwoods that stumps many flowering shrubs, and is notably deer-resistant. Give it moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and shelter from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaves; all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten and it should not be confused with the culinary star anise, Illicium verum.

Hammock sweet azalea is a large, summer-blooming native azalea of the Gulf Coastal Plain — the most heat-tolerant and latest-blooming of all eastern native azaleas, producing fragrant clusters of tubular, white (occasionally pink-tinged) flowers with a clammy, sticky texture in July and August, when summer heat makes gardening difficult and most flowering shrubs have long since finished blooming. Its natural habitat is the moist, shaded understory of hardwood hammocks, bay swamps, and magnolia-dominated wet forests from Florida to Louisiana, making it the most shade- and moisture-tolerant of all Gulf Coast native azaleas. In Gulf Coast landscape gardens, it fills a critical niche as a large, fragrant, summer-flowering shade shrub for moist, acidic woodland conditions — pair with ferns, Louisiana irises, and swamp spider lily in moist, acid-soil shrub borders for a true Gulf Coast hammock garden. The late summer bloom time and fragrant flowers attract hummingbirds and giant native sphinx moths that are still active in summer heat.

common_name: Harbor Dwarf Nandina (Classic Spreading Groundcover Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Harbor Dwarf is one of the longest-established and most reliable dwarf nandina cultivars, a low, spreading selection grown as a mass groundcover under trees, along foundations, and on slopes where its rhizomatous spread gradually knits together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat. New foliage emerges bronze-red and matures to blue-green through the growing season before turning red-orange in winter cold, giving reliable color change with almost no maintenance beyond an occasional cutting back of old canes. It tolerates deep shade better than most nandina selections, making it a dependable evergreen filler for difficult dry shade under mature trees, and unlike straight-species nandina it fruits only sparsely, reducing (though not eliminating) self-seeding.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Harbour Belle adapts to a wide range of soils and is drought tolerant once established, while tolerating substantial shade better than most broadleaf evergreen shrubs; Harbour Belle is a dwarf compact selection of Heavenly Bamboo (Nandina domestica), producing the characteristic Nandina feature set — pinnately compound leaves on cane-like stems, soft red new growth, summer green foliage, and brilliant red-orange to burgundy winter coloring — at half the size of standard nandina. The combination of multi-season foliage interest (red spring growth, green summer, then red-orange to burgundy in winter cold), adaptability to both sun and significant shade, drought tolerance once established, and the compact form that fits scale requirements of most residential plantings has made nandina in general — and compact forms specifically — one of the most heavily planted ornamental shrubs in the Gulf South. Harbour Belle's small size makes it particularly useful for low-growing foundation plantings, border edges, and mass planting under low windows where standard nandina would overgrow the site within 5–6 years. The fine-textured foliage and airy growth habit contrast well with coarser broadleaf companions like gardenias, hollies, and loropetalums.

common_name: Harbour Dwarf Nandina (Low-Growing Spreading Dwarf Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Harbour Dwarf is a distinctly low, spreading dwarf nandina (heavenly bamboo) selection reaching only 18–24 inches in height while spreading steadily wider by underground stolons — creating a slowly spreading, bamboo-textured groundcover mass with fine-textured, compound, pinnate foliage that turns shades of red, orange, and bronze in fall and winter. The fine, ferny texture of nandina foliage is unique among commonly grown shrubs — the small, lance-shaped leaflets create an almost grass-like visual lightness despite the woody, evergreen character of the plant. Unlike the large, upright nandina forms (which can reach 6–8 feet), Harbour Dwarf remains permanently low, making it appropriate for the front of foundation plantings, as a border edging, and as a shade-tolerant groundcover alternative to liriope or mondo grass. Fall and winter bring progressively more vivid red-orange coloration that intensifies after frost — some of the most reliable fall foliage color available in a compact evergreen shrub for Gulf South gardens. The spreading habit and shade tolerance make Harbour Dwarf one of the few ornamental woody plants useful as a groundcover under trees and in partially shaded borders. Extremely adaptable: tolerates drought, clay soils, and part shade once established.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hardy rubber tree is extremely adaptable and tolerates heat, cold, drought, and urban pollution better than most shade trees. Glossy, elm-like leaves that exude fine, elastic latex threads when torn give this tree both its common name and its most reliable identifying trait, and its bark, the source of du zhong, is one of the most widely used tonic herbs in traditional Chinese medicine, traditionally associated with supporting bone and joint health. A tough, adaptable, pest- and disease-resistant tree with no serious ornamental drawbacks, it makes a reliable, low-maintenance shade or street tree independent of any medicinal use, and is the only surviving species in its ancient plant family. Bark for medicinal use is typically harvested from mature trees using sustainable partial-strip techniques that allow the bark to regenerate rather than felling the tree.

Plant container specimens or root suckers in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; harlequin glorybower is a large, bold, East Asian deciduous shrub or small tree that provides the most remarkable autumn display of any ornamental tree or shrub in its zone range — the large, dark-purple flower buds open in late summer into clusters of pure-white, intensely fragrant, jasmine-like tubular flowers with long protruding stamens, and as the petals fall, the persistent calyxes remain and flush deep rose-pink to magenta, while the seed inside each calyx ripens to a brilliant, glistening, turquoise-blue to deep cobalt-blue, creating a simultaneous display of vivid blue berries in inflated red calyxes that is completely unlike anything else in the temperate landscape. The large, oval leaves smell unpleasantly if crushed. It tolerates partial shade, spreads by root suckers into colonies (which can be managed by mowing), and blooms most freely in full sun. The blue berries attract and feed birds throughout winter. 'Carnival' (yellow-variegated leaves) is an ornamental selection.

common_name: Harry Lauder's Walking Stick (Twisted Corkscrew Hazel, Contorted Filbert)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil with morning sun to light shade. Prune out any straight-growing rootstock shoots that emerge below the graft. Harry Lauder's Walking Stick (Corylus avellana 'Contorta') is one of the most prized ornamental shrubs in temperate horticulture, valued primarily for the extraordinary architectural quality of its winter branch structure. The plant is propagated by grafting the contorted cultivar onto straight European hazel (Corylus avellana) rootstock, and all woody growth above the graft union will be contorted; any growth from below the graft union will be normal straight hazel and must be removed as it appears. The contorted growth habit affects every branch and twig, producing a dense winter silhouette of spiraling, twisting branches that catches and holds frost, snow, and ice dramatically and creates complex shadow patterns on winter walls and garden surfaces. When bare of leaves, a mature Harry Lauder's Walking Stick is one of the most winter-interesting plants in temperate gardening — its corkscrew branches have inspired garden designers for generations as structural focal points in winter gardens. In spring, the contorted branches are draped with drooping yellow catkins (male flowers) before the large, slightly crinkled, typical hazel leaves emerge, adding a brief period of early-spring charm before the plant becomes a handsome but unremarkable leafy shrub for the rest of the growing season. The plant produces small nuts in fall, but nut production is typically sparse compared to standard hazel varieties.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Hartlage Wine sweetshrub is a sterile hybrid (Calycanthus floridus × C. chinensis) developed at JC Raulston Arboretum in Raleigh, North Carolina, that combines the best qualities of both parents into a superior, vigorous, large deciduous shrub with remarkable ornamental value — the outstanding flowers, produced in extraordinary abundance from May through August on a long season matched by few large shrubs, are large (2–3 inches across), multi-petaled, deep wine-red to burgundy, and produced on both old and new wood, maintaining color from late spring through summer. The large, broad, glossy leaves are more refined than those of the native sweetshrub. Unlike the common sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus), Hartlage Wine flowers reliably in partial shade and does not depend on heat or sun for good flower production. It is sterile and non-invasive. One of the finest and most adaptable flowering shrubs introduced in the late 20th century for zone 6–9 gardens, equally at home in sun or partial shade, and exceptionally free-flowering over its long bloom season.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; heart-leaf flame pea is a small Australian shrub of exceptional flower brilliance — producing in late winter and spring such an abundance of vivid, small, sweet pea-family flowers that a plant in full bloom appears entirely engulfed in a smothering cloak of the most vivid bicolor flowers: the standard petal brilliant orange-red to flame-red, the keel and wing petals a contrasting purple to deep violet with a small yellow blotch at the base, the combination of orange, purple, and yellow creating an intense, extravagant, tropical-colored display of remarkable saturation and vibrancy for such a small shrub. The small, heart-shaped to ovate leaves with holly-like, spiny-toothed margins (giving both the common name 'holly flame pea' and the species name cordatum = heart-shaped) provide an attractive, textured foliage background year-round. Native to the sandy soils of the Stirling Ranges and coastal heath of southwestern Western Australia, it requires the lean, well-drained soil conditions of its native habitat to thrive. One of the most brilliantly colored small shrubs available for the zone 9 garden.

Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix and grow in partial to full shade; heartleaf philodendron is a classic tropical vining houseplant and shade garden perennial with deep-green, glossy, distinctly heart-shaped leaves (3–4 inches at maturity, much larger when climbing in tropical conditions) on long, trailing stems that root readily at every node. It is considerably more shade-tolerant than pothos and produces a uniformly rich, velvety, dark-green appearance that remains attractive across a very wide range of light conditions — from bright indirect light down to quite dim interior corners. New leaves emerge with a bronze-copper tint before maturing to deep forest-green, a distinctive and attractive feature of the young growth. In zones 10–12 it covers the ground under trees and climbs tree trunks as a large-leaved epiphytic vine. Extremely easy to propagate — a single node cutting placed in water produces roots within days. 'Brasil' (yellow-green variegated center stripe), 'Micans' (velvety bronze-green), and 'Lemon Lime' (chartreuse) are popular cultivars. All parts toxic if ingested.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly watered, especially through the first two summers, and protect from deer, which browse the foliage and stems readily. Euonymus americanus is an open, airy, native deciduous shrub of eastern woodlands, grown chiefly for its remarkable fruit display: in fall, warty, bright crimson-pink seed capsules split open to reveal glossy orange-red seeds dangling on threads, giving rise to the descriptive common name 'hearts-a-bustin'.' Small, inconspicuous, greenish-white flowers appear in late spring, easy to overlook until the dramatic fruit show follows in September and October. The slender green stems provide winter interest and mild color even when bare. Best used as a specimen at the edge of a shaded woodland garden or native plant border where the fall fruit display can be appreciated up close, in zone 6–9.

common_name: Heaven Scent Gardenia (Exceptionally Fragrant Upright Gardenia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade, ideally near a patio, porch, or walkway where its fragrance can be fully appreciated. Heaven Scent is a Southern Living Plant Collection gardenia selected specifically for exceptionally strong, sweet fragrance, considered among the most powerfully scented gardenia cultivars available, carried on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub with glossy dark green foliage. Its manageable size fits foundation plantings and smaller beds better than some larger gardenia cultivars while still delivering an outsized fragrance impact. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves in insufficiently acidic soil, so feed with acid-forming fertilizer and maintain consistent moisture for the healthiest, most fragrant bloom.

Plant in virtually any well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to full shade; Nandina is one of the toughest and most site-adaptable ornamentals for Southern gardens, though it develops the best red fall and winter foliage color in full sun, and in heavy shade may remain more green year-round. Nandina domestica (heavenly bamboo — not a true bamboo) is an elegant, upright evergreen shrub native to China and Japan with fine-textured, pinnate (bamboo-like) foliage that emerges bronze-red in spring, turns green in summer, and becomes brilliant red to burgundy-red in fall and winter, especially in sun; large, pyramidal clusters of white flowers in May–June are followed by persistent clusters of bright-red berries that last through winter and provide exceptional wildlife value. The berries are relished by Cedar Waxwings and American Robins. Standard Nandina grows 4–6 feet tall; compact cultivars like 'Harbour Dwarf' (2–3 feet), 'Fire Power' (2 feet, intense red fall color), and 'Lemon Lime' (lime-green foliage) are popular. Note: Nandina berries are toxic to dogs and cats; berries may be invasive in some southeastern states — check local regulations.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge maple is exceptionally adaptable to poor soil, drought, pollution, and pruning, tolerating urban conditions better than most maples. Small, rounded, dark green leaves with softly lobed margins cover a dense, tidy, small-to-medium tree that tolerates heavy pruning and shearing exceptionally well, making it a traditional European choice for clipped hedges and formal allees as much as a freestanding shade or street tree, turning a modest but pleasant yellow in fall. Native to Europe and western Asia, it is remarkably tolerant of poor, compacted, alkaline urban soils, drought, and air pollution, performing reliably in difficult street tree and parking lot planting sites where more particular maple species struggle. It needs little supplemental care once established beyond routine pruning if grown as a hedge, and its small mature size and dense branching make it a versatile shade tree for a smaller residential lot.

common_name: Helene Rose of Sharon (White with Deep Red Veined Eye Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Helene bears crisp white, single flowers marked with a deep reddish-purple eye that radiates outward along the petal veins, a striking, high-contrast pattern distinct from the solid-eyed look of many other rose of sharon cultivars, blooming from midsummer into fall. Like its sibling introductions it is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection that sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older, seed-grown rose of sharon while remaining a tough, heat- and humidity-tolerant shrub. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

Plant in partial shade to deep shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with excellent drainage; Henry's anise is one of the finest shade-tolerant broad-leaved evergreen shrubs for gardens in zones 7–9, offering year-round glossy, lance-shaped, deep-green foliage with a distinct anise fragrance when crushed — a characteristic shared with the closely related native Florida anise (Illicium floridanum). Illicium henryi produces charming, star-shaped flowers from spring through early summer in shades of rose-red to deep carmine-pink, with petals arranged in the distinctive multi-layered pattern characteristic of the genus; the flowers are subtly fragrant and appear among the glossy foliage over an extended season. An outstanding plant for shady courtyards, woodland borders, and foundation plantings where a refined, deer-resistant, evergreen structure is needed; it pairs beautifully with Japanese maples, camellias, and Hydrangea quercifolia in the shade garden. CAUTION: all parts are toxic if ingested — do not confuse with culinary star anise (Illicium verum).

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Henry's anise tree is a Chinese evergreen shrub or small tree prized for its ability to thrive in deep shade — one of the relatively few large-growing broad-leaved evergreens that performs well in the dense shade beneath mature trees where most broadleaf shrubs languish. The large, glossy, dark green, willow-like leaves are aromatic when crushed. The flowers are rosy red to deep pink, star-shaped, and appear in late spring — more showy than those of the native Florida anise (I. floridanum) but less fragrant. Named for Augustine Henry, the Irish plant explorer who collected extensively in China in the late 19th century. Somewhat hardier than Florida anise, tolerating temperatures to 0°F in a sheltered spot. An excellent large screening shrub for shaded gardens in the Southeast.

common_name: Henry's Garnet Virginia Sweetspire (Fall Color Shade Shrub)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Henry's Garnet is the most widely grown and most celebrated Itea virginica cultivar — a superior selection chosen by Mary Henry of Gladwyne, Pennsylvania, for its outstanding combination of fragrant summer flowers, exceptional fall color, and adaptability to difficult growing conditions. In late June and July, the shrub produces 4–6 inch, drooping, bottlebrush-like clusters of small, fragrant white flowers that attract bees and butterflies. But Henry's Garnet's most remarkable attribute is its fall color — in September through November, the foliage transitions to vivid burgundy-red to deep garnet, one of the most reliable and intense fall color displays of any native shrub, maintained even in zone 9 where fall temperatures are mild. The fall color persists for 6–8 weeks — far longer than most fall-color shrubs. Henry's Garnet spreads by suckering to form a colony over years, making it effective as a mass planting for naturalizing, rain garden planting, and stream-bank erosion control. Unlike most fall-color shrubs that require full sun for good color development, Henry's Garnet develops excellent color even in partial shade — a notable advantage for shade gardens. The spreading habit and outstanding fall color with shade tolerance make it one of the finest native shrubs for zone 9.

Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Henryi is one of the oldest and most classic large-flowered clematis cultivars, producing enormous, creamy white flowers with conspicuous chocolate-brown stamens that create a striking contrast against the pale petals. Because it flowers mainly on old wood from the previous season, heavy pruning removes the coming season's bloom, so gardeners should limit pruning to removing dead or damaged stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole plant back as with Jackmanii-type clematis. It has been a garden favorite for well over a century for its dependable, large-scale white flower display.

Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; herald's trumpet is one of the most spectacular of all tropical and subtropical flowering vines — a native of the eastern Himalayan foothills and northern India that produces in spring (April through June) enormous, trumpet-shaped flowers of breathtaking scale: each individual flower is 4–5 inches long and 3–4 inches across at the opening, pure white, five-petaled, with a narrow tube flaring to a wide, rounded, slightly fragrant trumpet that resembles an Easter lily flower of exaggerated dimensions. These enormous white trumpet flowers are borne in large, clustered bunches of 6–20 at the ends of the stems, so that a mature vine in full spring bloom — covering a large pergola or two-story wall — presents hundreds of the enormous, pristine-white trumpets simultaneously in a display of singular tropical grandeur. The large, oval, glossy, dark-green leaves are bold and handsome year-round. The vine is very large-growing, reaching 30–50 feet on suitable permanent support, and is a decades-long commitment. In zone 9a it requires a warm, sheltered position and may suffer frost damage in severe winters but regrows. One of the ultimate ambitions of warm-climate gardeners — a vine you plant and tend for years to achieve an unforgettable eventual spectacle.

Hercules' Club is a large, dramatic native shrub or small tree of the coastal plain and piedmont of the southeastern United States, notorious for the massive, knobby, claw-like spines that stud the trunk and branches and make it instantly identifiable from a distance. A member of the citrus family (Rutaceae) and closely related to Sichuan pepper, the aromatic bark and leaves contain numbing, anesthetic compounds that were applied by many Native American peoples directly to sore gums and toothaches — earning it the folk name toothache tree — as well as used as a fish poison and in various medicinal preparations. A primary host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly, one of the largest butterflies in North America, Hercules' Club is an outstanding native choice for wildlife gardens in the Southeast. Plant in well-drained, moderately infertile, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established, it spreads by root sprouts and benefits from open, sunny, naturalized settings.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Heritage is the premier named cultivar of river birch — introduced by Earl Cully of Heritage Tree Nursery in Jacksonville, Illinois, and selected for outstanding bark exfoliation quality, larger leaf size, and superior heat tolerance compared to unselected species plants.
