The spectacular bark display is the tree's signature attribute: the outer bark exfoliates in large, curling, papery sheets throughout the year, revealing the inner bark in a complex palette of salmon-pink, cream, cinnamon-brown, and reddish-tan tones — a year-round ornamental effect that is one of the finest bark displays of any tree in cultivation. In winter when the tree is bare of leaves, the multi-trunked form with its layered, peeling, multi-colored bark is truly spectacular against a winter sky. Heritage is also one of the most heat-tolerant birches — unlike white or paper birch that decline in the heat of zone 7 and warmer, Heritage river birch thrives through zone 9 in moist to wet sites, making it the birch of choice for the Gulf South. It is highly resistant to bronze birch borer, which devastates most white birch species in the eastern United States. The naturally multi-trunked form and year-round bark display make Heritage an exceptional specimen and focal-point tree.

common_name: Heritage Rose (Classic David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1984, Heritage is one of the most beloved and enduring early English roses, carrying soft shell-pink, cupped, shallowly rosetted blooms with a distinctive lemony myrrh fragrance that helped define the fragrance profile many gardeners now associate with English roses. Its graceful, arching, densely foliaged shrub and reliably repeat-blooming habit from late spring through frost have kept it in continuous cultivation for decades, and it remains a benchmark for softness of color and fragrance among pink English roses.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light. Herme is a long-established, historic Camellia japonica cultivar with roots tracing back to Japan, producing semi-double flowers with an irregular, ever-varying marbled pattern of soft pink, deeper rose, and white, so that individual blooms on the same shrub display a range of patterning rather than an identical, uniform color. This unpredictable variegation has made it a favorite among camellia collectors for generations. It blooms in winter into early spring on an evergreen shrub with the same glossy, dark green foliage typical of the species, and benefits from consistent moisture, acidic soil, and protection from harsh afternoon sun.

Plant in moist, well-drained, average garden soil in partial to full shade; Hicks Yew is a columnar hybrid between English yew (Taxus baccata) and Japanese yew (Taxus cuspidata) that combines the deep-shade tolerance of its parents with markedly better cold hardiness, making it one of the most dependable evergreen conifers for foundation planting, screening, and formal hedging as far north as USDA zone 4. Its naturally upright, multi-stemmed, vase-shaped habit needs little corrective pruning to stay narrow, though it accepts shearing readily for a tighter formal hedge. The dark, glossy, flattened needles hold their color through winter, and female plants set small red arils in fall that attract birds, though the seed inside the aril and every other part of the plant contain toxic taxine alkaloids. Unlike most evergreens, Hicks Yew performs equally well on the shaded north side of a building as it does in full sun, and it tolerates urban pollution and heavy clay so long as drainage is adequate.

common_name: High Fragrance Camellia (Exceptionally Fragrant Blush-Pink Hybrid Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; High Fragrance is one of the most important fragrant camellia cultivars — a hybrid between Camellia japonica and the fragrant species C. lutchuensis that produces the elegant, refined flowers of japonica combined with a genuine sweet, jasmine-like fragrance that is absent from the vast majority of camellia varieties. Most camellia flowers, despite their beauty, are essentially scentless — the discovery that crossing with the fragrant C. lutchuensis could introduce lasting fragrance into hybrid offspring was a significant horticultural development. High Fragrance produces medium-sized, semi-double to peony-form flowers in soft blush-pink to white-with-pink tones in late winter to early spring — the same season as other camellias — with a sweet, clean fragrance detectable several feet from the plant under favorable conditions. The fragrance intensity is variable with temperature: warm, calm mornings amplify the scent; cold or windy conditions reduce it. The plant grows as a medium-sized, evergreen shrub with the characteristic glossy, dark-green camellia foliage. An outstanding choice for planting near entryways, patios, and garden seating areas where the fragrance can be appreciated. In zone 9, High Fragrance is a reliable perennial shrub that blooms most heavily in late January–March.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; High Hat camellia produces large, formal flowers on a compact, upright shrub. Large, formal double flowers open a clear, soft pink with neatly overlapping, evenly arranged petals in a classic, symmetrical form long favored by camellia show exhibitors, blooming over a long winter and early spring season on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub. Its reliable, high-quality flower form and manageable, upright habit have made it a long-standing favorite among camellia collectors and show growers seeking dependable, exhibition-quality blooms without a sprawling mature size. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid overhead watering which can spot the delicate petals, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Himalayan hydrangea is a large, vigorous shrub to small tree from the Himalayan foothills, producing broad, flat lacecap flower clusters in creamy white in early summer, larger and often earlier-blooming than many familiar garden hydrangeas. As the shrub matures over several years, the bark begins to peel and flake in attractive cinnamon-brown patches, giving it worthwhile winter interest well beyond its bloom season — a feature few other hydrangeas offer. Its eventual large size makes it best suited to a woodland-edge planting, the back of a large shrub border, or as a specimen with high, filtered shade from taller trees, rather than a small foundation bed. It flowers on the current season's growth, so any pruning to control size or shape is best done in late winter before new growth begins, without sacrificing that year's bloom. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, since hydrangeas wilt quickly when the soil dries out.

Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Himalayan indigo is a large, graceful, arching shrub or subshrub from the mountain forests and open slopes of the Himalayas, producing an extraordinary profusion of rose-pink to magenta-pink, tiny pea flowers in dense, pendulous racemes from June through September — covering the sweeping, arching branches so densely during the flowering peak that the individual branches are almost obscured by bloom. The elegant, pinnate foliage is soft-gray-green throughout the season, creating an attractive textural complement to the vivid flower clusters. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen and improves poor soils. Himalayan indigo is one of the finest long-blooming shrubs for full sun in temperate gardens — combining drought tolerance, extended bloom, attractive foliage, and a graceful weeping habit in a plant that is still relatively little-known outside specialist gardens. Prune hard to the ground or to 6 inches in late winter to maintain compact, vigorous, floriferous growth.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Hindu Rope hoya is slow-growing and blooms most reliably when left undisturbed and slightly pot-bound for years. Thick, waxy leaves curl and twist tightly along densely contorted stems that coil like braided rope, an unusual crinkled mutation of the common wax plant that gives this cultivar a sculptural, almost knotted texture unlike any other hoya, eventually producing the same fragrant, star-shaped pink flower clusters as the straight species once mature. Slow-growing and long-lived, it is a classic heirloom houseplant often passed down through generations, thriving for decades in the same pot with minimal repotting, since disturbing an established, pot-bound plant can set back or delay flowering for years. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright indirect light, and resist the urge to repot frequently, since this cultivar flowers best when left undisturbed.

common_name: Hino Crimson Azalea (Brilliant Red Small-Leaf Compact Kurume Azalea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Hino Crimson is a Kurume azalea cultivar producing one of the most vivid red flower displays of any small-leaf azalea — masses of brilliant, intense red single flowers in spring that cover the plant completely at peak bloom, creating a display significantly more vividly red than the pink-to-pink-red tones of most other azaleas. The very small leaves (typical Kurume fine texture) and compact, mounded habit make Hino Crimson one of the most refined and formal-looking of the spring-blooming azaleas — a tight, dense, naturally rounded shrub that requires minimal pruning to maintain its shape. The cold-hardiness of Hino Crimson (to zone 5) exceeds that of Southern Indica and most other azalea groups, making it adaptable to a broader geographic range, including the cooler portions of zone 9 where indica types can be borderline. In Gulf South zone 9, Hino Crimson is a reliable, long-lived evergreen foundation shrub that blooms dependably each March–April. The intense red color makes it particularly striking in mass plantings along walks and driveways where the simultaneous red bloom creates a powerful seasonal display. Planted where early morning sun can backlight the flowers, the vivid red becomes almost incandescent — one of the most spectacular light effects achievable in the spring garden.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun; holly olive (false holly, holly-leaved osmanthus) is a versatile Japanese evergreen shrub that combines two highly desirable landscape qualities that rarely coexist — the bold, spiny, holly-like foliage that deters deer and unwanted entry, and the extraordinarily fragrant, small, white flowers that perfume the autumn garden with a powerful, sweet, apricot-like scent similar to but distinct from the related tea olive (O. fragrans). The spiny, glossy, dark-green leaves closely resemble English holly leaves, creating a formal, polished effect in the landscape; several cultivars offer gold-, white-, or purple-tinted foliage. It tolerates partial shade, dry soil, and urban conditions far better than most broadleaf evergreens. 'Goshiki' (cream, green, and pink variegated), 'Rotundifolius' (small, rounded, spineless leaves), 'Purpureus' (deep-purple new growth), and 'Gulftide' (compact, cold-hardy) are widely grown selections. More deer-resistant than almost any comparable shrub due to the spiny foliage.

Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; holly-leaf sweetspire is an evergreen Chinese shrub with glossy, spiny-toothed, holly-like leaves that give year-round structure to a shaded border. In late summer it produces long, slender, pendulous racemes of small greenish-white flowers dangling like tassels or catkins from the branch tips, a bloom time and form unlike almost any other shade shrub and valuable for extending seasonal interest past the usual spring shrub display. It is somewhat less cold hardy and slower to establish than its deciduous North American cousin, Virginia sweetspire, so site it in a sheltered spot out of harsh winter wind in the colder part of its range. Mulch well and water during dry spells in the first two years, after which established plants tolerate normal garden conditions with only moderate care.

Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, dry to average soil in full sun; holm oak is the iconic evergreen oak of the Mediterranean Basin — a massive, dark, brooding, evergreen tree with small, dark green, holly-like leaves (hence both 'holm' from Old English 'holly' and the species epithet ilex meaning 'holm oak'). It forms the characteristic dark green groves and monte bajo of southern Europe and North Africa. In California, holm oak has been planted for over a century and shows excellent adaptation to the Mediterranean climate — drought-tolerant, long-lived, and providing deep, dense shade year-round. The acorns are small and bitter, but the related Holm oak variety (Quercus ilex subsp. ballota) from Portugal and Spain produces sweet, edible acorns eaten raw or roasted — the famous Spanish 'bellota' acorn eaten by Ibérico pigs. An excellent large evergreen tree for hot, dry climates in zones 7–10.

Honey locust is one of the most broadly adaptable native trees in North America, tolerating alkaline soils, periodic flooding, urban air pollution, road salt, and heat that defeat other trees — widely planted as a tough street and lawn tree in the form of thornless, podless cultivars developed from its natural variety inermis. The feathery, twice-pinnately compound leaves create dappled shade that allows turf and understory plants to grow beneath the canopy more easily than under most large shade trees; the fine-textured leaves also break down quickly in fall without raking. Wild trees produce massive, twisted, dark brown seed pods up to 18 inches long that contain sweet pulp historically eaten by wildlife and indigenous peoples, and formidable branching thorns several inches long; select thornless, seedless cultivars for most landscape uses. Native pollinators, especially short-tongued bees, visit the inconspicuous but very fragrant creamy-white flower clusters heavily in spring, making honey locust an underappreciated urban pollinator plant.

Honeycup (or Powdery Zenobia) is a stunning native shrub, native to wet pine savannas, pocosins, bog edges, and seepage slopes of the coastal plain from North Carolina to northern Florida, where it grows with fetterbush, inkberry, and swamp azalea in highly acidic, peaty, wet soils. In June and July it produces dangling clusters of lily-of-the-valley-scented, white, bell-shaped flowers on gracefully arching stems — the flowers are honey-sweet in fragrance and highly attractive to native bees. The distinctive glaucous (powdery blue-green) leaves are semi-evergreen to deciduous depending on the winter, and the shrub slowly spreads by stolons to form loose colonies. Grow in wet, highly acidic soil in partial shade; it is excellent companion to Atlantic white cedar, blueberries, and swamp azaleas in a native bog or rain garden planting. Avoid alkaline or dry conditions, which are fatal.

Propagate by air-layering or cuttings (this sterile hybrid sets no seed) or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Hong Kong orchid tree is a sterile hybrid flowering tree and the floral emblem of Hong Kong — one of the most spectacular flowering trees for zone 9–12, producing enormous, deep-rose-purple to magenta-crimson, orchid-like flowers up to 6 inches across that appear in great abundance from autumn through late spring on the arching branches, creating a brilliant and prolonged display of large, showy, fragrant tropical flowers at the cooler end of the year. The large, uniquely bilobed, rounded, butterfly-wing leaves (characteristic of all Bauhinia species) are attractive year-round. Because it is a sterile triploid hybrid, it does not set seed and has no invasive potential — unlike many other Bauhinia species that self-seed aggressively — making it the preferred choice for ecological responsible planting. It flowers for the longest season of any Bauhinia and is widely considered the most ornamental. Tolerates partial shade acceptably. Excellent as a specimen or small shade tree in the tropical or subtropical garden.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; hop tree is a native small tree or large shrub found naturally in woodland edges, river bluffs, and dry rocky hillsides from southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, highly unusual among small trees in its genuine shade-tolerance — it grows in understory conditions beneath taller trees where most ornamentals fail. The common names derive from its two most notable features: the distinctive, round, wafer-like seed capsules (samaras) that ripen in fall and were historically used as a substitute for hops in brewing, and the compound leaves with three leaflets that carry a strong, distinctive aroma when crushed. Clusters of small, greenish-white flowers in early summer attract many pollinators but are unshowy — the ornamental interest lies in the attractive trifoliate foliage, yellow fall color, and the striking, papery, disc-like fruits that hang in clusters and rattle in winter wind. Most importantly, it is the primary and preferred larval host plant of the giant swallowtail butterfly (Papilio cresphontes), North America's largest butterfly, and a significant host for the tiger swallowtail as well.

common_name: Hopi Crape Myrtle (Medium Pink Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hopi is a compact, semi-dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle that reaches 7–10 feet — smaller than the tree-sized Tonto and Sioux but larger than the truly dwarf compact selections — producing medium-pink to clear rose-pink flowers from July through September in dense, upright clusters. The clear, medium-pink flower color is one of the cleanest and most pleasing pinks in the crape myrtle palette — brighter and more saturated than the light lavender-pink of the large-tree Muskogee but softer and more feminine than the hot-pink Sioux. Hopi has perhaps the best mildew resistance rating of any National Arboretum crape myrtle, making it especially valuable in humid Gulf Coast climates where powdery mildew can be a persistent problem with older crape myrtle cultivars. The compact, upright-spreading habit with attractive exfoliating bark and reliable orange to red fall foliage provides year-round interest. Hopi's manageable size makes it one of the most versatile crape myrtles for typical residential lot sizes, appropriate for foundation plantings, screening masses, and specimen use without requiring restriction pruning that destroys the natural form. Remove only dead and crossing branches; never top.

common_name: Horsehead Philodendron (Oak Leaf Philodendron, Laciniatum Philodendron)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Horsehead Philodendron grows fastest and develops its most dramatic leaf lobing in consistent bright indirect light, though it tolerates lower light levels than many collector aroids without obvious deterioration. Philodendron pedatum is a climbing philodendron native to Venezuela, Trinidad, Guyana, and northern Brazil, readily identifiable by its uniquely shaped adult leaves — deeply and irregularly lobed into three to five distinct sections in a pattern that, viewed from certain angles, resembles the silhouette of a horse's head (hence 'Horsehead Philodendron') or the lobed shape of an oak leaf (hence 'Oak Leaf Philodendron'). The leaf shape is significantly more complex than most climbing philodendrons: a broad primary lobe is flanked by smaller lateral lobes, and the arrangement of these lobes relative to the petiole attachment creates a distinctive, almost sculptural leaf form that changes in complexity as the plant matures on a climbing support. The leaves are glossy, medium-green, leathery, and held on long petioles. Philodendron pedatum is one of the most available and most adaptable of the lobed-leaf climbing philodendrons, growing more vigorously and tolerating imperfect conditions better than the demanding collector types. It has been used extensively in hybridization, notably as a parent of the popular 'Philodendron Florida Green' and related Florida hybrid series. All parts are toxic.

common_name: Hot Lips Salvia (Bicolor Jame Salvia, Red-and-White Sage)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Hot Lips is one of the most popular and widely planted ornamental salvias for Gulf Coast gardens — a Salvia × jamensis hybrid (a cross between S. greggii and S. microphylla) producing a striking and unusual bicolor flower pattern: each small tubular flower displays pure white lower lip with red upper lip, creating a vivid two-toned effect that gives the plant its theatrical name. The bicolor pattern is highly variable and temperature-dependent — in cool weather (fall, spring) the flowers display more white; in heat they shift toward more red; some flowers may be entirely red or entirely white. This variability is part of the cultivar's charm — the same plant displays different flower color proportions through the seasons. Hot Lips blooms continuously from spring through fall in zone 9, with the most intense flower production in the cooler months of spring and fall. Hummingbirds are strongly attracted to the red tubular flowers. The compact, mounding habit stays 18–30 inches and is virtually maintenance-free — light trimming after each bloom flush encourages fresh growth and continued flowering. Unlike larger shrubby salvias, Hot Lips is scaled for small gardens and container culture. Extraordinarily drought-tolerant once established; excellent in rock gardens and full-sun mixed borders.

common_name: Hotspot Rose Autumn Sage (Compact Deep-Rose Salvia greggii Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Hotspot Rose is a compact Salvia greggii cultivar selected for a more refined, tidy habit than older autumn sage varieties — producing the same long-season rose-pink flowers and exceptional drought and heat tolerance as standard S. greggii but on a more compact, self-shaping plant of 18–24 inches that requires less frequent hard cutting back to maintain attractive form. The deep rose-pink to cerise-pink flower color is vivid and saturated — more intensely pink than the pastel pink of some selections — and maintains its color through the Gulf South summer heat without fading. In zone 9, Hotspot Rose blooms continuously from spring through hard frost with particularly heavy flushes in spring (March–May) and fall (September–November). The compact habit makes Hotspot Rose outstanding for defined border edging, container use, and mass plantings in small residential landscape beds where the larger older selections would be out of scale. Like all Salvia greggii cultivars, Hotspot Rose is attractive to hummingbirds and native bees throughout the bloom season and highly resistant to deer browsing. The compact habit means less aggressive annual cutback is required compared to large-growing types — remove the previous year's woody stems to 6 inches in late February to promote vigorous spring growth.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Howard McMinn manzanita needs excellent drainage and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot. Smooth, deep mahogany-red bark and glossy, rounded evergreen leaves cover a dense, mounding shrub topped with small clusters of pink-tinged white, urn-shaped flowers in late winter that are an important early nectar source for native bees and hummingbirds, followed by small berry-like fruit favored by birds. One of the most widely planted and reliably garden-tolerant manzanita cultivars, valued for its adaptability to a wider range of garden conditions than many finickier manzanita species while retaining the group's signature smooth red bark and drought tolerance. Water only during the first year or two of establishment, then rely on natural rainfall alone, and avoid summer water, rich soil, and heavy mulch piled against the trunk, all of which shorten the plant's life.

common_name: Hoya pubicalyx (Silver Pink Hoya, Purple Rain Hoya, Wax Vine)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a fast-draining, well-aerated potting mix; Hoya pubicalyx is one of the most vigorous and free-flowering of the commonly available Hoyas, producing its distinctive clusters of star-shaped flowers more readily than many other species. Hoya pubicalyx is a twining, semi-succulent epiphytic vine from the Philippines in the family Apocynaceae, producing long, trailing stems clothed in narrow, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves that are often lightly flecked or mottled with silver-gray spots — giving the species the common name 'Silver Pink Hoya.' The flowers are the defining ornamental feature: each umbellate cluster contains 20–40 individual star-shaped flowers in shades from deep burgundy-red to pink-purple (varying with cultivar and light intensity), each flower centered with a contrasting pink-white corona — the entire cluster has an almost candied, jewel-like appearance. The flowers exude a sweet, spicy, slightly chocolatey fragrance most intense in the evening. Multiple cultivars exist: 'Silver Pink' (dark burgundy-purple flowers), 'Red Buttons' (deep red flowers), 'Chimera' (variegated form). Like all Hoyas, the plant produces a milky latex sap when cut — avoid skin contact. Non-toxic to pets.

Huisache is the quintessential flowering shrub/small tree of the Gulf Coast prairies and south Texas brush country — in late winter and early spring, before the leaves fully expand, the tree explodes into thousands of brilliant golden-yellow, intensely fragrant pompom flowers that can be smelled from considerable distance and create one of the most spectacular natural wildflower spectacles of the Gulf Coastal Plain. The flowers are harvested commercially in the South of France for perfume production (the variety 'Cassia' provides notes in many classic French perfumes), and the honey produced from huisache nectar is highly prized among Texas beekeepers for its unusual floral sweetness. Trees grow rapidly in full sun in a wide range of soils including alkaline clay and caliche common to south-central Texas, making them well-suited for low-maintenance landscape uses in zone 8–11 where their winter-to-spring bloom fills the gap when little else is flowering. Armed with paired white spines — use caution when planting near walkways and children's play areas.

Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; Hummingbird is a naturally dwarf, spreading selection of the native Southeastern shrub summersweet, staying compact and dense where the wild species can grow considerably taller. In mid-to-late summer it produces upright spikes of small, intensely fragrant white flowers that draw bees and butterflies in large numbers, followed by attractive seed capsules that persist into winter. It spreads slowly by suckers to form a low colony over time, tolerates wet, poorly drained sites better than most shrubs, and is one of the more reliable flowering shrubs for shady, damp corners of the garden.

Plant acorns in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; Hungarian oak is one of the most impressive and stately deciduous oaks of southeastern Europe — a massive, broadly spreading tree with exceptionally large, deeply pinnately lobed leaves (up to 10 inches long with large, rounded lobes) that are among the largest of any oak. Native to the open parkland forests, mixed deciduous forests, and scrubland of the Balkan Peninsula, Hungary, Italy, and southeastern Europe. Has become an important ornamental tree in western European and British gardens for its bold, large-leaved texture and massive, spreading form. More tolerant of heavy clay soils and moderate drought than most large-leaved European oaks. Relatively fast-growing for an oak. In the UK, the hybrid with sessile oak (Quercus x hispanica 'Lucombeana', the Lucombe oak) is a very ornamental semi-evergreen cultivar derived from Hungarian oak. An outstanding specimen tree for large landscape sites where maximum leaf impact and bold texture are desired.

Plant in full to partial sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Hybrid Deutzia tolerates a wide range of soil types as long as drainage is adequate. In late spring the gracefully arching branches are smothered in clusters of white to pale pink flowers that make this compact 3–5 ft shrub one of the most floriferous in the garden. Prune immediately after flowering by cutting one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each year; this keeps the plant vigorous and prevents the centre from becoming congested. Foliage is notably clean and disease-resistant, making it an easy-care alternative to more demanding flowering shrubs.

Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid flowering quince (Chaenomeles x superba) is the cross between the Japanese flowering quince (C. japonica, dwarf) and the Chinese flowering quince (C. speciosa, large) — a group of widely grown, compact, early-spring-flowering shrubs producing an outstanding display of flowers in red, pink, orange, salmon, white, or bicolor combinations before or as the leaves emerge. The parent of many of the most commonly sold cultivars including 'Crimson and Gold' (red with gold stamens), 'Jet Trail' (white), 'Nicoline' (scarlet), and 'Pink Lady' (salmon-rose). Blooms very early in the season — one of the first shrubs to flower in late winter/early spring — and the flowers are frost-tolerant. The small, hard, yellow-green fruits (like tiny hard quinces) that follow are edible when cooked and used for jellies, jams, and flavoring in some Asian and European cuisines. Thorny stems create good wildlife cover. One of the most dependable and widely grown early-spring flowering shrubs in temperate gardens.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; hybrid witch-hazel is a cross between Japanese witch-hazel (Hamamelis japonica) and Chinese witch-hazel (H. mollis) and includes the most spectacular named garden cultivars of any witch-hazel — producing their strap-petaled, spidery flowers in January and February directly on leafless branches, providing color at the darkest time of year when almost nothing else is blooming. The flowers are heavily and sweetly fragrant and can be enjoyed cut indoors. Outstanding named cultivars include 'Arnold Promise' (clear yellow, most cold-hardy), 'Jelena' (luminous copper-orange), 'Diane' (deep red to garnet), and 'Ruby Glow' (copper-red). Fall foliage is outstanding in orange, red, and yellow. Hybrid witch-hazels are larger and more vigorous than either parent, eventually forming large multi-stem shrubs or small trees to 15 feet across.

common_name: Ice Chip Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile White Buddleja)
notes: Ice Chip is the white-flowered counterpart to Blue Chip in the dwarf, sterile Lo and Behold butterfly bush series, staying under three feet tall and wide while producing a continuous supply of pure white flower spikes from summer through frost. Its low, mounding, sterile habit avoids the self-seeding concerns associated with larger Buddleja davidii cultivars, fitting containers, small borders, and foundation plantings where standard butterfly bush would quickly outgrow the space. Like its siblings in the series it draws butterflies and hummingbirds heavily despite its small size, tolerates heat and drought well once established, and needs only the same annual hard cutback in late winter to stay compact and floriferous.

Plant rooted cuttings in average, well-drained soil and keep evenly watered the first season as the trailing stems root along their length and knit into a dense mat. Trim back hard in early spring if growth becomes leggy or if any solid-green shoots revert, since the gold coloring is less vigorous than the plain species. The rounded leaves are centered in bright gold with a narrow dark green margin, brightening shaded ground far more than typical periwinkle, and single lavender-blue flowers appear in spring. It is useful as a slow, low, colorful groundcover for erosion control or filling gaps under shrubs where little sun reaches the soil.

common_name: Illusion Emerald Lace Sweet Potato Vine (Finely Cut Lacy-Leaf Ornamental Vine)
notes: Illusion Emerald Lace stands apart from most ornamental sweet potato vine cultivars for its finely dissected, almost ferny bright green leaves, a delicate lacy texture that reads very differently from the broad, heart-shaped or lobed leaves of cultivars like Margarita or Blackie. The airy foliage trails and cascades over container edges without the visual heaviness of larger-leaved selections, making it a useful filler texture in mixed plantings alongside bolder companions. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it is just as heat-tolerant and fast-growing as other ornamental sweet potato vines through the peak of Gulf South summer, needing only occasional trimming to keep it in scale.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Incrediball is the improved Annabelle — a next-generation smooth hydrangea cultivar bred with significantly stronger, stiffer stems than the classic Annabelle that was notorious for stem flopping under the weight of the enormous flower heads in rain. The problem with Annabelle was that the giant 10–12 inch white flower heads would weigh down and collapse the flexible stems in wet weather, leaving the entire plant prostrate on the ground. Incrediball solves this with substantially stronger stems that hold the enormous flower heads upright even in heavy rain and wet conditions. The flower heads are similarly giant — up to 12 inches in diameter — in the same brilliant white as Annabelle, and the plant has the same new-wood blooming habit (can be cut back hard in late winter and still flowers prolifically the same season). In every practical characteristic, Incrediball is an upgrade over Annabelle: same giant white flowers, same performance in shade, same easy care, but with stems strong enough to support the flowers in all conditions. Like Annabelle, Incrediball is one of the most cold-hardy hydrangeas (to zone 3) and one of the most reliable bloomers across a wide range of conditions in zone 9 with afternoon shade.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil; Erythrina variegata is remarkably drought tolerant once established — deep, infrequent watering promotes deep root development, and established trees require little supplemental irrigation in subtropical conditions. Erythrina variegata (Indian Coral Tree, Tiger's Claw, or Variegated Coral Tree) is a large, fast-growing deciduous tree native to tropical coastal forests, mangrove edges, and tidal shorelines from the Indian subcontinent through Southeast Asia to the western Pacific islands, where its brilliant scarlet-to-orange, narrowly cylindrical pea-family flowers appear in dense terminal racemes on bare, thorny branches in the dry season before leaf-out — creating one of the most dramatic floral displays of any large tropical tree. The species epithet 'variegata' references a widely grown ornamental cultivar with bold yellow leaf variegation. The soft, lightweight, easily carved wood has been used across South and Southeast Asia for traditional canoe outriggers, floats, and knife handles, and the tree is deeply woven into Balinese Hindu ritual culture where it appears in temple gardens and ceremonial use. In Southeast Asian countries it is widely planted as a street tree and temple tree, blooming spectacularly in the dry season. A nitrogen-fixer in the legume family, it enriches soils around it. Excellent large specimen tree for tropical and warm subtropical gardens.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Indian Hawthorn (Raphiolepis indica) is arguably the most widely planted evergreen foundation shrub in Gulf Coast landscapes, carpeting suburban front yards from Houston to Jacksonville with its compact mounding form and clusters of fragrant pink or white apple-blossom flowers in February–April. The glossy, dark-evergreen leaves are leathery and handsome year-round; after bloom, small blue-black berries develop that attract mockingbirds and cedar waxwings. Dozens of named varieties exist in commerce ranging from 6-inch ground covers to 6-foot tall hedge plants: 'Olivia' (low-mounding, large white flowers), 'Eleanor Tabor' (pink flowers, dwarf), 'Clara' (white flowers, compact), 'Majestic Beauty' (upright, to 6 feet), and 'Indian Princess' (pink, very dwarf). Indian Hawthorn is exceptionally drought, heat, and salt spray tolerant — making it a top choice for coastal Gulf South gardens, highway medians, and HOA foundation beds that receive minimal irrigation or care. Entomosporium leaf spot is the primary disease in humid conditions; plant in locations with good air circulation and avoid wetting foliage with irrigation. Prune immediately after spring bloom to maintain shape without sacrificing the following year's flower buds.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Indian hawthorn tolerates part shade but blooms more heavily and stays more compact with at least 6 hours of direct sun. Rhaphiolepis indica is a rugged, compact, rounded evergreen shrub native to southern China that has become one of the most widely planted landscape shrubs in the Deep South, Gulf Coast, and California for good reason — it combines attractive dark-green, leathery, serrated leaves with clusters of fragrant, 5-petaled, white to deep-pink flowers in spring (and often again in fall), followed by small, blue-black berries that attract birds, all on a compact, tidy plant that requires minimal maintenance. It is outstanding for coastal landscapes — tolerating salt spray, poor sandy soils, and coastal wind exposure that defeats most shrubs. The cultivar 'Eleanor Taber' has deep-pink flowers; 'Ballerina' is compact with rosy-pink flowers; 'Spring Rapture' has rose-red flowers. Indian hawthorn is susceptible to Entomosporium leaf spot (especially in humid climates) — give plants good air circulation and avoid overhead irrigation to minimize this problem. Prune immediately after spring bloom only to shape.

common_name: Indian Laurel (Chinese Banyan, Laurel Fig, Cuban Laurel)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Indian Laurel is broadly adaptable to soil types but the aggressive surface roots require careful placement away from pavement and structures. Ficus microcarpa (Indian Laurel, Chinese Banyan, or Cuban Laurel) is the Ficus species most commonly used as a street tree in South Florida, Gulf Coast cities, and subtropical regions worldwide — lining downtown boulevards in Miami, Houston, New Orleans, and countless Gulf Coast municipalities with its massive, dense, dark-green canopy. In tropical climates, mature trees develop spectacular aerial roots that cascade from branches and eventually thicken into secondary trunks, creating the multi-trunked banyan tree form. A 150-year-old specimen can cover an acre of ground. The 'Green Island' cultivar (Ficus microcarpa 'Green Island') is a compact, slow-growing selection with small, rounded, thick leaves and a controlled habit (6–8 feet) that makes an outstanding shade-tolerant foundation or container plant without the invasive root system of the straight species. Ficus microcarpa is the primary host plant of the invasive fig gall wasp (Josephiella) and laurel fig thrips in some regions — consult local extension services before large-scale planting in natural areas.

Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest, as viability declines rapidly; plant one to two seeds per deep root-trainer pot or directly in the ground at a depth of 0.5-1 inch, covering lightly with moist soil. Germination typically occurs within 2-4 weeks in warm, humid conditions above 72°F, and seedlings should be watered consistently but not waterlogged during the first growing season. The Indian mast tree is prized for its dramatically columnar, weeping habit and its tolerance of heat, drought, and urban pollution once established, making it an outstanding choice for avenue planting, windbreaks, or as a vertical accent in tropical landscapes. Feed young trees monthly with a balanced fertilizer through the first two years to encourage rapid development of the characteristic tall, narrow silhouette.

growth_habit: South Asian timber and shade tree
notes: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile to average soil; Dalbergia sissoo is drought tolerant once established, fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root symbiosis, and can improve soil fertility on degraded or depleted sites — water regularly only in the first year of establishment. Dalbergia sissoo (Indian Rosewood, Sheesham, or Sissoo) is a large, fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing deciduous legume tree native to the Indo-Gangetic Plain foothills, riverine forests, and lower Himalayan slopes of India, Nepal, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan, where it is one of the most important and commercially valuable timber trees of South Asia. The dense, interlocked, dark-brown to reddish-brown heartwood is among the finest furniture, carving, flooring, and musical instrument timbers of the region, with extraordinary durability and beautiful figuring. A nitrogen-fixer in the legume family (Fabaceae), Dalbergia sissoo enriches impoverished soils through atmospheric nitrogen fixation and organic matter return. Small, fragrant, pale-pink to whitish pea-family flowers attract pollinators. Trees are widely planted across India, Pakistan, and the Middle East as street trees, windbreaks, and shade trees for their fast growth, nitrogen-fixing soil improvement, drought tolerance, and ornamental foliage with rounded, tri-foliate, bright-green leaflets. It has naturalized in parts of Florida and the Caribbean and can become invasive — plant with awareness of local invasive status.

Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun — inkberry is a native evergreen holly shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, growing naturally in bogs, pocosins, pine flatwoods, and moist woodland margins. It tolerates shade, wet soil, and flooding conditions that defeat most other shrubs. The small black berries in late summer and fall are consumed by dozens of bird species including wild turkeys, wood ducks, and bluebirds; bees (especially Melittidae oil-collecting bees) work the small white flowers in spring. It spreads steadily by suckering roots and can form dense, wildlife-shelter colonies over time. Named cultivars include 'Shamrock' (compact, mounding) and 'Densa' (dense form). An outstanding native evergreen for wet, acidic soils where Rhododendron and Kalmia cannot be grown. Plants are dioecious — both male and female plants are needed for berry production.

Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry is exceptionally tolerant of wet feet and periodic flooding, unusual among broadleaf evergreens, and also handles drier upland soils once established. Ilex glabra is a native evergreen holly of the wet pinelands, pocosins, and coastal plain wetlands of the eastern and Gulf Coast United States, valued in the landscape as a fine-textured, small-leaved, boxwood-like substitute that thrives in acidic, poorly drained soils where boxwood struggles. Small, inconspicuous white flowers in late spring give way, on female plants, to small black berries that persist into winter and are an important food source for songbirds. The dense, upright to rounded habit takes shearing well, making it a popular choice for a low hedge, foundation planting, or naturalistic screen in a partly shaded woodland-edge landscape. A tough, adaptable, wildlife-valuable native evergreen for difficult wet or acidic sites, zone 4–9.

Select a dry, rocky, or sandy site in full sun with excellent drainage — this prairie native will not persist in heavy or consistently moist soil. Scarify seeds with sandpaper and cold-stratify for 60 days before sowing, or propagate from softwood cuttings in early summer. Once established, this nitrogen-fixing shrub improves soil and needs little supplemental water. Clusters of small white flowers in late spring attract native bees and butterflies, making it a valuable addition to a wildlife garden.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; intermediate fothergilla is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between small fothergilla (F. gardenii) and large fothergilla (F. major), combining the best traits of both parents — the compact habit of the dwarf parent with the larger flower heads and superior fall color of the tall parent. The fragrant, bottlebrush-like white flowers emerge before the leaves in early spring, offering a spectacular display of creamy puffball blooms on bare stems. The summer foliage of the cultivar 'Blue Shadow' is an unusually intense blue-green — among the most striking blue tones of any deciduous shrub — before turning a fiery combination of red, orange, and yellow in fall. A superb specimen shrub for woodland gardens, foundation plantings, and native shrub borders in zones 4–8, combining especially well with azaleas, mountain laurels, and other acid-loving shrubs.

Plant this floribunda rose in spring in a hole amended with compost, keeping the graft at soil level in colder zones. Clusters of richly fragrant purple-plum blooms appear from spring through fall on an elegant upright form, making a bold focal point. Provide full sun, well-drained soil, and consistent moisture, watering at the base to keep foliage dry. Prune in late winter to shape the plant and deadhead spent clusters to encourage repeat flowering.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Invincibelle Spirit was a breakthrough introduction as the first pink-blooming cultivar of native smooth hydrangea (the species behind the classic white Annabelle), producing rounded clusters of soft pink flowers on a native plant traditionally available only in white. Like Annabelle, it blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter and still flower reliably the same year, and it rebounds quickly from winter damage in colder zones. Its stems are somewhat sturdier than old Annabelle types but can still benefit from light staking in a very rainy, exposed site. It is a good pollinator plant and, being a native species selection, tends to be adaptable and low-maintenance across a range of soil conditions.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Issai is a compact, dwarf beautyberry selection that reliably sets heavy clusters of bright violet-purple berries even on young plants, without needing the several-year establishment period some beautyberries require before fruiting well. Its small mature size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and smaller gardens where the full-sized native American beautyberry would grow too large. It flowers and fruits on new wood, so cutting the shrub back hard to a foot or so from the ground each late winter encourages vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production the following fall.

common_name: Ivy Leaf Morning Glory (Ivy Morning Glory)
notes: Nick or file seeds and sow directly after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence for the twining stems. Ipomoea hederacea (ivy leaf morning glory) is a native North American morning glory producing ivy-shaped, three-lobed leaves that immediately distinguish it from common morning glories with heart-shaped foliage; the 1.5-to-2-inch flowers are sky-blue to pale blue to violet with a white throat, appearing profusely from summer through frost. The ivy-shaped foliage is the key ornamental distinction — it creates a finer texture and more elegant twining pattern on fences and trellises than the typical morning glory. This species is native to the eastern US and tropics and naturalizes readily in disturbed soils, roadsides, and old fields; it self-seeds abundantly and can spread aggressively in the landscape. It is valuable as a wildlife plant — the flowers provide nectar for bumblebees and the seeds feed native sparrows and mourning doves through winter. Zone 9 and warmer: treat as a warm-season annual that self-seeds reliably.

common_name: Ixora (Flame of the Woods, Jungle Geranium)
notes: Plant in strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; ixora is one of the most popular tropical flowering shrubs in the world, producing dense, rounded clusters of small tubular flowers in brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and white nearly year-round in frost-free gardens and spring through fall in zone 9. The flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) are 3–4 inches across and attract butterflies throughout the bloom season. It is a slow-growing, compact shrub and one of the best choices for formal hedges and foundation plantings in tropical and subtropical landscapes. The main cultural challenge is soil pH: ixora demands strongly acidic conditions (pH 5.0–6.0) and in the alkaline limestone soils of Florida and the Gulf Coast, iron and manganese deficiencies cause chronic yellowing. Use acidifying fertilizer specially formulated for ixora and apply chelated iron if chlorosis appears. Avoid 'lollipop pruning' (shearing into balls) which reduces blooming — prune lightly by selectively removing branches.

Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; jacaranda is a South American deciduous tree that is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world — in spring, before or as the leaves emerge, the entire tree becomes covered in masses of large, tubular, lavender-blue to violet-purple flowers arranged in billowing panicles that transform the canopy into a breathtaking cloud of blue-purple. The flowering display lasts 6–8 weeks and the fallen flowers carpet the ground beneath the tree in a second violet display. The finely divided, fern-like, bright-green, doubly-pinnate leaves are attractive through the growing season. Jacaranda is the definitive 'purple flowering tree' of warm-climate landscapes worldwide — seen lining streets in Los Angeles, Johannesburg, Sydney, and throughout zone 9–11 in the southern United States. It is frost-sensitive, with established trees tolerating brief dips to approximately 25°F in zone 9 — tops may be killed by hard freezes, but established root systems often resprout. Requires a dry season to flower most reliably. An iconic specimen tree for zone 9–11 gardens.

Plant with roots shaded and cool (mulch well or shade the base with low companion plants) while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis, fence, or other support. Introduced in England in 1862, Jackmanii is one of the most enduring and widely grown clematis cultivars ever bred, producing an abundance of large, velvety, deep purple flowers from early summer into fall. Because it flowers entirely on new growth, it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned hard, back to about a foot from the ground, in late winter, which keeps the vine vigorous and full of bloom rather than leggy and bare at the base. It is a tough, adaptable, long-lived vine that has introduced generations of gardeners to clematis.

Plant in spring in moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade against a trellis, fence, or tree for support; Smilax smallii climbs by tendrils and can reach 10–20 feet, providing dense evergreen coverage in shaded areas. Jackson brier is the most ornamental of the native southeastern Smilax species, producing long, lance-shaped, glossy dark green leaves on gracefully arching, somewhat thorny stems; it is the 'smilax' of traditional Southern floriculture — the garlands of small-leafed, shiny green vine used to decorate churches, ballrooms, and mantles throughout the South for weddings and holiday celebrations for well over 100 years. Small, greenish-white flowers in early spring are not showy but are fragrant, and small blue-black berries in fall are important food for mockingbirds, catbirds, and other wildlife. Valuable as a native evergreen shade vine in zone 7–10 landscapes.

Jade Butterflies is a dwarf, shrubby ginkgo selection that stays a densely branched mound only a few feet tall, a striking departure from the towering size of the straight species, with distinctive fan-shaped leaves that are often partly fused or folded, giving them a butterfly-like shape that inspired the cultivar name. Like the species it turns a brilliant, uniform gold in fall, and as a male selection it produces no fruit, avoiding the notoriously foul-smelling seed litter of female ginkgo trees. Extremely tough, pest- and disease-free, and adaptable to poor soil, heat, drought, and urban pollution, it works well as a specimen shrub, foundation planting, or container subject where a full-sized ginkgo tree would be far too large.

common_name: Jade Plant (Money Tree, Friendship Plant, Lucky Plant)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to full sun in very well-drained, gritty succulent potting mix; Jade Plant tolerates lower light conditions than most succulents but develops the most compact, well-colored foliage with bright indirect light or morning sun. Crassula ovata is a succulent shrub native to the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces of South Africa, where it grows in rocky hillsides and dry scrub in dry, well-drained conditions. Over its decades of cultivation as an ornamental houseplant worldwide, it has become one of the most recognizable and widely-owned plants on earth — practically ubiquitous in offices, homes, and gardens across every continent. The thick, oval, glossy, jade-green leaves with red-edged margins and the stout, woody, trunk-like stems that develop over years give well-grown specimens a miniature tree appearance highly prized in bonsai aesthetics. In zone 10–11, established outdoor plants produce clusters of small, star-shaped, pink to white flowers in winter, creating a charming seasonal display. In Asian cultures, Jade Plant is considered a symbol of good luck, financial prosperity, and friendship — 'money plant' is one of its most common names in Chinese and Japanese contexts. Single leaves placed on gritty soil root readily within weeks, making it one of the most freely propagated of all succulents.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in bright indirect light to full sun; provide very strong, substantial support structure — jade vine becomes massive. Strongylodon macrobotrys (jade vine or tayabak) is one of the most spectacularly beautiful and rarest flowering vines in cultivation — a Philippine rainforest legume producing extraordinary, cascading, 3-to-5-foot racemes of 75–100 large, claw-shaped, iridescent jade-blue-to-turquoise-green flowers whose unique color is essentially unmatched by any other flower. The jade-green flowers have an almost translucent, gemstone-like quality in sunlight. Jade vine is critically endangered in its native Philippine rainforest habitat due to deforestation and the disruption of its specialized bat and sunbird pollinators. The vine is massive and powerful in ideal conditions — growing to 60–70 feet and requiring very substantial support. It blooms in late winter to spring after a cool dry period. It is extraordinarily difficult to grow outside of tropical conditions (zone 11–12) and is primarily a botanical garden specimen; very rarely available in the nursery trade. For true tropical enthusiasts only. An extraordinary rarity of the plant world.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; Jamaica dogwood is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks of South Florida, the Keys, and the wider Caribbean basin. A member of the legume family, this fast-growing native tree produces showy clusters of pink-and-white, pea-shaped flowers in spring before new leaves emerge, followed by distinctive four-winged seed pods, and its bark and roots contain compounds historically used by Caribbean fishers to stun fish, giving the tree its 'fishpoison' common name — a traditional practice not appropriate or legal for casual use today. Highly salt- and wind-tolerant, it is well suited to coastal landscaping in South Florida, tolerating the sandy, well-drained soils and salt spray of shoreline plantings with little supplemental care once established. Water regularly while young, and provide the full sun and coastal exposure this tough, fast-growing native tree tolerates well in its home range.

common_name: James Galway Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, or train the more vigorous stems upward for extra height. Introduced by David Austin in 2005 and named for the celebrated flutist, James Galway produces large, full, rounded rosette flowers in a soft, warm pink with a strong old-rose fragrance carrying hints of myrrh, held on sturdy, slightly arching canes clothed in glossy, disease-resistant foliage. It repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost and its vigorous, adaptable habit suits both a mixed border and, with support, a short climbing position on a fence or trellis.

common_name: Jane Magnolia (Little Girl Series Compact Late-Blooming Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Jane is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated hybrid magnolia from the U.S. National Arboretum's 'Little Girl' breeding series (a cross of Magnolia liliiflora 'Nigra' and M. stellata 'Rosea'), producing large, fragrant, reddish-purple, tulip-shaped flowers with white interiors on a compact 10-15 foot tree — small enough to fit a modest yard where a full-size saucer magnolia would eventually overwhelm the space. Its key advantage over many early-spring-blooming magnolias is timing: it flowers noticeably later in spring than star and saucer magnolias, which often lose an entire season's bloom to a late freeze that damages open flowers, so Jane's later bloom window helps it dodge that common frustration. It sometimes produces a light rebloom later in summer as well. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture and avoid heavy pruning, since magnolias generally need little routine shaping beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained soil in partial shade, giving each plant 4–6 feet of space; Japanese andromeda is a four-season evergreen shrub notable for chains of white urn-shaped flowers in early spring that hang like lily-of-the-valley, glossy red or bronze new growth that gradually matures to dark green, and persistent buds that decorate the plant through winter. Protect from afternoon sun in hotter zones to prevent leaf scorch; afternoon shade extends its range into zone 7 and 8. Prune lightly after flowering to shape; deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage stronger bud-set for the following year. All parts are toxic if ingested.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to part shade; Japanese anise is a slow-growing, densely leafy evergreen shrub native to Japan and Taiwan, closely related to Florida anise (Illicium floridanum) but with wider cold hardiness and glossier foliage with a strong, pleasant anise-clove fragrance when crushed. In spring it produces small, cream-white to pale-yellow star-shaped flowers with many narrow petals — understated but charming close up, with the same star pattern as culinary star anise (I. verum) though unrelated in flavor. The foliage is the primary landscape asset: thick, lustrous, deep-green leaves densely arranged on upright stems creating a solid, refined mound of evergreen texture in shade gardens where few alternatives exist. It is outstanding as a shade-garden shrub under large trees, as an evergreen screen in shade, and in combination with hostas, hellebores, and woodland ferns. CAUTION: all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — the seeds resemble and may be confused with culinary star anise.

Divide rhizomatous colonies or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Japanese ardisia (marlberry, senryo-alternative) is a low-growing, spreading, evergreen Asian shrub that forms a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover in shaded conditions — the toothed, glossy, oval leaves in whorled clusters give the plant a neat, refined appearance throughout the year. Small, white, nodding flowers in summer are followed by clusters of brilliant red berries that persist through winter and into the following spring, providing attractive color at a season when little else is colorful in the shade garden. Plants spread by underground stolons to gradually colonize shaded areas, creating dense, uniform coverage under trees and in woodland settings. Much more cold-hardy than the invasive coral ardisia (A. crenata) and native to similar garden conditions. 'Hakutsuru' (white berries), 'Chirimen' (crinkled leaves), and 'Nishiki' (variegated) are cultivar selections.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Japanese beautyberry produces the most vivid violet-purple berries of any ornamental shrub — small, glossy, jewel-like fruits clustered in dense rings along arching stems in late summer and fall, giving a color intensity that photographs cannot fully capture. The effect is stunning both in the landscape and in cut floral arrangements. The foliage turns light yellow in fall before dropping to reveal the berries even more prominently against the bare stems. Unlike American beautyberry (C. americana), which can reach 8–10 feet and become ungainly, Japanese beautyberry stays more compact at 3–6 feet and is better behaved in the border. White-berried ('Leucocarpa') and pink-berried ('Albibaccata') cultivars offer interesting color variations alongside the typical violet-purple.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Japanese boxwood is a heat- and humidity-tolerant relative of Korean boxwood long used across the Southern United States for clipped hedges, foundation plantings, and parterre-style formal gardens, valued for its small, glossy, rounded leaves and dense, easily shaped growth. It handles the long, hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season better than English boxwood, which often struggles in southern zones, though it still requires sharp drainage since all boxwoods are prone to root rot in soggy soil. Shear one to two times a year to maintain a formal shape, or leave it looser and prune selectively for a more natural look, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the main pest to monitor in Southern plantings.

Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Japanese camellia is the quintessential flowering shrub of the American South, producing large, formal, rose-like flowers in red, pink, white, and bicolor combinations in late fall through early spring — when almost nothing else is in bloom. Over 30,000 named cultivars exist, ranging from single-flowered (most cold-hardy) to fully double (most spectacular). In zone 8–9 it is one of the most spectacular ornamental shrubs available: a mature, large-flowered camellia in full January bloom, covered in hundreds of perfect flowers, is one of the most breath-taking sights in any garden. It requires strongly acidic soil and will show iron and manganese deficiency chlorosis in neutral or alkaline conditions. Prune immediately after bloom in late spring before the following year's buds set. Scale insects and petal blight are the primary concerns — improve air circulation and treat scale with horticultural oil in late winter.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese clethra is a multi-stemmed large shrub or small tree from Japan that surpasses the popular native summersweet (C. alnifolia) in ornamental impact at a larger scale. The most distinctive feature is the exfoliating, cinnamon-colored bark that peels in attractive layers on mature stems — providing striking winter interest. The long, arching racemes of fragrant white flowers in midsummer attract countless butterflies and bees. Excellent fall color in shades of yellow and red. More tolerant of dry soil than C. alnifolia once established. An underused, three-season ornamental shrub for shaded woodland gardens, native plant borders, and naturalized settings.

Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to full shade; Japanese euonymus is one of the most widely used evergreen hedge and foundation shrubs in the southeastern US and mild-climate gardens worldwide — valued for its exceptional tolerance of deep shade, salt spray, air pollution, and a wide range of soil conditions. The thick, glossy, dark green leaves with finely toothed margins are attractive year-round, and the many cultivars offer gold-edged ('Aureomarginatus'), silver-edged ('Argenteomarginatus'), and yellow-centered ('Aureus') variegated leaf forms. A key advantage over many evergreen alternatives is its tolerance of deep shade — growing and maintaining dense, attractive foliage even in the shade of buildings or under tree canopies where most evergreen shrubs become thin and leggy. The main pest is euonymus scale (Unaspis euonymi) — small white and gray scale insects that can defoliate and kill plants if left untreated. An essential versatile evergreen for shaded foundation plantings, formal hedging, and coastal gardens in zones 6–9.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in partial to full shade; Japanese evergreen oak (akagashi in Japanese) is one of the most beautiful and important evergreen forest trees of Japan, Korea, and China — a relatively small (by oak standards) evergreen tree with glossy, dark green, simple, lanceolate to elliptic leaves and attractive pale-brown, smooth bark. In Japan it is an important forest tree of the warm-temperate evergreen broadleaf forest (laurel forest) zone along the Pacific coast. More shade-tolerant as a young tree than almost any other oak — it can grow as a woodland understory tree under a partial canopy where most oaks would be severely light-limited. The name 'akagashi' (red oak) in Japanese refers to the reddish new growth rather than any classification similarity to North American red oaks. An excellent evergreen shade tree for southeastern US gardens where a refined, glossy-leaved evergreen tree (unlike the course evergreen oaks) is desired. Rarely available but rewarding when found.

Plant in spring or fall in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Japanese flowering crabapple is among the most disease-resistant and reliably floriferous of all crabapple species, making it a lower-maintenance choice than many ornamental crabapple hybrids. Malus floribunda is a graceful, wide-spreading Japanese crabapple growing 15–25 feet tall with an equal or greater spread, famous for its spectacular spring display of deep rose-red to carmine buds that open to single white to pale pink flowers so profuse they completely cover the arching branches, followed by tiny (1/4 inch) red-and-yellow fruits that wildlife relish through fall and winter. It has outstanding resistance to apple scab, fire blight, and powdery mildew compared to many hybrid crabapples. Best used as a specimen tree where its graceful, weeping habit and spring floral display can be appreciated; needs full sun to bloom well.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese holly is a versatile evergreen shrub with small, dark-green, crenate (scalloped-edge) leaves that superficially resembles boxwood but is unrelated — it tolerates the same shearing and formal shaping, making it a popular boxwood substitute in regions where boxwood blight is problematic. The fine-textured, dense foliage is outstanding for formal hedges, mass plantings, and foundation shrubs. Small black berries are produced in fall and persist through winter but are inconspicuous. Key cultivars include 'Helleri' (very dwarf, spreading mound to 3×5 feet), 'Green Island' (open, spreading habit to 3–4 feet), 'Compacta' (dense, globular, 4–6 feet), and 'Sky Pencil' (dramatically narrow, columnar, 6–10 feet tall but only 2 feet wide). Japanese holly tolerates shade better than boxwood and performs reliably in zone 5–9. In zone 9, mulch root zone in summer to prevent heat stress.

Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Japanese honeysuckle is an extremely vigorous, twining evergreen vine with intensely fragrant white-to-yellow tubular flowers from late spring through summer that are one of the most recognizable scents of southern summers. However, it is classified as invasive or noxious across much of the eastern US, where it smothers native vegetation in forest understories and disturbed areas. For most planting situations, consider the native alternative coral honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) which is not invasive, hummingbird-pollinated, and equally ornamental. Japanese honeysuckle is useful for erosion control on steep, disturbed slopes where invasiveness is less of a concern.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial to full shade; Japanese hornbeam is the most ornamentally distinctive of all the hornbeams — the relatively large, prominently veined, dark green leaves are deeply ridged with parallel veins and have strongly toothed margins, combined with an outstanding fruiting display of large, hop-like pendulous clusters of closely overlapping, fan-shaped bracts surrounding each tiny nut, creating one of the most ornamental fruiting displays of any hornbeam. The fruiting catkins hang in pendulous strings of tightly packed, flat-winged structures that give the branches a distinctive appearance in summer and autumn. More compact and shade-tolerant than European hornbeam — an excellent choice for smaller gardens and for partially shaded positions under taller trees. Excellent fall color (yellow to orange). An underused but refined and highly ornamental small ornamental tree for shaded garden settings.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens against a shaded wall, large tree, or fence in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Japanese hydrangea vine is a closely related, often superior alternative to the beloved climbing hydrangea (Hydrangea petiolaris), attaching to surfaces by aerial rootlets and producing broad, flat-topped flower heads in midsummer — the lacecap-type inflorescences display a ring of enlarged, sterile 'ray flowers' consisting of a single, large, white, heart-shaped bract, each elegantly proportioned and more refined than the comparable structures on climbing hydrangea. Like climbing hydrangea, it is slow to establish but ultimately vigorous and long-lived, covering large shaded walls in full deciduous leafy coverage by year 5–7. The fall foliage turns yellow before drop. 'Roseum' (rose-pink bracts) is a sought-after selection. Excellent for shaded north and east-facing walls.

Plant in well-drained, adaptable, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Japanese pagoda tree is a large, wide-spreading shade tree native to China (despite the common name 'Japanese') that produces large panicles of creamy-white, pea-like flowers in July and August — one of the very few large trees that blooms in mid to late summer when the landscape is starved for flowering trees. The flowers are produced in enormous numbers on mature specimens and are highly attractive to honeybees and native bees, making it a significant honey and pollen source. The flowers are followed by distinctive, bright-green, bead-like seed pods that remain on the tree through winter and ornamental even after the leaves drop. The bark is attractively furrowed and the overall form is graceful, with pinnate leaves giving light, dappled shade. Long planted as a sacred tree in China along temple approaches, it was brought to Europe in the 18th century and has been a standard urban street tree in Europe and North America for its drought tolerance, heat tolerance, and summer blooms. The cultivar 'Regent' grows faster and blooms more reliably at a younger age.

common_name: Japanese Pieris (Lily of the Valley Shrub, Andromeda)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in part shade; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity, and protect from harsh afternoon sun and winter winds in colder zones. Pieris japonica is an elegant, slow-growing evergreen shrub that earns three-season ornamental interest through brilliant red to bronze new growth emerging in spring (one of the most vivid of any evergreen shrub), cascading clusters of white to pink, urn-shaped flowers in February–April (often starting when snow is still on the ground), and long-persistent ornamental seed capsules that hang in drooping chains through winter. The flowers closely resemble lily-of-the-valley blooms at much larger scale. The glossy, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves provide handsome year-round structure. Cultivars range from compact ('Cavatine,' 2–3 feet; 'Valley Valentine,' red flowers) to large ('Forest Flame,' fire-red new growth); the species is somewhat deer-resistant and is fully evergreen in zones 5–8, making it outstanding for year-round structure in acidic-soil woodland gardens alongside azaleas and rhododendrons.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese pittosporum is one of the most widely planted foundation and hedge shrubs in Gulf Coast and southern California landscapes, prized for its dense, glossy, dark-green, rounded foliage arranged in attractive whorls, powerful fragrance of orange blossom from the creamy-white flowers in spring, and extreme adaptability to heat, drought, salt spray, poor soil, and shade. The compact selection 'Wheeler's Dwarf' (2–3 feet) is extremely popular for formal hedging and low foundation plantings. 'Variegatum' (gray-green with white margins) provides lighter foliage contrast. The shrub tolerates hard pruning and can be shaped into formal hedges, trained as a small tree, or left to grow in its natural rounded form. An essential utility shrub for zone 8–11 gardens.

common_name: Japanese Privet (Wax Leaf Privet, Wax Ligustrum)
notes: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil — Japanese privet is extraordinary in its adaptability, accepting clay, sand, alkaline soils, compacted urban soils, reflected heat, and neglect without significant decline — in full sun to partial shade; Japanese privet is the most widely planted hedge and screen shrub across the Gulf South, a vigorous, large-growing evergreen producing dense, glossy, waxy, dark-green leaves on stout stems that respond readily to shearing into formal hedges or can be allowed to grow into substantial multi-trunked small trees reaching 18 feet. White flower clusters in late spring have a distinctive, heavy fragrance that some find pleasant and others find objectionable; the flowers produce abundant blue-black berries in fall and winter that are consumed and spread by birds — a characteristic that has made ligustrum a serious invasive plant in natural areas across the Southeast and Gulf South. The berries are mildly toxic to humans and should be noted in gardens used by children. Despite its invasive potential, Japanese privet remains the dominant hedge plant in zone 9 residential and commercial landscapes due to its unmatched combination of heat tolerance, drought tolerance, adaptability, and fast growth. Alternatives for non-invasive hedging include Podocarpus macrophyllus, Ternstroemia gymnanthera, and Distylium.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial to full shade; Japanese rose is one of the most valuable flowering shrubs for shade — producing brilliant golden-yellow, rose-like flowers in early spring on gracefully arching, bright-green stems that are themselves ornamental through winter when the bark retains vivid chartreuse-green color. It spreads gradually by suckering to form colonies and is excellent for naturalizing in shaded areas, under trees, and on north-facing slopes where little else blooms. The double-flowered form 'Pleniflora' (pompom-like, globe-shaped flowers) is more commonly grown than the single species. 'Golden Guinea' (single flowers, larger) and 'Picta' (white-variegated leaves) are other notable cultivars. Bloom is most abundant in partial shade in hot-summer climates; full sun can bleach and shorten the flower display. Tolerates considerable root competition from trees.

Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; skimmia is a refined Japanese shrub with glossy, aromatic, evergreen leaves that provides three seasons of interest — fragrant white flower clusters in spring, persistent bright-red berries (on female plants) that remain decorative through winter, and handsome foliage year-round. It is one of the finest shade shrubs for dense-shade situations that defeat most flowering shrubs. The plant is dioecious — you need at least one male (often sold as Skimmia japonica 'Rubella' or 'Fragrans') for every three female plants to produce berries. Yellowing leaves indicate iron or manganese deficiency in alkaline soil; treat with chelated iron. Never allow plants to dry out — they wilt dramatically in drought.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Japanese snowbell is one of the most elegant and refined small ornamental trees for the garden, producing in late May and June an extraordinary display of pendant, pure-white, bell-shaped flowers hanging in rows beneath the horizontal branching — creating a layered, wedding-cake silhouette when viewed from below that reveals the full beauty of its blooms.
