Styrax japonicus is a graceful multi-stemmed or lightly branched small tree with excellent horizontal structure and clean, fine-textured dark-green foliage that turns yellow to red in fall; the cultivars 'Pink Chimes' and 'Carillon' offer weeping forms and pink-flushed flowers for smaller gardens. It performs particularly well as an understory tree beneath high-canopy oaks, planted where afternoon shade protects it from drought stress — it is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Virtually pest- and disease-free, making it an outstanding choice for zones 5–8 gardens seeking a refined, low-maintenance flowering tree of exceptional beauty.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese spirea is a tough, adaptable deciduous shrub that earns its place in the landscape through months of ornamental interest — colorful new foliage in spring (gold in 'Gold Flame', chartreuse in 'Gold Mound'), dense flat-topped clusters of pink to deep rose flowers in early summer, good fall color, and attractive twiggy winter form. Deadhead after first flowering and shear lightly to encourage a second flush of bloom. Hard rejuvenation pruning to 6–8 inches in early spring every 3–4 years keeps plants vigorous. Note that Japanese spirea is invasive in parts of the eastern United States; check local invasive plant lists and consider using native spiraea relatives (Physocarpus, Fothergilla) where appropriate.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; Japanese stewartia is widely considered one of the finest four-season landscape trees available, earning distinction in every month of the year: brilliant white, camellia-like flowers with orange stamens bloom in June–July during the quiet gap between spring and late-summer bloomers; large, leathery leaves turn orange-red in fall; and the stunning exfoliating bark reveals a patchwork mosaic of gray, orange-brown, cream, and reddish-brown that makes it arguably the most beautiful bark of any deciduous tree in temperate horticulture. The pyramidal growth habit is elegant and requires little pruning. Trees grow slowly but steadily to 20–30 feet over many decades and are extremely long-lived. Unlike the native Stewartias (S. ovata, S. malacodendron), Japanese stewartia is considerably more cold-hardy and easier to establish in most garden conditions.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Ternstroemia gymnanthera is a slow-growing, refined evergreen shrub from Japan and China that has been widely sold in the Gulf South nursery trade under the name 'Cleyera' — though it is botanically distinct from true Cleyera japonica. It produces dense, oval, waxy, dark-green leaves (emerging with distinctive bronze to wine-red new growth) on neat, naturally well-shaped plants with excellent ornamental appeal throughout the year. Small, creamy-white, fragrant flowers appear in summer beneath the foliage, followed by orange-red berries. The combination of beautiful new-growth color and outstanding shade tolerance makes it a valuable alternative to Red Tip Photinia in shaded situations where photinia would fail from disease. Ternstroemia grows slowly and requires no pruning to maintain an attractive shape, ultimately reaching 5–8 feet in typical garden conditions. Unlike Photinia, it is essentially free of serious pest and disease problems in zone 9 — an important advantage in Gulf Coast conditions. It is also deer-resistant. The cultivar 'Burnished Gold' has chartreuse-gold variegated leaves; 'Big Bronze' has exceptionally large, deep-bronze new growth. An outstanding but underutilized alternative to photinia, nandina, and ligustrum in partial to full shade settings.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Japanese tree lilac is the tree-form lilac of North American streetscapes and public gardens, valued for its extraordinary cold hardiness (to zone 3), its tolerance of urban stress, and its massive, creamy-white flower panicles that appear in June — two to three weeks after common lilacs — providing lilac-family bloom when the familiar spring shrubs have long finished. The panicles can reach 12 inches long and are produced in great abundance, creating a white-cloud effect in early summer. The scent is distinctive — not the sweet, classic lilac fragrance but a heavier, privet-like quality that some find pleasant and others less so. The bark is attractive and cherry-like on mature specimens, reddish-brown and lightly exfoliating. Highly resistant to powdery mildew (a common problem on common lilacs) and largely trouble-free in the landscape. The cultivar 'Ivory Silk' is a compact, heavy-blooming selection that is the most commonly available.

Plant on an extremely sturdy support structure in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Japanese wisteria is considered by many gardeners the most ornamental of the wisterias, producing extraordinarily long (up to 36 inches), pendant flower racemes in shades from white through lilac, violet, and purple — cascading down in waves of color in spring. The fragrance is sweet and pervasive. However, it is the most aggressive and potentially invasive of the wisterias in the American South (it is invasive in many southeastern states) — the native alternatives (W. frutescens, W. macrostachya) are strongly recommended for environmental responsibility. If growing Japanese wisteria, regular biannual pruning is essential to contain the plant and promote flowering. NOTE: all wisteria parts are toxic if ingested; the seeds particularly so.

Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese witch hazel is one of the parents of the widely grown Hamamelis x intermedia hybrid witch hazels (crossed with Chinese witch hazel H. mollis) — producing some of the most widely planted late-winter-flowering shrubs in the world. The species itself produces yellow to yellow-orange, ribbon-like, spidery petals on bare branches in late winter, earlier than most witch hazels, with a pleasant sweet fragrance. More heat-tolerant than the Chinese species, making it a better choice for zone 7–8 gardens in the southeastern US. The outstanding fall color of yellow to orange-red makes it a four-season ornamental shrub. Parent of many named cultivars and interspecific hybrids including 'Arnold Promise' (yellow, very fragrant), 'Jelena' (copper-orange), and 'Diane' (red) — among the most celebrated winter-flowering shrubs in horticulture. Excellent as a woodland garden shrub flowering in the dormant season when nothing else is in bloom.

common_name: Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink Loropetalum (Compact Purple-Leaf Fringe Flower)
notes: Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink is a compact member of the Jazz Hands loropetalum series, bred to fit small beds and container plantings while still delivering the deep burgundy-purple foliage and ribbon-like, spidery pink flowers the species is known for. Its dense, well-branched, rounded habit stays smaller than most loropetalum cultivars, holding good foliage color through the season with a heavy spring flower flush and scattered rebloom later on. It shares the easy care of other loropetalum selections, tolerating normal garden soil, heat, and humidity as long as drainage is good, and needs only minimal shaping right after its main bloom period to stay neat.

common_name: Jean's Appalachian Snow Dogwood (Anthracnose-Resistant White Flowering Dogwood)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Jean's Appalachian Snow is a University of Tennessee-bred flowering dogwood selected specifically for resistance to dogwood anthracnose and powdery mildew, two fungal diseases that have killed or badly disfigured flowering dogwoods across much of the humid South in recent decades, making disease-resistant selections like this one an increasingly important choice over older, more vulnerable cultivars. It produces the classic large, pure white bracts in early spring on a naturally graceful, horizontally branched small tree, followed by good fall color and red berries that feed birds. As an understory species, it performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, mimicking its native woodland-edge habitat. Mulch heavily around the root zone to keep soil cool and moist through Gulf South summer heat.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a site sheltered from full afternoon sun and drying winds, and keep the root zone consistently moist since hemlocks do not tolerate drought. 'Jeddeloh' is a dwarf, mounding selection of eastern hemlock with fine, soft, dark green needles on branches that radiate outward and slightly downward, forming the shallow central depression that gives nest-form conifers their name. Its slow growth and low, spreading shape suit it to rock gardens, shaded foundation plantings, and mixed dwarf conifer collections rather than screening, and, like all eastern hemlocks, it should be monitored for hemlock woolly adelgid in regions where that pest is established.

common_name: Jelena Witch Hazel (Copper-Orange Winter Witch Hazel)
notes: Jelena is widely regarded as one of the finest copper-orange witch hazel cultivars, its spidery, ribbon-petaled flowers opening a warm burnt-orange with a reddish flush toward the base of each petal, glowing against bare winter branches when little else in the garden shows any color. It carries some of the best fall foliage of any witch hazel cultivar as well, turning shades of orange, red, and yellow that echo the winter flower color, giving it real two-season value in a shaded border. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since witch hazel resents both drought and waterlogged soil.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Jerusalem sage is a robust, aromatic Mediterranean shrub producing some of the most distinctive and beautiful yellow flowers in the ornamental garden. The large, rounded leaves are covered in dense, soft, white-woolly hairs that give the entire plant a silvery-gray appearance and make it exceptionally drought-tolerant. In late spring and early summer, tall stems bear whorled clusters of vivid, brilliant-yellow tubular flowers arranged in stacked rings around the stem in tiers, giving a candelabra effect that is unique among flowering shrubs. The dried brown seed whorls persist attractively on the stems through winter and are ornamental in their own right. Native to rocky, dry hillsides throughout the eastern Mediterranean from Greece to Israel, it thrives in the hot, dry, alkaline conditions of Mediterranean-climate gardens, Gulf Coast landscapes, and dry borders where most ornamental shrubs would struggle. Combines beautifully with lavender, rosemary, and other silver-leafed Mediterranean plants.

Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; scarify seeds with sandpaper and soak overnight before sowing. Parkinsonia aculeata (Jerusalem thorn, palo verde, or retama) is a spectacular, fast-growing, native thorny tree of the Sonoran Desert and south Texas brushlands — one of the most drought-tolerant of all North American trees — producing cascading, bright-green, photosynthetic stems and flattened, grass-like leaf rachises (the true leaves are reduced to tiny leaflets that drop early) with a weeping, delicate, almost feathery texture. In spring and sporadically after rains, the tree is smothered in masses of bright-yellow, fragrant, pea-like flowers that are outstanding for bees and other native pollinators. The green stems photosynthesize year-round, even when leafless — an adaptation for the desert. Jerusalem thorn grows extremely fast (4–6 feet per year when young) and is one of the best trees for quickly establishing a windbreak, shade, or wildlife habitat in hot, dry, alkaline soils. Young plants are somewhat frost-tender; established trees survive brief drops to 15°F. The seed pods and green seeds are edible in traditional Indigenous and Mexican cuisines.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; jetbead tolerates deep shade and poor soil better than most flowering shrubs but self-sows readily, so deadhead spent flowers where volunteer seedlings are unwanted. Rhodotypos scandens is a tough, adaptable, deciduous shrub related to Kerria, with pleated, sharply toothed, opposite leaves and single, four-petaled white flowers in mid-spring followed by clusters of glossy, jet-black, pea-sized fruit that persist into winter and give the plant its common name. It is one of the most shade-tolerant flowering shrubs available, thriving in the deep, dry shade beneath mature trees where few other shrubs perform, and asks for essentially no maintenance once established beyond occasional renewal pruning. Because it seeds itself freely and can naturalize into nearby wooded areas in some regions, it is best used in a contained landscape bed rather than adjacent to natural woodland, with faded flowers removed before seed matures if spread is a concern.

common_name: Jim Dandy Winterberry Holly (Early Male Pollinator Winterberry)
notes: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, matching this male selection's early bloom time to an early-flowering female cultivar to ensure the berry set gardeners actually grow winterberry for. Jim Dandy itself produces no berries since winterberry is dioecious, but it is a compact, floriferous pollen source that stays proportionate to dwarf female cultivars rather than overwhelming them the way a full-size male can. Its small white spring flowers are inconspicuous but essential to fruiting nearby females. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

growth_habit: Florida Keys endemic coastal native shrub
notes: Plant Jacquinia keyensis in rocky, alkaline, well-drained to dry, sandy coastal soil in full sun to partial shade; it is highly adapted to salt spray, thin rocky substrate, and periodic drought, making it an excellent choice for coastal restoration plantings and coastal hammock gardens in the Florida Keys and extreme South Florida; water sparingly once established. Joewood is one of the rarest and most regionally restricted native shrubs in the United States — found naturally only in the Florida Keys and the southern tip of Miami-Dade County, where it grows in coastal hammock communities on porous, alkaline, marl and coral rock soils just above the tidal zone. The species is classified as Threatened in Florida due to habitat loss from development, sea-level rise, and invasive plant competition. Small, leathery, spine-tipped leaves, fragrant white star-flowers produced repeatedly through warm months, and distinctive hard, contorted wood give Joewood a distinct, sculptural appearance suited to both naturalistic coastal plantings and cultivated low-maintenance coastal gardens. It provides nectar for native bees and butterflies and fruit for migratory birds. A slow-growing plant that rewards patience with exceptional performance in otherwise challenging coastal conditions. Sourcing from Florida-native nurseries propagated from local ecotypes is strongly recommended to support regional genetic conservation.

Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; well-behaved and non-invasive, unlike Japanese honeysuckle. John Clayton is a yellow-flowered selection of native coral honeysuckle, discovered in Virginia and named for the 18th-century botanist, bearing long, tubular, clear yellow flowers instead of the species' typical scarlet-to-coral color, with a long bloom season from spring through fall and light rebloom. It provides the same long-tube nectar source ruby-throated hummingbirds rely on, while giving gardeners a color alternative to the more common red-flowered selections for pairing with other warm-toned plantings. Prune in late winter or just after a bloom flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood; semi-evergreen in mild Gulf South winters.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. John Nelson is a selected cleyera cultivar valued for denser branching and more compact, uniform growth than seed-grown plants, with the same glossy, oval, dark-green leaves that emerge bronze-red on new growth and small, fragrant, creamy flowers in summer followed by red berries. Its improved density makes it a stronger choice for screening and hedging than straight-species cleyera, while retaining the shade tolerance that makes the species valuable as an alternative to photinia or ligustrum in partly shaded Gulf Coast landscapes. It requires little pruning to hold an attractive form and is largely untroubled by pests or disease.

Give this compact clematis a modest trellis or obelisk to climb, keeping the root zone shaded and moist while the top growth flowers in full sun to light shade. Its claim to fame is an unusually long-lasting, fully double flower packed with narrow rose-pink petals layered into a tight rosette, blooming from early summer and often repeating into fall as temperatures cool. Because it flowers on both old and new stems, it needs only a light tidy-up in late winter rather than hard pruning, so remove dead or weak growth and leave the rest. The dense, ruffled blooms make it a standout specimen for a container trellis or small garden support.

Plant in lean, gravelly or sandy, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun and resist the urge to amend the planting hole or irrigate on a regular schedule; Joshua trees are adapted to the high-elevation Mojave Desert of California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah, where winter cold and summer drought are both part of the plant's natural rhythm. This unmistakable, multi-branched arborescent yucca is topped with rosettes of stiff, dagger-like blue-green leaves and can eventually reach 15-40 feet with a gnarled, candelabra-like silhouette that takes many decades to develop. Established trees are extremely drought tolerant and cold hardy into the single digits Fahrenheit, but they are notoriously slow-growing and intolerant of poor drainage, soggy soil, or excess summer humidity, which makes them best suited to arid inland gardens rather than the humid Gulf Coast. Like other yuccas, the creamy, waxy spring flower clusters depend on the yucca moth (Tegeticula synthetica) for pollination, and mature trees are a keystone habitat feature in their native range.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade. Jubilation is a Southern Living Plant Collection gardenia bred for exceptionally large, fully double, intensely fragrant white flowers on a plant more compact and reliably cold-hardy than many older gardenia cultivars, making it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller beds where a big gardenia bloom is still wanted. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer, and its improved cold tolerance extends dependable gardenia culture a bit further north than older selections allow. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves if the soil is not sufficiently acidic, so use an acid-forming fertilizer and keep soil consistently moist for the healthiest, most floriferous plant.

Bred at the Arnold Arboretum from Viburnum carlesii x V. bitchiuense, Judd viburnum was developed to keep the intense, sweet fragrance of Korean spice viburnum while gaining better vigor and disease resistance. Pink buds open to fragrant white to pale-pink flower clusters in mid-spring, followed by red fruit that ripens to black and reddish-purple fall foliage. Its dense, rounded, symmetrical habit needs little pruning beyond the occasional light shaping right after flowering, making it a low-fuss choice for a fragrant foundation planting or mixed shrub border.

common_name: Jude the Obscure Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1995, Jude the Obscure carries large, deeply cupped, golden-yellow blooms that pale toward the outer petals as they mature, famous for one of the strongest and most distinctive fragrances of any English rose, a rich, fruity scent often described as fresh guava. Its full, heavy flowers can nod on their stems, especially after rain, and it is a somewhat lax, medium-sized shrub best sited where its fragrance can be enjoyed up close, repeat-blooming from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Jungle Flame (Flame of the Woods, West Indian Jasmine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), humus-rich, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; acidify soil with sulfur if pH is above 6.0 — ixora is highly pH-sensitive and yellows rapidly in alkaline soil. Ixora coccinea (jungle flame or flame of the woods) is one of the most widely grown tropical landscape shrubs in South Florida, South Texas, Central America, and tropical Asia — prized for its dense, nearly year-round display of brilliant, dome-shaped flower clusters (corymbs) of small, tubular, four-petaled flowers in glowing shades of red, orange, salmon, pink, white, and yellow. Modern landscape cultivars include compact ('Nora Grant,' 'Super King,' 'Dwarf') and standard forms; the classic straight species produces vivid scarlet-red flowers. Ixora's critical cultural requirement is acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.0); in the alkaline soils common in coastal Florida and South Texas, plants develop interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between leaf veins due to iron and manganese deficiency) and decline unless soil is regularly acidified with sulfur or treated with chelated iron. The flowers are a nectar source for butterflies and hummingbirds; in traditional medicine (Ayurveda), various parts of the plant are used for a range of ailments. One of the most rewarding tropical shrubs where it is winter-hardy.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Kaleidoscope tolerates a wide range of conditions and is drought-tolerant once established; Kaleidoscope is a multi-season variegated abelia cultivar that earned recognition through All-America Selections and other awards for its exceptional year-round ornamental value — a compact (2–3 feet) mounding shrub that changes color through the seasons from spring's golden-yellow new growth through summer's bright green-and-yellow variegation to fall's spectacular orange, red, and burgundy tones. Small, tubular, white to pale pink fragrant flowers appear continuously from spring through fall, adding a floral dimension to the primarily foliage-based ornamental value. Abelia is one of the most butterfly-attractive landscape shrubs available — the small, tubular, nectar-rich flowers are visited by virtually all butterfly species present in zone 9 from spring through fall, making Kaleidoscope an effective pollinator garden plant that is also ornamental enough for formal landscape use. The compact habit, multi-season interest, and tolerance of partial shade make Kaleidoscope one of the most versatile small shrubs for Gulf South landscapes.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Kaleidoscope is the most celebrated and widely planted variegated abelia cultivar — named for its remarkable seasonal foliage color changes that shift through a wide range of colors through the growing season. The new spring growth emerges brilliant golden-yellow to chartreuse; through summer the leaves display yellow margins on green centers; in fall the foliage transitions to vivid orange, red, and burgundy-red — an essentially continuous foliage display that provides more sustained ornamental interest than almost any other compact landscape shrub. The small, white to pale-pink tubular flowers bloom prolifically from spring through frost, adding light fragrance and excellent butterfly and hummingbird value throughout the season. The arching, well-branched habit stays compact at 2.5–3.5 feet tall and wide with minimal pruning. Kaleidoscope won the award of the American Nursery & Landscape Association and has become one of the most popular landscape shrubs introduced in the early twenty-first century. Like all abelias, it is extremely tough — tolerating drought, clay soil, heat, humidity, and partial shade with minimal care. Essentially pest-free; deer-resistant. Prune lightly after spring bloom to shape; remove any all-green reverted shoots immediately to prevent them from overtaking the variegated growth.

Plant in average to sandy soil, tolerant of both seasonally wet and fairly dry conditions, in full sun to partial shade; Kalm's St. John's wort is a compact, rounded native shrub from Great Lakes shorelines and rocky lakeshores, valued for bright, sunny-yellow flowers with a prominent burst of long stamens that bloom over a long stretch of summer, set against fine-textured, blue-green foliage. Older stems develop attractive exfoliating, peeling bark that adds interest through winter after the leaves drop. It is remarkably adaptable to difficult sites — tolerating both periodic flooding and dry, sandy soil, as well as wind and some salt exposure — which makes it a useful, low-maintenance choice for rain gardens, pond and shoreline edges, and other spots with unpredictable moisture. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom; a light shearing in early spring keeps the mounded shape tidy and encourages fresh flowering wood. Pollinators, particularly bees, visit the flowers heavily.

Plant rooted cuttings in fall into sharply drained, humus-poor, acidic rocky or gravelly soil in a sheltered rock garden or trough, echoing the serpentine outcrops of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains where this Oregon endemic is found nowhere else on Earth. In spring it bears small, bright rose-pink, rhododendron-like flowers over a dense mound of tiny evergreen leaves, making it a prized miniature for alpine and rock gardens. It demands cool nights, high humidity, and drainage that never stays soggy, so raised beds or scree plantings suit it far better than ordinary garden soil.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, moist to average soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; kapok is one of the most recognized tropical trees in the world — the sacred World Tree (Ceiba) of Maya cosmology, the largest tree in Central American rainforests, and the source of kapok fiber (used historically to stuff life preservers, sleeping bags, and pillows before synthetic fills). The enormous, buttressed trunk with its distinctive large, pointed spines on the bark is unmistakable. The leafless tree produces masses of cream-to-white flowers for bat and moth pollination when the dry-season canopy is open. The seed pods split to release a mass of fine, silky kapok fibers that carry the seeds on the wind. The tree is the sacred national tree of Guatemala. In South Florida, a few mature specimens exist as landscape curiosities; it is better known as an indoor botanical garden and tropical greenhouse specimen.

common_name: Katharina Zeimet Rose (White Baby Rambler Polyantha)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Katharina Zeimet, introduced in 1901 and nicknamed the White Baby Rambler, is a compact polyantha rose bearing large clusters of small, pure white, lightly fragrant flowers almost continuously from spring through frost. Its low, dense, well-behaved habit makes it a reliable choice for borders, edging, and mass plantings, needing far less spraying and maintenance than many modern roses to look good all season. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and expect vigorous rebloom within a few weeks after each flush is spent.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; katsura tree is one of the most beautiful ornamental trees for four-season interest, producing small, heart-shaped, scalloped-edged leaves that move through a sequence of striking colors — emerging in spring with bronze-red or purplish new growth, maturing to clean blue-green through summer, then turning in autumn to brilliant shades of yellow, apricot, and pink. As the leaves fall they emit an extraordinary fragrance universally described as caramel, cotton candy, or freshly baked sugar — one of the most enchanting scents in the autumn garden. The tree also develops attractive, finely furrowed, shaggy russet-brown bark on older specimens that is ornamental through winter. Native to mountain forests of Japan and China, it grows as a graceful, pyramidal tree that softens with age, often with multiple ascending trunks. A magnificent specimen for a moist, partly shaded position where its four-season sensory qualities can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Katy Road Pink Rose (Found Texas Polyantha)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Katy Road Pink is one of the classic Texas 'found roses' rescued by rose rustlers from an old homesite along the road that gives it its name, and like most found roses it is grown own-root, making it far more resilient to freeze dieback than grafted roses since any new growth from the base is still the same good rose. It produces clusters of small, semi-double, clear pink flowers in nearly continuous flushes from spring through fall, on a compact, dense, twiggy shrub that needs almost no spraying to stay healthy through the Gulf South's humid summers. Give it an occasional light shaping and a spring feeding; otherwise it thrives on neglect, making it an outstanding low-maintenance landscape or hedge rose.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Kay Parris is a named Southern magnolia cultivar selected for its superior cold hardiness, narrow columnar form, and early and prolific bloom — a combination of attributes that makes it one of the finest magnolias for zone 6–10 residential landscapes. The naturally narrow, upright habit (20–30 feet tall with a relatively tight 10–15 foot spread) fits medium-sized residential landscapes better than the broadly spreading species without requiring the extremely compact size of Little Gem. Kay Parris begins blooming at young age, producing large (6–8 inch), intensely fragrant white flowers from May through September in zone 9. The cultivar was selected and named by nurseryman David Parris for his wife Kay. A notable characteristic is the exceptionally cold-hardy performance for a Southern magnolia — Kay Parris has been successfully grown into zone 6 with protection, significantly colder than most Southern magnolia selections. The leaves show the characteristic glossy dark-green upper surface and reddish-bronze to cinnamon undersurface. The narrow form suits planting near buildings, driveways, and in limited spaces where the standard Southern magnolia would eventually overwhelm the landscape.

Kentucky Coffeetree is one of the most architecturally dramatic of the eastern native trees, native to the bottomlands, river terraces, and moist upland woods of the central and mid-south United States from New York and Nebraska south to Tennessee and Oklahoma, immediately recognizable in winter by its massive, stout, few-branched silhouette, deeply ridged gray bark, and enormous, persistent, dark brown seed pods up to 10 inches long that hang through winter — one of the most bold and graphic of all bare winter tree forms. The enormous, doubly-pinnate leaves (up to 3 feet long and 2 feet wide) unfurl very late in spring and drop early in fall, giving it one of the shortest leafy seasons of any native tree; in late spring it produces hanging clusters of fragrant white flowers attractive to long-tongued native bees. The hard seeds were roasted and used as a coffee substitute by early settlers and Native American tribes (raw seeds contain toxic alkaloids destroyed by roasting); the pods were fed to pigs and cattle historically. Extremely drought-tolerant, pollution-tolerant, and adaptable to urban conditions once established; an outstanding underused native street and shade tree.

Select a site in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil that mimics its native rocky streambank habitat. Plant container-grown specimens in early spring, backfilling with a mix of native soil and compost. Water deeply each week during the first two growing seasons to encourage a deep root system. White flower clusters emerge in late spring and give way to blue-black berries that are a valuable food source for migrating and resident birds throughout autumn.

Kentucky Wisteria is the hardiest and most well-behaved of the native wisterias, native to the bottomland forests, streambanks, and moist woodland edges of the south-central United States from Illinois and Missouri south to Louisiana and Texas, producing in late spring (and often again in late summer) dense, fragrant, lavender-to-purple flower racemes 6–12 inches long that are visually spectacular on an arbor or pergola — and doing so while behaving far less aggressively than the invasive Japanese and Chinese wisterias that have escaped cultivation and naturalized throughout the southeastern United States. Named cultivars such as 'Blue Moon', 'Aunt Dee', and 'Thunderstruck' are reliable repeat-bloomers and are the preferred choice over seedlings, which may take years to bloom and produce inferior flowers. Unlike Asian wisterias, Kentucky Wisteria twines in a clockwise direction and is significantly less vigorous and easier to manage, though it still requires a strong support and annual pruning. Grow in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which promotes excessive foliage at the expense of flowers.

Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Kimi Moragne is a Hawaiian-bred plumeria cultivar producing flowers that blend soft pink outer petals with a warm yellow throat, a cheerful bicolor combination carrying the strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance prized for lei-making and garden display alike. It is a reliable, well-branched grower that produces flower clusters generously through the warm season. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to prevent stem rot. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, acidic, phosphorus-poor soil in full sun; king protea is South Africa's national flower — the most iconic member of the Proteaceae family and the largest protea species — producing extraordinary globe-shaped flower heads 8–12 inches across with ring upon ring of petal-like bracts in shades of pale silvery-pink to deep rose-crimson surrounding a central dome of silvery-gray florets, the whole resembling a vast artichoke or a jeweled crown. Blooms appear in late winter through summer on plants typically 3–7 feet tall and nearly as wide. It is the dominant species in the South African fynbos (heathland) and requires the same conditions — excellent drainage, lean, low-fertility, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic soil, full sun, and Mediterranean-style dry summers with winter moisture. Phosphorus toxicity from ordinary fertilizers or manure kills it rapidly. Outstanding as a cut flower of extraordinary longevity (lasts 2–3 weeks in a vase). Succeeds in California, coastal Southern California, and similar Mediterranean-climate warm-winter gardens.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; king's mantle (bush clock vine, royal purple thunbergia) is a West African evergreen shrub of the family Acanthaceae that produces large, trumpet-shaped, deep-purple to violet flowers with pale-yellow to white throats continuously from spring through late fall — the flowers are among the richest and most deeply saturated purple-blue of any flowering shrub available for the Gulf Coast and tropical garden. The dark, metallic, deep-purple flower color against the glossy, dark-green, oval leaves creates a striking combination that remains outstanding throughout the long blooming season. Unlike most purple-flowering tropical plants that demand full sun, king's mantle blooms acceptably in partial shade, making it particularly valuable for lightly shaded garden areas where comparable purple-flowered plants would fail. It grows as a mounding, arching shrub with woody lower stems and softer, freely-branching upper growth that flowers on new wood. In zone 9 it may freeze back but regrows reliably from the roots in spring. Excellent as a specimen, informal hedge, or color accent in the partial-shade border.

Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, or grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; Kiwi cordyline holds its variegation best out of the hottest afternoon sun. Long, strap-shaped leaves are edged in cream and pink over a green center with a distinct thin magenta margin at the very edge, a layered, multi-toned variegation pattern reminiscent of the fruit for which it is named, borne on an upright, cane-like stem typical of ti plants. Native to the Pacific Islands and long culturally significant across Polynesia, ti plant is a classic tropical landscape and container shrub in frost-free climates, valued for its bold, colorful, low-maintenance foliage that needs no deadheading or special care beyond routine watering. Water when the top inch of soil dries, protect from any frost, and cut back leggy canes to encourage bushier new growth from the base.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun. Kleim's Hardy is distinguished from most gardenia cultivars by its small, narrow, fine-textured leaves and smaller single-form flowers, giving it a more refined, delicate look than the bold, glossy-leaved standard gardenia. It also blooms earlier in spring than most gardenia cultivars and shows improved cold hardiness, letting it succeed in gardens at the cooler edge of typical gardenia range. Fragrance remains strong despite the smaller flower size, and the compact habit suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and smaller garden spaces. Consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential to avoid the chlorotic yellowing common to gardenias in alkaline conditions.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moisture-retentive, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; kobus magnolia is a Japanese native and the parent of many important magnolia hybrids, producing abundant, slightly fragrant, white flowers with 9–12 petals in early spring before the leaves emerge — similar to star magnolia but on a larger, more tree-like plant. One of the most cold-hardy of the Asian magnolias, reliably hardy to zone 4. The Loebner magnolia hybrids (M. x loebneri), crosses of kobus with star magnolia, are particularly valued for combining cold hardiness with early, profuse blooming and are among the most reliable magnolias for northern gardens. Kobus itself is a stately, large specimen tree when old, eventually becoming a wide-spreading tree of considerable grace. The bark produces fragrant compounds used in Japanese temple incense.

Set out plants in spring into acidic, well-drained soil high in organic matter, watering deeply and mulching to conserve moisture while the shrub establishes. Native to Korea, northeastern China, and Japan, it tolerates a range of light from partial shade to more open sites and is valued for blooming before almost any other woody plant in the garden, often while snow still lingers. Clouds of funnel-shaped rosy-lavender flowers cover the bare branches in very early spring, ahead of the leaves, making it a striking companion to snowdrops and early hellebores at the edge of a shaded border. It is one of the more cold-hardy deciduous rhododendrons and handles colder winters better than many broadleaf evergreen relatives.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean spice viburnum is arguably the most sweetly fragrant of all flowering shrubs — the dense, rounded heads of small pink buds opening to white flowers in early spring produce an extraordinary spicy-sweet perfume that fills the garden on warm spring days and can be detected from 50 feet away. The fragrance is strongest on still mornings and in the evening warmth. The rounded shrub is neat and symmetrical, reaching 4–5 feet tall and wide over many years, with dull dark-green leaves that turn wine-red to burgundy in fall where summers are not too hot. It performs best in zones 4–7 where winter cold is reliable — in zone 8 and warmer, it often fails to bloom well due to insufficient winter chilling hours and may decline over time. Site it where the fragrance can be fully appreciated: near the entrance, beside a path, or outside a frequently used window. Prune lightly if needed immediately after flowering to maintain shape.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean stewartia is a four-season specimen tree widely regarded as one of the most beautiful of all small ornamental trees. In summer, it produces large, white, camellia-like flowers with showy orange stamens over several weeks. As summer transitions to fall, the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and purple. In winter and spring, the intricate, flaking bark — peeling in irregular patches to reveal a mosaic of gray, orange, tan, and cinnamon — provides some of the most dramatic winter interest of any tree. The tree is pyramidal in youth and gradually broadens with age. More heat-tolerant than Japanese stewartia and slightly more adaptable to zone 8 conditions. One of the finest specimen trees for the transitional South, performing best in partial afternoon shade in zones 7–8.

Grow as a houseplant trained onto a moss pole or bark slab in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Korthals' shingle vine presses its juvenile leaves flat against a climbing support and needs that vertical surface to grow well. In its juvenile climbing stage, small, glossy, overlapping leaves press tightly flat against tree bark or a moss pole in a dense, shingled pattern, a distinctive growth habit shared with a handful of other aroid vines and prized by collectors for the tidy, textured wall of foliage it creates. As the vine matures and reaches better light, its leaves grow progressively larger and eventually become perforated, similar in appearance to a small monstera, once it is well established and climbing vigorously. Provide a broad, moist support such as a sphagnum-covered pole for the aerial roots to grip, mist regularly to keep humidity high, and be patient, since the shift from small shingling leaves to larger mature foliage can take considerable time.

Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kousa dogwood is a Japanese, Korean, and Chinese small deciduous tree that blooms approximately three to four weeks later than the native flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) — producing its characteristic four-pointed, star-shaped, white or pink bracts in June rather than April — and is considered by many gardeners to be even more ornamental over the full year. The pointed, white (occasionally pink) bracts surround the small true flowers in the center and remain attractive for 4–6 weeks. In late summer and fall, large, bumpy, pink-red, strawberry-like composite fruit clusters ripen and are edible (sweet, slightly grainy, and pleasant-tasting, used to make jam in Japan). The fall foliage is outstanding — purplish-red to scarlet. On mature specimens the bark becomes attractively mottled and exfoliating. It is significantly more resistant to dogwood anthracnose disease and dogwood borer than C. florida — one of the primary reasons for preferring it in areas where these pests are problematic. 'Milky Way' (very heavy flower production), 'Satomi' (deep-rose-pink bracts), and 'Wolf Eyes' (white-variegated leaves) are outstanding cultivars.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kramer's Supreme is one of the most significant Camellia japonica cultivars because it is reliably fragrant — a quality extremely rare in camellias, which are otherwise almost completely scentless. The large (4–5 inch), peony-form to informal double, vivid turkey-red flowers have a light but distinct, pleasant fragrance that is surprising in a camellia, making this cultivar uniquely valuable for gardens where fragrance is a priority. The flower color is an especially vivid, pure turkey-red without the blue-purple tones of Mathotiana — a clean, electric red that is among the most brilliant flower colors available for the winter garden. Kramer's Supreme blooms in midseason (November–February in zone 9), providing brilliant red winter color when few other shrubs are in bloom. Its exceptional cold hardiness (to zone 6, surviving temperatures to 10–15°F) makes it the most reliably winter-hardy red camellia cultivar, growing further north than most other japonica types. The upright to spreading habit grows 6–10 feet tall with regular pruning. In zone 9, Kramer's Supreme is an outstanding long-lived landscape shrub that requires only light pruning after bloom and supplemental iron (from acidic fertilizer) to prevent chlorosis in alkaline Gulf Coast soils.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Krimson Queen hoya colors most vividly in bright light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound. Thick, waxy, oval leaves are edged in broad creamy-white margins that blush distinctly pink in bright light, especially on new growth, growing on vigorous, twining vines that eventually produce rounded clusters of small, star-shaped, fragrant pink flowers with a deep red center from the same reusable flowering spurs year after year. One of the most popular variegated hoya cultivars for its reliable, colorful foliage even when not in bloom, it climbs or trails readily and rewards a bright window with steady growth and repeat flowering. Provide a trellis or hanging basket for the twining stems, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flowering spurs, which continue to rebloom for years.

common_name: Kumasaka Camellia (Cold-Hardy Rose-Pink Japanese Heirloom Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Kumasaka is a historic Japanese Camellia japonica cultivar producing rose-pink, rose-form double flowers with neatly overlapping petals, valued not only for its classic, elegant bloom form but for cold hardiness above average for the species, which has helped it remain in cultivation across a broader hardiness range than many other japonica cultivars. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in midseason and provides dense, glossy year-round structure. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

growth_habit: Australian native drought-resistant ornamental shade tree
notes: Plant Brachychiton populneus in full sun in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, deep soil (it develops a strong taproot); it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and adapts to alkaline, heavy clay soils that challenge most trees; avoid overwatering, especially in youth. Kurrajong is a superlative drought-tolerant ornamental tree for hot, dry climates — native to the slopes, foothills, and grasslands of inland southeastern Australia where it is drought and heat adapted. The leaves are remarkably variable on the same tree: some deeply multi-lobed, others simple and oval, giving the tree a naturally textured, organic appearance. The cream to white, cup-shaped flowers with red and purple interior spotting are produced in summer in clusters and are attractive up close. The woody seed pods (follicles) split to reveal yellow, edible seeds surrounded by irritating hairs — the seeds are roasted to remove the hairs and then eaten or ground into flour; Aboriginal Australians roasted the seeds as a significant food and ground the inner bark fiber for fiber and string. The fat-storing capacity of the young roots was also exploited as a water source in dry conditions. A valuable shade tree for Texas, the Gulf Coast, and dry-summer climates where it withstands drought, alkaline soils, and heat that defeat most ornamental trees. Moderately frost-hardy to about 18–20°F.

common_name: Kwanzan Flowering Cherry (Double Pink Ornamental Cherry)
notes: Kwanzan is the classic double-flowered ornamental cherry, its dense clusters of vivid rosy-pink, fully double, pompom-like blooms covering the bare branches in mid-spring before the bronze-tinted new leaves emerge, producing one of the showiest flowering tree displays available in a temperate garden. Unlike Yoshino cherry, Kwanzan sets essentially no fruit, avoiding fruit litter, and its vase-shaped, upright-spreading habit and reddish-bronze fall color add further seasonal interest beyond the spring bloom. Give it moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to minimize disease entry through large wounds, and expect a relatively short lifespan of 15-20 years typical of ornamental cherries, which are prone to canker and borer problems as they age.

This evergreen camellia shrub is best planted from a nursery specimen in fall or early spring in a location with morning sun and afternoon shade, sheltered from harsh wind. It thrives in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, so mulch the shallow roots and avoid planting too deeply. From winter into spring it bears playful blooms of white or soft pink streaked with red, with no two flowers alike. Water regularly during dry spells and prune lightly just after flowering to shape the plant.

Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, replicating the sphagnum bogs and boreal peatlands of the Great Lakes region and points north where this evergreen ericaceous shrub naturally grows. Clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are visited by bees and flies, while the dense, leathery, rust-fuzzed foliage provides year-round cover for birds along bog and wetland edges. Leaves are aromatic and were historically brewed as tea, though they contain compounds that are toxic to livestock if browsed in quantity, so this is a plant for wildlife habitat and ornamental bog gardens rather than for foraging. Best suited to a dedicated acidic bog garden alongside pitcher plants, sundews, and cranberry rather than average garden soil.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline, rocky or limestone-derived soil in full sun; Lacey oak is a Texas Superstar-designated Hill Country native, valued for smoky blue-green summer foliage that emerges with an attractive soft pink flush in spring, along with excellent resistance to oak wilt, the vascular disease that has devastated live oaks and red oaks across parts of Texas. It grows slowly into a graceful, moderately sized shade tree well suited to the alkaline, rocky, drought-prone soils of the Texas Hill Country and similar limestone-based Gulf South sites where many other shade trees struggle. Its slow, controlled growth rate also means a naturally strong branch structure that needs relatively little corrective pruning compared to fast-growing trees. Once established, it is highly drought tolerant and needs no supplemental irrigation in most climates within its range. Give it plenty of room and full sun to develop its best form.

common_name: Lady Clare Camellia (Large Semi-Double Rose-Pink Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Lady Clare, known in its native Japan as Akashigata, is a classic large semi-double camellia bearing loosely arranged, deep rose-pink petals surrounding a prominent, showy cluster of golden-yellow stamens, a looser and more informal look than fully double camellia forms. Its vigorous, spreading, somewhat weeping growth habit and large flower size have made it a long-standing favorite for Southern gardens and historic camellia collections, often trained as a specimen or espalier to show off its graceful branching. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it flowers in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9, when little else is in bloom. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

common_name: Lady Emma Hamilton Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2005, Lady Emma Hamilton produces vivid orange-red buds opening to peachy-orange, cupped blooms that darken toward the petal edges, carrying a strong, fruity, tea-like fragrance, on a compact, well-branched shrub whose new growth emerges an unusual deep reddish-purple before maturing to green. The combination of saturated warm flower color and dark young foliage gives it strong two-tone appeal, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Lady Margaret Passionflower (Red Hybrid Passion Vine)
notes: Give this fast-growing hybrid a wire trellis, obelisk, or fence in a warm, sheltered spot, and keep the soil evenly moist but well drained. It bears an abundance of small, richly colored deep red-and-pink flowers with a dark maroon-purple center almost continuously from late spring until frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds to the garden. In frost-free climates it stays semi-evergreen and can be left to cover a large structure, while in cooler areas it is best grown in a container and brought indoors or treated as a fast annual climber. Cut back hard in late winter where it is hardy to keep new growth vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Lady Vansittart Camellia (Variegated White-and-Pink Striped Camellia japonica)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Lady Vansittart is a historic Camellia japonica cultivar dating to the 1800s, prized for its semi-double flowers striped and marbled in white and rose-pink in an irregular, ever-varying pattern from bloom to bloom, occasionally producing solid pink or solid white flowers on the same plant, a trait long fascinating to camellia collectors. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in mid-season and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its striking winter and early spring flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Lady of Shalott Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2009, Lady of Shalott bears warm apricot-orange, tea-and-spice-scented blooms that open from red-orange buds into loosely cupped rosettes, held on strong, arching, thorny canes that resist bending in rain far better than many old-style roses. It is one of the most disease-resistant and heat-tolerant English roses available, holding up well to Gulf South humidity and blooming almost continuously from late spring through frost, and its vigorous growth allows it to be trained as a short climber against a fence or trellis if given support.

common_name: Lady of the Night (Night Jasmine, Brunfelsia americana)
notes: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Lady of the Night is one of the finest shade-tolerant fragrant shrubs for zone 9-11 Gulf Coast gardens, where its powerful nocturnal fragrance fills outdoor spaces on warm spring and summer evenings. Brunfelsia americana is an evergreen shrub from the Caribbean (Jamaica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Lesser Antilles) in the Solanaceae family closely related to Yesterday Today Tomorrow (B. pauciflora and B. australis). Its single-day flowers begin as pure white tubes and age through cream to pale yellow — the reverse color change from B. pauciflora's purple-to-white progression. The flower fragrance is released most powerfully after dark and is one of the most intensely sweet and complex fragrances in the plant world — often described as combining jasmine, vanilla, and gardenias — with a reach that can fill a large garden or patio on warm, still evenings. In zone 9, Lady of the Night blooms from spring through fall with peak flowering in late spring and early summer. The combination of shade tolerance and extraordinary nocturnal fragrance makes it one of the most valuable plants for shaded evening garden spaces, planted near patios, decks, and seating areas. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic — contain brunfelsamidine and other alkaloids causing neurological symptoms if ingested.

Plant rooted cuttings or small divisions in spring into acidic, gritty, well-drained soil in a cold, sunny, exposed site, matching the arctic tundra and the wind-scoured alpine summits, such as New Hampshire's Presidential Range, where this circumboreal dwarf shrub survives as a disjunct relict of the last ice age. In late spring it is covered in small, purple-violet, funnel-shaped flowers held just above tiny evergreen leaves, a striking miniature echo of its showy garden rhododendron relatives. It demands cool roots, sharp drainage, and reliable winter snow cover, making it a plant strictly for dedicated alpine troughs or high-elevation rock gardens rather than typical shrub borders.

Large Fothergilla is an exceptional four-season native shrub, native to the mountain forests and rocky slopes of the southern Appalachians from Virginia and North Carolina south to Alabama, producing fragrant, white, bottlebrush-like flower spikes of dense stamens in April and May before the leaves emerge — a display that rivals those of its close relative Witch Hazel (Hamamelis). Larger than Dwarf Fothergilla (F. gardenii), it grows 6–10 feet tall and wide and provides multi-season appeal through its dark green, blue-green tinged summer foliage, one of the finest fall color displays of any native shrub (crimson, orange, and yellow often appearing simultaneously on a single leaf), and attractive winter form. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; best fall color develops in full sun, but the plant tolerates partial shade and is easy to establish in typical native plant garden conditions. An outstanding choice for four-season structure in the southeastern native garden.

Large Gallberry is a robust evergreen native holly, native to the wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, bay swamps, and seepage bogs of the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, where it grows alongside inkberry, fetterbush, and pond cypress in permanently moist to wet, highly acidic, sandy or peaty soils. The glossy, dark green, leathery, spine-tipped leaves provide year-round evergreen structure; female plants produce abundant clusters of large black berries in fall and winter that are critical food for bluebirds, hermit thrushes, and other migrating songbirds. Like inkberry (Ilex glabra), Large Gallberry is important for native bees, producing copious nectar that supports early-season bee populations. Plant male and female specimens together for reliable fruiting; provide consistently moist to wet, highly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. An outstanding wildlife shrub for wet native gardens in the lower South.

common_name: Large-Leafed Pothos (Amplissimum Pothos, Silver-Stripe Epipremnum, Giant Pothos)
notes: Grow on a rough support in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained soil — Large-Leafed Pothos climbs rapidly on rough bark or moss poles and develops its most dramatically different adult-leaf form when given a vertical surface to ascend. Epipremnum amplissimum is a climbing, hemiepiphytic aroid in the Araceae family native to the Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, and parts of tropical Asia — a member of the same genus as the ubiquitous common Golden Pothos (E. aureum) but producing a strikingly different leaf form. In juvenile form, E. amplissimum produces standard small, heart-shaped pothos-type leaves. As the plant matures and climbs, the leaves transition to the distinctively adult form: long (12–24 inches), narrowly lanceolate, linear to lance-shaped leaves in dark green with a pale to silver-green central stripe along the midrib — a leaf form that looks almost nothing like the common pothos and is instead reminiscent of a narrow Philodendrum or large Scindapsus. This adult leaf form is quite unusual and ornamentally distinctive, making E. amplissimum one of the more interesting of the Epipremnum relatives for collectors of shade-climbing aroids. The plant grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and covers surfaces quickly. Propagates easily from stem cuttings. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.

Laurel Greenbriar is an evergreen native vine of moist woods, swamp margins, and thickets of the coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, climbing by tendrils to 30 feet or more with stiff, spiny stems and long, narrow, leathery evergreen leaves that make it the greenest plant in the winter understory forest. The small, dark blue-black berries are produced in clusters and are a critical winter food for wild turkeys, black bears, white-tailed deer, mockingbirds, and cedar waxwings when other food sources are exhausted. The spiny, interlocking stems create impenetrable thickets that provide ideal nesting and escape cover for ground-nesting birds, rabbits, and other small wildlife, and the tubers were historically eaten by Native Americans. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Laurel Greenbriar tolerates periodic flooding and deep shade once established, and requires a sturdy structure or tree to climb.

common_name: Laurel Oak (Diamond Leaf Oak, Swamp Laurel Oak)
notes: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; laurel oak is one of the most common and important native trees of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic coastal plain — a large, fast-growing semi-evergreen oak reaching 60–80 feet with a broad crown and distinctive narrowly elliptical, unlobed leaves resembling laurel or willow leaves. Unlike live oak and other southern oaks, laurel oak grows readily in the wet, poorly drained soils of floodplains, swamp margins, and pine flatwoods that define much of the Gulf Coast landscape. It provides outstanding wildlife value — the small acorns are eaten by wood ducks, deer, turkeys, squirrels, and many other species. The semi-evergreen foliage provides moderate winter screening. Laurel oak grows faster than live oak (3–5 feet per year when young) but is shorter-lived (60–80 years). An excellent shade tree for moist, low-lying Gulf Coast sites.

Plant in partial to full shade in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil; laurel-leaf greenbrier is an evergreen native vine of the Gulf Coastal Plain that uses tendrils to scramble through shrubs and trees, providing year-round cover and valuable black berries for wildlife from fall through winter. The long, lance-shaped, leathery leaves remain glossy dark green through winter, making it valuable for screening and structure in year-round southern gardens. It tolerates flooding, deep shade, and sandy coastal conditions. New shoots in spring are edible and have been used by Native Americans as a vegetable and starch source. The dried rhizomes yield a starchy food and historically formed the basis of a root beer-style drink. Use on fences and naturalized areas where it can spread without becoming a maintenance challenge.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; laurustinus is a Mediterranean evergreen viburnum that provides exceptional winter interest — the flower buds, held in flat-topped clusters, open from pink buds to white flowers from late winter through spring, providing bloom when nearly nothing else flowers in the garden. After bloom, the fruits pass through a striking metallic turquoise-blue phase before ripening to black, providing a second season of ornamental value. It is one of the most shade-tolerant and adaptable evergreen viburnums, performing well in partial shade, alkaline soil, and coastal conditions. 'Eve Price' (compact, deep-pink buds), 'Spring Bouquet' (compact, freely flowering), and 'Lisarose' (rich pink) are excellent cultivar selections.

common_name: Lavender Chiffon Rose of Sharon (Sterile Double-Flowered Lavender Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Lavender Chiffon bears large, soft lavender-blue flowers with a ruffled cluster of extra petaloids at the center that gives the bloom a fuller, semi-double appearance, opening from midsummer into fall on a tough, reliable, low-maintenance shrub. Like the other Chiffon-series rose of sharon, it is a sterile triploid, setting almost no seed and avoiding the volunteer-seedling problem common in older rose of sharon plantings. Its soft, cool flower color pairs well with warmer-toned summer perennials, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil with ease once established.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Le Vésuve is an antique China rose dating to before 1825, bearing cupped, double blooms in soft pink that deepen and blush toward the petal edges as they age and as temperatures rise, much like its garden companions Old Blush and Louis Philippe. It flowers in repeated flushes from spring through fall and, grown own-root as China roses traditionally were in old Southern gardens, regrows true from the base after a hard winter or storm damage. It asks for little beyond decent drainage and full sun, tolerating summer heat and humidity with minimal disease and only occasional light pruning to keep its naturally rounded shape tidy.

Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, dry to average soil in full sun; leadplant is one of the deepest-rooted plants in the world relative to its above-ground size — individual plants develop root systems reaching 15 feet or more into the soil profile, making it one of the most drought-tolerant and fire-adapted shrubs native to North America, and making any attempt at transplanting futile; it must be established from seed sown in place. Amorpha canescens is a low, spreading prairie shrub with distinctive silver-gray, densely canescent (canescens = gray-woolly) pinnately compound leaves that give the whole plant a soft silver-lavender cast; in late June and July it produces spectacular, dense, upright spikes of tiny, deep purple flowers with bright orange anthers, creating a vivid contrast with the silvery foliage that makes it one of the most ornamentally distinguished native prairie shrubs in North America — the plant's association with the deep, lead-gray soils of undisturbed prairie gives it the common name leadplant. It is a nitrogen-fixing legume, an indicator of high-quality, never-plowed prairie remnants, and an exceptional pollinator plant visited by native bumblebees, sweat bees, and mining bees; leadplant is slower to establish from seed than most forbs, taking 2–3 years to begin flowering, but is then extremely long-lived and essentially maintenance-free, resprouting vigorously from its deep root crown after fire or cutting — fire suppression is one reason it has declined in much of its range, and it responds well to periodic cutting or burning that mimics natural disturbance.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; leafy rose spreads by suckers into a low, dense colony and tolerates heat and humidity better than many species roses. Glossy, narrow, finely divided leaves cover a low, dense, suckering native shrub topped with fragrant, single, deep pink flowers through much of summer, an unusually long bloom season for a species rose, followed by small red hips valued by birds. Native to prairies, open woods, and stream banks of Texas, Oklahoma, and Arkansas, it tolerates the heat and humidity of the southern plains and Gulf South better than many other North American species roses, spreading slowly by root suckers into a dense, weed-suppressing colony useful for a bank or naturalistic planting. It needs no spraying or winter protection and thrives with minimal care once established.

Leather flower is a graceful native clematis from the moist woodlands and streambanks of the central and eastern United States, distinguished by its nodding, urn-shaped flowers of leathery, thick-textured red-purple to mauve petals — the unusual closed, pitcher-like floral form is adapted for specialist bee pollinators that force their way inside for nectar, preventing nectar robbing by smaller insects. Unlike many showy cultivated clematis, leather flower blooms from late spring through summer with a steady succession of individual flowers rather than one dramatic flush, keeping the vine attractive for months; the feathery, plumed seedheads that follow add ornamental value into fall and winter. Grow on a fence, through a native shrub, or along a trellis in the partial shade of a woodland edge; pair with native ferns, columbines, and spicebush for a layered understory planting. Cut back to 12 inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

Plant at the base of a trellis, fence, or open shrub in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; keep the root zone cool and moist with mulch while allowing the vine to climb into brighter light — the classic clematis principle of cool feet and a sunny head. Leatherflower is a native vine of stream banks, forest edges, and thickets across the eastern US, bearing unusually thick-petaled, nodding urn-shaped flowers in shades of pink to reddish-purple that do not open fully, creating a distinctive lantern-like appearance from late spring through summer. The flowers are followed by showy, globe-shaped clusters of feathery-tailed seeds that persist and provide winter interest. Prune back to 12–18 inches in late winter as the plant blooms on new growth.

Plant in acidic, consistently wet to constantly moist, peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; leatherleaf is a low, spreading, evergreen native shrub of northern bogs and peatlands, with small, leathery, scaly-textured, dull green leaves along arching stems that line up in tidy rows of small white bell-shaped flowers in early spring, often blooming while there is still ice at the bog's edge. It is one of the first shrubs to bloom in the northern wetland calendar and a valuable early nectar source for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Growing naturally in permanently saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic peat, it is a plant for a true bog garden or a rain garden basin engineered to stay consistently wet with acidic soil, not an ordinary moist border — it does not tolerate normal garden soil or drying out. Where conditions suit it, leatherleaf spreads slowly into low colonies and needs essentially no maintenance beyond leaving it undisturbed.

Leatherleaf viburnum is grown chiefly for its bold, coarse-textured evergreen foliage — long, deeply veined, corrugated dark green leaves with a felted gray-brown underside that give the shrub year-round structural presence. Flat clusters of creamy-white flowers open in late spring, followed by red berries that ripen to black by late summer if a second unrelated plant is present for cross-pollination. It makes an effective evergreen screen or backdrop shrub but tends to lose its lower leaves and look leggy with age, so it is best planted behind lower shrubs or perennials that can mask its base. Afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hot, sunny sites.

Plant nursery-grown container stock only in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherwood is notoriously difficult to propagate and transplant — purchase from reputable native plant nurseries and disturb the root system as little as possible. Dirca palustris is one of the most shade-tolerant, slow-growing, and long-lived of all native North American shrubs, persisting for decades in deep shade under mature forest canopies in moist, rich woodland soils from Newfoundland to Florida; tiny, pale-yellow, tubular flowers appear in late winter before any leaves on bare, supple branches that are so flexible and strong they cannot be broken by hand (giving rise to its common name), and small, olive-green, berry-like fruits ripen in late spring. The plant is extremely patient and will eventually form a graceful, rounded mound; it is an underused jewel for shaded native plant gardens and rain gardens in moist, acid forest soils.

scientific_name: Fothergilla x intermedia 'ALICE' (Legend of the Fall)
common_name: Legend of the Fall Fothergilla (Long-Holding Multi-Color Fall Foliage Hybrid)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. Legend of the Fall is an upright fothergilla hybrid bred for a heavy show of fragrant, honey-scented, bottlebrush-like white flower spikes in spring before the leaves emerge, followed by blue-green summer foliage that turns a spectacular, long-holding blend of red, orange, and yellow in fall — the display persists notably longer than in many older fothergilla selections. Its upright, four to five foot habit suits a shrub border, woodland edge, or foundation planting. Requires minimal pruning; simply remove dead or crossing wood after flowering if shaping is needed.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lemoine deutzia is a classic, cold-hardy hybrid valued for its profuse, pure white late-spring flower display. This historic French hybrid, bred by the renowned Lemoine nursery in the late nineteenth century, smothers its arching branches in dense clusters of small, pure white, star-shaped flowers in late spring, one of the most floriferous of the classic deutzia hybrids and a mainstay of cottage-garden and heritage shrub borders for over a century. Reliable and easy-care, it tolerates a range of soils and climates, providing a reliable flush of white bloom each spring with minimal maintenance beyond occasional renewal pruning. Prune immediately after flowering to shape and remove some of the oldest canes at the base periodically to keep the shrub renewed and full from the ground up.

common_name: Lemon Lime Nandina (Bright Chartreuse Compact Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Lemon Lime is a dwarf, mounding nandina selected for foliage that emerges bright chartreuse-lime rather than the red tones typical of most nandina cultivars, holding that fresh lime-green color through summer without the burgundy winter shift seen in other dwarf types. Its compact, dense habit and unusual color make it a useful accent for brightening a shaded bed or breaking up the heavier greens and burgundies of a typical foundation planting. Like other modern dwarf nandina selections it is sterile and produces no berries, avoiding the self-seeding that has made standard nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast, and it needs little pruning beyond removing occasional damaged canes.

common_name: Lennei Magnolia (Full-Petaled Deep Purple-Pink Saucer Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Lennei is a classic saucer magnolia cultivar valued for its unusually full, heavy-petaled flowers in a deep rose-purple on the outside with a paler, almost white interior, giving each bloom a rounded, goblet-like fullness distinct from the more open form of many other saucer magnolia cultivars. It flowers on bare branches in early to mid spring, somewhat later than Alexandrina, and grows into a broad, spreading, multi-stemmed small tree that needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood. Established trees are long-lived, low-maintenance landscape specimens, though a late hard freeze can still brown open flowers in an unusually cold spring.

Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun; Leslie Ann is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated sasanqua camellia with a long track record, having won the Ralph Peer Camellia Award back in 1961 and remaining a proven, reliable landscape performer in the decades since. It produces large, semi-double flowers combining pink, blush, and white in each bloom, opening from October through December when few other shrubs are in flower, and provides glossy evergreen structure through the rest of the year. Like other sasanquas it is more sun-tolerant and generally faster-growing than Camellia japonica, but still benefits from some afternoon shade and consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.

common_name: Let's Dance Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Bigleaf Hydrangea Series)
notes: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Let's Dance is a breeding series of compact, reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas that stay under 3 feet tall, considerably smaller than older mophead cultivars, while still flowering on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year. This reblooming trait means a late spring frost that kills the old flower buds does not prevent a good summer bloom, unlike older hydrangea cultivars that flower only once per year on old wood. Individual cultivars within the series vary in flower form (mophead or lacecap) and color.
