Flower color shifts with soil pH the way most macrophylla hydrangeas do, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since hydrangea's large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

common_name: Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Gulf South. Let's Dance Rhythmic Blue is part of the Proven Winners Let's Dance series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas, bred to flower reliably on new growth as well as on old wood, so a late freeze that damages the previous year's stems doesn't wipe out the whole season's bloom the way it can on older mophead cultivars. Its compact, rounded habit fits smaller foundation plantings and containers better than full-sized mopheads, and the large, rounded flower clusters shift from blue to pink depending on soil pH, staying truest blue in acidic soil amended with aluminum sulfate if needed. Deadhead spent blooms and prune lightly to shape in late winter, avoiding heavy pruning that would remove the current season's developing flower buds.

Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Lewis's mock orange is drought-tolerant once established and adapts to a wide range of soils including rocky slopes and thin, dry soils. Philadelphus lewisii is a native western North American shrub (state flower of Idaho) producing clusters of large, 4-petaled, pure-white flowers with a pronounced, sweet, citrus-orange fragrance in late spring and early summer — one of the most powerfully perfumed of all flowering shrubs. Unlike the commonly cultivated European species (P. coronarius), this native is more drougt-tolerant, cold-hardy, and has excellent wildlife value; it provides important cover and nesting habitat for birds, and the fragrant flowers attract butterflies and native bees. The multi-stemmed, arching habit is attractive even out of bloom.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving trees generous spacing for airflow, since crowding and poor drainage are the leading causes of the canker diseases that shorten this tree's life in humid climates. Leyland cypress is a fast-growing hybrid conifer long popular across the South for quickly establishing a dense, narrow, evergreen privacy screen, capable of adding 3 feet or more of growth per year in its early years to reach a mature height of 40–60 feet with soft, feathery, blue-green foliage. Its rapid growth rate made it the default screening tree for decades, but it is increasingly susceptible to fatal canker diseases in the Gulf South's heat, humidity, and heavy clay soils, particularly when planted too closely together or in poorly drained sites, so many extension services now recommend Green Giant arborvitae or other alternatives for new plantings in this region. Where Leyland cypress is already established or planted with excellent drainage and spacing, minimal pruning is needed beyond an occasional light shearing to maintain shape.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun; lignum vitae is frost-tender, extremely slow-growing, and native to South Florida hammocks and the Keys. Small, leathery, evergreen leaflets cover a dense, rounded canopy that bursts into a profusion of vivid blue-purple flowers, often several times a year, followed by bright yellow-orange seed capsules that split to reveal striking red-coated seeds, making it one of the most ornamentally distinctive native trees of South Florida. Its extremely dense, heavy wood — historically the source of the actual lignum vitae timber prized for its self-lubricating properties in ship propeller shaft bearings — reflects an exceptionally slow growth rate that has made wild populations vulnerable to historical overharvesting, so cultivated specimens from nursery-propagated stock help support the species. Extremely drought- and salt-tolerant once established, it thrives on poor, rocky, alkaline soil with essentially no supplemental care, making it a valuable, low-maintenance native specimen tree for a South Florida landscape.

Plant in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; avoid sites with late spring frosts as the flowers can be damaged in zone 5–6. Magnolia liliiflora is the wild lily magnolia of central and western China, a small, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree (8–12 feet) that produces distinctive, tulip-shaped flowers with deep purple-red to rose-magenta exteriors and white to pale lilac interiors from late March to May (late spring); it is the parent species crossed with M. denudata by Chinese and French horticulturalists to produce the beloved saucer magnolia (M. x soulangeana). The flowers are later-emerging than many magnolias and more reliably miss late freezes in zones 5–6. Grown as an elegant specimen or mixed border plant; 'Nigra' is the most widely grown cultivar, with deeper purple flowers than the species. The species has been cultivated in Chinese gardens for over 1,400 years.

common_name: Lime Sizzler Firebush (Variegated Chartreuse Hummingbird Shrub)
notes: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lime Sizzler is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated firebush selection with striking variegated foliage — leaves in bright chartreuse-lime with contrasting red-toned veining — that turns this reliable hummingbird shrub into a colorful foliage accent even between flushes of bloom. It keeps the tubular, red-orange flowers of the species, produced continuously from late spring through frost, which are a magnet for hummingbirds and butterflies throughout the long Gulf South growing season. In zone 9, it behaves as a root-hardy perennial in a well-protected, sheltered spot, dying back after a hard freeze and resprouting from the roots in spring, or it can be grown as a fast-filling warm-season annual shrub farther from the coast where winters are more severe. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, and prune out any winter-damaged wood in spring once new growth resumes.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Limelight is the most celebrated panicle hydrangea cultivar — a Dutch introduction that has become one of the most popular landscape shrubs in America in the early twenty-first century, distinguished from the classic PeeGee hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata) by its unique flower color: the large, cone-shaped flower panicles (10–12 inches long) open in a distinctive pale chartreuse-green rather than white, gradually changing to creamy white as they mature, then transitioning to dusty pink and finally parchment-buff as they age through summer into fall — providing nearly five months of evolving ornamental interest from a single set of flowers. The opening chartreuse color is particularly distinctive and unusual in the landscape — fresh, cool-looking, and completely unlike any other flowering shrub color. Limelight blooms on new wood and can be pruned hard in late winter to control size and encourage vigorous new shoots with maximum flower production. In zone 9, Limelight performs well in morning sun and afternoon shade; full day sun may cause wilting during peak summer heat. The large flower heads dry beautifully on the plant for fall and winter ornamental interest.

common_name: Limelight Prime Hydrangea (Compact Improved Lime-Green Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Limelight Prime carries the same fresh lime-green flower panicles that made the original Limelight one of the most popular panicle hydrangeas ever introduced, but on a somewhat more compact plant with stronger, more upright stems that better resist flopping under the weight of the large flower heads. The panicles age to soft pink and then tan through fall, extending the season of color well beyond the initial green flush, and because it blooms on new wood it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells for the fullest, most weather-resistant flower panicles.

Plant in rocky, calcareous, lean, very well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Limestone Milkvine is a native twining perennial vine of canyon edges, open rocky woodlands, and limestone outcrops in Texas and adjacent Oklahoma. It produces somewhat rough, heart-shaped leaves and small, dark maroon to brownish-purple, 5-petaled star-shaped flowers with a slight odor that attracts small flies as pollinators, followed by spindle-shaped seed pods that split to release wind-dispersed, plume-tailed seeds. Once established it is notably drought-tolerant and thrives without supplemental water in rocky, calcareous soils where most vines fail. It is an ecologically appropriate native vine for Texas Hill Country gardens seeking regionally adapted, low-water climbing plants.

Plant in moist, well-drained loam in partial shade to full sun; linden viburnum tolerates a wide range of soils and takes on some drought tolerance once its roots are established. The broad, felted, toothed leaves resemble those of a linden tree, giving the shrub its common name, and turn shades of russet and wine-red in autumn. Domed clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are followed, on cross-pollinated plants, by a heavy fall crop of glossy red berries that persist into winter and draw overwintering songbirds. Its dense, rounded form and reliable fruit set make it a good understory screening shrub for a woodland edge or shaded property line.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; lion's tail is one of the most visually striking tall sub-shrubs for warm climate gardens — a South African native producing from late summer through autumn and into winter (September through February in mild climates) long, upright, square-stemmed shoots bearing at regular intervals dense, globular whorls of velvety-textured, tubular, two-lipped, brilliant deep-orange to orange-scarlet flowers — the stacked orange rings of flowers arranged up the stem creating the 'lion's tail' silhouette that gives the plant its common name. Each individual flower is a vivid, velvet-textured, deep orange tube about 2 inches long projecting upward from the whorl, and a large plant in full bloom with multiple stems bearing stacked rings of vivid orange is one of the most spectacular displays in the subtropical garden. The color is a specific, saturated, warm orange-to-vermillion that attracts hummingbirds powerfully — migrating hummingbirds on the Gulf Coast flyway visit lion's tail repeatedly. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, requiring little supplemental water in zone 9 after the first season. Fast-growing from seed, potentially blooming in the first year. The traditional South African medicinal plant known as 'wilde dagga' (wild hemp) — no relation to cannabis.

common_name: Lipstick Plant (Lipstick Vine, Red Bugle Vine)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in fast-draining, well-aerated growing medium (an orchid bark mix or coarse potting soil with added perlite); Lipstick Plant is naturally epiphytic and requires excellent drainage to prevent root and stem rot. Aeschynanthus pulcher is a trailing, semi-succulent epiphytic vine from Malaysia and Java in the Gesneriaceae family — the same family as African Violets and Gloxinias. The common name comes from the flowers: vivid scarlet to red tubular blooms 2–3 inches long that emerge from dark maroon or dark brown tubular calyxes — the effect is precisely that of a red lipstick emerging from its case. The flowers are produced at the tips of the trailing stems (and sometimes along the stems) in winter-spring flush and sporadically throughout the year, and are an outstanding hummingbird attractant when the plant is grown outdoors in season. The stems are clothed in fleshy, glossy, dark-green, oval leaves that overlap along the stems. The cascading habit and attractive foliage make it excellent for hanging baskets and wall planters even when not in flower. Numerous hybrids and cultivars offer flowers in orange, yellow, pink, and bicolors in addition to the classic red.

common_name: Little Devil Ninebark (Dwarf Dark-Purple Foliage Ninebark)
notes: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; ninebark is an exceptionally tough native shrub tolerating clay, poor soil, and drought once established. Little Devil is a true dwarf ninebark selection, staying under 4 feet tall and wide — roughly a third the size of the straight species and more compact than even 'Diabolo' or 'Summer Wine' — while still producing the same deep purple-black foliage and clusters of small white to pale-pink spring flowers that draw native pollinators. Its small scale makes it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller mixed borders where full-size dark-leaf ninebark cultivars would be too large. Exfoliating bark on older stems adds winter texture; prune out the oldest stems at the base every 2–3 years to keep growth vigorous.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Gem is the single most important and most widely planted named cultivar of the Southern magnolia — a compact, narrow-form selection introduced by Warren Steed of Steed's Nursery in Candor, North Carolina, that has transformed the usability of this iconic Southern tree for residential landscapes. The standard Southern magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora) can reach 60–80 feet and 30–40 feet wide, making it a poor choice for typical modern residential lots. Little Gem reaches 15–25 feet tall with a dense, narrow spread of 7–10 feet — fitting foundation plantings, narrow screening situations, and typical residential lots that the species magnolia would overwhelm. Most remarkably, Little Gem begins blooming at 2–3 years of age — compared to 10–15 years for seed-grown species trees — producing medium-sized (3–4 inch), intensely fragrant white flowers from May through fall in zone 9 with periodic bloom throughout the growing season. The leaves have the characteristic deep green upper surface and rich cinnamon-brown woolly undersurface (indumentum) of the species. Little Gem also makes an outstanding espalier subject, pruned flat against a fence or wall to create a formal evergreen screen. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil; Southern magnolias dislike wet feet.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Little Henry Virginia Sweetspire performs well in the partial shade typical of the Gulf South understory, with good color and flowering in conditions too shaded for many ornamental shrubs; Little Henry (sold under the trade name 'Little Henry', patent name 'Sprich') is a compact selection of Virginia Sweetspire (Itea virginica), a native deciduous shrub of the Gulf South coastal plain that provides three distinct seasons of ornamental interest — fragrant white bottlebrush flower spikes in June–July, healthy green summer foliage, and an extraordinary fall color display of burgundy, orange-red, and crimson that persists for weeks longer than most shrubs in zone 9's mild autumns. The fragrant white flower spikes (4–6 inches long) appear in June when relatively few other ornamental shrubs bloom, attracting pollinators during a midsummer gap in the landscape flowering sequence. As a native Gulf Coast species, Virginia Sweetspire is perfectly adapted to the heat, humidity, and periodic flooding of Gulf South landscapes — tolerating wet soils along pond edges, creek banks, and low-lying areas where introduced landscape shrubs often fail. The compact scale of Little Henry makes the ornamental quality of the species accessible for residential landscapes where the spreading colonizing habit of the straight species would be inappropriate.

common_name: Little Henry Virginia Sweetspire (Compact Fragrant White Native Shrub for Partial Shade)
notes: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Henry is a compact selection of Virginia Sweetspire (Itea virginica) — one of the most valuable and reliable native shrubs for eastern North American shade and partial-shade gardens, providing three distinct seasons of ornamental interest in a small, manageable size suitable for mixed borders and foundation plantings. In late spring to early summer (May–June in zone 9), Little Henry produces long, arching, fragrant white flower racemes (3–4 inches) that droop gracefully from the branches, providing light sweetly-scented bloom when many shrubs have finished flowering. The summer foliage is clean, medium-green, and disease-free. Then in autumn, Little Henry delivers one of the most reliable and vivid fall color displays of any native shrub adapted to Gulf South conditions — the leaves turn scarlet, burgundy, purple-red, and orange, often holding the fall color longer than most other shrubs and providing persistent autumn interest through October and into November in zone 9. The compact habit (2–3 feet versus 4–5 feet for the standard species) makes Little Henry more versatile in typical garden settings. Virginia Sweetspire is native to moist woods and stream banks throughout the eastern US, including Gulf Coast regions, providing excellent ecological value — it is a larval host for several moths and provides wildlife habitat through the winter.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; keep evenly watered, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry, hot conditions. Little Honey is a compact, dwarf, golden-leaved sport of the classic native oakleaf hydrangea, Hydrangea quercifolia, selected for foliage that emerges bright chartreuse-gold in spring and holds strong golden color through summer before turning shades of orange-red in fall — a dramatic color echo of the oakleaf's already excellent native fall display. Creamy white, cone-shaped flower panicles appear in early summer, aging to soft pink, though the golden foliage is the primary draw of this compact cultivar, which stays considerably smaller than the species and fits well into smaller shaded gardens where a full-sized oakleaf hydrangea would be too large. An outstanding foliage-color accent for a partly shaded border, zone 5–9.

common_name: Little Joe Viburnum (Dwarf Native Walter's Viburnum)
notes: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart for a low hedge. Little Joe is a dwarf cultivar of Walter's viburnum, a Southeastern native shrub, selected for a naturally low, dense, mounding habit that tops out around 2-3 feet, dramatically smaller than the straight species, which can reach 10-20 feet as an untrimmed large shrub or small tree. Small, glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves (in the Gulf South, foliage often persists through mild winters) provide fine texture, and clusters of small white flowers appear in spring, followed by small red fruit that ripens to black and draws songbirds. Its compact size and native heritage make it a low-maintenance, wildlife-friendly choice for foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where the full-sized species would quickly outgrow the space. It tolerates a range of soil moisture from average garden conditions to occasionally wet sites, reflecting its native habitat in low woods and along streams, and needs little pruning to maintain its naturally tidy, compact form.

common_name: Little Lamb Hydrangea (Fine-Textured Panicle Hydrangea with Small Dainty Blooms)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; afternoon shade helps sustain flower quality through the hottest part of summer in zone 9. Little Lamb is a panicle hydrangea selected for smaller, more refined flower panicles made up of many tiny individual florets, giving the plant an airier, more delicate texture than the large, heavy blooms of cultivars like Limelight, and earning its name from the fluffy, lamb's-wool appearance of the massed small white flowers. Blooms open pure white in mid- to late summer and age to soft pink as temperatures cool in fall, held on sturdy stems that resist the flopping some large-flowered panicle hydrangeas suffer after rain. As with all Hydrangea paniculata, it blooms reliably on new wood, so hard pruning in late winter to shape the plant and encourage vigorous new growth does not sacrifice the coming season's bloom.

common_name: Little Lime Hydrangea (Compact Lime-Green Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Lime is the compact version of the celebrated Limelight hydrangea — a dwarf selection (3–5 feet) that produces the same distinctive chartreuse-to-cream flower panicles in a proportionate size for smaller residential garden spaces where the full-size Limelight (6–8 feet) would dominate. The flower color progression is identical to Limelight: opening chartreuse-green in midsummer, maturing to creamy white, and transitioning through pink to dusty rose and finally buff-parchment as the flowers age through summer into fall — providing a 4–5 month evolving color display from a single set of flower heads. Like all Hydrangea paniculata cultivars, Little Lime blooms on new wood and is pruned hard in late winter (to 12–18 inches) to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum flower production. This makes it essentially foolproof — unlike French hydrangeas that lose flowers if pruned at the wrong time, Little Lime reliably flowers on whatever new wood it produces after any pruning regime. In zone 9, morning sun with afternoon shade is preferred — sufficient sun for good flower production with heat protection during the intense Gulf South afternoon. The compact size makes Little Lime suitable for foundation plantings, smaller landscape spaces, and containers.

common_name: Little Lime Punch Hydrangea (Compact Pink-Red Aging Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Little Lime Punch is a compact panicle hydrangea that opens the same fresh lime-green flower panicles as its parent Little Lime, but ages through a more pronounced rosy-pink-to-red flush by late summer and fall, giving a bolder two-tone color progression on a plant scaled for a smaller border or foundation planting. Sturdy stems hold the flower heads upright without staking, and because it blooms on new wood it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells for the fullest panicles and the most vivid late-season color change.

common_name: Little Ollie Dwarf Olive (Fruitless Compact Landscape Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Ollie is a compact, naturally dwarf, non-fruiting selection of common olive, prized for the same fine-textured, silvery-gray evergreen foliage as full-sized olive trees but on a dense, easily maintained shrub that fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and containers far better than a full-scale olive tree. Because it produces little or no fruit, it avoids the dropped-olive mess and staining that can be a drawback of ornamental fruiting olives planted near hardscape. It is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soils, and needs only occasional shearing to maintain a tidy, rounded form, making it a low-maintenance evergreen backbone plant for xeriscape and Mediterranean-style landscapes.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Little Princess is a classic compact Japanese spiraea — a neat, mounding dwarf shrub staying 18–30 inches tall with a wider spread, producing masses of small, rose-pink flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) in late spring to early summer against mid-green foliage. Where Magic Carpet spiraea is grown primarily for foliage color, Little Princess is grown primarily for its prolific pink summer flower display — the small, densely packed flower heads cover the plant in a vivid pink display for 4–6 weeks and attract bees and butterflies intensively during bloom. The compact, mounding habit and fine-textured blue-green to medium-green summer foliage that transitions to orange-red in fall provide seasonal interest beyond the spring bloom. Shear lightly immediately after flowering to promote a second, lighter summer flush and maintain the naturally compact mounding form — cutting back by one-third after spring bloom encourages fresh new growth and often produces additional flowering in late summer. Little Princess is among the most cold-hardy Japanese spiraea cultivars, and its compact size and adaptability to clay and average soils make it one of the most practical and reliable deciduous flowering shrubs for zone 4–8 landscapes.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after the main bloom flush to tidy the mound and encourage a modest rebloom. Little Princess is a compact, mounded spirea grown primarily for its abundant clusters of rose-pink flowers that blanket the blue-green foliage in early summer, rather than for foliage color as with the gold-leaved spirea cultivars. Its dense, tidy, low habit suits it to low hedges, foundation plantings, and mixed borders where a reliable flush of pink summer bloom is wanted on a plant that stays in bounds without heavy pruning. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor soil and urban heat with minimal maintenance.

common_name: Little Quick Fire Hydrangea (Compact Early-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Little Quick Fire is a compact sport of Quick Fire hydrangea, keeping the same early bloom timing and unusually fast color change but on a dense, rounded shrub well under half the mature size of most panicle hydrangeas. White flower panicles open several weeks ahead of standard panicle hydrangeas in early summer, then shift to pink and finally deep wine-red within weeks, giving a long season of color change on sturdy stems that hold the flower heads upright without staking. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it tolerates a hard late-winter pruning to control size or renew an aging plant without sacrificing the coming season's bloom, and it takes more sun than mophead hydrangeas without wilting.

common_name: Little Quickfire Hydrangea (Compact Early-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate considerably more sun than bigleaf types. Little Quickfire is a compact sport of the popular Quickfire panicle hydrangea, offering the same trait of blooming several weeks earlier than most other panicle hydrangeas, with conical flower clusters opening white and aging to a rich pink-to-burgundy as the season progresses, but on a smaller-scale plant that fits foundation plantings and smaller beds where full-sized Quickfire would be too large. Unlike bigleaf hydrangeas, flower color is not affected by soil pH, and flower buds form on new wood, so it can be pruned back hard in late winter without sacrificing that year's bloom. Water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads in late winter to tidy the plant before new growth begins.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; little silverbell is the smallest of the native silverbells (Halesia), forming a shrubby small tree to 25 feet with the genus's characteristic white, bell-shaped flowers in spring before leaf-out. The flowers hang in clusters along the bare winter stems and create a charming early spring display. The fruits develop the distinctive winged structure typical of the genus. This species is native to the Gulf Coastal Plain and Piedmont from South Carolina to Texas and is better adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South (zone 9a) than the more commonly planted Carolina silverbell (H. tetraptera). An excellent native understory tree for partial shade in moist, acidic, woodland garden settings.

common_name: Little Spire Russian Sage (Compact Russian Sage)
notes: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Little Spire is a compact Russian sage cultivar that stays 18–30 inches — roughly half the height of standard Russian sage — making it manageable in typical residential borders where the full-size species (3–5 feet) would require staking and frequent division to remain attractive. The characteristic soft, lavender-blue, hazy flower spikes and silver-white, finely cut aromatic foliage are present in the compact form, creating the same misty, blue-silver cloud effect but in a more contained, neater habit. Russian sage is named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 1995 and remains one of the finest blue-silver perennials for full-sun, dry situations. The hazy lavender-blue flower spikes provide weeks of color from midsummer through fall, and the silver-white stems remain attractive through winter as a structural element in the garden. Strongly deer-resistant; exceptionally drought-tolerant once established; attracts bees and butterflies. The key challenge in zone 9 is the combination of summer heat and humidity — Russian sage succeeds with absolutely excellent drainage, lean soil, and good air circulation. In heavy clay or wet sites, it is short-lived or fails to establish. In well-drained, raised bed conditions or gravelly soils, it is reliably perennial in zone 9.

common_name: Little Woody Redbud (True Dwarf Vase-Shaped Redbud)
notes: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Woody is a genuine dwarf redbud, selected in 2000 by North Carolina plantsman Paul Woody, reaching only 10-12 feet at maturity with a tidy, vase-shaped form rather than the larger spreading canopy of the straight species. In early spring, the bare branches are covered in the classic rosy-pink, pea-like redbud flowers before the heart-shaped leaves emerge, providing the same spectacular native spring display as a standard redbud but scaled for a small yard, courtyard, or foundation planting. Water deeply during the first two years to establish the root system, then supplement only during dry spells once established. Prune lightly just after flowering if any shaping is needed.

Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; live oak is the defining tree of the Gulf Coast landscape, forming magnificent broad, sweeping canopies of twisted horizontal branches draped with Spanish moss, with a single mature tree providing habitat for hundreds of species of insects, birds, and wildlife. The leaves are semi-evergreen in zone 8 (dropping briefly in late winter as new leaves emerge) and evergreen in zone 9–10. It tolerates salt spray, sandy soils, and periodic drought once established and grows steadily — 1–2 feet per year when young. The small acorns are critically important fall and winter food for blue jays, wild turkeys, squirrels, and deer. Plant far from structures and utility lines — mature trees reach 40–60 feet tall with 60–100 foot spread. A heritage landscape tree meant for centuries.

Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich, peaty, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun — loblolly bay is a spectacular native evergreen tree of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic coastal plain bay swamps and wet pine flatwoods, producing 2.5–3 inch, pure white, camellia-like flowers with prominent gold stamens that appear from June through October in the hottest part of the summer when few other flowering trees bloom. The dark, glossy, evergreen leaves are handsome year-round; the bark is attractively furrowed and gray. It grows naturally in the acidic, peaty, frequently saturated soils of bay swamps, seeps, and wet flatwood depressions — conditions exactly matching an acidic, moist bog garden or the wet margins of a natural pond. It is closely related to the camellia family and equally demanding in its soil pH requirements; failure is almost always caused by insufficiently acidic soil. An outstanding native flowering tree for wet, acidic, shaded garden sites in zone 7–9.

Plant container-grown or bare-root seedlings in fall or early spring in average to moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; loblolly pine grows quickly on a wide range of soils and is the dominant commercial timber pine of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain. Long, dark green needles in bundles of three clothe a fast-growing, straight-trunked tree that can add two or more feet of height per year on a good site, eventually reaching well over 100 feet with a broad, rounded crown at maturity, making it one of the most economically important timber and pulpwood trees in the American South. It reseeds itself readily on disturbed and cutover ground and is a familiar, defining tree of the region's forests, providing habitat and seed for a wide range of birds and mammals including favored nesting habitat for red-cockaded woodpeckers in older stands. Give it plenty of room to reach full size, since it is not a small-yard tree, and avoid planting where ice storms or hurricane-force wind could bring down large limbs near structures.

Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Loebner magnolia is a hybrid between Magnolia kobus (Kobus magnolia) and M. stellata (star magnolia), combining the tree-like stature and vigor of the kobus parent with the larger, more numerous flower petals and earlier flowering of the stellata parent to produce a superior garden tree. In April the bare branches become covered with large, many-petaled, white to pale-pink, starry, fragrant flowers before the leaves emerge, creating a spectacular spring display. The cultivar 'Merrill' — vigorous, reliably flowering at a young age, and very cold-hardy — is the most widely planted and commercially available selection, and is considered one of the finest magnolias for zones 4–8. 'Leonard Messel' produces pale-pink to rose-purple flowers with typically 12 petals and is outstanding in a soft-pink color scheme. Both are superior to M. stellata in size, vigor, and visual impact. Tolerates partial shade and clay soil better than most magnolias. An excellent choice as a single specimen or small grove in lawns, borders, and naturalistic gardens.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; longstalked holly is a Japanese evergreen holly quite unlike the typical image of holly — the leaves are entire, smooth-margined, and spineless, with a glossy, dark green appearance resembling camellia leaves. The small, bright red berries are borne on unusually long, slender stalks (reflecting the name 'pedunculosa' — long-stalked) that hold the berries away from the foliage in a distinctive dangling display quite unlike any other holly. One of the hardiest broad-leaved evergreen hollies, tolerating temperatures to –20°F in zone 5 with protection. Excellent bird food: the bright berries attract thrushes, waxwings, and mockingbirds in fall and winter. A refined and underused evergreen screening shrub or small tree that adds elegant, season-long interest. Requires both male and female plants for berry set.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Longwood Blue bluebeard is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring. Aromatic, silvery-green foliage sets off dense clusters of vivid, true-blue, fringed flowers that wreathe the upper stems from late summer into fall, a bloom period that provides valuable late-season nectar for bees and butterflies when many other shrubs have finished flowering. Introduced by Longwood Gardens and prized for its especially rich, saturated blue flower color compared to older caryopteris cultivars, it is a compact, easy-care choice for the front or middle of a sunny border, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches from the ground in late winter, since it flowers on new wood and benefits from hard annual pruning to stay compact and floriferous.

common_name: Longwood Purple American Wisteria (Non-Invasive Native Wisteria Selection)
notes: Plant near a very strong trellis, pergola, or fence in full sun to partial shade; unlike the invasive Asian wisterias, this native selection is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. Longwood Purple, selected at Longwood Gardens, is a vigorous, heavy-blooming American wisteria cultivar with dense, fragrant, blue-purple flower clusters in late spring and good repeat bloom through summer, a reliability that seed-grown American wisteria does not consistently offer. It flowers at a younger age than seed-grown plants and responds well to pruning, staying more manageable than the aggressive Chinese and Japanese wisteria species widely sold. Prune twice yearly — once after the main spring bloom and again in late winter — to maintain size and encourage flowering spurs.

common_name: Louis Philippe Rose (Classic Deep South Heirloom China Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Introduced from China in the 1830s and long naturalized around old homesites and cemeteries across the Deep South, Louis Philippe is a classic 'found rose,' still turning up growing untended for a century or more with little care, testament to its exceptional heat tolerance, disease resistance, and toughness. It produces rich crimson-red, cupped, moderately fragrant blooms almost continuously through the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season, a trait that made China roses like this one especially valuable to Southern gardeners long before modern repeat-blooming roses existed. It thrives on neglect, needs only an occasional shaping prune, and is highly resistant to the black spot and powdery mildew that trouble many modern hybrid roses in humid climates.

common_name: Louise Odier Rose (Fragrant Warm-Pink Bourbon Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Louise Odier, introduced in 1851, is a classic Bourbon rose bearing warm rose-pink, cupped, densely petaled flowers with an exceptionally strong, rich fragrance, produced in generous flushes through the growing season on an upright, well-branched shrub. Bourbon roses like this one bridge the gap between antique once-blooming roses and modern repeat-flowering hybrids, and Louise Odier remains one of the most fragrant and reliable of the class for warm-climate gardens. Feed and water a bit more generously than tougher China or Tea roses, since Bourbons appreciate slightly richer soil, and prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued rebloom.

Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; nick the seed coat or soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination. Love-in-a-Puff (Cardiospermum halicacabum) is a delightful lightweight twining annual vine native throughout the tropics and subtropics including the Gulf Coast, where it scrambles through shrubs and fence wire producing a continuous display of tiny white flowers and its signature inflated, papery, three-winged seed pods that look exactly like miniature balloons or Japanese paper lanterns — the pods are responsible for the plant's whimsical common name. Inside each round green pod are three round, black seeds, each with a perfect white heart-shaped marking where they were attached to the pod wall — the 'heart seed' of the scientific name Cardiospermum. The vine is lightweight and delicate, climbing trellises, fences, and other plants to 8–10 feet by twining tendrils, never heavy or smothering. In zone 9–10, it naturalizes freely from dropped seeds. The leaves and seeds are used medicinally in Ayurvedic medicine for joint inflammation; research has identified anti-inflammatory compounds in the plant. An excellent, low-care vine for adding airy texture and charming seed pods to Gulf Coast gardens.

Plant transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Lucky series lantana is bred for a compact, uniform, mounding habit well suited to containers and small-space plantings. Clusters of small, brightly colored flowers in shades of yellow, pink, red-orange, and bicolor tones cover a dense, compact mound smaller and more uniform than older lantana selections, blooming continuously from late spring through frost and drawing butterflies and hummingbirds throughout the season. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives through the hottest, most humid part of summer with minimal care, tolerating poor soil and neglect far better than most bedding plants. It behaves as a root-hardy perennial in zones 8-11, dying back to the ground in a hard freeze and resprouting from the base the following spring, or is grown as a heat-loving annual further north.

Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Lydia broom forms a low, cascading mound of fine blue-green stems that is smothered in brilliant golden-yellow pea-shaped flowers for several weeks in late spring. It is exceptionally well suited to spilling over rock walls, covering dry slopes, or edging a gravel bed, and unlike some brooms it stays naturally tidy and compact without aggressive reseeding. Good drainage is essential — it declines quickly in heavy clay or soil that stays wet — but once sited correctly it needs almost no irrigation or fertilizer.

common_name: Lynn's Legacy Cenizo (Texas Superstar Reliable-Blooming Texas Sage)
notes: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline soil; Lynn's Legacy is a Texas Superstar-designated cenizo, discovered by plantsman Lynn Lowrey near Monterrey, Mexico, and selected because it blooms more consistently and for a longer stretch of the growing season than typical Leucophyllum cenizo, which famously flushes into bloom mainly around rain events. It shares the classic silvery, felted foliage that reflects heat and reduces water loss, along with clusters of lavender-purple tubular flowers, but with a more upright, slightly more refined growth habit than the common species. Never overwater, fertilize heavily, or amend the planting hole with organic matter, since excess moisture and rich soil are the most common causes of decline in cenizo. Outstanding for xeric, native, and wildlife gardens across zones 8-11.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Lynwood Gold is the most widely planted forsythia cultivar and perhaps the most familiar early-spring flowering shrub in American horticulture — a vigorous, upright-arching shrub that literally covers itself with vivid golden-yellow flowers in late February through March (in zone 8) before any leaves emerge, creating an explosive, golden-yellow color display that signals the end of winter. The flowers are produced on second-year wood along the entire length of the arching stems before any foliage appears — when in full bloom, a mature Lynwood Gold shrub is a mass of pure golden yellow visible from a considerable distance. This spectacle is the quintessential early spring garden moment in zone 5–8. Note: forsythia's flower bud hardiness is its limiting characteristic for zone 9 use — the flower buds require a period of cold dormancy and are damaged by extended warm winters in zone 9, where reliable flowering cannot be counted on every year. In zone 9, forsythia may flower well in cool-winter years and produce sparse bloom in mild winters. For zone 9 plantings, consider Karl Sax and Meadowlark cultivars with enhanced flower bud cold-hardiness, or accept the variable bloom performance of standard cultivars.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens on a trellis in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to partial shade; stephanotis is a twining vine from Madagascar prized for its waxy, pure-white, intensely fragrant tubular flowers in clusters from spring through summer — the flowers have one of the most exquisite perfumes in the plant kingdom and are traditionally used in bridal bouquets and leis. Keep the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged. The vine requires a period of cool, dry rest in winter (55–60°F) to set flower buds for the following season. Plants resent being moved once established; keep in the same pot or location for best performance. Grow outdoors year-round only in frost-free zones.

Plant in full sun in sandy, gravelly, or any extremely well-draining soil medium, since this Madagascar succulent tree rots quickly in heavy or moisture-retentive soil. Pachypodium geayi is very similar to and frequently confused with the more common Pachypodium lamerei in the nursery trade, but can be distinguished by its narrower, longer, more silvery-gray leaves with fine hairs along the margins, giving the crown a softer, more silvered appearance than lamerei's broader, glossier green leaves. Like its relative, it grows as a tall, spine-covered succulent column that is not a true palm despite the common name, eventually branching with age and producing fragrant, pinwheel-shaped white flowers at the stem tips on mature specimens grown in strong light. The milky sap is toxic and irritating to skin and eyes, so wear gloves when pruning or repotting, and site the sharp, spine-covered trunk away from foot traffic.

common_name: Madagascar Palm (Spiny Club, Club-Foot, Lamerei Pachypodium)
notes: Plant in full sun in sandy, gravelly, or any extremely well-draining soil medium — Madagascar Palm rots rapidly in heavy or moisture-retaining soils and must never sit in standing water. Pachypodium lamerei is a tall, columnar succulent tree native to the arid regions of southern Madagascar in the family Apocynaceae (the same family as Plumeria, Oleander, and Hoya), one of the most striking and distinctive succulents regularly available in the horticultural trade. Despite the common name 'Madagascar Palm,' it is not a palm at all — it belongs to no monocot group but is instead a tropical succulent adapted to the dry, spiny deserts of Madagascar. The plant grows as a tall, single column (branching occasionally with age) of silvery-gray to greenish, ridged stem covered along its entire length with clusters of three sharp, gray-white spines 1–2 inches long at each leaf scar — the spines and the architectural, column-like form create an immediate visual impression of a cactus from the American deserts but represent an entirely convergent adaptation on another continent. From the top of the column, a rosette of long, narrow, dark-green leaves appears in the growing season. On mature specimens, the column tip produces fragrant, white, pinwheel-shaped flowers (resembling Plumeria) — rare and prized in cultivation. The milky sap is toxic. A dramatic, architectural container specimen or landscape accent for hot, dry, zone 10-11 gardens.

common_name: Madame Galen Trumpet Vine (Less-Aggressive Orange-Red Trumpet Creeper)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun against a strong, permanent structure, since this vigorous woody vine becomes heavy over time and can damage weak supports or siding it is allowed to climb directly. A hybrid between American trumpet creeper and Chinese trumpet vine, Madame Galen produces abundant clusters of large, salmon-orange to apricot-red trumpet-shaped flowers through summer that are a favorite of hummingbirds. It is somewhat less prone to aggressive root suckering than the wild American species, though it still needs a firm hand with pruning to keep it in bounds and off of nearby structures. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease, and a hard pruning in late winter keeps the vine full and encourages the current season's flowering growth.

common_name: Madame Isaac Pereire Rose (Fragrant Bourbon Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, compost-enriched soil, and prune back by about a third after the main spring flush to encourage a strong repeat bloom later in the season. Bred by Garçon in France and introduced in 1881, Madame Isaac Pereire is a Bourbon rose renowned as one of the most fragrant roses ever raised, bearing very large, deeply cupped, ruffled blooms in a rich magenta-pink that release an intense, raspberry-like old-rose perfume detectable from a distance. Its vigorous, somewhat lax growth habit allows it to be kept as a large rounded shrub or trained as a short climber on a wall or pillar for extra height and better air movement through the dense foliage. Deadhead through summer to encourage the sporadic rebloom that follows its heavy spring display.

common_name: Madame Joseph Schwartz Rose (Ivory-Blush Sport of Duchesse de Brabant)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Madame Joseph Schwartz, introduced in 1871, is an ivory-white Tea rose blushed with soft pink that arose as a sport of the classic Duchesse de Brabant, sharing its parent's cupped, informal flower form, rich fragrance, and outstanding heat tolerance. Long grown as a 'found rose' in old Texas and Deep South gardens, it blooms in flushes almost continuously through the growing season and requires little care beyond a sunny, well-drained site and occasional light pruning after each flush. Its excellent disease resistance and easygoing nature have kept it a favorite in heirloom rose collections for generations.

common_name: Maggie Rose (Found Texas China-Bourbon Antique Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Maggie needs little beyond an occasional deep watering once established. Like many of the antique roses preserved through the Texas rose rustling movement, Maggie is a found rose, rediscovered growing untended at an old homestead and propagated from cuttings rather than traced to a known breeder or introduction date, and it is generally considered a China-Bourbon hybrid based on its growth habit and bloom. It produces richly fragrant, cupped, deep magenta-pink flowers in generous flushes from spring through fall on a vigorous, well-branched shrub that shrugs off Southern heat, humidity, and poor soil with the same toughness that let it survive decades of neglect at its original homesite. Its resilience and near-constant bloom make it an excellent low-input choice for a Gulf Coast heirloom border, and it asks for little beyond an occasional shaping prune after the heaviest spring flush.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Magic Carpet is one of the most spectacular compact spiraea cultivars for foliage color — a dwarf selection staying 12–24 inches tall that produces a dramatic seasonal foliage display beginning with vivid red-orange to scarlet new growth in spring, maturing to yellow-gold through summer, and transitioning to orange-red fall color. The three-season foliage interest — red spring, gold summer, orange fall — combined with pink summer flowers creates year-round ornamental value rarely matched by such a compact shrub. The flower heads are pink, produced in early summer above the colorful foliage, but the foliage is the primary ornamental feature. Magic Carpet's extremely compact size makes it outstanding for edging, mass planting as a colorful ground cover, container gardens, and foreground positions in shrub borders where larger spiraea would overwhelm. Like all Japanese spiraea cultivars, it is extremely tough and adaptable — tolerating drought, clay soil, urban conditions, and the heat of zone 9 with minimal care. Shear lightly after flowering and again in late summer to encourage fresh, colorful new growth. In zone 9, Magic Carpet tends to be slightly more compact than in cooler zones and performs best in full sun with good drainage. Deer-resistant once established.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Magnoliiflora is an antique Camellia japonica cultivar dating to around 1888, named for its smaller, semi-double, soft blush-pink flowers whose loosely arranged petals and prominent stamens give them a delicate resemblance to a small magnolia bloom, a distinctive form among the many fuller, more formal camellia types. It flowers later in the season than many other japonica cultivars, extending camellia bloom into late winter and early spring. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub provides dense, glossy year-round structure. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Majestic Beauty Indian Hawthorn (Tree-Form Large Indian Hawthorn)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Majestic Beauty is a hybrid Indian hawthorn selected for its unusually large mature size, growing into a substantial large shrub or small tree rather than the compact rounded mound typical of most Indian hawthorn cultivars, which makes it useful for screening, specimen planting, or a small flowering tree in coastal landscapes. In spring it produces abundant clusters of fragrant, light pink flowers followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds, all on glossy, leathery, disease-resistant foliage. It shares the species' outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soils, making it a strong performer in exposed coastal Gulf sites, though good air circulation helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

common_name: Major Wheeler Coral Honeysuckle (Best Native Hummingbird Honeysuckle Vine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Major Wheeler is widely considered the finest cultivar of native coral honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) — a vigorous, non-invasive, native vine producing intense scarlet-red tubular flowers in large clusters throughout the spring and early summer with rebloom through fall. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), Coral honeysuckle is well-behaved, manageable, and ecologically beneficial — a twining vine that climbs to 6–12 feet without smothering everything in its path, and one of the premier hummingbird plants in eastern North American gardens. 'Major Wheeler' was selected for exceptionally heavy and prolonged bloom compared to the straight species — the flower clusters are larger, more numerous, and the rebloom period more consistent, making it the overwhelming choice among coral honeysuckle cultivars for maximum ornamental and hummingbird value. The vivid red tubular flowers have no fragrance (unlike Japanese honeysuckle) but attract ruby-throated hummingbirds with exceptional consistency from spring through fall. The semi-evergreen, blue-green, oval leaves are attractive even when not in bloom. In zone 9, Major Wheeler performs best with afternoon shade protection during the hottest summers. Red berries persist into fall, providing late-season food for thrushes, mockingbirds, and other frugivorous birds.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with vertical support; Major Wheeler is widely considered the finest cultivar of trumpet honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) — the native American hummingbird vine — selected for its exceptionally prolific and long flower production. While the species is already outstanding for hummingbirds, Major Wheeler produces dramatically more flowers per season and repeats bloom flushes more reliably than unselected species plants. The 1.5–2 inch, tubular scarlet-to-coral-red flowers are produced in dense terminal clusters from spring through fall in zone 9, creating an almost unmatched hummingbird feeding resource — Ruby-throated hummingbirds visit repeatedly, and the vine at peak bloom will attract multiple hummingbirds simultaneously. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), trumpet honeysuckle is a well-behaved native that does not self-seed aggressively or spread invasively. The semi-evergreen foliage is attractive, with the characteristic perfoliate leaves (the vine stem appears to grow through the center of the leaf pairs) near the flowers. Major Wheeler is drought-tolerant once established and adaptable to a wide range of soils and light conditions from full sun to partial shade. The profusion of red flowers followed by small red berries provides exceptional wildlife value throughout the year.

Maleberry is a native deciduous shrub of wet, acidic soils across the eastern United States, found in pocosins, bog margins, wet flatwoods, and seasonally flooded stream banks from Maine south to Florida and west to Texas. The clusters of small, urn-shaped white flowers in late spring attract native bees and bumblebees, while the attractive fall foliage ranges from yellow to orange-red in appropriate sunlight. A member of the blueberry family (Ericaceae), Maleberry shares the extreme soil requirements of its relatives — strongly acidic, humus-rich, poorly drained to saturated conditions that would stress most landscape shrubs. Well-suited for wet, acidic garden settings including bog gardens, rain garden overflow zones, and moist native plant hedges in acid soil conditions, Maleberry is rarely cultivated but deserves wider use for challenging wet, acidic sites. Plant rooted cuttings in strongly acidic, moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in fall into well-drained, rocky to loamy soil in partial sun, matching the dry, open coniferous forest understory this species naturally inhabits across the Northern Rockies and Pacific Northwest. Mallow ninebark forms a dense, rounded mound of maple-like lobed leaves with clusters of small white to pinkish flowers in early summer that draw native bees and other pollinating insects. Its inflated seed capsules are eaten by songbirds through fall, while the foliage and twigs are browsed by deer and elk, making it an important component of wildlife habitat in dry western forests. Peeling, multi-layered bark gives the shrub interest through the winter months and shelter for overwintering insects.

common_name: Malvern Hills Rose (David Austin English Rambling Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, training the long, flexible canes over sturdy support such as an arch, pergola, or large fence, since Malvern Hills is one of the more vigorous, rambling David Austin introductions rather than a compact border shrub. Small, soft yellow, rosette-shaped flowers open in dense clusters in a single heavy flush in late spring, carrying a light, fresh fragrance, and the shrub's shade tolerance and vigor make it useful for covering a difficult structure or fence line that would defeat a less rambunctious climber. Prune immediately after the spring bloom to shape and remove old wood, since it flowers primarily on growth made the previous year.

common_name: Maman Cochet Rose (Large-Flowered Antique Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Maman Cochet, introduced in 1893, produces large, full, high-centered flowers in soft pink shaded with cream on the reverse of the petals, opening from long, elegant buds that made it a favorite cut flower and exhibition rose in its era. It remains one of the most widely planted and beloved Tea roses in old Southern gardens for its combination of exceptional bloom size, repeat flowering through the growing season, and the toughness and heat tolerance characteristic of Tea roses. Prune lightly after each flush to encourage continued rebloom, and expect strong resistance to black spot and powdery mildew even in humid Gulf Coast summers.

common_name: Mammy Croton (Dark Twisted-Leaf Red-and-Gold Croton Cultivar)
notes: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammy Croton is one of the most distinctive and recognizable croton cultivars — immediately identifiable by its strongly twisted, spiraling, contorted leaves that curl and spiral along their length rather than lying flat, creating an unusual three-dimensional texture unlike any other commonly available ornamental foliage plant. The leaf color is darker and more intensely red-dominated than Petra: deep, burgundy-red to red-and-gold coloring on a dark green base, with the red tones more predominant and the yellow more restricted to the midrib and splashes near the veins. The overall effect is a darker, moodier palette than the brighter, more orange-dominated Petra — making Mammy especially effective in tropical designs with other dark-leaved companions like black elephant ear, purple ti plant, and dark caladiums. In zone 9, Mammy is typically used as a warm-season container plant or annual-style tropical that is moved indoors before frost; in zone 10b-12 it grows as a permanent perennial shrub. The twisted leaf form is most pronounced in high light conditions — leaves in deep shade tend to become more flattened and less dramatically spiral. The unusual form makes Mammy Croton a striking conversation-piece plant in tropical container arrangements.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; mandevilla is one of the most popular tropical vines for patio containers in the United States, producing large, trumpet-shaped flowers 3–4 inches across in brilliant pink, red, or white from spring through frost. The climbing stems have glossy, dark green leaves that are attractive even out of bloom. Modern compact ('Sundaville' and 'Sun Parasol') series stay under 3 feet and are outstanding in large pots and hanging baskets. The larger vining types need a trellis or support and can reach 8–10 feet. Feed every 2 weeks with a bloom-booster fertilizer for maximum flower production. In zone 9–10 mandevilla may be left outdoors year-round in a sheltered location; in zone 8a bring inside at first frost and keep barely moist through winter. Very sap is milky white and mildly toxic — wear gloves when pruning.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; Manta Ray scindapsus climbs readily on a moss pole and develops larger, more richly marked leaves with vertical support. Thick, glossy, deep green leaves are marbled with irregular silver and gray patches and carried on distinctively winged, ridged petioles that give the plant a bold, slightly rugged texture compared to the smoother satin pothos more commonly sold. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it grows more vigorously and with larger foliage than many Scindapsus pictus cultivars once given a support to climb, making it a striking specimen for a moss pole in a bright room. Let the potting mix dry between waterings, provide bright indirect light for the strongest silver marbling, and mist occasionally to keep the thick leaves dust-free.

Plant in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; mapleleaf viburnum is exceptional among viburnums for its tolerance of both dry conditions and full shade — characteristics that together make it one of the most useful native shrubs for planting under established deciduous trees where root competition and low light challenge most plants. The maple-like leaves turn brilliant pink to rose-pink to crimson-magenta in fall, some of the most vivid fall color of any shade-tolerant shrub. Flat-topped white flower clusters in late spring attract native bees, followed by small dark blue-black berries (technically edible but not palatable) that are consumed by songbirds. Spreads slowly by rhizome to form naturalistic colonies; one of the best native shrubs for difficult dry shade situations.

common_name: Marble Queen Pothos (Heavily Variegated White-Green Pothos)
notes: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial shade, protected from direct hot sun which can scorch the pale variegated portions of the leaves. Marble Queen is a striking pothos cultivar with heart-shaped leaves marbled in bold patches of creamy white and green, a much more heavily variegated form than standard golden pothos, though the extensive white patches mean it grows more slowly and needs brighter light to stay vigorous and avoid reverting to plain green. It trails or climbs readily and is a popular hanging basket, shelf, or totem-trained houseplant, tolerating average indoor conditions and irregular watering better than most houseplants. In zone 9a it can summer outdoors in a shaded spot but must come indoors well before frost, since it has no cold tolerance.

Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Mardi Gras is a compact variegated abelia with green leaves edged in creamy white and flushed with rose-pink, especially on new growth and in cooler weather, giving the plant a colorful, festive look that lends the cultivar its name. It flowers over a long season from summer into fall with small, fragrant, pale pink to white tubular blooms attractive to pollinators, though the variegated foliage is the main ornamental draw. The dense, rounded, compact habit suits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and low informal hedges, and like other abelias it is tough and adaptable, tolerating heat, humidity, and drought once established with only light shaping needed after the main bloom flush.

common_name: Margarita Sweet Potato Vine (Brilliant Chartreuse Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine)
notes: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Margarita Sweet Potato Vine is a cultivar of ornamental sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) producing large, heart-shaped leaves in brilliant chartreuse to lime-green-yellow — one of the most luminous and versatile foliage colors available in an annual, capable of brightening dark garden areas and creating long-distance visual impact with its pure lime-yellow intensity. The heart-shaped leaves are larger and less lobed than 'Blackie', creating a softer, more flowing texture that contrasts well with both fine-textured annuals and bold-leaved tropical companions. 'Margarita' and 'Blackie' are the classic pairing in container and border compositions — the chartreuse and near-black create one of the most dramatic foliage contrasts available from annual plants, each color intensifying the visual impact of the other. The vigorous trailing habit (4–8 foot spread during Gulf South warm season) makes Margarita outstanding as a groundcover annual, as a trailer over pot edges and retaining walls, and as a weed-suppressing annual between permanent plantings. The chartreuse color illuminates shaded border edges and creates visual warmth in combination with cool blue-purple or coral-pink flowers. In Gulf South summer heat, Margarita vines grow rapidly enough to cover significant ground in 6–8 weeks from transplanting.

common_name: Marguerite Sweet Potato Vine (Chartreuse-Gold Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine)
notes: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Marguerite is the classic bright chartreuse-gold companion to the dark-leaved Blackie sweet potato vine, producing large, heart-shaped, glowing yellow-green leaves on fast-growing, trailing vines that quickly spill over the edges of containers, hanging baskets, and garden beds. Its vigorous, weed-smothering growth makes it a popular filler and spiller in mixed plantings, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought well once established, needing only occasional trimming to keep it from overwhelming smaller companion plants. Like other ornamental sweet potato vines, it produces edible tuberous roots, though the plant is grown almost exclusively for its foliage rather than as a food crop.

common_name: Marie Daly Rose (Thornless Louisiana China Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Marie Daly arose as a thornless sport of the beloved Cécile Brünner and was discovered and popularized in Louisiana, retaining that variety's dainty, shell-pink, sweetheart-shaped blooms and repeat flowering while dropping nearly all of the thorns from the canes — a real practical benefit for planting along paths, near doorways, or anywhere hands and clothing brush against the shrub. It grows own-root, dense, and bushy, and tolerates the heat and humidity of the Deep South with minimal disease pressure. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to encourage continued rebloom, and expect flowers in flushes from spring through fall in a mild Gulf Coast climate.

Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1888, Marie Pavié is a classic polyantha prized for producing dense clusters of small, fully double, blush-pink-to-white blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance unusual for such a compact rose. The tidy, rounded shrub blooms in flushes nearly year-round in mild climates and shows outstanding resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, requiring little to no spraying even in the humid Gulf South. Its modest size and dense, twiggy habit make it well suited to borders, low hedges, and containers, and it tolerates part shade better than most roses, though flowering is heaviest in full sun. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and to maintain shape; deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Mariesii doublefile viburnum develops its best horizontal, tiered branching structure with room to spread unpruned. Distinctly horizontal, layered branches are lined in spring with rows of flat, lacecap flower clusters held above the foliage on short stalks in a striking double row along each branch, giving the whole shrub a tiered, snow-covered appearance visible from a distance. One of the most architecturally striking flowering shrubs available, its strong horizontal branching habit provides four-season structural interest even without flowers, followed by red fruit that ripens to black and reliable burgundy fall color. Prune minimally and only to remove crossing or damaged branches, since heavy pruning disrupts the tiered branching pattern that is the plant's signature feature.

Marlberry is a handsome native evergreen shrub or small tree, native to the coastal hammocks, tropical hardwood forests, and pinelands of south Florida and the Keys, growing as a common and important component of the hammock understory layer in partial to full shade. It produces clusters of small white flowers from summer through fall, followed by clusters of round, glossy black berries that are one of the most reliable and abundant bird food sources in south Florida's hammock ecosystem — the berries are consumed by dozens of species of warblers, thrushes, vireos, and resident birds throughout fall and winter. An adaptable and attractive native shade shrub for zone 9b–11 landscapes, Marlberry fills the role of native understory shrub in conditions too shaded for most flowering shrubs, providing year-round evergreen structure, summer-fall blooms, and exceptional wildlife value. Important note: always confirm you are purchasing native Marlberry (Ardisia escallonioides) and not the look-alike invasive Coral Ardisia (Ardisia crenata), which has escaped cultivation and invaded Florida's native hammocks.

Marsh elder, also called high-tide bush, is a native deciduous shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coast salt marshes, growing precisely at the upper limit of regular tidal flooding — its common name 'high-tide bush' describes its ecological niche as the shrubby fringe that marks the upper boundary of the tidal marsh zone on both Atlantic and Gulf shorelines. Despite its unglamorous appearance for most of the year — a stiff, woody shrub with small, succulent leaves and inconspicuous late-summer flowers — marsh elder is ecologically critical: it provides nesting cover for marsh wrens, seaside sparrows, and clapper rails, and its seeds are consumed by dabbling ducks and shorebirds; it stabilizes the marsh-upland ecotone against erosion. In coastal restoration plantings along the Gulf, it is a primary native shrub for establishing the high marsh zone on restored or disturbed shorelines, often planted in combination with black needle rush (Juncus roemerianus) and saltmarsh cordgrass. It also serves as a windbreak and salt spray filter for adjacent upland plantings.

common_name: Martha Gonzales Rose (Compact Found Texas China Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart for a low border or mass planting. Martha Gonzales is a 'found rose' — a once-unnamed variety rediscovered growing in a Texas garden and identified and named for the woman who had grown and passed it down within her family — and it has become a favorite dwarf China-type rose valued for its compact, low-mounding habit rarely exceeding 2 feet, unusual among garden roses. It produces small, semi-double, brick-red blooms with a light fragrance in dense flushes almost continuously from spring through frost, and new foliage emerges with an attractive reddish tint. Like other China-type roses, it is exceptionally tolerant of heat and humidity and shows strong resistance to blackspot, needing no spray program even in the Gulf South. Its diminutive size makes it useful for edging beds, low borders, and containers where larger antique roses would overwhelm the space. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or twiggy growth; otherwise it needs very little maintenance.

common_name: Mary Helen Plumeria (Fragrant Golden-Yellow Hawaiian Plumeria)
notes: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Mary Helen is a popular Hawaiian-bred plumeria cultivar prized for large, rounded, deep golden-yellow flowers with a strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance, considered one of the best solid-yellow cultivars available for both garden display and lei-making. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to avoid stem rot. Established plants bloom heavily through the warm season with waxy, long-lasting flowers held in clusters at the branch tips. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes. Excellent drainage is the single most important requirement for healthy plumeria.

common_name: Mary Nell Holly (Upright Pyramidal Glossy Hybrid Holly)
notes: Mary Nell is a vigorous hybrid holly bred for a dense, upright, pyramidal form with glossy, deep green, lightly spined leaves and a heavy fall crop of bright red berries, making it a popular choice for a specimen tree, screen, or formal hedge. It grows faster than many broadleaf evergreens and holds its pyramidal shape with minimal pruning, tolerating Gulf Coast clay soils, heat, and humidity well once established. Give it well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune, if needed, in late winter or right after the main flush of spring growth to maintain size and shape without removing developing berries.

common_name: Mary Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Bred by David Austin and introduced in 1983 alongside Graham Thomas, Mary Rose carries loosely cupped, informal rosette flowers in a warm rose-pink with a light, sweet, old-rose myrrh fragrance, on a bushy, well-branched shrub that has remained a garden favorite for its dependable repeat bloom and forgiving nature. It tolerates a wider range of conditions than many English roses and continues flowering from late spring through frost with only routine care, making it a good starting point for gardeners new to growing old-fashioned-style roses.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mathotiana is one of the most enduring and widely grown Camellia japonica cultivars — a large-flowering formal double with rose-form to formal double, deep crimson to purplish-crimson flowers 4–5 inches across that are extraordinarily full and perfectly symmetrical. Mathotiana is sometimes called 'Purple Dawn' due to the purple-red to deep crimson color that distinguishes it from red camellia cultivars — the specific blue-red tone is unique and contributes to the flower's almost imperial visual richness. The flowers bloom in midseason (December through February in zone 9) on a vigorous upright to spreading plant that can ultimately grow 8–15 feet tall if unpruned. Mathotiana has been in cultivation since the early nineteenth century and is one of the foundational camellia cultivars — it has been in continuous cultivation longer than almost any other named japonica cultivar, reflecting its reliability, flower quality, and overall performance. In zone 9, Mathotiana performs as an exceptionally long-lived landscape shrub — camellia specimens of 50–100+ years are common in Southern historic gardens. Prune immediately after flowering (late winter/early spring) to control size and shape; avoid summer pruning that removes the following season's flower buds.

Plant in lean, dry, very well-drained soil in full sun; matilija poppy is one of the most dramatic and spectacular flowering perennials of the western United States — a large, subshrubby California and Baja California native producing glaucous, blue-gray, deeply cut foliage on stems reaching 5–8 feet, and from May through July, flowers of extraordinary size and beauty: pure white, papery-petaled, deeply crinkled blooms up to 9 inches across with a large, rounded, golden-yellow cluster of stamens at the center — the largest flowers of any native plant in North America. The size and purity of the white blooms, combined with the fragrant, crepe-paper quality of the petals and the golden center, make each individual flower an extraordinary sight, and a large, established clump in full bloom is a garden spectacle with few rivals. It evolved in the chaparral and canyon walls of southern California where fire triggers germination of the seeds, and it is perfectly adapted to summer drought, lean soil, and Mediterranean conditions. It spreads assertively by underground runners and can colonize large areas — useful for erosion control on dry slopes, but potentially problematic in small gardens.
