Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; May white azalea was only formally described in 1999 and remains uncommon in the nursery trade, so source plants from specialty native-azalea growers propagating from cultivated stock. Rhododendron eastmanii is a South Carolina native deciduous azalea producing clean white to pale pink, sweetly fragrant flowers in mid to late spring, later than the similar Piedmont azalea it was once confused with, and is one of the more recently recognized species in the eastern native azalea complex. Its clear white flowers and strong fragrance make it a choice addition to a native plant collection or woodland garden focused on regional biodiversity, and it associates well with other native azaleas, oakleaf hydrangea, and understory dogwoods. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and filtered light favored by other native deciduous azaleas.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Mayoi philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more deeply lobed leaves with vertical support. Slender, deeply three-lobed leaves have a gently ruffled, wavy margin and a narrow, elongated central lobe that give the foliage a wispy, almost windswept look distinct from the broader, rounder leaves of related climbing philodendrons. A relatively recent introduction to cultivation from Brazil, it has become popular with collectors for its fine texture and manageable size compared to some of the larger deeply lobed philodendron species, climbing steadily up a support without becoming unwieldy. Keep humidity moderate to high, provide bright indirect light, and let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

Meadow rose is the most cold-hardy and one of the most nearly thornless of all North American native roses — its species name 'blanda' means smooth, mild, or agreeable, referring to the nearly unarmed (spineless) character of mature stems that make it among the more garden-friendly of all native roses for areas near walkways. Fragrant, five-petaled, medium-pink flowers appear in June on arching stems, followed by small, orange-red hips that persist through winter and are consumed by ruffed grouse, mockingbirds, and a remarkable variety of songbirds. Native to the eastern and north-central United States from Maine to Colorado, it forms slowly spreading colonies by suckers and is among the first plants to colonize disturbed sites and woodland edges, providing excellent wildlife cover and erosion control. Like all native roses, it is host to native mining bees (Halictus and Andrena species) that collect rose pollen as a primary food source, and many moth species use Rosa as a larval host plant. Excellent for naturalizing in prairie and meadow borders, hedgerows, and native garden edges.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Merlot is a hybrid redbud, a cross involving Forest Pansy and Texas redbud (Cercis canadensis var. texensis) parentage, bred to combine deep wine-purple foliage with the smaller, glossier, more heat- and drought-tolerant leaves inherited from its Texas redbud heritage. The result holds its rich purple color better through summer heat than older purple-leaf cultivars, which tend to fade to green by midsummer, and shows improved resistance to leaf scorch in hot, humid climates like the Gulf South. Rosy-pink pea-like flowers cover the bare branches in early spring before the foliage emerges, followed by the season-long purple leaf display. Its more compact, rounded habit than standard redbud makes it well suited to smaller landscapes and foundation plantings. Provide afternoon shade in the hottest climates and well-drained soil, since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites; minimal pruning is needed beyond removing crossing or damaged branches in late winter.

common_name: Merlot Virginia Sweetspire (Compact Wine-Red Fall Color Shrub)
notes: Merlot is a compact, rounded selection of native Virginia sweetspire bred to fit smaller gardens than older cultivars like Henry's Garnet, staying under 3 feet tall and wide while still producing the drooping, fragrant, bottlebrush-shaped white flower spikes of early summer that draw bees and butterflies. Its namesake feature is fall color that turns a deep wine-red to burgundy earlier and holds longer than most Itea selections, giving reliable color even in the mild autumns of zone 9. Like other Virginia sweetspire cultivars it tolerates wet, periodically flooded soil far better than most shrubs and develops good fall color even in partial shade, making it a useful, well-behaved choice for a rain garden edge or a shaded foundation bed where space is limited.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; metallic-leaf begonia is a Brazilian shrubby begonia whose primary distinction is the extraordinary, burnished, metallic quality of its foliage — the large, asymmetric, heart-shaped leaves are deep olive-green to rich bronze-green in color but have a pronounced silvery-metallic sheen or gloss over the surface that catches and reflects light in a way that appears genuinely metallic rather than simply shiny, and the leaf surface is marked with prominent, dark-red to deep-purple veining that creates a vivid color contrast against the metallic-green ground. White hairs cover both leaf surfaces. The plant grows with an upright, branching, cane-forming habit and produces loose clusters of pale-pink flowers at the branch tips throughout the warm season. The metallic foliage is the primary ornamental feature and is most vivid in partial-shade conditions where direct light can catch the leaf surface at angles that maximize the metallic reflection. An excellent specimen for shaded tropical patios, conservatories, and zone 10–12 shade gardens.

Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Mexican anise tree has the most vividly colored flowers of the cultivated Illicium species and benefits from a sheltered site at the cooler edge of its hardiness range. Illicium mexicanum is a Mexican relative of the southeastern native Florida anise, grown for its glossy, aromatic, evergreen leaves and striking, star-shaped, deep wine-red to burgundy flowers produced over an unusually long season from spring into summer, showier and more prolonged in bloom than most anise tree species. Its rich flower color and dense evergreen habit make it a distinctive specimen or informal screen for a shaded border, tolerating deep shade better than most flowering evergreens. Give it consistently moist, acidic soil similar to camellia and azalea, and protect from hard freezes at the colder edge of its hardiness range.

Sow scarified seeds directly in warm soil after last frost, or nick the hard seed coat and soak overnight before planting in full sun in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil; Mexican bird of paradise grows rapidly to produce large clusters of brilliant orange-and-yellow or all-red flowers with long, showy stamens from summer through fall that are among the finest hummingbird plants in the Southwest and Gulf Coast. Highly drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in the heat, reflected sun, and dry conditions that challenge most other flowering shrubs. In zone 9 it may freeze to the ground in hard winters but regrows vigorously from the deep roots in spring; in zone 10–12 it is a large, semi-evergreen shrub. Prune hard in late winter to maintain shape and renew flowering vigor.

Sow scarified seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican bird of paradise is a Mexican native evergreen shrub or small tree in the pea family (Fabaceae) that produces upright racemes of bright, clear-yellow, five-petaled, ruffled flowers with showy long, red stamens on a nearly continuous basis from spring through frost — a bloom season that, combined with its tolerance of zone 8 cold and adaptability to dry, alkaline, calcareous soil, makes it one of the most reliably free-flowering large shrubs for Gulf Coast and southern Texas landscapes. It differs from the related red bird of paradise (Caesalpinia pulcherrima) in producing all-yellow flowers (vs. orange-red), being significantly more cold-hardy (to approximately 15°F in zone 8), and having a tidier, less aggressive growth habit. The fine-textured, bipinnate, ferny, dark-green, evergreen leaves remain attractive year-round. It tolerates partial shade significantly better than most drought-tolerant flowering shrubs. Excellent as a specimen, informal hedge, and xeriscape flowering tree in zone 8–11.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Mexican blood trumpet is a Mexican evergreen vine of the bignonia family that produces large, striking, trumpet-shaped flowers in a dramatic two-toned color combination — the flowers open from orange-red buds into large, flared trumpets in a vivid blood-red to orange-red outer color that fades inside through orange to a yellow throat, creating a warm, vivid, tricolored trumpet effect. The flowers are produced in dense clusters at the branch tips from spring through fall, with the primary flush in spring and a second in fall. The vine climbs by tendrils and can reach 20–30 feet on suitable support. It is more shade-tolerant than Pyrostegia venusta and blooms more reliably in partial-shade conditions, making it a good choice for lightly shaded arbors and structures where the flame vine would fail to produce its best display. Hardy to approximately 25–28°F in zone 9, with established plants typically recovering from frost damage by regrowing from the base. An excellent flowering vine for large arbors, pergolas, and walls in zone 9–12.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in partial to full shade; Mexican Buckeye (Ungnadia speciosa) is a native multi-stemmed large shrub or small tree indigenous to the limestone hills and cedar brakes of central and west Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, where it thrives in the dry shade beneath live oak canopies on thin, rocky, alkaline soils. The cloud of bright magenta-pink flowers that appears before the leaves in February–March is startling and beautiful — one of the earliest spring bloomers in the Gulf South native plant palette. The leathery, pinnately compound leaves (resembling the Ohio Buckeye's leaves) turn clear yellow in fall. The distinctive round, woody seed pods split open to reveal 1–3 shiny, mahogany-brown seeds resembling horse chestnuts — they are toxic (containing saponins and cytisine) and should not be eaten. Mexican Buckeye is extremely drought and alkaline-soil tolerant once established; it thrives where soils are too rocky and poor for most other ornamentals. The dense growth provides excellent cover and nesting habitat for mockingbirds and other cavity nesters. A superb native choice for dry shade situations in limestone-soil zone 7–10 gardens.

Plant Anisacanthus quadrifidus in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; once established it requires little supplemental water — it is highly drought-tolerant and actually performs better without irrigation in most Texas gardens; cut back hard in late winter to encourage compact, bushy growth and maximize summer flowering. Mexican Flame is one of the premier native hummingbird plants of Texas and the northern Mexico borderlands — a deciduous to semi-evergreen shrub that comes alive in the heat of summer and fall when little else is blooming, producing masses of brilliant orange-red tubular flowers on graceful, arching branches just when hummingbirds are fueling up for their fall migration. In zone 7–9 gardens, it dies back to the root crown after hard frost and re-emerges vigorously in spring; in zone 10 it may remain semi-evergreen. Several flower color variants exist: the most common has bright orange-red flowers, but yellow-flowered forms ('Yellow') are also available and equally valued for hummingbird gardens. A superb plant for xeriscape, wildflower, and native plant gardens throughout the Texas Hill Country, Gulf Coast, and adjacent regions — requiring no fertilizer, no regular irrigation once established, and minimal maintenance beyond annual pruning.

common_name: Mexican Flame Vine (Orange Glow Vine, Fireman's Cap)
notes: Root cuttings in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a fence or trellis; Mexican flame vine is one of the most spectacular winter-blooming vines for zone 9–11, producing dense clusters of bright orange, daisy-like flowers with contrasting yellow or orange centers from October through March — exactly the cool-season period when most other tropical vines have stopped blooming. The loose, twining stems 6–15 feet long bear small, dark green, slightly succulent leaves and are covered in vibrant orange blooms that attract butterflies. The orange color is exceptionally vivid and warm, excellent for combining with blue salvias or purple queen for autumn and winter color. In zone 8a it is killed to the ground in hard freezes but established root systems resprout reliably each spring to bloom again by mid-summer.

Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, rocky to gravelly, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Dasylirion longissimum requires excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water once established — it is highly drought and heat tolerant but will rot in poorly drained, wet, or clay soils. Dasylirion longissimum (Mexican Grass Tree or Toton Palm) is a dramatic, slow-growing architectural succulent in the Asparagaceae family native to the semi-arid highland mountains of Nuevo Leon, Coahuila, and Tamaulipas in northeastern Mexico, where it grows on rocky limestone slopes and ridges in full sun. Unlike the spoon-leaf Dasylirion species (D. wheeleri, D. texanum) whose leaves have serrated or spiny edges, D. longissimum is distinguished by its extremely long (to 6 feet), narrow, strap-like, essentially unarmed and smooth-edged leaves that radiate from the growing center in an enormous, perfect sphere — giving the plant an appearance of a giant teal-green sea urchin or porcupine. Over many years and decades, the plant develops a raised, cylindrical trunk beneath the leaf mass, eventually reaching 10–20 feet in old age. The flower stalk when it finally appears is a spectacular 10–15 foot spike covered with thousands of tiny cream flowers. Excellent for Southwestern desert gardens, xeriscape plantings, and architectural accent positions in hot, dry, alkaline-soil landscapes in zones 7–11.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Mexican Honeysuckle blooms most prolifically in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9 and actually benefits from afternoon shade during the peak of summer heat. Justicia spicigera is a large, soft-stemmed, fast-growing shrub from Mexico and Central America in the Acanthaceae family, closely related to the more commonly grown Jacobinia (Justicia carnea) and Shrimp Plant (Justicia brandegeana). The species' common name 'Mexican Honeysuckle' refers not to any botanical relationship with true Lonicera honeysuckles but to the nectar-rich tubular flowers, which are intensely attractive to hummingbirds and butterflies — the long, tubular, orange to orange-red flowers emerging from softly fuzzy, velvety calyxes are among the most reliable hummingbird attractants in the zone 9 garden. The flowers are produced in terminal spikes and bloom over an exceptionally long season, essentially year-round in zone 9b-10 with brief pauses between flush cycles. The large, soft, gray-green, velvety leaves give the plant an attractive textural quality even out of bloom. In Mexican folk medicine, Justicia spicigera leaves (Mohintli) have traditional uses as a blue dye plant and herbal remedy. Among the most underused but most hummingbird-effective shrubs for Gulf Coast partial-shade garden beds.

common_name: Mexican Lilac (Quick Stick, Mother of Cocoa)
notes: Plant container stock or large (2–4 foot) hardwood cuttings directly in the ground in spring; gliricidia establishes from large cuttings planted directly in the soil — a useful trait for creating instant living fence posts. Gliricidia sepium (Mexican lilac, quick stick, or mother of cocoa) is one of the most widely planted multipurpose tropical trees in the world — a Central American legume tree grown throughout the humid tropics for nitrogen fixation, living fences, shade for cacao and coffee plantations ('mother of cocoa' in Costa Rica), green manure, and fodder. The tree has an extraordinary capacity to root from large, dormant hardwood cuttings planted directly in the ground — a common practice for creating instant living fence posts that then leaf out and grow into full trees. In spring (usually January–March when dormant), the bare branches are covered with stunning clusters of bright pink-lavender pea-like flowers resembling redbud (Cercis) — one of the showiest tropical trees in bloom. The leaves and branches are nitrogen-rich and used as green mulch in organic farming; however, the leaves are toxic to mammals (including horses and dogs) if consumed in large quantities. CAUTION: Seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic to mammals — do not plant where livestock have access.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; Mexican orange blossom is one of the most popular fragrant evergreen shrubs for warm-climate gardens, producing clusters of pure white, star-shaped flowers with a powerful, sweet orange-blossom fragrance in spring and frequently reblooming again in fall. The glossy, trifoliate leaves are aromatic when crushed, releasing a sharp citrus-like scent. It is borderline hardy in zone 7 and may suffer leaf damage in hard freezes, but typically recovers vigorously from the root system — planting against a warm south-facing wall significantly improves winter survival. The compact cultivar 'Sundance' (golden-yellow foliage) and the more cold-tolerant 'Aztec Pearl' (narrower leaflets, very fragrant pink-tinged flowers) are excellent named selections.

Plant in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican redbud is a shrubby to small-tree redbud native to the rocky limestone mountains and canyon walls of west Texas (Big Bend country) and adjacent Mexico, distinguished from eastern redbud (C. canadensis) by its smaller stature, smaller and more rounded leaves with unusually wavy, scalloped margins, and greater tolerance of dry, alkaline, rocky soils. The bright magenta-pink spring flowers appear on bare branches before the leaves, like other redbuds. Heat, drought, and alkaline soil tolerance superior to eastern redbud makes it better suited to the dry limestone terrain of central and west Texas. A fine specimen shrub-tree for the xeric, alkaline, rocky garden in zone 9a where standard redbud struggles on thin, calcareous soils.

Plant container-grown specimens in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in bright filtered shade, protected from drying wind that shreds the soft fronds. Water generously and regularly, since it does not tolerate drought the way tougher landscape ferns do. Over years it develops a shaggy, fiber-covered trunk topped by a graceful crown of finely textured, soft-green arching fronds, making it one of the more elegant tree ferns for a shaded tropical courtyard or large container specimen in cooler climates.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexican white oak, also called Monterrey oak, is a Texas Superstar-designated shade tree native to both a small area of south Texas and much of northeastern Mexico, prized for a faster growth rate than most oaks along with attractive peach-to-bronze new spring growth that matures to glossy green. It is semi-evergreen to evergreen in mild winters, dropping and replacing its leaves quickly in late winter rather than standing bare for long, and tolerates heat, wind, and drought impressively well once established, making it a strong, adaptable shade tree choice for difficult urban and suburban Texas and Gulf South sites. Its faster growth compared to slower native oaks makes it useful where a newly planted landscape needs shade sooner rather than decades later. Give it plenty of room to reach its substantial mature size, and provide regular water during the first couple of years to establish a deep root system before easing off to only occasional supplemental irrigation.

common_name: Miami Crape Myrtle (Dark Pink Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Miami is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei hybrid releases, combining the flower power of common crape myrtle with the disease resistance and exceptional bark of Lagerstroemia fauriei. It produces abundant dark-pink flower clusters from summer into early fall on a tall, upright tree, and as it matures the outer bark exfoliates to reveal smooth, rich cinnamon-brown inner bark that becomes a major ornamental feature through fall and winter after the leaves drop. Its strong resistance to powdery mildew, the primary disease problem of straight Lagerstroemia indica cultivars, makes it a reliable choice for humid Gulf South summers. Its eventual height puts it among the larger crape myrtle selections, better suited to a specimen planting or street tree role than a small foundation bed. Never top or hard-prune the main framework; prune selectively in late winter only to remove crossing or crowded growth.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Middendorff weigela is the only yellow-flowered weigela species, distinct from the pink, red, and white tones of common hybrid weigela. Funnel-shaped flowers open a soft primrose-yellow marked with fine orange spotting in the throat, an unusual color among weigelas, which are overwhelmingly bred in shades of pink, red, and white, blooming on a compact, low-growing shrub native to cold woodland edges in northeastern Asia and Japan. Its distinctive yellow flower color and smaller stature compared to common hybrid weigela cultivars make it a worthwhile specialty addition to a shrub border or collector's garden seeking something beyond the usual pink and red weigela palette. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood like other weigela species.

Midnight Wine was the original dwarf dark-leaved weigela that later inspired the even smaller Fine Wine, staying under 18 inches tall and wide with dense, deep burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season. Clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers appear in a heavy late-spring flush that draws hummingbirds, and the low, spreading, mounded habit works well as a border edge, small-space accent, or mixed container planting where taller weigela cultivars would be out of scale. It is drought-tolerant and largely trouble-free once established, needing only a light shaping right after the main spring bloom and an occasional renewal cut to the oldest wood to keep growth vigorous.

common_name: Milky Way Kousa Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming White Kousa Dogwood)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Milky Way is an exceptionally floriferous kousa dogwood cultivar, its June flower display of creamy-white, pointed bracts so dense the branches appear covered in a blanket of white — a later bloom time than native flowering dogwood, extending the dogwood flowering season into early summer — followed in fall by raspberry-like red fruit that is edible and attracts wildlife, and by strong burgundy-red fall foliage color. As an Asian species, it is generally more resistant than native Cornus florida to the anthracnose and dogwood borer problems that trouble flowering dogwood in humid climates. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Millie Mac azalea is a selection of the Gulf Coast native orange azalea with distinctive white-edged flowers. A striking selection of the native Florida flame azalea, it produces fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers in warm gold and orange tones distinctly edged in crisp white, a bicolor pattern not found in the straight species, opening in mid-spring on bare branches before or just as new leaves emerge and filling the garden with sweet fragrance. Like other native deciduous azaleas, it thrives in the dappled shade and acidic, humus-rich soil of a woodland edge, providing important early-season nectar for native bees and swallowtail butterflies migrating through the Gulf South. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid heavy pruning since it flowers on the previous year's wood, and site in a location with good air movement to reduce fungal disease pressure.

common_name: Million Hearts Plant (Heart Leaf Dischidia, Rosary Dischidia)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade with exceptional drainage — Million Hearts Plant is a true epiphyte that rots quickly in heavy, moisture-retaining growing media. Dischidia ruscifolia is a small-leafed trailing epiphytic vine from the Philippines and Southeast Asia in the family Apocynaceae (the same family as Hoya and Stephanotis), producing thin, wiry, trailing stems clothed in pairs of tiny, heart-shaped, slightly fleshy, pale to medium-green leaves approximately half an inch across. The massed effect of hundreds of small green hearts cascading from a hanging basket gives the plant its popular common name — 'Million Hearts' — a name that perfectly captures the charming, delicate abundance of the foliage. As a true epiphyte from the humid forests of Southeast Asia, Dischidia grows naturally attached to rough tree bark in conditions of excellent air circulation, bright filtered light, and periodic drought — the small, slightly succulent leaves store water against dry periods between tropical rainstorms. Tiny, white, urn-shaped flowers appear sporadically along the stems. Multiple cultivars exist, including 'String of Nickels' (rounder, slightly larger leaves) and the slightly more compact 'Imbricata.' Non-toxic to pets and children.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; established mimosas tolerate drought, heat, salt spray, and poor soils far better than most flowering trees. Mimosa is a fast-growing, umbrella-shaped, deciduous tree valued for its finely divided, fern-like bipinnate foliage and its abundant clusters of fragrant, silky, pink pompom flowers produced from late spring through late summer, which are irresistible to hummingbirds and butterflies. The wood is weak and prone to storm damage, the roots can be aggressive near pavement, and the species is highly susceptible to Fusarium mimosa wilt, which can kill mature trees within a season or two. CAUTION: mimosa is classified as invasive throughout much of the southeastern United States, including the Gulf South, where it escapes cultivation readily along roadsides and disturbed woodland edges from its abundant, long-lived seed; gardeners in this region should weigh its ornamental value against its weedy tendencies and consider deadheading spent flowers before pods form.

common_name: Minerva Rose of Sharon (Lavender-Pink Red-Eyed Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Minerva bears large, single to semi-double, lavender-pink flowers with a bold reddish-purple eye at the center, opening over a long season from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Like its sibling introductions Aphrodite and Diana, it is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection that sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older, seed-grown rose of sharon while remaining tough and heat-tolerant. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; ming aralia (parsley aralia, wild coffee tree) is an Indo-Pacific tropical evergreen shrub in the ginseng family (Araliaceae) that produces some of the most intricately textured and refined tropical foliage available for shaded garden positions — the leaves are compound and deeply divided, with each leaflet further divided into multiple, small, toothed, crinkled, irregular segments that create a dense, feathery, parsley-like to fern-like appearance at close range and an impression of extraordinary, finely subdivided textural richness from a distance. The thin branches grow in a graceful, architectural, often slightly irregular pattern that resembles a natural bonsai. Ming aralia is frequently grown as an indoor specimen and shaped into bonsai form. Outdoors in zone 10–12 it grows into a substantial shrub or small tree to 15 feet with similarly intricate foliage at a much larger scale. The combination of shade tolerance, fine texture, and elegant form makes it one of the most useful and refined tropical foliage shrubs for shaded positions in the tropical garden.

Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade; Mini Monstera grows fastest in bright indirect light (3–6 feet from a sunny window) and develops larger leaves with more pronounced fenestrations when given good light and a climbing support. Rhaphidophora tetrasperma is a fast-growing, climbing tropical vine from southern Thailand and Malaysia that has become one of the most popular houseplants in the recent era of tropical plant collecting, despite being entirely unrelated to the true Monstera genus. It is sold in virtually every garden center and box store under the trade name 'Mini Monstera' because the deeply lobed, fenestrated, bright-green leaves bear a strong resemblance in miniature to Monstera deliciosa — the iconic 'Swiss Cheese Plant' — though R. tetrasperma leaves are smaller (4–8 inches) and thinner. The plant climbs by aerial roots, producing new leaves quickly and making it one of the fastest-growing popular tropical foliage plants. Each new leaf is larger than the last when the plant is given adequate light, warmth, and a climbing structure. Like Monstera, the leaf splits (fenestrations) are thought to be an adaptation for surviving high winds in the rainforest understory by reducing wind resistance on large leaves. Mildly toxic if chewed; the calcium oxalate crystals cause mouth irritation.

common_name: Mini Penny Hydrangea (Dwarf Reblooming Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Mini Penny is a dwarf sport of the widely grown, reliably reblooming Penny Mac hydrangea, retaining its parent's strong performance — flowering on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year — while staying considerably more compact, typically under 2 feet tall, making it well suited to small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-sized hydrangea would be too large. Because it reblooms on new wood, a late spring frost that damages old buds does not prevent a strong summer bloom. Flower color shifts with soil pH the way most macrophylla hydrangeas do, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

common_name: Miniature Wax Plant (Wax Bell, Beautiful Hoya, Hoya bella)
notes: Grow in bright indirect light to moderate shade — Miniature Wax Plant requires more light to bloom than its size suggests; place within 3 feet of a bright window for reliable flowering, while avoiding direct sun which burns the small leaves. Hoya lanceolata subsp. bella (commonly sold simply as 'Hoya bella') is a small, naturally pendant epiphytic Hoya from Myanmar (Burma) and the eastern Himalayas in the family Apocynaceae — one of the most compact and delicate of the commonly grown Hoyas. The slender, arching stems produce pairs of small, lance-shaped to oval, pale to medium-green, slightly succulent leaves about an inch long in an airy, cascading arrangement naturally suited to small hanging baskets and elevated containers. In bloom, the plant produces pendant umbels of 7–12 tiny, perfectly star-shaped, white flowers with a contrasting center corona of deep rose-purple — each individual flower less than half an inch across, but the massed effect of many clusters simultaneously in bloom creates a charming and delicate display. The flowers are lightly but pleasantly fragrant. Unlike the vigorous, twining large Hoyas, H. lanceolata subsp. bella has a naturally arching, pendant, non-climbing growth habit — it does not reach toward a support or twine but simply cascades downward in long, graceful arches. This makes it one of the finest small Hoyas for hanging baskets and elevated windowsill displays. Non-toxic.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; minniebush is native to high-elevation Appalachian forests and requires cool root conditions and excellent drainage, making it best suited to mountain and northern gardens rather than hot lowland sites. Menziesia pilosa is a compact, twiggy, deciduous heath-family shrub with soft blue-green foliage and clusters of small, urn-shaped, yellowish-white to pale pink flowers in late spring that hang beneath the new leaves, giving rise to the common name from their resemblance to tiny hanging bells. Fall color is a soft yellow to orange, and the fine-textured, mounded habit works well in a native rhododendron or azalea understory planting. It is rarely offered in the nursery trade and best grown from local ecotype seed or division by specialty native-plant growers, and it resents heavy clay or poorly drained soils.

common_name: Miss Kim Lilac (Compact Late-Blooming Fragrant Korean Lilac)
notes: Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and prune spent flower clusters right after bloom since next year's buds set soon after. Miss Kim is a compact selection of Manchurian lilac introduced from the US National Arboretum, prized for dense, rounded growth that stays smaller than common lilac, intensely fragrant lavender-purple flower clusters that open later and last longer, and foliage that turns burgundy-purple in fall. Its better tolerance of heat and humidity than Syringa vulgaris makes it one of the more dependable lilacs for the warmer edge of lilac-growing range, though it still wants a real winter chill to bloom well and struggles in the Deep South's mildest zones. Established shrubs are long-lived and low-maintenance, needing only post-bloom deadheading and an occasional renewal cane removed at the base to stay vigorous.

common_name: Miss Molly Butterfly Bush (Sterile Raspberry-Red Buddleja)
notes: Miss Molly was bred at North Carolina State University as part of a program to produce sterile, non-seeding butterfly bushes that avoid the invasive spread of older Buddleja davidii selections. It produces dense, conical flower spikes in a true, deep raspberry-red to cherry-red color that is unusually saturated for the genus, blooming continuously from summer through frost with minimal deadheading needed since it sets almost no viable seed. Its more compact habit than species butterfly bush makes it easier to fit into smaller borders, and like all buddleja it draws butterflies and hummingbirds in large numbers once established. It tolerates heat and drought well once its root system is established.

common_name: Miss Ruby Butterfly Bush (Sterile Rose-Pink Buddleja)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard to about 12 inches in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth. Miss Ruby is a North Carolina State University-bred sterile butterfly bush, producing dense, conical spikes of vivid rose-pink to magenta-red flowers continuously from summer through frost, with minimal deadheading needed since it sets almost no viable seed. Its more compact, well-behaved habit compared to older Buddleja davidii selections fits smaller borders while still delivering the heavy butterfly and hummingbird traffic the genus is known for. It tolerates heat and drought well once its root system is established, needing little care beyond the annual hard cutback.

common_name: Miss Ruby Loropetalum (Large Reblooming Purple Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it the 5–6 foot mature spread it needs to avoid constant shearing. Bred by the U.S. National Arboretum, Miss Ruby is a vigorous, large-growing loropetalum selected for foliage that emerges bright magenta-red and matures to a rich, dark burgundy-purple that holds its color through summer heat better than many older loropetalum cultivars, along with a heavy spring flush of frilly, ribbon-like hot-pink flowers and scattered rebloom into fall. Its larger scale suits it to hedges, screens, and background plantings rather than tight foundation spaces, and it tolerates both full sun (best color) and open shade. Prune, if needed, right after the spring bloom flush to avoid removing next year's flower buds.

Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun, where the soft, gray-green, ginger-scented foliage keeps its best color out of the harshest afternoon heat. Misty plume bush is a fast-growing southern African shrub that produces dense, upright plumes of small lavender-pink flowers in winter, when few other tender shrubs are blooming, making it valuable for extending color and pollinator forage into the cool season along the Gulf Coast. It tolerates poor, dry soil once established and needs little supplemental water beyond an occasional deep soak during extended drought. Cut the woody framework back hard in late winter after bloom to renew dense, bushy growth for the following season; in zone 8b the roots survive most winters even when the top is lost to frost.

common_name: Mme Antoine Mari Rose (Antique Heat-Tolerant Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Mme Antoine Mari is a classic Tea rose that has been passed along for generations among Southern rose collectors and preserved by the antique rose movement for its combination of soft blush-pink, high-centered, fragrant blooms with the vigorous, disease-resistant constitution characteristic of old Tea roses. Like other Tea roses it blooms repeatedly through the long, hot growing season and shrugs off the heat and humidity that stress many modern hybrid tea roses, needing little more than a sunny, well-drained spot to perform for decades. Prune lightly to shape after the main spring flush, and expect good resistance to black spot and powdery mildew compared with modern roses bred primarily for cooler climates.

Mohawk is a US National Arboretum introduction bred specifically to combine strong fragrance with outstanding fall color, two traits rarely found together in one viburnum. Dark red buds open in mid-spring to white, waxy, spicy clove-scented flower clusters that rival Korean spice viburnum for perfume but on a more vigorous, disease-resistant plant. Glossy dark green summer foliage turns brilliant orange-red in fall, and Mohawk shows notably better resistance to bacterial leaf spot than many other Burkwood viburnum selections. Site it near a walkway or window where the spring fragrance can be enjoyed, and give it room to reach its full rounded size without crowding.

Plant in dry, rocky, calcareous, alkaline to neutral, thin soil in full sun; Mohr's oak is a small, shrubby, semi-evergreen oak of the limestone hills and rocky grasslands of the Edwards Plateau and west Texas, forming extensive colonies by clonal spreading from rhizomes after fire — making it an important fire-resistant groundcover in Texas hill country landscapes. The small, leathery, pale green leaves are distinctive and remain on the shrub through most of the winter, contributing to the 'evergreen' characteristic of the Edwards Plateau landscape. Drought and heat tolerant in the extreme, naturally growing on the thinnest, rockiest limestone soils with summer rainfall supplementation only. The very small acorns are eaten by scaled quail, wild turkeys, and deer. Valuable for erosion control on dry, rocky, calcareous slopes in the hill country of central Texas.

Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Mongolian oak is one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant of all oak species, native to the boreal and temperate forests of northeastern China (Manchuria), Mongolia, Korea, and the Russian Far East where it is a dominant tree species in continental climates with extreme winter cold and hot, dry summers. In North American gardens, it offers an excellent alternative to overcup oak (Q. lyrata) or white oak for extremely cold climates in zones 3–4 where most oaks would be marginal. The leaves are large, distinctly lobed with very broad, rounded lobes and are clustered at branch tips in a manner reminiscent of daimyo oak. Fall color is yellow to orange-brown. One of the most underused oaks for extremely cold-climate gardens where shade trees are limited.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart to allow for its large, vigorous size. Introduced in France in 1891, Monsieur Tillier is a robust tea rose bearing large, loosely double blooms in variable shades of pink, salmon, and copper-tan, often several tones within a single flush, with a fruity tea fragrance. It is among the most drought-tolerant and vigorous of the old tea roses, capable of growing into a large shrub 5-6 feet tall and wide, and performs remarkably well in poor, sandy, or infertile soil where many modern roses struggle, a trait that made it a favorite for unattended cemetery and homestead plantings across the Deep South. It shows strong resistance to blackspot and thrives with minimal spraying in the humid Gulf South climate. Prune lightly in late winter to control size and remove dead or crossing wood, since Monsieur Tillier tolerates hard pruning better than many teas if size needs to be reduced.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Monstera Albo needs strong, consistent light on its white variegated sections, which cannot photosynthesize and rely on the green portions of each leaf. Large, deeply fenestrated leaves are boldly marked with irregular patches, streaks, or entirely half-white sectors of pure white variegation against the classic glossy green Swiss cheese plant leaf, a chimeric, genetically unstable pattern that varies unpredictably from leaf to leaf and has made well-variegated specimens among the most sought-after and expensive houseplants in the world. Because the white tissue contains no chlorophyll, plants with heavy variegation grow more slowly and are more prone to stress than solid-green monstera, and stems can revert to solid green or, less often, produce leaves with too little chlorophyll to sustain themselves. Provide bright indirect light to support the reduced photosynthetic area, prune out any fully white, unsustainable growth, and propagate stem cuttings that include at least some variegated leaf tissue to preserve the pattern.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Monstera Aurea needs strong, consistent light on its yellow variegated sections, which contribute less to photosynthesis than the green portions. Large, deeply fenestrated leaves are marked with bold, irregular patches of bright golden-yellow variegation against deep green, a warmer-toned counterpart to the more famous white-variegated Monstera Albo, similarly prized by collectors for its rarity and unpredictable, genetically unstable variegation pattern. Like other variegated monstera, plants with heavy yellow sectoring grow more slowly than solid-green plants and are more vulnerable to stress, and stems can revert to solid green over time if not selectively propagated from variegated growth. Provide bright indirect light, prune out any reverted all-green growth if maintaining variegation is the goal, and propagate from stem cuttings that retain variegated leaf tissue.

Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 8b–11; Montezuma cypress is the national tree of Mexico, closely related to but more heat-tolerant and less deciduous than bald cypress (T. distichum). In mild climates, it remains semi-evergreen or evergreen year-round — a significant ornamental advantage over the fully deciduous bald cypress. The ancient Tule Tree (El Árbol del Tule) in Oaxaca, Mexico — a Montezuma cypress — is considered the world's largest tree by trunk circumference at over 40 feet in girth, with an age estimated at 1,400–3,000 years. In zone 9–10 Gulf Coast landscapes, Montezuma cypress makes a superb massive shade tree for moist, low-lying areas and streambanks where its greater heat tolerance makes it more vigorous and longer-lived than the native bald cypress. Knees develop in wet conditions, providing habitat for numerous organisms.

common_name: Moon Bay Nandina (Compact Mounding Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Moon Bay is a compact, naturally mounding nandina selection staying 18–30 inches tall — smaller and more tightly formed than Gulf Stream or Harbour Dwarf, making it the most compact of the commonly available dwarf nandina cultivars. The graceful, fine-textured, finely divided foliage is a beautiful glossy-green through summer, turning vivid orange-red to scarlet-red in fall and winter when cold temperatures arrive. Moon Bay's compact, mounding form and outstanding fall/winter color combination make it an exceptionally practical and ornamental foundation shrub for zone 9 gardens where its reliability, low maintenance, and multi-season interest make it one of the most useful small evergreen shrubs in the landscape palette. Like all nandinas, Moon Bay is remarkably adaptable — tolerating clay, drought once established, heat, humidity, and partial shade without significant loss of performance or appearance. The foliage compound texture, graceful habit, and outstanding winter red color make it visually effective in all four seasons. Note: Nandina domestica berries are toxic to birds and the plant has invasive potential in some Gulf South natural areas — plant in contained garden settings away from natural areas.

common_name: Moon Vine (Large-Flowered White Night-Blooming Tropical Vine for Evening Gardens)
notes: Nick or soak seeds overnight, then direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Moon Vine (Ipomoea alba) is the classic evening and night garden vine — a tropical twining vine that produces extraordinarily large (4–6 inch), pure white, funnel-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and evening, perfuming the garden with a sweet, rich, jasmine-like fragrance that intensifies as darkness falls. The flowers are among the largest of any commonly grown annual vine and the pure white color reflects low light beautifully, appearing to glow under moonlight, porch lights, or landscape lighting — creating the ethereal moonlit effect that gives the plant its common name. Moon Vine is a rapid, enthusiastic climber, gaining 15–20 feet in a single growing season in warm Gulf South conditions — it covers fences, arbors, pergolas, and mailboxes with dense, large-leaved foliage and a continuous supply of evening flowers from mid-summer until frost. The flowers each last only one evening, but numerous buds open in succession for months of nightly bloom. In Gulf South zone 9, Moon Vine is grown as a warm-season annual from spring through fall. In zone 10–12, it grows as a perennial twining vine. The rapid growth and profuse bloom make it one of the most rewarding evening-garden plants for summer arbors and screens. Often combined with common morning glory (I. purpurea) to create a 24-hour floral display from the same genus.

common_name: Moonflower Vine (Night-Blooming White-Flowered Annual Ipomoea Vine)
notes: Nick seed coat or soak overnight; direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a sturdy trellis or arbor. Moonflower Vine is the large-flowered night-blooming cousin of morning glory — a tropical Ipomoea species producing enormous (4–6 inch diameter) white, saucer-shaped flowers with a sweet, tropical fragrance that unfurl rapidly at dusk and remain open through the night until midmorning, when they close as morning glories open. The dramatic daily opening — moonflowers can be watched as the buds spirally unfurl in minutes at dusk — is one of the most theatrical performances in the plant world. The very large flowers are pure white, satiny, with a star-shaped pattern visible in the petals, and the heavy, sweet, tropical fragrance carries well on still evening air, perfuming the garden and attracting sphinx moths (hummingbird moths) that are primary pollinators. Moonflower is a fast-growing, robust vine (10–15 feet per season) that covers a standard garden arbor or pergola quickly. The combination of its dramatic evening show and fragrance makes moonflower ideal for planting near outdoor dining or seating areas — evening patio dinners become special when the moonflowers open at dusk around the pergola. In zone 9–10, moonflower is a short-lived perennial that may persist between mild winters.

common_name: Moonlight Scindapsus (Treub's Scindapsus, Dark Form Scindapsus, Satin Pothos Relative)
notes: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, well-aerated aroid mix with a rough support to climb — Moonlight Scindapsus produces its most ornamental foliage in bright indirect to low light conditions and is an outstanding climbing shade vine for shaded indoor and outdoor tropical positions. Scindapsus treubii is a climbing, hemiepiphytic perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to Borneo, Java, and Southeast Asia — a member of the genus Scindapsus, which is closely related to but distinct from both Epipremnum (pothos) and Monstera, in the tribe Monstereae. The plant produces elongated, narrowly ovate leaves (4–6 inches long, distinctly narrow compared to S. pictus) on climbing stems that ascend with adhesive aerial roots. Two distinct leaf color forms have become highly popular in the collector aroid market: the 'Moonlight' form, which produces silver-green to pale sage-green leaves with a strong silver overlay that gives each leaf a luminous, silver-washed quality — and the 'Dark Form,' which produces leaves of a very deep, saturated dark forest-green to near-black, with a subtle, gunmetal blue-green iridescence in certain light. Both forms are striking and distinctly different from any common houseplant. The plant climbs readily when given a rough moss pole or bark board and develops larger, more lustrous leaves as it ascends. Moderately fast-growing in warm conditions. One of the most sought-after collector aroids of the past decade. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their full mature width to develop. Moonrock is a compact panicle hydrangea bred for exceptionally sturdy, thick stems that hold its dense, rounded flower panicles fully upright without staking, even after heavy rain — a common problem with older, larger panicle hydrangea cultivars. Flowers open creamy white in mid to late summer and age to a soft green before finishing pink-blushed in fall, giving a long season of changing color on a plant sized for smaller foundation plantings and mixed borders. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned back hard in late winter without losing that year's bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.

Moonseed is a deciduous, twining native vine of moist woodland edges, stream banks, and thicket margins throughout eastern North America, valued for its bold, broadly shield-shaped leaves and striking blue-black berries in fall. The crescent-shaped seed inside each berry inspired the common name and distinguishes it from the true wild grapes it resembles — the berries are highly toxic and must never be eaten. It spreads readily by underground rhizomes to form dense, colonizing patches, making it ideal for naturalizing moist, shaded slopes and stabilizing stream banks. Grow in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; it tolerates periodic flooding and deep shade better than most native vines.

Nick seed coat with sandpaper or soak overnight before sowing directly in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil after last frost; do not start indoors as tap root is damaged by transplanting. Ipomoea tricolor is the parent of the famous 'Heavenly Blue' morning glory, a fast-growing annual twining vine with heart-shaped leaves and large (3–4 inch), funnel-shaped flowers that open a vivid sky-blue or blue-violet each morning and fade to pink-purple by afternoon — one of the most startling and beautiful morning colors in the annual garden. Provide a trellis, fence, or other support to 8–12 feet; it will naturally scramble up any available structure. The seeds contain lysergic acid amides and are mildly toxic if eaten in quantity. Morning glories bloom most prolifically in lean, dry soil with minimal fertilization; rich soil produces excessive foliage.

common_name: Mosaica Copper Plant (Multi-Color Tropical Foliage Shrub for Gulf South Gardens)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mosaica is a cultivar of Acalypha wilkesiana (copper leaf, copperleaf, Jacob's coat) — a tropical shrub from the Pacific Islands grown primarily as a foliage plant for the extraordinary multi-color patterning of its large, broad leaves. The 'Mosaica' cultivar produces leaves with a complex, patchwork mosaic of copper, red-orange, bronze, gold-yellow, and reddish-purple tones — different colors appearing as irregular patches, blotches, and streaks across each leaf surface, creating a richly complex pattern that is genuinely different from plant to plant. The result in full sun is one of the most vivid and complex foliage colors available in a commonly grown landscape plant: a tropical tapestry of warm colors that creates intense visual interest in mixed subtropical plantings. Acalypha wilkesiana grows rapidly in Gulf South summer heat, reaching 4–6 feet in a single growing season when planted in warm soil with adequate nutrition. The inconspicuous catkin-type flowers are secondary to the foliage display. In zone 10–12, copper leaf is an evergreen perennial shrub. In zone 9, it grows as a warm-season annual — planted after the last frost and growing rapidly through summer and fall until frost kills it. The rapid growth and striking color make it one of the most effective single-season tropical foliage plants for Gulf South summer borders and container combinations.

common_name: Mound Lily Yucca (Spanish Dagger, Glorious Yucca, Soft-Tipped Yucca)
notes: Plant in full sun in excellent drainage; Mound Lily Yucca is larger than most garden yuccas and eventually forms a multi-stemmed shrub 5–10 feet tall; remove spent flower spikes after bloom; the species is slower-suckering than many yuccas and generally stays as a single or few-stemmed specimen for many years. Mound Lily Yucca is a large, architecturally bold native yucca of the southeastern United States coastal plain — one of the signature plants of the Atlantic and Gulf Coast dune systems, where it stabilizes sandy soils and provides year-round structural interest with its dramatic rosettes of broad, blue-green leaves. Unlike most garden yuccas, Yucca gloriosa grows to significant size over time, eventually developing a thick woody trunk or multi-stemmed shrub to 5–8 feet (sometimes 10 feet), with large rosettes of stiff, 2–3 foot leaves at the branch tips — creating a palm-like or tree-like silhouette unlike the low ground-hugging form of Yucca filamentosa. The common name 'Spanish Dagger' refers to the stiff, somewhat flexible leaf tip: while sharp, it is softer and less needle-like than the truly dangerous Y. aloifolia (Spanish Bayonet), making Mound Lily Yucca a somewhat safer choice for garden settings near walkways and play areas — though still requiring care. The dramatic 4–6 foot flower spike bearing hundreds of creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers appears in late summer to fall, creating one of the most spectacular flowering events of the late-season garden; the flowers are both edible and attractive to moths that pollinate them at night. Widely used in coastal landscape design for its salt tolerance and sandy-soil adaptation.

common_name: Mount Airy Fothergilla (Award-Winning Fragrant Bottlebrush Shrub)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in partial shade to full sun, and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. Mount Airy is a selection discovered at the Mount Airy Arboretum in Cincinnati, thought to be a hybrid between dwarf and large fothergilla, combining the compact, tidy habit of the smaller species with exceptionally heavy flowering and outstanding fall color. In April, before the leaves emerge, the shrub is covered in fragrant, honey-scented, bottlebrush-like white flower spikes made up of dense stamens, followed by attractive blue-green summer foliage that turns a spectacular blend of yellow, orange, and scarlet — often several colors on a single leaf — in fall. Its reliable performance, compact size, and multi-season interest have made it one of the most widely planted and highly rated fothergilla selections available, suited to a shrub border, woodland edge, or foundation planting. Requires minimal pruning; simply remove dead or crossing wood after flowering if shaping is needed.

Mountain Camellia is a striking native understory shrub or small tree, native to rich, moist, wooded slopes, ravine walls, and stream terraces in the southern Appalachians from Virginia and Kentucky south to Georgia and Alabama, blooming in July and August with large, white, five-petaled flowers bearing a prominent cluster of orange-tipped stamens. Larger than Silky Camellia (Stewartia malacodendron) and more cold-hardy (to zone 5), Mountain Camellia blooms later in summer when few other native shrubs are flowering, extending ornamental interest deep into the season. The smooth, exfoliating gray bark provides attractive winter interest, and the foliage turns shades of orange and red in fall. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade — it is somewhat more tolerant of garden conditions than Silky Camellia and establishes more readily from nursery transplants, though it is still slow-growing and long-lived.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; mountain devil is an Eastern Australian Proteaceae shrub of the Sydney sandstone heathlands that has become well-known for a botanical curiosity: the woody seed pods, when mature and dried, have a distinctive shape with two prominent, curved, tusk-like horns projecting from the opening of each follicle — the overall silhouette of the pod resembling a tiny devil or horned face, giving the plant its memorable and accurate common name. These distinctive horned seed pods have made mountain devil a popular dried-floral material in Australia; the pods are collected, sometimes dyed, and used in wreaths and arrangements. In the garden it is also a rewarding ornamental plant producing throughout the year (most heavily in late winter and spring) terminal clusters of 7 tubular, scarlet-red flowers with prominent, recurving, scarlet petals — vivid, hummingbird-attracting flowers of considerable color impact. Like all Proteaceae it requires excellent drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer. The combination of attractive red flowers and the remarkable, collectible, horned seed pods makes it a plant of multiple ornamental seasons.

common_name: Mountain Fire Japanese Pieris (Red New-Growth Andromeda)
notes: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in part shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind. Mountain Fire is grown chiefly for its brilliant fire-engine-red new growth in spring, considered among the most vivid of any Pieris cultivar, which matures to bronze and then glossy dark green as the season progresses. Cascading chains of small white urn-shaped flowers open in late winter to early spring before the new flush, giving two distinct ornamental moments. It is slow-growing and low-maintenance once established, needing little pruning beyond removing spent flower clusters.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade — mountain hydrangea from the mountains of Korea and Japan is a smaller, more elegant, and significantly more shade and heat tolerant cousin of the common bigleaf hydrangea (H. macrophylla), producing delicate, lace-cap or mophead flower clusters in blue, pink, or white (depending on soil pH and cultivar) in summer on compact, upright shrubs. It is more reliably heat tolerant than bigleaf hydrangea and flowers more consistently in zone 7–9 warm-climate gardens. Like bigleaf hydrangea, flower color shifts between blue and pink based on soil pH (blue in acidic soil, pink in alkaline) and is adjusted with aluminum sulfate applications. Outstanding cultivars include 'Blue Billow' (lacecap, blue), 'Preziosa' (mophead, pink aging to deep rose), and 'Tuff Stuff' (remontant). Its modest size makes it more practical than bigleaf hydrangea in smaller gardens.

Plant in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, avoiding afternoon sun in hot climates; mountain laurel is the state flower of Connecticut and Pennsylvania and arguably the most spectacular native flowering shrub in the eastern United States, producing dense clusters (corymbs) of intricate, bowl-shaped flowers in white, pink, deep pink, red, or bicolored patterns with contrasting star-like markings in late spring — each bud is geometrically folded like an origami flower before opening. The evergreen, lance-shaped leaves provide year-round interest and the gnarled, multi-stem growth habit becomes increasingly sculptural with age. It thrives in the dappled shade of pine and oak forests and is essential to the native woodland garden. Over 80 named cultivars offer great variation in flower color and plant size from dwarf (2 feet) to large (12 feet). All plant parts contain grayanotoxins and are toxic to humans and livestock.

Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mountain maple is the most shade-tolerant native maple in eastern North America, naturally growing as a small understory tree or large shrub in the deep shade of mixed northern hardwood forests, along rocky mountain streams, and on cool north-facing slopes. The upright flower spikes (distinctive among maples) appear in June after the leaves unfurl. Fall color is outstanding — brilliant scarlet and orange. This is an excellent choice for naturalizing in shaded woodland gardens in cooler climates and is critically important as winter food for moose, who browse the twigs and bark. Not heat-tolerant; best in zones 2-6 where summers stay cool.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly to moderately acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained soil in part shade; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity; avoid hot, dry, alkaline conditions. Pieris floribunda (mountain pieris or mountain fetterbush) is a native evergreen shrub of the high Appalachian Mountains of Virginia through Georgia — the North American counterpart to the widely grown Japanese pieris (P. japonica) — producing upright clusters (panicles) of small, white, urn-shaped flowers in March–April at the branch tips, with the characteristic red-to-bronze new growth that distinguishes the genus. Unlike the pendulous flower clusters of Japanese pieris, P. floribunda produces erect, branching flower panicles. The shrub is more compact and slower-growing than Japanese pieris, reaching 2–6 feet in maturity, and is somewhat more tolerant of deer browse. It is an excellent native alternative to P. japonica for acidic-soil woodland and shade gardens in the upper and mid-South. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — it is one of the classic poisonous woodland shrubs of the southern Appalachians. Note: in the lower South and zone 9, Japanese pieris (P. japonica) typically performs better in the heat.

Plant in well-drained to dry soil in partial shade to full sun; mountain sage is a large-leafed, shrubby Texas native salvia that lights up in fall with brilliant scarlet-orange tubular flowers precisely when migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds need fuel for their journey to Central America. The flowers are spectacularly hummingbird-attractive and among the showiest of all the fall-blooming salvias. In zones 9–11 it grows as a large, dense evergreen shrub 4–6 feet tall; in zone 8 it is killed to the ground by frost but typically regrows from the roots in spring. It tolerates the dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the Chihuahuan Desert and Hill Country, making it excellent for xeric Gulf Coast gardens with poor, calcareous soil.

Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; mountain silverbell is a large native deciduous tree of the southern Appalachian mountains that produces a spectacularly beautiful spring flower display in April and May, when the entire canopy becomes hung with thousands of small, nodding, pure-white, bell-shaped flowers that dangle in rows from the undersides of the leafing branches, backlit by new green leaves, creating one of the most delicate and ethereal spring effects of any native tree. The flowers are followed by decorative, four-winged, green to tan seed pods that persist through winter. In autumn the foliage turns clear yellow. Mountain silverbell grows naturally as a sub-canopy forest tree and is among the most shade-tolerant of all flowering trees — making it the ideal choice for planting under or alongside taller oaks, maples, and tulip poplars where most flowering trees would fail to bloom. The related Carolina silverbell (Halesia carolina) is similar but smaller; the mountain form (H. monticola, sometimes treated as H. tetraptera var. monticola) is the larger and more tree-like form. An outstanding native tree for the naturalistic woodland garden.

Stewartia ovata is a large, multi-stemmed, native Appalachian shrub to small tree producing some of the largest flowers of any native deciduous plant — white, camellia-like, five-petaled blooms up to 4 inches across with large, showy orange stamens and dark-purple anthers in June and July — as well as outstanding, multi-season ornamental interest from its handsome, peeling gray-tan-cinnamon mottled bark and brilliant red, orange, and purple fall foliage. Native to moist mountain forest understories from Virginia to Alabama, it is the most widely adaptable stewartia for eastern gardens and is slowly becoming available from quality native plant nurseries.

Mountain Sweet Pepperbush is a tall native understory shrub, native to the rich, moist, hardwood forests and mountain cove edges of the southern Appalachians from Virginia and North Carolina south to Georgia and Alabama, growing to 12 feet or more in deep, humus-rich mountain soils and producing fragrant white flower spikes in July and August that attract bumblebees and native butterflies. Distinguished from its coastal relative (Clethra alnifolia) by its greater height, more shade tolerance, and spectacular cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark that peels away in shaggy layers through the winter — an outstanding ornamental feature that rivals the most prized native bark textures. An excellent shrub for the shade garden in zones 5–8, where it tolerates conditions that defeat many other flowering shrubs; grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and mulch deeply with leaf litter to maintain consistent moisture.

growth_habit: species shrub rose grown for hips
notes: Choose a permanent site with full sun and good drainage, since this vigorous species rose grows into a large arching shrub that resents transplanting once established. Water regularly the first year and mulch to conserve moisture, then reduce supplemental watering as the deep roots mature. Deep crimson, single five-petaled flowers appear along the canes in early summer, followed by an outstanding display of large, flagon-shaped orange-red hips in fall that persist well into winter. It is best used as a specimen or background shrub where its size and structural form have room to shine.

common_name: Mrs. B.R. Cant Rose (Antique Southern Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, allowing 3-5 feet between plants since this vigorous tea rose can reach 6-8 feet in warm climates over time. Introduced in 1901 and named for the wife of an English rose nurseryman, Mrs. B.R. Cant became a mainstay of Deep South gardens and old cemeteries because of its extraordinary heat tolerance, vigor, and near-total resistance to blackspot, which lets it thrive in the humid Gulf South with no spraying. Large, cupped, silvery-pink double blooms with a rich tea fragrance appear in flushes from spring through the first frost, most heavily in cooler weather. Like most tea roses, it prefers to be left largely alone — minimal pruning beyond removing dead or damaged wood keeps the plant blooming reliably, since heavy pruning delays flowering and reduces the shrub's naturally graceful, arching form. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and neglect, which is why so many survive today in abandoned Southern homesites decades after they were planted.

common_name: Mrs. Dudley Cross Rose (Antique Cream-Blush Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Mrs. Dudley Cross is a classic Tea rose bearing pale yellow buds that open to soft cream flowers gently blushed with pink, produced in flushes almost continuously through the long, hot Gulf South growing season. Like other old Tea roses it is exceptionally vigorous, heat-tolerant, and disease-resistant, thriving with little more than a sunny, well-drained spot and occasional shaping, which has kept it in circulation among heirloom rose collectors and found growing untended at old homesites for generations. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued repeat flowering, and expect good resistance to black spot and powdery mildew compared with modern hybrid roses bred for cooler climates.

common_name: Mrs. Schiller's Delight Viburnum (Dwarf Dense Walter's Viburnum)
notes: Mrs. Schiller's Delight is one of the smallest and most tightly compact selections of native Walter's viburnum, forming a dense, fine-textured mound of small, glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves that stays well under 3 feet without regular shearing. Clusters of small white flowers open in spring, followed by small red fruit ripening to black that draws songbirds, on a plant scaled for low hedging, edging, and small foundation beds where even Little Joe would eventually need trimming to stay in bounds. Like other Walter's viburnum selections it tolerates a range of soil moisture, from average garden conditions to occasionally wet sites, and needs little pruning to hold its naturally tidy, rounded form.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; mugo pine tolerates poor, rocky, alkaline soil and windy, exposed sites better than most ornamental conifers, but resents heavy, wet clay. A European mountain native, it forms a dense, irregular, low-mounding to broadly spreading shrub of stiff, dark-green needles in bundles of two, useful as a foundation planting, rock garden anchor, or informal low screen where a tough, cold-hardy evergreen is needed. Growth rate and mature size vary considerably by seed source and named selection, so 'candle' (new growth tip) pruning in late spring is the standard technique for controlling size and maintaining a dense, compact form over time. It is notably heat-sensitive in humid, hot summer climates and performs best in cooler, drier regions than the Gulf South.

Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Multi Blue produces unusual, fully double flowers in rich blue-purple, the outer sepals surrounding a dense pompom of shorter, twisted, spiky inner petaloids that give each bloom a shaggy, almost anemone-like texture unlike the flat, single flowers of most clematis. It flowers in late spring to early summer on old wood with a possible lighter rebloom on new growth, so prune only lightly to remove dead or weak stems in late winter rather than cutting the vine back hard. Its unusual double form makes it a conversation-piece specimen for a trellis, arbor, or large container support.

common_name: Munchkin Oakleaf Hydrangea (True Dwarf Oakleaf Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Deep South. Munchkin is one of the smallest oakleaf hydrangea cultivars available, bred to bring the bold, deeply lobed foliage and cone-shaped white flower panicles of the species down to a true dwarf scale suited to small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-sized oakleaf hydrangea would quickly outgrow the space. Flower panicles open white in early summer and age to a soft pink, and the compact plant still develops the rich burgundy and orange fall foliage color and exfoliating bark the species is known for. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid pruning in fall, winter, or spring, which removes the coming year's blooms.

common_name: Munstead Wood Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Set plants in full sun with at least six hours of direct light and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply and regularly during the first year to build a strong root system. Prune back by about a third in late winter and remove spent blooms through the season to encourage repeat flowering. Deep crimson, richly fragrant double blooms with an old-rose form open in flushes from early summer to frost on this compact, bushy English shrub rose. Its dark, velvety petal color and strong scent make it a standout among David Austin's English rose introductions for borders and cutting gardens.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Muskogee is one of the most widely planted large crape myrtle cultivars, renowned for its soft, light lavender flower color — a cool, pale purple-pink that stands apart from the dominant pink and red tones of many crape myrtles and creates a particularly refreshing effect in the intense summer heat of the Gulf South. The flowers are produced in large clusters continuously from June through September in zone 9, covering the canopy with light lavender-purple throughout the peak summer season. Like Natchez (which it was developed alongside at the National Arboretum), Muskogee shows exceptional resistance to powdery mildew and retains attractive multi-trunked form when properly trained. The bark exfoliates to reveal mottled tan, gray, and cinnamon tones in late summer and fall. Fall leaf color transitions to orange-red, providing a third season of ornamental interest. Muskogee is a large-growing tree that can exceed 20–30 feet in height in zone 9 over decades, making it a true tree-scale specimen appropriate only for large planting spaces. Do not top or severely prune — always cut back only to lateral branches of similar diameter when any pruning is needed.

common_name: Mutabilis Rose (Butterfly Rose, Color-Changing China Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing plants at least 4-5 feet apart to allow for its eventual size, since Mutabilis can grow into a large, airy shrub 6-8 feet tall in warm climates over several years. Known as the Butterfly Rose for the way its single, five-petaled blooms seem to flutter above the foliage, Mutabilis opens flame-yellow, ages through pink, and finishes deep crimson, so a single established bush displays all three colors at once. As a China rose it blooms almost continuously from spring through frost with little deadheading required, and it is exceptionally resistant to blackspot and powdery mildew, making it one of the most reliable antique roses for the hot, humid Gulf South. It tolerates poor soil and some drought once established but flowers best and grows most vigorously with regular water and an occasional feeding. Prune lightly in late winter only to shape and remove dead wood, since Mutabilis flowers on both old and new growth and heavy pruning sacrifices bloom.

common_name: My Mary Azalea (Golden-Yellow Native Hybrid Azalea)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. My Mary is a Southern-bred native azalea hybrid prized for its clear golden-yellow flowers with a light, sweet fragrance, opening in a dense spring flush on a rounded, well-branched shrub that stays more compact than many native deciduous azalea species. Its clean yellow color and fragrance, combined with better heat tolerance than many Asian azalea hybrids, have made it a favorite for Southern woodland gardens wanting a native-type azalea in a warm color outside the typical orange-to-red native range. Keep the shallow root zone consistently moist and mulched, since deciduous azaleas resent both drought and waterlogged soil.

Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from the harshest afternoon sun where summers are hottest. My Monet is among the smallest weigela cultivars available, forming a tight, mounded plant under a foot tall with green leaves crisply edged in white, often blushing pink along the margins in cooler weather, topped with a modest flush of small pink flowers in late spring. Its diminutive scale suits it to rock gardens, border edges, and container plantings where a full-size weigela would be far too large, and its variegated foliage provides season-long interest well beyond the brief bloom period.
