Prune only lightly if needed, and remove any solid-green reverted shoots as soon as they appear to keep the variegation stable.

Plant in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 7–10; myrtle holly is a native evergreen shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, named for its unusually small, narrow, glossy leaves that strongly resemble those of true myrtle — quite different from the larger leaves of most native hollies. It grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, pond margins, bogs, and bay swamp edges throughout Florida and the Gulf Coast states, making it one of the most ecologically appropriate native shrubs for zone 9a moist-site plantings. The small, bright red to orange-red berries are highly attractive to bluebirds, yellow-rumped warblers, hermit thrushes, and other fruit-eating birds throughout winter. An underused native alternative to Japanese holly (I. crenata) that offers far greater wildlife value and superior adaptation to Gulf Coast conditions.

Myrtle oak is a small-leaved, evergreen scrub oak of the Florida Peninsula and adjacent Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, unique among native oaks for its distinctly myrtle-like, oval, entire (not lobed) leaves that are shiny and dark green above — so different in appearance from typical oak leaves that beginners often fail to recognize it as an oak. It grows in the hottest, driest, most nutrient-deficient white-sand scrub habitats of the Florida interior and coasts, forming dense thickets from ankle height to small tree size depending on fire history and site conditions; Florida scrub habitats maintained by periodic fire have low, clumping myrtle oaks while fire-suppressed scrub develops into tall, dense thickets. Like turkey oak, myrtle oak is a foundational component of the Florida scrub ecosystem, which hosts more endemic species per acre than almost any other habitat in temperate North America, including the federally threatened Florida scrub-jay that depends on scrub oaks as its primary food source. A valuable landscape shrub or small tree for dry, sandy, acidic sites in central and south Florida.

common_name: Mysore Clockvine (Dolls Shoes Vine, Indian Clockvine)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Mysore Clockvine grows vigorously in zone 9 conditions and produces its most spectacular bloom in fall through spring when temperatures moderate from summer heat. Thunbergia mysorensis is a large, vigorous, woody twining vine from the forests of southern India (Mysore, now Karnataka region), producing one of the most exotic and unusual flower displays of any tropical vine. The flowers are borne in long, pendulous racemes 12–18 inches in length that hang down from the vine canopy like earrings or chandeliers — each individual flower is two-toned, with reflexed outer petals in deep burgundy-red to maroon and a large, flaring, open throat in vivid golden-yellow, creating a striking color combination visible from a distance. The pendant flower clusters are specifically adapted for sunbird pollination in their native Indian forest habitat — the long, tubular corolla and dangling cluster position the flower perfectly for these hovering birds, and in zone 9, hummingbirds fulfill the same function with enthusiasm. In the US, Mysore Clockvine is grown as a spectacular pergola and arbor vine at botanical gardens (it is a signature plant at Balboa Park in San Diego and public tropical gardens nationwide) and is increasingly available at specialty nurseries for zone 9-11 home gardens.

common_name: Mysore Trumpetvine (Lady's Slipper Vine, Dolls Shoes)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; provide a very strong pergola or trellis — this vine grows vigorously and becomes very heavy; prune after flowering. Thunbergia mysorensis (Mysore trumpetvine, lady's slipper vine, or dolls shoes vine) is a spectacular evergreen climbing vine from the subtropical montane forests of southern India — particularly the Mysore region of Karnataka (where the common name originates) — and one of the most dramatically beautiful flowering vines in tropical horticulture. The vine produces long (12–18 inch), pendulous, racemose clusters of exotic, bicolor tubular flowers: deep red to burgundy-red on the outside with yellow-cream interiors and reflexed lobes, hanging in dense, eye-catching chains that resemble a row of dancing dolls or hanging slippers — hence the evocative common names. The flower clusters drape elegantly over pergolas, fences, and arbors, creating one of the most visually arresting and tropical-looking displays possible in a garden. The flowers are produced abundantly for months in warm climates and attract hummingbirds, bees, and sunbirds. The vine grows vigorously to 20–30 feet on strong support structures. Thunbergia mysorensis is becoming increasingly available through specialty tropical nurseries as awareness of its spectacular ornamental value spreads beyond its native range.

Plant in partial shade to filtered light — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; deep shade reduces flowering while full afternoon sun can cause leaf scorch; Mystery Gardenia (Gardenia jasminoides 'Mystery') is a large-flowered cultivar of one of the most fragrant of all flowering shrubs — producing the classic, intensely sweet, creamy-white gardenia flowers that have defined the concept of floral fragrance in American culture for generations. The 'Mystery' cultivar produces exceptionally large, fully double, pristine white to ivory flowers (4–5 inches across) against a backdrop of glossy, dark, evergreen leaves — creating a floral display of formal elegance and sensory intensity that few other ornamental shrubs can approach. The fragrance of gardenia flowers is one of the most recognizable and universally admired of any flowering plant — the complex, sweet, powdery-floral scent is distinctive and powerful enough to perfume an entire outdoor area when a mature, blooming gardenia shrub is nearby. In zone 9 gardenias thrive in the warm, humid climate that creates their ideal growing conditions — partial shade conditions that are abundant in the Gulf South landscape under pine and hardwood canopy providing exactly the situation they prefer. The combination of spectacular fragrant flowers, elegant glossy evergreen foliage, and cultural fit with zone 9's acid, partial-shade conditions makes Mystery Gardenia one of the most rewarding ornamental shrubs for Gulf South landscapes.

common_name: Nabob Abutilon (Deep Red Classic Flowering Maple)
notes: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Nabob is a longtime classic abutilon cultivar valued for its deep, velvety burgundy-red, bell-shaped flowers held against dark green, maple-shaped leaves, blooming nearly year-round in mild climates on an upright, well-branched shrub. Its rich, saturated flower color stands out among the typically softer pastel tones of many abutilon cultivars, making it a strong accent in mixed borders and large containers, and hummingbirds visit the pendant blooms regularly. In zone 8, expect frost dieback most winters, with plants often resprouting from the base if roots are mulched and protected; where hard freezes are common, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; nandina (heavenly bamboo) is one of the most widely planted landscape shrubs in the American South, prized for its four-season ornamental interest: delicate, feathery, compound foliage that emerges pinkish-bronze in spring, matures to bright green in summer, and turns brilliant scarlet-red in fall and winter; clusters of white flowers in late spring; and masses of bright red berries that persist through winter. It is extraordinarily adaptable, tolerating deep shade under trees, drought, poor soil, and heat with minimal care. Important ecological note: Nandina domestica is classified as invasive in many southeastern states as birds spread the seeds into natural areas; furthermore, the berries are toxic to cedar waxwings and other birds that eat them in large quantities. Select non-invasive, non-fruiting cultivars (compact 'Gulf Stream', 'Firepower', 'Fire Power', or dwarf 'Obsession Nandina') for residential use and avoid planting near natural areas. Compact cultivars at 2–3 feet are particularly useful for low-maintenance groundcovers in shade.

common_name: Nanho Blue Butterfly Bush (Compact Blue-Lavender Buddleja)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Nanho Blue is the most popular compact butterfly bush — a smaller-growing Buddleja davidii cultivar in the Nanho series reaching 4–5 feet tall and wide, compared to the 6–10 feet of standard-sized selections like Black Knight. The reduced size makes Nanho Blue appropriate for typical residential garden spaces where full-size butterfly bush would quickly overwhelm the surrounding plants. The flower color is clear lavender-blue to blue-violet — a cooler, more blue-toned color than many butterfly bush cultivars that trend toward red-violet and purple. The fine-textured, silver-gray foliage is particularly attractive in the Nanho series, with narrower, more delicate leaves than standard cultivars. Like all Buddleja davidii cultivars, Nanho Blue is extraordinarily attractive to butterflies — the honey-scented flowers attract admirals, swallowtails, and fritillaries through the summer. Deadhead regularly to extend bloom and prevent seed set. In zone 9, cut the entire plant back to 12–18 inches in February; vigorous new growth emerges quickly when temperatures warm. Butterfly bush is drought-tolerant once established and actually performs better in lean, somewhat dry soils — in rich, moist soil the growth is rank and floppy.

common_name: Nanho Purple Butterfly Bush (Compact Fine-Textured Buddleja)
notes: Nanho Purple is a compact selection from the Nanho series of butterfly bush, bred for a smaller mature size and finer-textured, narrower gray-green leaves than standard Buddleja davidii cultivars, fitting more easily into a mixed border without becoming an overwhelming presence. Its slender purple flower spikes are produced in abundance from summer through fall, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds just as reliably as larger cultivars despite the reduced plant size. In zone 9 it dies back over winter and should be cut back hard, to about 12 inches, in late winter to keep its naturally more compact habit tidy and to maximize summer bloom.

Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; narrowleaf cottonwood is the dominant riparian tree of mountain streams and rivers in the Rocky Mountain west, forming gallery forest along watercourses from Montana to New Mexico. The distinctively narrow, willow-like leaves set it apart from other cottonwoods, giving it a more refined, graceful appearance. In fall, the foliage turns brilliant golden-yellow — a signature of Rocky Mountain fall scenery, particularly in high-elevation valleys where large stands create sweeping landscapes of fall gold against pine forest. The tree provides critical nesting habitat for raptors, heron colonies, and songbirds in mountain riparian corridors. Hybridizes freely with plains cottonwood where ranges overlap, producing intermediate forms. A fast-growing pioneer species of mountain stream banks and flood plains in the intermountain west.

growth_habit: spectacular winter-flowering South African small tree
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Natal bottlebrush tree is a spectacular South African small tree or large shrub that produces in late winter, on bare leafless branches (flowering before the leaves emerge — a behavior called 'hysteranthous' that creates an unusually dramatic floral display against the bare winter framework of the tree), dense, cylindrical clusters of flowers in vivid scarlet to crimson-red, with prominent, projecting red stamens creating the brushy, bottle-brush-like texture. The individual flowers are composed primarily of conspicuous red stamens projecting from small scarlet sepals, creating the bottlebrush silhouette of the common name, and the color is an intense, clear, fire-engine red. A mature tree in full bloom — red bottlebrush clusters covering every leafless branch against the winter sky — is one of the most dramatically colorful winter spectacles in the zone 9 garden, and an irresistible feeding station for winter hummingbirds. The large, rounded, somewhat fig-like leaves that follow the flowers are also attractive. Related to Melianthus but without the strong odor. A choice specimen tree for warm gardens seeking a spectacular winter-blooming feature tree.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Natchez is widely considered the finest crape myrtle cultivar ever developed and is certainly the most widely planted — a National Arboretum hybrid of Lagerstroemia indica × L. fauriei introduced in 1987 that combines outstanding white flowers, four-season ornamental value, and exceptional disease resistance. From June through September in zone 9, Natchez produces massive clusters of pure white flowers continuously, creating a spectacular seasonal display that no other white-flowering summer tree rivals in the Deep South. In fall, the foliage transitions to brilliant orange-red — remarkable fall color for a Gulf Coast tree. But Natchez's most distinctive and lasting ornamental attribute may be its bark: the outer gray bark exfoliates in autumn to reveal rich cinnamon-brown, reddish-brown, and cream inner bark in a spectacular mottled pattern that makes the multi-trunked trunk one of the most beautiful in the tree world. The exfoliating bark is excellent as a winter feature when the tree is leafless. Natchez has outstanding resistance to powdery mildew — the primary disease problem of other crape myrtles. NEVER top (cut back major limbs) Natchez or any crape myrtle — this practice creates permanent, ugly knobby heads, destroys the tree's graceful form, and dramatically reduces its ornamental value without providing any benefit.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Natchez Crepe Myrtle thrives in summer heat and drought, requiring supplemental water only during establishment and extended dry periods once mature; Natchez is the flagship white-flowered introduction from the National Arboretum's landmark crepe myrtle breeding program, released in 1978 as one of the first L. indica x fauriei hybrids that combined the large, colorful flowers of L. indica with the disease resistance and refined exfoliating bark of the Japanese L. fauriei species. The extraordinary, exfoliating cinnamon-to-chestnut bark that peels to reveal cream, tan, and mahogany underlayers is arguably the most beautiful bark texture of any tree in the Southern landscape — providing striking ornamental interest throughout the fall and winter months long after the white flower clusters have dropped. The pure white flower clusters appear in midsummer (June–August), covering the entire canopy with massive, frothy white blooms before the foliage turns bronze-orange-red in fall. Natchez's combination of spectacular summer bloom, beautiful autumn color, exceptional winter bark, disease resistance, and adaptability to the heat and drought of zones 6–9 has made it one of the most widely planted ornamental trees in the American South for over four decades.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Natchez mock orange was bred in the South for good heat and humidity tolerance and performs reliably in Gulf South gardens. Large, pure white, four-petaled flowers smother the arching branches in late spring, filling the garden with an intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance that gives mock orange its common name, on a vigorous, upright shrub bred at Louisiana State University specifically for improved performance in hot, humid southern climates. Its strong Southern breeding heritage makes it a more reliable performer in Gulf Coast gardens than many older mock orange selections developed for cooler, drier climates, retaining good foliage quality through summer heat. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning sacrifices the next season's fragrant display.

common_name: Navajo Bright Red Autumn Sage (Vivid Red Salvia greggii)
notes: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Navajo Bright Red is part of the Navajo series of Salvia greggii selections bred for especially saturated, true-red flower color and heavy bloom production, covering the plant in vivid red, two-lipped flowers from spring through hard frost on a compact, rounded, semi-evergreen to deciduous subshrub. Like other Salvia greggii cultivars, it is exceptionally drought- and heat-tolerant once established and a reliable hummingbird and native bee magnet through its long bloom season. Cut back hard to 6–8 inches in late winter to promote fresh, dense growth and abundant spring flowering, and shear lightly after each flush to keep the plant tidy and blooming continuously.

common_name: Near East Crape Myrtle (Antique Soft-Pink Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Near East is an antique Lagerstroemia indica cultivar predating the modern mildew-resistant Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei hybrid series, valued for its soft, almost silvery blush-pink flower clusters and graceful, gracefully arching branch habit that gives it a softer silhouette than many stiffer modern cultivars. Older all-indica crape myrtles like Near East are more prone to powdery mildew than the newer hybrid series, so plant it with good air circulation and full sun exposure to minimize disease pressure in humid Gulf South summers. Its long bloom season from early to midsummer and attractive exfoliating bark give it multi-season appeal, and it has remained a fixture of historic Southern gardens for its distinctive antique color. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural form and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

Necklace Pod is a striking native coastal shrub, native to the sandy beaches, dunes, and coastal scrub of the Gulf and Atlantic coasts from Florida to Texas, the Caribbean, and tropical Americas, producing long, arching racemes of bright yellow pea-like flowers nearly year-round in frost-free areas that attract hummingbirds, butterflies, and large carpenter bees. The distinctive seed pods are constricted between each seed like a string of beads — giving the plant its common name — and the silvery-gray, velvety, compound leaves provide attractive texture against the beach landscape. One of the finest native plants for coastal stabilization and landscaping in zones 9–11, Necklace Pod tolerates salt spray, poor sandy soil, drought, and heat with equal ease, requiring virtually no care once established in a sunny, well-drained site. Caution: seeds are toxic if ingested.

Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to dappled light; Posoqueria latifolia benefits from consistent moisture and humidity — mulch heavily, water regularly, and protect from strong winds and salt spray. Posoqueria latifolia (Needle Flower Tree or Red Star) is an evergreen shrub to small tree native to humid tropical forests from southern Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean into South America, member of the Rubiaceae (coffee family), and one of the most ornamentally spectacular night-fragrant flowering trees of the tropics. The common name references the long, slender, needle-like flower tubes — each individual flower has a tube 4 to 6 inches long — held in large, globe-shaped terminal clusters that open white at night and release an intense jasmine-like fragrance evolved to attract long-tongued hawk moths (Sphingidae) as pollinators. The round, pale-yellow to orange fruits that follow are edible, mucilaginous, and eaten in some parts of its native range. Posoqueria makes an exceptional accent plant or large container specimen for humid subtropical and tropical gardens where it is a conversation-stopper in bloom; provide shelter, consistent moisture, and protection from frost for best results.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Needlepoint is a refined, upright Chinese holly cultivar valued for two outstanding characteristics: it is one of the most reliably self-fertile hollies (producing bright red berries without requiring a separate male pollinator), and it has narrower, more elegant leaves with a single prominent terminal spine rather than the multiple spines of typical Chinese holly. The reduced spine count makes it significantly more people-friendly than standard Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta) while maintaining excellent deer resistance and the characteristic waxy, deep-green, evergreen foliage. The heavy annual red berry crop is produced reliably from November through winter, providing outstanding wildlife value — berries are consumed by mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. The upright, pyramidal to oval habit grows 7–12 feet tall with a somewhat narrower spread, making it suitable for foundation plantings, hedges, and screening in spaces where the spreading Burford holly would be too wide. Needlepoint holly tolerates the full range of Gulf Coast conditions — clay soil, drought, heat, and partial shade — that challenge many landscape shrubs. Apply balanced fertilizer in spring; no regular pruning is needed beyond shaping immediately after the berry season ends in late winter.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Nellie R. Stevens is the most widely planted evergreen holly in the American South — a vigorous, broadly pyramidal tree-form shrub reaching 15–25 feet tall with a dense, naturally symmetrical form that requires minimal pruning to maintain its attractive shape. It is a hybrid of Ilex cornuta × Ilex aquifolium, combining the heat tolerance and gloss of Chinese holly with the cold hardiness and berry production of English holly. The dark, glossy, spiny evergreen leaves provide a rich, formal appearance year-round, and the plant produces abundant clusters of bright red berries from fall through winter that are highly attractive to cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and other wildlife. Nellie R. Stevens is considered partially self-fruitful — it sets fruit without a pollinizer, but nearby male hollies (any male Ilex cornuta or I. aquifolium) significantly increase fruit load. It is adaptable to a wide range of soil types and performs well in Gulf Coast clay soils once established. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant. In zone 9, Nellie R. Stevens is one of the most reliable large evergreen hollies, providing both year-round screening and spectacular winter berry displays.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Nellie Stevens Holly is a hybrid Ilex cultivar (believed to be Ilex aquifolium x Ilex cornuta) that has become one of the most popular evergreen screening trees and specimen hollies for the American South and transition zones — combining the large size and dense pyramidal form needed for privacy screening with exceptional heat tolerance and adaptability to Gulf South conditions. The large, glossy, dark green leaves with spiny margins create an impenetrable, formal-looking screen or hedge that requires minimal maintenance to maintain its naturally tidy pyramidal shape. In winter, heavily pollinated female trees are covered with large clusters of orange-red berries that persist through winter and are an important food source for robins, cedar waxwings, and other berry-eating birds. The combination of year-round ornamental value (evergreen foliage + winter berries), fast growth rate (2–3 feet per year in good conditions), and Gulf South adaptability has made Nellie Stevens one of the most planted ornamental trees across zones 6–9 for the past several decades.

Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, since Nelly Moser's flower color is prone to fading and bleaching in intense, all-day summer sun. Introduced in France in the 1890s, it remains one of the most recognizable clematis cultivars for its large, pale pink flowers boldly striped down the center of each petal with a deep carmine-rose bar. It flowers on old wood in late spring and can rebloom lightly on new growth later in summer, so pruning should be light, removing only dead or weak stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole vine back hard, which would sacrifice the main spring bloom.

common_name: Neon Flash Spirea (Compact Spirea with Vivid Magenta-Pink Flower Clusters)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, where flower color and density are strongest; light shade is tolerated but reduces bloom. Neon Flash is a compact, rounded Japanese spirea selected for unusually vivid, saturated magenta-pink flower clusters that stand out more strongly than the softer pink of older spirea cultivars, blooming heavily in late spring to early summer over blue-green foliage. Shearing the shrub back by about a third immediately after the main bloom flush tidies its shape and often prompts a second, smaller flush of flowers later in the season. Established plants are tough, drought-tolerant, and low-maintenance, tolerating poor soil and urban conditions well, and the compact size suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where a large, sprawling shrub would be unwelcome.

Net-leaf hackberry is the western species of hackberry, found on rocky canyon walls, limestone bluffs, and desert arroyo margins from the Texas Hill Country west to California and south into Mexico, where it often clings to near-vertical cliff faces and survives in conditions of extreme drought and heat. Its distinctive deeply veined, rough, sandpaper-textured leaves (the 'reticulata' means net-veined) and tolerance of alkaline limestone soils make it the hackberry for dry, rocky, alkaline landscapes of the southwest where eastern hackberry (Celtis occidentalis) is poorly adapted. Like all hackberries, it is a primary host plant for hackberry emperor and American snout butterflies, and its small, dark red to black berries are eaten by 30+ bird species including robins, mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and migrating thrushes. In south and central Texas and the southwestern states, it is an important native tree for dry, rocky, alkaline soil landscape situations and for restoring native woodland structure in arroyo and canyon habitats.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; netleaf leather flower is a slender native vine of the southeastern Coastal Plain that scrambles through shrubs and over fences with modest vigor. The unique, urn-shaped flowers have thick, leathery tepals in shades of dull purple with pale-veined markings — resembling tiny pitchers that hang from the vine stems in summer. Unlike the more showy garden clematis, this species is subtle and discovered on close inspection. The feathery seed heads that follow are silvery and attractive. The netted or reticulated (net-like) veins of the leaves give the species its name. This is one of the native leather flower clematis of the Gulf Coastal Plain (related to C. crispa and C. viorna) and a rare but valuable plant for a low-water, naturalistic southern garden.

common_name: New Harmony Elm (Disease-Tolerant Upright American Elm)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. New Harmony was released by the USDA National Arboretum as a companion selection to Valley Forge, chosen from the same disease-screening program for combining strong Dutch elm disease tolerance with a somewhat more upright, uniform growth habit that some growers prefer for street and boulevard plantings. Like other resistant American elm cultivars it restores the tall, graceful, arching form long associated with the species, and it has performed reliably in urban conditions including compacted soil, heat, and air pollution. Water deeply during the establishment years, prune early to encourage a strong central leader and well-spaced scaffold branches, and allow ample overhead and root space for the tree's eventual large size.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; New Jersey tea is a remarkable native shrub with one of the most interesting histories in American botany — the dried leaves were widely used as a tea substitute during the Revolutionary War when British tea was boycotted. The fluffy clusters of tiny white flowers in early summer are among the most important nectar sources in the native prairie and woodland edge, attracting dozens of bee species, skippers, and hairstreak butterflies. The roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility over time. This shrub is exceptionally drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established, thriving on rocky, infertile, dry soils where few shrubs succeed. The spring bee value alone makes it an outstanding native garden plant. It resents being moved after establishment, so site it correctly from the start.

common_name: New Mexico Privet (Desert Olive, Elbow Bush)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; once established, no supplemental irrigation is needed. Forestiera pubescens (New Mexico privet or desert olive) is a native Texas and New Mexico shrub — a member of the olive family (Oleaceae) producing olive-like, small (1/4-inch), blue-black drupes in fall that are eagerly consumed by migrating and resident birds, including mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings. The shrub is a multi-stemmed, densely branching, semi-evergreen plant with small, light-green, opposite leaves and tiny, inconspicuous, yellowish flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge. As a landscape plant, Forestiera pubescens is valued for extreme drought and limestone tolerance, dense wildlife-supporting structure, and use as a native hedge or screen plant that requires no supplemental water once established. It is an outstanding alternative to non-native privets (Ligustrum species) in dry southwestern and southern landscapes, providing equivalent screening value with native habitat benefits. The small, clustered fruits produced in fall are an important berry food source for fall migrants moving through the southwestern plains.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally within sight or scent of the coast; New Zealand Christmas tree is prized above all for its extreme tolerance of salt spray, wind, and sandy soil, thriving on exposed bluffs and beachfronts where few other flowering woody plants survive. Established plants are strikingly drought tolerant, drawing on deep roots once they are past their first year or two in the ground. Brilliant crimson, bottlebrush-like flower clusters cover the leathery, silver-backed leaves in a spectacular late-spring to early-summer display, and the plant can be maintained as a dense large shrub or screen with pruning, or allowed to develop into a picturesque small tree over many years. It is strictly a warm coastal plant, suffering damage below the high 20s F.

Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in spring after frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained, moist soil in zone 9–12; night-blooming jasmine is the most powerfully fragrant shrub for warm-climate gardens, releasing an almost overwhelming sweet tropical scent from small, tubular, white-to-yellowish-green flowers that open only after dark and fill the evening air for considerable distances. Flowers appear in clusters multiple times per year in frost-free climates, making it an exceptional plant for near patios, porches, and bedroom windows where the nocturnal fragrance can be enjoyed. Though not a true jasmine (it is in the nightshade family), its fragrance is incomparable; note that the plant is toxic if ingested. Prune lightly after each flowering flush to maintain a tidy, compact shrub form.

common_name: Nikko Blue Hydrangea (Classic Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nikko Blue is the most widely grown blue mophead hydrangea cultivar and a classic of the American garden — producing large (8–10 inch), rounded, fully double, sky-blue to cornflower-blue flower heads in early summer from June through August. The iconic blue mophead hydrangea flower is inseparable from the image of the classic American coastal and southern garden, and Nikko Blue has been the most popular blue mophead for decades. The characteristic pH-dependent color change is part of Nikko Blue's management: acidic soil (pH 5.0–5.5) produces the richest true blue; alkaline soil (pH above 6.5) produces pink. In Gulf South alkaline soils, amending with aluminum sulfate (2 lbs per 100 sq ft) and acidifying fertilizers in spring maintains the blue color. Nikko Blue blooms on old wood — meaning the flower buds form in late summer for the following year's bloom. This means the primary rule is: do NOT prune in fall, winter, or spring before bloom; prune only by removing spent flowers immediately after bloom to shape. In zone 9, Nikko Blue is evergreen to semi-evergreen and performs best in morning sun with afternoon protection from the intense Gulf South summer heat.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Nikko deutzia stays low and spreading rather than upright like most deutzia, making it useful as a flowering groundcover or low border shrub. This dwarf, mounding selection of slender deutzia forms a low, wide mat of fine-textured, dark green foliage that turns burgundy-red in fall, smothered in a profusion of small, star-shaped white flowers in mid to late spring. Its low, spreading habit sets it apart from taller deutzia cultivars, making it well suited to a foundation planting, low informal hedge, or the front of a shrub border where a flowering groundcover effect is wanted. It tolerates part shade better than many flowering shrubs while still blooming well, and needs only light pruning after flowering to maintain a tidy shape.

Bred in Poland by Władysław Noll, Niobe is one of the deepest, most saturated red large-flowered clematis cultivars widely grown, with velvety ruby-red 5 to 6 inch blooms set off by contrasting gold-yellow stamens that darken toward maroon as they age. It flowers heavily on old wood in late spring and early summer, then produces a lighter rebloom on new growth later in the season, so pruning should be light — just tidying and removing weak growth in late winter rather than a hard cutback. Like most clematis, it performs best with its roots kept cool and shaded while the vine climbs into full sun, a classic pairing achieved by underplanting with low groundcover or mulch.

Plant in well-drained, moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nippon spirea is a Japanese native and one of the finest white-flowering deciduous shrubs for the temperate garden — a rounded, arching shrub producing small, dark blue-green, oval leaves and in late spring through early summer, an exceptional display in which flat clusters of small, pure-white, button-like flowers cover every branch and arching stem so completely that the shrub appears to be draped in white lace, creating the characteristic mounded, snowdrift effect that earns the cultivar 'Snowmound' its name. The small, dark leaves provide an effective foil for the white flowers, and the contrast of the dark foliage and white bloom gives the plant a particularly fresh, clean appearance. Blue-green foliage color is distinctive throughout summer after bloom. Compact enough for foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders, it performs best with consistent moisture and full sun. Other cultivars include 'Halward's Silver' (lower and more compact) and 'June Bride' (particularly dense flower clusters). Widely used in residential landscaping across the northern United States.

Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade, spacing plants to allow the arching canes to form an informal thicket along a woodland edge, hedgerow, or streambank. Nootka rose is native to the Pacific Coast from northern California to Alaska, where it grows in open forest, coastal bluffs, and moist thickets. Its large, fragrant pink flowers, among the showiest of the wild roses, open in early summer and attract native bees, and the unusually large red hips that follow are an important winter food for grouse, thrushes, and small mammals as well as browse for deer. Dense, thorny growth also provides secure nesting habitat for shrub-nesting songbirds.

growth_habit: Norfolk Island Pacific coastal ornamental tree
notes: Plant Lagunaria patersonia in full sun in well-drained, lean, sandy or loamy soil; exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, coastal winds, poor soils, and drought once established — making it one of the best trees for beachfront and coastal gardens; CAUTION: the brown, dry seed pods contain fine, irritating hairs (similar to fiberglass) that cause significant skin, eye, and respiratory irritation — wear gloves and a mask when collecting or handling seed pods. Norfolk Island Hibiscus is a premier coastal street and garden tree for subtropical coastal areas — its dense, pyramidal crown, salt-spray tolerance, and resistance to sandy, nutrient-poor soils make it an ideal tree for challenging coastal garden sites where most other trees fail. The large, 3-inch, pale mauve-lavender flowers (resembling a subdued hibiscus) appear throughout spring and summer and are genuinely attractive; the tree forms a natural, neat, pyramidal shape requiring little pruning. Endemic to Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island — both tiny, remote South Pacific islands — it has been widely planted as a coastal amenity tree across Australia's eastern coast, California, Hawaii, and Florida. In the Gulf Coast zone 9–10 garden, it performs excellently in exposed coastal positions, along salt air-exposed roadsides, and in hot, sandy inland gardens. The sole species in its genus (Lagunaria), it represents an important isolated branch of the hibiscus family.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade, and protect young trees from frost, since foliage is damaged well above freezing. Despite the common name this is not a true pine but a member of the ancient Araucariaceae family, forming a strikingly symmetrical, tiered, pagoda-like silhouette with horizontal branches of soft, needle-like foliage that make it a favorite avenue and specimen tree along Florida, Gulf Coast, and southern California coastlines. It tolerates salt spray and sandy soils better than most conifers, but outside frost-free zones it is more commonly kept as a container specimen or houseplant, where it stays much smaller than the 100-foot trees seen in its native range and along tropical streets.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade protection in the hottest climates. North Star was bred for reliable winter color retention and cold hardiness beyond that of most boxwood cultivars, holding a good, even green through winter without the bronzing that afflicts many boxwoods in cold or intense sun, while its dense, rounded, naturally compact habit needs relatively little shearing to maintain a tidy form. It is a good choice for formal hedging, edging, and foundation plantings where consistent winter appearance matters as much as summer form. Boxwoods need well-drained soil, since they are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet sites; shear or hand-prune to shape in late winter or after the spring growth flush.

Plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; northern bayberry is a native, semi-evergreen shrub of eastern North American coastal areas that provides four compelling reasons for wider use: extraordinary tolerance of sandy, nutrient-poor, salty coastal soil where most shrubs fail; dense clusters of small, waxy, blue-gray berries along the stems that provide essential late-autumn and winter food for myrtle warblers (yellow-rumped warblers), tree swallows, and other migratory birds that depend on the high-fat bayberry wax for energy during migration; the rich, resinous, spicy-sweet fragrance of the leaves and berries that perfumes the landscape in warm weather; and the historical use of the waxy berries in traditional bayberry candle-making. Dioecious — plant both male and female plants for berry production. Nitrogen-fixing root associations with Frankia bacteria allow the plant to thrive in infertile soils without fertilization.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, deep loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; northern catalpa is one of the most bold and tropical-looking native trees of the central and eastern US — producing enormous, heart-shaped leaves (up to 12 inches long and wide), spectacular large clusters of white, orchid-like flowers with purple and yellow markings in early summer, and uniquely distinctive long, thin, bean-like seed pods ('Indian cigars' or 'catawba worms') up to 20 inches long that dangle from the tree through winter. The seed pods are entirely unique among North American trees. The catawba sphinx moth (Ceratomia catalpae) larva feeds exclusively on catalpa leaves and is so well-known as live fishing bait ('catalpa worms') that catalpa groves were historically planted near southern fishing ponds specifically to culture the caterpillars. The wood is exceptionally rot-resistant and was widely used for fence posts and railroad ties. A dramatic, fast-growing shade tree for large, open landscape areas.

Northern Prickly Ash is a native spiny shrub of open woods, thickets, and stream banks across eastern North America from Quebec south to the Gulf states, bearing paired spines at the branch nodes and aromatic compound leaves that release a sharp citrus fragrance when crushed. A member of the citrus family (Rutaceae) and close relative of the southern Hercules' Club, the aromatic bark contains numbing, anesthetic compounds that were applied by many Native American peoples — including the Ojibwe, Chippewa, and Cherokee — directly to sore gums for toothache relief; the bark was also used as a fish poison and to treat digestive ailments, earning the plant the folk name toothache tree. An important host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly in the northern portion of its range, where it often replaces the closely related Zanthoxylum clava-herculis as the primary larval host plant, Northern Prickly Ash provides dense, spiny nesting cover for birds. Plant in moist to moderately well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it spreads by root suckers to form thickets and is most useful in naturalized hedgerows and wildlife habitat plantings.

Set out bare-root or containerized saplings in early spring once the ground has thawed and workable, mulching well to retain moisture around the developing taproot. This fast-growing oak establishes a broad, rounded canopy that turns deep russet-red in autumn and casts dense summer shade over patios and large lawns. Its acorns mature in two seasons and feed deer, turkey, and squirrels, making it a cornerstone wildlife tree for parks and naturalized landscapes. Avoid heavy pruning after establishment since red oaks are more susceptible to oak wilt when wounded during the growing season.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nova Zembla is one of the most cold-hardy red-flowered rhododendron cultivars available, reliable in harsh winter climates. Bold trusses of vivid, true-red flowers with a subtle darker blotch open in late spring above large, dark evergreen leaves on a dense, rounded shrub, a classic old Dutch hybrid still widely grown for its dependable, exceptionally cold-hardy performance where less hardy red rhododendrons fail. Named for a remote Russian Arctic archipelago as an allusion to its extreme cold tolerance, it remains one of the standard red rhododendron choices for northern gardens, valued for its combination of hardiness and bold flower color. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, water during dry spells since shallow-rooted rhododendrons are sensitive to drought, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

common_name: Nuccio's Gems Camellia (Formal Double White Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nuccio's Gems is one of the most celebrated and award-winning Camellia japonica cultivars ever introduced — developed by Nuccio's Nurseries in Altadena, California, and recognized by the American Camellia Society for its exceptionally formal, regular, perfectly arranged double flowers of pure white with a very faint pink blush at times in cool temperatures. The flowers are consistently formal double in form — every petal is precisely arranged in concentric rings with mathematical regularity, with no stamens visible and no disorder of petals regardless of weather conditions. This consistency of form across different temperatures and conditions is the defining quality of Nuccio's Gems and the characteristic most prized by camellia enthusiasts. The blooms are medium-large (3.5–4.5 inches), long-lasting, and borne prolifically over a mid-season period from January through March in zone 9. The upright-growing shrub develops excellent deep-green, lustrous foliage and a clean, compact form reaching 6–10 feet. Like all C. japonica cultivars in zone 9, plant in dappled shade or morning sun with afternoon shade — the flowers burn in full afternoon sun. Mulch heavily, maintain consistent moisture, and feed with acid-forming azalea fertilizer in March and June. The pure white, perfectly formal flowers of Nuccio's Gems are considered among the finest white camellias available to American gardeners.

common_name: Nuccio's Pearl Camellia (Formal Double White-Blushed-Pink Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light. Nuccio's Pearl, from the renowned Nuccio's Nurseries camellia breeding program in California, produces exquisitely formal, tightly overlapping double flowers in soft white delicately blushed with pale pink along the petal edges, a refined color and form prized by camellia show exhibitors and collectors. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars it blooms in winter into early spring on a slow-growing, long-lived evergreen shrub with glossy, dark green foliage that provides year-round structure even when not in flower. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil, and protect from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can damage both the foliage and the delicate flowers.

common_name: Nuttall Oak (Pin Oak, Red River Oak)
notes: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, clay or heavy soil in full sun; Nuttall oak (Q. texana) is one of the most underused and underrated of all large southern oaks — a fast-growing (3–4 feet per year when young), majestic bottomland tree that reaches 60–90 feet with excellent scarlet fall color and one of the most important acorn crops of any oak, producing large (3/4 inch) acorns in abundance that are critical food for wood ducks, waterfowl, deer, squirrels, and turkeys. It is uniquely adapted to seasonally flooded, waterlogged clay soils where most trees cannot survive, making it the premier oak for wet, poorly drained sites, wet parking lot islands, and retention basin margins. Excellent fall color (brilliant scarlet) distinguishes it from most southern red-group oaks. Not to be confused with Q. nuttallii (same species, now synonymized as Q. texana).

Plant in lean, very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nuttall's linanthus is a California and Baja California native subshrub of the chaparral, producing exceptionally fine-textured, needle-like leaves that give the entire plant a distinctive, soft, feathery texture strongly reminiscent of heather or fine pine foliage — creating year-round textural interest before the plant flowers. In spring and early summer it produces small, tubular, five-petaled flowers in white to pale lavender carried in tight clusters at the branch tips, and on a mature, well-established plant, these flower clusters can be produced in sufficient abundance to create an attractive display against the distinctive, very fine, needle-textured foliage. Native to dry, rocky, chaparral habitats of the California Coast Ranges where it grows among other drought-adapted shrubs, it is well adapted to the Mediterranean-climate conditions of California and Gulf Coast gardens. The fine, needle-like foliage texture provides year-round structural interest in the dry garden that few other plants can match. Outstanding combined with other California native shrubs — ceanothus, manzanita, and salvias — in low-water native plant gardens.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Oakland Holly is a vigorous, fast-growing hybrid holly bred for a naturally narrow, upright, oval form that provides dense, formal screening in a noticeably smaller footprint than broader hollies such as Nellie R. Stevens, making it useful for property-line screens and narrow side yards where space is limited. The glossy, dark green, lightly spined evergreen foliage holds its color and density year-round with minimal pruning required to maintain a neat shape, and the plant produces small red berries in fall and winter that provide food for songbirds. It is heat- and humidity-tolerant, adapts well to Gulf Coast clay soils once established, and shows good resistance to the pests and diseases that can trouble other broadleaf evergreens. Established plants are reasonably drought-tolerant, though regular water during the first one to two years speeds establishment. Prune, if needed, in late winter or after the main flush of new spring growth to maintain the desired screen height and width.

Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; Oakleaf croton needs strong light to develop its best red and orange coloring. Deeply lobed leaves with irregular, wavy margins closely resemble an oak leaf in outline, a distinctive leaf shape among crotons that are otherwise typically grown for solid or strap-shaped foliage, colored in a mix of green, gold, orange, and red that intensifies with age and bright light. Its unusual leaf shape adds textural variety to a mixed tropical planting or croton collection where most other selections offer only color variation on similar strap- or oval-shaped leaves. Water when the top inch of soil dries, provide bright light for the fullest color development, and protect from any frost.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; oakleaf hydrangea is the premier four-season native flowering shrub for shade, offering showy white cone-shaped flower panicles in early summer that fade gracefully to dusty pink and tan and persist on the plant, then brilliant orange-red-purple fall foliage, and finally striking cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark on thick, architectural stems all winter. It is native to shaded ravines and woodland slopes in the Southeast. The shrub blooms on old wood — do not prune unless absolutely necessary, and only immediately after bloom. Named cultivars like 'Snow Queen' (large upright blooms), 'Pee Wee' (compact), and 'Ruby Slippers' (pink flowers) are widely available and all perform well in zone 8–9 gardens.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a trellis or hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; obovate hoya stores water in its thick leaves and prefers to dry out somewhat between waterings. Large, rounded, thick, waxy leaves are sometimes lightly speckled with silver and grow closely along vigorous, twining vines that climb or trail readily, eventually producing rounded clusters of small, fragrant, pale pink, star-shaped flowers with deep red-pink centers on mature growth. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it is a fast-growing, easy hoya well suited to a beginner, tolerating average indoor humidity and occasional missed waterings better than some finer-leaved hoya species. Provide a moss pole, trellis, or hanging basket for the twining stems, and avoid moving or pruning off flower spurs (peduncles), since the same spur reblooms repeatedly over the years.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Obsession is a distinctive compact nandina cultivar selected for its exceptionally vivid and sustained red winter foliage color — the leaves turn deep fire-engine red in fall and winter, holding this brilliant color for months, creating one of the most eye-catching winter shrubs in the Gulf South landscape. Unlike Firepower nandina (which turns bright orange-red in full sun and greenish in shade), Obsession maintains its rich red color even in partial shade positions, expanding its landscape use to partially shaded areas where Firepower often reverts to less colorful foliage. Obsession additionally produces clusters of red berries — a quality that Firepower lacks — providing bird food and additional ornamental interest through winter. The compact, upright-mounding habit stays 2–3 feet tall and wide with minimal pruning. Like all nandinas, Obsession is remarkably tough — tolerating clay, drought, heat, humidity, and partial shade that challenge many other ornamental shrubs. Note: Nandina domestica and its berries are toxic to birds and the plant is considered invasive in some Gulf South natural areas (particularly the Southeast) — plant in contained landscape settings rather than adjacent to natural areas, and deadhead flowers if self-seeding becomes a concern.

Plant container stock in fall as Pacific Northwest rains return, into well-drained soil that ranges from dry to moist, in partial shade to full sun near the coast. Oceanspray is a fast-growing, arching native shrub of forest edges and clearings from British Columbia to California, producing long, cascading plumes of tiny cream-white flowers in early summer that cover the shrub in a foam-like display visible from a distance. The abundant bloom is a magnet for native bees, butterflies, and beneficial wasps, and the dense thickets it forms provide excellent cover and nesting habitat for songbirds. It tolerates a wide range of soils and light conditions once established, making it a versatile hedgerow or restoration planting for Pacific Northwest gardens.

Oconee Azalea is a spectacular native deciduous azalea of dry to mesic upland oak-hickory and pine-oak woods of Georgia and South Carolina, producing some of the most vivid orange, red, and scarlet floral displays of any native North American shrub when it blooms in March and April — before or with the emerging leaves — providing a burst of intense color unlike any other native plant in the early spring landscape. The flowers are not fragrant but are intensely colored in shades of flame orange to deep scarlet, and the plant's natural occurrence is restricted to a relatively small area of the inner coastal plain and piedmont of the Carolinas, making it a regionally rare and culturally significant plant of considerable interest to azalea enthusiasts. A moderate-growing shrub that develops a naturally graceful, open, rounded form, Oconee Azalea provides superior wildlife value to most exotic azalea cultivars and supports native bumblebee queens emerging in early spring. Plant in well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to high, shifting shade; Oconee Azalea will not tolerate wet feet or alkaline soils.

Plant bare-root canes or container-grown stock in spring in extremely well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; ocotillo transplants most reliably as leafless bare-root canes set at the same depth they grew previously and watered in well, then left largely undisturbed. A cluster of tall, thorny, whip-like canes radiates upward from a woody base, remaining bare and gray for most of the year but flushing bright green with small leaves within days of a rain and shedding them again as the soil dries, an unusual drought-response cycle that can repeat several times a year. In late spring, bright orange-red, tubular flower clusters top each cane, providing an important early-season nectar source for hummingbirds migrating through the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Desert region it calls home. It needs essentially no supplemental water once established beyond natural rainfall, and its distinctive, gaunt, spiny silhouette makes it one of the most recognizable and dramatic accent plants for a desert xeriscape.

common_name: October Glory Maple (Late Red Fall-Color Red Maple)
notes: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun, and water deeply and regularly through the first two to three seasons to establish a strong root system before the tree can tolerate occasional dry spells. October Glory is one of the most widely planted red maple cultivars, prized for its dependable, brilliant red-to-scarlet fall color that develops later in the season than most red maple selections, extending fall color displays into late October and November in much of its range. Small red flowers appear on bare branches in late winter, an early sign of spring, followed by summer shade from a dense, rounded to oval canopy. It tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than many shade trees, including occasional wet or poorly drained sites, making it a versatile, fast-growing choice for a lawn specimen or street tree. Prune only to remove dead, damaged, or crossing branches, ideally in late fall or winter to avoid excessive sap bleeding.

common_name: October Glory Red Maple (Late-Season Brilliant Red Fall Color Maple)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. October Glory is one of the most widely planted red maple cultivars for its dependable, long-lasting, brilliant red fall color that develops later in the season than most maples, extending the fall color display after earlier-turning trees have already gone bare. It grows at a moderate-to-fast rate into a dense, rounded shade tree and tolerates a wider range of soil conditions, including occasional wet sites, than many other shade trees, making it a versatile choice for yards, streets, and parks. Like other red maples it has relatively shallow, fibrous roots that can compete with grass and nearby plantings, so avoid heavy underplanting close to the trunk and keep it well watered during establishment and drought.

Plant in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained to occasionally flooded soil in full sun to part shade; Myrica inodora tolerates prolonged wet, acidic, poorly drained conditions that challenge most ornamental shrubs, making it excellent for wet spots, pond margins, and rain gardens. Myrica inodora (odorless bayberry) is a seldom-cultivated native shrub of the Gulf Coastal Plain from Alabama to Florida and Louisiana, distinct from the common Southern wax myrtle (Morella cerifera) in its larger, glossier, darker-green, distinctly odorless leaves (as the name implies — wax myrtle leaves are distinctively aromatic when crushed; Myrica inodora leaves are not). It grows as a large evergreen shrub or small tree with an upright, irregular form, producing small, white, clustered flowers in spring and blue-gray, waxy berries in fall and winter that are consumed by Yellow-rumped Warblers and other berry-eating birds. It is less commonly available in native plant nurseries than M. cerifera but is superior for wet, acidic sites in the Gulf South, where it grows with greater vigor than most other native shrubs.

Ogeechee Tupelo is a native swamp tree of the coastal plain river bottomlands and freshwater swamps of Georgia and northern Florida, most abundant along the Ogeechee, Altamaha, and Suwannee rivers, where it grows in soils that are seasonally to permanently flooded. The large, oblong red drupes — sometimes called Ogeechee limes — are intensely sour and were historically used by Native Americans and early settlers as a substitute for lime in cooking and preserves; they remain a prized wild foraged ingredient in the modern era. The fragrant white flowers are the renowned source of prized tupelo honey, a light-colored, mild-flavored honey with unique fructose chemistry that resists crystallization and commands premium prices at market. Plant in permanently wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this species is intolerant of drought or alkaline conditions and grows best where roots reach permanent water.

Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy or alluvial soil in partial shade to full sun; Oglethorpe oak is one of the rarest native oaks in North America, known from only a handful of scattered populations in bottomland and ravine forests of northern Georgia and adjacent South Carolina — the total wild population numbers only a few thousand trees. Taxonomically unusual within oaks, it produces very small, rounded acorns on distinctively long stalks, and the leaves are large, dark green, and deeply lobulate with rounded tips. The species was not scientifically described until 1940, found in a ravine near Oglethorpe County, Georgia. Despite its extreme rarity in the wild, it grows vigorously in cultivation and has proven adaptable to a wider range of conditions than its limited natural distribution suggests. A conservation-worthy ornamental that horticultural planting can help save from extinction. Fast-growing and handsome, with good fall color and excellent form.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Ogon spiraea holds its bright gold foliage color best in full sun and greens up somewhat in shade. Fine, narrow, willow-like leaves emerge bright golden-yellow in spring and hold good color through summer before turning shades of orange and copper in fall, providing season-long foliage interest on a graceful, arching shrub that is also covered in small white flowers along bare branches in very early spring, ahead of the emerging gold foliage. Its combination of early spring bloom and vivid, long-lasting golden foliage makes it a valuable multi-season color accent for a mixed shrub border, standing out clearly against green-leaved companions from spring through fall. Prune lightly after flowering to shape, and provide full sun for the brightest, most sustained gold foliage color through the growing season.

Plant in moist, deep, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ohio buckeye is the state tree of Ohio and a striking native specimen tree with large, palmately compound leaves that emerge very early in spring and put on a vivid orange-red fall color display — often the first tree to color and drop leaves in autumn. Upright panicles of yellow-green flowers appear in April and May, attracting early-emerging pollinators, and ripen into the distinctive spiny husks that split to reveal the rich brown nuts that give the tree its name. All parts of the plant — bark, leaves, and especially the nuts — are toxic to humans, livestock, and dogs and should not be planted where children or grazing animals have access. Provide consistent moisture, especially during establishment, as it is poorly adapted to drought and will drop leaves early under heat stress.

common_name: Okame Flowering Cherry (Early Bright-Pink Heat-Tolerant Cherry)
notes: Okame is a hybrid flowering cherry bred from Taiwan cherry and Fuji cherry, prized for opening its single, vivid carmine-pink flowers earlier in spring than most other ornamental cherries and for tolerating heat and humidity noticeably better than Yoshino or Kwanzan, a real advantage in the Gulf South where many flowering cherries struggle and decline. Its smaller, more upright-vase-shaped habit fits a modest yard, and reddish-orange fall foliage color extends the season of interest beyond the early spring bloom. Give it moist, well-drained soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to limit disease entry through large wounds, and expect a shorter lifespan than longer-lived shade trees, typical of the flowering cherry group.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Oklahoma redbud is a Texas-native botanical variety of eastern redbud that is substantially more heat- and drought-tolerant than the standard eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis), making it the superior choice for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where summer heat and drought stress often cause the standard species to decline. The cultivar 'Oklahoma' was selected for exceptional dark rose-magenta to rosy-purple flower color — deeper and more saturated than the typical light pink-lavender of species redbud — and for glossy, leathery, rich dark-green leaves that are waxy-looking and more heat-resistant than the soft, matte leaves of the standard species. The flower display appears on bare branches in February–March in zone 9 and is spectacular — the vivid magenta-rose flowers cover the branches in dense clusters before the leaves emerge. The glossy-leaved foliage provides excellent summer interest and greater resistance to summer leaf drop than standard eastern redbud. Oklahoma redbud is smaller and more compact than the eastern species, reaching 12–20 feet tall and wide, making it appropriate for smaller residential landscapes. Superior drought tolerance, heat resistance, and adaptability to alkaline and clay soils make Oklahoma redbud one of the finest ornamental trees for zone 9.

common_name: Old Blush Rose (Parson's Pink China, One of the Oldest Cultivated Roses)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Old Blush is one of the four founding China roses brought to Europe in the late 1700s and is historically significant as one of the first roses to introduce genuine repeat bloom to Western rose breeding, which until then relied on once-blooming European roses. It produces semi-double, silvery-pink flowers that deepen in color with age and heat, blooming in flushes nearly continuously through the growing season, and remains a tough, easygoing garden rose with excellent heat tolerance and good resistance to black spot. Grown for over two centuries across the Gulf South, it needs little more than an occasional shaping prune and is a good choice for gardeners who want an authentic heirloom with real historical rose-breeding significance.

WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — site it away from areas where livestock, pets, or small children graze on foliage, and never burn the trimmings, since the smoke carries toxic compounds. Root cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; oleander shrugs off heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil, which is why it lines highway medians and beachfront properties across the Gulf Coast and Southern California. Clusters of single or double flowers in white, pink, red, salmon, or yellow appear almost continuously from late spring through fall on new wood, so prune lightly right after a bloom flush rather than in late winter. Cold snaps below the high teens can kill it to the ground in zone 8, but established plants typically resprout vigorously from the root crown.

common_name: Olivia Rose Austin (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Set plants in full sun with at least six hours of direct light and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply and regularly during the first year to establish a strong root system. Prune back by about a third in late winter and deadhead through the season to keep flushes of bloom coming. Olivia Rose Austin was bred by David Austin and named for his granddaughter, and it has become one of the most widely planted English roses for combining soft, cupped, blush-pink double blooms with a fruity fragrance and notably strong disease resistance compared to many older English rose cultivars, holding clean foliage through humid summers better than most. Its compact, bushy, well-branched habit makes it useful for smaller borders and mixed plantings where a full-sized shrub rose would be too large, and it repeats reliably from late spring through frost with regular deadheading.

common_name: Olympic Fire Mountain Laurel (Red-Budded Mountain Laurel)
notes: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Olympic Fire is a mountain laurel selection prized for exceptionally deep, wine-red buds that open to lighter pink flowers, giving a stronger two-tone contrast than the species' typical pink-and-white banding. It shares the species' gnarled, sculptural habit and evergreen foliage, making it a strong specimen or woodland-border shrub. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Orange Clock Vine (Brilliant Pure-Orange Continuous-Blooming Tropical Vine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Orange Clock Vine (Thunbergia gregorii) is an African climbing vine producing one of the most brilliantly pure-orange flower displays available in a commonly grown ornamental vine — the 1.5-inch, five-petaled, open-faced flowers are a vivid, saturated orange-to-apricot-orange with no dark center (the 'clock' of the common name refers to the open flower face), blooming in continuous succession from summer through frost. The pure, clean orange color without dark center markings or contrasting color zones creates a uniformly vivid orange effect that is quite different from Black-eyed Susan Vine (T. alata), which has a dark eye, or clock vines with throats of different colors. The fast-growing, twining stems cover trellises, fences, and arbors quickly — an established plant can produce a solid curtain of orange flowers across a 6–8 foot fence section. In zone 9, Orange Clock Vine grows as a warm-season perennial vine that may be killed by hard freezes but returns from the roots in protected positions with mulching; in zone 10-12, it grows as an evergreen perennial vine that blooms most of the year. The pure orange color makes it outstanding in tropical designs combining orange, yellow, and red — particularly effective with yellow allamanda, red mandevilla, and golden angel's trumpet for a warm tropical palette.

common_name: Orange Jessamine (Mock Orange, Chalcas, China Box)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Orange Jessamine is one of the most intensely fragrant shrubs available for zone 9 Gulf Coast and Florida gardens, producing multiple flushes of tiny, pure-white, star-shaped flowers throughout the warm months — the fragrance has been described as a combination of orange blossom and jasmine and is one of the strongest and most intoxicating scents in the subtropical plant world. Murraya paniculata is closely related to citrus (family Rutaceae) and is native from South Asia through southern China and into Malaysia; it has been naturalized in South Florida where it occasionally escapes into natural areas. The glossy, dark-green, aromatic foliage is attractive year-round; after the white flowers fade, small oval berries ripen from green to orange-red, adding additional ornamental interest. In zone 9, Orange Jessamine is an excellent fragrant hedge, privacy screen, or specimen shrub reaching 8–15 feet; it can also be maintained as a small tree with lower branch removal. It tolerates light shade well and performs admirably as a foundation shrub under building overhangs or in bright indirect light. Prune immediately after flowering to control size; the plant flowers on new wood. NOTE: Murraya paniculata is a host plant for citrus greening disease (Huanglongbing) and its import is restricted in some states — check local regulations before purchasing.

common_name: Orange King Bougainvillea (Warm Copper-Orange Bougainvillea Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Orange King is a bougainvillea cultivar producing bracts in warm copper-orange to apricot-orange tones — a distinctly different color character from the hot pinks and magentas of Barbara Karst or the scarlet-red of San Diego Red, offering instead a warmer, earthier color tone that reads more tropical and less vivid in the landscape. The orange-copper bracts combine particularly well with terracotta container materials, yellow walls, and companion plants in warm orange, yellow, and bronze tones. Orange King blooms in the same seasonal pattern as other bougainvillea cultivars in zone 9 — most heavily in spring and fall as temperatures moderate, with reduced bloom during peak summer heat and winter cold. The bract color in Orange King tends to fade to salmon-pink and peachy tones as the bracts age on the plant, creating a natural color progression from rich copper-orange at peak freshness to faded salmon-apricot as the bloom matures — a pleasing multi-tone effect during extended bloom periods. The growth rate and vigor are typical of bougainvillea: rapid once established in zone 9 conditions, capable of covering substantial wall or fence areas. The copper-orange color has become popular in Spanish Colonial, Mediterranean, and Southwestern landscape styles where the warm tones harmonize with stucco walls and warm architectural palettes.

common_name: Orangeola Japanese Maple (Cascading Orange-Red Lace-Leaf Maple)
notes: Plant in part shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and the harshest afternoon sun. Orangeola produces one of the most colorful seasonal displays among lace-leaf Japanese maples, with finely dissected leaves emerging brilliant orange-red in spring, deepening to bronze-red through summer, and finishing in a fiery orange-scarlet fall display, on a cascading, semi-weeping form that grows somewhat more upright than fully pendulous cultivars like Tamukeyama. Its strong, layered branching and vivid seasonal color changes make it a standout specimen near a patio or entry where it can be viewed up close through the year. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches.

Start seeds in moist potting mix after soaking 24 hours, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; orchid tree is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the subtropical world, producing large, pink-to-magenta 5-petaled flowers that truly resemble orchid blossoms from late winter to spring before or as the distinctive two-lobed (camel's foot-shaped) leaves emerge. Trees grow rapidly and begin flowering in 3–5 years, reaching 20–30 feet at maturity. They are relatively cold-hardy compared to other tropical trees, tolerating brief freezes to 22°F once established. Young trees require frost protection in zone 9 until the trunk reaches 4–5 inches in diameter. Prune after bloom to shape and remove any frost-damaged wood.

Root cuttings in warm conditions and train on a trellis or fence in full sun to part shade; orchid vine (butterfly vine) is a South American twining vine producing clusters of intricate, butter-yellow flowers with fringed, wavy petals that closely resemble small orchid flowers or the wings of a butterfly, giving the plant both its common names. The flowers are followed by samara-style winged fruits that are ornamental in their own right. Stigmaphyllon ciliatum grows rapidly to 10–25 feet and provides attractive coverage for fences, trellises, pergolas, and arbors with its somewhat heart-shaped, textured leaves and near-constant bloom from summer through fall. The unusual flower form makes it immediately recognizable and a conversation piece in the garden. Related S. littorale (Amazon vine) is more salt-tolerant and suitable for coastal Gulf Coast conditions. An excellent and underused tropical vine for zone 9–11 gardens.

Plant in fall in moist bottomland soils along Pacific Northwest streams, seasonal wetlands, or low-lying yards that stay damp through the wet season, since this is the only ash native west of the Rocky Mountains. Its broad, rounded canopy and compound leaves provide strong seasonal shade, turning yellow before dropping in autumn. It tolerates seasonal flooding and heavy clay soils better than most shade trees, making it valuable for riparian buffer and stormwater plantings. As with other native ashes, monitor for emerald ash borer as the pest continues to spread westward.

common_name: Oregon Grape Holly (Tall Oregon Grape, Mountain Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full shade; avoid exposed sites with afternoon sun or harsh winter winds, which cause foliage burn; protect with burlap in zone 5. Mahonia aquifolium is a Pacific Northwest native evergreen shrub with bold, leathery, pinnate leaves composed of 5–9 spiny, holly-like leaflets that are lustrous dark-green in summer and turn attractive bronze-purple to red-purple in fall and winter, especially in sun — a highly ornamental combination with the spring flowers and summer berries. Dense clusters of brilliant-yellow flowers cover the branch tips in March–April before most other spring-flowering shrubs, providing exceptional early-season pollinator value; the flowers are followed by clusters of blue-black, grape-like berries coated in blue-white bloom (powder) that ripen in August and are relished by many birds. The berries are edible (tart, high in vitamin C) and can be used for jelly or syrup; the roots and inner bark yield a yellow dye historically used by Indigenous peoples. The genus Mahonia is now often merged with Berberis by modern taxonomists.

Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oregon white oak (Garry oak) is the only native oak of the Pacific Northwest north of California, forming open oak savannas and woodlands from British Columbia to California. It is a slow-growing, long-lived, massive tree that can live over 500 years, developing deeply furrowed gray bark and massive, gnarled limbs with age. The oak savannas it creates support extraordinary biodiversity — over 200 species of bees use Oregon white oak, and it supports more invertebrate biodiversity per tree than any other northwest native plant. This ecosystem is now highly threatened, with less than 5% of original oak savanna remaining.
