The acorns are sweet and palatable, historically processed by indigenous peoples into acorn meal and flour. A landmark native tree for large-scale restoration planting in the Pacific Northwest.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; oriental cherry (Japanese flowering cherry) is the parent species of dozens of the most famous ornamental cherry cultivars in the world, including the double-flowered 'Kwanzan' (dark pink), 'Shirofugen' (white fading to pink), and 'Ukon' (pale yellow-green). In Japan, cherry blossom viewing (hanami) centered on this species and its cultivars is a centuries-old cultural tradition celebrating the brief but spectacular spring bloom. Most widely planted ornamental cherries in American gardens are cultivars derived from P. serrulata. The double-flowered cultivars produce no fruit (the extra petals replace stamens), limiting wildlife value, but the spectacle of spring bloom — covering the bare branches in clouds of pink or white — makes them among the most celebrated ornamental trees worldwide. Short-lived compared to some other ornamentals (25–30 years).

Plant rooted cuttings in warm soil after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; ornamental sweet potato grows extremely vigorously and may need periodic trimming to keep in bounds. Ipomoea batatas 'Tricolor' (ornamental sweet potato vine) is one of the most widely grown summer ornamental foliage annuals — a vigorous, trailing or mounding, tender perennial vine grown for its spectacular, large (3–5 inch), deeply lobed or heart-shaped leaves in bold foliage colors ranging from chartreuse to lime green ('Margarita'), deep burgundy-purple to nearly black ('Blackie'), and multicolored ('Tricolor' with pink, white, and green variegation). The plants trail vigorously up to 3–8 feet during the summer season and are used as groundcovers, in hanging baskets, and as 'spillers' in container combinations. Unlike edible sweet potatoes, the ornamental varieties have been selected for foliage rather than tuber quality, though the small tubers produced are edible. Ornamental sweet potato vine performs outstandingly in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers and is one of the few colorful trailing plants that maintains vigor through August heat. Note: the leaves and small tubers are mildly toxic to cats and dogs.

common_name: Osage Crape Myrtle (Semi-Dwarf Light Pink Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Osage was one of the earliest U.S. National Arboretum Indian-series crape myrtles, released in 1975, and remains valued for its light, clear pink flowers and especially smooth, glossy cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark, which many gardeners consider among the most attractive of any crape myrtle cultivar for winter interest. Its semi-dwarf, well-branched habit fits smaller landscapes better than some of the larger Indian-series introductions while still showing good resistance to powdery mildew. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ostbo Red is one of the deepest red-budded mountain laurel cultivars and needs the same acidic, well-drained conditions as other mountain laurels. Deep, rich red buds open to reveal cupped, saucer-shaped flowers with a paler pink interior, opening in intricate, crimped, origami-like folds typical of mountain laurel, one of the earliest and darkest-red cultivars bred by pioneering Pacific Northwest hybridizer Endre Ostbo in the mid-twentieth century. Native to the eastern United States, mountain laurel is an important broadleaf evergreen understory shrub, and this early red-flowered selection helped spark the modern wave of mountain laurel breeding for improved bud and flower color that followed in subsequent decades. Provide the same acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and dappled shade the species requires, mulch to keep roots cool, and avoid heavy pruning, since mountain laurel resents hard cutting back.

common_name: Otto Luyken Cherry Laurel (Dwarf English Laurel)
notes: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, and water regularly the first year to establish a dense root system before drier summers. 'Otto Luyken' is a compact, low-mounding selection of cherry laurel with narrower, glossier leaves than the species and abundant upright spikes of small white flowers in mid-spring, followed by small black fruits that birds favor. Its naturally tidy, spreading habit and shade tolerance make it one of the most reliable low hedges and mass foundation plantings for shaded entryways and woodland-edge borders, requiring only occasional shaping rather than regular shearing to stay dense.

Overcup oak is the definitive native tree for chronically wet, flood-prone sites across the Gulf Coastal Plain and Mississippi Alluvial Valley — its name refers to the unusual acorn, where the cup nearly completely encloses the nut, a characteristic unique among North American oaks. Trees are exceptionally flood-tolerant, naturally occurring in swamp forests, seasonally flooded bottomlands, and poorly drained clay flats where other oaks cannot survive periodic inundation, making it the native oak of choice for rain garden margins, detention basins, and low-lying wet areas. Mature trees develop deeply furrowed, blocky gray bark and a broad, spreading crown that provides excellent wildlife value: dozens of species of woodland birds and mammals rely on the mid-sized, nutritious acorns for fall and winter food. Overcup oak grows slowly but lives for centuries — use it as a lasting structural tree in native woodlands, riparian plantings, and large-scale landscape restorations.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Oyama magnolia is an East Asian deciduous magnolia that flowers in late spring to early summer (May–June) — well after frost risk has passed — producing pendant, nodding, cup-shaped, pure-white, intensely lemon-and-vanilla-fragrant flowers with a prominent central boss of deep crimson-red stamens that contrast dramatically with the white petals and give each flower a jewel-like center. The flowers nod downward on their stems and are best viewed from below or on a gentle slope, where their pendant display and scarlet centers are most visible. It is one of the very few magnolias that performs in genuine partial shade, blooms reliably in dappled light, and does not require full sun for good flowering — making it uniquely valuable for shaded woodland gardens where other magnolias would fail to bloom properly. The large, bold, bright-green leaves are themselves attractive. A refined, fragrant, and very different-looking magnolia suited to the naturalistic shade garden rather than the formal sunny border.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; PJM rhododendron is exceptionally cold-hardy and tolerates more sun than most large-leaved rhododendrons. Small, aromatic, dark green leaves turn an attractive plum-purple in cold weather, providing year-round color, and the shrub is smothered in a profusion of small, vivid lavender-pink flowers in very early spring, often the first rhododendron to bloom in a northern garden. Named for breeder Peter J. Mezitt and bred specifically for extreme cold hardiness, it tolerates far colder winters than most large-leaved rhododendron hybrids and adapts to more sun exposure, making it one of the most widely planted and reliable rhododendrons across the colder regions of North America. Mulch to keep roots cool, avoid planting in heavy or poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade along stream banks, pond margins, or in rain gardens; Pacific ninebark is a native riparian shrub of the Pacific Northwest excellent for stabilizing stream banks and moist slopes. Physocarpus capitatus is a large, vigorous, deciduous native shrub of western North American stream banks and moist slopes producing lobed, maple-like leaves, rounded clusters of small, creamy-white flowers in late spring, and ornamental, papery, red-bronze seed capsules in fall and winter; the exfoliating bark (which gives ninebark its name) peels in thin, multi-layered strips to reveal mahogany-colored inner bark, providing attractive winter texture. It is an important wildlife shrub, providing nesting cover, shelter, and browse for deer and elk; the flowers support native bees and butterflies. More vigorous and adapted to wet conditions than the eastern ninebark (P. opulifolius).

Transplant balled or container shrubs in fall into acidic, well-drained forest soil rich in organic matter, keeping the crown at grade and mulching with conifer needles or shredded bark. This is the dominant evergreen shrub layer beneath Douglas fir and redwood forests from British Columbia to California, so it thrives in dense to dappled shade and resents hot, exposed sites with reflected heat. Large trusses of pink to rosy-purple bell-shaped flowers appear in late spring above leathery, dark green leaves, giving structure and winter interest to a shaded native garden long after bloom. It is the state flower of Washington and pairs naturally with sword fern, salal, and huckleberry in a Pacific Northwest woodland planting.

Divide suckers or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda flower (scarlet clerodendrum, tower of gold) is a Southeast Asian tropical shrub that produces one of the most impressive flower structures of any tropical plant — enormous, upright, tiered panicles reaching 18–24 inches in height, composed of hundreds of small, intensely orange-scarlet, tubular flowers arranged in dense whorls that give the flower head the appearance of a brilliantly colored pagoda structure. The large, dark-green, boldly lobed leaves are themselves dramatic, and the entire plant creates a powerful tropical statement in summer and fall borders. It spreads steadily by underground suckers to form colonies, which can be controlled by mowing the perimeter. Hummingbirds and butterflies are strongly attracted to the flower heads. Semi-shade tolerant — performs well in dappled light under high canopy trees. In zone 9 top growth is sometimes killed by frost but resprouts vigorously from the root. 'Starburst' is a popular selection.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; painted buckeye is a native small tree or large shrub of the southeastern US Piedmont and Coastal Plain, naturally growing in the understory of moist woodland slopes and stream banks. It is the most heat-tolerant native buckeye, making it an excellent choice for southern gardens where the more common red buckeye (A. pavia) and Ohio buckeye (A. glabra) can struggle in summer heat. The pale cream to yellow flower clusters in spring attract ruby-throated hummingbirds and large bees. Like all buckeyes, the large, shiny seeds are toxic to humans and livestock, but are an important food source for squirrels which chew through the outer covering to reach the seed. The foliage often develops excellent yellow fall color.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Painted Lady philodendron holds its bright lime and yellow coloring best with strong, consistent indirect light. Glossy, heart-shaped leaves emerge a bright chartreuse-yellow speckled and streaked with darker green flecks, a lively, sunny leaf coloring that brightens a shaded corner far more than the deep greens typical of most climbing philodendrons, with the mottled pattern varying somewhat from leaf to leaf. A vigorous climber, it develops larger, more vividly patterned leaves when trained up a moss pole rather than left to trail, and its bright color makes an eye-catching contrast against darker-leaved houseplant companions. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the vivid yellow-green coloring, keep humidity moderate to high, and water when the top inch of potting mix has dried.

Plant at the base of a fence, trellis, or shrub where the roots can be shaded; shade the root zone with a stone or low groundcover while allowing the vine to climb into sunlight. Clematis versicolor (pale leatherflower) is a rare and seldom-cultivated native vine of the Ozarks and Interior Highlands of Missouri, Arkansas, and adjacent states, found on rocky, limestone-derived glades and open cedar-hardwood barrens in thin, alkaline soil; its urn-shaped or pendent, pale lavender to greenish-purple flowers (about 1 inch long) appear in midsummer after most other clematis have finished blooming, followed by large, globe-shaped, feathery seed heads that are attractive in fall. One of the leatherflower clematis group (Viorna section), sharing the nodding, urn-shaped flower form with C. crispa and C. pitcheri. Exceptionally drought-tolerant once established; grows naturally in dry, thin soils over rocky limestone and does not want summer irrigation. An outstanding rare native vine for dry, partially shaded garden settings.

common_name: Palibin Dwarf Korean Lilac (Compact Long-Lived Fragrant Dwarf Lilac)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, near-neutral soil, and prune only lightly right after bloom to remove spent flower heads, since Palibin naturally keeps a dense, rounded, proportionate form without regular shearing. This dwarf Korean lilac is smothered each spring in masses of small, intensely fragrant pale lavender-pink flower panicles that are proportionate to its compact size, unlike many lilacs where large blooms overwhelm a small shrub. Its naturally tidy habit, fine-textured blue-green foliage, and good resistance to powdery mildew have made it one of the most widely planted dwarf lilacs for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and low informal hedges. Like other lilacs it needs real winter chill to flower reliably and performs best at the cooler end of its hardiness range, but established plants are tough, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free.

common_name: Pam Puryear Turk's Cap (Pink-Flowered Native Turk's Cap)
notes: Plant in a bed with morning sun and afternoon shade, or in dappled light beneath trees, and water regularly the first season until the woody base is established. Discovered and popularized by Texas plantswoman Pam Puryear, this selection of the native Turk's cap bears the same twisted pink-red hibiscus-like blooms as the species but in a softer pink shade, opening continuously from late spring through fall. Hummingbirds visit the flowers constantly and songbirds eat the small apple-flavored fruits that follow, making it a dependable wildlife shrub for shady Gulf Coast gardens. It dies back in hard winters but resprouts reliably from the roots each spring.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Panama rose is a Cuban and Central American tropical evergreen shrub in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that produces rounded clusters of small, tubular, brilliant coral-orange to red-orange, five-lobed, fragrant flowers with a yellow eye, borne in profusion at the shoot tips from late spring through fall and intermittently at other seasons — the vivid coral-orange color and sweet fragrance combine to create an attractive and useful shade-tolerant flowering shrub for zone 9–11 gardens. The glossy, dark-green, oval, wrinkled leaves create an attractive foliage backdrop for the bright flowers. Panama rose is shade-tolerant for a tropical flowering shrub and performs acceptably in partial-shade conditions where most comparable orange-flowered shrubs would fail to bloom. It requires acidic soil and is sensitive to alkalinity. In zone 9 it is often damaged or killed by hard freezes but may regrow from established roots. An underused but excellent shade-tolerant flowering shrub for the Gulf Coast.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — panicle hydrangea is the most heat, sun, and cold tolerant of all hydrangeas, thriving from zone 3 to zone 9 in conditions that would stress or kill bigleaf hydrangeas. It blooms on new wood (unlike bigleaf hydrangeas that bloom on old wood), making it immune to late-frost damage to buds — simply prune hard in late winter and it will bloom reliably every year. The enormous, cone-shaped flower panicles (12–18 inches long) open white or cream in July–August and age to pink and then burgundy-parchment in fall, remaining attractive through winter. Modern cultivars like 'Limelight' (with chartreuse-green flowers), 'Little Lime' (dwarf), 'Quick Fire' (earliest to bloom), and 'Pinky Winky' (deep pink) greatly expand the ornamental range of the species. Flower color cannot be changed by soil pH, unlike bigleaf hydrangeas.

Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in early spring, ideally clustered in groups of three or more where the strikingly white, papery, exfoliating bark can be admired year-round against evergreens or dark backdrops. This fast-growing, relatively short-lived pioneer tree tolerates cold climates exceptionally well but struggles in prolonged heat and drought, so it performs best in northern gardens rather than the warmer end of its range. Its golden fall color and open canopy make it a favorite specimen for naturalized woodland edges, and the bark historically provided material for canoes and baskets. Keep roots consistently moist and mulched, since paper birch is prone to bronze birch borer when stressed by heat or drought.

Outside of Florida, plant Paperbark in full sun in moist to wet soils where its tolerance of flooding, salt spray, and periodic drought makes it an exceptional landscape tree for difficult sites. The distinctive spongy, white papery bark peels in thick layers year-round and is one of the most visually striking bark textures available in subtropical horticulture. Creamy white bottlebrush-like flower spikes appear multiple times per year and attract nectar-feeding birds and insects. This species is federally listed as invasive in Florida and must not be planted there; gardeners in other Gulf Coast and Pacific Coast subtropical regions should confirm local regulations before planting.

Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; paperbark maple is widely considered to have the finest bark of any temperate deciduous tree — the rich cinnamon-orange to mahogany-red outer bark peels in papery, tissue-thin curling sheets year-round, revealing layers beneath in a constantly changing mosaic that glows in winter sunlight. The trifoliate leaves turn blazing red-orange in fall, making it a multi-season treasure. It grows slowly to 20–30 feet over 30–40 years, making it appropriate for smaller residential landscapes. Originally from central China, it has been widely planted in the United States since the early 1900s and is reliable in zones 4–8. The combination of exceptional bark, good fall color, and small stature makes it arguably the single best ornamental tree for the four-season garden where space is limited.

Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; paperbush sets its silvery, silky flower buds in fall and holds them ornamentally through winter before opening in late winter, so avoid pruning after midsummer or next year's display will be lost. Edgeworthia chrysantha is a striking Asian shrub with a distinctive tiered, architectural branching structure and large, soft, blue-green leaves, producing rounded clusters of intensely fragrant, tubular, golden-yellow flowers that open from silvery, fur-covered buds in late winter to earliest spring before the leaves emerge. Its combination of bold winter structure, ornamental buds held through the cold months, and richly fragrant late-winter bloom makes it a premier specimen shrub for a shaded winter garden, best sited near a path or entrance where its fragrance can be appreciated. The bark has traditionally been used to make high-quality paper in Japan and China, giving the plant its common name, and it prefers a sheltered site out of harsh winter wind at the colder edge of its hardiness range.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty potting mix; parachute plant stores water in its succulent stems and tubers and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thin, wiry, trailing succulent stems bear pairs of small heart-shaped leaves and unusual, pale green flowers shaped like a tiny umbrella or parachute, complete with a fringe of fine hairs around the rim that trap small fly pollinators temporarily inside the flower before releasing them dusted in pollen. Native to South Africa, it grows from a small underground tuber that stores water and energy through dry periods, and its slender trailing stems make it a good candidate for a small hanging basket where its odd, whimsical flowers can be seen up close. Water only when the potting mix is fully dry, provide bright indirect light, and avoid overpotting this slow-growing tuberous vine.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; parsley hawthorn is the most delicate and ornamental of the southeastern hawthorns, distinguished by its exquisitely cut, deeply lobed leaves that truly resemble flat-leaf parsley — giving it an unusually fine, lacy texture among native trees. White flower clusters in spring are followed by small red berries in fall that provide wildlife food. It grows naturally as an understory tree in moist bottomland forests and shaded river banks throughout the Southeast and tolerates shade better than most hawthorn species. The gray-brown bark flakes to reveal attractive smooth orange-tan underbark. An underused native tree that deserves much wider garden use for its ornamental leaf texture and wildlife value.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly the first season and reducing frequency once the compact root system is established. Prune back by roughly a third in late winter to keep the mounded habit dense and encourage abundant new flowering shoots. Double, peach-to-coral blooms that fade to soft pink open in large clusters over low, spreading mounds of small glossy foliage, part of the Drift series developed by crossing groundcover and miniature roses. Its diminutive size and long bloom season from late spring to frost make it well suited to container plantings, rock gardens, and small-space borders.

Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial sun; pearl bush thrives in most average garden soils and tolerates clay provided drainage is adequate, but performs best with moderate supplemental irrigation during dry spells in its first two years. Exochorda racemosa is a multi-stemmed, arching Chinese ornamental shrub celebrated for its spectacular spring bloom: in April and May the entire plant becomes blanketed in pure white, five-petaled flowers borne in long racemes, rivaling any flowering shrub in the garden. Prune immediately after flowering if needed to maintain shape, as flower buds are set on the previous season's wood; removing up to one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each year keeps the plant vigorous and open.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; pearl bush is an underappreciated Asian flowering shrub producing, in mid-spring, an extraordinary display of pure-white flowers in rounded clusters that cover the plant so densely the individual flowers resemble a cascade of lustrous white pearls — a display that rivals the visual impact of the best spring flowering shrubs. The flowers are 5-petaled, circular, and exquisitely symmetrical, giving the plant its common name. Unlike many early-spring shrubs, pearl bush has a refined and elegant quality rather than blowsy exuberance. The cultivar 'The Bride' is a compact, densely flowering form that spreads wider than tall (3–4 feet tall, 4–6 feet wide) and has become the preferred selection for small modern gardens. It is long-lived and low-maintenance, requiring only light pruning immediately after flowering and an appropriate site that does not become waterlogged. An excellent alternative to spireas and deutzias for the spring border.

common_name: Pecos Crape Myrtle (Compact Pink Mildew-Resistant Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pecos is one of the more compact selections from the U.S. National Arboretum's mildew-resistant Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei breeding program, staying small enough for foundation plantings, smaller landscapes, and large containers where full-size crape myrtles would quickly outgrow the space. It produces abundant clear-pink flower clusters through summer on a dense, well-branched dwarf-to-medium shrub, along with the strong powdery mildew resistance characteristic of the fauriei-hybrid crape myrtles. Its small mature size means it needs little to no size-control pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter — never top or hard-prune crape myrtles, since this ruins the naturally graceful branching form. A dependable, low-maintenance choice for a smaller garden that still wants the long summer bloom crape myrtles are known for.

common_name: Pee Wee Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dwarf Oakleaf Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pee Wee is a compact dwarf selection of the native oakleaf hydrangea that stays only 2.5–4 feet tall and wide — dramatically smaller than the standard species that can reach 6–8 feet or more — making it appropriate for foundation plantings, smaller shade gardens, and situations where the full-size species would be overwhelming. Despite the smaller size, Pee Wee provides all the ornamental attributes that make oakleaf hydrangea outstanding: conical white flower clusters in late spring that age through pink to papery tan; deeply lobed, large, textured foliage that turns rich burgundy-red in fall in zone 9; and attractive exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark that provides winter interest. The flowers are proportionally smaller than the species but still conspicuous and attractive. Pee Wee is one of the few native shade shrubs that truly provides four-season interest in the Gulf Coast garden. Like all oakleaf hydrangeas, it blooms on old wood — never prune in fall or winter, trim only immediately after the main bloom period if shaping is needed. Pee Wee is outstanding for shaded rain gardens and areas with seasonal moisture variation.

common_name: Peggy Clarke Japanese Apricot (Double Deep-Pink Flowering Mume)
growth_habit: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree
notes: Peggy Clarke is a Japanese apricot selection grown almost entirely for its ornamental winter flowers rather than for fruit, bearing fully double, deep rose-pink blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on bare branches in the coldest part of winter, often January into February, when almost nothing else in the garden is flowering. Like the species it forms a graceful, small-to-medium, vase-shaped tree, and while it does set the small, sour, apricot-like fruit typical of Prunus mume, ornamental cultivars like Peggy Clarke are grown chiefly for the flower display rather than for a culinary crop. Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and prune to an open vase shape right after flowering to maintain form and encourage strong bloom the following winter.

Plant this vigorous climber from a potted or bare-root plant in spring, setting it in full sun with rich, well-drained soil at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence. It offers a cascading display of soft pink blooms and is renowned for thriving in tough conditions with minimal care, even shrugging off common rose troubles. Train the long canes horizontally to maximize flowering and water deeply while establishing. A fast grower that rewards patience with abundant bloom.

common_name: Penny Mac Hydrangea (Reliable Reblooming Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Penny Mac was an early and long-proven rebloomer among mophead hydrangeas, flowering on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year, which means a late spring frost that kills the old flower buds does not prevent a good summer bloom as it would on older mophead cultivars. Flower color shifts with soil pH the way most macrophylla hydrangeas do, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments if a particular color is desired. Keep soil consistently moist, since hydrangea's large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun along fences, trellises, and at woodland edges; peppervine is a native southeastern vine distinguished from grapes and other ampelopsis by its twice-compound leaves — the leaflets are themselves divided, giving the foliage a lacy, highly decorative texture quite unlike any other native vine. The small berries pass through shades of green, lavender, white, and finally dark purple-black as they ripen in fall — a stunning polychrome effect on the same cluster that makes this plant highly ornamental. The berries are important food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other fruit-eating birds in fall and winter. The plant tolerates partial shade better than most fruiting vines and is an excellent choice for naturalized areas in the woodland garden or at the edge of a forest.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Percy Wiseman is a compact yakushimanum-type hybrid well suited to smaller gardens than many larger rhododendron cultivars. Flowers open a soft peachy-cream fading to pale primrose-yellow with a hint of pink at the edges, a subtle, changeable color combination typical of the finest yakushimanum-heritage hybrids, on a compact, dense, mounding shrub with attractive, felted new growth. Its manageable mature size, exceptional flower quality, and the sturdy constitution inherited from its Rhododendron yakushimanum parentage have made it a multi-award-winning cultivar and a favorite for smaller gardens where full-sized rhododendrons would be too large. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid hot afternoon sun in warmer zones, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun in the warmest microclimates of zone 10–12; peregrina is a Cuban native with strikingly red star-shaped flowers borne in clusters nearly year-round, making it one of the most continuously blooming ornamentals in tropical and subtropical landscapes. Plants attract butterflies and hummingbirds avidly. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — the seeds in particular are very poisonous and should not be accessible to children or pets. Drought-tolerant once established. In zone 9 container culture, bring indoors to a bright location before frost.

Nick seeds and sow in early spring at the base of a trellis, fence, or shrub; perennial sweet pea is a vigorous, deep-rooted climbing perennial that produces small clusters of magenta-pink, rose, or white flowers from June through August — different in color and somewhat smaller than the annual sweet pea but with the same climbing, clasping, and twining habit. It climbs by tendrils to 6–10 feet and tolerates poor, dry soils and heat far better than the annual sweet pea, making it an easy-care perennial vine for difficult spots. Unlike the annual, it has no fragrance, a tradeoff for its tough perennial character. It self-sows readily and can naturalize on disturbed soil and roadsides. The 'White Pearl' and 'Red Pearl' selections provide specific flower color control. All parts of the plant are mildly toxic if consumed in large quantities.

common_name: Perfecto Mundo Hot Pink Azalea (Reblooming Sun-Tolerant Compact Azalea)
notes: Perfecto Mundo Hot Pink is a compact, reblooming azalea bred as a Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction with an emphasis on strong sun tolerance and dense, well-branched growth, producing vivid hot-pink flowers in flushes from spring through fall rather than the single spring bloom of traditional azaleas. Its compact size and tidy, mounded habit suit foundation plantings and mixed containers, and it needs minimal pruning to hold shape through the season. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving it more direct sun than older azalea types tolerate, and water deeply during dry spells to sustain the extended bloom cycle; light pruning right after the heaviest spring flush avoids removing developing buds for later color.

common_name: Perfecto Mundo White Azalea (Reblooming Sun-Tolerant Compact White Azalea)
notes: Perfecto Mundo White is a compact, reblooming azalea bred as a Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction, producing clean white flowers in repeated flushes from spring through fall on a dense, well-branched, sun-tolerant shrub. Its neutral flower color and tidy, mounded habit make it a versatile mixer in foundation plantings and containers alongside other colors, needing minimal pruning to hold shape through the season. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, giving it more direct sun than older azalea types tolerate, and water deeply during dry spells to sustain the extended bloom cycle; light pruning right after the heaviest spring flush avoids removing developing buds for later color.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Perle d'Or needs little beyond an occasional deep watering once it's established. Introduced in France in 1884, Perle d'Or is a classic polyantha rose closely related to the better-known Cecile Brunner, producing abundant clusters of small, high-centered, apricot-to-golden-pink blooms with a spicy-sweet fragrance held above neat, small foliage on a tough, twiggy shrub. It blooms in nearly continuous flushes from spring through frost, tolerates poor soil and Southern heat and humidity with minimal disease trouble, and its small flower size and clustered habit make it an excellent choice for cutting or for a low, informal hedge. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape the shrub and encourage vigorous new growth loaded with flower buds.

common_name: Perle des Jardins Rose (Fragrant Creamy-Yellow Antique Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Perle des Jardins, introduced in France in 1874, bears full, richly fragrant, pale creamy-yellow flowers that were prized historically as a cut flower and greenhouse florist rose before becoming a mainstay of heirloom garden collections. Like other Tea roses it repeats reliably through the growing season and tolerates heat and humidity with far less disease pressure than many modern hybrid teas, needing only a sunny, well-drained spot and occasional light pruning after each bloom flush. Its soft yellow color and strong fragrance make it a distinctive addition to an antique rose collection or mixed border.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Persian ironwood is one of the finest four-season ornamental trees available, native to the Alborz Mountains and Caspian lowlands of northern Iran where it grows as a dominant forest species. In late winter and very early spring (January–March), before any leaves appear, the branches are lit with clusters of tiny, brilliant-red staminate flowers — among the earliest flowers of any woody plant. The leaves that follow are large, wavy-edged, and glossy, producing some of the most spectacular autumn color of any tree in deep shades of scarlet, orange, yellow, and burgundy all simultaneously present on one tree. Through winter, the mottled, exfoliating bark in tones of gray, green, and brown creates a patchwork pattern similar to the London plane tree, giving outstanding year-round bark interest. The wood is among the hardest of all deciduous trees, hence its common name. Increasingly recognized as an outstanding landscape tree that offers something of interest in every season.

Plant in well-drained soil in full to partial shade — Persian ivy is more tolerant of deep shade than English ivy and produces dramatically larger leaves, up to 8–10 inches across, with a bold, tropical quality that makes it stand apart as a groundcover or climbing vine in shaded areas. The dark, leathery, heart-shaped leaves have a glossy surface and a pleasant resinous fragrance when handled. Unlike the widely planted English ivy (H. helix), Persian ivy is far less invasive and rarely escapes into natural areas in North America. The cultivar 'Sulphur Heart' features leaves with bold yellow centers and dark green edges, making it one of the most striking shade groundcovers available; 'Dentata Variegata' has cream-margined leaves. Berries are toxic — do not plant where children or pets may ingest them. Excellent on north-facing slopes and under dense tree canopies.

common_name: Peru Monstera (Karstenianum Monstera, Monstera sp. Peru)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Peru Monstera maintains attractive foliage in moderate indoor light and is more adaptable to typical room conditions than many of the collector Monsteras. Monstera sp. 'Peru' (sometimes called Monstera karstenianum, though this name has uncertain formal botanical status) is a compact climbing aroid from Peru and neighboring South American countries in the Araceae family, sold widely under the name 'Monstera Peru' in the houseplant trade. The leaves are its defining feature: small to medium-sized (typically 4–8 inches), dark green to nearly blue-green, rigidly leathery, and covered with a distinctive topographic texture — the leaf surface is not smooth but deeply embossed with a pattern of raised veins and sunken areas creating a strongly three-dimensional, almost crinkled or hammered-metal appearance. The leaves are glossy and intensely colored, and the rigid, structural texture of each leaf is the quality that makes the plant immediately recognizable among the many Monsteras now popular in cultivation. Unlike M. deliciosa and M. adansonii, Peru Monstera does not develop fenestrations (holes) even in maturity — the ornamental value is entirely in the texture and color of the solid leaf surface. It is generally adaptable to indoor conditions and grows at a moderate pace. All parts are toxic.

common_name: Petra Croton (Classic Multi-Color Bold-Foliage Tropical Shrub)
notes: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Petra is the most widely planted croton (Codiaeum variegatum) cultivar in the United States — the standard by which other crotons are measured, producing large, boldly lobed, leathery leaves with spectacular multi-color variegation in green, yellow, orange, and bright red that develops most intensely in high light. A single leaf may display all four colors simultaneously, with yellow at the midrib transitioning through orange to red at the leaf margins and green background — creating the kind of botanical fireworks impossible to achieve with any other commonly available ornamental. 'Petra' is named for its large, broadly lobed leaf form with relatively uniform multicolor patterning, distinguishing it from more narrowly-leaved or sparsely variegated croton selections. In zone 9, Petra is widely used as a warm-season container plant for patios and entryways, providing dramatic tropical foliage from April through October before being moved indoors to overwinter in a bright window or warm greenhouse. In zone 10-12, Petra grows as an evergreen perennial shrub to 4–6 feet with permanent outdoor planting. The spectacular foliage combines effectively with solid-color tropicals — red ginger, golden canna, purple confederate rose — where the multi-color leaves tie together the surrounding single-color plants.

common_name: Peve Minaret Bald Cypress (Dwarf Narrow-Conical Bald Cypress)
notes: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, though it also tolerates average well-drained garden soil once established. Peve Minaret is a dwarf, densely conical selection of the native bald cypress, growing to a fraction of the height of the species while retaining the same soft, ferny, deciduous foliage that turns rusty orange-brown in fall, making it a rare option for gardeners who want the character of a bald cypress in a small yard, foundation planting, or large container. Like the species it handles both flooded and ordinary soil with equal ease and needs little care once established beyond occasional watering during drought. Its compact, narrow form eliminates the need for the corrective pruning larger bald cypress selections often require near structures or power lines.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate far more direct sun than bigleaf types and are not affected by soil pH the way blue-and-pink mophead hydrangeas are. Phantom produces some of the largest flower panicles of any hydrangea cultivar, often 12–15 inches long, opening creamy white and aging to a soft pinkish blush, on a large, sturdy shrub whose thick stems hold the huge flower heads upright without flopping even after rain. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing that year's flowers, making size management straightforward for such a large-flowered cultivar. Water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads in late winter before new growth begins.

Plant seedlings in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; physic nut is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. All parts of the plant, especially the seeds, are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets. Thick, succulent stems and broad, lobed leaves cover a fast-growing, drought-tolerant shrub long used as a living fence across the tropics for its ease of propagation from simple stem cuttings, more recently studied worldwide as a source of biodiesel from the high oil content of its toxic seeds. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on poor, marginal soils with minimal care, but every part of the plant, particularly the oil-rich seeds, contains toxic compounds that cause severe illness if ingested by people or animals. Grow it as a hedge or specimen shrub in a location away from curious children, pets, or livestock, and handle pruned material with gloves, since the sap can irritate skin.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, avoiding direct sun, which scorches and bleaches the distinctive foliage. Picturata is an eye-catching aucuba cultivar with an unusual variegation pattern reversed from the more common gold-dust type: each glossy, leathery leaf has a bold splash of gold-yellow in the center surrounded by a dark green margin, rather than gold speckles scattered over green. Like other aucubas, it is one of the few broadleaf evergreen shrubs that thrives in deep, dry shade under trees where little else stays attractive, making it valuable for difficult shaded foundation plantings and understory beds. Female plants produce bright red berries in winter if a male aucuba is nearby for pollination; little pruning is needed beyond removing damaged or leggy stems in spring.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in dappled shade to light sun; the Piedmont azalea is among the most beautiful and fragrant of the native deciduous azaleas, naturally found in woodland edges and along streams from Virginia to Florida and Texas. The pale pink to white flowers with long, exserted stamens appear in early spring before or with the new foliage, giving the plant a delicate, open appearance very different from the dense evergreen hybrid azaleas. Unlike most garden azaleas it tolerates zone 9 Gulf Coast summers well. Prune only after flowering, removing no more than one-third of the plant at once; never shear. Amend soil heavily with compost and pine bark before planting.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Piedmont rhododendron is smaller in leaf and stature than catawba or rosebay rhododendron and tolerates more heat, making it a better choice for lowland southeastern gardens. Rhododendron minus is a compact, evergreen southeastern native with small, leathery, dark green leaves and clusters of pink to rose-purple, funnel-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, occurring naturally on dry rocky slopes and bluffs from the Carolinas into the Gulf South. Its smaller stature and greater heat and drought tolerance compared with the large-leaved mountain rhododendrons make it one of the more practical evergreen rhododendrons for lowland southeastern gardens, including well-drained Gulf Coast sites with some afternoon shade. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and avoid heavy, poorly drained clay, which this species tolerates poorly despite otherwise being one of the tougher rhododendron species for the Deep South.

common_name: Pig's Ear Plant (Round-Leaf Navelwort, Cotyledon orbiculata)
notes: Grow in full sun in fast-draining soil, watering deeply but infrequently and allowing the soil to dry between waterings to keep the fleshy stems from rotting. It forms a small, woody-based shrub over time, tolerating coastal wind and salt spray as well as drought. Thick, chalky gray-green paddle-shaped leaves often develop a reddish, crinkled margin in strong sun, giving the plant its pig's-ear common name. Clusters of dangling, tubular orange to red flowers rise on tall stalks above the foliage in summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators.

Plant Duranta erecta in fertile, well-drained, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun to partial shade; prune regularly to control size and shape — it can become a large, arching shrub or small tree without pruning; in zone 9, it dies back to the ground after hard frost but re-emerges in spring. CAUTION: Berries and leaves are toxic — do not plant where young children or pets have unsupervised access; the golden-yellow berries are attractive but cause severe gastroenteritis if ingested. Pigeon Berry is one of the most popular ornamental shrubs in Gulf Coast, tropical, and subtropical gardens for good reason — the cascading clusters of lavender-blue, tubular flowers with a fringed appearance (the 'sky flower') are produced in extraordinary abundance from spring through fall, creating a lavender haze that is irresistible to butterflies (particularly swallowtails, sulphurs, and monarchs) and hummingbirds. Following the flowers, clusters of bright golden-yellow berries persist through winter, providing excellent bird food for mockingbirds, robins, and thrushes — but the berries should not be eaten by people or pets. Several cultivars are available: 'Aurea' with golden-yellow foliage, 'Alba' with white flowers and yellow berries, and 'Golden Edge' with gold-margined leaves. In zone 10–12 it can become a large, sprawling shrub or small tree 15–18 feet tall without regular pruning.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; pincushion hakea is one of the most spectacular Australian shrubs — a large, erect shrub or small tree from southwestern Australia producing in autumn and winter remarkable, spherical, sea-urchin-like flower heads 2–3 inches across: dense, globular clusters of cream-yellow to pale-cream tubular flowers from which project numerous long, curved, crimson to bright-red styles — the combined effect of the cream flower and scarlet projecting styles creating the distinctive 'pincushion' or 'sea urchin' appearance from which the common names are drawn. The contrast of the cream-colored flowers and brilliant red styles is vivid and immediately eye-catching. The leaves are long, narrow, lance-shaped, blue-green to gray-green, providing a fine-textured, somewhat willow-like foliage year-round. Blooming in autumn and winter when few other dramatic flowers are available, it provides an exceptional, long-lasting (the flowers persist on the shrub for weeks) winter display and, in cultivation, proves to be a reliable hummingbird attractor. Like all Proteaceae, it requires excellent drainage, lean soil, and absolutely no phosphorus-based fertilizer.

Plant in gritty, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; pineleaf penstemon is a compact, woody-based, evergreen subshrub from the mountains of the American Southwest and northern Mexico, with narrow, needle-like leaves that persist year-round and give the plant its pine-like texture even when not in bloom. Slender, tubular, brilliant orange-red to scarlet flowers cover the mounding plants from late spring through summer and are outstanding hummingbird forage, reblooming readily if lightly sheared after the first flush. It is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant of all penstemons, thriving in rock gardens, dry borders, and gravel mulch plantings where excess moisture and rich soil would quickly rot it. Shear back lightly in early spring to remove winter-damaged growth and keep the mound dense and compact.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Cloud beautybush flowers most heavily in full sun and tolerates poor soil and drought once established. In late spring the entire arching, fountain-shaped shrub disappears beneath a dense, week-long cloud of small, bell-shaped, soft pink flowers with a yellow throat, a bloom so heavy it can obscure the foliage entirely, followed by bristly, bronze-pink seed capsules that add subtle texture into fall. Selected for its especially profuse, richly colored bloom compared to the species, it is an easy, tough, low-maintenance shrub once established, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil with minimal care, and its peeling, tan-brown bark provides winter interest after the leaves drop. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, removing some of the oldest stems at ground level each year to keep the shrub renewed and full from the base.

common_name: Pink Delight Butterfly Bush (Clear Pink Buddleja)
notes: Pink Delight is a classic, long-grown butterfly bush cultivar carrying long, dense, conical spikes of clear rose-pink flowers on a large, vigorous, arching shrub, one of the most reliable and widely available pink-flowered buddleja selections. The clean pink tone pairs easily with both cool and warm companion colors in a mixed border, and like other butterfly bush cultivars it draws swallowtails, monarchs, and hummingbirds heavily throughout its long summer-into-fall bloom season. In zone 9 it dies back hard over winter and should be cut to about 12 inches from the ground in late winter to encourage vigorous, floriferous new growth for the coming season.

Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, siting it in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Cornus florida f. rubra is the classic pink-flowering form of the native flowering dogwood, its showy pink to rose-pink bracts opening in early spring before the leaves fully emerge, followed by clusters of glossy red fall fruit that draw songbirds and bright red-purple fall foliage. Seedlings grown from this form show a range of pink intensity, so gardeners wanting a guaranteed, consistent shade of pink should choose a named, vegetatively propagated cultivar rather than seed-grown stock. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, since dogwoods are shallow-rooted and stressed by drought; prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Icicle camellia is valued for cold-hardy, reliable winter bloom in cold-tolerant camellia breeding lines. Semi-double to peony-form flowers open a soft, cool pink with a lighter, almost frosted edge to the petals, blooming reliably through the coldest part of winter on a vigorous, upright shrub bred from cold-hardy camellia lines developed to extend the range of camellia cultivation into colder climates than the classic Gulf South and coastal camellia belt. Its combination of improved cold tolerance and dependable winter flower production has made it a popular choice for gardeners at the northern edge of camellia hardiness wanting to grow this classic Southern shrub outside its traditional warm-climate range. Mulch well to protect roots through winter, provide the dappled shade and acidic soil all camellias require, and avoid planting in a site exposed to harsh winter wind.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Pink Jasmine blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9's summer climate, which can actually extend the blooming season. Jasminum polyanthum is a twining, evergreen vine native to the mountains of Yunnan province in southern China and Burma (Myanmar) at 5,000–9,000 foot elevations — a naturally cool-adapted plant that translates beautifully to zone 8–9 winter garden conditions. In late winter (January–March in zone 9), the vine produces clouds of intensely fragrant, star-shaped flowers that open white from deep rose-pink buds — the pink buds contrasting with the pure white open flowers creates a beautiful two-tone effect. The fragrance is intensely sweet and reminiscent of jasmine absolute — one of the most powerfully scented of all cultivated jasmines, detectable from remarkable distances on warm winter afternoons. A well-established vine covering a fence or arbor in full late-winter bloom is one of the most memorable garden sights of the zone 9 winter garden, drawing visitors to investigate the fragrance source. Pink Jasmine is also widely grown as a houseplant and patio container plant, where the fragrance of winter-blooming potted specimens fills indoor spaces. Listed as invasive in some Pacific island and mild coastal California locales where the climate allows year-round seeding.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; prune lightly after flowering flushes to maintain compact shape; CAUTION: All parts are toxic — do not ingest. Kopsia fruticosa (pink kopsia or Singapore rose) is a compact, tropical evergreen shrub in the Apocynaceae (dogbane) family — the same family as frangipani (Plumeria), vinca (Catharanthus), and allamanda — native to the forests and forest edges of Southeast Asia, particularly the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, and Indonesia. The shrub is an extremely popular and widely planted ornamental in Singapore, Malaysia, and tropical Southeast Asia, where it is one of the most recognizable roadside and garden shrubs. The flowers are similar in shape to periwinkle or frangipani flowers: five-petaled, pinwheel-shaped, 1–1.5 inch across, soft pink to rose-pink with a slightly darker center, produced in small clusters at the branch tips nearly continuously throughout the year in a warm, tropical climate. The effect is of a neat, clean, cheerful, softly-colored shrub covered in pastel-pink flowers year-round. The glossy, elliptic, dark-green leaves provide an attractive backdrop. Like most Apocynaceae, kopsia contains alkaloids (kopsingine and related compounds) that make all plant parts toxic if ingested; do not eat any part of the plant. A must-have for tropical gardens seeking reliable, long-blooming, moderate-sized ornamental shrubs.

Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained gritty soil in a cool site with some afternoon shade, mimicking the snowmelt-fed subalpine and alpine meadows of the Cascades, Sierra Nevada, and northern Rockies. Its heather-like needle foliage and nodding, bell-shaped pink flowers in early summer make it a favorite for high-elevation rock gardens and are visited by native bumblebees. It needs consistent moisture through the growing season and cool nights, so it is best suited to mountain or maritime climate gardens rather than hot lowland sites.

common_name: Pink Perfection Camellia (Shell Pink Camellia japonica)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Perfection is a classic, long-cultivated Camellia japonica cultivar — one of the most widely grown and beloved camellias in American Southern horticulture — producing perfectly formed, small to medium, fully double, shell-pink to pale-blush-pink flowers with tightly spiraling petals arranged in a formal decorative pattern of exceptional precision and beauty. The shell-pink color is softer and more refined than the deeper rose-pink of many camellias, with a cool, porcelain quality that has made Pink Perfection a perennial favorite for cut-flower use and formal garden settings. Bloom season in zone 9 runs from mid-season through late season (January through March), making Pink Perfection one of the later-blooming reliable japonica cultivars — an attribute that makes it more likely to miss the worst freeze events in zone 9. The growth habit is upright and moderately vigorous to 5–10 feet tall with dense, glossy dark-green evergreen foliage. Pink Perfection is considered one of the most reliable japonica camellia cultivars for zone 9 performance, with consistent flower production and good disease resistance. Fertilize with azalea-camellia specific acidic fertilizer in spring and fall; maintain 3–4 inches of pine bark mulch over the shallow root zone year-round.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in partial shade; pink porterweed (changeable porterweed, coral porterweed) is a large Central American tropical shrubby herb in the verbena family (Verbenaceae) that produces some of the most continuously attractive, hummingbird-visited, long-season flower display of any soft-wooded tropical perennial — it grows with a large, upright, somewhat sprawling, freely branching habit and produces at the tips of every shoot long, dense, spike-like, candle-like racemes in which the individual small, tubular, rich coral-pink to salmon-pink to deep-rose flowers open progressively from bottom to top of each spike, with each new flower opening daily for weeks. The vivid coral-pink color, continuous production of new spikes, and intense hummingbird and butterfly attraction make it one of the premier wildlife-garden plants for the Gulf South. Unlike the common blue porterweed (S. jamaicensis), which is a spreading groundcover, pink porterweed grows as a large, upright shrub. Killed by frost in zone 9 but regrows readily from established roots or from new transplants in spring.

common_name: Pink Powderpuff (Spectacular Tropical Small Tree with Giant Pink Pompom Flowers)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Powderpuff (Calliandra haematocephala) is one of the most visually spectacular flowering trees available for Gulf South zone 9b–12 gardens — a tropical South American legume tree producing large (3–4 inch diameter), perfect spherical pompoms composed entirely of long, bright pink to deep rose-red stamens, creating a flower display that looks like enormous powder puffs or fireworks suspended from the branches. The flower structure is unique: what appear to be the 'petals' are actually hundreds of long, silk-fine stamens arranged in a perfect sphere, each stamen tipped with a tiny bead of pollen — the combined effect of many stamens creating the full, lush, velvet-textured pompom that makes this plant immediately recognizable and unlike any other commonly grown flowering tree. The dramatic flowers appear in late winter through spring and often again in fall, hanging from branch tips in clusters that can cover the tree completely during peak bloom. In zone 9a, Pink Powderpuff is frost-sensitive and requires protection during hard freezes — many zone 9a gardeners grow it in large containers for easy winter protection, where it blooms abundantly. In zone 9b–12, it is a reliable, fast-growing evergreen tree. Hummingbirds visit the flowers for nectar; the long, silky stamens make it one of the most hummingbird-attractive trees in the tropical garden palette.

common_name: Pink Powderpuff (Surinam Powderpuff, Pink Mimosa Bush)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Pink Powderpuff thrives in the heat, humidity, and seasonal drought of zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, performing even better in zone 9b–11 where frost is rare. Calliandra surinamensis is a multi-stemmed tropical shrub or small tree native to Surinam and Brazil, producing the distinctive Calliandra flower type: spherical to semi-spherical clusters of numerous elongated stamens that collectively form a powder-puff appearance — in this species a beautiful bicolor combination of rose-pink at the outer stamen tips fading to white at the center. The individual flowers are small but borne simultaneously in numerous rounded clusters along the branches, and the overall effect of a plant in full bloom is a profusion of softly glowing pink puffballs distributed throughout the canopy. Flowers appear throughout the warm season in zone 9 and nearly year-round in zone 10-11. The feathery, twice-pinnate foliage is ornamentally attractive even out of bloom, giving the plant a delicate, lacy texture that contrasts beautifully with bold-leaved tropical neighbors. Highly attractive to hummingbirds, which probe the stamen clusters for nectar. Distinguishable from the Red Powderpuff (C. haematocephala) by its pink-and-white rather than solid red flowers and more compact habit.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Pink Silver hoya colors most vividly in bright indirect light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound. Narrow, dusky green leaves are heavily speckled with silvery flecks and flush pink to burgundy along the margins in bright light, growing on vigorous, twining vines that produce rounded clusters of small, dark maroon-pink, fuzzy-centered flowers with a musky, spicy fragrance most noticeable at night. A popular, fast-growing selection of one of the most variable hoya species, it tolerates a wider range of indoor conditions than many finer hoyas and rewards a sunny window with abundant, repeat blooms from the same flowering spurs. Provide a trellis or moss pole for climbing, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flower spurs, which rebloom for years.

Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; pink trumpet tree (formerly Tabebuia rosea, now Handroanthus roseus) is a large tropical deciduous tree native to Central America and northern South America that produces one of the most breathtaking spring flowering displays in the tropical world — in spring (late dry season), before or as the leaves emerge, the entire leafless tree becomes covered in large, funnel-shaped, lavender-pink to pale-purple-pink, trumpet-form flowers borne in dense, rounded clusters at every branch tip, transforming the canopy into a billowing cloud of soft-pink that is visible from great distances. The flowering display lasts 2–4 weeks, with the fallen pink petals carpeting the ground beneath the tree in a second display. The broad, palmate, compound, five-leaflet leaves are attractively tropical during the growing season. Pink trumpet tree is widely planted as a street and park tree throughout Central America, the Caribbean, and South Florida, where it is one of the most dramatic ornamental trees available for tropical zone 10–12 landscapes.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or fence in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; pink trumpet vine is a South African twining vine that produces large clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped flowers with red-striped throats from fall through early winter, filling a bloom gap when most vines have stopped flowering. The pinnate, deep-green glossy leaves are attractive throughout the growing season. The vine grows moderately (10–20 feet), is much less aggressive than Campsis radicans, and is suitable for structures that cannot support heavy, vigorous vines. Drought-tolerant once established. In zone 9 cut back frost-damaged stems in late winter; plants re-sprout reliably from the base.

Direct sow in dry, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pink wild bean is a native twining annual legume of dry, sandy coastal plain habitats from Long Island to Florida and Texas, producing small, rose-pink to pinkish-lavender flowers typical of wild beans followed by narrow seed pods. The seeds are eaten by bobwhite quail and other ground-foraging birds, making it a valuable wildlife plant for naturalistic meadow and coastal garden settings. As a native nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves soil fertility while providing summer flowering interest. The plant twines readily through other vegetation or on a small trellis. In zone 9a, it grows rapidly as a summer annual from seed and self-sows to perpetuate itself in appropriate dry, sandy soils.

common_name: Pink and White Shower Tree / Java Cassia
notes: Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and ample room for the tree's characteristically wide, horizontal branching structure; avoid sites with standing water or heavy clay. Java Cassia blooms most heavily when dry-season stress triggers flowering, so reduce irrigation in late winter before the expected spring bloom flush. The bicolor pink-and-white flowers open in waves across the canopy and are highly attractive to bees and butterflies. Stake young trees for the first one to two seasons to develop a strong central leader before the spreading canopy takes over.

common_name: Pinkie Indian Hawthorn (Classic Compact Pink Indian Hawthorn)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Pinkie is one of the oldest and most widely planted Indian hawthorn cultivars, a garden standard for decades, bearing soft pink flower clusters in spring above dense, glossy, leathery evergreen foliage, followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds. Its low, mounding, compact habit fits foundation plantings and low hedges, and it shares the species' reliable tolerance for salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils, a long-proven performer in coastal Gulf landscapes. Good air circulation between plants helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

Pinkshell Azalea is a beautiful and rare native deciduous azalea endemic to a small area of the Blue Ridge Mountains of North Carolina, where it grows on boggy hillsides, stream banks, and acidic seeps at elevations above 3,000 feet — one of the most restricted native azaleas in the eastern United States, known from fewer than 20 natural populations. The delicate, five-petaled, light to deep pink flowers borne in early spring before leaf emergence have a distinctive butterfly shape lacking the long floral tube typical of most azaleas, making the blooms uniquely recognizable among native azalea enthusiasts and adding exceptional elegance to the spring garden. Among the hardiest of all native azaleas, surviving USDA Zone 4 winters with ease, Pinkshell Azalea is a superb choice for northern gardens seeking a spectacular, native spring-flowering shrub for moist, partially shaded spots. Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation; it requires reliable moisture and high humidity to perform well, especially in warmer zones.

common_name: Pinky Winky Hydrangea (Two-Tone Pink-and-White Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Pinky Winky is a distinctive panicle hydrangea cultivar distinguished by its unusual two-tone flower display — the large, conical (12–16 inch) flower panicles open pure white in midsummer and then progressively change color from the bottom of the panicle upward, with the lower, older florets turning from white to deep pink to rose-red while the upper, younger florets remain white. This creates a striking bicolor effect of white-on-pink within a single flower head that provides weeks of ornamental interest as the color change progresses. The vigorous, upright-arching habit grows more vigorously than Limelight — Pinky Winky can reach 6–8 feet tall with strong, upright stems. Like all Hydrangea paniculata cultivars, Pinky Winky blooms on new wood and can be pruned hard in late winter to stimulate maximum new growth and flower production. It is among the hardiest of all hydrangeas (to zone 3) and tolerates clay soils, full sun (with adequate moisture), and some drought better than French hydrangeas. In zone 9, the pink color develops most intensely in cooler fall temperatures and may be less vivid in very hot summers.

common_name: Pinky Winky Prime Hydrangea (Compact Improved Bicolor Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Pinky Winky Prime carries the same distinctive two-tone flower panicles as the original Pinky Winky, with the lower portion of each panicle turning deep pink while the upper tip stays white, giving each flower head a bicolor effect as the bloom season progresses, on a more compact plant with stronger, more upright stems than the original cultivar. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, and its improved stem strength holds the heavy panicles upright through summer storms better than many older panicle hydrangea cultivars. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells for the fullest, most colorful panicles.

Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun to part shade, watering moderately from fall through spring and withholding water in summer when growth pauses. Aeonium haworthii (pinwheel aeonium) is smaller and more freely branching than the larger tree aeonium, forming a rounded, multi-stemmed shrublet topped with neat 4-to-5-inch rosettes of blue-green, spoon-shaped leaves edged in a fine red-pink line that gives the compact rosette its 'pinwheel' look. It shares the unusual reverse growing season of its genus, actively growing through cool, moist winters and going semi-dormant with reduced leaf turgor in hot, dry summers, when watering should be cut back sharply. This species is the parent of several popular variegated and colored cultivars, including 'Kiwi' and 'Tricolor', and readily branches from cut stems, making it easy to shape or propagate from tip cuttings. It suits rock gardens, mixed succulent containers, and coastal Mediterranean-style plantings in zone 9-11.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; pipevine is a vigorous native climbing vine with enormous heart-shaped leaves that creates a dense, lush shade canopy and unusual curved pipe-shaped brown flowers in late spring that lure and temporarily trap small flies as pollinators. It is the essential host plant for the stunning pipevine swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs exclusively on Aristolochia species — the caterpillars absorb aristolochic acids from the plant, making both larva and adult butterfly toxic to predators. Plant several vines together to provide enough leaf mass for the caterpillars. Train on a sturdy arbor, pergola, or fence; the vine can grow 20–30 feet and covers itself with tropical-looking foliage by midsummer. Cut back hard in late winter to control size.

Plant in dry, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pitch pine is one of the most fire-adapted trees in eastern North America, able to re-sprout from dormant buds in the bark after fire damage — a trait unique among northeastern pines. The New Jersey Pine Barrens, one of the most ecologically important and unusual ecosystems in the eastern US, is dominated by pitch pine, which requires periodic fire to maintain the open, scrubby canopy and prevent succession to other forest types. The tree produces pitch (resin) in extraordinary quantities — historically harvested for naval stores, tar, and turpentine. An extremely tough, gnarled, characterful tree for the driest, most infertile, fire-maintained habitats in the Northeast and Appalachians. Not suitable for zone 9 — limited to zones 4–7.

Pitcher's clematis is a native vine of the south-central United States — Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and adjacent states — producing nodding, pitcher- or urn-shaped flowers of purplish-blue to violet-blue with thick, recurved petal tips from May through August on a twining vine that scrambles through shrubs and fences with a restrained, manageable habit. Its distinctive flowers are adapted to specialist bee pollinators and are particularly visited by native metallic green sweat bees that navigate the closed floral tube; the feathery, silvery seedheads that follow persist into winter as the seed plumes expand and catch the light. As a species adapted to drier, alkaline limestone soils, Pitcher's clematis is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant of all native clematis, performing well in zones 7–9 where summer heat and occasional drought challenge other species in the genus. Cut stems back to 12–18 inches in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and prolific flowering the following season.

Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; plains cottonwood is the subspecies of eastern cottonwood (Populus deltoides) adapted to the semi-arid Great Plains, forming the iconic riparian forest galleries along the Platte, Republican, Arkansas, and other prairie rivers of the central US. In the treeless expanses of the Great Plains, cottonwood groves along rivers are biological oases — the only substantial tree cover across thousands of square miles of grassland. They support nesting red-tailed hawks, great horned owls, heron colonies, orioles, and dozens of other bird species that simply cannot exist without tree canopy in the open prairie. The brilliant yellow fall foliage is a spectacular landmark in an otherwise somber fall landscape. The female trees produce cottony seed release in early summer that can be messy — male plants are preferred in urban settings.

Planer Tree — also called Water Elm — is a small and uncommon native tree of permanently wet swamps, river floodplains, and cypress-tupelo bottomlands of the coastal plain from South Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, where it often grows in the understory beneath bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp cottonwood. The small, rough-textured leaves and warty, inconspicuous drupes superficially resemble those of the closely related elms, but the single nutlet with a distinctly rough, tuberculate surface is the diagnostic feature that separates Planera from Ulmus. Seeds should be collected and planted fresh in moist to wet, acidic soil under light shade, as viability drops quickly; container-grown nursery transplants are the most reliable method for establishing this species in cultivation. Planer Tree is rarely grown in ornamental settings but makes a distinctive small specimen for rain gardens, pond margins, and naturalized floodplain plantings where saturated soils and periodic flooding prevent most woody plants from thriving.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Pleniflora' suckers more vigorously than single-flowered kerria and is best given room to form a naturalized colony or planted where suckers can be mowed or pulled to control spread. This double-flowered kerria selection produces the same bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes as the species but with fully double, pompom-shaped, golden-yellow flowers in mid-spring that resemble small ranunculus blooms and last longer than the single form. It tolerates considerably more shade than most flowering shrubs while still blooming reliably, making it a good choice for a woodland edge, foundation planting, or naturalized shrub border, and its green stems provide subtle winter interest after leaf drop. Prune out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year to keep the colony vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Plum Gorgeous Loropetalum (Compact Deep Plum-Purple Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with at least a few hours of direct sun each day to bring out the deepest foliage color, since plants grown in heavy shade fade toward green. Plum Gorgeous is a compact, mounding loropetalum selected for rich, deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color through summer heat better than many older loropetalum cultivars, paired with bright pink fringe flowers that appear in a heavy spring flush and continue sporadically into summer and fall. Its manageable, rounded size fits foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders without the frequent shearing larger loropetalums need to stay in bounds, and the dark foliage makes an effective color contrast against golden or chartreuse companion plants. Loropetalums as a group are among the most heat- and humidity-tolerant flowering shrubs for the Gulf South and are largely trouble-free once established in well-drained soil; avoid waterlogged sites, which invite root rot.

common_name: Plum Passion Nandina (Deep Plum-Red New Growth Heavenly Bamboo)
notes: Plum Passion is a compact nandina selected for new foliage that emerges a deep plum-red to burgundy, maturing to green through the growing season before shifting back to purple-red tones in fall and winter cold, giving a longer window of rich color than many dwarf nandina cultivars that show red only in cool weather. Its dense, mounding habit fits foundation plantings and mixed borders without the tall, leggy cane growth of standard nandina, and like other modern dwarf selections it produces few or no berries, reducing the self-seeding that has made straight-species nandina invasive in parts of the Southeast. It needs little care beyond occasionally removing damaged canes to keep its naturally tidy shape.
