Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun — plumeria is a tropical American tree sacred in Buddhist and Hindu cultures, widely planted around temples throughout Asia and used in Hawaiian leis, and one of the most intensely fragrant of all flowering plants. The waxy, 4-inch flowers in white, yellow, pink, red, or multicolor combinations have a powerful sweet tropical scent that is strongest at night. Plumeria is deciduous (leafless in winter), drought tolerant, and thrives in heat — full sun and excellent drainage are its only requirements. In zone 9a it is widely grown in containers: bring indoors dry and leafless when temperatures drop below 40°F, store in a frost-free location, and return outdoors in spring. Hundreds of named cultivars are prized by collectors; the Singapore White (P. obtusa) is an evergreen species suited to zone 10+.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plumleaf azalea holds a unique distinction among native deciduous azaleas — it blooms in July and August, later than every other native azalea species, and is therefore in bloom when every other azalea in the garden has long finished. The large, brilliant orange-red (rarely yellow) flowers appear on the shrub in midsummer, providing color and hummingbird nectar in a season when the woodland garden often lacks bloom. This is one of the rarest native azaleas in the wild, found only in southwestern Georgia and eastern Alabama, but it is a superb and underused garden plant. It tolerates the heat and partial shade of zone 8–9 summers better than most native azaleas. Mulch heavily with pine bark to maintain soil moisture and acidity.

common_name: Pocomoke Crape Myrtle (True Dwarf Groundcover-Type Rose-Pink Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pocomoke is one of the true dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle selections, staying under three feet tall and wide, useful as a low border, mass planting, or large-scale groundcover rather than the shade-tree role most crape myrtles fill. It produces rich rose-pink flower clusters over a long summer season and, like other National Arboretum hybrids, shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Its very small mature size means it needs almost no pruning beyond removing dead wood, in sharp contrast to the standard practice of cutting back larger crape myrtles.

Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, mulching well since roots resent drying out; poet's laurel is an Asparagaceae relative of butcher's broom grown not for flowers but for its arching stems of glossy, dark green, leaf-like cladodes that are a mainstay of the florist trade for their remarkable vase life. Tiny greenish flowers in spring are followed, on pollinated plants, by orange-red berries that persist through winter and add interest to the deep-shade planting. Growth is very slow, with clumps taking several years to reach mature size, so treat new plantings as a long-term investment and avoid disturbing established clumps once they are settled in. It tolerates dry shade and heavy shade better than nearly any other broadleaf evergreen, making it valuable under mature trees where little else will grow.

common_name: Poinsettia (Mexican Christmas Star, Easter Flower, Noche Buena Garden Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun or morning sun with afternoon shade; prune heavily after blooming (January–February in zone 9) — cut plants back by one-third to one-half to prevent legginess and encourage compact growth and more prolific flowering the following winter; avoid any artificial light at night in October–November which will delay or prevent flowering since poinsettia requires uninterrupted long nights (14+ hours of darkness) to initiate flower (bract) color. Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) is primarily known as a holiday houseplant in most of the United States, but in zone 9–11 (tropical and subtropical Gulf Coast, California, Hawaii, Florida) it is a perennial garden SHRUB that grows 6–12 feet tall, often becoming a significant landscape element that blooms dependably every winter. In the wild, poinsettia is native to Mexico — particularly the Pacific coastal region of Taxco, Guerrero — where it grows as a semi-deciduous shrub or small tree 10–15 feet tall in the dry tropical forest and blooms in response to the shortening days of November–December, turning entire hillsides red with its bracts (the colorful parts are modified leaves, not petals — the true flowers are the small yellow structures at the center). The plant takes its common English name from Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first U.S. Ambassador to Mexico, who introduced it to the United States in 1825. In zone 9a, poinsettia grown outdoors blooms reliably from November through January with minimal care, and established plants develop woody trunks and can become large impressive shrubs. The characteristic that determines bloom timing is photoperiodism — poinsettia requires uninterrupted dark periods of 14 hours or more to initiate bract coloration, which occurs naturally as nights lengthen in autumn. Streetlights or interior lights shining on the plant at night will disrupt this cycle and delay or prevent coloring.

common_name: Polish Spirit Clematis (Vigorous Deep Purple Viticella Clematis)
notes: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Polish Spirit is a vigorous, free-flowering viticella-type clematis producing masses of rich, velvety deep purple flowers with a lighter central boss of cream-colored stamens, blooming heavily from midsummer into fall on a fast-growing vine that can cover a large trellis or scramble through a shrub or small tree in a single season. Because it flowers entirely on new growth, it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned hard, back to about a foot from the ground, in late winter, which keeps it vigorous and full of bloom rather than tangled and bare at the base. Its viticella parentage also gives it good resistance to clematis wilt, a fungal disease that troubles some large-flowered hybrid clematis.

Plant in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with good drainage, positioning the shrub where it receives filtered light and shelter from strong midday sun. Native to the Caucasus region and parts of eastern Europe, it has long been grown as a parent species of the hardy Ghent azalea hybrids and thrives in the same open woodland conditions those hybrids prefer. In late spring, clusters of intensely fragrant golden-yellow flowers open before or with the emerging leaves, filling a shaded garden with scent that carries much farther than the plant's modest size would suggest. Its narrow, willow-like leaves often turn shades of red, purple, and orange in autumn, adding a second season of color to a woodland border.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; poor man's rhododendron is a large, shrubby, perennial impatiens native to the cool, moist, highland forests and forest margins of East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda), where it grows to 4–6 feet in sheltered, moist situations and blooms almost without pause through the entire growing season. The common name 'poor man's rhododendron' refers to its remarkable capacity to produce continuous, abundant flower color in shade — filling the role that rhododendrons play in cool, acid, Pacific Northwest gardens — but in a warm-climate shade garden context where rhododendrons cannot grow. The flowers are the characteristic impatiens form — five-petaled, flat-faced, with a distinctive curved nectar spur — but much larger than the common bedding impatiens (Impatiens walleriana), reaching 1.5–2 inches across, in clear lavender-pink to soft pink to pale lilac and white. They are produced in continuous succession at the stem tips throughout the warmer months, a single plant carrying dozens of open flowers simultaneously when in full growing mode. In zone 9 it grows as a genuine, long-lived perennial shrub — not an annual — developing woody base stems over multiple seasons and increasing in size to form a large, leafy mound that fills a shady corner with continuous flower color and lush, rich, tropical-looking foliage. Requires consistent moisture and protection from midday sun; wilts quickly in drought or full-sun exposure. Outstanding for large, moist, shaded spaces in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens.

common_name: Popcorn Cassia (Peanut Butter Cassia, Candle Bush, Pois Puant)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Popcorn Cassia is adaptable to poor, sandy, or clay soils and tolerates drought once established in zone 9's hot summers. Senna didymobotrya is a large, fast-growing annual to short-lived perennial tropical shrub native to tropical Africa (Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia), extensively naturalized across the humid tropics as one of the most widely planted ornamental Senna species. The name 'Popcorn Cassia' or 'Peanut Butter Plant' comes from the extraordinary, strong, sweet, peanut-butter-popcorn scent released when the leaves are brushed or crushed — one of the most distinctive and surprising fragrances in the plant world, completely unlike the plant's golden appearance. The flowers themselves are produced in erect, candle-like spikes 6–12 inches long of bright golden-yellow petals emerging from dark brown to black overlapping buds that resemble a stack of poker chips — the visual contrast of black buds and gold flowers is dramatic and unique. The plant blooms from late summer through fall in zone 9 (August–November), providing late-season color when most other ornamentals are past peak. Note that all parts of the plant are toxic, particularly the seeds, which contain anthraquinones causing gastrointestinal distress.

common_name: Popcorn Drift Rose (Compact Groundcover Rose with Creamy-Yellow Blooms)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants to allow the low, spreading habit to fill in as a groundcover without crowding. Popcorn Drift is part of the Drift series of compact groundcover roses, a cross between full-sized groundcover roses and miniature roses that combines the disease resistance and toughness of landscape roses with a scale small enough for foundation plantings, borders, and containers. It produces clusters of small, semi-double, creamy-white to pale yellow flowers with a soft popcorn-like fullness continuously from late spring through frost, self-cleaning without the need for deadheading. Like other Drift roses it has strong resistance to black spot and other common rose diseases, needing only a hard cutback in late winter to renew growth and shape, making it one of the lowest-maintenance flowering shrubs available for sunny beds and slopes.

Popcorn is a viburnum selected for its rounded, ball-shaped white flower clusters, which resemble the doubled snowball-mophead form of the older Chinese snowball viburnum but appear on a plant with the stronger, more tiered branching structure typical of doublefile types. The dense clusters open lime-green and mature to pure white in mid-spring, smothering the horizontally layered branches, and the plant colors well in fall with burgundy-red foliage. Because most flowers are sterile, fruit set is light compared with lacecap doublefile forms, so it is grown primarily for its heavy floral display rather than for berries; give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade and ample room to develop its broad, spreading habit.

Plant Podranea ricasoliana in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with a very sturdy trellis, pergola, or wall to support its vigorous growth; train the initial stems to the support and allow to mature for 2–3 years before expecting heavy bloom; cut back in late winter to encourage compact, manageable growth and maximize flowering. Port St. John's Creeper is named for the coastal town in the Eastern Cape of South Africa near the Pondoland coast, where it scrambles over scrub and along forest margins. The large, broadly funnel-shaped flowers in soft rosy-pink to lilac-pink are produced in loose clusters at the branch tips from late spring through fall; individual flowers are 2–3 inches across, giving the vine a generous, lush appearance when in full bloom. It is similar to the more commonly grown Bignonia capreolata and related trumpet vines but with distinctly softer, more pastel coloring that blends beautifully with other plants. In zone 9, it dies back to the root crown after hard frost and re-emerges in spring; in zone 10–11 it grows as a large, semi-evergreen perennial vine reaching 15–20 feet or more. Butterflies visit the flowers and the vine is generally pest- and disease-resistant in suitable climates. A superb choice for pergolas, fences, walls, and large trellises in Gulf Coast subtropical gardens.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, saline-tolerant soil in full sun in tropical and near-tropical coastal areas; portia tree is a widely distributed pantropical beach and coastal tree in the hibiscus family, producing handsome, broadly heart-shaped leaves and large, yellow, hibiscus-like flowers with a dark maroon center that fade to purple-red as they age. Like beach hibiscus (Hibiscus tiliaceus), the flower color change occurs within hours on the same flower. The portia tree is one of the most salt-tolerant tropical trees available and has been widely planted throughout Pacific island communities for its high-quality, dense, decorative wood used in carving, furniture, and tool handles. The seeds, leaves, bark, and roots have various traditional medicinal applications across tropical Asia and Polynesia. In the US, suitable for south Florida and the warmest Gulf locations.

Plant acorns in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; Portuguese oak is the characteristic semi-evergreen oak of the western Mediterranean — a large, long-lived tree native to the Iberian Peninsula (Spain, Portugal) and northwestern Africa, growing in open forests, dry hillsides, and rocky slopes of the Mediterranean climate zone. Semi-evergreen in character — retaining most of its leaves through mild winters and shedding them in spring as new growth expands. The leaves are deeply lobed to entire, intermediate between deciduous and evergreen European oaks. Highly drought tolerant — one of the most drought-adapted of the European oaks, growing in areas with 12–20 inches of annual rainfall. Historically important in the dehesa (Spanish) and montado (Portuguese) agro-sylvo-pastoral systems — the open, grazed oak park-landscapes of Iberia that support unique biodiversity including Iberian lynx and black vultures. More heat and drought tolerant than English oak, suitable for Mediterranean-climate gardens of the US West Coast and similar warm, dry climates.

Root cuttings or plant in virtually any soil type — from dry, rocky, alkaline limestone to moist, sandy loam — in full shade to full sun — possum grape is one of the toughest native vines of the Gulf Coast and South Texas, a member of the grape family with succulent, deeply lobed, somewhat grape-like leaves on twining stems. The succulent stems store water, giving this vine exceptional drought tolerance even under large trees where root competition is intense and soil is bone dry. Small clusters of inconspicuous flowers in summer are followed by small, dark purple to black berries that are eagerly consumed by mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. It tolerates the deep shade under live oaks, cedar elms, and other large trees better than almost any other vine and is useful as a tough groundcover or fence cover for difficult, dry, shaded exposures. Deer avoid it. Deciduous in zone 7–8; semi-evergreen in zone 9–10.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; possum haw is a native deciduous holly of the Southeast naturally found in stream margins, swamp edges, and moist bottomland forests, valued for the brilliant orange-red berries that adorn bare branches all winter long after leaves drop in fall. It is an excellent alternative to winterberry (I. verticillata) for zone 8–9 gardens where winterberry can struggle with heat. Like all hollies, it is dioecious — both male and female plants are required for berry set, in a ratio of at least one male per five females. Cedar waxwings, robins, bluebirds, and mockingbirds rely on the persistent berries throughout winter. Named female cultivars like 'Warren's Red' and 'Fineline' are widely available.

Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun to partial shade; possumhaw adapts naturally to floodplains and stream banks and tolerates periodic inundation better than most landscape shrubs. Ilex decidua is a native deciduous holly of the southeastern and south-central US that delivers one of the most spectacular winter berry displays of any North American shrub — after the leaves drop in fall, the bare stems are completely covered in dense clusters of brilliant red to orange berries that persist through February, providing vivid color and abundant wildlife food throughout the dormant season. The berries are heavily utilized by cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and bluebirds during winter irruptions. A male pollinator plant (such as Ilex decidua 'Red Escort' or a male I. opaca) within pollinating distance is essential for berry set on female plants. Outstanding for naturalistic borders, rain gardens, and stream-bank plantings.

Post oak is one of the most drought-resistant and ecologically critical native oaks of the southeastern United States, forming a distinctive cross- or plus-shaped leaf outline (the 'stellata' — starry — refers to the star-shaped hairs on the leaf underside) that makes it immediately identifiable among the dozens of native oaks. Found on dry, sandy, or rocky ridges and uplands across its enormous range from New England to Texas, it is the characteristic oak of the 'post oak savanna' ecoregion of east Texas and the Cross Timbers region — a unique fire-maintained landscape of widely spaced oaks over a diverse grass and wildflower understory. The hard, rot-resistant wood was historically used for fence posts and barn sills (giving the tree its common name), and post oak acorns are among the most important mast crops for white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and dozens of bird species across the Southeast. Post oak supports over 500 species of Lepidoptera (moths and butterflies) as a larval host — making it one of the top native trees for butterfly and moth diversity in the region.

Plant in well-drained soil beside a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence, since this fast-scrambling vine needs support to weave through and will sprawl if left unstaked. Loose clusters of star-shaped white flowers with bright yellow centers open almost continuously from spring through fall in mild climates, giving off a light sweet fragrance especially in the evening. It is a vigorous, semi-evergreen climber that can be cut back hard in late winter to control its size and encourage fresh flowering shoots. Where winters bring hard freezes it dies back to the roots but often resprouts in spring, or it can be grown in a large container and moved to shelter.

Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix and grow in partial to full shade; pothos (devil's ivy, golden pothos) is the most widely grown and universally recognized houseplant in the world — a vigorous tropical vine from the Solomon Islands with glossy, heart-shaped, variably yellow-and-green or solid-green marbled leaves that trails or climbs on virtually any surface, rooting at the nodes to attach to trellises, moss poles, and textured walls. Its legendary low-maintenance character — tolerating low light, irregular watering, low humidity, and neglect that kills competing tropical plants — makes it the most appropriate choice for shaded interior spaces, covered porches, and areas of deep garden shade in zones 10–12, where it covers the ground or climbs trees. Stem cuttings root within days in plain water and can be transplanted to soil or left to grow in vases. Classified as an invasive species in some tropical regions (Hawaii, Florida) because of its ability to smother native vegetation outdoors in frost-free climates. Common cultivars include 'Golden Queen' (yellow-green variegated), 'Marble Queen' (white-splashed), 'Neon' (chartreuse), and 'N'Joy' (white and green). All parts toxic if ingested.

growth_habit: Indo-Pacific freshwater mangrove nocturnal flower tree
notes: Plant Barringtonia racemosa in moist to permanently wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun at the margins of ponds, streams, or in any reliably moist lowland position; in dry gardens, regular deep irrigation is needed; highly ornamental when in bloom at night. Powder Puff Mangrove is the freshwater counterpart to Barringtonia asiatica — smaller in overall size, preferring stream banks, pond margins, and freshwater mangrove zones rather than saltwater beaches, but equally spectacular in flower. The long, pendulous flower racemes (each 8–24 inches long) bear dozens of individual flowers that open at night, producing an exquisite display of white, brush-like, many-stamened flowers that fall by morning — the fallen stamens carpeting the ground or water below. The nocturnal blooming strategy reflects pollination by bats and hawk moths; the fragrance is sweet and distinctive. Throughout its vast range across tropical Asia and Africa, the bark, leaves, fruits, and seeds have numerous traditional medicinal applications — used for fever, skin conditions, rheumatism, and as a fish poison (similar to its coastal relative). The fruits are fibrous, oval, and float in fresh water for dispersal along rivers and streams. An outstanding ornamental for tropical water gardens, pond margins, and moist lowland positions in zone 10–12.

Prairie acacia is a native thornless (or nearly thornless) shrub of open prairies, rocky hillsides, and dry woodlands from Texas and Oklahoma to Arizona and south into Central America — one of the most ornamentally appealing of all native acacias due to its feathery, twice-pinnate leaves and profuse, creamy-white fluffy flower balls that emerge throughout summer and fall. As a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and builds soil organic matter through prolific leaf fall — traditionally it was valued as a fodder and soil improvement plant in tropical dry regions as well as for wildlife cover. The delicate, fernlike foliage is grazed by white-tailed deer and provides larval host resources for several butterfly species; the abundant seed pods attract quail, bobwhite, and songbirds in fall. In Gulf Coast gardens and south Texas habitat restorations, it is one of the more reliable, low-maintenance native shrubs for full sun in poor, dry soil — it dies back to the ground in cold winters in zones 7–8 but regrows vigorously from deep roots each spring.

Plant young trees in spring in well-drained, average to dry soil and full sun, giving the thorny, wide-spreading crown room in an open fencerow, savanna, or pasture edge planting. Prairie crabapple is more drought tolerant than many crabapples once established, reflecting its origin on the tallgrass prairie and midwestern plains. Its very fragrant, rose-pink blossoms open in late spring and are heavily worked by native bees, while the small, waxy, greenish-yellow fruit persists into winter and is eaten by foxes, raccoons, deer, and fruit-eating birds after repeated freezing and thawing softens it. Dense, thorny branching also offers secure nesting sites for grassland and edge-dwelling birds.

Plant in well-drained to slightly moist, sandy or loamy soil in full sun to light shade; prairie willow is one of the few willows adapted to dry upland sites rather than wetlands, making it valuable for stabilizing dry slopes and prairie edges. The fuzzy silver catkins emerge in earliest spring before the leaves — earlier than most other willows — providing critical pollen and nectar for queen bumblebees and early-emerging native bees. Prairie willow is an important larval host plant for the viceroy butterfly and several species of giant silk moths. The plant forms colonies through root suckering and tolerates fire.

Plant cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; prickly phlox is a native California shrub of chaparral, coastal sage scrub, and dry rocky slopes in the California Ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, producing densely needle-like, prickly foliage (much sharper and more aggressive than any true phlox) and profuse, bright rose-pink, five-petaled flowers that closely resemble garden phlox in spring. The combination of phlox-like flowers and needle-prickle foliage is unmistakable. Despite belonging to the same family (Polemoniaceae) as true phlox, it is in a different genus. A spectacular, California-native flowering shrub for dry, hot, well-drained gardens in zones 8–10, producing one of the showiest spring flower displays of any California native shrub. Excellent for slope stabilization, xeriscape, and fire-resistant California native gardens. Hummingbirds and native bees visit the flowers.

common_name: Pride of Augusta Carolina Jessamine (Double-Flowered Evergreen Vine)
notes: Plant against a sturdy trellis, arbor, mailbox post, or fence in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and train young vines onto their support until the twining stems take hold on their own. Pride of Augusta is a heritage double-flowered selection of Carolina jessamine, the southeastern native evergreen vine, bearing fully double, ruffled, deep golden-yellow flowers with a sweet fragrance that smother the vine in late winter to early spring, a showier and longer-lasting display than the single flowers of the standard species. Its glossy, twining evergreen foliage provides year-round cover for a fence or arbor even when not in bloom, and once established the vine is highly drought-tolerant and easy-care, asking for little beyond an annual light pruning after flowering to control size and shape. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where livestock or small children might be tempted to chew the foliage or flowers.

common_name: Pride of Barbados (Red Bird of Paradise)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — sandy, rocky, and even alkaline soils are acceptable; pride of barbados is one of the most spectacular flowering tropical shrubs for hot, dry, difficult sites, producing large showy clusters of exotic-looking flowers in brilliant shades of red-orange with long protruding red stamens (resembling a bird of paradise arrangement) over finely pinnate, lacy green foliage from summer through frost. It is exceptionally heat, drought, and poor-soil tolerant and blooms most prolifically in the hottest part of the summer when many other plants flag. The entire shrub is typically killed to the ground by hard freezes in zone 8 but regrows robustly each spring, often re-blooming within 60 days. In zone 9–12 it is woody and persistent, reaching shrub-tree size. Seeds germinate quickly after the hard seed coat is nicked or soaked. All parts are toxic if ingested. An outstanding butterfly and hummingbird plant for xeric, full-sun gardens.

common_name: Pride of Burma (Orchid Tree of Burma, Queen of Flowering Trees)
notes: Plant in partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Pride of Burma is one of the most demanding of all ornamental trees and requires the warm, humid, protected conditions of its native Myanmar habitat — consistently high humidity, warm temperatures year-round, shelter from drying winds, and fertile moist soil. Amherstia nobilis is an evergreen tree from the tropical forests of Myanmar (Burma), monotypic in its genus (the only species of Amherstia), and considered by many botanists and horticulturists to be the single most beautiful flowering tree in the world — a claim contested only by a handful of other extraordinary trees. The tree produces its flowers in pendant racemes hanging from the branch tips: each raceme carries 15–30 individual flowers of extraordinary complexity — vivid scarlet-red sepals, yellow-tipped petals, scarlet wings, arranged in a structure resembling an ornate tropical orchid flower in brilliant red and yellow. Each flower is 3–4 inches long; a single raceme in full development is among the most spectacular botanical displays in existence. The new leaves that emerge before the flowers are equally remarkable: they hang in long, copper-red to orange-pink, perfectly limp pendant tassels up to 3 feet long before gradually stiffening and turning green as they mature. Named in honor of Lady Amherst, wife of the Governor-General of India, who first preserved specimens for Western science in 1826.

common_name: Pride of Houston Yaupon Holly (Upright Berry-Producing Native Holly)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Pride of Houston is an upright, densely branched selection of native yaupon holly that, unlike the compact dwarf yaupon forms, is a female clone that produces abundant bright red berries prized for winter interest and wildlife value, holding well into the colder months. It grows into a substantial large shrub or can be pruned up into a small evergreen tree for use as a screen or specimen, and like all yaupon selections it is extremely tolerant of heat, drought, wind, salt spray, and poor soil, making it one of the toughest Gulf Coast landscape plants available. It needs only occasional shaping and no supplemental water once established.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pride of Rochester grows considerably taller and more upright than dwarf deutzia cultivars and needs room to reach its full arching, vase-shaped mature size. This heirloom nineteenth-century deutzia cultivar produces an abundance of double, pale pink-tinged white flowers packed densely along arching branches in late spring, one of the showiest bloom displays among old-fashioned flowering shrubs, followed by peeling, cinnamon-colored bark that adds winter interest. Its large size and old-fashioned charm make it a good choice for the back of a shrub border, an informal flowering hedge, or a specimen where its fountain-like form and heavy spring bloom can be fully appreciated. Renewal-prune a portion of the oldest canes to the ground right after flowering each year to keep the shrub vigorous and well-shaped over time.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; primrose jasmine is semi-evergreen in mild climates and cascades attractively over a wall or bank. Bright, semi-double, pale yellow flowers resembling small primroses open along arching green stems in late winter and early spring, larger and showier than the flowers of winter jasmine though sharing that relative's lack of fragrance and cascading, wall-draping growth habit. Its glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and long, arching canes make it a good choice for softening a retaining wall, bank, or trellis in mild-winter climates, providing an early, cheerful splash of yellow color when little else is blooming. Prune immediately after flowering to control size and shape, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and it tolerates hard pruning to rejuvenate an overgrown planting.

common_name: Princess Alexandra of Kent Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2007, Princess Alexandra of Kent produces rich, pure pink, cupped rosette flowers with a fresh tea fragrance that grows stronger as each bloom matures, on a vigorous, healthy, well-branched shrub with glossy, disease-resistant foliage. It is regarded as one of David Austin's more robust, easy-care introductions, tolerating heat and humidity well, and it repeat-blooms generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Princess Flower (Glory Bush, Purple Glory Tree, Brazilian Spider Flower)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic, organically rich soil; water consistently but ensure excellent drainage, as Tibouchina is intolerant of wet feet. Princess flower (Tibouchina urvilleana) is one of the most magnificent flowering shrubs for Gulf South and tropical gardens — a native of southern Brazil that produces enormous (3–4 inch), five-petaled, royal-purple flowers of a saturated, jewel-toned violet-purple color rarely found in any other woody plant. The flowers are borne singly or in small clusters at the branch tips continuously from summer through fall, with the heaviest bloom often in late summer and early fall; the large, soft, velvety leaves with their strongly ribbed texture add tactile and visual interest even when not in flower. Plants grow 4–15 feet depending on frost exposure and cultural conditions — in frost-free climates Tibouchina becomes a large shrub or small tree; in zone 9 where hard freezes occur, plants die back to the crown in cold winters and return as smaller shrubs each spring. The rich purple flower color pairs exceptionally well with golden or orange flowering plants, bougainvillea, and tropical foliage plants; Tibouchina is frequently used as a focal-point specimen shrub in Gulf Coast landscapes and performs well in large containers (12+ gallon) where it can be moved to frost protection in winter. Slightly acid soil (pH 5.5–6.5) with added organic matter is important for sustained health and heavy flowering — alkaline soil causes interveinal chlorosis.

Plant in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, with caution regarding invasive potential; princess tree is a Chinese ornamental tree that has become invasive across the eastern and southern United States, spreading prodigiously by wind-dispersed seeds into disturbed habitats, roadsides, riverbanks, and forest margins. The spring flower display is extraordinary — large, erect panicles of lavender-purple, foxglove-shaped flowers bloom in April before the very large, velvety, heart-shaped leaves emerge, creating a spectacular early spring display. The wood is prized in Japan as the finest, lightest, most resonant wood for musical instruments and traditional craft; female dolls and furniture are traditionally made from paulownia wood. Despite its beauty, plant responsibly — avoid locations near natural areas and never plant where it could escape cultivation into native habitats.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing generous room for the tree's wide, arching, classic vase-shaped canopy to develop. Princeton is a selection of American elm originally chosen in the 1920s for its fast growth, dense glossy foliage, and handsome symmetrical form, only to later prove one of the most Dutch-elm-disease-tolerant American elm selections available, which has made it the standard replacement elm for streets, parks, and campuses across much of the country. It restores the soaring, cathedral-like street-tree silhouette that made American elm so beloved before the disease devastated the species, while resisting infection far better than seedling-grown trees. Water deeply during establishment, provide good air circulation and avoid wounding the bark, since even resistant cultivars can occasionally succumb under heavy disease pressure, and prune to maintain a strong central structure while the young tree is developing its canopy.

common_name: Princeton Sentry Ginkgo (Narrow Columnar Seedless Male Ginkgo)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; ginkgo tolerates urban conditions, air pollution, and compacted soil better than almost any other large landscape tree, making it a favorite for street and parking-lot plantings. Princeton Sentry is a male ginkgo selection prized for a distinctly narrow, upright, columnar form that fits streets and tight urban spaces where a full-spreading ginkgo would be impractical, while still developing the species' brilliant, uniform golden-yellow fall color that drops in a dramatic, near-simultaneous leaf fall. As a male clone it never produces the malodorous, messy fruit of female ginkgo trees, avoiding the notorious smell and slip hazard those seeds cause on walkways. Slow-growing and exceptionally long-lived, ginkgo is essentially pest- and disease-free once established, needing only a deep, infrequent watering during extended drought and no routine maintenance beyond structural pruning while young to establish a strong central leader.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Profusion Beautyberry is adaptable to a range of light conditions and performs well in the partial shade typical of zone 9 landscapes under the filtered canopy of high-branched trees; Profusion is a cultivar of Chinese Beautyberry (Callicarpa bodinieri), producing one of the most spectacular and unusual fall fruiting displays of any landscape shrub — clusters of intensely violet-purple to magenta berries packed tightly in whorls along the length of the arching stems in September through November. The color of the berries is genuinely unusual — a saturated, electric, jewel-like violet-purple that has no equivalent among common native berrying shrubs, creating a fall display that stops observers who are unfamiliar with the plant. Profusion was selected for particularly heavy berry production compared to the straight species, bearing abundant clusters on vigorous, arching stems that achieve maximum visual impact in full fruit. The fall berry display works well in combination with the native American Beautyberry (Callicarpa americana), whose berries are a slightly different, more pink-magenta shade — the two species together providing a visual study in the range of violet-purple available within the Callicarpa genus. As a wildlife plant, beautyberry berries are consumed by at least 40 bird species across the US, making it a high-value habitat shrub for landscape designs focused on bird support.

common_name: Pugster Amethyst Butterfly Bush (Dwarf True-Purple Compact Buddleja)
notes: Pugster Amethyst is part of the dwarf Pugster butterfly bush series, bred for unusually thick, sturdy stems and large flower spikes on a plant that stays under two feet tall, a striking contrast to the tall, willowy growth of standard Buddleja davidii. It produces true purple-amethyst flowers continuously from early summer through frost, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds just as reliably as full-size cultivars despite its diminutive stature, and its low, dense habit fits containers, small borders, and mass plantings where larger butterfly bush would overwhelm the space. Like other modern Buddleja hybrids it is sterile and does not self-seed, and it needs only an annual hard cutback in late winter to stay compact and free-flowering.

common_name: Pugster Blue Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile Reblooming Buddleja)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pugster Blue is part of the Pugster series of dwarf butterfly bushes, bred to stay compact — under 2 feet tall and wide — while producing full-sized, densely packed, true-blue flower spikes on unusually thick, sturdy stems that hold up well without flopping. Unlike older Buddleja davidii cultivars, the Pugster series is bred to be sterile or very low-seeding, largely eliminating the self-seeding invasiveness concern associated with standard butterfly bush in parts of the country, so it can be planted more responsibly near natural areas. It blooms from early summer through frost with only light deadheading needed to keep flowers coming, and like all butterfly bush it is a strong draw for butterflies, particularly swallowtails and monarchs, as well as hummingbirds. In zone 9, plants die back partially in winter and resprout vigorously from the base in spring; cut back hard in late winter to encourage a full flush of new flowering growth. Its small stature makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, mixed perennial borders, or large containers where a full-sized butterfly bush would overwhelm the space.

common_name: Pugster Pink Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Pink Buddleja)
notes: Pugster Pink shares the same thick-stemmed, dwarf habit as the rest of the Pugster butterfly bush series, staying under two feet tall while still carrying large, dense flower spikes in a clear rose-pink, blooming continuously from early summer through frost. The compact, sturdy form fits small borders, containers, and foundation plantings where standard butterfly bush cultivars grow far too large, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds with the same intensity as full-size cultivars. It is sterile and does not self-seed like older Buddleja davidii selections, and needs only an annual hard cutback in late winter, to about 6-12 inches, to stay dense and floriferous.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in wet to seasonally flooded, poorly drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pumpkin ash is adapted to swamps and bottomlands and tolerates standing water far better than upland ash species. Named for the swollen, pumpkin-shaped base that often develops on trees growing in permanently flooded ground, this large wetland tree bears compound leaves and winged seeds typical of ash, providing food for wildlife and dense shade over the bottomland hardwood forests and cypress-tupelo swamps of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain. It is among the most flood-tolerant of all ash species, capable of growing in standing water for extended periods, making it valuable for restoring wet bottomland sites where few other large shade trees will survive. Like other native ash species it is vulnerable to the invasive emerald ash borer, so plant it as part of a diverse wetland tree planting rather than a monoculture.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Purple Allamanda requires full sun for best flowering and will produce fewer blooms in shaded conditions. Allamanda blanchetii (sometimes listed as A. violacea) is a large, vigorous, scrambling shrub or lax vine from Brazil, closely related to the common Golden Allamanda (A. cathartica) but producing rich rose-purple to magenta, trumpet-shaped flowers 3–4 inches in diameter rather than the familiar yellow. The flowers are stunning — the color a deep, saturated rose-magenta that is unusual among tropical vines — and are borne in successive flushes from late spring through frost in zone 9. Like its golden relative, Purple Allamanda has a sprawling, lax habit that can be trained on a fence or trellis by tying stems, or allowed to cascade down a bank or over a wall. The stems exude a milky white sap when cut, similar to the toxic latex of its relatives in the Apocynaceae family — this sap is a skin irritant and toxic if ingested, with all plant parts considered poisonous. In zone 9, Purple Allamanda is used as a warm-season annual or half-hardy perennial; in zone 10-11 it grows as a large, floriferous evergreen shrub that blooms nearly year-round.

Plant in spring or early fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; purple beautyberry performs best in partial afternoon shade in zone 7–8 which prevents leaf scorch while maintaining prolific berry production. Callicarpa dichotoma is the Asian counterpart to the native American beautyberry, producing a more compact shrub (3–5 feet) with arching branches and, in fall, spectacular clusters of vivid violet-purple berries so intense in color they seem almost artificial — these berries are among the most electric and eye-catching of any fruiting shrub in the temperate garden and are invaluable for fall color. The small, lavender flowers in summer are attractive to pollinators. Plant in groups of 3 or more for best berry set; prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and heavy fruiting. The berries are mildly toxic to humans.

common_name: Purple Diamond Loropetalum (Compact Deep-Purple Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water regularly the first season to establish before easing into a lower-maintenance routine. Purple Diamond is part of the First Editions breeding program and stands out among Loropetalum chinense cultivars for its unusually dense, rounded, naturally compact habit and consistently deep, dark purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season rather than fading to green, punctuated by frilly magenta-pink flowers in spring with scattered rebloom into fall. Its tidy, slow-to-medium growth rate makes it lower-maintenance than larger loropetalum cultivars, suiting foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders without frequent shearing. Prune lightly right after the spring flower flush if shaping is needed, since later pruning removes next year's flower buds.

Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; purple false eranthemum (Jacob's coat, eldorado) is a Pacific Islands tropical shrub grown for its spectacular, large, glossy, dark-purple to maroon leaves dramatically overlaid with scattered spots, streaks, and blotches of pink, rose, gold, and white — one of the most richly colored foliage plants available for tropical and subtropical gardens. The unusual combination of dark background coloration with bright-colored irregular markings creates a bold, jewel-like quality unlike any other landscape shrub. Small, pale-lavender to white, tubular flowers appear in terminal spikes throughout the year in frost-free climates but are secondary to the remarkable foliage. Excellent combined with chartreuse-leaved plants (golden pothos, lime coleus) for high-contrast tropical compositions. Grown as a houseplant in cool climates; in zone 10–12 it forms an outdoor foliage shrub of 2–4 feet. 'Tricolor' and 'Rubrum' are cultivar selections emphasizing different color combinations.

common_name: Purple Glory Tree (Brazilian Spider Flower, Princess Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, organically rich soil; Purple Glory Tree grows most vigorously in full sun but tolerates afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Tibouchina granulosa is a large, fast-growing tree from the Atlantic rainforest of Brazil, producing one of the most spectacular purple floral displays of any tree in the subtropical world. In late summer through fall, the entire canopy becomes covered with large (2–3 inch) royal purple to intense violet flowers borne in broad, flat-topped clusters at every stem tip — the effect is breathtaking, with a well-established specimen appearing as though it has been draped in a cascade of purple velvet. Each flower has prominent purple anthers on curved filaments that give the genus the common name 'Spider Flower.' The large, velvet-textured, dark-green, prominently ribbed leaves are attractive year-round. Tibouchina granulosa (the tree form) is distinguished from the shrubby Princess Flower (T. urvilleana, 6–10 feet) by its potential tree height of 25–40 feet in zone 10-11 and its tendency to develop a single dominant trunk. In zone 9, hard pruning after frost damage stimulates vigorous regrowth and heavy flowering on new wood. An outstanding specimen tree for subtropical Gulf Coast landscapes.

common_name: Purple Hyacinth Bean Vine (Ornamental Heirloom Lablab Bean Vine)
notes: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost near a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor — the vines can reach 10–15 feet and require support. Purple Hyacinth Bean (Lablab purpureus) is one of the most dramatic ornamental vines for the warm-season garden — a fast-growing tropical legume vine with multiple ornamental features occurring simultaneously: dark green leaves with deep purple veining and purple undersides, dense racemes of fragrant, bright magenta-purple pea-type flowers, and after flowering, spectacular flat, bright purple seed pods (2–3 inches long) that persist on the vine for weeks, contrasting strikingly with the continuing flowers and creating a multi-season display. The ornamental pod color is unusual in the plant kingdom — very few plants produce purple pods of this intensity, and the color display is most impressive in late summer and fall when the pods are most abundant. Hyacinth bean is one of the most popular annual vines in American Southern gardens where the long growing season allows it to reach its full potential; it is relatively tender and needs the warmth of a Gulf South spring to establish well. The seeds and pods are edible when cooked thoroughly (raw hyacinth bean contains toxic amounts of cyanogenic glucosides), and the plant is grown as a food crop throughout Africa and Asia.

Sow scarified seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; purple orchid tree is a South Asian deciduous to semi-evergreen flowering tree widely planted throughout zone 9–12 landscapes for its large, showy, fragrant, five-petaled, orchid-like flowers in shades of pink, lavender, purple, and white with crimson veining that appear in autumn through early winter — uniquely, the tree flowers most abundantly after dropping its large, rounded, bilobed leaves in late fall, so the spectacular flower display occurs on nearly bare branches for maximum visual impact. The flowers are followed by flat, woody seed pods that persist through winter. Bauhinia purpurea flowers in fall-winter (August–December in the Gulf South), while the related B. variegata flowers in late winter-spring — together they extend the Bauhinia flowering season. The young leaves and flower buds are edible and eaten in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking. It is one of the most reliable and easily grown flowering trees for zone 9–12 and germinates readily from seed, though seed-grown trees vary in flower color and intensity.

common_name: Purple Pillar Rose of Sharon (Columnar Narrow-Growing Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely to form a narrow, upright screen or leave as a single columnar accent. Purple Pillar is a distinctively narrow, columnar rose of sharon that grows as tall as the species while staying only 2–3 feet wide, an unusually upright form that fits tight side-yard beds, narrow entry plantings, and vertical accents where a normal spreading rose of sharon would not fit. It produces the same double, rich purple-violet flowers as other modern rose of sharon cultivars from midsummer into fall, on a shrub whose narrow silhouette makes it useful for privacy screening in a limited footprint. Prune in late winter to maintain the columnar form and encourage vigorous new flowering wood.

common_name: Purple Pixie Loropetalum (Dwarf Weeping Groundcover Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Pixie is a dwarf, strongly weeping Loropetalum cultivar with a radically different growth habit from standard upright loropetalum — growing very low (12–24 inches tall) but spreading wide (3–5 feet) with strongly pendulous, cascading branches that create an elegant, trailing, mounded groundcover form unlike any other commonly available ornamental shrub in the Gulf South. The weeping habit makes Purple Pixie exceptional for uses that standard upright shrubs cannot fill: draping over retaining walls and raised planter edges to create a cascading curtain of burgundy foliage, massing as a groundcover on slopes and banks that are difficult to maintain with upright plants, and providing low-growing, weed-suppressing cover in landscape beds where taller shrubs would block views. The same deep burgundy-purple foliage and bright magenta-pink spring flowers as standard loropetalum cultivars, produced on cascading branches that sweep naturally downward. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, tolerating heat, humidity, and the clay soils of the Gulf South. The very compact, spreading growth means minimal pruning is required to maintain the natural form — periodic tip-pruning to encourage density and remove any particularly vigorous upright shoots maintains the groundcover character.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Pixie is a breakthrough compact and weeping selection of the purple-leaved loropetalum that stays only 12–24 inches tall while spreading 3.5–5 feet wide, creating a distinctive low, mounding to weeping groundcover effect entirely different from the large-growing standard selections. The deep burgundy-purple foliage is among the darkest and most richly colored of any loropetalum cultivar — maintaining its vivid color through the growing season with more sun intensity increasing the purple intensity. Bright, deep pink fringe flowers appear in spring and intermittently through the season, providing color contrast against the dark foliage. The strongly weeping branch tips cascade down and outward, creating a softening effect at wall edges, raised planting beds, and container rims that the standard upright forms cannot provide. Purple Pixie is an outstanding container plant, groundcover on slopes, and edging plant where its low profile and weeping habit can be showcased. It is Zone Award from the Gulf Coast Plant Introduction Group and performs reliably in zone 9 heat without the pest and disease problems that affect some ornamental cultivars.

common_name: Purple Queen Bougainvillea (Rich Purple-Violet Bougainvillea Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Purple Queen is a bougainvillea cultivar producing bracts in rich, deep purple-violet to blue-purple tones — one of the more purely purple-toned bougainvilleas available, with bracts that lean toward violet-blue rather than the magenta-red of Barbara Karst or the scarlet of San Diego Red. The deeper, cooler purple tone has a different visual quality in the landscape — more sophisticated and less vivid than the hot pinks and reds, creating an elegant effect particularly effective with silver and gray foliage companions. Purple Queen has the same vigorous growth habit as other bougainvillea cultivars, capable of covering large wall areas or pergolas in favorable zone 9-11 conditions. The bloom response to humidity-following-drought, water stress promotion, and lean soil management applies equally to Purple Queen as to other bougainvillea cultivars — slightly stressing the plant consistently produces heavier flowering than well-fed and well-watered specimens. The purple bract color fades to mauve-pink as the flowers age on the plant, providing a naturally occurring color gradient from new vivid-purple bracts at the stem tips to older faded-mauve bracts closer to the main stems — an attractive multi-tone effect during extended bloom periods. Container-grown Purple Queen performs well on patios and in large planters where the root restriction actually promotes flowering.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; purple wreath is one of the most spectacular tropical flowering vines, producing cascading clusters 12–18 inches long of small, star-shaped violet-purple flowers with contrasting deeper purple calyces that remain decorative for weeks after the petals fall — the persistent purple calyces give the vine a second ornamental period. The rough-textured, sandpaper-like leaves give rise to the alternate name 'sandpaper vine.' Established plants bloom in a spectacular spring flush with intermittent repeat bloom through summer and fall. The woody vine can reach 20–40 feet and requires a large, sturdy support. It is drought tolerant once established and blooms most prolifically with minimal irrigation. A stunning specimen for zone 10–12 landscapes; in zone 9b it can survive in sheltered south-facing locations.

Purpureus is a false holly selection grown for new spring foliage that emerges deep purple-black before gradually maturing to dark green through the summer, giving a seasonal color shift on top of the spiny, holly-like leaf texture typical of the species. Like other Osmanthus heterophyllus cultivars it produces tiny, sweetly fragrant white flowers tucked among the leaves in fall, easy to miss by eye but obvious by scent, and it forms a dense, deer-resistant, evergreen screen or informal hedge with minimal maintenance. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the harshest afternoon exposure, and prune lightly to shape only after fall bloom.

Pussy Willow is the beloved harbinger of spring throughout eastern North America, a large native shrub or small tree native to wet meadows, swamp margins, streambanks, and moist thickets from Newfoundland to British Columbia and south to the Appalachians and Pacific Northwest, producing in February and March the large, plump, silvery-gray male catkins that are one of the most universally recognized signals that winter is ending. Male plants produce the showiest catkins (female catkins are smaller and less attractive); catkin branches cut in late winter and placed in water indoors immediately become a beloved floral display that reliably roots — the resulting rooted cuttings can be potted or planted directly in the garden. An important early pollinator plant, providing pollen to native bees, honey bees, and other emerging insects before virtually any other tree flowers; willows in general are one of the most important native pollinator plants in North America. Plant in wet to moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade near pond margins, rain gardens, or wet depressions.

Plant in very well-drained, deep sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; pygmy fringetree is a rare, federally listed endangered shrub endemic to the ancient sand ridges of central Florida, where it grows as a much smaller relative of the familiar white fringetree — a compact, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a small tree — producing the same delicate, fragrant, white, fringe-petaled flower clusters in spring on a fraction of the scale. Dark, olive-like fruit follows on female plants when a male is nearby for pollination. Because it evolved in the deep, fast-draining, nutrient-poor sands of Florida scrub, it needs sharp drainage and tolerates drought and poor soil far better than average garden conditions; wet feet or heavy clay are more likely to kill it than neglect. Grown occasionally by Florida native-plant specialty nurseries and used in native scrub restoration and low-water landscaping within its narrow natural range; site it in a lean, sandy, well-drained bed rather than a typical amended garden border.

Pyramid Magnolia is a rare native deciduous magnolia of the southeastern coastal plain, found in scattered populations in Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, and Texas, growing in moist, rich, well-drained soil in the understory of mixed hardwood forest — a much more restricted habitat than the closely related Fraser Magnolia (Magnolia fraseri), which it resembles closely but with a more pyramidal form and consistently smaller stature. White, cup-shaped flowers 3–4 inches across appear in April and May before or with the emerging leaves; the large, auriculate (ear-lobed) leaves and attractive pink-red fruit clusters provide multi-season interest similar to its Appalachian relatives. Among the least-known of the native magnolias in horticulture despite being well-suited to zone 7–9 gardens, Pyramid Magnolia is increasingly available from specialty native nurseries as interest in deciduous native magnolias grows. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, deeply amended soil in partial shade; protect from strong winds that damage the large leaves.

Plant root suckers or cuttings in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; quaking aspen is the most widely distributed native tree in North America, ranging from Alaska to Newfoundland and south through the Rocky Mountains to Mexico. Named for the distinctive trembling of the leaves on their flattened petioles in even the slightest breeze, the constant movement produces a shimmering, glittering effect that is uniquely beautiful. Aspen groves are clonal colonies — all trees in a grove are genetically identical, connected by a single underground root system. The famous 'Pando' clone in Utah is estimated to be 80,000+ years old and weighing over 6 million kilograms, potentially the oldest living organism on Earth. Brilliant golden-yellow fall color; white bark provides winter interest. Best in cool, moist climates of the northern states and mountain West; struggles in hot, humid southern areas.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide strong trellis, fence, or arbor support — queen wreath becomes a large, heavy vine. Petrea volubilis (queen's wreath or purple wreath) is a Mexican and Central American tropical vine producing some of the most spectacular flower displays of any vine in subtropical horticulture — cascading, wisteria-like racemes 10–18 inches long densely packed with tiny, star-shaped flowers in an extraordinary violet-purple color in spring, with a secondary flush after summer rains. Each individual flower consists of a larger, calyx-like structure that outlasts the true petals, persisting as a pale-blue to lavender star shape after the purple petals drop — creating two overlapping color displays as the raceme matures. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves (responsible for the common name 'sandpaper vine') are semi-evergreen. The vine climbs by twining and becomes very large and woody over time; mature plants require substantial support. In zone 9, it may be damaged by hard freezes but typically resprouts from the base. One of the most beautiful flowering vines for Gulf Coast trellises and fences.

common_name: Queen of Sweden Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2004, Queen of Sweden bears soft, pure pink, cupped rosette flowers with a light myrrh fragrance on an upright, narrow, well-branched shrub that stays notably tidy and self-supporting compared to more lax English rose cultivars. It is among the most disease-resistant of the David Austin roses, holding clean, healthy foliage through humid summers with minimal spraying, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost, making it a reliable choice for a narrow bed or formal border planting.

Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; queen's crepe myrtle (giant crepe myrtle, banaba) is a large tropical tree native to South and Southeast Asia that is the largest and most spectacular flowering member of the crepe myrtle family — it can grow to 40–60 feet in ideal tropical conditions and in summer and early monsoon season produces enormous, terminal panicles (12–18 inches long) of large, lavender-pink to rose-purple, crinkled, crepe-textured flowers in the characteristic crepe myrtle style, but at a scale dwarfing the common crepe myrtle (Lagerstroemia indica). The bark exfoliates in patches like all crepe myrtles, revealing a smooth, gray-beige inner bark surface that is ornamental year-round. The leaves turn brilliant red-orange in the dry season before falling. Banaba leaf extract has been intensively researched for its anti-diabetic properties and is widely sold as an herbal supplement, particularly in the Philippines, where the tree is called banaba. An outstanding flowering shade tree for zone 10–12 tropical and subtropical landscapes.

common_name: Queensland Trumpet Tree (Deplanchea, Four-Leaf Deplanchea, Yellow Cassod Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Queensland Trumpet Tree grows most vigorously and produces its best flower displays in full sun conditions. Deplanchea tetraphylla is a medium to large, evergreen tropical tree native to northeastern Queensland, Australia (Cape York Peninsula and adjacent Queensland rainforest margins) in the Bignoniaceae family, one of the outstanding ornamental flowering trees of northeastern Australia and one of the least known outside the botanical garden world. The tree has a distinctive, immediately recognizable appearance due to its whorled leaf arrangement: the large, broadly oval to obovate leaves (12–18 inches long) are arranged in precise whorls of four at each node rather than the alternating or opposite arrangement of most trees — giving the tree an architectural, tiered, symmetrical appearance. The flowers are spectacular: large, dense, terminal panicles of bright orange-yellow, tubular flowers crowded into massive heads at the branch tips, each individual flower about 1 inch long with five spreading lobes, produced in profuse display in spring to summer. The orange-yellow flower clusters at the tips of the whorled branches create a striking visual pattern — concentric rings of color and foliage. A rare but genuinely impressive zone 10-12 ornamental flowering tree that deserves wider planting in tropical and subtropical botanical gardens and large residential landscapes.

common_name: Quick Fire Hydrangea (Earliest-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea with Fast Color Change)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving this larger-growing selection plenty of room to reach full size. Quick Fire was notable as the first panicle hydrangea bred specifically to bloom several weeks ahead of standard types, opening white flower panicles in early summer that begin shifting to deep pink and finally wine-red within weeks rather than the months typical panicle hydrangeas take, giving a longer overall season of colorful interest from a single shrub. Its sturdy, reddish stems hold the maturing flower panicles upright well, and the extended color change from white through pink to red-purple keeps the shrub visually interesting from early summer into fall. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it tolerates hard pruning in late winter to control size or rejuvenate an older shrub without losing the coming season's flowers.

Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Quickfire earns its name by flowering several weeks ahead of most other panicle hydrangeas, opening white conical flower clusters in early summer that gradually age to deep pink and finally rich rose-red as the season progresses, giving a longer overall season of color than later-blooming types. Unlike mophead hydrangea, panicle types like Quickfire bloom on new wood, so a hard pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the coming season's flowers and instead encourages a strong flush of new flowering stems. Its sturdy stems hold the flower clusters upright well even in rain, and the plant tolerates more sun and drier soil than mophead hydrangeas once established.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; rain of gold (Galphimia glauca, shower of gold, thryallis) is a Central American and Mexican evergreen shrub widely planted throughout the Gulf Coast and south Florida for its extraordinarily prolonged display of brilliant, clear-yellow, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers borne continuously on the tips of every stem from early spring through frost — the plant is almost never out of bloom during warm weather and functions as a continuous-color shrub requiring virtually no deadheading or care. The flowers are arranged in loose, upright, golden racemes that create an effect of scattered gold stars across the dark-green, glossy, oval-leafed plant. It thrives in the intense heat and drought of zone 9–11 summers, asks for minimal water once established, and rewards benign neglect with the most extended bloom season of any Gulf Coast flowering shrub. It is cold-sensitive and root-hardy to approximately 25–28°F in zone 9 with protection. Excellent massed as a summer-to-fall flowering hedge, in median plantings, and as a low-maintenance xeriscape flowering shrub in hot, sunny areas.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can scorch the variegated foliage. Rainbow is a colorful sport of the native Appalachian shrub drooping leucothoe, with glossy, arching evergreen leaves splashed in cream, pink, and coppery-red that are showiest on new growth in spring and again in cool fall weather. Small, white, urn-shaped flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in spring, similar to its relatives in the heath family. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a graceful, cascading mound, making it a good textural companion for ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials, and benefits from an occasional thinning of old canes at the base to keep growth vigorous.

Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; provide strong trellis or fence support; the vine is frost-tender but regenerates from the root in zone 9. Quisqualis indica (Rangoon creeper, Chinese honeysuckle, or drunken sailor) is one of the most flamboyant and unique tropical flowering vines available for zone 9–12 gardens — native to the tropical forests of South and Southeast Asia (India through the Philippines) and now one of the most widely grown tropical ornamental vines worldwide. The vine's most distinctive feature is its color-changing flowers: the 2-inch, long-tubed, star-shaped, fragrant flowers open pure white on the first day, turn soft pink on the second day, and deepen to brilliant scarlet-red by the third day — so the vine simultaneously carries clusters of white, pink, and red flowers at all times, creating a tricolor display unlike any other garden plant. The flowers have a powerful, sweet, jasmine-vanilla-like fragrance that intensifies in the evening, making them extraordinary for garden areas where evening fragrance is desired. The vine is a vigorous grower (reaching 20–30 feet) and blooms prolifically in warm weather. In zone 9, the vine dies back to the root in hard freezes but regenerates vigorously in spring — effectively functioning as a semi-perennial.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis; Rangoon creeper is one of the most spectacular and fragrant of all tropical vines, producing pendant clusters of fragrant tubular flowers that open pure white, then change through pink to brilliant red over 3–4 days — the different-colored flowers at different stages create a stunning three-color display on the vine at all times during the long blooming season from late spring through fall. The sweet fragrance is strongest in the evening and carries widely on still air. In zone 8–9 established plants die to the ground in freezes but resprout vigorously in spring from the established root system. The vine can become very large in warm climates and may need annual pruning to keep manageable. Once established it is drought tolerant. The seeds are edible and have been used medicinally in Asia for centuries.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Ray Hartman ceanothus needs excellent drainage above all else and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot. A vigorous, large-growing hybrid between two California native ceanothus species, it produces masses of medium-blue flower clusters over glossy, deep green foliage in early spring, growing quickly into a substantial evergreen shrub or small multi-trunked tree that can be trained with a single leader for a more tree-like form. One of the most reliable and widely planted ceanothus hybrids in California native gardens, it tolerates poor soil and heat with essentially no supplemental water once established, and its abundant spring bloom is a major early-season draw for native bees. Water only during the first year or two of establishment, then withhold summer irrigation entirely, and prune lightly after flowering if shaping is needed.

Root cuttings and grow in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in part shade; red angel's trumpet is the most distinctive Brugmansia species — unlike the white, pink, and yellow angels' trumpets (B. x candida and relatives) that prefer warm conditions, B. sanguinea is native to the cool, cloud forest elevations of the Andes (5,000–11,000 feet) in Peru, Chile, Colombia, and Ecuador, producing exceptionally large, pendant, bicolored tubular flowers that are red-orange at the flared tip fading to yellow at the base, with a prominent green calyx. The flowers are in continuous production on established plants and are pollinated by hummingbirds in their native habitat — making them strongly attractive to hummingbirds in cultivation. The cool-preference nature makes it better suited to coastal California and mild Pacific Northwest climates than to tropical Gulf Coast summers, where afternoon shade, ample water, and well-drained fertile soil are essential. All plant parts are highly toxic; contain scopolamine, atropine, and related tropane alkaloids.

Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Red Bristle Philodendron produces its largest, most dramatically lobed leaves with adequate bright indirect light and a climbing support to grow upward. Philodendron squamiferum is a climbing philodendron from French Guiana, Suriname, and northern Brazil, one of the most immediately distinctive and recognizable collector philodendrons because of its unique combination of leaf shape and petiole texture: the leaves are large (10–18 inches), deeply and irregularly lobed into five distinct lobes (like an oak leaf or a flattened hand), rich dark green, with a thick, leathery texture — but the plant's most distinctive feature is the petioles (leaf stalks), which are covered in dense, soft, bristle-like red hairs or scales. These bright rust-red to coral-red bristled petioles are unique among commonly grown aroids and give the plant the common names 'Red Bristle Philodendron' and 'Hairy Philodendron.' The contrast between the dark green lobed leaves and the vivid red furry stems creates an ornamental effect quite different from the smooth-stemmed philodendrons that dominate the market. The species is generally adaptable and grows well in indoor conditions with moderate care. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; red buckeye is one of the finest native shrubs for the shaded garden, producing upright panicles of brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers in April and May precisely timed to the return of ruby-throated hummingbirds from migration. The flowers are visited almost exclusively by hummingbirds and are among the most important early-season hummingbird plants available. It grows naturally as a forest understory shrub throughout the Southeast and performs exceptionally well in zone 8–9 Gulf Coast gardens in partial shade. The glossy, palmate compound leaves are attractive all season but the plant goes fully dormant in summer heat — mark its location and interplant with later-season companions. The large, mahogany-colored seeds are toxic to humans and livestock.

Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Dragon Japanese maple holds its deep red color better in more sun than many other laceleaf cultivars, but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Finely dissected, lacy, deep burgundy-red leaves cover a compact, mounding, weeping laceleaf form that holds its rich color from spring through summer better than many older red-leaved cultivars, which often fade toward green by midsummer, before finishing with a bright crimson fall display. Its dense, cascading, umbrella-like habit makes it a striking specimen for a container, rock garden, or the front of a shaded border, providing structure and color even without flowers. Provide afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through summer heat.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Red Emerald philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops larger leaves when given vertical support. Glossy, elongated heart-shaped leaves in rich emerald green are set off by wine-red new growth, petioles, and stems, a classic color combination that made this one of the most widely grown climbing philodendrons since its introduction decades ago. As a true climbing aroid it develops larger, more mature foliage and stronger red coloring when trained up a moss pole or trellis rather than left to trail, and it grows quickly under good indoor light with minimal care. Wipe dust from the glossy leaves periodically, provide bright indirect light for the best stem color, and prune to control length and encourage branching.

Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; red escallonia produces glossy, aromatic, dark green leaves and clusters of small, tubular, crimson-red flowers over a long summer bloom season that draws hummingbirds and bees. It is a mainstay hedge and screening shrub of coastal California and Pacific Northwest gardens because of its outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, and fog, though it prefers more consistent moisture than a true desert xeriscape plant. Shear or hand-prune after the main flush of bloom to keep an informal hedge dense, and site it where air circulates freely to minimize leaf spot in humid coastal conditions.

common_name: Red Heart Rose of Sharon (Classic White with Red Center Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Red Heart is a classic, long-cultivated rose of sharon bearing large, single, pure white flowers with a bold crimson-red center, a simple but striking color combination that has kept it in continuous cultivation for generations. Blooming heavily from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub, it is tough, heat-tolerant, and easy to grow in average garden soil, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and encourage the current season's flowering wood.
