Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Hills azalea is native to the Gulf Coastal Plain of Alabama and Georgia and is well adapted to the heat and humidity of a Deep South garden. Rhododendron colemanii is a large, vigorous deciduous azalea only formally described in 2008 from the Red Hills region of Alabama and Georgia, producing intensely fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers in shades of cream, pale pink, orange, and yellow in late spring to early summer, with considerable variation in color among individual plants. As a genuine Gulf South native azalea, it is exceptionally well suited to zone 8–9 gardens where many other native azaleas struggle with heat and humidity, making it an excellent choice for a naturalized woodland border in the Deep South. It tolerates more heat than mountain-native azaleas but still needs consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil and the dappled light of a high pine or hardwood canopy to perform well.

Plant in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; red justicia is a compact, rounded Arizona and Sonoran shrub with small, bright green leaves and clusters of vivid red-orange, tubular flowers produced heavily in spring and again in fall, with lighter, sporadic bloom through summer in favorable conditions. It is a reliable, easy-care hummingbird plant for desert gardens, tolerating both reflected heat in full sun and the dappled light of a partially shaded courtyard or wash-side planting. Established plants are quite drought tolerant, though occasional deep watering during the hottest, driest stretches keeps the foliage fuller and encourages more consistent flowering. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to maintain a dense, rounded form, and expect frost damage to the top growth in a hard freeze, with recovery from the base typical the following spring.

Red Mangrove is one of the most ecologically important coastal trees in the subtropical and tropical Americas, forming the seaward fringe of mangrove forests along sheltered tidal coasts, estuaries, and coastal lagoons of Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean, where its arching prop roots create a complex three-dimensional habitat supporting hundreds of species of fish, invertebrates, birds, and reptiles. The species is viviparous — the seeds germinate on the parent tree itself, producing cigar-shaped propagules up to 12 inches long that drop into the water and drift with currents before anchoring in tidal mudflats and developing new trees. Red Mangrove forests provide irreplaceable ecological services including coastal erosion control, storm surge buffering, carbon sequestration, and water quality filtration; removing them is illegal in Florida and most coastal states. Plant nursery-grown material only in appropriate tidal coastal zones in full sun in Zones 9–11; Red Mangrove is cold-sensitive and should not be planted north of its natural range.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun for best fall color; red maple is one of the most widely distributed and commonly planted native trees in eastern North America, naturally ranging from Newfoundland to Florida and adaptable to an enormous range of soil moisture conditions from wet bottomlands to dry upland ridges. True to its name, red maple puts on a red display in virtually every season: tiny red flowers cluster on bare branches in late winter (often the earliest tree to bloom), red samaras (winged seeds) ripen in spring, the leaf stalks are red through summer, and fall foliage blazes in brilliant shades of orange-red to crimson. The samaras are consumed by squirrels, grosbeaks, and finches; red maple is also a significant larval host plant for the Cecropia moth and numerous other native insects. With a growth rate of 1.5–2.5 feet per year and wide site adaptability, it is one of the most practical large native shade trees for gardens of all sizes.

Set out container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; unlike the tree-form orchid trees (Bauhinia variegata and purpurea), this species is a loose, sprawling, non-invasive shrub with a scrambling habit that can be left informal as a mounding hedge or tied to a fence or trellis for a more vertical effect. Brick-red to orange, orchid-shaped flowers open in flushes from late spring through fall and draw butterflies and hummingbirds reliably. It thrives on neglect once established, tolerating heat, poor soil, and extended dry spells, and its twin-lobed leaves give it a soft, ferny texture even when not in bloom. Where winters dip into the low 20s F it dies back hard but usually resprouts from the base the following spring.

common_name: Red Porterweed (Cayenne Porterweed, Light Blue Snakeweed)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; very drought-tolerant once established; self-sows freely in warm climates. Stachytarpheta cayennensis (Cayenne porterweed or light blue snakeweed) is a tropical perennial shrub native to the Caribbean, tropical Americas, and Central America — closely related to the widely-grown blue porterweed (S. jamaicensis) and sharing its exceptional ecological value as a butterfly nectar plant. Like S. jamaicensis, it produces long, slender, erect spikes with small, individual flowers that open one at a time along the spike over an extended period — but the flowers of S. cayennensis are lighter blue to lavender-blue and slightly smaller than those of S. jamaicensis. Both species are among the highest-value plants in the tropical butterfly garden: the elongated flower spike design provides ideal perches for feeding butterflies, and the plant blooms nearly continuously in warm climates. Like S. jamaicensis, S. cayennensis is also used medicinally in tropical traditional medicine across its range — as an anti-inflammatory, antifungal, and general tonic herb in Caribbean and Latin American folk medicine. The two species are nearly identical in garden use and can be distinguished mainly by flower size and shade intensity. Often naturalized as a weed in disturbed tropical habitats worldwide.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; red powderpuff is one of the most dramatically beautiful flowering shrubs of the tropical and subtropical world, producing spectacular round clusters of deep crimson stamens that form feathery, silky balls 3–4 inches across — the individual flowers have no petals, only hundreds of brilliant red stamens that create the distinctive powderpuff effect. Blooms appear nearly year-round in frost-free areas and intermittently spring through fall in zone 9. The new foliage emerges in shades of copper and bronze before maturing to glossy dark green, providing an additional season of ornamental interest. An outstanding hummingbird and butterfly plant. Prune lightly after bloom cycles to maintain shape but avoid heavy pruning in fall; the plant blooms on old wood. A white-flowered species (Calliandra surinamensis, pink powderpuff) is also widely grown in Gulf Coast gardens.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Prince weigela is valued for holding its red flower color without fading in heat better than many older red weigela cultivars. Masses of vivid, true-red, trumpet-shaped flowers smother the arching branches in late spring, with a lighter rebloom often following in summer, on a vigorous, cold-hardy shrub with clean green foliage that provides a dependable backbone of bright color for a mixed shrub border. Its non-fading red flower color and strong cold tolerance made it a standard, widely planted weigela cultivar for decades, valued by gardeners for its reliability over showier but less hardy newer introductions. Prune immediately after the main spring flush to shape and encourage rebloom, since it flowers primarily on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Red Sister Ti Plant (Brilliant Red-Foliage Cordyline Tropical Accent)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to bright indirect light; Red Sister is the most widely planted ti plant (Cordyline fruticosa) cultivar in Gulf South landscaping — producing long, strap-shaped, arching leaves in brilliant burgundy-red to rose-red and magenta-pink tones that provide a year-round tropical foliage focal point in warm-climate gardens. The name 'ti plant' refers to the Pacific Islander cultural significance of Cordyline fruticosa, where the plant carries deep spiritual and traditional meaning and is widely used in ceremonial contexts throughout Polynesia and Hawaii. 'Red Sister' is one of the most intensely and uniformly red ti plant cultivars — the long, lance-shaped leaves (12–24 inches) are a rich, saturated red-magenta through much of the year, sometimes with lighter pink margins that create a luminous, two-tone effect. In zone 9b-12, Red Sister grows as a perennial tropical shrub reaching 3–6 feet with arching rosettes of foliage; in zone 9a, it is often used as a container plant moved indoors before frost or as a warm-season annual-style tropical replaced each spring. The bold red foliage creates outstanding contrast with green-foliaged tropical plants — ginger, elephant ear, bird of paradise — where the red provides the warm color accent that defines a classic tropical border composition.

Red Stopper is a native evergreen shrub or small tree of the subtropical coastal hammocks of the Florida Keys and Miami-Dade County, as well as much of the Caribbean, producing small clusters of edible red to black berries that are sweet and aromatic, relished by white-crowned pigeons, mockingbirds, and other subtropical fruit-eating birds. The glossy, elliptical leaves emit a spicy fragrance when crushed, typical of the Eugenia family, and the small, white, brush-like flowers attract native bees and butterflies. A component of the critically imperiled South Florida coastal hardwood hammock community, Red Stopper is an attractive, slow-growing landscape shrub for Zone 10–11 coastal gardens, providing wildlife value, year-round evergreen foliage, seasonal flowers, and colorful edible berries. Plant in well-drained, rocky to sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant in coastal settings.

common_name: Red Sunset Maple (Early Orange-Red Fall-Color Red Maple)
notes: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply through establishment to help the root system develop before the tree faces summer heat stress on its own. Red Sunset is a widely planted red maple cultivar selected for its uniform, upright-oval crown and consistently outstanding orange-red fall color, which typically develops earlier in autumn than October Glory, making the two cultivars useful companions for extending a red maple color display across several weeks. Like other red maples, it bears small red flowers on bare branches in late winter and grows at a moderate to fast rate into a dense, symmetrical shade tree well suited to lawns, streets, and parks. It adapts to a range of soil types, including occasional wet conditions, though it performs best with consistent moisture and acidic to neutral soil. Prune to remove dead or crossing branches in late fall or winter dormancy to minimize sap bleeding from cuts.

common_name: Red Tip Photinia (Fraser Photinia, Red Robin Photinia)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun with good air circulation; Red Tip Photinia is one of the most widely planted and most recognizable landscape shrubs in the American South — a large, fast-growing evergreen producing stunning flushes of brilliant scarlet-red new growth throughout spring and into summer, creating a spectacular multi-season display as the vivid red leaves mature to glossy dark green. This red new growth is the plant's defining ornamental feature and the reason for its extraordinary popularity. Flat-topped clusters of creamy-white flowers appear in spring. Red Tip Photinia grows vigorously to 10–15 feet tall but responds readily to shearing as a formal hedge at whatever height is needed. However, heavy shearing stimulates rapid new growth — which, while ornamentally attractive for its color, also provides dense, susceptible tissue for the plant's primary disease problem: Entomosporium maculatum leaf spot, which causes spreading purple-red spots with gray centers that disfigure and eventually defoliate plants in humid, warm climates. In zone 9, Entomosporium can be severe in dense plantings with poor air circulation. Planting in full sun with wide spacing and avoiding overhead irrigation reduces, but does not eliminate, the risk. The disease has significantly reduced Red Tip Photinia's use in zone 9 plantings since the 1990s; Ternstroemia gymnanthera is sometimes recommended as a disease-resistant alternative providing similar red new growth.

common_name: Red Turks Cap (Mexican Sleeping Hibiscus Shade-Tolerant Hummingbird Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Turk's Cap (Malvaviscus arboreus var. mexicanus) is a Gulf South garden classic and one of the most important hummingbird-attracting plants for the region — a robust, fast-growing shrub producing bright red, tubular, never-fully-opening flowers from summer through frost, the twisted petals and protruding stamens creating the distinctive 'sleeping hibiscus' appearance that gives the plant one of its common names. The flower form — a narrow, twisted tube of red petals rather than the open cup of a blooming hibiscus — is precisely adapted to hummingbird feeding: only a long bill can access the nectar at the base, making Malvaviscus one of the premier hummingbird plants for the Gulf South. The Mexican variety grows larger, more vigorously, and with larger leaves and flowers than the native Texas Turk's Cap (var. drummondii), reaching 6–9 feet in a single growing season in warm zone 9 conditions. One of the exceptional qualities of Red Turk's Cap is its extraordinary shade tolerance — unlike most flowering shrubs, it blooms prolifically in partial to deep shade, filling the critical niche of shade-tolerant flowering shrub that few Gulf South plants can occupy. Under large live oaks and pines, where most flowering plants decline, Turk's Cap thrives and blooms from June through December. In zone 9, the tops may be killed by hard freezes but plants return vigorously from the roots in spring. Excellent for naturalizing in large shade garden areas.

Plant in moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to full shade; red-osier dogwood produces its most vivid winter stem color in full sun but tolerates significant shade, making it one of the few native shrubs that lights up a shady winter garden with brilliant crimson branches. The white berries ripen in summer and are eaten by over 40 bird species, and the dense thicket provides year-round nesting cover. Rejuvenate the shrub every two to three years by cutting one-third of the oldest canes to the ground in early spring, since the brightest stem color comes from young growth. The stoloniferous habit forms broad colonies excellent for streambank stabilization and erosion control.

Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; redberry juniper is exceptionally drought-tolerant, adapted to the caliche and limestone soils of west and central Texas rangeland. Dense, scale-like, blue-green to gray-green foliage covers a shrubby, multi-trunked small tree that produces distinctive brick-red to copper-colored, berry-like cones rather than the more typical blue-gray of most junipers, making it easy to distinguish from the similar Ashe juniper it often grows alongside. Native to the rocky plains, canyons, and mesas of west and central Texas, New Mexico, and Oklahoma, it provides valuable cover and winter food for wildlife and tolerates the region's extreme heat, drought, and thin, rocky soils with ease once established. It is considered a rangeland-encroachment concern in some grazing contexts but remains a tough, low-water landscape choice for xeriscape plantings on difficult, rocky sites.

growth_habit: species shrub rose grown for foliage
notes: Set plants in well-drained soil amended with compost, in a spot with at least six hours of sun, and water deeply during the first growing season to establish a strong root system. Prune only lightly in late winter to shape the arching canes, since flowers form on both old and new wood. This species rose is grown chiefly for its plum-purple to blue-gray foliage on wine-red stems, with small single pink flowers in late spring followed by showy orange-red hips that persist into winter. It tolerates partial shade and poor soil better than most garden roses, making it a striking hedge or background plant.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into well-drained, gravelly to loamy soil in full sun to light shade, giving the upright, reddish-stemmed canes room along a streambank, open woodland edge, or recently cleared site. Redstem ceanothus is named for its distinctive maroon-red young bark, which stands out clearly against the surrounding forest even in winter. Dense conical clusters of fragrant white flowers open in late spring and are worked heavily by native bees, butterflies, and other pollinating insects, while deer and elk browse the twigs and foliage and grouse and small mammals eat the seed. It readily resprouts after fire or cutting, making it valuable early cover and forage in recovering forest habitat.

Plant in moist, very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; redvein enkianthus is an outstanding but underused deciduous shrub with four seasons of ornamental interest. In spring before the leaves emerge, pendulous clusters of small cream-to-pale-yellow bell-shaped flowers delicately striped with red veins are produced at branch tips — the striped pattern gives the species and cultivar names. The neat, whorled foliage arrangement on tiered branches creates an attractive, layered architecture through summer. In fall the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and yellow — among the best fall color of any flowering shrub. The upright, vase-shaped habit and slow growth make it suitable for smaller gardens. It thrives alongside azaleas, rhododendrons, mountain laurels, and other acid-loving shrubs in woodland settings, requiring the same culture: moist, acidic, organic, well-drained soil and partial shade. Performs best in zones 4–7 where reliable winter cold is available; marginally hardy in zone 8 in cool, shaded, moist sites.

common_name: Reine des Violettes Rose (Queen of the Violets Hybrid Perpetual)
notes: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and give the nearly thornless canes room to arch gracefully rather than crowding them against other shrubs. Bred by Millet-Malet in France and introduced in 1860, Reine des Violettes is a Hybrid Perpetual prized for its flat, quartered, old-rose-form blooms that open cerise-pink and mature to a striking violet-mauve unlike almost any other rose, carrying a strong, classic old-rose fragrance. It repeat-blooms through the growing season, though most heavily in spring, and its soft gray-green foliage and graceful, relatively thornless growth make it a favorite for cottage-style borders and cutting gardens. Prune lightly after the first flush to encourage further rebloom and remove any dead or crossing wood in late winter.

Plant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light; Renegade cordyline holds its deep burgundy color best with abundant light. Narrow, glossy leaves emerge nearly solid deep burgundy-red to near-black, one of the darkest and most saturated color selections among cordyline cultivars, forming an upright, cane-like clump that provides bold, season-long color contrast against green-leaved companions in a tropical or container planting. Its compact size and reliably intense dark coloring, holding well through the season without fading to green in reasonable light, make it a popular choice for adding a strong color anchor to mixed tropical containers and landscape beds in frost-free climates. Water when the top inch of soil dries, provide bright light for the deepest color, and protect from any frost.

Retama is one of the most spectacular native flowering trees of the Texas coastal region and Gulf South — its weeping, bright green photosynthetic stems and spine-tipped branches give it a distinctive architectural silhouette year-round, and in spring it erupts into cascading sprays of fragrant, bright yellow flowers with an orange-spotted petal that is so showy it has been called 'Jerusalem thorn' in the Anglo tradition and 'retama' in the Spanish South Texas culture. The photosynthetic green bark allows the tree to produce energy even during droughts when leaves (tiny, feathery leaflets on long, drooping rachises) may drop, enabling survival in extreme heat and drought that would kill most trees. Retama grows exceptionally fast — often 6–8 feet per year in good conditions — making it useful for rapid screening and shade creation in south Texas landscapes; it also serves as an important nectar plant for native bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds and provides nesting habitat for orioles and doves. The tree is armed with paired thorns and is not recommended near high-traffic areas.

Rheingold is a slow-growing, dwarf, rounded-to-conical arborvitae valued for foliage color that shifts through the seasons, emerging soft yellow-gold in spring, deepening to a rich old-gold through summer, and warming further to coppery bronze in fall and winter cold. Its compact form and long season of changing color make it a favorite specimen for rock gardens, mixed conifer beds, and foundation plantings where a small, slow-growing accent with year-round interest is wanted. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the best color development; like other arborvitae it prefers cooler climates and is not well suited to the extreme heat and humidity of the Deep South.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, setting the root ball slightly high with a thick mulch of pine bark or leaf litter over the shallow roots. Choose a site in dappled woodland shade or a boggy edge where soil stays cool and evenly damp, since this species naturally grows in bog margins, wet thickets, and open coniferous woods across the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. In May, before its leaves fully expand, the low twiggy shrub covers itself in clusters of rosy-purple flowers with an unusual two-lipped shape. It is one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant native azaleas and works well in a naturalized woodland or rain garden planting where taller shade trees keep the summer sun off its foliage.

Divide underground stolons or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; rice paper plant (Chinese rice paper plant) is a bold, dramatic Asian shrub that produces some of the largest leaves of any hardy to zone 8 plant — enormous, deeply lobed, palmate leaves that can reach 3 feet or more across on stems that rise to 6–15 feet, creating an instantly tropical, jungle-like effect with no equivalent in temperate gardening. The felted undersides of the leaves provide a contrasting silver-gray texture. The traditional Chinese paper used for making rice paper paintings is made from the pith of the stems. It spreads steadily by underground stolons to form expanding colonies, which can be managed by mowing around the perimeter; this spreading habit also makes it excellent for covering large areas. In zone 8, top growth is killed by frost but the plant rebounds from underground stolons vigorously each spring, often reaching 8–10 feet by summer. 'Steroidal Giant' is a selection with even larger leaves.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in partial shade; ring-cupped oak is a beautiful East Asian evergreen oak widely distributed from Japan through China, Korea, and the Himalayas — an important component of warm-temperate and subtropical Asian forests. The attractive, evergreen, lanceolate to oblong leaves have characteristic waxy, blue-gray (glaucous) undersides that give the species its name. The acorn cups have distinctive concentric ring-shaped ridges (hence 'ring-cupped'). More shade-tolerant than most oaks — an unusual characteristic that makes it appropriate for partially shaded sites where most oaks would struggle. In Japanese gardens it is used as a refined evergreen specimen tree. Adaptable to the warm, humid southeastern US climate in zones 7–9. The glossy, dark-green, evergreen foliage provides year-round interest. An underused Asian evergreen oak for southern US gardens where holm oak might also be grown.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, alkaline soil in full sun; Rio Bravo sage is a South Texas native shrub in the cenizo group, with small, silvery-gray, felted leaves and abundant lavender-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers that burst into bloom within a day or two of rain or a sharp rise in humidity, a trait that has earned cenizo shrubs the folk name 'barometer bush' across South Texas. It stays somewhat more compact than the widely planted Texas sage (Leucophyllum frutescens) and tends to flower even more heavily and reliably after rain events. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, it thrives in poor, rocky, or caliche soil that would stress most ornamental shrubs, needing only excellent drainage and full sun. Prune minimally and only to shape, since heavy shearing removes the natural silvery, rounded form and reduces the flush of bloom that follows each rain.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically flooded soil in full sun to light partial shade; river birch is the most adaptable and heat-tolerant native birch in North America, naturally occurring along streambanks and floodplains from New Hampshire to Florida and west to Kansas. Unlike the European white birch, river birch is highly resistant to the bronze birch borer and bronze birch clearwing, making it a far more reliable long-term landscape tree throughout most of the eastern US. The ornamental exfoliating bark — cinnamon to salmon-pink to creamy-white — peels in papery curls to reveal new inner bark throughout the year, providing outstanding four-season interest. River birch grows quickly (1.5–2 feet per year) and tolerates both wet, poorly drained soils and moderate drought once established, an unusually wide site adaptability. The small winged seeds are relished by chickadees, redpolls, and pine siskins in late winter.

common_name: Roald Dahl Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2016 and named for the celebrated children's author, Roald Dahl bears warm peachy-pink, cupped rosette flowers with a light, fresh tea fragrance, on a healthy, compact, disease-resistant shrub bred to hold clean foliage through humid summers with minimal spraying. It flowers freely and repeats reliably from late spring through frost, making it a dependable, easy-care choice for gardeners wanting classic English-rose form without a demanding maintenance routine.

common_name: Robin Holly (Bronze-Red New Growth Screening Holly)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Robin is a pyramidal hybrid holly notable for the striking bronze-red flush of its new spring growth, which matures to glossy dark green and contrasts attractively with the bright red berries produced later in the season when a compatible male holly is planted nearby for pollination. Its dense, upright form and moderate size make it a versatile choice for screening, hedging, and specimen use in the landscape, requiring only occasional shaping to maintain a neat outline. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, and consistent watering during the first couple of seasons speeds root establishment.

Plant in spring in well-drained upland soils or limestone-based ground where this slow-growing elm forms a narrow, pyramidal crown distinct from the vase shape of American elm. Distinctive corky wings often develop along its branches, giving winter interest that sets it apart from other native elms. Rock elm shows somewhat better resistance to Dutch elm disease than American elm, making it a worthwhile alternative for restoration plantings and long-lived shade in northern landscapes. Its exceptionally dense, heavy wood was historically valued for tool handles and shipbuilding, reflecting the tree's slow, sturdy growth habit.

common_name: Rock Rose (Texas Pavonia, Rose Mallow Pavonia)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas pavonia is one of the most outstanding native shrubs for the Gulf Coast garden — a compact, woody perennial shrub that produces a profusion of small (1.5 inch) single rose-pink flowers with yellow stamens continuously from spring through frost, with peak bloom in summer. Each individual flower lasts only a day, but the plant produces new flowers constantly for 6+ months, creating a long-lasting display. It tolerates alkaline soil, drought, and heat and actually blooms better under mild stress than in rich, moist conditions. Deer resistant and attractive to hummingbirds and butterflies. In zone 7–8, top growth may be killed by hard freezes but roots resprout vigorously in spring. Light pruning in late winter promotes compact, bushy growth.

common_name: Rockspray Cotoneaster (Low Spreading Fishbone-Branched Groundcover with Red Berries)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants tolerate drought, poor rocky soil, and wind, making this a reliable choice for slopes, banks, and low-maintenance beds where little else thrives. Rockspray cotoneaster is named for its distinctive herringbone or 'fishbone' branching pattern, with stiff horizontal branches that hug the ground and layer over each other as the plant spreads, studded with small glossy dark green leaves that turn red-orange in fall. Small white to pink flowers appear in late spring and are followed by abundant bright red berries that persist into winter, providing food for birds and strong seasonal color over bare or rocky ground. It needs minimal pruning beyond removing dead wood, and its low, wide-spreading habit make it a classic choice for cascading over walls and covering banks where mowing is impractical.

Plant in moist, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Rocky Mountain maple is a multi-stemmed native small tree or large shrub found from Alaska to New Mexico in canyon bottoms, streamside areas, and the cool slopes of the Rocky Mountains and Cascades. It is one of the most important browse plants for mule deer, elk, and moose in the West. The distinctive three-lobed leaves are bright green in summer, turning yellow, orange, and red in fall — a spectacular display in mountain settings. More drought-tolerant than most maples once established. The samaras are consumed by small birds and squirrels. Excellent for naturalizing in shaded, moist spots in western gardens and mountain landscapes where conditions suit its northern and montane origins.

Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs or scrambles into full sun to light shade. Rooguchi is a distinctive Japanese viticella-type hybrid bearing nodding, bell-shaped, thick-petaled flowers in deep purple-blue with a paler, twisted, recurved petal tip, a form entirely different from the flat, open flowers of most large-flowered clematis, blooming continuously from early summer into fall. Its lax, semi-climbing habit works well trained on a low trellis or obelisk, woven through a shrub, or left to sprawl at the front of a border, and unlike many clematis it flowers on new growth, so it can be cut back hard in late winter. Its long, prolific bloom season and unusual flower form have made it a favorite among clematis collectors and gardeners looking for something different from the typical large-flowered hybrids.

Take hardwood cuttings 6 to 8 inches long from dormant stems in late winter and root them in a sandy propagation medium with bottom heat. Alternatively, dig rooted suckers from established clumps in early spring and transplant directly to the desired location. Plant in full sun in well-drained, even poor or sandy soil, as rich conditions encourage excessive suckering at the expense of flowering. Install a root barrier if planting near walkways or structures, as this shrub spreads vigorously by underground stolons.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rose Creek is a compact, cold-hardy abelia cultivar selected for its tight, mounding growth habit (2–3 feet tall and wide), exceptional cold hardiness (reliably hardy to zone 5 with protection, zone 6 without), and profuse white flower production from spring through frost. The white, tubular flowers are produced on arching stems in clusters and have the characteristic sweet, light fragrance of abelia flowers that attracts butterflies and hummingbirds. The small, dark-green foliage turns attractive bronze-reddish in fall and winter, providing seasonal color change interest. Rose Creek is somewhat more upright and compact than standard Abelia × grandiflora and its smaller stature makes it appropriate for tight foundation positions and smaller garden spaces where standard abelia would become too large. Like all abelias, Rose Creek is remarkably adaptable — tolerating clay soils, drought, heat, humidity, and partial shade that challenge many flowering shrubs. Minimal pruning is needed — remove any winter-damaged stems in late winter and lightly shape immediately after spring bloom if size control is needed. Plant 3–5 for foundation borders or in masses for sweeping effect.

Plant in partial sun with rich, evenly moist soil; in hotter climates, afternoon shade helps prevent wilting and keeps the large leaves looking their best through summer. The enormous domed clusters of fragrant rose-pink flowers appear from July through September and are highly attractive to butterflies. Be aware that this shrub spreads aggressively by root suckers, especially in zone 9 and warmer — install a root barrier or remove suckers promptly to prevent unwanted spread. In zones 7 and 8 the top growth is often killed by frost but roots reliably resprout in spring; cut dead stems to the ground and apply a thick mulch layer over the root zone each winter.

common_name: Rose Glow Barberry (Mottled Pink-and-Purple Foliage Dwarf Barberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since the mottled pink-purple color develops most intensely with good light exposure. Rose Glow is a compact, thorny barberry cultivar valued for new growth that emerges deep purple heavily mottled and splashed with rose-pink and white, giving each shrub a distinctive marbled, variegated look that matures to a more uniform reddish-purple as leaves age through the season. Its dense, twiggy, thorned branching makes it useful as a barrier planting or accent, and small yellow spring flowers are followed by red berries that persist into winter. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and low-maintenance, needing only an occasional shaping prune, but because Japanese barberry seeds into wild areas and displaces native understory plants in much of the eastern and midwestern US, gardeners should confirm it is not restricted or invasive in their area before planting.

common_name: Rose of Venezuela (Scarlet Bouquet Tree, Brownea grandiceps)
notes: Plant in partial shade to dappled light in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Brownea grandiceps is a natural tropical forest understory tree that grows in the bright, filtered light beneath the forest canopy and performs best in garden conditions that replicate this environment. Brownea grandiceps is a medium-sized evergreen tree from Venezuela and adjacent Colombia in the family Leguminosae (Fabaceae), considered one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the tropical world — alongside Amherstia nobilis and Delonix regia — for the extraordinary quality and appearance of its flowers. The inflorescences are large, dense, spherical or dome-shaped heads of 50–100 individual tubular flowers, each 2–3 inches long, in vivid scarlet to orange-red with pale yellow stamens — the combined head is 8–14 inches across and resembles a massive, burning, scarlet cushion or bouquet emerging directly from the branch tips. The flowers are produced in successive flushes, primarily in spring and fall, and at peak bloom an established tree may carry dozens of the massive heads simultaneously. The emerging new leaves are equally spectacular: they appear as long, limp, silky, coppery-pink tassels hanging vertically from the branch tips before gradually stiffening and turning green — a phenomenon called 'juvenile leaf wilting' that occurs in many rainforest trees as a strategy to make young leaves unattractive to herbivores. Among the most prized ornamental trees in zone 10-11 tropical collections.

common_name: Rose of Venezuela (Scarlet Flame Bean, Mountain Rose)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; provide irrigation during dry periods. Brownea coccinea (Rose of Venezuela or scarlet flame bean) is a tropical South American tree widely regarded as one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the tropics — a standard in tropical botanical gardens worldwide precisely because of two extraordinary visual displays. The first: large, dome-shaped, tightly packed heads (capitula) of brilliant scarlet-red, tubular flowers — 6–10 inches across — that emerge directly from the branches and trunk (cauliflory), creating a dense, ball-like cluster of brilliant red against the green foliage. The second: the remarkable display of new leaf growth — young leaves emerge in hanging 'pendant' clusters, beginning as soft, limp, pale-pink to cream-colored 'ribbons' of young leaflets that hang limply below the branch tips before gradually stiffening, darkening to green, and taking their mature position. This juvenile 'drooping' display of new leaves is one of the most unusual and memorable sights in tropical horticulture. Brownea is in the legume family (Fabaceae) and is related to the flamboyant tree. In zone 10–12, it makes an outstanding specimen tree for tropical gardens, botanical collections, and large spaces where a genuinely rare and spectacular ornamental is desired.

Rosebay rhododendron (great laurel) is the largest native rhododendron in North America — capable of reaching 20–35 feet in the moist, cool, deep shade of Appalachian stream gorges and hemlock forests — and produces massive trusses of white to pale pink, spotted flowers in June and July, a month later than most other rhododendrons, making it the last and largest-flowered of all native flowering shrubs in the eastern forest. Its enormous, glossy, dark green leaves (up to 10 inches long) curl tightly during cold weather as a frost protection mechanism, a distinctive winter character; the dense, multi-stemmed growth creates impenetrable evergreen thickets in shaded stream valleys that are critical winter shelter for ruffed grouse, white-tailed deer, and black bears. It is the most shade-tolerant of all native rhododendrons — thriving in the darkest understory beneath eastern hemlock, where little else with ornamental value grows — and represents one of the few truly shade-tolerant, large-scale evergreen flowering shrubs for the eastern native garden. Grows slowly but long-lived; once established it requires minimal care in appropriate conditions.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rosemary grevillea is an Australian shrub named for its narrow, rosemary-like needle leaves (prickly to the touch) on arching, graceful stems that form a loose, airy, medium-sized shrub 3–6 feet tall. From late autumn through spring it produces clusters of spidery, deep-pink to crimson-red flowers in the distinctive grevillea style — curved, nectar-rich, toothbrush-shaped clusters that are irresistible to hummingbirds and honey-producing bees, providing critical winter nectar during the period when almost no other nectar source flowers in California and the Southwest. One of the most consistently winter-flowering garden shrubs in zones 8b–10. Drought-tolerant once established (requires no summer water in Mediterranean climates), long-lived, and largely pest- and disease-free in appropriate conditions. An essential plant for California native wildlife gardens and for year-round hummingbird habitat.

Roseshell Azalea is a fragrant native deciduous azalea of the northeastern United States and Appalachian Mountains, producing profuse clusters of deep rose-pink to light pink flowers with a strong, sweet clove-like fragrance that perfumes entire gardens in late spring — a quality unique among native azaleas that makes it an outstanding choice wherever fragrance is a garden priority. The most cold-hardy of all native azaleas, surviving USDA Zone 3 reliably, Roseshell Azalea grows in rocky, dry-to-moist, open woods, cliff edges, and forest margins from Quebec south to the Virginia mountains, tolerating somewhat drier and stonier conditions than most other native azalea species. The compact, naturally rounded growth habit, spectacular fragrant flowers, and brilliant orange-red to crimson fall foliage make this a superb multi-season native shrub for northern and mountain landscapes. Plant in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to high, shifting shade under deciduous trees.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Roseum Elegans is one of the most cold-hardy and widely adaptable rhododendron cultivars, tolerating heat, cold, and poor soil better than many fussier hybrids. Large, dense trusses of lavender-pink flowers with a faint orange-brown blotch cover this old, extremely reliable catawba rhododendron hybrid each late spring, backed by large, leathery, deep green evergreen leaves that provide year-round structure to a shaded border. Introduced in the nineteenth century and still one of the most widely planted rhododendron cultivars in North America, it owes its enduring popularity to exceptional cold hardiness, heat tolerance, and general toughness compared to more temperamental modern hybrids, thriving in a wider range of climates and soils. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid planting too deep or in poorly drained soil, and prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.

This hardy evergreen shrub produces clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped blooms in spring above lush foliage. Plant it in spring or fall in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and site it in dappled shade or morning sun. Keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist with a mulch of pine bark or leaves. Avoid deep planting, as the crown must stay near the surface. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape the plant.

Plant in partial sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with protection from harsh wind; Dipelta floribunda develops into a large arching shrub of 10–15 ft and needs generous space to display its full elegance. In late spring, fragrant pale pink flowers with distinctive orange-yellow throats cover the gracefully drooping branches in a display reminiscent of a giant Weigela. After the flowers fade, the papery, wing-like seed bracts persist through summer and add ornamental interest that extends the plant's season of appeal. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape, removing only the oldest and weakest stems; heavy pruning is unnecessary and detracts from the natural arching habit.

common_name: Rotunda Holly (Dwarf Chinese Holly, Mounding Chinese Holly)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rotunda is one of the most widely planted compact foundation shrubs in the Gulf South — a male Chinese holly selection with a dense, rounded, mounding form that stays compact (2–4 feet tall, slightly wider) without the frequent pruning that many other Chinese holly cultivars require to maintain shape. Rotunda does not produce berries (it is a sterile male clone) and is grown purely for its clean, dark-green, heavily spined foliage and reliable, slow-growing mounded form. The extremely sharp, multiple-spined leaves make Rotunda an outstanding security planting under windows and along boundaries — the spines deter entry more effectively than most other barrier plants. Despite the spiny leaves, Rotunda is one of the most versatile, trouble-free foundation shrubs in the Gulf South: it tolerates heavy clay, drought, heat, partial shade, and the year-round humidity without significant pest or disease pressure. In typical residential foundation plantings, Rotunda maintains a clean, tight mound for years with minimal to no pruning — a significant advantage over faster-growing hollies that require aggressive trimming 2–3 times per season. Deer-resistant; essentially maintenance-free in well-drained soil.

common_name: Rotundiloba Fruitless Sweetgum (Seedless Round-Lobed Sweetgum with No Gumballs)
notes: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; Rotundiloba is a naturally occurring seedless selection of American sweetgum, prized for producing the species' spectacular multicolored fall foliage display of yellow, orange, red, and burgundy-purple without the spiny seed balls that make standard sweetgum a nuisance on lawns, patios, and walkways. Its distinctive rounded, scalloped leaf lobes (rather than the pointed star shape of typical sweetgum) also make it easy to identify at a glance even before fall color develops. Like the species it grows into a large, handsome shade tree with a somewhat narrower, more upright habit than seed-grown sweetgum, transplanting readily when young and establishing quickly in the landscape. Because it sets no seed, it also does not provide the winter seed-ball forage that goldfinches and other birds rely on from wild sweetgum, a worthwhile tradeoff to weigh where wildlife value is a priority.

This French-bred cultivar is valued for its velvety, deep ruby-red blooms with contrasting cream-yellow anthers, produced in flushes from early to late summer. As a pruning group three vine, cut all stems back to a strong bud pair roughly twelve inches above the soil in late winter each year to keep growth vigorous and floriferous. It performs best with its roots shaded and cool and its foliage and flowers reaching into full sun on a trellis, fence, or through a shrub. Regular moisture and an annual topdressing of compost help sustain its rich color through the season.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; rough velvetseed is frost-tender and native to coastal hammocks and pinelands of South Florida. Rough, sandpaper-textured leaves cover a large shrub or small tree bearing small, fragrant, white to cream flowers followed by red berries that turn black as they ripen, providing food for a range of native birds and wildlife across its hammock and coastal scrub habitat. Well adapted to the poor, well-drained, often rocky limestone soils typical of South Florida's native plant communities, it tolerates both dry, sunny sites and the partial shade of a hammock understory, making it a versatile choice for naturalistic native landscaping. It needs little supplemental water or fertilizer once established and provides good wildlife habitat value with minimal maintenance.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; rough-leaf hydrangea is a large, bold-textured shrub from Asia that differs dramatically from the common mophead and lacecap hydrangeas — it produces enormous, velvety, felted leaves up to 10 inches long on stout stems covered with coarse hairs, giving the plant a distinctly tropical, textural quality. The large lacecap flower heads in midsummer bear pale lavender to purple fertile flowers surrounded by white to soft pink sterile ray flowers in a classic lacecap pattern, but on a much larger scale than Hydrangea macrophylla. The combination of the huge, rough-textured foliage and the lacecap flowers makes it an outstanding architectural shrub for woodland shade gardens. It performs better than mophead hydrangeas in zone 7–9 heat and humidity. The subspecies and cultivar 'Macrophylla' (also called villosa hydrangea) is the most widely grown selection. Provide consistent moisture and protection from drying winds.

Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — roughleaf dogwood is a tough, suckering native shrub or small multi-stem tree of southern woodlands, thickets, and stream edges, producing flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by pea-sized, creamy-white berries on red pedicels in late summer that are among the most intensely sought fruits by migrating songbirds. The rough-textured, opposite leaves turn attractive shades of maroon and wine-red in fall. It spreads by root suckers to form dense, multi-stem thickets that provide outstanding cover and food for wildlife year-round. Adaptable to dry, rocky, alkaline conditions unusual among dogwoods — an outstanding native for difficult southern sites where flowering dogwood (C. florida) struggles. Prune out oldest stems periodically to maintain vigor and an open, attractive form.

Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun for wildlife habitat restoration in naturalistic settings; roundleaf greenbrier is the most widespread and familiar Smilax species of eastern North American woodlands, forming nearly impenetrable thickets of stout, thorny, green-barked stems along forest edges, thicket margins, and disturbed moist areas. The rounded, shiny green leaves with prominent parallel veining are distinctive, remaining deep green through summer before turning a dull yellow in fall. The blue-black berry clusters persist through winter and are among the most important winter food sources for mockingbirds, catbirds, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and wild turkeys. Dense greenbrier thickets serve as critical nesting habitat, providing protection from predators that avoids entering the thorny tangles. Young shoots are eaten in spring. A foundational wildlife plant for large naturalized areas, woodland restorations, and edge habitats.

Plant in spring or early fall into moist, acidic, well-drained soil enriched with compost or leaf mold, siting it where dappled shade shields the flowers and foliage from harsh afternoon sun. Native to the mountain woodlands of Korea, Manchuria, and Japan, it naturally grows as an understory shrub and performs best with morning sun and afternoon shelter from taller trees. In mid-spring, fragrant pale pink flowers open just as the whorled, obovate leaves emerge, and those same leaves often turn attractive shades of orange and red in fall, giving the shrub two strong seasons of interest. Its tiered branching habit and unusually large, rounded leaves make it a distinctive specimen for a woodland garden rather than just a spring-bloom shrub.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; royal paulownia is the larger-flowered Chinese species of paulownia — a massive, fast-growing tree with enormous heart-shaped leaves (up to 18 inches) and spectacular large, fragrant, pale lilac-white, foxglove-shaped flowers in early spring (before the leaves emerge). The flowers are larger and paler in color than those of the more commonly planted princess tree (Paulownia tomentosa). One of the world's fastest-growing hardwood trees, capable of 10–20 feet of growth in the first year from seed and 8–15 feet per year subsequently in ideal conditions. The exceptionally light, strong, rot-resistant wood dries rapidly without warping and is highly valued in Japan (where it's called kiri) for making chests, musical instruments (koto), and wooden sandals. Produces billions of tiny seeds from its large, oval seed capsules — be vigilant about removing seed pods before they open to prevent invasive spread in moist eastern US forests where it has naturalized. More heat-tolerant than princess tree.

Royal Poinciana is widely considered the most spectacular flowering tree in the world, native to the dry deciduous forests of Madagascar and now naturalized throughout the tropics and subtropics, producing in late spring and summer an overwhelming canopy of enormous, brilliant scarlet-orange flowers with yellow-tipped petals that can completely conceal the wide-spreading, umbrella-shaped crown — a display so vivid that the tree is visible from miles away. The fine, bipinnate, ferny foliage provides delicate shade during the non-flowering months, and the dark brown seed pods (up to 2 feet long) persist through winter, rattling in the wind. In zones 10–11 it is reliably perennial, and in favorable coastal conditions may be semi-evergreen; it is killed to the ground by even light frost and therefore confined to South Florida, the Florida Keys, and other subtropical areas in the continental US. Grows extremely fast — up to 5 feet per year in good conditions — but needs 5–10 years to reach first flowering. Provide well-drained soil, full sun, and space for its wide-spreading roots and canopy.

common_name: Royal Purple Smokebush (Classic Deep Purple Foliage Smoke Tree)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, where drainage is excellent; smokebush dislikes heavy, wet soil. Royal Purple is the classic, most widely planted dark-leaved smokebush cultivar, producing rounded, deep wine-purple leaves throughout the growing season, often shifting to fiery orange-red in fall, combined with airy, wispy, pinkish-purple flower and seed plumes in summer that create the smoky, cloud-like haze giving the plant its common name. It is highly drought-tolerant once established and tolerates poor, lean soil better than rich, moist conditions, which can promote weak, floppy growth. Prune in late winter if a more compact, densely foliaged shrub is wanted, since hard pruning sacrifices the smoky flower plumes that year but produces larger, bolder leaves.

common_name: Royal Red Butterfly Bush (Deep Magenta-Red Buddleja)
notes: Royal Red is one of the older, most established butterfly bush cultivars, producing long, dense, conical flower spikes in an intense reddish-magenta-purple that reads as the deepest red available among widely grown butterfly bush colors, each with a small orange eye at the center of the individual florets. It blooms in heavy flushes from summer through fall on a large, vigorous, arching shrub that draws swallowtails, monarchs, fritillaries, and hummingbirds in significant numbers whenever it is in flower. In zone 9 it behaves as a woody perennial that dies back hard in winter and regrows vigorously each spring, so cut the entire plant back to about 12 inches in late winter to keep growth compact and maximize the coming season's flower production.

common_name: Royal Star Magnolia (Large White Star Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Royal Star is the premier star magnolia cultivar — selected for flowers significantly larger and with more petals (25–30 tepals per flower) than the standard Magnolia stellata species (12–18 tepals), creating a fuller, more sumptuous floral display in late winter to early spring. The flowers are pure white, intensely fragrant with a light vanilla-rose scent, and open from fuzzy silver-gray buds in late February through March (in zone 7–8) before any foliage appears — the bare branches covered with star-shaped, multi-petaled white flowers creating one of the most beautiful early spring floral spectacles of any woody plant. Royal Star also blooms approximately one week later than the species — a practical advantage since the open flowers of star magnolia are frequently damaged by late frosts in zone 4–7. The later bloom timing extends the frost-free blooming window significantly. Magnolia stellata and Royal Star are naturally slow-growing, multi-stemmed shrubs to small trees reaching 10–15 feet over many decades. In zone 9, star magnolia blooms very early but may struggle in the hottest, most humid portions — it performs best in zone 5–8 and in the cooler microclimates of zone 9a.

common_name: Rozannie Aucuba (Compact Self-Fruiting Female Japanese Aucuba)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where its solid deep-green, glossy leaves brighten deep-shade spots that stump most flowering shrubs. Rozannie is a compact, dense, rounded female Aucuba japonica selection prized for being reliably self-fertile, so it produces its clusters of glossy scarlet berries through fall and winter on its own, without needing a male plant growing nearby the way most Aucuba cultivars do. Its naturally tidy, mounding habit needs little pruning to stay in bounds, making it a low-maintenance choice for foundation plantings, woodland gardens, and shaded courtyards where year-round structure and winter berry color are wanted. It tolerates deep shade, dry shade once established, and heavy clay better than most broadleaf evergreens, and it is notably resistant to deer browsing.

common_name: Rubber Tree (Rubber Plant, Indian Rubber Fig)
notes: Grow in bright indirect light to part shade — Rubber Tree adapts to a wide range of light conditions from low indoor light to outdoor filtered sun, but grows fastest and develops the deepest foliage color in bright, indirect light. Ficus elastica is a tropical tree native to India (Assam, Meghalaya) and Malaysia that grows into a massive 100-foot banyan-form tree in its native habitat, producing aerial roots that descend to form additional trunks — in Indian forests, single trees can span an enormous area. In cultivation worldwide, it is one of the most popular large houseplants and patio container trees, prized for its large (8–12 inch), thick, glossy, dark green leaves that give the plant a bold, tropical presence. The standard green 'Decora' and 'Robusta' cultivars are joined by dark red-burgundy 'Burgundy' (nearly black leaves in high light), cream-edged 'Tineke', and the highly popular tri-color 'Ruby' (pink, green, and cream variegated). In zone 10-11 landscapes, planted outdoors it grows into a large canopy tree eventually. The common name refers to the milky latex sap — exploited commercially before the rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) replaced it as the primary natural rubber source in the 19th century. CAUTION: Sap is a serious skin and eye irritant; all parts toxic if eaten.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; 'Rubella' is a male-flowering selection grown for its ornamental winter buds and fragrant spring flowers rather than for berries, since it does not set fruit. This compact, mounding, evergreen skimmia selection is prized for its conspicuous red flower buds that form in fall and persist ornamentally through winter, opening in early spring into fragrant clusters of small white flowers with red-tinged anthers that scent the garden. Because 'Rubella' is a male clone it produces no berries itself, but it is an excellent pollinator for female skimmia cultivars grown nearby for their showy red winter fruit, and its dense, glossy foliage and winter buds provide year-round interest on their own. It thrives in deep shade where few flowering evergreens perform well, making it a valuable choice for a shaded foundation planting or woodland garden.

common_name: Ruby Falls Redbud (Weeping Purple-Leaf Dwarf Redbud)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting where its weeping branches can cascade freely. Ruby Falls combines two desirable redbud traits rarely found together — the deep, rich purple foliage of Forest Pansy and the graceful, cascading branch structure of a weeping cultivar — on a genuinely dwarf tree that typically stays under 10 feet tall, considerably smaller than most purple-leaf redbud selections. In early spring, the weeping branches are studded with the species' typical rosy-pink, pea-like flowers before heart-shaped, glossy purple leaves emerge and hold their color well into summer. Its small mature size and weeping form make it an excellent specimen for a small garden, foundation planting, or large container, where its cascading habit and dark foliage stand out against lighter-colored companions. Provide afternoon shade in zone 8-9 to help the purple foliage resist summer fading and scorch, and plant in well-drained soil since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.

common_name: Ruby Loropetalum (Compact Deep-Purple Foliage Gulf South Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Ruby is a compact Loropetalum chinense (Chinese fringe flower) cultivar producing deep, rich burgundy-purple to reddish-purple evergreen foliage throughout the year, punctuated by prolific flushes of bright magenta-pink, fringe-petaled flowers that create a vivid burgundy-and-magenta combination in spring (March–April) and sporadic rebloom through fall. At 4–6 feet with a similar spread, Ruby is one of the most manageable Loropetalum cultivars for typical residential borders and foundation plantings — the compact, rounded habit is more landscape-appropriate than the large-growing species which can reach 10–15 feet. The deep burgundy foliage holds its rich purple color well through the Gulf South summer without the greening that affects some purple-leaf shrubs in high heat. Loropetalum tolerates considerable drought once established and handles the acidic, often clay soils of the Gulf South coast without significant amendment. The spring bloom is one of the showiest shrub floral displays of the Gulf South spring garden — the combination of the bright magenta flowers against the dark burgundy foliage is visually stunning. Minimal maintenance required: prune immediately after spring bloom to maintain size and shape; avoid late-season pruning that removes flower buds developing for the following spring.

common_name: Ruby Slippers Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dwarf Red-Turning Oakleaf)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ruby Slippers is the most distinctive compact oakleaf hydrangea cultivar — selected not only for its reduced size (3–4 feet, compared to 6–8 feet for the species) but for its exceptional flower color change: the large, conical flower panicles open white in early summer and then turn progressively to deep rose-pink and finally rich ruby-red as they age through summer, providing an extended color display that ranges from pure white in June through rich rose-red by August. This color change from white to red is unique among oakleaf hydrangeas and gives Ruby Slippers a dramatically different appearance from the typical white-only oakleaf cultivars. Like all Hydrangea quercifolia cultivars, Ruby Slippers is a southeastern US native fully adapted to the heat, humidity, clay soils, and shade of the Gulf South — requiring no special care and developing excellent reddish-purple fall foliage color and cinnamon peeling bark for winter interest. The multi-season ornamental qualities, compact size, and distinctive red flower color make Ruby Slippers one of the most celebrated oakleaf hydrangea introductions of the early twenty-first century.

common_name: Ruby Snow Loropetalum (Variegated White-Flowered Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune out any solid-green reverted shoots as soon as they appear to keep the variegation stable. Ruby Snow is an unusual loropetalum grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, with new leaves emerging burgundy-pink and maturing to green heavily marbled and edged in cream-white, a striking departure from the solid purple or green foliage of most loropetalum cultivars, paired with clean white, ribbon-like spring flowers rather than the typical pink or magenta. Its compact, rounded habit and bright, contrasting foliage make it a strong accent or specimen plant where a bolder color break is wanted among evergreen shrubs. Prune lightly right after spring bloom if shaping is needed, since flower buds set on the current season's growth soon after.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade, though it tolerates more sun with consistently wet soil; keep evenly moist, since summersweet does not tolerate prolonged drought. Ruby Spice is a pink-flowered cultivar of the native summersweet, Clethra alnifolia, bred to hold a deeper, more saturated rose-pink flower color through its whole bloom period than older pink selections, which often fade toward white as the flowers age. In mid-to-late summer, dense, upright, bottlebrush-like flower spikes release an intensely sweet, spicy fragrance that carries well through the garden and draws heavy pollinator traffic from bumblebees, honeybees, and butterflies during a period when many other shrubs have finished blooming. The glossy, dark green foliage turns clear yellow in fall before drop. An outstanding fragrant, pollinator-rich choice for a partly shaded, consistently moist border or woodland-edge planting, zone 4–9.

Runner Oak is a low, colony-forming native shrub oak of the coastal plain sandhills and fire-maintained xeric scrub habitats of Georgia and Florida, spreading underground by rhizomes to form dense colonies of knee-high stems across expanses of pure white sand where larger trees cannot survive — making it superficially resemble a grass colony more than a tree. Despite its small stature, Runner Oak produces full-sized acorns that are a critical food source for Florida Scrub-Jays, gopher tortoises, and black bears in the imperiled scrub ecosystem where larger mast-producing oaks may be sparse. Highly adapted to fire, Runner Oak resprouts vigorously from its extensive underground rhizome system within weeks of a scrub burn and is a dominant component of the ground-layer plant community in many Florida scrub sites. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in infertile, pure, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun — Runner Oak requires the xeric, open, fire-maintained conditions of native scrub and will not thrive in more productive or shaded environments.

common_name: Rustica Rubra Magnolia (Later-Blooming Rose-Red Saucer Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Rustica Rubra produces deep rose-red, cup-shaped flowers with a paler interior, blooming somewhat later in spring than Alexandrina and Lennei, which gives it a real practical advantage in regions prone to late hard freezes that can blacken the open flowers of earlier saucer magnolia cultivars. The tree grows into a broad, spreading, multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub, requiring little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, and its rich color makes it a striking spring focal point once established. Give it a sheltered site with consistent moisture for the healthiest growth and most reliable annual bloom.

Rusty Staggerbush is a coarse-textured evergreen shrub or small tree, native to the dry, sandy, scrubby flatwoods, pine ridges, and xeric hammocks of the Florida peninsula and coastal plain from South Carolina to Alabama, distinguished by its large, leathery leaves with rust-colored (ferruginous) scales on the undersides that give the species its common name. In spring it produces clusters of white to pale pink, urn-shaped flowers typical of the heath family (Ericaceae), which are important nectar sources for native bees; the plant may grow 8–20 feet tall in ideal conditions, forming small trees in open scrub habitats. All parts are toxic if ingested by livestock — the 'staggerbush' name refers to the neurological symptoms caused in cattle that graze the foliage. Grow in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it is drought-tolerant once established and an important component of Florida scrub restoration plantings.

Establish in a hot, sunny spot with extremely well-drained, gritty or rocky soil; Sacramento Rose is native to desert mountain slopes and is uniquely adapted to alkaline, low-nutrient conditions that would stress most cultivated roses. Its unusual gooseberry-like divided leaves and bristly stems make it visually distinctive even when not in bloom. Water sparingly after the first season — established plants are highly drought-tolerant and resent overwatering. Propagate by taking semi-hardwood cuttings in early summer and rooting them in very gritty, low-fertility compost; seeds benefit from a warm stratification period followed by cold stratification before germination.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1839, Safrano is one of the oldest tea roses still in general cultivation and was long prized for its long, elegant, saffron-orange buds that open to loosely double, apricot-to-buff blooms with a rich, classic tea fragrance — the scent for which the entire tea rose class is named. Like other tea roses it flowers almost continuously from spring to frost, with the buds often considered more beautiful than the fully open bloom, and it shows good resistance to blackspot in the humid Gulf South compared with modern hybrid teas. The lightly arching, twiggy shrub works well in mixed borders or as an informal low hedge. Minimal pruning is needed — remove dead or crossing wood in late winter and avoid hard cutting back, which reduces the flush of bloom.

Set plants in full sun along the margins of ponds, ditches, or rain gardens where soil stays consistently moist to occasionally brackish, giving the twining stems something low to scramble over. Native to Gulf Coast marshes and estuary edges from Texas to Florida, it produces arrowhead-shaped leaves and funnel-form pink-lavender flowers through the warm months that attract bees and sphinx moths. It is an excellent choice for stabilizing damp, low-lying ground where few other flowering vines will thrive. Once rooted it tolerates both standing water after storms and short dry spells between rains.

Plant container-grown shrubs into moist, brackish, or occasionally flooded soil in full sun; saltwater false willow is a fast-growing, upright native shrub of Gulf and South Atlantic coastal marshes with narrow, slightly succulent leaves that tolerate salt spray and fluctuating soil salinity better than most woody plants. It is dioecious, with male and female flowers on separate plants, and produces small tufted seed heads in fall that support pollinating insects late in the season. Because it thrives in the low, wet, salt-influenced spots where many landscape shrubs fail, it is a practical screening or erosion-control choice along the back edge of a Gulf Coast property near a ditch, pond, or brackish waterway. It tolerates hard pruning if a denser, shorter form is wanted.

common_name: San Diego Red Bougainvillea (Vivid Scarlet-Red Large Vigorous Tropical Vine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; San Diego Red (also sold as 'Scarlett O'Hara' or 'Rosenka') is a large, vigorous bougainvillea cultivar known for its vivid scarlet-red to brilliant red bract color — one of the most intensely red bougainvilleas available, producing masses of brilliant red bracts that create a bold, high-impact tropical display when the vine is in full bloom. The bract color is described as more purely red (rather than the magenta-red of Barbara Karst) — a cleaner, more saturated crimson-to-scarlet tone that creates a different visual temperature in the landscape. San Diego Red is also noted as one of the more cold-hardy bougainvillea cultivars for zone 9 — surviving brief periods below freezing better than many other varieties, with some gardeners in zone 9a successfully maintaining it as a returning perennial with winter protection. Like all bougainvilleas, San Diego Red blooms most prolifically under slightly stressful conditions: periodic dry-down between waterings, lean soil without excessive nitrogen, and full sun exposure produce the heaviest flower display. The large, vigorous vine can reach 20+ feet on a wall or pergola structure in favorable conditions. Outstanding trained against a south or west-facing wall where reflected heat enhances bloom production and the structure protects the vine from cold north winds in zone 9 winters.

Sand hackberry (granjeno in south Texas) is a thorny native evergreen shrub of the lower Rio Grande Valley and south Texas brush country, producing small, yellowish-orange to red fruits abundantly year-round that are among the most important food sources for resident and migratory birds in the region — it is one of the top-ranked native plants for bird feeding in the Rio Grande Valley by wildlife managers and birders. The dense, thorny thickets provide impenetrable nesting and escape cover for green jays, Altamira orioles, and dozens of other brushland birds; the plant is a cornerstone of the native south Texas chaparral community. Hackberry emperor butterflies use this species as a larval host, and white-tipped doves, plain chachalacas, and chestnut-fronted macaws consume the fruits. In south Texas wildlife habitat gardens and Rio Grande Valley native plantings, granjeno is one of the highest-priority native shrubs for creating dense, self-sustaining wildlife habitat that provides food, cover, and nesting resources year-round without supplemental irrigation.

Sand live oak is a native evergreen tree of coastal sand dunes, scrub habitats, and sandy pinelands of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, closely related to live oak (Quercus virginiana) but distinctly adapted to excessively drained, nutrient-poor, acidic sands of ancient coastal terraces. It is distinguished from live oak by its smaller, more narrow leaves with rolled-under (revolute) margins, lower growth habit, and adaptation to dry sand rather than the moist, fertile soils favored by live oak. In coastal dune restoration and sandy barrier island plantings, sand live oak serves as one of the primary stabilizing species for ancient coastal plain sands, where it eventually develops into sprawling, wind-sculpted specimens of great character; it is more salt spray tolerant than live oak. Like all oaks, it supports an enormous diversity of native moths, butterflies, and beetles as larval hosts; its small acorns feed migrating wood ducks, and the dense evergreen canopy provides nesting habitat for many songbirds. A valuable evergreen tree for coastal sandy sites in zone 7–10 where typical live oak would not thrive.

Plant in dry, infertile, pure white to light-colored, acidic sand in full sun; sand pine is a Florida endemic of the ancient marine sand ridges and white sand scrub habitats of the Florida peninsula and coastal panhandle — one of the most ecologically specialized trees in North America. It is the primary tree of Florida scrub, growing in soil so nutrient-poor and drought-prone that it excludes virtually all other tree species. Two populations exist: a serotinous scrub variety (var. clausa) with cones that remain closed until opened by fire — releasing a mass of seeds after fire removes competing vegetation — and an open-cone variety (var. immuricata) along the Gulf Coast. The scrub habitat it creates is among the most biodiverse ecosystems in Florida, harboring endemic species including the Florida scrub jay, Florida mouse, and dozens of rare plant species. An extremely site-specific tree that should only be planted in authentic white-sand scrub conditions.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; sand-myrtle demands sharp drainage and is native to coastal-plain sandhills and rock outcrops, so amend heavy soils generously with coarse sand or grit before planting. Leiophyllum buxifolium is a compact, mounding, evergreen heath-family shrub with tiny, glossy, boxwood-like leaves that bronze attractively in winter, smothered in a profusion of small white to pink star-shaped flowers in mid-spring. Its fine texture and low, tidy habit make it a good substitute for boxwood in acidic-soil gardens, and it works well massed as a foundation planting, in a rock garden, or along a sunny woodland edge. Give it consistently sharp drainage and lean soil, since it is intolerant of wet feet or rich, heavily amended garden beds, and avoid fertilizing beyond a light acidic feeding in spring.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; sandankwa viburnum is the most widely used broadleaf evergreen hedge and screening shrub in Gulf Coast and central Florida landscapes — an easy-growing, tough, relatively drought-tolerant Japanese species that forms a dense, 5–8 foot mound of glossy, dark green, oval leaves and produces clusters of small, fragrant white to pale pink flowers in winter and early spring when few other shrubs bloom. The flowers are followed by red fruits that mature to black, attracting birds. It tolerates partial shade well and performs reliably in the heat and humidity that limits many northern shrubs in zone 8b–10 gardens. Widely used for foundation planting, privacy hedges, and screening in Florida and along the Gulf Coast; easy to shear to a formal shape or allow to grow naturally as an informal screen.

Plant in wet to moist, sandy or silty soil in full sun along stream banks, pond margins, and flood-prone areas; sandbar willow colonizes bare mineral soils and gravel bars faster than almost any other native woody plant, making it invaluable for erosion control and streambank stabilization following disturbance. The long, narrow silver-green leaves give the plant an elegant, fine-textured appearance that contrasts nicely with coarser riparian vegetation. Mature plants form dense thickets through aggressive root sprouting, providing nesting cover for warblers, wrens, and yellowthroats. The species is ecologically keystone in southwestern riparian corridors where it provides critical streambank structure and willow-dependent pollinator forage.
