Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, rocky, calcareous, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sandpaper oak is a small, shrubby to tree-like, semi-evergreen oak of dry, rocky, limestone slopes in west Texas and New Mexico, named for the distinctively rough, sandpaper-textured upper surface of the small, leathery, holly-like leaves with spiny teeth. It forms dense, thorny, impenetrable thickets in its natural habitat that serve as important cover for scaled quail, roadrunners, and various lizards in the Chihuahuan Desert. The small acorns provide food for wildlife in an arid region where food sources are sparse. A tough, dry-land shrub-oak for rocky, alkaline, exposed garden conditions in west Texas and the Southwest where most ornamental plants struggle. Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established. Can form a functional barrier hedge in harsh, exposed xeric conditions.

Plant in acidic soil that stays consistently wet to seasonally flooded, in full sun to partial shade; sandweed is a native wetland shrub of Gulf South pine flatwoods ponds, bog margins, and roadside ditches, with narrow, needle-like leaves and bright golden-yellow flowers with a prominent tuft of stamens blooming through summer. Older stems develop attractive reddish, peeling, exfoliating bark that adds winter interest after the leaves drop, giving the plant its 'peelbark' common name. It tolerates standing water for extended periods better than almost any other flowering shrub, making it a genuinely useful choice for the wettest part of a rain garden, pond margin, or low spot that floods after storms and stays soggy for weeks. Pollinators, especially bees, visit the flowers heavily through the long summer bloom season. Once sited in appropriately wet, acidic ground it needs very little care.

common_name: Santa Barbara Mexican Bush Sage (Compact Mexican Sage)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Santa Barbara is a compact selection of Mexican bush sage (Salvia leucantha) — a smaller, more garden-friendly alternative to the full-size species that can reach 4–6 feet. Santa Barbara stays 2–3 feet tall and wide, making it practical for smaller beds and borders where the full-size species would quickly become overwhelming. Like the species, Santa Barbara produces spectacular, long (6–12 inch) velvety-purple and white flower spikes from late summer through fall — the velvety-purple calyxes enclose small white flowers in a distinctive bicolor spike that is exceptional for late-season pollinator value and cut-flower use. The long, arching, purple flower spikes of Mexican sage provide the single most dramatic fall display of any commonly grown Gulf Coast perennial — no other plant matches the intensity and quantity of the purple-and-white flower production in September through November. Santa Barbara's compact habit blooms slightly earlier than the full-size species, making it more practical in zone 9 where the species sometimes misses the first frost deadline. Cut back to 12 inches after blooming; the plant regrows vigorously from the woody base. Drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free in well-drained soil.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Sapphire Showers is a trailing form of duranta, producing cascading stems draped in clusters of small, tubular blue-violet flowers over a long warm-season bloom period that draws butterflies and hummingbirds. Its spreading, arching habit sets it apart from the more upright, tree-like duranta cultivars often grown as small specimen trees, making it a good choice for hanging baskets, raised containers, or spilling over a low wall. In zone 9a it typically dies back to the ground after a hard freeze but regrows quickly from the roots the following spring in most winters; in colder zones it is best grown as a container annual or overwintered indoors.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sargent cherry is a Japanese species named for Charles Sprague Sargent, director of the Arnold Arboretum, and is one of the largest and most stately of ornamental cherries, developing into a substantial, wide-spreading tree with reddish-brown bark marked by horizontal lenticels. The flowers are deep pink, single, appearing in clusters in early spring — earlier than most Japanese cherries. The fall color is early and vivid — rich orange and crimson tones appearing weeks before most other trees. More cold-hardy and longer-lived than many ornamental cherries and a parent of several widely planted cultivars including 'Accolade'. The small, dark purplish-black fruits are eaten by birds. One of the finest and most substantial ornamental cherry species for long-term landscape use.

Sarvis Holly is a rarely cultivated native deciduous holly of moist, low-lying forests, wet woods, and stream margins of the coastal plain from South Carolina to Louisiana, producing clusters of small pink to red berries that ripen in late summer and fall and are avidly consumed by mockingbirds, bluebirds, robins, and other fruit-eating birds during the critical pre-migration feeding period. The name 'sarvis' is a folk rendering of 'serviceberry' or 'service tree,' reflecting the ripening time of its berries relative to other fall food sources. Less commonly cultivated than Possumhaw or Winterberry hollies, Sarvis Holly thrives in the wet, shaded conditions of bottomland forest and stream banks where larger hollies may struggle, and deserves wider use in native plant landscapes. Plant rooted cuttings in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; dioecious, so both sexes are required within pollinator range for berry set.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade to full sun; sasanqua camellias bloom in fall and early winter, earlier than Camellia japonica, and are more sun-tolerant and heat-hardy, making them the better choice for Gulf Coast gardens in zones 8–9. Single, semi-double, or double flowers in white, pink, red, and lavender provide vivid color from October through January when little else is in bloom. Unlike japonicas, sasanquas can be trained as espaliers against walls, used as hedges, or even grown as small specimen trees. Apply pine-bark mulch and acid-forming camellia fertilizer in spring. Petal blight and scale are the main concerns; improve air circulation and treat scale with horticultural oil in late winter.

Transplant root suckers or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average soil in full sun to partial shade; sassafras is a native eastern North American deciduous tree distinguished from all other trees by its uniquely variable leaf shape — individual trees simultaneously bear three distinct leaf shapes: simple oval leaves, mitten-shaped leaves with one lobe, and three-lobed leaves — all on the same tree, all with the same distinctive, pleasantly spicy-aromatic, root-beer fragrance when crushed. In spring, small clusters of yellow flowers appear before the leaves. The autumn foliage is among the most brilliantly colored of any native tree — turning orange, red, purple, and scarlet in a spectacular multi-color display. Dark-blue, olive-like fruits on red stalks feed many songbirds in fall. Sassafras was historically important in American commerce — root bark was the original source of sassafras oil and the primary ingredient of traditional root beer and filé powder (an essential Creole seasoning) — though safrole, the active compound, is now restricted as a food additive. Spreads by root suckers to form groves. An excellent native tree for dry, sandy, difficult sites where many trees fail.

common_name: Satin Pothos (Silver Philodendron, Silk Pothos, Silver Scindapsus)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade; Satin Pothos tolerates lower light than most variegated plants and can maintain attractive foliage color even several feet from a window, though growth slows considerably in dim conditions. Scindapsus pictus is a climbing tropical vine native to Southeast Asia — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Malaysia, Philippines, Sulawesi, and Sumatra — widely grown as a houseplant for its distinctive, heart-shaped, velvety-textured leaves decorated with irregular silver-gray patches and speckles. The silver variegation has an unusual quality: it appears slightly iridescent or three-dimensional against the dark, matte, blue-green base color, an effect created by air pockets beneath the leaf surface that scatter light — the same optical phenomenon that makes butterfly wings iridescent. The cultivar 'Argyraeus' has smaller, more compact leaves than the species with abundant fine silver spotting; 'Exotica' has larger leaves with more extensive, bold, irregular silver patches. Unlike true pothos (Epipremnum), Scindapsus has single leaves and no overlapping juvenile leaf stages when climbing. Its tolerance for low light, inconsistent watering, and indoor conditions — combined with the beautiful iridescent foliage — makes it a perennial houseplant favorite. Mildly toxic due to calcium oxalate.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water deeply and regularly through the first two years to establish before the tree can tolerate brief dry spells. Satomi is a classic pink-bracted Kousa dogwood cultivar, bearing large, star-shaped, deep rose-pink flower bracts in late spring after the leaves have emerged, later than native flowering dogwood, followed by raspberry-like red fruit in late summer that attracts birds, and finishing the season with reddish-purple fall foliage color. Kousa dogwoods bloom on a delay compared to native Cornus florida and show much better resistance to the anthracnose and borer problems that plague native dogwood in humid climates, making Satomi a reliable substitute where disease pressure has made native dogwood difficult to grow. Its attractive, exfoliating bark adds winter interest once the tree matures, and it works well as a specimen tree, understory planting, or focal point near a patio where its multi-season display can be enjoyed up close.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — saucer magnolia is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world for spring impact, producing enormous, tulip-shaped flowers (4–10 inches across) in shades ranging from deep rose-purple to pale pink to white, borne on bare branches before the leaves emerge in late winter to early spring. A single tree in bloom is visible from hundreds of feet away. The hybrid origin (M. denudata x M. liliiflora) combines cold hardiness and floriferous habit; named cultivars include 'Lennei' (deep rose-purple), 'Alexandrina' (pink and white), 'Brozzonii' (nearly white), and 'Rustica Rubra' (rich rose). The main risk in the South is late frost damage to early-opening buds in zone 5–7; in zone 8–9, this is rarely a problem and plants bloom reliably and abundantly. An outstanding focal point or specimen tree for the front landscape.

common_name: Sausage Tree (African Sausage Tree, Kigelia, Fetish Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Sausage Tree grows most vigorously in full sun with adequate water during establishment, becoming drought-tolerant in deep, well-drained soils once established. Kigelia africana is a large, wide-spreading, semi-evergreen tree native to tropical Africa (from Sudan and Ethiopia south to Namibia and South Africa) in the Bignoniaceae family (the trumpet vine family), widely known for producing one of the most extraordinary fruits of any tree. The fruits are enormous, cylindrical, sausage-shaped, hard-shelled, fibrous, gray-brown, and can reach 2 feet in length and 20 pounds in weight — each hanging individually from long, ropy, cable-like stalks attached to the branches, with multiple giant 'sausages' dangling from a single tree creating a surreal, prehistoric appearance. The flowers are deep maroon-red to brownish-red, large, bell-shaped, produced on long pendant racemes and opening at night to release a powerful, somewhat unpleasant odor that attracts bat pollinators — bats visit the flowers at night and transfer pollen between trees. The fruits require bat or other animal dispersal to germinate in the wild. The fresh fruits are toxic if consumed raw; however, the dried or roasted fruits have been used medicinally in traditional African medicine for centuries, and extracts are now investigated for pharmaceutical applications including wound healing and skin conditions. A dramatic, unmistakable specimen tree for large zone 10-11 tropical landscapes.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, acidic to slightly acidic soil — American holly adapts to a wide range of conditions but produces the densest berry crops in full sun with consistent moisture; Savannah is one of the most prolific and ornamentally outstanding cultivars of American Holly (Ilex opaca), the native evergreen holly that defines the winter ornamental landscape of the American East and Gulf South. Selected for heavy, consistent berry production, Savannah bears abundant clusters of bright red berries along every branch by November that persist through winter — providing both winter ornamental interest (the classic evergreen holly-and-berry combination) and critical food resources for overwintering birds including robins, cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and yellow-rumped warblers. American holly is the native counterpart to English holly (Ilex aquifolium), with dull rather than glossy leaves and a more open, pyramidal growth habit — less formal than English holly but fully hardy throughout the South and adapted to the heat and humidity that limits English holly below zone 6. Savannah's native provenance means complete adaptation to Gulf South soils, climate, and pest pressure without the cultural requirements or limitations of introduced hollies.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Savannah holly is a naturally occurring hybrid between Dahoon holly (Ilex cassine) and American holly (Ilex opaca) — both southeastern native hollies — producing a fast-growing, upright-pyramidal evergreen tree valued across the Gulf South for its rapid establishment, lighter, finer-textured foliage than other landscape hollies, and exceptional production of small, bright-red berries on female plants throughout winter. The relatively light-weight, less spiny leaves give Savannah a more graceful appearance than the coarser-textured hollies, and the gray bark is attractive. It grows faster than American holly and adapts to a wider range of soil conditions, including periodic wetness, that would stress other hollies. A single female Savannah holly laden with red berries in winter is one of the most attractive of all native evergreen trees for wildlife gardening — the berries are a critical winter food source for cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds. A male pollinator nearby is needed for consistent berry production; any compatible male Ilex opaca or I. cassine in the vicinity will serve. Excellent for screening, naturalizing, and as a specimen tree in the Gulf South.

Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; savin juniper is one of the most important ornamental junipers in the landscape industry — a low, spreading, multi-stemmed shrubby juniper of mountain slopes in central Europe and western Asia that has given rise to dozens of widely grown cultivars. The cultivar 'Tamariscifolia' (tam juniper) is one of the most widely planted low-growing evergreen shrubs in North American commercial landscaping. The species and cultivars tolerate heat, cold, drought, and poor soils, making them reliable low-maintenance groundcovers for banks, slopes, and sunny exposed sites. The foliage has a distinctly pungent, somewhat unpleasant odor when crushed — quite different from the pleasant cedar scent of most junipers. All parts are poisonous if ingested; the plant contains savin oil which historically caused miscarriages and was used as an abortifacient in herbal medicine — it should never be used internally. An excellent tough groundcover for full-sun, dry, difficult slopes.

Allow to naturalize in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in wildlife garden settings; saw greenbrier is a native evergreen vine of the southeastern US, producing stout, angular green stems armed with short, broad spines and thick, leathery, mottled-blotched dark green leaves. The small, shiny black berries in fall and winter are critically important food for mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and many other birds. The underground rhizomes form large, starchy masses that were roasted and eaten by southeastern Indigenous peoples; young shoots can be eaten as a cooked vegetable. Despite its ornamental berries and ecological importance, it is rarely cultivated — its stiff, sharp thorns and persistent rhizomes make it better suited to wildlife areas than manicured gardens.

Plant in sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — saw palmetto is one of the most ecologically important shrubs in the southeastern US, forming the dominant understory layer across millions of acres of Florida and Gulf Coast pine flatwoods and scrub. Individual plants are estimated to live 500–700 years, maintaining an enormous root system that stores carbohydrates and re-sprouts after fire within days. The cream-white flower clusters produce small black berries that are a primary food source for black bears, white-tailed deer, gopher tortoises, and more than 100 bird species. The berries are also harvested commercially as an herbal supplement for prostate health. Saw palmetto tolerates partial shade, salt, drought, and periodic flooding — it is one of the most resilient and valuable native plants for Gulf Coast habitat gardens. The saw-toothed petioles give it its name.

Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; sawtooth oak is an Asian oak (native to China, Korea, and Japan) widely planted throughout the southeastern and mid-Atlantic US as a fast-growing wildlife tree, producing large, chestnut-like acorns in heavy crops beginning at 5–8 years of age — far earlier than most native oaks. The long, narrow, chestnut-like leaves (reminiscent of chestnut rather than typical oak foliage) turn golden yellow in fall. The large acorns are eagerly consumed by deer, turkey, wood ducks, and other wildlife. Its fast growth rate, adaptability, and early, heavy acorn production make it the most widely planted non-native oak for deer and wildlife habitat planting in the Southeast. However, it can naturalize and potentially displace native oaks in some regions — use thoughtfully near natural areas.

common_name: Scarlet Beauty Virginia Sweetspire (Heat-Tolerant Morton Arboretum Selection)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Scarlet Beauty was selected at the Morton Arboretum for producing fragrant, drooping, bottlebrush-like white flower clusters in early summer followed by an especially vivid fall display that blends red, orange, and yellow, often several colors on a single leaf, and for tolerating a wider range of soil pH and heat than many other named Itea selections. Like other sweetspire cultivars it tolerates wet, periodically flooded soil better than most landscape shrubs, making it an excellent choice for a rain garden or low-lying moist spot in the Gulf South landscape. It spreads gradually by suckering to form a colony over time, useful for naturalizing or streambank stabilization. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood; it develops excellent fall color even in partial shade.

Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet honey myrtle is a medium-sized Australian shrub that produces in spring and early summer one of the most vivid and brilliant-red bottlebrush-type flower displays in the Melaleuca genus: dense, cylindrical, bottlebrush-like spikes of bright, true-scarlet to vivid red flowers composed of numerous stamen bundles projecting from the central axis, each cluster of stamens bright scarlet-red, the whole spike a dense, vivid, bristling cylinder of saturated red from 2–3 inches long. The flower color is among the most intense, pure reds of any commonly cultivated Australian shrub. Natural color variants also occur within the species — including salmon, pink, and purple-lilac forms — providing additional color options from the same species. Like other Melaleuca species it produces nectar that is highly attractive to honeyeating birds in Australia and hummingbirds in cultivation, the bottlebrush structure perfectly adapted for bird pollination by providing a stable perch while the bird probes for nectar. Somewhat more moisture-tolerant than many Australian natives, making it more adaptable to the wet summer conditions of the Gulf Coast in zone 9.

Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet morning glory (hummingbird vine) produces small, brilliant scarlet, tubular flowers with a yellow throat on vigorous twining stems — like a more compact, finer-textured version of the large garden morning glories, but with a much more intensely colored, tubular flower that is irresistible to hummingbirds and monarch butterflies. The distinctive ivy-shaped leaves (hederifolia = ivy-leaved) distinguish it from other red-flowered morning glories. Native to tropical Americas and naturalized throughout the subtropical US, it self-sows freely in zone 9 gardens where it provides a season-long display on fences, trellises, and shrubs. More drought-tolerant than many morning glories once established. An excellent hummingbird plant for warm-climate gardens that provides continuous summer color with minimal care.

Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average soil in full sun; scarlet oak is named for the spectacular, deep scarlet fall color — one of the most brilliantly red of all native trees, maintaining its color for 4–6 weeks in fall. The leaves are deeply cut with pointed lobes typical of the red oak group, and the deeply cleft sinuses extend nearly to the midrib, creating a dramatic, finely cut pattern. The tree is naturally adapted to dry, infertile, sandy or rocky upland sites where other oaks struggle, and is a pioneer species on disturbed dry slopes in the East. The acorns are a critical food source for squirrels, blue jays, wood ducks, and wild turkeys. Well-suited as a street tree and park tree in well-drained, slightly acidic urban soils. The spectacular fall color and attractive form make it one of the finest native oaks for landscape use.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; scarlet plumbago (red plumbago, rose-colored leadwort) is a Southeast Asian tropical shrub entirely different in character from the common, sprawling, blue Cape plumbago (P. auriculata) — it is an upright, non-climbing, softer-wooded tropical shrub that produces long, erect, terminal racemes of tubular, five-petaled flowers in a vivid, rich crimson-red to scarlet-red color, creating a striking and rarely seen red-flowered plumbago display that is particularly effective in the partial shade of a tropical garden. The flowers have the characteristic sticky calyx of all plumbagos and are produced in succession over a long season from spring through fall. The soft, broadly oval, bright-green leaves are larger and less glossy than common Cape plumbago. Scarlet plumbago is a distinctive and underused tropical shrub for zone 10–12 shade and partial-shade gardens, where it provides vivid red color in positions where most red-flowered tropical shrubs would fail to bloom adequately without more direct sunlight.

Scentlandia is a compact Southern Living Plant Collection selection of native Virginia sweetspire bred for noticeably stronger fragrance than older cultivars, packing dense, drooping, bottlebrush-shaped white flower spikes in early summer that perfume the air around a patio or walkway far more than the species. It stays low and mounded, well under 3 feet, with glossy summer foliage that turns burgundy in fall, and like other Itea selections it tolerates wet, periodically flooded soil far better than most flowering shrubs. Give it moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; it flowers and colors well even in a fairly shaded spot, making it a good fit for a small, fragrant shade bed in the Gulf South.

common_name: Scentless Mock Orange / Wild Mock Orange
notes: Plant in partial sun with good air circulation in well-drained to dry soil; unlike the common Mock Orange, this native species thrives in lean, rocky soils along woodland edges and bluffs without supplemental fertilization. The large, pure white four-petaled flowers appear in late spring and, while scentless, are showy enough to be a garden highlight and attract native pollinators. Allow ample space — established shrubs reach 6–10 ft in both height and spread and develop a bold, multi-stemmed arching form. Prune selectively after flowering, removing the oldest stems at the base every few years to rejuvenate the shrub and encourage strong new flowering wood.

common_name: Schillings Dwarf Yaupon Holly (Compact Rounded Native Holly)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Schillings Dwarf (also sold as Stokes Dwarf) is one of the most widely planted compact hollies in the Gulf South, a naturally dense, rounded, slow-growing selection of native yaupon that fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mass plantings without the constant shearing that fast-growing shrubs demand. Being a male selection it does not set the red berries of the species, but it more than compensates with an extremely low-maintenance, uniformly rounded habit and outstanding tolerance of heat, drought, wind, salt spray, and poor soil, making it a workhorse plant across coastal Gulf landscapes. Established plants need very little supplemental water and only occasional light shearing if a stricter formal shape is desired.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, allowing enough room for its arching, spreading branches to fill in as an informal hedge. Schip laurel carries narrower, smaller, more finely textured leaves than the species along with the same fragrant white spring flower spikes and dark fruit, but it was selected in the Balkan mountains for improved cold hardiness, so it holds up in colder winters that damage many other cherry laurel cultivars. Its dense, layered growth and tolerance of shade and shearing have made it a widely used privacy hedge and screening plant in the Pacific Northwest and mid-Atlantic where a fast, reliably evergreen barrier is needed.

Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), lean, sandy or gravelly, peaty soil in full sun; Scotch heather is the defining plant of the British moorlands — the vast open landscapes of Scotland, northern England, Wales, and Ireland carpeted with purple heather in August are among the most iconic and beloved landscapes in Europe. The genus Calluna contains only this single species, distinguished from the related Erica heathers by having the colored sepals (not petals) as the main display. Hundreds of cultivars exist in shades from white through pink, lavender, and deep purple, as well as double-flowered and golden-foliaged forms. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain compact, bushy plants — unsheared plants become leggy and open. Invaluable for dry, acidic, heathland-style gardens in appropriate climates. Late-summer (August) bloom provides nectar for migrating monarch butterflies, honeybees, and native bees during the fall migration period.

Plant in poor, sandy, or gravelly soil in a fully exposed, sunny location; Scotch Rose is one of the most wind and cold tolerant of all roses and actually performs poorly in rich or waterlogged ground. It spreads steadily by underground suckers to form a low, dense, weed-suppressing thicket, making it excellent for stabilizing dry banks and coastal dunes. The distinctive dark purple-black hips ripen in late summer and persist into autumn, providing food for birds. Propagate by detaching and replanting rooted suckers in early spring, or take semi-hardwood cuttings in mid-summer.

common_name: Scrambling Sky Vine (Purple Thunbergia, Blue Kenya Clockvine)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Scrambling Sky Vine thrives in zone 9 humid warmth and produces its best bloom in late summer and fall when daytime temperatures drop below 95°F. Thunbergia battiscombei is a scrambling, semi-woody tropical vine from East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda) in the Acanthaceae family, closely related to the widely-grown Bengal Clockvine (T. grandiflora) but producing smaller flowers in a richer, deeper purple-violet with a contrasting yellow-white throat. The flowers are trumpet-shaped, 2–3 inches in diameter, and borne singly on slender stems along the length of the twining vine — the deep violet-purple with the pale, open throat is one of the most saturated blues available in a tropical vine and blooms continuously from late spring through fall in zone 9. Unlike the enormous, vigorous T. grandiflora which can overwhelm a small space, T. battiscombei is more manageable in scale, typically reaching 10–15 feet and controllable with annual pruning. The common name 'Scrambling Sky Vine' reflects its habit of weaving its way through other shrubs and structures rather than climbing tightly around a support. An excellent choice for informal tropical gardens, butterfly gardens, and screening, where its continuous production of purple flowers provides months of interest.

common_name: Sea Green Juniper (Arching Fountain-Form Bright Green Juniper)
notes: Sea Green is a vigorous, arching juniper with bright green, fountain-shaped sprays of foliage that curve outward and downward in a graceful vase form, distinct from the flatter, more prostrate habit of many spreading juniper cultivars. Its bright, clean green color and fine texture make it a versatile foundation or mass-planting shrub, and it holds up well to the summer heat and humidity of the Gulf South, provided drainage is sharp. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and prune only to remove wayward branches, since its natural arching form is part of its appeal; avoid overhead watering late in the day to reduce the risk of foliage blight in humid weather.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Cerbera manghas tolerates brief coastal flooding, salt spray, and periodic waterlogging in its native coastal forest habitat — water regularly in establishment, then moderately once established. Cerbera manghas (Sea Mango or Pong-pong) is an evergreen tropical tree native to the coastal forests, mangrove margins, and beach strands from Madagascar and the East African coast through South Asia, Southeast Asia, and into the Pacific islands, where it is one of the quintessential components of coastal tropical forest. The tree produces clusters of large, intensely fragrant white flowers with a bright pink or red center tube, ornamentally comparable to frangipani, followed by large (3–4 inch), smooth, shiny, green-then-red ornamental fruits resembling a small mango — entirely toxic and not to be eaten. All parts of Cerbera manghas contain cerberin, neriifolin, and related cardiac glycosides among the most toxic plant compounds known; historically the seeds were used in trial-by-ordeal poison rites in Madagascar and across the Pacific. Despite its toxicity, Sea Mango is widely planted as an ornamental street and coastal tree throughout tropical Asia and the Pacific for its compact, attractive form, fragrant flowers, and colorful fruits; it is tolerant of salt, wind, and coastal conditions. Plant in locations inaccessible to children and livestock and always wash hands after handling.

common_name: Seacoast Marsh Elder (Beach Elder, Dune Marsh Elder)
notes: A low, succulent-leaved shrub of the primary and secondary dune zone, seacoast marsh elder grows just landward of sea oats where salt spray and burial by wind-blown sand are constant. Its fleshy gray-green foliage sheds salt efficiently, and its spreading root system helps knit loose dune sand together. Plant in full sun in pure beach sand with no irrigation once established; it is intolerant of rich garden soil or regular watering. Use it as a companion to sea oats and railroad vine in dune restoration plantings, where it fills the low, wind-scoured swales between larger grass clumps.

common_name: Seiryu Japanese Maple (Upright Green Lace-Leaf Maple)
notes: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Seiryu is unusual among lace-leaf Japanese maples for its upright, tree-like habit rather than the mounding or weeping form typical of most dissected-leaf cultivars, producing finely cut, bright green leaves on a vigorous, vase-shaped small tree that turns gold, orange, and red in a spectacular fall display. Its upright form and greater sun tolerance make it a good choice where a lace-leaf maple's fine texture is wanted but a low, spreading form does not fit the space. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; selloum is a bold, trunk-forming tropical aroid with massive, deeply and irregularly lobed leaves on long petioles that arch outward from a stout central stem, eventually developing a short, thick, above-ground trunk covered in old leaf-base scars as it ages. It is one of the most widely planted tropical foliage specimens in warm-climate landscapes, valued for filling large shaded areas with bold, architectural texture and requiring relatively little maintenance beyond removing old, yellowing lower leaves. Established plants tolerate brief light frost, with damaged foliage resprouting readily from the crown in spring even after a hard freeze kills the top growth back in zone 9. Provide ample room to spread, since a mature specimen can reach 6 feet or more in height and equal spread, and keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged during the growing season.

common_name: Seminole Crape Myrtle (Medium Pink Early-Series Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Seminole is a medium-pink flowering crape myrtle from the U.S. National Arboretum's early tribe-named breeding series, one of the longest-established selections still found in Southern landscapes, producing abundant crepe-textured flower clusters through the heat of summer on a dense, multi-stemmed shrub. As a straight Lagerstroemia indica cultivar rather than one of the later, more mildew-resistant indica x fauriei hybrids, it benefits from full sun and good air circulation to minimize powdery mildew pressure in humid climates. Its long track record and moderate size make it a familiar, dependable choice for a summer-flowering hedge, screen, or specimen shrub. Never top or hard-prune the main framework; prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or crowded twiggy growth and maintain the natural vase-shaped form.

common_name: Semmes Beauty Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large-Panicle Native Oakleaf)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. 'Semmes Beauty' was selected in Alabama for its exceptionally long, dense flower panicles, which open pure white in early summer and gradually flush to a rich rose-pink as they age, held on strong stems that resist flopping even after summer rain. The large, deeply lobed, oak-shaped leaves are proportionally bold to match the flower size and turn shades of bronze, maroon, and burgundy in fall, while the shrub's peeling cinnamon bark adds interest through winter. Because it blooms on old wood, prune only immediately after flowering, and site it where its substantial mature size can be accommodated as a woodland-edge specimen or informal shaded screen.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, limestone-based upland soil in full sun to partial shade; September elm tolerates the same range of soils as other native elms and needs little care once established. Unlike every other native elm, which flowers in late winter or very early spring before leafing out, this uncommon species flowers and sets its winged seeds in September and October, giving the tree its distinctive common name and making it easy to identify in fall when its papery samaras are conspicuous against the still-green foliage. Native to scattered limestone bluffs and upland woods across the mid-South and lower Midwest, it is considered rare and local throughout its range, making cultivated plantings valuable for conserving the species' genetic diversity outside isolated wild populations. Like other American elms it is susceptible to Dutch elm disease, though reportedly to a somewhat lesser degree than American elm, and provides the same wildlife and shade value as more common elm species where it can be sourced from a specialty native nursery.

common_name: Serissa (Tree of a Thousand Stars, Snow Rose)
notes: Grow in bright light with some direct morning sun, in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil kept evenly moist. Serissa is a small-leaved evergreen shrub from Southeast Asia grown for its tiny, glossy, dark-green foliage and its remarkably long, nearly year-round flush of small, star-shaped white flowers (double or single depending on cultivar) that gives the plant its common name; several popular variegated cultivars offer cream-white leaf margins for added interest. Like Fukien tea, it is a classic indoor and patio bonsai subject valued for naturally fine branching and a woody, gnarled trunk that develops quickly, but it shares a reputation for dropping leaves in response to sudden changes in light, temperature, or watering, so keep conditions as consistent as possible. Prune and wire young growth in spring and summer to train bonsai shape, feed lightly during active growth, and repot every one to two years into fresh, fast-draining mix.

Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, deep soil in full sun; sessile oak is the co-dominant great oak of Europe alongside English oak (Q. robur), but distinguished by its stalkless (sessile) acorns held directly on the twigs (whereas English oak acorns hang on long stalks). The two species hybridize freely wherever their ranges overlap, producing intermediate forms. Sessile oak tends to grow on better-drained, more acidic, hillside soils while English oak occupies clay vales and wetlands. The 'ancient oakwoods' of Wales, Ireland, Scotland, and the western Highlands are typically sessile oak — including the famous Wistman's Wood on Dartmoor and the ancient semi-natural oakwoods of the Lake District. The wood is highly valued for fine furniture, flooring, and wine and whiskey barrel staves. An exceptionally long-lived tree reaching over 1,000 years. Provides the full suite of habitat value as English oak for British and Irish wildlife.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; seven-son flower is one of the most underrated multi-season ornamental shrubs or small trees, native to central China and offering a remarkable sequence of interest from late summer through winter. Fragrant, small white flowers appear in clusters in late August and September — later than virtually any other woody shrub — followed by an unusual second display: the sepals surrounding the spent flowers enlarge and turn bright rose-red in October, extending the colorful season by several weeks and often mistaken for the flowers themselves. The exfoliating bark on mature stems peels in long, curling strips of gray, brown, and cream, creating striking winter interest similar to crape myrtle or birch. The bold, dark-green, distinctly veined leaves are tropical-looking for a hardy shrub. Adaptable to zones 5–9 and to a range of soil conditions, it combines late-season bloom, extended fall color, and ornamental bark in a single low-maintenance plant.

common_name: Shaina Japanese Maple (Dwarf Dense Red Maple)
notes: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Shaina is a dwarf, densely branched sport of the classic 'Bloodgood' Japanese maple, growing as a compact, rounded shrub-like small tree with the same deep maroon-red foliage color but reaching only a fraction of Bloodgood's mature size, making it a good fit for small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-size Japanese maple would eventually outgrow the space. Its tight branching and small, deeply lobed leaves give it a fine, dense texture that holds up well through the growing season before a bright scarlet fall display. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Shamrock inkberry is a compact selection that holds a denser form than the species without the legginess older inkberry cultivars develop. Small, glossy, spineless evergreen leaves cover a dense, rounded native shrub that serves as a broadleaf evergreen alternative to boxwood, tolerating wetter soil and more shade than boxwood while providing similar year-round structure for a foundation planting or low hedge. Native to wetlands and pinelands of the eastern and southeastern United States, it is more compact and less prone to the bare, leggy lower growth that plagues many older inkberry cultivars, and only female plants produce the small black berries valued by birds, requiring a male pollinator nearby for fruit set. Shear lightly if a more formal shape is wanted, and provide consistently moist, acidic soil, since inkberry tolerates wetter conditions than most broadleaf evergreens.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral or even alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; Shantung maple is a medium-sized Chinese maple of outstanding toughness and ornamental value — the young spring leaves emerge in shades of rich purple-burgundy before maturing to glossy, deep green, and the fall color is consistently a rich orange-red, comparable to red maple in intensity. It grows 20–30 feet with an upright-oval to rounded crown and is among the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant maples available, thriving in the hot, dry, alkaline conditions of the Great Plains and Southwest where most other maples fail. Unlike Norway maple, it is non-invasive and better-behaved in the landscape. 'Norwegian Sunset' and 'Pacific Sunset' (A. truncatum x platanoides hybrids) have been widely planted in street tree programs across the western and central United States for their exceptional adaptability.

common_name: Shasta Doublefile Viburnum (Compact Horizontal-Branching Flowering Viburnum)
notes: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; doublefile viburnum blooms on the previous year's wood and should be pruned, if needed, only right after flowering. Shasta is a compact, wide-spreading selection of doublefile viburnum, producing an exceptionally heavy display of pure white, flat-topped lacecap flower clusters held in tiers along strongly horizontal branches in spring, followed by red berries that ripen to black and attract birds, and burgundy-red fall foliage color. Its strikingly tiered, horizontal branching habit gives the shrub a distinctive architectural presence even out of bloom, and it spreads noticeably wider than it grows tall, so allow ample lateral space when siting it.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing plenty of lateral room for the wide, tiered, horizontal branching this cultivar is known for. Bred by the U.S. National Arboretum, Shasta is among the most spectacular doublefile viburnum cultivars, its strongly horizontal, tiered branches lined in spring with rows of flat, lacecap-like flower clusters so dense the branches appear snow-covered, followed by red berries that ripen to black and draw songbirds in late summer. Its wider-than-tall habit makes it a strong specimen for open lawn areas or the edge of a woodland garden where its architectural branching pattern can be fully appreciated from a distance. Prune only lightly and selectively right after bloom, since heavy shearing destroys the natural tiered structure that is the plant's chief ornamental asset.

common_name: Shawnee Brave Bald Cypress (Narrow Columnar Bald Cypress)
notes: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, though established trees also tolerate average well-drained garden soil once roots are developed. Shawnee Brave is a narrow, densely pyramidal selection of the native Southern bald cypress, holding a much more upright, columnar shape than the broadly spreading wild species, which makes it far better suited to street plantings, narrow side yards, and formal allees where space is limited. Like the species, it tolerates both flooded and ordinary garden soil with equal ease, developing the picturesque flared trunk base and soft, ferny, deciduous foliage that turns rusty orange-brown in fall before dropping. It is highly wind- and storm-resistant once established and essentially free of serious pests or diseases, making it an excellent long-lived specimen or street tree throughout the Gulf South.

Plant in acidic, consistently moist, well-drained to boggy soil in partial shade; sheep laurel is a low, compact native evergreen shrub of eastern bogs, barrens, and cutover woodland, closely related to mountain laurel but shorter and distinguished by its flowering habit — clusters of small, deep rose-pink, cup-shaped flowers appear along the stem below the current year's new leafy growth rather than at the branch tips, giving mature plants a distinctive layered look with new green growth rising above a band of bloom in early summer. It is a useful native shrub for the acidic, moist end of a woodland or bog garden and provides nectar for native bees and other pollinators. As the common names 'sheep laurel' and 'lambkill' warn, all parts of the plant contain grayanotoxins that are toxic if ingested by livestock and by people — keep it out of pastures and away from grazing animals, and do not consume any part of the plant. Prune lightly after flowering only if needed to shape; it resents heavy cutting.

Shingle Oak is a distinctive and underappreciated native oak of the eastern United States from New England south to Georgia and west to Kansas, immediately recognizable among oaks by its entire, unlobed leaves resembling those of a water beech — a surprising feature for an oak — making it an excellent conversation piece in any landscape. The dried leaves persist on the branches well into winter in a quality called marcescence, providing landscape texture and winter interest, while the abundant small acorns are a reliable annual mast crop for wood ducks, turkeys, white-tailed deer, and numerous songbirds. An adaptable and durable large shade tree for urban and suburban landscapes, Shingle Oak tolerates heavier clay soils and greater pH variability than many oaks, and develops a graceful, broadly pyramidal to rounded crown at maturity with modest fall color ranging from yellow to russet brown. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade.

Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to full shade; shining fetterbush performs remarkably well in wet, poorly drained conditions that challenge most ornamental shrubs, making it valuable for rain gardens, pond margins, and wet woodland settings. Lyonia lucida is an evergreen native shrub of the southeastern coastal plain with exceptionally handsome, glossy, dark-green, alternate leaves with a prominent revolute (rolled-under) margin that gives the plant a polished, refined appearance unusual in native shrubs; small, pink to white, urn-shaped flowers are produced in axillary clusters along the previous season's stems in March–April before many other shrubs flower, providing important early-season nectar for native bumblebees and other early-flying pollinators. The glossy foliage (the source of the epithet 'lucida,' meaning shining) is effective year-round and provides excellent winter interest. Shining fetterbush is native to wet flatwoods, bay swamps, and pocosins from Virginia to Florida and Louisiana and is an outstanding native choice for wet, acidic-soil sites in zones 7–10 where drainage is poor.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; shiny xylosma is grown chiefly for its glossy, bronze-red new growth maturing to lustrous bright green foliage rather than for its small, inconspicuous, fragrant greenish-yellow flowers, which are followed by black berries on female plants. It responds exceptionally well to shearing and is widely used as a formal or informal hedge, screen, espalier, or small patio tree in California, Texas, and Gulf Coast landscapes. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and urban conditions with ease, and the arching, somewhat thorny branches make it a useful barrier planting as well as an ornamental one.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Shishigashira is a compact, mounding sasanqua camellia noted for its unusually low, dense, wider-than-tall habit compared to the more upright growth of most sasanquas, making it useful as a large-scale groundcover, low hedge, or foundation planting. It produces semi-double, rose-pink flowers with ruffled petals in late fall into winter, later in the season than earlier-blooming sasanqua cultivars, extending camellia interest further into the cold months. Like other camellias it needs consistently moist, acidic soil and benefits from a layer of mulch to protect shallow roots and conserve moisture through the year.

common_name: Shoal Creek Chaste Tree (Classic Large-Spike Gulf South Vitex Selection)
notes: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Shoal Creek is the standard Gulf South chaste tree selection, chosen for noticeably longer, more densely flowered lavender-blue spikes and faster, more vigorous growth than seed-grown plants of the species. It blooms profusely on new growth from summer through fall, tolerating the heat, drought, and poor soil that defeat many other flowering shrubs, and the fragrant, gray-green palmately compound foliage adds a pleasant sage-like scent to the garden. Cutting back hard in late winter to 12-18 inches above ground produces vigorous new growth and the best flower display. It is a favorite of bees and butterflies through its long bloom season.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; shooting star is a Pacific Island tropical shrub of the family Acanthaceae grown primarily for its striking foliage — the oval to lance-shaped leaves are broadly variegated in an irregular blotch pattern of deep purple, green, cream, and ivory-white, creating a bold, multicolored effect that is ornamental year-round and serves a similar role to coleus in the shaded tropical garden. Periodically through the year, the plant produces loose clusters of small, tubular, white flowers with purple-spotted throats, adding to the display. The cultivated forms include purple-leaved and cream-variegated variants, all under the variable species classification. It requires genuine tropical warmth (zone 10–12) and resents cold temperatures — even brief chilling below 50°F can cause leaf discoloration and drop. Most effective in the warm, bright-shade microclimate of an established tropical garden, where its bold variegated foliage provides a strong mid-border accent. Excellent for shaded container plantings and outdoor tropical rooms in zone 10–12.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Shooting Star hoya has a more upright, shrubby habit than most trailing hoya species and benefits from light staking when young. Glossy, lance-shaped leaves clothe a semi-upright, shrubby plant that produces dramatic, dense clusters of dozens of small, narrow, swept-back yellow-to-white flowers with reflexed petals, resembling a burst of tiny shooting stars and giving the plant its common name. Native to Southeast Asian forests, it blooms more readily and at a younger age than many hoya species, and its shrubbier, less vining habit makes it a good choice for a floor or tabletop specimen rather than a hanging basket. Provide bright indirect light for reliable flowering, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flowering spurs, which rebloom for years.

common_name: Shooting Star Viburnum (Upward-Facing White Doublefile Viburnum)
notes: Shooting Star is a doublefile viburnum selected for lacecap flower clusters whose outer sterile florets twist and curl upward and outward as they mature, giving each cluster a starburst appearance rather than the flat, symmetrical disc of most doublefile types. It carries the same strongly tiered, horizontal branching habit as other doublefile selections, producing a heavy spring bloom followed by red berries that ripen to black and are readily taken by birds, with burgundy fall color to close the season. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade and allow generous width, since the layered branches spread further than the plant grows tall.

Show Off is a compact forsythia bred to flower along the entire length of every branch, from the base to the tip, rather than mainly at the branch tips as in older cultivars, producing an unusually dense, solid mass of golden-yellow flowers in late winter before the leaves emerge. Its smaller mature size, roughly half that of standard border forsythia, fits foundation plantings and smaller gardens without the annual hard pruning that larger forsythia cultivars need to stay in bounds. Like all forsythia, flower bud hardiness is the limiting factor outside its ideal cold-winter range — flower buds need a period of cold dormancy and can be damaged by extended warm spells in mild winters, so bloom performance in zone 9 varies from year to year depending on winter chill.

common_name: Showy Jasmine (Florida Jasmine, Yellow Jasmine Shrub)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil; Showy Jasmine is adaptable to a range of soil types and is more tolerant of clay soils than many ornamental shrubs. Jasminum floridum is a semi-evergreen to evergreen shrubby jasmine native to China (cultivated in Chinese gardens for centuries and naturalized in parts of the southern US, hence its occasional listing as 'Florida Jasmine'). Unlike the vining habit of most popular jasmines (J. officinale, J. polyanthum), Showy Jasmine grows as a compact, mounding, multi-stemmed shrub with arching branches and small, dark-green, glossy, trifoliate or 5-leaflet compound leaves. The bright yellow, 5-petaled, tubular flowers bloom in spring and sporadically through the warm season, providing cheerful color without the fragrance of white-flowering jasmines — the flowers are pleasantly scented but not as intensely aromatic as J. polyanthum or J. officinale. Showy Jasmine is one of the better-adapted jasmines for zone 9 Gulf South conditions — tolerating summer heat, humidity, and clay soils better than the more tender tropical species while providing reliable cold hardiness through zone 7 winters. It makes an excellent landscape shrub for partially shaded foundation plantings, mixed shrub borders, and parking lot islands.

Plant young trees in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, acidic soil and full sun to light shade, sited where summers stay relatively cool since this northern species declines in hot, humid regions. Showy mountain ash is native to boreal forests, rocky shorelines, and cold uplands across the northern United States and Canada, forming a small, rounded tree with flat clusters of white spring flowers that attract bees and other pollinators. The large, bright orange-red berry clusters ripen in early fall and persist into winter, becoming a magnet for migrating and overwintering cedar waxwings, pine grosbeaks, and other winter finches once softened by frost. Its open branching structure also provides good perching and nesting sites for songbirds.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; shrubby cinquefoil is among the toughest, most cold-hardy, and longest-blooming deciduous shrubs in cultivation — a circumboreal native of arctic and alpine regions of the Northern Hemisphere that produces a dense mound of fine-textured, small, pinnate leaves and, from late spring through autumn, a near-continuous succession of cheerful five-petaled flowers resembling small wild roses in yellow, white, cream, pink, or orange depending on the cultivar. The bloom season is exceptionally long — often six months in favorable conditions — making it one of the most reliably flowering shrubs per season of any woody plant in cold climates. It tolerates cold to zone 2, clay soil, alkaline soil, drought once established, and salt spray. Dozens of named cultivars are available including 'Goldfinger' (deep yellow), 'Primrose Beauty' (pale yellow), 'Abbotswood' (pure white), 'Pink Beauty' (soft pink), and 'Red Ace' (orange-red, which fades to yellow in heat). Outstanding for low-maintenance shrub borders, highway medians, and mass plantings in cold climates.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; shrubby germander is a standout evergreen Mediterranean shrub valued for its exceptional silver-white foliage that glows brilliantly in the sun. The entire plant — stems, leaves, and undersides — is covered in dense, white, woolly hairs that give it an almost luminous silver-white appearance in the garden, making it one of the most silver-foliaged of all hardy shrubs. From spring through summer it produces a long succession of two-lipped, pale-blue to lavender flowers with a prominent lower lip, carried singly in the leaf axils along the branches. Native to the western Mediterranean in Spain, Portugal, and North Africa, it thrives in lean, alkaline, well-drained soils and intense sun and is extremely drought-tolerant once established. It is widely used in Mediterranean-style, California, and Gulf Coast gardens as a specimen shrub, low screening hedge, or silver foliage accent. Responds well to shearing and can be kept as a formal hedge of 3-4 feet.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; shrubby penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, thriving in a rock garden or dry border. Small, evergreen, toothed leaves cover a low, woody-based, mounding subshrub that produces an abundant flush of large, vivid lavender-blue to violet flowers in late spring, native to rocky slopes, ridges, and open pine forests across the inland Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies. Its semi-woody, shrubby structure gives it more year-round garden presence than many herbaceous penstemons, holding a tidy mounded shape through winter, and its drought tolerance and rock-garden scale make it well suited to a xeriscape border or scree planting. Cut back lightly after flowering to maintain a compact form, and avoid rich soil or excess summer water, both of which shorten this dryland native's lifespan.

Shrubby St. John's wort is one of the most adaptable and cold-hardy native flowering shrubs of eastern North America — a rounded, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub that produces bright, butter-yellow five-petaled flowers with showy stamens prolifically in July and August, when the garden's early-summer bloom has faded and few other native shrubs are at peak flower. It grows naturally in a wider range of moisture conditions than most native shrubby Hypericums, tolerating both dry rocky slopes and moist, seasonally wet bottomland edges, making it one of the more versatile native shrubs for mixed landscape situations. Native bees — particularly specialist pollen collectors in the family Melittidae and Apidae — are the primary pollinators, attracted by the abundant pollen (this genus provides no nectar); the persistent, star-shaped seed capsules are ornamental through winter and consumed by some birds. An excellent choice for naturalistic shrub borders, rain garden edges, and native landscape plantings in the cold northern half of its range where golden St. John's wort is less reliably hardy.

Plant fresh acorns in fall or container trees in early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Shumard oak is the premier large native oak of the Gulf Coast and Deep South, growing faster than most oaks (2–3 feet per year when young) while developing into a large, long-lived specimen tree with spectacular deep red-to-scarlet fall color — one of the best oaks for fall color in zone 7–9 where many trees fail to color reliably. It tolerates brief flooding and clay soils better than many oaks, making it an excellent choice for urban and suburban landscapes in the South. The deeply lobed leaves with pointed tips are similar to pin oak but without the drooping lower branches. The acorns provide important fall food for turkeys, deer, and numerous bird species. An outstanding Gulf Coast street tree, shade tree, and wildlife tree.

Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Siberian pea tree is one of the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant nitrogen-fixing shrubs available, native to Siberia and northern China and reliably hardy to zone 2 — surviving temperatures of -50°F — making it invaluable for the most extreme northern climates where few other leguminous shrubs survive. The yellow pea flowers in spring are attractive and nectar-rich, providing early-season bee forage. The seed pods (up to 2 inches long) contain small seeds that are technically edible — they were eaten by indigenous Siberian peoples as a protein source in famine conditions — and are eaten by birds and small mammals. In permaculture design, Siberian pea tree serves as a cold-hardy nitrogen-fixing component for food forests, shelter belts, and northern homesteads. It is widely used for windbreaks and shelterbelt plantings on the northern Great Plains of North America and the prairie provinces of Canada. The weeping form 'Pendula' is sometimes grown as an ornamental grafted specimen.

Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Siebold's viburnum is a large, handsome, tree-like viburnum from Japan with bold, deep-green, leathery leaves and, in late spring, dense, rounded clusters of creamy-white flowers with a distinctive, somewhat pungent fragrance that carries on the air. The real show follows in late summer as the fruit clusters ripen through a striking sequence from green to pink to bright red and finally glossy black, all held on showy, persistent, contrasting red stalks (pedicels) that remain colorful even after the birds strip the berries. Give it room to grow, since with age it develops into a substantial small tree well suited to the back of a shrub border, a woodland margin, or as a specimen with high, filtered shade from taller trees overhead. Prune only to remove dead or crossing wood; the naturally handsome, layered branching habit needs little shaping. A tough, long-lived, four-season shrub for a partly shaded spot with room to spare.

common_name: Sierra Linda Autumn Sage (Compact Coral-Red Salvia greggii)
notes: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Sierra Linda is a compact, bushy Salvia greggii selection bred for a denser, more uniform mounding habit than the straight species, producing vivid coral-red, two-lipped flowers in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost. Its smaller, tidier scale suits foundation plantings, border edges, and mass plantings where a very drought-tolerant, long-blooming Texas native is wanted without the looser, more open growth of older Salvia greggii selections. It draws hummingbirds and native bees throughout its long bloom season; cut back hard to 6–8 inches in late winter to promote fresh, dense growth and abundant spring flowering, and shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep production continuous.

common_name: Sikes Dwarf Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact Oakleaf Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sikes Dwarf is a compact oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia) selected for its smaller, more manageable size — reaching 3–4 feet tall and wide — compared to the standard oakleaf hydrangea species that can grow 6–8 feet. Like the species, Sikes Dwarf has all the outstanding multi-season qualities that make oakleaf hydrangea the finest native flowering shrub for the Gulf South: conical white flower panicles from June through August that dry to tan-parchment and persist ornamentally through winter; large, distinctive oak-shaped leaves with outstanding reddish-purple to burgundy fall color; attractive cinnamon-orange peeling bark for winter interest; and excellent adaptation to the heat, humidity, clay soils, and partial to full shade of Gulf South gardens. Oakleaf hydrangea is native to the southeastern United States, making it perfectly adapted to zone 9 conditions without the special care that exotic hydrangea species may require. In deep shade (3 hours or less of sun), it flowers less but still provides outstanding foliage, bark, and fall color. The compact size makes Sikes Dwarf suitable for foundation plantings, shade borders, and garden positions where the full-size species would be too large.

Silk Bay is a Florida endemic member of the laurel family, native to the ancient, fire-maintained scrub habitats of the central and southern Florida peninsula, where it grows in pure white sand alongside Scrub Hickory, Florida Rosemary, and scrub oaks in conditions of extreme infertility and drainage. The leaves are smaller and silkier than those of the closely related Red Bay and Swamp Bay, with a distinctive silky pubescence on the undersides; small, dark blue-black drupes produced in summer and fall provide important food for Florida Scrub-Jays, fish crows, and migratory songbirds. Like all native bays in the genus Persea, Silk Bay is highly susceptible to laurel wilt disease, an exotic fungal pathogen spread by the redbay ambrosia beetle that has devastated native bay populations across the Southeast. Plant in extremely well-drained, infertile, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; this species demands perfect drainage and will quickly decline in heavy, wet, irrigated, or highly amended soils.

common_name: Silk Floss Tree (Palo Borracho, Pink Floss Silk Tree, Ceiba speciosa)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Silk Floss Tree is drought-tolerant once established and resents waterlogged conditions. Ceiba speciosa (formerly Chorisia speciosa) is a large, fast-growing ornamental tree native to the Gran Chaco and Atlantic Forest regions of South America (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay) in the family Malvaceae (the mallow family, which also includes Hibiscus and cotton). The tree is immediately identifiable at any age by its green to gray-green trunk studded with large, conical, bottle-shaped spines that cover the bark from ground to canopy — the spines function as water-storage adaptations during the dry season of its native habitat and create a sculptural, primeval appearance. In fall (October–November in zone 9), after the leaves have dropped, the bare, spiny branches produce an extraordinary display of large (4–6 inch), 5-petaled flowers in shades of bright pink to rose-magenta with a white and yellow-streaked center — a bloom so striking on leafless branches that the tree resembles a pink-flowering cloud when viewed from a distance. The large, oval seed pods that follow split open in late winter to release abundant silky white floss that carries the seeds on the wind. Established trees are impressively cold-tolerant — a remarkable quality in a tree with so tropical an appearance.

Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; silk tassel bush is a California native evergreen shrub or small tree producing some of the most dramatic winter catkins of any temperate plant — long, silky, pale gray-green to silver catkins that hang in cascading clusters from the branch tips of male plants from December through February, swaying in the winter wind and creating an arresting spectacle during the garden's emptiest period. On the male cultivar 'James Roof' (the most widely grown), these catkins can reach 14 inches long and are present in such abundance that the entire shrub seems draped with silver-gray fringe. Female plants produce grape-like clusters of purple berries if a male pollinator is nearby. The foliage is leathery, wavy-edged, and deep glossy green with woolly gray undersides, giving the shrub excellent texture year-round. Drought-tolerant once established and native to coastal California chaparral and mixed evergreen forest, it thrives in mild climates but resents excessive summer irrigation. An outstanding specimen for dry gardens, woodland edges, and shrub borders where winter interest is most needed.

Silky Camellia is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful native shrubs in North America, native to moist, acidic forest understories from Virginia and Tennessee south to Florida and west to Arkansas and Texas, where it blooms in May through July with large, pure white, five-petaled flowers featuring a central boss of deep bluish-purple filaments with yellow anthers — a combination found nowhere else in the native flora and reminiscent of a Japanese camellia. The flowers open sequentially over several weeks and are followed by attractive woody capsules; the fall foliage turns shades of orange and scarlet. Despite its beauty, Silky Camellia is notoriously slow-growing and slow to establish, taking many years to reach blooming size and resenting transplanting once established — but gardeners who invest the time and proper siting conditions are rewarded with a genuinely spectacular flowering shrub. Provide moist, deeply amended, acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; mulch heavily and water regularly during the first several years.

common_name: Silky Oak (Australian Silver Oak, Fern-Leaf Grevillea)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; silky oak is drought-tolerant and fast-growing — site with ample space. Grevillea robusta (silky oak or Australian silver oak) is a large, fast-growing Australian native tree from the subtropical rainforests of Queensland and New South Wales — one of the most widely planted and recognizable Australian trees in subtropical and warm-temperate regions worldwide. The tree produces extraordinarily beautiful, deeply pinnate to bi-pinnate, fern-like leaves with a silver-silky underside (the 'silky' in the name) that create a delicate, lacy, architectural texture rare in a tree of this size. In spring, the tree is covered with striking, elongated clusters of golden-orange to rusty-orange 'brush' flowers (each a typical Proteaceae flower with a long, curling style) that attract bees, butterflies, and in Australia, honeyeaters. In the US, silky oak is used as a street tree and large specimen in zone 8–11 Florida and California, where it grows rapidly to 50–80 feet. In India, silky oak is one of the most commonly planted shade trees on tea plantations, providing canopy shade for tea bushes (and its wood is the traditional material for Indian furniture in colonial-era designs). It tolerates lean, acidic soils and drought once established — very low maintenance once past establishment. CAUTION: Contact dermatitis reported in some individuals from handling leaves or wood.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; silver bush is a compact Mediterranean shrub of the bindweed family prized for its outstanding foliage — small, narrow, lance-shaped leaves so densely covered with fine, silky, silver hairs that the entire plant appears to be fashioned from spun silver, creating a brilliant, luminous effect in the hot, sunny garden. From spring through summer it produces successive flushes of typical bindweed-shaped flowers, each a pure white funnel with a faint pink exterior, emerging from distinctly pinkish buds and opening into clean white — the contrast of the metallic silver foliage and snow-white flowers being extraordinary. A Mediterranean cliff and limestone plant from rocky coastal scrub, it requires the same lean, dry, well-drained, sunny conditions as lavender and rosemary and performs best with no summer irrigation in appropriate climates. Outstanding in combination with other silver-leafed and drought-tolerant Mediterranean plants in water-wise gardens.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky coastal soil in full sun; silver buttonwood is a variety of buttonwood (Conocarpus erectus) distinguished by its striking silvery-gray foliage — the leaves are covered with fine, silky, silver-gray hairs (sericeus = silky) that give the entire plant a luminous, metallic quality unlike any other coastal plant. An outstanding ornamental for coastal landscapes in zone 10–11, it provides year-round silver foliage color with outstanding resistance to salt spray, drought, wind, and shallow rocky soils. Extremely tolerant of coastal exposure and one of the most salt-tolerant broadleaf trees for South Florida coastal plantings. Widely used as a coastal hedge, specimen shrub, or small tree in South Florida landscaping. The small, rounded flower clusters and button-like fruiting heads give the buttonwoods their common name. A native of coastal hammocks and mangrove transitions.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry between waterings. Crassula arborescens (silver dollar jade, silver jade plant) is a South African relative of the common jade plant, distinguished by larger, nearly circular, powdery blue-grey leaves edged in red that intensifies with bright light and cooler temperatures. It grows more slowly and stays more compact for longer than Crassula ovata, but over years develops a similar thick, woody, tree-like trunk and can be trained as a striking succulent bonsai in a shallow container. Propagate from stem or leaf cuttings allowed to callus for a day or two before rooting in dry succulent mix; established plants tolerate brief dry spells well but are quick to rot if left in soggy soil, especially in winter. Small pale-pink, star-shaped flower clusters may appear in late winter on mature specimens grown in strong light.

common_name: Silver Lace Vine (Russian Vine, Mile-a-Minute Vine)
notes: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; silver lace vine (Russian vine, or 'mile-a-minute' vine for its extraordinary growth rate — up to 15 feet per year) is one of the fastest-growing hardy vines available, capable of covering an entire structure, fence, or wall in a single growing season with dense, twining stems. In late summer and early autumn it produces masses of tiny white to pinkish-white flowers in enormous, frothy plumes covering the entire vine — creating one of the most spectacular displays of any vine in bloom, resembling a cloud of white foam or lace. Native to central Asia (Tajikistan and Afghanistan). Despite its aggressive growth, the vine dies completely to the ground in cold winters, making management easier in zones 4–6 than in milder climates where it may remain semi-evergreen. Valuable for quickly covering unsightly fences, walls, and structures where nothing else would grow fast enough. Do not plant near delicate or small plants it might overwhelm. Potentially invasive — check local status.

Plant divisions in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; silver lady fern (dwarf tree fern) is a Pacific Island native that is one of the most architecturally impressive of the smaller tropical ferns — it develops a short, stout, fibrous trunk topped by an elegant crown of spreading, once-pinnate, ladder-like fronds with smooth, glossy, dark-green pinnae that give the plant a clean, refined, almost tropical prehistoric quality. As the plant matures it resembles a miniature tree fern, with the arching crown of fronds rising from an increasingly taller fibrous stem, eventually reaching 3–4 feet in height with an elegant, sculptural silhouette distinctly different from the bushier, non-trunked appearance of most ferns. An excellent specimen fern for shaded tropical gardens, container plantings, and indoor bright-shade locations. More tolerant of dry indoor air than many tropical ferns. In zone 9, protect from frost — the crown is the most vulnerable part. 'Silver Lady' is the standard cultivar widely grown.

common_name: Silver Leaf Philodendron (Brandt's Philodendron, Olive Leaf Philodendron)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Silver Leaf Philodendron is adaptable to lower light levels than many collector philodendrons but produces its best growth and most vibrant silver leaf coloration with consistent bright indirect light. Philodendron brandtianum is a climbing philodendron from Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, and Peru, valued for its distinctive and unusually colored foliage: the heart-shaped to oval leaves emerge in shades of rich olive-bronze and mature to a striking combination of grayish-green base color overlaid with irregular patches and blotches of silver and pale gray, creating an iridescent, metallic quality in the leaf that is unusual among philodendrons. The contrast between the olive-toned base and the silvery markings is most visible in raking or indirect light and varies somewhat depending on growing conditions. The leaves are smaller than many philodendrons (typically 4–8 inches), giving the plant a neater, more compact form well-suited to hanging baskets and medium-sized containers. New leaves emerge on vivid red-pink petioles that fade to green as the leaf matures, adding further ornamental interest.
