Philodendron brandtianum is generally regarded as more adaptable and easier to grow than most collector aroids, tolerating imperfect humidity and temperature fluctuation with less damage to its appearance than the demanding velvet types. All parts toxic due to calcium oxalate.

Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to neutral or slightly acidic, fertile to average, deep loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; silver linden is distinguished from other lindens by the distinctive silver-white felt of dense, soft hairs on the undersides of the dark green leaves — when a breeze stirs the canopy, the alternating flash of dark green upper surfaces and brilliant silver-white undersides creates a shimmering, sparkling effect quite unlike any other tree. The heavily fragrant, creamy-white flowers in summer are powerfully honeyed and sweet — the flowers are harvested for linden flower tea (tilleul) across European countries, used as a relaxing, mildly sedative herbal remedy. The most heat- and drought-tolerant of the European lindens — surviving hot, dry summers in southeastern Europe better than other linden species. More adaptable to urban conditions (heat, air pollution, drought) than American basswood or littleleaf linden. An excellent street and shade tree where its large scale is appropriate. The silver leaf underside display when windblown is one of the finest effects of any ornamental tree.

Silver Maple is the fastest-growing of the native maples, native to the streambanks, bottomlands, and moist lowlands of eastern North America from New Brunswick to Florida and west to the Dakotas, producing a new flush of growth each season that can exceed 3 feet per year in rich, moist alluvial soil. It is among the first native trees to bloom in late winter (February–March), producing clusters of tiny red flowers on bare branches that are one of the most important early pollen and nectar sources of the year for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. The leaves are deeply lobed with silvery-white undersides that shimmer and flash in the breeze, creating a beautiful display in summer wind storms; fall color is modest — pale yellow to orange. The wood is softer and weaker than other maples and Silver Maple is prone to branch breakage in ice storms, making maintenance planning important; it is most appropriate for wet, low-lying sites near water where its moisture tolerance, fast growth, and wildlife value are assets. Keep away from foundations and sewer lines.

common_name: Silver Monstera (Siltepecana Monstera, El Salvador Monstera)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Silver Monstera is more tolerant of lower light than Monstera deliciosa but produces its best growth and most dramatic leaf size with consistent bright indirect light. Monstera siltepecana is a small-to-medium Monstera species native to southern Mexico (Chiapas, hence 'siltepecana' from the Siltepec region) south through Central America to El Salvador, producing one of the most striking examples of heterophylly (dramatic leaf-form difference between juvenile and adult stages) in the Araceae family. In the juvenile or trailing phase, the plant produces small (3–5 inch), elongated leaves with a distinctive silver or gray-blue metallic sheen overlaid on the dark green surface — silvery markings between the lateral veins that create an unmistakable iridescent effect, giving the species its common name 'Silver Monstera.' When provided a vertical climbing support and allowed to mature, the same plant produces dramatically larger adult leaves (12–24 inches) that develop fenestrations (holes) and lose the juvenile silver coloration entirely — a transformation so complete that juvenile and adult forms were historically treated as separate species. The juvenile silver form is what is sold commercially and is the reason for the plant's popularity. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

Plant stem cuttings in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic potting mix in bright indirect light to shade; allow the top inch to dry slightly between waterings. Scindapsus pictus (silver pothos or satin pothos) is a Southeast Asian tropical vine prized for its extraordinary leaf texture — heart-shaped, matte-surfaced leaves 4–6 inches long overlaid with an irregular, splashed pattern of silver spots and variegation that has a unique, almost luminous 'satin' quality unlike the shiny surface of true pothos (Epipremnum aureum). The silver spotting pattern varies from light splashing (in 'Argyraeus') to heavy, nearly complete silver covering (in 'Exotica' or 'Silver Splash'). In the wild, the plant climbs large trees in Southeast Asian rainforests, producing larger, more deeply patterned leaves as it ascends toward the canopy. In cultivation, it trails or climbs moderately and adapts well to hanging baskets, climbing poles, and shaded wall coverage in tropical gardens. CAUTION: Like most aroids, silver pothos is toxic to cats and dogs if ingested. It tolerates lower light levels than many tropical vines, making it particularly valuable for deeply shaded interior spaces.

common_name: Silver Saw Palmetto (Silvery-Blue Coastal Saw Palmetto)
notes: Plant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; saw palmetto tolerates poor, dry, or salty coastal soils exceptionally well once established. Silver Saw Palmetto is a striking silvery-blue-leaved form of the native saw palmetto, most commonly found naturally along coastal dunes, offering the same slow-growing, spreading, low-trunked or trunkless habit of the species with the added ornamental impact of icy-blue fan fronds that contrast beautifully with green landscape plantings. Like the species it is extremely tough, drought- and salt-tolerant, and long-lived, making it an excellent low-maintenance native accent for xeriscape and coastal Gulf South gardens. It is very slow-growing, so patience is needed for a young plant to reach a substantial size, and it requires almost no supplemental care once established beyond removal of old fronds.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Silver Sword philodendron climbs readily and develops larger, more elongated leaves with vertical support. Narrow, elongated, arrowhead-shaped leaves have a matte, silvery-blue-green cast and a soft, almost velvety sheen, a cool, muted coloring that stands out among the mostly solid green or variegated philodendrons more commonly grown. A selection of Philodendron hastatum, it climbs steadily up a moss pole, producing progressively larger, more elongated silvery leaves as the vine matures, and its understated, elegant color makes it a popular choice for a minimalist or monochromatic plant display. Provide bright indirect light to maintain the silvery sheen, keep humidity moderate to high, and let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

common_name: Silver Trumpet Tree (Caribbean Trumpet Tree, Golden Tabebuia, Aurea Trumpet)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to rocky, moderately fertile soil — Silver Trumpet Tree is highly drought-tolerant and performs beautifully in the sandy, alkaline soils common throughout the Gulf Coast and South Florida where many flowering trees struggle. Tabebuia aurea is a medium-sized, deciduous to semi-deciduous tree native to the dry forests and savannas of Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Argentina in the Bignoniaceae family, closely related to the widely-planted Pink Trumpet Tree (Handroanthus impetiginosus). In spring, after the dry season has caused leaf drop, the bare, silver-gray branches of Tabebuia aurea produce one of the most spectacular flowering displays of any flowering tree: masses of large, 3-inch, bright golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers covering every branch simultaneously before the new leaves emerge — the tree appears as a golden cloud against the sky when viewed from a distance. The palmate, silver-green, leathery compound leaves that emerge after flowering are themselves attractive in a silvery, semi-succulent way, explaining the common name 'Silver Trumpet Tree.' Tabebuia aurea is considered one of the best-performing and most cold-tolerant of the tropical trumpet trees for zone 9 Gulf South use, and established trees in Houston, New Orleans, and adjacent areas have produced reliably spectacular spring bloom displays for decades. The national tree of Venezuela.

common_name: Silver Waves Camellia (Large Ruffled White Anemone-Form Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Silver Waves is an Award of Garden Merit-winning camellia bearing large, semi-double to anemone-form flowers of pure white with gently ruffled, wavy-edged petals surrounding a center of golden stamens, a bold, textured flower form that stands out among the many flatter-petaled white camellia cultivars. It flowers over a long midseason window on a vigorous, well-branched shrub with the glossy, dark-green foliage typical of Camellia japonica. Its large, distinctive flowers make it a strong specimen or accent planting; prune, if needed, immediately after bloom in late winter or early spring, before next year's flower buds set.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; silverleaf hydrangea tolerates more sun and drier soil than smooth hydrangea once established, thanks to the reflective undersides of its leaves. Hydrangea radiata is a Southern Appalachian endemic closely related to smooth hydrangea (Hydrangea arborescens), distinguished by the brilliant silvery-white undersides of its leaves, which flash dramatically whenever the foliage moves in a breeze, topped by flattened clusters of small white flowers with a ring of showier sterile florets in summer. Its striking two-toned foliage effect makes it a distinctive choice for a shaded native shrub border, and its Appalachian mountain origin gives it good tolerance of the humid Southeast when given adequate shade and moisture. Prune out old wood in late winter as needed, since it blooms on new growth and tolerates hard pruning well if rejuvenation is needed.

common_name: Singapore Plumeria (White Frangipani, Evergreen Frangipani, Blunt Leaf Plumeria)
notes: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, preferably sandy or rocky soil; Plumeria obtusa is drought-tolerant once established and will rot in heavy, moisture-retaining soils. Plumeria obtusa is a tropical flowering tree native to the Caribbean islands (Cuba, Jamaica, Bahamas, Hispaniola) that has become one of the most widely planted ornamental trees throughout tropical Asia, particularly Singapore and Thailand, where it is now so ubiquitous in Buddhist temple gardens and public landscapes that it has acquired the common name 'Singapore Plumeria,' though it is not native to that region. Unlike the deciduous Plumeria rubra (the most widely planted frangipani in the US), P. obtusa remains evergreen year-round in frost-free climates, retaining its broad, glossy, dark-green, blunt-tipped leaves through all seasons — the specific epithet 'obtusa' refers to the rounded, blunt (obtuse) leaf tips that distinguish it from the narrower-tipped P. rubra. The flowers are pure white with a bright yellow center and produce the classic sweet, tropical frangipani fragrance that is among the most widely recognized flower fragrances in the world. The blooms appear at the stem tips in clusters and are borne for months in warm climates. The milky, latex sap that exudes from cut stems is irritating to skin and eyes. In zone 9, P. obtusa is most practical as a large container specimen brought in during winter.

common_name: Singapore Rhododendron (Indian Rhododendron, Senduduk, Malabar Melastome)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil — Singapore Rhododendron produces the most flowers in full sun but tolerates and grows attractively in partial shade, which suits its natural habitat as an edge and forest-margin species. Melastoma malabathricum is a fast-growing, evergreen, multi-stemmed tropical shrub native from India and Sri Lanka through all of Southeast Asia to Australia in the Melastomataceae family, widely grown throughout the tropical world as an ornamental flowering shrub for its prolific production of bright, showy, 5-petaled flowers in vivid magenta-pink to rose-purple. The flowers are large for a shrub (2–3 inches across), saucer-shaped, with five distinctly veined petals in intense magenta to hot pink and a central cluster of curved, two-toned stamens in yellow and purple — a flower with genuine ornamental impact. The plant blooms throughout the year in zone 10-11, never without flowers for long. The common name 'Singapore Rhododendron' reflects both its wide use as an ornamental in Singapore and the general resemblance of the flower to a tropical Rhododendron, though the plants are not botanically related. The ripe berries are edible (though they turn the mouth and teeth temporarily black — the genus name means 'black mouth' in Greek), sweet, and consumed in Southeast Asian traditional practice. A robust, reliable, and free-flowering ornamental shrub for zone 9b-11 warm, moist gardens.

Abelia uniflora is the wild Chinese species behind the many hybrid abelias common in cultivation, and it deserves far wider use in its own right for its graceful arching habit and long succession of single white-to-pink tubular flowers from summer into fall. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; it tolerates a range of soil types once established and is notably deer resistant. Propagate by softwood cuttings taken in early summer, rooting them in a moist perlite-peat mix under intermittent mist or a plastic tent. Light renewal pruning immediately after flowering encourages fresh branching and extends the bloom season without sacrificing the following year's flower buds.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; sinojackia is one of the rarest and most underused small ornamental trees in cultivation — a member of the Styracaceae family (relatives include Styrax and Halesia), it produces profuse, pure-white, star-shaped flowers with prominent yellow stamens in spring, blooming along the branches as the new leaves emerge and creating an effect reminiscent of a refined, smaller-scale Halesia carolina. Sinojackia xylocarpa is native to a restricted area of eastern China and is considered endangered in its native range, making cultivated plants in gardens an important contribution to ex-situ conservation. The flowers are followed by distinctive woody, beaked fruits that persist into winter and provide additional ornamental interest; the multi-stemmed habit and clean, oval leaves offer good fall color. An exceptional conversation piece for collectors and enthusiasts, best displayed as a specimen or focal point in a woodland garden where its delicate flowers can be appreciated at close range.

common_name: Sioux Crape Myrtle (Dark Pink Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Sioux is a medium-sized National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle producing deep hot-pink to rose-pink flower clusters from June through September — a vibrant, saturated pink that is warmer and more vivid than the typical light pinks common in older crape myrtle cultivars. The flowers are produced abundantly on an upright-spreading, multi-trunked tree reaching 15–20 feet in zone 9, providing both specimen tree and shade-tree functions for medium-sized residential landscapes. Like other National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, Sioux shows good resistance to powdery mildew compared to older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars. The exfoliating bark develops attractively with age, revealing warm tan to cinnamon tones beneath the peeling gray outer bark. Fall leaf color is orange-red. Sioux fills the important mid-sized slot between compact dwarf selections (under 10 feet) and the very large tree-sized Natchez and Muskogee, making it appropriate for typical suburban residential lot sizes where large-tree crape myrtles would eventually overwhelm the space. Remove any suckers that emerge from the base; lightly prune to remove crossing branches and dead wood only — do not top.

common_name: Sixteen Candles Summersweet (Dwarf Fragrant White-Flowered Clethra for Shade)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and mulch well to keep the shallow roots cool and consistently damp through summer heat. Sixteen Candles is a compact selection of native summersweet bred for dense, upright flower spikes that stand out from the foliage like small white candles, blooming in mid- to late summer with an intense, sweet fragrance that draws bees and butterflies from a distance. Its tolerance for wet, poorly drained soil and heavy shade makes it one of the more useful flowering shrubs for low spots, rain gardens, and woodland edges where few other shrubs bloom well, and its compact size suits smaller foundation plantings better than full-sized summersweet cultivars. Established plants sucker gently to form a dense colony over time and need little more than an occasional thinning of old canes to stay vigorous.

common_name: Sky Pencil Holly (Extremely Narrow Columnar Japanese Holly)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Sky Pencil is a striking Japanese holly selection with an extremely narrow, strictly upright, columnar growth habit unlike almost any other common shrub, reaching several feet tall while staying only a foot or so wide, which makes it a favorite for narrow side yards, tight entryway plantings, and repeated vertical accents flanking a doorway or path. The small, glossy, spineless leaves give it a refined, fine texture, and while it holds its narrow shape naturally, an occasional light shearing keeps individual plants uniform in a formal planting. It prefers consistently moist, well-drained soil, since it can struggle in soggy or very dry sites, and light staking when young helps prevent splaying in heavy snow or wind until the plant matures.

Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; deutzia blooms on old wood, so prune immediately after flowering in late spring by removing older canes at the base to renew the plant. Deutzia gracilis is a Japanese native deciduous shrub producing fountains of arching stems smothered in late spring with pure-white, star-shaped, 5-petaled flowers in upright, cylindrical racemes — one of the most reliably and abundantly flowering shrubs for temperate gardens. The slender, arching habit and prolific flowering make it ideal as a specimen, in groups, or as a flowering hedge in zones 4–8; the compact cultivar 'Nikko' (12–18 inches) is particularly useful as a groundcover or edging plant and offers outstanding red-purple fall color.

Slippery Elm is a large, somewhat coarser native elm than American Elm, native to rich, moist forest slopes, bottomlands, and upland woods throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to the Dakotas, named for the distinctive slippery, mucilaginous quality of its inner bark, which has been used medicinally for centuries as a demulcent (soothing agent) for sore throats, coughs, and gastrointestinal inflammation — the FDA has recognized the inner bark as a safe and effective over-the-counter demulcent. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves are distinctive and diagnostic for the species; the reddish, hairy leaf buds in late winter are among the first signs of life in the spring forest. While moderately susceptible to Dutch Elm Disease, Slippery Elm is adaptable to a wider range of soil conditions than American Elm, tolerating clay, limestone, and occasionally wet soils. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the coarse texture and broad shade make it a valuable native alternative to cultivated elms.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; small anise tree is more shade-tolerant and faster-growing than Florida anise (I. floridanum) and is especially effective as a tall, screening shrub in deep shade situations. Illicium parviflorum is a large, fast-growing, evergreen native shrub or small tree endemic to central Florida and historically occurring only in Volusia and Seminole counties, though now widely cultivated throughout the Gulf South for its outstanding performance as a screening plant in difficult shaded and wet conditions; it produces bright, lime-green to medium-green, aromatic, elliptic leaves and tiny, inconspicuous, pale yellowish flowers in spring. A workhorse screening shrub and hedge plant for zones 7–10 that can reach 8–15 feet tall quickly; it naturalizes along shaded stream banks, pond margins, and moist ravines.

common_name: Small-Flowered Cuphea (Candy Corn Cuphea, Micropetal Cuphea)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Small-Flowered Cuphea blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates partial shade and is more drought-tolerant than many tropical-looking ornamental shrubs once established. Cuphea micropetala is a compact, semi-woody, perennial shrub native to Mexico and Guatemala in the Lythraceae family, one of the most cold-hardy and ornamentally valuable of the approximately 260 Cuphea species for zone 8-11 gardens. The plant produces a dense, upright to somewhat mounding form with narrow, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves and an exceptionally free-flowering habit — producing dozens to hundreds of tubular flowers at the leaf axils simultaneously through the warm months from spring through fall. Each flower is a small (0.5-inch), tubular, slightly curved structure in orange to orange-red with a yellow-green tip — a bicolored orange-and-yellow pattern that strongly resembles a piece of candy corn, explaining the marketing name 'Candy Corn Plant' sometimes applied to this species. The nectar-rich, tubular, hummingbird-adapted flowers attract Ruby-throated, Rufous, and other hummingbird species reliably, with hummingbirds visiting and revisiting a flowering Cuphea micropetala plant dozens of times daily during migration. Greater cold hardiness (to zone 8) than most ornamental Cuphea species makes this a particularly valuable selection for zone 9 gardens. Non-toxic.

Sow seeds in spring directly into their permanent location or into deep containers to accommodate early taproot development. Plant in full sun in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil — this shrub thrives in poor, alkaline, or sandy conditions where most plants struggle. Once established it requires virtually no supplemental irrigation and tolerates wind, drought, and severe cold with ease. Use in mass plantings for erosion control, shelterbelts, or wildlife hedgerows across challenging exposed sites.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide a sturdy trellis, wall, or fence for climbing support. Bougainvillea glabra (smooth bougainvillea) is the species most commonly sold as 'bougainvillea' in the nursery trade — a vigorous, thorny, sprawling vine or shrub from Brazil producing masses of small, white, tubular true flowers surrounded by the magnificently colored bracts (modified leaves) in magenta, purple, red, orange, yellow, white, or bicolor combinations that are the ornamental feature of the plant. B. glabra differs from the common hybrid Bougainvillea spectabilis in having smooth (glabrous, as the name implies) stems and leaves vs. hairy stems and is generally considered more free-blooming and compact. Bougainvillea blooms most heavily after mild water stress in full sun; withhold water before anticipated bloom periods to trigger flowering. In zone 9, it may die back in hard freezes but resprouts vigorously from roots when established; in zones 10–12, it is a dramatic year-round bloomer. Stems are armed with sharp thorns; handle with heavy gloves.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; smooth hydrangea is the native parent of the enormously popular cultivars 'Annabelle' and 'Incrediball', which have transformed shade gardens with their enormous round white flower heads up to 12 inches across. Unlike oakleaf hydrangea, smooth hydrangea blooms on new wood — cut all stems to 12–18 inches in late winter for the strongest, most floriferous performance. It grows naturally along stream banks, woodland edges, and cliff faces across the eastern US and tolerates more shade and competition than most shrubs. If flower heads become too heavy for stems, cut back less severely the following year. Pollinators of many species use the tiny fertile flowers at the center of the flower heads.

Plant in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; smooth winterberry is a native deciduous holly of the Atlantic Coastal Plain, closely related to but slightly smaller and more southern-adapted than common winterberry (I. verticillata). The glossy leaves and more tapered, smooth-margined leaflets distinguish it from the more northern species. In fall, the bright orange-red to scarlet berries are produced in exceptional abundance — smaller than I. verticillata berries but often in denser clusters — and persist into winter. The plant grows naturally in bog edges, wet flatwoods, and pond margins from Maine south to Georgia, making it well-suited to zone 9a moist conditions where it is more reliable than its northern relative. The berries are critically important winter food for bluebirds, robins, and cedar waxwings. Like all hollies, the berries are toxic to humans.

Direct sow after frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; snail vine is a vigorous tropical vine from South America producing some of the most uniquely shaped flowers in the legume family — the petals are twisted into a tight spiral or snail-shell shape, creating a flower that looks as if it has been wound up like a corkscrew. The flowers are lavender-purple to pink and emit a rich, honey-vanilla fragrance that intensifies in the afternoon and evening. A rapid grower once established, covering a trellis or fence with lush, tropical foliage and weeks of unusual, fragrant flowers from midsummer through fall. Thomas Jefferson famously grew snail vine at Monticello, where he valued it as an ornamental and edible bean — the pods and seeds are edible. In zone 9a, it may perennialize in warm microclimates.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Swartzia madagascariensis is drought tolerant once established and adapted to seasonal dry conditions — water regularly in the first two years for establishment, then reduce to deep, infrequent watering or rely on seasonal rainfall in tropical climates. Swartzia madagascariensis (Snake Bean Tree or Worm Tree) is a large, semi-deciduous to evergreen legume tree native to the woodland savannas, miombo forests, and bushveld of tropical and sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal east through Ethiopia and south through East Africa to Zimbabwe and Mozambique, where it is recognized as one of the most distinctive fruiting trees of the African savanna by its extraordinarily long, pendulous, corded, snake-like or worm-like seed pods — each 18 to 36 inches long, twisted and constricted between seeds, hanging in spectacular cascades from the branches. The creamy-white and yellow flowers carried in dense clusters attract pollinators before the pods develop. The hard, heavy, dark-reddish-brown heartwood is highly valued as a traditional timber for construction, tool handles, musical instruments, and carving across the tree's range. The bark and roots are widely used in traditional African medicine for pain relief, wound healing, and anti-parasitic applications. An exceptional specimen tree for large tropical gardens, wildlife areas, and agroforestry systems.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; snow bush (snowbush, calico plant) is a Pacific Islands tropical shrub that produces some of the most elaborately variegated foliage available in tropical landscaping — the small, oval leaves are mottled, splashed, spotted, and streaked with white, pink, red, and green in patterns that vary from leaf to leaf and intensify in color through the growing season, creating a continuously shifting kaleidoscope of color. Young growth is especially vibrant, flushing pink and red before developing its characteristic multi-colored pattern. The cascading, arching branch habit creates a graceful, cottage-garden character despite the dramatic coloring. Excellent as a colorful accent in tropical mixed borders, as a container specimen, and as a vibrant informal hedge in zones 10–12. Full sun intensifies the coloring; partial shade softens it. Frost-sensitive — protect or bring indoors when temperatures approach 35°F. The cultivar 'Roseo-Picta' is the standard ornamental selection with the fullest color range.

common_name: Snow Flurry Camellia (Cold-Hardy White Ackerman Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with some protection from harsh winter wind in the coldest parts of its range. Snow Flurry is one of the most floriferous of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy Winter-series camellia hybrids, smothering its spreading, dense evergreen branches in small, white, anemone-form flowers with ruffled centers over a long fall-into-winter bloom season. Its Camellia oleifera parentage gives it notably better cold hardiness than standard Camellia japonica, letting gardeners at the colder edge of camellia range enjoy a heavy floral display that would otherwise be unreliable. The naturally spreading, slightly weeping habit also makes it useful for a low, wide evergreen groundcover-like planting rather than the more upright shape typical of most camellias. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom and prune lightly only to shape.

common_name: Snow Fountains Weeping Cherry (Cascading White-Flowered Dwarf Cherry)
notes: Snow Fountains is a compact, strongly weeping flowering cherry, its slender branches cascading nearly to the ground and smothered in small, single, pure white flowers in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge, giving a fountain-like effect that suits it well as a specimen near a patio or entry where its form can be appreciated up close. It stays considerably smaller than most flowering cherries, making it a good fit for a modest-sized yard, and its glossy green summer foliage turns orange-red in fall for additional seasonal interest. Give it moist, well-drained soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to shape and remove crossing branches, and expect the shorter lifespan typical of ornamental cherries, which are prone to canker and borer problems as they age.

common_name: Snow N Summer Asiatic Jasmine (Variegated White-Splashed Groundcover)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and mulch and water regularly until the low, twining stems knit together into a solid mat. Snow N Summer is a variegated sport of Asiatic jasmine bearing small, glossy leaves heavily splashed in white and cream over green, with new growth often flushed pink in cool weather, giving the groundcover noticeably brighter, more varied color than the plain species. It shares the same dense, weed-suppressing, low-maintenance habit prized in Asiatic jasmine, making it useful for lightening dry shade under trees, slopes, and other spots where mowing is impractical, though its variegated leaves are somewhat less vigorous and slower to fill in than solid green Asiatic jasmine. Shear back hard in early spring every couple of years to remove old woody growth and encourage dense, colorful new foliage, and watch for any all-green reverted shoots, cutting them out to keep the planting true to type.

common_name: Snow Queen Oakleaf Hydrangea (Upright Classic Oakleaf Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, allowing room for its full 5–7 foot spread at maturity. A Georgia-bred, Award of Garden Merit-winning selection introduced in the 1960s, Snow Queen is one of the most widely planted oakleaf hydrangea cultivars, valued for its unusually erect, well-branched flower panicles that stand upright rather than nodding, and its heavier-than-average flower production compared to the wild species. Flowers open white in early summer, age to a rich pink-bronze by late summer, and can be left standing through fall and winter for continued interest, while the bold, deeply lobed foliage turns brilliant shades of red, orange, and burgundy in fall before the shrub's cinnamon, exfoliating bark takes over as the winter feature. Blooms form on old wood, so prune, if needed, only in the weeks right after flowering.

common_name: Snow White Indian Hawthorn (Compact White-Flowered Indian Hawthorn)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Snow White is a compact Indian hawthorn cultivar producing abundant clusters of pure white flowers in spring, followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds, all on a dense, rounded mound of glossy, leathery, disease-resistant foliage. Its low, tidy habit fits foundation plantings, low borders, and coastal landscape beds, and it shares the species' outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, heat, and poor sandy soils, making it a dependable performer in exposed Gulf Coast sites. Good air circulation between plants helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

Snowberry is a low-growing, thicket-forming native shrub of North American forests and woodland edges, producing the remarkable clusters of pure white, waxy berries (technically drupes) in fall that gave the plant its name — the berries are striking against the bare winter stems, remaining on the plant through November and December as one of the last fruits visible in the winter woodland. The berries are technically mildly toxic to humans (containing saponins) but are consumed by birds including ruffed grouse, pheasants, and robins, as well as by black bears and other mammals; they were used medicinally by several indigenous tribes. Snowberry spreads freely by stolons to form dense, erosion-controlling thickets — excellent for stabilizing slopes and difficult, shaded problem areas where other shrubs struggle to establish. The small, pink tubular flowers in summer are a critical nectar source for hummingbirds and are also visited by native bees; the twinberry hummingbird (Calypte anna) in the west is particularly associated with Symphoricarpos species as a nectar plant.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, fast-draining, rocky soil in full sun, choosing a dry slope or open site similar to the burned or disturbed forest ground this species naturally colonizes across the mountain West. Snowbrush ceanothus fixes atmospheric nitrogen at its roots, allowing it to thrive in poor soils where it also improves fertility for neighboring plants. Its dense, fragrant clusters of small white flowers in early summer are among the most heavily visited native shrub blooms for bees, butterflies, and other pollinators, while deer and elk browse the evergreen foliage and small mammals and birds eat the seed. The thick, glossy leaves and low, spreading form also provide valuable cover for ground-nesting birds.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Snowflake oakleaf hydrangea is a superior selection of the native oakleaf hydrangea, distinguished by its remarkable double flowers — each individual floret in the large panicle cluster bears extra petals and sepals that give the entire flower head a dense, fully doubled appearance unlike the single-flowered species. The enormous, conical flower clusters can reach 12 inches long and are an extraordinary display in late spring and early summer in zone 9 (May–June). The flowers open pure white, age to soft rose-pink over several weeks, then become a papery tan-cream that persists through fall as attractive dried flower heads. Snowflake was selected and patented by plantsman Jeff Beasley of Piccadilly Farm in Georgia. The large, deeply lobed, oak-like leaves develop outstanding burgundy-red to reddish-purple fall color in September–October in zone 9 — exceptional for a shade shrub. The attractive exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Snowflake grows somewhat larger than the single-flowered species but retains the same outstanding adaptability to humid southeastern conditions.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; soaptree yucca is the state flower of New Mexico, an iconic desert grassland plant with narrow, flexible, blue-green leaves edged in white, curling fibers that top a slender trunk which develops slowly over many decades, eventually reaching tree height in old specimens. A tall, arching flower stalk rises well above the foliage in late spring, densely packed with creamy white, bell-shaped flowers pollinated exclusively by the yucca moth in an obligate partnership found throughout the genus. The roots and trunk contain natural saponins historically used by Native American and Mexican communities as a soap and shampoo substitute, the source of its common name. It is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant, requiring virtually no supplemental water once established, and makes a striking, slow-growing architectural specimen for xeriscape and desert-style landscapes.

common_name: Sodom Apple (Rubber Bush, Dead Sea Apple)
notes: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy dryland soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant; CAUTION: All parts are highly toxic; the milky latex causes severe skin and eye irritation — wear gloves and eye protection when handling. Calotropis procera (Sodom apple, rubber bush, or Dead Sea apple) is a drought-resistant tropical shrub native to the dryland regions of sub-Saharan Africa, the Sahel, North Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia — naturalized across warm, arid, disturbed habitats worldwide. The plant is related to and resembles crown flower (C. gigantea) but is typically smaller and better adapted to drier, harsher conditions. The most distinctive feature of C. procera is its unusual fruit: large (2–3 inch), perfectly round, hollow, inflated pods that look like smooth, apple-green, apple-shaped balloons — hence 'Sodom apple' (the reference to Sodom in the Dead Sea region where it is found). When ripe and dry, the pods burst open to release small seeds attached to long, silky, white, cottony fibers similar to milkweed floss; this floss has been used as stuffing material and in traditional rope-making. Small (1-inch), waxy, lavender and white, star-shaped flowers are produced abundantly. The milky white latex is extremely toxic and caustic — used historically as an arrow poison in Africa. Despite its toxicity, the fiber and bark have traditional uses across Africa and Asia.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Soft Caress is a revolutionary mahonia introduction from China — the first mahonia to produce completely thornless, soft, fine-textured leaves that can be touched without the painful spines that characterize traditional mahonias like Mahonia bealei and M. aquifolium. The soft, narrow, willow-like leaflets are arranged in the typical pinnate mahonia pattern but are smooth-edged and as soft to the touch as fine grass — making Soft Caress the first mahonia that can be used in foot-traffic adjacent plantings, children's play areas, and along pathways without hazard. The graceful, arching form (3–5 feet tall, similar spread) with cascading, fine-textured leaflets creates an exceptionally refined and unusual texture in the shade garden — unlike any other widely available shade shrub. In fall and early winter (October–December), Soft Caress produces racemes of bright-yellow flowers along the stem tips, followed by small, blue-black, powdery-coated fruits that are attractive to birds. The plant thrives in deep shade where few other shrubs grow well — performing under dense tree canopies that exclude even azaleas and camellias. Cold-hardy to the low-single-digits Fahrenheit, it is reliably perennial throughout zone 7–9. A landmark introduction for shade gardeners.

common_name: Soft Touch Holly (Spineless Dwarf Mounding Japanese Holly)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Soft Touch is a Japanese holly selection valued for its genuinely soft, spineless foliage, pleasant to brush against or work around unlike the prickly leaves of Chinese hollies, combined with a naturally dense, low, rounded mounding habit that stays tidy with little to no pruning. Its fine-textured, boxwood-like appearance makes it a popular low-maintenance substitute for boxwood in foundation plantings and low borders, especially in humid climates where boxwood can struggle with disease. It prefers consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil and tolerates a range of light conditions from partial shade to nearly full sun, needing only an occasional light shearing if a more formal outline is wanted.

Plant offsets or container-grown plants in spring in any well-drained to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and require virtually no maintenance once established. Yucca recurvifolia is among the most garden-friendly of all yuccas because its long, blue-green leaves recurve or droop gracefully at the tips rather than ending in a sharp point, making it safe to plant along walkways and in high-traffic areas; it produces tall (3–5 ft) spikes of large, creamy white, bell-shaped flowers in early summer that are pollinated by yucca moths and are dramatic and beautiful. The plant spreads slowly by offsets to form attractive colonies and is extremely tolerant of heat, drought, salt spray, and poor sandy soils — a nearly indestructible landscape plant for Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 gardens.

common_name: Sombreuil Rose (Antique White Climbing Tea Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor, allowing 4-6 feet for its climbing spread. Introduced in France in 1850, Sombreuil is a climbing tea rose bearing large, flat, densely quartered, creamy-white blooms tinged with the faintest blush of pink, carrying a light tea fragrance and considered one of the finest white antique climbers for its old-fashioned flower form. It blooms repeatedly from spring through fall, most heavily in spring, and performs reliably in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South with good resistance to blackspot compared to many climbing roses. Train the long canes horizontally along a fence or arbor rather than straight up a post, since horizontally trained canes produce far more flowering side-shoots than vertical ones. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to remove spent wood, saving any structural pruning for full winter dormancy.

Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and deadhead spent flower clusters through the summer to keep the rebloom cycle going. Unlike traditional weigela cultivars that flower only in a single spring flush on old wood, the Sonic Bloom series flowers on both old and new wood, producing a heavy spring display of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers followed by continued waves of bloom through summer into fall — dramatically extending the season of interest for a shrub usually valued for only a few spring weeks. Its hummingbird-attracting flowers and repeat bloom make it a strong choice where a longer season of color is wanted from a single shrub. Little pruning is required beyond removing dead or crossing branches, since rebloom on new wood makes timing far less critical than with old-wood-only weigela cultivars.

Plant in well-drained to dry, rocky, alkaline or neutral soil in full sun in zones 7–11; sorrelvine is a native Texas vine of the same family as grapes, naturally scrambling over limestone slopes, rocky draws, and caliche outcrops across central and south Texas. The trifoliate leaves superficially resemble poison ivy — enough to cause alarm — but sorrelvine has tendrils (poison ivy doesn't) and causes no skin irritation. The small black berries are eaten by birds but toxic to humans. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, with thickened roots that store water. In zone 9a it makes a vigorous summer vine that provides quick cover on a fence or trellis during the hottest part of the year. Dies back after hard frost but re-sprouts reliably from the base in spring.

Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; sourwood is a native American forest tree considered by many horticulturalists to be the finest small to medium-sized ornamental tree native to the eastern United States, offering four seasons of distinction: long, drooping panicles of small, white, lily-of-the-valley-like flowers in July and August (a rare native tree that flowers in midsummer when few other trees bloom); spectacular fall foliage in fiery scarlet-red to deep crimson — among the earliest and most vivid trees to color in autumn; persistent, creamy-white seed capsules that decorate the bare branches through winter; and elegant, slightly drooping branch tips that give the tree a graceful, somewhat weeping quality year-round. Sourwood honey (made by bees collecting nectar from the flowers) is considered among the finest American honeys. Strictly requires strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) and declines rapidly if planted in alkaline or compacted soils. Resents root disturbance after planting.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil; sourwood is among the most multi-season native trees of eastern North America, earning its place in the landscape with four distinct seasons of interest — it is a member of the heath family (Ericaceae) and one of the few trees in that family to achieve canopy stature. In July, when most trees offer nothing but foliage, sourwood erupts in long, arching, drooping panicles of small white urn-shaped flowers reminiscent of lily-of-the-valley — these are the primary source of the prized sourwood honey produced by Appalachian beekeepers, considered by many to be the finest American varietal honey. Fall color is nothing short of spectacular: leaves turn vivid scarlet to deep crimson while the persistent creamy seed capsules hang in graceful clusters, often coinciding with yellow foliage of neighboring trees for a striking contrast. The glossy, lance-shaped leaves have a pleasantly sour taste (hence the common name) and the tree's naturally layered branching habit provides excellent winter structure; it is exceptionally long-lived, low-maintenance, and virtually pest-free when sited in appropriately acidic soils.

Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in a location that receives partial shade, such as the edge of a woodland, streambank, or rain garden basin. Unlike most shrubs, this viburnum tolerates and even benefits from periodic inundation and clay soils. Water generously through the establishment period and maintain steady soil moisture thereafter — it will not perform well in dry conditions. White flower clusters open in spring and attract numerous native pollinators, while the dark blue fall berries are eagerly consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and other frugivorous birds.

common_name: Southern Catalpa (Cigar Tree, Indian Bean Tree, Hardy Catalpa)
notes: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, fertile soil in full sun; Southern catalpa is a fast-growing, bold-textured native deciduous tree of the southeastern United States — native to the Gulf Coastal Plain and Mississippi Delta region — producing enormous, heart-shaped, bright-green leaves up to 12 inches wide that create a dramatic tropical effect when backlit. In late spring and early summer, the tree produces spectacular upright clusters (panicles) of white, orchid-like flowers marked with yellow and purple spots, followed by distinctive long, narrow, cigar-like seed pods that reach 8–18 inches long and persist through winter, giving the tree its common names of 'cigar tree' and 'Indian bean tree.' The bold, tropical-looking foliage creates exceptional shade and the flower clusters are among the most beautiful of any North American native tree. The fallen flowers and seed pods can create some litter, so placement should account for cleanup. Southern catalpa is historically famous as catfish bait tree — the large catalpa sphinx moth caterpillars that feed on the leaves are prized as fishing bait. The tree adapts readily to the wide range of soil conditions found across the Gulf Coastal Plain, including heavy clay and periodically wet sites.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–5.5) soil amended with pine bark in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade; Southern Indica azaleas are the classic massive-flowering shrubs of Deep South gardens, producing spectacular displays of white, pink, red, lavender, or salmon flowers in spring that completely cover the plant. These are large, fast-growing plants — give them full mature-size spacing rather than planting them too close. They are much more heat- and root-rot tolerant than Northern azaleas and are specifically bred for Gulf Coast conditions. Mulch deeply with pine straw to maintain moisture and soil acidity. Prune immediately after flowering ends in spring, as next year's buds set on summer growth. Lace bugs are the primary pest — treat with systemic insecticide in late spring.

Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; southern live oak is the quintessential evergreen tree of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, forming massive, wide-spreading crowns with horizontal limbs draped in Spanish moss that define the character of the region. This long-lived giant is remarkably tough — salt spray, poor sandy soils, periodic flooding, and coastal winds are all tolerated once the tree is established, and mature trees are exceptionally drought-tolerant. The small, dark acorns are produced in generous quantities and are critically important food for wood ducks, mallards, squirrels, and deer. Acorn production begins at 25 years and peaks in trees 75 years and older, underscoring that this is a multigenerational planting that rewards patience with an irreplaceable landscape anchor.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; southern magnolia is the defining icon of the Deep South, a massive evergreen tree with leathery, glossy dark green leaves (with rusty-brown undersides) and enormous, intensely fragrant white flowers up to 12 inches across that open from May through September — among the largest flowers of any native North American tree. The tree is native to the coastal plain from North Carolina to Texas and is the state flower and tree of Mississippi and Louisiana. Compact cultivars like 'Little Gem' (20–25 feet, repeat-blooming) and 'Brackens Brown Beauty' make it accessible for smaller gardens. The cone-like fruit with brilliant red seeds is highly ornamental and provides important food for gray squirrels, turkeys, and songbirds. Plant away from foundations, driveways, and structures to allow for its eventual large size.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade at wetland edges, spring-fed areas, and depression swamps; southern spicebush is a federally threatened native shrub of the southeastern United States, growing naturally in small, disjunct populations in depression swamps, bay swamps, and spring-fed wet areas from Missouri to Florida. A close relative of the common spicebush (L. benzoin) but adapted to wetter conditions and deeper shade, it produces the same intensely aromatic, spicy-fragrant foliage and stems when crushed. Like common spicebush, it is the larval host plant for the spicebush swallowtail butterfly. The beautiful yellow flowers in early spring emerge before the leaves, and the bright red drupes in fall provide excellent wildlife food. Growing this plant in the garden directly supports conservation of a federally threatened species while providing exceptional wildlife value in shaded, wet-site conditions.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; southern sugar maple is the heat-tolerant, summer-drought-adapted southern counterpart to the familiar sugar maple (Acer saccharum), differing in smaller leaf size, lighter texture, and significantly greater heat tolerance, performing well in zones 7–9 where northern sugar maple languishes or dies in the summer heat. The fall color is outstanding — rich orange, red, and yellow tones that rival northern sugar maple in many years — providing some of the best native fall color in the South. The bark is more furrowed and less smooth than northern maple. Although not tapped commercially for syrup, the sap does contain sugar. A superb native shade tree for southern gardens providing habitat, fall color, and a graceful canopy that suburban northern sugar maples cannot achieve in the Gulf South.

Plant in any soil — wet or dry, acidic or alkaline, rich or poor, sun or deep shade — wax myrtle tolerates virtually every condition in zone 7–11 once established and is arguably the Gulf Coast's most versatile and valuable native shrub. The aromatic, evergreen foliage provides year-round screening and privacy; both male and female plants produce tiny waxy blue-gray berries that encrust the branches in fall and winter, providing essential food for yellow-rumped warblers, tree swallows, and many other bird species that can digest the high-fat wax. The root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil over time. Prune heavily at any time to maintain a desired size, or allow it to develop naturally into a multi-trunked small tree 15–20 feet tall. The aromatic leaves have traditional use as an insect repellent.

common_name: Souvenir de St. Anne's Rose (Sparse-Petaled Antique Bourbon Rose)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Souvenir de St. Anne's is a distinctive sport of the famous Bourbon rose Souvenir de la Malmaison, bearing the same soft blush-pink coloring but with far fewer petals, giving each bloom a loose, semi-double, almost single-rose appearance that reveals its golden stamens. It repeats reliably through the growing season and, like other Bourbon roses, performs well in the heat and humidity of Southern gardens with good disease resistance for an antique variety. Its more compact, well-behaved habit compared with many old Bourbons makes it a manageable choice for a mixed border or heirloom rose collection. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued repeat flowering through the season.

common_name: Souvenir de la Malmaison Rose (Classic 1843 Bourbon Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun with excellent air circulation in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1843 and named for the rose garden of Empress Josephine at Château de Malmaison, this Bourbon rose is famous for enormous, flat, quartered blooms in soft blush-pink packed with dozens of petals and a rich, classic old-rose fragrance considered among the finest of any rose. It blooms in flushes from spring through fall on a compact, sturdy shrub, but in the humid Gulf South its densely petaled blooms can 'ball' — swelling with trapped moisture and failing to open — so siting it where morning sun dries the foliage quickly and air moves freely improves bloom quality. It is more disease-resistant than most Bourbons but still benefits from being kept away from overhead irrigation. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to remove spent flowers and shape the plant, and avoid heavy pruning, which reduces flowering.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole or trellis in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; spade-leaf philodendron is a vigorous climber that develops its largest, most arrow-shaped leaves when given support to climb. Long, glossy, elongated arrowhead- or spade-shaped leaves with a distinctive quilted texture and pronounced veining are carried on a robust, fast-growing climbing vine that can quickly cover a moss pole or trellis with bold, tropical foliage. One of the classic old-fashioned philodendrons long grown as an easy, undemanding houseplant, it tolerates average indoor conditions and irregular watering better than many newer collector cultivars, making it a reliable choice for a floor specimen given room to climb. Wipe dust from the large leaves periodically, water when the top inch of soil dries, and provide a sturdy support as the vine matures and its leaves grow larger.

Start indoors and transplant to a sunny trellis or fence after last frost; Spanish flag is an unusual and showy Ipomoea vine producing one-sided clusters of tubular flowers that dramatically change color as they age — opening bright scarlet red at the tip of the cluster, fading through orange to yellow to white at the base, so that a single flower cluster simultaneously displays four different colors like a living color gradient. The palm-shaped, deeply lobed leaves are attractive even without flowers. The plant climbs quickly to 10 feet or more and blooms from midsummer through frost. It is an outstanding plant for adding tropical flair to a trellis, arbor, or fence and the constant succession of multicolored flower clusters is endlessly interesting.

Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Spanish rockrose is a close relative of the cistus family shrubs, native to dry, sandy, and rocky scrublands of the Iberian Peninsula, producing spreading mounds of gray-green to silver-gray aromatic foliage and in late spring through early summer, vivid bright-yellow flowers 1–2 inches across, each with a distinctive dark reddish-brown to purple-black basal blotch on each petal — a spot pattern producing a strong eye at the center of each flower in dramatic contrast to the yellow. The dark basal markings against clear yellow create a flower of considerable visual impact. Like the cistuses, each flower lasts only a day, but is replaced in rapid succession over several weeks. Often crossed with Cistus species to produce the hybrid genus x Halimiocistus, which shows the qualities of both parents. Outstanding for lean, dry, hot sunny gardens in zones 8b–10, particularly in combination with other Mediterranean scrub plants.

Spanish Stopper is an attractive evergreen native shrub or small tree, native to the coastal hammocks, scrub, and pinelands of south Florida and the Florida Keys, with a natural range extending through the Caribbean and tropical Americas. Small, oval, aromatic, dark green leaves densely clothe the branches and produce a thick, fine-textured screen when planted as a hedge; clusters of small white flowers in summer are followed by round black berries that are avidly consumed by mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings. Highly adaptable to a range of coastal conditions including salt spray, drought, and partial shade, Spanish Stopper is an excellent foundation plant, hedge, or specimen for south Florida and Gulf Coast landscapes in zones 9b–11. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants require little care and tolerate periodic drought with minimal stress.

Plant container or field-grown stock in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spicebush is one of the most shade-tolerant of all native shrubs and grows naturally as a dense understory shrub in moist, rich, deciduous forests — it is exceptional in deeply shaded garden spots where few shrubs thrive. Lindera benzoin is one of the most valuable native shrubs for wildlife gardens: the aromatic, spicy-scented foliage is the exclusive larval host plant for the spicebush swallowtail (Papilio troilus) and the promethea silk moth; small, bright-yellow flowers appear in late winter to early spring before the leaves, providing critical early nectar; glossy, red, waxy berries in fall are greedily consumed by migrating songbirds, especially wood thrushes and veeries; and brilliant yellow fall foliage lights up shaded woodland garden interiors. Dioecious — plant male and female for berries.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Jatropha is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most heavily in full sun. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — keep away from children and pets. Jatropha integerrima (spicy jatropha or peregrina) is a Cuban native tropical shrub producing dense, rounded clusters of brilliant scarlet-red, star-shaped flowers 1 inch across almost continuously throughout the warm months in zones 10–12, and reliably spring through fall in zone 9. The flowers are irresistible to butterflies (especially Sulphurs, Zebra Longwings, and Gulf Fritillaries) and hummingbirds, making it an outstanding wildlife plant for tropical gardens. The attractive, slightly lobed, dark-green to bronze-tinged leaves add ornamental interest between bloom flushes. Despite the toxicity of its seeds and sap (all Jatropha species contain toxic diterpenes), the plant is widely grown as a landscape shrub in South Florida, the Caribbean, and tropical regions; wear gloves when pruning. It grows rapidly from cuttings and can be trained as a small tree for greater impact.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, protected from direct hot afternoon sun, which scorches the fine variegation faster than it would plain green foliage. Spider Web is a striking variegated sport of the popular architectural shade shrub Fatsia japonica, with each large, glossy, hand-shaped leaf speckled in fine white flecks that give the whole plant a frosted, almost cobweb-dusted look distinct from the bolder white-edged variegation of other Fatsia cultivars. It brings dramatic tropical-looking texture to a deep shade bed where few other shrubs perform, and its bold foliage pairs well with ferns, hostas, and other fine-textured shade perennials as a contrasting anchor plant. Established plants tolerate the humid Gulf Coast summer well but appreciate protection from hard freezes in the colder parts of their range; a hard frost may damage foliage even where the roots survive and resprout in spring. Prune only to remove damaged or overly leggy stems, since Fatsia branches slowly and responds well to renewal pruning if it becomes overgrown.

Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Spider's Web' is less vigorous and more cold-sensitive than plain green fatsia, so give it a sheltered site or grow it in a container that can be moved for winter protection. This striking fatsia selection carries the same bold, glossy, deeply lobed, tropical-textured leaves as the species but heavily speckled and mottled with white, giving each leaf a frosted, web-like appearance that brightens a deeply shaded corner. Rounded clusters of small white flowers appear in fall on mature plants, followed by black berries, though the plant is grown almost entirely for its dramatic variegated foliage rather than its modest bloom. Because variegated growth is less vigorous than solid green fatsia, prune out any reverted all-green shoots promptly to keep the plant's variegation strong, and protect from hard freezes and drying winter wind at the colder edge of its range.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade, sheltered from late winter frosts; spike winter hazel is a Japanese species distinguished from other Corylopsis by the unusually long, cylindrical racemes containing up to 20 lemon-yellow flowers each — the longest pendulous flower clusters of commonly grown winter hazels. The flowers are slightly larger than those of C. pauciflora and carry a soft, sweet, cowslip-like fragrance that is particularly pleasant in the mild days of late winter and early spring. The purple-tipped stamens create a colorful contrast with the pale yellow petals. Leaves emerge with an attractive reddish-purple flush that matures to blue-green, turning golden yellow in fall. Hardy to zone 5, this is one of the more reliable winter hazels for cold-climate gardens. Combines beautifully with early-blooming witch hazels (Hamamelis) for an extended winter flowering display.

Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and remove the oldest flowered stems right after bloom to keep the compact shrub from becoming crowded at its base. Spilled Wine is a dwarf weigela roughly half the size of the species, producing dense, arching mounds of deep burgundy-purple foliage topped with a heavy flush of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds reliably. Its small stature and consistently dark foliage make it a strong color-contrast shrub for the front of a mixed border or foundation planting where a full-size weigela would be too large. It is tough and adaptable, tolerating a range of soils once established, with minimal pruning needed given its naturally compact, well-behaved habit.

common_name: Spineless Yucca (Soft Leaf Yucca, Giant Yucca)
notes: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Spineless Yucca is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives on neglect in appropriate conditions. Yucca elephantipes (also sold as Yucca gigantea) is a native of Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico that has become one of the most widely planted tropical accent plants in Gulf Coast zone 9–11 landscapes and a standard large houseplant and container specimen throughout the world. Unlike most yuccas whose stiff leaf tips can pierce skin (earning the family name 'needles and thread'), the Spineless Yucca's long, dark-green, strap-like leaves have soft, flexible tips that cause no injury — making it safe around children and pets and usable in high-traffic landscape situations where spiny yuccas would be hazardous. The plant develops multiple trunks over time, each eventually producing dramatic 3–4 foot spikes of creamy-white, pendant, bell-shaped flowers. It makes an excellent large container specimen for patios, entryways, and atriums where the bold form contrasts with fine-textured plants. When planted directly in the ground in zone 9b–11, it can grow to 30 feet with multiple branching trunks and a truly impressive specimen presence. Very popular in formal tropical and Mediterranean-style Gulf Coast landscapes.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, coastal soil in full sun; spiny black olive is a native tree of tropical coastal hammocks and scrub of south Florida and the Caribbean, not related to the olive (Olea) but named for the dark, fleshy, olive-like fruits. The tree has an attractive, fine-textured, weeping canopy with long, drooping branchlets bearing small, leathery, elongated leaves and (on young growth) short, stiff spines that have given it one common name. The small fruits are eaten by tropical birds. Well adapted to coastal conditions including salt spray, rocky limestone soil, and drought — all characteristic of the Keys habitat. Widely used as an ornamental and windbreak tree in South Florida coastal landscapes. A smaller relative of the commonly planted (and non-native) black olive (Bucida buceras), which is the dominant street tree of Miami.

Choose a sunny site with fast-draining, lean soil — rich or moist soils encourage weak growth and root rot in this chaparral native. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in late summer, or transplant nursery-grown starts in spring. Water only to establish during the first season, then reduce to occasional deep irrigation in summer. The spiny branches form an effective barrier hedge while the bright red berries draw birds throughout fall and winter.

common_name: Split-Leaf Monstera (Pinnatipartita, Peru Monstera, Broad-Leaf Monstera)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Monstera pinnatipartita transitions from its juvenile to its extraordinary adult leaf form most rapidly with adequate bright indirect light and a climbing support. Monstera pinnatipartita is a climbing aroid from Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia in the Araceae family, producing one of the most dramatically transformative leaf progressions in the genus Monstera — the group named for their 'monstrous' leaves. In the juvenile trailing or hanging phase, the plant produces relatively small (4–6 inch), simple, elongated, glossy dark-green leaves that give no indication of what is to come. As the plant climbs a vertical surface and matures, the leaves transform dramatically: they enlarge significantly and become deeply pinnately lobed — divided almost to the midrib into numerous (8–12 pairs or more) distinct lobes — creating a leaf structure that is deeply slashed rather than fenestrated (holed), with the individual lobes remaining attached to the central rib like a feather. The adult leaves, reaching 24 inches or more, are among the most striking in the genus. Monstera pinnatipartita is frequently confused in commerce with Monstera siltepecana (which is similar in juvenile form), Rhaphidophora decursiva (similar in adult form), and even Epipremnum pinnatum — accurate identification is helpful for appropriate care and expectation setting. All parts are toxic.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge. Spring Bouquet is a compact cultivar of laurustinus, prized for its dense, dark green, glossy evergreen foliage and abundant clusters of small, fragrant, pinkish-white flowers that open from reddish-pink buds in late winter and early spring, one of the earliest flower displays in the evergreen shrub border. Flowers are followed by small blue-black berries that add fall and winter interest and attract birds. Its naturally rounded, well-proportioned habit holds a tidy shape with far less pruning than many broadleaf evergreens, making it useful for foundation plantings, informal hedges, and mixed borders. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, though good drainage improves long-term performance, and it shows good resistance to the pests and diseases that trouble some other Southern landscape evergreens. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering to avoid removing the next year's flower buds.

Plant in well-drained soil, tolerant of poor, dry, chalky, or alkaline ground, in partial to full shade beneath established trees; spurge laurel is a low, rounded evergreen shrub notable for tolerating deep, dry shade better than almost any other flowering shrub, with glossy, leathery, dark-green leaves clustered near the branch tips and small, fragrant, yellow-green flowers tucked among the upper leaves in late winter, followed by black berries in summer. It asks for very little once established — no supplemental water in most climates and no feeding — making it a useful, low-maintenance evergreen for the difficult dry shade under mature trees where few flowering shrubs will grow at all. Every part of the plant, especially the berries and sap, is toxic if ingested, and the sap can cause skin irritation or blistering on contact, so wear gloves when pruning and site it away from children and pets. In parts of its introduced range, notably the Pacific Northwest, it has become locally invasive by self-seeding into woodland understories, so check local guidance before planting it and remove any unwanted seedlings promptly.

Direct sow after last frost, scarifying seed to speed germination, into sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining vines to climb; spurred butterfly pea tolerates poor, dry soil and needs no fertilizer. Slender, twining stems carry trifoliate leaves and showy, flattened, lavender-to-purple, pea-shaped flowers with a distinctive spurred keel from summer into fall, scrambling over low shrubs and fences or trailing as a groundcover where no support is available. Native to sandy pinelands, dunes, and open woodland edges across the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain, it is a larval host and nectar source for several native bee and butterfly species and fixes nitrogen in the lean, sandy soils it favors. It behaves as a perennial in zones 8-10 and dies back to the root in occasional hard freezes, resprouting readily from its woody crown the following spring.

Plant in moist to dry, acidic, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Hypericum hypericoides establishes readily in poor, infertile, acidic soils and is excellent for shaded edges, pine understory plantings, and woodland gardens — requires no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established in appropriate soil. Hypericum hypericoides (St. Andrews Cross) is a small, multi-stemmed, deciduous native shrub of the eastern and southeastern United States, ranging from New England south through Florida, west through Oklahoma and Texas, and into the Caribbean, where it grows in dry to moist pine flatwoods, sandhills, woodland edges, and stream banks. The common name and species epithet both reference the unusual cross-like arrangement of the 4 petals — unique among North American Hypericum species, all others of which have 5 petals — resembling the X-shaped cross of St. Andrew (the Saltire). Small, bright-yellow flowers appear prolifically in summer, followed by small, 2-valved capsules. A remarkably adaptable native shrub that performs well in both dry and moist conditions, acid soils, sandy substrates, full sun and deep partial shade — one of the most useful native shrubs for low-maintenance naturalistic planting in the Southeast. Valuable for pollinators, particularly native bees that collect pollen from the numerous stamens.

common_name: St. Cecilia Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 2.5-3.5 feet apart. Introduced by David Austin in 1987, St. Cecilia was among his earlier English roses and remains a favorite for its soft, blush-apricot, cupped, old-fashioned-looking blooms and strong myrrh fragrance, an unusual scent profile distinct from the classic damask or tea fragrances of most roses. The relatively lax, arching shrub blooms in flushes from late spring through fall and shows better disease resistance than many early English roses, though like most of the class it benefits from good air circulation and occasional attention to blackspot in humid climates. It works well in mixed borders and cottage-style plantings, where its graceful, informal habit and soft coloring blend easily with perennials. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage a compact shape and vigorous new flowering growth.

Staggerbush is a graceful native deciduous shrub of the coastal plain's moist to moderately dry, acidic soils from New England south to Florida and west to Texas, producing elegant, pendulous clusters of white to pink, urn-shaped flowers in May that hang gracefully from the branches before the leaves fully expand. The common name 'staggerbush' refers to the plant's toxicity to sheep and other livestock that consumed the foliage; like all Lyonia species, the leaves contain grayanotoxins (andromedotoxins) that cause staggering, drooling, and potentially fatal poisoning in grazing animals. Despite this toxicity, Staggerbush is an attractive ornamental native shrub with graceful spring flowers, attractive summer foliage, and modest red to orange fall color that supports native bees when in bloom. Plant in moist, well-drained to moderately wet, strongly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; keep away from livestock.

Divide root suckers or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; staghorn sumac is a fast-growing, large native shrub or small tree that provides one of the most spectacular multi-season landscape performances of any woody plant: bold, tropical-looking, compound leaves with 11–31 leaflets create a dramatic summer canopy; brilliant, fire-engine-red to orange-scarlet fall foliage among the most vivid of any temperate tree or shrub; fuzzy, cone-shaped clusters of deep-red, acidic berries (drupes) that persist through winter and provide critical food for ruffed grouse, robins, thrushes, bluebirds, pheasants, wild turkeys, and numerous other birds; and the distinctive, densely furry, brown-velvet branch tips that resemble the antlers of a stag in velvet — the most distinctive structural feature of any dormant shrub. Berries are used to make a pleasantly tart, pink lemonade-like beverage (sumac-ade) in indigenous and folk traditions. 'Laciniata' (cut-leaf/dissected foliage) is a particularly elegant ornamental cultivar. The suckering habit makes it excellent for erosion control on slopes.

Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; star magnolia is a Japanese deciduous shrub-tree that flowers earlier than virtually any other ornamental tree in the temperate garden — in late March to April (zone 5–7), or even late February to early March in milder zones, the still-bare, furry-budded branches burst open into masses of large, multi-petaled, pure-white (or pale-pink in 'Rosea'), star-shaped flowers with 12–18 narrow, strap-like petals that radiate in all directions from the center. The pure-white, star-like flowers cover every branch and create an extraordinary white cloud effect before a single leaf has emerged. It blooms 2–3 weeks before Magnolia x soulangeana and considerably earlier than most garden shrubs, making it the first dramatic flowering statement of the temperate garden year. The narrow petals give it a distinctive, finely structured appearance quite different from the cupped, tulip-flowered magnolias. It is smaller and more shrubby in habit than many magnolias. 'Royal Star' (late-flowering, avoiding late frosts, particularly large flowers), 'Waterlily' (pink-budded, white-opening, very fragrant), and 'Centennial' are excellent cultivars.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge or screen. Steeds is a classic Japanese holly cultivar valued for its dense, upright, multi-stemmed habit and small, boxwood-like, glossy dark green leaves without the conspicuous spines of many other hollies, making it a popular substitute for boxwood in humid Southern climates where boxwood is prone to blight and decline. It grows slowly into a formal, columnar-to-oval shape that tolerates shearing well, making it a good choice for low hedges, foundation plantings, and formal garden structure, though it also looks attractive left unpruned in its natural upright form.
