Small black fruit follows inconspicuous flowers, of little ornamental significance compared to red-berried hollies. It tolerates a range of soil conditions but performs best with consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil, and it shows good resistance to the pest and disease pressures that trouble boxwood in the Gulf South. Prune in late winter or after the spring flush if a more formal, sheared shape is desired.

Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, spacing plants to allow the shrub's suckering habit to fill in as a loose colony over time. Steeplebush is a small native shrub of eastern North American wet meadows, bogs, and pond margins, prized by pollinator gardeners for its dense, fuzzy, upright spikes of tiny rose-pink flowers that bloom from mid to late summer when many other nectar sources have faded. The felted, gray-woolly undersides of the narrow leaves distinguish it from its white-flowered cousin meadowsweet, and the persistent dried flower spikes and reddish-brown stems add winter interest. It thrives in rain gardens, pond edges, and other consistently damp, sunny sites where few woody ornamentals perform well, and requires minimal pruning beyond removing old canes in late winter.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Stellar Pink dogwood is a Rutgers-bred hybrid with strong resistance to dogwood anthracnose and borers, which trouble many flowering dogwoods. A hybrid between the native flowering dogwood and the Asian kousa dogwood developed at Rutgers University, it combines the classic large, showy, soft pink bracts of flowering dogwood with the improved disease and pest resistance of its kousa parent, addressing the anthracnose and borer problems that have devastated many straight Cornus florida plantings in recent decades. Blooming in mid-spring between the earlier flowering dogwood and later kousa dogwood bloom windows, it provides reliable pink flower color on a tough, adaptable small tree well suited to a woodland edge or specimen planting. Water during establishment and dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool, and avoid the anthracnose and borer problems common to straight dogwood species by choosing this resistant hybrid for new plantings.

Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun near the coast or partial shade inland; sticky monkeyflower is a resilient California chaparral and coastal scrub subshrub with narrow, sticky, resinous, dark green leaves and an extended bloom season of open-faced, snapdragon-like flowers ranging from cream and pale yellow through peachy orange to deep red-orange depending on the population. Flowers appear nearly year-round in mild coastal gardens, tapering off only during the hottest, driest part of summer, and are a favored nectar source for hummingbirds and native bees. It is drought-deciduous in harsh conditions, dropping leaves during severe heat or drought and flushing new growth with the return of cooler, wetter weather, so do not mistake dieback for plant failure. Lightly prune leggy stems after the main flowering flush to keep growth dense, and avoid regular summer irrigation once plants are established.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; stiff dogwood is a native multi-stemmed shrub of wetland margins and moist bottomland forests throughout the southeastern Coastal Plain, distinguished from gray dogwood (C. racemosa) by its more southern range and adaptation to moist to wet conditions. The flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers in spring attract many native bees and flies. The small, blue-black berries on red stems in fall are critically important food for numerous bird species including warblers, thrushes, and vireos during fall migration — one of the most productive native bird-food shrubs for the Gulf South. Spreads by root sprouts to form multi-stemmed thickets in wet conditions. An essential native shrub for wet, shaded garden margins and naturalistic wetland plantings in zone 9a.

Direct sow in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; stinking passionflower is a weedy, delicate annual vine producing small white to pale lavender passion flowers enclosed in intricate, hair-fringed bracts that resemble lace or mist around the flower — giving it the poetic alternative name 'love-in-a-mist'. The red to orange ripe berries enclosed in the lacy bracts are edible and consumed by birds and children. The plant is a larval host for the gulf fritillary butterfly, adding to its conservation value. The leaves have a slightly unpleasant odor when crushed (hence 'foetida') and the glandular hairs on the bracts are sticky and may trap small insects. Self-sows prolifically in zone 9 to naturalize as a charming summer vine, flowering continuously through the season until frost.

common_name: Strawberry Sundae Hydrangea (Compact Pink-Red Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their mature width to fill in. Strawberry Sundae produces conical flower panicles that open creamy white and quickly flush strawberry-pink from the base upward, creating a two-toned, sundae-like effect as the color moves up each flower cluster through summer, eventually deepening to a richer rose-red in fall. Its mid-size, well-branched habit fits mixed borders and foundation plantings without the bulk of larger panicle hydrangea cultivars. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be pruned back hard in late winter without losing that year's flowers; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.

common_name: String of Hearts (Rosary Vine, Chain of Hearts)
notes: Plant in well-drained, gritty potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial sun, allowing the soil to dry out between waterings. String of Hearts produces long, thin, trailing stems draped with small, heart-shaped, marbled gray-green and silver leaves, occasionally accented with a pink or purple blush, making it a favorite hanging basket and shelf plant that cascades gracefully over a container edge. It is a true succulent and rots quickly in overly wet, poorly drained soil, so err on the side of underwatering, particularly in winter when growth slows. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container that can be moved indoors or under cover during freezes, since it has very little cold tolerance, unlike more cold-hardy garden succulents.

common_name: String of Stars Hoya (Wax Vine, Linearis Hoya, Thread-Leaf Hoya)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Hoya linearis is somewhat more shade-tolerant than the succulent-leaved Hoyas but requires good light to bloom. Hoya linearis is a cascading epiphytic vine from the Himalayas of Nepal, Bhutan, northeastern India, and southwestern China, growing naturally on mossy tree branches and rock faces at cool elevations of 5,000–8,000 feet — one of the few Hoyas to originate from a genuinely cool mountain environment. The plant looks startlingly different from the typical Hoya: instead of thick, waxy, succulent leaves, Hoya linearis produces long, narrow, slightly hairy, soft-textured, thread-like leaves less than an inch long that are densely arranged along trailing stems, creating a cascading, fern-like or rosemary-like texture entirely unlike other popular Hoyas. Long stems hang in soft curtains from hanging baskets, creating an elegant waterfall of narrow foliage. In summer, the plant produces tight umbels of small, pure white, star-shaped flowers with a sweet, slightly waxy fragrance. The combination of unusual fine-textured foliage and delicate white flowers makes Hoya linearis one of the most distinctive trailing houseplants available, prized by Hoya collectors and general houseplant enthusiasts alike. Non-toxic to pets.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, cool soil in partial to full shade — striped maple is one of North America's most beautiful native understory trees, instantly recognizable by the striking vertical white-and-green striping on the young bark (giving it the alternate name 'snakebark maple' or 'moosewood'). The large, three-lobed leaves turn butter yellow in fall. It is a true understory specialist that grows naturally in the shade beneath taller hardwoods in cool, moist, acidic mountain forests — it is shade-tolerant enough to regenerate in nearly complete shade. Moose browse the bark in winter (giving the common name). Not suited to zone 7 and warmer, where the heat and humidity are too much for this cool-climate species. An outstanding ornamental tree for the shaded garden in zone 3–6, particularly in New England, the upper Midwest, and the Appalachian highlands. The ornamental bark is visible year-round and is spectacular.

Plant in any well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade — sugar hackberry is the primary Celtis species of the Gulf Coast and Deep South, better adapted to the heat, humidity, and occasional flooding of zone 7–9 than the common hackberry (C. occidentalis). The distinctive warty, corky-gray bark is unmistakable and one of the most interesting bark textures of any native tree. Small orange to purple-black berries in fall are among the most important food sources for migrating songbirds — more than 50 species consume the berries, including yellow-rumped warblers and hermit thrushes. The tree is the exclusive larval host for the hackberry emperor butterfly and American snout butterfly, two distinctive native butterflies wholly dependent on Celtis species. It tolerates urban conditions, compacted soils, drought, and alkaline pH remarkably well. A keystone wildlife tree for the Gulf Coast landscape.

Transplant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil away from road salt and compacted urban sites, since sugar maple is sensitive to both. This long-lived tree develops a dense, rounded crown prized for the brilliant orange and scarlet fall color that defines much of the eastern hardwood forest, and mature stands are the traditional source of maple syrup sap. It provides excellent shade for large residential and park settings but needs consistent moisture during establishment and should be kept out of confined urban tree pits. Give it room to grow undisturbed for decades, as it is intolerant of heavy pruning and soil disturbance near its roots.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sugar Shack Buttonbush thrives in the poorly drained, wet soils that defeat most landscape shrubs and is actually native to swamp and wetland margins; Sugar Shack is a compact cultivar of native Buttonbush (Cephalanthus occidentalis), introduced by Bailey Nurseries as a landscape-appropriate size selection of one of the most ecologically valuable native shrubs in North America. The extraordinary round, spherical, 1–1.5 inch white flower heads that appear in July–August are genuinely unusual — the flower ball is densely packed with tiny, long-tubed white florets with projecting styles that give the whole ball a pin-cushion or sputnik-like radiating texture unlike any other common landscape plant. This unusual flower structure is extremely attractive to butterflies (especially swallowtails and skippers), bumblebees, and other nectar-seeking pollinators — making Buttonbush one of the highest-value native pollinator plants available. The subsequent seed heads remain through winter as small, persistent brown balls that provide food for ducks, songbirds, and small mammals. As a native species adapted to Gulf Coast wetlands, Sugar Shack Buttonbush fills the specific niche of a flowering shrub for wet, low-lying sites that are often the most challenging spots in residential landscapes.

common_name: Sugar Tip Rose of Sharon (Variegated Sterile Pink Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Sugar Tip stands apart from other rose of sharon cultivars for its striking blue-green foliage crisply edged in creamy white, providing ornamental interest even before the double, soft pink flowers open from midsummer into fall. As a sterile selection, it sets little to no seed, avoiding the self-sowing weediness of older rose of sharon while adding season-long variegated foliage color that few other rose of sharon cultivars offer. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, making it a low-maintenance, multi-season shrub for a sunny border.

growth_habit: South African Cape fynbos signature shrub
notes: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; sugarbush is the most widely distributed and historically significant protea species — the signature Cape fynbos plant of the mountains and coastal hills of the Western Cape from which the Cape Floral Kingdom takes much of its iconic visual identity. The flower heads are typical protea form — a rounded 'artichoke' of overlapping bracts enclosing the central mass of flowers — in white to cream-white to pale pink, sometimes streaked or flushed with deeper pink or rose, each individual flower head 4–5 inches across. They bloom in winter and spring (May–October in South Africa) and produce so much sweet nectar that the common name 'sugarbush' refers to the honey-like sweetness that children and sugarbirds alike consume directly from the flower — the traditional source of 'proteabosse stroop', a traditional Cape syrup. The nectar production and flower structure are extraordinary among ornamental plants; in cultivation, hummingbirds visit the flowers repeatedly. The large, dried flower heads, with their sculptural, papery bracts, are a major cut-flower and dried-flower export from South Africa. A magnificent signature plant for zone 9 Mediterranean-climate gardens — requiring the specific drainage, lean soil, and low-phosphorus conditions of its fynbos habitat.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Summer Chocolate is a purple-leaved sport of mimosa selected for its deep bronze-chocolate, finely divided, fern-like foliage, which holds its dark color through the heat of summer far better than most other purple-leaved trees and provides a striking, season-long contrast to the pale pink, silky pompom flowers produced from early summer into fall. It is somewhat smaller and more restrained in habit than the straight green species, typically reaching 15-20 feet, and its weak, brittle wood still benefits from a sheltered planting site away from strong winds. Because it is grafted or vegetatively propagated onto known rootstock, Summer Chocolate is more predictable in size and color than seed-grown mimosas, but gardeners in the Gulf South should still watch for and remove volunteer seedlings, as the cultivar remains capable of setting viable seed.

Summer Snowflake is a doublefile viburnum valued for producing a strong flush of flat, white lacecap flower clusters in mid-spring and then continuing to open scattered new clusters sporadically through summer into early fall, a much longer bloom window than the single spring flush typical of most doublefile selections. Its growth habit is narrower and more upright than the wide-spreading species, fitting more easily into foundation plantings and smaller garden spaces, while still producing the tiered horizontal branching, red-to-black fall berries, and burgundy fall foliage typical of the group. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, and prune, if needed, only right after the main spring flush to avoid removing the buds that produce the later summer rebloom.

common_name: Summer Wine Ninebark (Compact Wine-Red Foliage Ninebark)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Summer Wine brings the same striking dark foliage color popularized by Diabolo into a considerably more compact plant, better suited to foundation plantings, smaller borders, and mass plantings where a full-sized ninebark would grow too large. The deep wine-red leaves hold their color well through the season, especially in full sun, and clusters of small white flowers in late spring add contrast before fading to reveal reddish seed capsules later in summer. It requires minimal care beyond occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems each year to maintain a full, vigorous shrub.

Root softwood cuttings in late spring or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; summersweet (sweet pepperbush) is one of the finest native shrubs for shaded, moist gardens, producing upright spikes of small, pure-white to pale-pink, intensely and deliciously fragrant flowers in mid- to late summer — filling a bloom gap when few shade-tolerant shrubs flower. The clean, lustrous, dark-green foliage turns bright golden-yellow to orange in fall. It suckers to form multi-stemmed colonies in suitable conditions. Excellent for stream banks, rain gardens, woodland edges, and shaded borders with consistently moist soil. 'Hummingbird' (compact, 2–3 feet), 'Ruby Spice' (deep pink flowers), and 'Sixteen Candles' are superb cultivars. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the fragrant flowers heavily.

common_name: Sun Mandevilla (Tropical Vine with Large Showy Summer Flowers)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sun Mandevilla (Mandevilla x hybrida, marketed under trade names including 'Sun Parasol') is a tropical climbing vine producing large (3–5 inch diameter), trumpet-shaped flowers in shades of brilliant red, deep pink, rose, pale pink, or white throughout the warm season. The large, glossy, dark-green leaves and continuous production of oversized, flamboyant flowers make mandevilla one of the most dramatically ornamental vines for Gulf South container gardens, trellis plantings, and patio displays. In zone 9, mandevilla grows vigorously through the warm season (April–November), producing continuous flowers without deadheading. The twining stems require a trellis, post, or support structure to climb — without support, mandevilla sprawls as a mounding container plant, which is also ornamentally effective. Zone 9b and 10 gardeners can treat mandevilla as a perennial vine that returns from the roots after mild winters; in zone 9a, the plants may be killed by severe freezes but return from persistent roots with mulch protection, or be overwintered as container plants in a frost-free garage or greenhouse. Red-flowered cultivars are attractive to hummingbirds. Container-grown mandevilla requires more frequent watering and fertilization than in-ground plants — use a balanced liquid fertilizer every 2 weeks through the growing season for best bloom production.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sun Parasol Crimson Mandevilla blooms most abundantly in full sun with consistent moisture; Mandevilla (Mandevilla x amabilis) is a tropical twining vine producing large, funnel-shaped flowers with five broadly overlapping petals in a classic five-lobed arrangement — the Sun Parasol Crimson selection bearing vivid crimson to deep rose-red flowers 3–4 inches across that create a striking, uninterrupted bloom display from late spring through frost. Mandevilla's combination of tropical flower size (far larger than most annual vines), glossy deep green foliage, continuous bloom without deadheading, and ability to quickly cover a trellis, pergola, or fence with an impressive tropical display makes it one of the most impactful ornamental vines for zone 9 summer gardens. The large, funnel-shaped flowers are hummingbird-attractive — the trumpet form, bright crimson color, and sweet nectar production make mandevilla a reliable hummingbird plant wherever hummingbirds occur. In zone 9's warm, humid climate, mandevilla performs as one of the finest summer flowering vines available — thriving in the heat that defeats many vine species and providing the tropical character that suits the Gulf South climate.

common_name: Sunny Knock Out Rose (Yellow Knock Out)
growth_habit: landscape shrub rose, Knock Out series
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply during the first season and then only during dry spells once established. Light shearing in late winter keeps the rounded shrub form tidy and encourages fresh bloom flushes through the season. Single, bright yellow flowers that fade to creamy white open continuously from spring to frost on this low-maintenance landscape shrub, part of the widely planted Knock Out series bred for disease resistance and repeat bloom without deadheading. Its compact size and self-cleaning flowers make it popular for mass plantings and foundation beds.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, where the foliage colors most brightly; in shadier sites the leaves stay more chartreuse-green than gold. Sunshine Ligustrum was selected as a sterile, non-flowering, non-fruiting sport of common Chinese privet specifically to provide the same tough, brightly colored foliage without the invasive seeding that has made the wild species a serious problem in Southern woodlands. Because it never flowers or sets berries, it channels its energy into dense, compact growth and vivid golden-yellow foliage color that holds through the heat of summer, making it a popular low hedge, mass planting, or color accent shrub. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease and needs only occasional shearing to maintain a tidy shape.

Plant in full sun in dry to average, well-drained soil typical of central US prairies; this species is native to open grasslands and woodland edges and does not tolerate wet feet or heavy shade. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and spreads by root sprouts to form a low thicket useful for erosion control and wildlife cover. Deep pink blooms appear in late spring to early summer and are followed by small, globe-shaped red hips that persist into winter, providing important food for birds. Propagate from hardwood cuttings in late autumn or by carefully digging and transplanting rooted root sprouts in early spring.

Supplejack is a vigorous native woody vine of bottomland forests, swamp margins, and moist woodland edges across the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States, climbing high into the forest canopy by twining and branching through the upper shrub and tree layers. Its flexible, wiry stems gave rise to the common name — the wood was historically used to make walking sticks, basket frames, and tool handles because of its exceptional suppleness and strength. Small, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers in late spring produce blue-black drupes that ripen in fall and are consumed by wood ducks, wild turkeys, and at least a dozen species of songbirds and small mammals, making supplejack one of the highest-value wildlife vines in the region. In naturalized woodland gardens or large-scale habitat restorations, allow it to climb through native trees and form dense thickets that provide both food and nesting cover; it is too vigorous for small spaces but invaluable for restoring native forest understory structure.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving some winter sun where possible to help harden off growth before hard freezes. Survivor is one of the toughest of Dr. William Ackerman's cold-hardy camellia hybrids, bred from Camellia oleifera crossed with Camellia japonica specifically to push reliable camellia flowering and foliage survival further north and into colder microclimates than the species alone can handle. It bears small to medium single white flowers in fall into early winter on a dense, twiggy, evergreen shrub, and its exceptional hardiness makes it a forgiving choice for gardeners at the colder edge of camellia country or in an exposed Gulf Coast site prone to occasional hard freezes. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer after bloom, keep the root zone mulched, and prune only lightly to shape immediately after flowering finishes.

common_name: Susan Magnolia (Little Girl Series Deep Purple-Red Compact Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Susan is one of the most widely planted of the 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, producing slender, elegant, deep reddish-purple buds that open into fragrant, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact, multi-stemmed tree suited to smaller gardens where a full-size saucer magnolia would eventually be too large. Its later bloom timing than star and saucer magnolias helps it avoid the late spring freezes that often damage earlier-flowering magnolias, and it is known to produce a light rebloom later in summer more reliably than some of its Little Girl siblings. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture, and avoid heavy pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

Plant in moist to wet, deeply acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to light sun; swamp azalea is the most fragrant of all native North American deciduous azaleas, producing intensely clove-spice-scented white flowers (often pink-flushed) in late June through July, extending the native azalea bloom season well into summer after all other species have finished. It grows naturally in swamps, bogs, stream banks, and wet woodland margins from Maine to Florida, and tolerates standing water better than any other Rhododendron. The plant spreads slowly by rhizome and root sprouts to form a colony; purchase container-grown propagated plants only. Mulch with pine bark or pine needle litter to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Never allow to dry out in summer.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun — swamp bay is a native evergreen tree of Gulf Coast wetlands, closely related to the edible bay laurel and redbay, with aromatic leaves historically used as a bay leaf substitute in Creole and Southern cooking. The glossy, elliptic evergreen leaves have a whitish-downy underside and are fragrant when crushed with the characteristic bay laurel scent. Small, yellowish-green flowers in spring attract native bees; dark blue-black berries feed songbirds and the palamedes swallowtail butterfly uses the foliage as a larval host. It grows naturally in cypress swamps, wet flatwoods, and bay swamps throughout the Gulf Coast and is one of the best choices for naturalizing in wet, low areas where other trees refuse to grow. The wood is durable and aromatic; the tree is long-lived and forms the canopy of classic southern bay swamp ecosystems.

common_name: Swamp Chestnut Oak (Basket Oak, Cow Oak)
notes: Plant in moist, rich, slightly acidic bottomland soil in full sun to partial shade; swamp chestnut oak is a magnificent large native oak of the rich bottomland forests of the Southeast, reaching 60–100 feet with a straight trunk and broad, open crown with large, chestnut-like leaves 5–9 inches long. The large, sweet acorns (up to 1.5 inches) ripen in a single season and are the largest, most palatable acorns produced by any American oak — they were eaten by Native Americans and early settlers and are readily eaten by deer, turkeys, squirrels, and wood ducks. The handsome, ridged, grayish bark and excellent fall yellow-orange color make this a valuable landscape tree where space permits. Tolerates seasonal flooding but also grows well in moist, well-drained upland soils. Somewhat more tolerant of partial shade when young than most oaks. A premier wildlife and landscape tree for zone 5–9.

Swamp Cottonwood is the wetland specialist of the cottonwood family, native to the permanently flooded swamps, blackwater river bottoms, and cypress-tupelo swamp margins of the southeastern coastal plain from Connecticut to Florida and west to Indiana and Oklahoma, where it tolerates deeper and more prolonged flooding than any other native cottonwood. Its leaves are distinctly broader and more rounded than those of Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides) — hence the species epithet heterophylla (variable-leaved) — and the tree often develops a tall, straight trunk in the competitive light environment of bottomland forest. Like other cottonwoods, Swamp Cottonwood is a fast-growing pioneer tree important for rapid canopy establishment in wetland restoration projects; it roots readily from hardwood cuttings pushed into wet soil in early spring. The cottony seeds of female trees are dispersed by wind and water in late spring and early summer. An excellent riparian tree for the restoration and naturalization of permanently wet bottomland habitats in zones 5–9.

Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp cyrilla (also called titi or leatherwood) is a distinctive multi-season native shrub of coastal plain bogs, swamp margins, and pocosins in the Southeast, producing long racemes of small white flowers in June and July that are intensely fragrant and among the most important summer nectar sources for native bees and the basis of the highly prized 'titi honey' produced by southeastern beekeepers. The semi-evergreen leaves turn brilliant orange-red in fall before dropping, and in warm winters may persist through spring. The plant is adapted to very acidic, poorly drained soils where it has little competition. An outstanding specimen for bog gardens, rain gardens, and acid pond margins in zone 7–9.

Swamp Doghobble is a graceful native deciduous shrub of moist to wet, shaded, acidic habitats along shaded stream banks, boggy swamp margins, and wet woodland understories of the eastern United States, producing fragrant, white, cylindrical flowers in drooping clusters along the stems in spring before the leaves fully emerge. Unlike the evergreen leucothoes, Swamp Doghobble is deciduous and displays outstanding orange, red, and purple fall foliage color that rivals the showiest cultivated shrubs. The arching, fountain-like growth habit and multi-season ornamental interest — spring flowers, attractive summer foliage, and brilliant fall color — make Swamp Doghobble a highly desirable native shrub for shaded, moist, acid garden settings. Plant in strongly acidic, moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Swamp Doghobble will not tolerate alkaline soil, drought, or prolonged direct sun.

Swamp Dogwood is a large, multi-stemmed native shrub native to wet thickets, streambanks, pond margins, and swamp edges throughout eastern North America from New Brunswick to Florida and west to Oklahoma, tolerating prolonged seasonal flooding and thriving in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. It produces flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in June and July that attract a wide variety of native bees and other pollinators, followed by striking porcelain-blue fruits on red-stemmed clusters that ripen in August and September and are eagerly consumed by over 40 species of songbirds, including wood thrush, catbirds, and warblers. The purplish-red winter stems provide attractive four-season interest, and the shrub suckers readily to form dense thickets that stabilize streambanks and provide excellent nesting cover for wildlife. An outstanding plant for wet native gardens, rain gardens, or bio-swales where its moisture tolerance is an asset rather than a compromise.

common_name: Swamp Jessamine (Rankin's Jessamine, Scentless Yellow Jessamine)
notes: Plant in partial shade in moist, acidic soil along a fence, trellis, or arbor; Swamp Jessamine twines to 10–20 feet and can cover a large support structure. Gelsemium rankinii is a native evergreen vine closely related to Carolina Jessamine (G. sempervirens) but adapted to entirely different habitat — wet, shady floodplains and swamp margins rather than dry, sunny slopes. The yellow, tubular, slightly fragrant flowers (though less intensely fragrant than G. sempervirens) appear in two distinct blooming periods: late winter–spring (like Carolina Jessamine) AND again in fall (October–December), making it a unique vine that provides yellow blooms in both early spring and late fall when few other plants are in color. The glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage is attractive year-round. Swamp Jessamine fills a specific ecological niche as a shade-tolerant, moisture-loving native vine for moist woodland settings in zone 6–9 where Carolina Jessamine would fail in the shade and wet conditions. CAUTION: Like all Gelsemium species, all parts of the plant are highly toxic — containing gelsemine and other alkaloids that can be fatal. Do not confuse with edible plants. Plant away from children and pets.

Swamp leather flower is a native clematis of the Gulf Coastal Plain, blooming from late spring through summer with distinctive nodding, urn-shaped flowers in soft lavender to blue-purple with flared, recurved petal tips that give the flowers a crisp, sculptural quality unlike any other vine — it is one of the finest ornamental native vines of the American South yet remains underutilized in cultivation. The vine is naturally found in swampy thickets, bottomland forests, and moist shrub borders from Virginia to Texas, making it ideally suited to rain garden edges, pond margins, and low-lying moist areas of Gulf Coast gardens that challenge other vines. Unlike many Clematis species, it handles the heat and humidity of the Gulf South reliably without the mildew and root rot problems that affect hybrid large-flowered types in zones 8 and 9. Plant through a native shrub or on a fence in partial shade; cut back hard to the ground each winter to maintain a neat, vigorous plant.

Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial sun along woodland edges, swamp margins, stream banks, or moist fence lines; swamp leatherflower is one of the most beautiful native vines of the Gulf Coast and southeastern US, producing delicate, nodding, urn-shaped flowers with flared, crisped petal tips in shades of lavender-blue to pale violet throughout summer. Unlike many clematis it thrives in poorly drained and seasonally flooded soils, making it invaluable for wet spots where other vines fail. It climbs by twining leaf petioles to 3–6 feet through shrubs, other vines, or light structures and pairs naturally with buttonbush, swamp rose, and Virginia willow in wet garden borders. The feathery seed heads are ornamental in fall. This species is best grown from nursery-propagated plants; purchase from reputable native plant nurseries as wild collection is discouraged.

Root stem cuttings directly in shallow water or moist mud, then transplant in spring along pond edges, marsh margins, or shallow standing water where this arching, semi-woody wetland shrub naturally forms dense colonies. Where its long stems arch over and touch water they root at the tip, gradually building thickets that stabilize soft shorelines and create rich cover and spawning habitat for fish, amphibians, and waterfowl. Showy magenta-pink flower clusters bloom in the leaf axils through summer and draw bees and other pollinators, while the tangled root mass filters runoff and reduces erosion along pond and marsh edges throughout the eastern US and Great Lakes basin. Give it full sun to partial shade and a spot that stays wet or seasonally flooded for best colonization.

Swamp Privet is a large, multi-stemmed native deciduous shrub, native to the riverine swamps, oxbow lakes, backwater floodplains, and cypress-tupelo swamps of the southeastern and mid-South United States from South Carolina to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas, tolerating prolonged inundation that few other native shrubs can survive. Inconspicuous yellow flowers appear in February and March before the leaves emerge, providing critical early-season nectar and pollen for native bees emerging from winter dormancy; small, dark blue-purple olive-like drupes ripen in summer and are avidly consumed by wood ducks, mallards, and other water-dependent birds. A valuable plant for the restoration and naturalization of wet bottomland and floodplain habitats, Swamp Privet tolerates prolonged flooding up to 4–6 months and is one of the few native shrubs that can establish in true swamp conditions. Plant male and female individuals together for fruit production; it requires no maintenance once established.

Swamp Rose is a robust, upright-arching native rose naturally found along stream banks, swamp margins, and moist open meadows from Nova Scotia to Florida, and is the most flood-tolerant of all native eastern rose species. Plant rooted cuttings in spring into moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 4 to 6 feet apart to accommodate their vigorous suckering habit. Deep rose-pink, 5-petaled, fragrant flowers 1.5 to 2 inches across appear on recurved-prickled arching canes from June through July, followed by round red hips that persist through winter and are eaten by dozens of bird species. Allow plants to spread naturally by suckers to colonize wet areas, stream banks, and rain garden berms where few other flowering shrubs will thrive.

Plant in wet to moist, acidic, peaty or humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; swamp titi is a native Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain shrub of remarkable ornamental and ecological value that is still underused in landscape horticulture. The long, drooping racemes of small white honey-scented flowers in late spring and summer are among the most important nectar sources for honey production in the Florida Panhandle, where 'titi honey' is a regional specialty. The semi-evergreen to evergreen, leathery leaves turn vivid red and orange in fall before dropping. It tolerates flooding, poor acid soil, and full sun in swampy conditions — exactly the site conditions where most ornamental shrubs fail. In zone 9a, it makes an excellent native screen in wet or poorly drained areas.

Swamp Tupelo is a dominant native tree of the permanent swamps, bay forests, and river floodplains of the southeastern coastal plain from Delaware to Florida and west to Texas, often growing alongside bald cypress and water tupelo in pure stands in the deepest, most permanently flooded low-lying land in the South. It is distinguished from the more upland Black Gum (Nyssa sylvatica) by its narrower leaves, preference for wetter conditions, and more southern distribution; in very wet sites it develops the distinctive swollen, buttressed trunk base characteristic of swamp-adapted trees. In fall Swamp Tupelo produces one of the finest foliage displays of any native tree — brilliant crimson, scarlet, and orange — providing spectacular autumn color even in the deep South where fall foliage is often muted. Small blue-black drupes in fall are consumed by a wide variety of birds and mammals. Plant in consistently wet to seasonally flooded, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates standing water better than almost any other native upland tree.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; swamp white oak is the premier large native oak for wet, clay-heavy, or periodically flooded sites — conditions where most other oaks decline. The exfoliating, peeling bark on the upper branches is a distinctive and attractive identification feature, revealing lighter bark beneath. The acorns are large, borne in pairs on long stalks (2–4 inches), and are among the most important fall-winter food for wood ducks (which nest in cavities of old trees), turkeys, deer, and dozens of other species. Fall color is yellow to bronze. The tree develops into a large, rounded specimen 50–60 feet tall with a broad, open crown. Its tolerance of wet, clay, compacted, and temporarily flooded conditions makes it an outstanding choice for low areas of the landscape, stream buffers, and rain gardens where it can manage stormwater.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline soil with the crown at or just below the soil surface; sweet autumn clematis explodes into bloom in late summer and fall with masses of small, starry white flowers that cover the vine in a frothy blanket of fragrance reminiscent of vanilla. The plant can grow 15–20 feet in a season once established and needs a strong trellis, arbor, or fence to climb. Prune back hard in late winter (cut to 12–18 inches from the ground) to control size and encourage vigorous new growth, since it blooms on current-season growth. Important note: sweet autumn clematis self-seeds prolifically and is considered invasive in portions of the eastern US; deadhead before seeds mature or remove seedlings promptly to prevent spread into wild areas. Excellent on chain-link fences, pergolas, and as a late-season screen.

Plant in moist to wet, acid soil in full sun to partial shade; this native magnolia naturally inhabits swampy lowlands and stream banks from Massachusetts to Florida and is one of the best large shrubs or small trees for wet areas in the southern garden. The creamy-white, lemon-scented flowers appear over a long season from late spring through summer, and the semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves (depending on winter severity) have a striking silver underside. In the Gulf South it can reach 30 feet as a multi-stemmed, nearly evergreen tree; in colder zones it is smaller and more deciduous. The red fruit clusters provide fall and winter food for songbirds and small mammals.

Sweet Birch is an elegant native birch of the Appalachian Mountains and northeastern North America, native to cool, moist, well-drained forest slopes and ravines from Maine and Ontario south through the Appalachians to Georgia and Alabama, distinguished from other birches by its dark, cherry-like bark (not peeling white or papery) and the intensely sweet, wintergreen fragrance released when the bark, twigs, or leaves are crushed — the essential oil methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) was historically distilled from the bark and twigs for flavoring and as a precursor to salicylic acid. Rich, golden-yellow fall color, pendant pollen catkins in early spring, and an attractive, slightly furrowed dark bark provide four-season ornamental interest in the woodland garden. Sweet Birch is host to dozens of native Lepidoptera species (caterpillars) and provides high-quality nesting habitat for cavity-nesting birds in mature specimens. Grow in cool, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; it is most appropriate for the cooler portions of its range and struggles in the heat of zones 7–8.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; sweet box is a refined, slow-growing, suckering Asian shrub with small, polished, lance-shaped leaves and inconspicuous tiny white flowers in late winter to early spring that produce one of the most intensely sweet vanilla-honey fragrances in the plant world — remarkable for their power from such small, unshowy blooms. Small, glossy black berries follow in late summer. The plant is entirely shade-adapted and makes an excellent low-maintenance, deer-resistant groundcover or fragrant foundation planting under trees where little else succeeds. 'Purple Stem' (Sarcococca hookeriana var. humilis) stays more compact at 18 inches. No significant pruning required.

Plant in partial to full shade in moist to dry, well-drained soil; Sweet Box is exceptionally tolerant of dry shade and root competition, making it one of the best low-growing shade shrubs for planting beneath established trees. Sarcococca confusa is a low, spreading, slowly suckering evergreen shrub in the boxwood family (Buxaceae) native to China, notable for producing its tiny but extraordinarily fragrant flowers in the dead of winter — December through February in zone 7–9 — when little else in the garden is blooming. The individual white flowers are barely noticeable: small tufts of stamens without petals, hidden among the glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves. But the fragrance they produce is intensely sweet and reminiscent of vanilla and honey, and on mild winter days it carries remarkably far from a planting, making Sweet Box one of the most valuable fragrant plants for the shade garden. After flowering, small black or red berry-like fruits provide additional ornamental interest and are eaten by birds. The plant spreads gradually by underground suckers to form a dense, ground-covering colony 2–3 feet high and 4–6 feet across over many years. Essentially pest- and disease-free, drought-tolerant in shade, and long-lived, it is among the finest low-maintenance shade shrubs available.

Choose a sunny spot with lean, well-drained soil; Sweet Briar thrives on chalky or limestone ground and the apple scent of its foliage is most pronounced in warm sun after a light rain. Propagate by hardwood cuttings taken in late autumn and rooted in gritty compost over winter. Avoid rich soils or heavy feeding, which promote excessive vegetative growth at the expense of flowers and hips. Thin old woody stems every few years to keep the plant open and productive, and wear heavy gloves — the hooked thorns are notably sharp.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Bronze Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Bronze-Purple Ornamental Vine)
notes: Sweet Caroline Bronze produces deeply lobed, ivy-like leaves in a warm bronze-purple, a softer, more finely cut alternative to the broad near-black leaves of the older cultivar Blackie, on a plant bred to be more compact and manageable in containers than earlier ornamental sweet potato vine selections. Its trailing stems cascade over pot edges and retaining walls, and the finely lobed foliage texture pairs well with both bold tropical companions and fine-textured annuals in a mixed planting. Give it well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; like other ornamental sweet potato vines it is extremely heat-tolerant and grows fastest in the peak of Gulf South summer, needing only occasional trimming to keep it in scale.

common_name: Sweet Caroline Light Green Sweet Potato Vine (Compact Chartreuse Ornamental Vine)
notes: Sweet Caroline Light Green carries bright chartreuse-green, deeply lobed foliage on a more compact, restrained vine than older lime-colored sweet potato vine cultivars, making it easier to keep proportionate in a mixed container rather than letting one plant take over the whole pot. The luminous foliage color brightens shaded corners and pairs naturally with cool blue and purple flowering companions or bold dark-leaved foliage plants for contrast. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates a bit more shade than most chartreuse foliage plants while still holding good color, and needs only occasional trimming to control its trailing spread through the heat of summer.

Plant young trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade, choosing an open site at a field or woodland edge where the rounded crown has room to spread. Sweet crabapple, native to the eastern and midwestern United States, produces intensely fragrant pale pink blossoms in mid-spring that draw large numbers of native bees and other pollinators before most other trees have leafed out. The small, hard, greenish-yellow fruit ripens in fall and often clings into winter, becoming an important food source for foxes, deer, and overwintering birds such as robins and cedar waxwings once it softens after frost. Its dense branching also offers good nesting cover for songbirds.

Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; sweet mock orange is a European deciduous shrub that produces one of the most intensely and purely sweet fragrances of any flowering shrub available to temperate gardeners — the large, pure-white, four-petaled flowers, borne in dense clusters along the arching branches in late May to June, fill the garden air with a sweet orange-blossom and honey fragrance that is produced in such quantity that a single established shrub can perfume an entire garden. The flowers have a simple, classic, white-on-white beauty that complements the fragrance perfectly. Individual flowers are relatively brief (2–3 weeks), but the overall display is impressive and the fragrance lingers. 'Aureus' has golden-yellow spring foliage that fades to chartreuse-green in summer; 'Variegatus' has white-margined leaves. It tolerates partial shade and clay soil better than most fragrant shrubs. Prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape and encourage vigorous flowering growth for the following year. One of the most valuable and time-tested fragrant flowering shrubs in the temperate garden tradition.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Sweet Olive performs best with at least 4 hours of sun but tolerates and even thrives in the dappled shade of open woodland gardens, where its fragrance is often more concentrated. Osmanthus fragrans is perhaps the most intensely fragrant shrub or small tree in temperate horticulture — its tiny, creamy-white to pale-apricot flowers, only a few millimeters across and produced in small axillary clusters, carry an extraordinarily powerful and sweet fragrance described variously as apricot, peach, jasmine, and vanilla that can perfume an entire garden on still evenings, carrying 50–100 feet from the plant. The fragrance blooms emerge in fall (September–November), often again in spring, and sporadically year-round in warm climates — the fall flush, just as the garden is losing other interest, makes it especially prized. In zones 8–10 it grows as an evergreen shrub or small multi-stem tree 6–20 feet tall; in zone 7 it may be semi-evergreen and die back to the roots in severe winters. The form 'Aurantiacus' has orange flowers with even more intense fragrance than the typical white-flowered form. Essential for zone 9 gardens.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; sweet viburnum is one of the most widely planted evergreen screening shrubs of the Gulf Coast, Deep South, and Florida — valued for its large, glossy, dark-green leaves, rapid growth rate, and the intensely fragrant white flower panicles produced in late March through May that fill the surrounding garden with a sweet, orange-blossom-like fragrance. After flowering, clusters of small fruits ripen from red to black and attract birds. The plant adapts equally well to full sun and part shade and grows rapidly to form a dense privacy screen or hedge 10–20 feet tall. It tolerates brief dips to 15°F but is most reliable from zone 8b southward. Shearing 2–3 times per year maintains it as a tight formal hedge; left unpruned it develops into a handsome large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with layered, spreading branches. The cultivar 'Emerald Lustre' offers especially large, deeply glossed leaves. One of the fastest and most reliable evergreen privacy solutions for Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes.

Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; sweetbay magnolia is more tolerant of wet, boggy soils than most magnolias and thrives in the heavy, seasonally wet soils common in southeastern gardens. Magnolia virginiana is the finest native magnolia for year-round SE gardens — semi-evergreen in zones 7–10 with smooth, blue-gray bark; large, glossy, dark-green leaves with silver undersides that flutter beautifully in the breeze; and creamy-white, lemon-scented flowers 2–3 inches across that open throughout summer, providing a long season of fragrance and pollinator value. The red, berry-like seeds in fall are consumed by birds, and the tree supports specialist Promethea silk moth and tiger swallowtail caterpillars; it grows naturally in swampy, streamside habitats from Massachusetts to Texas.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to part shade; avoid dry soil or full sun, which bleaches and scorches the leaves. Sarcococca hookeriana (Himalayan sweetbox) is one of the finest shade shrubs for temperate and mild-winter gardens — a compact, slowly spreading, Himalayan evergreen shrub producing small, glossy, narrow, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves on gracefully arching stems, and tiny, thread-like, white flowers of almost no visual impact but extraordinary fragrance in January–March, filling the winter air with an intense, vanilla-like perfume that is among the most powerful and pleasing of any garden plant in bloom. The flowers are followed by small, glossy, black drupes (berries) attractive to birds. Plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form tidy, weed-suppressing colonies. The variety humilis (dwarf form, to 24 inches) is lower and more spreading; var. digyna is slightly taller with narrower leaves. Sweetbox is superbly adapted to the dry shade and root competition under large trees — one of the most underused shrubs for difficult shaded spots. In zone 9, protect from afternoon sun and provide reliable summer moisture.

Divide root suckers in early spring or plant container specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy, infertile soil in full sun to partial shade; sweetfern is one of the most distinctive and characterful of all North American native shrubs — though it looks like a miniature fern with deeply lobed, linear, fern-like leaves, it is actually a nitrogen-fixing, aromatic shrub related to bayberry (Morella), not a fern at all. The leaves have a remarkable, intensely spicy-sweet, resinous fragrance when bruised or crushed — one of the most evocative natural scents of the northeastern American outdoors, instantly recognizable to anyone who has walked through sunny pine barrens, rocky slopes, and sandy blueberry barrens in summer. It thrives in extremely infertile, dry, sandy, acidic soils where virtually nothing else will grow, and is essential for naturalizing and stabilizing infertile, acidic slopes and disturbed areas. The nitrogen-fixing root system slowly enriches the surrounding soil, making it useful as a nurse plant for subsequent native plantings. Essentially impossible to transplant bare-root; always use container stock.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; sweetgum is one of the most visually spectacular native trees for fall color in the South, producing star-shaped leaves that turn a stunning mosaic of yellow, orange, red, and burgundy-purple — often all colors simultaneously on a single tree — rivaling the best maples in fall display. It is a major component of bottomland and upland forests throughout the eastern United States and grows rapidly into a large, pyramidal to oval tree. The distinctive spiny spherical seed balls (gumballs) that persist through winter provide important food for goldfinches, pine siskins, and purple finches but can be a nuisance underfoot on lawns; fruitless cultivars such as 'Rotundiloba' are available for situations where the seed balls are problematic. The sweetgum is one of the most ecologically important trees for wildlife in the Southeast.

common_name: Sweetheart Hoya (Heart Leaf Hoya, Lucky-Heart Plant, Valentine Hoya)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Sweetheart Hoya is more shade-tolerant than most succulents but produces its best growth and flowers (on mature vines) in bright indirect light; it will not flower in low light. Hoya kerrii is a succulent-leaved epiphytic vine native to the hill and montane forests of Southeast Asia (Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, southern China), belonging to the family Apocynaceae alongside other Hoyas and Dischidias. The common name 'Sweetheart Hoya' and the plant's enormous commercial popularity around Valentine's Day both derive from the uniquely heart-shaped leaves: thick, fleshy, dark-green, perfectly symmetrical cordate (heart-shaped) leaves that give the plant an immediately charming, gift-ready appearance. The single rooted leaf cuttings sold in tiny pots — ubiquitous in florist shops and garden centers every February — are cute but limited: because a single leaf has no axillary bud (node), it can root and survive indefinitely but can never produce new growth or develop into a full plant. Only stem cuttings with a node can develop into the full trailing vine, which in time produces small, white, star-shaped flowers in umbels with a faint sweet fragrance. The complete vine form, with its thick, overlapping heart leaves and occasional fragrant flowers, is the superior ornamental plant. Non-toxic to pets and children.

Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath established trees; adaptable to a range of soil textures as long as it is not waterlogged. Symplocos tinctoria (sweetleaf, or horse sugar) is a semi-evergreen to evergreen native shrub or small tree of southeastern woodlands, named for its distinctly sweet-tasting leaves — historically browsed eagerly by livestock (hence 'horse sugar') and once used by farmers as emergency fodder. In late winter to earliest spring, before or as new leaves emerge, the bare branches are lined with small, fragrant, pale yellow flower clusters that provide an important early nectar source for native bees at a time when little else is blooming. The foliage is a larval host plant for several moth species, including the striking io moth, adding real ecological value to a woodland garden planting. An underused, ecologically valuable native for the shaded understory of a southeastern woodland garden, zone 6–9.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; sweetshrub is an excellent native shrub for the woodland garden, producing unusual maroon-to-burgundy, many-petaled, strap-petaled flowers in late spring with a sweet, fruity, strawberry-spice fragrance that has been treasured for centuries — historically the dried flowers were placed in sachets and closets for perfuming linens. Fragrance intensity varies considerably among individuals, so select plants when in bloom or seek named fragrant cultivars like 'Athens' (buttery-yellow flowers) and 'Michael Lindsey'. The large, dark-green leaves turn butter-yellow in fall. Adaptable and low-maintenance once established; it suckers moderately to form a naturalistic clump.

common_name: Swing Low Distylium (Prostrate Groundcover Evergreen Shrub)
notes: Swing Low is one of the lowest-growing distylium selections available, spreading wide while staying under 18 inches tall, which makes it a tough, evergreen alternative to traditional shade groundcovers like liriope or mondo grass in beds too shaded for turf. Its small, glossy, leathery leaves resist deer browsing and stay attractive year-round, with new growth tinged bronze-red before maturing to green, and inconspicuous small red flowers appear in late winter without significant ornamental impact. Like other distylium selections it is remarkably adaptable, tolerating wet or dry soil, heat, humidity, and both full sun and deep shade with minimal disease or pest pressure, and needs only an occasional trim to keep its spreading habit in bounds.

common_name: Swiss Cheese Vine (Monkey Mask Plant, Adanson's Monstera)
notes: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade; Swiss Cheese Vine performs best with bright indirect light (2–4 feet from a sunny window) and will tolerate lower light than the larger Monstera deliciosa, though growth slows significantly in very dim conditions. Monstera adansonii is a tropical vine from Central and South America in the Araceae family closely related to but smaller-leaved than the iconic Monstera deliciosa. Its heart-shaped to oval, dark-green leaves are perforated by numerous oval holes (fenestrations) of varying sizes — the perforations develop naturally as the leaves expand and are thought to allow wind and rain to pass through without damaging the leaf in the turbulent rainforest understory. The fenestrated leaves, smaller than M. deliciosa (3–8 inches versus 12–18 inches), are nevertheless extremely ornamental and have made Swiss Cheese Vine one of the most popular and widely sold trailing houseplants in the current era of 'indoor jungle' interior design. The plant grows quickly in good conditions and can cascade several feet from a hanging basket or climb enthusiastically up a moss pole. In zone 10-11, it can be planted outdoors in deeply shaded, humid spots and will eventually climb trees to considerable height. All parts are mildly toxic if chewed.

Sycamore-leaf Snowbell is a beautiful native understory shrub or small tree, endemic to the limestone canyons, creek banks, and rocky woodland slopes of the Texas Edwards Plateau and Hill Country, where it grows in the shaded understory of live oak and Texas cedar elm woodlands in thin, alkaline, limestone-derived soils. In April and May it produces clusters of fragrant, white, pendant bell-shaped flowers similar to those of other snowbells (Styrax species), with the blooms arranged more openly than the closely related American Snowbell (Styrax americanus). The large, maple-like (plataniform) leaves are a distinctive characteristic that sets it apart from other native snowbells. An excellent shrub for Texas Hill Country native landscapes and limestone-soil gardens in zones 7–9, it is drought-tolerant once established in well-drained alkaline soil and requires no fertilizer or supplemental irrigation after the first two seasons. Source from specialty native Texas plant nurseries.

Plant in dry, rocky, very well-drained, acidic, lean soil in full sun on exposed ridges and slopes; table mountain pine is an Appalachian endemic restricted to dry, exposed, rocky ridge tops from Pennsylvania to Georgia, typically growing on south- or west-facing outcrops at elevations of 2000–4000 feet. The most distinctive feature is the armored cones — among the most ferociously spiny of any North American pine, with stout, curved, sharp spines on each scale. These serotinous cones remain closed on the tree for decades and require the intense heat of a wildfire to open and release seeds, an adaptation to the fire-maintained pine barrens community of dry Appalachian ridges. The tree has a gnarled, picturesque growth habit from constant exposure to wind and drought on rocky summits. Of limited garden use outside its native range but outstanding for naturalistic plantings on rocky, thin, dry, acidic slopes in Appalachian zones 4–7.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Taiwan cherry blooms in January through February in zone 8–10, producing small, bell-shaped (campanulata = bell-shaped) flowers in a vivid, deep cerise-pink to crimson-red — among the most intensely colored of all cherry blossoms. Unlike most Japanese ornamental cherries that require cold winters for satisfactory bloom, Taiwan cherry thrives in mild winters and requires minimal winter chill. It is the ornamental cherry of choice for gardeners in the Gulf South, Pacific Southwest, and other mild-winter areas where cold-requirement Japanese cherries languish. A hummingbird magnet — the intensely colored, nectar-rich flowers attract Anna's and rufous hummingbirds throughout their bloom period. The small, dark red fruits are edible though small and tart. Blooms in late winter before most other flowering trees.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tall stewartia needs consistent moisture and dislikes hot, dry conditions or root disturbance. Among the largest-growing of the stewartias, this Japanese species develops smooth, richly colored cinnamon-red exfoliating bark considered by many collectors to be the finest of any stewartia, alongside small white summer flowers and reliable orange-red fall color, all on a taller, more substantial tree form than most of its garden-scale relatives. Its combination of eventual larger size and exceptional bark color makes it a valuable specimen tree for a spacious woodland garden where its slow but steady growth into a true small-to-medium shade tree can be accommodated over the years. Provide consistent moisture, dappled shade, and acidic, humus-rich soil, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established, since stewartias establish and transplant slowly.

Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind and hot midday sun; Tama-no-Ura is a celebrated Japanese camellia cultivar discovered growing wild on the Gotō Islands off Nagasaki in 1947, bearing single, rich red flowers cleanly edged in white — a naturally occurring bicolor pattern that, unlike many mottled or streaked camellias, holds true and rarely reverts to solid color. The glossy, deep-green evergreen foliage provides year-round structure, and the plant blooms in winter into early spring, when few other shrubs are in flower. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it needs consistently moist but well-drained, acidic soil and benefits from a site with some shelter from strong afternoon sun, which can bleach and brown open flowers. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly after flowering only to shape, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.

common_name: Tamukeyama Japanese Maple (Weeping Red Lace-Leaf Maple)
notes: Plant in part shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and the harshest afternoon sun. One of the oldest and most reliable weeping lace-leaf Japanese maple cultivars in cultivation, Tamukeyama forms a low, dome-shaped, cascading mound of finely dissected, deep burgundy-red leaves that hold their color through summer heat better than most other red lace-leaf cultivars, a trait that has made it a Gulf South and Deep South favorite. Its wider-than-tall, mounding habit makes it a strong specimen for the edge of a pond, atop a slope, or spilling over a low wall. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially through the first few years, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches, preserving the natural cascading form.

common_name: Tangerine Beauty Crossvine (Native Apricot-Orange Tubular Flower Spring Vine)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Tangerine Beauty is a selected cultivar of crossvine (Bignonia capreolata), a native southeastern vine notable for its warm apricot-orange to copper-orange flower color — a softer, warmer tone than the typical red-and-yellow of the straight species. The 2-inch, tubular, trumpet-shaped flowers are produced in dense clusters along the vine in March–May, creating a spectacular spring display of orange-toned blooms that attract hummingbirds with exceptional consistency — the tubular flower form and warm color combination is highly attractive to ruby-throated hummingbirds during their spring migration through the Gulf South. Crossvine clings to surfaces with adhesive tendrils and disk-like holdfasts similar to Boston ivy — it can climb masonry, wood, and bark without a separate trellis. The semi-evergreen, compound leaves (two leaflets flanking a tendril) turn deep burgundy-red in winter cold, providing attractive winter foliage color before the spring bloom. Unlike many vines, Tangerine Beauty tolerates considerable shade — growing well on north-facing fences and under tree canopy where most flowering vines fail. The native origin makes it valuable for wildlife gardens: hummingbirds in spring, and specialist native bee species that visit the flowers. The vine is manageable in typical garden settings, growing to 10–20 feet rather than the 50+ feet of some other vines.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants generously to accommodate its large mature size. Tardiva is a classic, tall-growing panicle hydrangea cultivar, dating to the early 20th century, valued for flowering three to four weeks later than most Hydrangea paniculata selections, opening airy, loosely branched white flower panicles composed mostly of small fertile florets with scattered showy sterile florets in late summer that age to a soft pinkish-bronze through fall. Its later bloom time and more open, elegant panicle shape distinguish it from denser modern cultivars like Limelight, making it valued by gardeners who want hydrangea color extending into September and October. Like all panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood regardless of pruning timing, so it can be cut back hard in late winter to control size and encourage strong new flowering stems; the large habit also makes it useful as a big-shrub anchor at the back of a mixed border or as a small specimen tree when limbed up.

Plant in acidic, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; tarflower is a native evergreen shrub of Gulf South pine flatwoods and sandy scrub, blooming in late summer with clusters of fragrant, white-to-pink, sticky flowers whose petals are edged with tiny glandular hairs that exude a resinous, tar-like substance — hence the common name, and a genuine curiosity, since bees visiting the flowers often end up with a bit of sticky residue on their bodies. It is a fire-adapted plant of longleaf pine ecosystems, resprouting vigorously after burns in the wild, and is highly drought tolerant in the deep, fast-draining sand it evolved in. Grown occasionally by native-plant nurseries for wildlife gardens and low-water landscaping within its native range, it asks for little beyond sharp drainage and lean, acidic soil; rich garden soil or poor drainage are more likely to cause problems than neglect. Its long late-summer bloom period is valuable for native pollinators when many other shrubs have finished flowering.

Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Tasmanian tree fern is more cold-hardy than most tree ferns and can survive brief light frosts once established, but the growing crown should be mulched heavily ahead of any hard freeze. Dicksonia antarctica is a slow-growing but exceptionally cold-tolerant Australian tree fern with a thick, shaggy, fibrous trunk and a broad crown of dark green, leathery, arching fronds, forming a striking specimen for a sheltered shaded courtyard or woodland garden. It grows more slowly than Cyathea species, typically only an inch or two of trunk per year, but tolerates cooler, more temperate conditions and light frost better than most of its tropical relatives, making it the tree fern of choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of tree-fern-growing range. Keep the growing crown watered from above regularly, especially in dry weather, since the trunk has no true root system and absorbs much of its moisture through the fibrous trunk itself.

Tawnyberry Holly is a native evergreen holly tree of the Florida Keys, Miami-Dade rockland hammocks, and Caribbean islands, producing small clusters of tawny-orange to reddish-black berries that are eagerly consumed by white-crowned pigeons, mockingbirds, and other fruit-eating birds in the subtropical forests of southernmost Florida. Growing as a slender understory tree to small specimen tree in the hammock community, Tawnyberry Holly has glossy, dark green evergreen leaves and small, inconspicuous white flowers in spring. An important component of the rare Florida Keys and Miami-Dade pine rockland hammock community — one of the most imperiled plant communities in the United States — this species deserves wider cultivation as an ornamental holly in frost-free south Florida landscapes. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in Zone 10–11; both male and female plants are needed for berry production.

Plant in well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Grown for centuries in China for the edible oil pressed from its seeds, Tea Oil Camellia produces fragrant white flowers in late fall into winter and is notably more cold-hardy than the familiar ornamental camellias, tolerating temperatures well below what damages Camellia japonica or sasanqua. The glossy evergreen foliage and modest size make it a useful dual-purpose shrub for a partly shaded border, valued both as an ornamental flowering evergreen and, where enough plants are grown, for pressing the oil-rich seeds. It tolerates a range of light conditions from woodland shade to fairly sunny sites and needs the same acidic soil and good drainage as other camellias.

Plant in well-drained, mildly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, giving the shrub room to develop its open, arching, vase-shaped habit rather than crowding it against other plantings. Tea viburnum is grown chiefly for its heavy fall display of long-lasting, translucent orange-red berries that dangle from the branches on drooping stalks well into winter, set off by narrow, willowy leaves that turn bronze-red before dropping. The common name comes from the historical use of dried young leaves as a tea substitute in parts of China, though it is grown ornamentally today. Because it flowers on old wood, prune only right after the spring bloom to avoid removing the berries that follow; light shade during the hottest afternoon hours helps keep foliage from scorching in warmer parts of its range.

common_name: Teasing Georgia Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1998, Teasing Georgia bears deep yellow buds opening to cupped, rich yellow blooms that soften with age, carrying a strong tea fragrance, on long, arching canes that reach 8 feet or more when trained as a climber, or can be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. Its vigor and rich, saturated yellow color have made it one of David Austin's most popular climbing selections, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Techny Arborvitae (Broad Pyramidal Winter-Hardy Green Arborvitae)
notes: Techny is a broad, dense, pyramidal arborvitae grown for its reliable deep green color that holds through winter cold far better than many other Thuja occidentalis selections, which often bronze or yellow in freezing weather. Its wider, fuller pyramidal shape makes it a substantial specimen or privacy screen, slower-growing and more compact than towering cultivars like Green Giant, and it needs only light shearing, if any, to maintain a tidy form. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; arborvitae generally performs best in cooler climates and struggles with the intense heat and humidity of the Deep South, so it is best suited to the northern edge of its range.

common_name: Teddy Bear Magnolia (Compact Fuzzy-Backed Southern Magnolia)
notes: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Teddy Bear is a compact, densely pyramidal southern magnolia selection notable for its thick, glossy dark green leaves with dense, fuzzy cinnamon-brown undersides, a texture that gives the plant its name and provides striking contrast when wind or hand movement flips the leaves to show their reverse side. Its narrower, more upright form and smaller mature size than the massive straight species make it a practical evergreen specimen or screen for typical residential lots, while it still produces the large, fragrant, creamy white summer flowers magnolias are prized for. It requires little pruning to maintain its naturally tidy pyramidal shape and tolerates the same range of soil conditions as other southern magnolia selections.

common_name: Tess of the d'Urbervilles Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1998 and named for the Thomas Hardy novel, Tess of the d'Urbervilles bears dark crimson-red, rosette-shaped blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous, well-branched shrub with glossy foliage. Its rich, velvety red color and classic old-rose form and scent have made it a favorite among David Austin's darker-flowered introductions, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Texanum ligustrum tolerates heat, humidity, and heavy pruning well, a mainstay hedge shrub across the Gulf South. Broad, glossy, dark green, wax-textured leaves cover a dense, fast-growing shrub topped in early summer by conspicuous clusters of small white flowers with a strong, sweet scent some find pleasant and others find overpowering, followed by small dark berries that birds readily consume and disperse. A more compact, rounder-leaved selection than the straight species, it has long been one of the most widely planted hedge and screening shrubs across the warm, humid South, tolerating heavy shearing, heat, and drought once established, though it can self-sow aggressively and is considered invasive in some regions. Shear regularly to control size and maintain a formal hedge, and monitor for self-sown seedlings in naturalistic areas, since birds spread the berries widely.

Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained sandy soil in partial shade, keeping roots consistently moist but never waterlogged. Texas azalea is a deciduous native shrub of the West Gulf Coastal Plain, found wild in sandy pine woods and along shaded stream banks of East Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma, where it forms a mounding, spreading thicket of slender branches. In mid-to-late spring, after or alongside the emerging leaves, clusters of narrow, glandular, white to pale pink tubular flowers open with a distinctive lemony-spice fragrance that carries well beyond the plant. Because it flowers later than many spring azaleas, it extends the native azalea bloom season in a partly shaded woodland border, and it is a useful nectar source for late-season pollinators including sphinx moths.

Plant in well-drained, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas clematis is the only North American clematis species with urn-shaped, non-opening flowers in shades of scarlet to coral-pink — a dramatic departure from the typical flat, open clematis bloom. In its native Texas limestone hill country habitat, it scrambles through shrubs and along rocky slopes. The plant is one of the most drought-tolerant clematis species once established and thrives in the alkaline soils and intense heat of zone 8–9 where many clematis struggle. Its native-species hybrid offspring, including the popular 'Princess Diana' (coral-pink) and 'Duchess of Albany' (pink), are more widely available than the straight species but share its ornamental urn shape. Prune back hard in late winter as the vine blooms on new growth.
