Texas Dutchman's Pipe is a twining native perennial vine of moist, calcareous woodland edges and bottomland thickets in Texas and adjacent Oklahoma, recognized by its large, prominently net-veined, heart-shaped leaves and brownish-purple, pipe-shaped flowers that bloom from spring into early summer. It is a critical larval host plant for the Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor) in central and south Texas, and a single well-established plant can support multiple generations of caterpillars through a growing season. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline, limestone-based soil in partial shade to full sun; the plant spreads by underground rhizomes and will form a colonizing patch over time. It is an essential component of butterfly garden plantings for the Texas Hill Country, cross-timbers region, and adjacent areas with alkaline soils.

Texas ebony is one of the finest ornamental trees native to south Texas and northeastern Mexico, producing a dense, rounded crown of small, dark green compound leaves on thorny branches — the tree's extremely hard, black-brown heartwood (comparable in density to commercial ebony) is prized for wood turning and tool handles, and the species' name reflects this extraordinary wood quality. Clusters of fragrant, creamy-white to pale yellow flowers appear in summer and fall and are heavily visited by native bees and honeybees, producing a distinctive honey; the large, woody seed pods split open in fall to reveal shiny black seeds that are edible when roasted and were an important food source for indigenous peoples of the Rio Grande Valley. In south Texas (zone 9–10) it is among the most recommended native trees for year-round evergreen screening, wildlife habitat, and creating dense shade in landscapes — slow-growing but extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived once established. It also provides one of the most important nesting trees for the endangered ferruginous pygmy owl in the lower Rio Grande Valley.

Plant in well-drained, lean, even rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Texas lantana is a native alternative to the non-native common lantana sold at garden centers, with the same heat tolerance and butterfly-magnet qualities but a more compact, less rampant habit that doesn't pose the invasive risk of L. camara in tropical areas. The small, multi-colored flowers progress from yellow through orange to red as they age on the same cluster, creating a striking tricolor effect that attracts swallowtails, skippers, and monarchs all summer long. The plant is toxic to livestock and pets if ingested. In zone 8, it dies back to the root crown after hard freezes and regrows as a true perennial; in zones 9-11 it stays semi-evergreen. An excellent plant for hot, dry slopes, driveways, and sunny borders where heat and drought defeat most other plants.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Texas Lilac is a widely promoted vitex selection valued for its dense, fragrant, lavender-blue flower spikes and reliably strong performance under the extreme heat, drought, and poor soil conditions typical of Texas and Gulf South summers, where it has become a landscape staple as a tough, low-maintenance flowering large shrub or small tree. It blooms heavily on new growth from late spring through fall, with the fragrant, gray-green palmately compound foliage adding a light sage-like scent to the garden. Cut back hard in late winter to about 12-18 inches above ground each year to encourage vigorous new growth and the best flower display, and to keep the plant at a manageable size. Bees and butterflies visit the long-lasting flower spikes heavily.

Plant in alkaline to neutral, rocky or caliche, sharply drained soil in full sun; this aristocratic native evergreen shrub of the Texas Hill Country and desert Southwest is prized for its intensely fragrant violet-purple flower clusters that smell like Concord grape candy and appear in early spring. It is extremely slow-growing (6–12 inches per year), drought tolerant once established, and virtually pest and disease free. The distinctive woody seed pods contain bright red seeds that are highly toxic if eaten. Give it an excellent drainage and poor alkaline soil — rich, moist conditions cause root rot. An excellent foundation or specimen plant for Gulf Coast and zone 8–9 gardens where winter temperatures stay above 10°F.

common_name: Texas Olive (Mexican Olive, Anacahuita, Wild Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Texas olive is one of the most spectacular native flowering trees of the Rio Grande Plains and an outstanding ornamental for zone 8–11 gardens. The large, tropical-looking leathery leaves and stunning pure white, 2-inch funnel-shaped flowers with a yellow throat are produced year-round in warm weather, attracting bees, butterflies, and birds. The olive-like fruits ripen to white and are eaten by mockingbirds and other wildlife. The tree is semi-evergreen, holding its large velvety leaves in mild winters and dropping them only in cold or drought. It is highly drought tolerant once established and grows naturally on rocky limestone slopes, chaparral, and thorny brush country of the Rio Grande Plains. In zone 8a it may be killed to the ground in severe winters but resprouting from roots is common.

common_name: Texas Palmetto (Mexican Palmetto, Rio Grande Palmetto)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun; once established, Texas palmetto is drought-tolerant and requires little supplemental water. Sabal mexicana (Texas palmetto or Mexican palmetto) is the native palm of the lower Rio Grande Valley and the southernmost tip of Texas — the most cold-hardy of the larger Sabal species and the only palm native to continental Texas. It produces a massive, solitary trunk up to 50 feet tall topped with a globular crown of large, fan-shaped (palmate), blue-green fronds 4–6 feet across on 8-to-10-foot petioles; the base of old petioles persist on the trunk as a distinctive boot-like attachment giving the trunk a characteristic rough texture. The palm is closely related to the Cabbage Palm (Sabal palmetto) of the Florida/Carolina coast, but is larger and adapted to the limestone, alkaline soils of southern Texas and northern Mexico. It is the dominant palm of the Texas Gulf Coast and Rio Grande Valley and is important as an ornamental landscape tree, wildlife food source (fruits are eaten by numerous bird species including Hooded Orioles), and cultural symbol of the Rio Grande Valley. More cold-hardy than most large palms, surviving brief drops to 15°F when established.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — Texas redbud is the heat-and-drought-hardy western variety of our native eastern redbud, offering the same spectacular early spring bloom — dense clusters of magenta-pink pea-flowers covering every branch before the leaves emerge — with significantly improved performance in the rocky limestone soils, alkaline caliche, and intense summer heat of the western Gulf Coast and Edwards Plateau. The foliage is rounded, glossy, and notably thicker and more heat-tolerant than the standard species, holding up through brutal Texas summers without scorching. Selected cultivars like 'Oklahoma' (with very dark, glossy foliage and wine-red flowers) and 'Texas White' (clear white flowers) offer outstanding ornamental refinements over the species. An outstanding small patio or understory tree for dry, alkaline, sunny to lightly shaded garden sites in zone 6–9, requiring minimal water once established.

Plant in well-drained, rocky, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; Texas sotol is a dramatic native xeriscape plant of the Chihuahuan Desert and Edwards Plateau, forming a globe of many hundreds of narrow, finely toothed, spoon-based leaves with serrated margins and a distinctive dried-flower-arrangement appearance year-round. Established plants occasionally send up towering flower stalks 10–15 feet tall bearing dense clusters of small white flowers in summer, then produce fruit and seeds over the following months before dying back — the vegetative rosette survives and eventually produces another stalk. The base of the leaves was a critical food staple for the Chihuahuan people who roasted and ate the heart (similar to agave); the leaves are used to make sotol fiber and baskets. Slow-growing but extremely long-lived and virtually maintenance-free once established.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Texas White is a white-flowered selection of the Texas botanical variety of eastern redbud, combining the glossy, leathery, heat-tolerant foliage and superior drought resistance of Texas redbud with pure white spring flowers instead of the typical magenta-pink. The crisp white bloom against bare branches in late winter to early spring provides a striking contrast to pink- and purple-flowered redbuds nearby, and the same waxy, dark green summer leaves resist the leaf scorch and drop that afflicts standard eastern redbud in Gulf Coast heat. Like other Texas redbud selections it is well adapted to alkaline, clay, and rocky soils and needs little supplemental water once established, making it a reliable, low-maintenance small flowering tree for the Gulf South.

Take semi-hardwood cuttings in spring, treat with rooting hormone, and root in a warm, humid environment with bottom heat around 75 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit until a strong root system develops before transplanting. Choose a site with full sun, good drainage, and ample space, as this large tree can reach 20 to 30 feet tall and wide at maturity in frost-free climates. Water regularly during the first two years to establish deep roots, then reduce irrigation as the tree becomes more self-sufficient during dry periods. In zone 9, plant in a sheltered microclimate and mulch heavily at the base to protect roots if a rare frost threatens, as even brief freezes can cause significant dieback.

common_name: The Alnwick Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2001 and named for Alnwick Garden in Northumberland, The Alnwick Rose bears rich rose-pink, cupped rosette flowers with a strong, sweet old-rose fragrance, on a compact, rounded, well-branched shrub that fits smaller borders more easily than larger English rose cultivars. It repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost, and its dependable habit and strong fragrance have made it a long-standing favorite in David Austin's catalog.

The Champion Sunblush is an easy-care flowering rose shrub with brilliant, sun-kissed petals suited to both beginner and experienced gardeners. Set the plant in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, digging a hole wide enough for the roots and watering in well. Provide consistent moisture at the base to keep foliage dry, and mulch to conserve water and moderate soil temperature. Prune in late winter to shape the shrub and remove dead or crossing canes, and feed in spring as growth begins. Hardy in zones 5 to 9, it rewards steady care with repeat blooms through the season.

common_name: The Generous Gardener Rose (David Austin Climbing English Rose)
notes: Set plants in full sun to light partial shade with rich, well-drained soil, and provide a trellis, fence, or pergola if training it as a climber, since it flowers well trained flat against a support or left as a large, arching, informal shrub. Prune to shape in late winter, removing only crossing or damaged canes if grown as a climber, and deadhead through the season to encourage repeat bloom. The Generous Gardener is a David Austin rose valued for its large, cupped, soft blush-pink double flowers with a strong, classic old-rose fragrance carrying notes of musk and myrrh, produced in generous flushes from late spring into fall. It tolerates a bit more shade than most roses, making it a useful choice for a partly shaded fence or wall where a typical rose would bloom poorly, and its long, flexible canes make it easy to train horizontally to maximize flowering along a support.

common_name: The Pilgrim Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1991, The Pilgrim carries soft, clear yellow, deeply cupped rosette flowers with a strong myrrh fragrance, on long, arching canes that reach 8 feet or more when trained as a climber, or can be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. It was one of the earlier David Austin introductions to combine a strong yellow color with reliable repeat bloom and good disease resistance, and it continues to flower generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Introduced in England in 1876, The President remains one of the most reliable and widely planted large-flowered clematis more than a century later, prized for its rich purple-blue, star-shaped 5 to 6 inch flowers with contrasting reddish-purple stamens and silvery reverse petals that catch the light as they twist in the breeze. It reblooms twice in a season — a strong flush in late spring to early summer followed by a lighter repeat in late summer — and its long garden pedigree has earned it lasting popularity. As with other clematis, keep the roots cool and shaded (mulch or low companion planting works well) while the vine itself grows into full sun.

The Rising Sun redbud is a small deciduous tree prized for new growth that emerges in fiery apricot, orange, and gold before aging to lime and green. Site it in rich, well-drained soil where it receives morning sun and some afternoon shade in hot climates. Rosy-pink pea-like flowers cover the bare branches in early spring before the leaves unfurl. Water deeply during the first two years to establish the root system, then supplement only in dry spells. Prune lightly after flowering to shape the canopy.

Plant in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky soil in full sun; Thompson's yucca is a blue-gray-leafed native of the Trans-Pecos limestone mountains of west Texas — one of the most ornamental small to medium tree yuccas, developing a slowly lengthening trunk over many years and producing a symmetrical, rounded head of narrow, blue-gray, finely toothed leaves. Its blue-gray foliage is similar to Yucca rostrata but the plant stays somewhat more compact and typically doesn't develop as tall a trunk. The narrow, glaucous leaves create a fine-textured, spherical crown that is outstanding as a landscape specimen and combines well with native grasses, agaves, and other desert-adapted plants. In spring, impressive, branched flower spikes 4–6 feet tall bear numerous large, white, bell-shaped flowers. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert and adjacent ranges in Texas and Mexico, it is excellent for dry, alkaline, rocky landscape situations in zones 6–10.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; thorny elaeagnus is a large, vigorous, thorny, evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub from Asia with distinctive silvery-brown scales on the lower leaf surfaces that give the foliage an attractive metallic sheen. Small, intensely fragrant, white to cream-colored flowers appear in October–November — one of the few strongly scented fall-flowering shrubs — followed by reddish berries (edible but tart) in spring. It is extremely tough — among the most stress-tolerant shrubs for dry, salty, alkaline, or compacted soils and full shade — and fixes nitrogen through root nodules. Excellent for barrier hedges, windbreaks, and difficult dry or salt-spray sites in the Gulf South. 'Fruitlandii' (larger, more silver leaves) and 'Maculata' (golden-splashed variegation) are popular selections.

common_name: Thryallis (Galphimia, Rain of Gold, Golden Thryallis)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Galphimia glauca (commonly called Thryallis, Rain of Gold, or Golden Thryallis) is a Mexican and Central American shrub that is one of the most reliably blooming and low-maintenance flowering shrubs for Gulf Coast and South Texas zone 8–10 landscapes — producing a nearly continuous shower of small, five-petaled, bright golden-yellow flowers on terminal spikes from spring through fall (and sometimes year-round in zone 10+). The effect of hundreds of small golden flowers covering the fine-textured, blue-green foliage is spectacular and sustained, unlike many flowering shrubs that bloom only briefly. Thryallis tolerates heat, humidity, and drought exceptionally well once established, requires minimal fertilization, and is rarely bothered by pests or diseases — the combination of beauty, durability, and low maintenance makes it one of the finest choices for reliable color in challenging Southern landscapes. The shrub grows into a well-behaved, rounded mound (4–8 feet tall and wide over time) without aggressive spreading. Excellent as a specimen, mass planting, or informal hedge. Freezes to the ground in hard winters in zone 8 but resprouts from roots with vigor; essentially evergreen in zone 9b–12.

common_name: Thryallis (Shower of Gold, Rain of Gold)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after flowering to maintain compact shape. Galphimia gracilis (thryallis, shower of gold, or rain of gold) is a graceful, fast-growing, shrubby Mexican native in the Malpighiaceae family — one of the most reliably cheerful and floriferous flowering shrubs for zone 8–11 Gulf Coast and tropical gardens. The plant produces long, arching branches tipped with clusters of small (1/2-inch), five-petaled, brilliant golden-yellow flowers produced abundantly almost year-round in warm, frost-free climates — hence the evocative common names 'shower of gold' and 'rain of gold.' In zone 9–11, thryallis blooms nearly continuously from spring through fall, pausing only during the coldest months. The fine-textured foliage, graceful, fountain-like habit, and prolific golden flower production make it outstanding for mixed borders, foundation plantings, and as a flowering accent in drought-tolerant landscapes. It is also highly attractive to butterflies. Thryallis is more cold-hardy than many Mexican tropical shrubs, surviving brief dips to about 25°F once established in zone 8b; it dies back in cold winters but regrows from the root. A tremendously reliable and low-maintenance choice for hot, sunny, dry gardens throughout the Gulf South.

Thuja Green Giant is a fast-growing evergreen conifer widely used as a living privacy hedge, adding several feet of dense, rich green foliage each year. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants 5 to 6 feet apart for a continuous screen. Water regularly the first season to establish deep roots; once mature it tolerates heat, humidity, and brief drought. Its naturally pyramidal habit rarely needs pruning, though it takes shearing well if a formal shape is desired. It resists deer browsing and most pests.

Thuja Virginian is a compact arborvitae hybrid that offers the dense evergreen screening of Green Giant in a more manageable size for smaller yards. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water consistently through the first growing season to establish. Its tight, upright pyramidal form makes an excellent privacy hedge or specimen without heavy pruning. Mature plants tolerate heat and humidity and stand up to deer better than many evergreens. Mulch the root zone to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature.

Plant in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; Thunberg spirea is among the earliest-blooming of all spireas, opening masses of tiny, five-petaled white flowers along slender, arching branches in very early spring, often before or alongside forsythia, giving rise to its baby's-breath-like common name. Fine-textured, narrow blue-green leaves follow the bloom and often color soft yellow-orange in fall before dropping. The fountain-like, twiggy habit is best left unsheared and only lightly thinned right after flowering, removing a portion of the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the shrub airy and floriferous rather than dense and shaded out. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and is a reliable, low-fuss flowering shrub for foundation plantings, informal hedges, and mixed borders.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Thunberg's bush clover is one of the most spectacular late-season perennials available, producing dense, cascading wands of small, rosy-pink to rose-purple pea flowers in August and September — when almost nothing else in the garden is blooming with this abundance — on long, gracefully arching branches that create a weeping, fountain-like form of exceptional elegance. Each individual stem carries hundreds of small flowers in a dense, continuous spike, and a single established plant produces dozens of such stems that cascade toward the ground under their own weight, creating a foamy, waterfall effect of pink bloom that can span 5-7 feet. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves soil over time. Native to China and Japan, it dies back to the woody crown each winter and emerges late in spring, growing rapidly to blooming size by midsummer. Extraordinary for filling the late summer gap in the perennial border with a dramatic, long-lasting display highly attractive to bees and butterflies.

common_name: Thunder Cloud Texas Sage (Deep-Purple Compact Cenizo Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Thunder Cloud is one of the most compact and richly colored Texas sage (cenizo) cultivars — producing the species' characteristic silvery-gray, small, soft-textured foliage on a more restrained 3–4 foot plant, with deep purple-violet flowers that are more saturated and darker than the typical medium-purple of the species and many other cultivars. The compact habit makes Thunder Cloud proportionate for typical residential borders and containers where the sprawling, larger selections would overgrow the planting space. Like all cenizo, Thunder Cloud blooms in remarkable, synchronized flushes triggered by periods of high humidity or moisture after dry weather — the sudden appearance of masses of purple flowers across an entire planting following a rain or fog event is one of the most dramatic of Gulf South garden phenomena. The silvery foliage is attractive year-round — the pale gray-silver leaf color provides an effective contrast to green or dark foliage companions. Leucophyllum requires excellent drainage — in the humid Gulf South east of San Antonio/Houston, site in raised beds, berms, or rocky slopes where water moves away from roots quickly. Once established in appropriate drainage conditions, Thunder Cloud requires virtually no supplemental watering or fertilization. An outstanding choice for xeriscaping, reflected-heat positions, and caliche/alkaline soils where other ornamental shrubs struggle.

Thunderstruck Coral Boom is a fast-growing crape myrtle that produces large panicles of vivid coral-pink blooms from early summer into fall. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; more sun means more flowers and better mildew resistance. Its multi-season interest includes attractive exfoliating bark in winter and colorful fall foliage. Prune in late winter to remove crossing branches and shape the canopy, avoiding heavy topping. Water regularly while establishing, after which it becomes notably heat- and drought-tolerant.

Thunderstruck Rumblin' Red is a crape myrtle celebrated for its fiery red summer blooms and strong year-round interest. Site it in full sun in well-drained soil, where abundant light maximizes flowering and helps prevent powdery mildew. The dark-tinged foliage and smooth exfoliating bark add appeal beyond the long bloom season. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain a tree-like structure rather than topping it hard. Once established it is quite tolerant of heat and dry conditions, needing supplemental water only in extended droughts.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; thyme-leaf fuchsia is a Mexican cloud-forest species that appreciates cooler summer conditions and consistent moisture. Fine, small, thyme-like leaves clothe delicate, arching branches studded nearly year-round with small, slender, pale pink to rose-red flowers, giving the shrub an airy, refined texture distinct from the larger-leaved, gaudier hybrid fuchsias. Native to oak and pine-oak woodlands of Mexico and Central America, it is more heat-tolerant than many species fuchsias while still preferring the dappled shade and humidity of a woodland setting, making it a good choice for a shaded border in warmer climates where typical fuchsias struggle. Pinch growing tips periodically to encourage a bushy habit and continued bloom, and protect from hard freezes in marginal zones.

Propagate from softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings in summer, keeping them warm and humid until well rooted before potting on. Transplant to the garden only in frost-free zones 10-11, or grow in a large container in zone 9 and overwinter indoors above 55°F. Maintain consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and fertilize monthly with a balanced tropical-plant fertilizer throughout the growing season. The pinwheel-shaped white flowers bloom repeatedly in warm weather and are at their most fragrant in the evening, making this tree a standout near patios and entryways.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tibetan cherry from western China is grown almost exclusively for its extraordinary, burnished, mahogany-red to copper-brown bark that peels in horizontal strips to reveal gleaming, polished, metallic-looking new bark beneath — arguably the most ornamental bark of any tree in temperate gardening. The effect is amplified in winter sun when the bark catches raking light and glows like burnished copper. The flowers are white and relatively small, appearing with or just before the narrow, willow-like leaves in spring. The dark red fruits are small but attractive to birds. Position where winter sun will illuminate the trunk, and keep it clear of competing vegetation at the base. The bark develops its best coloring as the tree matures — young trees are less impressive. A specimen tree for its stem and bark character.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tiffany is a magnificent large-flowered Camellia japonica cultivar producing extremely large (4.5–5 inch), semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a distinctive warm orchid-pink to light lavender-pink color with slightly wavy, cupped petals surrounding a prominent cluster of bright-yellow stamens. The large, open, somewhat informal flower form and the distinctive orchid-pink color (neither the deep red of Mathotiana nor the pure pink of Debutante, but a warm intermediate with lavender tones) make Tiffany instantly recognizable and uniquely beautiful among red and pink camellia cultivars. Tiffany was selected from a seedling in California and has become one of the most popular and widely grown large-flowered japonica cultivars in American gardens. The blooms are produced mid to late season (January through March in zone 9) on an upright, vigorous shrub that can reach 6–12 feet with excellent annual growth rate. As with all Camellia japonica cultivars in zone 9, plant in dappled shade or morning sun with afternoon shade; consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential for healthy growth and maximum bloom production. Supplement iron with chelated iron fertilizer if leaves show yellowing between veins (chlorosis) — a common sign of iron deficiency in alkaline Gulf South soils.

common_name: Tiger Eyes Sumac (Golden Cutleaf Staghorn Sumac)
notes: Tiger Eyes is a compact sport of staghorn sumac selected for deeply cut, lacy, fern-like foliage that emerges chartreuse-yellow in spring, holds bright gold through summer on contrasting pink-red leaf stalks, then finishes with fiery orange-scarlet fall color, giving three seasons of striking foliage color on a shrub roughly half the size of the wild species. It still spreads by root suckers to form a colony over time, though far less aggressively than the species, and its fuzzy, cone-shaped red berry clusters persist into winter and feed birds. Give it some afternoon shade in hot climates, since the pale gold leaves scorch more readily than green foliage in intense summer sun; this cultivar is best suited to cooler regions and can struggle with the combination of extreme heat and humidity found deep in the Gulf South.

Tilt-A-Swirl is a bigleaf hydrangea whose mophead blooms shift through pink, red, and green as the season progresses, with flower color influenced by soil pH. Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil where it gets morning sun and shade during the hottest part of the day. Keep the soil consistently moist, especially in summer, as this species wilts quickly when dry. It blooms on old and new wood, so avoid heavy pruning; simply remove spent flowers and dead stems in late winter. Amend soil with aluminum sulfate for bluer tones or lime for pinker ones.

Tiny Tower is a very slow-growing dwarf Alberta spruce that keeps a naturally dense, narrow pyramidal shape without shearing, making it perfect for small gardens, entryways, and containers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and provide good air circulation to discourage spider mites, its main pest. Water regularly the first two seasons and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. In hot climates give it some afternoon shade to prevent needle scorch. Its compact evergreen form also serves as a living holiday tree.

Tiny Wine is a compact ninebark selection carrying the same deep wine-red to purple maple-like foliage as larger dark-leaved cultivars but on a rounded shrub roughly half the size, staying well under 5 feet tall and wide. Clusters of small white-to-pink spring flowers draw pollinators and are followed by reddish seed capsules, while the exfoliating bark provides winter interest once the leaves drop. Like other ninebarks it tolerates a very wide range of soil conditions, including clay and periodic flooding, and full sun brings out the darkest, richest foliage color; renewal-prune by removing some of the oldest stems at the base every few years to keep the plant full and vigorous.

common_name: Tipu Tree (Pride of Bolivia, Rosewood of Bolivia, Tipu)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Tipu Tree grows most vigorously in full sun and well-drained soil, becoming drought-tolerant once established. Tipuana tipu is a fast-growing, large, semi-evergreen to deciduous ornamental tree native to Bolivia, Argentina, and Brazil in the legume family (Fabaceae), monotypic in its genus. The tree has become one of the most widely planted street and shade trees in Mediterranean-climate cities worldwide (particularly in California, Spain, Argentina, South Africa, and Australia) and in zone 9-11 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes. In late spring to early summer, the tree produces its annual bloom: an explosion of small, pea-like flowers in rich apricot-yellow to golden-orange covering the entire canopy — the display can be so dense that the foliage is temporarily obscured by the flowers, and the falling petals create a golden carpet beneath the tree. The flowers are followed by distinctive single-winged samara seed pods that spin as they fall. The broad, spreading canopy (often exceeding the tree's height in spread) provides exceptional shade on large lawns and public spaces. The compound leaves — each composed of 13–21 paired leaflets — are a fine-textured, light green that dances in the breeze. A magnificent specimen tree for large residential and public zone 9-11 landscapes.

common_name: Tonto Crape Myrtle (Red Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tonto is a compact, semi-dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle cultivar reaching 8–12 feet — smaller than the large tree-form selections but larger than the truly dwarf compact types — producing rich fuchsia-red to magenta-red flower clusters from midsummer through fall. It occupies the important size category that bridges the gap between full-size landscape trees and dwarf shrub-form crape myrtles, making it appropriate for foundation plantings of large structures, medium-sized residential landscapes, and situations requiring a crape myrtle that provides substantial presence without becoming a full-scale tree. Tonto shows exceptional resistance to powdery mildew — one of the best in the National Arboretum series for disease resistance — and produces glossy, deep mahogany-red fall foliage color that is among the finest in any crape myrtle selection. The developing exfoliating bark provides winter interest. Tonto benefits from annual removal of small crossing and rubbing branches and removal of sucker growth from the base to maintain an attractive multi-stemmed form. The fuchsia-red flower color is particularly vivid against light-colored walls and combines boldly with contrasting white or silver companion plantings.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Toringo crabapple is a wild species used both as an ornamental tree and, historically, as breeding stock for many modern crabapple cultivars. Small, pink-budded flowers opening white cover this graceful, small Japanese species tree in spring, followed by tiny, pea-sized, red-to-yellow crabapples that persist into fall and provide food for birds, and the wild species has served as important parentage in breeding many modern disease-resistant flowering crabapple cultivars grown today. Its small mature size, graceful branching habit, and reliable disease resistance compared to many older crabapple cultivars make it a worthwhile small ornamental tree in its own right, not merely a footnote in crabapple breeding history. Water during establishment, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and prune minimally to maintain its naturally graceful form.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; tough bumelia (Alachua buckthorn) is a native evergreen shrub or small tree of north-central Florida's dry, sandy scrub and upland pine habitats — one of several Sideroxylon species native to Florida, related to the widespread tough buckthorn (S. tenax) of the Coastal Plain but with a more restricted distribution centered on Alachua County, Florida. Like other bumpelia/sideroxylon species, it produces leathery, elliptic, dark green leaves, small white flowers in clusters that attract pollinators, and small, oval, dark purple-black drupes that are eaten by mockingbirds, catbirds, and other fruit-eating birds. The spiny branches (typical of the genus) provide excellent nesting cover. An important but rarely cultivated native for the dry, sandy, acidic scrub gardens of north-central Florida.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; trailing abutilon has a naturally lax, arching to trailing habit and small, maple-shaped leaves, with distinctive pendant, lantern-like flowers combining a swollen red calyx and bright yellow petals that hang like tiny paper lanterns nearly year-round in mild climates. Its trailing growth makes it well suited to hanging baskets, cascading over a low wall, or loosely trained against a trellis or fence, where the flowers are best appreciated from below. Hummingbirds visit the tubular blooms regularly, and the plant flowers most heavily with consistent moisture and light monthly feeding through the growing season. In zone 8, expect frost dieback most winters, with the plant often resprouting from the base if roots are protected by mulch; where hard freezes are common, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

Lantana montevidensis is a sprawling, trailing, woody-based perennial groundcover shrub native to South America, producing a near-continuous succession of dense, rounded clusters of small, lilac-purple flowers from late spring through hard frost — one of the longest and most reliable bloom periods of any ornamental shrub in warm climates, while also serving as an important nectar source for butterflies and hummingbirds. Propagate from cuttings in a warm, bright location; once transplanted to full sun and well-drained soil, trailing lantana is highly drought-tolerant and heat-loving, making it ideal for dry slopes, rock gardens, raised beds, and hanging baskets where it will cascade attractively over edges. Note that Lantana montevidensis is considered invasive in parts of the Gulf Coast (Florida, Texas, and Hawaii) where it escapes cultivation into natural areas — always check local regulations before planting outdoors, and prefer growing it in containers in regions where it may naturalize aggressively. Shear plants back by one-third in early spring to encourage fresh, vigorous growth and prevent woody, leggy stems; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, particularly the unripe green berries, so plant with caution in gardens accessible to children or pets.

Plant rooted stem sections or nursery starts in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, letting the trailing stems spread and root along the ground to knit together a low, informal groundcover under trees. Trailing snowberry is native to open woods and coastal bluffs of the Pacific Northwest and California, where its sprawling form stabilizes soil on slopes and forest edges. Small pinkish flowers in early summer attract native bees, and the round white berries that follow are eaten by grouse, quail, and small mammals through the colder months. Its dense low cover also shelters ground-feeding birds and provides forage for browsing deer.

Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; Gardenia volkensii is deciduous in seasonal dry conditions — water regularly during the growing season but allow a pronounced dry rest in winter, mimicking its native seasonal-rainfall savanna habitat. Gardenia volkensii (Transvaal Gardenia) is a deciduous shrub or small tree native to the bushveld, miombo woodland, and seasonal savanna of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Kenya, and East Africa to the Mozambique coast, where it produces spectacular, large, creamy-white, 6–8-petaled flowers with a powerful sweet fragrance on bare branches in late winter and early spring before leaf flush — making it one of the most dramatic late-winter flowering trees of the African dry savanna. The trees produce oval to oblong, distinctively ribbed, green to yellow fruits, nutritious to wildlife including elephants, baboons, and hornbills, and used medicinally across its range for skin conditions, fever, and eye ailments. It is hardier to cold than Gardenia thunbergia, tolerating brief periods at or just below freezing in dry winter conditions, making it suitable for protected spots in zone 9. Excellent drought-tolerant specimen or fragrant accent plant for hot, dry, sunny gardens.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a prominent spot where the cascading, ground-sweeping branches can be fully appreciated. Traveller is a weeping selection of Texas redbud discovered as a chance seedling in Texas, grafted onto an upright trunk to create a small, umbrella-like specimen tree whose branches drape strongly downward, often trailing along the ground if left unpruned. It carries the same glossy, heat-tolerant leaves and superior drought and alkaline-soil tolerance as other Texas redbud selections, along with a dense flush of pink-magenta flowers on bare weeping branches in early spring. Because the graft union determines the tree's ultimate height and the weeping habit has no natural upright growth, stake young trees to develop a strong trunk and prune only to remove crossing or damaged branches, leaving the cascading form largely undisturbed.

Plant in well-drained, slightly lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; water moderately in fall through spring; withhold water in summer when the plant is dormant. Aeonium arboreum (tree aeonium or Irish rose) is a Canary Islands succulent remarkable for its unusual growth rhythm: unlike most succulents, aeoniums grow actively in cool, moist winters and go dormant in summer heat — the rosettes may drop most of their leaves and appear stressed in hot weather but revive with fall rains. The plant produces branching, succulent stems topped with large, flat rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves in bright green ('normal' form), or deep burgundy-purple to nearly black in the popular 'Zwartkop' (Black Rose) cultivar. Mature plants eventually produce a central rosette that elongates into a tall (2–3 foot) cone of small yellow flowers — after which that rosette dies (monocarpic), but side branches continue. The 'Zwartkop' cultivar with nearly black foliage is one of the most dramatically dark-leafed plants in horticulture. In zone 9, aeoniums perform well in the mild climate; avoid summer irrigation. An outstanding architectural container or rock garden plant.

common_name: Tree Marigold (Mexican Sunflower Tree, Wild Sunflower, Nitobe Chrysanthemum)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — Tree Marigold is one of the most fast-growing, adaptable, and drought-tolerant ornamental shrubs for zone 9-12 conditions and will establish vigorously in poor soil where many plants fail. Tithonia diversifolia is a large, fast-growing, woody-based perennial shrub native to Mexico and Central America in the Asteraceae family — not the annual marigold of the flower garden but a large, semi-woody to woody, perennial plant that can reach 10–15 feet in height in zone 9-12 and produces masses of bright orange-yellow, daisy-like flowers 3–4 inches across on the branch tips through fall and early winter. In zone 9, the plant cuts back to the ground in hard freezes and regrows vigorously from the root in spring; in zone 10-11, it forms a large, multi-stemmed shrub of impressive presence. The flowers are powerfully attractive to Monarch butterflies, Gulf Fritillaries, native bees, and hummingbirds — one of the most valuable late-season butterfly nectaring plants for zone 9-12 gardens. Beyond its ornamental value, T. diversifolia has attracted significant interest in organic agriculture as a 'biomass' green manure plant: the thick, succulent, nitrogen-rich foliage contains nutrients that, when cut and incorporated into the soil, release nitrogen and organic matter at rates comparable to commercial fertilizers. Used as a living mulch and soil-building green manure throughout tropical Africa. An outstanding, multipurpose native-range plant for zone 9-12 landscapes. Non-toxic.

Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil sited where the shrub's permanent woody framework won't need to be moved again, since tree peonies resent transplanting once established. Unlike herbaceous peonies, Paeonia suffruticosa keeps a permanent woody structure through winter rather than dying back to the ground, slowly building a gnarled, long-lived shrub that can outlive the gardener who planted it; its huge, often ruffled or double blooms up to 8-10 inches across open in mid-to-late spring, roughly a week or two ahead of herbaceous peonies, in shades of white, pink, magenta, and deep maroon-purple depending on the selection. Give the plant full sun where summers are mild, but afternoon shade and reliable moisture where summers turn hot and humid, since tree peony foliage and flower quality both decline under intense heat stress. Avoid heavy spring or summer pruning, since flower buds form on old wood the prior season; remove only dead or damaged wood, and apply a light annual topdressing of compost rather than high-nitrogen fertilizer to avoid lush, disease-prone growth.

The Tri-Color Dappled Willow is a fast-growing deciduous shrub whose new spring growth emerges in variegated green, white, and soft pink, with coral-red stems adding winter interest. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; it thrives in damp spots where many shrubs struggle. Prune hard in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of the brightest variegated foliage. Water generously, as willows are thirsty plants that dislike drying out. Grow it as a rounded shrub in a mixed border or shear it into a formal shape.

This is the standard, tree-form version of the tri-color dappled willow, grafted atop a single trunk to create a lollipop-shaped canopy of green, white, and pink variegated leaves. Plant in full sun to light shade in consistently moist, fertile soil where it can show off its cascading foliage. Prune the head in late winter to keep it dense and to renew the most colorful new growth. Keep the soil evenly moist, as willows demand regular water and tolerate wet feet. Remove any suckers that sprout below the graft to preserve the tree form.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Tricolor is a classic Japanese camellia cultivar bearing formal double flowers with neatly layered petals variably streaked and marbled in red, white, and pink, a variegation pattern that varies noticeably from bloom to bloom and even from year to year on the same plant depending on growing conditions. This unpredictable, ever-changing coloring has made Tricolor a favorite among camellia collectors for generations, since every flush of bloom offers a slightly different show. The dense, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage provides reliable year-round structure between bloom seasons. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it flowers in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; trident maple is a small to medium-sized Chinese maple that has become one of the most valued urban and street trees in temperate regions for its exceptional toughness, adaptability, and multi-season ornamental character. The distinctive three-lobed leaves resemble a trident in silhouette, turn brilliant orange-red to burgundy in fall, and the exfoliating orange-tan bark on mature specimens is decorative in winter. Trident maple is one of the most popular species for bonsai cultivation, where its small leaves, fine branching, and easily trained habit produce classical specimens. As a landscape tree it is tolerant of heat, drought, alkaline soil, and urban pollution far beyond most maples — making it the preferred maple for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where standard sugar maple and red maple often struggle in the heat.

Plant in bright indirect light to partial shade outdoors — Trinette Schefflera thrives in shade conditions where direct sun is absent or minimal, making it one of the most useful large foliage plants for covered patios, deep porches, and shaded landscape settings; Trinette is a variegated cultivar of Dwarf Umbrella Plant (Schefflera arboricola), producing the characteristic glossy, palmate, compound leaves of schefflera in a green-and-cream to yellow-green variegated form that provides significantly more ornamental interest than the plain green species. Each palmately compound leaf is composed of 7–9 leaflets radiating from a central point in the classic umbrella arrangement that gives the plant its common name, with the Trinette cultivar's cream-yellow variegation adding a bright, light-catching quality to the foliage that works especially well in shaded settings. As a patio or porch container plant in zone 9, Trinette Schefflera fills the role of a large, architectural foliage plant for shaded outdoor living spaces — providing a tropical, lush texture that transforms a covered porch or shaded patio into an outdoor room with lush, jungle-like plant material. The size and bold foliage make it a genuine statement plant for large containers on shaded patios, and it overwinters successfully as an indoor houseplant in bright indirect light.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; tropical dogwood (Ashanti blood, red flag bush) is a West African tropical shrub in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that creates one of the most spectacular and unusual flowering effects available in the tropical garden — the small, true yellow flowers are relatively inconspicuous, but each is surrounded by one or more greatly enlarged, modified, leaf-like, blood-red to rose-red calyx lobes (sepals) that function as the visual attractor, and in full flowering these large, papery, brilliantly colored bracts cover the entire plant in a mass of vivid red-orange or pink that resembles a bougainvillea in intensity. The Philippine white mussaenda (Mussaenda philippica) is a white-bracted form of similar effect. The bracts are produced most abundantly through the warm season. All parts of the plant are reportedly toxic if ingested. In zone 10–12 it grows as a large, evergreen, freely-branching shrub; in zone 9 it may be grown as a container specimen moved indoors in winter. An extraordinary tropical specimen for zone 10–12 gardens.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Dombeya wallichii is fast growing and responds well to pruning after flowering to maintain a compact form — cut back one-third of the plant after each bloom cycle to encourage bushiness and the next flush of blooms. Dombeya wallichii (Tropical Hydrangea or Pinkball Tree) is a large, fast-growing evergreen to semi-deciduous shrub or small tree native to Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, and the East African highlands, where it grows at elevations of 3,000–7,000 feet in forest edges, clearings, and disturbed habitats. The large, pendulous, globular clusters of pink to deep rose, 5-petaled flowers closely resemble oversized hydrangea flower heads and appear dramatically in winter and early spring, often nearly obscuring the large, velvety, heart-shaped leaves. The dried, spent flower clusters remain attractively on the plant for weeks after petal fall, persisting as papery, straw-colored globes. Dombeya is a consistent performer in zones 9–12, flowering reliably in winter when few other large flowering shrubs are in bloom — making it exceptionally valuable for winter interest in Gulf Coast, Florida, and Southern California gardens. Mulch well, maintain consistent moisture, and fertilize monthly during the growing season for best flowering. Plants freeze to the ground in zone 9a frost events but typically regrow rapidly from the root crown.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in zones 9-12; tropical snowball is one of the most spectacular flowering small trees for warm-climate gardens, producing enormous, round clusters of soft pink to deep pink flowers in late winter and spring when little else is in bloom. The large, heart-shaped leaves are bold and tropical. The pendant flower clusters hang like ornaments from the branches and are extraordinarily fragrant — filling the surrounding air with a sweet, honeyed perfume. Native to Madagascar, the tree is now widely planted in tropical and subtropical gardens worldwide. In zone 9, it may be damaged by hard freezes but typically re-sprouts vigorously from the base in spring, behaving as a large perennial shrub. It is a magnet for butterflies and bees. Prune after flowering to maintain a tidy shape.

common_name: Tropical Turk's Cap (Sleeping Hibiscus, Cardinal's Hat)
notes: Root stem cuttings in moist sand or plant divisions in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tropical Turk's cap is a Mexican species closely related to the native Turk's cap (Malvaviscus arboreus) but distinctly different — producing pendulous, elongated, deep red, twisted flowers 2–3 inches long that hang downward on long stalks rather than the upright flower of M. arboreus, giving it a more dramatic, drooping floral display. Like its relative, the flowers never fully open — they remain twisted into a tube, accessible only to hummingbirds whose long bills can reach the nectar at the base. Tropical Turk's cap is a large, fast-growing shrub reaching 6–10 feet with large, tropical-looking leaves and year-round bloom in frost-free areas, making it one of the most reliably productive hummingbird plants for zone 9b–12 gardens. It tolerates significant shade and grows vigorously under tree canopies where other flowering shrubs struggle. More frost-tender than the native species, requiring protection or regrowth from roots in zone 9a.

common_name: Trumpet Creeper (Trumpet Vine, Cow Itch Vine)
notes: Plant in poor to moderately fertile, well-drained to dry soil in full sun on a very sturdy support; never plant on wooden fences or near small trees as the vigorous vine can destroy them within a few years. Campsis radicans (trumpet creeper) is a native deciduous woody vine of exceptional ornamental value and hummingbird attraction — its large, trumpeted, 3-inch orange-red to scarlet flowers bloom prolifically in clusters of 4–12 from July through September on the current season's growth, creating an irresistible magnet for ruby-throated hummingbirds which are the primary pollinators. The vine climbs by clinging rootlets that attach firmly to masonry, bark, and wood and can scale heights of 20–40 feet or more. It is one of the most vigorous plants in American horticulture — spreading by root suckers and self-seeding freely — and should be sited with awareness of its potential to overtake its space: do not plant on wooden structures, near small trees, or where spread cannot be controlled. The cultivar 'Flamenco' has yellow-orange flowers; 'Crimson Trumpet' has deeper red flowers; 'Indian Summer' is more compact. Despite its vigor, trumpet creeper is extraordinarily valuable for wildlife and native garden plantings on large, sturdy supports.

Plant seedlings in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; trumpet tree is a frost-tender, fast-growing pioneer species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Large, distinctive, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves radiate from hollow, jointed stems on this extremely fast-growing Neotropical pioneer tree, which colonizes disturbed clearings and forest gaps throughout Central and South America, its hollow stems famously providing a home for symbiotic Azteca ants that protect the tree from herbivores in exchange for shelter and food. Growing many feet per year when young, it is one of the fastest-growing woody trees in the American tropics but is relatively short-lived and structurally weak, better suited to quickly establishing shade or a distinctive architectural specimen in a tropical garden than a long-term landscape anchor. Water regularly while young, provide full sun for the fastest growth, and expect a relatively short lifespan compared to slower, longer-lived tropical trees.

Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants against a very sturdy structure in full sun in any well-drained soil; trumpet vine is a vigorous native climber of the eastern US that attaches by aerial rootlets and can ultimately reach 20–40 feet, producing masses of large, brilliant orange-red trumpet flowers from midsummer through fall that are the single most effective hummingbird plant for zone 4–9 gardens during the critical midsummer period. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially indestructible, but its vigor must be respected — it spreads by suckers that emerge from the roots, can become invasive in some settings, and the aerial rootlets can damage masonry and wood siding. Prune aggressively in late winter to control size; it blooms on new growth so hard pruning never reduces flowering. The cultivar 'Flava' has clear yellow flowers; 'Crimson Trumpet' is a deep red.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some protection from hot afternoon sun; Tuff Stuff is a compact reblooming mountain hydrangea (Hydrangea serrata) bred by Proven Winners to flower on both old and new growth, so even if a hard late freeze damages the previous year's buds, the plant still produces a strong flush of lacecap blooms on new wood later in the season — a real advantage over bigleaf hydrangeas that bloom only on old wood and can lose an entire year's flowering to a bad spring frost. Flower color shifts with soil pH, from blue in acidic soil to more pink or purple tones in neutral to alkaline soil, the same way it does in bigleaf hydrangea. Mountain hydrangea is generally more cold-hardy and sun-tolerant than bigleaf hydrangea, and its compact size fits well into smaller foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders. Water regularly during dry spells, since hydrangeas wilt quickly in dry soil, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat.

The tulip poplar is a fast-growing native shade tree that reaches towering heights, with distinctive four-lobed leaves and cup-shaped, greenish-yellow tulip-like flowers in late spring. Give it a large, open site in full sun with deep, moist, well-drained soil, as its extensive root system needs room. Water regularly for the first few years to establish; mature trees are fairly self-sufficient. Its rapid growth makes it excellent for quick shade, though the soft wood benefits from a sheltered location. Foliage turns clear golden-yellow in autumn.

Plant in moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun to full shade; Turk's cap tolerates a wide range of soil conditions and is virtually maintenance-free once established. Malvaviscus arboreus (Turk's cap or wax mallow) is one of the most beloved and useful native shrubs of south Texas and the Gulf Coast — a large, sprawling, multi-stemmed shrub native from Florida through Texas and deep into Mexico and Central America, producing a continuous show of small, unique, hibiscus-like flowers whose petals never fully open but instead remain spirally twisted around the central column, creating a distinctive, turban-shaped, bright-scarlet-red 'Turk's cap' flower from late summer through fall. It is among the very best plants for attracting hummingbirds and butterflies to the Gulf Coast garden. What distinguishes Turk's cap ecologically is its outstanding shade tolerance — it blooms prolifically under large live oaks, in deep woodland margins, and in full shade where almost no other flowering shrub succeeds. It is also drought-tolerant, deer-resistant in many areas, and nearly carefree. The small, red berries are edible (mildly sweet, jelly-like) and can be used to make preserves; they are also consumed by wildlife.

common_name: Turk's Cap (Turk's Cap Mallow, Wax Mallow)
notes: Plant in spring in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to deep shade; Turk's Cap is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant native shrubs of the Gulf Coast and is also one of the most shade-tolerant flowering plants in the region. Malvaviscus arboreus var. drummondii (Turk's Cap) is a native perennial shrub of the Gulf Coast and Texas lowlands from Louisiana to Mexico, producing distinctive, red, partially-opened hibiscus-like flowers with petals that never fully unfurl (remaining curled around the prominent staminal column in the distinctive 'turban' or 'fez' shape that gives it the common name). The tubular, nectar-rich flowers are among the most important hummingbird food sources in Gulf Coast and Texas gardens from summer through late fall; native bees and butterflies also visit. Edible small red fruits follow the flowers and are eaten by mockingbirds and other wildlife. Dies to the ground in freezes north of zone 9 but re-sprouts from the root crown reliably. Outstanding for shaded gardens, natural areas, and wildlife plantings in zones 7–11.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to deep shade; Turk's cap is one of the South's most versatile and valuable flowering shrubs, producing bright red nodding flowers with tightly spiraled petals that never fully open (resembling a Turkish fez) from summer through frost — and in zone 9–10, flowering nearly year round. It is outstanding in dry shade under large trees where little else will bloom, and is equally at home in full blazing sun. Ruby-throated and rufous hummingbirds are its primary pollinators and mob the flowers from summer through migration. In zone 8 it dies back to the roots in hard freezes but re-sprouts reliably in spring and reaches full size by July. Do not overwater; it tolerates considerable drought once established.

Turkey oak is a native small to medium tree endemic to the scrub and sandhill habitats of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from Virginia to Louisiana — one of the most adapted trees in North America to the white, nutrient-deficient, excessively drained sands of the ancient coastal plain terraces where it forms nearly pure stands alongside longleaf pine and sand live oak. Its deeply 3–5 lobed leaves are large, glossy, and architectural — among the most decorative of all oak foliage — and turn vivid shades of red, orange, and burgundy in fall, providing exceptional autumn color even in warm climates where most oaks turn only dull brown. Turkey oak is the critical host tree for the Florida scrub-jay, one of the most endangered birds in North America, which depends on turkey oak acorns as its primary food; the tree is also habitat for dozens of rare invertebrates endemic to scrub habitats. In sandy coastal plain gardens with excessively drained, acidic, nutrient-poor soil — exactly the conditions that challenge most ornamental trees — turkey oak thrives with no supplemental care once established.

Tuscarora is a vigorous crape myrtle that bears long-lasting panicles of hot coral-pink flowers from midsummer into fall. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil to maximize bloom and reduce the chance of powdery mildew. Its smooth, mottled cinnamon bark and orange-red fall color extend the interest well past the flowering season. Prune only lightly in late winter to preserve its graceful vase-shaped structure rather than cutting it back hard. Established plants tolerate heat and drought, needing extra water mainly during long dry stretches.

common_name: Twilight Magic Crapemyrtle (Plum-Foliage Disease-Resistant Purple-Leaf Alternative)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Twilight Magic bears deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color through the heat of a Gulf South summer, providing dramatic contrast against clusters of fuchsia-pink blooms from summer into fall. It was bred with high resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew, holding its dark foliage cleanly through humid conditions that cause many purple-leaved landscape shrubs and small trees to decline or defoliate. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood, preserving the plant's natural form rather than heavily topping it.

Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where twinberry honeysuckle naturalizes readily along stream edges and under an open woodland canopy across its wide native range from Alaska south through the Pacific Northwest and Rockies. In spring the shrub bears small, paired, tubular yellow flowers tinged with red, followed in summer by shiny black berries held in pairs against a showy pair of deep red bracts — an unmistakable, almost theatrical fruit display that gives the plant its common name. The berries are bitter and unpalatable to people but are readily eaten by robins, waxwings, and other songbirds, and the shrub's dense, arching form provides valuable cover for nesting birds. It tolerates wet soil better than most shrubs sold for shade, making it a strong choice for the damp, low-light corners of a woodland or rain garden where few other flowering shrubs thrive.

common_name: Twist of Lime Abelia (Lime-and-Cream Variegated Abelia)
notes: Twist of Lime is an abelia selection grown chiefly for its foliage, small leaves margined in creamy yellow around a lime-green center, with new growth emerging flushed pink before settling into the mature variegated pattern, giving the shrub a bright, multicolored look through most of the growing season. It still produces the small, fragrant, white-to-pale-pink tubular flowers typical of abelia from late spring into fall on gracefully arching stems, and like other abelia cultivars it is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay soil, heat, humidity, and drought with minimal care once established. Prune lightly after the main flush of spring bloom if shaping is wanted, and watch for occasional reversion shoots of plain green foliage, which should be cut out to keep the variegation strong.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and remove spent flower heads through the season to encourage continued rebloom. Part of the Endless Summer collection, Twist-n-Shout is a reblooming lacecap hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, producing flat clusters of pink or blue fertile florets ringed by showy sterile ray flowers from early summer through fall, with the deep red-tinged stems adding fall and winter interest after leaf drop. Because it blooms on new growth as well as old, an errant late-frost or a hard pruning does not eliminate the whole season's flowers the way it does on old-wood-only cultivars, making it more forgiving for gardeners uncertain about pruning timing. Keep soil consistently moist — hydrangeas wilt readily in summer heat — and mulch to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature.

Sow scarified or overnight-soaked seed 1 inch deep into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, with a trellis, wire, or shrub for support; two-flowered everlasting pea is considered the most ornamental of the perennial peas, bearing pairs of exceptionally large, richly colored deep-pink to magenta flowers on each stem from early to midsummer — the blooms are substantially larger than those of the common everlasting pea (Lathyrus latifolius) and make a striking display on arches, obelisks, or through open shrubs. It spreads steadily by rhizomes and will naturalize freely in well-drained soils, forming sizeable clumps in time; site it where it can expand without crowding small neighbors. Like most perennial peas it is drought-tolerant once established and fixes its own nitrogen, performing best in lean rather than heavily enriched soils.

Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade; two-toned grape hyacinth stands apart from other muscari species through a striking, built-in bicolor effect on each individual spike: the lower portion of the densely packed raceme carries the typical, deep, dark-blue-violet to navy-blue, urn-shaped, fertile florets of the grape hyacinth type, while the upper portion of the same spike carries distinctly lighter, sky-blue to pale-blue, sterile florets that are more elongated and open — creating a natural two-toned spike that grades from dark violet at the base to pale sky-blue at the tip. This gradation of two distinct blues on a single small flower spike is botanically unique among commonly grown muscari and creates a more complex, interesting flower display than the single-toned spikes of M. armeniacum. A single broad leaf (vs the several narrow leaves of other species) gives the foliage a distinctive, lush quality. The bulbs increase steadily and naturalize in part shade under deciduous trees and shrubs, where the bicolor spring spikes create a particularly attractive display in the dappled light. An outstanding, underused grape hyacinth for the woodland garden.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; two-winged silverbell is a graceful southeastern native small tree that puts on one of the most charming spring flower displays of any native woody plant — in March and April, before or just as the leaves emerge, the pendulous branches are draped in clusters of pure-white, four-petaled, nodding bell-shaped flowers that dangle like delicate ornaments along every stem, providing exceptional early nectar for pollinators. Halesia diptera is distinguished from the more commonly grown Carolina silverbell (H. carolina) by its two-winged fruits rather than four-winged, and by its superior heat tolerance, making it the silverbell of choice for gardens in the Deep South and Gulf Coast regions where H. carolina struggles. The fruits that follow are decorative in their own right, persisting on the branches well into fall, and the clean oval foliage turns yellow in autumn before dropping. An outstanding specimen tree for woodland garden edges, naturalistic streamside plantings, and residential lawns in zones 5–9 where a refined, low-maintenance flowering tree of genuine native provenance is desired.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; umbrella magnolia is a distinctive native understory tree of the Appalachians and Southeast named for the pattern of its enormous leaves — 12–24 inches long — arranged in a dramatic whorl around the branch tips like the spokes of an umbrella, creating a striking bold-textured tropical effect in the shaded garden. The large creamy-white flowers (6–10 inches) in late spring have an unusual, slightly unpleasant fragrance but are still attractive from a distance. Red cone-like fruit clusters in late summer and fall are ornamental and eaten by songbirds. It grows naturally as a subcanopy tree in moist, acidic ravines and tolerates shade better than most Magnolia species, making it one of the few flowering trees that performs well in partial to light shade. The extraordinarily large leaves and exotic texture make it an excellent specimen in shaded woodland gardens.

Root stem tip cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun; umbrella plant grows rapidly to become a large, multi-stemmed tree in zones 10–12 with bold, palmate, compound leaves of 7–16 leaflets arranged like the ribs of an umbrella, creating a striking tropical silhouette. Mature trees produce dramatic, upright clusters of small red flowers that attract birds. Outdoors it can reach 40 feet tall; as a container plant or indoor specimen in filtered light it stays manageable at 4–8 feet. Plant has become invasive in Florida and Hawaii — consider the smaller, non-invasive Schefflera arboricola (dwarf schefflera) as an alternative in those states. Container plants tolerate low light exceptionally well.

common_name: Umbrella Tree (Octopus Tree, Queensland Umbrella Tree)
notes: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; CAUTION — invasive in Florida and Hawaii; do not plant near natural areas. Schefflera actinophylla (umbrella tree or octopus tree) is an Australian tropical tree that has become one of the most popular houseplants in the world while simultaneously becoming a serious invasive species in Florida and Hawaii. As a landscape tree in zone 10–12, it grows to an impressive 25–40 feet with a distinctive canopy of large, palmate (hand-shaped) compound leaves with 5–16 leaflets radiating like the ribs of an umbrella — each leaflet 4–10 inches long and glossy. The common name 'octopus tree' comes from the bizarre flowering structure: dark-red, finger-like flower spikes emerging from the branch tips like tentacles — striking in flower and producing small, dark-red berries consumed by birds (which has spread the plant into natural areas). As an indoor plant, the large-leafed forms create a bold tropical statement; 'Amate' is a popular, more compact cultivar. CAUTION: Listed as an invasive Category I exotic pest plant in Florida — do not plant near wild areas or waterways.

common_name: Valley Forge Elm (Highly Disease-Tolerant American Elm)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the tree room for its broad, classic vase-shaped canopy. Valley Forge was released by the USDA National Arboretum after extensive screening trials and stands out for having some of the strongest documented Dutch elm disease tolerance of any American elm cultivar, making it a leading choice for restoring the American elm to streets and parks where the species was once devastated by the disease. It grows quickly, often faster than other resistant cultivars, though its structure can be somewhat more open and irregular, so early formative pruning helps develop a strong central framework as the tree matures. Water deeply while establishing, avoid trunk and root wounds that can allow disease entry, and expect a large, long-lived shade tree well suited to the wide, open sites where American elm has always excelled.

Plant fresh acorns in fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; valley oak is the largest of California's native oaks, reaching 40–100 feet tall with massive, sprawling crowns up to 80 feet wide — widely regarded as one of the most majestic and iconic trees of California. It grows naturally in deep valley soils and oak savanna throughout California's Central Valley and coast ranges. Valley oaks can live over 600 years and develop massive, deeply furrowed, gray trunks and wide-spreading canopies of graceful, deeply-lobed leaves. The large acorns were the primary food staple of numerous California indigenous cultures. CRITICAL: never irrigate established valley oaks in summer — summer water near the root zone encourages Phytophthora root rot (sudden oak death) and kills otherwise healthy trees. Plant away from irrigated lawns and landscapes. A landmark tree requiring ample space but magnificent at maturity.

common_name: Van Houtte Sage (Van Houtte's Scarlet Sage, Red Velvet Sage)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Van Houtte Sage grows fastest in full sun but tolerates and even appreciates afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat, where it continues blooming through July–August when other sages shut down. Salvia van-houttei is a large, vigorous, soft-stemmed tropical sage from Brazil that produces some of the most theatrical and unusual flowers in the genus. The whorled flower spikes are covered with large, deeply-veined, velvety, dark burgundy-red to wine-colored calyxes that persist long after the scarlet corolla flowers inside them have fallen — the persistent, showy calyxes give the entire spike a dramatic deep-red to black-purple appearance and extend the ornamental interest of each bloom spike for weeks. The flowers themselves are tubular, bright scarlet, and intensely attractive to hummingbirds and large butterflies including swallowtails. The large, soft, dark-green, pebbly-textured leaves are aromatic and give the plant a bold, tropical presence even out of bloom. Van Houtte Sage is one of the most underused and undervalued of the tropical sages available for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens — combining long bloom season, hummingbird attraction, heat tolerance, and an exotic tropical appearance that rivals showier but less adaptable ornamentals.

common_name: Vanessa Bell Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2016 and named for the Bloomsbury Group painter, Vanessa Bell carries semi-double, soft butter-yellow flowers that fade toward cream as they age, with a fresh, tea-and-lemon fragrance, on a healthy, free-flowering, medium-sized shrub. Its semi-double form exposes more stamens than fully double English roses, giving a slightly looser, more relaxed look that also makes it useful to pollinators, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanhoutte Spiraea, commonly called Bridal Wreath, is one of the most beloved flowering shrubs in American horticulture — a large, wide-arching shrub that in April and May (zone 7–8) produces such a profusion of small, pure-white flower clusters along the entire length of each cascading branch that the branches appear covered with a white veil, creating the bridal wreath effect that gives the plant its common name. The arching, fountain-like form with flowers distributed along every branch tip is one of the most graceful and spectacular spring flowering shrub effects available in the northern and mid-South garden. Vanhoutte spiraea is a hybrid of Spiraea cantoniensis and S. trilobata that has been cultivated since the 1860s — more than 150 years of continuous popularity testify to its landscape merit. Unlike summer-blooming Japanese spiraea (S. japonica) cultivars that bloom on new wood, Vanhoutte blooms on old wood and must be pruned immediately after flowering — never in fall or winter, which would remove the following year's flower buds. In zone 9's heat, Vanhoutte performs best in zone 8 and colder; in the hottest parts of zone 9a, the summer heat can stress the plant.

common_name: Vanilla Spice Summersweet (Large-Flowered Fragrant White Clethra)
notes: Vanilla Spice was bred for unusually large flower spikes, nearly twice the size of the species, packed with small white, intensely sweet-scented flowers that open in mid-to-late summer and draw heavy pollinator traffic from bumblebees, honeybees, and butterflies during a period when many other shrubs have finished blooming. Like other summersweet selections it forms a dense, suckering, upright shrub with glossy dark-green foliage that turns clear yellow in fall, and its fragrance carries well through a partly shaded garden on a warm evening. Keep soil consistently moist in partial to full shade, since summersweet does not tolerate prolonged drought, and expect the shrub to slowly spread by suckers to form a colony over time, useful for naturalizing a moist, shaded area.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanilla Strawberry is one of the most spectacular and distinctive panicle hydrangea cultivars — producing enormous, upright, conical flower panicles (up to 12–16 inches long) that undergo a dramatic color transformation through the growing season: opening pure creamy-white in early summer, then progressively blushing from the base of each panicle upward from pink to vivid strawberry-red as summer advances, creating a bicolor white-and-strawberry effect that is unlike any other hydrangea.
