At peak color in late summer and early fall, the large panicles display a gradient from strawberry-red at the base through pink to creamy-white at the tip — an extraordinary color combination that has made Vanilla Strawberry one of the fastest-selling new shrubs since its introduction. The shrub grows 6–8 feet tall and 4–6 feet wide with a strong, upright habit and sturdy stems that support the heavy flower panicles without flopping — an advantage over some other large-flowered H. paniculata types. Like all H. paniculata, it blooms on new wood and is pruned hard in late winter. In zone 9, morning sun with afternoon shade produces optimal results — the intense strawberry-red color develops best with some direct sun but the flowers hold color better if protected from the intense afternoon Gulf South sun.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; varicolored angel's trumpet is an Ecuadorian species named for its distinctive flower color change — the enormous pendant trumpets open white and gradually transition through cream, peach, and apricot to a final orange tone as they age, so a single plant displays multiple flower colors simultaneously, creating an exceptional multicolor effect rare in tropical ornamentals. The flowers, up to 14 inches long among the largest in the genus, have a pleasant, sweet fragrance. Like all Brugmansia, all parts are dangerously toxic and the plant must be sited away from children and animals. The enormous, tropical-looking foliage and dramatic pendant flowers create the most architectural and dramatic tropical statement in the warm-climate garden. Heavy fertilization and consistent moisture are essential for maximum performance; drought or nutrient stress cause immediate flower drop.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. A long-established classic among variegated shrubs, Variegata weigela produces soft green leaves broadly edged in creamy white that brighten a mixed border all season, paired with clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds. The variegated foliage provides ongoing visual interest well beyond the relatively brief flowering period typical of weigela cultivars. It performs best with a light shaping prune right after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's wood, and is otherwise a tough, easy shrub tolerant of average soil and normal garden care.

Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near a sturdy trellis or arbor; variegated chocolate vine is a vigorous twining climber and needs a strong support, plus occasional pruning to control spread. Palmate, five-lobed leaves are irregularly splashed and marbled in creamy white, a bright variegated counterpart to the plain green species, twining vigorously up any nearby support and producing small, chocolate-scented, maroon-purple flowers in spring, occasionally followed by unusual sausage-shaped purple fruit with sweet, edible pulp in favorable conditions. Its vigorous, twining growth can become aggressive and self-seed in mild climates, so site it where its spread can be managed and monitor for volunteer seedlings, particularly since escaped chocolate vine has become invasive in parts of the eastern United States. Prune hard in late winter to control size and shape, and provide a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis strong enough to support its vigorous twining growth.

Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a trellis or fence for the twining stems; variegated confederate jasmine holds its cream-margined variegation best in bright light. Glossy, dark green leaves are irregularly edged in creamy white, often blushed pink on new growth in cooler weather, providing year-round variegated color even outside the plant's intensely fragrant late-spring flowering period, when small, pinwheel-shaped white flowers cover the twining vine with classic jasmine scent. Slightly less vigorous and cold-hardy than the plain green species, it still makes a fine trellis, fence, or mailbox-post vine in warm-climate gardens or a colorful container specimen further north, brought indoors or into a greenhouse for winter outside its hardiness range. Provide a support for the twining stems, water regularly during establishment, and prune after flowering to control size and shape.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegated pittosporum is one of the most reliable and widely planted foundation and landscape shrubs for zone 8–11 coastal and Gulf Coast gardens — a compact, rounded, evergreen shrub producing distinctive, leathery, spatula-shaped leaves in dark green irregularly edged and streaked with creamy white to gray-green variegation. The variegated foliage provides year-round visual interest and brightness in both full sun and partial shade conditions. In spring, the shrub produces small, creamy-white, intensely orange-blossom fragrant flowers — the fragrance is remarkably strong for such small flowers and perfumes the surrounding garden. Variegated pittosporum is among the most salt-tolerant and wind-tolerant of common landscape shrubs, making it exceptional for coastal exposures where most shrubs struggle with salt spray and marine wind. The compact, naturally mounding habit stays 3–5 feet tall and wide with minimal pruning, though it can be pruned to control size immediately after spring bloom. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; tolerates clay soil, alkaline conditions, and reflected heat from paving. Avoid wet, poorly drained sites where Phytophthora root rot can be a problem. Essentially pest-free in zone 9. The standard green species Pittosporum tobira grows larger and is also widely planted in Gulf Coast landscapes.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Variegatus is one of the oldest and most classic variegated false holly cultivars, its spiny, holly-like leaves crisply edged in creamy white around a dark green center, providing bright, reliable, year-round contrast in a shaded border without depending on bloom for interest. Tiny, sweetly fragrant white flowers appear tucked among the leaves in fall, easy to miss visually but noticeable by scent alone. Its dense, evergreen, deer-resistant foliage makes it a durable choice for shaded foundation plantings, informal hedges, and screens; little pruning is needed beyond light shaping after fall bloom.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection, mulching well to keep roots cool. Varnadoe is a selected form of Piedmont azalea (Rhododendron canescens), a widespread Gulf South and Southeastern native, chosen for an especially heavy flush of fragrant, pale pink flowers with prominent, showy stamens on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed shrub in early spring before the leaves fully emerge. Like other native deciduous azaleas, it is far better adapted to the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Deep South gardens than most Asian evergreen azalea hybrids, and its intense honeysuckle-like fragrance carries well beyond the plant itself. Site it at a woodland edge or under high pine or hardwood canopy, similar to the conditions where it grows wild along stream banks and bluffs.

Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; Boston ivy clings tightly to masonry surfaces and is difficult to remove once established, so site carefully. One of the original introduced forms of the classic ivy-league-covering vine, it produces smaller, more deeply three-lobed leaves emerging purplish-bronze in spring before maturing to glossy green and turning a spectacular scarlet-crimson in fall, clinging tightly to brick and stone with adhesive tendril discs to blanket entire building facades. Extremely vigorous and self-clinging, it needs no additional support once established but can grow large enough to obscure windows and gutters if not pruned, and removing an established planting from masonry can leave persistent tendril residue. Prune annually to keep growth away from windows, doors, and roof edges, and consider the vine's vigorous, decades-long coverage potential before planting against a valued building surface.

common_name: Veitchii Gardenia (Classic Florist Gardenia with Everblooming Double White Flowers)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Veitchii is the classic florist and corsage gardenia cultivar — the variety that shaped the public image of gardenia for most of the 20th century as the preferred white flower for corsages, wedding bouquets, and cut flower arrangements, valued for its perfectly formed, fully double, pure-white flowers and the intense, sweet, iconic gardenia fragrance that makes it one of the most recognizable flower scents in the world. The flowers of Veitchii are somewhat smaller than those of the larger-flowered 'Fortuniana' and 'Mystery' cultivars but are more precisely and symmetrically formed — tight spirals of white petals forming a perfect double flower that is simultaneously elegant and lush. The key practical advantage of Veitchii over earlier cultivars is repeat or continuous bloom (sometimes described as 'everblooming') — unlike once-blooming gardenias that flower only in spring, Veitchii produces flowers from late spring through summer and into fall, a trait that made it invaluable commercially. The intense gardenia fragrance is full and true across all blooming periods. The plant grows as a compact to medium evergreen shrub (3–5 feet) with the characteristically glossy, deep-green foliage of gardenia. In zone 9, Veitchii is somewhat cold-sensitive — mulching the roots and planting against a south-facing wall provides winter protection in zone 8–9a. Strongly acidic soil and iron availability are the most common cultural challenges.

common_name: Velvet Arrowhead (Wendland's Syngonium, Silver Goosefoot Plant, Dark Velvet Syngonium)
notes: Grow in full to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Velvet Arrowhead is one of the most shade-adapted and visually distinctive of the Syngonium species and thrives in the low-light conditions of a shaded porch, bright interior room, or understory garden in zone 10-12. Syngonium wendlandii is a climbing, rhizomatous tropical vine in the Araceae family native to Costa Rica and Central America, one of the most sought-after species in the genus for the extraordinary visual quality of its leaves. The leaves are a deep, saturated dark forest-green on their upper surfaces, with a broad, brilliant white to silver-white midrib and primary veins creating a dramatic two-tone pattern of dark and light. The surface of the leaf has a distinctly velvety texture from tiny surface papillae that scatter light in a way reminiscent of velvet fabric — making the leaves appear almost three-dimensional, like cut velvet or dark plush. Juvenile plants produce smaller, arrowhead-shaped leaves on compact, low-growing stems. As the plant matures and begins to climb a support, the leaves take on a larger, more broadly lobed form up to 10–12 inches across, with the white markings becoming even more pronounced. Syngonium wendlandii is one of the classic collector aroids now widely appreciated both as a houseplant and as a shaded outdoor container or landscape plant in frost-free climates. The deep shade tolerance, compact juvenile form, and extraordinary leaf pattern make it ideal for shade gardens and sheltered patios. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested — keep away from cats and dogs.

Transplant in spring into desert washes, irrigated yards, or streambank sites across the Southwest, where this drought-adapted ash tolerates alkaline soils and intense summer heat far better than eastern ash species. Its velvety young twigs and leaflets give the tree a soft gray-green texture, and its dense canopy makes it a popular fast-growing shade tree in arid urban landscapes. It benefits from periodic deep irrigation during establishment even though mature trees can survive on minimal supplemental water in wash habitats. Watch for emerald ash borer as its range continues to expand into the Southwest.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Venus is the US National Arboretum's most celebrated hybrid dogwood introduction — a first-generation hybrid between the native American flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) and the Chinese kousa dogwood (C. kousa) that produces flower bracts of extraordinary size: individual bracts (modified leaves surrounding the true flowers) reach 3–4 inches long, making the overall flower display twice the visual impact of either parent species. The enormous, pure-white, overlapping bracts create a spectacular late-April to May floral display (blooming slightly later than C. florida, extending the dogwood season) on a vigorous, upright tree. Venus inherits the best qualities of both parents: the early spring bloom timing and dense flowering of C. florida, combined with the superior heat tolerance, drought resistance, and disease resistance of C. kousa — specifically resistance to dogwood anthracnose that has devastated native C. florida populations. In zone 9, Venus performs reliably where native dogwood often struggles — the C. kousa genetics provide significantly better adaptation to Gulf South heat, humidity, and the summer conditions that stress C. florida. The large fruits that follow bloom are more showy than those of either parent. A landmark introduction for southern gardeners who love dogwoods.

common_name: Vera Cruz Rose Plumeria (Fragrant Deep Pink Plumeria)
notes: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Vera Cruz Rose is a widely grown, long-established plumeria cultivar producing rich, saturated deep pink flowers with a lighter blush toward the yellow-white center, carrying a strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance that intensifies in the evening. It is one of the more reliably vigorous and free-flowering pink plumeria cultivars, making it a popular choice for both garden specimens and lei-flower production in Hawaii. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to prevent stem rot. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade — vernal witch hazel is the earliest-blooming native Hamamelis species, opening its strap-petaled flowers in January through March while the plant is still dormant, even in the coldest conditions of zone 4–5. The flowers come in shades from pale yellow to orange to deep brick-red (dark orange-red in the commonly grown form) and have a sweet, spicy fragrance. Unlike the common witch hazel (H. virginiana), which blooms in fall, H. vernalis blooms in late winter and is the best native species for early-season pollinator value — providing nectar for early queen bumblebees and native mining bees on warm winter days. It is native to the gravel bars and rocky streambanks of the Ozarks and tolerates moist to wet conditions. The fall foliage is brilliant orange-yellow.

common_name: Vernal Witch Hazel, Ozark Witch Hazel
notes: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; vernal witch hazel is native to the Ozark plateau and grows naturally along stream gravels — it is more tolerant of dry, calcareous soils than H. virginiana and slightly more drought-tolerant once established. Hamamelis vernalis is among the first woody plants to bloom in late winter, producing intensely fragrant, small, yellow to reddish-orange, ribbon-petaled flowers on bare stems from January through March, filling the dormant winter garden with a spicy-sweet scent on any mild winter day; the flowers close when temperatures drop below freezing and reopen when temperatures rise, allowing them to survive late-winter freezes. The fall foliage is outstanding in shades of gold and orange; it is a major improvement over Asian witch hazels for naturalizing in eastern North American native gardens because it supports specialist witch hazel bees and other native insects.

Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; vetchleaf sophora is a spreading, elegant Chinese shrub in the pea family producing silvery-gray, pinnately divided foliage that has a delicate, fern-like texture throughout the season — and producing in May and June loose clusters of small, pale-blue to lilac-white pea flowers flushed with purple that are attractive to bees and butterflies. The combination of silvery, soft-textured foliage and subtle blue-white flowers gives the shrub a refined, mediterranean quality, somewhat resembling a drought-tolerant version of false indigo (Baptisia). It develops a somewhat stiff, twiggy branching structure that can be shaped to enhance the garden form, and the dried seed pods are ornamental in winter. Very drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in lean, rocky, alkaline soils similar to those of the Chinese highland slopes where it grows naturally — an excellent plant for dry, alkaline sites where most flowering shrubs perform poorly.

common_name: Victorian Lady Abutilon (Ruffled Pink Flowering Maple)
notes: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Victorian Lady bears large, ruffled, bell-shaped flowers in soft pink with darker pink veining, hanging gracefully from a tall, upright, well-branched shrub with maple-shaped leaves, blooming nearly year-round in mild climates. Its old-fashioned, cottage-garden charm and long bloom season make it a favorite for mixed borders and large containers where its upright habit fits better than trailing abutilon types, and hummingbirds visit the pendant flowers regularly. In zone 8, expect frost dieback most winters, with plants often resprouting from the base if roots are mulched and protected; where hard freezes are common, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

Introduced in France in 1899, this heirloom clematis bears bright carmine-red blooms with a paler central bar, fading slightly as they age through summer. As a pruning group three cultivar, cut all stems back hard to a strong pair of buds about a foot from the ground in late winter, which keeps the vine compact and floriferous. Provide a trellis, obelisk, or shrub to climb, and keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist. It flowers on new growth from midsummer into fall, making it a reliable companion for climbing roses that bloom earlier in the season.

common_name: Ville de Nantes Camellia (Red-and-White Marbled French Heirloom Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Ville de Nantes, introduced in France in 1910, is a distinctive antique Camellia japonica cultivar bearing loose, peony-form red flowers irregularly marbled and streaked with white, the notched, informal petal edges giving each bloom a slightly ragged, old-fashioned character unlike the smoother forms of many other camellias. It blooms in mid to late season on an upright, vigorous evergreen shrub that provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its unusual flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; vine maple is the most shade-tolerant native tree on the Pacific Coast, growing as a multi-stemmed understory tree or large shrub in the dense Douglas-fir and western red cedar forests of the Pacific Northwest from British Columbia to northern California. The circular, 7-9-lobed leaves turn brilliant orange, scarlet, and gold in autumn, making it one of the premier fall-color plants of the region. In deep shade, the stems often lean, twist, and arch to seek light, creating a sculptural form used in Japanese-inspired gardens. The small red flowers appear in spring and the winged samaras ripen in summer. It adapts better to garden conditions than most native Pacific Northwest trees and is excellent for shaded Pacific Coast gardens.

common_name: Vintage Jade Distylium (Compact Spreading Evergreen Shade Shrub)
notes: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Vintage Jade is a low, wide-spreading distylium selection that matures to roughly 3-4 feet tall but spreads 5-8 feet across, making it one of the most useful large-scale evergreen groundcover shrubs for difficult shady sites where azaleas, boxwood, and other traditional shade shrubs often struggle. Like other distyliums, it produces small, glossy, leathery, dark green leaves and inconspicuous, petal-less red-stamened flowers in late winter that add subtle color before most shrubs break dormancy. Its defining feature is extraordinary adaptability — it tolerates full sun, deep shade, wet or dry soil, and both acid and moderately alkaline pH with no serious pest or disease problems and virtually no pruning required to look tidy, and deer generally leave it alone. Because it spreads wider than tall, space plants according to their eventual width rather than the young nursery size, and use it in mass plantings, foundation beds, or as a substitute where foundation shrubs have failed in a heavily shaded spot.

common_name: Violet Iochroma (Violet Tubes, Blue Bells Shrub)
notes: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; in zone 9's intense summer sun, afternoon shade improves performance and prevents leaf burn. Iochroma cyaneum is a soft-wooded shrub in the Solanaceae family (related to Brunfelsia and nightshade) native to the Andes of Ecuador and Colombia, where it grows in moist montane cloud forests at 6,000–10,000 feet elevation. In zone 9 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes, it is grown for its spectacular pendant clusters of deep violet-blue, 1.5-inch tubular flowers that dangle from the branch tips in profuse flushes throughout the warm season. The deep, pure violet-blue color is among the most saturated blues available in a large tropical shrub — not lavender, not purple, but true rich violet-blue. The flowers are intensely attractive to hummingbirds, which hover at the pendant clusters throughout the blooming season. The plant grows quickly, reaching 6–10 feet by the end of its first full season. Prune back hard after each major bloom flush to encourage repeat flowering and a more compact, bushy habit. All parts of the plant are mildly toxic if ingested. An outstanding hummingbird and ornamental shrub for zone 9b–11.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; violet silverleaf needs excellent drainage and full sun to bloom well and rots in heavy, wet, or overwatered soil. Small, densely felted, brilliant silvery-white leaves cover a compact, rounded shrub that erupts into a profuse flush of rich violet-purple flowers following summer rains, a dramatic and reliable bloom response shared by other Texas silverleaf species and prized for the way it signals rainfall across the Chihuahuan Desert landscape it calls home. Native to limestone hills of the Trans-Pecos region and northern Mexico, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, needing no supplemental irrigation beyond natural rainfall, and its striking silver foliage provides season-long textural interest between bloom flushes. Prune lightly to shape if needed, avoiding heavy shearing which reduces the natural rounded form and flowering, and plant in the leanest, best-drained spot available.

Virgin's bower is the most widespread and cold-hardy of all native North American clematis, scrambling through shrubs and small trees along streams, roadsides, and woodland edges from Nova Scotia to Florida — in late summer it smothers its support in masses of small, four-petaled white flowers that are intensely fragrant and attract a spectacular diversity of native bees, wasps, beetles, and butterflies seeking late-summer nectar. After bloom, the flowers are replaced by feathery, silvery seed plumes that persist through fall and winter, creating a spectacular 'old man's beard' effect in the landscape — a three-season ornamental vine of understated elegance. While not as showy as large-flowered hybrid clematis, its fine-textured floral masses and subsequent silky seedheads provide months of changing interest with zero maintenance; it is drought-tolerant once established and pest-free. Self-seeds freely to form spreading colonies — allow it to naturalize in native shrub borders or along a fence where it can sprawl without becoming an obstacle.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; virginal mock orange is a classic, widely grown hybrid group prized for heavily double, intensely fragrant flowers. Large, semi-double to fully double, pure white flowers cover the upright, somewhat leggy branches in late spring, carrying an intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance that made this old hybrid group a mainstay of cottage and heritage gardens since the early twentieth century. Less refined in habit than some newer compact mock orange cultivars, it is grown chiefly for the strength of its fragrance and flower fullness, best sited toward the back of a border or near a window or path where the scent can be appreciated during its bloom period. Prune immediately after flowering, removing some of the oldest canes each year at the base to keep the naturally leggy shrub renewed and full at the bottom.

Plant in virtually any soil — wet or dry, rich or poor, sandy or clay — in full sun to deep shade; Virginia creeper is one of the most versatile native vines, blanketing fences, walls, trees, and arbors in deep shade where few other plants grow, and producing a stunning curtain of brilliant crimson-scarlet-burgundy fall color that is among the most vivid of any plant in the North American flora. The small dark blue-black berries that follow in fall are an essential food for migrating thrushes, waxwings, bluebirds, and woodpeckers. It clings by adhesive pads (not invasive roots), making it appropriate on stone and brick. The sap and berries are toxic to humans and can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals; the similar five-leaflet compound leaf distinguishes it from three-leaflet poison ivy. Prune aggressively in late winter to control size.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, poor, acidic soil in full sun; Virginia pine is a pioneer species of the mid-Atlantic and upper South, naturally colonizing dry, infertile, disturbed, and eroded sites where richer soils and better drainage favor other trees. It is a relatively small, irregularly shaped pine with short, twisted needles in pairs and persistent small cones that remain on the tree for years, providing seeds and cover for wildlife through winter. The tree's value for wildlife planting on poor soils is exceptional — it is a primary host for numerous moth and butterfly caterpillars, and the cone seeds are eaten by finches, chickadees, and other birds. Used extensively in reclamation planting on strip-mined land and abandoned agricultural soils in Appalachia and the Piedmont. Though not a timber tree, it serves as an important nurse tree that prepares infertile sites for succession to mixed hardwood forest.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — Virginia rose is one of the most ecologically valuable of all native roses, producing simple, five-petaled, clear pink flowers in late spring with a pleasant light fragrance, followed by the best hips of any eastern wild rose: large, bright red, glossy fruits that persist on the canes through winter and provide critical food for catbirds, mockingbirds, robins, and cedar waxwings. The foliage turns brilliant shades of red, orange, and burgundy in autumn — outstanding fall color for a shrub. It spreads by suckers to form dense, wildlife-valuable thickets in naturalistic settings, along fencerows, and at the edges of woodland, and tolerates salt spray, poor sandy soils, and moderate drought. Disease resistance is excellent compared to hybrid roses: no spraying required. Prune out oldest canes after flowering to keep the plant productive; remove suckers to control spread in small spaces.

Stewartia malacodendron is the most beautiful and rarest of the native stewartias, a slow-growing, multi-stemmed shrub to small tree of open forest understories in the coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and Texas, producing extraordinarily showy, wide-open, camellia-like white flowers 3–4 inches across with distinctive, dramatic, purple-blue stamens and dark-purple anthers in June and July — the most spectacular flowers of any stewartia. It also has handsome, flaking, mottled gray-and-cinnamon bark and brilliant red autumn foliage. A coveted collector's plant for shaded native woodland gardens.

Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full shade; Virginia sweetspire is an outstanding native shrub for difficult moist or shaded sites, producing long (2–6 inch) arching spikes of fragrant white flowers in early summer and then delivering some of the richest fall foliage of any native shrub — leaves turn crimson, scarlet, orange, and burgundy-purple and often hold into early winter long after most deciduous shrubs have dropped their leaves. The multi-stem arching habit is graceful year-round. Unlike many shade shrubs, it tolerates both periodically wet conditions and drought once established, making it excellent for rain gardens, woodland edges, and stream banks. 'Henry's Garnet' is the most widely grown cultivar, with outstanding wine-red to deep scarlet fall color and somewhat larger flower spikes than the species.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, acidic to slightly acidic soil — Walter viburnum naturally grows in the wet, acidic soils of coastal plain wetlands and is highly tolerant of flooding and poor drainage; Reifler's Dwarf is a compact cultivar of Walter Viburnum (Viburnum obovatum), a native Florida and Gulf Coast evergreen viburnum that provides exceptional ecological value as a wildlife food source while offering ornamental merit in difficult, wet, or shaded landscape conditions. The small, rounded, dark green leaves and compact habit create a dense, fine-textured evergreen shrub suitable for hedging, screening, and naturalistic plantings in the challenging moist-to-wet soil conditions where many landscape plants struggle. In late winter and early spring (February–March), Walter viburnum produces flat clusters of small white flowers that attract early-season pollinators before most other landscape shrubs begin blooming. The small, red-to-black fruits that mature in summer are eaten by dozens of bird species — making Walter viburnum a high-value wildlife plant for zone 9 landscapes designed to support native birds. The native provenance means Walter viburnum is adapted to the exact soil, climate, and pest pressures of the Gulf South without the cultural challenges of introduced alternatives.

Plant in moist to wet or well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Walter viburnum tolerates flooding, drought, clay, and sand — one of the most site-adaptable native shrubs for Florida and the Gulf Coast. Viburnum obovatum is a native Florida and Gulf Coast viburnum with small, leathery, dark-green, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves that give the plant a fine texture uncommon among viburnums; flat-topped, 2-to-3-inch clusters of small white flowers appear in February–March and are followed by red berries that ripen to black, providing outstanding value for songbirds including thrushes, mockingbirds, and waxwings through winter. The shrub ranges from 3–12 feet tall depending on conditions — compact in dry, sunny sites and larger in moist, shaded conditions — and responds well to pruning into a dense hedge or wildlife planting. The cultivar 'Mrs. Schiller's Delight' is a compact, 3–4 foot selection with proportionally small leaves, ideal for residential gardens. Walter viburnum is native to wet flatwoods, swamp margins, and stream banks from Virginia to Florida and is an outstanding choice for rain gardens, wet spots, and bird gardens in zones 7–10.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Walter's dogwood is a large shrub or small tree from central and northern China distinguished among dogwoods by its striking deeply furrowed, interlacing bark — among the most dramatically textured trunks of any dogwood — and by notable drought tolerance once established. The flat-topped clusters of small, creamy-white flowers in early summer are followed by blue-black berries consumed by birds. Like other Cornelian-cherry relatives, the fall color is an attractive red-purple. Significantly more drought and heat tolerant than flowering dogwood (C. florida) and less susceptible to dogwood anthracnose, making it a more durable choice for Southern gardens in zones 7–9 where C. florida often struggles. An underused specimen tree that deserves wider planting for its ornamental bark and adaptability.

Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; adaptable to both periodically wet and average garden soils, and tolerates shearing into a formal hedge as well as being left to grow into a graceful large natural shrub or small tree. Viburnum obovatum (Walter's viburnum) is a native evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub of wetland margins, stream banks, and hammocks across the Gulf South and Florida, distinguished from other native viburnums by its small, glossy, finely textured leaves that give it a refined, boxwood-like appearance even without pruning. In late winter to early spring, the branches are covered in small, fragrant, white flower clusters that draw abundant pollinators, followed by small red fruits that ripen to black and are readily eaten by songbirds. Its fine texture, evergreen habit, and tolerance of both hedge shearing and natural form make it one of the most versatile native shrubs for a Gulf South screen, hedge, or woodland-edge planting, zone 7–9.

Washington hawthorn is the most widely planted of all native North American hawthorns in cultivation — an exceptionally ornamental small tree with multiple seasons of interest: dense clusters of white flowers in May, glossy, deeply lobed leaves turning orange-red in fall, and abundant clusters of small bright red fruits that persist into winter. It is one of the highest-value wildlife trees available for the eastern garden: at least 20 species of birds consume the fruits, including cedar waxwings, robins, and bluebirds; the dense, thorny structure (1–3 inch curved thorns) provides nesting habitat for catbirds, thrashers, and kingbirds; and over 150 species of Lepidoptera use native Crataegus as larval host plants. Washington hawthorn adapts to urban conditions including soil compaction, air pollution, and alkaline pH better than most native landscape trees, making it suitable for street planting, parking lots, and urban parks where native trees are rarely successful. A top choice for combining year-round ornamental interest with maximum wildlife value in limited space.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; water jasmine (sacred Buddhist tree, wild water plum) is a Southeast Asian tropical evergreen shrub widely cultivated throughout the tropical world — particularly in Thailand, Cambodia, and Malaysia — both for its ornamental beauty and its deep spiritual significance, as it is traditionally planted at temples and sacred sites, and its dangling clusters of small, pure-white, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers with long filamentous corona lobes are used as Buddhist temple offerings. The flowers are produced continuously and profusely throughout the warm season on the drooping, fine-twiggy branches, with a sweet, delicate fragrance, creating a graceful, weeping, white-flowered effect. The plant belongs to the Apocynaceae (oleander family) and exudes a milky sap when cut; all parts are toxic if ingested. In addition to its garden use as a specimen and informal flowering hedge, wrightia is one of the preeminent tropical bonsai subjects, widely grown in competitive Southeast Asian bonsai culture. Excellent in containers and as a specimen in zone 10–12.

Water Locust is the swamp-adapted cousin of Honey Locust (Gleditsia triacanthos), native to the permanently flooded bottomlands, river swamps, and slough edges of the southeastern and south-central United States from South Carolina and Florida west to Illinois and Texas, where it tolerates standing water for extended periods that most other large trees cannot survive. Like Honey Locust it bears formidable branched thorns on the trunk and branches, but the seed pods are shorter and usually contain only one or two seeds rather than the many seeds in Honey Locust's long pods. The flat seed pods that fall into floodwater are buoyant and dispersed by currents, making Water Locust an effective natural colonizer of new bottomland habitats after flooding. A valuable riparian restoration tree for wet, bottomland habitats in zones 5–9, providing large tree structure in permanently flooded sites where bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp cottonwood grow as associates. Plant in full sun in wet, rich, slightly acidic alluvial soil.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun; water oak is one of the most common and fast-growing native oaks of the coastal South, easily identified by its distinctively variable leaf shape — three-lobed duck-foot leaves, paddle-shaped leaves, and narrow elliptic leaves can all appear on the same tree. It grows naturally in bottomland forests, wet stream banks, and moist upland soils from New Jersey to Texas and is among the fastest-growing oaks in the South (2–3 feet annually). The very small, nearly round acorns produced in enormous quantities beginning at 10–15 years are critically important for wood ducks, mallards, wild turkeys, squirrels, and deer. Water oak is smaller than live oak (40–70 feet) and better suited to residential landscapes where space is limited. It typically lives 60–80 years.

Plant in wet to seasonally flooded, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loamy bottomland soil in full sun to partial shade — water tupelo is one of the dominant trees of the Deep South's most iconic wetland ecosystems: the cypress-tupelo swamp. It develops a dramatically buttressed, swollen trunk base that allows gas exchange during prolonged flooding, standing in water for months at a time in the bottomlands of the Gulf Coast and Mississippi River corridor. The large, elliptic leaves turn brilliant orange, scarlet, and crimson in fall, making it one of the finest fall-color trees for wet sites. Clusters of small, oblong, dark blue to black fruit in late summer and fall are among the most sought by migrating birds. Water tupelo honey — gathered by bees from the small spring flowers — is renowned as a premium monofloral honey with an exceptionally delicate, fruity sweetness and crystallization-resistant properties. An outstanding large tree for naturalizing in wet, swampy, or bottomland areas.

common_name: Waterfall Japanese Maple (Vigorous Green Weeping Lace-Leaf Maple)
notes: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun, allowing plenty of lateral room for its cascading spread. Waterfall is a vigorous green weeping lace-leaf Japanese maple, its finely dissected, bright green leaves cascading over long, arching branches in a form that lives up to its name, turning brilliant gold to orange-yellow in a long-lasting fall display that is among the showiest of any green-leaf cultivar. Its wide, mounding, cascading habit makes it an outstanding specimen for the top of a slope, the edge of a pond, or any spot with room to let the branches drape naturally. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches.

Watson's Dutchman's Pipe is a slender, drought-adapted native perennial vine of desert washes, rocky canyon slopes, and scrubby edges in southern Arizona, New Mexico, and adjacent Mexico. It produces narrow, elongated leaves and distinctive, S-curved, brownish-purple pipe-shaped flowers that serve as an exclusive larval host for the Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor) — female butterflies seek it out specifically to lay eggs, and the caterpillars sequester the plant's defensive alkaloids for their own protection. Grow in dry, well-drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade; established plants are highly drought tolerant and should be watered only sparingly. This unassuming vine is among the most ecologically important plantings a Southwestern gardener can make for supporting native pollinators.

common_name: Wax Mallow (Turk's Cap, Mexican Turk's Cap)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average fertility, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wax mallow (the Texas Turk's cap) is closely related to Malvaviscus arboreus but distinguished by flatter, less deeply lobed leaves. Like its relative, it produces characteristic semi-tubular, never fully-opening, bright red flowers throughout the long Gulf Coast growing season — from summer well into winter in mild years. The nectar-rich flowers are a critically important hummingbird nectar plant in the Gulf South, visited constantly by ruby-throated and rufous hummingbirds throughout their migration. The small red fruits are edible fresh and can be used for jelly. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established; dies to the ground after hard freezes but regrows vigorously from the root in spring. An essential native plant for the hummingbird garden in zone 9a.

Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, lean soil in partial shade; wax plant (porcelain flower) is an East Asian tropical vining succulent of the milkweed family (Apocynaceae) that produces clusters of utterly distinctive, perfectly formed, waxy flowers — each cluster a spherical umbel of 20–40 small, star-shaped, pale-pink or white flowers, each flower centered with a smaller red-pink, five-pointed, star-shaped corona that gives the cluster an intricate, jewel-like appearance, and the entire flower cluster glistening with sweet, clear nectar droplets. The flowers are intensely fragrant, especially in the evening. The thick, succulent, oval, glossy, dark-green leaves on the twining stems provide attractive year-round foliage coverage. Flowering requires patience — established plants may take several years to bloom — and a cool, dry winter rest period (the opposite of most tropical plants) to initiate the process. Once blooming age is reached, it flowers reliably from the same spur-like peduncles that should never be removed. 'Krimson Queen' (white-cream leaf margins), 'Tricolor', and the double-flowered 'Compacta' are popular cultivars. A long-lived, low-maintenance succulent vine once established.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Wayet's hoya trails naturally and looks best allowed to cascade rather than staked upright. Narrow, pointed, deep green leaves often flush purple-red along the margins in bright light, growing densely along slender, gracefully trailing stems that produce small clusters of dark maroon-red, star-shaped flowers with a sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening. Native to the Philippines, it is a compact, easy-care hoya well suited to a hanging basket or shelf where its cascading stems can drape freely, and, like other hoyas, it blooms repeatedly from the same short flowering spurs, which should never be removed. Allow the potting mix to dry between waterings and provide bright indirect light for the best leaf color and most reliable flowering.

Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil, including dry, chalky, or alkaline ground, in full sun to partial shade; wayfaring tree is a large, rugged, deciduous viburnum long used for hedging and windbreaks across Europe, with felted, gray-green, textured leaves and flat clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring that develop into berries passing through red on their way to a final glossy black, so a single cluster often shows both colors together in late summer — a striking two-tone effect that also feeds birds. Fall color runs from yellow to deep red-purple. It is one of the toughest large viburnums available, shrugging off poor soil, wind, drought, and neglect once established, and works well as an informal hedge, screen, or woodland-margin shrub where a tidier plant would struggle. Prune right after flowering if shaping is needed; otherwise it needs very little routine care. The felted leaves and stems are a useful identification feature that distinguishes it from smoother-leaved viburnums.

Wedding Ring is a variegated boxwood selection whose small, glossy leaves are edged in creamy yellow around a green center, giving hedging or specimen plantings a lighter, brighter look than the solid dark green of standard boxwood cultivars. It holds a naturally rounded, dense habit and takes shearing well for those who want a crisper formal shape, though it can also be left to its own tidy form for a more relaxed planting. Give it moist, well-drained soil, protection from harsh afternoon sun in the Deep South, and watch for boxwood leafminer and boxwood blight, the two most significant pest and disease pressures on boxwood in Southern gardens.

common_name: Wee Bit Grumpy Hydrangea (Dwarf Reblooming Deep Blue-Purple Mophead Hydrangea)
notes: Wee Bit Grumpy is a dwarf, reblooming mophead hydrangea staying compact enough for a large container or small foundation bed, producing rounded flower heads that read as intense deep blue in acidic soil or purple-pink in more neutral to alkaline soil, following the same pH-driven color shift typical of macrophylla hydrangeas. Because it flowers on both old and new wood, a late spring freeze that damages the previous season's buds does not prevent a strong summer rebloom. Keep soil consistently moist in partial shade, since the leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning sacrifices the earliest old-wood flowers.

common_name: Weeping Blue Atlas Cedar (Sculptural Silvery-Blue Cascading Cedar)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, staking and training the central leader upright for the first several years if a taller, cascading form is desired, since left untrained this cultivar sprawls as a wide, undulating mound. Weeping Blue Atlas Cedar is a dramatic, sculptural conifer with long, weeping branches clothed in striking silvery-blue needles, prized as a specimen tree that can be trained into strikingly different forms — tall and serpentine, mounded and groundcover-like, or trained flat against a wall — depending on staking and pruning in its early years. Its bold color and highly individual, sculptural character make it one of the most dramatic focal-point conifers available, though its ultimate size and shape are unpredictable and shaped largely by the grower's training choices. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant and require little routine care beyond removing dead wood.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; weeping bottlebrush is an Australian evergreen tree that is one of the most spectacular flowering trees for the Gulf Coast and Deep South — in spring (primary bloom), and intermittently throughout the year, the long, arching, weeping branches become covered from tip to base with the plant's signature cylindrical, bright-crimson-red, bottlebrush-like flower spikes, each composed of hundreds of long, projecting red stamens with yellow tips that form the dense, brush-like structure for which the plant is named. The weeping habit and the brilliant red flower display against the fine-textured, narrow, willow-like, evergreen leaves make it one of the most visually impressive medium-sized flowering trees available for zone 8–11. It flowers most heavily in spring but continues to produce scattered bloom through summer and fall. Attracts hummingbirds and orioles with exceptional reliability. Drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established. Hardy to approximately 15°F in zone 8.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; in zone 9, afternoon shade protection extends the plant's cold hardiness and prevents leaf scorch during heat waves. Ficus benjamina is the world's most widely cultivated indoor tree and one of the most popular tropical landscape trees in zone 9b–11 Gulf Coast, Florida, and California landscapes, where mature specimens with their gracefully arching, weeping branches laden with small, glossy, pointed leaves create an elegant, tropical canopy. In warm climates, trees grow to 50–60 feet with an equally broad spreading crown. The smooth gray trunk often develops aerial roots in humid conditions. The plant produces small, inedible figs in zone 10-11 but rarely fruits in zone 9. Ficus benjamina is notorious indoors for dropping leaves when conditions change — any shift in light, temperature, humidity, or watering schedule triggers a stress response. For outdoor landscape use in zone 9b, choose a permanent location as transplanting established trees causes significant leaf drop. The aggressive root system can damage sidewalks, foundations, and underground utilities within 20-30 feet; avoid planting near hardscape or infrastructure. A spectacular specimen when given room and a frost-free site.

Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the leader upright when young if a taller, cascading specimen is wanted, since left unstaked this cultivar sprawls along the ground as a wide, low mound instead. Weeping Norway spruce produces long, pendulous branches draped in dark-green needles that cascade dramatically once the tree gains some height, making a dramatic, sculptural specimen whether trained tall and narrow or allowed to spread as a groundcover-like mound over a slope or wall. No two plants develop exactly alike, since the ultimate form depends on training and the individual habit of the grafted specimen, giving each tree a unique, almost bonsai-like character. Little routine pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood and guiding the leading shoot if a taller form is desired.

The Weeping Willow is a graceful, fast-growing shade tree with long, sweeping branches that trail nearly to the ground and sway in the slightest breeze. Plant in full sun in moist to wet soil, ideally near a pond or stream where its thirsty roots have ample water. Keep it well away from septic lines, drains, and foundations, as the aggressive roots seek out moisture. Water deeply and regularly, especially in dry spells and during establishment. Prune in late winter to remove crossing or damaged branches and to raise the canopy as it matures.

Plant in moist to dry, acidic to slightly alkaline, well-drained to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Weeping Yaupon is a dramatic, architecturally distinctive native holly cultivar with strongly pendulous, cascading branches that create an elegant weeping form quite unlike any other native landscape tree. The long, drooping branches cascade downward from the upright central leader, creating a columnar-weeping silhouette in winter and a dense, cascading curtain of small, glossy, dark-green evergreen leaves during the growing season. In winter when the female plant bears translucent red berries against the dark green foliage along the drooping branches, the display is spectacular. Weeping yaupon is a female Ilex vomitoria selection and requires a nearby male yaupon holly (the species or a male cultivar) within about 100 feet for reliable berry production. Like the species, Weeping Yaupon has extraordinary adaptability — thriving in the full spectrum of Gulf Coast conditions from seasonally flooded clay soils to dry sandy uplands, salt spray, alkaline soils, and both full sun and partial shade. It grows 12–18 feet tall with a cascading, somewhat narrow spread of 6–10 feet. The weeping form makes it outstanding as a specimen, accent, or garden focal point where its distinctive silhouette can be appreciated.

The Weeping Yoshino is a flowering cherry with gracefully cascading branches that in spring become a fountain of delicate, blush-white blossoms before the leaves emerge. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and provide good air circulation to limit fungal issues. Water regularly during establishment and mulch the root zone, keeping mulch away from the trunk. Prune only lightly right after flowering to maintain the weeping shape, as cherries are prone to disease through large cuts. It makes a spectacular focal point in a lawn or beside a patio.

Root cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; weigela is a Chinese deciduous flowering shrub that has been a cornerstone of the North American spring garden since the Victorian era — producing masses of trumpet-shaped, 1-inch flowers densely covering the arching branches in late May to June in shades ranging from deep crimson-red and rose-pink to pale pink and white, depending on cultivar, at the same time as azaleas and late lilacs, creating one of the richest spring flowering displays available in zone 4–8. Modern cultivars have dramatically expanded the ornamental value beyond the original species, adding dark-purple, burgundy, or gold foliage to the flowering display: 'Wine and Roses' (deep-purple foliage, bright-pink flowers), 'Midnight Wine' (compact, dwarf, burgundy leaves, rose-pink flowers), and 'Sonic Bloom' series (repeat-flowering from spring through frost) are standout introductions. It attracts hummingbirds reliably. Tolerates partial shade acceptably. One of the easiest and most adaptable flowering shrubs for the temperate garden.

common_name: Welch's Pink Beautyberry (Soft Pink-Berried American Beautyberry)
notes: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil. Welch's Pink is a selected color form of the native American beautyberry, bearing the same tight, globe-shaped berry clusters ringing the arching stems in late summer and fall, but in a soft rosy pink rather than the species' typical vivid magenta-purple, offering a gentler color option for gardeners who want the beautyberry effect with a different palette. Like the species it provides valuable late-season food for mockingbirds, robins, and other wildlife once the berries ripen, and the small, pale pink summer flowers attract pollinators. Prune hard in late winter, cutting back to within 6-12 inches of the ground, to encourage vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production, since berries form on new wood and unpruned plants can become leggy and sparse over time.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun in zone 10–12; West Indian mahogany is one of the most prized timber trees in the world — the original 'true mahogany' of the Caribbean cabinet-making tradition, producing close-grained, durable, reddish-brown wood used in fine furniture, musical instruments, and boat building since the 16th century. It is the state tree of the Dominican Republic. In south Florida and the Keys, it grows naturally in tropical hardwood hammock and is the only native mahogany in North America. Widely planted as a street and shade tree in Miami, it develops into a stately, large, semi-deciduous tree with a dense, spreading canopy. The large, hanging seed capsules split into five valves to release winged seeds. Critically endangered in its natural range due to centuries of timber harvesting; planting supports conservation of this culturally important species.

Set out container-grown plants in fall or early spring into loose, well-drained, acidic soil amended with leaf mold or conifer duff, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer. It grows naturally along streambanks and in open, partly shaded woods from California into southern Oregon, so give it filtered light beneath high canopy and steady moisture in its first few seasons while it establishes deep roots. Fragrant white to pale pink flowers with a yellow blotch open in early summer on a rangy, multi-stemmed shrub, and the scent carries well through a shaded border or informal woodland edge. Established plants tolerate summer drought better than most azaleas once their roots reach cooler subsoil.

Plant nursery-grown container specimens in fall into consistently moist, strongly acidic, peaty soil in partial shade, replicating the mountain bogs, fens, and streambanks from British Columbia and the Cascades south to California and east to the Rockies where this evergreen shrub grows wild. Rounded clusters of small white flowers open in early summer above aromatic, leathery, woolly-backed leaves, drawing bees and other pollinators, while the dense foliage offers year-round shelter in wetland habitats. Closely related to the eastern Labrador tea but distinct to western wetlands, it belongs in a dedicated acidic bog garden rather than ordinary garden soil, since both drying out and alkaline conditions are quickly fatal.

Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into consistently moist, acidic, gritty soil in a cool site with light shade, matching the rocky alpine and subalpine slopes of the Pacific Northwest and Sierra Nevada where it grows in mats fed by melting snowbanks. Its tiny, scale-like leaves densely clothe wiry stems, and in early summer it is studded with small white, bell-shaped flowers nodding on thread-like stalks, a classic sight of high mountain heather meadows. It is exacting about cool roots and steady moisture, making it best suited to a shaded scree bed, trough, or high-elevation native rock garden.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; western mountain ash prefers cooler mountain climates and struggles with heat and drought in lowland gardens. Flat clusters of small white flowers open in early summer above compound, fern-like leaves on this small native tree of high-elevation forests and mountain slopes across western North America, followed by bright orange-red berry clusters that persist into fall and winter, providing important food for grouse, waxwings, and other mountain wildlife. Its compact size and showy fruit display make it a good choice for a native mountain or high-elevation garden, but it is not well adapted to hot, humid, or low-elevation conditions far from its cool mountain forest habitat. Water during establishment and dry spells, and site in a location with cool summer temperatures and good air circulation for the best long-term performance.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; western redbud is the California and Great Basin counterpart of the eastern redbud, native to rocky hillsides, chaparral, and dry canyon walls throughout California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah. It is a distinctly different plant from eastern redbud in several ways: typically growing as a large, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a single-trunked tree (reaching 10-15 feet rather than 20-30 feet), with round rather than heart-shaped leaves, and substantially higher drought tolerance adapted to the dry-summer Mediterranean climate of the American West. In early spring, the leafless stems are covered in brilliant, vibrant magenta-pink pea flowers identical in form to eastern redbud, creating a breathtaking display. The round, deep-green summer leaves have attractive fall color. An outstanding California native for xeriscaping, wildlife gardens, and drought-tolerant landscapes, and increasingly valued as a garden plant in the Gulf Coast and Southeast where its heat tolerance is an advantage.

Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in average to dry soil and full to partial sun, spacing plants to allow the colony to spread naturally by underground rhizomes into a dense thicket. Western snowberry needs little care once established and tolerates heavy clay, drought, and harsh prairie winters better than most ornamental shrubs. Small pink-tinged bell flowers in early summer draw bumblebees and other native pollinators, and the waxy white berries that follow persist into winter, feeding sharp-tailed grouse, pheasants, and small mammals when other food is scarce. The dense, thicket-forming habit also provides valuable nesting and escape cover for grassland songbirds.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous to sandy soil in full sun; western soapberry is a native tree of the south-central US, growing on dry, rocky, calcareous plains and hills from Kansas and Missouri south to Mexico. The fleshy, translucent, golden-amber berries contain saponins — natural soap compounds — and are high enough in saponin concentration that the crushed berries lather in water and have been used historically as soap for washing clothes and hair by indigenous peoples. The fruits are technically toxic if eaten in quantity due to the saponins. The pale yellow-green fall foliage, persistent golden berries through winter, and handsome pinnate leaves provide multi-season ornamental interest. Excellent urban tree tolerating drought, heat, alkaline soils, and neglect — one of the toughest native trees for harsh, dry, calcareous landscape conditions in zone 9.

Choose a site that receives morning sun and afternoon shade, with fast-draining, rocky or sandy soil that stays dry in summer. This is the only Viburnum native to Oregon and California, and it is adapted to summer drought — avoid planting in lawn areas or anywhere that receives regular irrigation. Plant in spring, water to settle the roots, and then allow natural rainfall to take over after the first season. Clusters of white flowers in late spring attract native pollinators, and the dark berries that follow are eaten by western scrub-jays, towhees, and other Pacific coast birds.

common_name: Weyer's Butterfly Bush (Orange-Gold Globe-Flowered Buddleja Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, and cut the entire shrub back hard, to within a foot or so of the ground, in late winter each year, since flowers form on new growth and a severe annual pruning keeps the shrub compact and floriferous rather than large and leggy. Buddleja x weyeriana is a cross between the familiar purple butterfly bush (B. davidii) and the yellow-flowered B. globosa, combining the long, arching bloom season of the former with rounded, ball-shaped flower clusters closer to the latter, opening in shades of warm orange, gold, and apricot from midsummer through fall. Like other butterfly bushes it is a magnet for butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds, and its distinctive globe-shaped flower clusters and unusual color range set it apart from the more common purple- and pink-flowered Buddleja davidii cultivars. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established, and deadheading spent flower clusters through the season helps prolong the bloom display.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wheeler's Dwarf tolerates coastal salt spray, wind, and poor soil better than many broadleaf evergreens, making it a reliable low hedge or foundation plant in Gulf Coast landscapes. This dwarf pittosporum forms a dense, mounding shrub of small, glossy, leathery, deep-green leaves rarely reaching more than 2 feet tall, with clusters of small, cream-white flowers in spring that carry a strong orange-blossom fragrance detectable from several feet away, the trait that gives the species its common name of mock orange. Its naturally low, tidy habit needs little shearing to maintain shape, and it holds up well to both heat and the Gulf Coast's high humidity. Prune, if needed, right after the spring bloom to preserve next year's flowers.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white angel's trumpet is the most fragrant and widely grown Brugmansia species, producing pendant, white, trumpet-shaped flowers up to 12 inches long with an intensely sweet, heady tropical fragrance most pronounced in the evening — one of the most powerfully scented flowers of any tropical plant. The fragrance on a warm summer evening can perfume an entire garden. Multiple flushes of bloom occur throughout the warm season. Like all Brugmansia, all parts are dangerously toxic — do not grow where children or curious pets have access. In zones 9–10, it grows as a large semi-evergreen shrub; in zone 8 it dies to the ground in winter and re-sprouts from the base. Heavy feeding with balanced fertilizer and consistent moisture produce the largest and most prolific flowers. Widely available in both white and cream-to-pale-yellow double-flowered forms.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white ash is a magnificent native canopy tree of eastern North American forests, producing large, compound leaves that turn exceptional shades of yellow, orange, and deep burgundy-purple in fall — among the finest fall color of any native tree. IMPORTANT: White ash is critically threatened across its entire range by the emerald ash borer (EAB), an invasive beetle from Asia that has killed hundreds of millions of ash trees since its detection in Michigan in 2002; all native Fraxinus species in North America are vulnerable. Planting is still worthwhile in areas where USDA-approved biocontrol programs using parasitoid wasps (Tetrastichus planipennisi and others) are actively established, as these programs are showing meaningful suppression in treated areas. Consult your state forestry agency or Cooperative Extension service for current EAB biocontrol status in your region before planting. The historically important wood — used for baseball bats, tool handles, and furniture — and the tree's exceptional ecological value as a host for hundreds of native insects make white ash worth preserving wherever possible.

common_name: White Autumn Sage (Pure White Everblooming Salvia greggii Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; 'Alba' is the pure-white flowered cultivar of Salvia greggii (autumn sage), a Texas native subshrub that produces small, two-lipped, pure-white flowers in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost. The clean white color is distinctive in the Salvia greggii palette (which otherwise runs through red, pink, coral, salmon, and bicolor combinations) — providing a true white that is uncommon among drought-tolerant Texas native salvias and outstanding for brightening shaded edges of full-sun borders, for white-and-blue combinations with blue salvias (Blue Queen, Indigo Spires), and for white garden themes. 'Alba' has the same exceptional drought tolerance, heat performance, and wildlife value as the red-flowered Salvia greggii species — the white flowers attract hummingbirds, large carpenter bees, and numerous native bee species throughout the long bloom season. The semi-evergreen to deciduous shrub reaches 2–3 feet with a similar spread and benefits from a hard cutback to 6–8 inches in late winter to promote fresh, dense growth and abundant spring flowering. In zone 9, 'Alba' reliably overwinters and produces its best flowering in the spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) shoulder seasons; summer bloom continues in the heat but may be somewhat reduced. Light shearing after each main flush encourages continuous production.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil; 'Lactea' is a naturally occurring white-fruited selection of American beautyberry, identical to the wild species in habit, foliage, and pale lilac summer flowers but bearing clusters of translucent, ivory-white berries instead of the typical magenta-purple, for a strikingly different look against the same arching, deciduous stems. The pale berries persist into fall and are just as valuable to mockingbirds and other fruit-eating birds as the species type, though some gardeners note the paler fruit can be slightly less visible to foraging wildlife against green foliage. Because seed-grown plants frequently revert to the common purple-berried form, propagate only from rooted cuttings taken from a confirmed white-fruited plant to preserve the trait. Prune hard in late winter, as with the species, since flowers and berries form on the current season's new growth.

common_name: White Beautyberry (White-Berried Form of Native American Beautyberry Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; White Beautyberry is the white-fruited selection of Callicarpa americana — the native American beautyberry that is one of the most striking native fruiting shrubs of the Gulf South, now in the unusual and elegant white-berry form that provides a distinct ornamental alternative to the standard vivid-purple berry clusters. The white (ivory to pale cream-white) berry clusters of 'Alba' are arranged in the same dense, tightly-packed rings around the stems at each leaf axil as the purple species — the distinctive whorled ring pattern that makes beautyberry unmistakable — but the white color creates a different visual effect: quieter and more sophisticated in combination with dark green foliage, and particularly effective in evening garden settings or combined with dark purple or burgundy companions where the contrast is strong. The berry clusters are produced abundantly in August through November, persisting on the bare stems into winter after the leaves fall, providing food for at least 40 species of songbirds and game birds. The leaves of American beautyberry contain callicarpenal, a compound with documented mosquito-repellent activity that has long been used in folk tradition. Beautyberry grows as a loose, arching shrub that benefits from hard pruning in late winter — cutting back by one-third to one-half stimulates vigorous new growth that produces the most prolific berry clusters in the same year. Self-sows in favorable conditions.

Divide basal suckers or plant large container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; white bird of paradise is the giant tree-form relative of the familiar orange bird of paradise (S. reginae), developing massive, paddle-shaped, blue-green leaves up to 6 feet long on tall, bamboo-like trunks — producing a dramatic, tropical architectural effect in the landscape. The flowers are spectacular when they appear: large, boat-shaped spathe bracts of deep purple-blue cradle blue-and-white flower petals. The plant is extensively used as a dramatic indoor specimen (the most popular tropical foliage plant in US interior landscaping) and as an outdoor landscape focal point in zones 10–12. Tolerates partial shade and indoor low light better than most tropical trees, though outdoor plants in full sun are most vigorous. Outstanding as a large-scale specimen in courtyards, entrances, and pool gardens in zone 10–12 landscapes.

common_name: White Cedar (Pink Trumpet Tree, Variable-Leaf Tabebuia, Caribbean Lapacho)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil — White Cedar is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in the sandy, alkaline soils of coastal Gulf and Florida landscapes. Handroanthus heterophyllus (formerly Tabebuia heterophylla) is a medium-sized, semi-deciduous flowering tree native to the Caribbean islands (Puerto Rico, Hispaniola, Cuba, Jamaica, and the Lesser Antilles) in the family Bignoniaceae, the national tree of Puerto Rico. The species name 'heterophyllus' (variable leaf) refers to the variation in leaf form on individual trees — sometimes simple, sometimes 3-leaflet, sometimes 5-leaflet compound. In spring, the tree produces clusters of large (3–4 inch), trumpet-shaped flowers in soft lavender-pink to light rose-pink, blooming on bare or nearly bare branches before the new leaf flush — the delicate pink coloration is softer and more pastel than the vibrant magenta-pink of H. impetiginosus, creating a distinctly elegant bloom display. The tree is widely used in Caribbean and tropical American landscapes as a medium-sized flowering shade tree, and has proven successful in zone 9 Gulf South conditions where its relative cold tolerance, drought adaptability, and spring flower display make it one of the better choices among the many beautiful but sometimes tender Handroanthus trumpet trees.

common_name: White Chiffon Rose of Sharon (Sterile Double-Flowered White Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, since bloom occurs on new growth. White Chiffon bears large, semi-double, pure white flowers with a soft, ruffled cluster of extra petals at the center that gives each bloom a fuller, more anemone-like look than the typical single rose of sharon flower, blooming from midsummer into fall. As a sterile selection, it produces almost no seed, sidestepping the self-sowing weediness that has given older rose of sharon a mixed reputation, while still delivering months of clean white color from a tough, low-maintenance shrub. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established.

common_name: White Cloud Texas Sage (White-Flowered Cenizo Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; White Cloud is the white-flowered cultivar of Texas sage (cenizo, Leucophyllum frutescens) — producing the same outstanding silver-gray, small, soft, woolly foliage and the remarkable humidity-triggered synchronized blooming behavior as the purple-flowered species, but with pure white flowers that create an entirely different aesthetic. The white-flowered display is particularly striking against the silver-gray foliage — an all-silver-and-white combination that has a cool, refined quality in contrast to the warm purple-on-gray of standard cenizo cultivars. White Cloud's bloom response to humidity or rainfall (a sudden mass flowering of white across the entire shrub following a rise in relative humidity or rain event) is one of the most dramatic natural phenomena in southwestern ornamental horticulture. The white flowers pair beautifully with blue-purple companion plants (blue salvias, Russian sage) for a traditional blue-and-white planting combination, and with ornamental grasses whose warm golden tones provide contrast. Like all Leucophyllum, White Cloud requires excellent drainage and lean soil — excessive water and fertility produce soft growth and reduce the tight, silver-gray character of the natural plant. In zone 9 west of the high-humidity coastal zone (San Antonio area, central Texas), White Cloud is exceptionally hardy and reliable; in the humid Gulf Coast proper, good drainage is essential.

common_name: White Diamonds Hydrangea (Sturdy Upright White Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to reach its full mature size as a large specimen shrub or small tree form. White Diamonds bears large, conical, pure white flower panicles on strong, rigid stems that stay upright through summer storms without staking, aging to a soft pink blush by fall. Its vigorous, well-branched, tree-like habit can be trained as a small single- or multi-stem specimen tree as well as grown as a large shrub, giving it more design flexibility than more compact panicle hydrangea cultivars. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.

common_name: White Duranta (White-Flowered Golden Dewdrop Shrub with Golden Berries)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; White Duranta ('Alba') is the white-flowered form of golden dewdrop (Duranta erecta) — a widely grown tropical shrub native to the Americas that produces arching, cascading branches of small, white flowers (rather than the blue-purple of the species) followed by the showy strings of golden-yellow berries that give the plant its common name 'golden dewdrop'. The white flower and golden berry combination creates an elegant, clean color scheme distinct from the blue-and-gold of standard Duranta. Duranta is one of the most important butterfly and hummingbird plants for Gulf South gardens — the flowers attract monarch butterflies, queen butterflies, sulphur butterflies, and a wide range of native bees throughout the long bloom season (summer through fall), making it an outstanding pollinator plant in full-sun borders and along fence lines. The golden-yellow berry clusters persist through fall and are consumed by mockingbirds, catbirds, and other frugivorous birds. In zone 9, Duranta grows as a perennial shrub in protected locations, often killed to the ground by hard freezes but returning vigorously from the roots in spring. The fast-growing, arching habit means established plants can reach 6–8 feet in a single warm season. The berries are toxic if eaten — a caution for households with small children or pets that might be attracted to the colorful fruits.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; white enkianthus stays more compact than redvein enkianthus and works well as a foundation shrub or low hedge in an acidic-soil shade garden. Enkianthus perulatus is a compact Japanese shrub with fine-textured foliage and clusters of small, pure white, urn-shaped flowers dangling beneath the branches in mid-spring, followed by outstanding fall color that ranges from bright red to orange-scarlet, among the most reliable fall foliage displays of any acidic-soil shrub. Its smaller size compared with redvein enkianthus makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, low hedges, or the middle layer of an azalea and rhododendron border in partial shade. It needs the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil as its relatives and requires little pruning beyond removing any dead or crossing branches.
