Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; white fringetree is one of the most spectacular native flowering trees of the eastern United States, erupting in late April and May in airy, drooping panicles of pure-white, strap-like petals that give the effect of shimmering white fringe covering the entire canopy — often before or just as the leaves emerge, which amplifies the floral display dramatically. Chionanthus virginicus is dioecious: female plants produce loose clusters of olive-sized, blue-black, grape-like fruits in late summer that are highly attractive to birds, particularly thrushes, mockingbirds, and waxwings; male plants typically produce slightly showier and more fragrant flower clusters. Exceptionally adaptable to a wide range of soil types including clay, loam, and sandy soils, and tolerant of urban conditions, air pollution, and occasional flooding once established — making it an outstanding choice for residential landscapes, streetscapes, and naturalistic borders throughout zones 3–9. Grows slowly at 6–10 inches per year; patience yields a magnificent specimen that can live for decades with virtually no maintenance.

Direct-sow or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; white indigoberry (milkberry, prick-wood) is a spiny, evergreen native shrub of south Florida, the Caribbean, and coastal tropical Americas that is one of the most reliable and wildlife-valuable small shrubs for zone 9b–12 coastal and dry upland landscapes. Its small, white, fragrant, tubular flowers produce an indigo-blue to white, waxy berry that is a critical food source for mockingbirds, thrashers, bluebirds, and over thirty additional bird species — making it one of the most bird-attractive native shrubs of south Florida. The sharp, paired spines make it an excellent barrier hedge for security plantings, and the plant's extreme tolerance of salt spray, drought, and poor sandy soil makes it ideally suited to the harsh conditions of coastal landscapes where few other shrubs thrive. Slow-growing to 3–10 feet, it can be used as a hedge, a natural barrier, or allowed to grow as a specimen with an attractive, irregular branch structure. Largely absent from commercial nurseries but available from native plant nurseries.

Plant in well-drained, thin, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral oolitic limestone soil in partial shade; white ironwood is a rare native tree of the tropical hardwood hammocks of the Florida Keys, a member of the soapberry family (Sapindaceae) producing trifoliate compound leaves with small, leathery leaflets and small white flower clusters followed by black, fleshy fruits. The black fruit gives the tree its alternate common name 'inkwood.' The extremely hard, dense wood was historically used for construction and tool handles, and the tree is sometimes confused with paradise tree (Simarouba). Critically threatened in the wild due to habitat loss in the Keys, white ironwood is an important species for native plant restoration in the Florida Keys and extreme south Florida. The fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons and other subtropical birds. A conservation plant worth growing in appropriate south Florida native gardens.

Plant in moist, fertile, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; White Ixora requires consistent moisture, good drainage, and acidic soil — iron chlorosis (yellowing leaves) occurs in alkaline soils and should be treated with acidified water and chelated iron supplements. Ixora finlaysoniana (White Ixora, Petch Lan Fah in Thai) is an evergreen shrub native to Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam, grown throughout tropical Southeast Asia, South Asia, and the Pacific for its large, rounded corymbs of pure-white, tubular, 4-petaled flowers held above glossy, dark-green foliage — and for its notably stronger, sweeter honey-jasmine fragrance compared to the familiar red-flowered Ixora coccinea of commerce. White Ixora carries deep cultural significance in Thai Buddhism, where the white flowers are offered at temples, shrines, and merit-making ceremonies, and in Hindu ritual use across South and Southeast Asia. Plants bloom continuously in warm, humid conditions and respond well to light pruning after each flush to encourage dense, compact growth and continuous flower production. Excellent for hedges, foundation plantings, and container specimens in subtropical and tropical gardens.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; White Mandevilla blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9, where this combination can extend the flowering season through the hottest months. Mandevilla boliviensis is a twining tropical vine from Bolivia and Ecuador that produces pure white, 3-inch, funnel-shaped flowers with a contrasting yellow center — a clean, elegant color combination that pairs beautifully with other tropical colors or with purely white garden designs. The flowers are produced profusely and continuously throughout the warm months on vigorous, evergreen stems clothed in glossy, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves. White Mandevilla is the primary white species used in breeding the modern 'White' selections of Mandevilla sold in mass-market retail — though most commercial 'white' Mandevillas are actually complex hybrids combining M. boliviensis with other species for improved plant size and flower production. Like all Mandevilla relatives (family Apocynaceae), the plant produces a milky latex sap when cut that is irritating to skin and eyes. In zone 9, it is one of the finest annual or temporary perennial vines for rapid seasonal color on trellises and fences, growing 6–10 feet in a single season.

White Mangrove is the most frost-sensitive of the three Florida mangrove species, typically occupying the landward fringe of the mangrove forest on slightly higher ground that is less frequently inundated than the zones occupied by Red and Black Mangrove. Distinguished by its pale, yellowish-gray bark and distinctive pairs of salt-excreting glands (nectaries) at the base of each leaf, White Mangrove lacks the dramatic prop roots of Red Mangrove and the pneumatophore air-root mats of Black Mangrove, though small peg-like root structures occasionally develop in waterlogged conditions. The flowers attract native bees and produce nectar, and the dense canopy provides critical nesting habitat for ibis, egrets, herons, and spoonbills in Florida's coastal rookeries. Restricted to frost-free Zone 10–11 coastal settings in the United States, White Mangrove is protected under Florida law and should only be planted from nursery stock within the appropriate coastal habitat.

Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer, treating the basal cut with indole-butyric acid rooting hormone and maintaining high humidity and bottom heat of 75-85°F until rooting occurs in 6-10 weeks. Transplant rooted cuttings into fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in a warm, protected site and water thoroughly to settle the roots. Fertilize with a balanced slow-release fertilizer in spring and again in early summer, supplementing with a micronutrient drench if foliage yellows on alkaline soils. The intensely fragrant pure-white flowers are produced year-round in the warmest climates and peak in spring and summer; harvest individual blooms in the early morning for use in garlands or hair ornaments, as the fragrance is most potent just after opening.

Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; white mistflower is one of the most spectacular fall-blooming native shrubs of the Texas Hill Country and Gulf South, covering itself in dense clusters of pure white, fluffy, ageratum-like flowers in October–November just when most other plants are going dormant. The fragrant flowers are outstanding for butterflies and late-season pollinators, including migrating monarch butterflies that use them as a critical nectar source during the fall migration. The plant is semi-evergreen in mild winters. It grows naturally in the shade of limestone canyon walls and cedars, making it one of the more shade-tolerant native fall-blooming shrubs available. The common name 'mistflower' refers to the soft, misty appearance of the white flower clusters. Cut back by one-third in early spring to encourage compact, dense growth.

common_name: White Mussaenda (Philippine Mussaenda, White Flag Bush, Donna Luz)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; White Mussaenda grows most vigorously and blooms most heavily in full sun but tolerates and benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Mussaenda philippica is a large tropical shrub from the Philippines in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that has produced some of the most spectacular ornamental hybrids in tropical horticulture — particularly through the Philippine breeding program that developed the 'Dona' series (Dona Aurora, Dona Carmen, Dona Luz, Dona Esperanza) named in honor of Philippine First Ladies, in which the small, typically 5-petaled flowers are surrounded by greatly enlarged, pure white, snowflake-shaped sepals (not petals) that cover the entire branch tips in a cloud of brilliant white. The ornamental display comes entirely from these enlarged sepals, which function to attract pollinators to the small true flowers within — a strategy shared with bougainvillea and poinsettia. The Dona Luz cultivar has become one of the most widely planted tropical ornamentals in zone 10-11 landscapes worldwide for its exceptionally long bloom season (essentially year-round in zone 10-11), clean white appearance, and dramatic presence as a large specimen shrub.

Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white oak is one of the most majestic and ecologically important trees in eastern North America, growing slowly into a massive, wide-spreading giant with deeply furrowed gray bark and a broad, rounded crown that can span 80 feet or more. White oak acorns are widely recognized as the single most nutritious acorn for wildlife — lower in tannins than red oak acorns, they are eagerly consumed by white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, wood ducks, blue jays, and at least 180 other vertebrate species, making white oak the keystone wildlife tree of the eastern deciduous forest. The deeply lobed leaves turn attractive wine-red to russet-brown in fall. Growth is slow but steady — expect 12–15 inches per year — and the tree is exceptionally long-lived (centuries to over 500 years in natural settings). Despite the slow start, there is no native tree that surpasses white oak in landscape longevity, wildlife value, and grandeur.

Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after all frost danger has passed in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full to partial sun; white passionflower is frost-killed to the ground in zone 9 but reliably resprouts from the root, and is fully evergreen in frost-free zones 10-11. Passiflora multiflora is a vigorous native vine of Florida, the Caribbean, and Central America, producing an abundance of small, intricate white flowers with the characteristic passionflower structure that attracts pollinators throughout the warm season; it is a critical larval host plant for the Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterflies, making it an essential addition to Florida and Gulf Coast butterfly gardens. The vine climbs readily by tendrils and can be trained over a trellis or fence, or allowed to ramble as a groundcover in frost-free settings.

Root branch cuttings (allow cut ends to callus for 1–2 weeks) in gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; white plumeria (Plumeria alba) is the species native to the Caribbean and Puerto Rico, prized for its narrow leaves and pure white flowers with a yellow eye that are intensely fragrant with a sweet, tropical, honeysuckle-like scent. The flowers are the classic blooms used to make Hawaiian leis and Indian garlands (gajra). Grows as a deciduous to semi-deciduous shrubby tree in the tropics and subtropics; in zone 10 it loses its leaves during the cool dry season but is cold-sensitive and damaged below 32°F. Extremely drought-tolerant and resistant to most pests once established. An iconic tropical ornamental suited to containers for gardeners in cooler zones.

White Stopper is a native evergreen shrub or small tree, native to the coastal hammocks, tropical hardwood forests, and pineland edges of south Florida, the Florida Keys, and the Caribbean, known for its spicy, clove-like or cinnamon fragrance that can be detected from several feet away — the aromatic foliage distinguishes this species from most other Florida stoppers. Clusters of small, white, four-petaled flowers appear in summer and fall, followed by round berries that ripen from red to black and are an important food source for migrating songbirds in fall and winter. It grows to small tree size in protected hammock situations or can be maintained as a dense, evergreen hedge through pruning. White Stopper tolerates partial shade and is one of the most salt-spray-tolerant of the native Eugenia species, making it a versatile choice for coastal gardens in zones 9b–11 that need a fragrant, wildlife-supporting evergreen screen.

Plant container-grown nursery stock in spring into moist, strongly acidic, sandy peat along the edges of pocosins or seepage bogs in partial shade, replicating the fire-maintained wetland margins of the Cape Fear region of the Carolinas where this rare deciduous Kalmia is endemic. In late spring it produces small white, maroon-marked, urn-shaped flowers on bare stems just as the narrow leaves emerge, a charming and unusual look among garden Kalmia. Because it is a globally rare species of conservation concern, source only nursery-propagated plants and give it the same acidic, saturated conditions as its pocosin neighbors like sweetbay and fetterbush.

Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun along streams, pond banks, or low-lying wet areas; white willow is a large, fast-growing Eurasian tree widely naturalized in North America and historically among the most important medicinal plants in Europe, as the bark contains salicin — the precursor to aspirin. The undersides of the leaves are covered in fine white hairs that give the canopy a silvery shimmer in wind, making it highly ornamental near water. The cultivar 'Tristis' (golden weeping willow) is one of the most familiar weeping trees in temperate horticulture. Like all willows, it has extremely invasive roots that seek water and must be planted well away from foundations, septic systems, and underground pipes.

Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container on a moss pole in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; White Wizard philodendron needs strong indirect light to sustain its white variegation and resents cold, drafty conditions. Broad, dark green leaves are irregularly marked with bold patches and speckles of creamy white variegation on pale green petioles, closely resembling the similar 'White Knight' and 'White Princess' philodendrons but with somewhat lighter stem coloring, a distinction collectors watch for when identifying which particular white-variegated philodendron they have. As a climbing aroid it develops larger, more heavily variegated leaves when trained up a moss pole rather than left to trail, growing steadily under good light and warmth. Provide strong indirect light to maintain the white variegation, remove any fully white (chlorophyll-free) growth that will eventually decline, and keep humidity moderate to high.

Plant in partial shade to filtered light — camellias prefer the bright, indirect light of open shade under tall pines or high-branched trees, avoiding deep shade or full afternoon sun; White by the Gate is a registered Camellia japonica cultivar producing elegant white flowers in the formal double or peony form that represents one of the most refined and sophisticated floral displays available from any landscape shrub in zone 9's winter garden. The pure white flowers — whether formal double, semi-double, or peony form — provide a clean, luminous, refined contrast to the dark, glossy, evergreen foliage of the camellia shrub, creating a winter display of formal elegance that has made white camellias a staple of Southern estate and garden district plantings for generations. Camellia japonica is one of the defining landscape plants of the American Gulf South — thriving in the same partial shade, acidic, well-drained conditions that characterize the longleaf pine and mixed hardwood forests native to the region. The combination of large (3–6 inch) formal flowers in January–March when nothing else of comparable size or quality blooms in the landscape, glossy evergreen foliage year-round, and the exceptional longevity of well-sited camellias (specimens over 100 years old are documented in the Gulf South) makes camellia japonica cultivars essentially irreplaceable in zone 7–9 winter garden design.

White-leaf Leather Flower is a twining native perennial vine of moist woodland edges, stream banks, and thickets in the southeastern United States, instantly recognizable by the striking glaucous — blue-gray and waxy-white — undersurfaces of its leaves that flash silver whenever a breeze stirs the foliage. In spring it bears nodding, urn-shaped flowers with recurved purplish-pink to rose petals, followed by showy, feathery silvery seed heads in fall that extend the ornamental season well into winter. Grow in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, keeping the root zone cool and consistently moist; it climbs by twining leaf petioles and benefits from a sturdy support. The glaucous foliage sets it apart from all other native clematis and makes it a distinctive choice for moist fencerows and woodland garden edges in zones 5-9.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting where its cascading branches have room to arch downward without crowding. Whitewater is a weeping redbud cultivar whose branches cascade gracefully from a central leader, giving it a fountain-like silhouette distinct from the typical vase-shaped redbud form. In early spring, the bare, pendulous branches are covered in the classic rosy-pink pea-like flowers typical of the species, followed by heart-shaped leaves heavily variegated in white and cream over green, a striking combination that provides ornamental interest all summer rather than just during the brief spring bloom. Because variegated foliage photosynthesizes less efficiently than solid green leaves, growth is somewhat slower than standard redbud cultivars, and the tree stays more compact, making it a good choice for smaller landscapes or as a specimen near a patio where its cascading, patterned foliage can be appreciated up close. Provide afternoon shade in zone 8-9 to prevent leaf scorch on the variegated foliage, and plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are highly susceptible to rot in wet sites.

common_name: Wichita Crape Myrtle (Large Lavender-Flowered Tree-Form Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving this large tree-form cultivar plenty of room to mature. Wichita is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Indian-series crape myrtles, producing bright lavender flower panicles through summer on a large, upright tree, with richly colored cinnamon-to-mahogany exfoliating bark that provides striking winter interest once the leaves drop. Its size and vigor make it well suited as a specimen shade tree or street tree in larger landscapes rather than a foundation shrub. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed. Avoid severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

Wild Coffee is one of the most valuable native shade shrubs for south Florida and tropical hammock gardens, native to the dense, shaded understories of tropical hardwood hammocks, coastal hammocks, and pinelands from Brevard and Hillsborough counties south through the Florida Keys and into the Caribbean. Its large, glossy, strongly quilted or pleated dark green leaves with prominent veins are among the most attractive foliage textures in the Florida native palette, providing a lush, tropical appearance in deep shade where few other shrubs thrive. Small white flowers appear year-round, followed by clusters of bright red berries in fall and winter that are a vital food source for migrating warblers, robins, and thrushes. Despite the common name, it is not a true coffee (Coffea), though the plants share family membership; the berries are not edible by humans. An outstanding shade shrub for zone 9b–11 landscapes that fills the difficult deep-shade role with year-round beauty and wildlife value.

Direct sow after last frost in moist, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wild cucumber is a vigorous native annual vine of moist woodland edges, streambanks, and disturbed riparian areas across most of North America, climbing rapidly by branching tendrils over shrubs, fences, and small trees to produce a dense, large-leaved screen in a single season. The large, maple-like leaves create excellent temporary screening. Small, white, star-shaped male flowers in large, fluffy panicles are mildly fragrant and attractive to many small native bees. The distinctive, spiny, oval, cucumber-like fruits (about the size of a golf ball) are ornamental and give the plant both its common names — the inflated, papery fruits are balsam-apple shaped and resemble tiny cucumbers covered in soft spines. The fruits split at maturity to release 4 large, flat seeds. An excellent, fast-growing native annual for covering trellises, fences, or unsightly structures in partially shaded, moist locations.

Direct sow Zehneria scabra seeds in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a trellis, fence, or shrub for the slender tendrils to climb; water moderately and fertilize lightly during active growth; harvest decorative red fruits for displays or leave for birds. Wild Cucumber Vine is a vigorous, scrambling, African cucurbit vine in the Zehneria genus — a group of small, wild cucumbers native to Africa, Asia, and Australia that are less known than their cultivated relatives but often equally ornamental. The plant climbs by tendrils to 5–8 feet, producing small but numerous cream-white flowers followed by masses of tiny, glossy, oval fruits about the size of a grape that ripen from green through yellow to brilliant glossy scarlet-red, creating a cheerful, berry-like display. The fruits are not edible for humans (bitter) but are eaten enthusiastically by birds, making this an excellent plant for wildlife gardens. The rough-textured leaves (scabra means 'rough') are typical of the cucurbit family. In zone 9–12, it grows as a perennial vine from a persistent rootstock; in zone 8, it can be grown as a warm-season annual. Useful for quickly covering fences, trellises, and outbuildings in warm climates with minimal care, while providing ornamental value and wildlife support.

Plant in well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Gardenia thunbergia tolerates more sun than the common Gardenia jasminoides and is considerably more drought-tolerant once established — water deeply but infrequently, allowing the top few inches of soil to dry between irrigations. Gardenia thunbergia (Wild Gardenia or Woodland Gardenia) is a medium to large shrub or small tree native to the coastal forests and bushveld of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Tanzania, differing from the familiar florist gardenia in producing strikingly symmetrical, 8-petaled, white waxy flowers — intensely fragrant in the evening — on a naturally sculptural, dark-barked tree that can reach 20–30 feet. The large, hard, ribbed woody fruits are distinctive — oval, white-grey, prominently ridged, and woody-shelled — and have historically been used as snuff containers, children's toys, and a source of yellow to gold fabric dye across southern Africa. Unlike Gardenia jasminoides, which suffers in alkaline soils, G. thunbergia is somewhat more tolerant of soil variation. It is prized in warm-climate gardens for its refined branching habit, glossy foliage, and exceptional evening fragrance, and makes an outstanding specimen tree or large fragrant hedge in zones 9–11.

Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in late spring or summer, dipping the cut end in rooting hormone before inserting into a well-draining mix of perlite and peat. Transplant rooted cuttings outdoors in spring once nighttime temperatures reliably stay above 50°F. Gardenia thunbergia is more heat- and drought-tolerant than common gardenia, but consistent moisture during the first growing season promotes rapid establishment. Fertilize with an acid-formulated fertilizer in spring and midsummer to encourage lush foliage and the best display of its large, intensely fragrant white blooms.

Wild Lime is a native evergreen shrub or small tree of coastal hammocks, rocky pinelands, and scrub edges of southern Florida and coastal Texas, recognizable by its small, dark green leaflets attached to a winged rachis — a distinctive feature of the citrus family — that release a sharp lime fragrance when crushed. A critical host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly, the largest native butterfly in North America, Wild Lime provides the caterpillar's only food source in many south Florida hammock habitats, and its dense, spiny growth makes it an excellent barrier plant or habitat hedge in tropical and subtropical landscapes. The small, gland-dotted aromatic fruits and leaves are used in Caribbean folk medicine and regional cooking, and the plant's salt tolerance and drought-hardiness make it particularly valuable in coastal south Florida settings. Plant in well-drained, sandy to rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established plants require virtually no irrigation or maintenance in appropriate Zone 9b–11 landscapes.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; wild olive is the native North American member of the same genus as the prized Asian fragrant sweet olive (O. fragrans), and though its white flowers in late spring are smaller and less flamboyant, they carry a delicate, sweet fragrance and are borne abundantly on large shrubs or small trees in woodland settings. It grows naturally in moist, shaded coastal plain forests and ravine forests of the Southeast, making it well-suited to garden use under tall trees where it provides refined, glossy-leaved evergreen structure year-round. The small, dark blue berry-like drupes ripen in fall and provide wildlife food. Slow growing but extremely long-lived; excellent as a foundation shrub or informal hedge in shade.

Root cuttings in a moist, well-drained medium in warm conditions and transplant to the garden in spring once nighttime temperatures remain above 40 degrees F. Unlike the invasive Lantana camara, this native species is well-behaved and blooms with small white to pale lavender flower clusters nearly year-round in frost-free regions. The pungently fragrant foliage deters browsing by deer, and the blooms are a premier nectar source for swallowtails, skippers, and other butterflies. Water sparingly once established and prune lightly in late winter to shape the plant and encourage fresh flowering stems.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, thin, rocky, calcareous soil in full sun; wild tamarind is a striking native tree of subtropical south Florida, the Florida Keys, and the Caribbean, producing an exceptionally graceful, lacy, filtered-shade canopy of bipinnately compound leaves that resemble tamarind foliage. The tree forms a high, open canopy that provides filtered light — one of the best native trees for creating dappled shade in south Florida landscapes without completely blocking light. Small, fragrant, white pompom flowers in spring attract numerous pollinators. A nitrogen-fixing legume (like true tamarind) that improves soil fertility. The flat, papery seed pods persist through the dry season. Butterfly gardeners prize it as a host plant for large orange sulphur butterfly larvae. The finest native shade tree for zone 10 rocky, calcareous, limestone soil conditions where other trees struggle.

common_name: Wild Thing Salvia (Vigorous Hot-Pink Hybrid Sage)
notes: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and give this vigorous hybrid room to grow into a substantial, well-branched mound over its first two seasons. Wild Thing is a Texas A&M introduction resulting from a cross between Salvia greggii and S. microphylla, combining the best traits of both parents into a larger, more heat-tolerant plant that produces an especially heavy, near-continuous display of vivid hot-pink, two-lipped flowers from spring through frost. Its larger stature and exceptional bloom production make it a standout hummingbird and butterfly plant for a sunny border or mixed shrub planting, and like its parent species it is highly drought-tolerant once established, thriving on lean soil with minimal supplemental water. Cut back hard in late winter to renew growth and keep the plant from becoming woody and sparse at the base.

common_name: Will Fleming Yaupon Holly (Narrow Columnar Native Holly)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Will Fleming is a naturally narrow, strictly upright, columnar selection of the Gulf Coast native yaupon holly, discovered and named for a Texas landscape architect, and valued for providing the vertical accent of a formal columnar evergreen without any shearing or shaping required to maintain the shape. As a male selection it does not produce the red berries typical of yaupon holly, but its extreme drought tolerance, adaptability to both wet and dry soils, and complete indifference to heat and poor soil make it one of the toughest, most maintenance-free narrow accent shrubs available for Gulf Coast gardens. It works well as a narrow screen, foundation accent, or repeated vertical element along a walk or drive.

common_name: William Shakespeare 2000 Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2000 as an improved replacement for his earlier William Shakespeare rose, this cultivar carries deep velvety crimson-purple, fully double blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous shrub bred for markedly better disease resistance than the original 1987 introduction, which was notoriously prone to black spot. It repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading, and its dark, saturated color makes a dramatic accent among lighter companion plantings.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; willow oak is one of the most graceful and distinctive of the native oaks, bearing narrow, willow-like leaves that give the tree an unusually fine-textured, airy appearance very different from other oaks. It grows naturally in moist bottomland forests and upland slopes throughout the Southeast and is one of the most widely planted native oaks as a street and lawn tree, valued for its tolerance of urban soils, relatively fast growth (1–2 feet per year), and adaptability. The small acorns produced abundantly from age 15 onward are a critical food source for wood ducks, mallards, wild turkeys, and many songbirds. The fine foliage turns attractive golden-yellow in fall before dropping cleanly, and the tree's upright-oval form matures into a large, handsome landscape specimen.

Wilma Goldcrest is a lemon cypress with glowing golden-green foliage that releases a fresh citrus scent when brushed, and a narrow, upright form perfect for tight spaces. Grow it in full sun to keep the foliage brightest, in fast-draining soil that never stays waterlogged. In containers it stays around 3 to 5 feet, while in the ground in mild climates it can reach 10 feet. In zones colder than 7, grow it in a pot and bring it indoors near a bright window over winter. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and avoid soggy roots.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Wilson's magnolia is a Chinese deciduous magnolia introduced from Sichuan province by plant hunter E.H. Wilson in 1908 that produces, in May and June, the most exquisitely formed pendant flowers of any magnolia species — pure-white, circular, saucer-shaped, deeply cupped flowers about 3–4 inches across, with nine large, rounded, pure-white petals surrounding a magnificent, bold, central boss of deep crimson-red to rose-red stamens, hanging nodding on slender stalks from the tips of the branches so that they look directly downward, like ornamental lanterns. The brilliant contrast of the white petals against the vivid crimson stamen cone makes each flower a miniature work of art. Like M. sieboldii, it performs well in partial shade — making it particularly valuable for the woodland garden — and the late flowering season (May–June) means frost damage to the flowers is rare. A connoisseur's magnolia for zone 6–9 gardens seeking unusual shade-tolerant flowering trees. Closely related to and similar to M. sieboldii, distinguished by its slightly larger flowers and different leaf shape.

common_name: Wine and Roses Weigela (Dark Purple-Leaf Pink-Flowered Weigela)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Wine and Roses was a breakthrough weigela introduction for combining rich, dark burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season with abundant clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped spring flowers that stand out sharply against the dark leaves. Hummingbirds are drawn strongly to the tubular flowers, and the plant provides months of foliage-color interest even after the main spring bloom flush ends. It is generally trouble-free, tolerating heat and average garden soil well, and needs only a light shaping prune right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood and heavy pruning at the wrong time removes the next season's flower buds.

Winged Elm is a medium-sized native tree of dry to mesic upland woods, rocky slopes, fence rows, and disturbed roadsides across the southeastern and south-central United States from Virginia to Florida and west to Kansas, readily identified by the distinctive corky, wing-like ridges that develop along younger branches — a feature unique among eastern elms. The seeds ripen in early spring before the leaves emerge and must be sown fresh in moist, well-drained soil immediately upon collection, as germination viability drops to near zero within days of ripening; nursery transplants are the practical method for establishing this species. Winged Elm is among the toughest and most adaptable of the native elms, tolerating drought, compacted clay, alkaline soils, and periodic flooding, and shows some tolerance to Dutch elm disease, making it a useful native tree for difficult urban sites and naturalized roadsides. The vase-shaped canopy, small rough-textured leaves, and light-yellow fall color provide multi-season ornamental interest with minimal maintenance.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Winnifred Gilman sage needs sharp drainage and is more compact and better suited to smaller gardens than the species. Intensely aromatic, wrinkled gray-green leaves cover a rounded, well-branched shrub topped with dense whorls of vivid violet-blue flowers held on distinctive purple-black flower stalks, a strong color contrast that makes this one of the most popular selections of Cleveland sage grown in California native gardens. Its compact size compared to the straight species, combined with exceptional fragrance and a long bloom season that draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, makes it a standout choice for a sunny xeriscape border or native pollinator garden. It needs no supplemental water once established and resents rich soil, heavy mulch, or summer irrigation, all of which shorten its naturally long lifespan.

Plant this Mediterranean evergreen clematis in autumn with its roots shaded and cool while its ferny, sometimes bronze-tinted foliage climbs into brighter light above, the classic cool-roots-sunny-head rule relaxed here since the vine tolerates partial shade throughout. Nodding, bell-shaped cream to pale yellow flowers, often freckled maroon inside, open through winter into early spring when little else in the garden is blooming. It is a useful choice for softening a shaded wall or fence with off-season interest and a light almond scent in some selections. Prune lightly right after flowering to tidy growth without sacrificing next winter's buds.

Plant in sharply drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade and choose the site carefully — winter daphne resents transplanting and should be considered permanent once established. The intensely sweet fragrance of its pink-purple flower clusters from late winter to early spring is one of the most powerful and pleasant in the garden and can perfume the air for 20 feet or more. Excellent drainage is the single most critical cultural requirement; root rot in wet soil kills plants quickly and without warning, a phenomenon so common that gardeners joke that daphne 'dies for no reason.' Keep well-watered during dry spells in summer. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — handle with care and wash hands after pruning.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun with afternoon shade protection; Winter Gem is the most widely planted Korean boxwood cultivar — a tight, globe-forming selection that maintains exceptional dense, rounded form with small, dark-green, lustrous leaves that hold their color better than many boxwood cultivars through winter and summer. The deep, rich green color with a slightly glossy sheen is particularly attractive as a formal edging or clipped topiary subject. Unlike many Buxus sempervirens cultivars, Winter Gem shows markedly superior resistance to boxwood blight (Calonectria pseudonaviculata), which has devastated English boxwood plantings across much of the Eastern United States — this disease resistance is a major reason Korean boxwood cultivars have increased in popularity. Winter Gem tolerates zone 9 summer heat better than English boxwood selections, provided afternoon shade protects from the most intense sun. Boxwoods require well-drained soil — they are extremely susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet, poorly drained sites. No serious pests affect boxwood in Gulf Coast gardens except the boxwood leafminer, which causes blistering of the leaves; treat with systemic insecticide if infestation is severe. Shear or hand-prune to maintain desired formal shape in late winter or after spring flush.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter honeysuckle blooms on bare branches in late winter, filling the garden with fragrance well before spring. Small, creamy white, unassuming flowers open along the bare branches in late winter to very early spring, easy to overlook visually but releasing an intense, sweet, lemon-and-jasmine-like fragrance that carries a remarkable distance on a still winter day, making this shrub prized for scent rather than showy bloom. A large, rounded, semi-evergreen to deciduous shrub, it is best sited near a door, window, or path where its understated but powerful winter fragrance can be enjoyed up close during the coldest, least colorful part of the year. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, and note that it has naturalized and become weedy in some regions, so monitor for unwanted seedlings and consider a well-behaved native alternative where invasive spread is a local concern.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; winter jasmine tolerates poor soil and looks best cascading over a wall or bank where its arching stems can drape freely. Bright yellow, star-shaped flowers open along bare, arching green stems from late winter into early spring, well ahead of most other flowering shrubs, providing a welcome flush of cheerful color during the last cold weeks of winter dormancy despite lacking the fragrance of its jasmine relatives. Its long, sprawling, cascading stems root wherever they touch soil, making it a useful, tough groundcover for a bank or the top of a retaining wall where its arching branches can spill downward and its winter bloom can be appreciated from below. Prune immediately after flowering to shape and control spread, since it blooms on the previous year's wood, and it tolerates hard renewal pruning if the planting becomes overgrown.

common_name: Winter's Star Camellia (Cold-Hardy Orchid-Pink Ackerman Camellia)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through winter cold snaps. Winter's Star belongs to the Winter series of cold-hardy camellia hybrids developed at the U.S. National Arboretum, crossing Camellia oleifera into the hardier fall-blooming Camellia hiemalis lineage to combine dependable fall-into-winter flowering with markedly better cold tolerance than most camellias. It produces single, orchid-pink flowers with prominent golden stamens on a vigorous, spreading evergreen shrub, blooming over a long season from fall into early winter when few other shrubs are in flower. Feed lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer after the main bloom period, and prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends, since next year's buds set on the current year's new growth.

Plant in moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; winterberry is a spectacular native deciduous holly that produces brilliant red (or yellow or orange in some cultivars) berries that encrust every branch after leaf drop in fall, providing dazzling winter interest from October through February when birds finally strip them. It grows naturally in swamps, stream banks, and wet woodland margins and performs best with consistent moisture. This species is dioecious — you must plant both male and female plants, matching cultivars that bloom at the same time, to get berries. Named female cultivars like 'Winter Red', 'Sparkleberry', and 'Red Sprite' (compact) are widely available; match them with the appropriate male. Mulch to maintain soil moisture and acidity.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Wintergreen boxwood holds its green winter color better than many boxwood cultivars, which often bronze in cold weather. Small, glossy, bright green leaves cover a dense, rounded, exceptionally cold-hardy boxwood selection bred for reliable survival in harsh northern winters where many traditional boxwood cultivars suffer dieback, while retaining fresh green foliage color through the coldest months rather than the bronzing common in less hardy types. Its combination of superior cold hardiness and good winter color has made it a popular substitute for English boxwood in colder climates, used for low hedges, edging, and formal shapes much like its more tender relatives. Shear in late spring or early summer to maintain a formal shape, water during establishment and dry spells, and provide good air circulation to reduce the fungal disease pressure that affects many boxwood plantings.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a warm wall or in a sheltered spot near a path where its fragrance can be appreciated up close; wintersweet is an old Chinese garden shrub grown for one thing above all — intensely sweet, spicy fragrance from small, waxy, translucent pale-yellow flowers with maroon-purple centers that open on bare gray branches in the dead of winter, often during a warm spell between freezes, well before the glossy leaves emerge. A single stem cut and brought indoors will scent an entire room. The shrub itself is an unremarkable, rangy, multi-stemmed grower with plain foliage the rest of the year, so site it where winter interest matters and something else can carry the summer show, such as near an entry or a frequently used winter path. It tolerates partial shade but flowers most heavily with several hours of sun. Prune immediately after flowering, since next winter's buds form on the current year's growth; older plants can be renovated by cutting the oldest stems to the ground.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; American witch hazel is the latest-blooming native shrub, producing clusters of fragrant, spidery yellow flowers on bare branches from October through December — often while the leaves are still falling around the flowers. It is a stunning sight in the November woodland garden when nothing else is in bloom. Growing naturally as a multi-stemmed understory tree in moist woodland slopes and ravines across eastern North America, it tolerates full shade but blooms more heavily with some dappled light. The bark and leaves are the botanical source of witch hazel astringent. Allow it to grow naturally as a large multi-stemmed specimen; it resents heavy pruning. The seed pods pop open explosively to disperse seeds.

common_name: Wolf Eyes Kousa Dogwood (Variegated Dwarf Kousa Dogwood)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the variegated leaves. Wolf Eyes is a dwarf, slow-growing kousa dogwood grown as much for its striking foliage as its flowers, with leaves crisply edged in creamy white around a gray-green center, turning shades of pink and burgundy-red in fall, along with a modest early-summer flush of white bracts against the variegated backdrop. Its smaller mature size and dense, compact habit make it a strong specimen for smaller gardens or as a focal accent near a patio where the foliage can be appreciated up close. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Wollerton Old Hall Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes as a climber; prune lightly to shape after the main flush rather than hard-pruning, which sacrifices height. Introduced by David Austin in 2011, Wollerton Old Hall produces soft apricot-cream, cupped rosette flowers carrying one of the strongest myrrh fragrances of any English rose, on long, arching, thornier-than-average canes that can reach 10 feet or more when trained upright, or be kept as a large freestanding shrub with pruning. Its vigor, fragrance, and repeat bloom from late spring through frost have made it a favorite for both border and climbing use in warm-climate gardens.

common_name: Woman's Tongue (Siris Tree, East Indian Walnut)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established. CAUTION: invasive in Florida — do not plant near natural areas. Albizia lebbeck (woman's tongue or siris tree) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous-to-semi-evergreen tropical legume tree native to South Asia and tropical Africa, now widely naturalized throughout the tropics as both a valued shade tree and an invasive species. The plant is named 'woman's tongue' for its persistent, flat, tan, papery, 6–10 inch long seed pods that hold their seeds loosely and rattle loudly in the slightest breeze — the metaphorical association being obvious. As a landscape tree, Woman's Tongue is excellent: it grows rapidly (3–5 feet per year), provides dense, spreading shade, fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root bacteria, produces attractive cream-white, fragrant, powder-puff flower clusters in late spring, and is extraordinarily drought-tolerant on poor soils. The bark has traditionally yielded saponins used as a soap substitute in India. The wood is highly valued as a timber for furniture and construction in South Asia. IMPORTANT CAUTION: In Florida, coastal Gulf South states, and Hawaii, Albizia lebbeck is classified as an invasive exotic pest plant — it naturalizes in disturbed areas, roadsides, and natural areas aggressively. Do not plant in proximity to natural lands in Florida or coastal Gulf states.

common_name: Wood Rose (Yellow Morning Glory, Hawaiian Wood Rose)
notes: Direct sow scarified seeds in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; wood rose is drought-tolerant and vigorous once established — provide a very strong support. Merremia tuberosa (wood rose or Hawaiian wood rose) is a large, fast-growing tropical vine in the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae) native to Mexico and Central America, now naturalized and widely grown throughout the tropics. It produces large (3-inch), beautiful, pale golden-yellow, funnel-shaped morning glory flowers throughout the warm season. But the real treasure of wood rose is its extraordinary seed pod: as the flower fades and the fruit ripens, the calyx (the five-lobed green backing of the flower) expands and stiffens into a large, starfish-shaped, papery-woody structure 2–3 inches across, remaining on the vine to dry naturally. When fully dry, these calyces are deep chestnut-brown, rigid, and resemble intricately carved wooden roses — hence the name. The dried pods are highly prized in the craft and dried flower market, used in wreaths, arrangements, and floral crafts. Seed the pods during summer, collect in fall, and air-dry for use. In Hawaii, where the vine has naturalized widely, it is considered invasive in some native plant habitats. NOTE: Seeds may contain mildly psychoactive ergot alkaloids (similar to morning glory seeds) — do not ingest.

Plant rooted suckers or nursery stock in spring in average, well-drained soil and full to partial sun, allowing room for the thicket-forming shrub to spread by underground rhizomes into a dense, thorny colony. Wood's rose ranges from the Great Plains to the Pacific Coast and from Canada into Mexico, tolerating cold winters, drought, and poor soils better than most cultivated roses. Its fragrant pink single flowers in early summer feed native bees, and the bright red hips that follow persist through winter, providing critical food for grouse, pheasants, and songbirds along with browse for deer. The dense, prickly thickets also create some of the safest nesting cover available to grassland and shrubland birds.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone cool and shaded while allowing stems to climb toward light; woodbine is the native European honeysuckle celebrated in Shakespeare's writings and the source of the intensely sweet evening fragrance associated with English cottage gardens. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica), this species is non-invasive and suitable for planting in naturalistic gardens. The tubular flowers, creamy-white flushed with pink and purple, are exceptionally fragrant in the evening and attract hawk moths; the red berries feed warblers, thrushes, and other birds in late summer. Popular cultivars include 'Serotina' (late Dutch, deep purple outside), 'Graham Thomas' (creamy white aging to yellow), and 'Belgica' (early Dutch honeysuckle). Prune lightly after flowering to shape.

common_name: Woodbridge Rose of Sharon (Classic Rosy-Pink Red-Eyed Althea)
notes: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Woodbridge is one of the most popular and long-cultivated rose of sharon selections, bearing large, single, rich rosy-pink flowers with a deep red eye at the center, blooming prolifically from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its rich, saturated color and reliable heavy bloom have kept it a garden favorite for decades, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden soil with ease, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern.

Native to the scrub and stabilized secondary dunes of the Florida Panhandle and Gulf Coast, this rounded evergreen shrub produces silvery, resinous foliage and a showy flush of small yellow flower heads in mid to late fall. It is extremely drought and salt tolerant once rooted, thriving in deep, sterile beach or scrub sand where few other flowering shrubs survive. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and resist the urge to fertilize or irrigate beyond the first season. It works well massed on dune crests or in xeric coastal gardens where its fall bloom complements late-season grasses like muhly and bluestem.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; woolly butterfly bush is a compact, rounded Chihuahuan Desert shrub with small, felted, silvery-gray leaves densely covered in soft wool-like hairs, and small, tight, ball-shaped clusters of bright orange flowers in spring and again after summer rains. Unlike the fast-growing, sometimes weedy Buddleja davidii common in nurseries, this species stays naturally compact and slow-growing, making it far better suited to small xeriscape gardens and rock plantings without becoming leggy or invasive. Its dense silvery foliage and modest size pair well with agaves, yuccas, and other true desert plants in a mixed xeriscape border, and it is visited by butterflies and bees during its bloom periods. It requires excellent drainage and minimal water once established, needing only light shaping after flowering to maintain its naturally tidy, rounded form.

common_name: Woolly Congea (Shower Orchid Vine, Lilac Vine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; woolly congea is a vigorous vine requiring strong support and can become very large — provide a sturdy pergola or large fence. Congea tomentosa (woolly congea, shower orchid vine, or lilac vine) is one of the most spectacular and unusual tropical flowering vines available for zone 10–12 gardens — a native of Thailand, Myanmar, and Southeast Asian dry tropical forests where it scrambles over trees in the deciduous forest canopy. The ornamental display of congea is completely different from most flowering vines: the actual flowers are tiny and inconspicuous, but each small cluster is surrounded by three large, petal-like, woolly bracts (modified leaves) that are the true ornamental display. These bracts, 1–2 inches long, are produced in enormous quantities in dense, cascading clusters that cover the vine during the cool, dry season (winter to early spring in zone 10–12) — pale lavender-lilac when fresh, fading to silvery-white as they age. The overall effect of a flowering congea is one of cascading pale-lavender to white woolly clusters hanging in billowing masses from the vine — sometimes compared to a waterfall of lavender or a shower of lilac snow. The vine can reach enormous size (30–50 feet) on a large pergola or tree. After flowering, the silvery dried bracts persist attractively for weeks. A breathtaking and rare ornamental vine for large tropical gardens.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun with a sturdy support structure; woolly Dutchman's pipe is the southeastern US native species of Aristolochia, distinguished from A. macrophylla by its dense woolly coating of soft hairs on the leaves and stems — a beautiful textural detail. Like all native Aristolochia species, it is the exclusive larval host plant for the pipevine swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor), one of the most spectacular black-and-iridescent-blue native butterflies in eastern North America. A single established vine supports dozens of caterpillars each season. The unusual curved, yellowish-green to brown pipe-shaped flowers are insect-trapping devices that temporarily trap small flies for pollination. Twining stems reach 10–20 feet and provide rapid screening in partial shade. Highly recommended for butterfly gardens in zones 5–9, particularly in the Southeast where this species is native.

Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; woolly sweetspire is a native ericaceous shrub of wet, acidic Coastal Plain habitats — pocosins, bay edges, moist pine flatwoods, and the margins of Carolina bays — from Virginia to Georgia. The dense, white, fragrant flower racemes in midsummer are intensely perfumed and highly attractive to native bees, particularly bumblebees, which find the tubular flowers accessible. The woolly-textured leaves and stems (more densely hairy than C. alnifolia) give the plant a distinctive soft appearance. Fall foliage turns orange to red. As with all sweetspires, it thrives in moist, acidic woodland gardens and wetland edges — excellent for rain gardens and moist shade borders in zones 5–9. Spreads slowly by stolons to form colonies.

Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Xanadu is a compact, self-heading philodendron hybrid selected for its neat, rounded mound of deeply lobed, glossy dark green leaves that never develop the sprawling scale or trunk of full-sized selloum, making it far better suited to foundation plantings, mixed shade borders, and mass plantings in smaller garden spaces. It holds a tidy, symmetrical form with minimal care, needing only the occasional removal of an old lower leaf to stay attractive year-round in frost-free climates. Container culture works well anywhere, with plants moved indoors to a bright spot before the first frost in climates colder than its hardiness range. Established outdoor plantings tolerate brief light frost with foliage damage but generally recover from the crown, much like other tender aroids grown in zone 9.

Plant in full sun to full shade in virtually any well-drained to periodically wet soil — yaupon holly is among the most stress-tolerant of all native North American shrubs, thriving in sand, clay, limestone caliche, brackish coastal soils, and dry urban sites once established. Ilex vomitoria is the only native North American plant known to contain significant quantities of caffeine, and its dried leaves were used by Indigenous peoples of the Southeast to brew a stimulating ceremonial tea called 'Black Drink' — today it is being explored commercially as a sustainable source of caffeine for teas and beverages. Female plants produce masses of small, translucent-red (rarely yellow) berries that persist through winter and provide critical food for cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, bluebirds, and many other bird species. Outstanding cultivars range from large screening shrubs to weeping forms, dwarf groundcovers, and topiary specimens, giving landscape designers exceptional versatility with a genuinely native, wildlife-supporting plant.

Plant in spring or early fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Yeddo hawthorn is drought-tolerant once established and extremely tolerant of salt spray and coastal conditions, making it an outstanding choice for beachfront and coastal zone 8–10 landscapes. Yeddo hawthorn (R. umbellata) is the Japanese species of Raphiolepis, larger and slower-growing than the commonly sold Indian hawthorn (R. indica), with distinctly thick, leathery, very dark green rounded leaves and showy clusters of large, pure white fragrant flowers in spring followed by dark blue-black berries attractive to birds; the overall appearance is more refined and dramatic than other Raphiolepis. Excellent as a specimen plant, in foundation plantings, or as a formal hedge in coastal and Gulf Coast landscapes where salt tolerance is essential.

Yellow anise tree is a rare Florida native evergreen shrub endemic to the Ocala National Forest and surrounding central Florida scrub and flatwoods, closely related to Florida anise (Illicium floridanum) but producing small, inconspicuous yellow flowers rather than red ones — its primary appeal is its dense, lustrous evergreen foliage and exceptional shade tolerance that make it one of the finest screening shrubs for difficult deep-shade sites in Gulf Coast landscapes. All parts of the plant contain toxic compounds similar to true star anise (Illicium verum) and emit a strong, pleasant anise-like fragrance when crushed, making deer browsing rare — an excellent choice where deer pressure limits other evergreen shrubs. Plants grow moderately quickly into dense, mounding 5–10 foot specimens that provide excellent year-round privacy screening in shaded settings where hollies and other broadleaf evergreens might struggle; they tolerate periodic flooding and are well-suited to moist, organic soils. As a critically rare Florida endemic, yellow anise tree deserves wider use in horticulture throughout zones 7–10 wherever a tough, fragrant, shade-tolerant evergreen screening shrub is needed.

common_name: Yellow Bauhinia (Bell Bauhinia, St. Thomas Tree)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape. Bauhinia tomentosa (yellow bauhinia, bell bauhinia, or St. Thomas tree) is a deciduous to semi-evergreen shrub or small tree from the tropical dry forests and savannas of East Africa, India, and Sri Lanka — a member of the enormous Bauhinia genus (orchid trees) but markedly different in appearance from the more commonly cultivated purple orchid tree (B. variegata) and red orchid tree (B. blakeana). The flowers of B. tomentosa are distinctive and elegant: large (3–4 inch), bell-shaped with five petals that do not spread as broadly as other orchid tree flowers, colored a soft pale-yellow to cream-yellow with one petal bearing a dramatic deep-maroon to near-black central stain — a striking bicolor combination unlike any other Bauhinia. The leaves are the characteristic twin-lobed 'butterfly' shape shared by all Bauhinia species (resembling two joined leaves — the genus name honors botanist Gaspard and Johann Bauhin, twin brothers, for this two-lobed leaf). In zone 8–11, yellow bauhinia is a more compact and cold-hardy Bauhinia option than many tropical relatives, making it useful in zone 8b gardens that cannot support larger tropical Bauhinia species. The bark has traditional medicinal uses in Indian Ayurveda.

Plant in full sun in any well-drained to dry soil — sandy, rocky, alkaline, and poor soils are all acceptable; esperanza or yellow bells is a native flowering shrub and small tree of Texas, the Southwest, and Mexico that produces brilliant golden-yellow trumpet-shaped flowers in large clusters almost continuously from late spring through frost. It is among the most heat tolerant and drought resistant flowering plants available for zone 8–11 landscapes, thriving in conditions that challenge almost everything else. The showy flowers attract hummingbirds and butterflies prolifically throughout the summer. The cultivar 'Gold Star' is the most widely planted, selected for compact habit and extra-large flower clusters. Esperanza grows vigorously and may need annual cutting back in mild winters; in zone 9 it is woody and persistent year-round while in zone 8 it typically dies to the ground in winter and regrows from roots. It blooms on new wood, so frost damage sets back the plant temporarily, not permanently.

Yellow Birch is a graceful, long-lived native tree of moist, cool Appalachian and northeastern forests from eastern Canada south to the mountains of Georgia and Tennessee, distinguished by its golden-yellow to bronze, papery bark that peels in thin, curly horizontal strips and provides remarkable year-round ornamental interest. The young twigs and inner bark carry a distinctive sweet wintergreen fragrance from the natural methyl salicylate they contain, and the sap can be tapped in late winter for a birch syrup similar to maple syrup; the bark was historically distilled to produce oil of wintergreen. An important component of northern hardwood forest ecosystems, Yellow Birch provides critical nesting habitat for warblers, vireos, and thrushes while moose, deer, and snowshoe hares browse the twigs and bark through winter. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich, cool soil in partial shade to full sun; Yellow Birch demands consistently cool, moist conditions and is not suitable for hot, dry, or alkaline climates.

common_name: Yellow Bird of Paradise (Desert Bird of Paradise)
notes: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; yellow bird of paradise is a native of Argentina that has naturalized extensively in the American Southwest and Mexico, prized for its brilliant, eye-catching flowers — large, canary-yellow petals surrounding long, dramatic, brilliant-red stamens that extend 2–3 inches beyond the petals in striking contrast. The flowers appear in loose, upright clusters at the branch tips from summer through fall — a spectacularly colorful display during the dry season when many desert plants are dormant. The compound, ferny, blue-green foliage is attractive on its own. It is among the most drought-tolerant ornamental shrubs available, requiring virtually no water once established in desert climates, but can be grown throughout zones 8–11 with well-drained soil. Caution: it reseeds prolifically and has naturalized invasively in parts of the Sonoran Desert and adjacent areas; check local invasive status before planting in Arizona and southern New Mexico.

Plant in moist, fertile, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade — yellow buckeye is unusual among trees in that it actually performs better in partial shade than full sun, making it one of the best large native trees for the shaded garden. Native to rich mountain forests of the southern Appalachians, it produces beautiful upright clusters of yellow flowers in spring that attract hummingbirds and long-tongued native bees, and large smooth seed pods containing 1–3 mahogany-brown nuts with pale patches — striking ornamental fall fruit. The palmate compound leaves of 5 leaflets are among the first to emerge in spring and first to drop in fall (often by August in drought). It tolerates understory conditions and is frequently found growing as a subcanopy tree beneath tulip poplar and basswood. The nuts are toxic to humans but consumed by squirrels. Often considered the most beautiful of the North American buckeyes.

Scarify seeds before direct-sowing or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun; yellow flame tree (copper pod, copperpod) is a large tropical tree native to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia and widely planted throughout the tropical world as a street, shade, and ornamental tree of exceptional quality — it produces dense, spreading canopy of finely divided, bipinnate, feathery, dark-green leaves that create a graceful, filtered shade, and from summer through fall, produces large, upright, terminal and lateral panicles of vivid yellow, five-petaled, fragrant flowers that bloom in flushes and can blanket the canopy in golden yellow. After the flowers, the tree produces masses of distinctive, flat, winged pods that mature through russet-brown to bright copper-red, persisting ornamentally on the tree for months and giving it the common name 'copper pod'. The tree's fine foliage, yellow flowers, copper seedpod clusters, and attractive form make it ornamental across multiple seasons. It is fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, and widely used as a street tree in tropical cities across Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and South Florida.

Yellow honeysuckle is a native semi-evergreen vine of the Ozarks and Appalachian foothills, one of the most ornamentally beautiful of all American honeysuckles — its showy clusters of vivid golden-yellow to orange-yellow trumpet flowers in spring are magnets for ruby-throated hummingbirds during their northward migration and are also visited by long-tongued bumblebees and sphinx moths. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) that has escaped across the South, yellow honeysuckle is a well-behaved native that twines moderately and stays in bounds without smothering trees or shrubs; it is semi-evergreen in mild winters in the South. Small red berries ripen in summer and are eaten by mockingbirds and other fruit-eating birds. Train on a picket fence, stone wall, arbor, or through a native shrub border — it blooms most profusely in partial shade to full sun and combines beautifully with coral honeysuckle for extended bloom.

common_name: Yellow Ipe (Brazilian Trumpet Tree, Yellow Lapacho, Guayacan Amarillo)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Yellow Ipe is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in the sandy, well-drained soils common throughout Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes. Handroanthus serratifolius is a large, deciduous to semi-deciduous tree native to Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, and Brazil in the Bignoniaceae family, one of several South American species collectively called 'Ipê Amarelo' (Yellow Ipe) — celebrated as among the most spectacular flowering trees in the world. In late winter to spring, the tree drops its leaves and then, on the leafless branches, produces one of the most dramatic flower displays in all of the tree kingdom: the entire canopy simultaneously explodes in masses of large, 3-inch, brilliant golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers covering every branch without a single leaf to distract from the flower display — the tree appears from a distance as a cloud of pure, intense yellow gold. After the bloom, the new leaves emerge as the flowers fall, carpeting the ground with a golden layer of spent petals. The wood of Ipê (called 'ironwood' in lumber trade) is one of the hardest, most durable timbers in the world — rated Class A for marine and ground-contact use and used for heavy decking, bridges, and structural applications across South America and in exported form worldwide. In the ornamental world, the bloom display alone justifies the tree's cultivation in zone 9-12 landscapes.

Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, gritty, well-drained soil in a cool, partly shaded site, recreating the high alpine and subalpine slopes of the Cascades and northern Rockies where it often grows beside its pink-flowered relative. Clusters of small, urn-shaped, greenish-yellow to cream flowers open in early summer above dense needle-like foliage, and where the two species overlap they hybridize into an intermediate-colored form. Give it steady moisture and cool summers; it declines quickly in hot, dry, or poorly drained garden conditions.

common_name: Yellow Oleander (Lucky Nut, Be-Still Tree, Cascabela thevetia)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil; Yellow Oleander is drought-tolerant once established and will rot in heavy, consistently wet soils. Cascabela thevetia (formerly Thevetia peruviana) is a large, evergreen shrub or small tree from Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean in the Apocynaceae family — distantly related to Oleander (Nerium) and sharing its extreme toxicity. The plant produces long, narrow, deep green, glossy, lance-shaped leaves that densely clothe the arching stems, and bears funnel-shaped, slightly fragrant flowers 2–3 inches across in brilliant yellow — occasionally orange-yellow or peach in some forms. Flowering occurs year-round in zone 10-11 and from spring through fall in zone 9, with peak bloom in warm months. In tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, Yellow Oleander is one of the most commonly planted ornamental shrubs for hot, dry, full-sun landscapes — its combination of attractive foliage, continuous flowers, and extreme drought and heat tolerance makes it exceptionally useful. EXTREME CAUTION: All parts of Yellow Oleander contain highly toxic cardiac glycosides (thevetin A and B, neriifolin) that affect the heart — the large black seeds are particularly concentrated and have caused accidental poisonings and intentional toxicity events worldwide; do not plant where children, pets, or livestock have access.

Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; yellow passionflower is the most shade-tolerant native Passiflora species and is far less aggressive than maypop (P. incarnata), making it more suitable for smaller gardens and shaded areas. The flowers are smaller than other passionflowers but share the same intricate, layered structure — creamy yellow-green petals and a distinctive corona of filaments — and are visited by long-tongued native bees for nectar. Like all native Passiflora, yellow passionflower is a host plant for the larvae of gulf fritillary, variegated fritillary, and zebra longwing butterflies. The small dark purple fruits are eaten by birds. It grows naturally along shaded woodland edges, thickets, and roadsides throughout the southeastern US and is one of the best native vines for adding butterfly-host value to a shaded fence or trellis.

Plant container specimens in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; yellow trumpet tree is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the tropical and subtropical world, producing an explosion of brilliant golden-yellow trumpet-shaped flowers completely covering the bare branches in late winter to early spring before the new leaf flush — the brief but unforgettable show stops traffic when the tree is in peak bloom. Trees grow 15–30 feet tall and wide and tolerate drought, poor soils, and salt once established. Established plants are somewhat cold-hardy to 28°F for brief periods; young trees require frost protection in zone 9 until established. The wood is extraordinarily dense and durable, historically used for bow-making and tool handles.

common_name: Yellow Trumpet Tree (Yellow Tabebuia, Golden Tree, Ipe Amarelo)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, any-type soil including alkaline limestone soils in frost-free locations; yellow trumpet tree (Handroanthus chrysanthus, formerly Tabebuia chrysantha) is a semi-deciduous tree producing spectacular clusters of brilliant golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers in late winter before the new leaves emerge, creating a breathtaking solid-yellow canopy for one to three weeks — among the most stunning floral displays of any tree in the world. It is the national tree of Brazil (ipê amarelo) and commonly planted as a street and park tree in south Florida and along the Gulf Coast. Exceptionally drought-tolerant, hurricane-resistant, and adaptable to poor soils once established. Plant as a specimen in a lawn or as an avenue tree where its brief but extraordinary bloom can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Yellow Trumpet Vine (Chamberlain's Anemopaegma, Golden Bignonia)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Yellow Trumpet Vine blooms most prolifically in full sun and produces fewer flowers and more vegetative growth in shaded positions. Anemopaegma chamberlaynii is a vigorous, tendril-climbing, woody vine native to Brazil in the Bignoniaceae family, grown for its display of large, bright yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers that closely resemble those of Allamanda or the yellow form of Bignonia capreolata. The flowers are large (2–3 inches long), funnel-shaped to trumpet-shaped, bright golden-yellow, with five spreading, slightly frilled petal lobes — produced in terminal and axillary clusters throughout the spring and fall. The vine has attractive, pinnately compound leaves with 2 leaflets and a terminal tendril that grips supports for climbing. In zone 9-10 Gulf Coast conditions, Anemopaegma chamberlaynii is valued as a less common but ornamentally rewarding alternative to more frequently planted Bignoniaceae vines like Bignonia capreolata and Campsis radicans, producing the same general 'trumpet vine' aesthetic but in a pure, clear yellow. The genus name 'Anemopaegma' comes from the Greek for 'playing in the wind' — referring to the delicate, light movement of the flowers in a breeze. A handsome and underused flowering vine for zone 9-11 fences and arbors.

Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist soil in partial to full shade; yellowroot is a low, colony-forming native shrub of Appalachian stream banks and moist woodland slopes, grown for its ferny, compound foliage that provides attractive, fine-textured groundcover in shade, its drooping panicles of small maroon-purple flowers in early spring, and its outstanding orange-gold fall color. The roots and inner bark are vividly yellow from the alkaloid berberine (also found in goldenseal), historically used as a natural yellow dye and for medicinal purposes. As a groundcover, it spreads vigorously by rhizome to form weed-suppressing mats under trees, on moist slopes, and along shaded stream banks. One of the best native low-maintenance groundcovers for moist shade.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; yesterday today tomorrow (Paraguayan brunfelsia, Paraguay raintree) is a South American evergreen or semi-evergreen shrub whose flowers perform the unique trick of opening deep violet-purple on the first day, fading to lavender on the second, and turning pure white on the third — so that at any one time the shrub simultaneously displays all three color stages in a captivating three-tone effect that gives the plant its evocative common name. The intensely sweet, jasmine-like fragrance of the flowers is strongest in the evening. Brunfelsia australis is the hardier of the commercial species, surviving brief cold snaps to around 25°F in protected locations, making it more suitable for zone 8 than the less cold-tolerant Brunfelsia pauciflora. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, particularly the berries, and represent a significant risk to dogs who may be attracted to the fallen fruit. Thrives in the dappled light of an open tree canopy. Excellent as a fragrant specimen or informal hedge in warm coastal gardens.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) produces best performance.
