Brunfelsia pauciflora (yesterday today and tomorrow or morning noon night) is a Brazilian tropical shrub famous for one of the most charming color-change performances of any flowering plant — new flowers open deep violet-purple ('yesterday'), fade to lavender the next day ('today'), and become nearly white by the third day ('tomorrow') — creating a three-toned tapestry of violet, lavender, and white flowers simultaneously visible on the plant at all times, against a backdrop of glossy, dark-green, somewhat wavy leaves. The flowers are sweetly fragrant, especially in the evening. The shrub is compact (3–6 feet), with a naturally tidy form that requires little pruning; it blooms most heavily in spring and may rebloom after summer rains. In zone 9, it typically survives mild winters with light frost damage, rejuvenating vigorously in spring; protect from hard freezes below 28°F. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested; the berries are especially dangerous to children and pets.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; yesterday-today-and-tomorrow takes its name from one of the most enchanting flower color-change sequences in horticulture: the fragrant, flat-faced flowers open deep violet-purple ('yesterday'), fade to lavender ('today'), and turn white ('tomorrow') before dropping — so at any given moment a single plant displays all three colors simultaneously, creating a remarkable polychrome effect. The sweetly fragrant flowers appear in spring and intermittently through summer and fall. This attractive, moderate-growing evergreen shrub performs best in the bright shade of a pergola or lath house where it is protected from scorching afternoon sun. A critical caution: all parts of the plant are highly toxic to dogs, causing severe neurological symptoms including tremors and seizures — it should not be planted where dogs can access the fruit or flowers. Prune lightly after the main spring bloom flush.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; ylang-ylang is the source of one of the most important perfume ingredients in the world — the intensely fragrant yellow-green flowers with long, drooping petals are steam-distilled to produce the essential oil used in Chanel No. 5, Joy, and countless other perfumes. The scent is rich, heavy, and intensely sweet with notes of jasmine, narcissus, and banana. The tree grows remarkably fast — producing a graceful, weeping tropical specimen in just a few years — with pendulous branches and large, oval leaves. Flowers are produced year-round in tropical climates and are used fresh in garlands and as bedroom perfumers throughout Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Ylang-ylang is the national flower of the Philippines, where it is called 'poor man's perfume.' Only suited to outdoor culture in frost-free zone 10–12.

The Yoshino cherry is the classic flowering cherry famed for its spring canopy of fragrant, blush-white blossoms that open before the leaves emerge. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, giving it plenty of room for its broad, spreading crown. Water regularly while young and mulch the root zone, keeping the mulch off the trunk. Prune sparingly and only just after bloom, since cherries are susceptible to disease through large wounds. It provides light shade in summer and golden-bronze foliage in fall, making it a beloved landscape specimen.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. 'Yoshino' is one of the most widely planted Japanese cedar selections in American gardens because its dense, soft, blue-green foliage stays green through winter rather than turning the bronze-purple typical of the species, and its broadly pyramidal form and faster growth rate suit it well to screening and hedging. It reaches a moderate mature size compared with the towering wild species, making it a more practical choice for residential-scale privacy plantings while still providing the fine, feathery texture Japanese cedar is prized for.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yuletide is perhaps the most distinctive and widely grown Camellia sasanqua cultivar for its brilliant red flowers with a contrasting boss of bright golden-yellow stamens — a vivid red-and-gold color combination that perfectly matches the traditional holiday color palette, earning the cultivar its name. While most sasanqua camellias bloom in October–November, Yuletide blooms in December–January in zone 9, providing genuine holiday-season color at the precise time when few other plants are in flower. The single, bright red flowers with the prominent golden stamens are smaller than japonica flowers but produced prolifically, covering the upright shrub with vivid color during the typically brown and gray winter garden season. The compact to medium-sized, upright habit grows 5–10 feet tall with dense, small, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage. Yuletide tolerates more sun than most camellias — sasanqua types generally prefer more sun than japonica camellias — and performs well in 4–6 hours of direct sun with some afternoon protection. The late bloom season makes Yuletide less susceptible to freeze damage on open flowers than earlier-blooming camellias, though the flowers will be damaged by hard freezes below 28°F. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil pH for best performance.

common_name: Yuma Crape Myrtle (Lavender-Flowered Mildew-Resistant Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Yuma is a medium-sized crape myrtle from the U.S. National Arboretum's mildew-resistant Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei breeding program, producing generous clusters of soft lavender flowers through the summer on a well-branched, upright tree. Like its better-known siblings such as Natchez and Muskogee, it carries strong resistance to powdery mildew, the primary disease that plagues straight Lagerstroemia indica cultivars in humid climates, along with good fall foliage color and attractive bark as the tree matures. Its medium mature size makes it a versatile choice for a specimen tree in a moderate-size yard where the largest crape myrtles would eventually overwhelm the space. Never top or hard-prune the main framework, since this permanently disfigures the natural form; instead prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or crowded twiggy growth.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Yunnan camellia is less cold-hardy than Camellia japonica and best suited to zones 8-9. Prized among camellia specialists for producing some of the largest flowers of any camellia species, often eight inches or more across, with prominently veined, semi-double to fully double blooms in shades of rose-pink to deep red on a somewhat looser, more open-growing shrub than the denser, more familiar Camellia japonica. Native to the mountains of Yunnan province in southwestern China, it has been extensively hybridized with Camellia japonica to produce many of the largest-flowered modern camellia cultivars, though the pure species itself remains a coveted specimen for dedicated collectors. Provide the same acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and dappled shade other camellias require, protect from hard freezes given its somewhat reduced cold hardiness, and mulch well to keep roots cool and moist.

Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yunnan michelia is more compact and more shade-tolerant than banana shrub, its closer relative, and works well as a foundation shrub in filtered shade. Michelia yunnanensis (sometimes sold as Magnolia laevifolia) is a dense, compact, evergreen relative of magnolia from southwestern China, with small, glossy, deep green leaves backed in rusty brown felt and creamy white, cup-shaped, intensely fragrant flowers with a fruity, banana-like scent opening from furry brown buds in spring. Its naturally tidy, rounded habit needs little pruning to stay attractive, making it a low-maintenance evergreen specimen or informal hedge for a shaded courtyard or foundation planting in warm-climate gardens. It appreciates consistent moisture and acidic soil similar to camellia and azalea, and benefits from a wind-sheltered site at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.

Plant in well-drained to moderately moist soil and water regularly until established, after which the shrub shows good drought tolerance compared to other sweetspires. Long, arching racemes of fragrant white flowers appear in early summer, followed by excellent red to orange-red fall foliage color that holds late into the season. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a tidy shape and encourage branching, removing any dead or crowded stems at the base. Mulch annually to protect the root zone and retain soil moisture through the hottest months.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; yuzuriha is slow-growing and long-lived, so allow generous room for its eventual size and avoid siting it where later transplanting would be needed. Daphniphyllum macropodum is a handsome, coarse-textured evergreen shrub or small tree from Japan and Korea grown for its large, glossy, leathery, rhododendron-like leaves carried on distinctive red-tinged petioles, with inconspicuous flowers in spring and small blue-black fruit on female plants. In Japan the new leaves emerge only after the old ones drop, symbolizing generational succession, which gives the plant its common name and traditional use in New Year decorations. It makes a substantial, deer-resistant evergreen backdrop or specimen for a shaded border, tolerating deep shade better than most broadleaf evergreens, and needs little maintenance beyond occasional shaping once established.

common_name: Zhuzhou Loropetalum (Tall Vigorous Purple-Leaf Fringe Flower)
notes: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade for the deepest foliage color. Zhuzhou is one of the larger, more vigorous loropetalum selections, growing into a substantial evergreen shrub or small tree rather than the low, compact mounds bred more recently for foundation plantings, making it valuable where a tall screen or specimen with the same rich burgundy-purple foliage and fringy hot-pink spring flowers is wanted. It flowers heavily in spring with a lighter rebloom possible later in the season, and the deep foliage color holds well through summer heat given adequate sun. It tolerates a range of soil conditions once established and needs only occasional structural pruning to maintain a strong framework as it reaches its larger mature size.

common_name: Zinfin Doll Hydrangea (Deep Pink-Red Aging Panicle Hydrangea)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to reach its full 5–7 foot mature size. Zinfin Doll produces large, dense flower panicles that open white and quickly begin blushing pink, deepening over the following weeks to a rich wine-red by late summer and fall — a faster and more intense color transition than many other panicle hydrangea cultivars — on strong stems that hold the heavy flower heads upright. Its long season of shifting color, from white through pink to deep red, gives it multiple distinct looks across a single growing season on one plant. Because it blooms on new wood, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing bloom; water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads before spring growth begins.

common_name: Zuni Crape Myrtle (Compact Lavender-Pink Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Zuni is one of the smaller National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, producing lavender-pink flower clusters from summer into early fall on a compact, semi-dwarf tree well suited to smaller residential landscapes and foundation plantings. Like other National Arboretum hybrids it shows good resistance to powdery mildew, a common disease problem on older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars, and develops attractive exfoliating bark with age. Fall foliage turns shades of orange-red. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune only to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the plant.

Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; A4 macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued commercially for high oil content and cracking quality. One of the classic Hawaiian-selected macadamia cultivars developed for commercial orchards, it produces medium-sized nuts with a high proportion of premium-grade, whole-kernel cracking quality and rich, high oil content prized by processors, making it a benchmark variety in Hawaiian macadamia production for decades. Like other macadamias it needs consistent warmth, protection from frost, and several years of growth before reaching significant bearing age, along with a compatible cross-pollinator variety for the best nut set. Water regularly during nut development, allow nuts to mature and fall naturally before harvest, and provide the same warm, humid, frost-free conditions the species requires throughout the year.

common_name: AU Buck IV Chestnut (Auburn University Annual-Bearing Chinese Chestnut)
notes: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Buck IV is part of a numbered series (AU Buck I through V) of Chinese chestnut selections patented by Auburn University from open-pollinated seedlings of the AU-Cropper cultivar, chosen for blight resistance, precocious bearing, and dependable annual cropping rather than the alternate-bearing pattern common in seedling chestnut trees. It sets a medium to heavy crop of large nuts most years once established, and like other Auburn chestnut releases it is bred specifically to perform under the heat, humidity, and soilborne disease pressure of the Deep South. Space trees widely for a broad mature canopy and good air circulation, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar nearby, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful. Harvest nuts from the ground in September-October as the spiny burrs split open, and refrigerate cured nuts to sweeten the starches before eating.

common_name: AU-Cropper Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)
notes: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Cropper is a Chinese chestnut selection released through Auburn University's chestnut breeding program, developed specifically for reliable, precocious production under the heat, humidity, and disease pressure typical of Alabama and the broader Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that eliminated American chestnut from Eastern forests, and begins bearing meaningful crops within a few years of planting rather than the decade or more required by seedling trees. Nuts drop free of the spiny burr at maturity in September–October for easy hand or ground collection. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy and to maintain the air circulation that helps limit fungal disease pressure in humid Southern summers, and plant a second unrelated Chinese chestnut cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts are not reliably self-fruitful.

common_name: AU-Homestead Chestnut (Auburn University Southeastern Chinese Chestnut)
notes: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU-Homestead is a Chinese chestnut cultivar developed through Auburn University's chestnut improvement program as a companion release to AU-Cropper, selected for good nut quality and disease tolerance under the heat, humidity, and soil conditions typical of Alabama and the wider Gulf South. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it inherits strong resistance to chestnut blight, the introduced fungal disease that historically devastated American chestnut, and begins cropping within a few years of planting on a grafted tree. Space trees widely to accommodate the broad, spreading mature canopy typical of Chinese chestnut, and interplant with a second, unrelated named cultivar within pollination range, since chestnuts require cross-pollination for a full nut set. Harvest nuts from the ground in September–October as burrs split and drop, and store cured nuts refrigerated for the sweetest flavor, since chestnut starches convert to sugar during cold storage.

common_name: AU-Leader Chestnut (Auburn University Precocious Chinese Chestnut)
notes: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut cultivars for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU-Leader is a Chinese chestnut selection from Auburn University's chestnut improvement program, drawn from the same precocious, blight-resistant seedling population that also produced AU-Cropper and AU-Homestead, and was chosen for a strongly upright, single-leader growth habit that makes it easier to train and maintain than the sprawling form typical of many chestnut selections. Like its sibling releases it inherits good resistance to chestnut blight and begins bearing at a young age on a grafted tree. Nuts run large for a Chinese chestnut, averaging roughly a dozen grams each, and mature and drop free of the split burr in early-to-mid September, ahead of many other Southern-adapted cultivars. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy, and interplant with a second unrelated chestnut cultivar within pollination range for a full nut set.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kola nut is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. This West African rainforest tree bears large, star-shaped pods containing caffeine-rich seeds that are chewed fresh across much of West Africa as a stimulant and used ceremonially to welcome guests, and were historically the original flavoring source for early cola soft drinks before synthetic flavorings largely replaced them. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and need consistently warm, humid, partly shaded conditions similar to their native rainforest understory habitat, limiting cultivation outside the tropics to botanical collections and large frost-free properties. Water regularly, especially while young, and provide the dappled shade of taller companion trees where possible to mimic natural forest conditions.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 10–12; abiu (Pouteria caimito) is a tropical Sapotaceae tree native to the Amazon basin that produces smooth, glossy, bright lemon-yellow fruits with a custardy, translucent white flesh of exceptional sweetness — often described as tasting of caramel, vanilla, or crème brûlée — that clings to a small number of large seeds. The fruit is eaten fresh by scooping out the flesh, taking care to avoid the slightly sticky latex in the skin, which can irritate the lips if left in contact. Abiu is widely grown in Brazil and Queensland, Australia, where its productivity and flavor have made it one of the most popular exotic Sapotaceae fruits among tropical fruit enthusiasts. Trees respond well to regular fertilization with a balanced tropical fruit fertilizer and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development; mulch heavily to conserve soil moisture and maintain root health.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; avoid planting in frost-prone sites. Blighia sapida (ackee) is a West African tree that became the national fruit of Jamaica, where the arils (fleshy seed coverings) of the opened, ripe fruit are the key ingredient in Jamaica's national dish, ackee and saltfish. The three large, black seeds of each red ackee pod are surrounded by creamy-yellow, buttery, scrambled-egg-textured arils that taste mildly savory and are typically sautéed with salt cod, onions, and peppers. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: Unripe ackee (pods not fully opened naturally) contains hypoglycin A, a toxin that can cause Jamaican Vomiting Sickness — consume only the fully ripe arils after the pod has opened completely on the tree and seeds have developed fully. The ripe arils are nutritious, high in protein, fat, and niacin. The tree is an attractive, medium-sized evergreen with pinnate leaves and small white flowers. Fresh ackee is available in Jamaican and Caribbean communities in South Florida; canned ackee (already safely processed) is widely available.

Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Adams produces an abundant spring flush of deep rose-red buds opening to rose-pink flowers, followed by small, glossy, cherry-red fruit about half an inch across that persists into winter and draws robins, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. It is a reliably disease-resistant crabapple, showing good resistance to apple scab and cedar-apple rust that plague many older, less-improved cultivars, and its rounded, well-branched form makes it a dependable small flowering shade tree for a home landscape. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Adams Elderberry (Classic High-Yield Large-Cluster American Elderberry Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Adams is one of the oldest and most widely established named elderberry cultivars — selected from wild American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) populations and long used as the benchmark for comparison in elderberry cultivar trials. It produces large, flat-topped flower clusters (cymes) in June–July — among the largest of named elderberry cultivars — followed by heavy, pendant clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late August–September. Adams is valued not only for its direct productivity but as an exceptionally effective cross-pollinator for other cultivars: planting Adams near Bob Gordon, Nova, or other cultivars consistently boosts overall production across the planting. The heavy, well-formed berry clusters of Adams are well-suited to all standard elderberry processing: elderberry syrup (a popular immune support product), elderberry wine, elderberry jelly, and elderflower preparations from the spring flowers. The large flower clusters are among the most attractive of any elderberry cultivar for elderflower cordials, fritters, and other culinary uses. As with all American elderberry, Adams spreads vigorously by root suckers and can naturalize in favorable moist conditions — manage the suckering to maintain a defined shrub rather than a spreading thicket. In zone 9, elderberry performs best in the slightly cooler, moister areas — near water features or in low spots where soil moisture is consistent.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Adams Pearmain is a reliable, easy-to-grow classic English russet apple well suited to a home orchard. An old English variety first recorded in the early nineteenth century, it bears medium, elongated, pearmain-shaped apples with a dull red flush over a russeted yellow ground and dense, crisp, nutty-sweet flesh, ripening in mid-fall as a reliable, well-flavored traditional dessert apple. Its consistent, moderate cropping and good disease tolerance compared to some other classic English varieties have made it a dependable choice for a home orchard wanting an easy-to-grow heirloom russet-type apple. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a few weeks to a couple of months for the best rich, nutty dessert flavor.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; a very large tree requiring considerable space — suitable primarily for large tropical properties in zone 11–12. Treculia africana (African breadfruit or ize) is one of the most ecologically and nutritionally important food trees of West and Central Africa — a massive, buttressed tropical tree native to the humid forests of Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, DRC, and Central Africa, producing the largest fruits of any species in the breadfruit/jackfruit family (Moraceae). The enormous globose fruits (12–36 inches across, weighing 10–65 lbs) erupt directly from the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) and are technically similar to jackfruit or breadfruit in structure, but used very differently: unlike common breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis, where the flesh is eaten) and jackfruit (where the flesh is the food), in African breadfruit, the edible product is the starchy, protein-rich seeds embedded in the fibrous flesh. The seeds are extracted, boiled or roasted, ground into flour, fermented (to make ugba or ukpaka — a traditional condiment in southeastern Nigeria), made into porridge, or pressed for oil. The fermented seed product (ukpaka) is a major flavor ingredient in Igbo cuisine, used similarly to cheese or miso as an aged, complex-flavored condiment. African breadfruit seeds are exceptionally protein-rich (21%) compared to other starchy staples. The tree is too large and slow-growing for most home gardens but represents one of the most important indigenous food forest trees of sub-Saharan Africa.

Plant in moist to wet, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Dacryodes buettneri requires consistently high rainfall and humidity typical of tropical rainforest conditions — water abundantly during dry spells, mulch heavily, and maintain high organic matter content. Dacryodes buettneri (African Bush Mango, Ozigo, or Arbre à Beurre in French) is a large, emergent to canopy rainforest tree native to Gabon, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, and the Congo Basin forests, a member of the same Burseraceae genus as the widely grown African olive (Dacryodes edulis / Safou). Like safou, D. buettneri produces oblong, oil-rich fruits with thin, waxy skin ripening from green to dark-blue or black-purple, cooked (boiled or roasted) rather than eaten raw — the soft, creamy, rich, butter-like pulp develops a flavor somewhat reminiscent of avocado or a rich olive when heated. The fruits are an important food and oil source for forest-dwelling communities in Gabon and Cameroon, and the extracted fat is used for cooking and traditional personal care. Dacryodes buettneri is a tall-growing, high-humidity, tropical rainforest species best suited to humid equatorial climates in zones 11–12; it does not tolerate drought, salt, or cold and needs rich, moist, forest-type soils to perform well.

growth_habit: African dryland cucurbit ornamental fruiting vine
notes: Plant Kedrostis africana seeds or tuber sections in very well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; water sparingly during establishment and infrequently once growing — the large tuberous roots store water for extended dry periods; allow to dry down significantly in winter (the plant may appear dead); new growth emerges from the tuber in spring. African Cucumber is one of the most drought-adapted vines in the Cucurbit family — a member of the extraordinary African flora adapted to seasonal drought — growing from a large, knobby, water-storing tuber (caudex) that can persist underground through months-long dry seasons without any rainfall. Slender, twining vines emerge from the tuber in the wet season and bear small, deeply lobed leaves and clusters of tiny, exquisite, green-and-cream-striped oval fruits that look like perfect miniature watermelons as they develop, then ripen through yellow-orange to bright scarlet-red, splitting to reveal black seeds. In African folklore and traditional medicine, the tuberous roots and fruits of related Kedrostis species have various documented uses; the fruits are eaten by birds and mammals in the wild. The ornamental miniature fruits make it a conversation piece in the dry garden; it is well suited to succulent gardens, xeriscapes, and dry South Africa-inspired plantings in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep, sandy-loam to clay-loam soil in full sun; African locust bean is drought-tolerant once established and fixes nitrogen. Parkia biglobosa (African locust bean, dawadawa, or nere) is a massive, wide-canopied leguminous tree from the West African savanna and Sudan zone — one of the most economically and nutritionally important trees across a broad band of West Africa from Senegal to Ethiopia. The tree produces striking, spherical, red to orange pompom flower heads on pendulous stalks — spectacularly ornamental. The fruits are long pods containing seeds embedded in a dry, yellow, powdery, sweet pulp. The sweet pulp (high in sugar, vitamin C, and tannins) is eaten fresh or dissolved in water as a sweet drink. The seeds are the critical product: fermented over several days into dawadawa (called iru in Yoruba, ogiri-nono in Igbo, sumbala in Mande-speaking regions) — an intensely aromatic, deeply umami-flavored condiment with a pungent smell similar to very strong blue cheese or natto. Dawadawa is the essential flavoring in West African soups, stews, and sauces in the same way that fish sauce is essential in Southeast Asia — providing deep umami richness. The tree also fixes atmospheric nitrogen (Rhizobium symbiosis), improving soil fertility. A supremely important multi-use tree for tropical food forests in zone 10–12.

The African mango, or bush mango, is a large tropical tree grown for its mango-like fruit and especially its oil-rich seed kernel, called dika nut. It demands a hot, humid, frost-free climate with abundant moisture and deep, fertile soil. Plant in full sun with plenty of room, as mature trees become tall and broad. Trees are slow to bear from seed, so grafted stock fruits sooner; harvest the fallen fruit and dry the prized kernels.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; African mangosteen tolerates brief light frosts to about 28°F when established, making it considerably more cold-hardy than tropical mangosteen and viable in zone 9 sheltered locations. Garcinia livingstonei is an African native shrub or small tree grown for its small (1–2 inch), orange-yellow to orange-red, edible fruits with juicy, sweet-tart, apricot-like flesh and 1–3 large seeds; the flavor is pleasant and described as a combination of apricot and mango, and the fruits are eaten fresh, made into juices, and used to make a fermented beverage in southern Africa. Unlike tropical mangosteen (G. mangostana), which is notoriously difficult to cultivate outside the humid tropics, African mangosteen is adaptable, drought-tolerant when established, and significantly more cold-hardy — an excellent choice for Gulf Coast subtropical gardens in zones 9–11.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. African Pride is a popular commercial and home garden atemoya cultivar known for a more compact tree size and heavy, reliable fruit production compared to some other cultivars, making it a practical choice where space is somewhat limited. The rich, sweet, custard-like flesh is classic atemoya quality, and hand pollination in the morning hours, transferring pollen from male-stage to female-stage flowers, significantly improves fruit set and size. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the skin lightens in color, then let it finish ripening at room temperature for the best eating quality.

common_name: African Walnut (Gaboon Nut, Walnut of the Congo)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in part shade; African walnut is a slow-growing canopy tree for large properties in zone 11–12 humid tropics. Coula edulis (African walnut or Gaboon nut) is a large, slow-growing canopy tree of the humid tropical rainforests of West and Central Africa — native to Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Congo, and the DRC — and one of the most important wild nut-producing trees of the Central African forest zone. The tree produces small (1–1.5 inch), olive-to-cherry-sized, oval to round fruits with a thin, olive-like outer flesh and an extremely hard, woody shell inside (in the Olacaceae family, related to the African walnut group). The single kernel within the hard shell has a distinctly walnut-like flavor — nutty, oily, and rich — and is eaten fresh (raw), roasted in hot ashes, or boiled by forest communities across its range. The nuts are gathered from wild trees and are sold in markets in Cameroon, Gabon, and DRC as an important forest food product and source of income for forest-dependent communities. The high fat content (40–50%) makes the kernels calorie-dense and nutritionally valuable. Coula edulis is listed as a species of conservation concern in parts of its range due to overharvesting of wild nuts and habitat loss. A remarkable and entirely unknown tree outside West Central Africa.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; African wild mango grows as a large forest tree requiring considerable space in zone 10–12. Irvingia gabonensis (African wild mango, ogbono, or dika nut) is a large, canopy forest tree native to the humid tropical forests of West and Central Africa — particularly Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, Ivory Coast, and the Congo Basin — and one of the most economically important non-timber forest trees of the West African rainforest zone. The tree produces round to oval, 2–3 inch fruits that superficially resemble small mangoes externally (hence 'African wild mango') but are unrelated: the fruit flesh (mesocarp) is sweet, yellowish, edible, and pleasant, but it is the large, hard-shelled seeds inside that represent the primary economic and culinary product. The seeds (ogbono nuts or dika nuts) are dried, smoked, or processed into ground ogbono powder — the essential thickening and flavoring agent in Nigerian ogbono soup (also called draw soup for its slimy, mucilaginous texture) and related soups across the forest zone of West Africa. Ground ogbono has a distinctive, complex, slightly bitter, earthy-nutty flavor and contains mucilaginous compounds (similar to okra) that create the characteristic 'draw' texture of the soup. The seeds also yield dika oil (Gaboon chocolate), used in confectionery. The tree gained international attention as a weight-loss supplement ingredient (IGOB131 extract) in the 2000s, with preliminary studies suggesting effects on blood lipids.

common_name: Akane Apple (Tokyo Rose, Early Scab-Resistant Tart-Sweet Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible early-blooming pollinator. Bred in Japan from a cross of Jonathan and Worcester Pearmain and released in 1970, Akane produces small-to-medium, bright red apples with crisp, juicy, tart-sweet flesh reminiscent of Jonathan but with better resistance to apple scab. It ripens in late summer, ahead of most main-season apples, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early harvest without spraying heavily for disease. Fruit is best used fresh or in sauce shortly after picking, as it does not store as long as later-season varieties.

common_name: Alexandrian Laurel (Tamanu, Beauty Leaf, Beautyleaf, Kamani)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or rocky coastal soils — Alexandrian Laurel is one of the most salt-tolerant large trees available for tropical coastal gardens and is an outstanding choice for beachfront and coastal landscapes in zone 10-11. Calophyllum inophyllum is a large, slow-to-moderately growing evergreen tree native to coastal environments from East Africa through South and Southeast Asia to Australia and the Pacific Islands — one of the few tree species with a genuinely pan-tropical coastal distribution, adapted to sandy, saline soils and salt-laden coastal winds. The tree produces a broad, spreading, dense canopy of large (4–8 inch), glossy, dark-green, oval leaves with distinctive parallel lateral veins that converge at both the midrib and leaf edge — a leaf venation pattern so distinctive that it is diagnostic for the genus Calophyllum. In spring and summer, the tree produces small clusters of intensely fragrant, white, 4-petaled flowers with prominent yellow stamens — the fragrance is sweet, fresh, and carries on the breeze. The round, green fruits (1–1.5 inches) contain a nut that is pressed to yield tamanu oil — a thick, nutty, golden-green fixed oil traditionally used throughout Polynesia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific Islands for wound healing, skin care, and as a muscle pain remedy, and now widely used as a premium ingredient in natural cosmetics. The wood has been used for traditional outrigger canoes and structural timber throughout the Pacific.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; the Allegheny chinkapin is the smaller native cousin of the American chestnut and is fully resistant to chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) — making it an irreplaceable food plant in regions where the American chestnut was eliminated. It produces small but richly flavored sweet nuts enclosed in a spiny bur, just one nut per bur (unlike 2–3 per bur in true chestnuts); they are superb eaten raw or roasted. Forms a thicket-like shrub to small tree via root-sprouting and is heavily used by deer, turkeys, and squirrels as mast. Best performance is on well-drained, acidic upland soils; heavy or wet soils cause decline.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to more sun as the tree matures; Allegheny is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars selected by pawpaw breeder Neal Peterson from decades of evaluation work aimed at identifying the largest, best-flavored, and most productive pawpaw seedlings for named release. It produces good-sized fruit with the rich, complex banana-mango-custard flavor pawpaw enthusiasts prize, on a vigorous, dependable tree. As with all pawpaws, Allegheny is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar such as Susquehanna or Shenandoah planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set — pawpaw flowers are pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, so hand-pollinating with a small brush between two open flowers of different cultivars can meaningfully improve yield in a home planting. In zone 9, site trees where they get afternoon shade in the hottest years and expect best performance toward the cooler end of the zone.

Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in fall or spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Allegheny plum spreads by root suckers and forms thickets over time, useful for naturalizing on a slope or bank. Clouds of white flowers cover the thicket-forming branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, followed by small, dark purple, tart plums historically gathered by Appalachian settlers for jams and preserves, ripening in late summer on a small, suckering native tree found on dry ridges and rocky slopes of the central Appalachian region. Its suckering, thicket-forming habit makes it useful for stabilizing an eroding bank or naturalizing a difficult dry slope where its dense thicket provides wildlife cover as well as fruit. Water during establishment, then rely on natural rainfall, and allow it to sucker and spread if a naturalized thicket is the goal, or remove suckers to maintain a single specimen.

Divide root suckers or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade; Allegheny serviceberry is a native eastern North American multi-stemmed small tree of exceptional four-season ornamental value — in early spring (March–April), before the leaves emerge, the smooth gray-barked stems become covered with clusters of delicate, drooping, pure-white, star-shaped flowers that are among the first tree flowers of the year; the bronze-red emerging leaves turn green in summer; round, sweet, dark-purple, blueberry-like fruits ripen in June (hence an alternative common name 'Juneberry') and are edible, sweet, and excellent fresh, in pies, jams, and for drying like raisins; and the foliage turns vivid orange-red to burgundy in autumn. As a native understory tree that grows naturally at forest edges and in open woodlands, Allegheny serviceberry is one of the most shade-tolerant fruiting trees available and will produce a useful fruit crop in partial shade conditions where no other small fruit tree would bear productively. The ripe berries are eagerly sought by at least 35 species of birds. Excellent combined with witch hazels and native azaleas in a naturalistic woodland edible garden.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible plum cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set. Allred is a hybrid plum valued as much for its landscape impact as its harvest, holding rich red-purple foliage color through the growing season that rivals purpleleaf ornamental plums, while still producing sweet-tart, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed fruit good for fresh eating and preserves. Its dual-purpose nature makes it a good choice for a home orchard that also wants ornamental structure in the landscape. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that improves airflow and fruit quality.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Alma is a Texas-bred fig developed by Texas A&M University and released in 1974, bred specifically for the alkaline, calcareous soils and hot, humid summers of Texas. It is the most widely planted fig variety in Texas home gardens because of its exceptional adaptability to Texas soils, heat, and moderate drought tolerance. The fruit is small to medium, golden-tan to amber when ripe, with very sweet, rich, amber-colored flesh and a distinctive honey flavor superior to most brown-skinned varieties. Alma produces a very heavy main crop in August–October in zone 9. Skin is thin and the fruits are best eaten fresh or for preserves; they do not ship well, which is why Alma remains primarily a home and farmers' market variety. The tree produces few to no Breba (first-crop) figs but compensates with tremendous main-crop productivity. Trees are slightly cold-sensitive below 10°F; in zone 8, protect with mulch around the base in winter.

Almonds bloom earlier than almost any other tree fruit and are severely damaged by late spring frosts, which is why commercial production is limited to Mediterranean-type climates. Most varieties require a cross-pollinator — plant at least two compatible cultivars (Non-Pareil with Carmel or Price, for example). Trees thrive in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soils and are drought-tolerant once established. Harvest when the hulls split open and the shells dry and harden, typically in late summer; spread nuts to dry for two weeks before storing.

common_name: Alstonville Finger Lime (Commercial Australian Caviar Lime Cultivar)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since this rainforest-understory species tolerates and even benefits from some afternoon protection in hot inland climates. Alstonville is the leading commercial finger lime cultivar in Australia, selected for vigorous upright growth, heavier yields, and consistent production of glossy green, cylindrical fruit filled with pale green caviar-like pulp vesicles. It is self-fertile and bears at a younger age than most finger lime seedlings when grown on grafted rootstock. Harvest when fruit detaches easily with a gentle twist, and use the tangy pulp fresh as a garnish since it does not store well once opened.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Amazon grape is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the western Amazon basin, this fast-growing relative of cecropia trees bears grape-like clusters of purple, thin-skinned fruit with sweet, translucent, juicy pulp eaten fresh, unusual among tropical fruit trees for reaching bearing age within just a few years of planting rather than a decade or more. Its palmate, cecropia-like leaves and relatively quick growth to fruiting make it an appealing option for a tropical fruit collector wanting faster results than many slower Amazonian species, though it still needs consistent warmth and humidity to thrive. Water regularly, especially during establishment, and expect the first fruit clusters within three to five years under good growing conditions.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Spondias cytherea is fast-growing and drought tolerant once established — water deeply and infrequently in subtropical conditions; excellent performance in South Florida's calcareous soils and in Gulf Coast sandy soils. Spondias cytherea (Ambarella, Golden Apple, or June Plum) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous tropical tree native to the Society Islands of French Polynesia, spread throughout tropical Polynesia by Polynesian voyagers and later widely planted across tropical Asia, the Caribbean, Central and South America, and tropical West Africa. The oval, 2–3 inch, golden-yellow fruits have crisp, fibrous, firm, juicy, tart-sweet, aromatic flesh with flavors of unripe mango, pineapple, and apple — remarkably refreshing as a fresh fruit when ripe (golden-yellow), and extensively used green (firm, crunchy, very tart) as a condiment, relish, chutney base, and snack with salt, fish sauce, and chili across South and Southeast Asia. In the Caribbean (Jamaica) it is 'June Plum,' in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia 'Ambarella.' Trees are fast-growing — fruiting in 3–4 years from cuttings — and highly productive, dropping fruit that must be gathered regularly. One of the easiest tropical fruit trees to establish in zone 9b–12; an outstanding choice for South Florida, the Gulf Coast, and similar warm subtropical climates where it naturalizes readily.

common_name: Ambarella (June Plum, Golden Apple, Otaheite Apple)
notes: Plant in very well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; ambarella is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree native to Melanesia and widely cultivated throughout the Pacific islands, Caribbean, and Southeast Asia for its versatile fruit. The oval, golden-yellow to orange fruits are eaten at all stages: the crisp, acidic green fruit is popular in Southeast Asian salads, slaws, and pickles with a tart mango-apple flavor, while fully ripe fruits are sweeter and eaten fresh. The fibrous pit germinates reliably in a few weeks. Ambarella is one of the faster-fruiting tropical trees, often bearing within 2–3 years from air-layers. It drops leaves briefly in dry season. In zone 9a it grows in a large container (25+ gallon) and must be moved indoors or into a greenhouse before the first frost; in zone 10+ it is an outstanding productive landscape tree.

common_name: Ambersweet Orange (Cold-Hardy Early Hybrid Sweet Orange)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun; Ambersweet tolerates more cold than most sweet oranges and ripens very early, from October, extending the citrus season in areas at the cooler edge of the Gulf Coast citrus belt.

American beech is monoecious and wind-pollinated, but nut production is highly variable and irregular — large mast crops occur every 2–5 years, driven by weather patterns; at least two trees (ideally a grove) dramatically improves mast yield in any given year. The triangular beechnuts are sweet and nutritious, high in fat and protein, and valued by both wildlife and people; they are best eaten raw or lightly roasted and are traditionally used for oil extraction. Beech is extremely sensitive to soil compaction and grade changes around the root zone — construction damage is the primary killer of mature trees in urban settings. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained, acidic soil away from construction zones and plan for very long-term production: significant nut crops typically begin 10+ years after planting.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to full shade; American black currant is a native fruiting shrub found in moist woodlands and streambanks from Nova Scotia to Virginia and west to the Rockies, producing clusters of small, round, black-purple currants in July–August that are excellent for jams, jellies, juice, and wine. The fruit flavor is similar to European black currant but milder, without the strong 'cassis' musk of Ribes nigrum, making it more palatable to those who find European black currant too strong. Most importantly, it is one of very few fruiting shrubs that produces in deep shade, making it irreplaceable for woodland edible gardens where blueberries and most other fruit shrubs fail. The fragrant, small, white to yellowish tubular flowers in spring are attractive to hummingbirds and native bees. The foliage is attractively lobed and resinous-scented when brushed. American black currant is alternate host for white pine blister rust and should not be planted within 900 feet of white pines in susceptible regions — check with local extension before planting.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun — the American chestnut was once the dominant tree of the eastern forest, comprising 25% of all trees from New England to the Deep South and providing the primary mast crop sustaining deer, turkeys, bears, and passenger pigeons across millions of acres. The introduction of chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) from Asia in the early 1900s killed an estimated 4 billion trees within 50 years in the most catastrophic ecological disaster in American history. The root system of most trees survives and sends up shoots that grow to 10–20 feet before dying of blight — these sprouts can produce a small crop of nuts. The American Chestnut Foundation has developed blight-tolerant hybrid trees (about 94% American chestnut genetics) and restoration planting is actively underway. Planting American chestnut seedlings or blight-resistant hybrids is a meaningful conservation act; the trees grow fast, produce sweet nuts, and support 125 species of caterpillars.

Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; American hazelnut tolerates a wide range of soil conditions but produces the most nuts in full sun; it spreads by root suckers and should be allowed to form thickets for best wildlife habitat value. Corylus americana is a vigorous, multi-stemmed native shrub of eastern North American woodlands and thickets, producing small, round hazelnuts similar in flavor to European hazelnuts (C. avellana) enclosed in distinctive, toothed, leaf-like husks from August through October; the nuts are eagerly consumed by squirrels, blue jays, turkeys, and other wildlife. Long yellow-green male catkins appear very early in spring (February–March), providing one of the first pollen sources for emerging native bees, and the rounded, hairy leaves turn bright orange-yellow in fall. It is native, low-maintenance, and excellent for naturalizing into wildlife hedgerows and edible landscaping.

Collect seeds in autumn as soon as the berries ripen and sow immediately in a prepared bed or seed flat at a depth of about 1/4 inch, then allow winter temperatures to provide the necessary stratification sequence. Seeds will germinate in spring once soil warms; transplant seedlings to a permanent site in their second year when they have developed a robust root system. Choose a cool, moist site with well-drained, acidic soil and full sun to partial shade, reflecting this tree's preference for northern forests and high-elevation ridges. Consistent moisture during establishment is critical, as young trees are drought-sensitive; once established, they are exceptionally cold-hardy and low-maintenance.

Plant in deep, well-drained to average soil in full sun to partial shade; American persimmon is a tough native tree with striking blocky, alligator-hide bark and excellent fall color that produces small, intensely sweet, apricot-flavored fruits after the first hard frost when they become fully ripe and astringency disappears. The fruits are outstanding for puddings, breads, and fresh eating and are highly attractive to deer, foxes, opossums, and birds. Trees are quite drought-tolerant once established and will grow in poor, rocky, or clay soil where few fruit trees survive. Named female cultivars (Meader, Szukis, Yates, Pieper) with improved fruit size are grafted onto seedling rootstock — grow these for reliable, large-fruited production. Allow fruits to fall naturally after frost and collect from the ground before wildlife does.

Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; American plum is drought-tolerant once established and naturalizes readily in hedgerows and woodland edges. Prunus americana (American wild plum) is a native small tree or large shrub found across much of the eastern and central United States, producing clusters of fragrant white flowers in March–April before leaf emergence (a spectacular early-spring display that attracts native bees, especially mining bees and andrenid bees) followed by abundant 3/4-inch, red to orange-yellow plums in July–August. The fruits are quite tart when fully ripe but develop excellent plum flavor when fully ripe and dead-ripe, and are highly prized for jams, jellies, wines, and preserves; they were a staple food of many Native American peoples and European settlers. American plum spreads by root suckers to form thickets valuable for wildlife (providing dense nesting cover for songbirds and food for over 70 bird species), and has been extensively used as rootstock for grafting hybrid plum cultivars. It is among the most cold-hardy, drought-tolerant, and disease-resistant of all plums.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; American wild plum is a rugged native shrub or small thicket-forming tree that produces fragrant white flower clusters in early spring before the leaves emerge, then bright red or yellow-orange tart plums 3/4–1 inch in diameter in July through August. The thickets provide excellent wildlife cover and nesting sites. Wild plum suckers heavily and can naturalize into large hedgerows — a valuable feature in permaculture designs. The tart fruits are excellent for jams, jellies, sauces, and fruit leathers; deer, foxes, raccoons, and dozens of bird species rely on them. Tolerates drought, clay, alkaline soils, and extreme cold once established.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; amla is a deciduous small tree native to South and Southeast Asia, grown for its round, pale green, translucent fruits that are extremely high in vitamin C and intensely sour and astringent when fresh. The tree tolerates poor, rocky soils and considerable drought once established, and produces feathery, fine-textured foliage that drops in the dry season. Fruits ripen in fall to early winter and are typically pickled, candied, dried, or processed into juice, chutney, and the Ayurvedic preserve chyawanprash rather than eaten out of hand. Trees are usually grafted onto seedling rootstock for faster, more reliable bearing and are sensitive to hard freezes, restricting outdoor culture to the warmest parts of zones 9-11 or container growing elsewhere.

Plant a grafted tree in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving it plenty of room to reach its mature size and pairing it with a Type II pollinator cultivar for a good nut set. Amling is a Gulf South pecan cultivar valued for strong resistance to pecan scab, the humid-climate fungal disease that is the single biggest challenge to growing pecans without a heavy fungicide spray program in the Southeast, making it a lower-maintenance choice than older scab-susceptible standards. It bears a good crop of medium-sized, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality on a vigorous, productive tree. Young trees take several years to bear their first nuts and reach full production only after ten years or more; water deeply and regularly during establishment and through nut fill in late summer, since drought stress during fill reduces kernel quality. Provide deep, infrequent irrigation rather than frequent shallow watering to encourage a deep root system.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; anacua is a native south Texas and Mexico tree of the Rio Grande Plains and Gulf Coast, valued for its multi-season ornamental interest: fragrant white flowers in spring, followed by clusters of small orange-yellow fruits (edible, slightly sweet) in late spring and early summer that attract numerous birds. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves give the tree its secondary common name. The fruit is eaten by numerous bird species, particularly golden-fronted woodpeckers, white-tipped doves, and mockingbirds. Semi-evergreen in mild winters in zone 9a; may lose some leaves in hard freezes but re-leafs readily from the base or branch tips. An excellent, underused native tree for south and central Texas gardens providing year-round interest, wildlife value, and adapting well to the alkaline soils of the Edwards Plateau and lower Rio Grande valley.

common_name: Angel Red Pomegranate (Soft-Seeded Sweet Red Fresh-Eating Pomegranate)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Angel Red is a soft-seeded pomegranate variety — one of the most important distinctions in pomegranate selection for fresh eating. Standard pomegranate varieties (including Wonderful) contain hard, woody seeds at the center of each aril that some people find unpleasant to eat; soft-seeded varieties like Angel Red have soft, barely-noticeable seeds that allow the entire aril to be eaten without extraction, fundamentally changing the fresh-eating experience. Angel Red produces large, bright-red fruits with deep-red, juicy arils and rich pomegranate flavor — somewhat sweeter and less astringent than Wonderful at peak ripeness. The soft-seeded quality makes Angel Red excellent for fresh eating out of hand (where hard seeds are an obstacle), salads (where whole arils are used as a garnish), and for fresh juice where the softer seeds blend or press more easily. Like all pomegranates, Angel Red is self-fruitful, drought-tolerant, heat-adapted, and ornamentally attractive with showy orange-red flowers in summer and richly colored fall fruit. In zone 9, Angel Red ripens in October–November at essentially the same time as Wonderful — the harvest timing is similar but the eating experience is distinctly more accessible for fresh consumption.

common_name: Angelique Fig (Early Yellow French Heirloom Fig)
notes: Angelique is a centuries-old French heirloom fig, historically grown around Paris and known there as Angelique or Melette, that Thomas Jefferson brought to Monticello after seeing it cultivated abroad. It bears medium to large fruit with pale greenish-yellow, subtly striped skin and sweet, cream-colored flesh, ripening notably early in the season and extending the fig harvest before later-season cultivars come in. As a common-type fig it is self-fertile and produces without pollination, and its long history of wide cultivation across France attests to its adaptability across a range of soils and climates. In the Gulf South, Angelique's early ripening window helps growers bring in a crop ahead of the peak summer humidity that promotes fruit souring and splitting in later-maturing varieties.

Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator (one male per 6-8 females) on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Anna is a widely grown, reliably productive hardy kiwiberry cultivar valued for good vigor and heavy fruit set once a compatible male is nearby. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet, bright green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. As with all kiwiberry vines, plants take a few years to reach full bearing size but then produce heavily and reliably for decades. Prune hard each winter on a permanent framework of cordons to control the very vigorous twining growth and keep the fruiting wood renewed and productive, and install a sturdy trellis or pergola from the start, since mature vines and their fruit load become quite heavy.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; apple serviceberry is the most widely planted Amelanchier hybrid — a cross between A. arborea and A. laevis producing larger flowers and larger, juicier berries than either parent. In early to mid-spring, before or just as the leaves emerge, it produces a spectacular display of pure-white flowers in drooping clusters that are among the first flowers of the season for early native bees, mining bees, and other spring pollinators that emerge before many plants are flowering. The blueberry-like fruits that ripen in June are sweet, purple-black, and edible fresh, in pies, jams, and wine — they are exceptionally rich in antioxidants and have a pleasant flavor combining blueberry and mild almond notes. The fruits are intensely attractive to birds. In fall, the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and occasionally yellow, providing a final season of interest. Multi-season value: spring flowers, summer edible fruit, fall color, ornamental winter silhouette. Tolerates part shade and is among the most wildlife-valuable small trees available.

An aprium is an apricot-dominant hybrid with the sweetness of apricot and a hint of plum, often bearing a faint fuzz. Plant in full sun on light, well-drained soil in a frost-protected spot, since apricot-type blooms open very early. Many apriums are self-fruitful but crop more heavily with an apricot pollinator nearby. Prune in dry summer weather to limit disease and thin the fruit for good size.

common_name: Arbequina Olive (World's Most Popular Home Garden Olive, Compact Spanish Oil Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Arbequina is extremely drought-tolerant once established and actually produces better oil quality under moderate stress — do not over-fertilize or over-water; harvest olives in November–December when shifting from green to purple-black for oil; for table olives, harvest green in October–November and cure in brine for 6–12 months. Arbequina olive is the most widely planted olive variety in the world and by a large margin the most popular olive for home garden use globally — a small Spanish variety from the town of Arbeca in Catalonia that was historically confined to a small region of northeastern Spain before becoming a worldwide standard through its adoption in super-high-density olive plantations in California, Australia, Chile, and Argentina. The variety's global success derives from a combination of characteristics ideally suited to modern olive production: extremely compact habit (10–15 feet versus the 25–30 feet of traditional olive varieties), heavy and precocious bearing (producing significant crops in year 3–4 rather than the 7–10 years of traditional varieties on standard spacing), self-fertility (producing good crops as a single tree), low chill requirement (300–400 hours, allowing successful growing in zones 7–10), and excellent high-quality oil — mild, fruity, golden-colored oil with low acidity that is considered among the finest olive oils. For home gardeners, Arbequina's compact size makes it suitable for large containers, small gardens, and courtyard plantings where standard olive trees would be too large. The small, round olives (1–2g each) can also be table-cured in brine though the size is small by table olive standards.

common_name: Arbosana Olive (Compact Cold-Hardy High-Density Oil Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; avoid over-fertilizing or over-watering, since moderate stress improves oil quality. Arbosana is another small Spanish olive variety, alongside Arbequina, widely adopted in modern super-high-density olive orchards for its compact habit, precocious and heavy bearing, and good cold hardiness relative to larger traditional olive cultivars. The small fruit yields a well-regarded, balanced, mildly fruity oil, and the tree's naturally smaller size makes it practical for large containers and compact home landscapes, similar in scale to Arbequina but noted for handling occasional colder winter dips slightly better. Harvest olives as they shift from green to purple-black for oil production in late fall to early winter, or pick green and cure in brine for table olives. Established trees are drought-tolerant and need minimal fertilization.

Plant male and female vines (one male per 6-8 females) on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; prune heavily each winter to manage size. Actinidia kolomikta (Arctic beauty kiwi or kolomikta kiwi) is an East Asian kiwi vine native to the cold, humid forests of Siberia, northern China, Korea, and Japan — the hardiest of all Actinidia species, surviving temperatures to -40°F (USDA zone 3) with no winter protection. It produces abundant, smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruits (no need to peel) with green flesh, a flavor similar to full-sized kiwi fruit, and a slightly sweeter, more complex character — excellent fresh or in fruit salads, smoothies, and preserves. The vine is dioecious — plant at least one male per 6-8 female vines for pollination and fruit set. What makes Arctic beauty kiwi especially garden-worthy is the extraordinary variegated foliage of the male plants: in late spring and early summer, the new leaves emerge with spectacular patches and splashes of bright pink, cream-white, and green — rivaling any ornamental vine in beauty. Female vines are solid green but highly productive. A superb ornamental-edible vine for cold-climate gardens where fuzzy kiwi (A. deliciosa) cannot survive.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting in the warmest available microclimate for the first few winters. Arctic Frost is a satsuma mandarin selection bred for improved cold hardiness beyond standard satsuma cultivars, allowing mature trees to tolerate brief drops into the low 20s or upper teens Fahrenheit with only minor wood damage, when standard citrus of similar fruit quality would be killed to the ground. Fruit is sweet, low-acid, essentially seedless, and easy to peel, with the loose, glossy rind typical of satsumas, ripening in fall to early winter. Young trees need cold protection for the first two to three winters until established, but mature wood is notably tougher than most edible citrus. Like other satsumas, it is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, and it tends to bear well even as a young tree. Protect the trunk and graft union with mulch or wrap in the coldest years, and avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization in late summer, which can push tender new growth that is more vulnerable to an early freeze.

Plant young trees in full sun in deep, well-drained, rocky to sandy soil in spring; Arizona walnut (Juglans major) is a native walnut of the Desert Southwest, growing along canyon bottoms and mountain slopes in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and northern Mexico. The small, round, thick-shelled nuts are labor-intensive to crack but have excellent, rich flavor comparable to eastern black walnut — and have been a valued food of indigenous peoples of the Southwest (Apache, Navajo, Pueblo peoples) for centuries. More heat and drought tolerant than eastern walnuts, the tree is the dominant native walnut of the semi-arid West and an outstanding choice for dry-climate food-forest systems. It is also an important wildlife tree and rootstock for grafting cultivated walnuts in desert climates.

common_name: Arkansas Black Apple (Ozark Heirloom Dark-Skinned Keeper Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator variety. This late-1800s Ozark heirloom is famous for skin that darkens from deep red to nearly black in full sun, and for fruit that is rock-hard and tart at harvest but mellows into a dense, sweet, aromatic apple after two to three months in storage. Because of this, growers pick it in October and cellar it rather than eating it fresh off the tree. The thick skin and firm flesh make it an outstanding long-keeping cider and baking apple that was once a major shipping variety before modern refrigeration existed.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, raised or mounded soil in full sun with cold-air drainage; Armstrong satsuma is among the more cold-hardy satsuma selections and is a Gulf South dooryard favorite from Louisiana to coastal Texas. A bud-sport selection of Owari satsuma found in the Gulf South, it produces the same sweet, easy-peeling, nearly seedless fruit but ripens two to three weeks earlier, letting growers harvest ahead of the season's first hard freeze in marginal citrus climates. The compact, glossy-leaved, thornless tree is heavily productive and, like other satsumas, hardier to cold than most other mandarins, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit once mature. Mulch the root zone and wrap or cover young trees during hard freezes, and pick fruit as soon as it colors since satsumas hold poorly on the tree once ripe.

common_name: Aromatnaya Quince (Russian Quince Edible Fresh Without Cooking)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Aromatnaya is a Russian quince cultivar notable among quince types for fruit that is mild and pleasant enough to eat fresh, unlike most quince varieties that require cooking to be palatable due to their hard, astringent flesh. The pineapple-yellow fruit is intensely fragrant and still excellent for cooking into preserves and quince paste, but its unusually mild, less astringent flavor when fully ripe has made it popular with gardeners who want a more versatile quince. The tree is self-fertile, cold-hardy, and otherwise managed like other quince cultivars, benefiting from good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk.

common_name: Ascolano Olive (Large Mild Table and Oil Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Ascolano is an Italian-origin olive cultivar long grown in California for its large, thin-skinned, mild-flavored fruit — one of the highest-quality table olives available, with less bitterness before curing than most cultivars and flesh that separates easily from the pit. Its thin skin bruises more readily than firmer-skinned table olives such as Manzanillo or Sevillano, so fruit is best hand-harvested carefully rather than shaken or mechanically picked. Ascolano can be cured green or ripe black and also produces good-quality oil, though its lower oil content and thinner skin make it less common in commercial oil orchards. Trees are moderately vigorous and only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second, compatible olive cultivar nearby improves fruit set and overall yield. As with other olives, established Ascolano trees are notably drought-tolerant and adapt well to the alkaline, low-fertility soils common across much of the Gulf Coast and Texas.

common_name: Ashmead's Kernel Apple (English Heirloom Sharp-Flavored Russet Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Raised from seed around 1700 by Dr. William Ashmead of Gloucester, England, this is one of the oldest russet apples still grown and is treasured by cider makers and flavor enthusiasts for its intense, sharp, pear-drop sweetness balanced against high acidity. The medium, dull green-gold fruit is entirely covered in rough russet skin and looks unassuming, but the dense, dry, richly flavored flesh has made it a favorite of English apple connoisseurs for centuries. It ripens in mid-fall and its flavor improves somewhat with a few weeks of storage.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, allowing the shrub to form its natural dense, multi-stemmed thicket. Asian hazel is native to Siberia, Korea, northern China, and Japan and is exceptionally cold hardy compared with the European hazelnut, tolerating harsh continental winters that would damage most commercial filbert cultivars. It produces small nuts in short, bristly husks and is widely used by breeders working to develop cold-hardy, blight-resistant hazelnut cultivars for the northern United States and Canada by crossing it with European hazelnut.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 9–11; atemoya is a hybrid between the cherimoya (Annona cherimola) and the sugar apple (Annona squamosa), combining the better qualities of both parents — the large size and richly flavored flesh of cherimoya with the tropical heat tolerance of sugar apple. Atemoya is widely considered one of the finest-flavored fruits in the world, with a rich, creamy white flesh tasting of vanilla custard with notes of pineapple and coconut. It requires hand pollination in most US gardens — transfer pollen from flowers in the male stage to flowers in the female stage in the morning using a small brush. Plant grafted trees for faster fruiting (typically 2–3 years) rather than seedlings. Popular cultivars include 'Gefner' (nearly self-fruitful) and 'African Pride'. An outstanding subtropical fruit for South Florida and Gulf Coast gardens where winter temperatures stay above 28°F.

Cold-stratify seeds in damp sand in the refrigerator for four to six weeks before sowing in spring into deep pots to encourage taproot development before transplanting. Move seedlings to their permanent site while still young and small, choosing a spot in full sun with rocky, sandy, or otherwise fast-draining soil. Once established this tree is exceptionally drought-tolerant and long-lived, requiring no supplemental irrigation in Mediterranean or dry climates. Plant at least one male and one female tree to ensure fruit production, as this species is dioecious.

Atreano is a Portuguese fig notable for its pale yellow-green skin that stays light even when the fruit is fully ripe, which makes judging harvest timing by color alone unreliable; instead check for softening and a slight neck droop. The amber flesh is mild, honeyed, and low in seediness, making it a favorite for fresh eating among growers who find darker figs too intensely flavored. It is a vigorous, heavy-bearing tree well suited to warm Mediterranean-type and humid subtropical climates alike. Give it full sun, good drainage, and room to spread, since it can become a large, dense specimen if left unpruned.

Native to the semi-arid interior of Australia, this small-fruited citrus relative is among the most cold-hardy true citrus species available, tolerating brief dips into the high teens Fahrenheit once established, which makes it a worthwhile dooryard planting for zone 9a gardeners where standard limes struggle. The pea-to-marble-sized round fruits have a tart, intensely aromatic lime flavor and are used in marmalades, cordials, and as a lime substitute; the species is also valued by citrus breeders as rootstock and hybrid parent material for cold tolerance. Give it excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water once established, since it is adapted to low-rainfall conditions and resents wet feet more than most citrus.

The Australian finger lime bears elongated fruit packed with juicy, caviar-like vesicles that burst with tart citrus flavor, making it a chef's favorite. Native to rugged coastal Australia, this compact, thorny citrus is tough and adapts well to container culture. Grow from a potted tree in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and protect it from frost by moving it indoors in cold climates. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season and water steadily without letting roots sit wet.

common_name: Autumn Beauty Jujube (Qiyuexian, Early-Ripening Crisp Fresh-Eating Jujube)
notes: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in almost any well-drained soil; jujubes tolerate heat, drought, and poor soils better than most fruit trees once established. Autumn Beauty, also sold as Qiyuexian, needs only about 400 chill hours and stays compact at 8 to 10 feet tall, with attractive zigzag branching and glossy foliage that turns yellow in fall. The apple-crisp, subtly spicy fruit is prized for fresh eating when harvested at the crunchy green-to-tan stage, ripening earlier than many other Chinese jujube selections. Its low chill requirement and tolerance for hot, humid summers make it a good complement to Gulf Coast-adapted jujube selections like Li and Sherwood.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 9–11; babaco is a naturally occurring hybrid of two Andean Vasconcellea species, selected and cultivated in Ecuador for its large, distinctively five-angled, torpedo-shaped fruits that are entirely seedless — a parthenocarpic trait that makes it the only papaya relative that does not require cross-pollination for fruit set. The flavor is refreshing and tropical, combining papaya with pineapple and strawberry notes, with lower enzyme activity than mountain papaya so the fruit can be eaten fresh. The tree stays compact at 6–10 feet and fruits prolifically in zone 9. In zone 9a, provide frost protection below 28°F or grow in large containers moved indoors in winter. A novelty fruit tree that produces a steady supply of unusual, edible fruit without the gender complications of other Vasconcellea species.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; bacupari is slow-growing and may take 8–10 years to fruit from seed. Garcinia madruno (bacupari or madruno) is a Colombian and South American tropical fruit tree in the mangosteen family (Clusiaceae/Guttiferae) — related to the famous mangosteen (G. mangostana) and native to the cloud forests and tropical lowlands of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela. It produces small (1–2 inch), oval, bright-yellow to orange fruits when ripe, with thin, slightly resinous skin and white, juicy pulp with 1–3 seeds — the flavor is sweet-tart with floral-citrus notes similar to mangosteen but somewhat less complex. The tree is adapted to partial shade as an understory species in its native cloud forest habitat, making it one of the few tropical fruit trees that can be grown productively in partial shade. Bacupari/madruno is virtually unknown outside of Colombia and the Andean region where it is grown as a local specialty fruit. For zone 11–12 tropical gardeners seeking the most unusual and rare edible collectors' plants. Extremely rare in commercial availability.
