Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bacuri is a frost-tender Amazonian tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the Amazon and Brazilian cerrado regions, this large forest tree produces a thick-shelled, yellow fruit containing creamy, tangy-sweet white pulp considered one of the finest-flavored fruits of the Amazon, used fresh and in ice creams, juices, and preserves across northern Brazil, though the tree is notoriously slow to reach fruiting age. A relative of mangosteen in the same plant family, it shares that group's exacting climate requirements and very long juvenile period, often a decade or more before first fruiting, making it a specialty tree for dedicated tropical fruit collectors and botanical gardens rather than a quick home orchard planting. Water regularly during the long establishment period, and provide the warm, humid, consistently frost-free conditions the tree requires to eventually bear fruit.

common_name: Balaton Cherry (Hungarian Sour Cherry, Dark Sour Cherry, Sweet-Tart Cherry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Balaton is self-fertile; it ripens 7–10 days after Montmorency (late June to mid-July in Michigan and the northeastern states), producing large, dark red to mahogany-red fruits with dark red flesh and juice — unlike Montmorency's lighter flesh — with a distinctly sweeter and milder flavor that can be enjoyed fresh as well as used for processing. Balaton sour cherry is a Hungarian variety (from the Balaton region of Hungary, named for Lake Balaton) introduced to North American production through Michigan State University's cherry breeding and evaluation program in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming the most important new sour cherry variety introduced to the American market since Montmorency dominated the category throughout the 20th century. The primary distinction of Balaton from Montmorency is the fruit character: Balaton produces large (slightly larger than Montmorency), very dark red to nearly black fruits with dark red flesh and intensely colored juice, in contrast to Montmorency's lighter pink-red skin and clear to pale yellow flesh. This dark flesh and sweet-tart balance gives Balaton a distinct advantage for certain uses: the fruit can be eaten fresh (it is significantly sweeter and less acidic than Montmorency, approaching the level of fresh-eating quality), the juice is intensely pigmented for concentrated cherry products, and the fruit makes darker, richer-colored preserves and pies. MSU Extension has actively promoted Balaton as an alternative to Montmorency for Michigan commercial producers and home orchardists, particularly for growers wanting a second variety to extend the harvest window and access specialty markets.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soils better than most fruit trees and do well in raised beds or large containers where restricted roots encourage fruiting over rampant growth. Baldwin was developed at a University of Florida research station and selected specifically for resistance to souring, a common problem in the Gulf South and Florida where warm, humid weather during ripening lets yeasts and bacteria enter the open eye of the fruit and spoil it before harvest. The medium, brown-skinned fruit has sweet, pink-amber flesh and a closed eye that helps keep out rain and insects, giving Baldwin an edge over open-eyed varieties in humid climates. It produces a reliable main crop in late summer without needing a pollinator, and benefits from a thick mulch layer and occasional deep watering during dry spells.

Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with trellis or fence support; banana passion fruit produces elongated pale yellow-green fruits 2–4 inches long with a strong passion fruit flavor and abundant aromatic juice used in drinks and ice cream throughout the Colombian highlands, where it is called curuba. The soft-hairy three-lobed leaves and pendant pink tubular flowers attract hummingbirds and are highly ornamental; the vine tolerates light frost better than most passion fruits and grows best in mild, humid conditions rather than the hot lowland tropics. It has escaped cultivation in Hawaii and New Zealand where it is invasive — deadhead spent fruits to prevent self-seeding when grown in mild climates.

Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; banana passionflower is more cold-tolerant than most passionflowers, surviving brief frosts to about 27°F when established, and has been successfully grown in sheltered spots in zone 8b and even zone 8a. Passiflora mollissima is an Andean native cultivated throughout the Andes from Colombia to Bolivia for its edible, banana-shaped, yellow, oblong fruits (curuba) 3–5 inches long with juicy, bright-orange, passion-fruit-flavored pulp used in juices, ice cream, and desserts; it is one of the most commercially important passionfruit species in South America. The flowers are beautiful — long-tubed, rose-pink to coral-pink, with a reduced corona — and are pollinated by hummingbirds. It grows vigorously and is considered invasive in warm, humid climates outside its native range (especially Hawaii, New Zealand, and South Africa); confirm it is legal to grow in your area.

common_name: Banyan Tree (Bengal Fig, Indian Banyan, Strangler Fig)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in deep, well-drained soil with ample space — Banyan Tree is one of the largest living organisms on Earth and requires consideration before planting in any developed landscape. Ficus benghalensis is a massive evergreen fig tree native to the Indian subcontinent (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal), sacred in Hinduism and one of the national trees of India. The Banyan Tree has produced the largest tree canopy of any living plant species: the famous Great Banyan Tree in the Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden near Kolkata, India covers more than 4 acres with approximately 3,500 aerial prop roots and a canopy circumference of more than 1,500 feet. The tree's extraordinary growth mechanism — aerial roots that descend from the branches, root in the soil, and gradually thicken into secondary trunks capable of supporting additional branches — allows an individual tree to expand laterally without limit, progressively creating a multi-trunked 'forest' from a single genetic individual. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and Florida, Banyan Trees are major landscape and street trees. Small specimens are excellent as container bonsai or large indoor specimens in zone 9. The milky sap is irritating to skin. The small figs are eaten by birds but are not palatable to humans.

growth_habit: African iconic ancient dryland multi-use tree
notes: Plant Baobab in deep, freely draining, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; they are highly drought-tolerant once established and dislike any root waterlogging — excellent drainage is non-negotiable; water moderately during summer active growth and reduce or stop watering in winter when deciduous; container-grown Baobabs make striking bonsai or patio specimens for decades before size becomes an issue. Baobab is one of the most extraordinary trees on Earth — capable of living 2,000–5,000+ years (and possibly far longer), storing thousands of liters of water in its massive, spongy, swollen trunk, and providing food, medicine, fiber, and shelter for both people and wildlife across its native sub-Saharan Africa range. The large, white, bat-pollinated flowers open at night and are strongly fragrant; they are followed by the football-sized, hard, hanging fruits — known commercially as 'baobab fruit' or 'monkey bread' — containing dry, chalky-white pulp naturally rich in Vitamin C (6x more than oranges per weight), calcium, potassium, and antioxidants. The pulp, leaves, seeds, bark, and roots all have documented food and medicinal uses across Africa; commercial baobab fruit powder has grown into a global superfood industry. In zone 10–12, it makes a spectacular, extraordinarily long-lived specimen tree; young plants grow slowly but rewards patient gardeners with one of the planet's most remarkable organisms.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; barbados cherry (acerola, West Indian cherry) is a subtropical shrub or small tree that produces cherry-sized, three-lobed, bright red to orange-red fruits containing the highest natural concentration of Vitamin C of any food crop — approximately 65 times the Vitamin C of orange juice by weight. In south Florida, Texas Gulf Coast, and zone 9–11 climates, established plants produce three to four fruiting cycles annually, yielding heavy crops of sweet-tart, highly perishable fruits that must be processed immediately (fresh eating, juice, smoothies, frozen puree) as they deteriorate within hours of harvest. The plant is an attractive, dense, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub with small, pink, orchid-like flowers and is often grown as a fruiting hedge or informal screen. Productive and relatively pest-free in tropical and subtropical climates. 'B-17', 'Manoa Sweet', and 'Florida Sweet' are improved selections with larger, sweeter fruit.

Root cuttings in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Barbados gooseberry is one of the most botanically fascinating of all edible plants — a primitive cactus (family Cactaceae) that retains true persistent leaves unlike all other cacti, making it a living link between leafy plants and the succulent cacti. The woody, thorny scrambling vine can reach 30 feet when climbing, with oval, slightly succulent leaves and masses of fragrant white to pale pink flowers in fall. The yellow to orange fruits ripen to 0.75 inches with multiple seeds embedded in pulp with a pleasant acid-sweet, citrus-like flavor — used fresh, in jams, and as a vegetable cooked with rice in the Caribbean. The young leaves are edible as a potherb. In South America the leaves are consumed as 'ora-pro-nobis,' valued for their exceptionally high protein content (25% dry weight). An unusual and productive edible vine for frost-free gardens.

common_name: Barcelona Hazelnut (Barcelona Filbert, Pacific Northwest Commercial Filbert Standard)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Barcelona requires a companion pollenizer variety; the catkins (male flowers) shed pollen in late winter before the tiny female flowers emerge; nuts ripen in September–October and fall naturally when ripe — sweep them from the ground daily for best quality before mold develops. Barcelona hazelnut is the dominant commercial hazelnut (filbert) variety in the Willamette Valley of Oregon, which produces approximately 99% of the American commercial hazelnut crop and is the third-largest hazelnut production region in the world after Turkey and Italy. The variety was introduced from Spain (where it was a standard filbert cultivar) to the Oregon hazelnut industry in the late 1800s and quickly became the commercial standard because of its productive, consistent cropping, large nut size for the era, and good kernel quality. For over a century, Barcelona dominated Oregon hazelnut production so completely that the Oregon hazelnut industry and Barcelona hazelnut were essentially synonymous. The primary limitation of Barcelona — and the reason it has begun to be replaced by newer OSU-released varieties — is its extreme susceptibility to Eastern Filbert Blight (EFB), a canker disease caused by the native American fungus Anisogramma anomala that is devastating in the eastern United States where it is endemic but historically absent from Pacific Coast orchards. EFB reached Oregon in the 1990s, and its spread has prompted the Oregon hazelnut industry to shift toward the new EFB-resistant OSU varieties (Jefferson, Yamhill, others).

Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Barland is an exceptionally slow tree to reach bearing age, sometimes taking well over a decade. A classic Herefordshire perry pear long prized for producing exceptionally high-tannin, astringent juice that gives finished perry real structure and aging potential, it is considered one of the finest true perry pears despite, or because of, fruit far too harsh and bitter for fresh eating. Its notoriously slow growth to first bearing has always made it a tree planted for a future generation rather than quick reward, a tradition reflected in the old West Country saying about planting pears for one's heirs. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and mellow, then mill and press for perry.

common_name: Bartlett Pear (Williams' Bon Chrétien Pear, Williams Pear)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Bartlett (Williams' Bon Chrétien in Europe) is the most widely grown pear in North America and the world's most commercially important pear cultivar — the classic yellow, buttery, bell-shaped fruit that defines the word 'pear' in popular culture. The large, sweet, aromatic fruit with fine-grained, melting flesh ripens from late summer to early fall and is excellent fresh, canned, dried, and used in pies and preserves. Trees are moderately susceptible to fire blight (Erwinia amylovora), which can cause significant damage in warm, humid climates; planting on well-drained sites and applying copper during bloom reduces risk. Bartlett needs 600–800 chill hours and is best suited to zones 5–7 where winters reliably provide sufficient cold. For warmer zones 8–9, low-chill pears like 'Hood', 'Flordahome', and 'Orient' are more appropriate than Bartlett. Trees bear at 3–5 years and live for decades.

Collect ripe blue-black berries in midsummer and sow seeds fresh in fall, pressing them lightly into moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered outdoor bed or cold frame. Unlike most serviceberries that bear fruits in long clusters, Bartram's Serviceberry ripens single fruits or small groups of 2–4, making hand-harvest easy. This cold-hardy species thrives in cool, moist conditions resembling its native boreal and subalpine habitat; avoid planting in heavy clay or hot, dry sites. Established shrubs are trouble-free and begin producing their first meaningful berry crops within 2–5 years of transplanting.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade at forest edges and woodland understory positions; bay starvine is the native North American member of the Schisandraceae — the same family as the famous five-flavor berry (S. chinensis) of Chinese medicine. It grows in the moist, shaded ravines, stream bottoms, and rich forest understory of the southern Appalachians and adjacent lowlands, producing small red flowers in spring that require cross-pollination between male and female plants. The fruits, clustered like a miniature bunch of grapes on an elongated stalk, ripen red in late summer. The plant tolerates deep shade better than most fruiting vines, filling a valuable niche in shaded woodland garden designs. Though less medicinally celebrated than the Asian species, the native bay starvine has similar phytochemical constituents. A rare and beautiful native vine deserving wider use in woodland shade gardens.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; beaked hazelnut is distinguished from American hazelnut (Corylus americana) by the long, tubular, beak-like husk that encloses each nut — the 'beak' can be twice the length of the nut itself. The nuts ripen in late summer and are enthusiastically gathered by squirrels, chipmunks, turkeys, woodpeckers, and grouse; you must act quickly to harvest any for yourself. Plant two or more seedlings for reliable cross-pollination since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and often self-infertile. The catkins that appear in late winter before the leaves are an early source of pollen for native bees.

common_name: Beall Fig (Heirloom Gulf South Bronze Fig)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate a wide range of soils but produce their best fruit with consistent moisture during ripening. Beall is a long-passed-down heirloom fig from the Gulf South, maintained by home orchardists and fig collectors rather than through commercial nursery release, producing medium bronze-brown fruit with sweet, richly flavored, pink-to-amber flesh. Like most Gulf Coast heirloom figs, it is valued for its vigor and reliability under regional heat and humidity, ripening over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to control size and remove winter dieback, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system; established Beall trees tolerate the occasional hard freeze common to zone 8-9 winters, resprouting from the base if top growth is killed back.

Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Beaumont macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, but bears at a younger age than many macadamia cultivars. A hybrid between the two main macadamia species, this Australian-bred cultivar is widely planted for home gardens and smaller orchards because it begins bearing noticeably earlier than many other macadamia selections, often within three to four years, and produces large clusters of good-quality nuts on a moderately vigorous tree. Its relatively quick time to first bearing makes it a popular choice for home growers wanting a faster return than the decade-plus wait typical of some macadamia cultivars, though like all macadamias it needs consistent warmth and is easily damaged by frost. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and harvest nuts as they fall naturally from the tree when fully mature, since immature nuts do not ripen further once picked.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Beauty is one of the earliest-ripening Japanese plum cultivars, producing medium-sized, bright scarlet-red to crimson fruit with red-streaked yellow flesh in late spring — often the first plum available from the orchard in a given season. The flesh is sweet and juicy with good flavor for fresh eating, canning, and jam production. Beauty is partially self-fertile but produces best crops with a pollinizer nearby (Santa Rosa, Methley, or other Japanese plums). Its low chill requirement (approximately 250–400 hours) makes it well-adapted to zone 7–9, where it performs more reliably than higher-chill European plum cultivars. Trees are moderately vigorous and somewhat susceptible to brown rot, which can be managed with timely fungicide applications and prompt removal of infected fruit. Beauty ripens over an extended period of 2–3 weeks, reducing harvest pressure compared to plums that ripen all at once.

common_name: Ben Davis Apple (Mortgage Lifter Apple, New York Pippin)
notes: Ben Davis tolerates less-than-ideal soil and irregular watering better than most apples, making it forgiving for beginning orchardists or marginal sites. Introduced in the early 1800s and possibly of Kentucky or Tennessee origin, it became one of the most widely planted commercial apples in 19th-century America, prized for its precocious, heavy, reliable annual crops and its exceptional storage life rather than for outstanding fresh flavor, which is mild and somewhat bland compared to dessert apples. It remains of interest to homesteaders and heirloom growers today mainly for its toughness, productivity, and long keeping quality in cold storage.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in a frost-free location; bergamot orange is a small citrus tree grown almost exclusively in Calabria, Italy, for the essential oil extracted from the peel — the aromatic compound that gives Earl Grey tea its distinctive floral-citrus character. The fruit is yellow-green when ripe, roughly lemon-sized, and inedible raw due to intense bitterness. The peel oil is also used extensively in high-end perfumery, providing the top notes to Chanel No. 5 and countless other classic fragrances. In the garden it is an ornamental conversation piece; harvest peels from ripe fruit and dry them, or make a simple extract by steeping fresh peel in vodka. A reliable performer in zone 9–11 with minimal maintenance beyond regular citrus feeding.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Beurre Hardy is a vigorous, reliable tree well suited to a home orchard. A classic French dessert pear introduced in the early nineteenth century, its name meaning roughly buttery and hardy, it bears attractive bronze-russeted, greenish fruit with exceptionally juicy, melting, sweet flesh carrying a distinctive light rosewater aroma prized by pear connoisseurs, on a notably vigorous, reliably productive, and disease-tolerant tree. Its combination of rich flavor, vigorous growth, and good disease resistance compared to some other classic European pears has kept it in cultivation as a favorite home orchard variety for two centuries. Harvest while still firm and green in late summer to early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for a few days until the flesh yields slightly to gentle pressure near the stem.

common_name: Beverly Hills Apple (Very Low-Chill California-Bred Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible low-chill pollinator such as Anna, Dorsett Golden, or Ein Shemer. Beverly Hills was discovered as a chance seedling in Beverly Hills, California and remains valued today as one of the lowest-chill apples available, needing only around 300 chill hours, which lets it set fruit reliably even after the mild winters typical of the Gulf South where most standard apple varieties bloom poorly or not at all. Fruit is medium-sized, red-striped, with tart, crisp flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in mid to late summer. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good airflow and fruit quality in humid conditions.

Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; bigflower pawpaw is adapted to Florida scrub and sandhill habitat and requires sharp drainage, performing poorly in heavy or poorly drained soils. Asimina obovata is a Florida-endemic shrub or small tree grown for its large, showy, creamy-white, three-petaled flowers with a sweet fragrance in spring, followed by yellow-green, custard-fleshed fruit smaller than the common pawpaw but edible fresh. Its thick, leathery, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen leaves and drought tolerance make it a distinctive addition to a sandy-soil food forest or native pollinator garden in the Deep South, where it serves as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies just as its northern relative does. It needs excellent drainage and full sun to partial shade, tolerates poor, infertile sand, and should never be irrigated on a schedule suited to typical garden shrubs.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — bignay is a medium-sized tropical tree of Southeast Asia and the Pacific, producing spectacular long (12–18 inch) pendulous clusters of small (pea-sized) berries that ripen from green through red to deep purple-black in sequence on the same cluster, creating a striking multi-colored effect. The berries have a pleasant tart-sweet flavor with some astringency and are eaten fresh, made into wine, juice, and jam; in the Philippines bignay wine is a traditional fermented beverage. The tree is dioecious and shade-tolerant, growing naturally as an understory tree in mixed tropical forests. The polished, reddish-brown seeds (resembling small nutmegs) are made into decorative necklaces in the Philippines. An outstanding ornamental fruiting tree for zone 9b–12 gardens offering shade tolerance and dramatic fruiting clusters.

Plant rooted cuttings or air-layered trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bilimbi is more shade-tolerant than its close relative starfruit and is a good choice for partially shaded spots in tropical gardens, though it fruits best in full sun. Averrhoa bilimbi is a relative of carambola producing clusters of small (2–4 inch), cucumber-shaped, intensely sour, pale-green to yellow fruits that grow directly from the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) in a bizarre but highly productive display; the extremely tart fruit is rarely eaten fresh but is valued in Southeast Asian and Caribbean cuisine for its acidity in curries, preserves, pickles, and beverages, substituting for tamarind or lime. Trees fruit heavily multiple times per year in frost-free climates (zones 10–12) and can be grown in large containers moved indoors in zone 9; the pinnate leaves and clustered trunk fruits make it an ornamental specimen even when not fruiting.

common_name: Bing Cherry (Dark Sweet Cherry, American Commercial Cherry Standard)
notes: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Bing must be paired with a compatible pollinizer (Rainier, Lapins, or Black Tartarian) — Bing cannot cross-pollinate Stella, Lambert, or Napoleon; protect ripening fruit from birds using netting; avoid planting in poorly drained sites or low spots where frost collects; Bing ripens in late June to early July in the Pacific Northwest, the timing that has made it the dominant commercial cherry. Bing cherry is the most widely grown commercial sweet cherry variety in the United States — the cherry that defines what most Americans mean when they say 'sweet cherry' — a dark mahogany-red to nearly black, large, firm, heart-shaped variety with exceptionally sweet, complex flavor developed in Oregon in 1875 by Seth Lewelling on his fruit farm near Milwaukie, Oregon. Lewelling named the variety after his Chinese foreman, Ah Bing, in recognition of his contributions to the orchard — an unusual act of recognition for a Chinese immigrant worker in that era. The variety quickly spread from Oregon throughout the Pacific Coast commercial cherry-growing regions (the Columbia Basin of Oregon and Washington State, the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys of California) because its combination of large size, dark color, firm flesh, excellent sweetness, and good shipping characteristics made it ideal for the developing rail-shipped fresh fruit trade. Today, Bing accounts for more than 90% of the sweet cherry production in the Pacific Northwest and a major share of all American commercial sweet cherries. The characteristic Bing appearance — large, round to heart-shaped, very dark mahogany-red to black — is so iconic that 'a bag of Bings' has become synonymous with sweet cherries in American culture, and fresh Bing cherries in early summer represent one of the quintessential seasonal fruits of the American marketplace.

Clean seeds from ripe black fruits in late summer and sow immediately to take advantage of the warm-soil period before winter cold sets in; this two-phase stratification requirement is essential and skipping either phase will delay germination by a full year. Plant in moist, fertile soil near a stream bank or in a woodland clearing, reflecting its natural preference for riparian and marginal woodland habitats throughout northern Eurasia. Bird cherry grows vigorously once established and will naturalize readily, so site it where suckering can be managed or is welcome as a thicket for wildlife. Expect the first flower racemes by year four to six, filling the garden with a heavy almond-like fragrance in mid to late spring before the leaves fully expand.

Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a sturdy arbor, fence, or large shrub in well-drained sandy soil in full sun. Bird grape is a slender, thin-barked native vine of Florida hammocks, pinelands, and Gulf Coast scrub, distinguished from the related muscadine by its smaller leaves and less shaggy bark, and it climbs readily by tendrils once given support. Its small, sweet black grapes ripen over a long season and are eaten avidly by songbirds, making it a valuable addition to a wildlife hedge or fence line rather than a fruit crop for the table. It tolerates the heat, humidity, sandy soils, and periodic drought of the Gulf Coast better than most grape species, needing only occasional pruning to keep it in bounds.

common_name: Biriba (Wild Sweetsop, Rollinia, Lemon Meringue Fruit)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil; Biriba grows rapidly in zone 10–11 humid conditions and benefits from regular irrigation and fertilization to produce its heavy crops of large, distinctive fruits. Rollinia deliciosa (often treated as a synonym within the soursop genus: Annona mucosa) is a tropical fruit tree from the Amazon basin of Brazil, Colombia, and Peru, prized by tropical fruit enthusiasts for producing one of the most extraordinarily flavored and unusual-looking fruits in the Annona family. The fruits are large (4–8 inches), covered in soft, flexible, yellowish-green to golden spines or fingerlike projections that soften completely when ripe, and contain white, extremely juicy, sweet-tart flesh described as tasting like a combination of lemon meringue, vanilla custard, and banana — some connoisseurs consider it the finest-flavored of all the Annona relatives, surpassing cherimoya and soursop. The fruits ripen very rapidly (within 1–2 days of picking) and bruise at the slightest touch, making commercial distribution virtually impossible and confining the fruit almost entirely to home gardens and local markets in tropical growing regions. In zone 10–11 South Florida, Biriba is increasingly grown by rare-fruit enthusiasts and community gardens as a fast-growing, productive tree that rewards the patient gardener with extraordinary fruits unavailable in any market.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; bitter kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the humid rainforests of West and Central Africa, this understory to mid-canopy tree bears a fruit whose bitter, astringent seeds are widely chewed fresh across West Africa, valued both as a traditional stimulant, similar in cultural role to true kola nut, and as an important item in traditional hospitality and ceremony. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and require the warm, humid, shaded forest conditions of their native range to thrive, making this a specialty planting for tropical botanical collections, ethnobotanical gardens, or large frost-free properties rather than a typical home garden tree. Water regularly, especially while young, and protect from any exposure to direct hot afternoon sun, which the shade-adapted seedlings do not tolerate well.

Plant in moist to well-drained, fertile, loamy or clay soil in full sun; bitternut hickory is the most widely distributed hickory in eastern North America and one of the fastest growing, making it valuable as a canopy tree where time to a large shade tree is a priority. The nuts are notably bitter and unpalatable to humans (hence the common name), being too high in tannins for human consumption even after shelling — unlike the sweet-nutted shagbark and shellbark hickories. However, they are consumed by squirrels, deer, and wood ducks after additional caching and processing. The distinctive butter-yellow winter buds are an important winter identification trait. The golden-yellow fall color is attractive, and the tree provides superb canopy for native plant understories. One of the most moisture-tolerant hickories.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average tropical soil in partial shade to full sun in zone 10–12; black calabash is a tropical tree of the Bignoniaceae family (the same family as trumpet creeper and catalpa) native to Central American and Caribbean coastal forests, producing unusual, large, round-to-oblong, gourd-like fruits with extremely hard, black shells when mature. The hard shells are used throughout Central America and the Caribbean to make maracas, rattles, cups, bowls, and other traditional crafts and musical instruments — the same traditional use as the unrelated calabash gourd (Lagenaria). The fleshy inner pulp is eaten by bats and birds, which disperse the seeds. The flowers, which appear directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), are interesting botanical curiosities. Adapted to partial shade of tropical forest edges and hammocks. A rare conversation piece for south Florida collectors and native plant enthusiasts.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; black cherry is arguably the most ecologically important fruiting tree in eastern North America, supporting the larvae of over 400 species of moths and butterflies (more than almost any other tree genus), providing early-spring nectar in its white flower racemes, and producing thousands of small black cherries in summer that are consumed by over 70 species of birds — robins, waxwings, thrushes, catbirds, woodpeckers — as well as bears, foxes, and raccoons. The small black cherries are edible and intensely flavorful, traditionally used for cherry wine, jelly, and syrups. The wilted leaves and seeds contain prussic acid and are toxic to livestock. The bark has traditional medicinal use as a cough suppressant. A fast-growing native tree (2–3 feet per year) that can seed prolifically.

Black Genoa is a widely grown Italian heirloom producing purplish-black skinned fruit with deep amber-pink flesh and a rich, sweet flavor that many growers rank among the best dark-skinned figs for fresh eating. It is a reliably heavy producer of both an early breba crop on overwintered wood and a larger main crop on new growth, giving an extended summer-into-fall harvest in warm climates. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and prune in winter to control size, since trees can become quite large and dense without management. Long popular in California and Australian home orchards, it performs well in Mediterranean and humid subtropical climates alike.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — jackfruit is intolerant of waterlogged soil and will decline rapidly if the root zone remains saturated; Black Gold Jackfruit is a named, semi-dwarf cultivar of Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), the world's largest tree-borne fruit, selected for compact tree size and superior fruit quality — sweet, aromatic, deep yellow flesh with lower latex content than seedling trees, making the fruit more pleasant to prepare and eat. Jackfruit is one of the most nutritionally complete and calorie-dense tropical fruits: the ripe, sweet arils (seed pods) are eaten fresh and have a flavor combining banana, pineapple, and mango; the unripe green fruit, with its fibrous, neutral, meat-like texture, has become internationally popular as a plant-based meat substitute in pulled pork, tacos, curries, and other savory dishes. The combination of edible ripe fruit and valuable unripe culinary use gives jackfruit two entirely different roles in the kitchen — one as a sweet tropical fruit and one as a versatile vegetable protein. In the warmest zone 9 microclimates and zone 10 the semi-dwarf Black Gold produces a manageable ornamental and productive fruit tree that brings one of the most unique and globally significant tropical fruits into the home garden.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; black hawthorn is a widespread native of western North America from Alaska to California and east to the Rocky Mountains, producing distinctive shiny black fruits (rather than the red of most hawthorns) that ripen in late summer. The blackish-purple haws are sweet and flavorful, traditionally eaten fresh and dried by Pacific Northwest Native peoples including the Klallam, Nlaka'pamux, and many others. The thorny thickets provide exceptional nesting habitat for songbirds. White spring flowers attract numerous pollinators. The fruit is also made into jam, jelly, and wine. More tolerant of wet soils than most hawthorns and common along stream banks in its native range.

Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, rocky, or red clay soils in full sun; black hickory is the most drought-tolerant hickory native to Texas and the Coastal Plain, naturally inhabiting dry sandy uplands, rocky ridges, and sandstone hills where other hickories fail. The nuts are small and have thick shells relative to their edible kernel, but are consumed by squirrels, deer, wild turkeys, and other wildlife that provide the ecological services of seed dispersal. The dark, rough, blocky bark becomes increasingly distinctive with age. Like all hickories, black hickory is very slow to establish (most growth goes underground in early years as the taproot develops) but eventually becomes a long-lived, tough, low-maintenance tree well-suited to the challenging dry sandy soils of east Texas and Oklahoma. Important wildlife food tree for dry upland woodland habitats.

Black Ischia is a small-to-medium fig with near-black, purple-black skin that lacks a pronounced neck, opening to reveal strawberry-pink to red flesh with a rich, sweet flavor. Long grown on the Mediterranean island of Ischia and popularized in American gardens through heirloom fruit exchanges, it typically bears both a light early breba crop and a heavier main crop in warm climates. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and prune lightly in winter to maintain an open, easily harvested framework, since the thin skin bruises readily. It is valued by home growers for its rich flavor rather than shipping quality, making it best suited to dooryard planting rather than commercial production.

common_name: Black Jack Fig (Compact Semi-Dwarf Dark-Fruited Container Fig)
notes: Plant nursery trees or rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; prune in late winter to maintain size and shape. Black Jack is a compact, semi-dwarf fig tree — a sport or selection from the Brown Turkey class producing somewhat smaller stature (8–12 feet rather than the 15–25 feet of standard fig trees) while bearing large, richly flavored dark purple-black fruits. The moderate compact habit makes Black Jack one of the most practical fig varieties for residential gardens and particularly well-suited to large containers (20–25 gallon) for small spaces, patios, and areas where a standard-sized fig would be too large. The fruits are medium to large, elongated, with dark purple-black to near-black skin and deep strawberry-red flesh — a visually dramatic appearance that makes the fruits ornamentally attractive at the harvest stage. The flavor is rich, very sweet, and fig-like with deep, complex, sweet notes that improve when fruits are allowed to fully ripen on the tree (they should feel soft and droop slightly at the neck before harvest). Black Jack produces reliably in zone 7–11 with proper cold protection when young. In zone 9, the long, warm growing season allows excellent main crop development and often a bonus early-season breba crop.

Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Black Mission fig is the most widely grown commercial fig in California, introduced by Spanish Franciscan missionaries in the 1700s and now the cornerstone of the California fig industry. It produces two crops yearly in favorable climates — a breba crop on last year's wood in early summer, and a main crop in late summer to fall. The large, purplish-black figs have pink to reddish flesh with an intensely rich, complex, sweet-jammy flavor that is among the finest of all fig varieties. Excellent fresh, dried, or made into preserves. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and is relatively drought-tolerant once established. In humid climates, fruit splitting and souring can be problematic; select LSU Purple or Celeste for the Southeast.

The black mulberry is a slow-growing, long-lived tree bearing intensely flavored dark fruit far superior to that of white or red mulberries. Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a spot sheltered from cold winds. It is self-fertile, so one tree crops well, though the staining fruit is best sited away from paving. Prune only lightly in winter, as mulberries bleed heavily from large cuts.

growth_habit: West African edible black plum ornamental shade tree
notes: Plant Vitex doniana in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; highly drought-tolerant once established; prune young trees to develop good branching structure; the tree grows slowly at first then more vigorously once the root system is established. Black Plum is one of the most important multi-purpose trees of the African sahel and Sudan savanna zone — spread across a vast belt from Senegal and Gambia through Mali, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, and east to Sudan, Uganda, and Kenya. The sweet, date-like, purple-black fruits are eaten fresh throughout the region, made into local beverages, and dried for storage; the nutritional profile includes iron, calcium, and vitamins. Young leaves are cooked and eaten as a vegetable (especially important during the 'hungry season' before the harvest) and the leaves are also used medicinally for fever and rheumatism. The dense, golden-yellow heartwood is highly prized for furniture, carvings, drums, and mortars; a single tree can be worth significant sums in local markets. In the Sahel agroforestry system, Black Plum is a valued component of parkland farming systems (farmer-managed natural regeneration) where it provides food, shade for crops, fodder, and materials. An outstanding drought-tolerant shade tree for zone 10–12 dry tropical gardens.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in frost-free conditions; black sapote produces tomato-sized fruits with thin green skin that turns olive-yellow at full ripeness, concealing soft black pulp with a rich, sweet, chocolate-like flavor that famously resembles chocolate pudding — often eaten directly from the skin with a spoon. A relative of persimmons, it must be completely soft before eating; hard fruits are extremely astringent. Excellent used in smoothies, ice cream, mousses, and as a low-fat substitute for chocolate in baked goods. Trees are moderately fast-growing and begin bearing 3–5 years from transplant; an outstanding conversation piece and genuinely delicious tropical fruit for zone 10–12 gardens.

common_name: Black Spanish Grape (Lenoir Grape, Jacques Grape, Historic Gulf Coast Red Grape)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — Black Spanish is notably drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the thin, rocky soils of the Texas Hill Country; train on cordon system; prune in late winter; fruit ripens in July–August in the Gulf South; the small, dark blue-black berries are very juicy with moderate tannins and produce a robust, full-bodied red wine and excellent red grape juice. Black Spanish (also called Lenoir, after a French viticulturalist named Lenoir who promoted it, or 'Jacques' after a French settler who may have introduced it) is a historic American hybrid grape variety that has been cultivated in Louisiana, Texas, and the broader Gulf South since before the Civil War — one of the earliest wine grapes to be grown commercially in Texas. Its precise parentage is disputed (likely a complex hybrid of Vitis aestivalis or Vitis berlandieri with other American species, possibly with some vinifera ancestry from early French colonial plantings), but its performance characteristics are well-established: Black Spanish is exceptionally tolerant of Pierce's disease, heat, and drought. In the 19th century, when European settlers attempted to establish vineyards in the South with vinifera varieties, virtually all of these plantings failed within a few years due to Pierce's disease — but varieties like Black Spanish, which incorporated native American species with natural resistance, survived and produced fruit year after year. This made Black Spanish the cornerstone of the early Texas and Louisiana wine industries, and it remained the dominant red grape in Texas through much of the early 20th century. The wine produced is dark, deeply colored, with robust tannins and an earthy, slightly rustic character that is quite different from European reds but has its own distinctive appeal. Modern Gulf Coast winemakers continue to work with Black Spanish as a component of blended wines.

Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Black Tartarian is one of the oldest and most reliable sweet cherry cultivars in cultivation — an early-season cherry with large, dark mahogany-red to nearly black, heart-shaped fruit with sweet, rich, dark-red flesh. It ripens 1–2 weeks before Bing and is one of the first sweet cherries to mature in a given location. The fruit is softer than Bing or Rainier and does not store or ship as well, making it particularly suited to home garden production and immediate fresh consumption. Black Tartarian also serves as an excellent pollinizer for most other sweet cherry varieties. It was imported from Russia in the early 1800s and is one of the oldest sweet cherry cultivars still in commercial and home garden production. Trees are vigorous, relatively disease-resistant, and productive. Require 900+ chill hours; best suited to zones 5–8 in areas with reliable cold winters.

Black walnut is a native North American species grown primarily for its richly flavored nuts and valuable timber. It produces high concentrations of juglone in its roots, leaves, and hulls, which is toxic to many garden plants including tomatoes, peppers, apples, and blueberries; maintain a 50–80 foot buffer from sensitive plants. Trees are monoecious and partially self-fertile but cross well with a second tree. Hulls stain skin and clothing an indelible dark brown; wear gloves when husking. Nuts are ready when hulls are yellow-green to black and dent when pressed; cure for 2–3 weeks after husking.

Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Blakeney Red is a vigorous, self-fertile perry pear, but still crops more heavily with a second variety for cross-pollination. One of the most widely planted traditional English perry pears, originating in the Forest of Dean area of Gloucestershire, it produces a heavy, reliable crop of small, red-blushed pears on a large, vigorous, long-lived tree, valued by perry makers for moderate tannin and good juice yield that blends well in traditional West Country perry production. Unlike many perry pears, it is self-fertile, making it a more forgiving choice for an orchard with limited space for a dedicated pollinator tree, though a second variety still improves cropping. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, and let it sweat in a pile for a few days before milling and pressing.

common_name: Blanc du Bois Grape (Gulf Coast Pierce's-Disease-Resistant White Wine Grape)
notes: Train on a cordon trellis system in full sun; prune in late winter; Blanc du Bois ripens in June–July in the Gulf South, much earlier than northern grapes; the fruit is white-green to golden at maturity and produces crisp, fruity white wine with notes of melon, citrus, and tropical fruit; fruit can also be eaten fresh or made into juice. Blanc du Bois is the most important Gulf Coast white wine grape variety, bred by Dr. John Mortensen at the University of Florida's Levin College of Law agricultural breeding program (USDA-ARS Fort Pierce) specifically for the hot, humid climate of the American Southeast and Gulf South where European vinifera varieties cannot survive. The critical factor in Gulf Coast viticulture is Pierce's disease — a bacterial infection caused by Xylella fastidiosa spread by the glassy-winged sharpshooter leafhopper (Homalodisca vitripennis) — which kills European vinifera varieties (Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, etc.) within 1–5 years throughout the Gulf South. Blanc du Bois was developed as a complex hybrid incorporating Vitis champinii (heat-tolerant wild Texas grape) and other native American species to provide Pierce's disease resistance, while retaining enough vinifera quality characteristics to produce high-quality white wine comparable to European-style dry whites. The resulting wine is crisp, fruity, and aromatic with Muscat-like floral notes and good acidity — genuinely world-class for a Pierce's disease-resistant variety and the backbone of the emerging Gulf Coast wine industry. Blanc du Bois grapes ripen unusually early — in June to early July in zone 9a, compared to September ripening in northern vineyards — which allows harvest before the peak summer heat and humidity. Several Texas and Florida wineries produce award-winning Blanc du Bois wines that have helped establish the variety's reputation nationally.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Blenheim Orange is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it cannot pollinate other apples and needs two different diploid varieties nearby. An old English variety dating to the eighteenth century, it bears large, handsome, orange-red-flushed apples with dry, nutty, richly flavored flesh good for both fresh eating once fully ripe and for cooking, one of the classic dual-purpose apples that bridges the line between dessert and culinary use. As a triploid, it produces sterile pollen and requires two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination of itself and each other, a detail worth planning for before planting, and it makes a large, vigorous, long-lived tree. Harvest in mid-fall and let the fruit mellow in storage for a few weeks before eating fresh, since the flesh is at its best after a short period off the tree.

Blood orange cultivars (Moro, Tarocco, Sanguinello) develop their signature ruby-red flesh and juice through the accumulation of anthocyanins, a pigment triggered by cool nights during fruit development — temperatures between 40 and 50°F for several weeks from late autumn through midwinter produce the deepest coloring. In frost-free tropical climates the flesh remains orange with little anthocyanin. Trees are self-fertile, medium-sized, and managed identically to other sweet oranges: plant in well-drained soil, fertilize with a citrus blend three times per year, and irrigate deeply but infrequently. Harvest from late winter through early spring when the flesh has developed full color and the fruit is sweet.

Plant grafted stock in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; fertilize with citrus formula in late winter, late spring, and early fall. Citrus × sinensis 'Moro' (Moro blood orange) is the most intensely red-fleshed blood orange variety — a Sicilian mutation of sweet orange in which the flesh, juice, and sometimes the rind develop stunning deep-red to near-purple color from anthocyanin pigments produced in response to cool autumn nights. The 'Moro' cultivar produces the deepest, most intensely colored blood-red flesh and dramatic dark-red juice of any blood orange, with a distinctive flavor that combines sweet orange with a raspberry-berry overtone from the anthocyanins. In zone 9, the cool fall and winter nights (below 60°F) trigger the red pigment development; in warmer climates the color development is minimal. Blood orange juice makes extraordinary cocktails, salad dressings, and sauces. The 'Tarocco' variety (less cold-hardy, zone 10) produces the best flavor; 'Sanguinelli' is another reliable variety. Blood oranges ripen December through March in zone 9.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Bloomsweet is a grapefruit-like hybrid selected for cold hardiness beyond that of standard grapefruit cultivars, producing pale yellow, thin-skinned, juicy fruit with a mild, less bitter flavor than classic grapefruit and only a light blush of the typical grapefruit tang. The tree's improved cold tolerance, credited to its mixed parentage, has made it a popular choice for gardeners in the cooler parts of the Gulf Coast citrus belt who want grapefruit-style fruit without the cold sensitivity of true Citrus x paradisi selections. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree, sweetening further if left to hang after coloring fully. Give young trees winter protection for their first several years in zone 8, since even improved hardiness has limits; mature trees tolerate brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s F with minimal damage.

Give this large, coarse-leaved shrub a sheltered spot with dappled or half-day shade and consistently moist, rich soil, mimicking the Himalayan and Chinese forest margins it comes from. By autumn, established plants hang thick with startling metallic-blue, finger-like seed pods several inches long; split one open to reach the sweet, translucent, gelatinous pulp inside, which tastes something like watermelon or lychee, though the numerous black seeds must be spit out. It needs a male and female plant, or a self-fertile seedling, to set the curious pods reliably. Few other fruiting shrubs offer both genuine shade tolerance and such a conversation-starting harvest.

Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; blue bean shrub needs a second, genetically distinct plant nearby for reliable pod set and benefits from a sheltered site out of harsh drying wind. Decaisnea insignis is a striking, large, multi-stemmed shrub from the Himalaya and western China with big, compound, tropical-looking leaves and drooping clusters of small yellow-green flowers in late spring, followed by the plant's signature feature — dangling, metallic blue, sausage-shaped seed pods in fall that give rise to its unsettling common name. The pods split open to reveal a translucent, gelatinous, mildly sweet pulp around black seeds that can be eaten fresh, similar in texture and flavor to a mild melon, though it is grown mostly as a conversation-piece ornamental rather than a serious food crop. It prefers a woodland-edge setting with shelter from wind and consistent moisture, and its architectural form and unusual fruit make it a standout specimen in a shaded border.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun and provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous tendrils; blue passionflower is the most cold-hardy of the fruiting passion vines, tolerating brief dips to 10–15°F when established roots are protected by mulch. The intricate blue, white, and purple flowers with their alien-looking filament corona rank among the most striking summer blooms of any garden vine, followed by oval orange-yellow fruits that are edible but bland compared to commercial passion fruit — grow it primarily for the spectacular flowers and cold hardiness. Dies to the ground in zones 7–8 but regrows strongly from deep roots; do not remove dormant crowns too early in spring.

Train young plants onto a wall, pergola, or fence in part shade in spring, in fertile soil with reliable drainage, since this evergreen twiner from central China resents waterlogging even though it tolerates low light well. Small, fragrant purple-and-white flowers open in spring and are followed in a good year by sausage-shaped purple fruits with sweet, translucent pulp, though fruiting improves markedly when two plants are grown together. Its leathery, trifoliate evergreen leaves make it a valuable year-round screen for shaded boundaries where deciduous vines would leave a winter gap. Prune after flowering to control its vigorous twining growth.

common_name: Bob Gordon Elderberry (Kansas State University Very Large Fruit Elderberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Bob Gordon was selected by James Millican from a wild elderberry population in Kansas and released through Kansas State University — it produces some of the largest individual berries of any American elderberry cultivar, with berry diameter significantly exceeding the standard wild-type, and heavy, pendant clusters of dark purple-black berries that ripen in late summer. American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) is a vigorously suckering native shrub producing flat-topped, white flower clusters (cymes) in June–July — large, fragrant, and excellent for elderflower cordials, vinegars, and baked goods — followed by heavy clusters of dark purple-black berries in August–September used for elderberry syrup, wine, jelly, and juice. 'Bob Gordon' performs well in the humid heat of Gulf South zone 8-9 conditions, though elderberries prefer the slightly cooler and more reliably moist soils of zone 7-8 for maximum production. In zone 9, provide consistent moisture and afternoon shade protection to maintain health through summer. The very large berry size and heavy production make Bob Gordon one of the top choices for home and commercial elderberry production in the eastern US. Plants spread by suckers to form colonies — remove suckers regularly to maintain a well-defined shrub form.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Bonanza is a genetic dwarf apricot that naturally stays under six feet tall while still producing normal-sized, sweet, orange-fleshed fruit, making it one of the few apricots practical for a large container or a very small yard. Like most apricots it blooms quite early in spring, so a sheltered site away from low-lying frost pockets improves the odds of a good fruit set. The dense, compact form needs little pruning to maintain shape beyond removing crossing branches, and the tree is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator variety.

common_name: Bonnie Brae Lemon (California Heirloom Slender Lemon)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed, in a warm, well-drained, sunny site, giving this vigorous, somewhat thorny tree room to spread. Water consistently during establishment and avoid waterlogged soil, which quickly stresses lemon roots. Bonnie Brae produces distinctively long, slender, thin-skinned lemons with abundant tart juice and few seeds, and it can flower and fruit nearly year-round in mild climates. Once grown commercially in Southern California, it remains a sought-after heirloom for home growers who prize its exceptionally juicy fruit over its irregular, less market-friendly shape.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in zones 10-12; Booth is a long-established Florida cherimoya selection prized for reliable production and good-sized, conical, mildly ribbed fruit with rich, sweet, custardy white flesh and the classic tropical flavor blend of pineapple, banana, and vanilla. It has a reputation as one of the more dependable croppers among named cherimoya cultivars in Florida's warm, humid subtropical conditions, which can otherwise be a challenging environment for a species that prefers the cooler, drier climate of its Andean homeland. As with all cherimoya, hand-pollinate by transferring pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers with a small brush in the morning hours, since the flowers' protogynous timing makes natural self-pollination unreliable. Grafted trees bear within two to four years; protect young trees from frost and give them consistent moisture during fruit development.

Grow this understory shrub from the Colombian Chocó rainforest in a large pot of rich, moisture-retentive potting mix, since it wants filtered light and constant humidity rather than harsh full sun. It produces large, dense, brown fruits packed with a thick, tart pulp that is almost always processed into juice or preserves rather than eaten fresh. Because it is one of the most cold-sensitive fruiting plants grown by tropical fruit collectors, Gulf Coast and Florida growers keep it strictly as a greenhouse or sunroom container specimen and never leave it outside once temperatures dip toward 50°F. Consistent watering and high humidity are more important to fruit set than any particular soil type.

common_name: Bouche de Betizac Chestnut (Large-Nutted Blight-Resistant Hybrid Chestnut)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator chestnut within range for the best nut production, since yields improve substantially with cross-pollination even in partially self-fertile cultivars. Bouche de Betizac is a French-bred hybrid between European and Japanese chestnut species, combining the large, sweet, high-quality nuts prized in European chestnut cookery with meaningful resistance to chestnut blight, the disease that devastated native American chestnut populations and continues to threaten susceptible European chestnut plantings. It bears precociously, often producing a first crop within just a few years of planting, and continues with heavy, reliable yields of large, easy-to-peel nuts on a vigorous, productive tree. Its blight resistance and large nut size have made it a popular choice for both commercial and home chestnut orchards seeking a reliable, disease-tolerant alternative to susceptible pure European chestnut cultivars. Harvest nuts as burs split and drop in fall, collecting promptly to avoid rodent and insect loss.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Named for the former French colonial name of Réunion Island, where it was first cultivated after being introduced from Yemen, this historic Arabica coffee variety is one of the parent lines behind many modern specialty coffee cultivars and is still prized by growers and roasters for producing sweet, well-balanced, complex cups, though its lower yield compared to newer hybrid varieties has made it less common in large-scale commercial production. Like other Arabica coffees it grows best in the dappled shade of taller companion trees, mimicking its native highland forest understory habitat, and needs consistent warmth and moisture without ever standing in wet, waterlogged soil. Water regularly but ensure good drainage, provide filtered shade, and expect the first coffee cherry harvest after three to four years of growth.

A classic fig of Provence, Bourjassotte Grise bears medium-sized fruit with a distinctive grayish-brown to violet-tinted skin covering deep strawberry-red flesh with a rich, sweet, complex flavor long prized in French markets. The tree is moderately vigorous and reliably productive once established, generally favoring a single strong main crop over a heavy breba crop. Plant in full sun with good air circulation, since the thin skin is prone to splitting after heavy rain near harvest. It is best suited to long, warm-summer climates where the late-season fruit has time to fully ripen before cool weather arrives.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Bradley is a Florida-developed atemoya cultivar valued for ripening later in the season than Gefner, extending the atemoya harvest window into late fall and helping spread out the crop for home growers with more than one tree. Like other atemoya cultivars it produces rich, custardy, sweet flesh with tropical vanilla and pineapple notes, and benefits from hand pollination for the most reliable and largest fruit set. Harvest when fruit begins to soften slightly and the skin color lightens, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating.

common_name: Braeburn Apple (Crisp Aromatic New Zealand Sweet-Tart Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and provide a cross-pollinator, since Braeburn is not reliably self-fruitful. Discovered as a chance seedling near Motueka, New Zealand in 1952, it quickly became one of the most widely exported dessert apples of the late 20th century for its dense, crisp flesh and layered sweet-tart flavor with a faint spice note. Fruit ripens late in the season and colors in streaky red over a green-gold background; it keeps exceptionally well in cold storage, often holding good eating quality for months. Thin heavy fruit sets in early summer to improve size and prevent biennial bearing.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Bramley's Seedling is a vigorous, triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby and ample permanent space. Grown from a pip planted in Nottinghamshire, England around 1809, this is the definitive British culinary apple, producing very large, bright green, sharply tart fruit that cooks down into a smooth, fluffy puree prized above nearly all other apples for pies, sauces, and traditional English cooking, though it is far too acidic and firm-fleshed for most people's taste eaten fresh off the tree. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for cross-pollination, and it makes a notably large, vigorous, long-lived tree that benefits from ample permanent space and a sturdy semi-standard or standard rootstock. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fully ripe, and the acidic fruit stores exceptionally well through winter when kept cool, making it a valued keeper for a home cook's cooking apple supply.

growth_habit: Amazonian iconic edible nut canopy tree
notes: Plant Brazil Nut trees in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with adequate space for their ultimate enormous size; they require mycorrhizal fungi associations established in forest soil for optimal growth; fruiting does not begin until trees are 10–15 years old and requires the presence of orchid bees (Eulaema spp.) for pollination of their complex flowers — making commercial fruiting difficult outside the Amazon Basin. Brazil Nut trees are among the most ecologically important trees in the Amazon — their hard, 4-inch woody seed pods (cocos) fall from the canopy with enough force to be fatal, making harvesting genuinely dangerous; they are collected by harvesters who enter the forest after the natural fall season. The seeds (nuts) are extraordinarily rich in selenium — a single Brazil nut provides the recommended daily allowance — and are one of the world's most nutritionally dense foods. Brazil Nut is also an indicator of primary forest health: the trees only reproduce successfully in intact, undisturbed Amazonian rainforest where their Euglossine bee pollinators (attracted exclusively by certain orchid species) and agouti seed dispersers are both present. This extraordinary ecological dependency makes Brazil Nuts one of the best arguments for conservation of intact Amazonian forest, as deforestation eliminates both the trees and their irreplaceable ecosystem partners.

common_name: Brazil Nut Tree (Para Nut, Castanheiro do Para)
notes: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, moist to wet tropical soil; Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) is one of the largest trees of the Amazon rainforest, reaching 150 feet tall, and requires 10–20 years from seed to first fruiting in optimal conditions. The pods (actually large, woody capsules weighing up to 5 lbs) each contain 8–24 seeds (the 'nuts') and fall from height, posing a safety hazard — harvest sites require protective gear. The Brazil nut ecosystem depends entirely on the orchid bee (Eulaema sp.) for pollination and the agouti (a large rodent) for seed dispersal, making it nearly impossible to grow commercially outside its native ecosystem. Trees in south Florida and Hawaii produce limited fruit but are grown primarily as impressive specimen trees; the heavy, dense, rot-resistant wood is also extremely valuable.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in zones 9–11; Brazilian guava (also called cas in Costa Rica) is a small to medium-sized tree native to tropical America that produces heavy crops of small, round fruits with white, aromatic, pleasantly sour flesh — highly prized throughout Latin America for fresh-squeezed juice, fruit nectars, jellies, fermented beverages, and agua fresca. Unlike common guava, it shows considerable resistance to the devastating guava wilt fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. psidii) and is more tolerant of occasional frosts, making it a practical choice for gardeners at the cool edge of the tropical fruit range in zones 9–10. Trees begin producing in 3–6 years from transplant and fruit prolifically once established, often producing two crops per year in warm climates. Fruits drop quickly when ripe and should be harvested promptly or they will be taken by wildlife.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis) is a Polynesian staple food tree that has been cultivated throughout the Pacific and Caribbean for centuries, prized for its large, starchy fruit that can be roasted, boiled, fried, or dried into flour — providing a remarkably complete carbohydrate staple that sustained entire island civilizations. A single mature tree can produce 50–200 or more large fruits per year, yielding hundreds of pounds of nutritious food with minimal inputs. Most improved varieties are seedless triploids propagated from root suckers or cuttings; plant these for the fastest fruiting and best productivity. Trees are highly sensitive to frost and cold winds, but once established in a frost-free tropical location they are vigorous, long-lived, and capable of producing fruit within 3–5 years of planting.

Plant in rich, deep, well-drained, moist, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free tropical conditions; in south Florida, protect young trees from the rare hard freeze. Artocarpus camansi (breadnut) is the seeded ancestor of the seedless breadfruit (A. altilis) and produces large, spiny, oblong to round fruits 8–12 inches long containing 20–50 large, protein-rich seeds embedded in creamy, starchy, edible flesh; both the seeds and flesh are eaten. The seeds (when boiled, roasted, or ground into flour) are the primary food value of breadnut, tasting somewhat like chestnuts or macadamia nuts — they are a traditional protein-rich staple in the Pacific Islands and Philippines (where the tree is called 'kulo'). The flesh (ripe) is sweet and may be eaten similarly to breadfruit. The large, deeply lobed, tropical leaves and rapid growth rate make breadnut an impressive specimen tree in tropical gardens. Breadnut is native to New Guinea and the Philippines and widely naturalized in tropical America; it is closely related to jackfruit, durian, and the edible fig within the family Moraceae.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Breda Giant is a classic Dutch medlar selection prized for producing unusually large, russeted brown fruit on a small, gnarled, ornamental tree with showy white spring flowers and good fall color. Fruit is rock-hard and inedible at harvest in late fall and must be 'bletted' — stored in a cool place for several weeks after the first frosts until it softens and browns internally to a soft, spiced, wine-like custard texture before eating fresh or making jelly and butter. The tree is very cold-hardy, tolerates poor soils, and is largely pest- and disease-free, making it an easy, low-maintenance addition to a home orchard once its unusual harvest-and-ripen routine is understood.

The bronze loquat is grown both for its striking coppery new foliage and small, tart edible fruit. Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered position, as the flowers and young growth are frost-sensitive. Water regularly while establishing, then only during dry spells once mature. Prune after fruiting to shape the canopy and remove any frost-damaged tips.

common_name: Brown Select Satsuma (Premier Gulf Coast Satsuma Mandarin, Louisiana Commercial Standard)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil with full sun. Protect from frost below 28°F by covering young trees. Harvest October–November when fully orange. Brown Select Satsuma is a mandarin orange selection developed and popularized in Louisiana, where Satsuma mandarins have been grown commercially and in home gardens along the Gulf Coast since Japanese immigrants introduced the variety to Louisiana in the late 19th century. Satsuma mandarins (Citrus reticulata, specifically the 'Unshiu' or 'Satsuma' group) became an integral part of Gulf Coast culture — Louisiana's St. Bernard Parish and adjacent areas were once a significant commercial Satsuma production center, and Satsuma season (October–December) remains a beloved Gulf South annual event with home trees producing for family and community distribution. The name Satsuma comes from the Satsuma Province of Japan, where the variety was cultivated for centuries before reaching the United States. Brown Select's primary distinction from the more widely distributed Owari Satsuma is earlier ripening (Brown Select ripens 2–3 weeks earlier, in October rather than November) and what many Gulf Coast growers consider superior juice quality — slightly richer, sweeter, and with more complex flavor than Owari in typical Gulf Coast growing conditions. The tree is vigorous and productive under good culture, reliably producing heavy crops of 2-inch flattened-round fruits with loose, easy-peel skin, seedless flesh (typically zero to few seeds per fruit), and intensely sweet, juicy mandarin character. For zone 9 gardeners seeking a productive citrus tree, Brown Select Satsuma is often the first recommendation — earlier than most other mandarins, reliably productive, cold-tolerant enough for zone 9, and producing fruit of exceptional quality.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Brown Select is a distinctly early-ripening Satsuma mandarin developed and selected in Louisiana as an improvement on Owari Satsuma in terms of harvest timing — the trees produce ripe, full-flavored, easy-peeling mandarins in late September to October, making Brown Select the first commonly grown citrus to ripen in the Gulf South citrus season. The flavor at peak ripeness is comparable to Owari — sweet, aromatic, with the characteristic Satsuma complexity — but the earlier timing extends the homegrown citrus season by 3–4 weeks before Owari becomes ready. Brown Select carries the same exceptional cold hardiness as Owari (among the hardiest of all citrus to freezing temperatures) and the same practical advantage of loose, easily peeled skin and nearly seedless, juicy flesh. The combination of extreme cold hardiness, high productivity, and early ripening makes Brown Select specifically important to Gulf South citrus culture in the zones where winter cold is a genuine risk factor for citrus growing, and where starting the fresh fruit season as early as possible is valuable.

common_name: Brown Snout Apple (Herefordshire Bittersweet Cider Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Brown Snout is a late-ripening, reliably productive variety valued in traditional Herefordshire cider blends. A traditional Herefordshire, England cider apple named for the distinctive russeted, elongated end of its small, dull orange-brown fruit, it is a well-regarded bittersweet variety contributing good tannin structure and moderate sugar to a blended cider, and it remains a component of some well-known commercial English cider blends. It ripens late in the season, later than many other classic cider varieties, and stores reasonably well after harvest before milling, giving cider makers some flexibility in scheduling the press. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press once fully ripe, since the astringent fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

This cold-hardy fig tolerates temperatures near 10 degrees F, making it a good choice for cooler regions where most figs struggle. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and provide consistent moisture while fruit is developing for deep burgundy fruit with a pink center. In borderline zones, mulch heavily around the base or grow in a pot to overwinter in a protected spot. Prune in late winter to keep the tree at a manageable height and encourage a strong branching structure.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Brunswick is a common fig type requiring no pollinator and one of the most widely grown figs in the American South under various regional names. Brunswick (known throughout the southeastern United States as 'Magnolia fig' and occasionally as 'Madonna fig') is an old European fig variety that has been grown in Southern gardens for at least 150 years, widely distributed through cuttings exchanged between generations of gardeners in the Gulf Coast states; the very large (3–5 oz), pear-shaped to oblong fruits have thin, pale yellowish-green to bronze-green skin, prominent ribs, and dark amber to brownish-strawberry interior flesh with moderately sweet flavor and good quality. A vigorous, large-growing tree that tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers better than many European fig varieties. Excellent for preserves, fresh eating, and drying. Because of widespread cutting-sharing over generations, plants sold or shared under the name 'Magnolia fig' may vary somewhat; most are similar to or identical with Brunswick.

common_name: Brush Cherry (Magenta Brush Cherry, Australian Cherry)
growth_habit: tropical evergreen hedge and fruit shrub
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; shape with hedge shears for formal use or allow to grow naturally as a specimen. Syzygium paniculatum (brush cherry or magenta brush cherry) is an Australian native tree or large shrub in the rose apple family (Myrtaceae) — closely related to rose apple (S. jambos) and other Syzygium fruit trees — that has become one of the most widely planted evergreen hedge, screen, and topiary plants in zone 9–12 landscapes in Florida, California, and the Gulf Coast. The plant produces glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green new growth that flushes copper-red to bronze-red as it emerges — making it attractive year-round — and responds well to shearing into formal hedge shapes. It produces abundant, 1/2-inch, bright magenta-pink fruits in summer that are edible but primarily astringent and mild, with a rose-water and mild apple flavor; they are eaten fresh in small quantities, made into jams, or used in drinks. The flowers are fluffy, cream-white, and produced in clusters; they attract bees and butterflies. As a hedge plant, brush cherry is outstanding: it maintains dense, dark-green foliage, responds well to clipping, and is salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established. More widely available in the nursery trade in Florida and California than most other Syzygium species.

Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting two or more trees for reliable pollination.
