Buartnut is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between butternut (Juglans cinerea) and Japanese walnut or heartnut (Juglans ailantifolia), combining some of butternut's rich, oily flavor with heartnut's heavier and more reliable nut production. Because true butternut has been decimated across its range by butternut canker disease, buartnut is grown by nut enthusiasts in colder climates as a hardier, often more disease-tolerant alternative that still carries much of the butternut flavor profile.

This cold-hardy hybrid plum produces juicy reddish-purple fruit with a distinctive sweet, spicy flavor often compared to bubblegum. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and include a compatible pollinizer nearby since Toka also serves as an excellent pollinator for other plums. Water consistently during fruit set and thin heavy fruit clusters to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune in late winter to an open-center form for good light penetration and air flow.

Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in woodland garden settings; buckthorn bumelia is a native thorny shrub of the eastern Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, growing naturally in moist, mixed woodlands and forest edges from Virginia to Texas. Unlike the more drought-adapted gum bumelia, this species prefers moist woodland soils and grows in shade-adapted situations at woodland margins and in the forest understory. The small, black fruits in fall are eaten by numerous species of birds and the thorny branches provide valuable nesting habitat. A useful shrub for creating dense, bird-friendly hedgerows at the edge of native woodland garden designs in zones 6–9. The small white flowers in summer attract pollinators.

Buddha's hand is a citron variety bearing distinctive finger-like lobes that contain only aromatic peel with no juice or pulp; it is valued entirely for its intensely fragrant zest used in baking, cocktails, and as a natural air freshener. Trees are self-fertile and small enough to grow in 15–20 gallon containers, making them suitable for patios and sunrooms in colder climates; bring indoors before temperatures fall below 32°F. Fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer three times per year and maintain consistent moisture to prevent fruit drop. Harvest when the fingers have turned fully yellow and the fragrance is intense; fruit can be stored at room temperature for 1–2 weeks.

Sow fresh seed straight from a fallen cone into a deep container, since the large nut and long taproot make this towering Australian conifer resent transplanting once it is well rooted. Bunya pine takes many years to reach flowering and cone-bearing size but rewards patient growers with basketball-sized cones containing dozens of large, chestnut-flavored nuts that are traditionally roasted or boiled. Give it a wide, open site well away from structures, parking, and foot traffic, because mature cones can weigh more than twenty pounds and drop from a great height without warning. Young trees tolerate a light frost but need full protection for their first several winters in the coolest parts of their growable range.

common_name: Burkett Pecan (Large-Nutted West Texas Commercial Pecan)
notes: Discovered around 1912 as a chance seedling near San Saba, Texas, Burkett became one of the signature commercial pecan cultivars of the arid irrigated orchards of West Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. It produces a large, attractive, well-filled nut with excellent cracking quality that made it a favorite for retail and gift-pack sales under the Texas pecan label. Burkett performs best where humidity stays low, since it is notably more susceptible to pecan scab than modern disease-resistant cultivars and struggles in the humid Gulf South without an aggressive fungicide program. Give it full sun, deep soil, and reliable irrigation through nut fill, along with a compatible pollinator, for consistent large-nut production.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; bustic (false mastic) is a medium to large evergreen tree native to the tropical hammocks and rockland forests of south Florida and the Caribbean, producing a dense, spreading canopy of large, glossy, leathery leaves. The small, white, fragrant flowers are produced throughout the year in clusters, followed by small, yellow to orange edible fruits with a sweet, apricot-mango-like flavor. The fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons, gray catbirds, and numerous other birds as a critical food source in the south Florida hammock ecosystem. The wood is extremely hard and durable — historically used for railroad ties and boat building. A superb shade tree for south Florida native landscapes, providing an evergreen canopy, wildlife food, and attractive flowers. One of the characteristic dominant trees of the endangered Miami rock ridge hammock ecosystem.

Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer variety planted nearby, since Butte is not self-fertile. Butte is a mid-to-late blooming California commercial almond noted for its heavy, consistent bearing, semi-hard shell, and small, plump kernel, and it is frequently interplanted with Nonpareil as a reliable cross-pollinating partner. Its later bloom compared with Nonpareil reduces exposure to early spring frost damage in many California growing regions.

Butternut, or white walnut, produces rich, oily nuts with a milder, sweeter flavor than black walnut and is native to eastern North America. The species is severely threatened by Sirococcus clavigignenti-juglandacearum (butternut canker), so seek out canker-resistant cultivars or hybrids (butternut x heartnut crosses, or selections from university breeding programs) rather than straight-species seedlings. Like other walnuts, butternut is monoecious and partially self-fertile but benefits from a second tree nearby; it also produces juglone that can inhibit nearby sensitive plants. Harvest when the sticky, hairy green hulls begin to soften and turn yellow-brown in early to mid-fall; hull promptly and dry nuts for 2–3 weeks before cracking or storing.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination and best fruit set. Byrongold was released in 1985 by the USDA-ARS research station in Byron, Georgia, from Ozark Premier breeding lines, selected specifically to hold up better against the disease pressure common in humid Southeastern orchards while producing round, yellow-fleshed fruit with good eating quality. Its Southeastern breeding background makes it a solid choice for Gulf South home orchards facing the fungal and bacterial diseases that trouble many plum cultivars developed for drier climates. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that promotes airflow and reduces disease pressure.

growth_habit: Brazilian Atlantic Forest myrtaceous berry tree
notes: Plant Cabeludinha in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water consistently; maintain high organic matter; protect from hard frost below 28°F; harvest fruits when fully colored and give slightly to gentle pressure. Myrciaria glazioviana is one of the lesser-known but highly regarded wild fruits of Brazil's endangered Atlantic Forest — a small to medium-sized tree whose golden, hairy fruits are prized locally though almost unknown internationally. The fruits (roughly 0.5–1 inch diameter) are covered in short, fine hairs that give them a distinctly fuzzy appearance, unlike the smooth skin of the closely related jaboticaba (Myrciaria cauliflora). The pulp is translucent, juicy, sweet-tart, and grape-like in texture — excellent eaten fresh directly from the tree and used for juices, fruit wines, and liqueurs in the same tradition as jaboticaba. Unlike jaboticaba, Cabeludinha produces its fruits on the branch tips rather than cauliflorous directly on the trunk, giving a different fruiting habit. Growing naturally in the understory to mid-canopy of Atlantic Forest remnants, it tolerates partial shade better than full-sun species. Part of the rich Myrtaceae fruit tree diversity from Brazil that includes Cambuci (Campomanesia phaea), Grumixama (Eugenia brasiliensis), and Araçá (Psidium cattleianum), representing an extraordinary regional flora of underexploited edible berries.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — cacao is the source of chocolate, one of the world's most important food crops, and is an understory tree of the tropical rainforest that grows naturally in partial to deep shade. The unusual cauliflorous flowering habit (flowers and fruits growing directly from the main trunk and large branches rather than at branch tips) produces football-shaped pods in vivid yellow, orange, red, or purple at maturity, each containing 30–50 seeds (cocoa beans) embedded in sweet white pulp. The pulp is eaten fresh in cacao-growing regions; the seeds are fermented, dried, and processed to produce cocoa powder and chocolate. In South Florida and tropical zones, small cacao trees fruit in as little as 3–4 years and produce two crops per year. An exceptional specimen plant for the tropical garden that actually prefers shade over full sun.

common_name: Caddo Pecan (Scab-Resistant Productive Mid-Season Pecan, Type II Gulf South Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile soil in full sun; Caddo is consistently high-yielding and somewhat more scab-resistant than varieties like Desirable and Wichita in humid conditions; nuts are medium-sized (50–55 per pound) with excellent filling and flavor; a good choice for home orchards in the humid Gulf South where scab management is a primary concern. Caddo pecan is a USDA-released variety that has become an important recommended variety for the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States, particularly valued for its combination of reliable productivity, above-average scab resistance, and good nut quality in the hot, humid growing conditions of the Gulf South. In the humid pecan-growing regions of Louisiana, Mississippi, and coastal Texas, pecan scab disease (caused by the fungal pathogen Fusicladium effusum) is the primary limiting factor in pecan production — attacking leaves, shoots, and developing nuts in wet spring and summer conditions, reducing kernel quality and yield. Varieties with good scab resistance are substantially more forgiving for home orchardists who cannot maintain the intensive fungicide spray programs used by commercial producers. Caddo's above-average scab tolerance compared to Desirable (which is quite scab-susceptible in humid conditions) makes it a more practical choice for many Gulf South home orchards. The nuts are medium-sized with an attractive appearance, good kernel percentage (57–60%), and solid, sweet pecan flavor. Caddo is also considered a relatively good cross-pollinator as a Type II variety paired with Type I varieties in mixed plantings. Louisiana State University's AgCenter has included Caddo as a recommended variety for Louisiana pecan production for many years.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil — Calabash Tree grows most vigorously with full sun and regular water during establishment, then tolerates periods of drought in sandy and rocky soils once established. Crescentia cujete is a medium-sized tropical tree native to Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America, widely distributed by pre-Columbian peoples throughout tropical America as a utilitarian and sacred plant — the large, round, hard-shelled fruits of the calabash have been among the most widely used natural containers, bowls, cups, ladles, and musical instrument bodies across all cultures of the tropical Americas for thousands of years. The tree is immediately recognizable by its phenomenon of 'cauliflory' — flowers and fruits borne directly on the trunk and major branches rather than on the growing tips, a strategy that attracts bat pollinators that can access the flowers and fruits by hovering next to the trunk. The greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers open at night for bat pollination, and the mature fruits are perfectly round to slightly ovoid, 4–14 inches in diameter, hanging directly from the bark on short stalks. The fruit shell is extraordinarily hard when dried — traditionally cut in half for bowls, carved and decorated as art objects, or used as maracas. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida landscapes, the Calabash Tree is a distinctive tropical ornamental valued for its unusual fruiting display.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; calamansi is self-fruitful and produces small, round fruits year-round in warm climates. Citrofortunella microcarpa (calamansi, calamondin, Philippine lime) is a kumquat-tangerine hybrid that is the most important souring citrus in Filipino cuisine and widely used in Southeast Asian cooking generally; the tiny (1–1.5 inch), round, orange-rinded fruits with intensely tart, aromatic green to orange juice are used in Philippine cooking the way lemons and limes are used in Western cuisine — squeezed over virtually every savory dish, mixed with soy sauce as the ubiquitous sawsawan dipping sauce, squeezed over grilled meats, noodles, soups, and rice. The distinctive, intensely floral-tart flavor is quite different from standard lime or lemon. Bears fruit almost continuously in warm climates; highly ornamental with glossy foliage. Outstanding as a large container citrus that can be moved indoors in colder zones.

Calamondin is a hybrid between a kumquat and a mandarin orange, producing prolific small, sour-sweet fruits that are eaten whole like kumquats or used as a lime substitute in Southeast Asian cooking. The tree is self-fertile, nearly thornless, highly ornamental with fragrant white flowers, and among the easiest citrus to grow in containers — it tolerates indoor conditions better than most citrus. It tolerates brief dips to about 20°F when established. Fruit ripens from late autumn through spring; harvest when fully orange for best flavor, though the rind remains sweet while the flesh is tart even at the green-orange stage.

This ornamental citrus, a kumquat-mandarin cross, bears a heavy crop of small, round, tart fruit prized for marmalades and drinks. Grow in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and feed regularly with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In non-tropical climates keep it potted so it can move to a bright indoor spot before frost. Fragrant white blossoms and glossy evergreen leaves make it as decorative as it is productive.

common_name: California Black Walnut (Southern California Black Walnut)
notes: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; California black walnut is a multi-trunked, drought-adapted tree native to the coastal ranges and foothills of Southern and Central California, historically an important food source for indigenous peoples and still valued by native plant and wildlife gardeners for its small, thick-shelled, richly flavored nuts. It is far more heat- and drought-tolerant than eastern black walnut and has long been used as rootstock for grafting English walnut in California orchards because of its vigor and disease resistance. Trees are slow-growing and produce nuts within a juglone-rich root zone, so keep sensitive plants at a distance. Given its wild, spreading habit and long lifespan, it suits large properties, hedgerows, and wildlife plantings more than small home gardens.

This compact mandarin produces sweet, juicy, easy-peeling fruit and stays small enough for patios or sunny indoor rooms. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and water deeply but allow the top inch to dry between waterings. Feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season and protect from frost, moving containers indoors when temperatures drop. Light pruning after harvest keeps the canopy open and the tree productive.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil along a strong support; California wild grape is a vigorous, deciduous native vine of streambanks and canyons from Oregon to Baja California, grown both as a fast-growing ornamental shade vine and for its small, tart, blue-black grapes that ripen in early fall. Fruit is seedy and sharply acidic, used mainly for jelly, juice, and wine rather than fresh eating, and is an important wildlife food. The species is a parent of the widely planted, purple-leaved ornamental cultivars 'Roger's Red' and 'Rogers Red', and its rootstock has been used in grape breeding for drought and Pierce's disease tolerance. Once established, the deep-rooted vine is remarkably drought-tolerant and requires only annual dormant-season pruning to control its vigorous growth.

common_name: Calville Blanc d'Hiver Apple (French Culinary Heirloom Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Documented in France since the 1500s, Calville Blanc d'Hiver is one of the oldest named apple cultivars still grown and became the classic dessert and pastry apple of French cuisine, famously used in tarte Tatin and other traditional preparations. The irregularly ribbed, pale greenish-yellow fruit has a distinctive, complex, almost pineapple-like flavor and unusually high vitamin C content for an apple. It ripens quite late in the season and improves with several weeks of storage, but the tree can be a light or biennial bearer and benefits from a warm site and careful thinning.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full sun in zones 10–11; cambucá is a rare Atlantic Forest gem in the Myrtaceae family (closely related to jaboticaba) that produces large, round, yellow-green fruits directly on its trunk and major branches — a phenomenon known as cauliflory that makes the tree a striking spectacle when loaded with fruit. The thick-skinned fruits hold exceptionally sweet, white, juicy flesh with a fragrant, complex flavor described as a blend of mango and passion fruit, and are eaten fresh or made into artisanal jams and wines in the Brazilian coastal states where it is native. Cambucá prefers the high humidity and warm temperatures of its coastal rainforest home and performs best with regular deep watering and organic mulch kept away from the trunk. Seed must be planted fresh — sow immediately after extraction from ripe fruit, as viability falls dramatically within two to three weeks.

common_name: Cameo Flowering Quince (Double Peach-Pink Flowering Quince)
notes: Cameo carries fully double, soft peachy-pink flowers, a gentler pastel departure from the hot reds and oranges typical of most flowering quince cultivars, opening directly on the bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage. Its compact, rounded, largely thornless growth habit makes it easier to work around than older, thornier quince cultivars, and small yellow-green fruit follows the bloom, usable for jelly and preserves though not typically eaten fresh. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid cutting off next season's flower buds.

Plant in moist, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; camu camu (Myrciaria dubia) is a shrubby Amazonian Myrtaceae producing small, cherry-like, reddish-purple fruits with a powerfully acidic, cranberry-passion-fruit flavor that are virtually inedible raw due to their extreme sourness but are valued as one of the highest natural sources of vitamin C on earth — 20–60 times more vitamin C per 100g than oranges. The fruit is processed into powders, juices, and health supplements widely sold in health food stores; home production is possible in south Florida and Hawaii with specimens growing in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil or at pond edges. An outstanding addition to a food-forest understory in zone 10+, where it also provides white, fragrant flowers and attractive foliage.

Plant grafted trees or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Canada plum is the most cold-hardy of the native North American plums, surviving temperatures to -40°F and producing fruit reliably in zones 2–6 where most stone fruit trees would be killed by winter cold. Prunus nigra is a native small tree or large shrub of eastern and central Canada and the northern US producing prolific white flowers in early spring (before leaves) and medium-sized, oval plums ripening yellow to red to deep purple in late summer with a tart, wild-plum flavor excellent for jams, jellies, and sauce. Cross-pollinate with American plum (P. americana) or another Canada plum seedling for best fruit set; it also attracts wildlife heavily — the fruit is avidly eaten by bears, raccoons, foxes, and many bird species.

Plant in average, well-drained soil and stake young trees for their first year or two, since they establish quickly and grow at a moderate to fast rate. Canada Red is a selection of the native chokecherry whose new leaves emerge green in spring and gradually deepen to a rich burgundy-purple by summer, providing strong seasonal color alongside white spring flower clusters. It bears heavy clusters of small, tart, dark red-to-black cherries that are astringent fresh but make excellent jelly, syrup, and wine once cooked with sugar. Extremely cold-hardy and adaptable, it is a popular multi-purpose shelterbelt and specimen tree across the northern Plains and prairie provinces.

common_name: Canadice Grape (Cornell-Bred Red Seedless Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Canadice was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and is a dependable, heavily productive red seedless table grape, bearing compact clusters of small, sweet, mildly Labrusca-flavored berries on a vigorous, cold-hardy vine. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning early in the season to improve berry size and quality. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and insufficient winter chill limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil in frost-free conditions; candlenut (Aleurites moluccanus, kukui in Hawaiian) is an extremely versatile tree native to tropical Asia and the Pacific Islands, widely cultivated for its large, oily nuts that are a critical ingredient in Indonesian (kemiri), Malaysian, and Hawaiian cuisine — the roasted kernels are ground into pastes, sauces, and curries. Caution: raw candlenuts are toxic and mildly purgative due to saponins; always roast or cook before eating. The nuts have the highest oil content of any edible nut and burn like candles, giving the tree its common name; the oil was traditionally used for lighting, wood finishing, and skin care. The Hawaii state tree (kukui), with distinctive silvery-green foliage visible from a distance.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA pecan breeding program, Candy is valued for bearing precociously, often producing a crop within a few years of planting, well ahead of many older commercial cultivars. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality and a well-filled, attractive shell, and the tree tends to crop reliably from a young age rather than needing a long establishment period before its first real harvest. As with other pecans, supplement with zinc on alkaline soils and monitor for scab disease pressure in humid climates.

common_name: Cannonball Tree (Nagalingam, Sala Tree, Shivalinga Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil — Cannonball Tree grows most rapidly and blooms most prolifically in full sun with regular watering, becoming a dramatic, multi-season ornamental after 5–10 years. Couroupita guianensis is a large tropical tree native to tropical South America (Guiana, Venezuela, Peru, Brazil) in the Brazil-nut family (Lecythidaceae), famous for two simultaneous ornamental spectacles occurring directly on its trunk and branches. The flowers are produced year-round on long, pendant cauliflorous racemes (flower stalks) that hang directly from the trunk and major branches — each fragrant, complex, waxy flower 3–4 inches across with large, creamy-white to pale pink petals surrounding a modified stamen structure in pink, orange, and yellow that creates an exotic, orchid-like appearance. Simultaneously, the tree bears the previous season's fruits: enormous, perfectly spherical, hard-shelled, rust-brown fruits 6–12 inches in diameter (the 'cannonballs') that are attached in clusters to the same trunk racemes as the flowers — so the tree often displays flowers and fruits simultaneously. The fruits fall explosively when ripe, with a loud impact that explains the 'Cannonball Tree' name. In Hindu and Buddhist temple gardens throughout South and Southeast Asia (where the tree is sacred as the 'Shivalinga Tree' and 'Sala Tree'), the trunk-borne flowers and spherical fruits have profound religious symbolism.

common_name: Cape Elderberry (Bourtree, Southern Elder, Yellow Elderberry)
notes: Root stem cuttings in spring or autumn in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; plant in partial shade to full sun; cape elderberry (Sambucus australasica) is an Australian species native to Queensland and New South Wales rainforest edges and creek margins, producing large clusters of small, bright yellow berries (distinct from the dark purple-black of northern elderberries) that ripen in summer. The berries are edible when fully ripe and can be used in the same applications as European elderberries — jams, jellies, syrups, and wines — though they are reportedly less intensely flavored. The flowers are also edible as elderflower tea and fritters. An attractive subtropical alternative to common elderberry for zone 9–11 gardens, with similar wildlife value and similar requirements for moist, moderately fertile soil.

common_name: Cape Fear Pecan (Mid-Atlantic Southeastern Pecan, Type I Reliable Cross-Pollinator)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun; Cape Fear is a reliable medium-to-large nut producer with moderate scab resistance; it is widely adapted throughout the southeastern states from coastal North Carolina through the Gulf South; trees are vigorous and come into production in 5–7 years; supplement with zinc spray in spring. Cape Fear pecan is a variety developed by the USDA Pecan Breeding Program and named for the Cape Fear River valley of North Carolina, where the variety demonstrated particularly reliable production under the moderately humid coastal plain conditions of the mid-Atlantic South. The variety has proven broadly adapted throughout the southeastern states from eastern North Carolina through the Gulf Coast, performing reliably under a range of humidity levels and soil types typical of the coastal plain and river bottom land of the region. Cape Fear produces medium-to-large nuts (45–52 per pound) with good kernel percentage (57–61%) and solid pecan flavor — not the exceptional nut quality of Desirable or Wichita but consistent, reliable, and commercially acceptable. The variety's primary contribution to many home orchard designs is as the Type I cross-pollinator for the more challenging-to-fruit Type II varieties: since pecan varieties are strongly cross-pollinated (most nut set requires pollen from a different variety), placing Cape Fear alongside Type II varieties like Desirable, Wichita, Elliott, or Stuart ensures reliable pollination and heavier crops on both trees. Cape Fear is also the companion pollinator recommended in many pecan extension publications for home gardeners planting the newer precocious varieties like Pawnee.

The Cara Cara is a sweet, low-acid navel orange distinguished by its rosy-pink flesh and berry-like flavor. This adaptable citrus performs well in the ground in mild regions or in a large container that can be moved indoors where winters are cold. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil and feed it a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season. Water deeply but allow the top of the soil to dry between waterings, and protect it from frost.

common_name: Carlos Muscadine Grape (Classic Bronze Self-Fertile Wine-Quality Gulf South Muscadine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Carlos is the benchmark bronze muscadine cultivar — one of the most widely planted and historically important Gulf South muscadines, valued equally for fresh eating quality and as the primary variety for muscadine wine production in the Southeast. The medium to large, round grapes ripen to bronze-tan to bronze-gold color with thick skin and sweet, aromatic, musky flesh typical of the muscadine type; the flavor profile is somewhat more refined and balanced in acidity than many other muscadine cultivars, which is why Carlos is the preferred variety for wine production and has long been the standard against which other muscadines are evaluated. Muscadine wine from Carlos has a characteristic sweet, floral, musky quality — distinctively Southern and quite unlike any European wine style — with enough natural acidity to provide balance. Carlos is self-fertile with perfect flowers and is an outstanding cross-pollinator for female-flowered cultivars including Fry, Higgins, and others. The vines are vigorous and productive, disease-resistant to the fungal diseases (black rot, downy mildew, powdery mildew) that make growing European grapes nearly impossible in Gulf South conditions, and adapted to the heat, humidity, and long growing season of zones 6–10. Grapes ripen in August through September, with individual grapes in each cluster ripening sequentially. Excellent for fresh eating, juice, muscadine wine, jelly, and preserves.

common_name: Carmel Almond (Reliable California Pollenizer Almond, High-Production Soft-Shell Almond)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained fertile soil in full sun; Carmel is primarily planted as a companion and cross-pollinator for Nonpareil in commercial orchards but also produces its own crop of soft-shell almonds with good flavor; it ripens slightly after Nonpareil (mid-August); kernels are slightly smaller than Nonpareil but of good quality for snacking and roasting. Carmel almond is a UC Davis release developed specifically to serve as the ideal companion and cross-pollinator for Nonpareil — the two are now the most common planting pair in California commercial almond orchards, with the standard three-variety system often being Nonpareil + Carmel + Mission or Butte. Carmel's most important attribute in commercial production is pollination efficiency: its bloom time coincides precisely with Nonpareil, it produces abundant viable pollen, and it bears its own crop reliably and heavily — making it productive as both a pollinator and a production variety rather than just a sterile companion tree. The variety was developed at UC Davis by Floyd Zaiger and William Sims and has been important in the rapid expansion of California almond acreage since the 1970s because its reliable early bearing and high productivity complemented Nonpareil's commercial requirements. Carmel produces soft-shell almonds of moderate size with a sweet, mild almond flavor somewhat similar to Nonpareil — entirely acceptable for all uses including direct consumption, roasting, and confectionery — while its primary role remains as the preferred pollinator in the world's most important almond-producing region.

Carob is a slow-growing evergreen legume tree that fixes atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in dry, rocky, alkaline soils where few other fruits survive; it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established. Trees are dioecious — plant one male for every 8–10 female trees, or choose hermaphroditic cultivars such as Santa Fe and Clifford that produce fruit without a separate male. The long, dark-brown seed pods ripen in late summer and fall and are left on the tree to dry and sweeten; they are harvested when fully brown, dry, and the seeds rattle inside. Carob pods are sweet and chocolatey and used ground as a cocoa substitute or in stock feed.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, away from vegetable gardens and other sensitive plants since walnut roots exude juglone, a compound toxic to many other species. Carpathian refers to a cold-hardy strain of the common English (Persian) walnut originating in the mountainous Carpathian region of Poland, introduced to North America in the mid-20th century specifically because it tolerates far colder winters than typical English walnut selections from milder climates. The thin-shelled, easily cracked nuts have the classic mild, rich English walnut flavor, and the trees are large, long-lived, and productive once mature, typically beginning to bear within five to seven years of planting.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Carrie mango is prized for its compact size and rich flavor, making it a favorite dooryard tree in frost-free and marginal citrus climates. A Florida-bred seedling selection, it produces small to medium, fiberless fruit with deep orange flesh and an intensely rich, sweet, complex, almost spicy flavor that many home growers rate among the best-tasting mangoes available, though the skin stays mostly green even when ripe. The tree is naturally more compact and precocious than many mango cultivars, bearing at a young age and staying manageable in a home orchard or large container. Water deeply during fruit development and reduce irrigation as fruit nears harvest to concentrate sweetness; protect young trees from any frost, since mango is damaged by temperatures near freezing.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, acidic to neutral, infertile to average soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; cashew is native to northeastern Brazil and now cultivated throughout the tropics as one of the world's most important nut crops. The 'nut' is actually a large seed attached to the outside of a swollen, fleshy, pear-shaped 'cashew apple' (pseudofruit) which is edible fresh, juiced, or fermented into cashew wine. The seed shell contains urushiol — the same irritating compound in poison ivy — and must never be handled or roasted without protection. Commercial cashews are processed to remove this compound before the familiar pale nut is edible. The cashew apple, rarely seen in North America, is highly perishable and consumed fresh throughout tropical regions as a vitamin-C-rich refreshing fruit. In zone 9, treat as a container specimen moved indoors in winter.

common_name: Catawba Grape (Historic American Pink Wine and Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Catawba is one of the oldest named American grape varieties, discovered in North Carolina in the early 1800s and once the most widely planted wine grape in the country, producing distinctive coppery-pink to reddish-purple berries with the characteristic musky, richly sweet Labrusca 'foxy' flavor, used historically for sparkling and still wine as well as fresh eating and juice. It is self-fruitful and ripens in mid to late season. As a high-chill Labrusca type it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease pressure and insufficient winter chill limit its success; Gulf South growers do better with muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes.

common_name: Cedar Bay Cherry (Beach Cherry, Reinwardtiana Berry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; excellent salt and wind tolerance makes it outstanding for coastal gardens. Eugenia reinwardtiana (cedar bay cherry or beach cherry) is an Australian native Eugenia shrub or small tree from the tropical beaches, coastal scrub, and dry vine thickets of far north Queensland and the Northern Territory — one of the few Eugenia species native to Australia (most Eugenia, including the commercial Brazilian cherry group, are from the Americas). The plant bears small (1/2-inch), round, bright orange-red to scarlet fruits in clusters along the branches — similar in size and color to Surinam cherry (Eugenia uniflora) but with a different, distinctly sweet-acid, pleasant flavor without the resinous undertone characteristic of Surinam cherry. The fruits are eaten fresh as a snack and used in jams and beverages. Cedar bay cherry is especially valued in coastal tropical gardens for its outstanding tolerance of salt spray, wind, sandy soils, and coastal drought — growing naturally on exposed beaches and coastal headlands. The plant can be grown as a low shrub or allowed to develop into a small tree; it responds well to pruning for hedge use. The attractive, glossy, oval leaves and prolific berry production make it ornamentally pleasing. Very rare in cultivation outside tropical Queensland and the Pacific Islands.

Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; Celeste is the most popular and cold-hardy fig in the Deep South, producing small to medium, violet-brown figs with a honey-sweet, rose-pink interior that ripen mid-July through August. It is the standard home garden fig from Virginia to Texas and is considered by many to have the best flavor of any common fig variety. Figs fruit on second-year wood and on new growth late in the season — do not prune heavily in winter. Mulch roots in zone 7 to prevent root freeze-kill. Trees rarely need fertilizer and will produce heavy crops with minimal care once established. Other excellent Gulf Coast cultivars include 'Brown Turkey', 'LSU Purple', and 'LSU Gold'.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; plant both male and female trees for fruit production. Dovyalis hebecarpa (Ceylon gooseberry or kitambilla) is a Sri Lankan thorny shrub or small tree producing small, 1-to-1.5-inch, velvety, dark-purple to maroon fruits with an intensely tart, acidic flavor somewhat resembling a sour cranberry or gooseberry crossed with tamarind — extremely sour fresh but outstanding for jams, jellies, preserves, and syrups when sweetened. The plant is densely armed with sharp thorns and can be grown as an impenetrable security hedge while also producing edible fruit — a combination making it practically useful as a barrier plant in tropical gardens. In Sri Lanka, the fruits are made into a traditional preserve and the juice is used as a refreshing tart drink. The tree tolerates moderate drought and poor soils once established and can be used as a rootstock for grafting related Dovyalis species. It is dioecious — plant both male and female plants for fruiting. The compact form and spiny character make it useful as a living fence.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Champagne is a light greenish-yellow fig long grown in Texas dooryards, prized for its thin skin, amber-pink pulp, and very sweet, honeyed flavor that many gardeners rank above darker-skinned figs for fresh eating. It fruits on both old and new wood, giving a small early-summer breba crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer. Trees tolerate heat and humidity well and need little fertilizer once established, though a summer mulch layer helps even out soil moisture during fruit ripening. Protect young trees during hard freezes in the cooler end of its range; established plants regrow readily from the base after cold damage.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun in a warm, sheltered site; Chandler is a University of California Riverside pomelo selection prized for its very large fruit (often 4-6 pounds), thick pink-blushed rind, and sweet, low-acid pink flesh with relatively little of the bitterness found in some other pomelo types. The huge fruit takes a long season to mature, typically ripening in late fall to winter, and the tree needs a warm, essentially frost-free site to size and sweeten the crop properly, making it best suited to zone 9b-10 in sheltered microclimates or container culture that can be moved under cover for winter. The thick rind makes the fruit easy to peel and section by hand once cut open, and segments hold their shape well for fresh eating, salads, and citrus platters. Give young trees consistent moisture and wind protection, and expect the first meaningful crop several years after planting.

common_name: Chandler Walnut (California Commercial Standard Walnut, UC Davis Walnut)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Chandler benefits from cross-pollination though it will produce some crop alone; the large, thin-shelled nuts ripen in September–October and are harvested by mechanical knock-down or hand-collection when hulls begin to split; allow nuts to dry at 100°F for several days after harvest to reduce moisture content for storage. Chandler walnut is the most widely planted commercial English (Persian) walnut variety in California and among the most important walnut varieties in the world — released by UC Davis in 1979 from the UC Walnut Improvement Program as a selection with exceptional combination of large nut size, very thin shell, high kernel percentage (above 50%), and excellent kernel color and quality. California produces approximately 75% of the world's English walnut supply, and Chandler accounts for more than half of that production — making Chandler the single most economically important walnut variety on earth. The variety produces very large (28–30 mm), well-shaped nuts with a thin shell that cracks easily and yields plump, light-colored halves with mild, sweet walnut flavor and high oil content typical of premium English walnuts. The light kernel color (essential for premium market pricing, where darker kernels command lower prices) and consistent quality in the drying and processing process made Chandler the preferred commercial variety over the older standards (Franquette, Hartley, Serr). For home orchards in zones 6–9, Chandler delivers premium walnut quality with good productivity.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, sheltered from cold north winds; mulch well and protect young trees through their first few winters until established. Changsha is a small-fruited mandarin native to Hunan Province, China, valued above nearly all other citrus for its exceptional cold hardiness — mature trees have survived and fruited after temperatures well below 10°F, making it one of the few true mandarins that can be grown outdoors, unprotected, in the Gulf South and even into the coastal Southeast beyond typical citrus range. The small, flattened, deep orange fruits are intensely sweet with a rich, aromatic mandarin flavor, though they are notably seedy, which has historically limited commercial interest despite the outstanding flavor and hardiness. Changsha is widely used by cold-hardy citrus breeders and hobbyists both as a garden fruit tree in its own right and as breeding stock for hardier hybrid mandarins. A rewarding choice for Gulf South gardeners who want the flavor of a true mandarin from a tree that can survive outdoors through a hard winter, zone 8–10.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Chardonnay needs a long, warm growing season and consistent trellising and pruning to ripen fruit and produce quality wine grapes. The most widely planted white wine grape in the world, it produces tight clusters of small, thin-skinned green-gold grapes that adapt to a remarkably wide range of climates and winemaking styles, from crisp, mineral, unoaked wines in cool regions to rich, buttery, oak-aged wines in warmer ones. Vigorous and relatively easy to grow compared to some finicky wine varieties, it still requires careful canopy management, disease monitoring, and a well-drained site to reach commercial fruit quality, and benefits from professional pruning guidance for home vineyard growers new to viticulture. Train young vines to a permanent trellis system, thin fruit clusters if overcropping occurs, and harvest based on sugar and acid balance rather than a fixed calendar date, since ripeness timing varies significantly by site and season.

Che, sometimes called the Chinese mulberry, produces round, red, fig-like fruit with a mild, melon-melon flavor. It is drought-tolerant and adaptable once established, growing well in full sun on well-drained soil. Seedling trees can be thorny and slow to bear, so plant a grafted, female cultivar for earlier crops; a male tree nearby can improve set. Prune to keep it manageable and net the sweet fruit against birds as it ripens in autumn.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; chempedak is a close relative of jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), native to Southeast Asia from Indonesia to Thailand, producing large, barrel-shaped compound fruits borne directly on the trunk and main branches like jackfruit but typically smaller and sweeter. The fruits have a strongly aromatic, intensely sweet, almost fermented flavor that is more pronounced than jackfruit — considered by many Southeast Asian aficionados to be superior to jackfruit for fresh eating. The soft, yellow-orange arils surrounding the seeds are eaten fresh, fried in batter (a popular street food in Malaysia), or incorporated into desserts. The seeds are roasted or boiled and eaten. More tolerant of wet, poorly drained soils than jackfruit, making it suitable for sites that jackfruit would struggle in. An outstanding choice for tropical South Florida gardens seeking an alternative to the more common jackfruit.

Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Garcinia prainiana requires consistent moisture, high humidity, and protection from wind and cold — mulch well and water regularly throughout the growing season. Garcinia prainiana (Cherapu or Button Mangosteen) is an evergreen fruit tree endemic to the lowland and hill forests of Peninsular Malaysia and southern Thailand, member of the Garcinia family (Clusiaceae) and closely related to the famous Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana). The fruits are distinctive: small (1.5–2 inch), round, with thin, orange to mandarin-colored skin (not the thick, purple rind of mangosteen) that peels easily to reveal 4–5 segments of soft, sweet-sour, orange-to-white, juicy, aromatic pulp with a complex tropical flavor — often described as a blend of sweet orange, lychee, and tangy passion fruit. The tree is compact and ornamental with glossy, dark-green, opposite leaves, and suits smaller tropical gardens better than the slower-growing mangosteen. Like all Garcinia species, G. prainiana is slow-growing and requires patience — typically 5–8 years from grafted stock to first fruit. A prized and rarely exported tropical fruit tree for serious tropical fruit collectors in zone 10–12.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; cherimoya (Annona cherimola) was famously described by Mark Twain as "the most delicious fruit known to men," and it remains one of the most sought-after fruits in the world among tropical fruit enthusiasts, producing heart-shaped, scaly green fruits with a snow-white, custardy flesh of extraordinary sweetness and complexity — with flavors of pineapple, banana, vanilla, and cream all at once. Native to the Andean highlands of Ecuador and Peru, cherimoya prefers a mild, subtropical rather than hot tropical climate and performs best where summers are warm but not brutally hot, and winters are cool but frost-free. Hand-pollination is essential in cultivation: transfer pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers using a small brush or cotton swab in the morning for reliable fruit set. Grafted trees of selections such as 'Lisa,' 'Booth,' and 'McPherson' begin bearing in 2–4 years and produce superior fruit size and flavor compared to seedling trees.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; self-fertile but produces better with a second tree for cross-pollination; cherry plum is extremely adaptable and flowers early. Prunus cerasifera (cherry plum or myrobalan) is a small deciduous tree native to Western Asia and southeastern Europe — one of the earliest flowering Prunus species in spring, often opening white or pale-pink blossoms in late winter or very early spring even before peaches or almonds, creating a spectacular early-season display. The cherry-sized (3/4–1 inch) fruits ripen in summer in a range of colors from bright yellow to red to dark purple-black depending on variety, with sweet to sweet-tart, plum-like flesh that can be eaten fresh, cooked into jam, preserved as conserves, or fermented into wine or vinegar. Cherry plum is enormously important horticulturally as one of the primary rootstocks onto which commercial plum, apricot, and nectarine varieties are grafted. Several ornamental purple-leaved forms (particularly 'Atropurpurea' and the popular 'Thundercloud' and 'Purple Pony') are among the most commonly planted street and specimen trees in zone 5–9 landscapes for their deep maroon-purple spring foliage and masses of pink flowers. The species naturalizes readily and has escaped into the wild in parts of North America and Europe.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; cherry of the Rio Grande is a Brazilian Eugenia species prized by subtropical fruit enthusiasts for its exceptional flavor — the dark red to purple, oblong, cherry-sized fruits have a rich, complex flavor that blends cherry, wine, and grape notes with a slight aromatic complexity that is unique in the subtropical fruit world. It is one of the most sought-after specialty fruits for zone 9 food gardens. The dense, glossy, evergreen foliage is attractive year-round and the showy white flowers appear in spring. It grows as a medium shrub or small tree and tolerates partial shade well, making it suitable as an understory specimen in the food forest. The fruit ripens from May through June on the Gulf Coast and must be harvested promptly as it ferments rapidly after picking. In zone 9a it may need frost protection in hard winters; established plants recover readily. One of the top five subtropical fruits for Gulf Coast gardens.

Chestnuts require cross-pollination between at least two different cultivars or seedlings — plant them within 50 feet of each other for reliable nut set. American chestnut was devastated by blight, so choose blight-resistant Chinese, European, or hybrid selections (such as Dunstan Chestnuts). Trees strongly prefer acidic soils (pH 4.5–6.5) and perform poorly in alkaline or wet conditions. Harvest in fall when burs open and nuts fall; collect daily as nuts on the ground deteriorate quickly. Fresh chestnuts are perishable — refrigerate promptly and use or freeze within a month.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA breeding program, Cheyenne is notable for its smaller, more compact tree size compared to many pecan cultivars, along with excellent kernel quality and a high percentage of kernel to shell. It tends to bear at a younger age than older heirloom cultivars, giving growers an earlier return on a new planting, though it is more susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and benefits from good spacing and airflow. Its compact habit makes it a reasonable option where space is more limited than a full commercial pecan grove requires.

One of the hardiest figs available, Chicago Hardy can be grown down to Zone 5, where the tops may freeze back but resprout from the roots to fruit on new wood. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and mulch heavily over winter in colder regions to protect the crown. Water steadily while fruit develops for the best sweetness. In the coldest zones, grow it in a container that can overwinter in a garage or basement.

Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chickasaw plum thrives on neglect and is essentially care-free once established. Prunus angustifolia (Chickasaw plum or sand plum) is one of the most important native fruit plants of the Gulf Coastal Plain, East Texas, and Piedmont Southeast — a tough, fast-growing, suckering shrub or small tree producing abundant 1/2-to-3/4-inch, bright-red to orange-red or yellow plums in May–June that are tart-sweet and excellent for jellies, preserves, wines, and eating out of hand. The tree is one of the earliest flowering native plants of the Southeast, producing dense clusters of small white flowers in February–March (before the leaves emerge) that provide extremely valuable early nectar for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Chickasaw plum forms thickets by root suckers, creating dense, thorny hedgerows that provide outstanding nesting cover and food for a wide range of wildlife. It is self-fertile (though cross-pollination improves yields) and one of the most heat, drought, and disease-resistant of all stone fruits for southeastern gardens.

Plant in dry, well-drained, rocky soil in full sun on a site that mimics its native semi-arid mountain slopes of the northwestern Himalaya. Chilgoza pine is a slow-growing, long-lived five-needle pine with distinctive flaking, patchwork bark and is cultivated commercially in its native range for its large, thin-shelled, richly flavored pine nuts, among the most prized pine nuts in South and Central Asian cuisine. It requires cold winter dormancy and sharp drainage, and takes many years from planting to first significant cone production.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese box orange tolerates poor, sandy, and salt-affected soils and is commonly grown as a dense, thorny hedge in coastal and southern landscapes. This slow-growing, densely branched citrus relative carries small, glossy, boxwood-like leaves on stiff, thorny stems, with tiny, fragrant white flowers followed by small, dark, olive-black berries that are not palatable but are eaten by birds. Its dense, twiggy, thorn-armed growth makes it an outstanding impenetrable barrier hedge or foundation screen, and it shears well to a formal shape, tolerating heat, drought, and salt spray once established far better than most true citrus. Prune after the main spring flush to maintain a tight hedge form and remove any wayward growth.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun — Chinese chestnut is the blight-resistant alternative to the devastated American chestnut, producing sweet, edible nuts very similar to the native species. It grows naturally in China where it evolved resistance to the fungal blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) that destroyed American chestnuts, and is now the primary species used in chestnut restoration hybrids and in commercial chestnut orchards throughout the eastern US. The tree is medium-sized (30–50 feet), requires two or more trees for cross-pollination, and begins producing nuts within 3–5 years from a grafted tree. The burr-enclosed nuts ripen in fall and are harvested fresh for roasting, boiling, grinding into flour, and use in stuffings and desserts. Chinese chestnut wood is also blight-resistant and durable. An important and practical nut tree for the food forest and home orchard in zone 4–9.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade, giving the tree room to develop its narrower, more elongated leaves than other chestnut species. Native to central and southern China, Chinese chinkapin is a distinct chestnut species from Castanea mollissima, bearing small burs that typically enclose a single sweet nut rather than the two or three found in most chestnuts. It has been used by breeders exploring additional sources of blight tolerance and is planted both as a nut producer and as an ornamental shade tree in its native range.

This large subtropical tree, widely cultivated across southern China and Southeast Asia, produces olive-shaped drupes with an edible oily, nut-like kernel inside fibrous flesh that is traditionally pickled, candied, or cooked rather than eaten raw off the tree. It is unrelated to the Mediterranean olive but fills a similar culinary role in Chinese cuisine, where preserved and salted fruits are a common snack. Because it is only reliably hardy to around 25-28°F, treat it as an experimental planting for the warmest, most sheltered Gulf Coast sites, and expect a long juvenile period of many years before first fruiting from seed-grown trees.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Chinese quince (Pseudocydonia sinensis) is a small ornamental tree related to quince and pear but in its own monotypic genus, producing magnificent exfoliating bark (flaking in irregular puzzle-piece patches of green, cream, and tan like a camouflage pattern), beautiful pale pink spring flowers, and large, 6-inch, yellow, pear-shaped fruits in autumn with a powerful quince-like fragrance that fills a room. The fruits are too astringent to eat raw but make outstanding jelly, paste (membrillo), and syrup; the trees are also spectacular in fall when the leaves turn brilliant orange, red, and yellow. One of the most ornamentally distinguished small trees available for zones 5–9, combining beautiful bark, flowers, fruit, and fall color in a single specimen.

common_name: Chinese White Mulberry (Silkworm Mulberry, King White Mulberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mulberry tolerates a wide range of soil conditions once established. Morus multicaulis (Chinese white mulberry or silkworm mulberry) is the mulberry species most important to global sericulture (silk production) — the leaves are the sole or preferred food source for the silkworm (Bombyx mori), whose cocoons are processed into silk thread. The species is a distinct subspecies or variety within the Morus alba complex, selected over millennia in China, Japan, and Korea for large, tender, nutritious leaves with high silkworm productivity. It produces sweet, large, white-to-pale-lavender to white-pink fruits that ripen in early summer — slightly milder and sweeter than red mulberry, excellent fresh, in pies, jams, syrups, and wine. The tree is fast-growing and quite large, eventually reaching 20–30 feet with a spreading canopy that provides excellent summer shade. In zone 9, the large, sweet fruits ripen in May–June; the tree is deciduous and provides summer shade then winters interest with a distinctive, broadly spreading branch structure. An underused fruit tree for Gulf Coast food gardens where its heat and drought tolerance are genuine assets.

Chinkapin (Castanopsis chrysophylla, also called golden chinquapin) is a large Pacific Coast evergreen related to chestnuts and oaks, bearing small, intensely sweet nuts in spiny burs — often considered the finest-flavored nut native to the Pacific Northwest. Unlike American chestnut it is not susceptible to chestnut blight, making it a valuable blight-free nut tree for western gardeners. Trees are monoecious but require cross-pollination between at least two seedlings or distinct cultivars for reliable nut production; wind and insects both carry pollen. Burs take two years to mature and split open in autumn — collect nuts promptly before squirrels and jays claim the entire crop, and consume or freeze within a month as the small nuts dry out quickly.

Plant in well-drained to dry, calcareous or acidic soil in full sun; chinkapin oak is among the most drought-tolerant native oaks and the only species that thrives naturally on dry limestone outcrops and bluffs — a trait that makes it excellent for rocky, alkaline soils where most oaks fail. The toothed, chestnut-like leaves are distinctive and turn attractive gold and brown in fall. The sweet, small acorns are among the least bitter of any oak, maturing in a single season and consumed immediately by deer, turkeys, squirrels, and wood ducks. The tree adapts to a wide range of soils including limestone-derived clays, shallow rocky hillsides, and deep loams, making it one of the most landscapeable native oaks for challenging sites.

Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chocolate is a PVNA (Pollination Variant Non-Astringent) Japanese persimmon — a type that produces sweet, non-astringent, crunchy-when-firm fruit with distinctive brown ('chocolate') flesh when pollinated and seeds are present, but remains astringent if no seeds develop from lack of pollination. The presence of a pollinator tree (Gailey, Maru, or another male or seeded cultivar) within 50 feet allows Chocolate to develop its characteristic dark brown, sweet, crunchy flesh that can be eaten firm at the orange-yellow stage — unlike astringent types that must be soft. This firm-eating non-astringent quality (shared by Fuyu) makes Chocolate outstanding for fresh use, salads, and eating out of hand. The unusual brown flesh color — resulting from tannin-anthocyanin reactions stimulated by seeds — is distinctive and has no direct equivalent among common temperate fruits. With a pollinator nearby, Chocolate produces medium-large, flat to slightly rounded, orange fruits with brown flesh that are ready from late September through November in zone 9. Without a pollinator, fruits are astringent and must ripen soft (similar to Hachiya) before eating. For maximum enjoyment, plant Chocolate near another persimmon variety for cross-pollination.

common_name: Choctaw Pecan (Large-Nut Premium Gulf South Pecan, Type II Late-Season Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Choctaw is a late-season variety ripening in October–November, later than most other pecans; supplement with zinc spray in spring; Choctaw is somewhat susceptible to pecan scab in very humid coastal conditions and benefits from fungicide applications in wet years; best in zones 7–9 with adequate growing season length. Choctaw pecan is a USDA-ARS variety (released 1959) known primarily for producing some of the largest individual nuts of any commercial pecan variety, with nut counts typically running 35–40 per pound compared to the 50–60 nuts per pound typical of smaller varieties — in pecan marketing, where size commands premium prices, Choctaw's exceptionally large nuts give it distinct commercial value. The nuts are well-filled, with 60–64% kernel percentage, and the kernel quality is excellent — bright golden color, plump halves, and a rich, sweet buttery flavor. Choctaw has broader adaptation through the Gulf South than some varieties, performing reasonably well in the humid coastal plain from eastern Texas through the Florida Panhandle, though like most pecans it requires fungicide management for scab control in high-humidity years. The trees are vigorous and upright-growing, ultimately becoming very large specimens, and are somewhat slow to come into production compared to precocious varieties like Pawnee. The late ripening season (October–November) is an advantage in areas prone to early fall wet weather — the nuts are harvested and on the ground before the worst scab-spreading conditions of mid-fall. A prestige variety for home orchards and direct-market operations where extra-large nut size commands attention.

Plant in well-drained to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; chokecherry is one of North America’s most cold-hardy and adaptable native fruiting shrubs, ranging from Alaska to Tennessee and coast to coast. Fragrant white flower racemes appear in spring followed by clusters of small dark red to purple-black fruits in mid-summer. The astringent, very tart fruits are too acidic to eat raw in quantity but cook into outstanding jams, syrups, and wines with a flavor reminiscent of Concord grape; the juice has been used by indigenous peoples for centuries as a food, dye, and medicine. It suckers freely to form thickets, providing excellent wildlife habitat. Cultivars 'Schubert' and 'Canada Red' have striking purple summer foliage.

Remove the seed from its hard stone before sowing, then plant 1 inch deep in sandy, well-drained soil in a warm, sunny location once all frost risk has passed. This tree demands heat and full sun and will not tolerate waterlogged or heavy clay soils; raised beds or slopes with excellent drainage are ideal in marginal climates. Protect young trees from frost in zones 8 and 9 during their first few winters until the trunk thickens and cold hardiness improves. Fruit production begins within three to five years of transplanting and increases substantially as the tree matures.

Citron is an ancient citrus grown mainly for its thick, fragrant rind, which is candied or used in preserves. It is among the most frost-tender citrus, so grow it in full sun in the warmest possible spot or in a container to move under cover. Provide rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, feeding regularly during growth. Prune to remove the plant's stout thorns and dead wood, and harvest the large fruit when fully colored.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Clapp's Favorite ripens quickly once picked and bruises easily, so harvest and handle it gently. Bred in Massachusetts in the 1860s, it bears large, pale yellow-green pears blushed with red, similar in shape and flavor to Bartlett but ripening about two weeks earlier, with sweet, juicy, fine-textured flesh that made it a widely planted early-season dessert pear in American orchards for well over a century. Its early ripening extends the home orchard's fresh pear season ahead of the main Bartlett crop, though the fruit softens and turns mealy very quickly once ripe and bruises easily, so it needs prompt picking and careful handling compared to firmer, better-keeping pear varieties. Harvest while still firm and green in late summer, then ripen indoors at room temperature and eat promptly once the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

Clementines are sweet, seedless, easy-peeling mandarins that ripen in early winter. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, sheltered from frost, or in a large pot to overwinter under glass in cool climates. Some cultivars fruit more reliably without a cross-pollinator, which keeps them seedless. Feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season and harvest as soon as the fruit colors, since it holds only briefly on the tree.

Plant grafted stock in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; water deeply and infrequently once established; fertilize with citrus-formulated fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and early fall. Citrus × clementina (clementine mandarin) is the small, seedless, thin-skinned, intensely sweet mandarin orange known worldwide as the holiday tangerine — a hybrid of mandarin and sweet orange discovered in Algeria around 1900 by Brother Clément Rodier (for whom it is named). The clementine is distinguished from ordinary mandarins by its typically seedless fruits (in isolated plantings without cross-pollination), deep-orange, extremely glossy, smooth peel that peels effortlessly, and exceptional sweet flavor with minimal tartness. In zone 9, clementines ripen from November through January — the ideal cool-season ripening period that concentrates sugars. Trees are moderately compact and more cold-tolerant than many citrus types, surviving brief drops to 28°F when established. Plant only grafted trees (not seedlings) for true-to-type fruit and quicker bearing; trees typically bear first fruit 2–3 years after planting. A reliable, productive choice for Gulf Coast home orchards.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Clementine is the most widely grown and beloved easy-peel mandarin orange in the world — the source of the small, bright-orange, seedless (when grown without cross-pollination) tangerines marketed as 'Cuties' and 'Halos' in American grocery stores. The fruit is small (2–2.5 inches diameter), very easy to peel with virtually no pith, with 8–14 segments of rich, sweet, complex mandarin flavor and distinctive floral aroma. The thin, glossy, bright-orange rind peels effortlessly, making Clementines the most practical fresh-eating citrus for children and adults who want convenient, mess-free citrus. Fruit ripens in November through January in zone 9 — the holiday season — making it one of the most seasonal and eagerly anticipated citrus fruits. The tree is compact, well-shaped, and attractive, with glossy dark-green foliage and fragrant white spring flowers. Clementines can produce seeds if cross-pollinated by other mandarin or sweet orange varieties growing nearby — for seedless fruit, avoid planting near other mandarins, or select a seedless clementine variety. In zone 9, Clementines should be sited in warm, protected locations and protected from temperatures below 28°F. Apply citrus fertilizer three times annually: February, May, and September.

This semi-dwarf grapefruit-pomelo hybrid produces juicy, sweet-tart, low-acid fruit on a compact tree ideal for patios or small yards. Grow in full sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and water deeply while letting the surface dry between waterings. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season for good fruit development. Move container trees to a bright indoor location before frost, as grapefruit is cold-sensitive.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained to seasonally wet, sandy, alkaline, or coastal soil; coco plum is a versatile South Florida and Caribbean native that ranges from a 3-foot groundcover to a 15-foot shrub depending on the cultivar and site conditions. The round to oval fruits ripen to white, red, or dark purple depending on variety and are eaten fresh when ripe — they have starchy, mildly sweet, coconut-flavored flesh around a large seed — or made into jam and jelly. The seed kernel contains a fat that is extracted for cosmetics in South America. Coco plum is both a valuable wildlife plant, supporting many birds and butterflies, and one of the few edible natives for South Florida's challenging alkaline, salty, and wet conditions. Tolerates periodic flooding and salt spray better than almost any other fruiting plant.

Start seeds in warm, moist mix at 75–85°F indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moist soil after soil warms; cocona (Solanum sessiliflorum) is a tomato relative from the Amazon basin of Colombia, Peru, and Brazil, producing 2–4 inch yellow to orange fruits that resemble a slightly fuzzy tomato with a pleasant, acidic, tomato-citrus flavor widely used in Amazonian cuisine for juices, jams, and salsas. The plants are large-leafed and fast-growing, producing fruit 6–9 months after transplanting in suitable tropical conditions. Rich in iron and an important component of the diet of indigenous Amazonian peoples; increasingly available as a specialty crop in Florida and Hawaii. Thrives in humid tropical conditions with good rainfall or irrigation.

Plant container-grown seedlings in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; coconut palm is the most widely cultivated and economically important palm tree in the world — a single tree provides coconut fruit (with meat, milk, water, and oil), fibrous husk (coir), palm fronds (for thatching and weaving), and palm heart, making it one of the most useful food trees in human history. In zone 10–12 Florida, Hawaii, and tropical coastal areas it grows to 30–60 feet with a gracefully curving trunk and a spreading canopy of long, feathery fronds. Trees begin producing coconuts 6–10 years after planting and can remain productive for 70–80 years. Excellent salt tolerance makes it one of the best trees for coastal landscapes. 'Malayan Dwarf' cultivars are shorter, earlier fruiting, and moderately hurricane-resistant. Growth is faster in deep, moist, sandy soil with access to groundwater. Extremely frost-sensitive — any freezing temperature causes permanent damage; restricted to southernmost Florida and Hawaii in the US.

Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; Coe's Golden Drop needs a compatible European plum or gage pollinator and blooms late, helping it dodge some spring frosts. An English gage-type dessert plum bred in Suffolk in the late eighteenth century, it is celebrated by connoisseurs for exceptionally rich, honeyed, sweet flesh inside a translucent golden-yellow skin often blushed pink in full sun, generally considered one of the finest-flavored dessert plums grown, though the tree is a notoriously shy and unreliable bearer compared to workhorse varieties like Victoria. Its late bloom period helps it escape some late spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering plums, but it still benefits from a warm, sheltered site to ripen its sugars fully and from a compatible pollinator, since it does not reliably self-pollinate. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and be patient with its lighter, less predictable crops in exchange for exceptional dessert flavor.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade — coffee is an attractive, glossy-leaved tropical shrub or small tree native to the forest understory of Ethiopia, grown worldwide in tropical highlands for the seeds (coffee beans) contained inside the red or yellow 'cherry' fruits, which ripen 9–12 months after the heavily fragrant white flowers bloom. As an ornamental plant it is outstandingly handsome: the dark green, glossy, waxy leaves are beautiful year-round; the clusters of jasmine-scented white flowers in spring are intensely fragrant; and the red coffee cherries are decorative and visually striking in fall and winter. Coffee is a genuine shade plant, preferring filtered light under taller trees rather than full sun, which scorches the leaves and stresses the plant in warm climates. In zone 10–11 it can be grown outdoors permanently; in cooler zones it is a remarkable large container plant for bright indoor spaces or protected outdoor areas in summer.

common_name: Coffee Plum (Indian Plum, Rhoea Plum, Puneala Plum)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in frost-free tropical conditions; coffee plum (also known as Indian plum or Puneala plum in India and Sri Lanka) is a Southeast Asian Flacourtia related to governor's plum but distinctly different — producing attractive clusters of small red to deep red-purple fruits with a sweet-acidic, slightly astringent flavor reminiscent of sour plum combined with cherry. The name 'coffee plum' is used in southern India where it is made into jams and pickles and eaten fresh when fully ripe. Often hermaphroditic and self-fertile, making it easier to grow than most Flacourtia species. An attractive thorny shrub with glossy leaves, useful as a security hedge in subtropical gardens.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Cogshall mango's naturally dwarf habit makes it one of the best mango cultivars for small yards and container culture. A compact Florida seedling selection related to Carrie, it bears small to medium fruit with fiberless, deep orange, richly sweet flesh and a distinctive flavor often compared to butterscotch, borne heavily on a tree that stays notably smaller than most mango cultivars even at maturity. Its dwarf habit and heavy, reliable bearing make it a favorite for gardeners with limited space who still want full-sized mango flavor, and it responds well to being kept pruned and compact in a large container. Reduce irrigation as fruit approaches harvest to concentrate flavor, and protect young trees from any frost or freeze.

common_name: Col de Dame Blanc Fig (Neck of the Lady Fig)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to average soil in full sun; Col de Dame Blanc performs best with reflected heat from south or west-facing walls and requires genuine summer heat to ripen its fruit fully — not recommended for cool-summer Pacific Northwest climates. Col de Dame (literally 'neck of the lady' in Catalan, for the fruit's distinctive elongated, graceful neck) is a group of heirloom Spanish figs from the Catalonia region particularly associated with the town of Sitges; the Blanc (white) form produces elongated, pear-necked, greenish-white to pale yellow fruits with exceptionally thin skin and almost liqueur-like white interior flesh with a concentrated honey sweetness and complex figgy aroma that experienced fig growers frequently describe as among the finest flavors of any variety. A common fig type requiring no pollinator. Less cold-hardy and less vigorous than many commercial varieties but the extraordinary flavor rewards the extra attention; increasingly popular among American fig collectors and now more readily available from specialty nurseries than a decade ago.

This cold-tolerant pomegranate bears vibrant red-fruited crops and handsome orange-red flowers on a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it thrives in heat and tolerates drought once established. Water deeply but infrequently, easing off as fruit ripens to prevent splitting. In the colder end of its range, site it against a warm south wall and mulch the base for winter protection.

common_name: Colossal Chestnut (European-Japanese Hybrid Chestnut, California Large Chestnut, Giant Chestnut)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile loam in full sun; Colossal requires cross-pollination; harvest nuts in October when burrs open and nuts fall naturally; collect promptly from ground; Colossal chestnuts are among the largest available — single nuts can reach 30+ grams, comparable to the best Italian and French chestnuts — with sweet, creamy flesh excellent for roasting, marrons glacés, and fresh cooking. Colossal chestnut is a hybrid of European sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa) and Japanese chestnut (Castanea crenata) developed in California in the late 1800s by Felix Gillet, a French-born nurseryman who operated the Nevada City Nursery in northern California and imported and trialed numerous European and Asian chestnut varieties and crosses. The variety became the standard commercial chestnut in California and the Pacific Northwest, where it grows vigorously in the mild, well-drained soils of the region and produces exceptionally large individual nuts — among the largest of any named chestnut variety, comparable to the finest Italian and French chestnuts in size and flavor. The large nut size (a single nut can weigh an ounce or more) and good flavor — sweet, starchy, and rich — make Colossal the variety of choice for specialty fresh-market chestnut sales, marron glacé (candied whole chestnuts), and roasting.
