It has been widely planted in California's chestnut-growing regions (Nevada County, the Sierra Nevada foothills) and in Oregon and Washington for commercial and home production.

Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun; common hawthorn is an exceptionally tough small tree or large shrub valued for its dense thorny habit providing excellent wildlife cover, profuse white spring flowers, and abundant red berries (haws) that feed birds through winter. The haws are edible — mildly flavored, slightly mealy, and high in antioxidant flavonoids — and are used to make jellies, wines, and medicinal syrups with a long history in European herbal medicine. Tolerates urban pollution, heavy clay, coastal exposure, and severe pruning. For hedging, plant 18 inches apart and shear twice yearly; the dense spiny habit makes a stock-proof barrier within a few years.

Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun; Conadria is a common fig type (no pollinator needed) and one of the most productive figs per tree, bearing heavily in its second and third years. Conadria was released in 1955 by USDA fig breeder Ira J. Condit from the Riverside California station after decades of fig selection work; it was selected for exceptional fruit quality combined with high yields, producing large (3–5 oz), turbinate, greenish-white to pale yellow fruits with strawberry-pink interior flesh and very sweet, rich flavor comparable to the finest White Adriatic and Calimyrna types. Outstanding for fresh eating and particularly excellent for drying, producing firm, sweet dried figs with good shelf life. A vigorous, upright, productive tree that performs exceptionally in hot, dry Western climates (Central Valley California, Arizona, Texas, Gulf Coast) and ripens reliably in the main crop (August–October). Somewhat more heat-tolerant than many high-quality white figs.

common_name: Concord Grape (American Blue Grape, Slip-Skin Grape, New England Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter — Concord is cane-pruned, leaving 2 strong canes per vine; fruit ripens in September in most zones; Concord is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator; the berries slip easily from their skins ('slip-skin'), which facilitates juice making but means they are not firm enough for shipping. Concord grape is the foundational American table and juice grape, developed in 1849 by Ephraim Wales Bull in Concord, Massachusetts, from a chance seedling of Vitis labrusca — the native American 'fox grape' species of the northeastern forests. Bull spent six years selecting seedlings for fruit quality from a wild Labrusca vine growing on his property before exhibiting the named variety at the Massachusetts Horticultural Society in 1853, where it immediately attracted attention and within decades became the most widely planted grape in the United States. The Concord grape flavor — simultaneously musky, sweet-tart, and intensely 'grapey' in a way that European vinifera grapes are not — became the defining American grape taste through Welch's grape juice (first produced in 1869 to provide an unfermented communion grape drink by Dr. Thomas Welch) and the ubiquitous grape jelly that made the PB&J sandwich a cultural icon. The flavor compound primarily responsible for the characteristic Concord aroma is methyl anthranilate, a naturally occurring ester found at high concentrations in Labrusca-type grapes and essentially absent from European vinifera varieties. Concord is a seeded grape (seeds are a minor inconvenience for fresh eating but irrelevant for juicing and jelly making) producing large, round, blue-black berries in substantial clusters in mid-to-late September. The vines are cold-hardy to -20°F and require 100–150 chill hours, which are met in zones 4–8 but rarely in zones 9+.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Concorde benefits from a compatible pollinizer such as Conference or Comice for best fruit set. Bred in England from a cross of Conference and the richly flavored Doyenne du Comice, it combines the best traits of both parents, producing long, slender, Conference-shaped fruit with the sweeter, more aromatic dessert flavor of Comice, on a tree that is notably more compact and easier to manage in a home garden than either parent. Its excellent flavor, attractive fruit shape, and good storage life have made it an increasingly popular modern addition to home orchards, particularly where garden space favors a smaller, more manageable tree. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature, since pears ripen best off the tree rather than left to soften on the branch.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Conference sets a reasonable crop on its own but yields much better with a compatible pollinizer such as Comice or Bartlett. The single most widely grown pear in the United Kingdom and one of the most recognizable European pears, it bears reliable, heavy crops of long, tapered, bronze-russeted fruit with sweet, juicy, fine-textured flesh that stores and ships notably well compared to more delicate dessert pear varieties. Its partial self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and good disease tolerance compared to some other European pears have made it a standard, forgiving choice for a home orchard, though a second variety nearby still meaningfully boosts yield. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the characteristic sweet, juicy texture, since pears ripen from the inside out and are best picked underripe from the tree.

Contender is a disease-resistant, cold-hardy, self-pollinating peach that produces abundant medium-to-large juicy freestone fruit across many climates. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water consistently during fruit development. Thin young fruit to about 6 inches apart to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune annually in late winter to an open-center shape for light penetration, and apply dormant sprays as needed to manage common peach diseases.

Coolidge is a self-fertile pineapple guava selection, useful where only one plant can be grown. Set it in full sun on well-drained soil and water consistently through the fruiting season for the best crop. It tolerates coastal conditions and light frost once established, and can be grown as a shrub or clipped hedge. Fruit is ripe when it drops naturally, so gather it daily from the ground beneath the plant.

common_name: Coratina Olive (High-Polyphenol Southern Italian Oil Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Coratina is a Southern Italian olive cultivar from Puglia prized for producing intensely robust, bitter, peppery oil with exceptionally high polyphenol content — among the highest of any commonly grown olive cultivar — making it a favorite for growers and consumers seeking a bold, health-forward oil rather than a mild table experience. The tree is vigorous, heat-tolerant, and productive, and has performed well in warm-climate US oil-olive trials outside its native Mediterranean range, including in parts of the Southeast. Harvest early, while fruit is still green to just turning color, for the most intensely peppery, high-polyphenol oil; later harvest mellows the flavor but reduces polyphenol content. Coratina is largely self-fruitful, though yields improve with a second compatible cultivar nearby. Established trees are drought-tolerant and, like most olives, thrive on benign neglect once past the first two establishment years, needing supplemental water mainly during prolonged dry spells at fruit set.

Plant acorns in fall in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; cork oak is the source of virtually all wine and champagne cork in the world — the extraordinarily thick, spongy, deeply furrowed outer bark is harvested every 9–12 years from mature trees (a process called 'cork stripping') that does not harm the tree, as the bark regenerates completely. Portugal and Spain produce about 80% of the world's cork. The tree is an evergreen with a broad, spreading canopy and small, evergreen, slightly holly-like leaves. First cork harvest is typically at age 25 years; subsequent harvests every 9–12 years for the remaining 150–200 years of the tree's life. In California, cork oaks have been grown for over a century as ornamentals and heritage trees, thriving in the Mediterranean climate. An interesting tree with historical and economic significance for home gardeners in zones 7–10.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; cornelian cherry tolerates a wide range of soil conditions. Cornus mas (cornelian cherry dogwood) is a large, multi-stemmed European and Asian shrub or small tree producing one of the very earliest spring flower displays of any hardy plant — tiny, bright-yellow flowers clustered in small, button-like heads that cover the bare branches in February–March (often while snow still falls) before any other spring-blooming shrub. The flowers are followed by oval, cherry-like fruits that ripen to deep scarlet-red in August, tasting like a tart-sweet cranberry crossed with a sour cherry — used in jams, jellies, liqueurs (the Georgian chacha), and sauces throughout Eastern Europe and the Caucasus, where the sour flavor is prized in cooking much like tamarind. The tree is also fall-ornamental with excellent red-pink fall foliage and attractive peeling bark. 'Golden Glory' and 'Redstone' are widely grown cultivars. At the warm edge of its range (zone 8), it grows best with afternoon shade and consistent moisture; it is marginal in zone 9 and does best in the cooler northern parts of zone 8.

common_name: Cortland Apple (McIntosh × Ben Davis Cross, Non-Browning Salad Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cortland is an excellent cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties including McIntosh; ripens mid-season (September–October); the non-browning flesh makes it uniquely valuable for salads, charcuterie boards, and fresh-cut preparations where apples must remain attractive for hours without discoloring. Cortland apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1915 from a cross of McIntosh and Ben Davis — two of the most important apple varieties of the early 20th century. Cortland inherits McIntosh's aromatic, sweet-tart flavor character in a larger, firmer fruit with significantly better keeping quality than McIntosh. However, Cortland's most famous and unique characteristic is the slow-browning tendency of its flesh when cut: while most apple varieties brown rapidly after cutting due to enzymatic oxidation, Cortland flesh is notably slower to brown, making cut pieces remain white and attractive for much longer than most varieties. This property makes Cortland uniquely valuable for fresh preparations where apple slices need to remain appealing: fresh fruit platters, salads, charcuterie boards, and school lunch boxes where the apples won't be eaten immediately after cutting. The fruit is large, round, red over greenish-yellow skin with very white, juicy, tender flesh and the characteristic McIntosh aromatic quality. It is an excellent cross-pollinator for most other apple varieties due to its abundant, viable pollen. A classic in northeastern U.S. home orchards.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollinator flowering at the same time, since Cot-N-Candy sets fruit poorly on its own. This Zaiger Genetics aprium, an apricot-plum interspecific hybrid weighted mostly toward apricot, looks much like a fuzzy-skinned apricot but carries noticeably sweeter, richer, more aromatic flesh thanks to its plum parentage. It ripens early in the stone fruit season, giving a jump on the summer harvest, and is generally grown and pruned like a standard apricot, with an open-center form and moderate annual pruning to renew fruiting wood. Because apricots and apriums bloom very early, plant in a site protected from the latest spring frosts, which can damage the flowers before fruit ever sets.

common_name: Cox's Orange Pippin Apple (World's Finest Eating Apple, English Dessert Apple Standard)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with good air movement; Cox's Orange Pippin is highly susceptible to apple scab and powdery mildew in humid climates — a preventive spray program or planting in the dry Pacific Northwest is strongly recommended; it requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in October when fully colored and giving slightly to pressure, then store 4–6 weeks to allow flavor to fully develop. Cox's Orange Pippin is the variety most consistently named by apple connoisseurs worldwide as the finest-flavored dessert apple in existence — a small to medium English heirloom discovered as a seedling by retired brewer Richard Cox in his garden at Colnbrook Lawn in Slough, Berkshire, England around 1825, and distributed commercially from 1850 onward. The flavor at peak ripeness is extraordinarily complex and rich by apple standards: intense, spicy-sweet, aromatic, with distinct notes of pear, mango, honey, and fresh nuts that no other apple variety precisely replicates — and which Cox's defenders argue no modern commercial variety (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) can equal in flavor depth and complexity. Cox's became the dominant apple of British gardens and orchards for 150 years and remains the benchmark of the English fresh-eating apple tradition. In the United States, Cox's is most successfully grown in the maritime Pacific Northwest (Oregon and Washington's western valleys, similar in climate to England) where the cool, moist summers allow the apple to develop its characteristic complex flavor without disease pressure overwhelming the susceptible trees. In the humid eastern states, disease resistance is a significant challenge that requires diligent management.

Crabapples bear small, tart fruit excellent for jelly and serve as reliable pollinizers for dessert apples. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing disease-resistant selections to limit scab and rust. They are extremely cold-hardy and adaptable, tolerating a wide range of soils. Prune in late winter to maintain an open canopy, and harvest the high-pectin fruit after the first firm color develops.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun on a strong, large-scale support, since this East Asian ornamental grape climbs vigorously by tendrils and can quickly cover an arbor, pergola, or old tree. It is grown chiefly for its huge, heart-shaped, deeply veined leaves, which can reach 10 inches or more across and turn spectacular shades of crimson, scarlet, and purple in autumn, rivaling any deciduous tree for fall color. Small, fragrant flowers in late spring are followed by clusters of small, dark purple grapes that are edible but seedy, tart, and generally considered better for jelly or wildlife forage than fresh eating. Because of its exceptional vigor, Crimson Glory Vine needs a sturdy, generously sized structure and room to run, and benefits from hard annual pruning in late winter to control size and encourage the largest, most colorful leaves the following season.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. CrimsonCrisp comes from the same Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois breeding program that produced GoldRush and Enterprise, carrying genetic immunity to apple scab along with resistance to cedar-apple rust and fire blight, making it a strong low-spray choice for home orchards in humid climates where scab is a constant pressure on susceptible varieties. The medium-size fruit has deep crimson-red skin over crisp, dense, juicy flesh with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor, ripening in early-to-mid fall — earlier than the late-season GoldRush and Enterprise, giving a staggered harvest when planted alongside them. It stores reasonably well under cool conditions, though not as long as the latest-ripening disease-resistant selections. Thin fruit clusters to one apple per cluster in late spring to improve size and reduce limb breakage.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Criollo cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Considered the finest-flavored and rarest of the three main cacao varieties, Criollo (Spanish for 'native' or 'creole') produces pale, thin-shelled pods with mild, complex, low-bitterness flavor prized by fine chocolate makers, but the tree is notably more susceptible to disease and lower-yielding than the hardier Forastero variety that dominates most commercial cacao production worldwide. It requires the warm, humid, sheltered understory conditions of a tropical rainforest, ideally grown beneath taller shade trees, and demands more careful disease management than more robust cacao types, making it a specialty planting for dedicated chocolate enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors rather than an easy home crop. Provide consistent shade, humidity, and warmth, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity.

common_name: Cripps Pink Apple (Pink Lady, Late-Season Low-Chill Sweet-Tart Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator, since this cultivar is not self-fertile. Bred by John Cripps in Western Australia from a cross of Golden Delicious and Lady Williams, it is marketed commercially as Pink Lady and is among the latest-ripening apples grown, often left on the tree into late autumn to fully develop its rosy-pink blush and dense, crisp, sweet-tart flesh. Its lower chill requirement compared to classic northern apples makes it one of the more workable dessert apples for warmer growing regions. Fruit stores exceptionally well and resists browning better than many varieties once cut.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Croisic is a French fig variety named for the coastal commune of Le Croisic in Brittany, notable primarily for its prolific breba crop — the early-season figs produced on previous year's wood that ripen in late May to early June in zone 9, weeks ahead of the main crop figs on most other varieties. The early-ripening breba figs are medium to large, with a yellow-green to yellow skin and amber to orange-tinged flesh with a mild, honey-sweet flavor. In zone 9 the Croisic fig provides the earliest fresh fig harvest of the season and is particularly valued by gardeners who want to extend the fig-eating season by starting early. The main crop figs on new wood ripen in August–September and are similar in quality to the breba crop. In zone 9 the mild winters and long growing season allow Croisic to produce heavy breba crops — the consistently warm temperatures maintain the tree's vigor for prolific breba production.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving this compact-growing selection room to branch out into a small, rounded tree. Unlike typical seedy sugar apples, this cultivar sets fruit that are largely seedless or nearly so, with the same custardy, sweet, segmented flesh that makes the species popular across south Florida dooryards. It defoliates in cool weather and is killed back by hard frost, so Gulf Coast growers favor sheltered south-facing walls or grow young trees in containers that can be moved into a garage during freezes. Hand pollination with a small brush in the early morning often improves fruit set, since natural pollinators can be scarce in home gardens.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part to full shade; cupuassu requires consistent moisture and high humidity and will not tolerate any frost or prolonged dry periods. Theobroma grandiflorum (cupuassu) is a Brazilian Amazon rainforest relative of cacao (T. cacao) producing large, 8-to-12-inch, oblong, woody fruits borne directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflorous), each containing 20–50 seeds surrounded by a thick, creamy-white, intensely fragrant pulp with a flavor combining chocolate, pineapple, banana, and guava — considered by many food scientists to be one of the most complex and delicious tropical flavors in the world. The pulp is used to make juices, ice creams, yogurts, and confectioneries throughout Brazil, where it is the second most important Amazonian fruit after açaí. The seeds can be fermented and processed into a chocolate-like product ('cupuaçu butter') and are the basis of a proprietary chocolate-substitute trademarked as 'cupulate.' Growing cupuassu outside zones 11–12 requires a greenhouse; at the frontier of zone 10b, protected microclimates may support growth. A rare and extraordinary specialty fruit for true tropical enthusiasts.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Curtis is an old, Florida Panhandle-origin pecan cultivar valued for its outstanding resistance to pecan scab and other humid-climate fungal diseases, making it one of the most reliable low-spray options for Deep South home orchards. The nuts are smaller than many modern commercial cultivars but well filled, with good flavor, and the tree bears consistently and precociously once established. Because of its disease tolerance and long track record along the Gulf Coast, Curtis is frequently recommended as a dependable, low-maintenance pollinator and production tree for home growers who do not want to run a fungicide spray program. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring.

Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; custard apple is a deciduous to semi-evergreen Annona tree producing round to heart-shaped yellow-green to brownish fruits 3–4 inches in diameter with a reticulated (net-patterned) skin. The creamy white flesh inside is sweeter and softer than sugar apple, with a custard-like texture and a mild, slightly musky flavor. It is the Annona most widely grown across tropical Latin America, the Caribbean, and South Asia, where it is known variously as bull's heart, corazon, nona, and anon. Hand-pollinate flowers using a small brush in the morning to transfer pollen between flowers on the same tree; like other Annona species, the stigma and anther are not receptive at the same time.

Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Czar is self-fertile, reliably productive, and one of the earliest-ripening European plums. An English culinary plum introduced in the 1870s, it bears heavy, reliable crops of dark purple-black, medium-sized fruit ripening notably earlier in the season than most other European plums, with tart, firm flesh that holds together well for cooking, canning, and jam-making even though it is somewhat less sweet than a fresh-eating dessert plum. Its self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and early ripening have made it a longstanding favorite for a productive, low-maintenance home orchard plum, particularly where an early culinary crop is wanted ahead of the main plum season. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit for better size, since it often sets a very heavy crop.

D'Anjou is a vigorous, productive European pear yielding sweet, juicy fruit excellent for fresh eating, baking, and canning. Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and include a different pear variety nearby for cross-pollination. Water consistently during fruit development and prune in late winter to a central-leader form. Harvest the fruit while still firm and ripen it off the tree in cool storage for the best texture.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site with well-drained soil and a compatible pollinator; D'Arcy Spice needs a warm season to develop its distinctive flavor and can be a shy, unreliable bearer. A rare old English apple originating in Essex in the late eighteenth century, it bears small, dull green-brown, unassuming-looking russeted apples that belie a uniquely rich, warm, nutmeg-and-spice-like flavor unlike any other apple, prized by heirloom enthusiasts and considered one of the most distinctively flavored traditional English dessert apples. It is a late-ripening, long-keeping variety that develops its best spiced flavor only after a period of storage, but the tree can be an unreliable, biennial bearer and needs a warm, sheltered site to ripen and flavor the fruit well, making it better suited to a favorable microclimate than an exposed site. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a month or more before eating, since the distinctive spiced flavor develops and intensifies in storage.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Dabinett is reliably productive and a good choice for a first cider-apple planting. Originating in Somerset, England, this small, red-flushed apple is one of the most widely planted bittersweet cider apples in both traditional English cider and the modern American craft cider industry, valued for contributing soft, rounded tannin and moderate sugar that blends smoothly with sharper or more acidic varieties. Unlike the temperamental Kingston Black, it is a reliable, consistent, heavy-bearing tree that ripens late in the season and tolerates a range of growing conditions reasonably well, making it a popular starting point for home cider orchardists. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the small, tannic fruit is grown exclusively for cider rather than fresh eating.

The damson is a hardy, self-fertile culinary plum whose tart, astringent fruit shines in jams, gins, and preserves. It thrives even on heavier soils and in exposed positions where dessert plums struggle. Plant in full sun to partial shade and keep young trees weed-free and mulched. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in summer; expect reliable heavy crops after three to four years.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; prune to open center form after harvest. Prunus domestica 'Damson' (Damson plum or Blue Damson) is an ancient, small-fruited European plum type — distinct from both Japanese plums (P. salicina) and common European plums in being smaller, more astringent, and more intensely flavored when raw, but superb when cooked or preserved. The small (1-inch), oval, blue-purple to nearly black fruits ripen in late summer through fall with a rich, complex, winelike, slightly tannic flavor that becomes sweet and luscious when cooked with sugar. Damson plum is the traditional fruit of English damson jam, damson cheese (a firm fruit paste), damson gin (sloe-gin equivalent made with damsons rather than sloes), and damson wine. The Shropshire Damson is the most celebrated English variety; Merryweather is the largest-fruited commercial type. Damson trees are notably hardy, long-lived, disease-resistant, and productive — often naturalizing at hedgerow edges across England — and require less winter chill than Japanese plums. Generally self-fertile or partially self-fertile; a pollination partner improves yields.

Plant grafted or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; damson is more self-fertile than most plums and often sets good crops without a pollinator, though cropping improves with cross-pollination from another plum. Prunus instititia is the wild source of the cultivated damson, a small tree or large shrub producing small, oval, blue-black to purple plums in late summer with dense, richly flavored, astringent flesh quite distinct in character from the sweet, fresh-eating Japanese plums; damsons are the traditional plum for cooking, being too astringent to eat in quantity raw but transforming into superb jam (damson jam is one of Britain's most prized traditional preserves), jelly, cheese, wine, and gin. The tree is extremely long-lived, hardy, and productive even in cold, exposed, and acid soils where other plums fail.

Plant grafted nursery trees in full sun, well-drained soil; fertilize with a citrus fertilizer 3 times per year (February, May, September). Dancy is the original American tangerine — named for Col. George L. Dancy of Orange Mills, Florida, who cultivated this variety beginning around 1867, making it one of the oldest named tangerine cultivars in the United States. For over a century, 'Dancy tangerine' was synonymous with 'tangerine' for most Americans — it was the predominant commercial tangerine grown in Florida and the citrus most commonly associated with Christmas stocking traditions, the holiday season timing of its December–January ripening. The fruits are medium-small, oblate, and deep orange-red at maturity with a distinctively loose, easily peeled 'zipper-skin' — the loose skin peels away from the flesh with minimal effort, releasing the fruit in clean, separate segments. The flavor is the classic tangerine profile: tart, sweet, aromatic, and intensely citrus with the characteristic spicy-sweet note that distinguishes tangerines from oranges. Dancy has substantial seeds (8–15 per fruit), which reduces its appeal compared to modern seedless mandarin hybrids; however, the intense traditional tangerine flavor is considered by many to be unmatched by the sweeter but blander modern seedless types. Trees are productive and long-lived in zone 9–11.

common_name: Dapple Dandy Pluot (Dinosaur Egg Red-Fleshed Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible plum or pluot pollinator such as Santa Rosa or Flavor Supreme, since Dapple Dandy is not reliably self-fruitful. Bred by Floyd Zaiger, this pluot, an interspecific plum-apricot hybrid weighted mostly toward its plum parentage, is instantly recognizable by its greenish-yellow skin dappled with maroon-red splotches, which gave rise to its Dinosaur Egg nickname, and by the vivid magenta-red flesh inside that is exceptionally sweet with a rich, complex flavor many tasters rate among the best of the pluot varieties. Fruit ripens over a fairly long midsummer window, giving a spread-out harvest rather than one concentrated picking, and the tree is otherwise managed much like a standard plum, with dormant pruning to an open center and thinning of heavy fruit sets to improve size. Its moderate chill requirement fits mild-winter Southern gardens better than many traditional European plums.

Plant in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; Darlington oak is a medium-sized semi-evergreen oak of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, often confused with the closely related laurel oak (Q. laurifolia) that grows in moister soils. The elliptical leaves are semi-evergreen to evergreen in the deep South, making this an excellent year-round shade and wildlife tree for zone 8–10 landscapes. Like most oaks, it produces abundant small acorns that provide essential food for wild turkeys, wood ducks, blue jays, and white-tailed deer. It is one of the most commonly encountered oaks in dry upland portions of the Florida peninsula and the Gulf Coastal Plain, thriving in the kind of deep, dry, infertile white sand that challenges most trees. An excellent canopy tree for naturalistic landscapes in the coastal Southeast where heat, drought, and sandy soils limit tree choices.

Plant in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; date plum is a medium to large tree native from the Caucasus and Mediterranean to eastern Asia, producing small (1/2–1 inch) yellow to blue-black persimmon fruits in October–November that resemble tiny plums and have a sweet, date-like flavor — hence 'date plum.' The fruit contains high tannin levels when unripe (astringent like American persimmon) but becomes sweet after frost or extended hanging on the tree. Historical records suggest the fruit may be the legendary 'lotus fruit' of Homer's Odyssey that made Odysseus's sailors forget their homes. The tree is highly ornamental with glossy, dark-green leaves that turn yellow and red in fall, interesting orange bark on mature specimens, and small, attractive cream-colored flowers. More cold-hardy than Asian persimmon and easier to establish in temperate gardens, it is used as a rootstock for kaki persimmons.

Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; dattock is a forest tree that benefits from some shade protection when young. Detarium senegalense (dattock or sweet detar) is a tall leguminous tree from the coastal forests, gallery forests, and moist woodland savannas of West Africa — native across Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Ivory Coast, Ghana, and Nigeria. The tree produces round to slightly flattened, 1–1.5 inch, thin-shelled fruits containing large, flat, hard seeds embedded in sweet, brown, fibrous, edible mesocarp with a distinctive sweet-acid, almost tamarind-like flavor. The fruits are exceptionally rich in vitamin C (up to 100 mg per 100g — roughly twice that of orange juice), and are eaten fresh as a pleasant sweet-sour snack across rural West Africa. The hard seeds contain a starchy meal used in traditional foods. The tree yields a useful timber and a resin used in traditional medicine. In Senegal, the sweet detar fruits are particularly popular and are sold in local markets. Sweet detar (D. senegalense) is the sweet-fruited species, distinguished from bitter detar (D. microcarpum), which has similar fruits but with an unpleasantly bitter taste — an important distinction for edibility. A largely unknown and underexplored fruit tree outside West Africa.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Dauphine is a French fig variety named for the Dauphiné region of southeastern France, producing large, round to flattened fruits with violet to brown-purple skin and pink to reddish-amber flesh with a rich, sweet, mild flavor. The large fruit size (2–3 inches) is among the biggest in the fig world and makes Dauphine figs particularly impressive for fresh eating and market presentation. The vigorous, productive tree performs well in zone 9 heat and provides abundant harvests of the large, handsome fruits from August through September. Dauphine figs are best eaten fresh at peak ripeness; the large size can lead to cracking if late-season rains arrive during ripening. The French Dauphiné region has a tradition of fig cultivation in its milder southern valleys, and Dauphine represents the large-fruited table fig tradition of this region. In zone 9 the Gulf Coast conditions closely approximate the warm, humid conditions of the Dauphiné valleys.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Davidson's plum grows naturally as a rainforest understory tree and requires protection from direct hot afternoon sun. Davidsonia pruriens (Davidson's plum or ooray) is a rainforest understory tree native to the tropical and subtropical rainforests of Queensland, Australia — one of the most commercially important fruits in the Australian native food industry. The tree is notable for its highly unusual growth habit: the large (1.5–2.5 inch), dark-purple to burgundy-black, plum-like fruits grow directly from the trunk and main branches in dense clusters (cauliflory), similar to cacao and jaboticaba. The fruits are intensely, mouth-puckeringly tart — far too sour to eat fresh in quantity without processing — but with extraordinary depth of flavor that has made them the darling of Australian native food chefs and product makers. Davidson's plum jam, Davidson's plum sauce (excellent with game, lamb, and dark meats), Davidson's plum sorbet, Davidson's plum wine and gin, and Davidson's plum dried food products are among the most celebrated products of the native food movement. The fruits are extremely rich in antioxidants — anthocyanins, ellagic acid, vitamin C — with a deep, complex, sour-fruity character that processing and sweetening reveals as intensely flavorful. Hardy to light frost in zone 9, Davidson's plum is increasingly available from Australian specialty nurseries.

Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant at least one other named elderberry cultivar nearby, since elderberries set a far heavier crop with cross-pollination than they do alone. Davis is a selected American elderberry cultivar grown for its broad, flat clusters of small white flowers in early summer, useful for elderflower cordial and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer that are cooked into syrup, jelly, and wine rather than eaten raw. Like other American elderberry cultivars it spreads by root suckers to form a multi-stemmed thicket if left unmanaged, so remove unwanted suckers each season to keep the planting to a defined shrub. Elderberry prefers consistently moist soil and performs best in a low spot or near a downspout where it won't dry out during summer heat; prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the shrub vigorous and productive.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Davis is one of the oldest widely propagated named pawpaw cultivars, selected by Michigan pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis in the mid-20th century from wild seedling trees and long valued for its consistent, reliable production and good flavor. Fruits are medium-sized with smooth, pale yellow, fiber-free flesh and a rich, sweet, banana-custard flavor, though the seeds are somewhat larger in proportion to flesh than in some newer cultivars. Davis ripens in the early-to-mid part of the pawpaw season and, alongside cultivars like Sunflower and Taytwo, played a foundational role in the mid-20th-century revival of interest in pawpaw as a cultivated fruit. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, since pawpaw's natural pollinators (flies and beetles, drawn to the maroon flowers' faint carrion scent) are often scarce in home gardens.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with excellent drainage; Day is one of the most cold-hardy avocado cultivars available, an important trait for Gulf South growers pushing avocado culture north of the traditional Florida and California ranges. A Mexican-race avocado selected in the mid-Atlantic for cold tolerance, it bears small, thin-skinned, rich, high-oil fruit with the anise-scented foliage typical of Mexican-race avocados, ripening in late summer to early fall on a tree reported to tolerate brief dips into the mid-teens Fahrenheit once well established. Like all avocados it demands sharp drainage and will not tolerate wet feet, so plant on a mound or raised bed in heavy Gulf Coast soils, and protect young trees with frost cloth during their first several winters. Its cold hardiness makes it one of the more realistic avocado choices for gardeners in zone 8b who want to attempt the crop outside the classic Florida-Texas-California avocado belt.

common_name: Delaware Grape (Historic Small-Berried American Pink Wine Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Delaware is a historic American grape dating to the mid-1800s, producing small, tightly clustered, pink-red berries with notably high sugar content and a delicate, sweet, wine-quality flavor considered superior to many other Labrusca-type grapes of its era, and it remains valued today for both fresh eating and wine and juice production. It is self-fruitful and matures in midseason. As a high-chill Labrusca type it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy dryland soil in full sun; one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available — tolerates 3–6 months of complete drought once established. Balanites aegyptiaca (desert date, heglig, or soap berry tree) is a thorny, slow-growing tree native to the arid and semi-arid regions of sub-Saharan Africa, the Sahel, and the Middle East — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important trees of the African drylands, found from Senegal and Mauritania east through Sudan and Ethiopia and into the Arabian Peninsula. The tree produces oval, olive-sized, yellow-brown to dark-brown fruits (drupes) with fleshy, oily mesocarp that is sweet-bitter with a date-like character; the fruits are eaten fresh, used to flavor traditional porridges, fermented into beer, and pressed for oil. The seed kernel yields an edible oil used in cooking and as a skin preparation. The bark, leaves, and fruit rind contain saponins traditionally used as soap — hence 'soap berry tree' — and in traditional fish stunning for fishing (the saponins narcotize fish). The tree has extensive traditional medicinal applications across Africa (treatment of malaria, diabetes, skin conditions) and is increasingly studied for bioactive compounds. One of the premier trees for the dryland agroforestry systems of the Sahel, where it withstands extreme drought, poor soils, and degraded conditions that defeat most other trees.

Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun against a south-facing wall in cooler climates to maximize heat accumulation; Desert King is a San Pedro type that requires no pollinator for its reliable breba crop but benefits from caprification for main crop development in warm climates. Desert King is the dominant fig cultivar in Pacific Northwest gardens (Oregon, Washington, British Columbia) where it excels for its large, spectacular breba crop (early summer, June–July) that ripens reliably without the extended heat required by most other figs; the very large (3–6 oz), flattened-turbinate fruits have thick, green to greenish-yellow ribbed skin and dark strawberry to amber-red interior flesh with rich, sweet flavor. In warm climates (California, Gulf Coast) it also produces a substantial main crop in August–October. Among the most cold-hardy of all quality fig varieties, surviving to about 10–12°F when established and dormant. A vigorous, large tree that requires space; well-suited to training as an espalier against south-facing masonry walls.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun; Desirable is the most widely planted named pecan cultivar in the United States and the benchmark against which other commercial varieties are measured. Developed by the USDA and released in 1940, it produces large, well-filled nuts (50–55 per pound) with an excellent kernel percentage (58–62%) and superb flavor — considered by many pecan growers to be the highest-quality commercial pecan available. It is a consistent, reliable producer in zone 7–9 and well-adapted to the Gulf Coast South from Texas to Georgia. The principal challenge is susceptibility to pecan scab disease (Fusicladium effusum) in humid climates — in very humid areas like coastal Louisiana and Mississippi, it may require fungicide protection in wet years. Space trees widely: pecans ultimately become very large trees (60–80 feet tall, 40–60 feet wide) that shade out everything below. Supplement with zinc spray in spring; pecan is notorious for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils.

common_name: Diamond Grape (Moore's Diamond, Historic White American Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Diamond, also known as Moore's Diamond, is a white American grape introduced in the 1880s, producing greenish-yellow berries in compact clusters with a mild, sweet flavor much less pronounced in the musky 'foxy' Labrusca character than many other American grapes, making it a pleasant fresh-eating and juice grape as well as a wine grape valued for delicate white wines. It is self-fruitful and ripens in early to midseason with good vigor and disease resistance for its type. As a high-chill Labrusca-derived grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Discovery is one of the earliest apples of the season and does not store for long once picked. Bred in Essex, England in the mid-twentieth century, this bright red, crisp early-season apple is prized for being one of the first dessert apples ready to eat each year, typically harvested in late summer well ahead of most other varieties, with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart white flesh that occasionally shows an attractive pink-tinged blush just under the skin. Its early ripening and reliable, moderate cropping have made it a popular home garden choice for gardeners eager for the first fresh apple of the season, though the fruit is best eaten within a few weeks of picking rather than stored long-term. Harvest in mid-to-late summer as soon as fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat promptly for the best crisp texture and flavor.

Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Named for the noted Arnold Arboretum horticulturist, Donald Wyman produces a heavy spring flush of white flowers from pink buds, followed by small, bright red fruit that persists on the branches well into winter, often until the following spring, providing months of ornamental interest and emergency food for birds during lean winter weeks. It is a vigorous, wide-spreading, disease-resistant crabapple with good resistance to apple scab, making it a dependable, low-maintenance flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches, giving it room to reach its considerable mature spread.

common_name: Dorset Golden Apple (Ultra-Low-Chill Gulf Coast Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Dorset Golden is one of the two or three apple cultivars with the lowest chill requirements that can be reliably grown in Gulf South zone 9 gardens — requiring only 100–200 chilling hours (hours below 45°F) for adequate dormancy break and fruit set. This ultra-low chill requirement makes Dorset Golden one of the very few apples that can be grown productively in the Gulf South where total winter chill hours range from 200–600 hours in zone 9, often falling short of the 700–1,000+ hours required by standard northern apple varieties. Dorset Golden originated as a chance seedling in the Bahamas — an unexpected confirmation that apples with very low chill requirements can produce high-quality fruit in tropical and subtropical climates. The fruit is medium to large, golden-yellow with a light blush, and has a firm, crisp texture with a good balance of sweetness and mild acidity — far superior in flavor to most other low-chill apple varieties. In zone 9, Dorset Golden ripens in June — exceptionally early for a full-sized apple. It is partially self-fertile but produces larger crops when cross-pollinated with Anna (another ultra-low-chill variety). For Gulf South apple growing, pair Dorset Golden with Anna for reliable cross-pollination.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along forest edges, stream banks, or open lowlands; dotted hawthorn is among the showiest of the eastern native hawthorns, producing broad, flat-topped clusters of white flowers in spring that are excellent pollinator forage, followed by heavy crops of round, dull-red to yellow haws distinctively spotted with pale lenticels — the 'dots' that give the species its name. The persistent haws are eagerly consumed by cedar waxwings, robins, grouse, and foxes through fall and early winter, making this one of the most productive wildlife trees in its native range. It forms a dense, thorny canopy well suited to wildlife hedgerows or naturalized areas where its formidable spines can serve as a living fence. Seeds require double dormancy and may take two full seasons to germinate; container-grown transplants establish most reliably.

common_name: Double Take Orange Flowering Quince (Thornless Double-Flowered Quince)
notes: Double Take Orange carries fully double, ruffled, camellia-like flowers in bright orange, opening directly on the bare stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, and was specifically bred to be thornless, unlike the sharply spined branches of traditional flowering quince. Because the flowers are fully double and largely sterile, the shrub produces little to no fruit, putting its energy entirely into the showy bloom display rather than fruit set, and making it easier to handle for pruning, cutting for arrangements, or planting near a walkway. Extremely tolerant of poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering to avoid removing next season's flower buds.

Plant in full sun to light shade in any fertile, well-drained to moist soil; downy hawthorn (Crataegus mollis) is among the largest-fruited native hawthorns in the eastern United States, producing abundant clusters of large, red-orange fruits (haws) nearly 3/4 to 1 inch across in late summer — far more substantial than most hawthorn species — that are suitable for making jelly, jam, and fruit leather with a pleasant, apple-like flavor. The tree itself is large and spreading with downy (hairy) leaves and branchlets and spectacular white flowers in spring. An outstanding wildlife tree providing critical food for over 100 species of birds and mammals, and exceptional browse habitat for deer and rabbits. The thorny branches also provide nesting protection for songbirds.

Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike the colonial serviceberry (A. canadensis), this species develops a single trunk to form a graceful multi-season small tree with spectacular clouds of white flowers in early spring, blueberry-like fruit in June, and brilliant orange-red fall foliage. The sweet berries ripen all at once in early summer and are excellent fresh, dried like raisins, or used in pies and jams; birds compete fiercely for the crop. Prune to remove crossing branches in late winter; do not top the tree. Cedar-apple rust and fire blight are potential problems in humid climates — ensure good air circulation around the canopy.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Traced to a tree found growing on Florida's Gulf Coast in the 1830s and later propagated commercially in 1892 by A. L. Duncan, this is the oldest named grapefruit cultivar still grown today and the ancestor of most modern seedless grapefruit varieties. The pale yellow, white-fleshed fruit is notably seedy by modern standards, but its tart, deeply flavored juice is prized by grapefruit enthusiasts and is still used in breeding programs for flavor quality. The tree is vigorous, productive, and among the more cold-tolerant grapefruit selections, making it a reasonable choice at the cooler edge of the grapefruit-growing range.

common_name: Dunstan Chestnut (Blight-Resistant American-Chinese Chestnut Hybrid, Food Forest Nut Tree)
notes: Plant two or more trees for cross-pollination; harvest nuts in September–October when burrs split and nuts fall naturally. Dunstan Chestnut is a hybrid between American chestnut (Castanea dentata) and Chinese chestnut (Castanea mollissima) that was developed by plant breeder Robert Dunstan beginning in the 1950s after he obtained blight-resistant American chestnut seedlings identified by plant pathologist Arthur Graves. Dunstan crossed these blight-resistant American chestnut trees (which retained their blight resistance while displaying more American-type tree form) with Chinese chestnut to create offspring that combined the superior nut quality, upright tree form, and improved blight resistance of the selected parent material. The Dunstan Chestnut is commercially distributed by Chestnut Hill Nursery in Alachua, Florida — itself a significant note, as Alachua/Gainesville, Florida is in zone 9, confirming that Dunstan Chestnut grows in zone 9 conditions. The nuts are large to very large (often 1 inch diameter), sweet, richly flavored — closer to American chestnut quality than Chinese chestnut — and produced in large quantities in well-established trees. Chestnuts have significant nutritional value: high in complex carbohydrates (unusual among tree nuts, which are typically high in fats), relatively low in fat, and with a flavor and texture that makes them excellent roasted, boiled, pureed into soups and stuffings, or ground into flour for baked goods. Chestnut trees are also long-lived, productive wildlife food trees: the nuts are consumed by deer, turkey, squirrel, and many other wildlife species, making Dunstan Chestnut valuable for food forest and wildlife habitat plantings in the Gulf South.

common_name: Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut (American-Chinese Hybrid Chestnut, Blight-Resistant Eastern Chestnut)
notes: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy loam or loamy soil in full sun; Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut is self-fertile; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity; harvest nuts in September–October when burrs split open and chestnuts fall; gather from ground promptly as ground moisture causes rapid spoilage; refrigerate fresh nuts within days of harvest since they are perishable. Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut represents one of the most important advances in American chestnut restoration, developed by Dr. Robert Dunstan of Greensboro, North Carolina in the 1950s and 1960s after discovering a surviving American chestnut tree in Ohio (the Graves tree) that appeared to have some natural resistance to the chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) that wiped out approximately 4 billion American chestnut trees from the eastern forest between 1904 and 1950. Dunstan crossed this apparently blight-resistant American chestnut with Chinese chestnut (Castanea mollissima), which has co-evolved with the blight fungus in Asia and carries true genetic resistance, to produce a hybrid combining the large size and straight timber form approaching American chestnut with the blight resistance of the Chinese parent. The Dunstan Hybrid produced nuts with excellent size and sweet flavor — closer to American chestnut sweetness than to the less-flavorful Chinese chestnut — while demonstrating substantially better blight resistance than standard American chestnut. Dunstan Hybrids have been widely planted in the southeastern and Mid-Atlantic states for orchard nut production, wildlife habitat (deer, turkey, and squirrels relish chestnuts), and as a productive native-type chestnut for home orchards where the formerly dominant American chestnut once grew.

Plant in dry, sandy, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), infertile soil in full sun; dwarf hawthorn is one of the few native woody plants genuinely adapted to the challenging conditions of pine barrens and sandhills, where richer soils and supplemental moisture will actually harm it by promoting overly lush growth susceptible to disease. Unlike all other native hawthorns, which bear flowers in corymbs, this species bears a single white flower at each thorn tip in spring — an unusual and botanically distinctive habit. The small, round red haws that follow are an important food source for songbirds in the dry-woods habitats where little else fruits abundantly. Its thicket-forming habit makes it useful as a wildlife brush pile and nesting cover in naturalized dry-soil gardens and restorations.

Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade — small-flower pawpaw is the native pawpaw of the southeastern coastal plain, growing in the dry understory of longleaf pine flatwoods and open, sandy woodlands from Virginia to Florida and west to Louisiana. It is more shade-tolerant and drought-tolerant than the common pawpaw (A. triloba) and produces smaller but similarly flavored fruits — small oblong yellow-green pawpaws 1–2 inches long with the characteristic sweet, custard-like tropical flavor of the familiar large pawpaw. Like all Asimina species, it is the exclusive larval host plant for the zebra swallowtail butterfly, which depends entirely on Asimina for its caterpillars. The small maroon flowers in early spring resemble the larger common pawpaw flowers. A valuable native plant for the shaded, dry woodland garden in the Southeast, supporting both edible fruit production and butterfly habitat.

Sow seeds in fall directly into a prepared bed with lean, well-drained soil, pressing them just below the surface and allowing winter cold to provide the stratification needed for spring germination. Dwarf Serviceberry spreads aggressively by root sprouts and will form dense thickets over time, so site it where naturalized spread is welcome rather than in manicured borders. The profuse white spring flowers provide early nectar for pollinators, and the sweet blue-black berries that follow are among the first wild fruits to ripen each summer. Established colonies are highly drought-tolerant and require virtually no maintenance, making this shrub an outstanding choice for habitat restoration, erosion control, or low-maintenance edible landscaping.

Plant in partial shade with morning sun in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Eastern Prince is a self-fertile cultivar of Schisandra chinensis, the 'five-flavor berry' used for centuries in Chinese and Russian herbal medicine and prized in its native forests for fruit and foliage said to combine sour, sweet, salty, bitter, and pungent notes in one berry. The twining vine bears small, waxy white flowers in spring followed by long, pendant clusters of glossy red berries in late summer, best used for juice, tinctures, syrup, and jam rather than fresh eating due to their intense tartness. Because it is perfect-flowered rather than dioecious, Eastern Prince fruits reliably without a separate pollinator vine, making it far more practical for small gardens than seed-grown schisandra. Provide sturdy support and consistent moisture, and mulch to keep roots cool.

Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pouteria campechiana benefits from regular water during fruiting but tolerates brief drought once established — maintain good drainage and avoid standing water around the root zone. Pouteria campechiana (Egg Fruit, Canistel, or Tiesa) is an evergreen or briefly deciduous tree native to the tropical forests of Central America — Guatemala, Belize, Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula — and introduced throughout the Caribbean, South Florida, the Philippines, Southeast Asia, and tropical West Africa. The fruit is one of the most distinctive of the sapote family: ovoid to pear-shaped, 2–4 inches long, with smooth, waxy, vivid orange to golden-yellow skin, and dense, dry, smooth, richly sweet orange-yellow flesh with a starchy texture remarkably similar to a hard-boiled egg yolk — sometimes described as sweet potato crossed with pumpkin pie. The flesh is eaten fresh, made into egg fruit nog, smoothies, ice cream, jam, and pies; it is particularly popular in Cuba, the Philippines, and South Florida ethnic markets. Trees require grafted or air-layered specimens to fruit true-to-type and within 3–5 years; seedling trees may take 6–8 years to fruit. A productive and adaptable tropical fruit tree for South Florida, the Gulf Coast, and similar warm subtropical climates.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Egremont Russet is partially self-fertile but crops best with a compatible pollinator, and it is one of the more reliably disease-resistant older English apples. The most widely grown and best-known russet apple in Britain, dating to the nineteenth century, it bears medium, dull golden-brown, rough-skinned fruit with dense, crisp, distinctively nutty, slightly sweet flesh that is prized by connoisseurs and pairs especially well with cheese. Its good resistance to scab and canker compared to many other classic English apples has kept it a popular, relatively trouble-free choice for a home orchard wanting a true old-fashioned russet apple. Harvest in early-to-mid fall and eat fresh from the tree or after a short period of storage, since russet apples generally do not keep as long as some smooth-skinned dessert varieties.

common_name: Ein Shemer Apple (Very Low-Chill Gulf South Apple for Zone 8-9)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most apples, Ein Shemer was selected in Israel specifically for regions with mild, short winters and thrives where classic high-chill apples like Red Delicious or Fuji fail to break dormancy properly. The medium, yellow-green fruit is mild and sweet with a soft, quick-to-ripen texture, best eaten soon after picking rather than stored long term. It ripens early in the season, generally ahead of most other low-chill apples, and its abundant, well-timed bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator in a mixed low-chill apple planting. This is one of the more dependable apple choices for zone 9a gardens along the Gulf Coast.

common_name: El Dorado Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Low-Chill Nectarine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, El Dorado is a genetic dwarf nectarine that naturally grows to only six to eight feet, a fraction of a standard tree's size, while still producing full-sized, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit. Its low chill requirement of around 300 hours lets it fruit reliably in mild-winter regions like the Gulf South where standard nectarines often fail to break dormancy evenly. The compact size makes it an excellent choice for large containers or small yards, though the dense, naturally rounded canopy still benefits from light annual thinning to let light into the interior. Fruit ripens in early summer and is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator.

Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Elliott is a Florida-origin pecan variety selected for commercial production in the humid Gulf Coast Southeast because of its outstanding resistance to pecan scab disease — the most economically damaging disease of pecans in the humid South. While Stuart and Desirable require protection in rainy years, Elliott produces consistent yields without fungicide programs in most Gulf Coast locations, making it the variety of choice for low-spray and organic home orchards in zone 8–9. Nuts are smaller than Desirable or Stuart (60–70 per pound) but kernel quality is excellent — thin shells, high kernel fill (55–60%), and very good flavor. Elliott is a late-season variety, maturing in October–November after most other varieties. Its smaller stature (60–70 feet mature) compared to some pecan giants also makes it slightly more manageable. An excellent choice for humid coastal and transitional zone 9 gardens where disease pressure is high.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Ellison's Orange ripens in late summer to early fall and is best eaten within a few weeks of harvest. Bred in Lincolnshire, England from Cox's Orange Pippin parentage, it bears medium, yellow-green apples flushed with red and carrying rich, aromatic flesh with a distinctive light aniseed note layered over classic Cox-like sweetness, a flavor combination that has made it a favorite among English apple enthusiasts seeking something a bit different from the standard dessert apple. It ripens earlier in the season than its famous Cox parent and is a somewhat easier, more forgiving tree to grow well, making Cox-like flavor accessible to gardeners without ideal conditions for true Cox's Orange Pippin. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat within a few weeks for the best distinctive aromatic flavor.

Plant an air-layered or grafted tree in acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, choosing a sunny site protected from strong wind. This cultivar is grown for its unusually large, thin-shelled fruit with sweet, juicy flesh and a smaller seed than many other lychee selections. Established trees handle brief dips into the upper 20s better than young trees but still benefit from overhead frost protection or covering during hard freezes on the Gulf Coast. Lychees need a period of cool, dry weather to initiate flowering, which makes fruiting inconsistent in the humid Gulf South even though the trees themselves can be grown successfully.

common_name: Empire Apple (McIntosh × Red Delicious, Cornell Commercial Release Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Empire requires a cross-pollinator; fruits ripen in September–October with medium to large, deep red to nearly all-red skin and crisp, firm, creamy-white flesh; Empire stores significantly better than McIntosh — refrigerated fruits hold quality for 3–5 months — making it preferable for wholesale and storage. Empire apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1945 from a deliberate cross of McIntosh and Red Delicious, and released for commercial planting in 1966 — named for 'The Empire State' of New York to honor the variety's state of origin. The cross combined the aromatic, sweet-tart character and eating quality of McIntosh with the firmer flesh and better keeping quality of Red Delicious, achieving an apple that outperformed both parents in commercial viability: Empire is significantly firmer than McIntosh (which quickly becomes soft and mealy after harvest), stores considerably longer under refrigeration, and maintains its crispness and good flavor for months. Today Empire is one of the most important commercial apple varieties in New York State — which produces the second-largest apple crop in the United States — and is widely planted throughout the northeastern states and eastern Canada. For home gardeners, Empire's earlier bearing age (compared to Northern Spy), reliable productivity, and superior storage compared to McIntosh make it an excellent choice for the home orchard where both fresh-eating and winter storage apples are desired.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; English hawthorn is the traditional hedgerow hawthorn of Britain and Europe, historically used to create stockproof field boundaries and now cultivated primarily for its spectacular late-spring flower display. The popular double-flowered cultivar 'Paul's Scarlet' (Crimson Cloud in North America) produces vivid deep pink to red double flowers that smother the thorny branches before the leaves fully emerge. The small red fruits (haws) ripen in fall and are consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and numerous other birds. The thorny dense habit makes it one of the most effective wildlife-friendly hedging plants for gardens. More susceptible to leaf blight diseases than native American hawthorns in humid summer climates.

English walnuts are monoecious — male (catkins) and female flowers occur on the same tree — and most cultivars are partially self-fertile, though a second tree improves yields. The tree produces juglone, a chemical that inhibits growth of many plants beneath its canopy; avoid planting near vegetables, berries, or sensitive ornamentals. Grafted Carpathian-strain trees are more cold-hardy and begin fruiting in 4–7 years; seedling trees may take 10+ years. Harvest in fall when hulls begin to crack and turn dark; remove husks promptly and cure nuts for 2–3 weeks before storing.

Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby; Ennis is susceptible to eastern filbert blight and best suited to the drier Pacific Northwest growing region. A classic Oregon hazelnut cultivar prized for producing exceptionally large, high-quality kernels favored by the fresh-eating and confectionery trade, it has long been a benchmark large-nut variety even as newer blight-resistant cultivars have gained ground in commercial orchards. Like older Pacific Northwest hazelnut cultivars bred before eastern filbert blight resistance was a priority, it is quite susceptible to that serious fungal disease and performs best in the relatively dry summer climate of western Oregon, struggling with disease pressure in humid eastern growing regions. Plant a compatible pollinator variety within range for good nut set, and monitor closely for filbert blight cankers, pruning out infected wood promptly if the disease appears.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program and released in the early 1990s, Enterprise is immune to apple scab and resists fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it a strong choice for low-spray or organic orchards. The medium-large, dark red fruit is crisp, firm, and sweet-tart with flavor that holds up well and even improves somewhat in storage. It ripens late in the season and keeps for several months under cool conditions.

common_name: Esopus Spitzenburg Apple (Thomas Jefferson's Favorite Rich-Flavored Heirloom Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating in Esopus, New York in the 1700s, this heirloom became famous as the reported favorite eating apple of Thomas Jefferson, who planted it at Monticello. The bright red-orange fruit, dotted with pale russet, has firm, yellow, intensely rich and spicy-sweet flesh that many consider among the finest-flavored of all apples, though the tree can be a shy, uneven bearer compared to modern commercial varieties. It ripens in mid-to-late fall and keeps reasonably well in cold storage, developing more complexity over several weeks.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate; Etrog citron (Citrus medica 'Etrog', also spelled 'Esrog') is the specific cultivar of citron used for the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles), where it serves as one of the Four Species (arba minim) central to the religious observance — a use with over 2,000 years of continuous documented history, making it one of the oldest cultivated citrus varieties still grown for a specific purpose. The fruits are very large (4–8 inches long), yellow, highly aromatic, with a very thick, white-fleshed rind and very little juice; the entire fruit, including the extraordinarily thick, sweet, resinous peel, is the primary edible product, commonly candied, used in liqueurs and confections, or made into jam. The strongly ribbed, warty, irregular shape and intense, complex citrus-resin fragrance make etrog citron immediately distinctive. Ritual-quality etrogs (used for Sukkot) must meet specific halachic requirements — fully yellow, unblemished, with the pitam (style/stigma) intact at the blossom end — and command very high prices. Etrog trees are quite ornamental, with large leaves and dramatic fruit, but are tender and need winter protection in most of zone 9.

common_name: Eureka Lemon (Standard Lemon Tree, Four-Season Lemon)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Eureka is the standard lemon cultivar in American commercial production and one of the most widely grown home-orchard lemons in zone 9–11 — a vigorous, nearly thornless tree that is truly everbearing, producing lemons year-round with peak crops in winter and spring. The classic medium-to-large, yellow lemons have thin, smooth skin, high juice content, classic lemon acidity, and excellent fragrance — the gold standard of lemon flavor for culinary use. The everbearing production habit means there is nearly always some fruit on the tree in zone 9, even if the heaviest crops come in winter and early spring. The tree reaches 8–15 feet with glossy, aromatic leaves and fragrant white flowers that bloom repeatedly throughout the year. Eureka is slightly more cold-sensitive than Lisbon lemon and significantly more cold-sensitive than mandarins or kumquats; temperatures below 28°F for more than 4 hours can cause fruit and leaf damage. In cooler parts of zone 9, Lisbon lemon (more cold-tolerant) or Meyer lemon (much more cold-tolerant) may be better choices. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually; iron and zinc deficiencies are common in alkaline soils and should be corrected with chelated micronutrient sprays.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Eureka is a long-established Southern astringent persimmon valued for its reliable heavy production and good cold tolerance compared to many Asian cultivars. The medium, flattened, deep orange-red fruit must fully soften after ripening before eating, since the tannins in unripe flesh are strongly puckering, but once jelly-soft it turns richly sweet and custardy, excellent fresh or baked into puddings and breads. Trees are self-fruitful, precocious, and tend to bear reliably once established, with fruit typically ripening from October into November after color develops fully.

Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; European hazel is wind-pollinated and requires at least two genetically different plants (or two named cultivars) for reliable nut production — one plant alone may produce few or no nuts. Corylus avellana is the hazel of European woodlands and hedgerows, grown for millennia for its nutritious hazelnuts (cobnuts and filberts in commerce); flexible, coppiced stems have been used for furniture, wattling, and charcoal production since prehistoric times; and the soft, round catkins that dangle from every bare stem in February and March are one of the earliest and most important pollen sources of spring for emerging native bees, including queen bumblebees and early Andrena mining bees. The large, rounded leaves turn golden-yellow in fall; the twisted cultivar 'Contorta' (Harry Lauder's Walking Stick) is a popular ornamental selection. Plant two different cultivars for best nut yield.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a lime-flavored citrus, tolerating temperatures that would kill true Key lime and Persian lime trees outright. Eustis limequat was developed in Eustis, Florida, in 1909 by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle as a cross between Key lime and kumquat, aiming to combine the tart, aromatic lime flavor with the cold hardiness of kumquat, one of the toughest edible citrus species. The resulting small, oval, yellow-gold fruit has a genuinely lime-like tart flavor along with an edible, sweet-tart rind in the kumquat tradition, making the whole fruit usable — sliced fresh, juiced, or preserved in marmalade — without peeling. The compact tree bears prolifically and tolerates cold that would damage or kill a true lime, making it one of the few practical ways to grow lime-flavored citrus in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 outside the true lime-growing range. Protect young trees through their first few winters; mature wood handles cold considerably better. Harvest fruit once it colors up gold, and use promptly, as limequats do not store as long as some other citrus.

Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Eversweet is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant once established, requiring little irrigation in most Gulf Coast settings after the first year; harvest when fruits are fully colored (rosy-orange to red skin) and sound hollow when tapped; fruits are sweet enough to be eaten with minimal mess. Eversweet is a distinctive pomegranate variety unlike any other in its combination of extreme sweetness, very soft (almost absent) seeds, and clear non-staining juice. Most pomegranates have deep red to crimson arils producing intensely colored red juice — the juice stains are notorious and pomegranate processing indoors is typically done over the kitchen sink with care to avoid contact with clothing. Eversweet breaks this rule: the arils are a soft rose-pink rather than deep red, and the juice they produce is clear to very light pink rather than the deep crimson of standard pomegranates, and crucially, it does not stain permanently. This characteristic makes Eversweet a more family-friendly choice for fresh eating, especially with children, and allows pomegranate eating and juicing without the usual mess concerns. The flavor is very sweet with low acidity — milder and less complex than Parfianka or Wonderful, but consistently rated among the sweetest pomegranates available. The seeds are extremely soft and virtually undetectable when eating the arils fresh. The exterior of the fruit is more orange-pink than red, making it visually distinct from other varieties at harvest.

Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — figs are adaptable to a wide range of soils but require good drainage; Excel is an LSU (Louisiana State University) AgCenter-developed fig cultivar released specifically for Gulf South production, selected for its large, distinctively yellow-skinned fruit with rich amber flesh and the high resistance to fruit souring that is a serious problem for figs in the humid Gulf Coast climate. While traditional Southern figs like Celeste and Brown Turkey are prone to splitting and souring in rainy, humid conditions at harvest time, Excel was specifically bred for improved resistance to these problems — producing firmer skin that resists splitting and reduces the entry of yeasts that cause souring. The large, sweet fruits have an extremely rich, complex, honey-fig flavor that is the archetypal fresh fig experience — one of the most sophisticated and complex flavors of any temperate fruit. Figs are the quintessential Gulf South home fruit tree: tolerant of heat, humidity, and occasional drought once established, self-fruitful (no cross-pollination required), highly productive, and producing fruit of exceptional quality that cannot be found in stores (fresh figs ship and store very poorly, making the homegrown experience irreplaceable).

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Excel is a modern Louisiana-bred pecan cultivar selected for strong resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum), the humid-climate fungal disease that plagues many older commercial cultivars along the Gulf Coast, reducing or eliminating the need for fungicide sprays in home plantings. It produces large, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality and ripens relatively early, helping it escape late-season disease and weather pressure. Because of its disease tolerance, Excel is increasingly recommended for Gulf South home orchards where spray programs are impractical.
