Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and watch for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils, correcting with a foliar zinc spray in spring.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Fairchild is a Panama-origin mango named for plant explorer David Fairchild and grown widely in South Florida dooryards for its small, dense, naturally dwarf-tending habit that suits small yards and container culture better than most mango cultivars. Fruit is small to medium with mild, sweet, fiberless flesh and a gentle flavor that is a good introduction to mango for those used to only supermarket varieties. The tree's compact growth and tolerance for hedging or pruning make it especially practical for zone 9 gardeners who want to keep a container specimen small enough to move indoors or into a greenhouse before winter cold arrives. Reduce irrigation as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor and protect the tree from any frost, since mango wood is damaged even by brief cold exposure.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fairchild tangerine is a Clementine x Orlando tangelo hybrid developed by USDA breeders in 1964, producing deep reddish-orange, medium-sized (2.5–3 inch) fruits with rich, sweet-tart, spicy-aromatic tangerine flavor — one of the most intensely flavored mandarins available. The skin is thin, slightly rough, and adheres somewhat to the flesh (tighter than most loose-skinned mandarins but peels relatively easily by hand); fruits typically contain 6–12 seeds, which is a trade-off for the exceptional flavor. Fairchild is one of the earlier-ripening mandarins in the California/Gulf South season, ripening November through December, and is an excellent choice for gardeners who want full-size mandarin flavor earlier in the season than the late-ripening Honey or Murcott types. The tree is medium-sized (8–14 feet), well-branched, and productive under good conditions with a cross-pollinator present. Trees in zone 9 should be sited in the warmest available microclimate as Fairchild is somewhat cold-sensitive; it tolerates brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established but young trees need frost protection in the first 2–3 years.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; established feijoas tolerate drought but produce better fruit with regular moisture during flowering and fruit development. Acca sellowiana (feijoa or pineapple guava) is a South American evergreen shrub native to southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and northern Argentina, producing exceptionally ornamental flowers in May — petals of white and crimson with red stamens that are edible and sweet, often harvested from the ground — and unique oval fruits in fall that have an intensely aromatic, tropical, pineapple-guava flavor unlike any other temperate-climate fruit. The silvery-green leaves with white undersides are attractive year-round; the plant is exceptionally cold-hardy for a subtropical fruiting plant, tolerating 12–15°F and making it viable throughout the Gulf Coast, the Southeast, and mild West Coast gardens. Most selections require two plants for cross-pollination, though self-fertile cultivars like 'Coolidge' and 'Pineapple Gem' are available.

Fignomenal is a true dwarf fig reaching only 2 to 3 feet, making it ideal for containers and small patios while still producing full-sized sweet fruit. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil and water consistently, easing off as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor. Its compact size makes it easy to move indoors to a cool bright space for winter in colder regions. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove weak wood. Feed during the growing season for steady production of its self-fertile crop.

Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing at least 10–15 feet from other plants to allow for the naturally wide-spreading form; filbert (Corylus maxima) is the large-fruited European hazelnut, distinguished from Corylus avellana by its longer tubular husk that completely encloses the nut, and is the parent of many named cultivars including 'Butler', 'Ennis', and 'Tonda di Giffoni'. A multi-stemmed deciduous shrub that bears pollen-heavy catkins in late winter while fully dormant — one of the earliest signs of spring — with small red pistillate flowers that require wind cross-pollination from a second genetically distinct plant to set nuts. Harvest when husks begin to brown and nuts release easily; dry in a single layer before storage to prevent mold.

Finger lime is an Australian rainforest citrus producing cylindrical finger-length fruits filled with spherical pulp vesicles that burst on the palate like caviar — highly prized in fine dining as a garnish. Grafted trees are strongly preferred over seedlings, which are slow to fruit and thorny; grafted plants begin fruiting in 2–3 years and are more manageable in size. The tree is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator; it performs well in containers and espalier forms. Fruit ripens in late autumn through winter; harvest when the skin (green, yellow, red, or black depending on variety) is fully colored and the fruit releases easily with gentle pressure — avoid overripening, as the vesicles lose their pop.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected and released by Texas A&M's citrus breeding program in 1987 from the Rio Red lineage, Flame produces medium-large, seedless fruit with intensely red-pigmented flesh and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. It is one of the reddest-fleshed grapefruit cultivars commercially grown and holds its color reliably even in warmer winters that can wash out the blush in older red grapefruit types. Fruit matures from late fall through winter and holds well on the tree, allowing a long, flexible harvest window.

Flame Red Seedless is a vigorous grape producing sweet, juicy, ruby-red seedless berries in large clusters. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil and provide a strong trellis or arbor to support the heavy vining growth. Train a permanent trunk and cordons the first years, then prune hard every dormant season to a few productive spurs or canes, as grapes fruit on the current year's growth. Water steadily while fruit swells but reduce moisture as harvest approaches for sweeter grapes. Good air circulation helps prevent mildew.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the more cold-hardy fig cultivars available, reliably resprouting from the roots after winters that kill back the top growth of less hardy varieties. Flanders is an old Belgian fig cultivar long grown in home gardens and small orchards for its dependable production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber flesh and good flavor, and for its resilience in marginal fig-growing climates where winter cold is a limiting factor. It typically produces a modest breba (early summer) crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and the fruit holds reasonably well against splitting in humid weather. Its cold tolerance makes it a valuable choice for gardeners at the northern edge of the fig range, or in a Gulf South garden where an occasional hard freeze is a risk, zone 6–10.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and site it away from the latest spring frost pockets, since aprium flowers open very early and are vulnerable to late cold snaps. Flavor Delight was among the first apriums released by Zaiger Genetics, and it remains valued for ripening earlier than almost any other stone fruit hybrid, giving gardeners a fresh, sweet, apricot-flavored fruit well ahead of the main summer harvest. The reddish-blushed, apricot-like skin covers dense, aromatic, low-acid flesh, and a compatible pollinator, such as an early-flowering plum, pluot, or aprium, is needed nearby since it is not reliably self-fruitful. Prune and thin as for a standard apricot, removing crossing interior branches in the dormant season and thinning heavy fruit sets in spring to improve final size.

common_name: Flavor Grenade Pluot (Firm Late-Season Green Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a second plum or pluot variety nearby for pollination, since Flavor Grenade sets fruit poorly on its own. Another of the Zaiger Genetics pluot introductions, Flavor Grenade keeps its green skin even at full ripeness, which can make judging harvest timing tricky for gardeners used to color-based cues, but the crisp, exceptionally firm, deep red-streaked flesh holds its sugary, tangy-sweet flavor for days after picking better than most stone fruit, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fruit that doesn't turn to mush a day after ripening. It ripens later in the season than most pluots, extending stone fruit harvest into late summer, and the moderately vigorous tree is managed and pruned much like a standard plum. Thin heavy fruit sets in late spring to improve final fruit size.

common_name: Flavor King Pluot (Reddish-Purple Sweet Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollinator, since Flavor King is not self-fruitful. This Zaiger Genetics pluot ripens to a deep reddish-purple skin over intensely sweet, dark red flesh with very little tartness, making it one of the sweeter pluot selections and a favorite for fresh eating out of hand. It ripens in mid-to-late summer, after earlier pluots like Flavor Supreme have finished, extending the harvest window for gardeners growing more than one pluot variety. As with other pluots, thin heavy fruit sets in late spring to improve final size and quality, and prune in the dormant season to an open center to let light into the canopy.

common_name: Flavor Supreme Pluot (Original Red-Fleshed Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a compatible plum or pluot pollinator nearby, since Flavor Supreme does not set a reliable crop on its own. Bred by Floyd Zaiger and one of the earliest pluot introductions, Flavor Supreme is still considered by many fruit growers to have the finest flavor of the whole pluot group, with mottled dark red-and-green skin over intensely sweet, richly flavored, deep red flesh that drips juice when fully ripe. It ripens early in the pluot season, and fruit left to color fully on the tree develops noticeably better flavor than fruit picked while still firm and greenish. Thin the heavy early fruit set to improve final size, and manage the tree with the same dormant pruning to an open center used for standard plums.

Flavortop is a fast-growing nectarine producing large, juicy, well-balanced freestone fruit that ripens in mid to late summer. Plant it in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, avoiding low frost pockets that harm early bloom. It is self-fruitful, so one tree will bear without a partner. Prune yearly in late winter to an open-center form for light and airflow, and thin developing fruit to boost size and prevent limb breakage. Provide steady water while fruit develops, and manage peach leaf curl with dormant sprays if needed.

Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; fleshy hawthorn tolerates a range of soils and is thorny, so site away from foot traffic. Clusters of white spring flowers cover this thorny native small tree, followed by unusually large, juicy, bright red fruit for a hawthorn, historically gathered and eaten fresh or made into preserves by Indigenous peoples and early settlers across its native range in the northern and central United States and Canada. Like other hawthorns it provides valuable dense, thorny cover for nesting birds and small wildlife, along with fall fruit that persists into winter as a food source when little else remains available. Water during establishment, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and prune to remove crossing or damaged branches while avoiding the sharp thorns.

Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Flordahome is a University of Florida-developed pear cultivar requiring only 150–200 chill hours — the lowest chill requirement of any commonly available pear cultivar, making it the primary choice for zone 9b, zone 10, and any warm-winter location where standard pear varieties (which require 600–1000+ chill hours) consistently fail to bloom and fruit adequately. Flordahome produces medium-sized, yellow-green, round fruits with mild, sweet flesh that ripens in early summer — often in June in zone 9 — earlier than most other pear varieties. The fruit quality is pleasant but not as buttery or complex as high-chill European pears; it is best enjoyed fresh at peak ripeness or processed into preserves and sauces. Plant with Hood or Orient pear for cross-pollination — Flordahome is not self-fertile and requires a pollinizer. Fire blight resistance is moderate; preventive copper sprays at bloom reduce fire blight incidence in humid Gulf South climates. Flordahome trees grow vigorously in zone 9 and may need pruning to maintain manageable size — prune annually during dormancy to develop and maintain an open-center structure.

common_name: Florida King Peach (Large Low-Chill Yellow Freestone Peach)
notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Florida King is one of the premier low-chill peach cultivars for the Gulf South — a large-fruited, yellow-fleshed, freestone peach that produces high-quality fruit with approximately 450–500 chill hours of cold requirement, making it adapted to the winter climate of zone 8–9a where higher-chill northern peach varieties fail to break dormancy properly. The large fruits (2.5–3 inches diameter) have golden-yellow skin with an attractive red blush, yellow-orange flesh, small pit (freestone type), and excellent sweet peach flavor. Florida King ripens in May in zone 9 — one of the earliest major peach harvests, ahead of the intense summer heat that can reduce quality in later-ripening cultivars. Like all peaches, Florida King must be thinned aggressively after set: thin to one fruit every 6–8 inches on each branch to allow the remaining fruits to develop to full size — unthinned trees produce large numbers of small, inferior fruits. Prune annually in late winter (February in zone 9) to maintain tree size at 10–12 feet, promote new wood development on which next season's crop will form, and open the canopy to air circulation that reduces disease pressure. Peach leaf curl and brown rot are the primary disease challenges in the humid Gulf South — preventive dormant sprays with copper fungicide are standard practice.

Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Florida soapberry is a native tree of the Florida Peninsula, growing naturally in upland sandy forests, sandhills, and dry flatwoods. Like its relative western soapberry (S. drummondii), it produces fleshy, translucent, amber fruits high in saponins that lather in water and have been used as natural soap. The pinnately compound leaves turn yellow in fall. Florida soapberry tends to be smaller and more restricted in distribution than western soapberry, naturally adapted to the sandy, acid, well-drained soils of Florida's uplands rather than the calcareous plains soils of the central US. The fruits are eaten by mockingbirds and robins. An underused drought-tolerant native for sandy, dry garden conditions in Florida and adjacent Gulf States where its multiple seasons of interest — spring flowers, fall color, and persistent amber fruits — make it a useful ornamental native.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida strangler fig is the only native fig species of the continental United States (excluding Hawaii), naturally occurring in the subtropical hammocks and rockland of south Florida and the Keys. In nature it begins as an epiphyte — a seed dropped by a bird into a tree crotch germinates and sends aerial roots down to the soil that eventually engulf and 'strangle' the host tree. As a free-standing garden tree it simply grows as a magnificent, large-canopy evergreen. The small yellow-orange figs are eaten by an extraordinary variety of wildlife — dozens of bird species, Florida panthers, and raccoons — making the strangler fig one of the most ecologically productive trees in south Florida. The dense canopy provides important nesting habitat for raptors. A keystone species of the south Florida hammock ecosystem.

Plant in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; flowering quince is one of the earliest-blooming ornamental shrubs of the temperate garden — producing brilliant flowers in red, scarlet, orange, salmon, pink, or white directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter and very early spring (February–March in the mid-South), often through snow. The dense, interlocking thorny growth makes it an impenetrable barrier hedge as well as an ornamental specimen. After the flowers, the shrub produces hard, green to yellow-green quincelike fruits 2–3 inches across that are not particularly palatable raw but make excellent jelly, preserves, and liqueurs — a quality long exploited in Japanese and Chinese cuisine. The fruits are high in pectin, which makes them particularly valuable for preserving, and have an intense quince fragrance when ripe. Extremely cold-hardy, drought-tolerant once established, and adaptable to a wide range of soils. The many named cultivars span the full color range from pure white ('Jet Trail') to deepest blood-red ('Crimson and Gold').

Flying Dragon is a dwarf, contorted selection of trifoliate orange with curved thorns and twisting stems, valued both ornamentally and as a size-controlling rootstock. It bears the same small, aromatic fruit and shares the species' extreme cold hardiness. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where its sculptural winter silhouette is a feature. Prune minimally to preserve the natural twisting form, and use the tart autumn fruit for preserves.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Forastero cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. The hardiest, highest-yielding, and by far the most widely grown of the main cacao varieties, accounting for the large majority of the world's chocolate supply, it produces thick-shelled pods with a stronger, more straightforwardly bitter and less nuanced flavor than the rarer Criollo type, but far better disease resistance and productivity that make it the backbone of commercial cacao farming across West Africa and Brazil. Easier to grow than Criollo, it still requires the same warm, humid, shaded rainforest understory conditions typical of all cacao, ideally interplanted beneath taller banana or other shade trees as is traditional in cacao agroforestry systems. Provide consistent shade, humidity, and warmth, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches bearing maturity and its first pod harvest.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Forelle is a smaller, ornamental-looking pear well suited to a home orchard with limited space. An old German heirloom pear whose name means trout in German, a reference to the distinctive red speckles that cover its bright yellow skin as it ripens, giving the fruit a striking, ornamental appearance quite different from most solid-colored pears, with crisp, sweet, juicy flesh good for fresh eating. Its small, attractive, speckled fruit and moderate tree size have made it a popular choice for a home orchard wanting an ornamentally distinctive dessert pear alongside its good eating quality. Harvest while still firm and green-yellow in early-to-mid fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for a few days until the flesh yields slightly near the stem.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Forkert is a classic Mississippi pecan cultivar valued for its thin, papery shell that cracks out easily in large, whole kernel halves, along with rich flavor and good kernel percentage. It bears precociously and produces consistent crops in the Gulf South, though like many older cultivars it benefits from a fungicide program in wet years to manage pecan scab. Forkert is commonly recommended alongside scab-resistant cultivars in home orchard plantings to diversify harvest timing and pollination. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring on alkaline soils.

Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full to partial sun; provide a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence from the start, as fox grape is a vigorous vine that can reach 30 feet and requires strong support to realize its full fruit production potential. Vitis labrusca is the native northeastern grape species that gave rise to the Concord, Catawba, and Niagara cultivated varieties; it produces large, round, purple to amber grape clusters with the characteristic musky, distinctly "foxy" flavor in September and October, beloved by wildlife and humans alike. The dense summer canopy provides excellent nesting habitat and cover for songbirds, and the ripe fruit draws foxes, raccoons, deer, turkeys, and a wide array of frugivorous birds including mockingbirds, catbirds, and thrushes.

common_name: Foxwhelp Apple (Historic English Bittersharp Cider Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Foxwhelp is an old, variable seedling-origin variety, so named-clone stock is preferable to seed-grown trees for predictable fruit quality. One of the oldest documented English cider apples, traced back to seventeenth-century Herefordshire, it is a classic bittersharp valued for high acidity balanced with substantial tannin, producing a sharp, vigorous, long-keeping cider prized by traditional cider makers for its aging potential. Its long history has led to several slightly different clonal strains circulating under the same name, so sourcing named, virus-indexed nursery stock rather than seedlings gives the most reliable fruit quality. Harvest in early-to-mid fall, notably earlier than many other classic cider apples, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

common_name: Franquette Walnut (Late-Leafing French Walnut, Frost-Safe Walnut, Isère Valley Walnut)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Franquette requires cross-pollination; the late leafing habit means the catkins emerge significantly later than standard varieties — reducing spring frost damage that can eliminate the entire nut crop in frost-prone sites; Franquette ripens late (October–November), producing medium to large nuts with moderately thin shells and good flavor. Franquette walnut is a French variety with origins in the Isère department of southeastern France, where it was grown as a commercial production variety long before California walnut production began, and was one of the first named walnut varieties introduced to the Pacific Coast of North America in the 1870s and 1880s when California's walnut industry was developing. The variety's most important attribute is its late-leafing phenology — Franquette emerges from dormancy 3–4 weeks later in spring than most other walnut varieties, including Chandler, Hartley, and Serr. This late emergence is critically important in frost-prone regions: walnut catkins (male flowers) and developing leaves are extremely frost-sensitive, and an unexpected late spring frost at the critical bloom period can eliminate the entire nut crop for the season — a problem that Franquette largely avoids due to its delayed bud break. This characteristic made Franquette the variety of choice for sites at higher elevations, more northerly latitudes, or valleys prone to late spring frosts where earlier varieties fail too frequently. Franquette also serves as an important cross-pollinator for Chandler and other protogynous varieties in commercial orchards.

Frantoio is a renowned Italian olive prized for producing high-quality oil and rich, dark fruit that ripens mid-season. This evergreen brings old-world Mediterranean character to the garden and tolerates heat and drought once established. Grow a young tree in full sun with lean, well-drained soil, watering sparingly since olives dislike wet roots. Prune to an open framework for light and air, and in marginal climates grow it in a container to shelter from hard freezes.

Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Frederick is a vigorous purple-fruited passionfruit cultivar valued for heavy production of aromatic, tart-sweet fruit on fast-growing vines. Like other purple passionfruit types it fruits within the first year from a rooted cutting or grafted plant, considerably faster than seed-grown vines, and ripe fruit drops naturally from the vine when ready to pick. Vines are vigorous climbers and need sturdy support along with regular tip-pruning to keep growth directed and manageable rather than sprawling. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily going into winter, since purple passionfruit types are more cold-sensitive than the hardier Possum Purple selection and a hard freeze can kill the vine to the ground or outright.

common_name: Fredonia Grape (Early Blue Concord-Type Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system, leaving a couple of strong canes per vine. Fredonia was bred at the Geneva, New York agricultural research station specifically to ripen earlier than Concord, giving gardeners in shorter-season climates a reliable blue slip-skin grape with the same rich, musky-sweet 'foxy' Labrusca flavor prized in grape juice and jelly. It is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator, producing large clusters of blue-black berries in late summer to early fall. Because it is a high-chill Labrusca type, it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease-tolerant muscadines or hybrid bunch grapes are more reliable choices.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Freedom was released by Cornell University's Geneva breeding program and is field-immune to apple scab, one of the most damaging fungal diseases of apple in humid climates, while also showing high resistance to cedar apple rust and powdery mildew. The medium-large, red-striped fruit is crisp and juicy with a tart, tangy flavor good for fresh eating and cooking, and it stores reasonably well for a few months under cool conditions. Because it needs so little disease-management spraying, Freedom is a strong choice for a low-input or organic home orchard. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety for good fruit set, and harvest once fruit has developed full color and comes away easily from the spur with a gentle twist.

Frost is a hardy peach bred for cooler climates, offering sweet, juicy fruit and notable resistance to peach leaf curl. Plant it in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and it tolerates spring frosts better than many varieties. It is self-fruitful, producing a crop from a single tree. Prune annually in late winter to an open-center shape and thin the young fruit to improve size. Water deeply during fruit development for the best harvest.

common_name: Frotscher Pecan (Frotscher's Egg Shell, Historic 1840s Louisiana Pecan)
notes: Frotscher, sometimes recorded historically as Frotscher's Egg Shell, was selected and propagated near New Orleans in the 1840s, making it one of the earliest pecan cultivars ever given a name and grafted for orchard use, decades before most of today's commercial cultivars existed. It produces a notably large, thin-shelled nut with a high kernel percentage typical of the old Louisiana river-bottom selections that first drew commercial attention to pecans as an orchard crop. Give it deep, moist bottomland-type soil and full sun, and expect a large, spreading tree that needs a compatible pollinator for consistent nut set. Because of its age and rarity today, Frotscher is grown mostly by pecan-history enthusiasts and heritage orchards rather than commercial growers, who favor newer scab-resistant selections.

Fuji is a Japanese-bred apple beloved for its exceptionally sweet flavor and crisp, dense texture that stores well. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil, and provide a compatible pollinating apple nearby since Fuji is not self-fertile. Prune each dormant season to a central-leader or open form for light and air, and thin fruit clusters to improve size. Water consistently during establishment and dry spells. Fuji ripens late in the season, so allow ample time on the tree for full sweetness.

Fukushu is a compact kumquat producing small oval citrus with an edible sweet rind and tart flesh, well suited to container growing. Grow it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and water when the top inch dries, avoiding both drought stress and soggy roots. In climates with frost, keep it potted so it can move to a bright indoor spot for winter. Feed regularly with a citrus fertilizer during active growth. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit.

common_name: Fuyu Persimmon (Non-Astringent Flat Asian Persimmon for Gulf Coast)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fuyu is the most popular non-astringent Asian persimmon for home garden production — producing flat, tomato-shaped, medium-large (4–6 oz), deep-orange fruits that can be eaten while still firm, like an apple, without the intense mouth-puckering astringency that makes other persimmons (including Hachiya) inedible until fully soft. The flat shape, firm texture when ripe, sweet flavor, and brilliant orange color make Fuyu the most practical and versatile fresh-eating persimmon. Fuyu ripens in October–November in zone 9, producing fruit after the summer growing season has ended and providing sweet, colorful fresh fruit at a time when few other locally grown fruits are available. The attractive deciduous tree puts on a spectacular fall display of orange to red fall foliage as the persimmons ripen — a visual combination that is outstanding in the autumn landscape. Fuyu is self-fruitful (does not require a pollinator tree) and produces reliable annual crops on mature trees with minimal pest and disease pressure. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and require minimal fertilizer input — excessive nitrogen encourages vegetative growth at the expense of fruit production. Japanese persimmons (D. kaki) require approximately 100–200 chill hours — readily accumulated in Gulf South winters — making Fuyu well-adapted to zone 9 production.

Fuyu is a non-astringent persimmon whose sweet, firm fruit can be eaten crisp like an apple while still firm. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil; it is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit develops, then it tolerates some drought. Prune in dormancy to build a strong framework, since heavy fruit can break branches. The fruit ripens in fall and holds on the tree well after the leaves drop, creating an ornamental display.

Plant a grafted specimen in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, choosing a warm, sheltered site out of harsh drying winds since young leaves are sensitive to cold snaps. This widely grown Thai-origin selection produces heavy clusters of sweet, low-acid, deeply ribbed fruit and tends to bear more prolifically than seedling carambola trees. Because established wood can suffer damage below the upper 20s, Gulf Coast growers plant it in the warmest microclimate on the property or keep smaller trees in containers that can be moved under cover during freezes. Regular irrigation through fruit development produces juicier, less fibrous fruit.

common_name: GA-866 Jujube (USDA Chico Sweet Crisp Jujube)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most fruit trees once established, and thrives in the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season. GA-866 originated at the USDA Plant Introduction Station in Chico, California, from an unrecorded cross evaluated during the agency's mid-1900s jujube trials, and was never given a formal cultivar name before the breeding program was discontinued — growers and nurseries have since propagated and sold it simply under its USDA accession number. The fruit is elongated and plump, ripening to a shiny reddish-brown skin with dense, crisp, apple-like flesh and a concentrated sweetness that many growers rate among the best-flavored jujubes for fresh eating. Compared with the more common Li and Lang cultivars it remains relatively rare in commerce, but it is valued for strong drought and cold tolerance, high yields, and good disease resistance. Space trees to allow for their naturally upright, somewhat thorny, suckering growth habit, and remove root suckers as needed to keep the planting in bounds.

Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, siting a compatible Type-2 pollinator such as Zinner nearby for good nut fill, since pecans are wind-pollinated and most cultivars set a much heavier crop with a cross-pollinator. Gafford is a Type-1 pecan valued by Gulf South growers for its notably strong resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that causes the most consistent yield losses for pecan growers in humid regions and drives the need for regular fungicide spraying on susceptible cultivars. Its disease resistance makes it a lower-maintenance choice for home orchards without a commercial spray program. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect the tree to take several years to reach bearing age before producing consistent annual crops.

Gala is a widely grown apple with a sweet, mild flavor and firm, crisp flesh that suits fresh eating and cooking alike. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil and include a compatible pollinating apple nearby, as Gala benefits from cross-pollination. Prune every dormant season for structure and light, and thin fruit clusters to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Water steadily during establishment and dry periods. Gala ripens in late summer to early fall, earlier than many other apples.

Plant Galip Nut in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in zone 10–12; water regularly during establishment; large trees are fairly drought-tolerant when established; harvest nut clusters when the outer drupes turn dark purple-black. Canarium indicum produces clusters of dark purple, almond-sized drupes resembling large olives, each enclosing a very hard, triangular-ridged shell containing a single cream-colored kernel of exceptional quality. The kernels are rich (approximately 70% fat) with a sweet, mild, buttery flavor reminiscent of a combination of almonds and macadamia nuts — widely considered among the finest edible nuts of the Pacific region. They are eaten fresh directly from the shell, roasted over fire, and processed into oil for cooking and for use in traditional body oil preparations. Galip nuts are the single most important indigenous tree nut of Papua New Guinea, traded widely in coastal markets, and of growing international interest as a specialty nut crop. The large trees (reaching 60–80 feet in their native forest habitat) are also highly valued for their straight-grained, durable timber. Closely related to the Pili Nut (Canarium ovatum) of the Philippines, which is also commercially grown; both species deserve wider cultivation in tropical Pacific and Caribbean gardens.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; plant multiple trees for cross-pollination as the species is polygamous. Garcinia cambogia (gambooge or Malabar tamarind) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Malabar Coast of India and Sri Lanka, producing small (2–3 inch), distinctively pumpkin-ribbed, yellow-orange, extremely sour fruits. The fresh fruit pulp is too acidic to eat raw, but the dried rind (kokum or kodampuli, depending on region) is an essential souring agent in Kerala, Konkani, and Sri Lankan coastal cooking — adding a fruity-tart, slightly sweet tartness to fish curries, sambars, and the famous Goan sol kadhi coconut drink. The dried rind is also used in Sri Lankan fish preparations and as a food preservative in traditional coastal cuisine. The fruit rind gained enormous international attention in the 1990s–2010s as a weight-loss supplement ingredient: it is the primary natural source of hydroxycitric acid (HCA), which was heavily marketed as a fat-burning compound — though clinical evidence for significant weight loss has been mixed. The tree is also the source of gamboge resin (from incisions in the bark), a yellow pigment historically used as a watercolor pigment. The tree needs multiple trees for fruiting as it is polygamous (different trees have different flower types).

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; gandaria prefers consistent moisture and excellent drainage. Bouea macrophylla (gandaria or Marian plum) is a Thai, Malay, and Indonesian tropical fruit tree in the mango family (Anacardiaceae) — closely related to mango (Mangifera) and producing small (1–1.5 inch), oval, egg-shaped fruits with a thin, smooth skin progressing from bright green through yellow-orange to golden when fully ripe, surrounding a large seed. The fruit's flavor profile is remarkably mango-like — fragrant, sweet-tart, resinous — but in miniature form; the flesh is juicy, fibrous, and intensely aromatic. Unripe fruits are highly acidic (like green mango) and are used as a souring agent in Thai and Malay curries, fish dishes, and the Thai-Malay salad-style dish 'rujak.' Ripe fruits are sweet enough to eat fresh. The tree is dense, compact compared to true mango, with large, glossy, dark-green leaves and clusters of small cream flowers. Gandaria is extremely popular in rural and home gardens of Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand but is almost completely unknown in Western horticulture. For tropical zone 11–12 gardeners seeking unusual, genuine Southeast Asian fruits.

This genetic dwarf peach tops out around 4-6 feet, making it ideal for large containers or tight yards while still yielding full-size, sweet yellow freestone fruit. Site it in full sun with well-drained soil and give it consistent moisture through the growing season. Thin the young fruit to about 6 inches apart so remaining peaches size up well. Prune lightly in late winter to keep an open, vase-shaped canopy, and expect a harvest beginning two to three years after planting.

common_name: Garretson American Persimmon (Early Golden Seedling Selection)
notes: Garretson is a named selection of the native American persimmon, raised as a seedling of the well-known 'Early Golden' cultivar and valued for its large, deep-orange, richly sweet fruit. Like most American persimmon selections it is primarily pistillate (female), so fruit set is heaviest when a seedling or named male tree is planted within pollinating range, though occasional male flowers on some branches can allow limited fruit set on their own. Fruit ripens in early October and, like all American persimmons, needs to fully soften after frost before it loses its mouth-puckering astringency and becomes honey-sweet. Garretson is cold-hardy into zone 4 and, thanks to the species' deep taproot and tolerance of heat, humidity, and poor soils, also thrives through the Gulf Coast's long, hot growing season.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Gaziantep is a Turkish jujube selection prized for very large fruit and performs well anywhere Chinese jujube cultivars thrive. Named for the jujube-growing region of southeastern Turkey, this selection produces unusually large, oblong fruit with crisp, sweet, apple-flavored flesh at the green-mature stage, among the biggest fruit sizes seen in jujube collector plantings, sweetening and wrinkling further if left to ripen to full brown maturity. The tree shares the toughness typical of the species — tolerant of heat, drought, poor soil, and light frost once dormant — and bears at a young age with minimal care once established. Harvest fruit in successive pickings from the crisp green-mature stage through the fully wrinkled, date-like brown stage depending on preferred texture and sweetness, and prune lightly in winter to control the tree's naturally twiggy, zigzag growth habit.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gbanja kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. The more widely commercially cultivated of the two main kola species, this West African rainforest tree produces large pods of caffeine-rich seeds that are the primary source of kola nuts in international trade, chewed fresh as a stimulant and once used as a flavoring base for early cola beverages before synthetic flavorings took over. Like its relative Cola acuminata, it requires many years of warm, humid, partly shaded growing conditions to reach bearing age, restricting realistic cultivation outside the tropics to specialty botanical or ethnobotanical plantings. Water regularly, especially during establishment, and provide filtered shade to replicate the tree's native rainforest understory habitat.

common_name: Gefner Atemoya (Nearly Self-Fruitful Popular Home Garden Cultivar)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Gefner is the most widely planted atemoya cultivar for home gardens, valued for setting a reasonable crop with less hand pollination effort than most other cultivars, since it is considered nearly self-fruitful under good conditions, though hand pollination still improves fruit set and size. The rich, creamy white flesh has the classic atemoya flavor of custard, vanilla, and tropical fruit notes, and the tree bears at a relatively young age once grafted. Fruit ripens in fall and should be picked when it just begins to soften and change from green to a slightly yellow-green color, then allowed to finish ripening at room temperature indoors.

Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Geneva is a hardy kiwiberry cultivar selected at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station, part of a long-running kiwiberry breeding and evaluation program aimed at improving fruit size, flavor, and reliability for cold-climate growers. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet green flesh and good classic kiwi flavor. As a university-trialed selection, Geneva offers more consistency in fruit quality and vine performance than many seedling-grown kiwiberry vines sold without named cultivar status. Prune hard each winter on a permanent cordon framework to control the vigorous twining growth, provide sturdy trellising from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within pollinating range for good fruit set.

Introduced from Genoa, Italy, this productive lemon bears juicy, tangy fruit much like Eureka. Give it at least 8 hours of sun, fast-draining slightly acidic soil, and a dedicated citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In zones colder than 9 grow it in a container and move it indoors near a bright window before frost. Water deeply but let the top inch of soil dry between waterings to avoid root rot.

common_name: Geo Pride Pluot (Early Red-Skinned Plum-Apricot Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and plant a compatible plum or pluot pollinator nearby for good fruit set. Geo Pride is one of the earlier-ripening pluots from Zaiger Genetics, opening the pluot harvest with attractive bright red skin over firm, juicy, sweet-tart flesh that holds up well to picking and handling. Its early season makes it a useful complement to later pluot varieties like Flavor King or Flavor Grenade in a garden with room for more than one, spreading pluot harvest over a longer stretch of summer. Manage the tree as a standard plum, with dormant-season pruning to an open center and spring thinning of heavy fruit sets to improve final size and sweetness.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Gerardi Dwarf is a naturally compact mulberry selection that stays a fraction of the size of standard mulberry trees — often kept as low as 3–6 feet with pruning — while still producing full-sized, sweet, juicy dark berries typical of good mulberry cultivars, making it one of the few mulberries genuinely practical for a small yard, large container, or spot under bird netting. It is self-fertile, so a single plant fruits without a pollinator, and its small stature allows the whole canopy to be netted against birds, which is otherwise the biggest challenge in mulberry growing since ripening fruit is intensely attractive to them. Prune annually in late winter to maintain the compact form and to encourage a flush of new fruiting wood, since mulberries fruit on both old and new growth. Harvest by gently shaking ripe branches over a sheet or tarp, since ripe mulberries detach easily and bruise if hand-picked one at a time; fruit ripens over several weeks rather than all at once, extending the harvest season.

Plant in deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun with an extremely sturdy support capable of handling 8-pound fruits; giant granadilla produces the world's largest passion fruits — 6 to 12 inches long and weighing up to 8 pounds — with whitish-yellow skin, a thick edible rind used as a vegetable, and seedy interior pulp that makes refreshing juice and drinks popular across tropical Latin America. The vine is extraordinarily vigorous, growing 30–50 feet annually, and requires rigorous pruning after harvest. Flowers measure 4–5 inches across with a remarkable corona of purple, white, and pink filaments. In Central America, the unripe fruit rind is cooked as a vegetable in soups and stews; the ripe pulp is eaten fresh or juiced.

common_name: Ginger Gold Apple (First-of-the-Season Crisp Yellow-Green Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator such as Gala or Fuji. Found as a chance seedling near a Golden Delicious orchard in Nelson County, Virginia after Hurricane Camille in 1969, the tree was named for the discoverer's wife, Ginger Harvey. It is prized as one of the very first apples ready to harvest each year, well before Gala, with crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh that resists browning after slicing. The pale yellow-green skin sometimes develops a light pink blush in full sun. Because the fruit softens quickly once ripe, it is best picked promptly and used within a few weeks rather than stored long term.

Ginkgo is dioecious — only female trees produce the edible nut, but a male is needed nearby for pollination; purchase named female cultivars (Tit, Megi, Oishi) or graft known female wood to avoid planting only males, which cannot be sexed until first flower at 20+ years. The outer fleshy seed coat (sarcotesta) smells powerfully of rancid butter when ripe and contains urushiol-related compounds — wear gloves when handling and process outdoors; the inner cream-colored nut inside the hard shell is the edible portion. Harvest when the fleshy coating has turned yellow-orange and fallen from the tree in autumn; clean immediately, dry the shells, and roast or steam before eating. Do not eat ginkgo nuts raw or in excessive quantities — they contain 4-O-methylpyridoxine, which is toxic in large amounts.

common_name: Gloria Grande Pecan (USDA Scab-Resistant Shade-and-Nut Pecan)
notes: Released by the USDA pecan breeding program, Gloria Grande was selected specifically for outstanding resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that devastates susceptible cultivars in the humid Southeast. It forms an unusually large, vigorous, long-lived tree, which has made it popular as a dual-purpose shade-and-nut planting for home landscapes and parks as well as orchards in high-scab-pressure regions. The nut itself is medium in size and only fair to good in kernel quality compared with top commercial dessert cultivars, so Gloria Grande is chosen more for reliability and low spray input than for exceptional eating quality. Plant it in full sun with deep soil and a compatible pollinator, and expect a tree that shades a wide area at maturity, so allow generous spacing from structures and other trees.

common_name: Gold Nugget Mandarin (Late-Season Seedless UC Riverside Mandarin)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Gold Nugget, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, produces small, bumpy-skinned, essentially seedless mandarins with rich, sweet flavor, notable for ripening later in the season than most mandarins, which extends fresh citrus availability into late winter and early spring. The medium-sized tree is well suited to container culture in areas cooler than its hardiness range. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality.

Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released in 1994 from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois breeding program, GoldRush carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with strong resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it one of the most reliable choices for growers who want to avoid a heavy fungicide program. The yellow-green, russeted fruit is quite tart and firm at harvest in October but mellows over weeks of cold storage into a dense, complex, honey-sweet apple that keeps for months, rivaling many classic long-keeping heirlooms. Pick late and store cool for the best eating quality.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Developed at Michigan State University for reliable cropping in colder apricot-growing regions where most cultivars bloom too early and lose their crop to frost, Goldcot combines good winter hardiness with a comparatively later bloom time that improves the odds of a successful harvest. The medium, deep orange, firm-fleshed fruit is sweet and well flavored, suitable for fresh eating, canning, and drying, and ripens in mid-summer. The tree is self-fruitful and productive, making it a dependable choice for northern home orchards that struggle with more tender apricot varieties.

Plant in moist to moderately dry, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; golden currant is a broadly adaptable native shrub of western and central North America producing intensely fragrant yellow flowers in spring — fragrant with a spicy clove-like scent that carries in the air, giving rise to the alternate common name 'clove currant' — that are followed in summer by round currants ripening from red to black-purple, sweet-tart and edible fresh or made into jelly, jam, and wine. The spring floral fragrance is among the most remarkable of any native shrub, detectable at a distance on warm spring days. The attractive foliage turns red and orange in fall. Unlike European black currant (Ribes nigrum), golden currant has no unpleasant 'catty' flavor and produces a pleasant, gently flavored fruit. It is one of the most important nectar sources for early hummingbirds and long-tongued native bees in the western states. Drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to part shade, and much more garden-friendly than many currant species.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; provide a very sturdy trellis or pergola — mature vines are extremely vigorous and heavy; one male plant pollinates up to 8 female plants. Actinidia chinensis (golden kiwi or yellow kiwifruit) is a separate species from the common fuzzy kiwifruit (A. deliciosa), native to the forests of central and eastern China — though the two species are closely related and sometimes hybridized commercially. The golden kiwi is distinguished from fuzzy kiwifruit by its smooth, thin, golden-yellow to bronze skin (no fuzzy brown hairs), golden-yellow to bright-orange-yellow flesh, and distinctly sweeter, tropical, less acidic flavor profile with notes of mango, papaya, and vanilla in addition to the classic kiwifruit taste. Golden kiwis are now among the most commercially valuable kiwifruit worldwide; the New Zealand-bred 'Zespri SunGold' variety (patented) dominates the premium market, but non-patented gold kiwi cultivars are available to home growers. Like fuzzy kiwifruit, A. chinensis is a vigorous deciduous vine requiring a substantial support structure, annual dormant pruning, and separate male and female plants (dioecious). It is somewhat less cold-hardy than A. deliciosa and requires mild winters without late spring frosts to protect the early-emerging shoots.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; golden mombin is fast-growing and may produce fruit within 3–4 years from cuttings. Spondias dulcis (golden mombin, ambarella, or June plum) is a Polynesian and Melanesian tropical fruit tree — widely cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and tropical Americas — producing oblong, golden-yellow, 2-to-4-inch fruits that ripen to orange-yellow with a fibrous central pit and flesh with a flavor combining mango, pineapple, and tart apple. The fruits are eaten fresh when ripe, or green (unripe) as a crisp, tart, mango-like condiment in curries, chutneys, and salads across Southeast Asian cuisines — particularly popular in Vietnam and Cambodia where unripe ambarella is eaten with salt, chili, and sugar. The tree is fast-growing and highly productive once mature, often requiring thinning of the heavy crop to prevent limb breakage; it is semi-deciduous in seasonal climates. The leaves are also edible as a vegetable in some Pacific Island cuisines. In zone 9, grow as a container plant or in the most frost-protected locations, bringing indoors or covering when frost threatens.

common_name: Golden Nugget Loquat (Large-Fruited Sweet Named Loquat Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Golden Nugget is one of the best-fruiting named loquat cultivars for Gulf South gardens — producing larger, sweeter, better-quality fruits than seedling loquats with the same outstanding adaptability to Gulf Coast conditions that makes loquat one of the most reliable subtropical fruit trees for zone 8b–9. The round to oval, deep golden-orange fruits are substantially larger than typical seedling loquat (1.5–2 inches diameter compared to 1–1.5 inches for seedlings) and have excellent sweet flavor with a mild, tropical quality. Loquats bloom in fall and winter (November–January in zone 9) and ripen fruit in early spring (February–March) — providing fresh tree fruit at a time when virtually no other locally grown fruit is available. The winter flowering is the primary limitation of loquat production in zone 9: the flowers and young fruit are frost-sensitive, and a hard freeze during the fruit development period can eliminate the entire crop. In years without hard freezes, Golden Nugget produces heavy crops of high-quality fruit. The evergreen tree is attractive year-round with large, bold, dark-green leaves and is suitable for use as a landscape tree as well as a fruit producer. Loquat tolerates a wide range of soils, partial shade when necessary, and is highly adapted to Gulf Coast humidity and heat.

This columnar Fruit Snacks apple grows tall and narrow, producing sweet snack-size fruit in as little as 2 feet of width, perfect for patios and small gardens. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and provide a compatible apple pollinator blooming at the same time. Water regularly the first two seasons while roots establish. Its naturally slim habit needs minimal pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average soil — tolerates drought, poor soils, and coastal conditions once established; governor's plum is a thorny tropical small tree or large shrub from Africa and Asia producing prolific clusters of small (1/2–1 inch) dark red to purple-black fruits with a flavor blending cherry and plum with pleasant tartness. One of the most reliable and productive tropical fruit plants for the subtropical home garden, fruiting heavily from a young age with minimal care beyond adequate drainage. The spiny branching habit makes it a formidable security hedge. Fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe, made into jams, jellies, and juices, or fermented into alcoholic beverages in East Africa.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Flacourtia indica is drought tolerant once established, adaptable to a wide range of soil types including lateritic and calcareous soils, and grows vigorously with minimal care — prune to shape after fruiting and to maintain desired height. Flacourtia indica (Governor's Plum, Ramontchi, or Madagascar Plum) is a thorny, fast-growing, many-branched shrub or small tree native to tropical and subtropical Africa and South Asia from Madagascar, the East African coast, and sub-Saharan Africa east through India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia to the Philippines. The small (0.5–1 inch), round to slightly flattened fruits ripen from green through red to deep red-purple or nearly black, with tart-sweet, juicy, dark-red flesh eaten fresh, made into jams, jellies, syrups, and fermented into wine across its broad native range. The flesh is astringent when underripe but richly sweet-tart and plum-like when fully ripe. Governor's Plum is a tough, adaptable, undemanding fruiting plant tolerant of poor soils, drought, alkalinity, and partial neglect — an excellent productive hedgerow plant or edible security hedge plant for zone 8–11. The plants are dioecious (separate male and female trees required for fruit set). Naturalized and sometimes invasive in tropical regions outside its range.

common_name: Grand Frost Lemon (Cold-Hardy Zone 8b Culinary Lemon)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing a warm, sheltered spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter protection. Grand Frost is a University of Georgia release bred for improved cold tolerance, extending reliable in-ground lemon culture into zone 8b gardens where standard lemon varieties struggle to survive most winters. It bears bright yellow, classically tart, aromatic fruit typical of a good culinary lemon, ripening over an extended season on a vigorous, thorny tree. For Gulf Coast gardeners in the cooler parts of the region, Grand Frost offers a realistic path to growing lemons outdoors with only modest winter protection.

The iconic tart green Granny Smith is prized for baking and long storage as well as fresh eating. It needs a long, warm season to fully ripen and a second apple variety nearby for pollination. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and water consistently while the tree establishes. Prune in late winter to maintain an open canopy that ripens fruit evenly and improves air circulation.

Grapefruit is self-fertile and produces best in the warmest citrus climates — the prolonged heat of south Texas and southern California delivers better sugar development than coastal or inland zones 9. Trees are large and vigorous; allow 20–25 feet between them and avoid overcrowding with other trees. Ruby Red and Flame are popular pink-fleshed varieties with good cold tolerance for zone 9. Fruit takes 12–18 months from bloom to full ripeness; taste-test from late autumn onward — the peel may remain slightly greenish even when the juice is sweet.

Plant in dry, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid summer irrigation once established, since this California foothill native is adapted to long, hot, dry summers and thin, mineral soils. Gray pine has an open, sparse, gray-green crown and produces very large, heavy cones armed with hooked spines that contain large, oily, edible seeds long harvested by California Indigenous peoples as a staple food. It is one of the most drought-tolerant pines suitable for a nut crop and grows slowly but steadily on marginal sites unsuited to most other nut trees.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade; green hawthorn — especially the cultivar 'Winter King' — is one of the finest native small trees for four-season ornamental value and wildlife habitat. In spring the tree is covered with small white flowers that are excellent bee forage; in fall the foliage turns burgundy-orange; and in winter the persistent glossy orange-red berries shine against bare branches well into February, providing critical food for cedar waxwings, robins, and thrushes. The tree has a vase-shaped form with slightly pendulous branches and is relatively free of the fireblight and cedar-apple rust that plague many hawthorns. The thorns are formidable — plant away from walkways. Excellent as a wildlife garden specimen or fall/winter focal point.

Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun; Green Ischia is a common fig type (no pollinator required) and typically produces both a reliable breba crop and a main crop. Green Ischia (also called Ischia Verde or simply 'Ischia') is one of the oldest continuously documented fig cultivars in European cultivation, with recorded references going back to at least the 16th century — one of the ancient Italian figs associated with the island of Ischia in the Bay of Naples. The small to medium, round to pear-shaped fruits have greenish-yellow skin that turns to golden-yellow when fully ripe; the interior flesh is pale amber to strawberry-amber with excellent sweetness and mild, delicate fig flavor with a gentle honey note. A two-crop variety that typically produces a moderate breba crop in early summer and a more abundant main crop in August–September. The small tree size (usually 8–15 feet with mature girth) makes Green Ischia more manageable than large fig varieties and an excellent choice for container culture in zones north of 7 where frost protection is needed. Outstanding fresh and dried.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 9–11; green sapote is a Central American relative of the mamey sapote, producing large, round fruits with an olive-green skin and a rich, caramel-flavored orange flesh that is eaten fresh, in milkshakes, and in ice cream. It is less commonly cultivated than mamey sapote but produces equally delicious fruit and is somewhat more cold-hardy — able to tolerate brief dips to 28°F with some defoliation but surviving in protected locations in zone 9b. The fruits ripen in winter, providing fresh tropical fruit at a time when most trees are bare. In zone 9a, plant against a south-facing wall or in the warmest microclimate available and protect from frost when young. Grafted trees from named selections begin fruiting in 3–5 years.

Greengage is an old European dessert plum prized for its honeyed, amber-green fruit. Give it a warm, sheltered site with fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil to ripen its sugars fully. Many greengage selections benefit from a compatible European plum pollinator planted within about 50 feet. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit for best size and sweetness.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis or head-trained system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Grenache is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant, well suited to hot, dry growing climates. One of the most widely planted red wine grapes in the world, it produces high sugar levels even in scorching heat, yielding fruity, medium-to-full-bodied red wines and, when picked earlier or pressed gently, some of the world's finest dry rosés, particularly from southern France's Rhône Valley and Spain, where it is also known as Garnacha. Its thin skin and upright growth habit make it well suited to traditional bush-vine (head-trained, unstaked) cultivation in hot, arid climates, requiring minimal irrigation once its deep root system is established. Consider head-training rather than a full trellis system in very hot, dry climates for traditional bush-vine culture, and monitor sugar levels closely since it can ripen quickly and lose acidity if left too long in hot weather.

Plant in well-drained soil of almost any pH in full sun; Grenada is a long-cultivated heirloom pomegranate variety passed down through Central Texas homesteads and nurseries, valued for combining good cold hardiness with the classic sweet-tart flavor and deep-red arils of a fully flavored pomegranate, unlike some ultra-hardy selections bred mainly for toughness over taste. Plants bear as a multi-stemmed large shrub or can be trained to a small single-trunk tree, produce showy orange-red trumpet flowers over a long season that attract hummingbirds, and are extremely drought-tolerant once established, needing little supplemental water beyond the first year or two. Fruit ripens in September and October, signaled by a hollow sound when the fruit is tapped and skin that has taken on full color; harvest promptly once ripe, since fruit left too long on the plant is prone to splitting after rain. Prune out root suckers to maintain a tidy shape and remove crossing interior branches each winter to keep the canopy open for good fruit coloring and air circulation.

common_name: Grimes Golden Apple (West Virginia Heirloom Parent of Golden Delicious)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Discovered as a chance seedling on Thomas Grimes' farm in Brooke County, West Virginia in the early 1800s, this heirloom is historically significant as the presumed parent of Golden Delicious, one of the most commercially important apples of the 20th century. The medium, deep yellow fruit has dense, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh with a wine-like richness that many old-apple enthusiasts consider superior to its more famous offspring. It ripens in early-to-mid fall and was historically valued both fresh and for cider, keeping reasonably well in a cool cellar.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — grumichama is a beautiful small-to-medium Brazilian Eugenia producing glossy, deep burgundy-to-black cherries (3/4 inch) with sweet, soft, slightly acidic flesh and 1–3 seeds, eaten fresh, made into preserves, or used in beverages. The trees are ornamental year-round with attractive smooth, pinkish-brown peeling bark, handsome dark glossy leaves, and masses of white flowers before fruiting. Unlike many tropical fruits it tolerates partial shade and moist conditions and has some cold hardiness to about 28°F. The fruits are produced in late spring and are consumed enthusiastically by birds. Closely related to jaboticaba and surinam cherry, the grumichama is one of the finest but least known of the Brazilian Eugenia fruits, producing a fruit that resembles a cherry in size and sweetness.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; guaba is a frost-tender rainforest and riverbank tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Closely related to and grown much like the more familiar ice cream bean, this fast-growing tropical legume tree produces long, ribbed pods containing seeds wrapped in the same soft, sweet, cotton-candy-like white pulp eaten fresh straight from the pod across Central and South America, though its pods and pulp are typically somewhat smaller than its larger relative. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it enriches surrounding soil and is commonly used as a fast-growing shade tree in coffee and cacao agroforestry systems throughout its native range. Water regularly, especially while young, and expect a few years of growth before the tree reaches significant pod production.

common_name: Guabiyú (Uruguayan Guabiju, Black Cherry of the Forest)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; guabiyú (Myrcianthes pungens) is a subtropical rainforest tree of southern South America producing small, round, deep purple to black berries in clusters, with a sweet, aromatic, cherry-like flavor and a pleasant Myrtaceae fragrance — consumed fresh, in jams, juices, and liqueurs throughout its native range. The tree is more cold-hardy than most Myrtaceae relatives, tolerating temperatures down to 25°F (-4°C) when established, making it potentially the most cold-tolerant South American Myrtaceae and an excellent candidate for zone 9 Gulf Coast fruit gardens. The attractive, reddish-barked tree also provides ornamental value year-round with glossy leaves. A growing interest among Gulf Coast gardeners and subtropical fruit collectors.

Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral or alkaline soil in full sun; gum bumelia is a thorny native small tree or large shrub of dry uplands, rocky hillsides, and dry woodlands across the south-central US from Kansas to Florida. The small, black, olive-like fruits are edible and mildly sweet — consumed by numerous birds including mockingbirds, thrushes, and cedar waxwings — making it an outstanding wildlife plant for dry, sunny, naturalistic landscapes. The thick, spiny branches provide secure nesting habitat for mockingbirds and other cavity-nesters and the dense crown offers excellent cover. The milky sap was historically chewed as gum by Indigenous peoples (hence 'gum elastic' and 'gum bumelia'). Extremely drought tolerant and long-lived. The thorny habit makes it effective as an impenetrable wildlife hedge or barrier plant.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil of any fertility — gumi fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root symbiosis with Frankia bacteria, improving the surrounding soil and feeding itself even in infertile, sandy, or rocky ground. The shrub produces silvery-speckled dark red to cherry-red fruits in early summer that are sweet-tart with a slight astringency that some compare to a tangy cherry; they are excellent eaten fresh, dried, or made into preserves and juice. The fragrant creamy-yellow flowers in spring attract pollinators. Unlike its invasive relative autumn olive (E. umbellata), gumi is a well-behaved garden shrub that doesn't spread aggressively. It makes an excellent companion plant in food forests and permaculture systems, enriching the soil for neighboring fruit trees and shrubs.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Hachiya is the classic large acorn-shaped astringent Japanese persimmon, with deeply orange 6–12 oz fruits harvested in late October and November that must fully soften (bleten) to jelly-like consistency before eating — frozen overnight or left on the counter for 1–3 weeks achieves this, producing a rich honeyed, spiced flavor. Excellent for making Japanese dried persimmon (hoshigaki), baked goods, puddings, and purées. Trees are remarkably drought-tolerant once established, require minimal spraying, and bear reliably in warm temperate to subtropical gardens — one of the most rewarding and lowest-maintenance fruit trees for zones 7–10.

Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; hackberry is among the most adaptable native trees, thriving in urban heat, clay soils, drought, flooding, and alkaline conditions that defeat many other species. The small dark-purple berries that ripen in September–October have a sweet, date-like flavor and are edible directly from the tree; the thin skin is nutritious and the sweet pulp surrounds a hard seed. The berries are a critical fall food source for over 50 bird species, including cedar waxwings, robins, bluebirds, and many migrating warblers. The distinctive corky bark warty growths are a natural feature, not a disease. Excellent choice for difficult urban sites or as a wildlife anchor tree.

common_name: Hall's Hardy Almond (Cold-Hardy Almond, Northern Almond, Zones 5-8 Almond)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, deep soil in full sun on a protected slope or elevated site to reduce late spring frost damage to blossoms; Hall's Hardy blooms later than standard almonds, reducing but not eliminating frost risk to flowers; harvest nuts in September when hulls split; the small to medium kernels have a mild almond flavor but thicker shells than California varieties — crack-in-shell type. Hall's Hardy almond occupies a unique market niche as essentially the only widely available almond variety for cold-climate gardeners in zones 5–8 of the northeastern and Midwestern United States, where the low temperatures that standard California almonds cannot survive and the late spring frosts that kill the early-blooming California almond flowers make standard almond production impractical or impossible. Hall's Hardy is believed by many pomologists to be a hybrid between Prunus dulcis (almond) and Prunus persica (peach) rather than a pure almond — it demonstrates characteristics of both parents, including cold-hardiness exceeding pure almond by a substantial margin, later bloom time, and nuts with a thick shell and moderate almond flavor. These characteristics — while reducing the quality compared to premium California almonds — allow Hall's Hardy to produce viable almond-type nuts in zone 5–8 climates where no standard almond variety will survive reliably. The nuts are smaller and have a thicker shell than Nonpareil or Mission, with a mild but acceptable almond flavor that is usable for cooking, baking, and direct consumption. For cold-climate home orchardists interested in growing their own almonds, Hall's Hardy is essentially the only viable option.

common_name: Hamlin Orange (Early Cold-Hardy Sweet Orange, Standard Florida Juice Orange)
notes: Plant grafted tree in full sun, well-drained soil; protect from frost in zone 9 when young. Fruit in October–December. Hamlin Orange is the most commercially important sweet orange in Florida — the variety that produces the majority of Florida's fresh-squeezed and not-from-concentrate orange juice, and the dominant early-season orange in Florida commercial groves. The variety was discovered as a chance seedling in Glenwood, Florida in 1879 by A.G. Hamlin, who recognized its value and began propagating it; the combination of very early ripening (October–December harvest, months ahead of navel oranges), excellent cold hardiness for a sweet orange, prolific bearing, and high-quality juice made Hamlin rapidly popular among Florida citrus growers. The fruit is medium-sized, round, smooth-skinned, thin-skinned, with pale orange-yellow to bright orange exterior. The flesh is tender, very juicy, with excellent sweet-acid balance and nearly seedless character (typically 1–3 seeds per fruit) — qualities that make Hamlin ideal for juicing, where seed count affects yield and flavor extraction. Hamlin's cold hardiness is one of its most significant practical attributes for zone 9 gardeners: it is more reliably cold-hardy than navel orange, Valencia, or most other sweet orange varieties, making it the recommended choice for zone 9a plantings where severe freezes are possible. Established trees in good health can survive temperatures to 26°F briefly without significant damage, though young trees and flowers are more sensitive.

Hardired is a cold-tolerant, self-fertile nectarine known for smooth-skinned, freestone fruit and good resistance to bacterial spot and brown rot. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and thin the fruit to about 6 inches apart for larger nectarines. Prune each late winter to an open-center vase shape to maximize light and airflow. Consistent watering during fruit development keeps the flesh juicy and sweet.

common_name: Hardy Chicago Fig (Widely Grown Cold-Hardy Home-Garden Fig)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and mulch well over the root zone. Hardy Chicago is one of the most widely planted fig cultivars for home gardens across the country, prized for dependable, heavy production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, strawberry-red pulp, along with unusual root hardiness that allows it to resprout from the base and still produce a crop even after a winter cold enough to kill the top growth to the ground. This resilience has made it a favorite starter fig for gardeners in climates on the edge of reliable fig hardiness, though in the milder winters of the Gulf South it typically grows as a full, unpruned multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Harvest figs when they soften, droop on the stem, and develop full color, picking every day or two during the height of the season since ripe figs do not store well.

common_name: Hardy Orange (Trifoliate Orange, Japanese Bitter Orange)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; hardy orange is deciduous (unusual for citrus) and leafless in winter. Poncirus trifoliata (trifoliate orange or hardy orange) is the most cold-hardy member of the citrus family — a deciduous, thorny Chinese shrub or small tree that survives temperatures to -10°F when dormant, making it the only citrus relative that can be grown permanently outdoors through USDA zone 5. The small, 1.5-to-2-inch, round, yellow fruits resemble a tiny orange but are intensely bitter and unpleasant raw (high limonin content) — technically edible as marmalade or preserves if the bitterness is accounted for, but not for fresh eating. The plant's primary horticultural importance is as a dwarfing, cold-hardy rootstock for grafting edible citrus — trifoliate orange rootstock limits tree size, improves cold hardiness, and increases fruit quality in grafted sweet oranges, grapefruits, and mandarins. As an ornamental, it is a thorny barrier or specimen plant with fragrant white flowers in spring (before the leaves emerge), attractive yellow fall fruits, and interesting green-barked, zig-zag winter branch structure. A novel cold-climate citrus curiosity.

common_name: Harry Masters Jersey Apple (Bittersweet Cider Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Harry Masters Jersey is a reliable, productive variety well suited to traditional cider blends. A West Country English cider apple prized for producing consistently high-tannin, well-structured bittersweet juice, it is one of the workhorse varieties of traditional Somerset and Devon cider blends, valued more for the reliable quality of its juice than for the tree's ornamental qualities.
