Its medium-sized, dull red-flushed fruit is grown exclusively for milling and pressing, and it pairs well in a blend with sharper, more acidic apples to round out the finished cider's structure. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is far too astringent for fresh eating.

Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing enough room for a large, vigorous, spreading canopy. Hartley is a long-established English walnut variety recognized for its large, elongated, smooth-shelled nuts and light-colored, mild-flavored kernel, and it was for decades a mainstay of California commercial walnut orchards. It has been largely replaced in new plantings by more disease-tolerant modern varieties, but mature Hartley trees remain productive and are still valued for nut size and quality in older orchards and home gardens.

Hazelnuts require cross-pollination and are wind-pollinated, so plant at least two different cultivars within 20 feet of each other; pollen is shed in late winter before leaves emerge. American hazelnut (C. americana) is hardier and more disease-resistant than European types; many gardeners grow hybrid selections for both traits. Eastern filbert blight (Anisogramma anomala) is a serious fungal disease in the eastern United States — choose blight-resistant cultivars such as Jefferson or York for eastern plantings. Harvest in late summer when nuts begin to fall from the husks on their own.

Heartnut is a variety of Japanese walnut bearing distinctively heart-shaped nuts that crack open cleanly along a suture to release a whole kernel — unlike black walnut, which requires significant effort to extract meat. Trees are monoecious and partially self-fertile but yield better with a second tree; they begin bearing in 4–7 years from grafted stock. Heartnut is notably less allelopathic than black walnut, making it more garden-friendly as a specimen tree. Nuts fall in clusters in late summer to early fall; hull and dry for 2–3 weeks before cracking and storing.

Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Hendre Huffcap is one of the more precocious perry pears, bearing somewhat sooner than many other traditional varieties. A well-regarded Herefordshire perry pear producing large, elongated, aromatic fruit for the type, it yields fragrant, medium-tannin juice that makes for a softer, more approachable perry than the harshest bittersharp varieties, contributing floral aromatics valued by perry makers seeking a more delicate finished blend. Its comparatively earlier bearing age and good, consistent yields have made it one of the more commercially popular traditional perry pears for new plantings. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and develop aroma, then mill and press for perry.

Plant grafted named-variety trees in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained bottomland soil in full sun; hicans are natural and intentionally bred hybrids between pecan (Carya illinoinensis) and various hickory species (most commonly shagbark or bitternut), combining traits of both parents — the nuts are usually larger and easier to crack than hickory but with a richer, more complex flavor than straight pecan, with less oil and a firmer, drier kernel. Trees are typically very vigorous and disease-resistant, combining pecan's productivity tendency with hickory's cold hardiness and adaptability. Suitable for zones 5–9 where pecan may be too tender or unreliable; an excellent choice for nut tree diversification in humid eastern forests. Requires cross-pollination from pecan or a compatible hickory nearby.

common_name: Himrod Grape (Cornell-Bred White Seedless Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Himrod was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and remains one of the most widely planted seedless table grapes for home gardens in cooler climates, producing loose clusters of amber-green, honey-sweet, crisp berries that ripen early in the season. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

common_name: Hog Plum (Wild Olive, Seaside Plum, Tallow Wood)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil — tolerates poor, rocky, and alkaline soils exceptionally well once established; hog plum is a pantropical shrub or small tree with strongly fragrant white flowers and small oval fruits that ripen from green to yellow-orange then red, with thin skin, juicy sour-sweet flesh, and a large oily seed. The fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe but is very sour; it makes excellent jellies, juices, and fermented drinks popular across sub-Saharan Africa, the Caribbean, and coastal Brazil. The seeds contain a high-quality oil used for cooking and cosmetics in West Africa. A superb drought- and salt-spray-tolerant fruiting hedge plant for coastal gardens.

common_name: Honey Jar Jujube (Small Sweet Early Chinese Jujube)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Honey Jar is among the earliest jujubes to ripen (mid-August in many areas, 3–4 weeks before Li and Lang); the small fruits are best consumed fresh at peak ripeness rather than dried; trees are moderately compact compared to other jujube varieties. Honey Jar is widely regarded as the sweetest-tasting jujube variety available in American nurseries — the fruits are small (about 3/4 to 1 inch), round, and at perfect ripeness have a flavor described as pure concentrated honey with very little acidity and no bitterness, earning the variety its descriptive name. The small size, while meaning less fruit per piece, is actually an advantage in fresh eating situations where you want to pop a whole fruit in your mouth without cutting — Honey Jar is the jujube equivalent of a cherry tomato or Champagne grape, perfectly sized for snacking directly from the tree. The early ripening season (mid-August in zones 6–8, somewhat earlier in zone 9a) makes Honey Jar valuable for extending the fresh jujube harvest over the longest possible season when planted alongside the mid-season Li and the late-season Lang — a three-variety planting can provide fresh jujubes from late July through October. The trees are somewhat more compact than Li and Lang, making Honey Jar a good choice when space is limited. Cross-pollination with Lang or Li improves fruit set on Honey Jar trees significantly.

Honey mesquite is the defining native tree of Texas plains and prairies, a thorny, nitrogen-fixing legume of unmatched drought resilience that has sustained both wildlife and indigenous cultures of the semi-arid Southwest for thousands of years — its sweet, nutritious seed pods were ground into mesquite meal (pinole) by many Southwestern and Gulf Coast tribes and are the source of distinctively flavored mesquite honey produced by Texas beekeepers from the abundant, fragrant yellow catkin flowers in spring and summer. The hard, dense wood is the premier smoking wood for Texas barbecue and is also used in flooring, furniture, and decorative woodworking; charcoal from honey mesquite burns hotter and longer than most other hardwoods. Honey mesquite is an important wildlife tree: the pods are consumed by deer, javelinas, coyotes, and dozens of bird species; the canopy provides nesting habitat for doves, mockingbirds, and scissor-tailed flycatchers across Texas ranchlands. Long-paired spines on the branches can be hazardous — site away from foot traffic, but within wildlife habitat and native plantings it is invaluable.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in the warmest available location in full sun; Honey tangerine (also called Murcott or Murcott honey mandarin) is one of the most intensely flavored and sweetest commercial citrus varieties — the name 'Honey' reflects its extraordinary sugar content (Brix up to 14–16) and rich, honeyed, complex flavor that combines mandarin aromatics with tangerine sweetness and a characteristic mild tartness. The fruit is medium-sized, deep orange, with thin, peelable skin and tender, very juicy flesh. Ripening in January–March, Honey tangerines extend the citrus season into late winter and early spring when other citrus is winding down. They have seeded flesh (unlike some modern mandarins) but flavor more than compensates. Trees are productive and attractive landscape specimens; they can have alternate-bearing tendencies (heavy crop one year, lighter the next) that are managed by thinning in the on-year. Feed with citrus fertilizer; protect from temperatures below 28°F. Florida produces commercial quantities in Polk and Highlands counties.

Honeycrisp is beloved for its explosively crisp texture and balanced sweet-tart flavor, and it is notably cold-hardy. It needs a compatible pollinating apple variety and thrives in cooler northern climates. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and water steadily through the season. Thin fruit clusters and prune in late winter to promote large, well-colored apples and reduce disease pressure.

growth_habit: East Asian small-fruiting Garcinia ornamental tree
notes: Plant Garcinia oblongifolia in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to dappled sun; maintain consistent soil moisture and avoid prolonged drought; protect young plants from temperatures below 32°F; established trees tolerate light frost. Hong Kong Garcinia is one of the more cold-hardy Garcinia species — adapted to the subtropical climate of South China and Hong Kong where winters can be cool with occasional brief frost — making it more tractable in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens than strictly tropical Garcinias. The ornamental value is high: the tree has a neat, dense, compact form with attractive, glossy, oblong, dark-green leaves and produces small clusters of bright orange-red fruits that are decorative on the tree. The fruits have a sweet-sour, juicy, translucent-white pulp somewhat resembling a small mangosteen in flavor — less rich than Purple Mangosteen but pleasant and refreshing. The tree is appreciated in Hong Kong and southern Chinese traditional culture both as an ornamental and for the edible fruits; it also has traditional medicinal uses in Chinese herbal medicine, particularly the dried rind of the fruit (similar to Garcinia cambogia). Relatively uncommon in Western cultivation but deserves wider planting in humid subtropical gardens as a hardy, attractive alternative to more tropical Garcinias.

common_name: Hong Kong Kumquat (Hong Kong Wild Kumquat)
notes: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a container to shelter indoors in winter; Hong Kong kumquat tolerates light frost once established but is best treated as tender outside zones 9-11. This dense, twiggy, thorny shrub from the rocky hillsides of southern China and Hong Kong bears masses of tiny, pea- to marble-sized round fruit with thin, sweet, edible rind wrapped around intensely tart, seedy pulp, best nibbled whole rather than juiced. It flowers and fruits abundantly even as a small potted specimen, making it a popular choice for bonsai and container citrus collections as much as for the fruit itself, and its fine, small-leaved habit distinguishes it from the larger-leaved kumquats grown for eating fresh. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season, water deeply but infrequently, and prune lightly after fruiting to maintain shape.

Plant grafted trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them to accommodate the tree's naturally compact, spreading form. Howard is a widely planted California commercial English walnut variety valued for its lateral bearing habit, which sets nuts along the length of each branch rather than only at the tips, boosting yields per acre. It produces a light-colored, high-quality kernel and buds out later than older varieties such as Hartley, reducing the risk of spring frost damage to the crop.

common_name: Hyakume Persimmon (Gosho, Nearly Non-Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hyakume, also sold as Gosho, is a large, flattish Japanese kaki persimmon cultivar notable among astringent-type persimmons for a distinctive trait — when the flowers are pollinated and seeds form, the flesh develops streaks and flecks of brown, sugary tissue, and fruit with enough of this coloring can be eaten firm and crisp like a non-astringent type rather than requiring full softening. Unpollinated fruit without seeds remains fully astringent until soft-ripe, so planting near another kaki cultivar for pollination noticeably improves the eating experience. The fruit is large, pale orange, and mild-flavored with a pleasant, slightly spiced sweetness once the brown sugar-flecking develops. Trees are vigorous, productive, and, like most Asian persimmons, largely trouble-free once established, tolerating heat and a range of soils well. Harvest in fall as fruit colors fully; taste-test a fruit or two to judge whether the crop has enough pollination-driven flecking to eat crisp, or whether it needs to soften fully before eating.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — ice cream bean is a fast-growing Central and South American legume tree producing enormous pods (12–30 inches long) filled with white, cottony, sweet pulp that wraps the seeds and tastes unmistakably of vanilla ice cream. The white pulp is eaten fresh directly from the pod; it melts on the tongue with a sweet, mild, creamy vanilla flavor that surprises everyone who encounters it for the first time. Beyond the extraordinary fruit, ice cream bean is a nitrogen-fixing legume that improves soil fertility, an excellent shade and windbreak tree (growing 30–40 feet), and a valuable component of agroforestry systems throughout the tropics. The fragrant white flower pompoms attract hummingbirds and native bees. It grows rapidly in the frost-free tropics and sub-tropics, beginning to fruit in 2–3 years from seed.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the hardiest citrus species available, surviving winter conditions that kill standard lemons and limes outright. Citrus ichangensis (Ichang lemon, or Ichang papeda) is a wild citrus species native to the mountainous borderlands of China, prized by cold-hardy citrus breeders and enthusiasts as one of the parents behind many of today's cold-tolerant citrus hybrids, thanks to its unusual combination of true citrus flavor and genuine winter hardiness. The rough-skinned, lemon-like fruit is highly acidic and aromatic with a distinct floral note, used much like a true lemon for juice, zest, and flavoring rather than fresh eating out of hand. Its glossy, deep green, notably large-winged leaves and modest thorns give it strong ornamental value even apart from fruiting. A rewarding choice for gardeners in the Gulf South and Southeast who want to grow citrus outside the usual protected range, and a useful parent plant for anyone interested in breeding hardier citrus hybrids, zone 7–10.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Ichang Papeda (Citrus ichangensis, Ichang lemon) is a wild citrus species from the mountains of central China near Yichang on the Yangtze River — the hardiest true citrus species, capable of surviving brief temperatures near 0°F and making it valuable for cold-climate citrus experimentation far beyond the normal range. The large, fragrant, lemon-yellow fruits are highly aromatic but extremely acidic and seedy, used for juice, fragrance, and culinary flavoring rather than fresh eating. The distinctive winged petioles on the leaves identify the plant and give it an interesting ornamental appearance with an almost tropical look. In zone 9 Ichang Papeda grows vigorously and produces abundant, highly aromatic fruit with a distinctive floral-citrus fragrance used in Chinese cooking and perfumery. Ichang Papeda is a parent of the Yuzu lemon hybrid and has contributed cold hardiness to many important citrus breeding programs; it thrives in zone 9 as an ornamental citrus tree with exceptional cold insurance.

common_name: Illinois Everbearing Mulberry (Long-Season Red Mulberry Hybrid, Eastern Standard Mulberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Illinois Everbearing is self-fertile; the trees are fast-growing and begin bearing in year 2–3; fruit ripens over an extended 4–6 week season (June–July in zones 5–7) rather than dropping all at once; the long harvesting period makes it practical to collect ripe fruit repeatedly from the ground or by shaking branches. Illinois Everbearing mulberry is a naturally occurring or deliberately selected hybrid of Morus alba (white mulberry) and Morus rubra (red mulberry) that was selected and propagated in Illinois in the mid-20th century and subsequently became the standard recommended mulberry variety for home orchards in the eastern and midwestern United States. The variety combines the key qualities of both parent species: from Morus rubra, it inherits superior fruit flavor — significantly more complex and berry-like than the often bland white mulberry — along with better fresh-eating quality; from Morus alba, it inherits cold-hardiness to zone 4 and adaptability to a wide range of soils and climates. The most practically important feature reflected in its name is the extended ripening season — berries mature gradually and drop over a period of 4–6 weeks rather than all ripening within 1–2 weeks as many mulberry seedlings do. This extended season makes it much more manageable for home fruit harvesting and wildlife feeding, and reduces the dramatic mess that concentrated mulberry drop can create on driveways, paths, and patios. The fruit quality is good: long (1–1.5 inch), dark red to black-purple berries with sweet, mild, pleasant mulberry flavor — not as intensely sweet as Pakistan Mulberry but far superior to most seedling trees.

growth_habit: Brazilian Caatinga native dryland fruit tree
notes: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to stony, poor to average soil; Spondias tuberosa is exceptionally drought tolerant — the underground water-storage tubers allow the tree to survive months of total drought; overwatering or waterlogged soil is fatal. Spondias tuberosa (Imbu, Umbú, or Umbuzeiro) is a drought-deciduous, small to medium tree endemic to the Brazilian Caatinga (semi-arid thorny scrubland) of the northeastern states of Pernambuco, Bahia, Sergipe, Piauí, and Ceará — one of the most important and beloved wild fruit trees of the Brazilian Northeast. The tree's defining ecological adaptation is remarkable: a system of massive, water-filled, carrot-to-sweet-potato-sized underground storage tubers (technically water-storing roots) that can accumulate hundreds of kilograms of water, allowing the tree to survive the brutal, multi-month droughts of the Caatinga and burst into fruit production with the first rains — typically January through March. The small (1–1.5 inch), round, pale-yellow to yellow-green fruits have juicy, sweet-sour, tropical, mango-lychee-like pulp eaten fresh, made into the beloved Brazilian drink umbuzada (fruit pulp boiled with milk and sugar), jams, and fermented into Caatinga wine. The tree has become a symbol of northeastern Brazilian cultural identity and food resilience. Spondias tuberosa is well adapted to dryland gardens in zone 9–11 where excellent drainage and full sun are provided; it is one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available.

common_name: Improved Brown Turkey Fig (Larger-Fruited Brown Turkey Selection)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Improved Brown Turkey is a selection of the classic Brown Turkey fig valued for producing somewhat larger, bronze-brown fruit with sweet, amber-pink flesh compared to standard Brown Turkey, while keeping the same dependable cold hardiness and heavy, reliable production that has made Brown Turkey one of the most widely planted figs in home gardens. Like other figs it bears on both old and new wood, giving an early breba crop in late spring followed by the main crop in late summer, and it needs minimal care beyond routine mulching and occasional pruning to control size. In colder zones, grow in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun, and mulch around the root zone to help protect against winter root injury in the northern part of its range. Improved Celeste is a selection of the classic Celeste fig chosen by growers for producing noticeably larger fruit than the standard cultivar while retaining Celeste's honey-sweet, rose-pink flesh and thin, violet-brown skin, along with its reputation for exceptional cold hardiness and dependable, heavy production in Deep South gardens. It ripens over the same mid-July through August window as standard Celeste and requires the same minimal care — established trees rarely need fertilizer and produce well without spraying. As with all Celeste-type figs, the small, closed eye at the base of the fruit helps deter souring insects and fruit spoilage common in open-eyed fig varieties in humid climates.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — Meyer lemon requires excellent drainage, regular deep watering during the growing season, and full sun for maximum fruit production; Improved Meyer Lemon is the most widely grown home lemon tree in the United States — a hybrid between a true lemon (Citrus limon) and a mandarin or sweet orange (possibly Citrus sinensis) that produces fruit with significantly less acidity and more sweetness than commercial lemons, combined with a distinctively rich, complex, floral lemon fragrance that makes it the preferred fresh lemon for culinary applications requiring the full flavor profile rather than pure acidity. The thin, smooth, deep yellow to orange-yellow skin is edible and aromatic, zesting beautifully for baking applications where the combination of lemon oil and zest from a Meyer produces a more complex, rounded result than commercial Eureka or Lisbon lemons. The combination of cold hardiness (extending the range further north than most citrus), compact tree size (6–10 feet), heavy and recurrent fruit production, beautiful flowers, and superior culinary quality has made Meyer lemon the definitive home citrus tree across zones 8–11.

A younger, bushier form of the classic Improved Meyer, this lemon-orange hybrid produces sweet-tart, thin-skinned fruit on a compact plant well suited to pots. Grow in full sun with fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and feed with citrus fertilizer during active growth. Let the top inch of soil dry between deep waterings to prevent root rot. Bring it indoors to a bright window before frost in cooler zones.

Improved Meyer is a low-maintenance lemon-orange hybrid that bears masses of fragrant, sweetly tart fruit, and it is nearly thornless and disease-resistant. It fruits reliably even for beginners and works beautifully as a container specimen. Provide full sun, fast-draining acidic soil, and regular citrus feeding through the growing season. In cold-winter areas keep it potted and move it indoors near bright light before the first frost.

Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most almond cultivars, Independence is self-fertile and can produce a good crop as a solid block planting without a separate pollenizer variety or heavy reliance on pollinator bees during bloom. It produces a semi-hard shell nut comparable in size and quality to Nonpareil, blooms later than many traditional varieties, and has become popular with growers seeking to reduce pollination costs and frost risk.

common_name: Indian Almond (Tropical Almond, Beach Almond, Sea Almond)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil — Indian Almond is extremely drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established, making it one of the best trees for exposed coastal sites in zone 10-11. Terminalia catappa is a large, deciduous to briefly deciduous tropical tree of uncertain original native range (possibly the Malay Archipelago and Indian Ocean Islands) that has been transported and naturalized throughout tropical coastlines worldwide by human action over millennia, now found on virtually every tropical coast from South and Southeast Asia through the Pacific Islands, tropical Africa, the Caribbean, Central America, and South Florida. The tree has a distinctive tiered, horizontal branching pattern that creates a naturally formal, layered silhouette. Large, glossy, oval leaves (8–12 inches) turn spectacular shades of red, orange, and crimson before dropping twice per year (briefly deciduous in dry or cool periods), a display of fall color unusual in the tropics. The fruits are oval drupes (1.5–2 inches) containing a hard inner kernel that, when extracted and dried, has an almond-like flavor and is eaten throughout Asia and the Pacific — though the extraction requires significant processing. The large leaves are prized in aquarium and aquaculture for their tannins, which lower pH, release antimicrobial compounds, and replicate conditions of tropical black-water streams favored by certain fish.

Plant in well-drained, lean to average, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun in zones 9–12; Indian jujube is one of the most widely cultivated fruits of the tropical and subtropical world, producing abundant crops of round to oval fruits that ripen from green to yellow, red, or purplish-black depending on cultivar — eaten fresh when crisp and apple-like, or dried when they become wrinkled and date-like in flavor. It is more heat-adapted and tolerant of alkaline soils than Chinese jujube, making it suited to south Texas, the Rio Grande Valley, and Gulf Coast zone 9–10 gardens. The fruit is one of the most important traditional fruits of South Asia, the Middle East, and West Africa, and is now gaining attention in the US as a dual-season crop that produces prolifically even under drought stress. Named cultivars such as 'Umran', 'Gola', and 'Seb' are selected for large fruit size and superior flavor.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Flacourtia jangomas is drought tolerant once established and adaptable to a wide range of soils including lateritic, sandy, and slightly calcareous soils — water regularly only in establishment. Flacourtia jangomas (Indian Plum, Paniala, or Paniyala) is a thorny shrub or small tree native to South Asia from India and Sri Lanka east through Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, and Malesia, cultivated and semi-wild in village gardens and homestead agroforestry systems across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia for its clusters of small (0.5–1 inch), round, red-to-deep-purple, juicy fruits. The fruits are sweeter and less astringent than F. indica when fully ripe — tasting of a mild plum with slight tartness — and are eaten fresh, made into jams, chutneys, pickles, and preserves. Ripe fruits stain dark purple-red and can be fermented into a mild wine. The plant is dioecious (male and female on separate plants); at least one male tree is required among a group of female plants for fruit set. Flacourtia jangomas is very similar in growth habit and care to F. indica and makes a productive, low-maintenance fruiting shrub or edible hedge plant for zone 8–11 gardens in warm, sunny, well-drained conditions.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade on dry, rocky upland slopes or brushy hillsides across the northern Great Plains and Great Lakes region; interior serviceberry is a cold-hardy, drought-tolerant clump-former that slowly spreads by root suckers to create a dense thicket of arching stems. White flowers in early spring emerge before the leaves and provide critical nectar for early native bees and overwintered butterflies when few other sources are available. The blue-black berries that ripen in early summer are sweet, flavorful, and high in antioxidants — excellent for fresh eating, jams, and pies, and consumed eagerly by fruit-eating birds before most gardeners can harvest them. It is one of the hardiest serviceberries available, making it a top choice for prairie-edge and windbreak plantings in zones 2–4 where other fruiting shrubs cannot survive.

common_name: Interlaken Grape (Cornell-Bred Early White Seedless Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Interlaken was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station as one of the earliest-ripening seedless table grapes available, producing sweet, crisp, pale green-gold berries in compact clusters well ahead of most other seedless varieties, an advantage for gardeners in shorter-season climates wanting a head start on the grape harvest. It is self-fruitful and, like other seedless grapes, benefits from cluster thinning to improve berry size. As a high-chill grape it performs best in cooler regions and is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters limit its success; Gulf South growers should choose muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

Plant on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Issai is a self-fertile hardy kiwiberry cultivar, a rare trait among Actinidia arguta selections that are normally dioecious and need a separate male vine for pollination. This makes Issai a practical choice for a small garden with room for only one vine, though yields still improve somewhat with a male pollinator nearby if space allows. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten skin and all, with sweet green flesh and classic kiwi flavor, ripening in late summer to early fall. Issai also tends to fruit at a younger age than many hardy kiwi selections, often within two to three years of planting rather than the longer wait typical of the species. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous, twining growth and keep fruiting wood renewed, and provide a sturdy support structure from the start, since mature vines become heavy.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Izu is a compact, early-bearing non-astringent persimmon well suited to smaller home gardens and containers. A Japanese non-astringent cultivar related to Fuyu, it bears small to medium, flattened, sweet fruit that can be eaten crisp like an apple straight off the tree, ripening earlier in the season than most other non-astringent types. The naturally small, dense, spreading tree bears at a young age and stays compact even without heavy pruning, making it one of the better persimmon choices for a limited-space garden or large container. Persimmons need little spraying or care once established; thin heavy fruit set in early summer to prevent limb breakage and improve fruit size.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in deep, fertile, consistently moist, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), well-drained soil; jabuticaba is one of the most spectacular food plants in the world, producing dark purple to black grape-like fruits that burst directly from the bark of the trunk and major branches in a phenomenon called cauliflory, which causes the whole tree to turn dark with fruit clusters several times per year in its native Brazil. The fruits are eaten fresh within a day or two of harvest (they ferment rapidly on the tree), pressed into wine, or made into jelly and liqueur. The skin is thick and slightly astringent while the white flesh is sweet, gelatinous, and fragrant with a flavor suggesting muscadine grape. In zone 9 the tree benefits from a sheltered position and protection when temperatures dip below 26°F. Though extremely slow to fruit from seed — sometimes 5–10 years — air-layered or grafted plants can bear in 2–3 years.

Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) is a fast-growing tropical tree from India and Bangladesh that produces the world's largest tree-borne fruit — massive, spiky green-to-yellow pods weighing 10–80 pounds that hang directly from the trunk and main branches in a spectacular display of cauliflory. The flesh (arils) surrounding each seed is sweet, fragrant, and fiber-rich, eaten fresh when ripe or cooked as a meat substitute when unripe — a use that has made jackfruit globally popular as a plant-based protein source. Trees grafted from superior selections begin fruiting in 3–4 years and can produce 100–200 fruits per year on mature specimens. Plant in well-drained soil, as jackfruit is highly susceptible to root rot in waterlogged conditions; once established, trees are moderately drought-tolerant and grow vigorously in the humid tropics.

Plant in deep, well-drained soil enriched with compost, choosing the warmest and most wind-protected spot available since this tree resents any chill below the mid-40s. Keep the root zone consistently moist during establishment and expect a large, glossy-leaved tree that eventually bears heavy, applesauce-scented fruit with a pale, custard-like pulp. On the Gulf Coast it is realistically grown only in the warmest coastal pockets of south Florida or in a large container that can be moved into a greenhouse for winter. Young trees should be protected from any frost, as even brief freezes can kill wood back to the ground.

Plant in well-drained, thin, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Jamaican caper (formerly Capparis cynophallophora) is a native Florida and Caribbean shrub or small tree related to the Mediterranean caper (Capparis spinosa), sharing the family's distinctive flowers — large, white, nocturnally fragrant blooms with numerous long, showy purple stamens that create a shaving-brush or firework appearance. The flowers open at night and are gone by mid-morning, attracting moths and long-tongued bees. The fruit, which resembles an elongated sausage, splits to reveal brilliant orange-red flesh containing the seeds — an attractive food source for white-crowned pigeons and other subtropical birds. A salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant native for coastal and hammock-edge gardens in south Florida. The young flower buds could theoretically be pickled like Mediterranean capers but this use is not traditionally practiced.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; James Grieve is a reliable, heavy-blooming pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties. Bred in Edinburgh, Scotland in the late nineteenth century, it bears medium, yellow-green apples flushed with red stripes and juicy, tender, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall as one of the more reliable early-to-mid-season dual-purpose apples for a cooler climate. Its good cold hardiness, heavy and reliable annual bearing, and value as a strong cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties have kept it a widely planted favorite in home orchards across the British Isles and other cool-summer regions for well over a century. Harvest in late summer once fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat within a few weeks, since the tender flesh does not store especially long.

growth_habit: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree
notes: Plant grafted Japanese Apricot in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; prune to open vase shape after fruiting; harvest fruits green-yellow when firm for pickling (umeboshi), or wait for full yellow ripeness for eating fresh or making ume liqueur. Prunus mume is revered in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean culture as the herald of spring — its fragrant, five-petaled flowers in shades of white through deep rose appear January–March, often while snow still falls, making it one of the most poetically celebrated trees in East Asian art and literature. The fruits, called ume (Japanese) or mei (Chinese), resemble apricots but are sharply sour when ripe due to high citric acid content; they are almost always processed rather than eaten raw. Traditional umeboshi preparation involves salt-pickling the green fruits with red shiso leaves to produce a strongly sour, salty Japanese condiment used in rice balls, with noodles, and as a digestive aid — extraordinarily long-lasting, with some umeboshi aged decades or more. Umeshu (ume liqueur, often called plum wine) is made by steeping whole green fruits in shochu spirits with sugar. Many named ornamental cultivars exist with double flowers and deep pink to red color; fruiting varieties for culinary use include 'Nanko' and 'Kairyou Ouseibai'.

Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; Japanese chestnut is critically important in chestnut breeding programs as a source of resistance to chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica), the fungal disease that virtually eliminated the American chestnut from eastern North American forests in the early 20th century. While Japanese chestnut is not immune to the blight, it carries resistance genes that allow infected trees to survive and produce nuts despite infection — a trait intensively incorporated into breeding lines for blight-resistant American chestnut restoration. The nuts are large (often larger than American chestnut), sweet, and excellent roasted or boiled in Japanese cuisine. Japanese chestnut has been cultivated in Japan for over 2000 years and is the source of many cultivated varieties. Requires cross-pollination; plant two or more trees.

Sow cleaned seeds in fall and be patient, as double dormancy means most seeds will not sprout until the second spring; mark the bed clearly and keep it weeded during the waiting period. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are adaptable to a range of soil types and tolerate summer heat better than its European relative Cornus mas. The clusters of tiny yellow flowers that stud the bare branches in late winter are among the earliest blooms of the year, providing a vital nectar source for early pollinators; the cherry-like fruits that follow ripen to bright red by midsummer and are edible fresh or made into jams and wines. With age, the exfoliating bark develops an ornamental patchwork of grey, brown, and orange, making this a genuinely four-season specimen plant for gardens across a wide range of climates.

Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun; Japanese flowering quince is tough and adaptable, tolerating clay, drought, and pollution once established — excellent for slopes, hedges, and difficult urban sites. Chaenomeles japonica is a compact, thorny, deciduous shrub that blooms in early spring before the leaves expand (often in February–March in mild climates), producing a spectacular display of vivid orange to scarlet-red, five-petaled flowers on bare stems — some of the earliest and most vivid spring color in the garden; the flowers provide critical early nectar for overwintered and emerging queen bumblebees. The hard, fragrant, yellow-green, apple-like fruits that follow in autumn are too astringent to eat raw but make outstanding jelly, quince paste (membrillo), and homemade quince wine with excellent flavor and natural pectin content. More compact and cold-hardy than the larger C. speciosa.

The evergreen Japanese loquat offers handsome, bold foliage and clusters of sweet-tart, apricot-like fruit that ripen in spring. It flowers in autumn, so late frosts can damage the developing crop in colder zones. Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil and water regularly while young. Thin fruit clusters for larger loquats and prune lightly after harvest to shape the canopy.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained to moderately moist soil; Japanese quince (Chaenomeles japonica) is a compact, thorny, deciduous shrub native to Japan, producing masses of brilliant red-orange to scarlet flowers on bare winter-spring branches — one of the most vivid early spring-flowering shrubs available. The small, apple-scented, greenish-yellow fruits that follow are too astringent to eat raw but make excellent jelly, jam, and cordial with a flavor combining quince, lemon, and apple; very high in pectin and requiring no added pectin when making preserves. The thorny habit makes it an effective barrier hedge. Extremely adaptable and long-lived, thriving in a wide range of soils and tolerating air pollution, drought, and neglect; a reliable garden shrub with multiple seasons of interest.

Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the Japanese raisin tree is an unusual and little-known deciduous tree from East Asia cultivated for its fleshy, branched fruiting stalks (peduncles) that swell and become sweet, raisin-like, and edible in fall when the actual seeds have dropped. It is the peduncles — not the small, round seeds — that are consumed; they have a mild, sweet flavor resembling dried figs or raisins and have been used in Japan, China, and Korea both as a food and as a traditional remedy for alcohol intoxication and liver protection. The tree is an attractive ornamental with large, tropical-looking leaves and fragrant white flowers in summer. In zone 9, it may bloom and fruit erratically due to insufficient winter chilling; it performs best in zones 6–8 where winter cold is reliable. An excellent and unusual fruit tree for the adventurous edible landscape.

Plant fresh nuts in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile, loamy soil in full sun; Japanese walnut is an impressive large nut tree from the mountains of Japan, Hokkaido, Honshu, and Sakhalin — closely related to Persian walnut (Juglans regia) but growing in colder climates and producing rounder, harder-shelled nuts. The trees are immediately distinguished by their enormous compound leaves (the largest of any walnut — up to 4 feet long with 11–17 leaflets) and by the sticky glandular hairs covering young growth and fruit husks. The nuts are round to slightly oval, with a very hard, thick shell and rich, oily kernel. The variety 'cordiformis' (heartnut) produces a distinctively heart-shaped nut that cracks more easily than the round-nutted species. Used in Japanese cuisine and for nut oil. Like all walnuts, releases juglone from its roots that can inhibit many nearby plants. The closely related Manchurian walnut (J. mandshurica) is even hardier. An excellent, ornamental, large-canopy nut tree for cooler northern gardens.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Jaune de Deux Saisons (Yellow of Two Seasons) is a French two-crop fig producing yellow-green to golden-yellow fruits in both the breba (early summer) and main crop (fall) seasons — one of the most productive two-crop fig varieties for home gardens because both crops are of comparable quality and size. The medium-sized, round to slightly pear-shaped fruits have golden-yellow skin and pale amber to pink-tinged flesh with a mild, honeyed sweetness and delicate flavor. The yellow color is distinctive and immediately identifiable among darker-skinned varieties. Two-crop figs like Jaune de Deux Saisons are particularly valuable in zone 9 where the long warm season allows both crops to mature fully — the breba crop in June provides early-season figs while the main crop extends harvest into October. The golden color makes this fig outstanding for fresh presentations and pale fig jam.

common_name: Java Olive (Tropical Chestnut, Bastard Poon Tree)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; a fast-growing tree that requires ample space. Sterculia foetida (Java olive or poon tree) is a large, fast-growing tropical tree native from East Africa and India through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, producing an impressive display of distinctive, star-shaped, woody, bright-red seed pods 4–6 inches across that split open dramatically to reveal 5–18 shiny black seeds with a high (55%) oil content. The common name 'Java olive' refers to the traditional use of the seeds as cooking oil and food in Java and other Indonesian islands — the seeds have a mild, slightly bitter, nutty flavor when roasted and can be pressed for a high-quality edible oil similar to olive oil in fatty acid composition. CAUTION: Raw seeds contain cyclopropene fatty acids that are mildly toxic; seeds should be roasted or heated before consumption. The tree has striking large, palmate leaves and produces flowers with a distinctive unpleasant odor ('foetida' = stinking) that attracts pollinating flies. An unusual specimen tree for large tropical landscapes where few food trees provide such dramatic seed pod displays.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; Java plum (Syzygium cumini), also called jambolan or jamun, is a large, fast-growing evergreen tree from India and Southeast Asia in the Myrtaceae family that produces dense clusters of small, oblong, deep purple to nearly black fruits with a distinctive flavor that is simultaneously sweet, tart, and astringent — with a tongue-staining purple juice widely used in wines, vinegars, syrups, and preserves across South and Southeast Asia. The astringency is due to tannins that diminish when the fruit is fully ripe; fruits are also eaten fresh with a pinch of salt, which tempers the bitterness and heightens the sweetness. Java plum has a long history in Ayurvedic medicine, with seeds, bark, and fruit used in preparations for diabetes management, digestive complaints, and other conditions. Trees are vigorous, moderately drought-tolerant once established, and remarkably adaptable — growing in a range of soil types — but produce the best fruit quality with regular moisture and full sun.

common_name: Jefferson Hazelnut (OSU Premium Large-Nut EFB-Resistant Filbert, OSU 2009 Release)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jefferson hazelnut requires a companion variety for cross-pollination; nuts ripen in September–October and drop naturally; harvest promptly from ground and dry immediately at low heat to cure and extend shelf life; Jefferson's large, well-filled nuts are suitable for roasting, confectionery, and fresh consumption. Jefferson hazelnut was released by Oregon State University in 2009 — named after Thomas Jefferson, who was an enthusiastic hazelnut grower at Monticello — and represents the flagship of OSU's first generation of EFB-resistant hazelnut varieties. Among the OSU 2009 releases, Jefferson stands out as the variety with the largest nut size and highest kernel quality comparable to the longtime commercial standard Barcelona, while adding the critical Eastern Filbert Blight resistance that Barcelona lacks. In Oregon and Washington State hazelnut orchards, Jefferson is being planted as a replacement for Barcelona both in existing orchards where EFB has arrived and in new plantings where EFB resistance is now considered standard. In the eastern United States, Jefferson has opened hazelnut production to a region that was essentially unable to grow commercial European hazelnuts due to the endemic EFB — Mid-Atlantic and Midwestern university variety trials show Jefferson performing strongly under heavy EFB pressure that devastates Barcelona in just 2–3 seasons. The nuts are large, round to oval, with a clean, thin shell and excellent sweet hazelnut flavor — considered among the best-tasting of any named variety, justifying the Jefferson name's association with culinary excellence.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Jiro is the most widely grown non-astringent Japanese persimmon cultivar in California, Asia, and the Gulf South — producing large, slightly flattened, bright orange-red fruits that can be eaten crisp, firm, and crunchy directly from the tree without waiting for softening, making them much more approachable than astringent persimmons (like Hachiya) that must be fully soft before eating. The non-astringent quality means Jiro persimmons are eaten like apples — sliced, eaten fresh, added to salads, or simply eaten out of hand with no waiting for ripeness. The sweet, mild, honey-like flavor is pleasant and distinctive. In zone 9, Jiro ripens in October–November, adding late-season ornamental color when the bright orange fruits hang on the increasingly bare branches after leaf drop — a striking autumn display that has made ornamental persimmons popular landscape trees. The tree is naturally well-shaped and attractive with excellent fall foliage color. Jiro requires very little care once established — it is drought-tolerant, highly pest-resistant, and adapts to clay soils that challenge many fruit trees. One of the most productive and reliable fruit trees for Gulf South landscapes.

common_name: John Rick American Persimmon (Large Sweet Indiana Persimmon Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun, ideally with a male American persimmon seedling or another pollinator cultivar nearby to ensure reliable fruit set; drought-tolerant once established. John Rick is a long-cultivated named American persimmon selection out of the Midwest, valued among heirloom fruit-tree collectors and permaculture growers for its large, richly flavored fruit and dependable productivity once a pollinator is present. The fruit ripens in fall and, as with all American persimmons, needs a hard frost or full ripening on the tree to shed its astringency, after which the deep orange flesh turns intensely sweet, custardy, and rich with notes of caramel and dried fruit. It is commonly grafted onto native persimmon rootstock and grown alongside other named cultivars in mixed persimmon plantings to guarantee cross-pollination and a heavier crop. A good choice for zone 5–9 growers assembling a diverse American persimmon collection.

Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; pair with a second, genetically distinct elderberry cultivar within cross-pollinating range for a full crop, since John's does not set well on its own. John's is one of the oldest named Canadian elderberry selections, long grown as a classic pollinator and companion cultivar for Adams in commercial and home elderberry plantings — the two cultivars were historically recommended together as a standard cross-pollinating pair for decades before more recent university releases like Bob Gordon and Wyldewood became available. The tall, vigorous shrub produces large, flat-topped flower clusters in early summer, valued for elderflower tea, cordial, and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer used for jams, syrups, wine, and traditional elderberry preparations. Its long track record and reliable vigor make it a solid, time-tested choice for a home elderberry planting, especially paired with Adams for cross-pollination, zone 3–8.

Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy desert soil; jojoba is a remarkable desert shrub native to the Sonoran Desert of Arizona, California, and Mexico whose seeds produce a liquid wax (not technically an oil) used extensively in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and lubricants as a spermaceti whale-oil substitute. The seeds are edible but contain a waxy compound (simmondsin) that causes nausea if eaten in quantity; indigenous peoples roasted or ground them into a paste. The shrub is among the most drought-tolerant woody plants in North America, surviving on 10 inches of rainfall annually, and provides important cover and food for desert wildlife. Excellent for erosion control and dryland restoration in zone 8–11.

common_name: Jolico Cornelian Cherry (Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)
notes: Plant bare-root or container-grown Jolico in early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade, giving it room to grow into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Jolico is an Austrian selection prized for its unusually large, pear-shaped, bright red fruit, up to twice the size of the wild species, produced on a plant that still tolerates the dappled light of a woodland edge better than most fruiting shrubs. The tart-sweet, cranberry-like fruit ripens in late summer and is traditionally cooked into jams, syrups, and sauces, though fully ripe fruit can also be eaten fresh. A part-shade planting slows ripening slightly but the shrub remains healthy and productive, making Jolico a good fit for the partly shaded fringe of an edible landscape.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Jonafree was bred by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative program to capture the classic tangy-sweet flavor of the old Jonathan apple in a tree resistant to apple scab, powdery mildew, fire blight, and cedar apple rust, sparing home growers the heavy fungicide schedule that susceptible heirloom apples like Jonathan itself require. The medium-sized, bright red fruit has crisp, juicy flesh with the familiar sprightly Jonathan flavor, good for fresh eating, sauce, and baking. Because it combines classic flavor with broad disease resistance, Jonafree is a good choice for gardeners who love old-fashioned apple flavor but want a low-spray, low-maintenance tree. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur.

common_name: Jonagold Apple (Jonathan × Golden Delicious, Best-Flavor Commercial Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; because Jonagold is triploid, plant it with two compatible diploid pollinator varieties — it needs two compatible pollinators and cannot pollinate other trees itself; thin fruit clusters in late spring for maximum size; Jonagold ripens mid-to-late season (October) producing very large fruit with outstanding sweet-tart flavor. Jonagold is widely considered one of the best-tasting apple varieties in the world — a cross of Jonathan and Golden Delicious developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1943 and released in 1968. The variety combines the aromatic, spicy sweet-tart character of Jonathan with the sweetness and crispness of Golden Delicious, resulting in very large, yellow-orange to red-blushed apples with exceptional, complex flavor that many apple connoisseurs consider among the finest eating apples available. Jonagold has become particularly important in European apple markets — it is one of the most widely planted apple varieties in Belgium and the Netherlands, and is highly regarded throughout European specialty apple production — in part because its substantial size and richly complex flavor profile make it stand out at specialty and farmers' market venues. In the United States, Jonagold is less prominent commercially than varieties with better storability (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) but widely recognized among apple enthusiasts as a flavor benchmark. An important practical consideration: Jonagold is a triploid variety (three sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two) — its pollen is sterile, meaning it cannot pollinate other apple trees and requires two compatible diploid varieties for its own fruit production.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Julie is a small, dwarf-habit mango of Caribbean origin, especially beloved in Jamaican and Trinidadian dooryard gardens for its compact size, precocious bearing, and intensely sweet, fiberless, deep orange flesh with a distinctive rich flavor that fans consider among the best of any mango. Because it stays notably smaller than most mango cultivars, Julie is one of the better choices for zone 9 gardeners growing mango in a large container that can be sheltered through winter rather than risking an in-ground planting. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars and flavor, and protect trees from any frost, since even brief freezing temperatures can damage or kill mango wood.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; june plum (ambarella) is a fast-growing tropical fruit tree of the Pacific Islands and Southeast Asia, producing clusters of oval green-to-yellow fruits 2–3 inches long that are consumed at all stages of ripeness. Unripe fruits are prized throughout Asia and the Caribbean for their crisp, tart flesh, used in fresh salads, pickled condiments, and green mango-style preparations; ripe fruits are sweet-tart with a fibrous spiny seed and are eaten fresh or juiced. The tree is extremely fast-growing (10–15 feet in the first 2 years), the leaves are edible as salad greens when young, and the tree propagates easily from large hardwood cuttings that fruit in 2–3 years. It thrives in zone 9b–12 as a reliable, low-maintenance, highly productive tropical fruit tree and is one of the best 'beginner' tropical fruits for warm-climate gardens.

Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before they can handle full sun. KSU-Atwood is a Kentucky State University research program release bred from Atwood x Overleese parentage, chosen for consistently large, well-filled fruit with rich, sweet flesh and a relatively low seed count for the species. Trees are vigorous and productive once established, ripening their crop in the midseason window and holding fruit quality well compared to many wild seedling trees. Because pawpaws are not self-fertile, interplant with a second unrelated cultivar within about 50 feet and consider hand-pollinating with a small paintbrush during the brief, unpleasant-smelling maroon bloom, since the flies and beetles that pollinate pawpaw in the wild are often scarce in home gardens.

Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil, shading young trees for their first year or two before they can tolerate full sun. KSU-Benson is a Kentucky State University pawpaw research program release, selected alongside sibling cultivars like KSU-Atwood for good fruit size and flavor from the university's decades-long regional germplasm evaluation program. Trees are vigorous and productive once established, bearing medium-to-large fruit with smooth, rich, custardy flesh in the late-summer harvest window typical of named pawpaw selections. Because pawpaws are not self-fertile, interplant with a second, genetically distinct cultivar within about 50 feet, and consider hand-pollinating with a small paintbrush during the brief, faintly unpleasant-smelling maroon bloom, since the flies and beetles that pollinate pawpaw in the wild are often scarce around home gardens.

common_name: Kadota Fig (Italian Honey Fig, Dottato Fig)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Kadota is one of the oldest known fig cultivars, documented in Italian records since at least the 16th century and known as Dottato or Dottato Bianco in Italy, where it has been cultivated around Naples and in Calabria for over 400 years. The American name 'Kadota' is an Anglicized corruption of 'Dottato.' The fruits are small to medium, rounded, pale green to yellowish-white at maturity (not turning brown like most figs) with amber to violet interior flesh that is seedless (no viable seeds) and extraordinarily sweet — among the highest sugar content of any fig. The nearly seed-free flesh is ideal for fig preserves, dried figs, and fresh eating. Kadota is self-fertile, drought-tolerant, and among the most productive figs per tree. It is the most widely used commercial fig in California's Central Valley canning and drying industry. The pale, golden-green skin requires learning when it is ripe — pick when it bends at the stem and yields gently to pressure, the skin turns a barely perceptible yellowish hue, and the neck softens. Excellent for the Gulf Coast Zone 9 garden.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Kakadu plum requires excellent drainage and tolerates seasonal drought — water only in establishment first year, then rely on rainfall in tropical monsoonal climate. Terminalia ferdinandiana (Kakadu plum, gubinge, or billygoat plum) is a small to medium-sized deciduous tree native to the open woodland and savanna regions of the Northern Territory and northwestern Western Australia — and the producer of what is recognized as the single richest natural source of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in the world. The small (1/2–1 inch), round, pale-green to olive-colored fruits contain an extraordinary 1,000–5,300 mg of ascorbic acid per 100g fresh weight — 20 to 80 times more vitamin C than oranges and roughly 100 times more than most commercial fruits. Aboriginal Australians across the Top End and Kimberley have eaten Kakadu plums as a traditional food and medicine for at least 65,000 years. The fruits are also remarkably high in ellagic acid and other polyphenol antioxidants. In contemporary Australian native food and cosmetics industries, Kakadu plum extract has become one of the most sought-after botanical ingredients for antioxidant skincare products, functional foods, and vitamin C supplements — and Kakadu plum jam, sauce, and fruit purée are premium native food products sold across Australia and internationally. The tree adapts well to tropical and subtropical low-humidity conditions with good drainage.

Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Kalamata olive needs a Mediterranean-type climate with dry summers and tolerates only brief light frost. Native to and named for the region around Kalamata, Greece, this classic dual-purpose olive cultivar produces large, almond-shaped, deep purple-black fruit famous worldwide when brine-cured for eating, along with good-quality oil, making it one of the most recognizable named table olive varieties globally. Like other olives it thrives on neglect once established, tolerating poor, rocky, alkaline soil and long dry summers far better than regular watering and rich soil, and needs a genuinely Mediterranean-type climate with wet winters and hot, dry summers to fruit and ripen well. Raw olives straight from the tree are intensely bitter and inedible; fruit must be cured through brining, salt-curing, or lye processing before eating, a process requiring several weeks depending on the method used.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in a warm, frost-free site; Kampong Mauve is a striking sugar apple selection with a distinctive dusty pink-to-mauve blush over its bumpy, segmented skin, standing out visually from the typical pale green sugar apple, while the sweet, creamy, custard-textured white flesh inside is classic sugar apple in flavor and texture. It is more cold-sensitive than cherimoya or atemoya and needs consistently warm, essentially tropical conditions to thrive, making it best suited to south Florida, south Texas, and similarly frost-free zones, or container culture that can be moved under cover in cooler areas. Hand-pollination with a small brush, transferring pollen between flowers in the evening or early morning when they are receptive, significantly improves fruit set in home garden settings where the tree's natural beetle pollinators may be scarce. Harvest when the segments on the fruit begin to separate slightly and the fruit softens, and eat promptly since ripe sugar apples do not store well.

Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost, in a sheltered, sunny spot, since this cultivar can be shy-bearing in cooler coastal fog belts and benefits from reflected heat. Keep soil evenly moist and feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season to support its dense, spreading canopy. Kara fruit ripens late, often improving in flavor if left on the tree into late winter, developing a rich, aromatic sweetness with a soft, slightly fragile peel. It is a favorite among California backyard growers for its dessert-quality flavor, though it ships poorly and is rarely found in stores.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, sandy or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; karanda is a thorny, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree from India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia — widely used throughout South Asia as an impenetrable security hedge and as a productive fruit shrub. The small, oval fruits (1/2 to 1 inch) ripen from green through white to pink and finally red-purple or black, with the white stage being particularly popular for pickling (used extensively in Indian pickles, chutneys, and preserves) while the ripe red-black fruits are eaten fresh or used for jams. The fruits have a mild, slightly tart flavor when ripe. Extremely drought and heat tolerant — one of the tougher fruiting shrubs for hot, dry gardens in zones 8–11. More cold-tolerant than natal plum (Carissa macrocarpa), making it useful in the warmer parts of zone 8 where natal plum would be damaged. Exudes a milky latex sap when cut — wear gloves when pruning. Forms an excellent thorny security hedge.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent moisture during the growing season — starfruit requires full sun and adequate water for consistent fruit production; Kary Starfruit is a superior sweet cultivar of Carambola (Averrhoa carambola), a tropical fruit tree originally from Southeast Asia that produces the distinctive 5-ribbed, translucent yellow-orange fruits that create the characteristic star cross-section when sliced. Unlike commercial starfruit varieties selected for high acidity and sour flavor, Kary was selected specifically for sweet eating quality — lower oxalic acid content, higher sugar content — producing fruits that are genuinely enjoyable eaten fresh without the puckering tartness that characterizes inferior varieties. The crisp, juicy flesh with a mild, sweet, tropical flavor combined with the visually stunning star-shaped cross section makes Kary starfruit both an eating and a culinary presentation fruit of first quality. In the warmest, most frost-protected zone 9 microclimates, starfruit can be grown successfully as a landscape tree with both ornamental value (pretty pink flower clusters, handsome tropical foliage) and substantial fresh-fruit production — providing a tropical fruit experience that very few other fruit trees can offer in zone 9.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Katy, bred in Sweden and also sold as Katja, produces attractive, bright red, crisp apples with a pleasant, slightly tart, sweet flavor, ripening in mid to late summer, well ahead of most main-season apples. Its moderate chill requirement makes it one of the apple cultivars sometimes recommended for the milder end of Southern apple-growing country, though it needs somewhat more winter chill than the very lowest-chill Florida-bred selections. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to keep the canopy open for good air circulation.

common_name: Katy Apricot (Low-Chill Gulf South and Texas Apricot)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, ideally on a slight slope or elevated site where cold air drains away from the blossoms during late-winter frosts. Bred by Zaiger Genetics in California and selected specifically for regions with mild winters, Katy is one of the more dependable apricots for Texas and the Gulf South, where most northern apricot cultivars fail to set fruit due to insufficient winter chilling. It blooms quite early, so late cold snaps remain the main risk to the crop even though the tree itself tolerates the region's warm winters well. Fruit is medium, orange-blushed, and sweet-tart, ripening in late spring to early summer, and the tree is self-fruitful, needing no separate pollinator.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — Kei Apple tolerates poor, sandy, alkaline, and mildly saline soils and is extremely drought-tolerant once established. Dovyalis caffra is a large thorny shrub or small tree native to the coastal thornveld and thicket of South Africa's Eastern Cape province, named for the Kei River region where it grows wild. The formidable 2-inch spines make it one of the most impenetrable barrier plants available for zone 9 — a mature hedge is impassable to deer, livestock, and intruders. The small, round fruits (3/4 to 1 inch diameter) ripen in summer (July–September in zone 9) to a bright golden-yellow or amber color with paper-thin skin and juicy, very acidic pulp that is rarely eaten fresh but makes extraordinary jams, jellies, chutney, and preserves with a distinctive bright, tart flavor combining notes of apricot, plum, and citrus. The glossy, willow-like evergreen foliage is ornamentally attractive year-round. Kei Apple can be grown as a specimen tree (2–4 trunks) or planted 4–6 feet apart and clipped into a dense, absolutely impenetrable hedge. Drought tolerance, extreme heat resistance, and salt spray tolerance make it valuable for coastal Gulf South gardens.

Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Ken's Red is a New Zealand-bred hardy kiwiberry cultivar notable for its smooth skin blushed red-purple over green, distinguishing it visually from the plain green skin of most kiwiberry cultivars, with sweet green flesh and rich kiwi flavor inside. Fruit ripens in late summer to early fall and is eaten whole without peeling, like other kiwiberries. As with all Actinidia arguta selections, plants need a few years to reach full bearing size but then crop heavily and reliably for many years once established. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous twining growth, train onto a permanent trellis or pergola from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within range for consistent pollination and fruit set.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kepayang is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Raw seeds and unprocessed plant parts contain cyanogenic compounds and must be properly fermented and processed before eating. This large Southeast Asian rainforest tree produces football-sized fruit containing large seeds that, after a traditional fermentation and boiling process to remove naturally occurring toxic compounds, become the famous kluwak or keluak used to flavor the dark, earthy Indonesian dish rawon and Peranakan ayam buah keluak. The raw seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic and must never be eaten without proper traditional processing, which involves burying, boiling, and fermenting the seeds over an extended period to render them safe. Grow only as a specialty tree for a large tropical property or botanical collection, and never attempt to process or consume the fruit without expert traditional knowledge of the detoxification method.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; kepel fruit is slow-growing and best suited to zone 11–12 humid tropical conditions with consistent moisture. Stelechocarpus burahol (kepel fruit or burahol) is one of the world's most unusual and historically remarkable fruit trees — a medium-sized tropical tree in the custard apple family (Annonaceae) native to Java, Indonesia, where it has been deeply associated with the royal courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta for centuries. The rounded, deep-brown, plum-sized fruits emerge cauliflourously in dense clusters on the trunk and main branches, and have a pleasant, sweet, melon-custard apple flavor. What makes kepel fruit uniquely extraordinary, however, is its documented effect on body chemistry: eating the fruits causes the sweat, breath, and urine of the consumer to take on a floral fragrance — reportedly reminiscent of violets or jasmine — for several hours. This effect was so prized in Javanese royal culture that kepel trees were traditionally planted exclusively in the gardens of the Kraton (royal palace), and common people were reportedly forbidden to grow or eat the fruit. The active compounds are thought to be terpenoids that are metabolized into aromatic volatiles excreted through the skin and kidneys. Kepel is extremely rare in cultivation outside Java; it is categorized as a vulnerable species due to limited habitat and restricted cultivation history.

Kerman is the standard commercial female pistachio cultivar grown across California's Central Valley, chosen for its large nut size and heavy production once mature, though trees can take 7-10 years to bear a full crop. It needs the same demanding climate as the species overall: 700-1000 hours of winter chill combined with long, blisteringly hot, low-humidity summers to fill and split the shells properly, which makes it a poor fit for humid Gulf Coast gardens even where winter cold is adequate. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil and expect strong biennial bearing, with a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter one the next. A male pollinator such as Peters must bloom at the same time and be planted nearby, since pistachio is wind-pollinated and entirely dioecious. Harvest when hulls loosen and nuts show the characteristic natural shell split, typically in early autumn.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; ketembilla (Ceylon gooseberry) is a thorny, multi-stemmed shrub from Sri Lanka producing small (1/2 to 1 inch diameter), round, reddish-purple to deep purple fruits with a tart, acidic, gooseberry-like flavor that makes them outstanding for jams, jellies, preserves, and syrups — not particularly pleasant raw due to their sharp acidity, but among the best tropical fruits for processing. The plant is heavily thorned and makes an impenetrable hedge — widely used in Sri Lanka and tropical gardens for security hedging. Requires both male and female plants for fruit (dioecious). Grows quickly in warm, humid, well-drained conditions. The tart fruits are exceptionally high in vitamin C. In Florida it is occasionally grown as a specialty fruit and hedge plant. Underutilized as a jam fruit in the US — the intense, tart purple jam from ketembilla rivals the finest domestic berry jams.

Key lime is a small, thorny tree distinct from the larger Persian lime (Citrus latifolia) — its fruit is smaller, more aromatic, more acidic, and nearly seedless at full yellow ripeness. It is self-fertile and bears prolifically in truly tropical conditions; the tree is damaged by any frost and requires zone 10–11 for outdoor culture, though it adapts well to large containers for zone 9 growers who can move it inside. Harvest fruit while still light green to yellow-green, before it turns fully yellow; yellow fruit is riper and less acid but also more perishable. Apply citrus fertilizer three times per year and ensure excellent drainage to prevent root rot.

Key lime, also called Mexican lime, produces small, intensely aromatic and juicy fruit beloved for pie, drinks, and marinades. This tender, somewhat thorny citrus stays compact and grows readily in a container that can shelter indoors in cold weather. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with excellent drainage and feed it a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply, letting the top of the soil dry between waterings, and protect it from any frost.

A younger, compact form of the Key lime, this semi-tropical evergreen produces small, juicy green limes nearly year-round, famous for Key lime pie. Grow in full sun with fast-draining acidic soil and feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply, letting the surface dry between soakings to avoid soggy roots. Its small size makes it perfect for patio pots that can be sheltered indoors in cold weather.

Kieffer is a tough, adaptable pear valued for its heavy crops of crisp, gritty fruit that is excellent for canning, cooking, and preserves. It shows strong resistance to fire blight and tolerates a wide range of climates. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and water regularly while establishing. Prune in late winter to build a strong scaffold and allow light into the canopy for even ripening.

Killen is a named native persimmon selection valued for its exceptionally sweet, blemish-free orange fruit and its self-fruitful habit, meaning a single tree can set a crop without a separate pollinator planted nearby. It is a somewhat smaller-statured American persimmon, typically maturing around 25 feet, which makes it easier to fit and harvest in a home orchard than many seedling-grown native persimmons. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, Killen fruit remains firm and astringent until fully ripened and softened by autumn frosts, after which it turns rich, sweet, and custard-like. The tree is drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to a wide range of soil types, and well suited to the long, humid growing season of the Gulf Coast.

Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Kimbrough is a cold-hardy satsuma mandarin selection developed and evaluated by the Louisiana State University AgCenter — selected specifically for superior cold hardiness compared to standard Owari satsuma, making it the recommended satsuma cultivar for zone 8a–8b gardens where occasional hard freezes occur. Satsuma mandarins are the most cold-hardy commonly grown citrus — Kimbrough extends the cold hardiness envelope even further, surviving brief exposure to 14–18°F without permanent damage when grown in well-drained soil (saturated roots dramatically reduce cold tolerance). The fruit is easy-peeling, seedless, and has the classic sweet-tart satsuma mandarin flavor that ripens early (October–November) — delivering fresh citrus fruit months before oranges and before the most demanding winter cold arrives in the Gulf South. In zone 9, Kimbrough satsumas perform reliably with minimal cold protection. Satsumas are fast to bearing — often producing some fruit in the second or third year — and are moderate-sized trees that fit comfortably in residential landscapes. Plant in the warmest, most protected microclimate (south-facing, near a wall or fence) for zone 8 plantings.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; King of the Pippins is a strong, reliable pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties, though it can bear biennially if not thinned.
