An old variety of uncertain French or English origin dating to at least the eighteenth century, it bears attractive orange-red-striped apples over a golden ground, with crisp, aromatic, sweet-sharp flesh that made it a widely planted commercial dessert apple across Europe for generations before more modern varieties took over the market. Its strong, abundant bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties in a mixed home orchard, though the tree has a tendency toward biennial bearing, alternating heavy and light crop years unless fruit is thinned in a heavy year. Harvest in mid-fall and eat within a couple of months, since it does not keep quite as long as some other classic dessert varieties.

common_name: Kingston Black Apple (Classic English Bittersharp Cider Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Kingston Black is notoriously shy-bearing and susceptible to scab, so site it in an open spot with good air circulation. Originating in Somerset, England, this small, dark red-purple apple is the most celebrated of the true single-variety, or vintage, cider apples, prized as a rare bittersharp carrying both the tannin and acid balance needed to produce a complex, well-structured cider entirely on its own without blending. Its fruit is far too astringent and acidic for fresh eating, but its combination of tannin, sugar, and acid in a single apple has made it the benchmark variety against which other cider apples are measured. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and expect a light, sometimes biennial crop, since Kingston Black is well known among cider makers for being a difficult, temperamental tree to grow well.

common_name: Kinnard's Choice Apple (Tennessee Heirloom Dessert Apple)
notes: Grow as a standard tree in deep, well-drained soil and thin fruit clusters to improve size and reduce limb breakage in heavy years. Kinnard's Choice originated in Tennessee in the 19th century and has long been prized by Southern heirloom apple collectors for its rich, aromatic, exceptionally sweet flesh, considered by many old-timers to be among the best-flavored dessert apples of the region. It ripens in late summer to early fall and is primarily grown today by small orchardists and heritage-fruit enthusiasts rather than commercial producers.

common_name: Kinnow Mandarin (King x Willowleaf Hybrid Tangerine)
notes: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost danger has passed, choosing a well-drained site with at least eight hours of direct sun and protection from cold winds. Water deeply and regularly during establishment, then taper to consistent moisture during fruit development while avoiding standing water. This vigorous mandarin hybrid produces deep orange, intensely sweet-tart fruit with numerous seeds and a tight peel, ripening in mid to late winter. It tolerates brief dips into the high 20s F once established but performs best where winters stay mild, making it a favorite in low-desert and Gulf Coast citrus plantings.

common_name: Kiowa Pecan (Precocious Large-Nut Type I Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with room for a large mature canopy. Kiowa is an Oklahoma State University release prized by home orchardists for its precocity, bearing well ahead of most named pecan varieties, and for its very large, attractive, thin-shelled nuts with excellent bright kernel color and good fill. It is a Type I pollinator, so pair it with a Type II variety for cross-pollination and heavier yields. Scab pressure is moderate; in the humid Gulf South a fungicide program during wet springs helps protect nut quality, while drier inland sites see less trouble. Thin overcrowded nut clusters in heavy-bearing years to reduce alternate bearing and keep nut size consistent season to season.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–7.0) soil; Kishu mandarin (Kishu mikan) is a tiny Japanese mandarin producing small, round, intensely sweet, completely seedless fruits — typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter, roughly the size of a large grape. The combination of total seedlessness and extraordinary sweetness makes Kishu the darling of high-end specialty markets, where the small size makes it a perfect one-bite citrus snack. The paper-thin skin peels effortlessly in a single piece, and the flavor is intensely sweet with rich tropical complexity that surpasses most commercial mandarins. Trees are compact and manageable at 6–10 feet, well-suited to zone 9 and container growing. Kishu ripens in December–January, slightly earlier than most clementine-type mandarins. Although small trees, they bear prolifically and a single established tree can produce hundreds of fruits. Avoid planting in frost pockets where cold air settles.

Direct sow or transplant in warm soil in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; provide trellis support; kiwano tolerates more drought than most cucurbits once vines are established. Cucumis metuliferus (kiwano or African horned melon) is an extraordinary African cucurbit producing one of the most visually dramatic fruits in horticulture — an oblong, 3-to-5-inch fruit covered in prominent, rigid, pointed spines (horns), ripening from green to brilliant deep orange-gold that looks almost artificial in its intensity. The jelly-like interior flesh is lime-green and gelatinous, with a mild, refreshing flavor combining hints of banana, cucumber, and lime. Kiwano is grown commercially in New Zealand, Kenya, and California for specialty markets and upscale grocery stores where the exotic appearance commands premium prices. The fruit is eaten by scooping out the jelly-like flesh with a spoon, used in tropical fruit salads, blended into smoothies, or used as a dramatic edible vessel for other foods. As an annual vine, it is easy to grow in zone 9 summers — direct sow after the last frost, provide trellis support, and harvest when the skin turns deep orange. The vines are vigorous and productive under heat.

Korean pine is a large, ornamental five-needle pine that produces the large, wingless pine nuts commonly sold in Asian markets — seeds are bigger than those of Italian stone pine and have a rich, buttery flavor. Trees are monoecious and bear cones that ripen over two growing seasons; significant cone production typically begins at 15–25 years from seed. Cones are harvested in early autumn when the scales begin to separate; spread cones on tarps to dry and then beat or tumble to dislodge seeds. The outer seed coat must be cracked to access the edible kernel, which is high in oil and should be refrigerated or frozen to prevent rancidity.

Koroneiki is a productive Greek olive celebrated for generous harvests and a compact, easygoing habit that suits both orchards and patios. Its small fruit yields a robust, high-quality oil, and the silvery evergreen foliage lends year-round Mediterranean charm. Grow a young tree in full sun with sharp drainage and minimal water once established. Prune to keep light reaching the interior, and where winters are cold, grow it in a pot to move to shelter during freezes.

Kumquats are the hardiest of the citrus family and the only ones whose entire fruit — sweet peel and tangy flesh — is eaten whole. They are self-fertile and well-suited to container growing in zones 7–8, where they can be overwintered indoors. Unlike other citrus, kumquats go dormant more readily in winter, which improves their cold hardiness. Fruit ripens from late autumn through winter; harvest when fully orange and sweet-peel is prominent.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Kuwini mango is similar in requirements to common mango but more frost-sensitive. Mangifera odorata (Kuwini mango or fragrant mango) is a species in the Anacardiaceae family related to common mango (M. indica), native to the Malay Peninsula and the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, producing small to medium-sized, oval, green to yellowish fruits with extraordinarily intense mango-floral fragrance — the most powerfully aromatic of all Mangifera species. The fresh fruit has a strong turpentine-floral aroma detectable at a considerable distance, with yellow-orange flesh that is significantly more fibrous than commercial mangoes and with more resinous flavor notes. While less pleasant to eat out of hand than polished commercial mango varieties, Kuwini is prized in Malaysia and Indonesia for juice, juice blends, mango lassi-type drinks, ice cream, and traditional sambal sauces where the intense fragrance shines through processing. The skin of the fruit also yields a yellow dye. The tree is also notable as one of the parents in the natural hybrid origin of common mango's wild ancestors. In zone 11–12 tropical fruit collections, Kuwini is a valuable diversity addition for those wanting the full spectrum of Mangifera species. Very rare in cultivation outside Southeast Asia.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; LSU Gold is a golden-yellow fig cultivar developed by the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center's renowned fig breeding program — one of several outstanding cultivars released by LSU specifically for Gulf Coast garden conditions. The medium-sized fruits have golden-yellow to amber skin and rich, sweet, amber-colored flesh with excellent flavor and lower acidity than common brown-skinned fig varieties. The golden skin and rich, honey-sweet taste make LSU Gold particularly attractive for fresh eating and fresh presentations where the unusual color adds visual appeal. LSU Gold ripens with a main crop in July through September in zone 9 and often produces a lighter breba (early crop) in June. LSU-developed figs are specifically selected for performance in the hot, humid Gulf South — resistance to fig mosaic virus, quality fruit production in high heat and humidity, and productivity in the long Gulf South growing season. Figs are among the easiest and most productive fruit trees for Gulf Coast gardens — drought-tolerant, naturally pest-resistant, fast to bearing (often fruiting in the second year from cuttings), and requiring minimal care beyond keeping the soil moist during fruit development. Propagate easily from dormant hardwood cuttings taken in late winter.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; LSU Purple fig was developed by Louisiana State University specifically for the Gulf Coast and Deep South, where high humidity, summer rains, and soil fungal diseases typically prevent figs from performing as reliably as in Mediterranean or California climates. It produces an abundant main crop in summer of medium-sized, deep purple-skinned figs with a rich, sweet, dark-red interior. The variety has superior resistance to fruit splitting and souring — common problems in humid regions where rain during ripening ruins the crop on other varieties. It ripens earlier than most, avoiding the worst of hurricane season. An outstanding choice for zone 8‑9 gardeners in the humid Southeast.

common_name: LSU Scott's Black Fig (Mississippi-Grown Deep Red-Fleshed Fig)
notes: Plant a rooted cutting or container tree in spring after frost danger in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soil but reward good drainage and consistent moisture during fruit development. Scott's Black is a fig developed by the LSU AgCenter's fig breeding program in the 1950s and, like its siblings LSU Gold and LSU Tiger, was selected specifically for vigor and fruit quality in hot, humid Gulf South conditions. The self-fertile tree produces small to medium figs with deep purple-to-black skin and intensely flavored, strawberry-pink flesh, ripening on a late main crop from September into October. Scott's Black stands out for continuing to produce good-quality fruit into cool, rainy fall weather after many other fig varieties have finished for the season.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; like its LSU AgCenter sibling releases, LSU Tiger fig was bred specifically to perform reliably in the humid, disease-prone conditions of the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Its most distinctive feature is its striking immature fruit — young, unripe figs are boldly striped in yellow-green and dark green, giving the variety its 'Tiger' name — before ripening to a bronze-brown skin with sweet, richly flavored, amber-to-strawberry-colored flesh. The variety carries useful resistance to fruit splitting and souring, common problems for figs grown where summer rains fall during ripening, and its ornamental striped immature fruit makes it a conversation piece in the garden even before harvest. A good choice for Gulf South growers who want the LSU program's disease resistance along with a visually distinctive fruit, zone 7–11.

Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to the juglone this species releases into the surrounding soil. Lamb is a named black walnut selection valued by nut growers for combining good kernel percentage and cracking quality with strong, consistent annual bearing, an important trait in a species that can otherwise produce heavily only every second year. Like other grafted black walnut cultivars, it grows into a large, long-lived shade tree over time, so it is best suited to a large property, orchard row, or field edge rather than a small home garden. Nuts drop in a thick, dark, staining husk in early fall that should be removed promptly to prevent kernel discoloration, and grafted trees typically begin bearing within six to ten years, considerably sooner than seedling trees. Rake and dispose of fallen husks away from lawns and walkways, since they stain concrete and skin on contact.

common_name: Lang Jujube (Pear-Shaped Chinese Jujube, Large Late Jujube)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — jujubes thrive in poor, alkaline, rocky soils where other fruit trees fail; Lang and Li are the classic companion pair for maximum fruit set; harvest fruits when they turn from green to mahogany-red and reach full size; air-dry excess harvest at room temperature for preserved 'dried dates.' Lang jujube is one of the two most important cultivated jujube varieties in American horticulture, planted alongside Li jujube (the other dominant variety) throughout the jujube-growing regions of the United States. Lang differs from Li in fruit shape and season: where Li produces round to oval fruits that ripen relatively early, Lang produces elongated, pear-shaped to teardrop-shaped fruits that are noticeably larger than Li (typically 1.5–2.5 inches long) and ripen later in the season. The larger, more elongated fruit shape of Lang also makes it particularly excellent for drying into Chinese-style red dates (hong zao / hóng zǎo), where the pear shape produces attractive elongated dried fruits with a pleasant chewy texture and concentrated honey-sweet flavor. Cross-pollination between Lang and Li is well-documented to significantly increase fruit set on both trees, making them the classic companion pair for backyard jujube plantings — planting one of each type provides mutual pollination benefits that result in substantially heavier crops than either variety planted alone. Like all jujubes, Lang is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant, thriving with no supplemental irrigation once established in most of the country. An exceptional choice for zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardeners who want a reliable, low-input fruit tree.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Langsat is more shade-tolerant than most tropical fruit trees and performs well with overhead canopy protection when young, mimicking its native understory forest environment. Lansium parasiticum (formerly L. domesticum) is a medium tropical tree native to the Malay Peninsula, the Philippines, and Indonesia, where it is one of the most beloved native fruits — at once common enough to be sold from roadside carts throughout Southeast Asia and exotic enough to be a premium market item in Japan and specialty stores. The fruits are produced in long, grape-like clusters directly on the main trunk and branches (cauliflory), each fruit a small (1–2 inch) oval, pale yellowish-tan berry with thin, papery skin. Inside are 3–5 segments of translucent, juicy, sweet-tart flesh with a flavor variously described as combining grape, grapefruit, longan, and rose water — extraordinarily refreshing in tropical heat. The 'Duku' form (sometimes listed separately) produces larger, thicker-skinned, sweeter fruits than the standard Langsat; 'Longkong' is a selected clone from Thailand with very sweet, thin-skinned fruits highly valued in Southeast Asian markets. Virtually unavailable commercially outside Southeast Asia and rare specialty markets, Langsat is a coveted addition to zone 11 South Florida tropical fruit gardens.

Lapins is a self-fertile sweet cherry producing large, firm, dark-red fruit without needing a pollinator, ideal for smaller gardens. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and water steadily as fruit develops. Prune in late winter or after harvest to keep an open canopy and reduce disease. Netting the tree near ripening helps protect the crop from birds.

Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — adapted to seasonally dry African bushveld. Ximenia caffra (large sourplum or wild sourplum) is a thorny deciduous shrub or small tree from the dry savannas, bushveld, and woodland margins of eastern and southern Africa — native across South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Tanzania, and Kenya. The plant produces small (1-inch), oval, single-seeded drupes that ripen from green to bright orange-red to scarlet, with very tart, astringent, vitamin C-rich flesh surrounding a large seed — eaten fresh across rural sub-Saharan Africa (often with salt to balance the sourness), and made into jam, chutney, beer, and preserved sour fruit drinks. The seed kernel has an almond-like flavor and is pressed for Ximenia oil (sour plum oil), one of the most sought-after African cosmetic oils, with excellent skin-conditioning properties rich in long-chain polyunsaturated acids — increasingly used in high-end African cosmetics, hair oils, and skin care. Distinguished from the smaller X. americana (tallow wood) by its larger fruits, larger leaves, and preference for drier, more seasonal climates. As a water-wise shrub for zone 9–11 gardens, large sourplum is extremely tough and attractive, with white, almond-scented flowers in spring.

growth_habit: Caribbean Lauraceae wild avocado relative tree
notes: Plant Beilschmiedia pendula in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; harvest fruits when fully colored and give slightly to gentle pressure. Laurel Avocado is one of numerous wild Lauraceae fruit trees related to the cultivated avocado — in the Beilschmiedia genus, distributed across tropical Asia, Africa, and the Americas. The Caribbean species B. pendula produces fruits that closely resemble small avocados in appearance and texture: oval to pear-shaped, 2–3 inches long, with dark greenish to purple-black skin and green, oily, smooth-textured flesh surrounding a single large seed. The flavor is avocado-like but distinctly different — the laurel-family heritage shows in a subtle aromatic note reminiscent of bay leaves, giving the fruit a more complex character than standard avocado. Eaten fresh with salt and lime, used in local Caribbean cooking as an avocado substitute, and occasionally used to press for oil. The tree grows naturally in humid Caribbean forest and coastal woodland environments and tolerates periodic flooding better than cultivated avocado. Of interest as a potential rootstock for avocado cultivation research and as a wild relative for avocado breeding programs.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Laxton's Superb is a reliable, cold-hardy alternative to Cox's Orange Pippin for gardeners wanting similar flavor from a more forgiving tree. Bred in Bedfordshire, England in the early twentieth century from a Cox's Orange Pippin and Wyken Pippin cross, it bears medium, red-flushed russeted apples with rich, aromatic, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh reminiscent of its famous Cox parent, but on a tree that is notably hardier, more reliably productive, and more forgiving of less-than-ideal growing conditions than the notoriously finicky Cox. Its combination of excellent Cox-like flavor and much easier garden performance has made it a favored choice for gardeners wanting classic English dessert apple flavor without Cox's demanding cultural requirements. Harvest in mid-fall and store for a few weeks to a couple of months, during which the flavor continues to develop and improve.

Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Leccino is one of Italy's most widely planted olive cultivars, valued for producing smooth, mild, buttery oil with low bitterness and pungency compared to more robust Tuscan cultivars like Frantoio, and for its comparatively good tolerance of cold winters and root rot among Italian olive selections, which has made it a popular choice in warm-temperate American olive trials including in the Southeast. Trees are vigorous, spreading, and heavy-bearing, typically beginning meaningful production within four to six years of planting. Harvest olives from green through purple-black depending on the oil style desired — earlier harvest yields a greener, more peppery oil, while later harvest gives a milder, more buttery result. Leccino is only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second, compatible olive cultivar nearby improves fruit set and yield. Established trees tolerate drought and poor, alkaline soil well, needing supplemental water mainly during the first two years and during fruit development in dry summers.

Lemons are self-fertile and can bloom and fruit year-round in frost-free climates; Eureka and Lisbon are the commercial standards, while Meyer lemon is hardier (damaged below 22°F) and better suited to containers in cooler climates. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and fertilize with citrus-specific fertilizer three times per year. In zones 8–9, grow in large containers and bring indoors when temperatures drop below 28°F. Fruit is ready when fully yellow, slightly soft, and the rind is thin — do not wait for it to fall off the tree.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; lemon aspen grows as a rainforest understory tree and performs best with some afternoon shade protection. Acronychia acidula (lemon aspen) is an Australian native rainforest tree from the tropical and subtropical rainforests of northeastern Queensland — one of the most distinctive flavor ingredients in Australian native cuisine and a rising star of the Australian native food industry. The tree produces small (1/2–3/4 inch), round, pale-yellow to white fruits with highly aromatic, intensely concentrated lemon-pine-eucalyptus flavor — a unique, complex, bright citrus character that is entirely different from true lemons (Citrus limon) but provides a distinctively clean, intense, herbal-citrus punch that chefs value highly. The flavor profile is often described as lemon with eucalyptus, thyme, and pine notes — a complexity that normal citrus lacks. Lemon aspen is entirely unrelated to true citrus but has evolved a remarkably similar citrus flavor independently through different chemistry. The fruits are too intense and sharp to eat fresh in quantity but are used in small amounts as flavor accents in dressings, seafood sauces, marinades, desserts, and beverages — both fresh and as preserves, oils, and freeze-dried powder. Commercially produced lemon aspen products are increasingly available in Australian specialty food stores and international gourmet markets.

growth_habit: Central American small citrus-flavored Garcinia fruit
notes: Plant Garcinia intermedia in fertile, moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; provide consistent moisture throughout the year — Garcinia species do not tolerate prolonged drought; protect from cold below 40°F, especially in youth; dioecious species (both male and female plants needed for fruiting, or select self-fertile named varieties if available). Lemon Drop Mangosteen is one of the most exquisitely flavored of all Garcinia fruits — smaller than the Purple Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) but with a uniquely intense, sweet-tart, citrus-dominant flavor profile quite different from other Garcinias. The bright golden-yellow to orange, golf-ball-sized fruits contain translucent-white, juicy pulp segments of remarkable flavor — combining intense lemon, lime, and sweet tropical fruit notes in an almost sherbet-like profile. In Central America, the fruits are eaten fresh, used in drinks, and made into preserves; the yellow skin contains bitter compounds similar to other Garcinias and is not eaten. In zone 10–12 gardens and collections, Lemon Drop Mangosteen grows as a slow-growing, handsome ornamental tree with attractive, glossy, dark-green leaves; fruiting begins after 5–7 years from seed. An excellent greenhouse tree in cooler climates.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; lemon guava (yellow-fruited variety of strawberry guava) produces small, round to oval, yellow-skinned fruits with white flesh and a sweet, aromatic, guava-strawberry-lemon flavor that is milder and less acidic than the red-skinned strawberry guava (var. cattleyanum). The glossy, dark green, evergreen leaves and attractive smooth bark are ornamental year-round. Fruits eaten fresh, used in jams, jellies, and juices. Like the red strawberry guava, it is extremely adaptable and has become seriously invasive in Hawaii's native forests and in parts of Florida and the Caribbean, where it forms dense thickets that displace native vegetation. In cultivation outside of tropical areas (zone 8), it is well-behaved; in zone 9–11 it should be monitored for self-seeding. Birds are the primary seed dispersers. More cold-tolerant than tropical guava, growing in zone 8 with some frost protection. The lemon-yellow skin makes ripe fruits easy to identify for harvest.

common_name: Lemonade Berry (Lemonade Sumac, California Lemonade Berry)
notes: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, lean soil in fall or early spring; lemonade berry is a coastal chaparral shrub of southern California prized for edible red-orange berries (technically drupes) covered in a sticky, tart coating — the berries can be soaked in cold water for 15–30 minutes to make a refreshing, pink, lemonade-like drink that indigenous Chumash and Cahuilla peoples have used for centuries. The berry flavor is strongly acidic and lemony with a resinous undertone. Absolutely drought-tolerant once established, thriving on coastal rainfall with no supplemental water after the first year — an ideal California-friendly landscape plant combining edibility with low maintenance and excellent wildlife value. Makes an attractive hedge or screen and tolerates salt spray.

Li is a large-fruited jujube cultivar producing sweet, apple-crisp fruit that can be eaten fresh or dried like dates. It thrives in hot summers and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and neglect once established. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; a second cultivar such as Lang nearby improves fruit set. Prune in late winter to remove suckers and thin the canopy, and harvest when the fruit turns fully brown.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Liberica coffee grows as a larger tree than arabica and needs more space; tolerates slightly drier conditions than arabica. Coffea liberica (Liberica coffee or barako) is the rare third major commercial coffee species — a larger, bolder, more assertive plant than arabica (C. arabica) or robusta (C. canephora). Native to the lowland forests of Liberia and West Africa, C. liberica is a substantial tree reaching 20–35 feet (much taller than the 10–15 foot arabica shrub), with large, glossy leaves, large white flowers, and large, asymmetric, elongated coffee fruits (cherries) containing unusually shaped, irregular beans. The flavor of Liberica coffee is perhaps the most controversial in the coffee world: strongly fruity with jackfruit-like, slightly funky, floral-aromatic, sometimes smoky notes — entirely different from the clean, nuanced arabica profile or the bold-bitter robusta profile. Some specialty coffee drinkers consider Liberica's complex, funky, tropical fruit character uniquely wonderful; others find it off-putting. Liberica coffee is of particular importance in the Philippines, where it is known as barako (from a Tagalog word for a virile bull) and has strong cultural identity as the traditional Filipino coffee — once produced in significant quantities on Luzon until coffee rust devastated plantations in the 1880s. Today barako is a prized specialty product in the Philippines.

common_name: Liberty Apple (Disease-Resistant Organic Apple, Cornell Scab-Free Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Liberty is self-unfruitful and requires a nearby apple of a compatible variety for pollination; in disease-resistant plantings, pair with Freedom or Enterprise for cross-pollination; Liberty ripens in October producing medium to large, red-blushed fruit with good sweet-tart flavor — quality significantly above what one might expect from a disease-resistant variety. Liberty apple is a Cornell University-developed disease-resistant variety (released 1978) that has become one of the most important apple varieties for home organic production in the eastern United States, where the humid climate creates severe pressure from the four major apple diseases — apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew — that require intensive fungicide spray programs to manage on standard susceptible varieties like Fuji, Gala, and McIntosh. Liberty's multiple-disease resistance package was assembled through deliberate crosses at Cornell that combined resistance genes from multiple sources: the apple scab resistance comes from Malus floribunda 821 (the same source as the PRI disease-resistant breeding program), while fire blight and rust resistance come from other wild Malus species in the parentage. The result is an apple variety that can be grown essentially spray-free in home gardens — a significant advantage for organic-minded gardeners — while still producing attractive, well-flavored fruit that compares favorably with commercial varieties. The fruit is medium to large, red-striped over yellow-green skin, with crisp, juicy, moderately sweet flesh and a pleasant balance of sweet and tart flavor. Liberty has been the recommended variety for organic home orchards from Cornell Extension for over 40 years.

common_name: Limbertwig Apple (Old Fashioned Southern Appalachian Heirloom)
notes: Stake young trees loosely, since the cultivar takes its name from the distinctively supple, drooping branches that bend rather than break under a heavy crop. Limbertwig is really an old Southern Appalachian family name covering many closely related strains, so trees sold under this name can vary somewhat, but all share a rich, spicy-tart flavor that many growers feel improves after a few weeks in storage. It was a dooryard and cider staple across the Southern mountains through the 19th century and is still sought out by heirloom orchardists for its complex, old-fashioned flavor and long keeping quality.

Key lime (C. aurantiifolia) is the most cold-sensitive common citrus and is reliable only in zones 10–11; Persian lime (C. latifolia) is somewhat hardier and suits zone 9 in sheltered spots. Both are self-fertile and produce almost continuously in warm climates with adequate water. Container culture in a large pot (25+ gallons) allows limes to be grown farther north and moved indoors during frost. Fruit is best harvested while still green and fully sized — if left to yellow on the tree it becomes dry and flavorless.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; limeberry is frost-tender and best suited to sheltered dooryard plantings in zones 9b-11 or large containers moved indoors for winter further north. This small, thorny, trifoliate-leaved citrus relative bears intensely fragrant, orange-blossom-scented white flowers nearly year-round in frost-free climates, followed by small, oval, deep-red fruit with a sweet, thin skin over lime-tart, mucilaginous pulp traditionally used in preserves and candies rather than eaten fresh. Long grown as a dooryard and hedge plant across the tropics and subtropics, it tolerates shearing well and makes a fragrant, fine-textured, thorny barrier planting or specimen shrub near a patio where its flower scent can be enjoyed. Protect from frost, water regularly during dry spells, and prune lightly after flushes of bloom to maintain shape.

Limequat is a Key lime × kumquat hybrid combining the intense lime flavor of Citrus aurantiifolia with the cold hardiness of Fortunella, tolerating temperatures down to about 20°F — the hardiest of the lime-flavored citrus. Like kumquat, the entire fruit — sweet edible peel and sour juice pulp together — can be eaten whole or sliced into drinks and salads. Trees are self-fertile, compact, and well-suited to container culture in zones 7–8, where they can be moved indoors during hard freezes. The small oval to round fruits ripen from green to yellow in autumn through winter; harvest when fully yellow for the sweetest peel, or use while still green for the most intense lime flavor.

Lisbon is a vigorous, cold-tolerant lemon that fruits heavily and produces classic tart, juicy fruit almost year-round in warm regions. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and keep the graft union above the soil line. In zones colder than 9, grow in a pot that can be moved indoors or to a bright greenhouse for winter. Feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer during active growth and water deeply but allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Thin fruit lightly on young trees so the branches are not overloaded.

common_name: Litchi Tomato (Morelle de Balbis, Sticky Nightshade)
notes: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; wear gloves when handling — plants are densely spiny. Solanum sisymbriifolium (litchi tomato or morelle de Balbis) is a South American tomato relative producing small (1/2-to-3/4-inch), bright-red berries resembling tiny tomatoes, enclosed in a spiny, papery calyx that peels back to reveal the glossy red fruit at maturity — the resemblance to lychee fruit when partially enclosed in its papery husk gives the plant its common name 'litchi tomato.' The flavor is sweet-tart, similar to a cherry tomato but with a distinct floral undertone; fruits are eaten fresh, used in jams, pies, and salsas, or dried. The plants are extremely productive in warm climates, bearing prolifically from midsummer through frost. The entire plant is covered with numerous, sharp, reddish-orange spines on stems, leaves, and calyces that make handling without gloves painful; despite this deterrent, the plants are interesting and productive specialty edibles. CAUTION: Like all nightshades, the leaves, stems, and unripe berries are toxic; consume ripe fruits only. The spiny character makes litchi tomato a useful barrier or living fence plant.

Little Miss Figgy is a naturally dwarf fig reaching only about 4 to 5 feet, making it ideal for patios and small gardens. It produces sweet, deep-purple figs on new growth, often with a light second crop later in the season. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water consistently while fruit is sizing up. In zones below 7, grow it in a container and move it to an unheated garage or shed during hard freezes. Prune lightly in late winter to shape the plant and encourage fruiting wood.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to occasionally wet soil in full sun along river banks, flood plains, or moist forest margins; littlehip hawthorn is one of the most graceful of the southeastern native hawthorns, with an elegant form, attractive spatula-shaped to shallowly 3-lobed leaves, and masses of tiny (1/4-inch) brilliant red haws that ripen in fall and persist on the branches well into winter. The persistent fruit crop is exceptionally valuable to winter-resident thrushes, cedar waxwings, and other berry-eating birds when larger food sources have been exhausted. White flower clusters in spring provide pollen and nectar for native bees and early butterflies. The tree's smaller stature relative to other hawthorns makes it well suited to suburban wildlife gardens and riparian restoration plantings where a medium-scale fruiting tree is needed.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; littleleaf sumac is a small-leaved, drought-adapted native shrub of the Chihuahuan Desert and Edwards Plateau of west and central Texas, recognized by its unusually tiny compound leaves with small, dark green, heat-tolerant leaflets. White flowers in early spring before leaf emergence are followed by small, sticky, tart red berries that are edible as a lemonade-like beverage (native peoples soaked them in water to make a refreshing drink, similar to other Rhus species). The persistent small red fruits are important food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other desert birds through summer. Outstanding fall color — brilliant orange-red — followed by attractive winter structure. An extremely drought and heat tolerant native shrub for xeric, rocky, alkaline gardens in central and west Texas and adjacent areas.

common_name: Lomanto Grape (Texas Hill Country Disease-Resistant Bunch Grape)
notes: Lomanto traces its parentage to the pioneering hybrid grape breeding work begun by T.V. Munson in Denison, Texas, which focused on combining native American Vitis species with European vinifera to create grapes tough enough for Texas heat, drought, alkaline soils, and Pierce's disease pressure. It bears clusters of small to medium dark red-black berries used mainly for juice, jelly, and home winemaking rather than fresh eating, with a tart, distinctly grapey flavor. Plant it on a sturdy trellis in full sun on well-drained soil, including thin, rocky, or alkaline sites where many other grapes struggle, since its American parentage gives it good drought tolerance and root vigor once established. It is a solid choice for home growers in the Texas Hill Country and greater Gulf South who want a low-input bunch grape without the spray program vinifera varieties demand.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Longue d'Aout is an old French heirloom fig variety named for its August ripening season, producing distinctive elongated, pear-to-tear-drop-shaped fruits with violet to purple-brown skin and amber to pink-tinged flesh with a sweet, mild, honey-fig flavor and very few seeds. The unusual elongated shape (2–3 inches long, narrowing to a pronounced neck) makes this variety immediately identifiable among more common round-fruited fig varieties and creates an elegant presentation at table. Longue d'Aout is a main-crop variety producing its primary harvest in August–September in zone 9. It grows as a moderately vigorous tree with good productivity once established. This variety is well-regarded in French fig traditions and has been grown for centuries in the south of France; its elongated form makes it particularly distinctive for display and specialty market use.

common_name: Louisiana Sweet Satsuma (Gulf South Cold-Hardy Mandarin)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and give young trees frost cloth protection on the coldest nights until they are several years established. Louisiana Sweet is a satsuma mandarin selection grown and promoted along the Gulf Coast for combining good cold hardiness with consistently sweet, low-acid flavor even in years when cooler, cloudier falls can leave other citrus tart. Fruit is medium-sized, nearly seedless, and easy to peel, ripening in the standard satsuma window from October into December ahead of most other citrus. As with all satsumas, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization late in the season, which delays the hardening off trees need to withstand winter cold, and mulch well to protect the root zone.

Sow fresh seeds in fall directly into sandy, well-drained soil, as Low Serviceberry is adapted to dry, rocky ground and performs poorly in rich or consistently moist conditions. Winter cold provides the stratification seeds need, and seedlings emerge in spring when soil temperatures warm to 40–55 degrees Fahrenheit. This spreading, colony-forming shrub is excellent for naturalizing slopes, stabilizing sandy soils, and providing wildlife habitat; allow adequate space for root-sprouting colonies to develop. Expect the first berry crop 2–5 years after transplanting; the sweet, dark blue fruits ripen in midsummer and are relished by birds and mammals.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun in a frost-free location; lucuma is a Peruvian fruit tree native to the Andean valleys, where it has been cultivated since ancient times and was called the 'Gold of the Incas.' The large, oval fruits (3–4 inches) have a dry, starchy, bright orange-yellow flesh with an extraordinary flavor — intensely sweet with a rich, complex caramel-maple-sweet potato quality that is completely unlike any familiar fruit. The taste is so distinctive and rich that lucuma powder (dried, ground lucuma flesh) is used as a natural sweetener and flavoring for ice cream, smoothies, pastries, and confections in Peru, where lucuma ice cream outsells chocolate and vanilla in many surveys. The flavor is particularly popular as a low-glycemic sweetener alternative. Fresh lucuma is eaten locally in Peru and Chile but ships poorly, so it is rarely found fresh outside its home region. An exceptional specialty fruit tree for collectors in frost-free zones.

Macadamias are self-fertile but cross-pollination between two or more varieties meaningfully increases yields; grafted trees start bearing at 3–5 years, while seedlings can take 10–15 years. The tree prefers well-drained, slightly acid soil (pH 5.5–6.5) and is sensitive to root disturbance — plant without disturbing the root ball. Trees produce racemes of cream-white flowers that fall and create a slippery surface; harvesting is done by collecting nuts that have dropped naturally as the green husk splits and the nut falls. Shell and dry nuts for 3–4 weeks before cracking; the shells require a commercial or heavy-duty nut cracker as they are among the hardest of any food nut.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; protect from frost below 26°F until established; plant 2+ varieties for cross-pollination and better yields. Macadamia integrifolia (smooth-shell macadamia) is one of the world's most celebrated nut trees and the only major food crop originating in Australia — native to the subtropical rainforests of southeast Queensland. The macadamia nut is universally recognized as one of the finest-flavored nuts in the world: round, ivory-white, buttery-smooth, with an extraordinarily rich, creamy, sweet flavor unlike any other nut. The fat content (75%) is predominantly monounsaturated, making macadamia oil one of the most desirable culinary and cosmetic plant oils. The smooth-shell species (M. integrifolia) is the primary commercial macadamia — most Hawaiian, Australian, South African, and Kenyan commercial orchards are primarily or entirely M. integrifolia or its hybrids. Trees are evergreen, grow slowly to 25–35 feet, produce dark-green, glossy, leathery leaves, and begin bearing in 5–7 years from grafted stock. The extremely hard shell (requiring 300+ psi to crack) requires a specialized macadamia cracker. Zone 9b–11, damaged below 26°F. Hawaii, California, and South Florida can grow macadamia commercially; zone 9a gardens can succeed with protected sites.

common_name: Macoun Apple (Beloved Northeast Eating Apple, McIntosh-Type Geneva Station Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic fertile soil in full sun; requires cross-pollinator; thin biennial crops by hand-removing half the fruit clusters in early summer to encourage annual bearing; Macoun ripens October and must be harvested at peak ripeness — slightly soft at the stem end, fully red, and with characteristic spicy aroma — as it deteriorates quickly after peak. Macoun apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva from a cross involving McIntosh, and named for W.T. Macoun, Dominion Horticulturalist of Canada who made significant contributions to fruit breeding and evaluation — released in 1923, making it roughly contemporary with McIntosh's commercial rise. Among apple connoisseurs of the northeastern United States, Macoun occupies a unique status: it is considered by many the finest-eating apple of any variety available in New York and New England, with a complex, spicy-sweet, intensely aromatic flavor at peak ripeness that exceeds even McIntosh in intensity and depth. The fruit is medium-sized, dark red (often nearly all-red with a purple-red hue at full maturity), with pure white, tender, very juicy flesh and the characteristic McIntosh floral fragrance amplified. Macoun's intense flavor comes with a significant limitation: the variety has a very short window of peak eating quality — typically 1–2 weeks at the height of ripeness in October — after which the flesh softens rapidly and flavor diminishes. This poor keeping quality has limited Macoun's commercial viability but made it a cult variety among farmers' market customers who know to seek it out during its brief peak season.

Grow this Cuban-origin, grafted mamey sapote cultivar in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing plenty of room for a large, long-lived tree. It is valued by south Florida growers for reliably producing smooth-skinned fruit with dense, sweet, salmon-pink flesh often compared to sweet potato or pumpkin custard. Young trees are noticeably cold-tender and can lose leaves or twigs at temperatures in the mid-30s, so Gulf Coast growers stick to the warmest coastal locations or grow smaller trees in large containers that come indoors for winter. Mature trees take several years to bear their first crop, and fruit is harvested firm and then ripened off the tree at room temperature.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. One of the earliest widely planted named pecan cultivars, dating to the early 1900s, Mahan is known for producing exceptionally large nuts, among the biggest of any pecan cultivar, though the kernel fill and disease resistance lag behind modern breeding selections. It remains of historical interest and is still grown in some older orchards and by collectors of heirloom pecan varieties for its striking nut size, even though it has largely been superseded commercially by higher-yielding, more scab-resistant cultivars.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mahlab, or mahaleb cherry, is a small ornamental cherry species native to the Mediterranean and Middle East, grown far more for the fragrant kernel inside its small, bitter cherry pits than for the fruit's thin, tart flesh, which is not typically eaten fresh. The dried, ground kernels — called mahlab or mahleb — have a distinctive bitter-almond, floral, faintly cherry aroma used to flavor Middle Eastern, Greek, and Mediterranean pastries and breads, including Greek tsoureki, Cypriot flaounes, and Middle Eastern ka'ak. To harvest the spice, collect ripe pits, crack them to remove the kernel inside, and grind the kernels just before use, since their aroma fades quickly once ground. The tree itself is small, fragrant-flowered in spring, and notably drought- and alkaline-soil-tolerant, which is also why it is widely used as a rootstock for grafting sweet and sour cherries in regions with dry, calcareous soils unsuited to standard cherry rootstocks. It tolerates heat and poor soil well once established.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun; mahua is drought-tolerant once established and thrives on poor soils. Madhuca longifolia (mahua or Indian butter tree) is a large, slow-growing tropical tree native to the forests of central and southern India, deeply woven into the culture and economy of indigenous tribal communities across Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Madhya Pradesh. The tree provides multiple distinct food, economic, and cultural products: the fleshy, sweet, cream-colored flowers (corollas) that drop prolifically in spring are edible and extremely sweet — they are eaten fresh (tasting like a mild honey-flower combination), sun-dried and used as a sweetener, fermented into mahua wine, and distilled into mahua liquor, one of India's most important traditional tribal spirits and an important livelihood product. The seeds contain 30–40% mahua butter (a semi-solid vegetable fat) with a composition similar to cocoa butter, used in traditional cuisine, soap-making, and cosmetics. The leaves provide fodder; the bark and flowers have Ayurvedic uses. Mahua is considered a 'tree of life' by many Indian adivasi (tribal) communities — the flowers are economically critical, often constituting a significant fraction of tribal household income in forest villages. A remarkable tree with enormous cultural depth and genuine multiple-use value.

common_name: Maiden Blush Apple (Early American Heirloom Dual-Purpose Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator, since Maiden Blush is not reliably self-fruitful. First noted in New Jersey in the late eighteenth century, Maiden Blush became one of the most widely planted American heirloom apples of the nineteenth century for its striking pale lemon-yellow skin marked with a rosy pink blush on the sun-exposed side, a color pattern early writers likened to a blushing cheek. The crisp, tart-leaning flesh cooks down into a pale, delicately flavored sauce and dries well, while a fully ripe apple mellows enough for pleasant fresh eating, making it a genuinely dual-purpose variety by the standards of its era. It ripens over a fairly early late-summer window and does not keep as long in storage as later-season heirlooms, so plan to use or process the crop within a few weeks of picking. Thin heavy fruit set in early summer to improve size and reduce biennial bearing.

common_name: Malabar Chestnut (Money Tree, Guiana Chestnut, Saba Nut)
notes: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained to seasonally wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Malabar chestnut is best known to most people as the ornamental 'money tree' with braided trunks sold as a houseplant across the world, but it is also a genuine food plant producing 12-inch oval pods filled with 20–25 large, edible seeds that taste remarkably like chestnuts or roasted peanuts when cooked — the seeds can be roasted, boiled, or ground into flour, and the young leaves and flowers are edible as vegetables. As a landscape tree in zone 9b–12 it can reach 30–40 feet in the ground with a spreading tropical canopy, but is easy to keep pruned to 10–15 feet. The large, palmate leaves and buttressed trunk give it outstanding ornamental character. Native to the seasonally flooded forests of Central and South America, it tolerates both dry periods and extended flooding — a rare combination that makes it valuable for challenging low-lying sites.

common_name: Malay Apple (Mountain Apple, Jambu Bol, Rose Apple Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Malay Apple grows most rapidly with regular watering and fertilization in the warm humid conditions of zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida. Syzygium malaccense is a large, fast-growing, evergreen fruit tree native to Malaysia and the Indonesian islands, now cultivated throughout the tropics from the Pacific Islands to Central America, Africa, and the Caribbean. The tree is doubly ornamental: in spring, it produces spectacular displays of crimson-red to deep rose-purple flowers that emerge directly from the bark of the trunk and major branches (cauliflory), creating an extraordinary effect of flowers growing from the wood — dozens to hundreds of 1-inch flowers with brush-like clusters of bright crimson stamens covering the trunk in a fiery display. These flowers are followed by the fruits: dark red to magenta, pear-shaped, 2–3 inch fruits with white, spongy, mildly sweet flesh and a faint floral flavor — eaten fresh throughout Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands and used in jams and beverages. The tree is an important crop and dooryard fruit tree throughout tropical Oceania and Southeast Asia. The Hawaiian name 'Ohia Ai' (mountain apple) reflects its long cultivation history in the Hawaiian Islands. In zone 10-11 South Florida landscapes, it serves as both an ornamental shade tree and a productive home fruit tree.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Malbec prefers warm, sunny conditions and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than many other red wine grapes. Originally a minor Bordeaux blending grape in France, this deeply colored red variety found its true expression in the high-altitude vineyards of Mendoza, Argentina, where abundant sunshine and cool nights produce the rich, plush, dark-fruited wines with soft tannins that have made Malbec Argentina's signature grape and an internationally beloved red wine style. It is somewhat prone to coulure (poor fruit set in cool, wet spring weather) and benefits from a warm, sheltered site with reliable sunshine through flowering and fruit set. Provide full sun and a warm site sheltered from late spring cold snaps, prune to a moderate crop load for the best concentration, and harvest when tannins are ripe alongside sugar development.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; mamey apple is a large, stately fruit tree native to the Caribbean, Mexico, and northern South America, producing round to oval fruits 3–8 inches across with a thick, rough, bitter brown-russet skin enclosing firm, apricot-orange to yellow flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavor suggesting apricot, vanilla, and almond — quite unlike most other tropical fruits. The flavor is complex and distinctive: the outer flesh directly under the skin can be slightly bitter, while the inner flesh is sweet and aromatic. The tree is magnificent as a landscape specimen — densely leafy, with thick, glossy, oval leaves and a formal, dome-shaped crown. Small, white, fragrant flowers appear on the branches directly. The timber is dense and valuable. Not to be confused with Mamey Sapote (Pouteria sapota), an entirely different fruit despite the similar name. Mamey apple was a staple food of the Taino people of the Caribbean before European contact and was described by Columbus's men. It is now primarily grown in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; mamey sapote (Pouteria sapota) is a majestic Central American tree in the Sapotaceae family that produces one of the most beloved tropical fruits in Caribbean and Latin American cuisine — a large, russet-brown, football-shaped fruit with vivid salmon-to-brick-red flesh of exceptional richness, sweetness, and smooth texture, often compared to a pumpkin-sweet potato-almond fusion. The fruit is eaten fresh, blended into milkshakes and batidos (a staple across Miami's Cuban community and throughout the Caribbean), made into ice cream, and used in desserts. Only grafted trees of named selections should be planted, as seedling trees can take 10–15 years to fruit and produce variable quality; grafted trees begin bearing in 3–5 years. Mamey sapote is moderately drought-tolerant once established but produces larger, higher-quality fruit with consistent irrigation and regular fertilization with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer.

common_name: Mammoth Black Twig Apple (Paragon, Arkansas Black Twig)
notes: Give this vigorous tree plenty of room and prune annually to keep the spreading, upright canopy open to light and air. Originating in Arkansas in the 1830s as a Winesap seedling, Mammoth Black Twig became a popular commercial apple across the South and lower Midwest for its large size, dark red color, and firm, tart-sweet flesh that stores well into winter. It is a distinct cultivar from the unrelated Arkansas Black and is grown today mainly by heirloom orchardists and collectors seeking a taste of 19th-century Southern apple culture.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free climates; mamoncillo (Spanish lime, quenepa, genip) is a large tropical tree native to Central America and the Caribbean that produces clusters of golf-ball-sized green fruits with a brittle outer skin concealing a translucent, salmon-colored pulp clinging tightly to a large seed. The flavor is a unique combination — simultaneously sweet-tart, tropical, and faintly lime-like with a passionfruit quality — that is utterly distinctive among tropical fruits. Fruits are eaten by biting through the skin and sucking the pulp off the seed, which is the traditional way to consume them across the Caribbean. They are also made into juice, fermented into wine, and processed into candy. Mamoncillo is an important street-food fruit in Puerto Rico, Colombia, Cuba, and throughout the Caribbean, where it is eaten fresh out of hand in large quantities. The tree is drought-tolerant once established and very long-lived.

Mandarins (including tangerines, clementines, and satsumas) are the most cold-hardy of the common sweet citrus, with satsumas surviving to about 15°F and thriving in zone 8. Most are self-fertile, though some varieties set more fruit with a compatible pollinator nearby. Fruit tends to ripen earlier in the season than oranges — from October through January depending on variety — and the loose peel and sweet-tart flavor make them popular for fresh eating. Avoid overwatering, as mandarins are somewhat drought-tolerant and susceptible to root rot in wet soils.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Citrus reticulata is the species encompassing all mandarins, tangerines, satsumas, clementines, and most mandarin-type hybrids — a diverse group of loose-skinned, easily peeled, aromatic citrus originating in Southeast Asia and southern China that includes hundreds of named varieties ranging from tiny, seedless clementines to large, deeply flavored Ponkans. As a group, mandarins are the most cold-hardy common citrus (Satsuma types tolerating temperatures to 18–22°F when established) and one of the most adaptable to Gulf South conditions, performing well in zones 8b–11 where sweet oranges or grapefruit might struggle with cold or humidity-related issues. Key mandarin varieties for Gulf South gardens include Satsuma (most cold-hardy), Owari Satsuma, Owens Navel, Clementine, Ponkan, Murcott (Honey mandarin), and Dancy tangerine. Most mandarins ripen November through February, and the loose skin that peels easily by hand makes them the most user-friendly fresh citrus. The species is very adaptable to container culture, making it practical for zone 8 gardeners who want moveable citrus.

common_name: Manzanilla Olive (Spanish Table Olive Standard, Green Martini Olive, Seville Table Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Manzanilla is extremely drought-tolerant once established; harvest for green table olives in October when fully sized but still green; harvest for black table olives in November–December when fully ripe; home-cured Manzanilla olives require brine treatment for 6–12 months to remove bitter oleuropein before eating. Manzanilla (meaning 'little apple' in Spanish, for the round fruit shape) is the dominant commercial table olive variety in the world — the variety behind the iconic green olives stuffed with pimentos found in cocktail jars and martini glasses throughout the Western world, and a major component of Spanish, American, and Mexican table olive production. Its origin is in the Seville region of Spain (particularly the province of Huelva), where it has been the foundation of the Spanish table olive trade since the 1800s, and it was introduced to California (where it is called 'Manzanillo') in the 19th century with California's Spanish-mission heritage, becoming established in the central California olive-growing regions (Fresno, Madera counties) and eventually as the dominant commercial table olive variety in the United States. The olives are medium-sized, round to slightly oblate, with firm, meaty flesh and a relatively small pit that makes them ideal for stuffing — the characteristic American 'green olive' of commercial production is almost always a Manzanilla cured at the green stage. The trees are medium-sized (15–25 feet), productive, and adapted to a wide range of California and Gulf South conditions with adequate drainage and minimal rainfall during the ripening period.

Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Manzanillo is a classic Spanish olive cultivar and the most widely grown table olive variety in the world, valued for its large, plump, meaty fruit with a favorable flesh-to-pit ratio that makes it the standard choice for brine-cured green and black table olives found in grocery stores worldwide. The tree bears heavily and reliably, and while it can also be pressed for oil, its primary use and reputation is as a table olive. Harvest green in fall for green-cured olives, or let fruit ripen to black for black-cured olives, then cure in brine or lye solution for several weeks to months to remove natural bitterness before eating; olives are inedible straight off the tree. The tree grows to a more traditional, larger size than modern compact cultivars, so allow ample space.

Plant in full sun in deep, rich, consistently moist, well-drained tropical soil; marang (Artocarpus odoratissimus) is a close relative of breadfruit and jackfruit, native to Borneo and Mindanao, producing rounded, yellow-green fruits about the size of a small jackfruit with an extremely sweet, creamy white flesh surrounding large, edible seeds — many who have tasted it rank it among the finest tropical fruits, with a rich, sweet, almost vanilla-custard flavor with a fragrant aroma. The seeds are also edible when cooked (roasted, boiled, or ground) and have a pleasant chestnut-like flavor. Strictly tropical and not tolerant of any frost; best suited for south Florida and Hawaii collections and food-forest enthusiasts in zone 11+. Less well-known outside Southeast Asia but increasingly available from specialty nurseries.

Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Marbrite is an Italian fig cultivar bearing medium-sized figs with pale green to yellow-green skin and sweet, translucent amber to white flesh, a lighter-colored departure from the deep pink and red interiors of Gulf Coast standards like Celeste and Brown Turkey. It typically produces two crops in warm climates: a smaller breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer, followed by a larger main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Figs fruit on both second-year wood and current-season growth, so avoid heavy winter pruning, which removes the breba crop; light shaping after the main harvest is sufficient. Trees are vigorous and productive once established and rarely need fertilizer, though a layer of mulch over the root zone helps in zone 7-8 where occasional hard freezes can damage unprotected roots. Harvest when fruit softens and the neck bends over, since figs do not ripen further once picked.

common_name: Marcona Almond (Spanish Queen of Almonds, Round Blanched Premium Almond)
notes: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile soil (calcareous or sandy loam preferred) in full sun; Marcona requires a companion pollenizer variety; harvest in late summer when hulls begin to split; the round, flat kernels are best roasted in olive oil and sea salt in the traditional Spanish preparation — the rich, buttery texture of roasted Marcona is distinctly different from any California variety. Marcona is a Spanish almond variety traditionally grown along the eastern Mediterranean coast of Spain (the Valencian Community and Murcia region) that has become known internationally as the 'queen of almonds' for its extraordinarily rich, buttery flavor and distinctive round, flat shape that makes it immediately recognizable on a charcuterie board or tapas spread. The flavor difference between Marcona and California varieties (Nonpareil, Mission, Carmel) is significant and immediately apparent to tasters: Marcona has a much higher fat content and a softer, more buttery texture with a sweeter, more intensely almond-flavored profile — often described as having hints of marzipan and fresh sweetness that California varieties cannot replicate. The traditional preparation — blanched (skin removed), roasted in olive oil, and salted — is the standard presentation in Spanish tapas and increasingly common in American specialty food and charcuterie culture. Marcona's very low chill requirement (200–300 hours) makes it the almond most adapted to warm-winter zones 8–10 where standard California varieties may also grow, but Marcona's flavor sets it apart for culinary use. Not as productive as California commercial varieties in California growing conditions.

Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. Bred in France from a cross of European and Japanese chestnut, Marigoule combines good resistance to chestnut blight and ink disease with large, easy-to-peel nuts and a precocious habit, often bearing within a few years of planting. It has become a popular choice in North American chestnut orchards specifically because its hybrid vigor and disease tolerance let it thrive where the straight American chestnut has been devastated by blight. The tree is moderately vigorous and more compact than a full-sized American chestnut, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or food forest planting.

common_name: Marsh Grapefruit (Seedless White Grapefruit, Marsh Seedless)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Marsh grapefruit (introduced commercially around 1860 from a seedling found in Florida) is the foundational white grapefruit of the citrus industry — virtually all seedless white grapefruits sold commercially today are Marsh or descended from it. The large, round, pale-yellow fruits (4–5 inches diameter) are nearly or completely seedless (a major practical advantage over older seedy varieties like Duncan), with pale-cream to light-yellow flesh, balanced sweet-tart grapefruit flavor, and abundant juice. The flavor is the benchmark classic grapefruit flavor — moderately tart with characteristic bitterness from naringin — excellent eaten fresh (halved and sectioned with a serrated spoon), juiced, or used in salads and cocktails. The large tree (15–20 feet when mature, larger on vigorous rootstocks) is cold-hardier than many citrus and can tolerate brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established. Marsh grapefruit is the parent of most modern grapefruit varieties, including Ruby Red (a bud sport of Marsh) and Thompson Pink. Ripens November through May in Florida; the fruits hold on the tree exceptionally well, improving in flavor through winter.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil of any type — Marula is remarkably adaptable to poor, sandy, or rocky soils and intensely drought-tolerant, thriving in conditions that challenge most fruit trees. Sclerocarya birrea subsp. caffra (Marula) is a large, spreading, deciduous African fruit tree native to the woodlands and savannas from Ethiopia and Nigeria south to South Africa, famous throughout sub-Saharan Africa as one of the most important traditional food and beverage trees of the continent. The plum-sized fruits (1–1.5 inches diameter) ripen in December–March in South Africa; in zone 9 they ripen in late summer–fall. When ripe, the thin, pale yellow skin covers soft, extremely juicy, intensely aromatic flesh with a rich, complex flavor combining tropical fruit notes reminiscent of mango, pineapple, and lychee — prized fresh, fermented into a traditional beer, and distilled into the popular Amarula Cream liqueur (produced commercially in South Africa). The large, brown, extremely hard seeds inside each fruit contain edible kernels with a rich, nutty flavor and high oil content used in traditional African cosmetics. Elephants travel great distances to feed on fallen marula fruits, giving rise to the folklore that they become inebriated — a myth, though the fruits do ferment rapidly when fallen. Marula is increasingly grown as an edible landscape tree in zone 9b–11.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Marumi is one of the oldest kumquat cultivars grown, producing small, round fruit with thin, sweet, edible skin surrounding a tarter, seedier pulp, eaten whole rather than peeled. It is among the more cold-hardy kumquats and, being a naturally small, dense shrub, adapts well to container culture and can be moved under cover during hard freezes in the cooler parts of its range. Fruit ripens in winter and holds on the tree for weeks without dropping, giving a long, flexible harvest window; established plants are otherwise low-maintenance and require only routine citrus fertilizing.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil — including rocky, limestone-based soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; Maya nut (Brosimum alicastrum) is a towering canopy tree in the Moraceae family that the ancient Maya and other Mesoamerican peoples relied upon as a critical famine food for thousands of years, with seeds that are extraordinarily nutritious — high in protein, calcium, potassium, iron, zinc, and B vitamins — and can be boiled, roasted, dried, and ground into flour. The ripe purple-skinned fruits are also edible fresh, with a sweet, fig-like flavor, and the abundant leaves serve as high-quality livestock fodder. Trees are long-lived, moderately drought-tolerant once established, and grow naturally in limestone-rich soils where other fruit trees may struggle. Though primarily a large timber and food tree rather than an orchard crop, Maya nut is gaining recognition as an exceptionally valuable multipurpose agroforestry species, with first seed harvests typically beginning 5–10 years after planting.

Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to occasionally flooded soil in full sun; mayhaw thrives in the heavy, wet, acidic soils of the Gulf Coast plain that frustrate most fruit trees. Crataegus aestivalis (mayhaw) is the iconic native fruit tree of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, producing small (1/2-to-3/4-inch), bright-red to orange-red, apple-like fruits in April–May (hence 'may haw' — haw is an old name for hawthorn fruit) that are traditionally harvested by spreading sheets under the tree or raking from the water's surface when the tree grows over ponds and bayous. Mayhaw jelly is a Southern culinary tradition — the vivid, translucent, coral-red jelly with a unique tart-sweet, apple-berry flavor is considered a regional treasure and a gift-worthy specialty product throughout Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi. The tree is also highly ornamental — producing masses of white flowers in February–March (often among the first spring blossoms), followed by the distinctive April berry crop, then good fall foliage color. Named cultivars for improved fruit production include 'Big Red,' 'Crimson,' 'Super Berry,' and 'Texas Star.' Mayhaw grows naturally in wet bottomland forests, bayou margins, and pond edges throughout the Gulf Coastal Plain.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw naturally grows in wet bottomlands and tolerates seasonal flooding. Crataegus opaca (Western mayhaw or May haw) is a native hawthorn of the Gulf Coastal Plain — a small to medium deciduous tree growing in the wet, seasonally flooded bottomlands, bayous, and boggy depressions of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia. It is the source of one of the most prized and distinctively Southern traditional preserves: mayhaw jelly, made from the small (1/2-inch), bright-red to orange-red, apple-flavored fruits that ripen in April and May (hence 'mayhaw' — haw ripening in May). Mayhaw jelly has a uniquely mild, apple-quince-like flavor with subtle floral notes that makes it a beloved regional specialty — spread on hot biscuits, it represents the taste of the Gulf South spring. The fruits must be harvested from the ground or water (they drop when ripe, sometimes into shallow water) and are processed immediately — too sour and dry to eat fresh, but exceptional for jellies, preserves, and syrup. Many improved fruiting cultivars have been selected in Louisiana, Texas, and Georgia; 'Super Berry,' 'Texas Star,' and 'Crimson' are productive modern selections. Mayhaw is notably tolerant of wet soils and occasional flooding, making it valuable for rain gardens and wet spots in Gulf Coast landscapes.

Direct-sow seeds or plant transplants in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil against a trellis, fence, or arbor; maypop is one of the most ornate native vines of the Southeast, producing intricately structured lavender-and-white flowers all summer followed by fragrant, egg-sized, yellow-green edible fruits that ripen in fall and make excellent juice and jam with a tropical guava-like flavor. The vine spreads vigorously by underground runners and can colonize an area quickly — provide a sturdy trellis and monitor spread, or allow it to naturalize along a fence row. Maypop is the sole or primary host plant for Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterfly larvae in the Southeast, making it one of the most ecologically valuable native plants for zone 5–9 pollinator gardens. Despite top growth dying back in zone 5–7, the deep roots re-emerge dependably each spring.

common_name: McIntosh Apple (Mac Apple, Original Red Apple, Northeastern Apple Classic)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; McIntosh requires cross-pollination; ripens early season (early September in New York), making it the first major commercial apple of the fall; fruit should be harvested when fully red and slightly soft to pressure — McIntosh doesn't firm up like later-season apples and is at its best when slightly tender and very aromatic. McIntosh apple is the foundational variety of the northeastern American apple industry and for decades was the dominant commercial apple in New England, New York, and eastern Canada. The variety was discovered as a chance seedling on John McIntosh's farm in Dundas, Ontario (near present-day Morrisburg) around 1811 — one of the most consequential accidental apple discoveries in North American horticultural history. The young seedling was found growing on his property, probably a wild seedling from a previous homestead planting, and John McIntosh and his son Allan grafted and propagated the tree beginning around 1835, eventually distributing trees throughout eastern Canada and New England. McIntosh produces distinctively aromatic fruit with a characteristic sweet-tart flavor and very soft, juicy, bright white flesh that is immediately recognizable to anyone who grew up in the Northeast. The red-green skin deepens to full red with harvest, and the flesh is softer than modern popular apples (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) — McIntosh is what older generations mean when they say 'the way apples used to taste' — a tender, juicy, very fragrant apple with complex flavor. McIntosh is also the primary parent of many important modern apple varieties including Cortland, Empire, Jonamac, Macoun, and others.

Plant female vines with at least one male Actinidia arguta pollinator on a strong trellis or pergola in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Meader is a hardy kiwiberry cultivar bred at the University of New Hampshire and named for horticulturist Elwyn Meader, selected for exceptional cold hardiness and a shorter growing season requirement that lets it ripen fruit reliably even in northern New England summers. Fruit is smooth-skinned and grape-sized, eaten whole without peeling, with sweet green flesh and good kiwi flavor, ripening earlier in the season than many other kiwiberry selections. This early ripening and strong cold tolerance make Meader a dependable choice anywhere the growing season is on the short side for other hardy kiwi cultivars. Prune hard each winter to control the vigorous twining growth, train onto a permanent trellis from planting, and keep a compatible male vine within pollinating range for consistent fruit set.

common_name: Meech's Prolific Quince (Classic American Heirloom Quince)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Meech's Prolific is a nineteenth-century American heirloom quince, long documented in historic US pomology references as one of the heaviest-bearing and most reliable quince cultivars available, producing large, bright golden-yellow, intensely fragrant fruit prized for preserves, jelly, paste, and baking. As the name suggests, it is notably precocious and prolific, often bearing well within just a few years of planting and continuing to crop dependably year after year. Like all quince the fruit is hard and astringent raw and is meant to be cooked, which transforms the pale flesh to a rosy pink and develops the complex floral-honey flavor quince is prized for. Prune in late winter to an open vase form for good air circulation, which is the best defense against fire blight, the primary disease risk for quince in humid regions. Harvest in fall once fruit has turned fully golden and developed its characteristic strong perfume; quince stores well in a cool location for weeks after picking.

Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Meiwa is the sweetest and most widely recommended kumquat cultivar for fresh eating — a round-fruited kumquat (distinct from the oval Nagami kumquat) with notably sweeter, thicker, nearly non-acidic edible skin and sweet-tart flesh.
