The sweet skin makes Meiwa kumquats the superior choice for eating whole — both skin and flesh are consumed together, and the sweetness of the Meiwa skin dramatically reduces the puckering tart bite that makes Nagami less pleasant for casual snacking. The small, round, golden-orange fruits appear in clusters on a compact, attractive, evergreen tree that makes an outstanding ornamental specimen even when not in fruit. Kumquats are among the most cold-hardy true citrus — surviving to 18–22°F — which makes them excellent choices for the entire Gulf South and even zone 8b gardens with minor winter protection. The trees are naturally compact and can be maintained at 6–10 feet for easy harvesting. Meiwa kumquat fruit is excellent fresh, sliced in salads, made into marmalade, and candied. The attractive, shiny, dark-green foliage and white, fragrant flowers make it an excellent landscape specimen year-round. Excellent container plant for patios and small gardens.

common_name: Melogold Grapefruit (UC Melogold, Sweet White Grapefruit)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Melogold is a pomelo x white grapefruit hybrid developed by the University of California alongside Oro Blanco from the same breeding program (both released 1980), but with a subtly different flavor — where Oro Blanco has a pomelo-forward character with slightly dry, mealy flesh, Melogold has juicier flesh and a flavor closer to a very sweet, very mildly bitter grapefruit, with somewhat more grapefruit character and slightly more juice than Oro Blanco. Like Oro Blanco, Melogold lacks the bitter naringin flavanone that makes standard grapefruit bitter, but retains more of the characteristic grapefruit aroma and slight tartness, making it a good bridge between grapefruit lovers and those who normally avoid grapefruit bitterness. The large, greenish-yellow to pale-yellow fruits (4–6 inches) ripen October through February and must be tasted to judge ripeness since the skin stays green or pale yellow even when fully ripe. The very large tree is suitable for large home landscapes and the Southern California and Gulf Coast climate in zones 9–11.

Melrose arose as a chance seedling discovered near Melrose Plantation in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, and was propagated for its unusually precocious habit of bearing a full crop years earlier than most named pecan cultivars. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil with plenty of room to spread, and provide a cultivar with an opposite pollen-shed pattern nearby to ensure full nut set. The medium-sized, well-filled nuts crack out easily and have good flavor, making Melrose a popular dooryard and home-orchard choice across the Gulf South even though it can show more scab susceptibility than newer disease-resistant releases in very humid seasons. Because it fruits so young, growers often use Melrose as a filler tree between longer-lived cultivars, removing it once the permanent trees begin bearing.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Methley is one of the best Japanese plum cultivars for warm climates — a highly productive, self-fertile tree requiring only 250–350 chill hours (hours below 45°F), making it one of the most reliable plum choices for zone 8–9 Gulf Coast gardens where most other plum cultivars fail due to insufficient winter cold. The medium-sized fruit has red-purple skin and distinctive red flesh with a sweet-tart, juicy flavor. Methley is an early-season plum that ripens in May or June in zone 8–9, which allows the harvest to be completed before summer heat and disease pressure peak. It is also an effective pollinizer for many other Japanese plum cultivars. Trees are vigorous and productive, beginning to bear 2–3 years after planting. Prune annually after harvest to maintain tree structure and control size. A consistent performer in the Gulf Coast South where it is one of the standard recommendations from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension.

Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; Mexican pinyon is the most widely distributed of the Mexican pinyon pines — a three-needle pinyon (three needles per bundle, distinguishing it from the two-needle Colorado pinyon) of the dry mountain ranges of Mexico and into trans-Pecos Texas, southeastern Arizona, and southern New Mexico. The most important commercial pine nut tree in Mexico and an important food plant for Indigenous peoples of northern Mexico. More heat-tolerant than Colorado pinyon, extending into warmer, drier climates of zones 6–9 in the Southwest — an excellent xeriscape tree for hot, dry Texas Hill Country, west Texas, and similar climates where Colorado pinyon is marginally hardy. The nuts are smaller than Colorado pinyon nuts but comparable in flavor and nutritional quality. Slow-growing but long-lived — old trees develop picturesque, gnarled forms on rocky, exposed slopes. An underused edible landscape tree for dry southwestern gardens.

common_name: Mexican Plum (Big Tree Plum, Creek Plum)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Mexican plum tolerates rocky, shallow, limestone soils that defeat most fruit trees. Prunus mexicana (Mexican plum or big tree plum) is the largest native plum of Texas and a landscape-worthy ornamental tree as well as a valuable food plant — more tree-like in form than the suckering Chickasaw plum, growing to 15–25 feet as a single-trunked specimen with attractive, exfoliating, reddish-brown bark. The 1-to-1.5-inch, dark-red to purple-red plums ripen in August–September with a rich, sweet-tart flavor excellent for jams, jellies, preserves, and fresh eating. Clouds of fragrant white flowers smother the bare branches in February–March, making it one of the most spectacular early-flowering native trees in the Texas landscape. Mexican plum is self-fertile, requiring no cross-pollination; it is also one of the most limestone and drought-tolerant of the native plums, thriving in the alkaline, rocky soils of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Post Oak Savanna. Wildlife value is high — the large fruits are consumed by deer, foxes, raccoons, and many bird species.

Meyer lemon is a natural hybrid between a lemon and either a mandarin or sweet orange, resulting in a thinner-skinned, less acidic, and more cold-tolerant fruit than standard lemon varieties; it tolerates brief dips to about 22°F once established. It is self-fertile, blooms nearly year-round in frost-free climates, and is exceptionally well-suited to container culture — a 20-gallon pot allows the plant to be moved indoors in zones 7–8. Plant in fast-draining citrus mix or well-amended garden soil and fertilize with citrus-specific fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and midsummer. Fruit is ripe when the skin turns deep golden-yellow and yields to gentle pressure; the rind is thin and zests well for culinary use.

Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; midland hawthorn tolerates heavier clay soils and partial shade better than common hawthorn. Crataegus laevigata (midland hawthorn or English May) is a native European hawthorn species closely related to — and often confused with — common hawthorn (C. monogyna), but botanically distinguished by having 2–3 styles per flower (instead of one in C. monogyna), deeply lobed but less deeply cut leaves, and preferring the partial-shade, moist-soil woodland-edge habitat rather than open scrub and hedgerows. Both species are called 'May' or 'May blossom' in England, referring to the masses of white (or in cultivated forms, pink or red) flowers in May that were traditionally brought into homes for May Day celebrations. The deep-red to scarlet fruits (haws) are similar to those of C. monogyna: small, oval, containing 2–3 seeds, with a mild, floury, slightly sweet-tart flavor. In European herbal tradition, hawthorn berries and flowers are among the most important cardiovascular herbs — widely used in European phytomedicine for mild heart conditions, improving coronary blood flow, and supporting healthy blood pressure. The double-flowered pink ornamental forms ('Paul's Scarlet' and 'Rosea Flore Pleno') are among the most popular ornamental flowering trees in British gardens.

common_name: Miho Satsuma (Early Compact Gulf South Satsuma)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Another early-ripening Japanese satsuma selection similar in season to Okitsu, Miho has become one of the most commonly sold satsuma cultivars in Gulf Coast nurseries because of its naturally compact, rounded growth habit and dependable early crop of small, sweet, essentially seedless fruit. Fruit typically colors and ripens in October, ahead of standard-season satsumas, with loose rind that peels away easily in segments. The tree's smaller stature also makes it a good option for large containers that can be moved under cover during hard freezes.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Minneola tangelo is a hybrid of Duncan grapefruit and Dancy tangerine developed by USDA breeders at the University of Florida in 1931, producing the largest and most dramatically flavored tangelo available — large (3–4 inch diameter), deep reddish-orange fruits with a characteristic knobby protrusion at the stem end (giving them the nickname 'Honeybell' from their bell-like silhouette) and intensely aromatic, sweet-tart juice that is considered by many citrus enthusiasts to be among the finest citrus flavors of any variety. Minneola typically ripens January–March in Florida and California (one of the latest-ripening citrus), and the fruits hold on the tree for 2–4 weeks allowing flexible harvest. The skins peel easily (a peel-and-eat citrus), and the flesh separates into 10–12 clean segments with very few seeds. The tree is medium-sized (8–15 feet), moderately vigorous, and somewhat cold-hardy for a tangelo. Minneola requires cross-pollination — plant a Temple orange, Dancy tangerine, or Orlando tangelo within 50 feet for adequate fruit set; trees planted alone may produce poorly. Outstanding for Gulf Coast gardens in zone 9–11.

Mirabelles are small, round, golden plums famed in Lorraine for tarts and eau-de-vie. Plant in full sun on fertile, free-draining soil and provide shelter from late frosts that can damage the early blossom. Most are self-fertile, so a single tree will crop, though a European plum companion boosts yields. Thin the abundant fruit set and prune lightly in summer to keep the canopy open.

common_name: Mission Almond (Texas Mission Almond, California Mission, Hard-Shell Commercial Almond)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mission is partially self-fruitful but benefits from a companion variety; harvest in late August to September — later than Nonpareil — when hulls split naturally; the thick, hard shell requires a nutcracker rather than the light hand pressure sufficient for Nonpareil; kernels are round, plump, and darker than Nonpareil with a richer, slightly more intense almond flavor. Mission almond (also called Texas Mission) is one of the oldest continuously grown named almond varieties in California, historically associated with the California Spanish mission system and possibly introduced to California with Spanish colonization in the late 1700s — though the exact origins are contested. It was one of the first California almond varieties to reach commercial significance and for many years was the second most planted California variety after Nonpareil. Mission's hard, thick shell — a significant disadvantage for fresh-cracking and processing — became an asset in the shell-on almond market, where the hard shell protects the kernel during shipping and storage, and in the roasted-in-shell specialty market. Mission almonds also have a distinctly different flavor from the mild Nonpareil — slightly richer, with a more intense almond character — making them preferred by some specialty roasters and confectioners. The variety's later bloom time (1–2 weeks after Nonpareil) reduces spring frost risk at the critical blossom stage, a practical advantage in frost-prone almond sites. In Texas, Mission is the primary recommended almond variety where it often goes by the name 'Texas Mission.'

The Mission olive, first cultivated in California, is a versatile favorite valued for both flavorful oil and classic table olives. It is a hardy, resilient evergreen that adapts to a range of conditions and delivers reliable harvests for home growers. Plant a young tree in full sun with well-drained soil and water sparingly once it establishes. Prune for an open canopy and good airflow, and in cold-winter regions grow it as a container specimen that can be sheltered from hard freezes.

Plant young container or bare-root trees in full sun in deep, well-drained, moderately fertile to fertile soil in spring; mockernut hickory is the most common hickory in the eastern United States and among the most beautiful, with dramatic large compound leaves that turn brilliant golden-yellow in fall. The nuts are enclosed in a very thick husk (giving the 'mockernut' name — the husk 'mocks' the nut inside), and the kernel is small but has a rich, full, classic hickory flavor. A critical wildlife tree, providing extremely high-value mast for deer, turkey, squirrels, and many other species; the very dense, strong, flexible wood is commercially valuable for tool handles and sporting goods. An outstanding native shade tree for large properties that also provides excellent wildlife food.

Grow this heavy-bearing grafted sapodilla cultivar in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing it well away from structures since mature trees become quite large and dense. It is grown commercially in south Florida for producing abundant crops of medium-sized fruit with grainy, malt-and-brown-sugar-flavored flesh once fully ripened off the tree. Established trees tolerate brief light frost better than many tropical fruits but still suffer leaf and twig damage below the upper 20s, so Gulf Coast growers reserve it for the warmest zones or keep young trees containerized for winter protection. Fruit must soften fully before eating, as unripe sapodilla is astringent with latex.

common_name: Money Maker Pecan (Historic Late-1800s Prolific Pecan)
notes: Selected in the closing years of the 19th century, Money Maker earned its name from its reputation as a remarkably prolific bearer, often setting such a heavy crop that nut size and shell thickness suffer without regular thinning or fertilization. It was one of the mainstay commercial cultivars of the early Gulf South pecan industry before scab-resistant 20th-century releases largely replaced it in new plantings. The nuts are small to medium with a moderately thick shell, and the tree is more prone than modern cultivars to biennial bearing if not managed with attentive fertility and crop-thinning practices. Today it is grown mainly in older heritage orchards and by collectors interested in preserving historic pecan germplasm.

Plant in moist to wet, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; money tree tolerates periodic flooding and poor drainage. Pachira aquatica (money tree or Malabar chestnut) is a Central American tropical tree famous in two quite different contexts: as a beloved ornamental houseplant (braided trunk forms sold under the 'money tree' name, associated in Feng Shui with prosperity) and as a significant wild and semi-cultivated food tree in its native tropical Central and South American habitat. The tree produces large, distinctive, 5-to-7-fingered, palmate leaves and spectacular, large (8–12 inch), creamy-white flowers with hundreds of long, red-tipped, brush-like stamens — one of the showiest flowers of any tropical tree. The large, woody fruits contain edible seeds (Malabar chestnuts) with a nutty flavor when roasted or boiled — eaten throughout Central America as a nutritious food. Braided trunk forms (produced by braiding multiple young seedlings while soft) have become extremely popular houseplants worldwide. In zone 10–12, money tree grows as a large landscape tree; in zone 9, it requires frost protection.

growth_habit: specialty vine fruit / natural sweetener crop
notes: Grow this dioecious perennial vine on a strong arbor or fence, planting at least one male vine for every six to eight female vines to ensure fruit set. The round green fruits, picked in autumn and dried, contain mogrosides that make them intensely sweet with none of the calories of sugar, and gardeners in zone 8-10 areas often treat the vine as a cut-back perennial that resprouts from the crown after light winter dieback. It prefers rich, well-drained soil high in organic matter and benefits from the same humid summer heat that suits muscadine grapes. Home use is mainly for steeping into tea or extracting a home sweetener rather than fresh eating, since the raw fruit is bitter until dried and cured.

Plant Monkey Jack in deep, fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zone 10–12; water well during establishment and dry seasons; harvest fruits when they turn golden-yellow and yield to gentle pressure — use gloves as the latex sap stains skin and clothing. Artocarpus lacucha produces round to irregularly shaped compound fruits 3–6 inches across — structurally similar to small jackfruits, formed from fused fruitlets on a central core — with golden-yellow to orange-red skin studded with small bumps and sweet-sour, aromatic, slightly astringent yellow flesh. The flavor is described as a complex blend of mango, pineapple, and slightly acidic tropical notes; the fruits are eaten fresh, pickled, cooked in curries, and used in chutneys and preserves throughout its native range. The starchy seeds are also edible when boiled or roasted, similar to jackfruit seeds. Various parts of the tree are used in traditional Ayurvedic and Thai medicine — the bark yields a yellow dye used for dyeing Buddhist monk robes in Thailand and Myanmar. A productive and ornamentally handsome tree for large tropical gardens, with attractive compound leaves and interesting fruits hanging from the main trunk and larger branches.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; monkey jack is more shade-tolerant than jackfruit and suited to multi-story food forest understory planting. Artocarpus rigidus (monkey jack, pingan, or terap hutan) is a tropical Artocarpus species from the lowland dipterocarp forests of Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines — one of several dozen Artocarpus species in the breadfruit and jackfruit genus, most of which produce edible composite fruits through cauliflory (fruiting on the trunk and main branches). Monkey jack produces round to oval, 2–4 inch composite fruits with a spiny-bumpy, green exterior and orange-yellow, sweet, somewhat sticky flesh surrounding multiple seeds. The flavor is sweet, fruity, and pleasant when fully ripe, though less refined in flavor than the closely related cempedak (A. integer) or jackfruit (A. heterophyllus). It is primarily a forest fruit eaten opportunistically in Malaysia and Indonesia rather than a major cultivated crop, and is notable mainly to tropical fruit collectors and ethnobotanists documenting the edible Artocarpus species of Borneo. As a garden tree, monkey jack is smaller and more manageable than jackfruit, with good shade tolerance making it useful in food forest designs. Restricted to zone 11–12 humid tropics.

Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun with plenty of room, since this striking Chilean and Argentine conifer eventually becomes a very large, unmistakable tree with thick, reptilian, spirally arranged branches covered in sharp, overlapping, scale-like leaves — an architectural specimen unlike anything else commonly grown. Native to the cool temperate rainforests and volcanic slopes of the southern Andes, it is the sacred tree of the Indigenous Mapuche and Pehuenche peoples, whose name for the tree, pehuen, gave the Pehuenche people their name as "people of the pehuen," reflecting the tree's central place in their diet and culture for millennia. Female cones take about three years to mature and release large, edible, chestnut-like seeds (piñones) that are traditionally roasted, boiled, or ground into flour, but a tree needs both a male and female cone-bearing tree nearby and several decades of growth before it produces a nut crop, making it a multigenerational planting rather than a quick food source. It tolerates cold well but resents the sustained summer heat and humidity of the Gulf South, performing best in cool-summer, mild-winter climates such as the Pacific Northwest or higher elevations.

common_name: Monstera (Swiss Cheese Plant, Fruit Salad Plant)
notes: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in deep to bright indirect shade; monstera is one of the world's most recognizable houseplants in temperate climates but grows as a large, vigorous outdoor vine in zone 10–12, where it can climb 20 feet or more up trees, walls, and structures by aerial roots. In the wild it migrates from deep shade toward brighter light as it matures, producing the characteristic deeply lobed and perforated leaves only in brighter conditions — deeply shaded plants have smaller, unlobed juvenile leaves. The edible 'fruit' is actually a cone-like cluster of hexagonal segments that ripens from the base upward over 10–12 months; fully ripe segments slip off cleanly and taste like a blend of pineapple, banana, and coconut. Unripe fruit contains calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense mouth irritation — harvest only segments that have separated naturally from the base.

Montmorency is the classic self-fertile tart pie cherry, so a single tree will crop heavily on its own. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, avoiding frost pockets that damage the early bloom. It is more compact and cold-hardy than sweet cherries, making it well suited to northern gardens. Prune to an open center in late winter and net the ripening fruit against birds.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Selected for reliable production and notably good resistance to pecan scab, a fungal disease that is a major limiting factor for pecan growing in humid Gulf Coast climates, Moreland has long been a dependable choice for growers in Louisiana, Mississippi, and neighboring states where less resistant cultivars require heavy fungicide programs. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality, and the tree is a consistent annual bearer under good management, making it a solid choice for growers prioritizing lower-input disease tolerance over maximum nut size.

common_name: Morello Cherry (English Morello, Dark Sour Cherry, Culinary Sour Cherry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun or partial shade; Morello is self-fertile; the dark red to nearly black fruits ripen in late July to August — later than most sweet cherries — and are very tart, intended for cooking, preserves, and culinary preparations rather than fresh-eating; harvest when fully black for maximum color in jams and liqueurs. Morello cherry is the classic European culinary sour cherry — a dark-skinned, dark-fleshed variety with deep red to nearly black skin and dark red juice that distinguishes it from the clear-juiced Montmorency type — grown for centuries in English, Dutch, and German cottage gardens as the primary cherry for preserves, pies, tarts, cherry brandy, and the fermented cherry preparations traditional in continental Europe. The dark flesh and juice of Morello give it distinct advantages over Montmorency in certain culinary applications: cherry jam, jelly, and liqueurs (including the famous Schwarzwälder Kirschwasser of the Black Forest and the maraschino cherry liqueur of Central Europe) derive their deep red-purple color from Morello's dark pigments, producing a dramatically richer-colored product than would result from clear-juiced cherries. Morello is also notable for being one of the few cherry varieties that will bear adequate crops in partial shade — a practical advantage in British and northwestern European cottage gardens where full sun is not always available. The fruit is very tart at all stages of ripeness, with a complex sourness and rich cherry flavor that intensifies with cooking and makes it the definitive variety for traditional European cherry cookery.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Moro is the deepest-colored blood orange cultivar — a Sicilian selection producing dramatic, dark crimson to near-black flesh with a striking red-streaked rind exterior. The flavor is distinctly more complex than standard sweet oranges, with a pronounced berry-like, raspberry-blackberry tone layered over the sweet orange base — a flavor unlike any other citrus. The deep red color comes from water-soluble anthocyanin pigments that develop only when cool nights (below 55°F) occur during fruit development; in very warm winters the flesh may show less red coloration but still produces the characteristic flavor. In zone 9, Moro blood oranges ripen in December through February — the coolest months — when the anthocyanin development is most favorable. The small to medium, round to slightly oval fruits have a thin, smooth rind. Blood oranges are highly valued in cooking for their dramatic color in fresh-squeezed juice (which turns deep ruby-red to purple), salad dressings, sauces, and cocktails. The juice color provides a culinary application that no other citrus can replicate. Protect from temperatures below 28°F; site in thermally protected areas of zone 9 gardens.

common_name: Morris Burton American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Seedless Indiana Persimmon)
notes: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and undemanding of fertile soil. Morris Burton is a named American persimmon cultivar out of Indiana grown for its combination of dependable cold hardiness, early bearing age, and consistent production of medium, seedless orange fruit without requiring a nearby male tree. The fruit ripens in mid-fall and, like other American persimmons, must fully soften on the tree or after a hard frost to lose its raw astringency, at which point the flesh turns sweet, thick, and richly flavored — excellent fresh, or processed into persimmon pudding, bread, and butter. Its good cold tolerance and self-fruiting habit make it a popular choice for northern-edge persimmon growers and for gardeners who want a single reliable tree without pollination logistics, in zone 5–9.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for citrus, with mature wood able to withstand temperatures well below what standard sweet orange trees survive, thanks to trifoliate orange parentage. Morton citrange is a hybrid between trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) and sweet orange, bred primarily to extend cold-hardy citrus growing further north than standard oranges allow. The fruit is tart, seedy, and more acidic than a true sweet orange, generally used for juice, marmalade, or as an ade rather than fresh eating out of hand, though well-ripened fruit mellows considerably. Trees show the trifoliate parent's deciduous or semi-deciduous habit in colder winters and small, three-part leaves, along with light thorns typical of trifoliate hybrids. Because of its unusual hardiness, Morton citrange has been of particular interest to cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing the edible citrus range into zone 6-7, well beyond where standard citrus survives. Protect young trees for the first few winters; established trees are considerably tougher. Harvest fruit once fully colored for the best balance of sweetness and acidity.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mountain papaya is a cool-climate relative of common papaya from the Andes of Colombia and Ecuador, adapted to elevations of 5000–10,000 feet where it tolerates light frost to 28°F — considerably more cold-hardy than the common papaya (Carica papaya). The small, yellow-green fruits are high in papain enzymes — even higher than common papaya — and must be cooked before eating, as the raw fruit is too enzyme-active to eat comfortably. Cooked, the flesh is used in jams, jellies, and stews throughout the Andes. In zone 9, mountain papaya can be grown outdoors year-round and provides a more climate-appropriate alternative to common papaya. The plant is dioecious; obtain plants of both sexes for fruiting.

Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun — mountain soursop is the larger-fruited relative of common soursop (Annona muricata), native to the rainforests of the Amazon basin, and is considered more vigorous and faster-fruiting than its more common relative. The spiny, ovoid fruits (3–6 inches) have white, fibrous, juicy flesh with a strong tropical flavor used to make juice, ice cream, and desserts similar to soursop. The tree is faster-growing than common soursop and shows slightly greater cold tolerance. Like all Annona species, the flowers produce heat and attract beetle pollinators overnight — cross-pollination with another tree improves fruit set significantly. The handsome, large, dark-green glossy leaves make it an attractive ornamental even when not in fruit. A productive, fast-bearing tropical fruit tree for zone 9b–12 gardens.

growth_habit: Mediterranean and Middle Eastern wild pistachio tree
notes: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, lean, rocky or sandy soil; Pistacia atlantica is remarkably drought tolerant and thrives in conditions too harsh for most fruit trees — avoid clay, overwatering, and excess fertility, which promote lush growth at the expense of drought adaptation and cold hardiness. Pistacia atlantica (Mt. Atlas Pistachio, Mastic Pistachio, or Bene) is a large, long-lived, drought-adapted deciduous to semi-evergreen tree native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia, and extending across the Middle East to Central Asia — the wild pistachio tree most widely used as the cold-hardy rootstock upon which commercial Pistacia vera (edible pistachio) varieties are grafted, conferring exceptional drought tolerance, deep-rooting habit, and disease resistance to the scions. The tree itself produces small clusters of small, pea-sized, resinous, edible nuts resembling tiny pistachios — edible and pistachio-flavored when roasted, historically used as a seasoning and oil source across the Middle East and North Africa. Pistacia atlantica is also the source of a gum-resin historically used as a primitive chewing gum and incense in the Middle East. As an ornamental landscape tree, it is exceptional: extremely long-lived, deeply drought-tolerant, with elegant pinnate foliage and spectacular orange-red-purple autumn color in cooler climates. Planted in California's pistachio-growing regions as a street and shade tree for its drought tolerance.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Garcinia dulcis is slow-growing and prefers consistent moisture. Garcinia dulcis (mundu or sweet mangosteen) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Philippines, Indonesia, and Malaysia — a member of the mangosteen family (Clusiaceae) and related to the famous mangosteen (G. mangostana) but distinctly different in fruit character. Mundu produces round, golf-ball-to-tennis-ball-sized fruits with smooth, thin, golden-yellow to orange-yellow skin and bright-yellow, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh with a flavor profile combining apricot, mango, and a slight citrus note — pleasant, refreshing, and more accessible in flavor than mangosteen's complex floral-tropical character. The yellow latex (gamboge) in the skin and pith is mildly bitter and slightly resinous (as in all Garcinia species) — peel carefully and avoid including the skin in the edible flesh. Mundu is significantly easier to grow than true mangosteen, which is notoriously difficult and slow; mundu is faster-maturing, more forgiving of less-than-perfect conditions, and more productive. The tree is also useful as a rootstock for grafting true mangosteen in regions where mangosteen is difficult to grow on its own roots. In the Philippines, the fruit is eaten fresh and made into jam; the large seeds contain a fat used in traditional cosmetics.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Murcott honey tangerine (also called Murcott mandarin, Honey mandarin, or Spring mandarin) is one of the most intensely flavored mandarins available — a complex tangor (mandarin x sweet orange hybrid) with deep reddish-orange skin, extremely sweet, rich, honey-like juice with excellent aromatic complexity, and medium-thick skin that peels relatively easily. The fruits are medium-sized (2.5–3.5 inches), slightly flattened, and typically contain 15–25 small seeds, which is a trade-off for the exceptional flavor profile that many citrus enthusiasts consider the finest of all mandarin types. Murcott ripens late in the season (January–March in Florida; February–April in California), and the fruits hang on the tree well, gradually increasing in sweetness through the winter; the tree can be used as a reliable late-season fresh citrus source when earlier varieties have finished. The California Citrus Research Board markets Murcott as 'Honey mandarin' and sells significant quantities at premium prices. Trees are moderately cold-sensitive (damaged at 28°F) and are best in the warmest sites in zone 9.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Muscat grapes are among the oldest cultivated grape varieties and are unusual for producing wines that actually smell and taste distinctly of fresh grapes. One of the oldest and most widespread grape families in the world, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains is prized for its intensely floral, distinctly grapey aroma, unusual among wine grapes for producing wine that actually smells and tastes like fresh table grapes, used to make everything from light, lightly sparkling Moscato d'Asti to sweet fortified dessert wines. The grapes are also excellent eaten fresh off the vine, giving this variety dual value as both a wine and table grape in a home garden setting. Provide full sun and good air circulation, thin clusters if fruit set is heavy to concentrate the distinctive floral aromatics, and pick based on desired sweetness level, since Muscat can be used for both dry and sweet wine styles depending on harvest timing.

Plant against a sturdy arbor, fence, or large tree in well-drained soil in full sun; mustang grape is one of the toughest and most vigorous native grapes of Texas and the Gulf South, tolerating extreme heat, drought, poor soil, and disease pressure that eliminates most cultivated bunch grapes in the region. Leaves have a distinctive dense white to rust-colored woolly underside, and the vine climbs aggressively by tendrils, quickly covering large structures if not managed. Small, tart, dark purple to black grapes ripen from midsummer into fall and are prized locally for jelly, juice, and wine once sweetened, though the juice is intensely acidic and the skins can irritate skin and eyes on contact, so handle fresh fruit with care. Prune hard each winter to control size and improve air circulation, since the vine's vigor can quickly overwhelm nearby structures and trees if left unchecked.

common_name: Mutsu Apple (Crispin, Large Honeyed Japanese-Bred Apple)
notes: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible diploid pollinator varieties nearby, since triploid cultivars cannot pollinate themselves or each other. Bred in Aomori Prefecture, Japan from a cross involving Golden Delicious and released in the late 1940s, Mutsu produces very large, greenish-yellow fruit with dense, juicy flesh and a rich, honeyed sweetness that intensifies in storage. It is sold in Britain and parts of Europe under the name Crispin. The tree is vigorous and productive, and the fruit holds its shape well when baked, making it a favorite for pies alongside fresh eating.

Plant in dry, sandy, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nantucket serviceberry is one of the most compact and low-growing serviceberries in cultivation, native to coastal pine barrens, heathlands, and sandy outwash plains from Cape Cod and Nantucket south through the mid-Atlantic — conditions that most other fruiting shrubs find inhospitable. Its small scale makes it one of the few fruiting native shrubs suited to tight urban lots or coastal cottage gardens where larger serviceberries would overwhelm the space. White flowers appear in early spring and sweet blue-black berries ripen in early summer, attracting catbirds, robins, and warblers. Because it is endemic to a restricted range and specialized habitat, sourcing plants or seed from reputable native plant nurseries rather than wild-collecting is strongly encouraged to protect remaining natural populations.

Start seeds in warm, moist seed mix at 75–80°F; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in a location sheltered from strong afternoon sun, as the large tropical leaves burn easily. This Andean highland fruit naturally grows at elevations where temperatures rarely exceed 85°F — it prefers the cool tropics and will struggle in humid Gulf Coast summers; maritime California and high-altitude zones 9–10 are ideal. The orange, tomato-like fruits are covered with soft hair when immature and ripen over several months; the intensely tart, aromatic pulp is used for juices, smoothies, and ice cream in Colombia and Ecuador. Prune to remove dead or crossing branches after harvest.

common_name: Natal Orange (Kaffir Orange, Spiny Monkey Orange)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; very drought-tolerant once established; the thorny nature deters browsing animals. Strychnos spinosa (Natal orange, spiny monkey orange, or kaffir orange) is a thorny deciduous tree from sub-Saharan Africa — native to the savanna, bushveld, and dry woodland regions of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and eastward to Kenya and Tanzania. The tree bears the most remarkable fruits in the genus: large (3–4 inch diameter), perfectly round, hard-shelled, bright yellow-green when ripe, strongly resembling oranges externally despite being completely unrelated (in the Strychnaceae family). IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: Unlike Strychnos nux-vomica (the strychnine tree, which has highly toxic seeds), S. spinosa fruit pulp is edible — the sweet-acid, jelly-like, cream to yellow flesh surrounding the large seeds inside has a pleasant, fruity, somewhat date-like flavor and is widely eaten in rural southern Africa. The seeds are bitter and should be avoided. The extremely hard shell of the dried fruit has been used for millennia as a container, bowl, and decorated gourd throughout sub-Saharan Africa. The roots, bark, and leaves have extensive traditional medicinal applications in southern African herbalism. A remarkably tough, drought-resistant tree for dry subtropical collectors' gardens in zone 9–11.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the Washington Navel is the world's most widely grown eating orange, identifiable by the small secondary fruit (the 'navel') embedded in the blossom end of each fruit. Navel oranges are seedless, easy to peel, and have exceptionally rich, sweet, non-bitter flavor when fully ripe. They ripen in winter (November through March), making them a precious fresh fruit at a time of year when few other fruit trees are bearing. Trees are self-fruitful and require no pollinators. Feed monthly with a citrus fertilizer, maintain good drainage, and protect from frost — even brief exposure to 28°F will damage fruit. In zone 9 the trees are hardy but fruit may be damaged in hard freezes.

Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Nellie Kelly is a purple passionfruit cultivar popular in Australian and subtropical home gardens for its combination of good disease resistance, heavy cropping, and rich, tangy flavor. The vine grows quickly and begins fruiting within its first year, producing abundant deep-purple fruit that drop naturally from the vine when ripe. Give the vigorous vine a sturdy trellis or fence and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage lateral branching, which increases the fruiting wood. In zone 9, site it in the warmest, most sheltered spot in the garden and mulch heavily over winter, since purple passionfruit types tolerate cold less well than the hardier Possum Purple hybrid and can be killed back or outright by a hard freeze.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, choosing a site that mimics the pine flatwoods and scrub where this pawpaw grows wild. Large, fragrant, creamy-white to maroon flowers open in spring before or alongside the new leaves, followed by yellow-green, custard-fleshed fruit that ripens smaller than common pawpaw but is sweet and edible fresh. The shrub spreads slowly by root suckers into low colonies and tolerates the sandy, low-fertility, seasonally wet-then-dry soils typical of the Gulf Coast pine belt far better than most fruiting shrubs. It is also a larval host for the zebra swallowtail butterfly, adding pollinator and wildlife value to a native fruit or naturalized planting.

common_name: Newtown Pippin Apple (Albemarle Pippin, Thomas Jefferson's Apple, First American Exported Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Newtown Pippin requires a cross-pollinator; the greenish-yellow to yellow fruit with some russet ripens very late (October–November) and benefits from 4–6 weeks of cold storage before eating, during which the flavor mellows, sweetens, and develops complex aromatic notes; an outstanding cider apple as well as a fresh eating variety. Newtown Pippin is one of the oldest American apple varieties in continuous cultivation, discovered as a chance seedling in the early 1700s in what was then the town of Newtown on Long Island, New York (now the neighborhood of Elmhurst in Queens), and is distinguished by a historical record rivaling any apple variety in the world. Benjamin Franklin shipped Newtown Pippin to England as early as the 1750s, where it was received with acclaim; it was later selected as the apple to be presented to Queen Victoria in the early 19th century — and became so popular in England that the British Parliament waived the apple import duty on American Newtown Pippins, the only American apple to receive such distinction. Thomas Jefferson planted Newtown Pippin at Monticello, where the variety is now called 'Albemarle Pippin' for its long association with Albemarle County, Virginia, and still grown in the restored Monticello orchard today. The fruit is medium-sized, greenish-yellow to yellowish with russet patches, with crisp, dense, moderately tart, richly flavored flesh that becomes complex and aromatic after storage — nutty, slightly spicy, and quite unlike most commercial varieties. An important cider variety as well.

common_name: Niagara Grape (White Concord, Golden Grape, American White Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun in well-drained soil; train to a 4-arm Kniffin system or similar; cane-prune in late winter; Niagara ripens 1–2 weeks before Concord in most regions (late August to early September); the berries are pale green to amber-gold at full ripeness, very juicy, with the classic musky Labrusca fragrance and flavor. Niagara is the second most important American Labrusca grape after Concord, developed in Lockport, New York in 1872 by C.L. Hoag and B.W. Clark as a cross of Concord and Cassady — two Labrusca-type grapes. Where Concord produces blue-black fruit with the iconic musky-sweet Concord flavor, Niagara produces pale green to golden-amber fruit with an equivalent but distinct flavor: the same Labrusca 'foxiness' but in a lighter, more delicate package that is closer to traditional white grape flavors when eaten fresh, yet unmistakably American in its musky, aromatic character. Niagara has been widely grown in the northeastern and midwestern states since its introduction and is the standard white-fruited companion to Concord in home vineyards across the grape belt of New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, and similar regions. The grapes are seeded (like Concord) with the same slip-skin characteristic — the skin separates easily from the pulp — and produce excellent fresh-eating fruit, white grape juice (with a distinctive musky-sweet flavor that distinguishes American white juice from European-style products), and white jellies and preserves with a characteristic Labrusca fragrance. The vines are vigorous and highly cold-hardy, equivalent to Concord in frost resistance, and similarly require adequate chilling hours that limit their usefulness in zones 9+.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Nichols is a fig selection developed in Louisiana and long grown across the Gulf South for its reliable production of medium-large, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber-pink flesh, along with good cold hardiness that lets it recover well after occasional hard freezes common at the northern edge of fig-growing country. Like other figs it fruits on both old and new wood, giving an early breba crop in late spring followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and needs minimal care once established beyond an annual mulch layer and light pruning to manage size. Established plants regrow readily from the base if winter cold kills back the top growth in an unusually harsh year.

Plant in full sun with good air movement, since this large, vigorous tree was historically valued for its toughness and reliability rather than fussy care. Nickajack was one of the most widely planted apples in the antebellum and postbellum South, grown from the Appalachians to Texas for its large greenish-red fruit, dependable annual crops, and good keeping quality in a root cellar. Flavor is mildly subacid rather than showy, making it best suited to cooking, drying, and cider as well as fresh eating once fully ripe.

common_name: Noble Muscadine Grape (Large Dark-Purple Self-Fertile Gulf South Muscadine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Noble is one of the most widely planted and highly regarded purple muscadine grape cultivars for Gulf South home gardens and small vineyards — a vigorous, productive vine producing large (1–1.5 inch), round, deep purple-black to dark purple grapes with thick, slightly tough skin and sweet, musky, richly flavored flesh that is the definition of classic muscadine flavor. Muscadine grapes (Muscadinia rotundifolia) are the grape of the American Southeast — a separate species from European and California wine grapes, native to the coastal plain from Florida to Virginia, and extraordinarily well-adapted to the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Gulf South summers that devastate Vitis vinifera varieties. Noble bears perfect (hermaphroditic) flowers and is self-fertile, a major advantage over the older cultivars that required a male or bisexual pollinator; it is also an excellent pollinator for female-flowered cultivars like Fry and Higgins. The large grape clusters ripen in August–September and are harvested individually as grapes ripen separately within each cluster — a distinctive feature of muscadine harvesting. Noble is used for fresh eating, juice, jelly, wine, and vinegar. The thick skin and seeds are the main characteristics distinguishing muscadine from table grapes — some people find them unpleasant, while others consider them inseparable from the authentic flavor experience. Noble wine produces a characteristically sweet, richly flavored muscadine wine very different from European wine styles.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Noire de Caromb is a French dark-skinned fig from the Caromb commune in Vaucluse, Provence — part of the rich fig heritage of Provence where the warm, dry Mediterranean climate has sustained diverse fig cultivation for millennia. The medium-sized, round to slightly flattened fruits have very dark purple to nearly black skin and deep red-to-garnet flesh with an intensely rich, complex, sweet flavor with pronounced winey depth that characterizes the best Provençal dark figs. Noire de Caromb is considered one of the finest-flavored dark-skinned fig varieties by European fig enthusiasts, though it remains less well-known in North American markets than brown Turkey or Celeste. In zone 9 the Gulf Coast heat produces fig flavor of excellent quality, and Noire de Caromb performs well in the long, warm growing season. Its primary advantage over more common dark-skinned figs is the depth and complexity of flavor.

Plant in well-drained sandy, rocky, or infertile soil — including saline and coastal soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; noni (Morinda citrifolia) is a small, fast-growing evergreen tree in the Rubiaceae family native to Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands that has been one of the most important plants in Pacific Islander traditional medicine for over 2,000 years, with virtually every part of the plant — fruit, leaves, bark, seeds, and roots — used in traditional preparations throughout Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia. The distinctive, lumpy, pale greenish-white to translucent fruits have an extremely pungent, cheese-like odor when ripe that makes them challenging to consume fresh, yet the juice has become a globally marketed health supplement product worth billions of dollars annually, prized for antioxidant compounds including iridoids, scopoletin, and various polysaccharides. Trees produce fruit year-round in frost-free tropical conditions, bear their first crop remarkably quickly — within 1–2 years of transplanting — and are exceptionally drought-tolerant once established, requiring irrigation only during establishment. Noni is one of the most salt- and wind-tolerant of all tropical fruit trees, making it well suited to coastal planting in South Florida and the Gulf Coast.

common_name: Nonpareil Almond (California Commercial Standard Almond, The World's Almond)
notes: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Nonpareil requires two cross-pollinating companion varieties for fruit set; irrigate deeply but infrequently once established; harvest in late July to August when hulls split open naturally; shake trees to dislodge nuts and allow to dry on tarps for 1–2 days before hulling and drying. Nonpareil is the most widely planted almond variety in the world and the variety that defines the global almond market — approximately 40–50% of California's almond production, which itself supplies roughly 80% of the world's almonds, comes from Nonpareil trees, making it the single most economically important tree nut variety on earth. The variety was selected in California in the 1870s by A.T. Hatch and propagated by Sexton & Lewelling Nurseries of San Leandro, California, quickly becoming the commercial standard because of its combination of easily-shelled, very thin shell, high kernel percentage (around 62–65%), excellent kernel quality (smooth, flat shape ideal for processing and sliced almonds), and early ripening that opens the harvest season before other varieties. Nonpareil kernels set the price benchmark in global almond markets — the Nonpareil grade commands the highest premiums for direct consumption, whole roasted almonds, and retail packaging because of the variety's consistent appearance, mild sweet flavor, and thin, papery shell. The variety is not self-fertile and requires two companion varieties with overlapping bloom times for reliable nut set.

Plant container-grown trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil, as this compact selection stays smaller and denser than standard Nagami kumquat. Water deeply during dry spells and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat. Nordmann bears an abundance of small, oval, orange fruit with sweet edible skin and tart flesh, and unlike standard Nagami it produces few to no seeds, making it easier to eat out of hand. It is among the more cold-hardy true citrus types, tolerating brief drops into the upper teens F once mature, and is popular for Gulf Coast and lower Southeast gardens.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; North Star is a naturally dwarf tart cherry developed at the University of Minnesota that reaches only 8–12 feet tall — significantly smaller than standard sour cherry trees — making it manageable for home gardens and usable on semi-dwarfing rootstocks for even smaller trees. The fruit is tart, dark-red, with a short stem that makes hand harvesting easier than Montmorency. It is self-fertile, needing no pollinizer, and is exceptional for its hardiness — surviving zone 3 winters reliably. Like all tart cherries, North Star fruit is used primarily for pies, jams, juices, and preserves rather than fresh eating, but the intense cherry flavor is prized in those applications. Trees bear heavily and begin producing within 2–3 years of planting. North Star is more disease-resistant than sweet cherries, requiring less intensive management. An excellent choice for the northern home orchard where sweet cherries may be unreliable.

Plant bare-root or container trees in deep, well-drained soil with a full sun exposure and ample room for a broad, spreading canopy. This California native walnut tolerates heavier soils, summer heat, and some drought better than English walnut, and was historically the dominant rootstock onto which commercial English walnut orchards in California were grafted. Left ungrafted, it produces a heavy crop of small, thick-shelled, strongly flavored nuts that are more work to crack than commercial walnuts but valued for wildlife forage and rootstock breeding.

common_name: Northern Spy Apple (Classic New York Pie Apple, Late-Season Northeastern Heirloom)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pair with McIntosh, Cortland, or Empire for cross-pollination; thin fruits in June for maximum size; Northern Spy ripens October–November — later than almost all other apple varieties — producing very large, greenish-yellow to red-striped fruits with exceptional crispness, complex sweet-tart flavor, and outstanding keeping quality. Northern Spy apple was discovered as a chance seedling in East Bloomfield (Ontario County), New York around 1800, taking its unusual name from political associations of the era; it was introduced to the nursery trade in the 1840s and rapidly became one of the most important commercial and home orchard apples of the northeastern United States and Canada. The variety has characteristics that make it consistently beloved by serious apple enthusiasts: very large size (sometimes exceeding one pound per fruit), exceptional crispness and juiciness, a complex, rich sweet-tart flavor with floral notes that compares favorably with any modern variety, and excellent keeping quality (fruits store 3–5 months under proper conditions). Northern Spy is the definitive pie apple of the northeast American tradition — the variety that old-time New England and New York pie recipes specify by name — because its firm flesh holds structure through baking and its tart, complex flavor creates an extraordinary pie filling. The trees are notably long-lived and become very large, with documented trees 150+ years old still producing; the long juvenile period (5–10 years to significant bearing) is a trade-off for extreme longevity.

common_name: Nottingham Medlar (Classic Bletted European Medlar Tree for Unusual Jelly and Wine)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nottingham Medlar is the best and most widely grown cultivar of one of the most unusual and historically significant fruits in the European garden tradition — the medlar (Mespilus germanica) is a small deciduous tree that produces brown, apple-like fruits with an open calyx end that must undergo 'bletting' (controlled softening through frost damage and fermentation) before becoming edible. Freshly picked medlar fruits are hard, astringent, and unpleasant; after bletting — either on the tree after frosts or stored in a cool location for several weeks — they transform into soft, brown, date-like paste with a rich, wine-like flavor combining apple, date, and brown sugar notes that is quite unlike any other fruit. Bletted medlar flesh is used for medlar jelly (a beautiful, rose-colored preserve with complex flavor), medlar wine, and eaten fresh as a confection. The tree itself is ornamentally beautiful: a small, naturally gnarled and picturesque deciduous tree (10–15 feet) with large white flowers in spring, handsome broad leaves that color well in autumn, and the unusual open-calyx brown fruits hanging from the branches through fall and into winter. The late-season beauty and ancient cultural history — medlar appears frequently in medieval and Renaissance English literature and was a common kitchen-garden tree for centuries — give this fruit exceptional interest for historically minded gardeners. Zone 9 is at the warm edge of its range.

common_name: Nova Elderberry (Early-Ripening High-Yield Canadian Elderberry Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Nova is a Canadian elderberry cultivar developed by Agriculture Canada that produces large, dense, heavy berry clusters ripening one of the earliest in the American elderberry season — typically 7–10 days earlier than Adams and other mid-season cultivars. The large, heavy clusters of very dark purple-black berries — dense and pendant when fully ripe — combine good fresh eating quality with excellent processing characteristics for elderberry syrup, juice, wine, and jelly production. Nova produces abundant flat-topped flower clusters in June–July, providing one of the most productive native pollinator resources in the early summer garden — elder flowers are visited by extraordinary numbers of native bees, small native bees, and beneficial insects that use the pollen and nectar. The compact cyme structure of Nova clusters makes harvesting somewhat easier than looser-clustered varieties. Nova's combination of early ripening, high production, and compact plant habit (slightly smaller than some other cultivars at 5–10 feet) makes it a practical choice for home gardens. As with all American elderberry, Nova spreads by root suckers to form colonies — plan for the suckering habit and remove suckers regularly to maintain the desired planting footprint.

Plant container-grown trees in spring once the danger of frost has passed, siting them in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and room for a moderately vigorous canopy. Provide steady irrigation through bloom and fruit set, and fertilize with a balanced citrus formula during the growing season. Nova produces deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with a rich, honeyed flavor that ripens early in the mandarin season, though a pollinator variety nearby improves fruit set and reduces seediness. It suits home orchards across Florida, the Gulf Coast, and coastal California where winters stay above the low 20s F.

Nutmeg Hickory is the rarest of the true hickories native to North America, found scattered in moist to wet bottomlands, alluvial flats, and river swamps of the southeastern coastal plain from South Carolina west to southeastern Texas, where it reaches its greatest abundance in Louisiana and Mississippi. The round, dark nuts — resembling nutmegs in shape and borne in thick, 4-parted husks — are smaller than those of most hickories but are relished by squirrels, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys, and were historically gathered and eaten by Native Americans. Plant fresh nuts directly in fall in deep, moist, slightly acidic loamy soil in full sun, allowing 90–120 days of cold stratification over winter before spring germination; the deep taproot that forms in the first growing season makes older trees virtually impossible to transplant. Trees grow steadily in bottomland soils and develop spectacular golden-yellow fall color and deeply furrowed gray bark that make them outstanding additions to naturalized floodplain or riparian plantings.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; O'Rourke is a fig developed by the LSU AgCenter and named for Dr. Ed O'Rourke, the Louisiana fruit breeder who led decades of fig research at LSU. Released in the late 20th century, it was bred specifically for Louisiana and Gulf Coast conditions, where the challenges of summer rain, humidity, and insect pressure at the eye (ostiole) cause fruit souring and internal pest damage in many standard varieties. O'Rourke has a distinctively tight, nearly closed eye that greatly reduces fruit souring caused by rain entering the ostiole and internal splitting — making it one of the best varieties for humid Gulf Coast gardens. Fruit is medium-sized, greenish-yellow to tan at maturity with amber-pink flesh, very sweet with complex fig flavor. The breba crop on old wood in June is modest; the main crop in August–October is abundant. Trees are vigorous and well-adapted to heavy clay soils when drainage is adequate.

common_name: Oconee Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Southeastern Pecan, Type I Mid-Season Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained to moderately moist fertile soil; Oconee is a mid-season variety (ripening October in the Gulf South) with large nuts and good kernel fill; its scab resistance makes it particularly valuable in the humid southeastern states from Virginia through the Gulf Coast; trees are moderately vigorous and productive. Oconee pecan is a University of Georgia-developed variety (released in the 1990s) that has become one of the most highly recommended pecan cultivars for the southeastern United States, specifically bred and selected for performance under the humid conditions, disease pressure, and climate of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf South. The breeding program at the University of Georgia's Tifton Campus has focused on developing pecan varieties with significantly improved scab resistance compared to the older standard commercial varieties (Desirable, Stuart, Schley) while maintaining nut quality comparable to those benchmarks — and Oconee represents one of the successful outcomes of this program. The nuts are large (40–48 per pound), well-filled, with good kernel percentage (58–62%), and produce a clean, sweet, buttery pecan flavor that compares favorably with the best commercial varieties. Oconee's most important attribute is its considerably better scab resistance than Desirable or Schley in the humid conditions of Georgia, Alabama, and the Gulf South — in UGA variety trials under disease pressure, Oconee consistently shows significantly lower scab infection rates on leaves and shucks, resulting in cleaner nuts and more consistent yields without the intensive fungicide programs that scab-susceptible varieties require. A premier choice for home orchard planting throughout the Gulf South.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected at Japan's Okitsu horticultural research station as an early-ripening sport of common satsuma, this cultivar produces small, flattened, deep-orange fruit that colors and sweetens several weeks before standard satsuma, often ready by October. The seedless, loose-skinned segments are tender and richly sweet with low acidity, and the compact tree bears reliably from a young age. Its early ripening window makes it especially useful in areas where an early hard freeze can threaten later-maturing citrus.

common_name: Old Home Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant European Pear)
notes: Plant in full sun with good air circulation, and prune lightly since vigorous new growth is the most blight-susceptible tissue on a pear tree. Old Home was released by USDA breeders in Oregon in the early 20th century and is famous chiefly for its outstanding resistance to fire blight, the disease that devastates most European pears in the humid Southeast, and it is widely used as a parent of blight-resistant rootstocks as well as a scion cultivar in its own right. The medium-sized, yellow-green fruit is firm and good for canning and baking, and a second pear cultivar such as Bartlett or Moonglow should be planted nearby for reliable pollination.

The olive is a slow-growing Mediterranean evergreen with silvery foliage, gnarled character, and small fruit ripening from green to black. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and needs a stretch of winter chill to set fruit well. Plant in full sun in fast-draining, even rocky soil and water deeply but infrequently once established. In zones below 8, grow it in a large pot and move it to a cool, bright indoor space during hard freezes. Prune in late winter to open the canopy and cure the fruit before eating, as fresh olives are bitter.

Plant Couepia polyandra in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; trees begin fruiting at 5–8 years and can produce heavy crops of excellent-quality fruit once mature. Olosapo is a member of the Chrysobalanaceae family (relatives of coco plum) native to the Pacific coastal lowlands of Mesoamerica, where it is a traditional food tree in local communities in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Costa Rica. The russet-brown to olive-green, oval fruits (resembling a small russet potato externally) contain very rich, creamy, yellow-orange flesh surrounding a single large seed; the texture is smooth and buttery, not unlike a ripe avocado, and the flavor is sweet and complex — combining notes of sweet potato, almond, and a mild tropical richness. The fruit is eaten fresh out of hand (removing the thin skin) or processed into beverages. The tree produces attractive, large, oval, glossy leaves and clusters of small white flowers followed by the distinctive fruits. Rarely seen outside its native range but considered by those who know it to be one of the finest-flavored Pacific coast Mesoamerican fruits; deserving wider cultivation in zone 10–12 tropical gardens in Florida, Hawaii, and southern California.

common_name: Olympian Fig (Exceptionally Cold-Hardy Brown-Skinned Productive Fig)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Olympian is a fig cultivar noted for exceptional cold-hardiness and reliable productivity — it is one of the hardiest named figs commercially available, surviving temperatures well below those that damage other cultivars, making it the preferred choice for gardeners at the northern edge of fig culture (zone 6-7) and an extremely reliable fruiting tree throughout zone 8-10. The medium to large fruits have brown to brown-violet skin, amber flesh with reddish tones, and a pleasant sweetness — not as dramatically flavored as Violette de Bordeaux but consistently good and productive. Olympian typically produces a breba (early summer) crop on previous year's wood in addition to the main crop on current year's wood, extending the harvest season. The cold-hardiness advantage of Olympian is most significant in zone 9a and northward, where occasional cold snaps below 20°F would damage less-hardy cultivars; in zone 9b-10, it provides a comfortable margin of cold tolerance safety. Self-fertile, like all common figs, and a vigorous, productive tree that begins bearing in its second or third year from planting. The large, distinctive lobed leaves of all figs provide attractive tropical-looking foliage through the growing season. Figs produce two crops in warm climates: the early breba crop in June and the main crop in late summer through fall.

Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Opal is self-fertile, precocious, and among the earliest dessert plums to ripen. A Swedish-bred dessert plum from a Victoria and Oullins Golden Gage cross, it bears reliably heavy crops of medium, reddish-purple fruit with sweet, juicy, richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening notably early in the plum season, well ahead of Victoria, which makes it a valued choice for extending the home orchard's fresh plum harvest earlier into summer. Its good cold hardiness relative to many English and French plum varieties, combined with reliable self-fertile heavy cropping and precocious young bearing, has made it a popular choice for colder-climate home orchards across northern Europe and the northern United States. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit clusters to improve size in a heavy-cropping year.

Sweet oranges (Citrus sinensis) are self-fertile; navel oranges and many blood oranges are seedless because they are parthenocarpic. Most oranges need warm nights to develop sweetness and cannot be grown outdoors north of zone 9; the Hamlin and Navel types are slightly more cold-tolerant. Fruit can stay on the tree for weeks to months after ripening, extending harvest, but may re-green in warm weather without losing quality. Apply a balanced citrus fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and midsummer for best production.

common_name: Orange Frost Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Changsha-Satsuma Hybrid Mandarin)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, ideally in a sheltered, south-facing spot near a wall or structure for extra winter warmth; Orange Frost is a Texas Superstar-designated cold-hardy mandarin, a hybrid between Changsha tangerine and satsuma bred to survive colder winters than standard satsuma varieties can tolerate, extending reliable in-ground citrus growing into zone 8 with proper siting and young-tree protection. It produces small, sweet, easy-peel orange fruit with the classic satsuma-type flavor in fall and early winter. Young trees still need frost protection — cover or use string lights on hard-freeze nights for the first several winters — but a well-established, mature tree in a good microclimate can survive cold snaps that would kill less hardy citrus outright. Water deeply and regularly during establishment and fruit development, and avoid heavy fertilizing late in the season, which can push tender new growth vulnerable to frost.

common_name: Orange Quince (Classic Round Golden American Heirloom Quince)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Orange Quince is a long-established American heirloom cultivar producing large, round, golden-orange fruit with a strong, sweet fragrance, among the most widely planted quince cultivars in home orchards for its reliable production and good flavor when cooked into preserves, jelly, and paste. Like other quince it is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, blooming with attractive pale pink flowers in spring before the hard, aromatic fruit develops and ripens in fall. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and needs only routine pruning to maintain an open form that allows good air circulation, which helps reduce fire blight, the main disease concern for quince in humid regions.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and site a compatible pollinizer citrus within about 50 feet since Orlando sets poorly on its own. This USDA-bred hybrid of Duncan grapefruit and Dancy tangerine, developed in Orlando, Florida, produces medium-sized, deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with juicy, mildly sweet flesh that ripens in midseason, generally ahead of its offspring cultivar Minneola. The tree is vigorous, moderately cold-hardy for a tangelo, and productive once established. It is one of the parent cultivars behind several modern tangelo hybrids but is less commonly planted itself today, making it a good candidate for home orchards seeking classic mid-century Florida citrus.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Orleans Reinette is a classic French dessert apple that stores well and develops fuller flavor after a few weeks off the tree. An old French variety documented since the eighteenth century, it bears medium-to-large, golden-orange, russet-dappled apples with dense, rich, nutty-sweet flesh long considered among the finest-flavored dessert apples grown in continental Europe, comparable in reputation to Cox's Orange Pippin in Britain. Its excellent, complex flavor and good keeping qualities have kept it a favorite of European apple connoisseurs and heirloom orchardists for centuries, even as it remains less widely known in North America than its English counterparts. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for several weeks to a couple of months, during which the rich, nutty flavor continues to deepen.

scientific_name: Citrus grandis x C. paradisi 'Oro Blanco'
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oro Blanco ('White Gold' in Spanish) is a remarkable hybrid of pomelo (Citrus grandis) and white grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) developed by University of California breeders in the 1950s and released in 1980, producing pale greenish-yellow to yellow fruits that appear externally unripe but are actually fully ripe and extraordinarily sweet — completely lacking the bitter notes of standard grapefruit due to the absence of the flavanone naringin, the compound responsible for grapefruit's characteristic bitterness. The result is a large citrus (slightly larger than grapefruit) with thick, spongy peel, white, juicy flesh, and a flavor that is pure sweet citrus without any bitterness — outstanding for people who love grapefruit flavor but dislike the bitterness, and for those who take medications contraindicated with grapefruit. Fruits ripen October through February (one of the earliest-ripening grapefruits) and hold on the tree for months; the thick peel insulates the flesh and extends storage life. The large tree (12–18 feet) is handsome in the landscape and produces heavily. A superb and under-known citrus for Gulf South zone 9 gardens.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil with consistent deep watering during the growing season — Oroblanco citrus requires full sun, good drainage, and regular irrigation for fruit production; Oroblanco is a grapefruit-pomelo hybrid (Citrus x paradisi) developed at UC Riverside specifically to combine the large, sweet, low-acid flesh of pomelo with the familiar grapefruit flavor profile — producing a fruit that is distinctly sweeter and less bitter than standard white or pink grapefruit while retaining the clean, refreshing citrus character that makes grapefruit family fruits distinctive. The large, pale yellow-green to yellow fruit (5–6 inches in diameter) has a thick rind and abundant, juicy, very pale yellow-white flesh with the reduced bitterness that makes Oroblanco accessible to consumers who find standard grapefruit too bitter without sugar. Oroblanco is one of the most productive and consistent hybrid citrus varieties for zone 9 — the combination of large fruit size, high juice content, and notably superior eating quality compared to bitter grapefruit types makes it a practical and rewarding home citrus tree in the warm, protected microclimates of zone 9 where adequate winter temperatures allow year-round outdoor culture.

Plant in virtually any well-drained soil in full sun — osage orange is extraordinarily tough and tolerates drought, flooding, extreme heat, alkaline soils, heavy clay, and compaction better than almost any other large deciduous tree; it was originally native to a small area of Texas and Oklahoma but was spread across much of North America in the 19th century for use as a living fence (a hedge of osage orange is literally 'horse-high, bull-strong, and hog-tight'). The dense, thorny branches form impenetrable barriers; the orange-colored heartwood is one of the most rot-resistant and hardest of any American wood, traditionally used for fence posts, bows (the tree's French name 'bois d'arc' means 'bow wood'), and railroad ties. The large, lumpy yellow-green fruits (osage oranges or hedge apples) are not edible for humans but are consumed by squirrels and, historically, by mammoths and ground sloths — the tree is a relic of the Pleistocene megafauna era.

Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and pair with a compatible pollinator of the opposite pollen type for full production, since pecans do not reliably self-pollinate. Osage belongs to the USDA pecan breeding program's family of cultivars named for Native American nations, developed to give growers better disease resistance and more consistent bearing than many older heirloom pecans, particularly in humid regions where pecan scab is a persistent problem. It produces medium-sized, good-quality nuts with a solid kernel percentage on a tree that begins bearing at a relatively young age for a pecan. As with other pecans, deep, well-drained soil and a large amount of room to grow are essential, since mature trees can eventually reach well over sixty feet with a comparably wide canopy. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poor kernel fill.

common_name: Osborne Prolific Fig (San Francisco Bay Fig, Cool-Climate California Fig)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Osborne Prolific is drought-tolerant once established and requires minimal fertilization; prune in late winter to maintain desired size; fruits ripen brownish-purple to dark reddish-purple and should be harvested when completely soft and sweet — they do not store or ship well and are best eaten immediately. Osborne Prolific is an heirloom California fig variety of unknown but apparently pre-1900 California origin, named for and associated with the nursery trade of the San Francisco Bay Area region where it became the standard recommended fig for maritime and cool-summer Pacific Coast gardens. Its primary distinguishing attribute is its ability to ripen fruit adequately in the cool, foggy summers of the Pacific Coast, where the heat units accumulated from May through October are significantly lower than in the Sacramento Valley or Central Valley fig-growing regions — conditions under which varieties like Calimyrna, Kadota, and Brown Turkey may fail to fully sweeten or ripen the main crop before autumn. Osborne Prolific's adaptation to cool conditions appears to involve both earlier ripening of the main crop and a reliable breba (first) crop in early summer that provides fruit even if the main crop is delayed by a cool summer. The fruits are medium-sized, brownish-red to dark reddish-purple, with amber to strawberry-pink flesh and an excellent rich, sweet, honey-fig flavor that is considered one of the finest of any California fig variety.
