Very productive and reliable — living up to the 'Prolific' in its name — it is also a good choice for mild-winter coastal gardens in the Southeast.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; tolerates short dry periods once established. Phyllanthus acidus (Otaheite gooseberry or star gooseberry) is a pantropical small tree native to Madagascar and widely grown throughout Southeast Asia, India, and the Caribbean, producing dense clusters of tiny (1/2-inch), deeply ribbed, 6–8 angled, pale cream to yellow fruits that grow directly from the branches and main trunk in a striking display of cauliflory. The fruits are extremely sour and high in vitamin C — almost inedibly tart fresh — but excellent when cooked with sugar to make preserves, pickles, chutney, and a distinctive sour relish used in Filipino and Southeast Asian cooking as a souring agent (similar to tamarind) in soups, stews, and curries. In India, the fruits are pickled in salt and used in rice dishes. The tree is ornamental in its own right — the delicate, deciduous, compound-leafed branches resembling fine fern fronds contrast with the heavy clusters of waxy fruits on the bare branches. In zone 9, the tree may be damaged by hard freezes but usually recovers from the roots. A neglected tropical food tree that produces abundantly with minimal care in warm climates.

The Owari satsuma is the early bird of citrus, ripening juicy, seedless, easy-peel mandarins in early winter. It is among the most cold-tolerant citrus, making it a good choice for growers in warm-temperate regions or in containers that overwinter indoors. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply but allow the surface to dry between waterings, and give some frost protection during hard cold snaps.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, sandy loam soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Owari Satsuma is the most widely grown mandarin in the Gulf Coast region and one of the best-adapted citrus for zones 8–9 where its exceptional cold hardiness (among the hardiest of all edible citrus) allows reliable production in climates that would damage other mandarin varieties. The medium-sized, flattened-globe fruits with loose, easily peeled orange skin and nearly seedless, exceptionally sweet, aromatic flesh begin ripening in October — well before navel oranges and most other citrus — providing fresh homegrown citrus through December from a single, low-maintenance tree. The loose peel (puffy skin that separates easily from the fruit segments) makes Satsumas the easiest-to-eat citrus variety for fresh consumption, requiring no knife and no mess — a significant practical advantage over oranges and grapefruits. Owari Satsuma's cold hardiness has made it the standard citrus for the Gulf South, where it is grown commercially in Louisiana and Texas as well as throughout zone 9 home gardens.

Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Own Choice macadamia is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, valued for its naturally compact, easy-care habit. This Australian-bred cultivar is prized for a naturally more compact, self-shaping growth habit that needs little pruning to maintain a manageable size compared to larger, more sprawling macadamia varieties, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or smaller property with limited space. It produces reliable crops of good-quality, high-oil-content nuts and, like other named macadamia cultivars, benefits from cross-pollination with a second variety planted nearby to maximize nut set. Water regularly, especially during nut development, and allow nuts to fall naturally from the tree at full maturity before collecting and drying them for storage or cracking.

Plant in well-drained, acidic, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; Ozark chinkapin is a native chestnut relative endemic to the Ozark Highlands of Arkansas and Missouri, historically less severely impacted by chestnut blight than the eastern American chestnut and still producing viable nuts in remnant populations. The tree occupies a niche on dry, rocky, acidic Ozark ridges where it was a valuable food resource for both wildlife and people — the sweet, thin-shelled nuts were gathered and eaten raw, roasted, and dried for winter storage. Like other American Castanea species, it is threatened by chestnut blight, though some individual trees show variable resistance. Conservation organizations actively collect seeds from resistant individuals for propagation and restoration. The nuts are smaller than Japanese chestnut but excellent in flavor, with a rich, sweet taste.

common_name: Ozark Premier Plum (Large Red Japanese-Type Plum)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and thin developing fruit to about 4–6 inches apart along the branch to encourage larger size and prevent limb breakage from a heavy crop. Developed in Arkansas and long a favorite in Southern orchards, Ozark Premier is a vigorous Japanese-type plum producing very large, round, red-skinned fruit with firm, juicy, amber-yellow flesh and a rich, sweet-tart flavor that holds up well for fresh eating, canning, and preserves. It ripens in mid to late summer and is partially self-fruitful, though yields improve significantly with a second compatible plum variety nearby for cross-pollination. The tree is vigorous and productive with moderate disease resistance for the region, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South home orchards where lower-chill plum selection is important. Prune annually in late winter to maintain an open center for good light penetration and fruit quality.

common_name: PA Golden Pawpaw (Pennsylvania Selection with Rich Golden Flesh)
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; PA Golden is a Pennsylvania-origin pawpaw selection prized for its rich, deep golden-yellow flesh, smooth fiber-free texture, and intensely sweet, tropical flavor that many growers rank among the best-tasting named cultivars available. The medium-to-large fruits ripen over a relatively long window in the mid-to-late season, and the tree is a consistent, productive bearer once established. Because of its outstanding flavor and reliability, PA Golden is one of the more widely recommended cultivars for new home pawpaw plantings. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, and plant with a second distinct cultivar such as Sunflower, Shenandoah, or Susquehanna for cross-pollination.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Packham's Triumph is a vigorous, productive tree valued for reliable cropping. Bred in New South Wales, Australia in the nineteenth century from a Bartlett seedling, it has become one of the most important commercial pear varieties in the Southern Hemisphere and a significant global export pear, bearing knobbly, irregular, pale green fruit that ripens to yellow-green with sweet, juicy, Bartlett-like flavor and notably good storage and shipping qualities. Its productive, reliable bearing and adaptability to a somewhat wider climate range than more cold-demanding European pears have made it a valued choice for warmer-winter home orchards seeking a Bartlett-type dessert pear. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the best sweet, juicy dessert texture.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Developed by USDA researchers in Orlando, Florida in 1963 from a cross of Minneola tangelo and Clementine mandarin, Page produces small, deep reddish-orange fruit with very sweet, richly flavored, easy-peeling segments. The compact, dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be moved to shelter during hard freezes. Fruit ripens from December into February, and the tree benefits from thinning in years of especially heavy fruit set to maintain size.

common_name: Pakistan Mulberry (Giant Mulberry, Long Mulberry, Sweet Giant Mulberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pakistan Mulberry is drought-tolerant once established; trees bear in year 2–3 from transplant; fruit ripens May–June, producing very long (2–3 inch), deep red to black-purple mulberries with extraordinary sweetness — far more intensely sweet than red or white mulberry; spread a sheet under the canopy and shake branches to harvest ripe fruit. Pakistan Mulberry is a named selection of Morus macroura (the long mulberry of South Asia and Central Asia) introduced and popularized in American home orchards in the late 20th century, valued almost entirely for its exceptional fruit size — the berries of Pakistan Mulberry are dramatically longer than any other mulberry variety, with ripe fruits reaching 2–3 inches in length, nearly twice the length of the longest standard mulberries. This extreme length gives Pakistan Mulberry a visual impact unlike any other berry and a practical advantage in harvesting and fresh eating — the long, cylindrical berries are easy to pick individually and contain more juice and sweetness per fruit than shorter mulberries. The flavor of ripe Pakistan Mulberry is exceptional: intensely sweet, deeply fruity, and far richer than the wild red or white mulberry, with a complex sweetness that improves significantly on the flavor of seedling-grown mulberry trees. The trees are large and vigorous (30–40 feet on standard, smaller with pruning), adapting well to the hot summers of the Gulf South, central California, and the lower Midwest. In zone 9a, Pakistan Mulberry performs very well and has become one of the most-sought specialty fruit trees at Gulf Coast nurseries.

Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; pale pawpaw is a shrubby member of the custard apple family endemic to dry sandhills, sandhill scrub, and dry oak-pine woodland of northern and central Florida and southern Georgia — a very different habitat than the moist bottomlands of common pawpaw (A. triloba). The white flowers with pale cream to white petals are produced before leaf emergence, showy against the bare stems in late winter to early spring. The small, oval fruits are edible and custard-flavored like common pawpaw but smaller. The larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus) feed exclusively on Asimina species, making all pawpaws critically important for this distinctive butterfly. A rare and threatened species in its native Florida sandhill habitat, valuable for ecological restoration of dry, sandy, native ecosystems.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; palillo prefers consistent moisture and excellent drainage. Campomanesia lineatifolia (palillo or yellow guabiroba) is a Colombian, Peruvian, and Ecuadoran tropical fruit tree in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) — the same plant family as guava, feijoa, and jaboticaba — producing small, round to oval, bright-yellow-orange fruits with smooth, thin, aromatic skin and a small quantity of cream to golden, very fragrant, sweet-rich flesh surrounding a few small seeds. The flavor is described as combining guava, mango, and custard in one fruit — aromatic, sweet, with pronounced tropical fragrance. The fruit is eaten fresh or made into juice, ice cream, and preserves; it is an important traditional food of indigenous Andean communities in Colombia and Peru. The genus Campomanesia encompasses many species of native Brazilian and South American myrtle-family trees — some famous (like guabiroba, C. xanthocarpa), most virtually unknown outside their native regions. Palillo is the Colombian and Peruvian name for C. lineatifolia; the tree is an important ornamental in Bogotá urban parks. Extremely rare in cultivation outside South America.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally sheltered from strong wind; Panache, also sold as Tiger Fig for its striking green-and-yellow striped skin, is a French heirloom fig grown as much for its ornamental fruit as for eating, with each ripe fig displaying bold longitudinal stripes over deep red, strawberry-jam-colored flesh. The breba (first) crop on old wood tends to be the more strongly striped and ornamental of the two annual crops, while the main crop on new wood ripens later in the season with slightly less pronounced striping. Fruit is sweet but not among the richest-flavored figs, so it is often grown as a conversation piece and fresh-eating novelty alongside more productive workhorse varieties like Celeste or Brown Turkey. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and control size, and protect young plants from hard freezes their first few winters, since Panache is somewhat less cold-hardy than common Gulf South fig standards.

common_name: Panache Tiger Fig (Ornamental Yellow-Green Striped Fig with Strawberry-Like Flavor)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Panache (Tiger Fig, Strawberry Fig) is one of the most visually distinctive and ornamentally beautiful fig cultivars — producing medium-sized fruits with unmistakable yellow-to-green and darker-green vertical striping on the skin that resembles the pattern of a tiger or the appearance of a watermelon rind, creating an arresting visual display unlike any other commonly grown fig. The striped skin pattern is formed by differential ripening of the fruit skin, with the yellow portions ripening ahead of the green stripes and both shifting gradually toward gold-and-green as the fruit matures. The interior flesh is light strawberry-red to pale rose — the flesh color and an unusually sweet, almost strawberry-like flavor that gives 'Strawberry Fig' its other common name. The ornamental quality of Panache at all stages of fruit development makes it an outstanding specimen tree for edible landscape use — the striped fruits hanging in clusters from late summer through fall are genuinely decorative. Production is somewhat lower than some other cultivars — Panache prioritizes flavor quality over quantity. In zone 9, Panache is grown successfully as a standard landscape fig tree; it is somewhat less cold-hardy than varieties like Celeste and may need frost protection below 20°F.

This extremely fast-growing pioneer tree bears small, soft, cotton-candy-sweet red berries almost continuously in warm weather, often fruiting within its first year or two from seed. It tolerates poor soil and drought once established but is reliably hardy only in zone 10-11, so Gulf Coast growers farther north typically grow it in a large pot that can be sheltered indoors during freeze events. Fruit is eaten fresh, dropping by the handful onto the ground when ripe, and it draws strong bird and wildlife interest, making it a useful fast-establishing pollinator and wildlife planting in warm-climate food forests.

Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Panama Red is a purple-red-skinned passionfruit selection valued for producing larger fruit than many standard purple passionfruit types, with rich, aromatic, tart-sweet pulp well suited to both fresh eating and juicing. The vigorous vine climbs quickly and begins bearing within its first year from a rooted cutting, dropping ripe fruit naturally from the vine when ready to harvest. Provide sturdy support and pinch new growth periodically to keep the vine directing energy into fruiting wood rather than unchecked vegetative sprawl. In zone 9, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily each winter, since this cultivar shares the cold sensitivity typical of purple passionfruit and can be damaged or killed by a hard freeze.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Panamint is a low-chill freestone nectarine developed for mild-winter growing regions, producing medium-to-large, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit with a sweet-tart balance typical of good dessert nectarines. Its comparatively low chilling requirement lets it flower and fruit reliably in areas like the Gulf South and lower South where standard high-chill nectarines fail to leaf out and bloom evenly. The tree is self-fruitful and ripens in early-to-mid summer; thin fruit to four to six inches apart along the branch in years of heavy set to improve size and reduce limb strain.

common_name: Paradise Nut (Zabucajo, Monkey Pot, Sapucaia Nut)
notes: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic, deep soil; Paradise Nut Tree grows best in conditions that approximate the humid, fertile soils of its native Amazonian rainforest habitat — deep, moist, well-drained, organic-rich soil with regular rainfall. Lecythis zabucajo is a large, majestic tropical tree from the Amazon Basin (Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, Brazil) in the Brazil-nut family (Lecythidaceae), grown for its edible seeds and as a remarkable ornamental specimen. The tree is closely related to the Brazil Nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and produces similar large, round, woody pods — but with a crucial difference: the pod of L. zabucajo has a natural operculum (lid) that opens at maturity to release the seeds, while the Brazil Nut pod does not open and must be cracked. The open-lidded pods ('monkey pots') have a narrow neck opening that is a natural primate trap: a monkey can reach in and grab a nut, but cannot withdraw its closed fist, and must release the nut or remain trapped — a phenomenon documented and described by naturalists since the 16th century. The Paradise Nuts themselves — large, brown, oily, rich — are considered by those who have tasted both to be superior to Brazil Nuts in flavor and richness. In zone 10-11 collections and botanical gardens, L. zabucajo is grown as both an edible nut tree and an ornamental specimen for its year-round beauty, including attractive pink flowers.

Plant in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 10–12; paradise tree is a multipurpose tropical tree from Central and South America producing large, pinnately compound leaves that create a lush, tropical canopy effect. Small, fragrant, yellowish flowers produce clusters of small, dark purple olives containing seeds with 60–75% oil content — one of the highest vegetable oil contents of any plant, approaching the palmitic/oleic profile suitable for both food use and biodiesel production. The tree is extremely fast-growing (20+ feet per year in tropical conditions), drought-tolerant once established, and being actively developed as a low-input bioenergy crop in tropical developing countries. The red-and-yellow immature fruits and the dark purple ripe fruits are ornamentally attractive. Of very limited landscape use in the US outside zone 10–11 Florida, but grown as an agroforestry specimen.

common_name: Parfianka Pomegranate (Central Asian Premium Pomegranate, Soft-Seeded Supreme)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate drought, alkaline soils, and heat — ideal for zone 9a; harvest when the skin deepens to full deep red and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped (late September–November in the Gulf South); Parfianka arils are strikingly deep red and the juice intensely colored. Parfianka is a Central Asian pomegranate variety (originally from Uzbekistan or the broader Turkestan region, where pomegranates have been cultivated for millennia) that has become the acknowledged gold standard of pomegranate flavor among American pomegranate enthusiasts, consistently winning blind tasting competitions at California Rare Fruit Growers Society events and receiving the highest ratings in UC Cooperative Extension pomegranate variety trials. The arils are brilliant deep crimson-red — darker and more richly colored than Wonderful (the commercial standard) — and have a flavor combination that separates Parfianka from other varieties: intensely sweet with balanced acidity, complex fruity aromatics, and remarkably soft, almost undetectable seeds. The seed softness (characteristic of the 'soft-seeded' varieties from Central Asia) means the arils can be eaten whole without the crunching sensation that bothers some pomegranate consumers. The juice is vivid deep red, exceptionally flavorful, and produces the finest pomegranate juice of any commercially available variety. For zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardeners willing to invest in the best possible fresh-eating pomegranate, Parfianka is the clear first choice — a tree that rewards with the finest-quality pomegranates available in home production.

common_name: Parson Brown Orange (Oldest Commercial Florida Sweet Orange)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Parson Brown is the earliest-ripening common sweet orange, ready from October, and is notably more cold-tolerant than later-season Florida oranges, which historically made it valuable for the northern edge of the citrus belt.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Passe Crassane ripens very late and needs weeks of cold storage before the gritty flesh softens and sweetens. A classic French winter pear bred in Normandy in the mid-nineteenth century, it was for generations the standard Christmas and New Year's market pear across France, bearing large, round, russeted fruit with dense flesh that is notably gritty and unpalatable straight off the tree but softens into rich, sweet, fine-textured flesh after a long period of cold storage. Its very late ripening and exceptional keeping ability once properly stored made it historically important for extending the fresh pear season deep into winter, well after other varieties had finished. Harvest quite late in fall while still very hard, store cool for many weeks, then finish ripening at room temperature until the flesh softens fully before eating.

Plant Herrania mariae in deep to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil with consistently high humidity; maintain soil moisture year-round; protect from all frost and dry winds. Pataste is a close relative of cultivated cacao (Theobroma cacao) in the same subfamily Byttnerioideae, sharing cacao's characteristic cauliflorous pod production — the colorful, oval to elongated pods emerge directly from the trunk and major branches rather than at the branch tips. The pulp surrounding the seeds is white, translucent, and sweet (similar to cacao pulp, eaten fresh or fermented for beverages); the seeds themselves are bitter and high in theobromine like cacao, and have historically been used by Amazonian peoples as a cacao substitute or mixed with true cacao for chocolate preparation. Herrania is a genetically diverse cacao relative of significant interest to cacao breeders for disease-resistance genes, and several species produce viable chocolate-flavored pods. Growing in the deep, humid, understory shade of Amazonian forests, Pataste is adapted to conditions of very high humidity, no frost, and dappled to deep shade — making it a perfect choice for shaded positions in zone 10–12 tropical gardens where true cacao may grow poorly in full exposure.

Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Pawnee is one of the finest pecan cultivars for the Gulf South — a USDA Agricultural Research Service introduction that has become one of the most widely planted pecans in the region for its combination of outstanding nut quality, large nut size, excellent kernel percentage (55–57%), early maturity, and partial scab resistance. Pawnee's most significant attribute is its very early maturity: it ripens 2–3 weeks earlier than Desirable, Stuart, and other standard cultivars, meaning Pawnee nuts are falling in late September to early October in zone 9 — well ahead of the alternating wet/dry weather cycles of mid-fall that cause many pecan cultivars to develop scab and quality losses. The large, thin-shelled nuts have excellent quality with bright, sweet-tasting kernels and very good percentage fill. Pawnee is a Type II pecan (protandrous pollen shedding) — it produces pollen when its own female flowers are not yet receptive, requiring cross-pollination from a Type I cultivar (like Desirable) for maximum yields. This cross-pollination requirement is easy to meet in the Gulf South where multiple pecan cultivars are commonly grown in close proximity. Pawnee is moderately susceptible to pecan scab — preventive fungicide applications during leaf-out and through spring are important in humid Gulf South conditions.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zones 9–12; peanut butter fruit earns its name from the distinctive flavor of the ripe orange-red fruits — the flesh surrounding the seeds has a rich, somewhat sticky texture and flavor uncannily reminiscent of peanut butter, combined with subtle sweet notes. Native to Peru and the Andes, this ornamental shrub is surprisingly adaptable to Gulf Coast conditions in zones 9–11, where it fruits prolifically on an almost continuous basis in warm seasons. The small, bright yellow flowers are attractive and produced repeatedly throughout the year in warm climates. The fruit are eaten fresh from the shrub or used in smoothies, ice cream, and desserts throughout South America. Unusually shade-tolerant for a fruiting tropical — it can produce reasonably well in the bright filtered light beneath a high canopy, making it valuable for partially shaded garden positions.

common_name: Peanut Butter Fruit (Amazon Peanut Butter Tree, Peanut Butter Plant)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Peanut Butter Fruit is adaptable to a range of soil types and is moderately drought tolerant once established, performing reliably in zone 9b-12 as an evergreen fruiting shrub-tree. Bunchosia glandulifera is an evergreen to semi-deciduous, large shrub to small tree native to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, and the Amazon basin in the Malpighiaceae family — the same family as Acerola (Malpighia emarginata), from which the distinctive wing-petaled yellow flowers of Bunchosia are recognizable. The plant produces ovate, dark-green, glossy leaves and clusters of small (0.5-inch) yellow flowers with the characteristic wing-petaled (fringed petal margin) form typical of the Malpighiaceae. The flowers are followed by oval fruits, 1–1.5 inches long, that ripen progressively from pale green through yellow-orange to deep red-orange. The ripe flesh of Bunchosia glandulifera fruit is thick, sweet, slightly dry in texture, and has a flavor that is remarkably and unmistakably reminiscent of smooth peanut butter — sweet, rich, and nutty, without any actual peanut content. The fruit can be eaten fresh at the ripe orange-red stage (before it becomes overripe), blended into smoothies, used as a natural sweet spread on crackers, or incorporated into desserts. Plants are highly productive in warm climates and begin fruiting within 1–2 years from a large transplant or seedling. An unusual and genuinely delicious tropical fruit for zone 9b-12 gardens. Non-toxic.

common_name: Peanut Butter Fruit (Silver-Leaved Bunchosia, Gold Cherry)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Peanut Butter Fruit grows and fruits well in partial shade, making it useful for under-story tropical food garden positions under larger fruit trees. Bunchosia argentea is a fast-growing, evergreen shrub or small tree from Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia in the family Malpighiaceae, widely grown as a dooryard fruit tree throughout tropical America and increasingly available in South Florida and zone 10-11 Gulf Coast fruit collections for one of the most remarkable flavor descriptions in the tropical fruit world: the flesh of the ripe fruit has the precise taste and texture of smooth commercial peanut butter — sweet, nutty, slightly dry, and unmistakably peanut-like, despite having no botanical relationship to Arachis hypogaea (the peanut). The fruits are small (half to 1 inch), oval to oblong, and ripen from yellow-orange to orange-red, produced in clusters along the branches from the warm months. A single ripe Bunchosia argentea fruit consumed fresh is a memorable culinary experience — the resemblance to peanut butter is genuine and immediate. The plant is a rapid grower that begins bearing fruit within one to two years of planting and produces through the warm months. The silver leaf undersides (the 'argentea' — 'silvery') give the plant an attractive bi-colored appearance. An excellent, unusual addition to any tropical or subtropical home food garden.

Pecans are protandrous or protogynous depending on variety — pollen shed and receptive female flowers rarely overlap on the same tree — so always plant at least two cultivars of opposite types (Type I with Type II) to ensure cross-pollination. Northern varieties (Hark, Kanza, Lakota) are bred for shorter growing seasons and suit zones 5–7; southern varieties need 250+ frost-free days. Pecans are heavy zinc feeders; apply zinc foliar spray in spring if leaves show rosette symptoms. Harvest when shucks split open in autumn and nuts fall freely.

Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; pecans require at least 30–40 feet of space in all directions and are best suited to large properties with deep, loamy soil. Carya illinoinensis (pecan) is the iconic native nut tree of the American South and Southwest — the only major North American nut to have achieved worldwide commercial importance — producing sweet, buttery, thin-shelled nuts from September through November that are consumed fresh, candied, in pies (pecan pie is the most iconic Southern dessert), and in a vast range of confectioneries and baked goods. The pecan is native to the Mississippi-Ohio River basin and Gulf Coastal Plain, reaching 60–100 feet tall and living for centuries; established trees are drought-resistant and incredibly long-lived. Two trees with different bloom times (Type I — shedding pollen before receptive to it; Type II — the opposite) are needed for reliable cross-pollination and maximum nut production. Named varieties for the Gulf South include 'Desirable,' 'Candy,' 'Caddo,' 'Cheyenne,' 'Kiowa,' and 'Oconee' — all selected for disease resistance to pecan scab, the primary disease problem in humid southeastern climates. The trees also have significant wildlife value as a mast crop for deer, turkeys, and squirrels.

Plant Pepino Dulce in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; water consistently and feed monthly with balanced fertilizer; stake or cage as plants sprawl; harvest fruits when fully colored and aromatic, giving slightly to gentle pressure. Solanum muricatum is a domesticated Andean crop related to tomato, potato, and eggplant — one of the less commonly grown members of the Solanaceae family that produces a genuinely delicious and distinctive dessert fruit. The oval fruits, ranging from 2–4 inches long, develop beautiful purple streaking on a pale yellow base as they ripen, and the flesh has a mild, sweet flavor combining melon, pear, and cucumber notes with very low acidity — a refreshing warm-season treat eaten fresh, chilled, or in fruit salads. Propagation from stem cuttings is faster and more reliable than from seed, yielding fruiting plants within the same season; plants grown in zone 9–11 behave as short-lived perennials and may be cut back after fruiting for regrowth. In frost-prone zones it is grown as a warm-season annual from transplants started indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost.

growth_habit: Brazilian Cerrado iconic oilseed and fruit tree
notes: Plant Caryocar brasiliense in deep, well-drained, sandy, acidic, very lean cerrado soil in full sun; the tree is adapted to nutrient-poor savanna soils and performs poorly in rich, fertilized conditions; water moderately during establishment, then sparingly — it is drought-adapted. CAUTION: the inner seed coat (endocarp) is covered with sharp spines; eat the oily flesh from the outside of the seed coat with extreme care, using a scraping motion, or you will be impaled. Pequi is an ingredient of such cultural importance in Minas Gerais and the Cerrado of central Brazil that it has been called 'the soul of sertanejo cooking.' The intensely aromatic, golden-yellow oily flesh surrounding the spiny inner stone is eaten by scraping with the front teeth — a culturally specific technique that everyone from the region knows — in dishes like Galinhada com Pequi (chicken and rice with pequi), pamonha, and various cerrado preparations. The flavor is extraordinary and polarizing: powerful, complex, unmistakably distinctive, combining notes of ripe mango, roasted nuts, pungent tropical cheese, and a rich, almost buttery oiliness. The fruit oil is pressed for cosmetics, cooking, and traditional medicine. A crucial food for wildlife in the Cerrado: jaguars, tapirs, and many birds consume the fallen fruits. The tree is the symbol of Minas Gerais state and a cultural keystone of the cerrado region.

Perry pears are tannic, high-acid cultivars grown to ferment into perry, the pear equivalent of cider. These are famously long-lived, slow-to-fruit trees that eventually reach great size, so give them ample space and patience. Plant at least two varieties for pollination in deep soil and full sun. Little pruning is required once a strong framework is established; harvest the astringent fruit slightly underripe and let it sweat before pressing.

Persian Bearss is a prolific, thornless lime producing juicy, seedless fruit perfect for cooking and drinks. It is one of the more cold-tolerant limes but still needs protection below freezing. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and keep the graft union above the soil line. Water deeply and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, feeding with a citrus fertilizer during active growth. In zones colder than 9, grow in a large pot that can move to a bright indoor location for winter.

Plant in excellent drainage in full sun; Persian lime is the lime sold in virtually every grocery store worldwide — the standard 'lime' of commerce in the United States and Europe. The large, seedless, thick-skinned fruits (much larger than Key lime) are harvested green and provide the characteristic lime flavor of margaritas, guacamole, and countless beverages. Unlike Key lime, Persian lime is technically a triploid (3 sets of chromosomes), which makes it seedless and somewhat more vigorous and cold-tolerant than Key lime. It produces fruit year-round in tropical climates and has peak seasons in spring and fall in zone 9. Trees are also more cold-tolerant than Key lime (surviving to 26°F vs. 28–30°F for Key lime) and are larger and more productive under zone 9 conditions. Feed 3–4 times yearly with a complete citrus fertilizer; supplement with chelated micronutrients if leaves show yellowing. Freeze protection below 28°F is recommended; wrap trunks with frost cloth or move container trees indoors.

common_name: Peter's Honey Fig (Small Yellow-Green Sweet Fig)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate poor soil but grow and fruit best with consistent moisture during fruit development. Peter's Honey is a fig cultivar collected and popularized among southern fig enthusiasts for its small-to-medium, pale yellow-green fruit with a honeyed, richly sweet flavor that belies its modest size and unassuming skin color. The tree is productive and vigorous, producing a light breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer followed by a heavier main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Because the fruit does not need to color up to signal ripeness, harvest by feel — ripe figs soften and the neck droops — rather than by color change. Prune in late winter to control size and remove any winter-killed tips, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system through Gulf Coast summers.

Peters is the standard male pollinator paired with Kerman and other female pistachio cultivars in commercial and home orchards; it produces no nuts itself but times its pollen shed to overlap with Kerman bloom, which is essential since pistachio is entirely wind-pollinated and dioecious. Grow it under the same demanding regime as female pistachio trees: deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, 700-1000 winter chill hours, and hot, dry summers, conditions that make the species a poor match for humid climates regardless of cultivar. In a home planting, a single Peters tree, sited centrally or upwind of the prevailing spring breeze, is usually enough to pollinate several female trees. Because it carries no fruit load, Peters tends to grow a bit more vigorously and can be pruned harder to keep its canopy from overtopping the females it is meant to serve.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Petite Aubique is a French compact fig variety producing small to medium, teardrop-shaped fruits with violet to brown skin and amber flesh — a mild, delicate, honey-sweet flavor suitable for fresh eating and preserves. The compact tree habit (smaller than most standard fig varieties) makes Petite Aubique one of the better options for container growing in large pots or half-barrels on patios and decks. The smaller plant size does not compromise productivity significantly; established container-grown Petite Aubique can produce 50–100 fruits annually. The small fruit size (1–1.5 inches) makes them a good all-in-one fresh-eating fig — no slicing required. In zone 9 the compact habit and full-sun requirement make it an excellent choice for warm south-facing walls or enclosed courtyards where reflected heat can accelerate ripening. The name 'Petite Aubique' is also found in the literature as 'Petite Grise,' indicating possible synonym use in some regions.

Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — figs are adaptable to a wide range of soils but require good drainage and at least 8 hours of sun for maximum fruit production; Petite Negra is a naturally compact, dwarf fig cultivar producing small, round to pear-shaped fruits with dark purple to nearly black skin and amber to red, rich, sweet flesh — delivering the characteristic fresh fig flavor at a manageable plant scale that makes fresh fig production accessible to gardeners with limited space. The dwarf habit (3–5 feet in the ground, 2–3 feet in containers) is the primary distinguishing feature: Petite Negra produces full-sized, high-quality fruit on plants small enough to grow as container specimens on patios, to fit in small garden beds, or to overwinter indoors in containers in marginally cold climates. Container-grown fig culture allows gardeners outside the traditional fig belt (zones 7–10) to grow figs by moving plants indoors or into garages during winter; zone 9 gardeners can grow Petite Negra in the ground as a permanent, productive perennial shrub or in large containers for patio display. The self-fruitful nature (no cross-pollination required) and rapid return to bearing (often in the first or second year) make Petite Negra one of the most immediately rewarding fruit plants available.

common_name: Picholine Olive (French Dual-Purpose Table and Oil Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Picholine is a classic French olive cultivar from the Languedoc region, valued as a dual-purpose variety producing both high-quality table olives — elongated, firm, green-cured olives with a distinctive nutty flavor — and good oil with a peppery, herbaceous character typical of southern French olive oils. The tree is notably vigorous and relatively cold-hardy for an olive, tolerating brief winter dips better than some more tender cultivars, which has made it a popular choice for marginal olive-growing climates. Harvest green in fall for classic Picholine table olives, curing in a lye or brine solution over several weeks to remove bitterness, or allow fruit to ripen further for oil pressing in early winter.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to move under cover before frost; Pickering is a Florida-bred mango descended from Alampur Baneshan, developed as a compact, heavy-bearing dooryard cultivar for home gardeners with limited space. Fruit is medium-sized with a rich, sweet, aromatic, fiberless flesh and a flavor many growers rank among the best of the Florida dooryard mangoes, ripening over a fairly long summer window that extends the harvest compared to single-flush cultivars. Its naturally compact size and tendency toward heavy annual bearing make it a strong choice for zone 9 gardeners planning to grow mango in a large container that can be sheltered through winter. Reduce watering as fruit approaches ripeness to concentrate flavor, and protect the tree from any frost or freeze, since mango wood is damaged even by brief cold snaps.

common_name: Picual Olive (World's Most Planted Oil Olive, Jaén Spain Olive, Stable High-Polyphenol Olive)
notes: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Picual is extremely drought-tolerant once established; harvest for oil production in November–December when olives shift from green to purple-black; Picual oil is known for its stability and resistance to oxidation — it keeps significantly longer than most olive oils and maintains its flavor profile without going rancid. Picual olive is the most widely planted olive variety in the world, accounting for approximately 20% of total global olive production — concentrated primarily in the province of Jaén in Andalusia, Spain, which alone produces more olive oil than the entire country of Greece. The variety's global dominance is built on a combination of practical attributes: very high oil content (22–27% by weight, among the highest of any variety), exceptional oil stability and shelf life (Picual oil has very high oleic acid and polyphenol content that makes it resistant to oxidation — a critical commercial advantage since most olive oil goes rancid within 1–2 years), strong cold-hardiness relative to other major varieties, and vigorous, productive trees adaptable to the challenging calcareous, poorly-drained soils of the Spanish meseta. Picual oil has a distinctive flavor profile: robust, fruity, slightly bitter and peppery in the fresh-pressed (unfiltered) state — characteristics that reflect its high polyphenol content (polyphenols provide both the peppery sensation and the health benefits of olive oil). For home oil production, Picual's high oil content and excellent stability make it the most efficient variety for pressing, and its robust flavor is well-suited to the strong tastes associated with premium extra-virgin olive oil.

common_name: Pieper American Persimmon (Named Female Midwestern Persimmon Cultivar)
notes: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained to average soil; Pieper is adaptable to clay, sandy, or poor soils and very drought-tolerant once established; harvest by collecting fallen fruits from the ground after frost softening — fruits that separate easily from the calyx are ready; ripe fruit is completely soft and uniformly orange. Pieper is a named American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) selection that has been propagated through Midwestern and eastern nurseries as a reliable female cultivar with above-average fruit size and consistent productivity — characteristics that distinguish it from seedling trees of variable quality. American persimmon is a dioecious species, meaning most trees produce only pollen (male) or only fruit (female), so named female cultivars like Pieper must be planted alongside a male tree or a self-fertile cultivar (Meader) for reliable cropping. Pieper produces medium to large American persimmon fruits (1.25–1.75 inch) that ripen in October–November following hard frosts, developing the characteristic sweet, honey-apricot flavor of excellent American persimmon at peak ripeness. The trees are vigorous, drought-resistant once established, and productive across the range of Midwestern soils — making them a practical native fruit for home orchards where Asian persimmon would be marginally hardy.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in zones 10-12; Pierce is a California-selected cherimoya cultivar valued for its smooth-skinned, relatively small-to-medium fruit that ripens later in the season than many other named selections, helping extend the cherimoya harvest window into winter. The white, custardy flesh is very sweet with the classic pineapple-banana-vanilla flavor typical of good cherimoya, and the fruit's smaller size makes it convenient for single-serving eating. Like all cherimoya, hand-pollination by transferring pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers with a small brush in the morning greatly improves fruit set, since the flowers' timing rarely allows a single flower to self-pollinate and natural pollinators are scarce outside the tree's native Andean range. Grafted Pierce trees begin bearing within two to four years and need protection from frost while young.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in sandy, well-drained soil; pigeon plum is a native Florida and Caribbean understory tree related to sea grape (Coccoloba uvifera) that produces dark purple, grape-like fruits in hanging clusters that ripen in fall and winter — an important food source for birds and wildlife. The small fruits have a thin, sweet skin covering minimal flesh around a large seed, similar to wild grape, and are used in the same ways as sea grape fruits: fresh eating, jelly, wine, and juice. The tree is highly salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, and pollution-resistant, making it valuable for coastal landscapes where other fruit trees struggle. Leaves are evergreen and smaller than sea grape. Best suited to south Florida and the Keys outdoors; zone 9a requires frost protection.

Pignut Hickory is a stately, long-lived native nut tree, native to the dry to mesic upland forests and ridges of eastern North America from Ontario and New England south to Florida and west to Kansas, where it is a dominant component of the oak-hickory forest communities of the eastern United States. The small, pear-shaped nuts — borne in thin, pear-shaped husks that split into four sections at maturity — are intensely bitter to humans but form a critical fall and winter food source for white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, squirrels, blue jays, and wood ducks, making Pignut Hickory one of the most ecologically important native nut trees in the eastern forest. Rich, golden-yellow fall foliage and deeply furrowed gray bark provide ornamental interest in all seasons; the hard, dense wood is among the toughest and most shock-resistant of any North American tree. Direct sow fresh nuts in fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the deep taproot that forms in the first year makes mature trees virtually impossible to transplant.

Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained tropical soil; pili nut (Canarium ovatum) is the premier nut crop of the Philippines, producing large, elongated, olive-shaped brown nuts with an extremely rich, buttery, almond-cashew flavor and high oil content (70–80% fat, similar to macadamia) that many food experts rank among the most delicious nuts in the world. The tree is a close relative of elemi resin trees and produces fragrant, semi-translucent resin used in varnishes. Nuts are eaten raw, roasted, candied, or pressed for cooking oil; the pulp surrounding the nut shell is also edible, used in Filipino cuisine for cooking and flavoring. Increasingly cultivated in Hawaii and south Florida as a high-value specialty nut crop by tropical fruit enthusiasts.

Plant in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; pin oak is the most widely planted native oak in urban landscapes because of its symmetrical pyramidal form, fast growth (1–2 ft/year when young), ease of transplanting, and tolerance of clay and periodic flooding. The deeply lobed leaves turn brilliant red in fall, and the tree retains many of its dead lower branches in a distinctive downswept arrangement — a characteristic silhouette. Pin oak strictly requires acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5); in high-pH soils the tree develops iron chlorosis with yellowing leaves and declining vigor. Avoid high-pH soils or amend with elemental sulfur before planting. The small acorns are among the most important wildlife foods in eastern North America, consumed by over 100 bird and mammal species.

Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil — this tree tolerates periodic flooding better than most fruit trees and thrives in Gulf Coast bottomland conditions; pineapple mayhaw (Crataegus opaca) produces the largest fruits of all native mayhaws — round, bright red, 1-inch berries with a distinctive fruity, pineapple-like aroma that distinguishes it from the more common Eastern mayhaw (Crataegus aestivalis). The tart, cranberry-like berries ripen in April–May and are prized across the Deep South for mayhaw jelly, syrup, and wine; an excellent crop in zones 6–9 Gulf Coast gardens. Largely overlooked by commercial horticulture despite the outstanding jelly quality; a critical food source for wildlife including cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and wood ducks.

common_name: Pineapple Orange (Classic Florida Sweet Orange with Aromatic Juice, Historical Commercial Variety)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil with full sun. Water regularly in establishment year; tolerates some drought once established. Harvest January–March when rind is fully orange and fruit is fragrant. Pineapple Orange is one of the historically significant Florida orange varieties that shaped the state's commercial citrus industry in the late 19th and early 20th centuries — at its commercial peak, it was one of the leading sweet orange varieties grown in central Florida's ridge region, particularly in Polk and Orange Counties where the well-drained sandy loam soils and warm nights produced the highest-quality fruit. The name refers to the distinctive pineapple-like aroma of freshly squeezed Pineapple Orange juice — a volatile ester profile distinct from other orange varieties that creates a complex aromatic quality prized by juice connoisseurs. Florida horticulturists identified the variety in the 1860s–1870s as particularly valuable for its juice quality, and it became an important commercial variety until it was gradually displaced by Navel oranges (which offer better fresh-eating convenience with their seedless character) and Valencia oranges (which hold on the tree longer for extended harvest seasons). Despite its loss of commercial dominance, Pineapple Orange remained a beloved home garden and specialty variety in Florida, maintained by homeowners and small growers who valued its juice quality over the commercial virtues (navel convenience, Valencia storage) that made other varieties dominant. For zone 9a Gulf Coast gardeners, Pineapple Orange remains one of the most rewarding sweet orange varieties for home juice production — the fruit sets reliably in zone 9's warm winters, ripens to exceptional sweetness and flavor in January–March when fresh citrus is most welcome, and the tree's moderate size makes it manageable in home landscapes.

common_name: Pineapple Quince (Fragrant Sweet Large-Fruited Quince for Gulf South Preserves)
notes: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pineapple Quince is the most popular and widely grown quince cultivar in North America — producing large, round to pyriform, golden-yellow fruits with a distinctive sweet, pineapple-like fragrance and flavor that sets it apart from tarter, more typical quince. Quince (Cydonia oblonga) is one of the oldest cultivated fruits, native to the Caucasus region and grown throughout the Mediterranean for millennia — the golden fruit of ancient mythology may have been a quince rather than an apple. The raw fruit is astringent and usually not eaten fresh, but becomes transformed by cooking: quince turns a beautiful ruby-red to deep rose color when cooked slowly with sugar, developing a rich, sweet, floral flavor for quince paste (membrillo), quince jelly, and quince preserves that are among the most distinctive of tree-fruit preparations. 'Pineapple' is selected for sweeter, less astringent raw flavor than most quince — it can be eaten fresh when fully ripe (golden-yellow with red cheeks), though cooking still brings out the most complex flavor. The spring bloom — large, cup-shaped, pale pink to white flowers — is ornamentally beautiful and provides excellent bee forage. In zone 9, quince performs best in the cooler, northern parts of zone 9 (zone 9a) where it receives adequate winter chilling (150+ hours below 45°F); southern zone 9 may provide insufficient chilling for reliable fruiting.

common_name: Pink Trumpet Tree (Rosy Trumpet Tree, Pink Tabebuia)
notes: Plant container-grown specimens in full sun in well-drained soil; pink trumpet tree (Tabebuia rosea) is one of the most spectacular flowering trees of the tropics, producing masses of large, pink to lavender-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late winter to early spring when the tree is briefly leafless — creating a breathtaking cloud of color before new leaves emerge. Native to Central America and widely planted across the Caribbean and Gulf Coast, it is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and thrives in the alkaline limestone soils of south Florida. The wood is among the hardest and most durable of any tropical tree. Plant as a specimen tree, street tree, or focal point; the brief but spectacular bloom period makes it one of the most admired flowering trees in zone 10–12 landscapes.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinot Gris is a genetic mutation of Pinot Noir and shares that variety's preference for cooler growing climates. A pinkish-gray-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir, this white wine grape produces two distinctly different wine styles depending on region and winemaking approach: light, crisp, neutral wines when labeled Pinot Grigio in the Italian style, or richer, more aromatic, fuller-bodied wines when labeled Pinot Gris in the Alsatian French style. It shares much of Pinot Noir's cold hardiness and preference for cooler climates, along with a similar susceptibility to fungal disease in humid conditions, requiring attentive canopy management for airflow. Prune for an open canopy to reduce disease pressure in humid climates, and decide on harvest timing based on the intended wine style, since earlier picking favors the crisper Pinot Grigio style and later picking favors richer Pinot Gris character.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinot Noir prefers cooler growing regions and is notoriously demanding, susceptible to fungal disease and sensitive to heat and site conditions. One of the world's most celebrated but challenging red wine grapes, it produces thin-skinned, tightly clustered grapes prone to rot in humid or wet conditions, making it best suited to cooler, drier climates with good air circulation rather than hot, humid regions like the Gulf South. Its thin skins and tight clusters demand vigilant canopy management, leaf pulling for airflow, and prompt disease treatment, and it is generally considered one of the more difficult grape varieties for a home vineyard to grow successfully compared to more disease-resistant hybrid grapes. Site vines on a well-drained slope with good air movement, prune for an open canopy to reduce humidity around the fruit, and monitor closely for powdery and downy mildew through the growing season.

Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; pinyon pine is the most ecologically and culturally important small tree of the American Southwest — the source of the highly prized and commercially valuable piñon nuts (pine nuts) that are a cornerstone of both Native American foodways and southwestern cuisine. A two-needle pine (two needles per bundle) forming dense, round-crowned, picturesque small trees in the classic piñon-juniper woodland that dominates millions of acres of the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin at 4,500–8,000 feet elevation. Pinyon nut harvests are a major economic and cultural event across the Southwest — harvested by Native peoples and marketed commercially for centuries. The large, wingless nuts are rich in protein, fat, and calories. Drought tolerant to an extraordinary degree — essentially requiring no supplemental irrigation once established in appropriate Southwest climates. Trees live 200–1,000 years. Pinyon jays are entirely dependent on pinyon nuts as their primary food source. An excellent, slow-growing, low-water landscape tree for hot, dry, rocky gardens in zone 4–8.

Pistachio is dioecious — you must plant at least one male tree (typically Peters variety) for every 8–10 female trees; pollen is wind-carried. The tree requires 700–1000 chill hours in winter and blisteringly hot, dry summers (100°F+ is ideal) to ripen nuts properly, making it poorly suited to humid or mild-summer climates. Trees are extremely drought-tolerant and actually prefer alkaline, well-drained soils. Nuts are ready when hulls turn from green to red-pink and slip off easily; harvest by shaking limbs and collect nuts off tarps laid below.

Plant in full sun in rich, moist but well-drained, slightly acidic soil in frost-free conditions; pitomba is a small to medium Brazilian Eugenia producing clusters of golden-orange round to ovoid fruits about cherry-sized with smooth thin skin and juicy sweet-acidic orange flesh surrounding a single large seed — the flavor blends apricot, mango, and peach with a pleasant tartness. Trees are slow to mature but once established bear heavy crops excellent eaten fresh, juiced, or preserved as jams. Slightly more cold-tolerant than many tropical Eugenias, tolerating brief dips near 30°F on established trees. A rewarding and unusual addition to the zone 10–12 food garden.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Pixie Crunch, also released as Co-op 33 from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program, combines genetic immunity to apple scab with a naturally denser, more compact growth habit than most other apple varieties, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards or higher-density plantings where a full-size tree would be too much. The fruit is medium-size, crisp, and juicy with a lively sweet-tart flavor and good storage quality, ripening in the fall alongside other mid-season scab-resistant varieties. Because the tree naturally stays more compact, it requires somewhat less aggressive pruning to control size than typical apple varieties, though annual pruning to maintain an open canopy and good light penetration is still recommended for fruit quality and disease control in humid climates.

common_name: Pixie Mandarin (California Heirloom Seedless Late-Season Mandarin)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Pixie is a longstanding California heirloom mandarin valued for small, easy-peel, essentially seedless fruit with rich, sweet flavor, and for an unusually late ripening window that stretches into spring and even early summer, well past when most other mandarins have finished, giving a long tail to the citrus season. The tree tends to be moderately vigorous with a somewhat spreading habit. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality.

The pluot is a complex plum-apricot hybrid skewed toward plum, prized for intensely sweet, richly flavored fruit. Plant in full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and provide a suitable Japanese plum or another pluot for cross-pollination. Train to an open vase form and thin fruit to 4-6 inches apart to prevent overbearing. In cold regions protect the early blooms from frost, as flowering can precede that of many plums.

Pomelo is the largest citrus fruit — often the size of a large cantaloupe — and the ancestor of the grapefruit. It is less bitter than grapefruit, with a sweeter, milder flavor, and a very thick pith that insulates the segments. Trees are self-fertile but cross-pollination with another variety increases fruit set. Pomelos require heat to develop sweetness and need a longer season than most citrus — fruit set in spring is ready from October through February of the following year. Apply citrus fertilizer three times annually and maintain consistent moisture during fruit development; drought stress during sizing causes dry, pithy fruit.

Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 10–12; pond apple (Annona glabra) is a native Florida Annona that holds the distinction of being the only member of its genus adapted to flooded, swampy, and periodically inundated soils — growing naturally along the edges of ponds, marshes, and Everglades sloughs where it often forms dense thickets. The round to oval, apple-sized fruits are bland compared to other Annonaceae relatives, with a pale yellow to cream custard-like flesh that is edible but not widely prized for fresh eating; they are consumed by wildlife and occasionally used in preserves or as rootstock for grafting more flavorful Annona species such as cherimoya and soursop. Trees reach 20–40 feet at maturity and produce dense, evergreen canopies well suited to wildlife habitat, riparian buffers, and edible landscape plantings in consistently wet, low-lying sites. Pond apple requires no irrigation once established in suitable wet conditions and is tolerant of brackish water and poor, waterlogged soils.

Ponderosa is a lemon-citron hybrid famous for enormous, grapefruit-sized, thick-skinned fruit with tart, seedy flesh. It is compact and free-fruiting, making it a rewarding container tree for patios and sunrooms. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and keep the graft union above the soil surface. Water deeply, letting the surface dry between waterings, and feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In zones colder than 9, bring the pot indoors to a bright spot before frost arrives.

common_name: Ponkan Mandarin (Chinese Honey Orange, Taiwanese Mandarin)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ponkan (also called 'Chinese Honey Orange', 'Warnurco', or 'Batangas' in the Philippines) is one of the most widely grown mandarin varieties in the world, dominant in China, Taiwan, Brazil, Japan, and throughout Southeast Asia — though less well known in North America than Satsuma or Clementine types. It produces large (3–4 inch diameter), round to slightly flattened, loose-skinned fruits (the skin slips off in large intact pieces much more easily than tighter-skinned mandarins) with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid juice and deeply orange, highly fragrant flesh divided into 10–13 segments with typically few seeds. The flavor profile emphasizes sweetness and intense mandarin aroma more than tartness, making Ponkan distinctively different from the more acid Clementine and Satsuma — excellent for people who prefer very sweet citrus. Ripens November through January in subtropical climates. The tree is medium-large and productive under good subtropical conditions in zone 9–11; it is moderately cold-hardy (tolerates brief temperatures to 26–28°F when established). An outstanding landscape and edible tree for Gulf South gardens.

common_name: Portugal Quince (Large Highly Aromatic Heirloom Quince)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ideally in a warm, sheltered spot; Portugal is an old European heirloom quince long grown in American heritage orchards, prized above most other quince cultivars for its very large, intensely aromatic fruit and, uniquely among quinces, flesh that cooks down to a rosy-red color with a smoother, less gritty texture than most quince varieties — traditionally considered the finest quince for jelly and paste making. It is a somewhat shier, slower bearer than heavier-cropping cultivars like Meech's Prolific or Orange, and performs best with a warm site and attentive care in its early years, but the exceptional fruit quality has kept it in cultivation for centuries despite more productive alternatives. As with all quince, fruit is hard and astringent raw and must be cooked to develop its rich, honeyed, floral flavor. Prune to an open form for good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk, and harvest in fall once fruit turns golden-yellow and is strongly fragrant.

Train this vigorous, purple-fruited passion vine onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, watering deeply during dry spells to keep production steady. It is grown for its noticeably better cold tolerance than typical yellow passion fruit selections, often resprouting from the root crown after the top growth is cut back by a freeze. On the Gulf Coast growers mulch the root zone heavily going into winter and treat the vine as a root-hardy perennial that regrows each spring even where hard freezes are common. Ripe fruit, which drops naturally from the vine, has an intensely aromatic, tart-sweet pulp used fresh or for juice.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum (also called smooth witherod) is a native shrub of swamp margins, streambanks, and wet coastal plain forests that provides one of the most remarkable fall berry displays of any native shrub. The berry clusters ripen in stages through August–November, with individual berries changing from apple-green to blush-pink to rose to blue-black on the same cluster simultaneously — creating a stunning multi-colored mosaic of color that extends for weeks. The berries provide essential fall nutrition for migrating and resident birds. The glossy, deep green leaves turn burgundy-red in fall. The cultivar 'Winterthur' is particularly floriferous and berry-laden. Plant in rain gardens, bog borders, or any consistently moist location.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun at fruiting age; Potomac is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected by breeder Neal Peterson for dependable, heavy production alongside good flavor and size — a combination that has made it a popular choice for growers who prioritize consistent yield in a home or small-orchard planting. The rich, custardy flesh has the classic pawpaw flavor profile reminiscent of banana, mango, and vanilla custard, best eaten fresh once the fruit yields to gentle thumb pressure and has developed full aroma. As with all pawpaws, Potomac is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and full fruit set. Pawpaws thrive as an understory tree when young, so give newly planted trees light shade for the first year or two before they adjust to more direct sun, and provide steady moisture through establishment.

Prairie Fire is an ornamental crabapple that puts on a spectacular show of magenta spring blossoms followed by fiery fall foliage and small persistent fruit that feeds birds. Disease-resistant and adaptable, it makes a durable landscape tree for cold and temperate gardens. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches, and enjoy the tiny fruit as wildlife forage or for jelly.

common_name: Prairie Flameleaf Sumac (Texas Sumac, Limestone Sumac)
notes: Plant in full sun in alkaline, rocky, well-drained limestone or caliche soil; prairie flameleaf sumac (Rhus lanceolata) is the primary sumac of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau, a large shrub to small tree with narrow, willow-like leaflets that turn brilliant flame-red in fall — one of the best fall color plants native to Texas and the Gulf Coast. The small, densely clustered red berries can be used to make a tart sumac lemonade or dried and ground as a spice, and are a critical winter food source for birds across the Gulf Coast. Exceptionally heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and adapted to the shallow, alkaline limestone soils of central and south Texas where other plants struggle. Provides dense thicket habitat for wildlife and butterfly larval host for several species.

An English heirloom selected for reliability in cool, short-season climates, Preston's Prolific produces medium-sized, brown-purple fruit with sweet amber flesh and is prized for setting a dependable breba crop even where summer heat is limited. Plant in full sun against a south-facing wall or in a warm microclimate to maximize ripening in marginal areas, and mulch the root zone well for winter protection. It fruits readily on both old and new wood, so light annual pruning to remove crossing branches is usually all that's needed. This cultivar is a good choice for gardeners in cooler temperate regions who want fruit without a heated greenhouse.

common_name: Prilop Pecan (Historic Scab-Resistant Texas Native Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar nearby. Prilop originated as a native pecan seedling growing along the Lavaca River south of Halletsville in Lavaca County, Texas, and was propagated and preserved by grafters after the original tree was destroyed in a 1940 flood; it is sometimes also found under the names Steffek or Kallus after growers who helped keep the selection in circulation before wood was sent to the USDA-ARS pecan collection. Like many Texas native-type selections, Prilop produces a smaller nut than large modern commercial cultivars but is notably scab-resistant, an important trait for low-spray home orchards in the humid Gulf South, and it was recognized as a Texas Pecan Show state champion native selection. It remains a solid, low-maintenance choice for East Texas and similar Gulf Coast growing conditions, though it is generally considered less productive overall than higher-yielding modern releases like Caddo or Oconee. Correct zinc deficiency with a spring foliar zinc spray and water deeply during nut fill in late summer for the best kernel development.

Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil, shading young trees for their first couple of seasons before exposing them to full sun. Prima 1216 is one of the oldest named pawpaw selections still in commerce, originally chosen from wild Michigan trees by pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis decades before the modern named-cultivar boom, and it remains valued for early, reliable ripening and consistent, medium-sized fruit with mild, smooth-textured flesh. It tends to bear at a younger age than many other named selections, making it a good anchor tree for a new pawpaw patch. Interplant with a genetically distinct cultivar such as Sunflower or Wabash for cross-pollination, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom if fruit set seems light in early years.

Plant Princess Persimmon in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; minimal pruning needed — mainly to shape; the tiny fruits persist through winter and are best left for ornamental effect and wildlife. Diospyros rhombifolia is a gem of the East Asian ornamental plant palette — a compact, slow-growing tree or large multi-stemmed shrub that transforms dramatically in autumn. The tiny round persimmon fruits (barely 0.5 inch across) ripen to vivid orange-red and are produced in such abundance that entire branches become festooned with bright baubles, creating one of the most spectacular ornamental displays of any small tree in the autumn and early winter garden. The fruits are technically edible once fully ripe and soft — very sweet, but seedy and small — though most gardeners leave them for wildlife and ornamental effect. Autumn foliage also turns attractive shades of red-orange before leaf drop, leaving the brilliant fruit display on bare branches well into winter. An excellent subject for container growing, bonsai, and small garden spaces where a larger persimmon tree would be impractical. Dioecious (male and female plants separate) — fruiting plants are female; ensure at least one male plant is within pollination range for reliable fruit set.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Priscilla was introduced in 1972 by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program and rates very resistant to apple scab while also resisting fire blight and cedar apple rust, letting a home orchard get by with little or no fungicide spraying. The medium-sized, red-striped fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall. As one of the earlier disease-resistant apple releases, Priscilla helped establish the case that good disease resistance and good eating quality did not have to be a trade-off. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and harvest once fruit has developed full color and separates easily from the spur with a gentle twist.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois program, Pristine is immune to apple scab and shows good resistance to fire blight and powdery mildew, making it a dependable low-spray choice for an early crop. The clear yellow, medium-sized fruit has crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh best enjoyed fresh soon after picking, since it does not store as long as the program's later-season siblings. Its early ripening extends the home orchard's harvest window well before fall apples come in.

Prolific is a self-fertile, cold-hardy hardy kiwi bearing sweet, grape-size fruit with smooth green skin you can eat whole, no peeling required. Train the vigorous vine onto a strong trellis or arbor in full sun with rich, well-drained soil. Water consistently during the growing season and prune in winter to control its rampant growth and encourage fruiting spurs. Fruit typically arrives two to three years after planting.

Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained tropical soil; pulasan (Nephelium ramboutan-ake) is a close relative of rambutan (Nephelium lappaceum) native to the Malaysian peninsula, producing clusters of oval, red fruits with short, thick, blunt protuberances (versus rambutan's long, flexible hairs) — distinguishing it from rambutan at a glance. The white, translucent, sweet, juicy flesh is widely considered sweeter and better-flavored than rambutan, and the seed of pulasan is also edible (unlike rambutan's bitter seed) — roasted or boiled with a flavor similar to cocoa or almond. A premium tropical fruit rarely available commercially outside Southeast Asia; highly prized by tropical fruit collectors. Requires high humidity, consistent moisture, and no frost.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil; purple chokeberry (Aronia prunifolia) is a naturally occurring hybrid between black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) and red chokeberry (Aronia arbutifolia), often found growing where the two parent species overlap. The dark purple to purple-black berries are intermediate in size and flavor between the parent species, with very high anthocyanin content (among the highest of any berry), strong tart-bitter flavor excellent for juices, jams, and wine, and exceptional antioxidant properties that have driven significant commercial interest. The shrub offers year-round interest: white flowers in spring, dark glossy leaves in summer, brilliant red to purple fall color, and persistent berries attractive to birds through winter.

common_name: Purple Heart Pomegranate (Deep Purple-Red Aril Pomegranate)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate drought, alkaline soils, and heat, harvesting when the skin deepens to full color and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. Purple Heart bears fruit with a deep purple-red skin blush and arils that run notably darker than the bright ruby-red of most pomegranate cultivars, with rich, sweet-tart flavor and juice that stains a deep, saturated purple-red. Its striking dark coloring makes it a distinctive choice among pomegranate cultivars both for fresh eating and for juice with an unusually deep color. Prune to an open, vase-shaped form in the early years and remove root suckers regularly, since pomegranates sucker readily from the base; established trees are long-lived and require little routine care.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a strong trellis or chain-link fence; the purple passion fruit vine grows rapidly and requires physical support for the tendrils. Unlike the cold-hardy native maypop (P. incarnata), this is a true tropical vine that produces the familiar large, purple, wrinkled fruits of commerce, intensely aromatic with sweet-tart yellow pulp. Fruits ripen and fall to the ground when ready — simply collect them from the ground. In zones 9b–11 plants produce heavily twice yearly, in spring and fall. The spectacular 3-inch flowers with purple, white, and yellow corona filaments are among the most intricate in the plant world and are visited by bumblebees, which are the most effective pollinators.

Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a fence, trellis, or wire support; allow some room for root sucker spread. Passiflora incarnata (purple passionflower or maypop) is the cold-hardy native passionflower of the eastern United States, producing the most extraordinarily ornate flowers in temperate horticulture — each 3-inch flower displays five white petals and five sepals framed by a crown of lavender to purple, fringed, radiating filaments arranged in concentric rings, the whole structure appearing more like an alien artifact than a flower. Flowers bloom from June through September and are followed by edible, golf-ball-sized, yellow-green to orange fruits (maypops) with a sweet-tart, guava-like flavor used for jams, jellies, and drinks. The vine is the obligate host plant for Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterfly larvae — caterpillars consume the leaves, making it exceptional for butterfly gardens. Passiflora incarnata is cold-hardy to zone 5 (dying to the ground in winter but resprouting vigorously from roots), and in zones 7–10 it is virtually indestructible once established, spreading from root suckers.
