Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple-leaf plum (cherry plum) is a small Asian ornamental tree and one of the most widely planted landscape trees in North America for its combination of very early white to pale pink spring flowers — often blooming in February in zones 7–9 — and the dramatic burgundy-purple foliage retained through the summer. The species itself has green leaves, but the purple-leaved cultivars 'Atropurpurea', 'Thundercloud', 'Krauter Vesuvius', and 'Newport' are among the most common ornamental trees in American residential landscaping. Small, round, yellow to red plums are produced in summer and are edible, making acceptable jam and jelly. Self-sows readily and some cultivars can become invasive outside gardens in mild climates. Short-lived compared to other ornamental trees (15–25 years) but very fast-growing and reliably floriferous.

Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Qing is a widely planted Chinese chestnut cultivar selected for strong resistance to chestnut blight, dependable annual production, and a manageable, relatively compact tree form compared with seedling Chinese chestnuts; nuts are medium-large, glossy mahogany-brown, and sweet, dropping free of the burr for easy harvest in September-October. It is a mainstay of southern nut-orchard and food-forest plantings because it tolerates heat and humidity far better than American or European chestnut, sets a heavy crop at a young age, and shows good resistance to the ambrosia beetle and gall wasp pressure that troubles many other chestnut selections in the Gulf South.

Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun with at least two different cultivars for cross-pollination; rabbiteye blueberry is the blueberry of the Gulf Coast South — native to the coastal plain from Texas to Florida and naturally adapted to hot summers, mild winters, and the low-chill conditions (below 45°F hours) that prevent highbush blueberries from fruiting reliably in zone 8–9. The name 'rabbiteye' refers to the pale, pinkish color of the unripe berries before they turn deep blue-purple at maturity. Plants are large, vigorous, and long-lived — potentially producing for 40–50 years — with spring flowers that attract early native bees, summer berries that ripen over an extended period from May through August depending on cultivar, and attractive red-orange fall foliage. A fundamental food plant for Gulf Coast edible gardens that produces abundantly with minimal care in appropriate acidic soil conditions. The primary challenge in the Gulf Coast is achieving and maintaining the necessary soil acidity; soil acidification with sulfur or planting in raised beds filled with peat, pine bark, and acidic compost is often necessary.

common_name: Rainier Cherry (Blushing Cherry, Yellow Sweet Cherry)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Rainier is considered the premium sweet cherry cultivar — producing large, blush-yellow to golden-red fruit with creamy yellow flesh that is exceptionally sweet, almost honeylike, with delicate flavor considered superior to the firmer, darker varieties. It was developed at Washington State University in 1954 and named for Mount Rainier. The firm, thick skin makes Rainier more resistant to cracking than some sweet cherries, but the pale color means bird damage can be severe — netting is often necessary. Rainier requires 700–800 winter chill hours (hours below 45°F) to fruit reliably, limiting it to zones 5–8; in warmer climates, performance is inconsistent. A pollinizer (Bing, Black Tartarian, or Lapins cherry) planted within 50 feet is necessary for full crop production. Prune during dormancy to maintain an open-center or modified central-leader form. Bears fruit on spurs that persist for many years — avoid pruning productive spur wood.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–11; rambai is a medium-sized Southeast Asian fruit tree in the Phyllanthaceae family that produces large, pendulous clusters of small, grape-like fruits — ranging in color from pale yellow to deep pink or red — borne on the branches and trunk in the cauliflorous habit shared by many tropical rainforest species. The translucent, sweet-tart flesh surrounds relatively large seeds and is eaten fresh or made into juices, wines, and pickles across Myanmar, Bangladesh, Thailand, and Malaysia, where the fruit is a beloved seasonal treat sold in local markets. Trees are dioecious, meaning separate male and female trees are required for fruit production, so plant at least two seedlings or obtain a confirmed female tree grafted onto a rootstock. Maintain high humidity and consistent moisture for best growth, and apply a thick layer of organic mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist throughout the year.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; plant at least one male and one female tree for fruit production — rambai is dioecious. Baccaurea motleyana (rambai or rambeh) is a tropical Southeast Asian fruit tree native to the humid lowland forests of the Malay Peninsula, Thailand, and Borneo — closely related to langsat (Lansium domesticum) in lifestyle and fruit appearance, though in a different botanical family (Phyllanthaceae). The tree produces long, pendulous clusters of small (1–1.5 inch), thin-skinned, yellow to pale-orange fruits directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), similar in habit to cacao and jackfruit. The sweet-acid, translucent-white, jelly-like flesh has a pleasant, mild, tropical flavor — somewhat sweet, gently tart, with a slight astringency when slightly underripe. Rambai is eaten fresh in Malaysia and southern Thailand, and is also used in traditional cooking and beverages. The tree requires genuinely hot, humid, tropical conditions without frost — suitable only for zone 11–12 in the continental US (extreme South Florida, Hawaii). It is dioecious, requiring both a male and female tree for fruit production; grafted female trees are occasionally available from specialty tropical nurseries. Almost entirely unknown outside Southeast Asia in cultivation; an exceptional and very rare find for the dedicated tropical fruit collector.

Rangpur lime is actually a mandarin-lime hybrid (not a true lime) prized for its mandarin orange appearance, intensely sour juice, and significantly greater cold-hardiness than Key or Persian limes, making it a practical choice for zone 8 citrus gardens and container culture. It is self-fertile, productive as a single tree, and bears fruit nearly year-round in warm climates; fruit ripens to a deep orange-red color similar to a tangerine. Use the juice as a direct substitute for regular lime juice in cocktails, marinades, and curries — it is slightly more complex and aromatic. Harvest when the fruit has turned fully orange-red and yields to gentle pressure; fruit can be held on the tree for several weeks after ripening without significant quality loss.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Rebecca's Gold is one of the older named pawpaw selections, predating the modern Peterson Pawpaw cultivars and long maintained in pawpaw germplasm collections for its rich, deep-golden flesh and excellent sweet flavor. It is a productive, reliable tree that has stood the test of decades of cultivation among pawpaw enthusiasts and collectors, valued alongside historic selections like Overleese and Sunflower as part of the foundation on which today's larger-fruited cultivars were bred. As with all pawpaws, Rebecca's Gold is self-incompatible and needs a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination and fruit set; hand-pollinating between two open flowers of different cultivars with a small brush can improve yield where natural fly and beetle pollinators are scarce. Provide consistent moisture through the first two seasons while the shallow root system establishes, and expect the tree to fruit within four to eight years from a grafted start.

common_name: Red Delicious Apple (Hawkeye Apple, Most-Planted American Apple, Classic Red Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Red Delicious requires cross-pollination from a compatible diploid apple variety; harvest when the background color turns fully yellow-green under the red and the calyx basin softens slightly — Red Delicious harvested too late becomes mealy, while picked at proper maturity it is firm and pleasantly mild. Red Delicious is the most historically planted apple variety in the United States, dominating American commercial apple production for most of the 20th century and serving as the iconic image of an apple in American culture — the deep red, elongated, five-pointed shape was for decades what millions of Americans pictured when they thought 'apple.' The variety originated as a chance seedling discovered by farmer Jesse Hiatt on his farm near Peru, Iowa around 1872; Hiatt named it 'Hawkeye' and sent samples to a Stark Brothers Nurseries competition in 1893, where it won first prize and was renamed 'Delicious' (later 'Red Delicious' to distinguish it from Golden Delicious). Over the following century, commercial selection pressure for maximum red color and long shelf life produced the modern market strains with deep, all-red skin and elongated shape — but these selections simultaneously reduced the flavor quality that made the original Hawkeye notable. By the early 2000s, Red Delicious had become widely criticized for waxy skin, mealy texture, and mild flavor — a cautionary example of how breeding for appearance at the expense of eating quality can undermine a variety's standing. However, heritage strains and home-grown Red Delicious harvested at correct maturity are noticeably better than commercial examples. Highly productive and disease-tolerant in its home range of zones 5–8.

Plant seedlings in deep, well-drained upland soil in full sun, allowing room for a tall, straight-trunked tree. Red hickory is a native eastern North American species closely related to pignut hickory, distinguished by its reddish twigs and a husk that splits more readily and completely from the nut at maturity. Its kernels are notably sweeter and less bitter than those of true pignut hickory, and the tree is a valuable wildlife mast producer as well as a source of dense, strong wood.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; jaboticabas are slow-growing and may take 5–8 years to first fruit but eventually produce multiple crops per year. Plinia trunciflora (red jaboticaba or jaboticaba vermelha) is one of several species in the jaboticaba group of Brazilian native fruit trees — distinct from the commonly cultivated Plinia cauliflora (the dark-purple or black jaboticaba) by producing smaller fruits that ripen red to deep ruby-red rather than purple-black, with thinner skin, slightly sweeter flavor, and a somewhat shorter delay before first flowering after planting in good conditions. Like all jaboticabas, P. trunciflora produces its fruits cauliflourously — directly on the bark of the trunk and main branches, covering the tree's lower structure with dense clusters of round, grape-like fruits that appear to erupt directly from the wood, creating one of the most visually spectacular fruiting displays in subtropical horticulture. The fruits are eaten fresh or made into wine, liqueur, and jam in Brazil; they are thin-skinned enough that the entire fruit (including the somewhat tannic skin) can be popped into the mouth. Jaboticabas produce multiple crops per year in warm, humid conditions. P. trunciflora is noted as marginally more cold-tolerant than some jaboticaba relatives, making it a candidate for protected zone 9 microclimates.

common_name: Red Jewel Crabapple (Upright White-Flowered Red-Fruited Crabapple)
notes: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Red Jewel produces pure white spring flowers from pale pink buds, followed by an abundant crop of bright, glossy red, jewel-like fruit that holds on the branches into winter, providing striking color against bare branches and snow long after most ornamental trees have finished their season of interest. Its narrower, more upright-oval form than many crabapple cultivars fits smaller landscapes and tighter planting spots where a wide-spreading crabapple would not fit. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; shows good resistance to common crabapple diseases.

Plant large hardwood cuttings directly in well-drained soil in full sun — red mombin is a small tropical plum tree of Central America and the Caribbean notable for two things: the flavor of its egg-shaped, wine-red to dark purple fruits (a thin skin over sweet-tart orange flesh with an enormous seed, eaten fresh or in agua fresca throughout Mexico and Central America where it is called 'jocote') and its ability to propagate from large cuttings stuck directly in the ground — even fenceposts made from the wood can sprout. The deciduous tree drops its leaves in the dry season, then blooms and leafs out simultaneously in the rainy season. It is remarkably drought tolerant and is grown in poor, dry soils throughout the tropics. The small reddish fruits ripen over a long season and are consumed by birds and wildlife. An excellent low-water, easy-care tropical fruit tree for zone 9b–12.

Plant in moist to dry, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; red-flowering currant is a Pacific Northwest native shrub and one of the most spectacular early-spring-blooming shrubs for Pacific Coast gardens, producing pendulous clusters of deep rose-red to carmine-pink flowers in March and April before the leaves emerge. It is the first major nectar source for returning rufous hummingbirds on their northward spring migration, and hummingbirds converge on flowering specimens in large numbers. The timing of its bloom — earliest of any showy ornamental shrub in coastal Pacific Northwest gardens — combined with its value to hummingbirds and other early pollinators makes it ecologically as well as ornamentally outstanding. The flowers are followed by small, blue-black, bloom-covered berries attractive to birds. The maple-like, aromatic leaves are attractive through summer and the shrub develops an open, graceful form. Highly drought-tolerant once established and naturally adapted to the summer-dry Pacific Coast climate. The cultivar range includes colors from white through all shades of pink to deep crimson.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Redfree was released by the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois cooperative breeding program in 1981 and is field-immune to apple scab while also resisting the other major fungal and bacterial apple diseases, making it one of the most reliably low-spray apples available. It ripens earlier than most disease-resistant varieties, giving a mid-to-late-summer crop of medium-sized, bright red, crisp, juicy fruit with a mild, sweet flavor good for fresh eating. Because it is one of the earliest scab-immune apples to ripen, Redfree is a good choice for gardeners who want disease resistance without waiting until fall for the harvest. Plant with a compatible pollinator variety and pick fruit once it has developed full color and separates easily from the spur.

common_name: Reliance Grape (Cold-Hardy Pink Seedless Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune heavily each winter using a cane-pruning system. Reliance was bred at the University of Arkansas and is prized for its outstanding cold hardiness among seedless grapes, along with medium-sized pink-red berries that are sweet, tender-skinned, and easy to eat fresh off the cluster. It ripens in midseason and is self-fruitful, though thinning clusters improves berry size and vine longevity. Because it needs sustained winter chill to perform well, it is best suited to northern and mid-South gardens rather than the humid, mild-winter Gulf Coast, where muscadines and Pierce's-tolerant hybrids are more reliable.

common_name: Reliance Seedless Grape (Red Seedless Home Garden Grape, Hardy Seedless)
notes: Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun; spur-prune in late winter to 2 buds per spur; Reliance is self-fruitful; fruit ripens mid-August in most zones; the medium-sized, rose-red to red berries are seedless, tender-skinned, and sweet with a mild, pleasant flavor more subtle than Concord; excellent for fresh eating, fruit salads, and home winemaking. Reliance seedless grape is a University of Arkansas-bred red seedless table grape (released 1982, bred by James Moore) that became the most widely planted cold-hardy seedless home garden grape in the United States, filling a genuine need for a sweet, seedless fresh-eating grape that could be grown reliably in zones 4–8 where the California-bred Thompson Seedless and Flame Red Seedless (developed for California's mild winters and low humidity) perform poorly or inconsistently. The breeding background of Reliance includes multiple American Labrusca and hybrid species crosses selected for cold-hardiness, which gives the variety a very cold-tolerant profile — mature canes are hardy to -15°F and the variety tolerates late spring frosts reasonably well. The berries are medium-sized, red-rose to medium red (lighter than dark blue varieties like Mars), round to slightly oval, and truly seedless with a tender, non-slip skin (unlike the slip-skin character of Concord and Niagara). The flavor is sweet, mild, and pleasantly fruity without the strong Labrusca 'foxiness' of slip-skin varieties — closer to the flavor profile of commercial seedless grapes but with its own mild aromatic quality. Reliance is a productive, reliable variety that earns its place as the standard seedless home garden grape for most of the northern and central United States.

common_name: Republic of Texas Lime (Cold-Hardy Thornless Lime)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, or grow in a large container that can be sheltered during hard freezes; Republic of Texas is a nearly thornless lime of uncertain hybrid parentage that has become a favorite dooryard and patio citrus across the Gulf South because it is noticeably more cold-tolerant and heat-tolerant than true Key lime, while still delivering a strongly aromatic, classic lime flavor. Trees are vigorous, heavy-bearing, and begin fruiting young, producing abundant small to medium, thin-skinned, seedy fruit that ripens from pale green to yellow — harvest while still green for the brightest acidity, since fully yellow fruit turns sweeter and less lime-like. It is self-fertile and does not need a pollinizer. In zone 9a, site trees against a south-facing wall for extra winter protection and wrap or cover young trees during freeze events; established in-ground trees recover from light freeze damage by resprouting from the trunk. Fertilize with a citrus-specific blend three times during the growing season and keep the root zone mulched but not piled against the trunk.

Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Revival is an American-Chinese hybrid chestnut developed as part of the blight-resistant breeding lineage that also produced the well-known Dunstan chestnut, combining some of the American chestnut's tree form and nut quality with the Chinese chestnut's resistance to chestnut blight. Trees bear precociously, often within a few years of planting, and produce medium to large, sweet nuts that drop free of the burr for easy harvest in fall. Because it carries genuine blight resistance rather than simply avoidance, Revival can be planted with more confidence in areas with a history of chestnut blight pressure than pure American chestnut. Good heat tolerance makes it a reasonable choice for Gulf South food-forest and small-orchard plantings, though as with all chestnuts, well-drained soil and good air circulation help minimize disease pressure in humid summers.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; riberry can be pruned as a formal hedge or left to grow as a specimen small tree. Syzygium luehmannii (riberry or small-leaf lillypilly) is an Australian native rainforest tree from the subtropical and warm-temperate rainforests of New South Wales and Queensland — one of the most commercially important of the Australian lilly pilly (Syzygium) species in the native food industry. The tree produces abundant clusters of small (1/2-inch), teardrop-shaped, vivid magenta-crimson fruits, and is one of the most prolific and reliable fruiting lilly pillies in the genus. The riberry flavor is unique and highly prized: sour, fruity, and sweet with distinctive warm cinnamon-clove spice notes from the high eugenol content — a flavor combination with no equivalent in European or American fruits. In Australian native food (bushfood) cuisine, riberries are used in jams, sauces, wines, ice creams, vinegars, and as a garnish for savory dishes — particularly with game, lamb, and cheese. As a landscape plant, riberry is compact, attractive, and responds very well to formal clipping into hedge shapes; the coppery-red new growth flushes make it ornamentally outstanding. Its combination of ornamental and food value makes it one of the best lilly pillies for zone 9–12 edible landscapes.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Ribston Pippin is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby. Raised in Yorkshire, England around 1707 and one of the two parent varieties of the famous Cox's Orange Pippin, it bears medium, orange-red-flushed, lightly russeted apples with rich, aromatic, sharp-sweet flesh that made it one of the most celebrated English dessert apples of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries before its own offspring largely eclipsed its popularity. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination, and it can be a somewhat biennial, uneven bearer from year to year. Harvest in mid-fall and store for a few weeks, during which the rich, sharp flavor continues to develop and mellow slightly.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Riesling is one of the more cold-hardy classic wine grapes and performs well in cooler climates unsuited to many other vinifera varieties. Late-ripening, aromatic, and capable of producing wines ranging from bone-dry to intensely sweet depending on when the grapes are picked, it retains bright, food-friendly acidity even at high sugar levels, a hallmark that has made it one of the most versatile and food-pairing-friendly white wine grapes grown worldwide. Its relatively high tolerance for winter cold makes it a realistic choice for home vineyards in cooler regions where more tender vinifera varieties struggle to survive, though it still needs a long growing season to fully ripen. Prune for an open canopy to promote airflow and reduce disease pressure, and consider harvest timing carefully, since flavor and sweetness profile change significantly the longer fruit hangs on the vine.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, the warmest available location; Rio Red is a grapefruit cultivar developed at Texas A&M University through irradiation mutagenesis of Ruby Red stock and released in 1984 — and has since become the dominant commercial grapefruit variety in Texas, replacing both Ruby Red and Star Ruby on most commercial acreage. The fruit is the gold standard for Texas red grapefruit: large, with yellow skin blushed deep red-pink, and flesh that is deep crimson-red, very sweet (low acidity), with complex flavor and very few seeds. Rio Red's flesh has the deepest, most consistent red color of any commercially significant grapefruit variety, a characteristic valued by both fresh market buyers and for appearance when halved. The trees are vigorous and productive. Feed with citrus fertilizer 3–4 times annually and supplement with zinc and manganese chelate if leaves show deficiency symptoms on alkaline soils. Protect below 28°F. In zone 9 the long hot summers develop excellent sweetness and color in the fall crop.

Plant in moist to well-drained, fertile, loamy soil in full sun along riverbanks, fences, and arbors; riverbank grape is native to streambanks and forest edges across most of North America, from Quebec to Texas, and is one of the most cold-hardy wild grapes — surviving to zone 2. The small, highly fragrant flowers in spring are intensely honey-scented and attract numerous pollinators. The small, blue-black, tart grapes ripen after the first fall frost (hence 'frost grape'), becoming slightly sweeter and less astringent with cold exposure. This species has been critically important in wine breeding — it is a parent of numerous cold-hardy wine grape cultivars including 'Marquette', 'Frontenac', and 'Frontenac Gris' developed for cold northern climates. Also an important source of phylloxera-resistant rootstock for European wine grapes.

Plant nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes, in a sunny, sheltered location with well-drained soil enriched with organic matter. Keep the root zone evenly moist during establishment and reduce watering slightly as fruit begins to color to concentrate sugars. Robinson bears loose-skinned, richly flavored orange fruit that ripens earlier than most mandarins, often by early fall, but it tends toward seediness unless grown in isolation from other citrus. It is popular with Florida and Gulf Coast home growers for its dependable early harvest and moderate cold tolerance.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in part shade; robusta coffee grows naturally as an understory shrub and performs best with afternoon shade in hot climates. Coffea canephora (robusta coffee or Congo coffee) is the second major commercial coffee species, accounting for approximately 40% of world coffee production — ranking second only to arabica (C. arabica) but distinctly different in origin, physiology, flavor, and agricultural use. C. canephora is native to the humid tropical forests of central and West Africa (particularly the Congo Basin region — hence 'Congo coffee'), where it grows as a spreading, multi-stemmed understory shrub. Robusta coffee has several significant differences from arabica: it is more disease-resistant (particularly to coffee leaf rust — Hemileia vastatrix — the devastating fungal disease that has devastated arabica crops worldwide); it is more drought-tolerant; it contains approximately twice the caffeine content of arabica (2–4% vs. 1.2–1.5%); and it can be grown at lower elevations and in hotter, more humid climates than arabica. These traits make robusta the preferred crop for hot, humid, lower-elevation tropical regions including Vietnam (the world's largest robusta producer), India, Ivory Coast, Uganda, and Indonesia. The flavor profile of robusta — stronger, more bitter, earthier, with woody and chocolate-cocoa notes — suits espresso blends (where it adds body and crema), instant coffee, and cold brew. In zone 10–12 gardens, both coffee species can be grown for home production and as ornamental shade-tolerant specimens.

common_name: Rome Beauty Apple (The Baking Apple, Ohio Heirloom Baker, Rome)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Rome Beauty is the classic baking apple and benefits from being cooked rather than eaten fresh — its firm, low-acid flesh holds structure beautifully under heat; harvest in October when fully colored deep red, typically after McIntosh and Empire are finished; baked whole apples with butter and brown sugar are the signature preparation. Rome Beauty (often sold simply as 'Rome') is an Ohio heirloom apple discovered as a branch sport on a seedling tree near Rome, Ohio (Lawrence County) by Joel Gillett around 1816, propagated by his neighbor Alanson Gillett, and introduced to the nursery trade in the 1840s where it rapidly became one of the most important American commercial apples of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The variety has an unusual characteristic that defines its culinary use: the flesh is relatively low in acid and somewhat dry in texture compared to most eating apples, which means it is not the most interesting variety for fresh consumption but becomes exceptional when baked — the firm flesh holds its shape without collapsing, the mild, sweet flavor concentrates under heat, and the large round shape makes it the ideal vessel for a whole baked apple filled with butter, sugar, and spices. For a century, 'Rome' and 'baking apple' were nearly synonymous in American cookery. The round, symmetrical, deep red to all-red appearance also made Rome Beauty particularly popular with retailers when unblemished fruit mattered; a barrel of large, perfectly round, uniformly deep-red Romes was among the most visually impressive of any apple variety.

Romeo and Juliet are a pair of compact, extremely cold-hardy bush cherries that produce sweet, robust fruit good for snacking and baking. Plant both varieties near each other in full sun with well-drained soil to improve cross-pollination and yields. Space plants 5-8 feet apart and water consistently while young to establish strong roots. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain an open, productive shape. These dwarf trees stay small enough for backyard gardens and fruit reliably even in harsh winter regions.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Ronde de Bordeaux (Round Bordeaux) is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region producing small, round, dark-purple to nearly black-skinned fruits with brilliant deep red to garnet-colored flesh — one of the most richly colored of all fig varieties. The dark skin and brilliant interior make Ronde de Bordeaux a spectacular fresh eating fig and an equally attractive fig for jam and preserves where the deep color produces richly-hued products. The flavor is very sweet, rich, and slightly winey with the complexity associated with dark-skinned fig varieties. The compact tree habit makes Ronde de Bordeaux one of the most practical figs for home gardens and container growing — it produces prolifically despite its modest size. It is an early-maturing variety with the main crop ripening in late July–August in zone 9, among the earliest of the dark-skinned European fig types. This fig has become very popular among fig enthusiasts in zone 9 and zone 10 for its combination of early ripening, outstanding flavor, and manageable tree size.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; rose apple (Syzygium jambos) is a medium-sized evergreen tree in the Myrtaceae family native to Southeast Asia that produces waxy, pale yellow to cream or blush-pink, oval fruits with a uniquely crisp, crunchy texture and a delicate, unmistakable flavor of rose water — floral, lightly sweet, and aromatic in a way unlike any other fruit. The fruits are primarily eaten fresh out of hand, and their distinctive rose fragrance also makes them popular for flavoring drinks, syrups, and desserts across Southeast Asia and the Caribbean. The tree produces spectacular ornamental flower clusters of long, creamy-white stamens resembling shaving brushes before fruit development, making it a dual-purpose landscape tree. Rose apple is adaptable, moderately fast-growing, and performs well with consistent moisture and regular balanced fertilization.

Train on a cordon trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Roucaneuf is a complex French-American hybrid grape carrying genes from several wild American Vitis species alongside European vinifera, giving it real resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European wine grapes across the humid Gulf South within a few seasons. It is one of a small group of Pierce's-disease-resistant varieties recommended by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for gardeners and small growers in the region who want to make wine or juice without the constant disease losses that come with standard vinifera grapes. Harvest clusters once berries have colored and developed good sugar content, and expect the vigorous vines to need regular summer pruning to manage growth in a warm, humid climate.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; M. tetraphylla is slightly more cold-tolerant than M. integrifolia and may succeed in protected zone 8b sites. Macadamia tetraphylla (rough-shell macadamia or prickly-leaf macadamia) is the second of the two commercially important macadamia species — closely related to the smooth-shell macadamia (M. integrifolia) but distinguishable by its prickly-edged leaves arranged in whorls of four (the species name 'tetraphylla' means 'four-leaved'), and by the rough, ridged texture of its nut shell. Both species produce equally delicious, buttery, rich macadamia nuts with the same world-class flavor, and in commercial macadamia production, the two species and their hybrids are grown side by side with little practical flavor difference noted by consumers. The practical distinction for home growers is cold tolerance: M. tetraphylla is marginally more cold-hardy than M. integrifolia, typically tolerating temperatures of 24–26°F in established trees — potentially extending the range to protected zone 8b–9a microclimates in warm-wall or frost-pocket-free sites. M. tetraphylla is also slightly smaller in tree size. Both species benefit from cross-pollination, and planting one of each species is commonly recommended to ensure good nut set.

Harvest berries when fully dark blue-black and extract seeds by mashing and rinsing before sowing in fall into lean, well-drained soil in a sunny outdoor bed. The round, coarsely toothed leaves that give this species its name are a useful identification feature as seedlings mature through their first growing seasons. Roundleaf Serviceberry tolerates shallow, rocky soils and gravelly barrens far better than most shrubs, making it a strong candidate for challenging landscape sites. Plants begin bearing their sweet, dark berries within 2–5 years of transplanting and attract a wide variety of frugivorous birds during the midsummer ripening period.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Roxburgh fig grows rapidly and produces large clusters of edible figs. Ficus auriculata (Roxburgh fig or timla fig) is one of the most ornamentally dramatic and useful fruiting figs in tropical horticulture — a large, fast-growing tree from the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia producing the largest leaves of any commonly cultivated Ficus: enormous (12–24 inch), rounded, dark-green, slightly hairy leaves with a bold, tropical texture that gives the plant a genuinely dramatic visual presence, resembling a cross between a giant philodendron and an elephant ear. The figs are equally remarkable: large (1.5–2.5 inch), distinctly ribbed, brownish-red when ripe, produced in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and older branches (cauliflory) — the same unusual fruiting pattern as jackfruit. The figs are sweet, moist, seedy, and pleasant to eat fresh when ripe, with a mild, sweet flavor; they are also eaten as a cooked vegetable when unripe in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking (stewed, pickled, or curried). In Himalayan and hill-station gardens in India, Roxburgh fig is grown as a major multi-use tree; in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens, it is an outstanding bold-textured ornamental that also produces an edible crop.

common_name: Roxbury Russet Apple (Oldest Documented American Apple Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. First recorded in Roxbury, Massachusetts in the 1630s, this is the oldest apple cultivar documented as having originated in North America, predating the country itself by well over a century. The medium, dull yellow-green fruit is almost entirely covered in rough golden-brown russet, with firm, crisp, sweet-tart flesh well suited to fresh eating, cider, and long winter storage, since the thick skin sheds moisture slowly and resists shriveling. It ripens in mid-fall and was historically prized precisely because it kept so well through the winter months before refrigeration existed.

Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Royal Raindrops is a distinctive ornamental crabapple with deeply cut, purple-red, finely serrated foliage unlike the broad, rounded leaves of most crabapple cultivars, opening with a heavy flush of magenta-pink spring flowers followed by small, persistent red fruit that hangs on into winter as forage for birds. It shows strong resistance to the fungal diseases — apple scab, fire blight, cedar-apple rust — that plague many older crabapple cultivars, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a small flowering shade tree. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; the small, hard fruit persists well into winter, providing months of ornamental and wildlife value beyond the spring bloom.

common_name: Ruby Red Grapefruit (Original Texas Pink Grapefruit, First US Plant Patent Recipient)
notes: Plant grafted tree in full sun, deep well-drained soil; mulch for moisture retention. Protect from frost in zone 9. Ruby Red is the original pink/red-fleshed grapefruit variety and one of the most historically significant citrus varieties in American horticulture: it holds the distinction of being the first variety to receive a US plant patent, issued February 4, 1930 (US Plant Patent 1), when Bonnie Nance's discovery of a pink bud sport on a Thompson grapefruit tree in Weslaco, Texas in 1929 was submitted by Stark Brothers Nursery. The story of Ruby Red begins in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas — one of the finest grapefruit-producing regions in the world — where the combination of warm days, cool nights, and alkaline soil produces grapefruit of exceptional sweetness and flavor. Ruby Red's pink flesh coloration comes from lycopene (the same pigment in tomatoes and watermelons) — a pigment that accumulates in the fruit's flesh during the cool nights of the growing season. The variety has less red pigmentation than its descendants (Rio Red and Star Ruby, which were developed specifically for deeper coloration), but it was the original breakthrough that made pink grapefruit a distinct commercial category. The fruit is large (3–5 inches), mildly fragrant, with blushed pink skin and sweet, mildly acidic, aromatic flesh that made pink grapefruit the preferred fresh-eating grapefruit variety in American markets through the mid-20th century.

Plant in well-drained soil including poor sandy or salty soils where few shrubs survive; rugosa rose is extraordinarily tough and requires almost no maintenance once established. The intensely fragrant single or semi-double flowers in magenta, pink, or white bloom repeatedly from late spring to fall, followed by the largest and most nutritious rose hips of any commonly grown species — orange-red to scarlet tomato-shaped hips up to 1 inch in diameter that are exceptionally rich in vitamin C. Hips are harvested after the first frost when fully soft and red for rosehip tea, syrup, jam, and wine. The dense, thorny habit makes an excellent barrier hedge. Remove only dead wood; avoid hard pruning, which disrupts repeat flowering.

Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained, fertile soil in humid tropical lowland conditions; rukam is a large Southeast Asian fruiting tree in the same genus as governor's plum but bearing larger, rounder fruits (3/4–1 inch) with dark red to purple-black skin and acidic flesh that sweetens with full ripeness and can be eaten fresh or preserved. A handsome ornamental tree with large glossy leaves, it is grown in home gardens across Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines as both ornamental and fruit tree. Much less commonly grown than governor's plum but produces superior fruit quality and larger individual fruits. Slow to bear from seed — grafted plants fruit several years earlier.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; rusty blackhaw is one of the most beautiful and underused native fruiting shrubs of the Southeast, producing spectacular flat clusters of creamy white flowers in early spring, followed by clusters of dark blue-black berries with a raisin-like, sweet-tart flavor that can be eaten fresh or used for jelly and wine. The leaves have rusty-red fuzzy undersides (giving the species name) and turn deep burgundy-red in fall. It grows naturally on dry, rocky, limestone slopes and woodland edges and is extremely drought tolerant once established. The berries provide fall food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and thrushes. It can be trained as a specimen shrub or allowed to develop into a small multi-trunk tree.

common_name: Sacred Fig (Bodhi Tree, Peepal Tree, Bo Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Sacred Fig grows vigorously in tropical and subtropical conditions and should be sited away from all structures, pipes, and paving. Ficus religiosa is a large, semi-deciduous fig tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, one of the most sacred plants in human history. It is the tree under which Siddhartha Gautama achieved enlightenment, becoming the Buddha, at Bodh Gaya in present-day India — an event considered so significant that the tree, and its descendants propagated from that original specimen, are venerated throughout the Buddhist world. The plant is equally sacred in Hinduism and Jainism. Its distinctive heart-shaped to ovate leaves have an extraordinarily elongated drip tip — sometimes 2–3 times the length of the leaf blade — that evolved to channel water rapidly off the leaf surface in the heavy monsoon rains of its native habitat. These trembling, long-tipped leaves create a distinctive rustling sound in the slightest breeze, a quality noted in both botanical and spiritual literature. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and Florida, Sacred Fig is grown as a significant landscape specimen and street tree. In zone 9, it is best maintained as a large container tree or bonsai subject, moved to protected locations in winter. Small, inedible figs are produced and consumed by birds.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; young trees benefit from partial shade and consistent moisture. Dacryodes edulis (safou, African pear, or bush butter tree) is one of sub-Saharan Africa's most culturally and nutritionally important indigenous food trees, native to the humid tropical forests of West and Central Africa — particularly Cameroon, Nigeria, Gabon, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The fruits are produced in large pendant clusters directly on the branches: deep purple-blue to violet, oval-oblong, 2–4 inches long, resembling a fat olive. The fruit is not eaten raw — the hard, firm flesh must be boiled or flame-roasted to soften, at which point it transforms into a rich, buttery, smooth, avocado-like consistency with a unique, savory-nutty flavor profile. The fruit pulp contains 35–55% oil with a composition similar to olive oil and palm oil combined, making safou one of the most calorie-dense and nutritionally complete forest fruits in Africa. It is also a significant protein source compared to most fruits. In its native range, safou is widely eaten alongside corn, cassava, and plantain as a major dietary fat source, and is sold extensively in West African urban markets. Outside Africa, safou is almost entirely unknown but is gaining interest as a potential food security crop and agroforestry tree in tropical regions worldwide.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Saijo is an astringent Japanese persimmon of Japanese origin — widely considered one of the finest-flavored of all persimmon cultivars, with elongated, narrow, yellow-orange to orange fruits and exceptional rich, honey-sweet flavor that persimmon enthusiasts describe as superior to any non-astringent variety. Saijo is astringent when firm — meaning the fruit must fully ripen and soften to a jelly-like texture before the astringency disappears and the full sweetness and flavor develop. This is not a defect but a different style of persimmon use: fully ripe Saijo is spooned from the skin like a pudding. Saijo ripens in September to October in zone 9, requiring only 100–200 chill hours, making it one of the lowest-chill persimmon cultivars and extremely well adapted to Gulf Coast climates. The tree is handsome, drought-tolerant once established, and remarkably free of serious pests and diseases — one of the easiest fruit trees for Gulf South gardens. The striking orange fruit and vivid orange fall foliage create exceptional ornamental value in the landscape. Saijo can be dried (hoshigaki) to make the traditional Japanese dried persimmon candy — a process that concentrates the intense natural sweetness into a complex, mellow confection.

common_name: San Piero Fig (Teardrop Purple Italian Fig)
notes: San Piero is a vigorous heirloom Italian fig, also grown under the synonym names Turkish Brown and Negro Largo, prized for its medium-to-large teardrop-shaped fruit with deep purple skin and richly sweet, strawberry-pink flesh. As a common-type fig it sets a reliable crop without pollination, typically producing a light early-summer breba crop and a heavier late-summer main crop. The tree is notably vigorous and productive, reaching 15-25 feet if left unpruned, but responds well to hard annual pruning to keep it manageable in home orchards and containers. San Piero tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity well and is closely related to the fig widely sold in warm-climate nurseries as 'Brown Turkey', sharing much of that cultivar's toughness and reliability.

Plant in sandy, gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; sand grape is a compact, shrubby wild grape native to gravel bars and rocky streambanks across the south-central United States, distinguished from most other native grapes by its low, bushy, non-climbing to weakly climbing habit and small, glossy, coarsely toothed leaves. The small, dark purple-black berries are tart and seedy, generally more valuable to wildlife and home winemakers blending with sweeter grapes than for fresh eating on their own. Its greatest significance is historical and genetic: sand grape's exceptional drought tolerance and resistance to grape phylloxera made it one of the key wild American species used to breed phylloxera-resistant rootstock in the late 19th century, helping save European wine grape production after the phylloxera epidemic devastated Old World vineyards. In the garden or native planting, it is a tough, low-maintenance vine well suited to lean, sandy, or rocky sites where other grapes struggle, and it provides food and cover for wildlife.

Sand Hickory is a native nut tree specially adapted to the dry, sandy, acidic soils of pine-oak barrens, sandhills, and upland forest margins across the southeastern coastal plain from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Kansas, where it thrives in conditions too infertile and dry for most other nut trees. The compound leaves are distinctively pale and silvery-hairy on the undersides — a useful field character separating it from the similar Pignut and Mockernut hickories — and produce brilliant gold fall color. Nuts are moderately thin-shelled with mildly bitter to slightly sweet kernels eaten by squirrels, white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, and black bears; direct sow fresh nuts in fall at 2–3 inch depth in sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, allowing 90 days of cold stratification before spring germination. Once established, Sand Hickory is highly drought-tolerant and requires no supplemental irrigation, making it the ideal native nut tree for dry, infertile, xeric sites.

The sand pear is a vigorous, disease-resistant Asian pear species valued for its gritty, juicy fruit and tolerance of hot, humid summers. Plant two compatible cultivars for cross-pollination in full sun and deep, well-drained soil. Train young trees to a central leader and thin fruit clusters to one per spur to improve size. Its strong fire-blight resistance makes it a dependable choice where European pears fail.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangiovese is a late-ripening variety that needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature. The most widely planted red wine grape in Italy and the backbone of Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino, and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, it produces medium-bodied, high-acid, savory red wines with notes of tart cherry and dried herbs that pair especially well with food, reflecting the grape's central role in Tuscan cuisine and culture. It is a genetically variable and somewhat finicky grape, with dozens of recognized clones differing in cluster size, vigor, and quality potential, making clone selection an important consideration for a home vineyard planting. Prune to manage its naturally vigorous growth, thin fruit clusters if needed to concentrate flavor, and be prepared for a long hang time on the vine, since it ripens later than many other red varieties.

Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Barbara macadamia is somewhat more cold-tolerant than Macadamia integrifolia cultivars but still needs a largely frost-free climate to thrive. A rough-shelled macadamia cultivar selected in coastal California, it belongs to the Macadamia tetraphylla species, which is generally hardier and better suited to California's cooler coastal climate than the smooth-shelled Macadamia integrifolia cultivars more commonly grown in Hawaii and Australia, producing flavorful, high-quality nuts with a thicker, more difficult-to-crack shell. Its improved cold tolerance relative to other macadamia species has made tetraphylla cultivars like this one the more practical choice for California growers outside the warmest coastal microclimates. Water regularly during nut development, provide the most sheltered, frost-free site available, and allow nuts to mature and fall naturally before harvest and shelling.

Plant this popular Japanese plum in deep, well-drained loam and full sun, setting the graft union a few inches above the soil line. Though partially self-fruitful, yields improve dramatically with a second Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination. Prune to an open-center vase shape during the dormant season to admit light and air. Thin heavy fruit sets to 4-6 inches apart to size up the crop and prevent limb breakage.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile loam; Santiam is an Oregon State University release bred for strong resistance to eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that has devastated susceptible hazelnut orchards, while also carrying blight-immune 'Gasaway' resistance genetics distinct from some earlier resistant releases, which helps slow the disease's ability to overcome a single resistance source when multiple resistant cultivars are planted regionally. Trees are moderately vigorous and productive, bearing medium-large, round, good-flavored kernels well suited to both fresh eating and processing. Like other European hazelnuts, Santiam needs winter chilling and is intolerant of the hot, humid, disease-pressured conditions of the Gulf South, performing best in the Pacific Northwest and other cool-summer, moderate-winter regions. Because hazelnuts are self-incompatible and pollinated by wind-borne pollen in late winter, plant with a bloom-compatible pollinizer cultivar for a reliable crop, and expect the first significant harvest around year four to five after planting.

Santol is a fast-growing Southeast Asian tree bearing round, downy fruit with sweet-sour, cottony pulp surrounding large seeds. It requires a hot, humid, frost-free climate and deep, fertile, well-drained soil with steady moisture. Plant in full sun, allowing ample space for the large canopy to develop. Grafted trees fruit within a few years; harvest when the skin turns yellow and use the pulp fresh or in preserves and candies.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — including sandy, rocky, and calcareous soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) is a long-lived, slow-growing Mesoamerican tree that ranks among the most drought- and wind-tolerant of all tropical fruit trees, making it exceptionally well adapted to South Florida's coastal sandy soils, salt air, and seasonal dry periods. The small to medium-sized, rough brown-skinned fruits reveal a translucent, grainy, caramel-brown flesh of extraordinary sweetness — often described as tasting of brown sugar, pear, and malt — that must be fully ripe and soft before eating, as unripe fruits are astringent from tannins. Grafted trees of selections such as 'Prolific' and 'Tikal' begin bearing in 4–6 years; seedling trees may take 8 years or more. The tree also has historical industrial significance as the source of chicle, the natural latex once used as the base of chewing gum, harvested by the Mesoamerican chiclero tradition for centuries.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; sapucaia requires genuinely tropical conditions and a long time to first fruiting — a tree for patient collectors in zone 11–12. Lecythis pisonis (sapucaia or paradise nut) is a massive canopy tree of the tropical rainforests of Brazil, Venezuela, and the Guianas — in the lecythis family (Lecythidaceae), closely related to Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and sharing its remarkable botanical story. The tree produces large, barrel-shaped, very heavy woody capsules (4–6 inches wide) that remain on the branches and open via a detachable 'lid' at the top — these are the famous 'monkey pots' or 'monkey cups': animals (monkeys, squirrels, agoutis) reach into the narrow opening to grab the nuts, but if they grab too many, their fist is too large to withdraw, trapping them. The nuts inside (5–40 per capsule) are considered by nut connoisseurs to be superior to Brazil nuts: milder, creamier, less waxy, with an exceptionally smooth texture and rich flavor, very high in healthy fats similar to macadamia oil composition. Sapucaia nuts are almost entirely unknown in commerce despite their exceptional quality, because they do not store as well as Brazil nuts (the high oil content means they go rancid quickly) — making them a fresh-nut delight available primarily near their source. A magnificent collector's tree for zone 11–12 tropical gardens.

Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil; saskatoon (Amelanchier alnifolia) is the primary serviceberry of the Great Plains and Canadian prairies, producing abundant clusters of sweet, blueberry-flavored, dark purple berries in June that have been one of the most important food plants of the North American plains — used fresh, dried, and in pemmican by indigenous peoples including the Cree, Assiniboine, and Blackfoot, and now commercially cultivated across western Canada as 'saskatoon berries' for pies, jams, and wine. One of the most cold-hardy edible berry shrubs available, surviving to -40°F. Named cultivars including 'Thiessen', 'Smoky', and 'Martin' produce particularly large, sweet fruits. An outstanding prairie food-forest plant and edible landscape shrub.

Plant Satin Leaf in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees tolerate brief cold to 28°F; protect young plants from hard frost; no significant pruning required. Chrysophyllum oliviforme is among South Florida's most striking native trees, instantly recognized by the extraordinary bicolor leaves — dark glossy green above and covered with dense, copper-golden, silky hairs below — that shimmer and catch light dramatically when wind moves through the canopy. The tree grows in South Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks alongside Gumbo Limbo, Strangler Fig, and Pigeon Plum, and is a highly recommended native alternative to non-native ornamental trees for South Florida landscapes. Small clusters of tiny white flowers give rise to small, dark purple, oval fruits (less than 1 inch) — technically edible and sweet when fully ripe, similar in structure to small star apples (in the same family), though the thin flesh makes them a minor snack rather than a major crop. The fruits are enthusiastically consumed by mockingbirds, robins, and migrating warblers in winter. An excellent shade tree for South Florida native gardens, providing year-round color interest through the glinting copper undersides of its foliage.

The satsuma is a nearly seedless, cold-hardy mandarin that ripens early and peels with ease. It survives brief dips near the low twenties Fahrenheit once established, making it the best citrus for marginal areas. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and protect young trees during hard freezes. Harvest promptly when the rind colors, as the fruit puffs and loses quality if left too long on the tree.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Sauvignon Blanc is vigorous and productive but benefits from canopy management to control its naturally sprawling growth. One of the world's most popular white wine grapes, it produces small, thick-skinned green grapes prized for wines with pronounced herbaceous, citrus, and 'green' aromatic character that vary noticeably by growing region and ripeness at harvest, from grassy and tart in cool climates to tropical and riper in warmer ones. Vigorous and adaptable to a range of soils and climates, it is one of the more forgiving wine grapes for a home vineyard, tolerating moderate disease pressure better than some of its more delicate relatives. Prune to control the vine's vigorous, sprawling growth habit, thin leaves around fruit clusters to promote airflow and even ripening, and harvest based on flavor and acid balance rather than a fixed calendar date.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade in zones 7–10; scarlet kadsura is a semi-evergreen to evergreen twining vine native to Japan, Korea, and southern China, valued for exceptional seasonal interest across multiple seasons: glossy, dark green, leathery leaves that may turn burgundy in cool weather; small, pale yellow, fragrant flowers in summer; and spectacular, showy clusters of scarlet-red, coral-like fruiting bodies in fall — each cluster up to 2 inches in diameter and resembling a bunch of tiny rubies. The fruits are edible and used in traditional Chinese medicine. It grows naturally in shaded forest understories and tolerates deep shade better than most fruiting vines — one of its most valuable garden traits. An outstanding shade vine for zone 7–10 gardens where its combination of handsome evergreen foliage, fragrant flowers, and dramatic red fruit clusters provides year-round ornamental interest in difficult, shaded positions.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Schley became one of the foundational commercial pecan cultivars of the 20th-century South and is still valued for its thin, easily cracked papershell and rich, high-quality kernel. It has been widely used as a parent in breeding programs that produced many of today's more disease-resistant cultivars, since it passes along excellent nut quality even though the tree itself is fairly susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and may need fungicide protection in wet years. It remains a good choice in drier pecan-growing regions or where scab pressure is manageable.

Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; screwbean mesquite is immediately recognizable by its uniquely coiled, spiral seed pods — tightly twisted into a tight helix resembling a screw or corkscrew — unlike the straight or gently curved pods of other mesquites. The common name 'tornillo' (Spanish for screw) reflects this distinctive pod shape. The pods are edible, sweet, and nutritious, and were processed into food by Sonoran Desert indigenous peoples. The tree grows naturally along desert washes and dry riverbanks of the Southwest, tolerating the highly alkaline, sometimes saline soils of desert floodplains. The cream-colored flower spikes are fragrant and heavily visited by native bees. Increasingly rare in some areas due to agricultural development of desert floodplains. A distinctive, drought-tolerant native for desert Southwest gardens with excellent wildlife value.

Scrub Hickory is a rare and imperiled native nut tree endemic to the ancient, fire-maintained Florida scrub habitats of the central Florida ridge, where it grows in pure white sand soils of extremely low fertility that are inhospitable to most other plants. A small tree rarely exceeding 25 feet, it produces small, round, thick-shelled nuts with bitter kernels that are eaten by Florida Scrub-Jays, fox squirrels, gopher tortoises, and other scrub wildlife, making it a keystone component of the Florida scrub food web. Plant fresh nuts in fall in pure, infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained soil in full sun — excessive water, clay, or organic matter quickly kills this species. In cultivation, Scrub Hickory performs best in open xeric settings that mimic native scrub conditions, and benefits from the periodic, low-intensity fire that characterizes and maintains the Florida scrub ecosystem.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Scuppernong is a bronze-skinned muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) that is arguably the oldest cultivated grape in North America — the original 'Mother Vine' on Roanoke Island, North Carolina, is estimated to be over 400 years old and still produces fruit. It is the ancestral cultivar of the entire muscadine grape industry in the southeastern United States. Scuppernong grapes are large (1–1.5 inches), round, bronze-green to golden when ripe, with a distinctively musky, sweet, complex flavor very different from European grapes — they are used for fresh eating, wine, juice, and preserves. Muscadines are extremely well-adapted to the hot, humid Gulf South, where they naturally resist Pierce's disease, black rot, and other diseases that devastate Vitis vinifera grapes. Vines are vigorous and long-lived, requiring a strong overhead arbor or high-wire trellis. Harvest in late August–September when berries drop from the cluster at a touch. Prune heavily each winter, leaving only short spurs on the permanent arms.

growth_habit: Southeast Asian coastal ornamental fruit tree
notes: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Syzygium grande is fast-growing and tolerates brief waterlogging and coastal conditions — water regularly in establishment, then water deeply and infrequently once the tree is established. Syzygium grande (Sea Apple or Jambu Bol) is a large, handsome, fast-growing evergreen tree native to the coastal and freshwater-edge rainforests of the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, Sumatra, and the Philippines — one of the most important and beautiful tropical street and shade trees of Singapore and Peninsular Malaysia, where it is widely planted in parks, streets, and public spaces as one of the city's signature urban trees. The tree is spectacular in flower: enormous, cloud-like masses of small, white, 'powder-puff' flowers (characteristic of the Syzygium genus) cover the tree canopy in brilliant white floral displays multiple times per year. The round, green-to-pink-red fruits — 1–2 inches across, resembling small apples — are crisp, watery, mildly sweet, and edible fresh in the same way as the related rose apple (Syzygium jambos), though less flavorful. The fruit is also attractive to birds and wildlife. Syzygium grande is among the fastest-growing and most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the large Syzygium species and is well-suited to the humid tropical climate of coastal south Florida and Hawaii.

Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; seagrape is one of the most iconic plants of Florida and Caribbean coastal areas — a native evergreen shrub or small tree with enormous, nearly round leaves 6–12 inches across with distinctive red veining that deepen to a rich burgundy in winter. It grows naturally in coastal dune scrub and maritime hammocks, one of the very few trees adapted to grow in pure beach sand with salt spray exposure. The clusters of grape-like fruits ripen to deep purple in late summer and fall, eaten fresh (moderately tart) or made into jelly and wine. Seagrape is critical habitat for coastal wildlife and an important sea-turtle nesting beach plant; it is legally protected in Florida — never collect from wild populations. It is used extensively as a hedge, screen, and windbreak in zone 10–11 coastal gardens.

Seckel is a small, intensely sweet American dessert pear often called the sugar pear. It shows useful resistance to fire blight and crops reliably in home orchards. Plant a second European pear such as Bartlett nearby for cross-pollination, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil. Train to a central leader, thin the abundant fruit, and pick while still firm to ripen in cool storage.

Collect ripe fruits in autumn and extract seeds, then sow directly in a prepared outdoor seedbed or in deep pots left outside to receive natural winter chilling. Seeds require 90–180 days near freezing to break dormancy and will not germinate reliably without this cold period. Transplant seedlings to their permanent location in well-drained soil once they reach 6–12 inches tall, ideally in their second or third year. Patience is essential: trees take 7–15 years to bear their first crop of small, astringent sorbets, which soften and sweeten after a frost or brief bletting period.

Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Sevillano is a Spanish-origin olive cultivar known in California and other American growing regions as the classic large-fruited table olive, producing some of the biggest olives of any commonly grown cultivar — prized for canning and curing as whole table olives rather than for oil, where its low oil content is a disadvantage. Trees are vigorous and grow considerably larger than compact modern cultivars like Arbequina, so give Sevillano plenty of room to reach its full spreading form. Harvest green for classic Spanish-style brine-cured green olives, or allow fruit to ripen to black for a milder cured product; either way, fresh-picked olives are intensely bitter and must be cured in lye or long brine soaks before they are palatable. Sevillano is only partially self-fruitful, so planting a second olive cultivar nearby improves both fruit set and yield. Established trees are drought-tolerant and long-lived, tolerating the alkaline, low-fertility soils typical of much of the Gulf Coast and Texas Hill Country.

Shagbark hickory is a stately native North American tree recognized by its exfoliating, shaggy gray bark; it produces small, round nuts with thin shells and exceptionally sweet, richly flavored kernels prized over pecans by many nut connoisseurs. Trees are monoecious and wind-pollinated; two or more trees improve nut set but a single tree can produce modest crops. Seedlings bear unpredictably and may take 10–20 years to fruit; grafted improved selections (Grainger, Wilcox) begin bearing in 5–7 years. Nuts drop in autumn when the four-sectioned husk splits open; collect promptly before squirrels take them and cure for 2–3 weeks before cracking.

common_name: Shangri-La Mulberry (Everbearing Compact Gulf South Mulberry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shangri-La is a compact, everbearing mulberry selection valued for Gulf South gardens where the combination of heat tolerance, low chill requirement, extended fruit production, and moderate size makes it one of the most practical fresh fruit trees for zone 9 home landscapes. The long, cylindrical, dark-purple to black fruits (1.5–2 inches) are sweet, juicy, and excellent for fresh eating, jam, jelly, and freezing — the rich, complex mulberry flavor is one of the finest of any easily grown fruit tree. 'Shangri-La' fruits over an extended season (typically March through June in zone 9, with some additional fall fruiting) rather than in a single compressed flush — providing weeks of fresh mulberry harvest rather than an overwhelming glut. The tree's smaller mature size (8–12 feet compared to 20–30 feet for seedling mulberries) makes it manageable in typical home landscapes and allows netting to protect fruit from birds, which are very competitive with human harvesters for mulberry fruit. Mulberries in the Gulf South require very few chill hours (100–200 hours) and fruit reliably in warm winters that defeat other tree fruits. Established trees are highly drought-tolerant and require minimal care — the most significant maintenance is the control of surface root spread and the cleanup of fallen fruit on paved surfaces.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Shasta Gold is a University of California-developed mandarin hybrid combining the superior flavor of Murcott mandarin with improved disease resistance and the late-season ripening of Encore — producing large, orange, flattened fruits with a very low seed count (typically 2–5 seeds), deep-orange flesh, and a rich, complex sweetness that many citrus experts rate among the finest mandarins available. The fruit holds on the tree without internal quality loss for 6–8 weeks after ripening (January–March), allowing extended harvest over a long window. The moderate-sized tree is easy to manage and produces heavy crops once established. In zone 9 Shasta Gold benefits from afternoon heat reflected from walls or pavement to ensure full fruit ripening; place against a south-facing wall in marginal locations. Trees are typically grafted onto trifoliate or flying dragon rootstock for cold hardiness.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep, sandy-loam soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — shea is a true savanna tree adapted to seasonal drought; requires decades to reach full production. Vitellaria paradoxa (shea tree or karite) is one of the most culturally and economically important trees in sub-Saharan Africa — a long-lived (200–300 years), slow-growing deciduous tree native to the dry savanna and Sudan zone from West Africa east to Uganda and Ethiopia. For millennia, shea has been a tree of extraordinary importance: the large seeds (shea nuts) yield shea fat (shea butter or karite butter), a solid, ivory-colored fat with exceptional cosmetic properties — outstanding skin and hair moisturizing ability, high stearic acid content, resistance to rancidity — that has become one of the most sought-after cosmetic ingredients worldwide and is also a major cooking fat and chocolate substitute in West African cuisine. Shea butter is one of the primary cooking fats across the West African Sahel. The sweet, green, plum-like fleshy fruit surrounding the shea nut is also edible fresh — tasting mildly sweet with a date-like softness. The tree is considered sacred in many West African cultures and is legally protected in several countries — it may not be cut down without authorization. Almost never cultivated outside Africa due to its extremely slow growth and extremely long time to first production (15–30 years from seed); a truly generational investment tree.

Plant in deep, moist but well-drained bottomland or alluvial soil in full sun, allowing ample space for this eventually massive tree; shellbark hickory bears the largest nuts of any hickory — up to 2.5 inches wide — with a rich, sweet, buttery flavor prized as the finest native hickory nut. It is a slow-growing but very long-lived bottomland tree of river floodplains; young trees may require 5–10 years before setting significant crops, but established trees become reliable producers for 150 years or more. The bark develops characteristic loose, curling, shaggy plates even more pronounced than shagbark hickory. Plant in deep organic-rich soil with consistent moisture; drought stress in the first few seasons significantly delays establishment and nut production.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade when young (seedlings require shade protection) transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Shenandoah is one of the finest named pawpaw cultivars — selected by Kirk Pomper at Kentucky State University for its large, sweet, beautiful fruit with vanilla-custard flavor and minimal strong aftertaste that characterizes some inferior seedling-grown trees. Pawpaw (Asimina triloba) is the largest tree fruit native to North America, producing fruits 3–6 inches long with yellow-green skin, creamy-yellow flesh, and a unique tropical flavor reminiscent of banana, mango, and vanilla custard combined — sometimes called 'the custard apple of the North.' Shenandoah was specifically selected for mild, sweet flavor without the bitterness or sourness that reduces the palatability of some pawpaw seedlings. The large, heavy fruits ripen in September–October in zone 7–8 and must be picked when they yield slightly to pressure — they do not ripen off the tree well and have a very short shelf life (2–3 days at room temperature, 2–3 weeks refrigerated). Pawpaws require cross-pollination from a different named cultivar; two or more plants are needed for reliable fruit production. The flowers have a faint unpleasant odor to attract fly and beetle pollinators — supplemental hand pollination or adding flowering road-killed meat near the trees during bloom significantly improves fruit set. In zone 9, pawpaw performs in the northern portions; the deep South's heat and lack of winter chill can limit performance.

common_name: Sherwood Jujube (Louisiana Jujube, Gulf Coast Large-Fruited Jujube)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Sherwood is vigorous and productive in the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate where some Chinese jujube selections may show reduced vigor; harvest at the red-mahogany stage for best fresh eating; the round, relatively large fruits are excellent for fresh eating and air-drying. Sherwood jujube is a Gulf Coast-adapted variety that originated as a chance seedling in Louisiana — making it an American selection rather than one of the Chinese-originated varieties (Li, Lang, Honey Jar) that dominate the market. This local origin is significant: the Sherwood tree's parents were jujubes that had already adapted to the climate of coastal Louisiana over multiple generations, and the resulting variety demonstrates the kind of humid-heat tolerance and disease resistance that matters in zone 9a and Gulf Coast conditions. Jujubes are generally very adaptable and drought-tolerant, but Chinese selections optimized for the dry summers of northern China sometimes show reduced performance in the hot, humid summers of the Gulf South. Sherwood's local Louisiana heritage makes it a logical first choice for Gulf Coast gardeners wanting to diversify beyond the standard Li and Lang combination. The fruits are large (comparable to Li), round, and flavorful at full mahogany-red maturity. Trees are vigorous and productive with good disease resistance in humid conditions. An important variety for preserving and developing Gulf Coast-adapted jujube germplasm.

common_name: Shinko Asian Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Russet Japanese Pear)
notes: Set the bare-root tree in well-drained soil with the graft union above grade, then train to an open-center or central-leader form and thin developing fruit to one per cluster for larger size. Shinko is prized among Asian pear growers for its unusually strong resistance to fire blight, a major limitation for pear culture in humid climates, while still producing sweet, mildly tangy, crisp bronze-russeted fruit. Harvest in late summer to early fall once the fruit slips easily from the spur, and expect a productive, long-lived tree once established.

Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; shortleaf fig is the native banyan tree of south Florida and the Florida Keys — a hemiepiphytic strangler fig in the Moraceae family that begins life as an epiphyte in the crevices of trees or walls before sending down aerial roots that fuse around the host, eventually forming a trunk that can outlive the original host. Related to and similar in growth habit to the more commonly planted Florida strangler fig (Ficus aurea), shortleaf fig is distinguished by its somewhat smaller, more oval-rounded leaves with a distinctive drip tip. The small, rounded figs produced on short stalks are consumed by white-crowned pigeons, mockingbirds, and other subtropical birds. A critically important food source for south Florida's native bird community. More cold-sensitive than strangler fig, and restricted to zone 10–12. Used in native-plant gardening in Dade and Monroe Counties for habitat restoration.

Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun on a sturdy support, since this is a vigorous twining vine related to kiwifruit; silver vine is best known in the West as a potent feline attractant, with dried leaves, wood, and galls used in cat toys because most cats respond to its nepetalactol compounds even more strongly than to catnip. Left to grow, it produces heart-shaped leaves that often develop a distinctive silvery-white blaze in summer, small white fragrant flowers, and yellow-orange fruit on female vines pollinated by a male plant; the normal fruit is edible though mild and rarely prized, while galled fruit caused by a gall wasp has a long history of use in traditional Japanese medicine. Because the vine is very vigorous and twining, give it a sturdy arbor or fence well away from smaller plants it could overwhelm, and expect enthusiastic garden cats to rub, chew, and roll on any part of the plant they can reach, which can slow young vines' establishment.

Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Silverhill, named for the jujube-growing community of Silverhill, Alabama, is a heat- and humidity-adapted selection well suited to Gulf South conditions.
