This historic American jujube selection traces to the early twentieth-century Gulf Coast jujube plantings around Silverhill and Fairhope, Alabama, where USDA plant introductions from China were trialed and locally adapted decades before jujube saw its recent surge in popularity. It bears medium, round to oval fruit with crisp, sweet, apple-like flesh at the green-mature stage, sweetening further and wrinkling like a date as it ripens to mahogany-brown, and the tree is notably tolerant of the humid, disease-prone summers that can trouble jujube varieties bred for drier climates. Once established the tree is extremely drought-tolerant, largely pest-free, and requires only light pruning to maintain an open shape; harvest fruit in stages from crisp-green through fully wrinkled-brown depending on preferred texture.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting it in a warm microclimate such as near a south-facing wall in the cooler parts of its range. This satsuma selection takes its name from the historic citrus-growing community of Silverhill in Baldwin County, Alabama, once a center of satsuma production shipped north by rail in the early 20th century. Like other satsumas, the small, deep-orange fruit is essentially seedless with loose, easy-to-peel skin and sweet, mild flesh, ripening from October into December. The tree is notably cold-hardy for a satsuma, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once mature, which made it a mainstay of small Gulf Coast dooryard orchards.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; simpson stopper is a Florida-native small tree or large shrub with flaking cinnamon-colored bark, glossy dark green oval leaves, and small white flowers with prominent stamens that have a pleasant spicy fragrance — the flowers are followed by small, orange to red, berry-like fruits that are edible and have a pleasantly spicy, aromatic flavor used for wildlife food, flavoring, and nibbling fresh. The peeling bark is one of the most distinctive features, revealing warm salmon-cinnamon tones beneath. Native to the coastal hammocks, pine rocklands, and tropical hardwood hammocks of South Florida and the Florida Keys, it is exceptionally well-adapted to the calcareous, well-drained soils of peninsular Florida and tolerates salt spray, drought, and partial shade. An important nectar source for butterflies and the berries are eaten by many species of birds and wildlife, making it an outstanding Florida native wildlife plant for landscapes in zone 9b–11.

Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to very dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; singleleaf pinyon pine is the botanical oddity of the pine family — the only pine in the world with one needle per fascicle (bundle) rather than the 2–5 needles typical of all other pines. The stout, curved, single needle is one of the most distinctive identification features in the western flora. The dominant tree of the Great Basin at mid-elevations — forming the classic Nevada and Utah basin-and-range piñon-juniper woodland with Utah juniper (Juniperus osteosperma) across millions of acres of the intermountain West. Produces large, wingless, edible pine nuts (piñon nuts) comparable in size and quality to the two-needle pinyon's nuts — both species' nuts are harvested commercially and by Native peoples. The nuts are an essential fall food for many Great Basin birds and mammals, including pinyon jays, Clark's nutcrackers, and mule deer. An exceptional xeriscape tree for hot, dry, rocky Great Basin and Mojave-edge gardens.

common_name: Sioux Pecan (High Kernel-Percentage Type I Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sioux, released from the USDA breeding program in Texas, produces small to medium nuts but is valued for an exceptionally high kernel percentage and rich, sweet flavor that makes it a favorite among home growers for eating fresh out of hand. Its smaller, more manageable tree size compared to old-line pecans like Stuart makes it a good fit for home orchards with limited space. It is a Type I pollinator and needs a Type II variety nearby for good nut set. Scab susceptibility is a real concern in humid Gulf Coast conditions, so Sioux performs best in drier inland areas or with a fungicide spray program during wet springs; irrigate deeply during nut fill for the best kernel quality.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring in sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; slimleaf pawpaw is adapted to dry, sandy pinelands and needs sharper drainage than the common pawpaw of the eastern woodlands. Narrow, willow-like leaves and creamy white to pale yellow, nodding flowers set this small shrubby tree apart from the common pawpaw, and it bears small, fragrant, yellow-green fruit with the characteristic custardy pawpaw flavor, though smaller and less commonly harvested than named common pawpaw cultivars. Native to the fire-maintained sandhill and scrub habitats of Florida, Georgia, and the western Gulf coastal plain, it is well adapted to the region's characteristic dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soils and periodic natural fire, resprouting readily from its root system after top damage. It serves the same role as other pawpaws as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies and needs little supplemental water once its extensive root system is established in sandy soil.

Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in spring in any well-drained soil — poor, thin, alkaline, or rocky — in full sun to partial shade; blackthorn is one of the most adaptable and tough woody plants available, tolerating exposure, drought, poor soil, and neglect. Prunus spinosa is a very thorny, dense, suckering European native shrub that flowers brilliantly in early spring with masses of small, white blossoms on bare black stems before the leaves appear, creating a spectacular display; the flowers are followed by small (1/3–1/2 inch), round, blue-black fruits (sloes) with a white bloom, astringent flesh, and complex flavor that is unpalatable raw but transforms with frost and sugar into excellent jams, jellies, wine, and the essential ingredient of sloe gin. The dense, thorny thickets provide superb nesting habitat for birds and small mammals. Harvest sloes after the first frost for best flavor.

Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; small viburnum is an underused evergreen to semi-evergreen native of Florida and the Gulf Coastal Plain, valued for its small, glossy, spoon-shaped leaves, masses of tiny white flower clusters in early spring before most plants awaken, and the bright red to dark purple-black drupes that provide exceptional wildlife food in summer and fall. Unlike many large viburnums, small viburnum stays naturally compact, to 6–8 feet in cultivation, and responds well to pruning — it can be maintained as a low hedge or specimen shrub. Very drought tolerant once established despite its riparian origins. The cultivar 'Mrs. Schiller's Delight' stays under 3 feet with particularly glossy foliage. An excellent choice for shaded understory positions and moist areas in zone 8–10 landscapes.

Plant in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; smooth sumac is the most cold-hardy North American sumac, naturally colonizing roadsides, old fields, and dry slopes throughout most of the continent. It is distinguished from staghorn sumac (R. typhina) by its smooth stems — staghorn has velvety, fuzzy new growth resembling a stag's antler in velvet. The brilliant, fire-engine-red fall color of smooth sumac is among the most spectacular of any native shrub, often turning color before most other plants. The large, upright, cone-shaped clusters of fuzzy, dark red berries persist through winter and are critically important food for numerous birds including robins, catbirds, mockingbirds, and cedar waxwings. Spreads by root suckers to form thicket colonies — an excellent native for erosion control on dry slopes but needs containment near formal gardens.

common_name: Smyrna Quince (Classic Large Fragrant Turkish Quince)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Smyrna is one of the classic Old World quince cultivars, originating in Turkey and long grown commercially in the eastern Mediterranean, producing large, golden-yellow, intensely fragrant fruit prized for preserves, quince paste (membrillo), and poaching, since the hard, tart flesh is rarely eaten raw. The tree is self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator, and blooms with attractive pale pink spring flowers before setting fruit that ripens in fall. Quince trees are generally low-maintenance once established, tolerating a range of soil types, though good air circulation helps reduce fire blight risk in humid climates.

Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; soap tree is a small evergreen to semi-evergreen tree of the Caribbean and south Florida with pinnately compound leaves and clusters of small white flowers followed by translucent, fleshy, amber fruits containing high concentrations of saponins — natural soap compounds. The crushed or moistened fruits lather readily in water and have been used throughout the Caribbean for centuries as soap for washing clothes and hair. Unlike the more common western soapberry (S. drummondii) of the southern plains, soap tree is a subtropical to tropical species better adapted to the hot, humid conditions of south Florida. The fruits are also used in some ayurvedic traditions and in natural cleaning products. A drought-tolerant, low-maintenance native tree providing both ornamental interest and functional soap production for eco-conscious gardeners in zone 9–11.

Plant in well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; soapberry is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, alkaline soils. Sapindus saponaria (wingleaf soapberry or wild China tree) is a native Texas, Caribbean, and tropical American tree producing clusters of small, round, translucent, amber-gold berries in fall that contain saponins — the natural soap compounds that give the genus its Latin name (Sapo = soap, Indus = Indian, originally referring to 'soap nut from the New World'). When the berry flesh is worked with water, it creates a genuine, biodegradable, soap-like lather that has been used by indigenous peoples and settlers for washing clothes, hair, and skin for centuries; the berries are the same 'soapnuts' sold in natural products stores as a biodegradable laundry detergent. The tree is a handsome, medium-sized shade tree with pinnately compound leaves, small white flowers, and attractive amber berries that persist into winter. The hard, black seeds inside the berries have traditionally been used as beads. Outstanding for low-maintenance, drought-tolerant landscaping in the Gulf South, especially on alkaline soils.

common_name: Somerset Redstreak Apple (Historic Bittersweet Cider Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Somerset Redstreak is a vigorous, spreading tree that benefits from a wide planting spacing. A traditional West Country English cider apple distinct from the unrelated old Redstreak variety once famous in Herefordshire, it produces a reliable crop of medium, red-streaked bittersweet fruit valued by cider makers for good, well-balanced tannin and juice yield in a full-flavored traditional English-style cider blend. Its vigorous, spreading growth habit and reliable annual bearing have kept it in cultivation in traditional Somerset cider orchards for generations, even as many other historic regional varieties have become rare. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

Plant Annona purpurea in full sun in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; water regularly during establishment and during fruiting; the tree is more drought-tolerant than Cherimoya or Sugar Apple once established; hand-pollinate flowers with a small brush during the female phase (when petals are slightly opening) to ensure fruit set, as natural pollinators may be absent outside the native range. Soncoya is the largest of the commercially relevant Annona fruits — with individual fruits commonly weighing 2–5 kg and occasionally much more — distinguished from the better-known custard apples by its dark-green, spiny surface (resembling a chestnut or sea urchin) and very dense, deep-orange to apricot-yellow flesh. The aroma is powerful and characteristic: sweet, musky, and fruity, sometimes described as a combination of mango, pineapple, and vanilla custard. The flesh is eaten fresh with a spoon scooped from the halved fruit; the flavor is very sweet and rich, though the large brown seeds must be removed. Soncoya is native to tropical dry forests of the Pacific coast of Central America and Mexico, making it better adapted to a pronounced dry season than most other Annonas; it performs well in zones with a dry winter season (zone 10–12 in Florida, Hawaii, and South Texas). Rarely seen in cultivation outside its native range but occasionally available from rare fruit nurseries.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with consistent moisture during the growing season; Soncoya is intolerant of frost and prolonged waterlogging but handles the heat and humidity of tropical climates better than its relative cherimoya. The large, spiny, orange-brown fruits weigh up to several pounds each and develop on the branches and trunk; they are ready to harvest when the skin begins to soften and the segments start to separate. The orange, fibrous interior pulp is most commonly processed into drinks, sorbets, and frozen desserts rather than eaten fresh due to its strong flavor. Hand pollination with a small brush, transferring pollen between flowers on different trees, can significantly improve fruit set.

The sour or Seville orange yields bitter, aromatic fruit that is the classic base for marmalade and its fragrant blossoms for perfume. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, protecting it from frost, and note that it is also widely used as a hardy, disease-resistant rootstock. Water deeply and feed during the growing season for steady growth. Harvest the deeply colored fruit in winter and use the tart juice and peel rather than eating it fresh.

growth_habit: Colombian tropical sapote Malvaceae fruit tree
notes: Plant Quararibea cordata in fertile, moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; water consistently throughout the year, maintaining soil moisture without waterlogging; the tree grows rapidly under good conditions and can begin fruiting in 3–5 years from a good-sized transplant. South American Sapote (chupa-chupa in Amazonian Colombia, where the name likely derives from the act of sucking the sweet flesh off the large seed) is one of the truly outstanding tropical fruits — combining the rich creaminess of mamey sapote with the bright tropical flavor of ripe apricot and mango in a way that is entirely its own. The orange-fleshed, salmon-skinned, football-sized fruits produced in large quantities on mature trees are eaten fresh out of hand or blended into juices, shakes, and ice creams. The tree is in the Malvaceae family (related to chocolate and kapok) and shares the fast growth and large size of its relatives. Fruiting is precocious for a tropical tree — beginning at 3–5 years from a good-quality transplant — and production can be heavy, with large trees bearing hundreds of fruits per season. Currently little-known outside Colombia and adjacent Amazonian countries but considered by tropical fruit enthusiasts as one of the best-tasting of all Neotropical fruits; wider cultivation in zone 10–12 tropical gardens is warranted.

common_name: Southern Bartlett Pear (Low-Chill Gulf Coast Bartlett Sport)
notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Southern Bartlett is a chance sport of the classic Bartlett pear discovered on an old Louisiana homestead and selected specifically for its low chilling requirement, letting it set fruit reliably in the mild Gulf Coast winters that leave standard Bartlett trees short on the cold hours they need to flower well. It bears the same classic bell-shaped, buttery, sweet pear fruit familiar from Bartlett, ripening in mid to late summer. Like most European pears grown in the humid South, it remains more vulnerable to fire blight along the immediate Gulf Coast than truly blight-resistant Southern selections such as Warren or Ayers, so prune out and destroy any blighted shoots promptly and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth blight favors. Harvest while still firm and green-yellow, then ripen off the tree at room temperature for the best buttery texture and flavor.

Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; very drought-tolerant once established — one of the most adaptable native shrubs for difficult sites. Viburnum rufidulum (southern blackhaw or rusty blackhaw) is a native deciduous shrub or small tree of the southeastern United States — found naturally in dry rocky woods, cedar glades, roadsides, and forest edges from Virginia south to Florida and west to Texas — and one of the most ecologically important and underused native fruiting shrubs for Gulf Coast wildlife gardens. The plant is distinguished from blackhaw (V. prunifolium) by its larger size, glossy dark-green leaves, and the distinctive rusty-red to reddish-brown fuzz (rufidulum = rusty) that covers the buds, new twigs, and leaf undersides. It produces large, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in spring, followed by large clusters of 1/3-inch, dark blue-black drupes (berries) in fall. The berries have a remarkable, sweet, prune-raisin-like flavor when fully ripe after frost — uniquely pleasant among native berries, and used by indigenous southeastern peoples for food. Birds (especially mockingbirds, bluebirds, and cedar waxwings) consume the fruit enthusiastically. The plant provides outstanding fall color (glossy burgundy-red), excellent winter bark interest, and remarkable drought tolerance — among the most xeric-adapted native shrubs for alkaline, rocky, and dry sites in the Southeast.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; southern crabapple is the native crabapple of the southeastern United States, producing a spectacular display of intensely fragrant pink flowers in early spring and small (1/2–1 inch) yellow-green to red crabapples in late summer and fall. The crabapples are too tart to eat fresh but make outstanding jelly, cider, and preserved fruit with excellent pectin content. The flowers are superb for native bees; cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and deer consume the fruit through fall and winter. It tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 better than most crabapple cultivars and produces cleaner foliage with fewer disease problems in the warm South. A self-fertile tree, so only one is needed for fruit.

Plant in well-drained to dry, acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; southern red oak is a dominant canopy tree of the southeastern US Coastal Plain and Piedmont, thriving in the dry, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy soils that characterize much of the region. The distinctive leaves have a broadly lobed base with a narrow middle and a multi-lobed apex — sometimes described as bell-shaped — turning dark red in fall. The tree is a significant mast producer with small, round, bitter acorns consumed by deer, wild turkeys, squirrels, and many other wildlife species. It is more drought-tolerant and better adapted to dry sandy soils than northern red oak (Q. rubra), making it a preferred choice for tough Coastal Plain sites. Historically valuable as a timber tree and important in the ecology of southeastern pine-oak communities.

common_name: Southern Sensation Seedless Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Table Grape)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Southern Sensation is a Texas Superstar-designated table grape, a joint release from Texas A&M and University of Arkansas breeding programs, bred to combine yellow, thin-skinned, seedless fruit with strong flavor and years of demonstrated resistance to Pierce's disease — the bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European-type table grape varieties within a few years across the humid South and has long limited backyard grape growing in Texas and the Gulf region. It has outperformed standard seedless varieties like Flame Seedless in regional trials specifically for disease survival and fruit quality in southern conditions. Prune to a permanent cordon system in late winter, and thin crowded fruit clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation, which helps reduce fungal disease pressure in humid weather.

common_name: Spanish Cherry (Bakul, Bullet Wood, Tanjong Tree)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy soil in full sun; Spanish cherry is slow-growing but long-lived and very low-maintenance once established. Mimusops elengi (Spanish cherry, bakul, or tanjong tree) is a slow-growing, long-lived tropical evergreen tree native to India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia, and the Pacific Islands — one of the most beloved ornamental and fragrance trees of the Indian subcontinent. The tree produces small (1/2-inch), white, star-shaped flowers with deeply fringed petals that emit an extraordinarily intense, sweet, jasmine-like fragrance — particularly at night. Remarkably, the fragrance of the flowers intensifies dramatically as they dry: fallen bakul flowers can perfume an entire courtyard for days after dropping, and dried bakul flowers are strung into garlands, threaded into women's hair (a classic Indian tradition), used in temple offerings, and dried for pot-pourri and perfume production. The sweet-acid, olive-sized, orange-red to orange fruits (the 'Spanish cherry') are edible — sweet, slightly astringent, with a pleasant, mild flavor — eaten fresh or used in preserves across the plant's native range. The hard, dense wood (bullet wood) is extremely durable. In zone 10–12 tropical gardens, bakul is an outstanding shade tree and long-term ornamental investment valued as much for its fragrance as its appearance.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil; Melicoccus bijugatus is drought tolerant and adapted to calcareous, rocky, and coastal soils typical of the Caribbean — water regularly only in establishment and during flowering and fruit set. Melicoccus bijugatus (Spanish Lime, Genip, Mamoncillo, Quenepa, or Limoncillo) is a large, stately, long-lived evergreen tree native to Colombia, Venezuela, and the Lesser Antilles, now widely naturalized and cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Central America, and parts of Florida and Hawaii. The common name 'Spanish Lime' describes the fruit's appearance — small (1–1.5 inch), perfectly round, lime-green, thin-shelled, resembling a small lime — but the flavor is a sweet-sour, tropical, guava-lychee combination with firm, translucent salmon-to-orange jelly-like pulp clinging tightly to the large seed. Fruits are sold in street markets in enormous clusters of hundreds — eaten by cracking the thin shell between the teeth and sucking or scraping the juicy pulp from the seed. Spanish lime is one of the most beloved street foods and market fruits of the Caribbean, Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Colombia. The ripe fruits are also made into juice, jams, wine, and fermented beverages. Trees are dioecious (separate male and female plants), so plant at least one male per several females for fruiting. Very long-lived — specimens 100+ years old still fruit productively. Well adapted to South Florida's alkaline limestone soils where many tropical fruits perform poorly.

Plant in well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), poor to average sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; sparkleberry is the largest native blueberry relative in the Southeast, growing to 25 feet as a gnarly, multi-trunked small tree with distinctive exfoliating gray-brown bark that reveals warm cinnamon-red underbark — one of the most ornamental native bark patterns in southern woodland plants. The white bell-shaped flowers in spring are followed by small, persistent dark black berries that, while dry and astringent compared to commercial blueberries, are eagerly consumed by wood thrushes, mockingbirds, foxes, and other wildlife throughout fall and winter. It grows naturally in dry, sandy upland forests and longleaf pine savannas. An outstanding specimen tree for dry, sunny or partly shaded naturalistic landscapes.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Spartan is a cold-hardy, reliably productive apple well suited to northern climates. Bred in British Columbia, Canada in the 1920s from a McIntosh and Yellow Newtown Pippin cross, it bears medium, deep purple-red apples with crisp, snow-white, juicy flesh and a sweet flavor with the light, distinctive tang inherited from its McIntosh parent, ripening in early-to-mid fall as a reliable, attractive dessert apple. Its excellent cold hardiness, reliable annual bearing, and good disease resistance compared to many other apples have made it a longstanding favorite for northern and Canadian home orchards where more tender varieties struggle. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once fruit colors up deeply and pulls easily from the spur, and expect good storage life of a couple of months under cool conditions.

common_name: Spice Zee Nectaplum (Genetic Dwarf Nectarine-Plum Hybrid)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, Spice Zee is a genetic dwarf nectaplum, a nectarine-plum interspecific hybrid, that naturally stays compact enough for a large patio container or small-yard planting while still bearing full-sized, sweet, richly flavored fruit with a flavor many describe as somewhere between a nectarine and a plum. The reddish-purple young foliage in spring, aging to bronze-green, makes it an attractive small ornamental tree even outside of fruiting season, and its self-fertile flowers mean a single tree can set a full crop without a second pollinator. Fruit ripens in early summer, and the naturally dense, rounded canopy benefits from light annual thinning to keep light reaching the interior and to manage fruit size.

Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Spring Snow is prized for producing essentially no fruit at all, a genetic trait that makes it a popular choice where the messy fruit drop of ornamental crabapples is unwelcome — around patios, walkways, and driveways — while still delivering the classic crabapple spring show of dense, fragrant, pure white flowers covering the tree before the leaves fully emerge. Its clean, tidy habit and lack of fruit litter have made it one of the most widely planted flowering crabapples for urban and residential landscapes. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches; watch for occasional fire blight and apple scab in humid climates.

Plant grafted trees in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; star apple is a highly ornamental tropical fruit tree native to the West Indies, producing beautiful round fruits 2–4 inches across in purple or green skin with a distinctive star pattern in the cross-section of the white, gelatinous, sweet, milk-filled flesh — the 'star' that gives the fruit its name. The leaves are distinctively two-toned: dark glossy green above, silky golden-bronze beneath, creating a shimmering display when the breeze moves through the canopy. The fruit is eaten fresh by cutting in half and scooping the sweet, creamy flesh; the latex in the skin and rind is astringent and should not be consumed. Grafted trees begin producing in 3–5 years. The sweet, mild flavor is a favorite in the Caribbean and South Florida. An outstanding ornamental and fruiting tree for zone 10–12 gardens.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; star gooseberry is a productive tropical fruit tree widely grown throughout Southeast Asia and the Caribbean, bearing clusters of ribbed, waxy, pale yellow to white drupes — each resembling a miniature star when cut cross-section — directly on the trunk and older branches in a distinctive cauliflorous pattern. The tart, acidic fruit has a crisp, translucent flesh somewhat reminiscent of a sour apple or green gooseberry and is consumed fresh (with salt and chili in Southeast Asia), pickled, candied, or made into jams and juices. Trees reach 10–30 feet in frost-free conditions but are easily maintained smaller through pruning. In zone 9 they may be damaged by frost below 28°F but typically recover from light frost damage at the root. Prolific bearers that fruit twice yearly in good conditions. The unusual trunk-fruiting habit and fine-textured, pinnate foliage are ornamental assets in the tropical garden. A worthwhile and underused edible tree for zone 9–11 gardens.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in the warmest location with maximum sun exposure; Star Ruby is a red-fleshed grapefruit variety developed by Texas A&M University through irradiation mutagenesis and released in 1970 — the variety that set the standard for deep-red, sweet, low-acid grapefruit. Texas Rio Grande Valley grapefruit production is dominated by Star Ruby and its offspring Rio Red (1984), both producing the deep ruby-red flesh and low-acid, sweet flavor that made Texas red grapefruit internationally famous. The fruits are large, with thin, yellow-blushed skin and deep crimson flesh that is sweeter and less bitter than white grapefruit — so sweet they are often eaten without added sugar. Star Ruby requires a long, hot growing season to develop maximum sweetness and color: in zone 9, summer heat is critical. Trees are vigorous, productive once established, and moderately cold-tolerant to about 26°F. Feed with citrus fertilizer (especially nitrogen and zinc) 3–4 times per year. An excellent landscape tree in warm zone 9 that provides both ornamental value and substantial food production.

Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring after frost risk has passed in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; purchase grafted trees for earlier bearing — seedling trees may take 5–7 years to fruit while grafted trees can bear in 1–2 years after planting. Averrhoa carambola is a tropical Southeast Asian fruit tree producing the unique, deeply 5-ridged, golden-yellow, translucent fruit known as starfruit or carambola that when sliced crosswise yields the distinctive five-pointed star shape; the fruit ranges from very tart to sweet depending on cultivar and is excellent fresh, in fruit salads, as a garnish, and in tropical beverages. Trees bloom and fruit multiple times per year in tropical climates, producing an almost continuous harvest in zones 10–11; in zone 9 they need frost protection and may lose leaves in cold winters but often recover. Sweet cultivars 'Arkin', 'Kari', and 'Fwang Tung' are the most popular for home orchards.

This evergreen woody vine is unusual among fruiting plants for genuinely preferring shade to partial shade, making it one of the few climbers suited to a north-facing wall or the dim understory of a garden pergola. Train the twining stems onto a trellis or fence and be patient, since named or grafted plants fruit far sooner than seedlings, which can take years to bear. In autumn the vine produces oblong purple fruit similar to its relative akebia, splitting to reveal a sweet, milky-white pulp studded with small black seeds that is eaten fresh by hand in Japan. Plant two vines for best pollination and fruit set, since a single plant fruits sparsely on its own.

common_name: Stayman Apple (Stayman Winesap, Rich Wine-Flavored Keeper Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby. Discovered in Kansas in 1866 by Dr. J. Stayman as a seedling of the older Winesap apple, this cultivar keeps the tangy, wine-like flavor of its parent in a larger, more productive fruit. The dark red skin covers dense, juicy flesh that holds up well in storage and in cooking, and the tree has long been a Mid-Atlantic and Southern favorite for cider and pie making. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once the background color turns from green to yellow-green.

common_name: Stella Cherry (First Self-Fertile Sweet Cherry, Canadian Self-Fertile Cherry)
notes: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Stella is self-fertile and will set a crop without a pollenizer — it will also cross-pollinate many other sweet cherry varieties as a companion tree; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting; Stella ripens mid-season (late June to early July) producing large, dark red to nearly black fruits with good sweet flavor. Stella sweet cherry was bred by Dr. Karl Lapins at the Summerland Research Station in British Columbia, Canada, and released in 1968 — it became historically significant as the first widely available self-fertile sweet cherry variety, a characteristic that transformed home garden cherry growing by eliminating the requirement for two compatible cherry trees with overlapping bloom times. Before Stella, growing sweet cherries required careful selection of compatible pollinating pairs (cherry pollination compatibility is complex and variety-specific), which limited practical cherry growing to gardeners with space for at least two trees and the knowledge to select compatible varieties. Stella's self-fertility made sweet cherries accessible for single-tree planting in small gardens throughout its zone range. The fruits are large (similar to Bing in size), dark red to nearly black at full ripeness, with firm, juicy, sweet flesh and excellent flavor — somewhat less complex than Bing by some evaluations, but reliably good and productive. Stella also serves as a pollinizer for most other sweet cherry varieties, making it a valuable companion in mixed plantings where Bing or other varieties need cross-pollination.

common_name: Steuben Grape (Cornell-Bred Spicy Blue Table Grape)
notes: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil, pruning heavily each winter with a cane-pruning system. Steuben was bred at Cornell University's Geneva, New York agricultural experiment station and is grown for its blue-black, slip-skin berries with a rich, spicy-sweet, almost wine-like flavor that many growers consider superior to Concord for fresh eating, though it also makes excellent juice and jelly. It is a reliable, productive vine that ripens in midseason and stores unusually well for a labrusca-type grape. As a high-chill northern grape, it is not recommended for the Deep South, where Pierce's disease and mild winters favor muscadines or Pierce's-tolerant hybrid bunch grapes instead.

Stone pine is the classic Mediterranean umbrella-form pine grown for the large, richly flavored pine nuts (pignoli) used in pesto, pastries, and Middle Eastern cuisine; it is monoecious, self-fertile, and pollen-heavy — individual trees produce both male and female cones. Cones take three years to mature from pollination to seed release, so a productive tree has three overlapping cone crops at any given time. Harvest brown, closed cones by hand or after they fall naturally in late autumn, then sun-dry or gently heat them until the scales open and release the papery-shelled nuts inside. The tree thrives in sandy, well-drained, alkaline to acidic soil and is extremely drought-tolerant once the taproot is established.

Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava (cattley guava, cherry guava, purple guava) is a Brazilian evergreen small tree or large shrub that produces small, round, dark-red to burgundy-purple fruits about 1 inch in diameter with a distinctive strawberry-guava flavor — sweet, aromatic, and mildly acidic — that are excellent eaten fresh, made into jams, jellies, juice, and desserts, or dried. The fruits ripen from late summer through fall and fall when fully ripe, making harvest simple. The plant is one of the most attractive year-round fruiting shrubs for zone 9–11, with smooth, mottled, tan and brown peeling bark, glossy, thick, oval, dark-green leaves, and small, white, fragrant guava flowers that precede the fruit. Hardy to approximately 22°F, it is more cold-tolerant than tropical guava (Psidium guajava). However, strawberry guava is listed as a highly invasive species in Hawaii and parts of Florida, where it spreads rapidly in natural areas, and should not be planted near natural habitats in those regions. In drier Gulf Coast areas it is better behaved and is a productive, attractive, low-maintenance small fruit tree.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; strawberry guava is a highly productive and flavorful small fruit tree or large shrub that produces abundant crops of 1-inch round fruits in red (the classic form) or yellow (Psidium cattleyanum var. lucidum, lemon guava) with an intensely sweet, slightly strawberry-like flavor — arguably the finest-flavored guava species, often preferred over the larger common guava by people who taste it. The glossy, dark-green evergreen leaves and smooth, mottled reddish-brown bark provide year-round ornamental value. In zone 9 it may suffer light frost damage but typically recovers well. It is extremely drought, heat, and poor-soil tolerant once established and produces fruit with minimal care. Important note: strawberry guava is listed as one of the world's 100 worst invasive species in subtropical humid regions — do not plant where it can escape to natural areas in Hawaii, Florida, and similar climates. In drier Gulf Coast locations it is less problematic.

Plant in poor, very well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the strawberry tree is a beautiful, slow-growing Mediterranean evergreen that produces clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers in fall and winter simultaneously with the ripening of the previous year's strawberry-like red and orange fruits — a unique garden spectacle of flowers and ripe fruit coexisting on the tree. The rough-textured red fruits are edible but taste nothing like a strawberry: they are mealy, mildly sweet, with a somewhat gritty texture, best used for jams, jellies, and wine rather than eating fresh (the name refers only to their appearance). The bark is a beautiful cinnamon red and exfoliating. The dwarf cultivar 'Compacta' stays 5–6 feet; 'Elfin King' is an ultra-compact form. Excellent drought-tolerant, deer-resistant evergreen for zone 7–10.

Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stuart is an old heirloom pecan variety originating in the Gulf South before the Civil War and one of the most historically important named pecans — it was among the first varieties to be systematically propagated by grafting and was widely planted throughout the Southeast from the 1880s through mid-20th century. Nuts are very large (45–50 per pound) with an excellent kernel percentage, rich flavor, and attractive appearance that made Stuart the standard commercial variety for much of the 20th century. Though partially supplanted by more scab-resistant modern varieties in humid commercial orchards, Stuart remains extremely popular for home planting in zone 7–9 because of its large, beautiful nuts, adaptability to a wide range of soils, and long productive lifespan — well-established Stuart trees may continue producing heavily for 100+ years. The principal weakness is moderate scab susceptibility in very wet years; in most zone 9 home orchards, this is manageable without spraying. An excellent choice for the Gulf Coast gardener who wants large, flavorful nuts from a landscape tree.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Sturmer Pippin needs a long, warm growing season to ripen and store well, and performs best where autumns stay mild. Bred in Suffolk, England in the early nineteenth century from a Ribston Pippin and Nonpareil cross, it bears firm, greenish-yellow apples with dense, crisp, sharply flavored flesh that ripens very late in the season and keeps exceptionally well, sometimes into late winter or early spring under good storage conditions, making it one of the longest-keeping traditional apples grown. Its late ripening and long storage life made it especially popular in Southern Hemisphere growing regions like Australia and New Zealand, where the extended warm autumn allows the fruit to mature fully; in cooler, shorter-season climates it can struggle to ripen well before frost. Harvest as late in fall as the season allows, letting the fruit hang as long as possible, and store cool for a remarkably long keeping period.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Success was among the important early named pecan cultivars that helped establish the commercial pecan industry in the South, valued in its day for good nut size and quality. It has largely been replaced in modern commercial orchards by more disease-resistant, higher-yielding cultivars, since it is fairly susceptible to pecan scab and other diseases common in humid climates, but it remains of historical interest and is still found in older plantings and heirloom nut collections.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sudachi is self-fruitful and produces tiny, green fruits that are harvested before they ripen to yellow for the most aromatic juice. Sudachi (Citrus sudachi) is a small, intensely aromatic souring citrus virtually unknown outside Japan but recently gaining attention in American culinary circles for its exceptional flavor; native and endemic to Tokushima Prefecture on Shikoku island (which produces approximately 98% of Japan's sudachi), the small (1–1.5 inch diameter), round, green fruits are always used before they ripen to yellow when their intense, fragrant juice and zest are at peak. The flavor is tart, fragrant, and floral with a complexity and intensity that surpasses lime or lemon — used by Japanese chefs exclusively for its aromatic quality as a garnish squeeze over grilled fish, mushrooms, soba noodles, and in ponzu sauce alternatives. Virtually unavailable commercially outside Japan; growing your own is the only way to access fresh sudachi in the US.

Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season; Sugar Belle is a University of Florida-bred mandarin cross prized for its distinctive bell-like shape, deep orange rind, and rich, intensely sweet, honeybell-style flavor, combined with better cold tolerance and canker resistance than many older mandarin varieties. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree without becoming puffy or losing flavor, giving a longer harvest window than many mandarins. Water deeply but let the soil surface dry between waterings, mulch to protect the root zone, and provide frost protection for young trees during their first couple of winters until they gain size and hardiness.

Plant in dry, well-drained, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sugar bush is an evergreen sumac native to chaparral and dry, rocky slopes of the California Coast Ranges and Baja California, one of the most reliable and ornamental drought-tolerant shrubs for California-climate gardens. The large, bold, leathery, ovate leaves are folded lengthwise like a taco shell — a distinctive feature that sheds rain and reduces water loss. The small, red, waxy-coated berries produced in summer are coated with a tart, malic-acid-rich white sugar that was mixed with water by indigenous peoples to make a refreshing, lemonade-like drink — hence the common name 'sugar bush.' A cornerstone shrub for California native and Mediterranean-climate gardens, providing year-round evergreen screening, early spring flowers for native bees, summer berries for birds, and outstanding drought tolerance. Never irrigate in summer once established — it prefers natural summer drought.

Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most fruit trees once established. Sugar Cane is a jujube cultivar valued for its exceptionally high sugar content and crisp, refreshing texture, similar to biting into a small, sweet apple, best enjoyed fresh at the green-to-mahogany transitional stage when both sweetness and crunch are at their peak. Fruit can also be left to fully ripen and wrinkle on the tree for a chewy, date-like texture and flavor if a different eating quality is preferred. The tree is largely self-fertile, extremely low-maintenance, and one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available, making it a good fit for the hot, dry margins of a Gulf South orchard.

common_name: Sugar Tyme Crabapple (Fragrant Pink-Bud White-Flowered Crabapple)
notes: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Sugar Tyme is a heavy, reliable bloomer, its deep pink buds opening to abundant, fragrant white flowers each spring, followed by a persistent crop of small, bright red fruit that holds through winter and draws birds when other food sources are scarce. It is one of the most disease-resistant crabapple cultivars available, showing strong resistance to apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew, which has made it a widely recommended low-maintenance choice by extension services across many regions. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

Plant in well-drained to average soil of any pH in full sun; summer grape is one of the most widespread wild grape species in eastern North America, climbing high into the forest canopy from New England to Florida and west to Nebraska. The large, deeply lobed leaves resemble European wine grape leaves and provide dense, ornamental screening on arbors and fences. Clusters of small, blue-black, seedy but sweet-tart grapes ripen in late summer to fall and are consumed by over 90 species of birds and mammals. The grapes are edible for humans and have been used to make juice, jelly, and wine — they are tart when underripe but improve after frost. Summer grape is a host plant for multiple moth and butterfly species including the grapeleaf skeletonizer. Prune back in late winter to a few buds on the main stems to encourage fruiting shoots.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sumo mandarin — sold under the trademarked name 'Sumo Citrus' in North America and known as 'Dekopon' in Japan and 'Shiranui' by its cultivar name — is a premium mandarin hybrid (Kiyomi tangor x Ponkan mandarin) developed in Japan and widely considered one of the finest fresh mandarin fruits in the world: extraordinarily sweet (very high Brix), completely seedless, easily peeled with thick, bumpy, loose skin, and so large (typically 3–4 inches in diameter) that a single fruit is a generous one-person serving. The characteristic topknot bump at the stem end and enormous size make Sumo instantly recognizable in markets, where it commands premium prices ($3–5 per fruit or more). The flavor is intensely sweet with very low acid and a honey-like aromatic quality unlike any other mandarin, and the peel comes off in large easy-to-remove sections. Sumo/Dekopon trees are slow to come into full production (4–5 years from grafted trees to reliable crops), somewhat demanding in their cultural requirements, and require fruit thinning to produce the signature large fruits — but the result is exceptional. A wonderful specialty tree for zone 9–11 home orchards and edible landscapes.

common_name: Sunburst Tangerine (Deep Orange-Red Florida Hybrid Mandarin)
notes: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Released by the USDA in 1979 from a cross of Robinson and Osceola mandarins, Sunburst produces medium-sized fruit with a strikingly deep orange-red rind and sweet, juicy, richly flavored flesh with relatively few seeds. It is one of the more widely planted modern mandarin cultivars in Florida and the Gulf South because of its dependable, heavy annual production and attractive fruit color. The tree bears young and can overbear, so removing some fruit in spring helps maintain fruit size and reduce alternate-year bearing.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, full sun at maturity; Sunflower is a named pawpaw cultivar selected in Ohio from wild seedlings notable for its large, somewhat self-fertile nature (better fruit set when grown alone than most pawpaw cultivars), medium-large fruit size, and rich, sweet, yellow-gold flesh with excellent banana-custard flavor. The 'sunflower' name refers to both the yellow-gold flesh color and the cultivar's tendency to produce better solo fruit set than most pawpaws, though production is still significantly improved with a cross-pollinator. Sunflower's partial self-fertility is its most important practical attribute for gardeners who have space for only one tree — it will produce some fruit without a pollinator while most other pawpaw cultivars produce little or none. The medium-to-large fruits (4–6 oz average) have green to yellowish-green skin that softens slightly and turns more yellow-toned when fully ripe; the rich, sweet, banana-custard flesh is among the most popular of named pawpaw selections. Harvest by feel rather than appearance — ripe pawpaws yield to gentle pressure like a ripe peach. As with all pawpaws, the very short post-harvest shelf life (2–5 days at room temperature) makes them a specialty fruit for home gardeners and local direct-sale; they cannot be commercially distributed through standard grocery supply chains.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunki is an exceptionally cold-hardy sour mandarin, tolerating brief dips into the low teens F once well established, well beyond what a standard satsuma or sweet orange survives. The small, seedy fruit is too tart and sour for most people to eat fresh, but it makes excellent marmalade, ade, and juice for cooking, and the tree's extreme hardiness has made it one of the parents behind many of the cold-hardy citrus hybrids bred for the Southeast. Sunki is also planted specifically as a dwarfing, cold-tolerant rootstock for grafting less-hardy scion varieties, which is how many home gardeners in zone 7-8 encounter it even without seeking out the fruit itself. Give young trees winter protection for their first few years; mature, well-established wood is considerably tougher. Harvest fruit once fully colored, and expect to use it in the kitchen rather than eating it fresh off the tree.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are drought-tolerant but produce best fruit with consistent moisture during the fruiting period. Eugenia uniflora is a glossy-leaved evergreen shrub or small tree native to tropical South America, widely naturalized in Florida, the Gulf Coast, Hawaii, and subtropical regions worldwide; the deeply ribbed, round, eight-segmented fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally to deep red or nearly black, with a distinctive sharp-sweet, resinous flavor that is immediately distinctive — excellent fresh when fully ripe (dark red to black stage), in juices, jellies, ice cream, and fermented beverages. The foliage is beautifully aromatic when crushed. It is commonly planted as a fast-growing hedge or screening shrub in zone 9–12 and has become naturalized (and invasive in some areas of Florida). Hardy to about 28°F; protect from frost in zone 9a.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Susquehanna is one of the flagship 'Peterson Pawpaws' — the group of named cultivars selected and introduced by Neal Peterson from decades of pawpaw breeding aimed at developing the largest, sweetest, and most productive cultivars available. Susquehanna produces some of the largest individual pawpaw fruits of any named cultivar, with exceptional fruits reaching 12–16 ounces — two to three times the average size of a good seedling-grown pawpaw — on a productive, healthy tree. The extraordinarily large fruit size, excellent sweet flavor with rich banana-custard-vanilla character, and low seed-to-flesh ratio (maximum edible flesh per fruit) make Susquehanna the top choice among pawpaw enthusiasts seeking maximum yield from a home orchard planting. Cross-pollination from Shenandoah, Wells, or another unrelated cultivar is required for reliable production — plant two or more different named cultivars within 50 feet. Because pawpaw flowers have an unusual pollination mechanism (receptive to pollen only briefly, with fly/beetle pollinators), hand-pollination using a small brush to transfer pollen between flowers at different stages significantly improves fruit set. In zone 9, pawpaws perform in the northern portions of the zone; deep South heat and insufficient winter chilling can limit production in zones 9b and warmer.

Harvest berries in early autumn and mash to separate seeds from pulp, then rinse seeds thoroughly before sowing to remove germination inhibitors in the flesh. Sow in a prepared seedbed or deep containers left outdoors to experience natural winter cold, which substitutes for manual stratification. Swedish Whitebeam is exceptionally adaptable and tolerates coastal winds, compacted urban soils, and exposed hillsides better than most ornamental trees. Move seedlings to their permanent site by the second year, choosing a location with full sun and good drainage where the tree can develop its distinctive white-backed foliage.

Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving them toward full sun as they mature. Sweet Alice is a historic Indiana-origin pawpaw prized for exceptionally large, sweet fruit with a mild, low-astringency flavor that many tasters rank among the best of the older named selections, though it can bear somewhat irregularly compared to more modern, heavier-cropping cultivars. Trees are vigorous with the typical pyramidal pawpaw habit and glossy drooping foliage, and they tolerate the wet-but-drained bottomland soils pawpaw favors in the wild. Because pawpaws require cross-pollination, plant Sweet Alice with a genetically unrelated cultivar such as Shenandoah or Wabash, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during bloom to improve fruit set in home settings where natural pollinators are scarce.

common_name: Sweet Calabash (Sweet Granadilla, Hard-Shell Passion Fruit)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide very strong trellis or arbor support. Passiflora maliformis (sweet calabash or sweet granadilla) is a passionflower native to the Caribbean islands and northern South America that produces one of the sweetest and most intensely aromatic of all passionfruits. The fruits are rounded to slightly apple-shaped, roughly 2–3 inches across, with a hard, woody, yellow-brown to dark-brown shell when ripe (much harder than purple or yellow passionfruit shells), protecting an extremely sweet, aromatic, orange-yellow pulp with a flavor that combines passion fruit, apricot, and guava with a honeyed sweetness rarely found in cultivated passionfruits. The hard shell makes it less susceptible to insect damage than thin-shelled species, and the fruits can be stored for weeks at room temperature. To eat, crack the hard shell and scoop out the aromatic pulp with seeds; the juice is excellent mixed with water as a tropical drink. Sweet calabash is prized in Caribbean home gardens and is occasionally grown in tropical botanical gardens worldwide; it remains very little known in commercial cultivation despite its outstanding fruit quality. The attractive, divided leaves and intricate blue-and-white flowers are typical of the genus. In zone 10–12, the vine is vigorous and productive in full sun.

common_name: Sweet Frost Mandarin (Cold-Hardy Seedless Changsha-Type Tangerine)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, siting them in a warm microclimate for extra protection during the coldest nights. Sweet Frost is a University of Georgia release bred from Changsha tangerine specifically to make a hardier, more dependable citrus for gardeners as far north as zone 8b, well beyond where most mandarins survive outdoors. The small to medium fruit is easy-peeling and notably sweeter and less seedy than standard Changsha, ripening in fall into early winter. Mature trees have shown better cold tolerance in trials than satsuma, making Sweet Frost a strong option for pushing citrus culture into the cooler fringes of the Gulf Coast.

Plant in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun with wire or trellis support; sweet granadilla is widely considered the sweetest and most delicately flavored of all passion fruits, with a brittle hard shell that rattles when ripe and a translucent sweet-gelatinous interior pulp eaten with a spoon — the dominant commercial species in Colombia, Peru, and Venezuela. It differs from P. flavicarpa in preferring cool highland conditions (3,000–8,000 feet elevation in the tropics, or mild Mediterranean climates); excessive heat reduces sugar content significantly. Harvest when the shell becomes brittle and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. A single established vine on a strong trellis can yield 100 or more fruits per season.

Sweet lime yields mild, low-acid fruit prized in South Asia and the Mediterranean for fresh juice. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, protecting it from any frost, or keep it in a large pot to shelter indoors in cold climates. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season and water deeply but infrequently. Harvest when the rind turns pale yellow-green and the fruit yields slightly to pressure.

growth_habit: tropical Southeast Asian cauliflorous fruit tree
notes: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; plant at least one male and one female tree for fruiting — Baccaurea dulcis is dioecious. Baccaurea dulcis (sweet rambai or jentik-jentik) is a small tropical fruit tree from the humid lowland forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula — one of the sweetest and most pleasant of the Baccaurea fruit species (the species name 'dulcis' means sweet in Latin). The tree is a compact size compared to other Baccaurea relatives, making it somewhat more suitable for home tropical gardens. Like other Baccaurea species, the fruits are cauliflorous — forming in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and main branches in the distinctive pattern shared with cacao, jackfruit, and related tropical trees. The small (1/2-inch), round to oval fruits ripen to yellowish to orange-red with thin skin and translucent, white, jelly-like flesh; the flavor is genuinely sweet and mild, with less of the tartness characteristic of other rambai relatives (B. motleyana). The tree is dioecious, requiring both male and female plants for fruit production. Sweet rambai is largely unknown in cultivation outside its native Borneo and Malaysian range; a rare collectors' fruit tree for dedicated tropical fruit enthusiasts in zone 11–12.

Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting and avoid low, frost-prone planting sites. Sweetheart is a Canadian-bred sweet cherry from the Summerland research station in British Columbia, valued for being self-fertile — unlike Bing and many other sweet cherries, it sets a reliable crop without a separate pollinizer tree, making it a practical choice where space allows for only one cherry tree. It ripens notably late in the sweet cherry season, extending fresh harvest well after earlier cultivars like Bing and Rainier have finished, with medium-large, bright red, firm, sweet fruit of good flavor. The tree is vigorous and productive, and its self-fertility combined with late ripening has made it a popular choice for home orchards and small commercial plantings alike. Provide consistent moisture during fruit development to avoid cracking, especially if rain falls as fruit nears full ripeness.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Swingle citrumelo is a grapefruit x trifoliate orange hybrid that became the standard commercial citrus rootstock across much of Florida and the Gulf South after older rootstocks succumbed to citrus blight and tristeza virus, valued for disease resistance, cold hardiness well beyond standard sweet orange, and good compatibility with most common scion varieties. Its own fruit is bitter, seedy, and essentially inedible, so it is used as understock for grafting a named orange, grapefruit, mandarin, or lemon variety rather than being grown for fruit. Trees show trifoliate-influenced foliage with small, three-part leaves and light thorns, especially on young wood. Home gardeners most often encounter Swingle citrumelo already grafted beneath a named citrus at the nursery rather than planting it directly, but it can also be grown from seed to produce rootstock trees for home grafting projects.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Syrah (called Shiraz in Australia and South Africa) is a vigorous, heat-loving variety well suited to warm growing regions. This bold, deeply colored red wine grape produces small, dark-skinned berries that yield rich, full-bodied wines with dark fruit, pepper, and smoky notes, thriving in warm, sunny climates from France's Rhône Valley to Australia's Barossa Valley where it has become that country's signature red grape under the Shiraz name. Vigorous and generally reliable in warm regions, it tolerates heat well but is susceptible to bunch rot in humid conditions, making canopy management for airflow important in more humid growing areas. Train to a trellis system that supports its vigorous growth, thin fruit if overcropping to concentrate flavor, and provide full sun and warmth for the best ripening.

Start seeds in warm, moist potting mix at 75–80°F and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from cold wind and afternoon heat; tamarillos are frost-sensitive but also dislike sustained temperatures above 90°F, thriving best in cool subtropical climates such as coastal California, highland tropics, or mild maritime zone 10. The smooth-skinned red or yellow egg-shaped fruits ripen 18 months from seed and have a rich, complex flavor — tangy and tomato-like — excellent in salsa, chutneys, smoothies, and cooked dishes. Shallow roots make the tree drought-sensitive; water deeply but infrequently. Prune after harvest to maintain a manageable 6–8 foot height.

common_name: Tamopan Persimmon (Large Ringed Chinese Astringent Persimmon)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Tamopan is a distinctive Chinese persimmon cultivar known for its unusually large size and a visible constriction ring around the middle of the fruit that gives it a pumpkin- or acorn-like shape unlike most other persimmons. The deep orange fruit is strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point the flesh becomes sweet, thick, and custard-like, well suited to fresh eating and baking. The tree is vigorous and productive, and because individual fruits can grow quite large and heavy, thinning excess fruit helps prevent broken branches in a heavy year.

common_name: Tanenashi Persimmon (Large Seedless Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tanenashi is the most widely planted Japanese persimmon cultivar in the American South — an astringent persimmon variety that produces large (3–4 inch diameter), round to slightly conical, bright orange-red fruits without seeds when grown without pollination. The seedless quality is one of Tanenashi's most important practical attributes — all commercial packing persimmons are seedless, and home-garden fresh eating quality improves without seeds in the soft, jellylike flesh. As an astringent persimmon, Tanenashi must be fully ripe (soft, completely yielding to pressure, like a water balloon) before eating or the tannins create an unpleasant mouth-puckering sensation; picking at the orange-red but still-firm stage and allowing to ripen at room temperature completes the conversion. The rich, sweet, pumpkin-like flavor of a fully ripe Tanenashi has no equivalent in temperate fruits. In zone 9, Tanenashi ripens in October through November and is one of the finest fall orchard fruits for the Gulf South — virtually pest-free, drought-tolerant once established, and producing heavily within 3–5 years of planting. The tree itself is ornamental: attractive dark-green summer foliage, spectacular orange-red fruit display in fall, and good fall foliage color before leaf drop.

The tangelo is a juicy, loose-skinned cross between a mandarin and a grapefruit or pomelo, often bearing a distinctive neck at the stem. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil in a frost-protected location, and note that some cultivars set better crops with a pollinizer nearby. Water deeply and feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Harvest when the fruit is fully colored and heavy with juice, typically from midwinter onward.

common_name: Tango Mandarin (Seedless Afourer-Type UC Riverside Mandarin)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Tango, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, is a seedless sport of the popular Afourer (W. Murcott) mandarin, bred specifically to stay seedless even when planted near other citrus, unlike its parent which becomes seedy from cross-pollination, while retaining the same rich, sweet-tart flavor and easy-peel skin. It ripens in winter, providing fresh citrus during the cooler months. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season.

A tangor is a mandarin-sweet orange hybrid, combining easy peeling with rich, full orange flavor. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and protect it from frost, which readily damages leaves and fruit. Apply a balanced citrus feed in spring and summer and mulch to conserve soil moisture. Harvest when fully colored and sweet, and prune lightly after cropping to remove crossing or weak wood.

common_name: Tarocco Blood Orange (Italian Half-Blood Sweet Orange)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above freezing, in full sun with deep, well-drained soil. Water deeply and consistently through the growing season, and expect the best red pigmentation where winter nights are cool but frost-free, as in coastal and inland California valleys. Tarocco fruit is nearly seedless with tender, aromatic flesh streaked or fully blushed red-purple and a flavor prized for its balance of sweetness and berry-like tang. It is considered the finest-flavored of the widely grown blood oranges but is more cold-sensitive than standard sweet oranges.

Tasty Red is a narrow, columnar apple that produces sweet, bite-sized red fruit with a refreshing crunch while taking up very little space. Its upright growth habit makes it ideal for containers, patios, and small yards, and several can be planted close together. Set the tree in full sun with well-drained soil and water regularly during establishment. Plant a second apple variety nearby for cross-pollination and better yields. Minimal pruning is needed thanks to the naturally compact columnar form.

Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Taynton Squash is among the oldest documented perry pear cultivars and one of the largest, most long-lived trees in the group. Named for the village of Taynton in Gloucestershire and documented since at least the seventeenth century, it is considered one of the oldest surviving named perry pear cultivars in England, producing a reliable crop of small, mid-tannin fruit on a tree capable of growing to an immense size and living for well over a century under good conditions. Its ancient pedigree and reliable cropping have kept it in cultivation in traditional Gloucestershire perry orchards continuously since long before named fruit varieties were commonly propagated by grafting elsewhere in Europe. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry.

Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving toward full sun once established. Taytwo is a historic Ohio-origin pawpaw selection long grown for its heavy, dependable production and medium-sized fruit with good, smooth-textured flavor, and it remains one of the most widely planted older cultivars for home orchards because it crops reliably even in cooler seasons. Vigorous, cold-hardy trees form the classic pyramidal pawpaw shape and tolerate the deep shade of establishment years better than most fruit trees, though full sun once mature produces the heaviest crops. Because pawpaws will not self-pollinate, plant a second unrelated cultivar such as Sunflower or Susquehanna nearby and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the maroon spring bloom for the most consistent fruit set.

Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with some wind protection, since Temple is more cold-sensitive than sweet oranges. First found growing in Jamaica and brought into Florida commerce in the early 1900s, it is classed as a tangor, a natural mandarin-orange hybrid, and produces a deep reddish-orange, easy-peeling fruit with an exceptionally rich, aromatic, sweet flavor that many consider superior to either parent type. It ripens January through March, later than most satsumas, giving a late splash of fresh citrus in the garden. Trees are moderately vigorous and benefit from regular citrus fertilizer and consistent moisture during fruit development.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Tempranillo is an early-ripening variety, an advantage in regions with shorter growing seasons or early fall rains. Spain's noble red wine grape and the foundation of Rioja and Ribera del Duero, its name derives from the Spanish word 'temprano' (early), reflecting its tendency to ripen earlier than many other red varieties, producing medium- to full-bodied wines with notes of red fruit, leather, and tobacco that develop further complexity with oak aging. Its earlier ripening window makes it a practical choice for regions with shorter growing seasons or a risk of early autumn rain damaging late-ripening varieties still on the vine. Prune to a moderate crop load for concentrated flavor, provide full sun and good air circulation to reduce disease pressure, and take advantage of its earlier harvest window in climates where fall weather can be unpredictable.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, poor to moderately fertile soil; terebinth is an ancient Mediterranean tree whose small red fruits (similar to tiny pistachios) have been consumed since prehistoric times and are still eaten in Greece and Turkey, where they are roasted, ground into a coffee-like drink, used to flavor spirits, and pickled in brine. The tree also historically yielded the original terebinth resin (turpentine) used in ancient medicine and as a paint vehicle. Closely related to the pistachio (Pistacia vera) and sometimes used as a pistachio rootstock. Extremely drought-adapted, thriving on poor limestone hillsides where little else will grow. The autumn foliage turns brilliant red before leaf drop.

growth_habit: Mediterranean wild fruit and spice tree
notes: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or limestone-derived soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — a true Mediterranean xerophyte. Pistacia terebinthus (terebinth or turpentine tree) is an ancient wild Mediterranean tree in the cashew family — the wild relative of the commercial pistachio (P. vera) — native to the dry hillsides, maquis, and garrigue scrublands of the Mediterranean basin from Portugal and Morocco east through Turkey and the Levant. The terebinth is one of the most historically significant trees of the ancient world: it appears in the Hebrew Bible (the 'elah' of the story of David and Goliath), in Greek mythology, and throughout classical Mediterranean literature. It produces small (1/4-inch), olive-shaped drupes that dry from red to dark brown-purple — the 'terebinth berries' or 'menengiç' used in Turkish cuisine as a traditional spice and, most distinctively, as a caffeine-free coffee substitute: roasted and ground terebinth berries are brewed exactly like coffee (menengiç kahvesi — terebinth coffee), producing a thick, rich, slightly bitter, nutty, resinous beverage beloved in southeastern Turkey and the Levant. The tree also produces a historical resin (Chian turpentine) used in medicine and varnishes in antiquity. As a garden plant, terebinth is an attractive, hardy, drought-tolerant Mediterranean small tree or large shrub with graceful pinnate leaves turning brilliant red-orange in autumn.

Plant in well-drained, rocky to sandy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; once established, Texas black persimmon requires little to no supplemental water. Diospyros texana (Texas black persimmon or Mexican persimmon) is a native small tree or large shrub of rocky Texas Hill Country limestone and the brushlands of south Texas and northern Mexico, producing small, 1-inch, round, jet-black fruits in July–September that taste intensely sweet — like dark plums or figs with a honey-like richness — and stain everything they touch with deep-purple-black juice (historically used as a fabric dye by Native Americans and early settlers). The tree is highly ornamental in addition to its fruit value: an attractive, multi-stemmed form with flaky, pale-gray bark that exfoliates to reveal silvery, cream, and pale-orange patches; small, glossy, semi-evergreen leaves; and outstanding fall-winter structural interest. It is adapted to full sun and extreme drought and alkaline soils where most fruit trees struggle. Wildlife (deer, wild turkey, quail, and many bird species) consume the fruits eagerly. Texas persimmon is dioecious (separate male and female trees needed for fruit); plant at least one male per 3–5 female trees.

Plant in well-drained, rocky, chalky, or limestone-derived soil in full sun in central and south Texas; Texas black walnut is the small, drought-tolerant walnut native to the rocky limestone hills and creek drainages of central Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico. Unlike the towering eastern black walnut (J. nigra), this species stays at 20-30 feet with a spreading, multi-stemmed habit. The small nuts are round and dark-shelled with a proportionally small but edible, walnut-flavored kernel — historically gathered and cracked by Indigenous peoples and early settlers. The tree produces juglone in its roots and leaves like all walnuts, inhibiting the growth of some nearby plants, especially tomatoes, peppers, and certain other species. An excellent native tree for dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the Texas Hill Country and adjacent areas where eastern black walnut cannot thrive.

common_name: Texas Blue Giant Fig (Large Purple-Black Texas Fig)
notes: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; figs benefit from consistent moisture during the fruiting season to size fruit well and avoid splitting. Texas Blue Giant is a large-fruited fig popular among Texas and Gulf South fig growers, producing sizeable, deep purple-black fruit with sweet, richly flavored strawberry-red flesh on a vigorous, spreading tree. Its large fruit size and dark, attractive skin color make it a favorite for fresh eating and preserving, and the tree is well adapted to regional heat and humidity, cropping over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to manage its vigorous size and remove any winter dieback, and mulch heavily to protect the shallow root system through summer heat and occasional winter cold snaps.

common_name: Texas Everbearing Fig (Texas Everbearing Brown Turkey)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; established Texas Everbearing figs are drought-tolerant and require minimal care; protect roots with 4–6 inches of mulch in zones 7–8 where temperatures occasionally drop below 15°F. Texas Everbearing is a fig variety specifically selected and propagated in Texas for its exceptional performance in the hot, humid climate of the Gulf Coast and Central Texas, where it is the most commonly grown and recommended home garden fig; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension has long listed it as a top variety for the region. The medium to large, pear-shaped fruits have brownish-purple to brown skin (similar to but distinct from standard Brown Turkey) with strawberry-pink to amber flesh; the flavor is rich, honeyed, and sweet with the characteristic caramel-fig quality characteristic of the best common-type figs. As an everbearing type, Texas Everbearing produces two crops: breba fruits on previous year's wood in early summer (June) followed by the main crop on current season's wood from late summer through frost (August–November); this extended fruiting season is a practical advantage over single-crop types for home garden production. Excellent fresh, dried, or preserved; very productive in Gulf Coast zone 8–10 conditions.

Plant container-grown trees or hardwood cuttings in spring in dry to moderately moist, rocky, sandy, or caliche soils in full sun to light shade; Texas mulberry once established is highly drought-tolerant and requires no supplemental irrigation in zone 7–10. Texas mulberry is a small native tree or large shrub (8–20 feet) of the dry Hill Country, Trans-Pecos, and Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and New Mexico, with smaller leaves and a more drought-tolerant constitution than any other native American mulberry; the sweet, dark purple to black mulberries ripen in late spring and are an extremely important food source for numerous bird species including cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and orioles, as well as mammals from foxes to deer.
