Excellent as a water-conserving landscape tree for dry zone 7–10 gardens where conventional mulberries may struggle; the fruit is edible and excellent fresh or in pies and preserves.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; Texas persimmon is a small native multi-trunked tree of the Texas Hill Country and Rio Grande Plains with distinctive smooth, peeling gray bark revealing white-green underbark (one of the most beautiful native bark patterns in the Southwest). The small round fruits ripen jet black in August–September and are intensely sweet when fully ripe, though the black pulp stains everything permanently — including lips, fingers, and clothing. They are eaten fresh, dried, or cooked into syrup and are an important food for coyotes, bears, gray foxes, and birds. The tree is extremely drought tolerant once established and requires alkaline, well-drained soil. Both male and female trees are needed for fruit production.

Texas Pink is a pomegranate valued for its large rosy-pink blushed fruit and its ornamental, gnarled bonsai-like bark and bright orange-red flowers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, allowing plenty of room for the shrubby tree to develop. Once established, it is quite drought-tolerant and needs only occasional deep watering. In zones colder than 7, grow it in a patio container and move it to shelter over winter. Prune to a single trunk or multi-stemmed form and thin fruit to improve size.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline, limestone-based or rocky soil in full sun; Texas pistache is a handsome small multi-trunked native tree of the limestone canyons of southwest Texas and northeast Mexico, prized for one of the most spectacular fall color displays of any native Texan woody plant — the compound leaves turning brilliant shades of orange, red, and scarlet before dropping. Small red fruits are eaten by birds and wildlife, and the tree is often suggested as a superior native alternative to the widely planted Chinese pistache (Pistacia chinensis). It is extremely drought tolerant once established and well suited to xeric landscapes, parking lot edges, and small residential lots in zones 7–10. Growth is slow to moderate, so purchase the largest container specimen available for faster landscape impact.

common_name: Texas Scarlet Flowering Quince (Compact Red-Orange Flowering Quince)
notes: Texas Scarlet is a compact, spreading flowering quince selection covering itself in brilliant red-orange flowers directly on the bare, twiggy stems in late winter and very early spring, well before the leaves emerge, making it one of the earliest color displays of the gardening year. Its low, mounding habit stays well under 4 feet, more manageable than many older flowering quince cultivars, and small yellow-green, quince-scented fruit follows the bloom, edible when cooked into jelly or preserves though rarely eaten raw. Extremely adaptable to poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and quite drought-tolerant, it blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinator cultivar planted within about 50–60 feet for reliable cross-pollination, since hazelnuts require wind transfer of pollen between genetically compatible trees. Theta was developed by Oregon State University's hazelnut breeding program and released with strong resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that has devastated susceptible hazelnut orchards, allowing more reliable production without the intensive disease management older, susceptible cultivars require. It produces medium to large, well-filled, high-quality nuts on a vigorous, productive tree, harvested in early fall as they naturally drop from the husk. Hazelnuts perform best in regions with cool, humid growing seasons and moderate winter chill, making them a better fit for the upper South and Pacific Northwest-like climates than the hot, humid Deep South, where summer heat and disease pressure limit success. Rake and collect fallen nuts promptly to prevent rodent loss and mold.

common_name: Thomas Black Walnut (Classic Large-Nutted Eastern Black Walnut)
notes: Plant grafted trees into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from vegetable gardens and shade-sensitive plants since black walnut roots exude juglone, a compound toxic to many other species. Thomas is one of the oldest and most widely planted named black walnut cultivars, selected in Pennsylvania in the 1880s and still valued for its consistently large, well-filled nuts, relatively thin shell, and good cracking quality compared with wild seedling trees. The vigorous, long-lived tree needs several years to reach bearing age but then produces reliably for decades, with nuts maturing and dropping in fall for hulling, curing, and cracking. Keep young trees watered during establishment, and protect the trunk from mower and string-trimmer damage; mature trees need little care beyond an occasional light fertilization and removal of any dead or crossing limbs.

Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a fruiting citrus, tolerating hard freezes that would kill standard citrus outright, though a sheltered microclimate still improves fruit set and tree vigor. Thomasville citrangequat is a three-way citrus hybrid — a cross of citrange (trifoliate orange × sweet orange) with kumquat — developed by USDA citrus breeder Dr. Walter Swingle in Thomasville, Georgia in the early 20th century specifically to push the boundary of cold-hardy edible citrus northward out of Florida. The small, oval, orange-yellow fruits have an aromatic, tart-sweet, marmalade-quality flavor with edible skin in the kumquat tradition, best used for marmalade, candying, or juice rather than fresh peeling and eating. The tree also carries attractive small trifoliate-influenced leaves and light thorns, and its extreme hardiness has made it a mainstay of cold-hardy citrus hobbyist plantings from the Gulf Coast through the Southeast. A rewarding novelty citrus for growers pushing the cold edge of the citrus range, zone 7–10.

Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Thorn is a reliably productive, widely grown traditional Gloucestershire perry pear. One of the classic Three Counties perry pears traditionally grown across Gloucestershire, Herefordshire, and Worcestershire, it produces a reliable crop of small, hard, astringent fruit prized for well-balanced tannin and good juice yield, and it remains a component of a number of well-regarded commercial English perry blends. Like most true perry pears it is grown solely for fermenting into perry rather than fresh eating, and it shares the group's characteristically slow growth to first significant bearing. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil from rocky to clay; three-leaf sumac (Rhus trilobata) is a wide-ranging, cold-hardy western sumac producing small, sticky, red-orange berries used identically to lemonade berry — soaked in water to make a tart, refreshing beverage — and was one of the most important wild food and medicinal plants of western Native American tribes from the Great Plains to California. The flexible young branches were traditionally used for basket weaving by many indigenous peoples. Exceptional for erosion control on dry slopes, with beautiful orange-red fall color, excellent wildlife value, and extraordinary drought tolerance. Does not sucker aggressively. The common name 'skunkbush' refers to the strong, somewhat pungent smell of the crushed foliage.

Plant Akebia trifoliata at the base of a sturdy trellis, pergola, or fence in partial to full sun; plant two or more seedlings of different genetic origin for cross-pollination and reliable fruiting; water regularly; harvest pods in autumn when they split open along the seam. Three-leaf Akebia is a fascinating edible ornamental vine producing unusual fruits that are rarely seen outside Japan and China but are gaining interest among adventurous Western growers. The pale purple to lavender sausage-shaped pods (3–5 inches long) split open in autumn to reveal sweet, translucent white pulp — the pulp is eaten fresh by scooping around the embedded seeds, which are not eaten. The flavor is mildly sweet, subtle, and aromatic — not intensely flavored but pleasantly unique. Beyond the fruit, young spring shoots are blanched and eaten as a vegetable (akebi no tsuru) in Japanese mountain cuisine. The intricate, three-leaflet foliage on twining stems is ornamentally attractive, and the small, dark purple flowers in spring are fragrant with a vanilla scent. A related species, Akebia quinata (Five-leaf Akebia), is very similar but with five leaflets and is widely grown ornamentally — both are vigorous and need substantial support.

Plant in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 5–9; threeleaf akebia is closely related to the more commonly grown fiveleaf akebia (A. quinata) but is distinguished by having only three leaflets per leaf (vs. five in A. quinata) and generally larger fruits — the sausage-shaped, blue-purple pods can reach 4–5 inches long in good specimens. The pale purple, vanilla-fragrant flowers in spring are striking and ornamental. The ripe fruits split open along one side to reveal white, jelly-like pulp surrounding black seeds — the pulp is eaten fresh, tasting sweet and somewhat like lychee, while the empty pods are used as a vegetable in Japan. A vigorous, somewhat twining vine that can be invasive in some regions; grow on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence where its vigor can be managed by pruning. A productive edible vine for the partial shade garden in zones 5–9.

common_name: Tonda Gentile delle Langhe Hazelnut (Piedmont Hazelnut)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and provide a compatible pollenizer variety nearby, since this hazelnut is not self-fertile. Tonda Gentile delle Langhe is the classic hazelnut of Italy's Piedmont region, celebrated for its round shape, thin shell, and rich, sweet, highly aromatic kernel that is the traditional standard for fine chocolate-hazelnut confections. Like most European hazelnut cultivars it is quite susceptible to eastern filbert blight in humid North American climates, so it performs best in drier growing regions or where the disease pressure is low.

common_name: Toyo Nishiki Flowering Quince (Multicolor Pink-White-Red Flowering Quince)
notes: Toyo Nishiki is a classic flowering quince cultivar famous for producing white, pink, and red flowers all at once on the same branch, and sometimes even within a single blossom, an unpredictable multicolor mix that makes each spring's bloom slightly different from the last. It flowers directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter into early spring ahead of the foliage, forming a large, vigorous, arching shrub, and small yellow-green, quince-scented fruit follows the bloom, valued for jelly and preserves rather than fresh eating. Highly adaptable to poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil once established and notably drought-tolerant, it makes an effective thorny barrier hedge in addition to its ornamental value.

Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, allowing 15-25 feet between trees for their eventual size. Trazels are named for their parentage — a cross between the native American hazelnut (Corylus americana) and the Turkish tree hazel (Corylus colurna) — combining the American parent's cold hardiness and blight resistance with the Turkish parent's strong single-trunk, tree-like growth habit, unlike the suckering thicket form typical of most hazelnuts. This tree form makes Trazels far easier to manage in an orchard row or as a landscape specimen than shrubby hazelnut types, and their resistance to Eastern filbert blight — a fungal canker disease that has devastated commercial plantings of European hazelnut (C. avellana) across much of the eastern and midwestern United States — makes them one of the more dependable hazelnut options outside the Pacific Northwest. Nuts are borne in husked clusters and ripen in late summer to early fall; because most Trazel seedlings show variable nut size and quality, growers select and propagate individual trees for improved nut characteristics. Plant two or more seedlings for best pollination, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and largely self-incompatible.

Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Solanum betaceum grows fast but has brittle branches — provide wind protection and stake when young; water deeply and regularly and fertilize monthly for maximum fruiting; prune after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new productive growth. Solanum betaceum (Tree Tomato or Tamarillo, syn. Cyphomandra betacea) is a fast-growing, soft-wooded, small tree in the Solanaceae (nightshade) family native to the semi-arid and sub-humid Andean highlands of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Colombia, and northern Chile at elevations of 5,000–10,000 feet. The tree produces prolific clusters of glossy, egg-shaped, thin-skinned fruits — deep red, orange, or yellow depending on cultivar — with tangy-sweet, intensely flavored flesh combining tomato, passion fruit, and tropical notes, surrounding a central core of dark-purple seeds. Tamarillos are extensively eaten fresh (the skin is typically removed), made into juice, jams, chutneys, salsas, and cooked sauces across Ecuador, Peru, Colombia, and especially New Zealand, where the industry was developed from Andean introductions in the mid-20th century. Trees fruit prolifically in 1–2 years from transplants, providing remarkable returns for a tree-fruit crop. The plants are susceptible to tobacco mosaic virus, cold below 28°F, and water stress — they perform best in cool, frost-light subtropical conditions (zone 8b–10) with consistent moisture. Named a 'new world food' candidate for its high vitamin C, antioxidant, and nutritional content.

The hardy trifoliate orange is a deciduous citrus relative bearing small, aromatic, seedy fruit used for marmalade and flavoring. Remarkably cold-tolerant, it survives well below freezing and is widely used as a dwarfing rootstock for other citrus. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; its dense, fiercely thorny growth makes an effective barrier hedge. Harvest the downy yellow fruit in autumn, using the tart juice and rind rather than eating it fresh.

common_name: Tropic Sweet Apple (Large Sweet Low-Chill Gulf South Apple)
notes: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tropic Sweet is a University of Florida low-chill apple introduction specifically developed for production in zone 8–10 gardens where chill hours are insufficient for standard northern apple cultivars. With only 150–200 chill hours required, Tropic Sweet is adapted to the winter climate of zone 9a where standard apple varieties cannot break dormancy properly. The fruits are large, round, yellow with a light blush, and distinguished by outstanding sweetness with very low acid content — a flavor profile that differs from the balanced sweet-tart quality of northern apples and appeals strongly to those who prefer sweet, mild apples. Tropic Sweet ripens in June in zone 9 — the June ripening window is well ahead of most summer fruit production and provides fresh orchard fruit at a time when few other tree fruits are ready. Like all low-chill apples, Tropic Sweet performs best when cross-pollinated with another low-chill cultivar such as Dorsett Golden or Anna. Proper dormant pruning (in late January–February) and fire blight management (preventive copper sprays during bloom) are the primary cultural practices for Gulf South apple production. The outstanding sweetness and large size make Tropic Sweet one of the finest fresh-eating apple choices for Gulf South gardeners willing to manage fire blight, which is the primary disease challenge in the humid Gulf South climate.

Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger has passed, in a warm, sunny site with well-drained soil, since this cultivar was selected for reliable fruiting in low-heat, low-humidity climates. Water regularly during establishment and reduce slightly as fruit matures to help concentrate flavor. Trovita produces medium-sized, thin-skinned oranges with juicy, sweet flesh and fewer seeds than many Valencia-type oranges, ripening in winter to early spring. Originating as a Washington Navel sport bred for desert and coastal Southern California conditions, it remains a dependable choice where summer heat is moderate.

common_name: Tung Oil Tree (China Wood Oil Tree)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; tung oil tree is a Chinese tree cultivated throughout zone 8–11 for its seeds, which yield tung oil — a fast-drying, water-resistant drying oil used extensively in paints, varnishes, wood preservatives, and wood finishing products. The spring flower display is spectacular — large clusters of white flowers with red or pink veining cover the bare branches before leaf emergence, followed by bold, large, heart-shaped leaves. The golf-ball-sized fruits contain 3–7 seeds with 50–60% oil content. The entire plant is poisonous if consumed — the seeds, leaves, and oil are toxic. The Gulf South has abandoned remnant tung orchards from a failed commercial industry of the mid-20th century. Now a naturalized, occasionally invasive ornamental/landscape tree notable for its spring flower show. Caution: all plant parts are toxic.

Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, even dry or compacted soil in full sun; Turkish hazel is the most drought-tolerant and urban-adaptable of all hazelnuts, renowned in the horticultural trade as one of the few large nut trees that tolerates dry, alkaline soils, compacted city conditions, and air pollution — a remarkable feat for any tree. It is used as a rootstock for grafting cultivated filbert and hazelnut varieties, and the straight species produces small edible nuts enclosed in deeply fringed husks. The distinctive corky, deeply ridged bark and broadly pyramidal form make it an ornamental specimen tree even when not in nut. Long-lived and very low-maintenance; used extensively in European forestry and urban planting programs.

Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Typica coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Considered the original Arabica coffee variety from which nearly all other Arabica cultivars ultimately descend, having spread from Yemen through European colonial cultivation to become the ancestral genetic base of the world's coffee industry, it is still valued today for its classically sweet, clean, well-balanced cup quality despite its taller, more open growth habit and lower yield and disease resistance compared to modern hybrids. Its lanky, open branching habit and susceptibility to coffee leaf rust and other diseases have led most commercial growers to switch to higher-yielding, more disease-resistant hybrid varieties, but heirloom Typica plantings remain prized by specialty coffee producers for their traditional flavor profile. Provide the same dappled shade, consistent moisture, and good drainage other Arabica coffees need, and expect the first harvest after three to four years of growth.

Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season; US Early Pride is a modern navel orange selection bred for an early ripening window, often ready for harvest well ahead of standard Washington navels, and produces sweet, low-seed, easy-to-peel fruit with the classic navel form. Water deeply but allow the soil surface to dry between waterings, and mulch to protect the shallow root zone from summer heat. Give young trees frost protection through their first winters, and expect a light first crop within a few years of planting a grafted tree, building to full production as the tree matures.

scientific_name: Citrus paradisi x Poncirus trifoliata x Citrus sinensis 'US-119'
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a protected spot such as a south-facing wall for extra winter buffering in zone 8-9 gardens. US-119 was developed by USDA breeders from a cross of citrumelo and sweet orange, giving it roughly one-quarter trifoliate orange parentage and correspondingly greater cold tolerance than a true sweet orange, while retaining a genuinely sweet, orange-like flavor rather than the sharp bitterness typical of many trifoliate hybrids. Fruit has a smooth, attractive orange peel, relatively few seeds, and juicy flesh with just a hint of the trifoliate parent's distinctive aftertaste. Because of its unusual hardiness for citrus with real dessert-orange flavor, it has become popular among cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing sweet citrus north of the traditional growing range; protect young trees through their first few winters, since mature specimens are considerably tougher.

Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ussurian pear tolerates temperatures to -40°F and is the hardiest pear species available, making it the only viable pear for zones 2–3 where European pears cannot survive. Pyrus ussuriensis is a large, ornamental, extremely cold-hardy pear species from northeastern China and Siberia; it bears masses of white flowers in early spring before the leaves, followed in fall by small (1–2 inch), round, green to yellow-green, gritty-fleshed fruits with a rough texture that are best cooked or used for preserves rather than fresh eating. Its primary agricultural value is as a rootstock for grafted pear varieties and as a breeding parent for cold-hardy pear cultivars (e.g., 'Ure', 'Rescue', 'David', 'Nova') developed by Canadian and university breeders for the northern Great Plains. The glossy, dark-green leaves turn brilliant red in fall, making it an outstanding ornamental even where fruit quality is secondary.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun to light shade; Utah serviceberry thrives in dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the West and Great Basin where other serviceberries would fail. Amelanchier utahensis is a native shrub of dry foothills, rocky slopes, and canyon walls from the Great Basin west, producing white spring flowers, small (1/3 inch) dark-blue berries with a sweet, mild, blueberry-like flavor in early summer (ripe very early, often by late May-June), and outstanding fall color in shades of orange and red. The berries are an extremely important wildlife food — essentially every frugivorous bird and mammal in the arid West relies on serviceberries during the brief ripening window. Extremely drought- and cold-hardy, this is the recommended serviceberry for xeric and high-altitude western gardens. Use for wildlife plantings, erosion control, and native landscaping.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; pomegranate is highly drought-tolerant once established and performs well on minimal irrigation in well-drained Gulf South soils. Utah Sweet is valued for pink-tinged skin and pulp with a notably sweeter, less tart flavor than the widely grown Wonderful pomegranate, along with softer, more tender seeds that make the arils easier to eat fresh without the firmer crunch typical of many other pomegranate cultivars. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will fruit, though yields can improve with cross-pollination from a second cultivar. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit is developing, then ease back as fruit nears ripeness to help prevent splitting, and harvest when the fruit gives a dull, metallic sound when tapped.

Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; uvaia (Eugenia pyriformis) is a beautiful Brazilian Myrtaceae tree closely related to Surinam cherry and pitanga, producing pear-shaped to round yellow fruits about 1 inch in diameter with a juicy, aromatic, sweet-acidic flesh — the flavor is often described as a complex blend of passion fruit, citrus, and Eugenia aromatics with a pleasant acidity that makes the fruit excellent fresh, as juice, in ice cream, and as jams. The tree has attractive bronze-red new growth and small white flowers. Increasingly popular among Brazilian native fruit enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors in south Florida and Hawaii; one of the finest of the genus Eugenia for flavor. Fruits appear in clusters along the branches and trunk.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun in the warmest available location; Valencia is the world's most important juice orange and the benchmark orange of Florida's commercial citrus industry. The medium-large, thin-skinned, deep-orange fruits mature in March–June — uniquely late for citrus, which is why Valencia becomes the dominant fresh-market and juice orange in late spring when all other oranges have finished. The juice is abundant, sweet-tart, and intensely flavored. Valencia is known for re-greening: mature ripe fruit turns orange during cool weather, then re-greens as temperatures warm in spring — this does not affect juice quality but can confuse growers expecting a uniformly orange skin. In zone 9, Valencia is one of the most cold-tolerant sweet oranges and often survives temperatures to 25°F with minimal damage; below 20°F the tree may be severely damaged. Feed with citrus fertilizer (including zinc, iron, and manganese) three times per year and maintain a 3–4 inch citrus mulch ring. Excellent fresh or for juice.

common_name: Van Deman Quince (Historic USDA-Named Heirloom Quince)
notes: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Van Deman is a historic American quince cultivar named for USDA pomologist Henry E. Van Deman, documented in older state and federal pomology references among the notable named quince selections grown in American orchards in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It produces large, aromatic, golden-yellow fruit with the classic hard, tart flesh that transforms into a fragrant, rosy-pink preserve or paste once cooked with sugar. Like other quince, it is self-fertile, needs no separate pollinator, and begins bearing within a few years of planting on a young tree. Prune to an open vase form for good air circulation, which is the primary defense against fire blight, the main disease risk for quince in humid climates. Harvest fruit in fall once it has turned fully golden and developed its strong, characteristic perfume, and store in a cool, dry spot, where quince keeps considerably longer than most tree fruit.

common_name: Variegated Pink Lemon (Pink Eureka Lemon, Eureka Variegated Pink)
notes: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Variegated Pink Lemon (sold as 'Pink Eureka Lemon' or 'Eureka Variegated Pink') is a striking sports mutation of the standard Eureka lemon, valued both as a productive lemon and as a highly ornamental landscape or container specimen. The foliage is distinctively variegated in green and cream-white patterns that remain attractive year-round; the unripe fruits are dramatically striped in green and yellow (somewhat like a watermelon in miniature), and the flesh is pale pink when cut — a surprise and visual delight that makes this lemon memorable and photogenic. As the fruit ripens to full yellow, the pink-flesh color fades but remains just slightly pink in fully ripe fruit; the flavor is standard Eureka lemon — tart, aromatic, excellent for culinary use in anything requiring fresh lemon juice, zest, or slices. Production is good but somewhat lighter than standard Eureka. An outstanding choice for container culture, ornamental edible gardens, and any setting where visual interest in the plant matters as much as production.

common_name: Velvet Apple (Mabolo, Butter Fruit, Kamagong Fruit Tree)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Velvet Apple grows most vigorously in full sun but tolerates and often benefits from afternoon shade protection in the intense heat of zone 9-10 summers. Diospyros blancoi is an evergreen fruit tree from the Philippines in the family Ebenaceae (the ebony and persimmon family), producing one of the most striking and unusual fruits in the tropical fruit world. The ripe fruits are perfectly round (3–4 inches in diameter), covered in a dense coat of fine reddish-brown to coppery velvet-soft hairs — like an incredibly large, round, red-brown cherry with velvet skin — from which the common name 'Velvet Apple' derives. Beneath the velvety skin is a firm, creamy-white to pink flesh with a sweet, mild flavor combining banana, cream, and mango notes and a dry, slightly astringent texture similar to some persimmons. The fruits have a striking, pungent odor when freshly harvested that many people find unpleasant (sometimes compared to ripe cheese or onion), but this odor dissipates with ventilation and does not affect the pleasant flavor of the flesh. In the Philippines, the tree is doubly valued: for its edible fruit and for its heartwood (called 'kamagong' — Philippine ebony), one of the hardest and heaviest woods in Southeast Asia, used for fine furniture and tool handles. The tree is also an ornamental specimen with glossy, dark-green foliage.

Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep, well-aerated soil in full sun; velvet mesquite is the dominant mesquite of Arizona desert grasslands and saguaro cactus country, nearly identical to honey mesquite (P. glandulosa) but more densely hairy (velutinous) on the leaves and pods, tolerating the extreme heat and seasonal drought of the Sonoran Desert. The long, flat, tan seed pods mature in late summer and are very high in sugar and protein — edible by humans (ground into mesquite flour), consumed by coyotes, javelinas, deer, and dozens of bird species. The fragrant, cream-colored flower spikes in spring attract swarms of native bees. Deep taproots (up to 60 feet) access groundwater far below the surface. An important nitrogen-fixing tree that improves soil fertility. The aromatic wood produces some of the finest barbecue smoke in the world — prized for smoked meats throughout the Southwest.

common_name: Ventura Strawberry Fig (Adriatic-Type Red-Fleshed California Fig)
notes: Ventura Strawberry is a California selection within the Adriatic group of fig cultivars, named for the deep red, berry-like color and flavor of its flesh rather than for any trait of its skin. Fruits are medium-sized with dark purple-black skin and a thick, juicy, red interior that carries a distinct strawberry-like sweetness; as with other Adriatic types it sets a dependable main crop without needing pollination. The tree performs well in hot, sunny conditions and has become a sought-after specialty selection among Southern fig collectors for its rich flavor and productivity. Grow it as you would other common-type figs, in full sun with excellent drainage, and expect the first fruit within two to three years of planting a rooted cutting.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — figs produce best in lean conditions and can become overly vegetative in rich, heavily fertilized soil; Verte de Bordeaux is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of southwestern France, producing small to medium, pear-shaped fruits with green to greenish-yellow skin that remains green even when fully ripe — a distinctive appearance that surprises consumers expecting a ripe fig to be darker. The deep burgundy-red interior flesh has an intensely rich, wine-like, complex sweetness that fig connoisseurs often rate among the finest flavors in the Ficus carica species. The petite size (1–2 inches) and striking green skin with deeply colored interior make it a specialty market favorite. In zone 9 Verte de Bordeaux produces consistently and handles the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers well. The green skin can be confusing to novice growers who may pick the fruit too early — harvest when the neck of the fig bends and the fruit softens.

Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Victoria is self-fertile and does not require a second variety for pollination, though a pollinator improves yield. The single most widely grown plum in England and one of the best-known European dessert plums in the world, it bears heavy crops of large, oval, red-blushed yellow fruit with juicy, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, and its reliable, self-fertile heavy bearing has made it a standard first-choice plum for a home orchard with room for only one tree. Its very heavy crops often require significant hand thinning of young fruit to prevent limb breakage and to improve the size and quality of the remaining plums. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, thin crowded fruit clusters, and support heavily laden branches in a good fruiting year.

common_name: Victoria Red Grape (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Table Grape)
notes: Train on a trellis system in full sun in well-drained soil; prune in late winter. Victoria Red is a seeded red table grape that has survived over 25 years of extreme Pierce's disease pressure at the Tarkington Vineyards test site near Victoria, Texas, making it one of the few table grapes with genuinely sustained tolerance to the disease that otherwise makes grape growing across the Gulf Coast so difficult. It produces large, sweet clusters with sugar levels reaching up to 25 brix, eaten fresh, dried into raisins, or made into juice. Because it was bred specifically for hot, humid Texas and Gulf Coast conditions, it needs none of the intensive spray programs required to keep Pierce's-disease-susceptible European grapes alive in the region. Harvest clusters once berries have colored fully and taste sweet, since grapes do not continue ripening after picking.

common_name: Vidal Blanc Grape (Vidal 256, Cold-Hardy French-American White Wine Grape)
notes: Vidal Blanc, officially Vidal 256, is a French-American hybrid bred from Ugni Blanc and Seibel 4986 that has become one of the most widely planted white wine grapes in the eastern and southern United States for its combination of productivity, cold hardiness, and good fungal-disease tolerance. It produces heavy clusters of thick-skinned, golden berries late in the season, valued both for crisp dry table wines and for late-harvest or ice-wine-style dessert wines where hard freezes concentrate the sugars. Train it on a high-wire cordon or Geneva double-curtain system in full sun, and prune to manage its vigorous, fruitful growth, which can overcrop and require cluster thinning for best wine quality. Like most French-American hybrids, Vidal Blanc carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance, so southern extension programs generally recommend it for the upper and middle South rather than the most Pierce's-disease-prone Gulf Coast counties.

Plant nursery trees in spring once frost danger has passed, in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil, allowing space for a nearly thornless, densely foliaged canopy. Provide even moisture throughout the year and protect young trees from hard freezes with covers or trunk wraps. Villafranca bears Eureka-type lemons that are medium-sized, juicy, and nearly seedless, produced almost continuously in warm climates with a heavier main crop in winter. Long grown in Florida and the Gulf Coast as a dooryard favorite, it is valued for producing well even under humid, subtropical conditions that can trouble other lemon cultivars.

common_name: Villard Blanc Grape (Seyve-Villard 12-375, French-American Hybrid White Wine Grape)
notes: Villard Blanc, registered as Seyve-Villard 12-375, is one of the classic French-American hybrid wine grapes bred in the early 20th century by Bertille Seyve and Victor Villard to combine vinifera-quality fruit with the fungal-disease resistance of American parentage. It produces large clusters of greenish-white berries that ripen into a crisp, aromatic dry white wine and has historically been planted across the humid eastern and southern United States, where straight vinifera varieties struggle with black rot, downy mildew, and powdery mildew. Train vines on a cordon or high-wire trellis in full sun with good air movement, and prune hard each winter, since Villard Blanc is a vigorous grower that needs canopy management to ripen fruit well and avoid disease pressure in wet years. It carries only moderate Pierce's disease tolerance compared with purpose-bred Gulf Coast hybrids, so it performs best in the upper and middle South rather than the most humid Gulf Coast counties.

common_name: Violette de Bordeaux Fig (Negronne Fig, Petite Negri Fig)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Violette de Bordeaux (called Negronne in California and known as Petite Negri in some American nurseries) is a small-statured French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of France — one of the most beloved fig varieties among connoisseurs because of its extraordinary flavor. The small (1.5–2 inch), deep purple-violet to nearly black berries have blood-red interior flesh with a rich, complex, intense sweetness with strawberry-raspberry undertones — a flavor profile significantly deeper and more complex than larger, milder figs. The tree's compact size (6–8 feet tall and wide) makes it an ideal container specimen for patios, balconies, and small urban gardens where a standard fig would overwhelm the space. Violette de Bordeaux is the go-to container fig recommended by specialty nurseries. The skin is quite thin and fruits bruise easily, limiting its commercial shipping potential but making it perfect for eating fresh off the tree. In zone 9, it fruits reliably August–October and can be moved into protected areas during cold snaps in zone 9a.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Violette de Sollies has Protected Designation of Origin (AOP) status as the primary fig of Sollies-Pont commune in Var, Provence — the most commercially important fig production area in France. It accounts for approximately 80% of French commercial fig production and is the fig you encounter in French supermarkets and on French cheese boards. The large, round to pear-shaped fruits have dark violet to nearly black skin and deep red to garnet flesh with an exceptionally creamy, melt-in-the-mouth texture and rich, complex sweetness. The PDO designation reflects the specific microclimate of the Var region and the care taken to produce the variety at optimal quality. Violette de Sollies is a fall-ripening variety, producing its main crop in September–October in zone 9 — later than most other figs and extending the fresh fig season into autumn. The exceptional flavor quality and French culinary prestige make it a premium choice for zone 9 gardens where the warm fall provides ideal ripening conditions.

common_name: Virginia Beauty Apple (Spicy Russeted Virginia Heirloom)
notes: Plant in a sheltered but sunny site and prune to an open canopy to help the fruit color and to control the tree's tendency toward biennial bearing. Virginia Beauty is a late-19th-century Virginia heirloom noted for its striped red skin, patches of russet, and distinctively spicy, aromatic flesh that improves in flavor during a few weeks of storage. It has long been a favorite among Southern heritage orchardists for fresh eating and cider, prized as much for its complex flavor as for its keeping ability into winter.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, transitioning to fuller sun as the tree matures; Wabash is one of the named Peterson Pawpaw cultivars, selected from Neal Peterson's long-running breeding program for its combination of large fruit size and notably vigorous, healthy tree growth. Fruit has the classic rich, tropical pawpaw flavor — often described as a cross between banana, mango, and custard — with good flesh-to-seed ratio. As with all pawpaws, Wabash is self-incompatible and requires a second, unrelated named cultivar planted within about 50 feet for reliable pollination; hand-pollinating between two different cultivars' open flowers with a small brush improves fruit set in home gardens where natural fly and beetle pollinators may be scarce. Mulch young trees well and keep soil consistently moist through the first two seasons, since pawpaw's shallow, fleshy root system is intolerant of drought while establishing; mature trees are considerably more drought-tolerant.

Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-protected conditions; wampee (wampi) is a Chinese subtropical fruit tree in the citrus family (Rutaceae) producing large drooping clusters of small, round, yellowish-white to golden fruits about the size of a large grape, with a thin, slightly oily skin and aromatic, translucent flesh that ranges from sweet to pleasantly acid-sweet, with a distinctive, complex, resinous-floral fragrance from essential oils in the skin. The flavor profile has notes of citrus, lychee, and a slight bitterness that makes it uniquely refreshing. Native to South China and widely grown in southern China, Vietnam, and Thailand, it has been cultivated for over 2,000 years and is a significant regional fruit crop in Guangdong. The fruits are eaten fresh, made into preserves and wine, and the essential oil from the rind is used in Chinese medicine and as a fragrance. It grows well in the humid subtropics of zones 9–11 and is more compact and manageable than many tropical fruit trees.

Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; requires consistent rainfall or irrigation during fruit development. Mangifera caesia (wani mango or binjai) is a large Mangifera species native to the humid lowland rainforests of Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula — one of the most important traditional fruit trees of Sarawak and Sabah (Malaysian Borneo), where it is planted around villages and sometimes bears enormous quantities of fruits. The fruits are remarkable: large (4–6 inches long), elongated-oblong to kidney-shaped, pale green to yellowish-white when ripe — larger on average than common mangoes — with white to pale-yellow flesh. The flavor is more distinctly turpentine-acidic than common mango, with a sweetness that varies considerably by seedling; selected clones can be mild and pleasant. The flesh is rather fibrous and the skin is not eaten. In Sarawak, wani fruits are sold fresh in markets and eaten as a fresh fruit, in rujak (spicy fruit salads), and processed into pickles. The bark and young leaves have traditional medicinal uses in Malaysian herbal medicine. Wani requires a genuinely tropical, hot, humid, low-frost-risk climate and is suitable only for zone 11–12 in the continental United States (extreme South Florida, Hawaii). A collectors' fruit tree for the most dedicated tropical fruit enthusiast.

Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Warren is an outstanding southern heirloom pear discovered in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, by T.O. Warren around 1960 — a chance seedling that produces buttery, very sweet, nearly grit-free fruit with the silky texture of a fine European dessert pear. This exceptional fruit quality, combined with good fire blight resistance (the most devastating pear disease in humid southern climates), has made Warren one of the most highly regarded pear varieties for the Gulf South in recent decades. Most European pears are highly susceptible to fire blight (Erwinia amylovora), the bacterial disease that kills branches and causes heavy losses in hot, humid climates — Warren's relative resistance makes it a practical choice where standard European pears like Bartlett routinely fail. The medium-to-large, greenish-yellow fruits ripen in August in zone 9 and require off-tree ripening (store at room temperature after harvest) to reach their full, buttery sweetness. Plant with Hood or Kieffer for cross-pollination. Warren is not always easy to find at nurseries but is available from regional southern specialty nurseries and bare-root mail-order sources.

common_name: Washington Navel Orange (Classic Seedless Navel Orange)
notes: Plant grafted trees in full sun in well-drained soil, keeping the graft union above the soil line, and water deeply and regularly while the tree establishes its root system. Washington Navel traces to a bud sport discovered in Bahia, Brazil in the early 1800s and became the foundation of the California citrus industry after Eliza Tibbets planted budwood from it in Riverside in 1873; it remains the standard by which other navel oranges are judged, prized for its large, easy-peeling, essentially seedless fruit with sweet, richly flavored flesh and the small secondary "navel" fruit embedded at the blossom end. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree for weeks without losing quality, but the tree itself is notably more cold-sensitive than many other sweet oranges, so gulf coast growers outside the mildest coastal pockets should plant it in a warm microclimate or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover during hard freezes. Fertilize lightly but regularly through the growing season and thin out crossing or dead wood in late winter to keep the canopy open.

common_name: Water Apple (Watery Rose Apple, Bell Fruit)
notes: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; water apple tolerates periodic waterlogging and is well-suited to wet, low-lying areas. Syzygium aqueum (water apple or watery rose apple) is a Southeast Asian tropical fruit tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Indonesia that produces the most 'watery' of all the rose apple relatives — distinctive, bell-shaped to pear-shaped fruits (1.5–2 inches long) in white, pale pink, or red, with an extremely high water content (as the name suggests), a thin, glossy skin, crisp texture, and a very mild, barely-sweet, cucumber-like flavor. The fruit is refreshing rather than richly flavored — in tropical heat, the high water content makes water apple a thirst-quenching fruit eaten fresh as a hydrating snack, cut into slices and served with salt and chili, or made into a light agua fresca. The tree is notably tolerant of wet soils and periodic flooding compared to other Syzygium species — it grows naturally along stream banks and in seasonal swamps in its native habitat. It is distinctly different from the rose apple (S. jambos) in its smaller, lighter, more watery fruit, smaller tree size, and tolerance of wet conditions. Widely grown in home gardens throughout Southeast Asia and the Philippines.

Water Hickory is the hickory of the riverine swamps, bottomland hardwood forests, and floodplain edges of the southeastern coastal plain, native from Virginia to Florida and west to Illinois and Texas, where it grows alongside bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp chestnut oak in the seasonally flooded alluvial soils of river terraces and floodplain edges. Its small, thin-shelled nuts are very bitter and not generally eaten by people, but they are an important food for wood ducks, squirrels, and wild turkeys in bottomland habitat — waterfowl consume large quantities of the nuts that fall into flooded bottomland pools in fall. Like all hickories, Water Hickory is slow-growing but extremely long-lived, with the deep taproot making transplanting nearly impossible after the first year of growth; direct-seed into the permanent planting site in fall for best results. Grow in moist to periodically flooded, rich, slightly acidic alluvial soil in full sun — the only hickory species reliably tolerant of extended seasonal flooding.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; water rose apple is a tropical Asian Syzygium closely related to the wax jambu (S. samarangense) and produces similar bell-shaped, hollow fruits that are crunchy, mildly sweet, and extremely refreshing with a high water content — as the name suggests. The fruits range from white to pale pink and are eaten fresh as a cooling fruit, particularly popular in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines where they are sold by street vendors. The tree is medium-sized and can be kept more compact than many tropical fruit trees. It bears fruit prolifically in the tropics and is beginning to appear in specialty tropical fruit nurseries in Florida. In zone 9a, grow in a large container and move indoors in winter; the fruits are produced year-round in frost-free conditions.

Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wax apple thrives in tropical lowland conditions with high humidity and warm temperatures year-round. Syzygium samarangense (wax apple or Java apple) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Andaman Islands, widely cultivated throughout Southeast Asia for its distinctive, pear-shaped to bell-shaped fruit with thin, waxy, translucent red to deep-red (or white, green, or pink depending on variety) skin, crispy, spongy, mildly sweet flesh, and a hollow, air-filled core with a rose-water scent — the fresh eating experience is unlike any other fruit, refreshingly crisp and very mildly sweet. The tree is evergreen with large, oval, glossy leaves and produces clusters of showy white to pale-pink, brush-like flowers (typical of the Myrtaceae family) followed by fruits in clusters. In the United States, wax apple cultivation is primarily limited to southern Florida and Hawaii; in zone 9, container culture or greenhouse growing is required. Named varieties include 'Jambu Air' (very dark red, sweet) and 'Pearl' (white-green, milder flavor).

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Wells is a named pawpaw cultivar selected from a wild tree in Maryland — valued for its exceptionally large fruit size, excellent sweet flavor with classic banana-custard character, and good productivity. Wells produces some of the largest pawpaw fruits of any named cultivar, with individual fruits commonly weighing 6–12 ounces and occasionally larger — a significant attribute for a species where fruit size varies enormously between seedling selections. The large, heavy fruits have creamy-yellow flesh with minimal fiber, full banana-vanilla custard flavor, and a smooth texture that makes them outstanding for fresh eating and pawpaw-based recipes (ice cream, smoothies, bread, beer). Wells ripens mid-to-late season (late September to early October in zone 7–8, slightly earlier in zone 9) and requires cross-pollination from a different named cultivar such as Shenandoah or Susquehanna for maximum fruit set. The very short shelf life inherent to all pawpaw fruit (2–4 days at room temperature, up to 2 weeks refrigerated) limits commercial distribution but is not a problem for home gardeners harvesting on demand. Hand-pollination with a small brush during the brief flowering window significantly improves fruit set in home orchard settings where natural fly and beetle pollinators may be scarce.

growth_habit: Tropical American food and timber tree
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hymenaea courbaril is drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry periods once established — water regularly in establishment years, then rely primarily on rainfall in tropical conditions. Hymenaea courbaril (West Indian Locust, Jatobá, or South American Locust) is a massive, long-lived, evergreen to semi-deciduous tree native to the Caribbean islands, Central America, and tropical South America from Mexico through the Amazon Basin, where it is one of the dominant canopy trees of seasonally dry and humid tropical forests. The tree produces large, hard, oblong, woody, dark-brown pods enclosing a dry, starchy, sweet-sour, floury pulp around the seeds — an important traditional food of indigenous peoples throughout its range, eaten directly, ground into flour for bread and porridge, or fermented into beverages. The pulp is nutritionally dense, rich in carbohydrates, protein, and calcium. Hymenaea courbaril is also one of the primary historical sources of Jutahy (or jatobá) copal resin, exuded from the trunk and roots as a hard amber-colored substance used in traditional varnishes, incense, and folk medicine for respiratory conditions and skin ailments. The extremely dense, hard, durable heartwood — among the hardest commercial timbers of the Americas — has been used for heavy construction, flooring, furniture, and tool handles for centuries. A very slow-growing, exceptionally long-lived tree requiring 10+ years to first fruit.

common_name: Western Schley Pecan (Widely Planted Southwestern Irrigated Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety, and provide consistent irrigation during nut fill, since this cultivar was developed for and performs best under the irrigated growing conditions of the arid Southwest. Often simply called Western in the trade, it produces a thin-shelled, well-filled nut with good flavor and has become one of the most heavily planted commercial pecan cultivars in New Mexico, Arizona, and West Texas orchards. It shows somewhat better tolerance of drier climates than many Southeastern-bred cultivars but still performs acceptably in the more humid Gulf South when given good air circulation and disease management.

common_name: White Adriatic Fig (Classic Italian Green-Skinned Honey-Flavored Jam Fig)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Adriatic is a classic Italian fig cultivar grown commercially in California (it is the primary variety used for dried figs and fig paste in California production) and traditionally cultivated in Gulf South kitchen gardens for its exceptional fresh-eating quality. The medium-to-large fruits have green-to-yellow-green skin at full ripeness with amber to light strawberry-rose interior flesh of unusually high sweetness and a clean, honey-like flavor that ranks among the most highly regarded of all common fig varieties for fresh use. The flavor of fully ripe White Adriatic fresh from the tree — warm, sweet, delicate — is the benchmark against which many other figs are judged. The thin skin is part of what makes the fresh flavor exceptional; it also means ripe fruits are delicate and should be harvested promptly before rain or excess humidity causes splitting. White Adriatic is a vigorous, productive fig tree that typically begins bearing in its second year from planting and reaches full production by year 3–5. In Gulf South zone 9, the main crop ripens in late July through September; a breba (early) crop may develop on previous year's wood in June in years when the wood survives winter undamaged. Self-fertile, requiring no pollinators. Best eaten fresh within a day or two of harvest; or made into fig preserves and jam where the delicate honey flavor is retained.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; White Genoa is an Italian light-skinned fig producing medium to large, greenish-yellow to pale gold fruits with amber to pink-tinged flesh and a mild, sweet, delicate flavor — one of the milder-flavored fig varieties, with a honey-sweet taste that lacks the robust winey complexity of dark-skinned varieties but is exceptionally appealing for fresh eating by people who find strong fig flavor too intense. The pale skin and light flesh of White Genoa produce an elegant presentation as fresh fruit or in light-colored preserves; it makes an outstanding pale-gold fig jam. It is widely grown in Australia and California where it performs well in Mediterranean-type climates and is considered one of the best light-skinned figs for fresh eating. In zone 9 and the Gulf Coast, White Genoa performs comparably to its reputation in warm Mediterranean climates. The light-colored fruits are prone to souring and cracking if they crack near the eye in wet weather; plant in locations with good air circulation.

Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; white jaboticaba (also called yellow jaboticaba) is a Brazilian species of jaboticaba producing smaller fruits than the common jaboticaba (Plinia cauliflora), with the distinctive yellow-green to white skin of the ripe grape-like fruits distinguishing it from the deep purple-black common jaboticaba. Like all jaboticabas, the fruits grow caulifloresly — directly on the trunk and main branches of the tree rather than on the branch tips — creating the remarkable, otherworldly spectacle of hundreds of fruits clustering directly on the bark. The flavor of white jaboticaba is sweeter and less astringent than the more common purple types, with a delicate, pleasant muscat-like sweetness. Used for fresh eating, jams, and fruit wines. Rare and highly prized even in Brazil, much rarer outside its native range than the common jaboticaba. A prized collector's fruit for zone 9–11 gardens where unusual tropical fruits are cultivated.

common_name: White Marseille Fig (White Fig of Marseille)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor, dry soils better than most fruit trees and perform well in raised beds and large containers where root pruning encourages fruiting. White Marseille (also spelled 'Marseilles') is one of the oldest fig varieties in documented cultivation, known in European gardens since at least the 16th century and praised in early horticultural literature for its sweet, honey-like flavor; the medium to large, turbinate fruits have pale greenish-yellow to creamy-white skin and translucent white to pale amber interior flesh with a mild, delicate sweetness and gentle fig fragrance unlike the darker, richer intensity of dark figs. A common fig type that requires no pollinator; produces a reliable main crop (August–September) and often a smaller breba crop in early summer. Excellent container and espalier candidate; protect from frost below 15°F as a large container specimen that can be moved indoors.

common_name: White Marseilles Fig (Lattarula Italian Honey Fig, Sweet Golden-Fleshed Mediterranean Fig)
notes: Plant nursery trees or rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; prune in late winter to shape. White Marseilles is one of the oldest documented fig varieties in European cultivation — referenced in 17th-century English garden literature and grown continuously in Mediterranean European gardens for centuries under various local names including Lattarula (Italian, meaning little bottle), Blanche (French), and White Marseilles (English, after the port city of Marseilles from which it was widely distributed). The fruit is medium to large, turbinate (pear-shaped) to round, with pale green to yellowish-green skin that becomes translucent amber-green at full ripeness — visually distinctive from the dark-skinned black and brown figs that are the most common fig types sold in American nurseries. The flesh is pale amber, extremely sweet and rich with a honey-like quality — the Lattarula name acknowledges the syrupy honey character of the ripe fruit — and the flavor is described as one of the finest among common fig varieties, with a complex sweetness that surpasses the simpler flavor of standard commercial brown turkey types. White Marseilles performs well in the warm, long growing seasons of zone 8–10, where the extended summer gives the main crop time to fully develop the honey concentration that distinguishes it.

White mulberry is a fast-growing, exceptionally hardy tree bearing sweet, mild fruit and historically grown to feed silkworms. It tolerates drought, heat, and poor soils, thriving in full sun in a very wide range of conditions. Plant a fruiting cultivar rather than a fruitless ornamental, and site away from walks since the ripe fruit drops freely. Prune in winter to control size, and expect abundant crops within a few years.

Sow cleaned seeds directly into a nursery bed in autumn, covering lightly with 1/4 inch of soil; the distinctive white-felted leaves of seedlings make them easy to identify and separate from weeds in spring. Whitebeam is notably tolerant of shallow, alkaline, and chalky soils, making it one of the few ornamental fruiting trees suited to difficult chalk downland conditions. Grow in full sun for the most compact habit and the best berry production; established trees are drought-tolerant and require little supplemental watering except during prolonged dry spells. Allow five or more years from seed for the tree to reach flowering size and begin producing its scarlet autumn berries.

common_name: Wichita Pecan (Western High-Quality Pecan, Type II Commercial Pecan)
notes: Plant in deep (4+ feet), well-drained loam or sandy loam in full sun; Wichita is very productive and precocious, bearing significant crops at 5–6 years after planting, earlier than most other varieties; supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring to prevent zinc deficiency; in humid southeastern conditions, Wichita is susceptible to pecan scab and may require fungicide protection. Wichita pecan is one of the most widely planted commercial pecan varieties in the southwestern United States — the dominant variety in the major commercial pecan production areas of western Texas and New Mexico where supplemental irrigation is available and the dry summer climate limits scab disease pressure. The variety was released by the USDA in 1959 and quickly achieved widespread planting in the irrigated orchards of the West Texas Pecan Belt (around San Saba, San Angelo, and the Pecos River region) and New Mexico's Mesilla Valley, where the combination of hot days, cool nights, low humidity, and fertile alluvial soils creates ideal pecan-growing conditions. Wichita produces large to very large nuts (40–45 per pound) with excellent kernel percentage (58–62%) and an exceptional, rich buttery flavor — consistently rated among the highest-quality pecans for flavor by tasting panels. The kernels are plump and well-filled, bright golden-yellow in color, and have the mild, sweet, buttery flavor characteristic of high-quality western-grown pecans. Wichita is a Type II protogynous variety — meaning the pistillate (female) flowers become receptive before the pollen is shed — so it requires pairing with a Type I variety for reliable pollination. Early-bearing, high-quality, and widely available — Wichita is an excellent choice for zone 8–9 home orchard plantings where summer humidity is not extreme.

Plant pits in fall in a sunny, well-drained spot with slightly acidic to neutral soil; this heat-tolerant native plum performs exceptionally well in the southeastern and south-central United States where many other plums fail. Thin seedlings to the strongest individual and allow it to develop naturally; wild goose plum will begin producing fruit within three to six years from a strong seedling and often spreads via root suckers to form a productive thicket. Cross-pollination with another wild plum or a compatible named variety will significantly improve fruit set and yields of the flavorful red-yellow fruits. This species is an important parent of many named southern plum varieties and provides early spring blooms that are a critical food source for native pollinators emerging from winter.

Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; exceptionally drought-tolerant once established — a true bushveld species. Vangueria infausta (wild medlar or African medlar) is a deciduous shrub or small tree from the dry savanna and bushveld regions of eastern and southern Africa — common across South Africa, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Mozambique, and Kenya in seasonally dry habitats. The plant produces round to slightly flattened, 1–2 inch fruits that ripen from green to yellowish-brown, with soft, sweet-acid, mealy flesh and 4–5 large seeds. The flavor when fully ripe is pleasant — sweet with fruity-acid notes somewhat reminiscent of a tart apple-medlar — and the fruits are eaten fresh throughout rural sub-Saharan Africa, as well as dried into a concentrated fruit leather, fermented into traditional beer, or made into jams and sauces. The tree is highly drought-resistant, adapted to seasonally dry and poor soils of the African bushveld, making it a candidate for water-wise agroforestry in dry subtropical climates. The leaves, bark, and roots have extensive use in southern African traditional medicine. As an ornamental and food plant in zone 9–11 dry climates, wild medlar is a low-maintenance, wildlife-friendly tree that produces an edible crop under difficult conditions.

Harvest fruits in late autumn and clean the seeds free of pulp before sowing 1/4 inch deep in a nursery bed; expect germination to be slow and potentially staggered over one to two springs, as wild service tree seeds are notoriously variable in their dormancy. Grow in well-drained loamy or clay soil in full sun to light shade, as this species thrives on the woodland edge in its native European habitat. The russet-brown berries are astringent when first ripe but become sweet and date-like after frost or bletting; harvest after the first hard frost for the best flavor. This rare woodland indicator species is long-lived and slow-growing, rewarding patience with outstanding maple-like autumn foliage and excellent value for pollinators and wildlife.

Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes, in a sunny, sheltered location with well-drained soil, since this older California cultivar performs best with reliable summer heat. Water deeply and regularly, and thin heavy fruit set to reduce the tree's tendency toward alternate bearing. Wilking produces deep orange, richly flavored fruit with a loose peel late in the mandarin season, and its flowers are notably fragrant. Though largely superseded commercially, it survives in heritage collections and backyard orchards as a parent of several modern mandarin hybrids, including Kinnow.

common_name: William's Pride Apple (Very Early Disease-Resistant Dark Red Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also a product of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding effort, William's Pride carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with resistance to fire blight, cedar-apple rust, and powdery mildew. The dark red, medium fruit ripens unusually early, often before the Fourth of July in warmer growing areas, with crisp, aromatic, mildly tart flesh. Because it softens fast after ripening, plan to harvest over a short window and use the fruit fresh rather than storing it.

common_name: Winesap Apple (Virginia Heirloom Keeper Apple, Self-Fertile Cider Apple)
notes: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Winesap is self-fruitful but yields improve with a cross-pollinator; harvest in October–November when deep red and firm; Winesap is an outstanding storage apple — sound fruits keep 3–6 months in a cool root cellar (32–40°F) while maintaining flavor and crispness far longer than most modern varieties. Winesap is one of the great classic American apple varieties, documented in Virginia since at least 1817 and possibly earlier, with origins that suggest development in New Jersey in the late 1700s before spread throughout the Shenandoah Valley and Appalachian apple-growing regions that became its primary production territory. The variety has a characteristic that made it enormously valuable before refrigeration: extraordinary keeping quality — Winesap apples stored in a cool root cellar or spring house could remain crisp, tart, and flavorful from harvest in October through March or April of the following year, making Winesap the standard winter apple of Appalachian farmsteads for generations. The fruits are medium-sized, deep red to almost black-red with yellow-green patches, with firm, dense, creamy-yellow flesh and a distinctive spicy-winy flavor with pronounced tartness and aromatic quality — unlike the mild sweetness of most modern commercial apples. Winesap is excellent for fresh eating (for those who appreciate tart, complex flavor), cider making, cooking, and drying. Its self-fruitfulness and cold-hardiness make it a practical single-tree orchard choice for zones 5–7.

common_name: Winged Passion Fruit (Fragrant Granadilla, Sweet Calabash, Red Passion Fruit)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and provide a sturdy trellis or fence; established plants fruit more reliably than recently transplanted ones, so patience through the first season is required. Passiflora alata (winged passion fruit) is a Brazilian passion fruit species that stands out from the more commonly grown P. edulis for two extraordinary qualities: its flowers and its fruit fragrance. The flowers are among the most beautiful of any Passiflora — large (3–4 inches across), deeply colored in crimson-red sepals with purple-and-white banded corona filaments, strongly fragrant, and produced in profusion from summer through fall. The aroma alone makes this an exceptional garden plant. The large, oval to oblong fruits (3–5 inches long) are distinctly fragrant when ripe, with a sweet, aromatic, tropical scent often described as more complex and perfumed than standard purple passion fruit (P. edulis); the golden-orange interior pulp is sweet and aromatic with a flavor that is mellower and less acidic than standard passion fruit, more approachable for fresh eating. The vine grows vigorously in zone 9–10, covering trellises and fences rapidly with glossy dark green leaves that have distinctly winged (four-angled) petioles — the characteristic that gives the species its common name. Pollination by large bees (especially carpenter bees) or hand-pollination improves fruit set. One of the most rewarding edible passion fruits for Gulf Coast gardens where it performs as a true perennial.

Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil in spring; winged sumac (Rhus copallinum) is the most widely distributed sumac in the eastern United States, recognizable by the distinctive 'wing' of tissue along the central leaf stem, and producing brilliant, glossy clusters of small red berries that can be used to make sumac-ade (sumac lemonade) or dried and ground as a tart, tangy spice similar to Middle Eastern sumac (Rhus coriaria). The fall foliage color of winged sumac is among the most spectacular of any native shrub — blazing scarlet, orange, and crimson in October — making it a superb ornamental as well as a food plant and wildlife species. High-value wildlife shrub providing critical late-season fruit for birds (songbirds, turkeys, quail) and dense thicket cover.

common_name: Winkler American Hazelnut (Blight-Resistant Native Hazelnut Selection)
notes: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Winkler is a long-cultivated named selection of the native American hazelnut, valued in nut-breeding circles for its strong natural resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that devastates the larger-nutted European hazelnut (Corylus avellana) across much of its Eastern US range. Because of this resistance, Winkler has been widely used as breeding stock for filbert-blight-tolerant hybrid hazelnuts, and it can also be grown directly as a small, multi-stemmed shrub for a reliable, low-input nut crop. Nuts are smaller than European hazelnut but flavorful, ripening in late summer to fall and often eaten by wildlife if not netted or harvested promptly. Like other hazelnuts, Winkler is not self-fertile and needs a second, genetically distinct hazelnut planted nearby for pollination and nut set — wind, not insects, carries the pollen, so plant within about 20 feet for reliable results. The shrub suckers over time to form a multi-stemmed thicket; thin out old wood periodically to keep the planting productive and easy to harvest.

common_name: Winter Grape (Graybark Grape, Sweet Mountain Grape)
notes: Plant dormant cuttings or bare-root vines against a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Winter grape is a vigorous, high-climbing native vine of river bottoms, thickets, and woodland edges across the Gulf South, bearing small, tart black grapes that ripen unusually late, often persisting on the vine into fall, which gives the plant its common name. Its dense, gray, felted young growth and strong disease and heat tolerance have made native populations valuable in grape breeding programs seeking rootstock resilient to Gulf Coast humidity and pests. In the home landscape it is best used as a screening or wildlife vine on a large arbor, since it grows quickly and needs annual pruning to control its size.

Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Winter Nelis ripens very late and needs a period of cold storage before it develops its best flavor. An old Belgian variety introduced in the early nineteenth century, it bears small, unassuming, dull green-russeted fruit that belies exceptionally rich, sweet, aromatic flesh once properly ripened, and it was among the most widely planted winter dessert pears in nineteenth-century American orchards for its outstanding flavor and long storage life. Unlike fall-ripening pears such as Bartlett, it needs weeks of cool storage after harvest before the flesh softens and the rich flavor fully develops, rewarding patience with one of the best-flavored of all winter pears. Harvest while still hard and green in mid-to-late fall, store cool for several weeks to a few months, then finish ripening at room temperature for a few days before eating.

Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; witherod is a multi-season native shrub of wet woodland edges, swamp margins, and boggy thickets from Newfoundland to Florida, producing flat-topped clusters of small, white flowers in spring, followed by berries that go through an extraordinary color sequence as they ripen from early summer through fall: green, then pink-salmon, then red, then blue, and finally blue-black, with the multiple colors sometimes present simultaneously on a single cluster. The fully ripe blue-black berries are edible and have been eaten by Indigenous peoples and settlers — they have a sweet, raisin-like flavor, giving rise to the name 'wild raisin.' The fall foliage turns brilliant red to burgundy-red, often among the best fall color of any viburnum. Outstanding for moist sites, rain gardens, and naturalistic plantings where its tolerance of consistently wet soil is invaluable. The fruit is an important wildlife food for migrating birds in fall.

Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; witherod viburnum is a native shrub of moist, acidic habitats across eastern North America — bog edges, streambanks, moist meadows, and pond margins from Newfoundland to Alabama. The berries pass through an extraordinary sequential progression of colors as they ripen — starting green, then turning through pink, blue-pink, and finally blue-black — so that clusters simultaneously display three or four colors. The fully ripe blue-black berries, called 'wild raisin,' are edible and sweet enough to eat raw or dried. Spectacular scarlet to burgundy fall foliage adds further season-long interest. Plant 2 or more plants of different clones for improved berry set. An exceptional wildlife shrub offering berries for over 30 bird species and the flowers feed numerous native bees and pollinators.

common_name: Wolf River Apple (Giant Wisconsin Heirloom Baking Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating near the Wolf River in Fremont, Wisconsin in the mid-1800s, this heirloom is famous chiefly for the sheer size of its fruit, with individual apples sometimes weighing over a pound and reportedly large enough that a single apple can fill a whole pie. The pale yellow-green skin blushed with red covers soft, mild, mellow flesh that is better suited to baking and sauce than fresh eating, since the flavor is pleasant but unremarkable on its own. The tree is extremely cold-hardy and vigorous, and its dramatic fruit size has kept it a curiosity and conversation piece in heirloom orchards for generations.

Pomegranate 'Wonderful' is the most popular home-garden variety, forming a large shrub or small tree that produces glossy red fruit filled with tangy-sweet, ruby-colored seeds. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it is self-fertile, so a single plant will fruit. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit is developing, then reduce as fruit ripens to prevent splitting. In climates colder than zone 8, grow it in a large container and move it to a protected spot over winter. Prune in late winter to shape and remove suckers, and harvest fruit in fall when it colors up and sounds metallic when tapped.

common_name: Wonderful Pomegranate (Classic Large Deep-Red Gulf South Pomegranate)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Wonderful is the dominant commercial pomegranate variety of California and the standard against which all other pomegranate varieties are evaluated — producing very large (10–16 oz), round, deep-red to scarlet-red fruits with a thin, hard rind enclosing hundreds of ruby-red arils (the juicy, seed-containing sacs) with a complex tart-sweet, deeply flavored, astringent juice that defines the classic pomegranate flavor profile. The ornamental quality of pomegranate is exceptional — showy orange-red flowers (May–July in zone 9), then large, jewel-colored fruits that ripen to deep red-purple by October–November. Pomegranate is an ancient cultivated fruit (documented cultivation for 4,000+ years) that is one of the most drought-tolerant, heat-adapted, long-lived fruit trees available for Gulf South gardens. In zone 9, pomegranate thrives in the hot summers and mild winters — requiring only 150–200 chill hours — and established trees are remarkably long-lived, with historic specimens surviving 50–100+ years with minimal care. The ornamental summer flowers and autumn fruit make pomegranate as valuable as a landscape specimen tree as it is as a fruit producer. Self-fruitful (does not require a pollinator) and resistant to most pests and diseases common in Gulf South gardens. Harvest fruit when the exterior skin has fully colored and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped.

Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average, neutral to slightly acidic soil; Casimiroa tetrameria tolerates brief light frost once established — provide winter irrigation in dry climates and mulch the root zone against cold.
