Casimiroa tetrameria (Wooly-leaf White Sapote or Matasano) is an evergreen to briefly deciduous tree native to the highlands of central Mexico and Guatemala, closely related to the more widely cultivated White Sapote (Casimiroa edulis) and distinguished by its distinctively velvety-woolly leaf undersides (the species name 'tetrameria' references the 4-merous flowers, while the woolly leaves differentiate it visually from C. edulis). The smooth, round to oval, 2–3 inch, green-skinned fruits contain creamy-white to cream-yellow, smooth, dense, rich, sweet flesh with a buttery-custard flavor and soft, satiny texture — eaten fresh, chilled, or pureed into smoothies and ice cream. Casimiroa tetrameria is considered by some tropical fruit enthusiasts to produce sweeter, richer fruit than the common white sapote, and the tree shows somewhat improved cold tolerance, performing well in zone 9 with good drainage. Graft onto Casimiroa edulis rootstock for earlier fruiting and better uniformity. The seeds contain mildly sedative alkaloids (casimiroin) and should not be eaten; wash hands after seed handling.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Worcester Pearmain ripens in late summer and is best eaten promptly, since it does not store for long. Bred in Worcestershire, England in the nineteenth century, it bears bright crimson-red, medium apples with crisp, white flesh carrying a distinctive light strawberry-like aroma and flavor that sets it apart from most other dessert apples, ripening in late summer as one of the more colorful and distinctively flavored early-season varieties. Its attractive bright color and unusual, well-loved fruity flavor have made it a longstanding favorite for fresh eating straight from the tree, though the fruit softens and loses its best texture within just a few weeks of harvest. Harvest in late summer once fruit colors up fully and pulls easily from the spur, and eat promptly for the best crisp texture and distinctive flavor.

common_name: Xie Shan Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Chinese Satsuma Mandarin)
notes: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and protect young trees with frost cloth for their first several winters until they gain size and cold hardiness. Xie Shan is a satsuma mandarin selection out of China favored by cold-hardy citrus enthusiasts and Gulf South growers for beginning to bear at a young age and setting unusually heavy crops of small to medium, easy-peel, seedless, sweet fruit that ripen early in the fall citrus season. The compact, naturally dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be given winter protection in the coldest zone 8 locations. As with other satsumas, fruit quality and cold tolerance improve once the tree is well established, so give young trees consistent water and a balanced citrus fertilizer through their first few growing seasons.

common_name: Yamhill Hazelnut (OSU EFB-Resistant Compact Hazelnut, Eastern-Adapted Filbert)
notes: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Yamhill requires a cross-pollinator (Jefferson, Wepster, or another EFB-resistant OSU variety); it is semi-compact and tends to produce a shorter, multi-stemmed bush form; nuts ripen September and fall naturally — harvest promptly from the ground; Yamhill typically begins bearing in year 3–4, earlier than some older varieties. Yamhill hazelnut is an Oregon State University variety released in 2009 from the OSU hazelnut breeding program — one of the first wave of EFB-resistant named hazelnut varieties developed specifically to allow hazelnut production throughout the eastern United States, where Eastern Filbert Blight (Anisogramma anomala) has prevented the success of standard European varieties including Barcelona. The OSU breeding program incorporated EFB resistance from the wild Turkish hazelnut (Corylus colurna) and other resistant species into productive, quality-fruited cultivars adapted to commercial and home hazelnut production. Yamhill's EFB resistance is now documented in variety trials throughout the mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states where EFB pressure is severe, showing dramatically better survival and production than Barcelona and other susceptible varieties. Yamhill tends to have a compact, bushy habit (shorter than Barcelona) and produces medium-sized, round nuts with good flavor and moderate kernel percentage — suitable for home fresh use, roasting, and processing. The combination of EFB resistance, compact habit, and earlier bearing age than older varieties makes Yamhill one of the most important hazelnut releases for home orchardists east of the Cascades.

Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Yarlington Mill blooms early, so avoid frost pockets that could damage the spring flowers. Named for a mill in Somerset, England, near which the original seedling tree was found, this attractive pink-blushed apple is a classic bittersweet cider variety producing soft, mellow tannin and good juice volume, widely planted both in traditional West Country English cider orchards and in newer American craft cider plantings. Its early, showy pink spring bloom makes it ornamentally attractive as well as productive, and it is a consistent, moderately vigorous bearer that combines well with sharper or bittersharp varieties in a cider blend. Harvest in mid-fall once fruit drops readily, and mill and press promptly, since the fruit is grown for cider rather than fresh eating.

common_name: Yates American Persimmon (Heavy-Bearing Virginia Persimmon, Wildlife Persimmon)
notes: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Yates American persimmon is drought-tolerant and productive in a wide range of conditions including poor and clay soils; harvest fruits from the ground after frost softening in October–November; the heavy fruit production of Yates makes it particularly attractive for wildlife plantings, permaculture food forests, and home orchards where a sustained fall crop of native fruit is valued. Yates is a named American persimmon cultivar known primarily for its exceptional productivity — consistently producing heavy crops of medium-sized fruits that ripen and drop over an extended period in October and November, making it valuable for both human harvest and as a wildlife-attracting planting throughout the mid-Atlantic and southeastern states. The extended fruit-drop period provides a sustained food source for deer, raccoons, foxes, opossums, and many songbirds rather than a brief burst of fruit, making Yates a popular choice in wildlife habitat plantings and food forest designs where the ecological role of the persimmon is as important as human harvest. For human use, the fruits are medium-sized (1–1.5 inch), deep orange to reddish-orange at maturity, with the intensely sweet, slightly grainy, honey-apricot flesh characteristic of excellent American persimmon after frost softening — a quality that exceeds most commercial fruit in richness when fully ripe. The trees are extremely adaptable across the range of Virginia and mid-Atlantic climates from zone 4 through 9.

Plant in dry, sandy or rocky, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun along the Coastal Plain; yellow haw is a rare and botanically distinctive native hawthorn prized for its fall display of attractive yellow to greenish-yellow, pear-shaped to rounded haws that are notably sweeter and more palatable than those of most other hawthorns. Its spring flowers provide nectar for early native bees, and the fruit is consumed by mockingbirds, brown thrashers, and other birds that frequent the dry, sandy-woods habitats where this species thrives. It performs best in lean, well-drained soils and is intolerant of heavy clay, standing water, or overly enriched garden beds. Yellow haw's rarity in the wild makes cultivating it from locally sourced seed a valuable contribution to the conservation of Coastal Plain plant diversity.

common_name: Yellow Mangosteen (Mysore Gamboge, Yellow Gamboge, Egg Tree)
notes: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Yellow Mangosteen grows best in the filtered light and moist, rich conditions of its native South Asian forest habitat and benefits from shade protection during establishment. Garcinia xanthochymus is an attractive, medium-sized, evergreen tree native to the Western Ghats and Mysore region of India and adjacent Burma (Myanmar) in the family Clusiaceae — the same family as the famous Purple Mangosteen (G. mangostana). The tree has a naturally elegant form: a pyramidal to columnar crown of large, glossy, deep-green, lance-shaped leaves that hang in graceful, slightly pendant arrays from the branches. In summer, the tree produces smooth, round to slightly oval fruits 2–4 inches in diameter with bright golden-yellow skin when ripe, containing 1–4 large seeds surrounded by soft, translucent, sweet-sour, juicy pulp. The flavor is distinctive — a complex sweet-sour combination reminiscent of both apricot and tamarind, refreshing as a fresh fruit and excellent in juices, jams, and chutneys. Yellow Mangosteen is considered by tropical fruit enthusiasts to be more adaptable to cultivation outside the tropics than the famously difficult Purple Mangosteen — it tolerates a somewhat wider range of soil conditions and performs in zone 10 where G. mangostana struggles. Also grown as an ornamental specimen tree for its attractive form and handsome foliage.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; yellow mombin (hog plum) is a large deciduous tropical tree of Central and South America and the Caribbean producing clusters of small, oval, golden-yellow fruits, 1–2 inches long, with a distinctive sweet-tart, highly aromatic tropical flavor that combines elements of mango, plum, and passionfruit with a resinous, citrus-like quality. The thick, waxy skin encloses a small amount of translucent yellow flesh surrounding a large seed. In the Caribbean, Central America, and tropical Brazil, the fruit is eaten fresh, made into juice, agua fresca, ice cream, wine, and vinegar — Spondias mombin juice is a major street beverage in countries like Colombia, Costa Rica, and Brazil. The tree is fast-growing, highly drought-tolerant once established, and tolerates a range of soil conditions from light sandy to heavy clay. It is distinct from the ambarella (S. dulcis) and red mombin/jocote (S. purpurea).

common_name: Yellow Passion Fruit (Golden Passion Fruit, Maracujá Amarelo)
notes: Sow seed just below the surface in warm starting mix and maintain 75–85°F for germination; yellow passion fruit is the world's most commercially cultivated passion fruit, producing golf-ball- to lemon-sized yellow-skinned fruits with intensely fragrant, tart orange-yellow pulp that is the basis of most commercial passion fruit juice. A rampant perennial vine to 30 feet, it needs a very sturdy trellis or fence and frost-free conditions; train two or three main canes horizontally along wires and allow laterals to cascade. Flowers require cross-pollination between two genetically distinct plants, or hand-pollination outside the tropics where native bee pollinators are absent. Harvest when fruit begins to show yellow color and drops easily from the vine.

growth_habit: Southeast Asian ornamental small-fruit persimmon tree
notes: Plant Diospyros decandra in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly throughout the year; protect from temperatures below 40°F; harvest fruits when they reach full yellow color and have a slight give to finger pressure — they should be non-astringent even when firm, unlike temperate persimmons. Yellow Persimmon is an underappreciated tropical fruit tree that deserves far wider cultivation than it currently receives outside Southeast Asia. Unlike the more widely known Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki) which is astringent when underripe, Yellow Persimmon (madan in Thai, 'ten stamen' in English — referring to its ten stamens vs. 16 in D. kaki) produces small, round, bright-yellow fruits that are sweet and non-astringent even when firm, and have a honey-sweet, mildly vanilla-flavored flesh. The fruits are eaten fresh in Thailand and throughout Indochina as a dessert fruit, and the tree is planted as both an ornamental (handsome, glossy-leaved, with fragrant, cream-white flowers) and a fruit tree in village gardens. The tree grows as a medium-sized, evergreen shade tree in the tropics, producing fruits that ripen over an extended season from late summer through winter. An excellent rare fruit tree for zone 10–12 tropical and subtropical gardens seeking both ornamental beauty and unusual fresh fruit.

common_name: Yellow Transparent Apple (Very Early Translucent-Skinned Russian Apple)
notes: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Introduced from Russia in the 1870s, Yellow Transparent is one of the earliest-ripening apples grown in North America, producing pale, almost translucent yellow-green skin over soft, tart, juicy flesh that cooks down quickly into a smooth sauce. Because the thin skin bruises easily and the fruit does not store, it is best picked directly for immediate use in pies, sauce, and fresh eating rather than for the fruit bowl. The tree is notably cold-hardy and productive, and its extremely early ripening has long made it a favorite for the first homemade applesauce of the year.

Plant in full sun in deep, fast-draining, even poor or rocky soil; yellowhorn is a small deciduous tree native to northern China where it grows on dry hillsides, and it is notably drought tolerant once established but intolerant of wet feet or heavy, poorly drained clay. In spring it puts on a striking floral display of white, horse-chestnut-like flower panicles marked with red-to-yellow throats, followed in late summer by leathery green seed capsules that split open to release large, dark, chestnut-flavored seeds edible raw or roasted. Trees need several years of establishment before producing a meaningful nut crop, and while broadly self-fertile, planting more than one seedling improves pollination and yield. Give it a full-sun, well-drained site away from irrigation runoff or low spots where water collects.

Plant grafted trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; shagbark hickory develops a long taproot and transplants best while young and dormant, with minimal root disturbance. A named selection prized among nut tree enthusiasts for producing thinner-shelled, easier-to-crack nuts with excellent sweet flavor compared to typical wild shagbark hickory seedlings, which often have very thick, difficult shells that discourage home processing despite the excellent nut quality. Like all shagbark hickories it is a large, long-lived forest tree distinguished by its shaggy, peeling bark and needs considerable time, often a decade or more, before reaching significant nut-bearing maturity, making it a true multi-generational planting. Provide deep, well-drained soil and full sun, protect the young tree's long taproot from damage during transplanting, and be prepared for a long wait before the improved, easier-cracking nuts this selection is known for become available in quantity.

common_name: York Elderberry (Largest-Cluster American Elderberry, New York Station Release)
notes: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun; York elderberry is drought-tolerant once established but produces better with consistent moisture; prune back to 6–12 inch stubs in late winter every 2–3 years to rejuvenate; harvest berry clusters in August–September when fully ripe and deep purple-black; process or cook berries within days of harvest as raw elderberries contain cyanogenic compounds and must be cooked for safe consumption. York elderberry was released by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in the mid-20th century as part of an American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) improvement program aimed at developing varieties with larger, more consistently sized berries and heavier individual clusters compared to wild-harvested elderberries. York is noted for producing some of the largest individual berry clusters of any named American elderberry variety — the flat-topped cymes (berry clusters) of York regularly reach 10–12 inches across and bear very heavy loads of ripe berries at the dark purple-black ripening stage. The individual berries are also somewhat larger than those of Adams and many other named varieties. This large cluster size and individual berry size make York an excellent choice for home elderberry production where maximum yield per plant and ease of harvest (larger clusters are faster to pick) are priorities. York ripens approximately 2 weeks after Adams, making the York + Adams combination the standard planting recommendation for home elderberry operations wanting to extend the harvest window and ensure reliable cross-pollination between the two varieties. All elderberry processing requires cooking — raw elderberries contain sambunigrin, a cyanogenic glycoside that is destroyed by heat; cooked elderberries are used for syrup, juice, jam, jelly, and elderberry wine.

Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; yuzu is self-fruitful and produces better with cross-pollination, though single-tree production is adequate. Yuzu (Citrus junos) is a Japanese and Chinese citrus species of great antiquity, prized throughout East Asian cuisine — particularly in Japanese cuisine — for its extraordinary aromatic zest and juice that has a flavor profile unlike any other citrus: intensely fragrant, complex, floral-tart with notes of grapefruit, mandarin, and pine. The rough, bumpy, medium-sized (2–3 inch diameter) yellow fruits are rarely eaten whole but their zest and juice are foundational in ponzu sauce, yuzu kosho, miso soup, hot pots (nabe), cakes, and flavoring sake. Yuzu trees are extremely thorny (the thorns can be 3–4 inches long) and slow to begin fruiting (5–8 years from seed; 3–5 years from grafted trees) but among the most cold-hardy of all citrus, surviving to 14–17°F. Now widely available as grafted plants and grown by American chefs and home gardeners.

Establish this Chilean rainforest vine in part shade against a sheltered wall or trellis in spring, in fertile, humus-rich soil, since it is less cold-hardy than its Asian Lardizabalaceae relatives and appreciates protection from harsh winter wind. Deep maroon-purple flowers appear in winter, and because plants are typically dioecious, both a male and female specimen are needed to set the dark purple, sausage-shaped fruits filled with sweet white pulp. Its thick, glossy, evergreen trifoliate leaves make an unusual dense screen for shaded courtyards in mild coastal climates. Water regularly during establishment, then allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings once mature.

Set out grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, moving toward full sun once established. Zimmerman is an Ohio-origin pawpaw selection known for very sweet, richly flavored flesh with a notably low seed count for the species, making the fruit easier to eat fresh than many wild seedlings. It ripens in the midseason window and produces medium to large fruit on a vigorous, cold-hardy tree with the classic pyramidal pawpaw form and large, tropical-looking drooping leaves. Because pawpaws will not set fruit from their own pollen, interplant Zimmerman with an unrelated cultivar such as Susquehanna or Taytwo, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief spring bloom to improve fruit set in home orchard settings.

Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Zinfandel thrives in warm climates and is prone to uneven ripening within a single cluster, requiring careful harvest timing. Genetically identical to the Croatian variety Crljenak Kaštelanski and Italy's Primitivo, this vigorous red wine grape produces loose clusters of thin-skinned, sweet grapes that ripen unevenly on the same bunch, with green, pink, and fully ripe purple-black berries sometimes present simultaneously, a quirk growers must manage carefully to avoid overripe, raisined fruit alongside underripe berries at harvest. Vigorous and productive in warm, sunny climates, it also produces the pink blush wine known as White Zinfandel when pressed with minimal skin contact, making a single variety the source of two very different wine styles. Manage canopy density to promote even ripening, monitor clusters closely as harvest approaches given the variety's uneven ripening tendency, and provide full sun and heat for the best sugar development.

Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, siting a compatible Type-1 pollinator such as Gafford nearby, since pecans are wind-pollinated and cross-pollination between a Type-1 and Type-2 cultivar produces much better nut set than a single cultivar alone. Zinner is a Type-2 pecan valued for combining good resistance to pecan scab with a notably thin, easy-cracking shell that yields plump, high-quality kernels, making it appealing for home growers who want good disease resistance without sacrificing nut quality. As with other scab-resistant cultivars, it is a lower-maintenance choice for Gulf South home orchards without a regular commercial fungicide program. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, and expect several years of growth before the tree reaches consistent bearing age.

Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade or full sun in cooler climates; Prunus africana requires the cool, moist conditions of montane forest environments — it performs poorly in hot, humid tropical lowlands and is best suited to highland subtropical and warm-temperate climates. Prunus africana (African Cherry, Pygeum, or African Plum) is a large, slow-growing, evergreen tree native to the montane forests of sub-Saharan Africa — occurring on nearly every major mountain range from Mt. Cameroon and the Ruwenzori to the Ethiopian Highlands, Drakensberg, and Kilimanjaro above 1,500m elevation — and listed on CITES Appendix II due to severe overharvesting of its medicinal bark. The bark contains a rich complex of phytosterols (beta-sitosterol, beta-sitostenone), ferulic acid esters, and n-docosanol with well-documented anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects on prostate tissue — making standardized Pygeum bark extract one of the most widely prescribed botanical medicines in France, Germany, and Italy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms. The annual global trade in Prunus africana bark exceeds 4,000 metric tons, putting wild populations under severe pressure across its range. Cultivating nursery-grown trees (which require 8–15 years to produce harvestable bark) is a sustainable alternative to wild collection. The small, cherry-like, red-to-black fruits are edible but very bitter; primarily a timber and medicinal tree.

Grow in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, humid, wind-protected location; African nutmeg is a mid-sized rainforest tree of West and Central Africa closely related to custard apple, notable for its unusual pendulous, ribbon-like, spiraling flowers followed by large round woody fruits the size of a grapefruit. Inside each fruit, numerous seeds embedded in aromatic pulp are dried and grated much like true nutmeg, imparting a similar warm, slightly bitter, musky-spicy flavor used in West African soups, rice dishes, and traditional remedies. Because seedlings take many years to reach bearing size, it is best suited to permanent agroforestry plantings or large tropical gardens rather than short-term cultivation, and young trees should be shaded and kept consistently moist during establishment.

growth_habit: South African traditional medicinal aromatic shrub
notes: Plant Artemisia afra in well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; avoid rich, wet soils which produce lush but less aromatic and medicinally active foliage; prune back hard each spring to maintain compact, bushy form; propagate easily from cuttings in late spring. African Wormwood is the cornerstone of South African traditional herbal medicine — a deeply aromatic, silver-grey-green shrub with finely divided leaves and a characteristic powerful, camphor-dominated fragrance that is instantly recognized across southern Africa. Traditional use includes steaming the crushed leaves in a bowl of hot water for inhalation to relieve cold and flu symptoms; drinking infusions (umhlonyane tea) for fever, malaria, coughs, and stomach complaints; and rubbing the leaves on the body as an insect repellent. The plant is used by practitioners of all major South African healing traditions — Zulu izinyanga, Xhosa izangoma, Cape Malay bonesmiths — and is sold in enormous quantities at traditional medicine markets (muthi shops) throughout the country. Research has confirmed antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic activity of various leaf extracts. The plant is hardy, attractive, and easy to grow in any warm, dry garden position; it makes an excellent border shrub for drought-tolerant Mediterranean-style gardens in zone 8–11. Related to the Northern Hemisphere wormwoods (Artemisia absinthium, A. annua) but distinct and more cold-hardy than expected for an African species.

Plant seedlings in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aidan fruit tree is a frost-tender West African tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to West African forests, this legume tree bears distinctive long, dark brown, four-winged (tetrapterous) pods filled with an intensely aromatic pulp used as a seasoning in soups and stews across Ghana and Nigeria, known as prekese, and long valued in traditional medicine for its aromatic properties. A member of the pea family, it fixes nitrogen in the soil like many of its legume relatives, and its distinctive winged seed pods make it an interesting specimen tree for a tropical botanical or ethnobotanical planting in frost-free climates. Water regularly while young, and expect pods to be harvested for seasoning once the tree reaches bearing maturity after several years.

CAUTION: for short-term use only, contraindicated in pregnancy and intestinal obstruction; can cause cramping or electrolyte imbalance with overuse. Nick or soak the hard seed coat before starting indoors 6-8 weeks ahead of the last frost, then transplant into full sun and sandy, fast-draining soil once nights stay warm. Leaves and pods contain sennosides and are dried for the classic short-term stimulant laxative used in traditional and modern medicine alike.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — allspice is a tropical Caribbean tree native to Jamaica and Central America, the source of the spice whose dried unripe berries combine the flavors of cloves, cinnamon, and nutmeg in a single berry (hence 'allspice'). The large, glossy, aromatic leaves also contain significant allspice flavor (used to wrap jerk meats in Jamaica). The tree is medium-sized (30–40 feet at maturity) with attractive smooth, exfoliating bark and fragrant white flowers. Allspice is a dioecious tree — both male and female plants are needed for fruit production, though the leaves of either sex can be harvested for culinary use. In South Florida it grows well outdoors in zone 10–11; in zone 9 it requires a container that can be moved to frost protection. An extraordinary ornamental, aromatic, and culinary tree for warm gardens.

Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Amarillo is a trademarked hop variety with proprietary status limiting commercial rhizome availability. Discovered as a chance seedling in Washington's Yakima Valley in the 1990s and named for its bright golden-orange color, this widely used American aroma hop delivers pronounced orange citrus and floral notes that became a defining character of American pale ale and IPA styles through the 2000s and remains a brewer favorite for its distinctive, bright citrus aromatics. Its exact genetic parentage was kept proprietary for years, and while cuttings are now more widely available to home growers, tracking down true, correctly identified Amarillo rhizomes can still be more difficult than sourcing more common commercial hop varieties. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and provide full sun and consistent moisture through the growing season.

Plant container-grown trees in spring in compost-enriched, consistently moist, well-drained soil, sited with protection from cold wind and, ideally, afternoon shade in hotter climates. Native to subtropical rainforest gullies of coastal New South Wales and southeast Queensland, this glossy-leaved tree contains one of the highest natural concentrations of anethole of any plant, giving the dried, ground leaf an intensely sweet licorice-anise flavor. Use the dried leaf in baking, fruit desserts, herbal tea blends, and as a striking substitute anywhere star anise or fennel seed is called for; it can be clipped and kept as a large shrub in gardens where space is limited.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; annatto (achiote) is a tropical American shrub known worldwide as the natural source of the orange-red pigment used to color cheese, butter, smoked fish, and countless processed foods — the intensely colored seeds inside the spiny red seed pods are ground or infused in oil to make the widely used Latin American spice paste. The seeds color and flavor rice, tamales, soups, and sauces in Latin American and Filipino cuisine. The attractive plant also produces large pink-lavender flowers similar to single roses followed by striking, bristly bright-red seed pods in clusters. A striking ornamental and useful spice shrub for zone 10–12 gardens; in zone 9a it may be grown in a large container and protected from frost.

common_name: Ashanti Pepper (West African Black Pepper, Uziza)
notes: Train cuttings up a post, tree trunk, or trellis in fertile, well-drained soil with light shade, especially while young; Ashanti pepper is a woody perennial climber native to the West and Central African rainforest that is prized for two distinct products from the same plant. The young, peppery-aromatic leaves, known as uziza leaf in Nigeria, are chopped fresh into pepper soups and stews, while the dried unripe fruit, uziza seed, is ground as a pungent, more intensely hot substitute for true black pepper. Harvest leaves lightly and repeatedly once the vine is established; fruit clusters ripen from green to red over several years as the plant matures. Mulch well and water during dry spells, since the species comes from consistently humid forest conditions.

Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; Assam tea is the large-leaved, tropical botanical variety of the tea plant, native to the hot, humid Assam region of northeastern India, and is the source of the malty, full-bodied character prized in classic Assam and many English breakfast-style black teas. Compared to the small-leaved China variety (Camellia sinensis var. sinensis) more commonly grown in cooler climates, Assam tea grows faster, produces larger leaves, and tolerates heat and humidity better, but it is noticeably less cold-hardy, making it a better fit for the warm, humid Gulf South than for northern tea gardens. Begin harvesting the tender top two leaves and a bud once plants are three to four years old and well established; frequent light plucking encourages a dense, bushy, more productive shape. Provide consistent moisture, since tea plants are sensitive to drought stress, and mulch well to keep roots cool and the acidic soil moist.

Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Australian rosemary is a coastal Australian native shrub from the mint family that closely resembles culinary rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis) in appearance — with narrow, whorled, needle-like leaves, a similar upright to spreading habit, and small tubular flowers — but is not used as a culinary herb and is generally more drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and adaptable than true rosemary. The flowers are white to pale lavender, produced nearly continuously through the year in mild coastal climates, providing a steady nectar source. It is one of the most reliable evergreen flowering shrubs for hot, dry, coastal zones 8–11, tolerating conditions of salt spray, poor soil, and extended drought that defeat most ornamentals. Widely planted in California coastal landscaping as a rosemary substitute where salt exposure makes true rosemary struggle. The cultivar 'Wynyabbie Gem' has more consistent lavender-mauve flowers; 'Morning Light' has cream-variegated foliage.

Plant Terminalia bellirica in deep, well-drained, fertile, moderately moist soil in full sun; the tree grows large and needs space to develop its wide-spreading crown; water during establishment and in dry periods, though mature trees are somewhat drought-tolerant. Baheda (vibhitaki in Sanskrit — meaning 'that which removes disease') is one of the three foundational plants in Triphala (Sanskrit: 'three fruits'), the cornerstone polyherbal formula of Ayurvedic medicine used for thousands of years across India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. Triphala — consisting of equal parts Amla (Phyllanthus emblica), Haritaki (Terminalia chebula), and Baheda (Terminalia bellirica) — is the most widely used compound herb in Ayurveda, prescribed as a rejuvenating tonic, digestive aid, gentle laxative, and general health formula. The dried rind of Baheda fruits is particularly high in tannins (gallic acid, ellagic acid, chebulagic acid) with demonstrated antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and hepatoprotective activity in research studies. Baheda's traditional Ayurvedic indications include respiratory conditions (bronchitis, asthma, cough), hair loss, eye diseases, and digestive disorders. The tree is also valuable for its hard, durable timber and as a shade and avenue tree in India; it produces inconspicuous cream-white flower spikes and later the characteristic ridged, oval grey-green fruits. An important tree for gardens serving South Asian communities in zone 10–12.

common_name: Bay Rum Tree (West Indian Bay, Bay Laurel of the Caribbean)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; the leaves can be harvested year-round for culinary and aromatic use. Pimenta racemosa (bay rum tree or West Indian bay) is a small to medium-sized aromatic evergreen tree native to the Caribbean islands — particularly Puerto Rico, the Lesser Antilles, and the Virgin Islands — in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae), closely related to allspice (P. dioica). The glossy, elliptic, leathery leaves of P. racemosa are extraordinarily aromatic when crushed or steam-distilled — yielding 'bay oil' or 'bay rum oil,' a complex essential oil rich in eugenol (clove-scented), myrcene, and chavicol, with warm, spicy, clove-bay character. Bay rum oil is the defining ingredient in traditional West Indian bay rum — a classic men's aftershave, hair tonic, and skin care product used throughout the Caribbean since the mid-19th century and still produced in the Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico today. The same leaves can be used as a culinary herb: dried or fresh leaves add a warmer, more complex, clove-tinged bay flavor to Caribbean stews, soups, and marinades compared to Mediterranean bay laurel. Small, white, fragrant flowers are produced in panicles, followed by small, black, spice-flavored berries. An outstanding aromatic tree for zone 10–12 gardens that combines culinary, aromatic, and cultural heritage.

common_name: Betel Pepper (Betel Vine, Paan Leaf, Sirih)
notes: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with a support for climbing — Betel Pepper grows most luxuriantly in the warm, moist, shaded understory conditions similar to its native habitat and will languish in full sun or dry soil. Piper betle is a perennial, climbing vine in the Piperaceae family native to South and Southeast Asia — the same genus as black pepper (P. nigrum) — and one of the most culturally and economically significant plants in the traditional medicine and daily life of South and Southeast Asia. The plant produces heart-shaped, glossy, smooth, dark-green leaves on a climbing, node-rooting vine that ascends trees and structures by adhesive root pads. The leaves are the harvest product: fresh betel leaves (called 'paan' in South Asian tradition) are harvested and used in the preparation of the traditional South Asian chewing combination of areca nut (from Areca catechu), slaked lime, and betel leaf — a preparation with mild stimulant effects consumed by hundreds of millions of people across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia. Beyond this traditional use, fresh betel leaves are used as a cooking wrapper, an herbal digestive, and in various ethnobotanical and Ayurvedic applications throughout the Asian traditional medicine systems. The leaves contain chavicol, eugenol, and other phenolic compounds that contribute their distinctive flavor and mild bioactivity. Grown in zone 10-12 as a permanent perennial shade vine, or as an annual-treated container plant in zone 9. Non-toxic in culinary amounts.

growth_habit: West African culinary medicinal bitter shrub
notes: Root Gymnanthemum amygdalinum (Bitter Leaf) stem cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; plants establish quickly and grow vigorously in warm climates — prune regularly to maintain a compact, shrubby form and encourage dense, tender leaf production; older stems become woody and less productive. Bitter Leaf (formerly Vernonia amygdalina) is arguably the most important vegetable shrub in West and Central African cuisine — a fast-growing, multi-purpose plant grown in every kitchen garden from Nigeria to the DRC, valued equally as a culinary ingredient, medicinal herb, and forage plant. The leaves contain bitter sesquiterpene lactones (vernodalin, vernomygdin) that give the plant its distinctive medicinal and flavor properties; for culinary use, fresh leaves are washed thoroughly, squeezed and kneaded repeatedly in water, and the liquid pressed out to reduce bitterness to a palatable level before adding to soups, stews, and sauces. The squeezed leaves add a distinctive savory, slightly bitter depth to Ofe Onugbu (Igbo bitter leaf soup with cocoyam and assorted meats) and other traditional dishes. In tropical Africa, the plant is also used to treat malaria, diabetes, fever, and intestinal parasites; research has identified antihelminthic and hypoglycemic compounds. In zone 9–12, Bitter Leaf grows as a perennial shrub reaching 4–8 feet; in cooler areas it can be grown as an annual in a large container.

Plant rooted cuttings in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with a support structure or trellis — black pepper is the world's most traded spice and a shade-tolerant climbing vine native to India's Malabar Coast, where it grows as a climbing epiphyte in the forest understory. In tropical gardens (zone 10–12) the vine climbs 10–30 feet up a tree or post, producing clusters of peppercorns that start green, turn red when fully ripe, and are picked at different stages to produce green pepper (fresh), black pepper (dried unripe), red pepper (ripe), and white pepper (ripe, hull removed). The vine requires warmth, humidity, and consistent moisture. As a container plant in zone 8–9 gardens, it makes an attractive tropical accent vine moved indoors for winter. A genuinely rewarding home-grown spice for warm-climate gardeners.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; black sage is one of the dominant shrubs of California coastal sage scrub — a white-flowered, strongly aromatic native sage with dark green, wrinkled, very fragrant leaves that produce a characteristic camphor-sage scent that perfumes the California coastal air on warm days. The clusters of small, white to pale lavender flowers in spring are exceptionally attractive to native bees — black sage is one of the most important native bee plants in California, producing abundant nectar and pollen particularly for bumble bees, carpenter bees, and many solitary native bees. The dried seed capsules (nutlets) are eaten by seed-eating birds and small mammals. Completely drought-tolerant once established, requiring no summer irrigation in coastal California gardens. The aromatic leaves can be used as a culinary sage substitute, with a flavor described as a blend of culinary sage and camphor. An essential native for California habitat gardens.

Plant in moist to wet, peaty, slightly acidic to neutral, poor, boggy soil in full sun to part shade; bog myrtle requires consistently moist to wet conditions and does not tolerate drought; fixes nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis. Myrica gale (bog myrtle or sweet gale) is a deciduous aromatic shrub native to the peat bogs, wet heathlands, and lakeshores of northern North America, northern Europe, and northern Asia — found from Labrador and Maine across Canada to Alaska, and from Ireland and Scotland east through Scandinavia and Russia. The small, lance-shaped, blue-green leaves are intensely aromatic when crushed — a warm, sweet, resinous, herbal fragrance combining elements of bay, eucalyptus, and spice — that has been exploited for culinary and brewing purposes for thousands of years. Before hops (Humulus lupulus) became the universal bittering agent in European beer in the late Middle Ages, bog myrtle (along with other herbs in the 'gruit' mixture) was the primary flavoring of European ale — recorded in historical documents as far back as the 5th century CE. Gruit ale is currently experiencing a major revival in craft brewing, with bog myrtle used in traditional Scottish, Scandinavian, and craft brewery gruit beers. The leaves are also used to flavor Scandinavian aquavit, Scottish whisky cocktails, and gin botanicals. The plant naturally spreads by rhizomes in wet soils and fixes nitrogen through Frankia bacterial symbiosis. A unique and historically significant herb plant for pond edges and bog gardens in zone 1–6.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; buchu is one of the most important medicinal plants of the South African Cape fynbos and one of the few Cape plants to have achieved significant international commercial significance as a herbal supplement. The small, oval, dark-green leaves are powerfully aromatic — the fresh or dried leaf releasing a strong, distinctive, somewhat blackcurrant-minty-spicy scent from oil glands visible as transparent dots in the leaf surface. In traditional San and Khoikhoi medicine, and later in European colonial medicine, buchu was used primarily for urinary tract and kidney complaints, and dried buchu leaf extract is still sold today as a supplement for urinary health and anti-inflammatory purposes. As a garden plant it is a neat, bushy, heather-textured small shrub of the fynbos type — small, oval, aromatic leaves on fine stems — that produces in spring small, white, five-petaled flowers in moderate quantity. The aromatic foliage is the primary ornamental and practical value. Excellent for a dedicated medicinal herb garden or Cape fynbos planting in zones 8–11 where its drainage and lean-soil requirements are met.

common_name: Bushy Lippia (White Lippia, Lemon Verbena Relative)
notes: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established. Lippia alba (bushy lippia or cidreira in Brazil) is a sprawling, aromatic, semi-woody perennial shrub from South America and the Caribbean, native from Mexico south to Argentina, that has become one of the most widely used and important medicinal herb teas throughout Latin America. The leaves have a pleasant, complex aroma ranging from lemon-mint to spearmint-citrus to slightly camphor-herbaceous depending on the chemotype (several distinct essential oil chemotypes exist: carvone-type, linalool-type, and citral-type, each with different scent profiles). In Brazil, where it is called 'erva-cidreira' or 'falsa melissa,' it is the most popular folk remedy for anxiety, nervous tension, insomnia, and digestive upset — sold fresh in markets and as a prepared tea in pharmacies. Throughout South and Central America, the leaves are used as a flavoring herb for desserts, drinks, and savory dishes. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, Lippia alba is ornamental, drought-tolerant, and virtually pest-free. The small, pale-lavender to white flowers attract pollinators. It is distinct from lemon verbena (Aloysia citrodora, formerly Lippia citriodora) but closely related and in the same family (Verbenaceae).

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; camphor tree is a majestic, aromatic evergreen tree from China and Japan, the source of natural camphor extracted from the wood and leaves. Every part of the tree contains camphor and 1,8-cineole, giving the foliage a powerful medicinal scent when crushed. It is an important timber, medicinal, and aromatic tree in traditional Asian culture. In the American South (particularly Texas and California), it is a common large shade tree planted for its ornamental value and fragrant foliage. NOTE: Camphor tree is classified as invasive in Florida and should not be planted there; it is suitable for other Gulf Coast states. The berries are consumed by birds but the plant as a whole is toxic to humans. Provides exceptional shade and is remarkably drought tolerant once established.

Direct sow Senna alata seeds (scarify or nick seed coat before sowing to improve germination) in full sun in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; plants grow very rapidly in warm conditions and can reach 4–8 feet in a single season; deadhead spent spikes to prolong blooming and cut back hard in late winter to prevent woodiness. Candle Bush is one of the most dramatic flowering shrubs of the tropics and subtropics — its upright, glowing flower spikes are truly candle-like before the bright-yellow, butterfly-shaped individual flowers open, giving the plant an almost magical quality in the garden. It is a pan-tropical species now naturalized throughout the tropics worldwide, spread from its likely South American origin. In traditional medicine across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, a leaf paste or extract is applied topically to treat ringworm, athlete's foot, and other fungal skin infections — giving rise to the common name 'Ringworm Bush'; the antifungal compound chrysophanol has been isolated from the leaves. The plant is also an important butterfly host plant, particularly for sulphur butterflies (Catopsilia spp.) whose caterpillars feed on the leaves. In zone 9, it self-sows readily and may re-establish from seed each year after frost kills the tops; in zone 10–12, it grows as a woody perennial shrub.

common_name: Cape Snow Bush (African Rosemary, Wild Rosemary)
notes: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; prune after flowering to maintain compact shape. Eriocephalus africanus (Cape snow bush or African rosemary) is a native South African fynbos shrub with needle-like, silver-grey, intensely aromatic leaves — the leaves have a fresh, camphor-pine aroma similar to rosemary but with distinctly South African floral-herbal notes. The plant is used in Cape Malay traditional cooking and South African herbal medicine as a seasoning and medicinal herb: the dried leaves flavor lamb stews, braai (barbecue) marinades, and herbal teas; the essential oil is used in aromatherapy for respiratory conditions. Common name 'Cape snow bush' derives from the small, fluffy, white seed heads that cover the plant in late summer, giving a snow-dusted appearance. As a landscape plant, Eriocephalus africanus is outstanding for hot, dry, lean, well-drained soils where European rosemary often struggles with root rot — it has superior drought tolerance and performance in alkaline coastal soils. The cultivar 'Silver Beads' is grown as an ornamental for its exceptionally silvery foliage. An excellent substitute for rosemary in challenging dry garden conditions.

Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to sandy, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; caper bush is a Mediterranean cliff-dwelling plant that rots in rich, moist, or poorly drained soil and thrives on neglect once established. Sprawling, spiny stems carry rounded, fleshy, blue-green leaves and large, showy, white-to-pink flowers with a prominent burst of long purple stamens, opening for just a single day each but produced continuously through the hot summer months. The edible product is the unopened flower bud, hand-picked daily at pea size and brine- or salt-cured into the tangy, briny capers used in Mediterranean cooking; unpicked buds open into flowers and later develop into a caper-berry fruit that can also be pickled. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established, it is well suited to a rock wall, dry slope, or container where poor soil and reflected heat are assets rather than liabilities, and it dies back to the root in hard freezes, resprouting the following spring in marginal zones.

WARNING: bark must be harvested only from mature (8+ year old) trees and aged at least a year before use — fresh, unaged bark causes severe cramping and should never be used directly off the tree, and long-term laxative use is discouraged due to dependency and electrolyte loss risk. Transplant dormant bare-root or potted stock in fall or early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of an understory site, mimicking its native Pacific Northwest forest habitat. This slow-growing native tree is the traditional source of cascara bark, a classic stimulant laxative once aged properly.

Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; chaparral sage (purple sage) is a large, aromatic California native shrub of the southern Coast Ranges, producing distinctive white-woolly (leucophylla = white-leaved) leaves that reflect harsh summer sunlight and reduce water loss — an adaptation to the extreme summer heat and drought of California chaparral. The lavender-purple flowers in late spring to early summer are striking and produce abundant nectar for native bees and hummingbirds. One of the 'allelopathic' California sages — the plant releases volatile chemicals that inhibit the germination of competing plants around it, creating a distinctive bare zone between the sage canopy and the surrounding grassland. The famous 'elfin forest' scent of California chaparral comes largely from this species and coast sage (S. apiana). Essential for authentic California coastal sage scrub plantings.

Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 8b–11; Chinese cinnamon is the source of most commercial cinnamon sold in the United States — the cassia bark sold in grocery stores as 'cinnamon' is typically the bark of this or related Cinnamomum species rather than true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum). The inner bark is harvested by stripping the outer bark from young shoots and allowing it to dry into the familiar quills. Chinese cassia has a stronger, more pungent flavor with higher coumarin content than the mild, sweet Ceylon cinnamon — a trait that limits consumption quantities but makes it the preferred spice for strongly-flavored applications. In zone 9 gardens, this attractive evergreen tree or large shrub provides handsome, dark green, three-veined leaves and an aromatic quality throughout the year. Harvest bark from branches 2–3 years old for optimal flavor concentration.

common_name: Chinese Prickly Ash (Flatspine Prickly Ash, Sichuan Pepper Relative)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; wear thick gloves when harvesting or pruning due to sharp thorns. Zanthoxylum simulans (Chinese prickly ash or flatspine prickly ash) is a thorny deciduous shrub from eastern and central China — one of several Zanthoxylum species used as sources of the Sichuan pepper-type spice in Chinese cooking, alongside the more commonly cultivated Z. bungeanum (Sichuan pepper) and Z. piperitum (Japanese sansho). Like its famous relatives, Z. simulans produces small, red, split-open seed husks (pericarps) after the black seed falls out; these husks contain hydroxy-alpha-sanshool and related sanshool compounds that cause the unique 'ma' (numbing-tingling) sensation of Sichuan cooking — a distinctive electric, oscillating numbness of the tongue and lips, combined with floral, citrus, and spicy aromatic notes. Z. simulans is more cold-hardy than the primary Sichuan pepper (Z. bungeanum) and is one of the species sometimes sold as 'Sichuan pepper' in the US market. The fresh husks, dried husks, and sometimes the young leaves are all used as aromatic seasonings. As a garden plant, it is an attractive, fast-growing thorny shrub with fragrant compound leaves that provides hedging function while producing a useful spice crop.

common_name: Christine's Choice Tea (Cold-Hardy Southeast Tea Cultivar)
notes: Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal, especially in hot Gulf South summers; Christine's Choice is a tea cultivar selected and named by Camellia Forest Nursery in North Carolina from Southeast-grown seedling stock, chosen specifically for vigorous, reliable growth and good leaf quality in the humid, hot-summer conditions of the American Southeast rather than for the extreme cold tolerance bred into Sochi-type selections. It is a popular choice for home tea growers from the Carolinas through the Gulf Coast who want a productive plant adapted to regional humidity and disease pressure rather than one optimized for northern cold snaps. Leaves and growth habit are typical of small-leaved China-type tea, suitable for green, oolong, or black tea processing depending on how the harvested leaf is handled. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old, and mulch well to protect the acid-loving root system.

Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Citra is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in 2007 and quickly becoming one of the most sought-after and widely used hop varieties in modern craft brewing, this vigorous climbing bine produces resinous, aromatic cones with a distinctive tropical fruit, citrus, and gooseberry character that helped define the juicy, hazy IPA styles that have dominated craft beer for over a decade. Like other hops it is a perennial vine that dies back to the ground each winter and regrows vigorously each spring, needing a sturdy tall support and full sun to reach its full trellis height and cone production. Train young bines up the support as they grow, harvest cones in late summer when they feel dry and papery and spring back after being squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season for the best cone development.

Plant Syzygium aromaticum (Clove Tree) in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic, deep loamy soil in full sun; requires consistent moisture year-round and high humidity; protect from all frost and cold winds; harvest flower buds (cloves) when they turn from green to light pink but before they open — dried immediately after harvest to the familiar dark-brown clove. Clove is one of the most historically significant spice plants on Earth — the dried, unopened flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum, native exclusively to the North Maluku (Spice Islands) of Indonesia, were so extraordinarily valuable in the medieval spice trade that they were literally worth their weight in gold in European markets. The trade in cloves drove European exploration and colonialism throughout the 15th–17th centuries; the Banda Sea spice islands' control by the Dutch VOC was among the most economically significant monopolies in history. Today, Zanzibar (Tanzania), Indonesia, and Madagascar are the primary producers. The essential oil eugenol (80–90% of clove bud oil) is the source of clove's characteristic powerful aroma; it is used in dentistry as a topical analgesic, in perfumery, and as a food flavoring. The whole spice is used in biryani, mulled wine, pumpkin spice blends, pickling, and traditional medicine worldwide. A large, handsome, aromatic evergreen tree with attractive red-flushed young growth and cream-white flower clusters when not harvested.

common_name: Clove Vine (Cipo Cravo, Cipó Cravo, Panama Clove Vine)
notes: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with strong climbing support — Clove Vine grows vigorously and its stems will clothe a fence, trellis, or tree in dense, attractive foliage once established. Tynanthus panurensis is a woody, liana-climbing vine native to the Amazonian regions of Peru, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, and Ecuador in the Bignoniaceae family, known not primarily for its flowers (small, tubular, cream to white, produced in axillary clusters) but for one of the most remarkable aromatic properties of any tropical climbing plant: the bark, stems, and wood of the vine smell powerfully, precisely, and unmistakably of cloves — the familiar spice from Syzygium aromaticum — when cut, scraped, or bruised. The fragrant compound responsible is eugenol, the same aromatic phenol that gives true cloves their characteristic fragrance, occurring in Tynanthus panurensis as a convergent natural chemistry that produces an olfactory experience nearly identical to the spice. Throughout the Amazon Basin, the bark of T. panurensis is harvested and macerated in spirits (rum, cachaça, or aguardiente) to create 'licor de cipó cravo' (clove vine liqueur) — a traditional tonic drink used medicinally and consumed recreationally with an unmistakable clove-spice flavor. A genuinely unique aromatic plant for zone 10-12 tropical garden enthusiasts interested in useful and ethnobotanically significant plants.

Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; common myrtle is one of the oldest cultivated plants in human history — sacred to Aphrodite, woven into Roman bridal wreaths, and mentioned in the Old Testament — a Mediterranean evergreen shrub with small, intensely aromatic leaves (releasing a fresh, clean, camphor-like fragrance when brushed), white flowers with prominent yellow stamens in summer, and small, round, blue-black berries in autumn. All parts of the plant are aromatic and culinary: the leaves are used to flavor meats and poultry in Sardinian and Corsican cuisine (similar to bay leaves), the berries are edible with a resinous, slightly gin-like flavor and are used to flavor liqueurs and as a spice in traditional Mediterranean cooking. The plant is compact and shapeable into hedges, topiary, and formal geometric shapes. Both leaves and berries are used in myrtle liqueur, particularly the Sardinian Mirto. It grows well in zone 8–10 with dry summers and is an excellent plant for Gulf Coast and California gardens with mild winters.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant; the most flavorful and intense of all thyme-related herbs. Thymbra capitata (conehead thyme, also known as Coridothymus capitatus or sold as Thymus capitatus) is a compact, thorny-based, perennial aromatic subshrub from the dry Mediterranean hillsides of Spain, Portugal, the Balearic Islands, and extending east through the Mediterranean basin. It is one of the most intensely aromatic herbs in the Mediterranean flora — the small, crowded, stiff leaves and pink flower heads (arranged in the characteristic rounded 'cone' clusters that give the plant its name) contain very high concentrations of carvacrol and thymol, the same aromatic compounds found in both thyme and oregano, but at higher concentrations than either cultivated thyme or Greek oregano. The flavor is powerfully savory, hot, and intensely aromatic — making it highly valued as a culinary herb (used as a substitute for oregano in Spanish cooking), as one of the traditional components of Mediterranean za'atar blends, and as a source of essential oil. In Israel and the Levant, dried conehead thyme is an important za'atar component. The plant requires perfectly drained, lean, alkaline, sun-baked conditions — overwatering or clay soil will kill it. In zone 8–10 Mediterranean-climate gardens, it is long-lived, decorative, and worth growing as a specimen culinary herb.

common_name: Costa Rican Mint Bush (Jamaican Mint Bush, Minty Savory)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pinch regularly to maintain bushy form and encourage leaf production; propagate by stem cuttings. Satureja viminea (Costa Rican mint bush or Jamaican mint bush, also known as Clinopodium vimineum) is a tropical perennial shrubby herb from the mountainous regions of Jamaica, Costa Rica, and Central America — notable for producing one of the most intensely and cleanly 'minty' fragrances of any plant in the Lamiaceae (mint) family, far exceeding true peppermint (Mentha x piperita) in the purity and strength of the mint-eucalyptus aroma. The aromatic compound profile is dominated by pulegone and other menthane-family compounds that create the characteristic cool, clean mint sensation. As a garden plant in zone 9–12, Costa Rican mint bush grows as an upright, multi-branched, woody-based shrub with small, oval, intensely aromatic leaves and small white to lavender flowers attractive to bees and butterflies. The leaves are used as a fresh mint substitute for teas, cocktails (authentic mojito-style drinks in parts of Central America), and culinary uses wherever fresh mint flavor is desired. The plant tolerates light shade and thrives with regular trimming in tropical and subtropical gardens. Hardy to about 28–30°F; useful in containers in zone 8.

Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cotton lavender requires superb drainage — it will rot in wet or waterlogged soil and performs poorly in humid climates without excellent drainage. Santolina chamaecyparissus is a low, aromatic, silvery-gray, evergreen Mediterranean subshrub with dense, coral-like, deeply cut foliage that emits a strong, somewhat pungent, herbal scent when brushed; it produces small, button-like, bright-yellow flower heads on long, slender stems in mid-summer. In the traditional European herb garden, it was used as a low hedging plant in knot gardens and formal herb borders (the silver foliage contrasting beautifully with the green of boxwood and rosemary), and the dried leaves were used as a moth repellent for linen closets. Shear after flowering to maintain a neat, compact shape and prevent woodiness; takes well to clipping.

Plant in well-drained, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun; culinary sumac (Rhus coriaria) is the source of the brilliant deep-red, intensely tart spice used throughout Middle Eastern cooking as the primary acidifying agent before lemons became available. The dried, ground berries coat kebabs, top hummus, season fattoush salad, and form the backbone of za'atar spice blend. Harvest berry clusters (drupes) in late summer when fully red and dark but before rain softens them; dry completely before grinding. This species is distinct from the ornamental staghorn sumac (Rhus typhina) of North American gardens — culinary sumac is a Mediterranean species grown specifically for its tart, lemony fruit. The shrub is extremely drought-adapted and well-suited to zone 7–10 gardens.

Propagate from stem cuttings taken in late spring or summer rather than from seed, as germination is erratic and slow; root cuttings in clean sand and transplant rooted starts in spring into dry, lean, sandy, slightly acidic, very well-drained soil in full sun. Avoid clay, enriched, or moisture-retentive soils, as the species is endemic to sandy and gravelly river bars along the Big South Fork and upper Cumberland River system in Tennessee and Kentucky, where it is federally listed as threatened. Dense mats of wiry, upright stems bear tiny, needle-like, intensely rosemary-scented leaves and masses of small, pale pink to lavender, 2-lipped mint flowers in spring; the entire plant releases a strong fragrance when brushed. An outstanding native aromatic subshrub for rock gardens and sandy borders in zones 5-8 where its narrow habitat requirements of sharp drainage, lean soil, and full sun can be met.

Plant in moist, deep, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade with a trellis or fence to climb; dang shen is one of the most important tonic herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine, used as an energy-building adaptogen and substitute for the more expensive Panax ginseng. The twining, climbing vine produces pale greenish-yellow bell-shaped flowers with purple-veined interiors in summer. The thick, fleshy taproot is harvested after 3-5 years and used in soups, teas, and tonic preparations throughout China, Korea, and Japan. Modern research confirms adaptogenic compounds in the root that support energy and immune function. The plant dies back in winter and re-emerges from the root in spring. Grow in a position where the deep taproot will not be disturbed.

Plant in moist, deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with a trellis, fence, or shrub to climb; deodeok, known as sha shen in Chinese medicine, is a twining East Asian vine grown for its thick, aromatic, ginseng-scented taproot, which is a well-known ingredient in Korean cuisine, roasted, grilled, or pounded and seasoned as a savory side dish (deodeok-gui and related preparations) and also used in traditional herbal tonics. The vine climbs by twining stems clothed in soft blue-green leaves and produces distinctive bell-shaped flowers, greenish outside and dramatically mottled maroon-purple within, that hang facing downward through mid to late summer. Unlike its close relative dang shen (Codonopsis pilosula), deodeok's root has a stronger, more resinous, distinctly aromatic flavor that intensifies with the plant's age, and roots are traditionally harvested at three years or older for the best culinary and medicinal quality. Grow it where the deep root can develop undisturbed, and provide support for the twining vine to climb.

Plant root divisions or hardwood cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; eleuthero is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and tolerates drought once established. Eleutherococcus senticosus (commonly marketed as Siberian Ginseng, though not a true Panax ginseng) is a thorny, deciduous shrub of northeastern Asia that is one of the most studied adaptogenic medicinal plants; its root bark is used in clinical herbalism as a tonic to improve stress resilience, physical endurance, and immune function, with hundreds of published studies supporting its use in Russian and Chinese traditional medicine. The dried root bark is made into tea or tincture; harvest bark from roots of 3–5 year old plants in autumn. The plant is fully hardy, grows readily in cool northern climates, and is far easier to cultivate than true ginseng. Note: consult a qualified herbalist before medicinal use.

Plant in sandy, well-drained, dry, acidic soil in full sun; false rosemary is a stunning native shrublet of the Florida Panhandle and Gulf Coastal Plain that looks remarkably like culinary rosemary but is a separate genus in the mint family. The needle-like foliage has a pleasant resinous-minty fragrance when crushed, and the plant produces masses of lavender-pink flowers in spring. In its native Florida scrub habitat, it grows on the most droughty, infertile white sand where almost nothing else survives. It is a critically rare and threatened species in the wild due to habitat loss from development. Growing false rosemary in Gulf Coast gardens both provides an ornamental plant suited to the region's sandy soils and supports the conservation of a plant under severe pressure in the wild. Needs excellent drainage above all else — no standing water ever.

Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in a frost-free location; in zone 9 and cooler, grow in large containers that can be moved indoors or to a greenhouse in winter. Passiflora vitifolia is a spectacular tropical passionflower vine native to Central and South America producing three-lobed, grape-like leaves (giving the species its name) and the showiest flowers in the genus — brilliant scarlet-red, 4-inch flowers with a striking corona of white-tipped, red filaments in the center; it blooms nearly continuously in tropical climates. The edible fruits are small, oblong, and yellow-green when ripe with a sweet-tart, grape-like flavor. It is one of the finest tropical passionflowers for greenhouse culture and large patio containers, with some of the most intensely colored and beautiful flowers in the genus; it requires warm temperatures year-round.

Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; green santolina requires the same excellent drainage and sunny, dry conditions as gray santolina but has slightly more tolerance of humidity and moisture. Santolina rosmarinifolia (syn. S. viridis) is a green-leaved counterpart to the familiar gray cotton lavender; it produces feathery, bright-green, rosemary-like foliage with a similar strong, herbal, camphor-like scent and equally bright-yellow button flowers in summer. The contrasting use of gray (S. chamaecyparissus) and green (S. rosmarinifolia) santolinas is a classic technique in traditional knot garden design; the green species' brighter, more vivid foliage makes it excellent as a companion to silver or purple-leaved plants in formal herb plantings. Shear after flowering to maintain shape.

Establish rooted cuttings in spring under the dappled shade of taller trees, since this caffeinated Amazonian holly is naturally an understory species requiring humid, warm, tropical conditions with well-drained but consistently moist soil. Traditionally grown alongside cacao and coffee in Kichwa agroforestry plots of Ecuador, guayusa produces glossy, elongated leaves that are harvested young, lightly toasted or sun-dried, and steeped into a stimulating morning tea richer in caffeine than yerba mate. Light harvesting can begin about a year after planting, with full annual yields developing as the tree matures over roughly five years.

Plant stem cuttings 6–8 inches long directly in moist, moderately fertile soil in spring; provide trellis or tree support — guduchi is a vigorous climber. Tinospora cordifolia (guduchi or giloy) is one of the three most revered medicinal plants in Ayurvedic medicine (the others being ashwagandha and shatavari) — a tropical Indian climbing vine that has been used continuously in Ayurvedic medical practice for over 3,000 years. Modern research has identified numerous bioactive compounds including tinosporin, berberine, and various alkaloids and glycosides with anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, antipyretic, and hepatoprotective properties. The stem is the primary medicinal part — consumed as a decoction, powder, or extract. The plant is a vigorous, twining vine with broad, heart-shaped, bright-green leaves resembling a large morning glory vine in appearance. In India, a respected folk tradition holds that guduchi plants growing on neem trees (Azadirachta indica) — absorbing constituents from the host — have enhanced medicinal potency. The plant naturalizes readily in tropical and humid subtropical climates; it spreads vigorously and may require management to prevent overgrowth in frost-free zones.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; provide a trellis or support structure; propagate by stem cuttings. Gymnema sylvestre (gymnema, sugar destroyer, or gurmar — Hindi for 'destroyer of sugar') is a woody climbing vine native to the tropical dry forests of central and southern India and Sri Lanka, famous in both traditional medicine and modern nutritional science for one of the most remarkable food interactions known in botany. The fresh leaves of gymnema contain gymnemic acids — triterpene saponins that temporarily bind to and block the sweet taste receptors on the tongue — causing a complete, reversible suppression of the ability to taste sweetness for 1–2 hours after the leaves are chewed. After chewing gymnema leaf, eating sugar tastes like sand, honey tastes like nothing, chocolate loses all sweetness, and sweet fruits taste only of their sour or astringent components — a dramatic, repeatable, pharmacological food interaction. This property has given gymnema both its ancient role in Ayurvedic medicine (used for 2,000+ years for 'sweet urine' — now understood as diabetes) and modern research interest: clinical studies suggest gymnemic acids may reduce sugar absorption in the intestine and support healthy blood glucose management. Gymnema is now one of the most widely sold botanical supplements for blood sugar support worldwide. In zone 9–12, it grows as an ornamental vine with elliptical leaves and small, yellow, tubular flowers.

Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; haritaki is a frost-tender tropical and subtropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. One of the most revered trees in Ayurvedic medicine, called the 'king of medicines,' it is a deciduous forest tree native from India to Southeast Asia bearing small, ribbed, olive-like fruit that is dried and used as one of the three fruits in the classic Ayurvedic formula triphala, valued in traditional practice for digestive support among many other uses. The tree needs many years of growth before fruiting begins and ultimately becomes a substantial shade tree, making it a long-term planting suited only to large tropical properties, botanical collections, or dedicated medicinal orchards rather than a typical home garden. Water regularly while young, reduce watering once established, and expect a long wait before the first harvestable fruit crop.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with trellis or other support for climbing; Smilax ornata is adaptable to a range of conditions including full sun with consistent moisture and deep shade — mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and supply organic matter to the root zone. Smilax ornata (Honduran Sarsaparilla, Zarzaparilla) is a thorny, woody, perennial climbing vine in the Smilacaceae family native to humid tropical forests, forest edges, and riparian corridors of Central America — particularly Honduras, Guatemala, Mexico (Veracruz and Chiapas), Cuba, and Jamaica — where it climbs through the understorey using tendrils. The long, aromatic, reddish-brown rhizomes are the authentic source of 'true' sarsaparilla flavoring — the complex, vanilla-anise-wintergreen root flavor historically used in 19th-century American sarsaparilla beverages and root beer before artificial flavors displaced it. Medicinally, sarsaparilla root was a major export from Central America and the Caribbean to European pharmaceutical markets in the 16th–19th centuries for treatment of syphilis, psoriasis, rheumatism, and as a blood-purifying tonic. Modern phytochemical research confirms anti-inflammatory steroidal saponins (sarsasaponin, smilasaponin) in the rhizomes. The rhizomes are harvested by carefully digging, removing a portion, and replanting the crown; the vine regenerates. Excellent shade-tolerant medicinal vine for forest-garden and woodland-garden settings in zones 7–11.

Plant seedlings or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, extremely well-drained, rocky soil in full sun; Indian frankincense is a dryland tree that needs sharp drainage above all else and is realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Native to dry, rocky hills across India, it is tapped for its fragrant resin, which hardens into aromatic amber 'tears' burned as incense and used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine, closely related to the African and Arabian frankincense trees that supply the resin of biblical and ancient trade fame. The papery, peeling bark and sparse, compound leaves give the tree an open, drought-adapted silhouette suited to a xeriscape or succulent-collection planting in frost-free climates, where it can be grown as much for its unusual form as for eventual resin tapping. Water sparingly, provide maximum sun and heat, and avoid any risk of standing water at the roots, which quickly kills this dryland species.

common_name: Indian Mulberry Root (Bai Ji Tian, Morinda Root)
notes: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; harvest roots after 3–5 years. Morinda officinalis (bai ji tian or Indian mulberry root) is a trailing and climbing vine from southern China and Southeast Asia in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) — one of the 50 fundamental herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and a plant used continuously in Chinese medical practice for over 2,000 years. The medicinal part is the dried root (bai ji tian in Chinese, meaning 'a hundred joints stretching to the sky') — starchy, slightly sweet, mildly warming — used in TCM specifically to tonify (strengthen) Kidney Yang energy, treating impotence, infertility, lower back and knee pain and weakness, fatigue, and osteoporosis from a TCM perspective. It is one of the principal herbs in many male reproductive tonifying formulas (like the classic Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan). The root contains anthraquinones, polysaccharides, and flavonoids with studied effects on testosterone levels, bone density, and adaptogenic activity. As a garden plant in zone 8–12, it is an attractive, semi-woody vine with glossy, ovate leaves and small white flowers in rounded clusters, followed by compound, white, aggregate fruits similar to noni (M. citrifolia) but smaller. Quite different from commercial noni in use and chemistry despite being in the same genus.
