Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining stems; Indian sarsaparilla is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Slender, twining stems carry narrow, leathery leaves with a whitish midrib and small, purplish-brown flowers, but the plant is grown chiefly for its long, aromatic, cinnamon-scented roots, traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine and as a flavoring agent similar to true sarsaparilla, to which it is not closely related botanically. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and light levels once established, scrambling over low supports or trailing from a container, and roots are typically harvested for use after at least a year or two of growth. Water moderately, allowing soil to dry somewhat between waterings, and protect from any frost, which damages both foliage and roots.

Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indian snakeroot is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Wild populations are heavily overharvested and vulnerable across much of its native range, so source only nursery-propagated plants. Glossy, whorled leaves and small clusters of white flowers followed by small purple-black fruit grow on a compact forest-understory shrub native to South and Southeast Asian shade, historically significant as the original plant source of reserpine, one of the first modern drugs used to treat high blood pressure, and long used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine before that. Because unsustainable wild collection has made the species vulnerable across parts of its range, cultivated plantings from nursery-propagated stock, whether in a botanical collection or a home shade garden in a frost-free climate, help take pressure off remaining wild populations. Provide consistent warmth, humidity, and shade, and never attempt to self-medicate with plant material, since reserpine and related alkaloids have a narrow margin of safety and require professional medical guidance.

common_name: Japanese Pepper Vine (Fuji Kadsura, Asian Pepper Vine)
notes: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; provide trellis or tree trunk support. Piper kadsura (Japanese pepper vine) is a Japanese and East Asian climbing vine in the pepper family (Piperaceae) — related to true black pepper (P. nigrum) but native to the humid, shaded forests of Japan, China, and Korea. The plant produces attractive, heart-shaped, deeply veined, dark-green leaves with conspicuous venation and a mildly spicy pepper aroma when crushed. Small, string-like flower spikes produce tiny, red to dark-purple peppercorns-like berries in fall that are mildly peppery-spicy and have been used as a seasoning and traditional medicine ingredient in East Asian cuisine and herbal practice. The vine climbs by adhesive stem roots similar to Virginia creeper and can attach to rough stone, brick, and wood surfaces. As a shade-tolerant ornamental vine for zone 9–12, it provides year-round interest with its attractive foliage and subtle fruiting display. Used in Japanese herbal medicine (kampo) for joint pain and circulation. Extremely rare in Western horticulture.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; makrut lime is grown primarily for its distinctive double-lobed leaves, which are the indispensable aromatic herb of Thai and Cambodian cooking, used in curries, soups, and stir-fries to impart an intensely floral, citrusy perfume that no other herb can substitute. The bumpy, knobbly green fruit has very little juice but extremely aromatic zest used in marinades and Thai curry pastes. Leaves can be harvested whenever new growth appears; young leaves have the strongest flavor. In containers (the most practical approach north of zone 9), use a quality potting mix, fertilize monthly with citrus fertilizer spring through fall, and overwinter indoors in a bright window above 50°F.

Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, and keep soil consistently moist through the tree's slow multi-year establishment. Kokum is dioecious, so both male and female trees are needed for fruit, and it is native to the moist forests of India's Western Ghats. The purple-rind fruit is sun-dried into the deep reddish-black souring spice used throughout Goan and Konkani cooking, such as kokum curry and solkadhi, and pressed into kokum butter; fresh pulp is also boiled into a tart, cooling summer syrup.

Plant in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 9–12; Korintje cinnamon is an Indonesian species from Sumatra that is actually the most commonly sold type of cinnamon in the United States under the generic label 'cinnamon' — accounting for the majority of commercial cinnamon imports. Named for Kota Kerinci in Sumatra, it produces thick, dark-brown bark quills with a strong, mildly sweet flavor intermediate between Ceylon and Chinese cassia cinnamons. The bark is harvested from trees 3–4 years after planting by stripping young branches; coppicing the trees stimulates new shoot production for repeated harvests. Like all commercial cinnamon, the attractive, broad, three-veined leaves are also aromatic when crushed. In zone 9–11, it grows well outdoors as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree; regular harvesting of branches maintains a bushy, productive form suitable for the home garden.

Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon myrtle is an Australian native rainforest tree with the most intensely concentrated lemon fragrance of any plant on Earth — the essential oil content of the leaves (95% citral) vastly exceeds that of lemon balm, lemon verbena, or lemon thyme. Fresh or dried leaves are used in cooking exactly as lemon is used, in teas, baked goods, sauces, marinades, ice cream, and fish dishes, with a clean, pure lemon flavor that holds up better to heat than actual lemon juice. It is increasingly popular as a culinary specialty herb in Zone 9–11 gardens in the US, particularly in coastal California and the Gulf Coast. The shiny, oval, evergreen leaves are attractive year-round, and small clusters of white flowers appear in summer. It makes an excellent large container specimen in colder zones that can be moved to protection before frost. Harvest leaves fresh as needed or dry for long-term use.

Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil; littleleaf linden (Tilia cordata) is one of the most important medicinal trees of Europe, grown primarily for its fragrant, pale yellow flower clusters (collected with the distinctive wing-like bract) that are dried to make tilleul tea — one of the classic European herbal teas with a pleasant mild flavor and traditional use for relaxation, sleep, cold and flu, and anxiety. The flowers, which appear in June-July, are intensely attractive to bees and are considered one of the finest sources of honey in Europe; linden honey is a premium product. The tree itself is magnificent, developing deeply furrowed bark and a broad, rounded crown that provides excellent shade. Leaves are edible as salad greens in spring when young and tender.

Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; protect from temperatures below 28°F. Citrus hystrix (makrut lime, formerly and controversially called kaffir lime) is a Southeast Asian citrus grown primarily for its extraordinary, hourglass-shaped double leaves — two leaves joined end to end — which have an intensely aromatic, complex lime-floral fragrance unlike any other citrus and are indispensable to the flavor profiles of Thai, Indonesian, Cambodian, and Lao cuisines. The fresh or dried leaves flavor curries, soups (Tom Yum), coconut-milk dishes, and rice; they are among the most important flavoring ingredients in Southeast Asian cooking. The small, warty, dark-green, rough-skinned fruits are highly acidic and used primarily for their zest (makrut lime zest is a key ingredient in Thai curry pastes) rather than their juice. The plant is an extremely popular container herb in Thai and Southeast Asian communities across the Gulf South — grown in pots for easy access to fresh leaves year-round and brought indoors when cold threatens. Makrut lime is also used in some natural beauty products for its essential oil.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Malabar nut, known as vasaka in Ayurvedic medicine, is a fast-growing evergreen shrub from South Asia long used in traditional respiratory remedies, with the leaves brewed into teas and syrups historically employed for coughs, bronchitis, and asthma-like symptoms. The plant forms an attractive, dense, leafy shrub with large, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves and showy white flowers marked with purple-veined lower lips, produced in short spikes mainly in spring, that attract pollinators despite the plant's primary reputation as a medicinal rather than ornamental subject. It tolerates a range of light conditions from partial shade to nearly full sun and adapts well to average garden soil once established, needing only routine watering during dry spells. In the Gulf South, Malabar nut can be grown as a woody perennial shrub in sheltered zone 9 gardens, cut back hard after a hard freeze to resprout from the base, or grown further north as a container specimen brought indoors for winter. Prune periodically to maintain a bushy shape and encourage fresh leaf growth for harvest.

Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; mastic tree is the source of the original mastic gum — the resinous, pine-scented exudate collected by scoring the bark of trees on the Greek island of Chios, used for at least 2,500 years as a chewing gum, food flavoring, incense, varnish, and medicine. Greek mastic ('Chios masticha') is a protected designation of origin product used in the liqueur Mastika, Greek chewing gum, breads, pastries, and Turkish delight. As a landscape plant, mastic tree is an outstanding drought-tolerant, evergreen shrub for Mediterranean-climate and Gulf Coast gardens, producing aromatic, glossy, pinnate leaves and small clusters of red to black berries that attract birds. It is excellent for coastal gardens due to its salt tolerance and thrives in the hot, alkaline, well-drained conditions of the Texas Hill Country and Gulf Coast. A relative of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera).

common_name: Mexican Bay Leaf (Mexican Avocado Leaf, Hoja de Aguacate)
notes: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; harvest leaves as needed throughout the growing season and dry for storage. Persea drymifolia (Mexican bay leaf or hoja de aguacate) is a Mexican and Central American tree in the avocado family (Lauraceae) grown primarily for its strongly aromatic leaves, which have a complex, distinctive fragrance and flavor combining anise (star anise), cinnamon, and sassafras. The leaves are not related to European bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) but occupy a similar culinary role in southern Mexican cooking — they are an essential, non-substitutable ingredient in Oaxacan mole negro, tasajo, estofado, and tamales, where they are toasted on a comal (griddle) before use to intensify their flavor and then added whole to slow-cooked dishes. The trees also occasionally produce small, avocado-like fruits that are inedible but closely resemble tiny avocados. In zone 9–11, the tree grows as a small to medium ornamental specimen; the leaves can be dried and stored for use. Dried Mexican bay leaves can be purchased at Mexican grocery stores but fresh-from-the-tree leaves are far more fragrant. A unique culinary herb tree that no serious Oaxacan cooking enthusiast should be without.

Lippia graveolens is the true oregano of Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking — a shrubby, woody perennial native to dry, rocky hillsides from northern Mexico through Central America whose strongly aromatic, slightly rough-textured leaves have a more intense, earthy, and complex flavor than Mediterranean oregano (Origanum vulgare), making it the preferred herb in authentic salsa, mole, chili, and carne asada recipes. Propagate from semi-hardwood stem cuttings, which root readily in moist perlite or sand; Mexican oregano is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in full sun, hot conditions, and lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil — rich, moist soils reduce essential oil concentration and can cause root rot. In zones 9-11 it grows as a multi-stemmed shrub 2-4 feet tall, bearing small, white, tubular flowers attractive to bees and butterflies throughout the warm season; in zone 9 a hard freeze may kill top growth, but established plants typically regrow vigorously from the roots in spring. Harvest leafy branch tips at any time during the growing season; the flavor is most concentrated just before flowering and the leaves dry well, intensifying in aroma much like Mediterranean oregano.

Poliomintha longiflora is a strongly aromatic shrubby herb native to the Chihuahuan Desert and south Texas, widely prized in Mexican regional cuisine as the true 'Mexican oregano' — its flavor is more complex and citrusy than Mediterranean oregano and is considered essential for authentic mole sauces, tamales, and chili con carne. Plant in the hottest, driest, most well-drained spot in the garden; once established it requires little to no supplemental water and thrives on neglect in rocky, alkaline soils. The long, lavender-pink tubular flowers produced from summer through fall are highly attractive to hummingbirds and are among the best late-season nectar sources in xeric gardens. In zone 9 and warmer the plant is evergreen and can be harvested year-round; in zone 7-8 it may die back to the roots in hard winters but re-sprouts reliably in spring.

Transplant young trees in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this fast-growing, drought-tolerant evergreen from the Peruvian Andes develops graceful, weeping, willow-like branches and clusters of small berries that ripen from green to bright rose-pink. The dried berries are sold commercially as pink peppercorns and add a fruity, mildly resinous heat to pepper blends, sauces, and infused oils, though botanically the tree is unrelated to true pepper (Piper nigrum). Handle fresh fruit and sap with care, as some people develop mild skin or respiratory irritation, and check local regulations before planting, since molle is classified as invasive or restricted in parts of California and the desert Southwest.

Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Mosaic is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in 2012, this vigorous, high-yielding American hop produces cones with an unusually complex aroma profile combining tropical fruit, citrus, pine, and berry notes all at once, living up to its name by contributing a shifting mosaic of different flavor impressions depending on how it is used in a beer recipe. Its complexity and versatility across both bittering and late-addition aromatic brewing uses have made it one of the most in-demand hop varieties among craft brewers since its release, commanding premium prices and frequently being in short supply. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season.

Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; litsea grows naturally as an understory tree in subtropical forest and tolerates partial shade well. Litsea cubeba (mountain pepper, fragrant litsea, or maychangberry) is a small to medium-sized deciduous to semi-evergreen tree in the laurel family (Lauraceae) native to the subtropical mountain forests of central and southern China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. The tree produces small (1/4-inch), round, pepper-like black fruits (cubeba = resembling cubeb pepper) with an extraordinarily intense, clean, lemon-floral-citrus aroma — one of the most concentrated natural sources of citral (60–80% of essential oil content), the same aromatic compound found in lemongrass (Cymbopogon), melissa, and other citrus-scented plants. The essential oil of L. cubeba (may chang oil or litsea oil) is extracted commercially and used extensively in high-end perfumery, soap, and cosmetic formulations, and as a natural food flavoring. The dried fruits can be used as a spice — adding a bright, lemony, floral-pepper note to dishes — in a culinary style similar to Sichuan pepper or pink peppercorn. In Taiwan and southern China, the fruits, leaves, and bark are used in traditional mountain tribal cuisine as a distinctive aromatic spice. The tree also has documented antimicrobial activity from citral. It performs well in zone 8–11 subtropical gardens as an aromatic specimen or food forest understory tree.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist. Tasmannia lanceolata (mountain pepper or Tasmanian pepperberry) is a native Australian alpine shrub from the cold, moist rainforests and alpine heathlands of Tasmania, Victoria, and New South Wales — the most important native Australian spice plant and a signature ingredient of contemporary Australian native cuisine. Both the black, ripe berries and the dried, ground leaves are intensely peppery-hot, with a heat that is initially sharp and then evolves into a prolonged, warming burn distinct from black pepper's heat — the primary pungent compounds (polygodial and drimanyl acetate) belong to a different chemical class from piperine (black pepper's heat compound) and interact differently with the tongue. The dried leaves have a complex, eucalyptus-clove-pepper aroma and are used in Australia as a seasoning rub for lamb, game, and seafood; the berries are used whole or crushed as a distinctive peppercorn substitute. Mountain pepper has become a centerpiece of the Australian 'bush tucker' (native food) movement and is increasingly available in gourmet food markets internationally. The plant is dioecious — plant male and female shrubs for berry production. In cultivation outside Australia, it requires cool, moist, acidic, shaded conditions.

Plant in well-drained, lean to fertile soil in full sun in a frost-free location; neem is one of the most multipurpose trees in tropical horticulture, revered for thousands of years in India where virtually every part of the tree is used: the seeds yield neem oil, widely used as an organic pesticide and insect repellent containing azadirachtin, a potent botanical insecticide; the leaves are used medicinally for their antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic properties; young shoots and leaves are eaten as a bitter vegetable in some South and Southeast Asian cuisines; and the twigs are traditionally used as disposable toothbrushes (chew sticks). The tree itself is a spectacular ornamental — fast-growing with a broad, spreading crown of dense, pinnate leaves and clusters of fragrant white flowers beloved by bees. It is one of the most drought-tolerant trees available and tolerates alkaline, poor soils that support little else. The organic pesticide market for neem oil products has created significant commercial cultivation in Florida and Hawaii.

common_name: Negro Pepper (Grains of Selim, Ethiopian Pepper, Hwentia)
notes: Plant seedlings in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with full sun to partial shade, giving the tree ample room since it eventually reaches a slender, tall canopy form. Negro pepper is an aromatic evergreen tree native to the humid lowland forests and savanna transition zones of West and Central Africa, grown for its finger-like, slightly twisted seed pods that are sun-dried and often smoked before use. The dried pods and their small seeds carry a warm, smoky, camphor-and-pepper flavor used whole or ground in West African soups, stews, and spice blends, and are also valued in traditional medicine and smoked-fish preparation. Because it is slow to bear, most growers outside Africa treat it as a long-term agroforestry or specimen tree rather than a quick spice crop; young trees benefit from light shade and should be protected from strong wind while establishing.

Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, lean to average soil in full sun; New Zealand tea tree is one of the most important plants of Maori tradition and modern apiculture — the intensely antibacterial nectar from manuka flowers produces the famous manuka honey, scientifically documented for its exceptional wound-healing and antibacterial properties. The leaves were used by Maori as a medicinal tea. In the garden, manuka is a handsome small to medium shrub covered in masses of small, open flowers — white in the species, pink to deep crimson in many cultivars — in late winter through spring. The tiny, heather-like aromatic leaves are evergreen. Many ornamental double-flowered cultivars are available ('Martini', 'Red Damask', 'Crimson Glory') that are showy but produce less nectar for bees. Full drainage is essential — root rot in wet soil is the primary cause of failure.

Plant in moist, average to rich soil in partial to full shade; northern spicebush is one of the few large shrubs truly native to the forest understory, making it invaluable for shaded landscapes. The tiny yellow flowers in early spring appear before the leaves and provide early nectar for native bees; the brilliantly yellow fall foliage is outstanding. Bright red, oil-rich berries on female plants in fall are devoured by migratory thrushes and are the primary larval host plant for the spicebush swallowtail butterfly. The dried berries are edible with a complex allspice-bay-pepper flavor once used as a colonial-era spice — they can replace allspice in recipes. All parts are intensely aromatic when crushed.

Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; oak-leaf geranium is a boldly distinctive scented-leaf pelargonium species prized for two features — its unusually large, deeply lobed, oak-leaf-shaped leaves (which give the plant its species name quercifolium, Latin for 'oak-leaved') and the strong, pungent, bitter-almond to balsamic fragrance released when the sticky, glandular leaves are handled, distinctly different from the rose or citrus notes of other scented pelargoniums. The leaves are large and rough-textured compared to most pelargoniums, sticky to the touch, and the plant becomes a large, somewhat gawky but aromatic shrub in warm climates. Small rose-pink to magenta flowers appear in spring and summer. Used in the fragrance industry and in potpourri for its balsamic notes. In zones 9–11 it can grow into an impressive specimen shrub with an overwhelming presence when the foliage is disturbed in the breeze. 'Fair Ellen' is a widely available cultivar with particularly deep-cut, decorative leaves. A plant grown more for fragrant-foliage effect than ornamental flowers — one of the most botanically interesting of the diverse scented pelargonium group.

Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in full sun; Padang cassia grows vigorously once established in frost-free conditions and begins producing harvestable bark on young shoots within 2–3 years after planting. Cinnamomum burmannii is an Indonesian native and the species that provides the majority of "cinnamon" sold in North American grocery stores and spice jars; it is harvested by stripping the bark from young branches and allowing it to dry into the familiar quills, and has a strong, sweet-spicy, slightly more pungent flavor and higher coumarin content than true Ceylon cinnamon (C. verum). The tree is an attractive, medium-sized, evergreen with oval, three-veined, cinnamon-scented leaves and can be grown as a landscape ornamental in zone 9–10; harvest bark from young shoots 1–2 years old and re-coppice to regenerate the plant cyclically for ongoing production.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; water sparingly — established plants need summer dry conditions to thrive. Salvia leucophylla (purple sage or coastal sage) is a California native aromatic shrub from the coastal sage scrub and chaparral communities of coastal and inland California. The plant produces aromatic, wrinkled, silver-gray to white-felted leaves with a strong, distinctive fragrance — more complex and resinous than common garden sage (S. officinalis), with additional notes of camphor, eucalyptus, and warm spice. The soft, gray foliage creates a beautiful silvery landscape effect, especially dramatic when paired with purple lavender and other Mediterranean-climate plants. In late spring through early summer, it produces whorled clusters of pink to light-purple flowers on white-felted stems — both fragrant and attractive to hummingbirds and bumblebees. Purple sage is a classic plant of the California chaparral and is notable for producing volatile allelopathic compounds (camphor, 1,8-cineole) from its leaves that inhibit the germination and growth of competing plants beneath its canopy — a natural herbicide effect. The leaves are traditionally used by California indigenous peoples for ceremonial smudging, and can be used as a culinary sage substitute (though stronger). Drought tolerance once established is extreme.

Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial shade to full sun; red bay is the native American aromatic bay of the coastal Southeast and Gulf Coast, producing glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves with the same aromatic oils and culinary bay-laurel fragrance as the Mediterranean bay laurel (Laurus nobilis) — the leaves are used identically in Southern cooking for seasoning gumbos, soups, stews, and bean dishes. In fact, red bay has traditionally been used in Gulf Coast cuisine (particularly in Louisiana) for generations as the local bay leaf. It is a fast-growing native tree of coastal hammocks and stream margins that provides excellent wildlife value — the blue-black fruits are important food for migrating songbirds, and the palamedes swallowtail butterfly uses red bay as its exclusive larval host plant. Tragically, laurel wilt disease (spread by an invasive ambrosia beetle) has killed the vast majority of red bay trees throughout the Southeast — consult local extension services before planting.

Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in frost-free zones (10–12) or grow in containers that can be protected from frost in zones 9 and below. Passiflora coccinea is a Brazilian tropical passionflower vine with large, heart-shaped to deeply lobed, oblong leaves and brilliant scarlet, orange-red, or vermilion flowers with a prominent corona of white-banded filaments from late spring through fall in tropical climates; it is one of the finest plants for attracting hummingbirds in tropical gardens. The small, edible fruits are yellow-green when ripe with soft, sweet, aromatic pulp. Related to P. vitifolia but with somewhat different leaf shape and flower proportions; both are outstanding for tropical garden collections and large container culture. Excellent on arbors, fences, and trellises in frost-free climates.

Soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to soften its hard coat, sow into acidic, sandy, low-fertility soil, and grow seedlings on for about two months before transplanting into their permanent full-sun position. Rooibos is a fine-needled legume shrub found only in South Africa's Cederberg mountains, where hot dry summers and cool wet winters shape its narrow native range. Harvested stems are cut, bruised, and left to oxidize before drying, turning the leaves the deep red-brown that gives the naturally caffeine-free, sweetly earthy tea its color and name.

Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Saaz is a lower-yielding traditional variety compared to modern high-alpha hops. One of the original four European 'noble hop' varieties, grown for centuries in the Žatec region of Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), it imparts the mild, spicy, earthy, floral bitterness that defines classic Czech and German pilsner beer styles, a subtle character quite different from the bold citrus and tropical fruit notes of modern American hop varieties. It is a lower-yielding, more disease-susceptible variety than many modern hybrid hops, reflecting its long, unimproved heritage, and rewards patient, attentive growing rather than the vigorous, high-output performance of newer cultivars. Train young bines up a sturdy support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and expect a lighter yield than modern high-alpha varieties in exchange for its classic, historic flavor profile.

Plant seedlings in spring alongside a compatible host plant (sandalwood is a partial root parasite and needs a nearby host tree or shrub to thrive) in well-drained soil in full sun; realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. This slow-growing tropical tree produces the fragrant, dense, oil-rich heartwood prized for centuries in incense, perfumery, and religious ceremonies across South and Southeast Asia, but the tree must be interplanted with a suitable host species from an early age, since its roots form haustoria that tap into a neighboring plant's roots for water and nutrients even as it also photosynthesizes on its own. Decades of growth (typically fifteen years or more) are needed before the valuable, densely aromatic heartwood develops in commercially useful quantity, making it a long-term, multi-generational planting rather than a quick garden project, and wild populations have historically been overharvested, making legally sourced plantation-grown seedlings the responsible choice. Water young trees regularly during establishment, choose a nitrogen-fixing or otherwise compatible host species to plant alongside it, and be prepared for a very long wait before any wood harvest.

Plant in well-drained, lean, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun in zones 8–11; shrubby blue sage is a woody native salvia of southern Texas and northern Mexico, producing bright lavender-blue flowers in loose terminal spikes over a very long season — from early spring to hard frost in warm climates — making it one of the most persistently flowering native sages in the South Texas garden. The strongly aromatic, gray-green, woolly-felted leaves have a distinctive strong fragrance and have been used traditionally in Mexico as a tea herb (mejorana is a traditional name in northern Mexico). The shrubby, semi-evergreen habit and extreme drought tolerance make it valuable as a foundation plant or informal hedge in alkaline, dry landscape conditions where few shrubs thrive. Consistently attractive to migrating hummingbirds, monarch butterflies, and native bees throughout its long blooming season.

Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sichuan pepper (not related to black pepper or chili peppers) is the dried husk of the fruit of Zanthoxylum shrubs, whose defining characteristic is a numbing, buzzing sensation on the tongue caused by the compound hydroxy-alpha-sanshool — a sensation called ma (tingling/numbing) that is the foundation of the ma-la (numbing-spicy) flavor profile of Sichuan Chinese cuisine. Harvest the small red fruits in fall when fully ripe, then dry and separate the husks from the black seeds — only the husks are used, as the seeds are bitter and gritty. The shrub is spiny and produces attractive clusters of small red fruits on female plants. Plant at least one male for pollination.

Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Simcoe is a patented, trademarked hop variety with licensing restrictions on commercial propagation. Released in the early 2000s, this high-alpha dual-purpose hop delivers a distinctive combination of passionfruit and pine aromas alongside earthy, dank undertones that became a signature flavor of the West Coast IPA style, and its high alpha acid content also makes it effective as a clean bittering hop. Its unique aroma profile and versatility for both bittering and late-addition dry-hopping uses have made it a foundational variety in modern American craft brewing since its introduction, prized enough that supply is often constrained relative to brewer demand. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture and full sun through the growing season.

Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; Sochi is a cold-hardy tea cultivar originally developed for the Black Sea coastal tea-growing region of Russia, the northernmost commercial tea-producing area in the world, and is widely sold in the US specifically because it tolerates significantly colder winters than typical tea plants, with reports of surviving briefly into the single digits °F once well established. This makes it the go-to choice for tea growers in cooler zones than the Gulf South, such as the mid-South and lower Appalachians, though it also performs well in the milder winters of zone 8–9. Leaves and growth habit are similar to standard small-leaved China-type tea, suitable for the same green, oolong, or black tea processing depending on how the harvested leaf is handled. Begin light harvesting of the top two leaves and a bud once plants are well established at three to four years old, and mulch heavily to protect the acid-loving root system through winter in the colder end of its range.

common_name: Spanish Thyme (Jamaican Oregano, Puerto Rican Oregano)
notes: Plant rooted cuttings in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; harvest stems frequently to maintain compact, bushy growth. Lippia micromera (Spanish thyme or Jamaican oregano) is a small, woody, aromatic shrub native to the dry limestone hills of Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, producing small, densely crowded, grey-green, strongly thyme-oregano scented leaves. The plant occupies the culinary niche of thyme and oregano in Caribbean cooking — the dried or fresh leaves are used in jerk seasoning blends, seasoning rubs for meats and fish, and traditional Caribbean herbal teas (sooshal, orosul). It is notably more drought- and heat-tolerant than either European thyme (Thymus vulgaris) or Mediterranean oregano (Origanum vulgare), making it well-suited to hot, dry, tropical and subtropical gardens where those herbs struggle. Lippia micromera belongs to the verbena family (Verbenaceae) and is distinct from Plectranthus amboinicus (Cuban oregano, also sometimes called 'Spanish thyme') — both are Caribbean oregano substitutes but from unrelated plant families. The essential oil is rich in thymol and carvacrol, the same primary compounds responsible for thyme and oregano's characteristic aroma. Excellent in containers in subtropical gardens.

Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring into humid, acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil sheltered from wind, ideally with morning sun and afternoon shade. True star anise is a slow, long-lived subtropical evergreen native to southern China and northern Vietnam that needs six to eight years of consistent warmth and humidity before it forms its first harvestable star-shaped seed pods. Pods are picked while still green, then sun-dried until they turn the familiar deep reddish-brown, and are essential to Chinese five-spice powder, pho broth, and mulled wine. Do not confuse it with the toxic ornamental anise relatives (Illicium floridanum, I. anisatum) sold for landscaping — only I. verum pods are safe to eat.

Root stem cuttings containing 3–4 nodes in moist, organic, fast-draining medium in part shade; hand-pollinate the flowers as they open; harvest beans after 9 months on vine when tips turn yellow. Vanilla tahitensis (Tahitian vanilla) is a separate species from the dominant commercial vanilla (Vanilla planifolia) — distinguished botanically and aromatically by several key differences: the beans are shorter, plumper, and contain more moisture; the primary aromatic compound is heliotropin (piperonal) — a floral, anise-cherry compound — rather than the vanillin-dominated aroma of V. planifolia; and the overall scent profile of Tahitian vanilla beans is more complex, fruity, and intensely floral, with distinctive cherry, anise, and licorice notes absent from Mexican or Madagascar vanilla. These aromatic differences have made Tahitian vanilla the preferred choice of French pastry chefs and many gourmet bakers for delicate preparations where the distinctive floral complexity can shine — French vanilla ice cream, pastry creams, and fine chocolates. Tahitian vanilla is grown primarily in Tahiti and French Polynesia, with smaller production in Papua New Guinea. Like V. planifolia, V. tahitensis requires hand-pollination in cultivation outside its native range, as the natural pollinators (specific bees and hummingbirds) are absent. The vine climbs strongly on trees or supports in humid tropical conditions.

Plant in well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; water regularly as tea plants are sensitive to drought but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Camellia sinensis is the plant species from which all true tea is made; the young leaves and leaf buds ('flush') are harvested and processed differently to produce green tea (unoxidized), oolong (partially oxidized), or black tea (fully oxidized) — the same plant, processed differently. Home tea gardens are feasible in zones 7–10 where the plant grows as a reliable evergreen shrub; in the Gulf Coast and Southeast United States (zone 8–10) it performs particularly well in the moist, acidic conditions similar to its natural subtropical mountain habitat in China and Southeast Asia. Begin harvesting the tender top two leaves and a bud once the plant is 3–4 years old and 2–3 feet tall; regular harvesting keeps the plant productive and bushy. Small white flowers in fall are fragrant.

Plant Melaleuca alternifolia in full sun to light shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to occasionally wet soil; it tolerates periodic waterlogging and moderate drought once established; prune after flowering to maintain shape and encourage dense growth; harvest leaves in late summer to early fall when terpinen-4-ol content is highest. Tea Tree is the world's most commercially important medicinal Melaleuca — grown on a large scale in the coastal plains of northeastern New South Wales, Australia, where its essential oil is steam-distilled from the leaves and young stems. Tea tree oil is one of the most thoroughly researched of all plant essential oils, with well-documented antibacterial (effective against MRSA and other resistant strains), antifungal, and antiviral properties; it is used in skin care products, toothpastes, wound antiseptics, and household cleaning products worldwide. In the garden, it is an attractive small tree or large shrub with papery, peeling whitish bark, fine needle-like leaves, and showy cream-white bottlebrush flower spikes that are excellent for native bees and other pollinators. Tolerates poorly drained and seasonally wet soils better than most ornamentals, making it useful in low-lying areas of Gulf Coast gardens; it performs best in zone 9–10 in the United States. Caution: tea tree oil is toxic if ingested and should not be used internally.

Transplant container-grown trees in spring into loamy, well-drained soil with a near-neutral pH, in full sun to partial shade; established trees tolerate brief light frost better than true tropical cinnamon relatives. The glossy, distinctly three-veined leaves carry a warm cassia-cinnamon-clove aroma entirely different from true bay laurel and are picked and sun-dried once the tree is a few years established. Tejpat is essential to North Indian garam masala, biryani, and dal tadka, and should not be substituted with Mediterranean bay leaf, which lacks its cinnamon character.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this thorny, deciduous, high-elevation Himalayan relative of Sichuan pepper is markedly more cold-hardy than its lowland cousins, tolerating winters at elevation across Nepal and northern India. The dried, husked berries deliver an intense citrus-grapefruit aroma alongside the characteristic tongue-tingling numbness of the genus, and are ground fresh for Nepali achar, momo dipping sauces, and spice blends. Harvest ripe berry clusters in autumn and dry them whole before grinding just before use to preserve the volatile citrus notes.

Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic, forest-type soil in partial shade to deep shade; Eurycoma longifolia requires the warmth, humidity, and consistent moisture of a tropical rainforest environment — avoid cold, drought, or standing water, and provide forest-floor-type organic mulch to mimic its natural habitat. Eurycoma longifolia (Tongkat Ali, Longjack, or Malaysian Ginseng) is a slender, dioecious, understory tree native to the lowland and hill dipterocarp rainforests of Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo, Vietnam, and the Philippines, recognized as the most commercially important and widely exported medicinal plant of Southeast Asia by trade value. The long, slender, deeply penetrating taproots — sometimes over 6 feet long and difficult to harvest — are the medicinal part, dried, powdered, and used in traditional Malay, Indonesian, and Vietnamese medicine as a bitter tonic for fatigue, stress, fever, and debility. Modern phytochemical research has identified quassinoids (eurycomanone) and other bioactive compounds with adaptogenic, testosterone-supporting, anti-fatigue, and antimalarial properties, driving a large international dietary supplement industry. Tongkat Ali is now one of the most over-harvested wild medicinal plants in Southeast Asia — Malaysia has established cultivation standards and sustainable harvesting programs to prevent wild population collapse. Cultivation from seed is slow; plant in deep, organically rich, moist, shaded conditions similar to rainforest understory.

Plant in fertile, well-drained, sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; true cinnamon (Ceylon cinnamon) from Sri Lanka is considered the 'real' cinnamon of culinary tradition — lighter, sweeter, and more delicate than the cassia cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia) sold in most North American supermarkets. True cinnamon has very low coumarin content compared to cassia, making it safer for regular consumption. The cinnamon spice is harvested from the inner bark of shoots cut from coppiced trees — the thin bark curls into the familiar quills as it dries. In the home garden, the tree provides an ornamental, fragrant, tropical presence; the young leaves can be used as a bay leaf substitute. In zones 9 and below, grow in a large container and harvest leaves and small stems for culinary use. Coppice regularly to keep the plant at a manageable size.

Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; nutmeg is a true tropical rainforest tree that needs consistent warmth, humidity, and shelter from wind and is only realistic outdoors in frost-free zone 11 or as a large container specimen kept above 60°F year-round elsewhere. Native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia, this evergreen tree bears apricot-like fruit that splits open to reveal a hard seed wrapped in a bright red, lacy covering; the seed itself is dried and ground into nutmeg, while the red aril is separately dried and ground into mace, making a single fruit the source of two distinct spices. Trees are dioecious, so both a male pollinator and a female fruiting tree (or a grafted tree combining both) are needed for fruit production, and trees typically take seven to nine years to begin bearing and up to twenty years to reach full production. Grow in the dappled shade of taller trees as it would experience in its native rainforest understory, keep humidity high, and protect from any cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit.

Plant stem cuttings in coarse, well-drained, slightly acidic organic bark mix in heavy shade with a support structure for aerial roots to climb — vanilla is the only edible-fruiting orchid and the world's second most expensive spice (after saffron), native to the tropical forest understory of Mexico and Central America where it climbs into the forest canopy in deep shade. The pale yellow-green flowers open one at a time for only a few hours and in most cultivated gardens must be hand-pollinated (the natural pollinators, stingless bees of the genus Melipona, are restricted to Mexico). Successfully pollinated flowers develop into the familiar vanilla bean pods (technically seed capsules) over 9–10 months. After harvest, the pods undergo a complex curing process (blanching, sweating, drying) to develop the characteristic vanilla flavor from the compound vanillin. An extraordinary container or greenhouse specimen for warm-climate gardeners who want to grow their own vanilla extract.

Plant stem section cuttings in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to part shade; water sparingly — Cissus quadrangularis is drought-tolerant and susceptible to root rot in wet soils. Cissus quadrangularis (veldt grape or harjora) is a tropical African and Asian succulent vine that looks unlike any typical grape-family plant (Vitaceae) — it produces thick, fleshy, distinctly four-winged-square (quadrangular = four-cornered) green stems segmented at intervals like bamboo nodes, with small, deciduous, kidney-shaped leaves and tiny clusters of red berries at the nodes. The plant is primarily known not as a food or ornamental but as one of the most important plants in Ayurvedic medicine — it is called 'harjora' in Sanskrit (literally 'bone-joiner') and is used for more than 2,000 years to accelerate fracture healing, treat osteoporosis, joint pain, and as a bone-strengthening tonic. Scientific studies have confirmed that extracts of C. quadrangularis stimulate osteoblast (bone cell) activity and accelerate bone mineralization. It is widely sold as a supplement in India and, increasingly, in Western natural health markets. In the garden in zone 9–12, Veldt grape is an ornamental curiosity — the square, succulent, bright-green stems and climbing or trailing habit make it an unusual specimen for a succulent or tropical garden.

Nick or soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to break the hard seed coat, then direct-sow shallowly into well-drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun once the site is frost-free; this arid-zone Australian shrub tolerates drought, poor soil, and salinity once established. The ripe, dried seed pods are harvested, roasted, and ground into wattleseed, an Aboriginal bushfood staple with a nutty, roasted-coffee, caramel flavor used to season breads, ice cream, and native spice blends. Prune lightly after seed harvest to maintain a manageable shrub form and encourage a fuller next season's pod set.

Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; minimal care once established. Morella cerifera (southern wax myrtle or bayberry) is one of the most ecologically important and garden-useful native shrubs of the Gulf Coastal Plain, native from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Texas and Oklahoma. The aromatic, semi-evergreen to evergreen leaves (crushed, they release a distinctive bayberry-bay-spice fragrance) are used dried in wreaths, sachets, and as a flavoring herb similar to bay laurel in coastal Southern cooking. The small, silvery-waxy, blue-gray berries produced on female plants are the basis of bayberry candle wax — melted from the berries and cast into candles with the distinctive bayberry fragrance beloved in New England and Colonial American tradition. Wax myrtle is among the most adaptable native plants for Gulf Coast gardens: it tolerates salt spray, wet conditions, drought, poor soils, and coastal conditions equally well, making it outstanding for beach landscapes, rain gardens, wet corners, and dry banks alike. The plant fixes nitrogen through root symbiosis with Frankia bacteria (actinorrhizal nitrogen fixation), improving soil fertility. As a screening shrub, hedge, or small tree, it grows rapidly (2–3 feet per year when young) to 10–15 feet. Native birds eat the waxy berries and nest in the dense foliage.

Root softwood cuttings in early summer or layer low branches, then plant out in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Distinct from the common ornamental hybrid forsythia, this species is grown for its fruit capsules, harvested green or ripe and used in traditional Chinese medicine formulas said to clear heat and support the body during colds and sore throats. Prune right after spring flowering so next year's fruiting wood has time to develop.

common_name: West Indian Vanilla (Pompona Vanilla, Vanillón, Big-Leaved Vanilla)
notes: Plant in partial shade to bright indirect light in moist, well-drained, organic-rich medium — West Indian Vanilla climbs most vigorously on rough-textured supports in conditions that approximate its native tropical forest habitat: bright, filtered light, consistent warmth, and humid air with good drainage at the roots. Vanilla pompona is a hemi-epiphytic climbing orchid vine native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean islands, and northern South America in the Orchidaceae family, closely related to the commercially dominant Vanilla planifolia but producing shorter, thicker, more barrel-shaped vanilla pods with a distinctly different, somewhat sweeter aromatic profile. As with all Vanilla species, the vine climbs by clasping aerial roots to tree bark or other rough surfaces, can reach impressive lengths (30+ feet), and produces axillary clusters of the characteristic large (2-inch), greenish-yellow to pale yellow vanilla orchid flowers — each lasting only a single day, requiring prompt hand pollination in cultivation to set the pods. The pods (the 'vanilla beans' of commerce) take 9–12 months to mature after pollination, then must be cured through a weeks-long process of sweating, drying, and conditioning to develop the characteristic vanilla aroma. Vanilla pompona has been used as an alternative and supplement to V. planifolia in commercial vanilla production, particularly in the Caribbean, and is more resistant to the Fusarium root rot disease that threatens V. planifolia plantations. An interesting food plant for zone 10-12 tropical gardens with appropriate climbing structures.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, rocky or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; trim lightly after flowering to maintain compact form. Micromeria fruticosa (white micromeria, white za'atar, or zuta levanit) is a small aromatic subshrub native to the dry rocky hillsides, terra rossa soils, and limestone outcrops of the Eastern Mediterranean — particularly Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, and the Palestinian territories. The plant has distinctive small, oval, white-hairy (tomentose) leaves with a soft, felted texture, giving the plant an overall white-gray appearance; hence 'white' za'atar or zuta levanit. The fragrance and flavor are unique: a gentle, warm, herbal-thyme character with a subtle mint and tea-like undertone — softer and more delicate than either thyme or savory. In Israel and the Levant, M. fruticosa is one of the most beloved traditional herbal teas, prepared by infusing fresh or dried leaves in hot water; it is believed to be calming, digestive, and to relieve cold symptoms. It is also one of the plants historically used in za'atar spice blends in the Levant, where different communities have distinct formulations using various combinations of Origanum syriacum, Thymbra spicata, Satureja thymbra, and M. fruticosa. A delightful low-growing groundcover for sunny, dry, Mediterranean-climate gardens.

common_name: Wild Yam (American Wild Yam, Colic Root)
notes: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to dappled shade, giving the twining vine a fence, shrub, or trellis to climb. Wild Yam is a native North American woodland vine long used in traditional herbal medicine, historically valued for its knotty rhizome, which contains diosgenin, a plant steroid compound that served as an early industrial source for synthesizing progesterone and other steroid hormones; despite folk claims, the raw rhizome is not directly hormonally active when eaten and is not a food crop like true cultivated yams. In the garden it is grown chiefly as a native woodland vine for naturalized shade plantings, valued for its heart-shaped leaves, twining habit, and small, inconspicuous summer flowers followed by distinctive three-winged seed capsules in fall. It spreads slowly by rhizome once established and tolerates a range of shaded conditions, making it a good choice for a low-maintenance native groundcover vine at a woodland edge.

Trichostema lanatum is a stunning California native evergreen shrub in the mint family, prized for its intensely aromatic narrow leaves and dramatic spikes of electric-blue flowers wrapped in showy woolly purple-violet calyxes that bloom from spring through summer and draw hummingbirds and native bumblebees in abundance. Propagate by softwood cuttings rather than seed, and plant out in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun — this plant will not tolerate clay, wet soils, or summer irrigation once it is established. It is native to the dry chaparral and coastal sage scrub of southern California and performs best in California-style dry gardens in zones 8-10. Excellent drainage is the single most important factor for long-term success; plants sited correctly are long-lived and largely care-free.

Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yabukita tea is a cold-hardy cultivar bred in Japan and tolerates more winter cold than many other tea cultivars. Developed in Shizuoka Prefecture in the early twentieth century and released commercially in 1953, this cultivar became so dominant in Japanese tea production that it now accounts for the large majority of all tea grown in Japan, prized for its balanced, clean, slightly sweet flavor well suited to sencha and other steamed green tea styles. Its relatively good cold hardiness compared to many tea cultivars, combined with reliable yields and disease resistance, made it the standard choice for Japanese tea farmers for decades and a natural benchmark against which newer Japanese tea cultivars are still compared. Harvest the youngest leaves and unopened buds by hand in spring for the highest-quality tea, and prune the shrub into a rounded hedge form typical of commercial tea cultivation to encourage dense, flush new growth.

common_name: Yaw Weed (Wild Indian Mulberry, Cheese Shrub)
notes: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; drought and salt-spray tolerant once established. Morinda royoc (yaw weed or wild Indian mulberry) is a native North American coastal shrub in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) — related to noni (Morinda citrifolia) and producing very similar compound, syncarpous white fruits (multiple small flowers fuse into a single fleshy structure), though much smaller and with a less objectionable odor than commercial noni. It is native to the coastal hammocks, shell middens, sandy beaches, and disturbed coastal areas of South Florida, the Florida Keys, the Caribbean islands, and the coastal Gulf of Mexico. The plant has a distinctly scrambling or climbing growth habit, with the stems leaning on and scrambling through other shrubs. The roots yield a traditional reddish-orange dye used by Caribbean indigenous peoples; the leaves and bark have traditional medicinal uses in Caribbean herbal medicine for skin conditions and fevers — the 'yaw weed' name refers to use for yaws (a tropical bacterial infection). As a native coastal landscape plant, yaw weed is exceptionally salt, drought, and wind tolerant — suitable for difficult coastal conditions where little else grows. The fruits are edible but not palatable fresh; birds eat them readily, providing wildlife habitat value.

Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, rocky or gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; avoid overwatering — this plant demands dry conditions. Satureja thymbra (za'atar savory, pink savory, or thyme-leaved savory) is a compact, woody-based perennial from the dry limestone hillsides, macchia scrub, and garrigue of the Eastern Mediterranean — native to Greece, Turkey, Cyprus, Lebanon, and Israel. It is one of several specific plants that go into the za'atar herb blend of the Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean — alongside Origanum syriacum, Thymbra spicata, and Micromeria fruticosa — and is also used independently as a culinary and medicinal herb. The flavor of S. thymbra is warm, complex, and intense: more resinous and thyme-like than common summer savory (S. hortensis), with oregano notes and a subtle bitterness that adds depth to za'atar blends, grilled meats, and herb breads. The plant forms a neat, mounding, evergreen (in mild winters) subshrub with small, deep-green, aromatic leaves and pink to light-purple flowers that attract bees abundantly in early summer. It performs well in Mediterranean-climate gardens (zone 8–10) with excellent drainage and lean soil — exactly the conditions found on Greek island hillsides.
